question:
A patient presents after an automobile versus pedestrian accident and is found to have an open ankle 
fracture dislocation with diminished distal pulses. 
The patient is prepped for an emergent reduction 
under procedural sedation. He is placed on a cardiac 
monitor with capnography and pulse oximetry. His 
vital signs are within normal limits, and his oxygen 
saturation is 100%. Airway equipment is available 
at the bedside. Which of the following describes the 
NEXT step?

options.text: Remove supplemental oxygen as it can delay the

englishExplanation:
13.  The answer is A.  (Chapter 37) It is appropriate to 
administer a short-acting analgesic agent prior to the procedure when time permits. Shorter-acting agents (such 
as fentanyl and morphine) are preferred to drugs with a 
longer duration of action (such as hydromorphone) to 
minimize postprocedure respiratory depression. Begin 
procedural sedation after the last dose of analgesic has 
reached its peak effect (3–5 minutes for IV morphine and 
2–3 minutes for IV fentanyl). Despite its potential to delay 
the recognition of respiratory suppression, supplemental 
oxygen reduces the incidence of hypoxemia and has no 
adverse clinical effects and should therefore be utilized in 
procedural sedation.

الفخ: الخيار D بيقترح إزالة الأكسجين المكمّل، وهاد غلاط لأن الأكسجين بيقلل احتمال الـ hypoxemia وما إله adverse clinical effects. والخيار B (hydromorphone) أطول مدة فبتزيد خطر respiratory depression بعد الإجراء. والـ sedation ما بتبلّش قبل ما يعمل الـ fentanyl أعلى تأثير.

question:
Which of the following should be corrected prior to 
the administration of propofol?
englishExplanation:
15.  The answer is C. (Chapter 37) Propofol can produce 
hypotension as a result of both negative inotropy and 
vasodilatation. Hypotension is more common in hypovolemic patients and those with severe systemic disease or 
multiple comorbidities. Hypovolemia should be corrected 
before propofol administration.

question:
Which of the following is TRUE regarding chronic 
pain syndromes?

options.text: Allodynia is an exaggerated response to a normally painful stimulus.
Fibromyalgia is characterized by muscular pain
Hyperalgesia is pain from a normally nonpainful
Transformed migraine is a syndrome in which

correctAnswer: Transformed migraine is a syndrome in which
englishExplanation:
17.  The answer is D. (Chapter 38) Transformed migraine 
is a syndrome in which common migraine headaches 
transform into a chronic pain syndrome, most commonly 
from medication overuse, including barbiturates, opioids, and NSAIDs. Pain may be more similar to tension 
headache with tenderness and tension of scalp musculature. Fibromyalgia is widespread muscular pain involving greater than six body areas out of 19 total regions and 
a symptom severity score of 5 or more for fatigue, sleep 
disturbance, and cognitive dysfunction (e.g., forgetfulness, inability to concentrate or recall simple words or 
numbers, confusion, and associated nonmuscle pain 
symptoms). Hyperalgesia is an exaggerated response to a 
normally painful stimulus. Allodynia is pain from a normally nonpainful stimulus.

question:
A 45-year-old woman presents for acute on chronic 
right-sided neck pain that is constant, dull and occasionally shooting. She has not had any trauma. She 
has point tenderness that produces reproducible pain 
in the right trapezius muscle, no muscle atrophy and 
poor range of motion in the right shoulder due to 
pain. History and examination are otherwise unremarkable. You review the patient electronic medical 
record and see that she has recently had X-rays and 
magnetic resonance imaging (MRIs) of the cervical 
spine and right shoulder that were normal. You perform a trigger point injection, which provides some 
pain relief to the patient. The patient requests a pain 
medication prescription for discharge and states that 
scheduled oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs 
(NSAIDs) have not been controlling her pain. Which 
of the following is the MOST APPROPRIATE medication for this patient?
englishExplanation:
18.  The answer is C. (Chapter 38) This patient has a myofascial pain syndrome. Pain symptoms include constant, 
dull, occasionally shooting pain, which does not typically 
follow nerve distribution. Signs include trigger points in 
area of pain, absence of muscle atrophy and poor range 
of motion in the involved muscle. Primary treatment for 
myofascial pain syndromes includes oral NSAIDs and 
topical diclofenac patch for single site of pain. Secondary 
treatment is amitriptyline. Long-acting controlled-release 
opioids for noncancer pain such as OxyContin, fentanyl 
patches, or methadone should not be prescribed from the 
emergency department. Outpatient opioids for patients 
with acute exacerbation of chronic noncancer pain should 
be avoided in the emergency department.
arabicExplanation:

الفخ: أكتر خطأ هو إنك تصرف Oxycodone أو fentanyl patch أو methadone من الـ ED، وهاد غلط كبير. الـ long-acting controlled-release opioids ما بينفع تصرفها من الـ emergency department، والـ opioids كـ outpatient بتاع acute exacerbation of chronic noncancer pain لازم تتجنب. ولا تنسى الـ trigger point injection اللي عملتها.

question:
A 50-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 2 
diabetes mellitus presents with bilateral chronic foot 
pain described as constant burning and aching pain. 
On examination, gentle touch to the feet produces 
severe reproducible pain. The patient has decreased 
two-point discrimination. Which of the following is 
the primary pharmacologic treatment for this patient?
englishExplanation:
19.  The answer is B. (Chapter 38) This patient has painful diabetic neuropathy. The symptoms of painful diabetic 
neuropathy are symmetric numbness associated with 
burning, electrical, or stabbing pain in lower extremities. Patients may have hyperesthesia, dysesthesias, and/
or deep aching pain. Pain may be provoked with a gentle touch to the skin in the areas of abnormal sensation. 
Duloxetine is the primary treatment for diabetic neuropathy. Pregabalin and gabapentin are secondary treatments 
of painful diabetic neuropathy. Carbamazepine is the primary treatment for trigeminal neuralgia.

question:
Which of the following is TRUE regarding aberrant 
drug-related behavior?

options.text: A personal history of illicit drug and alcohol
Dental pain is a common complaint of patients
Teens trying illicit drugs for the first time are

correctAnswer: A personal history of illicit drug and alcohol
englishExplanation:
20.  The answer is A. (Chapter 38) A systematic review 
of the literature found that the only consistent predictor of aberrant drug-related behaviors in chronic pain 
patients is a personal history of illicit drug and alcohol 
abuse. The most common complaints of patients who 
attempt to obtain opioids from the emergency department are (in order of highest to lowest frequency) back 
pain, headache, extremity pain, and dental pain. When 
aberrant drug-related behavior is confirmed or suspected 
in the emergency department, it should be documented 
in the chart, stating only the facts. Concerns about opioid overuse can be documented without diagnosing the 
patient with “drug-seeking behavior,” which may not be 
appropriate without evidence of illegal behavior. In 2012, 
17% of the teens trying illicit drugs for the first time used 
prescription opioids, second only to marijuana.

question:
A 30-year-old man presents with acute dental pain. 
He reports that his oxycodone prescription from 
another hospital was stolen and requests a refill. 
Examination is unremarkable. Which of the following describes a recommended practice for appropriate opioid prescribing in the emergency department 
when you suspect aberrant drug-related behavior?

options.text: Prescribe opioids to patients whose medications
Provide an opioid prescription for a patient presenting with dental pain whose examination
Refill a prescription for a patient who has lost
Search for the patient’s name in a prescription

correctAnswer: Search for the patient’s name in a prescription
englishExplanation:
21.  The answer is D. (Chapter 38) It can be challenging 
to identify patients with aberrant drug-related behavior. 
The patients with this disorder may present with a wide 
range of complaints including back pain, headache, tooth 
pain, extremity pain, and panic attack to name a few. 
Practitioners are encouraged to review the prescription 
drug monitoring program database before prescribing a 
discharge medication in order to help identify patients 
who are abusing or overusing prescription drugs. Other 
strategies for managing aberrant drug-related behavior in 
the emergency department include the following. Inform 
patients that report their prescription or pill bottle was 
stolen that this is a police issue and recommend that the 
patient call the police to rectify the matter. Perform a local 
nerve block and refer to a dentist any patient presenting 
with dental pain whose examination demonstrates dental 
caries only. Establish a policy that no lost opioid prescriptions will be filled and notify patients of this policy as they 
receive prescriptions.

question: Which statement comparing volume control (VCV) and pressure control ventilation (PCV) is NOT true?

options.text: Volume control guarantees a stable minute volume.
Pressure control's decelerating flow can improve alveolar recruitment.
For the same peak inspiratory pressure, VCV results in a higher mean airway
Pressure control limits peak airway pressure, which may protect against
Adaptive modes like PRVC aim to combine the benefits of both.

correctAnswer: For the same peak inspiratory pressure, VCV results in a higher mean airway
englishExplanation:
Analysis of the False Statement:
Statement C is incorrect, making it the right answer. In Pressure Control Ventilation
(PCV), the ventilator rapidly pressurizes the circuit to the set limit and maintains it,
creating a 'square' pressure waveform. In Volume Control Ventilation (VCV) with
constant flow, pressure rises linearly as the lungs fill, creating a 'triangular' or

'ramp' waveform. Mathematically, the area under the pressure-time curve determines Mean Airway Pressure. For the same Peak Inspiratory Pressure (PIP) and inspiratory time, the square wave of PCV has a significantly larger area than the triangular wave of VCV. Therefore, PCV generates a higher mean airway pressure, which
generally improves oxygenation.
Comparison Summary:
VCV guarantees tidal volume but results in variable pressures (risk of barotrauma)
and uses constant flow (risk of flow starvation). PCV limits pressure (safety) and
uses decelerating flow (better distribution) but results in variable volume if compliance changes.
Clinical Pearl
Mean Airway Pressure Comparison:
The square pressure waveform in PCV results in a higher mean airway pressure for
a given peak pressure compared to the triangular waveform of VCV. This increase in
mean airway pressure correlates with improved alveolar recruitment and
oxygenation.
Volume Control Advantages:
The primary advantage of VCV is the guaranteed tidal volume, which ensures a stable minute ventilation and predictable PaCO2 control, regardless of changes in lung
mechanics.
Pressure Control Disadvantages:
The main disadvantage of PCV is that the delivered tidal volume varies with changes
in pulmonary compliance and resistance. A decrease in compliance or increase in
resistance will result in a lower tidal volume, potentially leading to hypoventilation.
Flow Pattern Physiology:
PCV utilizes a decelerating flow pattern. As the lung fills and alveolar pressure rises,
the pressure gradient driving flow decreases, causing flow to taper off. This is considered more physiological and improves gas distribution to lung units with different time constants.
Adaptive Modes (PRVC):
Pressure-Regulated Volume Control (PRVC) is a dual-control mode that delivers
breaths with a decelerating flow pattern (like PCV) but automatically adjusts the inspiratory pressure limit breath-by-breath to achieve a target tidal volume (like
VCV).
Flow Starvation Mechanism:
In VCV with constant flow, the inspiratory flow rate is fixed. If a patient's inspiratory demand (drive) exceeds this set flow, they experience 'flow starvation', resulting in a scooped-out appearance on the pressure-time scalar and increased work of
breathing.
Equation of Motion Application:
The Equation of Motion (Pressure equals Flow times Resistance plus Volume divided by Compliance) explains ventilator graphics. In VCV, Pressure is the dependent variable; in PCV, Volume and Flow are the dependent variables.
Impact of Compliance Changes:
In VCV, a reduction in lung compliance (e.g., worsening ARDS, pneumothorax)
leads to higher peak airway pressures to deliver the set volume. In PCV, the same
reduction in compliance leads to a lower delivered tidal volume while peak pressure
remains constant.
Driving Pressure Significance:
Driving pressure (Plateau Pressure minus PEEP) represents the strain applied to
the lung parenchyma. It is a stronger predictor of mortality in ARDS than tidal volume or PEEP alone. In PCV, the driving pressure is the set inspiratory pressure
above PEEP.
Alveolar Recruitment Mechanism:
The sustained pressure of the PCV square waveform recruits collateral channels
(Pores of Kohn) and maintains patency of alveoli with slow time constants, improving oxygenation compared to the transient peak pressure of VCV.

ليش: في الـ PCV البنت بسرعة بترفع الضغط للـ set limit وبيضل ثابت، فبيطلع شكل مربع. أما في الـ VCV مع constant flow الضغط بيزيد linearrily مع امتلاء الرئتين، فبيطلع شكل مثلث. الـ mean airway pressure بتعتمد على المساحة تحت منحنى الضغط مقابل الوقت. بنفس الـ peak inspiratory pressure ونفس وقت الشهيق، المربع مساحة أكبر من المثلث، يعني الـ PCV بيدّي mean airway pressure أعلى وبتحسّن الـ oxygenation. ولهاد السبب العبارة C غلط.
الفخ: الخيار D بيخلطك لأن الـ PCV بيحدّ من الـ peak pressure، بس معناه إن الـ mean airway pressure عنده أعلى لا أقل. تذكّر إن مربع أكبر مساحة من مثلث لنفس القمة، والخيار E صح لأنه بجمع مزايا الاثنين.

question: Regarding the functional differences of the pediatric airway, which of the following is FALSE?

options.text: The small diameter of the airway means that resistance to airflow is significantly
The narrowest portion is the glottic opening between the vocal cords.
Infants are obligate nasal breathers for the first few months of life.
The trachea and chest wall are highly compliant, leading to an increased work of
A large occiput causes passive neck flexion when lying supine, potentially obstructing the airway.

correctAnswer: The narrowest portion is the glottic opening between the vocal cords.
englishExplanation:
Anatomy: The Narrowest Point:
Classic teaching describes the infant airway as funnel-shaped, narrowing at the
cricoid cartilage. While recent MRI data suggests the glottis may be anatomically
narrower in the transverse dimension, the cricoid cartilage is a complete, non-distensible ring. Unlike the glottis, which can distend to accommodate a tube, the
cricoid sets the functional limit for the diameter of an endotracheal tube. Therefore,
the cricoid is clinically regarded as the functional narrowest point in children (making Option B false), whereas in adults, the glottis is the narrowest point.
Airway Resistance:
Resistance is inversely proportional to the radius to the power of four (Poiseuille's
Law). The small baseline diameter of the paediatric airway means even minor mucosal oedema (e.g., 1 mm) significantly reduces the cross-sectional area and dramatically increases the work of breathing.
Mechanics of Breathing:
Infants have a highly compliant chest wall due to cartilaginous ribs. During respiratory distress, the generation of negative intrathoracic pressure causes chest wall recession (paradoxical breathing), reducing tidal volume and efficiency. This contrasts
with the rigid adult chest wall.
Physiological Differences:
Infants are obligate nasal breathers until approximately 3-6 months of age.
Obstruction of the nares (e.g., secretions, NG tubes) can precipitate respiratory failure. Additionally, a relatively large occiput causes neck flexion in the supine position, requiring a shoulder roll to maintain a neutral airway.
Clinical Pearl
Cricoid is the Functional Narrowest Point:
Although the glottis may be anatomically narrower in transverse section, the cricoid
cartilage is a fixed, non-distensible ring. It acts as the functional limiting factor for
endotracheal tube size to prevent subglottic ischaemia.
A Little Swelling is a Big Problem:
Because of Poiseuille's law, 1 mm of circumferential edema in an infant's airway can
reduce the cross-sectional area by over 75%.
Infants are Nose Breathers:
Infants are obligate nasal breathers. Nasal obstruction from secretions or stenosis
can cause severe respiratory distress; ensure patency of the nares immediately in
the distressed infant.
'Floppy' Chest and Trachea:
The highly compliant paediatric chest wall is prone to recession during inspiration.
This inefficiency increases the work of breathing and predisposes to rapid fatigue
compared to adults.
Positioning is Key:
The prominent occiput in infants causes passive neck flexion and airway obstruction
when supine. Place a roll under the shoulders (not the head) to align the axes in a
neutral position.
Rapid Desaturation:
Children have a higher metabolic rate (oxygen consumption 6-8 ml/kg/min vs 3
ml/kg/min in adults) and a lower functional residual capacity (FRC). This results in
precipitous desaturation during apnoea.
Closing Capacity vs FRC:

In infants, closing capacity often exceeds FRC during tidal breathing, leading to airway closure and atelectasis even in healthy states. Maintenance of PEEP is critical
during mechanical ventilation.
Epiglottis Morphology:
The paediatric epiglottis is relatively large, floppy, and omega-shaped. It is angled
more posteriorly over the laryngeal inlet compared to the flat, erect adult epiglottis,
often necessitating a straight blade for direct laryngoscopy to lift it directly.
Vagal Tone Dominance:
The paediatric myocardium is highly sensitive to hypoxia and vagal stimulation
(e.g., laryngoscopy, suctioning), leading to profound bradycardia. Cardiac output is
rate-dependent due to a relatively fixed stroke volume.
arabicExplanation:

question:
Which of the following options correctly pairs a fire class with its corresponding
combustible material?

options.text: Class A - Flammable liquids like gasoline or paint.
Class B - Combustible materials such as wood, paper, and fabric.
Class C - Flammable gases like hydrogen, butane, or methane.
Class D - Fires involving cooking oils and fats.
Electrical Fire - A permanent classification for any fire involving electronics.

correctAnswer: Class C - Flammable gases like hydrogen, butane, or methane.
englishExplanation:
BS EN 2 Classification System:

Under the UK/European standard BS EN 2, fires are classified by fuel type:
•Class A: Organic solids (wood, paper, textiles). •Class B: Flammable liquids
(petrol, diesel, paint). •Class C: Flammable gases (butane, hydrogen, methane).
•Class D: Flammable metals (magnesium, lithium). •Class F: Cooking oils and
fats (deep fat fryers).
Note: This differs from the US (NFPA) system where Class C refers to electrical
fires.
Electrical Fires:
Electrical fires do not have a specific letter designation under BS EN 2. They are
fires involving live electrical equipment. Once the power source is isolated, the fire
is reclassified according to the burning material (usually Class A). Carbon Dioxide
(CO2) extinguishers are the primary choice for live electrical equipment.
Clinical Pearl
International Classification Differences:
Fire classification systems vary internationally; notably, Class C denotes electrical
fires in the US (NFPA) but flammable gases in the UK/Europe (BS EN 2). Matching
the extinguisher agent to the specific fuel type remains the universal safety
principle.
ABC Extinguishers:
While Dry Powder (Blue label) extinguishers are rated for Class A, B, and C fires, BS
5306-8 generally prohibits their use indoors (including hospitals) due to the risk of
respiratory irritation and sudden reduction in visibility.
Class D Fire Management:
Water must never be applied to Class D (metal) fires, as it causes violent explosive
reactions with burning metals like magnesium or lithium. Specialised dry powder
(e.g., M28 or L2) is required.
Class F Fire Management:
Water applied to Class F (cooking oil) fires flashes to steam instantly, causing burning oil to disperse explosively. Management requires a Wet Chemical extinguisher
(Yellow label) or fire blanket to saponify the oil and seal the surface.
Hospital Fire Safety - RACE:
Rescue anyone in immediate danger. Alarm by pulling the fire alarm and calling for
help. Confine the fire by closing doors. Extinguish (if safe) or Evacuate.
UK Extinguisher Colour Coding:
Extinguishers in the UK are identified by a coloured band: Water (Red), Foam
(Cream), Dry Powder (Blue), CO2 (Black), and Wet Chemical (Yellow). In critical
care areas, CO2 is preferred for electrical equipment to minimize damage.

The Fire Triangle in ICU:
The ICU environment is high-risk due to the 'Fire Triangle': Fuel (alcohol gels,
drapes), Heat (diathermy, lasers), and Oxygen. Oxygen enrichment significantly
lowers the ignition temperature of materials and increases flame velocity.
Surgical Fire Risk:
Alcohol-based skin preparations must be allowed to dry completely before using
diathermy or electrosurgery. Pooling of solution in the umbilicus or drapes creates a
high-risk fuel source, particularly in oxygen-enriched environments.
Medical Gas Isolation:
In the event of a major ICU fire, the isolation of medical gas supplies (oxygen/air) is
a critical decision usually reserved for the senior charge nurse, consultant, or fire officer, as it has immediate life-threatening consequences for ventilated patients.
Evacuation Strategy:
ICU evacuation follows a progressive horizontal strategy: moving patients horizontally to an adjacent fire-safe compartment (behind fire doors) is preferred over vertical evacuation, which is resource-intensive and hazardous for critically ill patients.
MRI Fire Safety:
Standard ferrous fire extinguishers must never be taken into the MRI environment
due to the projectile risk from the magnetic field. Specific non-magnetic (usually
aluminium) MRI-conditional extinguishers are required.

question: Which statement about the interpretation of serum ferritin levels is FALSE?

options.text: In an otherwise healthy individual, a serum ferritin < 30 µg/L is highly specific for iron deficiency.
Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant, and its level can be significantly elevated by inflammation, masking an underlying iron deficiency.
In a patient with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and anemia, a ferritin level of 150 µg/L definitively rules out iron deficiency.
In early pregnancy, a ferritin level < 15 µg/L is indicative of depleted iron stores.
To diagnose iron deficiency in an inflammatory state, a higher ferritin cutoff (e.g., <100 µg/L) is used, often in combination with a low transferrin saturation (<20%).

correctAnswer: In a patient with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and anemia, a ferritin level of 150 µg/L definitively rules out iron deficiency.
englishExplanation:
**Analysis of the False Statement:**
   - Option C is FALSE.
   - In Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD), ferritin behaves as an acute phase reactant and is frequently elevated due to inflammation, reducing its specificity for iron deficiency.
   - NICE NG203 recommends diagnosing iron deficiency in CKD if ferritin is <100 µg/L, OR if ferritin is 100–800 µg/L with a Transferrin Saturation (TSAT) <20%.
   - Therefore, a ferritin level of 150 µg/L does not rule out iron deficiency; the patient may have functional iron deficiency indicated by a low TSAT.
  **Ferritin Thresholds in Health and Pregnancy:**
   - In otherwise healthy individuals, a low ferritin is highly specific for iron deficiency.
   - NICE CKS and British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines cite <30 µg/L as diagnostic.
   - In pregnancy, the British Society for Haematology also defines iron deficiency as ferritin <30 µg/L; a level <15 µg/L (Option D) represents severe depletion and is unequivocally diagnostic.
  **Inflammatory States:**
   - Inflammation stimulates hepcidin production, which blocks iron absorption and release from macrophages, raising serum ferritin.
   - In inflammatory states (CKD, Heart Failure, Critical Illness), standard cutoffs are insufficient.
   - Guidelines mandate evaluating TSAT alongside ferritin.
   - A TSAT <20% indicates iron restricted erythropoiesis even if ferritin is normal or elevated (up to 300-800 µg/L depending on the specific pathology).
  **Inflammation Falsely Elevates Ferritin:**
   - Interpret ferritin with caution in the presence of elevated CRP or chronic inflammatory conditions; 'normal' levels may mask absolute or functional iron deficiency.
  **In Inflammation, Check TSAT Too:**
   - In chronic disease (CKD, Heart Failure), rely on Transferrin Saturation (TSAT).
   - A TSAT <20% suggests iron deficiency even if ferritin is >100 µg/L.
  **A Low Ferritin is Always Iron Deficiency:**
   - A low ferritin level is very specific for iron deficiency, regardless of inflammatory status.
   - Inflammation can only make it falsely high, not falsely low.
  **Pathophysiology of Anemia of Chronic Disease:**
   - The combination of an inflammatory block on iron utilization (high hepcidin degrad ing ferroportin) and potential true iron deficiency is the basis for the anemia of chronic disease.
  **Heart Failure Thresholds:**
   - NICE NG106 recommends intravenous iron for heart failure patients with ferritin <100 µg/L, or ferritin 100–299 µg/L if TSAT <20%.
  **Soluble Transferrin Receptor (sTfR):**
   - Unlike ferritin, sTfR is not an acute-phase reactant.
   - Elevated sTfR levels can help distinguish true iron deficiency anemia (high sTfR) from anemia of chronic disease (normal sTfR) in complex inflammatory cases.
  **Hepcidin Mechanism:**
   - Hepcidin is the master regulator of iron homeostasis.
   - It binds to ferroportin (the cellular iron exporter) causing its internalisation and degradation.
   - This prevents iron release from macrophages and absorption from the gut, leading to the 'reticuloendothelial block' seen in inflammation.
  **Functional vs Absolute Iron Deficiency:**
   - Absolute iron deficiency is defined by depleted stores (low ferritin).
   - Functional iron deficiency occurs when stores are normal or high (normal/high ferritin), but iron cannot be mobilised fast enough to meet the demands of erythropoiesis, typically due to inflammation or use of Erythropoiesis Stimulating Agents (ESAs).
  **Oral Iron Resistance:**
   - In inflammatory states with high hepcidin, oral iron absorption is blocked at the ente rocyte level.
   - This explains why intravenous iron is often required in CKD, heart failure, and critical illness, as it bypasses the gut absorption block.
  **Reticulocyte Haemoglobin Content (CHr):**
   - CHr (or Ret-He) measures the haemoglobin content of reticulocytes, providing a snapshot of iron availability for erythropoiesis over the last 48-72 hours.
   - Unlike ferritin, it is not an acute-phase reactant and is a sensitive marker for functional iron deficiency.

ليش: الخيار C هو العبارة الغلط، لأن ferritin behaves like an acute phase reactant وبيطلع عالي مع الالتهاب ومن ضمنه chronic kidney disease. فـ ferritin 150 ug/L ما بتستثني iron deficiency أبداً، لأن NICE NG203 بتحكي إنه في CKD بتنشخّص iron deficiency إذا ferritin أقل من 100 ug/L، أو إذا ferritin بين 100 و 800 مع transferrin saturation أقل من 20%. يعني لازم تقرأ TSAT مع ferritin معاً.
الفخ: الخيار B عن ferritin كـ acute phase reactant صحيح، والخيار D عن pregnancy صحيح لأن أقل من 15 يعني استنزاف شديد. الفخ الحقيقي إنك تستبعد iron deficiency من ferritin مرتفع، بينما لازم دايماً تبص على TSAT مع ferritin معاً.

question: An obese patient (BMI 45 kg/m²) is lying supine for a general anaesthetic. How is their closing capacity (CC) and functional residual capacity (FRC) expected to change, and what is the clinical implication?

options.text: Both CC and FRC increase, improving ventilation.
The FRC increases, and the CC decreases, reducing the risk of atelectasis.
The FRC decreases significantly, while the CC is relatively unchanged, leading to the FRC falling below the CC.
There is no significant change in either parameter.

correctAnswer: The FRC decreases significantly, while the CC is relatively unchanged, leading to the FRC falling below the CC.
englishExplanation:
**Pathophysiology of FRC Reduction:**
   - Obesity causes a restrictive lung deficit primarily through mass loading of the chest wall and cephalad displacement of the diaphragm by abdominal contents.
   - This significantly reduces the Functional Residual Capacity (FRC), specifically the Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV).
   - The supine position further reduces FRC by increasing abdominal pressure on the diaphragm, and general anaesthesia reduces FRC by relaxing diaphragm tone and altering chest wall mechanics.
  **Determinants of Closing Capacity:**
   - Closing Capacity (CC) is the sum of Residual Volume (RV) and Closing Volume (CV).
   - It represents the lung volume at which small airways independent zones begin to close due to elastic recoil forces overcoming airway pressure.
   - CC is primarily determined by age (increasing linearly with age due to loss of elastic recoil) and is relatively independent of body habitus.
   - Therefore, in obesity, CC remains stable while FRC decreases.
  **The FRC-CC Relationship:**
   - The critical physiological threshold is when FRC falls below CC.
   - In this state, airway closure occurs during normal tidal breathing (not just forced expiration).
   - This creates areas of low V/Q ratios and intrapulmonary shunt, leading to absorption atelectasis and rapid arterial desaturation, as blood flows through non-ventilated alveoli.
  **FRC vs CC Relationship:**
   - The critical physiological derangement in obesity is FRC falling below Closing Capacity (CC).
   - This causes airway closure independent zones during tidal breathing, leading to shunt and hypoxemia.
  **Exponential Desaturation:**
   - Safe apnoea time is drastically reduced in obesity due to the combination of reduced oxygen reservoir (low FRC) and increased oxygen consumption (high metabolic rate).
  **Positioning is Vital:**
   - The 'ramped' or 'head-up' position (sternal notch aligned with external auditory mea tus) offloads the diaphragm, improving FRC and prolonging safe apnoea time for intubation.
  **PEEP Requirement:**
   - Positive End-Expiratory Pressure (PEEP) is essential to maintain end-expiratory lung volume above Closing Capacity.
   - Zero PEEP (ZEEP) should be avoided in obese patients under anaesthesia.
  **Recruitment Manoeuvres:**
   - Alveolar recruitment manoeuvres are frequently required after induction or circuit disconnection to reopen collapsed lung units, followed by sufficient PEEP to prevent re-collapse.
  **Extubation Strategy:**
   - Extubation should occur with the patient fully awake and in a semi-recumbent or sitting position to maximise FRC and minimise airway obstruction risk.
  **Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome:**
   - Defined by BMI >30 kg/m² and awake arterial hypercapnia (PaCO2 >6.0 kPa) in the absence of other causes of hypoventilation.
   - These patients have blunted central respiratory drive and are at high risk of post-operative respiratory failure.
  **Chest Wall Compliance:**
   - The reduction in total respiratory compliance in obesity is primarily driven by reduced chest wall compliance (due to adipose tissue mass and resistance), whereas lung com- pliance remains relatively normal unless significant atelectasis develops.
  **Closing Capacity Determinants:**
   - Since CC increases with age and FRC decreases with obesity, the older obese patient represents the highest risk phenotype for intraoperative gas exchange deterioration.
  **Opioid Sensitivity:**
   - Obese patients, particularly those with Obstructive Sleep Apnoea (OSA), exhibit increased sensitivity to the respiratory depressant effects of opioids.
   - Multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia is the standard of care.
  **Reverse Trendelenburg:**
   - Tilting the entire operating table head-up (Reverse Trendelenburg) is more effective than simple back-up positioning for improving respiratory mechanics in obese patients during surgery, as it displaces abdominal contents caudally.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: السمنة بتعمل mass loading على جدار الصدر وبيزح diaphragm لفوق، وهاد بيقلّل FRC بشكل كبير وخصوصاً في وضعية supine ومع general anaesthesia. أما Closing Capacity فمعتمدة على العمر و Elastic recoil مو على body habitus، فبتبقى تقريباً نفسها. لمّا الـ FRC ينزل تحت الـ CC، الهوا بيسكّر في tidal breathing العادي، وهاد بيسبّب low V/Q و intrapulmonary shunt و absorption atelectasis ونزول سريع في saturation.
الفخ: الخيار D بيقول إن الـ CC والـ FRC بينقصوا مع بعض، والخيار B بيقول إن الـ FRC يزيد، وهما غلط. افصل: الـ CC سببها فقد Elastic recoil مع العمر، واللي بينزل مع السمنة هو الـ FRC بسبب ضغط البطن على الـ diaphragm.

question: A 45-year-old farmer presents with a one-week history of high fevers, severe headache, myalgias (especially in the calves), and conjunctival suffusion (red eyes without discharge). He reports cleaning out a barn that was flooded after recent heavy rains. Labs show elevated creatinine and liver enzymes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
**Diagnosis:**
   - The clinical picture is classic for Leptospirosis (Weil's disease).
   - Key features include the epidemiological risk (farmer, floodwaters/rodent urine), specific symptoms (severe calf myalgia, conjunctival suffusion), and organ dysfunction (hepatorenal syndrome).
   - Conjunctival suffusion (redness without exudate) occurs in up to 55% of patients and is a specific sign.
  **Pathophysiology:**
   - Leptospirosis is a zoonosis caused by the spirochete Leptospira interrogans.
   - Transmission occurs via direct contact with urine from infected animals (rats, cattle) or contaminated water/soil entering through skin abrasions or mucous membranes.
   - The underlying mechanism involves widespread small vessel vasculitis and endothelial damage, leading to capillary leakage and organ hypoperfusion.
   - The incubation period is typically 7-12 days.
  **Management:**
   - Treatment involves supportive care (renal replacement therapy may be required) and antibiotics.
   - For severe disease, IV benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone is recommended.
   - Doxycycline is used for milder cases or prophylaxis.
   - Patients should be monitored for the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction upon initiating antibiotics.
  **Think Water and Rodents:**
   - The classic exposure is contact with freshwater or soil contaminated with animal (especially rodent) urine.
   - Think of farmers, sewer workers, and whitewater rafters.
  **Conjunctival Suffusion is a Key Sign:**
   - This is bilateral eye redness without purulent discharge, and it's highly suggestive of leptospirosis.
  **Weil's Disease:**
   - Remember this severe form of leptospirosis, characterized by the triad of jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage.
  **Biphasic Illness:**
   - The illness can have two phases: an initial flu-like phase followed by a more severe immune-mediated phase.
  **Treatment is with Antibiotics:**
   - Initiate antibiotics empirically if suspicion is high.
   - Severe disease is treated with IV Benzylpenicillin or Ceftriaxone.
   - Mild disease is treated with oral Doxycycline.
   - Treatment should ideally start within 5 days of symptom onset.
  **Diagnostic Window:**
   - In the first week (septicemic phase), PCR of blood or CSF is the diagnostic test of choice.
   - Serology (IgM ELISA/MAT) typically becomes positive only after the first week (immune phase).
   - Urine PCR may remain positive for weeks.
  **Jarisch-Herxheimer Reaction:**
   - Be alert for an acute inflammatory reaction (fever, tachycardia, hypotension) shortly after starting antibiotics, caused by the release of endotoxins from dying spirochetes.
   - This is common in spirochetal treatments (Syphilis, Lyme, Leptospirosis).
  **Laboratory Findings:**
   - Expect elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels due to myositis, which helps distinguish leptospirosis from viral hepatitis.
   - Thrombocytopenia is also common and contributes to the haemorrhagic risk.
  **Differential Diagnosis:**
   - Differentials include Hantavirus (prominent respiratory or renal failure, rodent exposure), Dengue (retro-orbital pain, rash, travel history), and Malaria (cyclical fevers, travel history).
   - Conjunctival suffusion and severe calf pain are specific discriminators for Leptospirosis.

question: A 21-year-old college student was in an altercation 15 minutes prior and presents with a painful right hand. Physical exam reveals a right hand with several bite and puncture marks. The range of motion is intact. There is no warmth or erythema. Local exploration reveals lacerations deep in the subcutaneous tissue but no joint involvement. A radiograph is unremarkable. What is the preferred treatment choice?

options.text: Thorough wound irrigation and primary closure
Thorough wound irrigation, prophylactic antibiotics, no closure
Thorough wound irrigation, sterile dressing and healing by secondary intention

correctAnswer: Thorough wound irrigation, prophylactic antibiotics, no closure
englishExplanation:
Thorough wound irrigation, prophylactic antibiotics, no closure
Expl anation
A. Admission for IV antibiotics
In this case, the patient is unlikely to already have an infective process as the altercation was 15 min prior to presentation. If the wound is showing signs of infection
(e.g. warmth, erythema, discharge, or limited joint mobility), then aggressive treatment, including admission and IV antibiotics is warranted.
B. Thorough wound irrigation and primary closure
Primary wound closure should be deferred in closed fist injuries but bite injuries to
other areas of the body can be treated as regular lacerations.
C. Thorough wound irrigation, prophylactic antibiotics, no closure
All wounds should receive thorough debridement and washout but human bite
wounds are particularly susceptible to infection due to the numerous pathogenic
bacteria of human oral flora. Common organisms are Streptococcus anginosus, S.
aureus, and Eikenella corrodens. Frequently, wounds are polymicrobial.
Prophylactic antibiotics are warranted, and typically suture repair is not advised.
Further information:
Eilbert W. Chapter 52. Mammalian Bites. In: Walls RM, Hockberger RS, Gausche-
Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical Practice. 10th ed.
Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
D. Thorough wound irrigation, sterile dressing and healing by
secondary intention
Wound irrigation, dressing and healing by secondary intention is not sufficient in
the case of a closed fist injury with human bite. These injuries are very susceptible
to infection and should receive prophylactic antibiotics.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الخيار C هو الأنسب، يعني غسل thorough للجرح مع prophylactic antibiotics وبدون closure. المريض وصل قبل 15 دقيقة من الخناقة وما في عنده علامات infection، يعني لسّه ما في infection process. عضّات الإنسان فيها بكتيريا فلورا الفم مثل Streptococcus anginosus و Staphylococcus aureus و Eikenella corrodens، وغالباً polymicrobial، فـ prophylactic antibiotics ضرورية، والخياطة مو مستحسنة عادة بهيك مواضع.
الفخ: الخيار A بالدخول و IV antibiotics بيجي بس لو في دفء واحمرار أو إفراغ أو تقييد حركة المفصل، وهاد مش موجود عنده. والخيار B خياطة أولية مؤجلة في closed fist injuries وعضّات الإنسان بشكل عام.

question: A 32-year-old woman presents after she cut her hand on a steak knife while washing the dishes six hours ago. She says she had a tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccination within the past three years. Physical examination of the right hand shows a 1.5 cm linear laceration at the base of the thumb on the palmar side of the hand with no active bleeding. Which of the following is the most important action to prevent wound infection in this patient?

options.text: Copious wound irrigation with tap water
Keeping the wound dry for 72 hours

correctAnswer: Copious wound irrigation with tap water
englishExplanation:
Copious wound irrigation with tap water
Expl anation
A. Avoidance of suture closure
Superficial lacerations caused by clean objects may undergo primary closure up to
6-8 hours from the time of injury. Wounds on the head and face may be closed up to
24 hours from the time of injury. Copious wound irrigation is the most important
step in preventing wound infections.
B. Copious wound irrigation with tap water
Copious wound irrigation is the most important step in preventing wound infections. Tap water is just as effective as sterile saline for wound irrigation.
Reference: Lammers, R and Aldy, K, "Principles of Wound Management" in
Roberts, James R, Catherine B. Custalow, Todd W. Thomsen, Jerris R. Hedges.
Roberts and Hedges' clinical procedures in emergency medicine and acute care, 7th
edition, 2019.
C. Keeping the wound dry for 72 hours
This is a common practice, but there is no evidence that getting a superficial laceration wet increases the risk of infection. Sutures can be uncovered and allowed to get
wet within the first 24 to 48 hours without increasing the risk of infection. Initial copious irrigation of the wound is the most important step in preventing wound
infection.
D. Oral cephalexin for five days
Prophylactic systemic antibiotics are not necessary for healthy patients with clean,
non-infected, non-bite wounds. The most important step in preventing wound infections is copious irrigation.

الفخ: الخيار D antibiotic لمدة 5 أيام مش لازم لجرح نظيف، والخيار A رفض الخياطة مش لازم لأن السطحية النظيفية ممكن تنخيط لحد 6-8 ساعات. ركّز على الغ copious irrigation كأهم خطوة.
