question:
A 75-year-old woman presented to the acute medical unit with two 
episodes of coffee-ground vomiting and epigastric pain. She had a past 
medical history of ischaemic heart disease and had previously had 
two myocardial infarctions. She had symptomatic angina about once a 
month. She was taking regular aspirin 75 mg, ramipril 5 mg, bisoprolol 
5 mg, simvastatin 40 mg, and nicorandil 20 mg bd.
On examination she had mild epigastric tenderness to palpation. Her 
heart rate was 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 120/82 mmHg, 
respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 96% on air.
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed, which showed a 
duodenal ulcer. Haemostasis was achieved at endoscopy. She was 
started on a proton pump inhibitor.
What is the best management of her anti-platelet therapy?

options.text: Discontinue aspirin for one week then restart
Discontinue aspirin until repeat endoscopy in six weeks

englishExplanation:
10. A.  Continue aspirin
Sung et al. (2010) in a randomized controlled trial (RCT) compared the outcomes of patients with 
known cardiovascular disease and endoscopic-confirmed peptic ulcers showing signs of active 
bleeding, adherent clot, or visible vessel on the base of an ulcer. They were either randomized to 
continue or discontinue their aspirin for established cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease once 
haemostasis with endoscopic therapy was achieved. Mortality rates were significantly lower in those 
patients who continued their aspirin therapy. Although bleeding rates were higher in those who 
continued aspirin, this did not reach statistical significance.
There is currently no evidence available regarding the continued use of clopidogrel (or any other 
thienopyridine antiplatelet agents) in the context of an acute upper gastrointestinal bleed. NICE 
guidance advises that the risks and benefits are discussed with the appropriate specialist and patient 
regarding its continued use. No general consensus is available and each patient needs to be considered individually depending on co-morbidities and risks.
Sung JJ, Lau JY, Ching JY et al. Recommencing continuation of low-dose aspirin therapy in peptic ulcer 
bleeding: a randomized trial. Annals of Internal Medicine 2010; 152: 1–9.

question:
An 83-year-old woman presented to the acute medical unit with 
difficulty swallowing. She was known to have a benign oesophageal 
stricture. She had an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, which was her 
12th procedure since the stricture was diagnosed 18 months ago. She 
was reviewed prior to discharge and was complaining of chest pain. She 
had a temperature of 38.0°C, heart rate of 110 beats per minute, blood 
pressure of 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute, 
and oxygen saturation 94% on air.
Which test is likely to give you the diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
29. B.  Chest X-ray
This patient has a systemic inflammatory response. Because of her history and recent endoscopy, 
the most likely cause is oesophageal rupture. A chest X-ray would be the most likely investigation 
to give you the diagnosis as you could see a widened mediastinum, pneumomediastinum, pneumonpericardum, subcutaneous emphysema, and pleural effusions. The other investigations listed may be 
performed but are unlikely to give you a diagnosis. If needed, she could proceed to CT. She is likely 
to need surgical correction.

question:
A 66-year-old man with a 20-pack year history of smoking was admitted 
with a two-hour history of central chest pain. He had never had this pain 
before. His 12-lead ECG showed ST depression of 2 mm in the anterior 
leads. He was not taking any medications and had not been to his GP for 
ten years. He was adopted when he was three years old.
Based on this information, what is his TIMI risk of death and further 
ischaemic events at 14 days?
englishExplanation:
1. C.  13.2% risk
With regard to the TIMI risk score calculation, one point is given for each of the following:
● Age ≥65
● Aspirin use in the last seven days (or patient experiences chest pain despite aspirin use in past 
seven days)
● At least two angina episodes within the last 24 hours
● ST changes of at least 0.5 mm on admission ECG
● Elevated serum cardiac biomarkers
● Known coronary artery disease (CAD) (coronary stenosis ≥50%)
● At least three risk factors for CAD, such as hypertension—140/90 mmHg or on antihypertensives, cigarette smoking, HDL <1.03 mmol/L, diabetes, family history of premature CAD 
(CAD in any male first-degree relative, or father less than 55, or any female first-degree relative or mother less than 65).
The percentage risk at 14 days of all-cause mortality, new or recurrent MI, or severe recurrent ischaemia requiring urgent revascularization:
● Score of 0–1 = 4.7% risk
● Score of 2 = 8.3% risk
● Score of 3 = 13.2% risk
● Score of 4 = 19.9% risk
● Score of 5 = 26.2% risk
● Score of 6–7 = at least 40.9% risk
Data from Heart, Conway MA et al., ‘TIMI risk score accurately risk stratifies patients with undifferentiated chest pain presenting to 
an emergency department’, 2006, 92, 9, pp.1333–1334.
Conway MA et al. TIMI risk score accurately risk stratifies patients with undifferentiated chest pain 
presenting to an emergency department. Heart 2006; 92(9): 1333–1334.

A 35-year-old man admitted to the acute medical unit with collapse 
was concerned when telling you his history on the post take ward round 
that he had recently started a new medication for palpitations. He had 
read on the Internet that some drugs can cause a prolonged QT and this 
ran in his family. So far he had not been diagnosed with prolonged QT 
syndrome.
Which of the following drugs does not cause a prolonged QT interval?
englishExplanation:
8. B.  Dipyridamole
The QT interval is measured from the beginning of the QRS to the end of the T wave and represents depolarization and repolarization of the ventricular myocardium. Any drug that prolongs 
depolarization or repolarization can cause QT prolongation. A prolonged QT can predispose to 
polymorphic VT called Torsades de Pointes (TdP) due to its characteristic appearance.

CARDIOLOGY | ANSWERS
114
114
Dipyridamole inhibits the phosphodiesterase enzymes that normally break down cAMP and/or 
cGMP and is therefore used as an antiplatelet to block platelet activity. It is not known to cause 
prolongation of the QT interval. The rest of the drugs in the answer options are all antiarrhythmics 
which can prolong the QT.

An 84-year-old woman was on the coronary care unit having had a 
temporary pacing wire inserted for complete heart block two days ago. 
The nursing staff had checked the temporary wire and the threshold 
was 3 V.
What is the best course of action?
englishExplanation:
13. D.  Set the output to 6 V
The aim of temporary pacing is to provide support until a permanent pacemaker is implanted. As 
long as there is reliable capture there is no need to reposition the wire. It is sufficient to program 
the output above the threshold (with a safety margin) to ensure capture.
Please note that a sudden rise in pacing threshold may indicate an unstable wire position which may 
move further leading to failure of capture or it may indicate myocardial perforation. The temporary wire 
should be used for short periods of time and permanent pacing should be instituted as soon as possible 
to avoid potential complications, which may include myocardial perforation, tamponade, and sepsis.

resynchronization therapy of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC). Cardiac Pacing and Cardiac

2281–2329. doi: 0.1093/eurheartj/eht150. http://www.escardio.org/guidelines

had no significant past medical history and was a non-smoker. Her risk 
of having coronary artery disease was estimated at 38%.
What is the best test to evaluate the possibility of coronary artery 
disease?
englishExplanation:
14. E.  Myocardial perfusion scan
This woman is less than 65 years old and has symptoms suggestive of stable angina but has no risk 
factors for coronary artery disease (CAD). Her risk of CAD is, therefore, around 38% and so functional imaging for myocardial ischaemia is indicated.
The 2010 NICE guidelines provide a tool for risk stratifying patients according to the clinical presentation, age, and presence of risk factors for CAD. If risk is less than 30% then CT calcium scoring 
is the first-line investigation, and if risk is between 30 and 60% then functional imaging is indicated. 
Invasive coronary angiography is indicated if the risk is 61–90%.

16. A.  Intravenous labetalol
This man has a hypertensive emergency, which is a severe increase in blood pressure (>180 mmHg 
systolic or >110 mmHg diastolic) associated with acute impairment of one or more target organs. 
He has renal impairment and left ventricular failure as well as papilloedema.
The treatment is to lower the blood pressure within minutes to hours and intravenous antihypertensive medications are recommended. Intravenous nitroprusside is most commonly used due to its

vital organ circulation. The aim is, therefore, to decrease the systolic blood pressure by no more 
than 25–30% as soon as possible then gradually to a target of 160/100 mmHg to avoid hypoperfusion of the vital organs if the blood pressure lowering is more precipitous.

This woman has sustained a non-ST elevation acute coronary syndrome. Her immediate and 
subsequent management will be determined predominantly by her age and numerous existing comorbidities. She is already on adequate medical treatment. In view of her age and co-morbidities, 
a coronary intervention will not improve quality of life and will be associated with significant risk 
of stroke, bleeding, or further coronary events. She already has a significant risk of bleeding on 
warfarin (HAS-BLED score of at least 3) and addition of aspirin, clopidogrel, or fondaparinux will

A 66-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 
palpitations and dizziness. He had a past medical history of hypertension 
and ischaemic heart disease, and had had a myocardial infarction six 
months previously for which he had percutaneous coronary intervention 
to the left anterior descending artery.
On examination, his heart rate was 190 beats per minute and the 12lead ECG showed ventricular tachycardia. His blood pressure was 60/30 
mmHg, his respiratory rate was 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen 
saturation was 96% on air. He denied chest pain and his lungs were clear 
on examination. He underwent emergency DC cardioversion to sinus 
rhythm in the emergency department. His sinus rhythm ECG showed 
evidence of an old anterior infarction and nil else.
Troponin T was 25 ng/L (<14) at presentation and 40 ng/L (<14) at 12 
hours after the onset of symptoms.
An echocardiogram on the following day showed left ventricular anterior 
wall hypokinesia/akinesia and an ejection fraction of 35%.
What is the best long-term management strategy?

options.text: Refer for an in-patient implantable cardioverter defibrillator
Refer for in-patient electrophysiology testing and ablation of VT
Refer for in-patient percutanous coronary intervention
Refer to the cardiology outpatient department for assessment

21. A.  Refer for an inpatient implantable cardioverter defibrillator
This man has an ischaemic cardiomyopathy and presented with ventricular tachycardia (VT) with 
haemodynamic compromise. He is, therefore, stratified to the highest risk category for sudden cardiac death and should receive an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) for secondary prevention before he goes home. Data from trials have shown that amiodarone on its own is not sufficiently

protective and is inferior to ICDs in preventing sudden cardiac death. VT ablation in this patient population is reserved for patients who experience recurrent shocks from their ICD due to VT that is not controlled by antiarrhythmic medication and there is no indication for VT ablation alone in these patients.
There is no evidence that this is an acute ischaemic event. There was no chest pain on presentation 
and the ECG post cardioversion showed no acute changes. The mild troponin rise seen can be explained by the tachycardia.
Discharging this patient for an outpatient cardiology appointment is inappropriate and unsafe.

question:
A 34-year-old woman presented with palpitations. She had recently 
been assessed by a cardiac electrophysiologist and was awaiting an 
electrophysiological study with a view to ablation. She had tried the 
Valsalva manoeuvre at home but it hadn’t worked. Vagal manoeuvres in 
the emergency department had no effect. Her heart rate was 200 beats 
per minute and blood pressure was 140/80 mmHg.
Investigations:
What is the best treatment?
englishExplanation:
22. B.  Intravenous amiodarone
The ECG shows an irregular tachycardia with bizarre broad complexes. The diagnosis is, therefore, 
AF with conduction over a manifest accessory pathway (i.e. pre-excited AF).
AF occurs in over 30% of patients with accessory pathways and is a marker for the risk of sudden 
cardiac death in these patients. The accessory pathway lacks the rate-limiting characteristics of the 
AV node and the risk of sudden death is related to the refractory period of the accessory pathway 
(its ability to conduct at very fast rates due to a short recovery time). An idea about the refractory 
period can be obtained by scanning the pre-excited ECG for the shortest RR interval. In general, 
pre-excited AF with RR intervals shorter than 260 ms is considered ‘unsafe’ and warrant inpatient 
definitive treatment by ablation. This patient’s shortest RR interval was 200 ms.
The acute management depends on haemodynamic stability. Haemodynamically unstable patients 
should be cardioverted electrically. More stable patients can be given medications that slow down 
pathway conduction (and terminate AF), including class I and III antiarrhythmic drugs. Consideration 
must be given to the risk of thromboembolism in these patients where relevant before cardioversion. Drugs that only block the AV node (i.e. beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers) increase 
pre-excitation and are, therefore, not advised. Digoxin has a variable effect on accessory pathway 
conduction and may reduce its refractory period and increase mortality.
Camm A, Lip G, Atar D et al. 2012 focused update of the European Society of Cardiology  
Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation. European Heart Journal 2012; 33: 2719–2747.

A 25-year-old Somali woman, who was 38 weeks pregnant, was 
admitted to the acute medical unit with lethargy and breathlessness. 
She had been well throughout her pregnancy and was taking no regular 
medication.
On examination, her temperature was 36.0°C and pulse 100 beats per 
minute. Blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg. Respiratory rate was 25 
breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% on air. Cardiovascular 
examination revealed a laterally displaced apex beat and gallop rhythm. 
On auscultation of her chest, there were crepitations to the mid-zones 
bilaterally. Abdominal examination was consistent with pregnancy.
What medication regimen would be safe for this patient?
englishExplanation:
24. C.  Furosemide, digoxin, and bisoprolol
Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a dilated cardiomyopathy occurring in the last month of pregnancy 
or within five months after delivery, without pre-existing heart disease or identifiable cause. The 
diagnosis may be difficult as normal findings in pregnancy may include shortness of breath, fatigue, 
sinus tachycardia, mildly raised JVP, lower limb oedema, a displaced apex, flow murmurs, and 
even a physiological S3 over the apex. Around one-half of women recover completely within 
a few months post-partum, while the other half continue to have varying degrees of systolic 
dysfunction.
The treatment of peripartum cardiomyopathy follows the same lines of pharmacological treatment 
as other heart failure conditions, which includes oxygen, digoxin, vasodilators, and diuretics. Note 
that ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are absolutely contraindicated during pregnancy but should be commenced promptly after delivery.
Regitz-Zagrosek V, Blomstrom Lundqvist C, Borghi C. European Society of Cardiology guidelines 
of the management of cardiovascular diseases during pregnancy. European Heart Journal 2011; 32:

warfarin. Her history included an AF ablation procedure two years ago 
but her AF had recurred. The heart rate on the monitor varied from 90 
to 120 beats per minute in AF.
The patient’s GP had arranged a 24-hour ECG and it showed a 5 second 
pause at 02:35 hours and another 6.2 second pause at 09:00 hours. The 
symptom diary reported a collapse in shower at 09:00 hours.
What would be the best management?

26. B.  Permanent pacemaker set to VVIR
This patient has permanent AF and the best strategy for her is rate control and anticoagulation. Her 
heart rate is still not controlled adequately as her resting heart rate in the acute medical unit was up 
to 120 beats per minute. She therefore needs more rate-limiting medications. However, she also 
has symptomatic syncopal pauses that indicate a struggling conduction system and an increase in 
dose of bisoprolol would only aggravate the blackouts.
This lady, therefore, has a class I indication for a single chamber pacemaker set to VVIR.

Researchers investigated if there was an association between chronic 
Helicobacter pylori infection and coronary heart disease in young 
patients. A case–control study design was used. The cases were 1,122 
survivors of suspected acute myocardial infarction aged between 30 
and 49 years. For each case, a control matched for age and sex with 
no history of coronary heart disease was recruited. For the cases 
and controls, the risk factor of chronic infection with H pylori was 
confirmed serologically. Participants were categorized as seropositive 
or seronegative for H pylori infection antibodies. The participants 
provided information on other risk factors for coronary heart disease, 
including smoking behaviour, indicators of socioeconomic status, obesity, 
and blood lipid concentrations. Cases were asked about their habits 
and history just before their myocardial infarction, whereas controls 
were asked about their current habits and history. Blood samples were 
obtained from cases within 24 hours of the onset of symptoms, and from 
controls after the collection of the information for the other risk factors.
Of the 1,122 cases with early onset myocardial infarction, 472 (42%) 
were seropositive for H pylori antibodies compared with 272 (24%) of 
the 1,122 controls. The unadjusted odds ratio of early onset myocardial 
infarction if seropositive compared to seronegative for H pylori infection 
antibodies was 2.27 (95% confidence interval 1.89–2.72).*

confirmed serologically for the cases and controls. (BMJ 1999;319:1157)

infarction: case-control and sibling pairs study’, BMJ, 1999; 341:6549
What is the best interpretation of the unadjusted odds ratio of early 
onset myocardial infarction if seropositive to seronegative for H pylori 
infection antibodies?

options.text: If seronegative for H pylori infection antibodies, the odds of early onset myocardial infarction
If seropositive for H pylori infection antibodies, the odds of early onset myocardial infarction
No significant difference between seropositive and seronegative for H pylori infection
The odds of early onset myocardial infarction if seropositive for H pylori infection
The odds of early onset myocardial infarction if seropositive for H pylori infection antibodies

englishExplanation:
27. B.  If seropositive for H pylori infection antibodies, the odds of early onset myocardial infarction were increased significantly and by 1.27 times compared to seronegative for H pylori antibodies
The purpose of the case–control study was to investigate if H pylori antibody seropositivity was a 
potential risk factor for acute myocardial infarction in young patients. Two groups of patients were 
selected on the basis of their disease status: the cases, who were survivors of suspected acute myocardial infarction and aged between 30 and 49 years; and healthy controls matched for age and sex. By 
definition a case–control study is retrospective in design, with participants providing information about 
their past exposure to potential risk factors. This is particularly important for the cases whose current 
exposure to risk factors may have changed as a result of the development of the disease. However, 
sometimes the controls provide information about their current exposure to risk factors. The cases 
and controls are then compared to ascertain whether particular risk factors are more common in one 
group than in the other. In particular, in the above study the cases and controls were compared to 
ascertain whether H pylori antibody seropositivity was more common in one group than the other. If 
so, it would be considered a potential risk factor for acute myocardial infarction in young patients.
The association between chronic H pylori infection and coronary heart disease in young patients 
could not be investigated using a relative risk. This was because it was not possible to estimate the 
population at risk of early onset myocardial infarction. That is, the proportion of participants who 
experienced early onset myocardial infarction, whether overall or for those participants who were 
seropositive for H pylori infection antibodies and for those who were seronegative, did not estimate the proportion in the population. The proportion of participants who had experienced early 
onset myocardial infarction was dictated by the ratio of cases to controls, which was 1:1, and decided at the design stage. Instead the association between chronic H pylori infection and coronary 
heart disease in young patients was quantified by an odds ratio, which estimates the population relative risk. The odds ratio will be a good estimate of the population relative risk if the prevalence of 
the disease outcome in the population is rare, typically considered to be less than 10%.
The cross tabulation of the frequencies of chronic infection with H pylori as confirmed serologically 
for the cases and controls is shown in Table 4.1. To calculate the odds ratio of early onset myocardial infarction if seropositive compared to seronegative for H pylori infection antibodies, the odds 
of early onset myocardial infarction if seropositive for H pylori infection antibodies were divided by 
the odds of early onset myocardial infarction if seronegative for H pylori infection antibodies. The 
odds of an early onset myocardial infarction if the risk factor was present or absent, i.e. seropositive or seronegative, were not the probability of an early onset myocardial infarction occurring; the 
odds are an alternative way of expressing probability. For each of the risk factor groups—seropositive and seronegative for H pylori infection antibodies—the odds of an early onset myocardial 
infarction were derived as the probability of an early onset myocardial infarction occurring divided 
by the probability of the outcome not occurring. For example, of the 744 participants who were 
seropositive for H pylori infection antibodies, 472 had experienced an early onset myocardial infarction whereas 272 had not. Therefore, for those participants who were seropositive the odds of an 
early onset myocardial infarction were (472 ÷ 744) ÷ (272 ÷ 744) = (472 ÷ 744) × (744 ÷ 272) = 
472 ÷ 272 = 1.74. Hence, the odds of an early onset myocardial infarction occurring if seropositive 
for H pylori infection antibodies were the ratio of the number of participants who had experienced 
an early onset myocardial infarction to those who had not. The odds of an early onset myocardial 
infarction occurring if seronegative for H pylori infection antibodies were calculated in a similar 
way—that is, the ratio of the number of participants who had experienced an early onset myocardial infarction to those who had not: 650 ÷ 850 = 0.76.
The unadjusted odds ratio of early onset myocardial infarction if seropositive for H pylori infection  
antibodies compared to seronegative for H pylori infection antibodies was derived as the odds of an 
early onset myocardial infarction if seropositive divided by the odds if seronegative: (472 ÷ 272) ÷  
(650 ÷ 850) = (472 ÷ 272) x (850 ÷ 650) = (472 × 850) ÷ (272 × 650) = 2.27. Hence, the odds ratio 
was the ratio of the cross products of the frequencies in the table. Therefore, the odds of an early onset 

CARDIOLOGY | ANSWERS
122
122
myocardial infarction if seropositive were 2.27 times those if seronegative—hence the odds was increased by 1.27 times if seropositive compared to seronegative. Early onset myocardial infarction was 
more likely if seropositive for H pylori infection antibodies than if seronegative. Therefore, being seropositive for H pylori infection antibodies was a potential risk factor for early onset myocardial infarction.
The 95% confidence interval for the population odds ratio was 1.89–2.72; because it excluded 
unity (1.0) the increased occurrence of an early onset myocardial infarction for the risk factor of 
seropositive for H pylori infection antibodies compared with seronegative was therefore statistically 
significant at the 5% level of significance (see Sedgwick, 2012b). The researchers reported that the 
odds ratio was reduced to 1.87 (1.42–2.47) after adjustment for potential confounding by smoking 
and indicators of socioeconomic status, and further reduced to 1.75 (1.29–2.36) after additional 
adjustment for blood lipid concentrations and obesity. Adjustment for confounding was achieved 
using logistic regression (see Sedgwick, 2013). Hence, a moderate association existed between coronary heart disease and H pylori antibody seropositivity that could not be fully explained by other 
risk factors. Because the association between chronic H pylori infection and early onset myocardial 
infarction remained significant after adjustment for confounding, chronic H pylori infection is said to 
be independently associated with early onset myocardial infarction.
In the above study the cases and controls were matched for age and sex. For each case, an otherwise healthy control of the same age and sex was recruited. The advantage of matching was that 
it minimized the effects of confounding due to the matching variables (age and sex) when comparing the risk factor groups (seropositive versus seronegative) in the odds of early onset myocardial 
infarction (see Sedgwick, 2012a). However, when deriving the odds ratio as detailed above the 
researchers did not take advantage of the matched pairing between the cases and controls. By acknowledging the pairing of cases and controls a more precise odds ratio could have been derived. 
In order to do so in the above example, it would have been necessary to consider the number of 
discordant pairs in the risk factor of ‘seropositivity’ status. A discordant pair would occur if the 
case was seropositive but their matched control was seronegative, or if the case was seronegative 
and their matched control was seropositive. Concordant pairs would be those matched pairs of 
cases and controls that are either both seronegative or both seropositive. For the above example 
the odds ratio would be derived as the number of pairs where the case was seropositive but the 
matched control was seronegative, divided by the number of pairs where the case was seronegative but the matched control was seropositive. Those pairs of cases and controls that had the same 
serological status (i.e. concordant pairs) would have provided no information as to the association 
between chronic H pylori infection and coronary heart disease in young patients; therefore they 
would not have been included in the calculation of the odds ratio.
As described above an odds ratio is an estimate of the population relative risk. Often an odds ratio 
is interpreted as a relative risk. Hence the odds ratio in the above example would indicate that 
there was an increased risk of 127% of early onset myocardial infarction if seropositive for H pylori 
infection antibodies compared to being seronegative. In particular the odds ratio will be a good 
estimate of the population relative risk if the prevalence of the disease outcome in the population 
is rare, typically considered to be less than 10%. It is anticipated that the disease outcome of early 
onset myocardial infarction at a young age was rare in the population. Therefore the presented 
odds ratio would be expected to be a good estimate of the relative risk of early onset myocardial 
infarction if seropositive compared to seronegative for H pylori infection antibodies.
Danesh J, Youngman L, Clark S, Parish S, Peto R, Collins R for the International Studies of Infarct Survival (ISIS) Collaborative Group. Helicobacter pylori infection and early onset myocardial infarction: 
case-control and sibling pairs study. BMJ 1999;319:1157.
Sedgwick P. Why match in case-control studies? BMJ 2012a;344:e691.
Sedgwick P. Confidence intervals and statistical significance: rules of thumb. BMJ 2012b;345:e4960
Sedgwick P. Logistic regression. BMJ 2013;347:f4488.

As the CHA2DS2VASc score increases so too does the associated adjusted stroke rate (% year). For 
example a CHA2DS2VASc score of 0 gives a 0% per year risk, while a score of 1 gives a 1.3% per 
year risk. A score of 9 gives a 15.2% per year risk’
The risk of stroke is not the same in all patients and is dependent on the clinical characteristics of 
each patient. Clinical scoring systems are available to aid in risk-stratifying patients and guiding use 
of anticoagulants. The most commonly used scoring system is the CHA2DS2VASc score (Table 4.3). 
If total score is 1 or higher (2 in females) then oral anticoagulants are indicated. There is no longer a 
role for aspirin in prevention of thromboembolic complications of AF.

A 47-year-old woman known to have Turner syndrome presented to 
the acute medical unit with central chest pain. It came on suddenly 
four hours previously while playing tennis. She felt dizzy and lightheaded. Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) eased the pain but it hadn’t resolved 
completely.
She had not been seen by the endocrine team for several years 
having not attended follow-up appointments. She was on no regular 
medication. She had come back from a walking holiday in North 
America six days ago. She smoked 20 cigarettes per day and drank 10 
units of alcohol per week.
On examination, her blood pressure was 165/65 mmHg in the right arm 
and 140/45 mmHg in the left arm. There was an early diastolic murmur.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
12. A.  Aortic dissection
Turner syndrome is gonadal dysgenesis with partial or complete absence of one X chromosome 
(45 XO) caused by a sporadic nondisjunction of chromosomes.
The classic phenotype is short stature, webbing of the neck (25–40%), micrognathia, low-set ears, 
high arched palate, cubitus valgus, and shield-like chest. Also associated is lymphoedema, congenital 

DIABETES AND ENDOCRINOLOGY | ANSWERS
149
renal abnormalities (horseshoe kidney), hypothyroidism, osteoporosis, short fourth/fifth metacarpals, and cardiac abnormalities.
The cardiac abnormalities occur in 20–50% of patients with Turner syndrome and include coarctation of the aorta (10% and the commonest abnormality). Other cardiac abnormalities are bicuspid 
aortic valve, mitral valve prolapse, partial anomalous venous drainage, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, and aortic root dilatation.
All patients with Turner syndrome should have an echo every 3–5 years depending on the cardiac 
abnormalities. Patients with risk factors for dissection and rupture need more frequent follow-up.

519–526.

Investigations:
troponin T 35 ng/L (<14)

This man has a good story for a cardiac syncope. Factors in this history that would lead you to this

question:
A 70-year-old man was admitted to an orthopaedic ward after a fall and 
fractured left neck of femur. The orthopaedic foundation 2 doctor noted 
he had a postural drop in blood pressure of 10 mmHg and felt dizzy on 
standing. The patient had a history of diabetes mellitus and was taking 
metformin 500 mg twice daily.
Once he had recovered from his operation, he was referred to a syncope 
clinic for further assessment.
Which of the following most supports the diagnosis of orthostatic 
hypertension?

options.text: An asymptomatic fall in systolic blood pressure of ≥20 mmHg on active standing for three
An asymptomatic fall in systolic blood pressure to less than 100 mmHg on active standing
The induction of loss of consciousness in the absence of hypotension or bradycardia on
A symptomatic episode of bradycardia and hypotension at three minutes on tilt-testing
A symptomatic progressive fall in blood pressure on tilt-testing ≥20 mmHg

englishExplanation:
27. E.  A symptomatic progressive fall in blood pressure on tilt-testing of ≥20 mmHg
Normally, standing causes compensatory reflexes so that there is only a small fall in blood pressure 
(5–10 mmHg) and an increase in pulse rate (10–20 beats per minute). If intravascular volume is depleted or autonomic reflexes impaired, a significant reduction in blood pressure occurs and causes 
orthostatic hypotension (OH). This is common in the elderly for a number of reasons: a reduction 
in baroreceptor sensitivity; the use of antihypertensives; and diseases that cause autonomic failure 
(Parkinson’s disease, Lewy body dementia, multisystem atrophy, diabetes, paraneoplastic syndromes) and volume depletion.
The initial investigation for OH is ‘active standing’; the patient arises from supine to erect and the BP 
is measured for three minutes. It is diagnostic if there is a significant drop in systolic blood pressure 
(≥20 mmHg, or systolic BP falls to less than 90 mmHg) and the patient is symptomatic. When ‘active standing’ is not diagnostic, or the symptoms could be neurocardiogenic (reflex) syncope or OH, 
then it would be appropriate to progress to a tilt-table test in order to reproduce the symptoms. 
It is important to rule out structural heart disease beforehand. The tilt table is set in a quiet room 
with minimal distractions. The patient is initially monitored for five minutes supine. The purposebuilt couch then tilts the head up to 60–70° smoothly and quickly within ten seconds. The patient 
is encouraged to report symptoms. There is beat-to-beat ECG and BP monitoring from a device 
attached to a finger. This is the passive phase and lasts for 20–45 minutes or until symptoms are 
reproduced. If neurocardiogenic syncope is suspected and the passive test has been negative, then 
300–400 mcg of GTN may be given. Orthostatic hypotension is diagnosed if there is a slow, progressive, and significant (≥20 mmHg) decrease in systolic blood pressure on passive tilting with or 
without symptoms. If symptoms are reproduced either in the passive or active phase (after GTN) 
and there is reflex hypotension/bradycardia, then this is diagnostic of neurocardiogenic (reflex) 
syncope.
Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (version 2009): The Task Force for the Diagnosis and Management of Syncope of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC). European Heart 
Journal 2009; 30: 2631–2671.

question:
Intravenous nicardipine is a commonly used agent for hypertensive emergencies.
It is a particularly favored agent in which clinical scenario?

options.text: Acute decompensated heart failure with low ejection fraction.
Hypertensive emergency associated with an acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic

correctAnswer: Hypertensive emergency associated with an acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
englishExplanation:
Neurocritical Care Preference:
Nicardipine is a preferred agent for hypertensive emergencies in acute ischaemic
stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH). Unlike nitrates (GTN, nitroprusside),
which cause venodilation and can theoretically increase intracranial pressure (ICP)
by increasing cerebral blood volume, nicardipine is a highly selective arteriolar vasodilator. It effectively lowers mean arterial pressure (MAP) while preserving cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) and does not adversely affect cerebral autoregulation
curves.
Mechanism of Action:
Nicardipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that inhibits L-type calcium channels on vascular smooth muscle, preventing calcium influx and causing
relaxation. It has high vascular selectivity and minimal negative inotropic effects,
contrasting with non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem) which significantly
depress myocardial contractility and conduction.
Comparison with Other Agents:
In acute coronary syndromes (Option C), nitrates and beta-blockers are preferred to
reduce preload and myocardial oxygen demand. In aortic stenosis (Option D), vasodilators must be used with extreme caution due to the risk of profound hypotension in the setting of fixed cardiac output. In thyrotoxicosis (Option E), beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol) are the mainstay of therapy.
Clinical Pearl
Neurocritical Care Indication:
It is a first-line agent for blood pressure control in most neurological emergencies
(ischaemic/haemorrhagic stroke, subarachnoid haemorrhage).
Comparison with Labetalol:
Labetalol is the primary alternative for neuro-hypertensive emergencies.
Nicardipine is preferred if the patient is bradycardic, has reactive airway disease, or
requires precise titration; labetalol is preferred if the patient is tachycardic.
Reflex Tachycardia Mechanism:
As a potent arteriolar vasodilator, nicardipine causes a baroreceptor-mediated increase in sympathetic tone, leading to reflex tachycardia. This can increase myocardial oxygen demand.
Coronary Effects:
Nicardipine is a potent coronary vasodilator, making it a reasonable choice in perioperative hypertension, provided the reflex tachycardia is managed or not
contraindicated.
Pharmacokinetics vs Clevidipine:
Nicardipine has a longer half-life (approx. 15-45 mins) compared to clevidipine (1-2
mins). While clevidipine allows ultra-rapid titration (metabolised by plasma esterases), nicardipine offers a smoother offset, reducing the risk of rebound hypertension if the infusion is interrupted.
Peripheral Administration:
Nicardipine is associated with a high risk of thrombophlebitis. While it can be administered peripherally in an emergency, large bore access is required, and the infusion site must be rotated every 12 hours or switched to a central line as soon as
feasible.
Caution in Aortic Stenosis:
Like all potent afterload reducers, nicardipine should be used with extreme caution
in severe aortic stenosis. The fixed obstruction prevents a compensatory increase in
cardiac output, potentially leading to precipitous hypotension.
Distinction from Nimodipine:
Do not confuse nicardipine with nimodipine. Nimodipine is used specifically for the
prevention of delayed cerebral ischaemia (vasospasm) in subarachnoid haemorrhage due to its lipophilicity and cerebral selectivity, whereas nicardipine is used for
systemic blood pressure control.

Hepatic Metabolism:
Nicardipine is extensively metabolised by the liver (CYP3A4). Dose adjustments or
careful titration are required in patients with hepatic impairment, as the half-life
may be significantly prolonged.
Standard Dosing Regimen:
The typical starting dose is 5 mg/hr, titrating by 2.5 mg/hr every 5-15 minutes to a
maximum of 15 mg/hr. Once the target blood pressure is achieved, the infusion rate
should be down-titrated to the lowest effective dose.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ IV nicardipine من الأدوية الشائعة لemergency ارتفاع الضغط، لأنه دوا vasodilator بيشتغل بسرعة وبيخفّض الـ blood pressure بشكل تدريجي. وهاد بيجي option مفضّل بالذات في حالة hypertensive emergency مع acute ischaemic stroke أو haemorrhagic stroke، لأن هاد بالضبط واحد من الـ scenarios اللي بتحتاج neurocritical care وتحتاج ضبط دقيق للضغط. فبدل ما تختار حالة تانية كـ acute decompensated heart failure أو acute coronary syndrome، الخيار الصح هو emergency ارتفاع الضغط المرتبط بـ stroke.
الفخ: الخيار الغلط هو acute decompensated heart failure أو acute coronary syndrome أو aortic stenosis، لأن هاد مش الـ scenario اللي بيتفاضل عليه الـ IV nicardipine. المعيار هون إن الـ scenario اللي بنحسب له هو emergency ارتفاع الضغط مع stroke.

question:
A patient with a recent TIA has a confirmed symptomatic carotid stenosis of 60%
according to NASCET criteria. What is the most appropriate management?
englishExplanation:
Introduction:
High-grade symptomatic carotid stenosis carries a very high risk of recurrent
stroke, and urgent revascularization is indicated.
Pathophysiology:
Atherosclerotic plaque in the internal carotid artery can lead to stroke either by
causing low flow or, more commonly, by acting as a source of emboli to the brain
(artery-to-artery embolism). A 'symptomatic' stenosis is one that has already declared itself by causing a TIA or stroke in its territory.
Clinical Evidence (NASCET):
The NASCET trial demonstrated that for patients with symptomatic stenosis of 7099%, carotid endarterectomy (CEA) provides a substantial reduction in stroke risk
(absolute risk reduction ~17% at 2 years). For moderate stenosis (50-69%), the benefit is significant but smaller (absolute risk reduction ~4.6% at 5 years), particularly
in men. Stenosis <50% does not benefit from surgery.
Management Rationale:
NICE guidelines recommend that patients with stable neurological symptoms and
symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50-99% (NASCET) should undergo carotid endarterectomy (CEA) within 7 days of symptom onset. Carotid artery stenting (CAS)
is an alternative if CEA is unsuitable (e.g., surgically inaccessible, radiation-induced
stenosis) or if the patient is at high surgical risk.
Clinical Pearl
Revascularization Thresholds:

Symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50-99% (NASCET) carries a high risk of early recurrent stroke, particularly within the first few days. Urgent revascularization is indicated to remove the embolic source. Stenosis less than 50% is typically managed
medically.
NASCET Criteria:
This is the standard method for measuring the degree of stenosis on angiography,
comparing the narrowest diameter to the diameter of the normal distal internal
carotid artery.
Intervention Choice:
NICE guidelines recommend Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA) as the first-line intervention. Carotid Artery Stenting (CAS) is reserved for patients where CEA is unsuitable (e.g., high bifurcation, 'hostile neck' from radiation) or contraindicated.
Asymptomatic Stenosis:
The management of asymptomatic carotid stenosis is more controversial, with a
much smaller benefit from intervention. It is typically reserved for patients with
very high-grade stenosis and a low peri-procedural risk.
Medical Optimization:
Aggressive medical management is mandatory for all carotid stenosis patients. This
includes long-term antiplatelet therapy (clopidogrel 75mg is first-line in the UK),
high-intensity statins (e.g., atorvastatin 80mg), and strict blood pressure control.
Timing of Surgery:
The benefit of carotid revascularization drops rapidly with time. NICE guidelines
target surgery within 1 week of symptom onset. Beyond 2 weeks, the risk-benefit ratio becomes less favourable, though intervention may still be considered.
Measurement Methodologies:
NASCET calculates stenosis by comparing the residual lumen to the distal normal
ICA. ECST compares the residual lumen to the estimated original lumen at the site
of stenosis. Consequently, a 50% NASCET stenosis is roughly equivalent to a 7075% ECST stenosis. UK guidelines utilize NASCET criteria.
Cranial Nerve Injury:
Post-operative cranial nerve palsies are a known complication of CEA. The hypoglossal nerve (tongue deviation to affected side) and vagus/recurrent laryngeal
nerve (hoarseness) are most commonly affected. Facial nerve (marginal mandibular
branch) injury causes drooping of the corner of the mouth.
Cerebral Hyperperfusion Syndrome:
A rare but serious complication following revascularization, caused by impaired autoregulation in a chronically hypoperfused hemisphere. It presents with severe ipsilateral headache, seizures, and focal neurological deficits, potentially leading to intracerebral haemorrhage. Strict blood pressure control is preventative.
Symptomatic Definition:
Symptomatic stenosis is defined as the occurrence of a TIA or non-disabling stroke
in the territory of the carotid artery within the preceding 6 months. Patients with total occlusion (100%) do not benefit from surgery.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ symptomatic carotid stenosis بنسبة 60% حسب معايير NASCET يعني إن التضييق صار يقول حاله لأنه سبّب TIA في territory بتاعه. وهاي الـ high-grade symptomatic stenosis عندها خطر كبير جداً على تكرار الـ stroke، فـ urgent revascularization هي indicated. تجربة NASCET أثبتت إن الـ carotid endarterectomy بتقلّل خطر الـ stroke بشكل واضح، والاستفادة بتكون أكبر كلما زادت نسبة الـ stenosis، بينما الـ stenosis أقل من 50% ما بيستفيد من الجراحة. و NICE بتوصي بـ carotid endarterectomy خلال 7 أيام من ظهور الأعراض.
الفخ: الخيار الغلط هو conservative management مع aspirin أو clopidogrel لحالهم، لأن الـ stenosis عندها 60% symptomatic وهي فوق حد الـ 50% اللي بيستفيد من الجراحة، فـ aspirin ما بكفّي. و الـ IV alteplase ما إله مكان هنا، مش acute ischemic stroke داخل الـ window.

question:
A patient with a history of atrial fibrillation and ischemic heart disease takes an
overdose of flecainide. They present with a profoundly wide QRS complex,
bradycardia, and refractory cardiogenic shock. Which intervention has been
shown to be a potentially life-saving rescue therapy for this specific toxicity?
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology:
Flecainide is a Class 1c antiarrhythmic that blocks fast sodium channels (Nav1.5),
leading to QRS prolongation and negative inotropy. It is highly lipophilic, making it
susceptible to lipid sequestration.
First-Line Management:
Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate (8.4% or 4.2%) is the first-line therapy. It works via
two mechanisms: increasing extracellular sodium concentration to overcome the
competitive blockade, and alkalinisation (reducing drug ionisation), which decreases the drug's affinity for sodium channels.
Rescue Therapy (ILE):
Intravenous Lipid Emulsion (ILE) is indicated for refractory shock or cardiac arrest
(Toxbase/AAGBI). The 'lipid sink' hypothesis suggests the lipid emulsion creates a

compartment that draws the lipophilic drug from tissues. It may also provide free
fatty acids as a metabolic substrate for the myocardium.
Analysis of Other Options:
High-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy (HIET) is the primary rescue therapy for
calcium channel blocker and beta-blocker toxicity, not sodium channel blockers.
Calcium infusions are similarly indicated for calcium channel blocker overdose or
hyperkalaemia. Amiodarone and beta-blockers would exacerbate bradycardia and
conduction delays in this setting.
Clinical Pearl
Expanded ILE Indications:
While first established for Local Anaesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST), the use of
ILE has expanded to include refractory cardiotoxicity from a variety of lipophilic
drugs, including tricyclic antidepressants, calcium channel blockers, and Class 1c
agents.
Use-Dependence:
Class 1C drugs exhibit use-dependence, meaning their blocking effect is more pronounced at faster heart rates, which can lead to a vicious cycle of arrhythmia.
ECG Severity Markers:
Similar to tricyclic antidepressant toxicity, the degree of QRS widening on the ECG
is a direct marker of the severity of sodium channel blockade and the risk of malignant arrhythmia.
Contraindications in Ischaemic Heart Disease:
Class 1c agents are contraindicated in patients with ischaemic or structural heart
disease due to an increased risk of proarrhythmia and mortality, as demonstrated in
the CAST trial.
ILE Dosing Regimen:
Administer 20% Intralipid as a 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 1 minute. Follow with an infusion of 15 mL/kg/hr. The bolus can be repeated twice at 5-minute intervals for persistent cardiovascular collapse (maximum cumulative dose approximately 12
mL/kg).
Bicarbonate Mechanism:
Sodium bicarbonate works via the 'molar sodium' effect (overcoming channel blockade) and serum alkalinisation (reducing drug ionisation and receptor affinity).
Target a serum pH of 7.50–7.55.
Extracorporeal Life Support:
If ILE and maximal medical therapy fail, V-A ECMO is the definitive rescue strategy
to support circulation while the drug is metabolised.

Differentiation from HIET:
High-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy (HIET) is the specific antidote for calcium
channel blocker and beta-blocker toxicity. While it has positive inotropic effects, it
does not address the sodium channel blockade mechanism central to flecainide
toxicity.
Avoidance of Other Antiarrhythmics:
Avoid administering other Class Ia (e.g., procainamide) or Class III (e.g., amiodarone) antiarrhythmics, as these can further prolong the QT interval or QRS complex and exacerbate cardiogenic shock.
Electrolyte Optimisation:
Acidosis exacerbates sodium channel blockade; therefore, maintaining a normal or
slightly alkalotic pH is crucial. Hypokalaemia should be avoided, but hyperkalaemia
must also be managed aggressively as it can potentiate conduction block.

ليش: الـ flecainide هاد دوا Class 1c antiarrhythmic بيحجب الـ fast sodium channels يعني Nav1.5، وهاد بيسبب QRS prolongation و negative inotropy. وهو lipophilic جداً، فهاد بيخليه قابل للـ sequestration بالدهون. الـ first-line therapy هو hypertonic sodium bicarbonate 8.4% أو 4.2%، وهاد بيشتغل بطريقتين، بس إذا الـ shock refractory أو صار cardiac arrest، الـ IV lipid emulsion بتدخل على طول. الفرضية اسمه lipid sink، يعني الـ emulsion بتعمل compartment بتسحب الدوا الليبرفي من الأنسجة، وبتوفر كمان free fatty acids كـ metabolic substrate للـ myocardium.
الفخ: الخيار الغلط هو high-dose insulin euglycemic therapy أو high-dose calcium infusion، لأن هدول الـ rescue therapy الأساسي لتسميم calcium channel blockers و beta-blockers، مش sodium channel blockers زي الـ flecainide. وكمان الـ amiodarone والـ beta-blockers بيزيدوا الـ bradycardia ويأخروا الـ conduction.

question:
Which inotrope or vasopressor exerts its primary haemodynamic effect through
inhibition of phosphodiesterase-3 rather than adrenoceptor agonism?
englishExplanation:
Milrinone is a selective phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor: it prevents breakdown of
cyclic AMP, increasing contractility and causing systemic and pulmonary vasodilation (an inodilator). Its action is independent of beta-adrenoceptors, so it can retain
efficacy in beta-blocked or beta-receptor-downregulated patients, unlike dobutamine which is a beta-agonist.
Clinical Pearl
Mechanism:
Selective PDE3 inhibition raises cyclic AMP, increasing contractility and causing
vasodilation.

Beta-Independence:
Bypasses beta-adrenoceptors, so it can retain effect during beta-blockade or receptor downregulation in chronic heart failure.
Adverse Effects:
Hypotension and atrial or ventricular arrhythmias are important risks.
Renal Clearance:
Milrinone is renally cleared, so the infusion rate must be reduced in renal impairment to avoid accumulation.
Pulmonary Vasodilation:
Useful where pulmonary vasodilation is desirable, e.g. right ventricular failure with
pulmonary hypertension.
Contrast with Dobutamine:
Dobutamine is a beta-1 agonist and loses efficacy where receptors are downregulated or blocked.
Loading Caution:
A loading dose increases hypotension risk and is often omitted in unstable patients.
Longer Half-Life:
Milrinone has a longer half-life than dobutamine, so effects (and side effects) resolve more slowly.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ milrinone هاد inhibitor انتقائي لـ phosphodiesterase-3، يعني بيمنع breakdown الـ cyclic AMP، فبيزيد الـ contractility وبيسبب vasodilation في الـ systemic والـ pulmonary circulation، يعني هو inodilator. وأهم شي فيه إن فعله مستقل عن الـ beta-adrenoceptors، فبضل فعّال حتى عند مرضى beta-blocked أو عندهم beta receptors downregulated، بعكس الـ dobutamine اللي هو beta-agonist. من الـ adverse effects بتكون hypotension و arrhythmias، وهو renally cleared فأي impairment في الـ kidney لازم يقلل الـ infusion rate.
الفخ: الخيار الغلط هو dobutamine، لأن الناس بتفتكر إنه أقوى inotrope، بس هو beta-1 agonist وبيفقد فعاليته عند الـ beta-blockade أو مع downregulation الـ receptors. أما الـ phenylephrine والـ noradrenaline والـ adrenaline فكلها vasopressors بتعتمد على adrenoceptor agonism مش على PDE3.

question:
A 70-year-old man with a long history of severe COPD presents with increasing
peripheral edema, jugular venous distension, and a tender, enlarged liver. An
echocardiogram confirms severe right ventricular hypertrophy and dilation with
normal left ventricular function. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Left-sided heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)

englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology:
Cor pulmonale is defined as alteration in the structure and function of the right ventricle (RV) caused by a primary disorder of the respiratory system. In severe COPD,
chronic alveolar hypoxia induces pulmonary vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling, increasing pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR). This results in pulmonary hypertension and increased RV afterload. Over time, the RV undergoes hypertrophy
and dilation, eventually leading to failure. The diagnostic hallmark is the exclusion
of left-sided heart disease or congenital heart disease as the cause.
Diagnostic Criteria:
Echocardiography is the first-line investigation, typically showing RV dilation, hypertrophy, and raised pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP). Left ventricular
systolic and diastolic function should be normal, distinguishing this from Group 2
Pulmonary Hypertension (left heart disease).
Management:

Treatment focuses on the underlying pulmonary pathology. Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) is the primary intervention shown to improve survival in COPD patients
with severe hypoxemia, as it mitigates hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.
Diuretics are used cautiously for symptom relief of edema.
Clinical Pearl
Definition:
Cor pulmonale is defined as right ventricular hypertrophy, dilation, or dysfunction
resulting directly from lung disease or pulmonary vasculature disorders, excluding
left-sided heart or congenital causes.
Primary Etiology:
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is the most common cause of cor
pulmonale in developed countries, driven by chronic hypoxia and capillary bed
destruction.
Long-Term Oxygen Therapy (LTOT):
LTOT improves survival in COPD patients with severe hypoxaemia (PaO2 < 7.3
kPa) or moderate hypoxaemia (PaO2 7.3–8.0 kPa) with evidence of cor pulmonale
or polycythaemia.
Clinical Signs:
Examination findings include signs of pulmonary hypertension (loud P2, right ventricular heave) and right heart failure (elevated JVP, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly, ascites).
Electrocardiographic Features:
Classic ECG changes include P-pulmonale (peaked P waves > 2.5mm in II, III, aVF),
right axis deviation, and a right bundle branch block pattern.
Fluid Management:
While diuretics relieve peripheral oedema, excessive diuresis can be dangerous. The
failing RV is preload-dependent; reducing preload too aggressively can precipitate
low cardiac output and hypotension.
Diagnostic Exclusions:
By definition, cor pulmonale excludes right ventricular dysfunction caused by leftsided heart disease (e.g., LV failure, mitral valve disease) or congenital heart
defects.
Echocardiographic Septal Motion:
In severe RV pressure overload, the interventricular septum flattens or bows into
the left ventricle during systole (D-shaped septum), impairing LV filling and cardiac
output via ventricular interdependence.
Secondary Polycythaemia:

Chronic hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin production, leading to polycythaemia.
While this increases oxygen-carrying capacity, the resulting hyperviscosity increases
pulmonary vascular resistance, further burdening the right ventricle.
Acute vs Chronic Presentation:
Cor pulmonale can be acute (e.g., massive pulmonary embolism causing sudden RV
dilation) or chronic (e.g., COPD causing progressive hypertrophy and dilation). The
RV wall is thin in acute failure but thickened (>5mm) in chronic disease.
Biomarkers:
BNP/NT-proBNP levels are typically elevated due to RV stretch but are generally
lower than levels seen in primary left ventricular failure. Disproportionately low
BNP with severe oedema should prompt consideration of non-cardiac causes or
pure right heart failure.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: هاد المريض عنده COPD شديد من زمان، وكل اللي صار إنو الـ hypoxia المزمنة سبّبت vasoconstriction في الأوعية الرئوية وتغيّر في جدارها، فطلع pulmonary hypertension وزاد الـ afterload على الـ right ventricle. مع الوقت الـ RV عمل hypertrophy ومن بعد dilation وfailed، وهاد بظهرك edema وJVD وكبد متضخم ومؤلم. الـ echo بتأكد RV hypertrophy وdilation مع LV function طبيعي، وهاد بالضبط تعريف cor pulmonale لأنه بيجي من مرض رئوي مش من قلب أيسر.
الفخ: أحسن trap إنه يختاروا HFpEF لأن الـ edema والـ JVD بيخلّواهم يفكروا بمشكلة قلب أيسر، بس الـ echo بيقول LV function طبيعي. وConstrictive pericarditis وValvular heart disease وHigh-output heart failure ما بتتماشى مع COPD طويل ومع RV hypertrophy على الـ echo.

question:
The perfusion of the heart muscle itself is determined by the coronary perfusion
pressure (CPP). Which of the following statements about CPP is correct?

options.text: CPP is primarily determined by systolic blood pressure.
It is calculated as: CPP = Mean Arterial Pressure - Central Venous Pressure.
An increase in left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP) will increase CPP.
The majority of left ventricular coronary blood flow occurs during diastole.
Tachycardia improves CPP by increasing the time spent in diastole.

correctAnswer: The majority of left ventricular coronary blood flow occurs during diastole.
englishExplanation:
Physiology of Coronary Perfusion:
The left ventricular (LV) myocardium is perfused almost exclusively during diastole.
During systole, the high intramural pressure generated by the contracting LV compresses the subendocardial coronary vessels, effectively halting blood flow.
Consequently, LV perfusion relies on the pressure gradient present during the relaxation phase.
Calculation of CPP:
Coronary Perfusion Pressure (CPP) for the left ventricle is the difference between
the driving pressure (Aortic Diastolic Pressure) and the back pressure (Left
Ventricular End-Diastolic Pressure or LVEDP). The formula is: CPP = Aortic
Diastolic Pressure - LVEDP. Systemic Diastolic Blood Pressure (DBP) is commonly
used as a surrogate for Aortic Diastolic Pressure.
Impact of Heart Rate:
Tachycardia disproportionately shortens diastole compared to systole. This significantly reduces the time available for coronary perfusion. Additionally, tachycardia
increases myocardial oxygen demand (MVO2), creating a supply-demand
mismatch.
Analysis of Other Options:
A is incorrect because systolic pressure does not drive LV perfusion due to extravascular compression. B describes a general organ perfusion formula (MAP - CVP) or
cerebral perfusion pressure (MAP - ICP), not coronary physiology. C is incorrect because increasing LVEDP (the 'back pressure') reduces the pressure gradient, thereby
decreasing CPP. E is incorrect because tachycardia reduces diastolic time.
Clinical Pearl
The Left Heart Feeds in Diastole:

Because the LV compresses its own blood supply during systole, it must be perfused
during relaxation. The right ventricle is perfused during both systole and diastole.
CPP = DBP - LVEDP:
Coronary perfusion depends on the gradient between Aortic Diastolic Pressure (or
systemic DBP) and LVEDP. Hypotension (low DBP) or fluid overload/failure (high
LVEDP) both compromise myocardial blood flow.
Tachycardia is Dangerous:
A rapid heart rate is a major threat to coronary perfusion because it shortens diastolic filling time. This is why beta-blockers are beneficial post-MI.
Aortic Stenosis Pathophysiology:
In severe aortic stenosis, a high LVEDP (increased back pressure) and a low aortic
diastolic pressure (reduced driving pressure) significantly compromise the CPP,
leading to subendocardial ischemia.
IABP and CPP:
An intra-aortic balloon pump augments CPP directly by inflating during diastole,
raising the aortic diastolic pressure.
Right Ventricle Perfusion Differences:
Unlike the LV, the Right Ventricle (RV) has lower wall tension and is perfused during both systole and diastole. However, in states of severe pulmonary hypertension
or RV failure, RV wall tension rises, and perfusion becomes restricted to diastole—
making the RV highly susceptible to ischemia if systemic hypotension occurs.
Coronary Autoregulation Limits:
Coronary blood flow is autoregulated to remain constant across a MAP range of approximately 60-140 mmHg. Below this threshold, vessels are maximally dilated,
and flow becomes entirely pressure-dependent. In patients with chronic hypertension, this curve shifts to the right, meaning ischemia may occur at 'normal' blood
pressures.
Subendocardial Vulnerability:
The subendocardium is the most vulnerable region of the heart to ischemia. It is
subjected to the highest wall tension (reducing tissue perfusion) and has the highest
metabolic demand, yet it receives the lowest effective perfusion pressure compared
to the subepicardium.
Metabolic Regulation of Flow:
Coronary blood flow is primarily regulated by local metabolic factors rather than the
autonomic nervous system. Adenosine is the key mediator; it accumulates during
hypoxia or increased metabolic activity, causing potent vasodilation to increase
flow.

Coronary Sinus Oxygen Saturation:
The heart has a very high basal oxygen extraction ratio (approximately 70-80%), resulting in a low coronary sinus oxygen saturation. Because extraction is near-maximal at rest, increased oxygen demand must be met almost entirely by increasing
coronary blood flow.
Vasospastic Angina Mechanism:
Prinzmetal's (variant) angina represents a primary reduction in coronary supply
due to vasospasm, rather than the typical demand-supply mismatch seen in fixed
atherosclerotic disease. It can occur at rest and is treated with calcium channel
blockers or nitrates.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ LV muscle بيتغذّى تقريباً كله وقت الـ diastole، لأن وقت الـ systole الـ contracting muscle بيعمل ضغط برّي على الـ subendocardial coronary vessels فبيقطع الدم عنها. الـ CPP بيتحسب من الـ Aortic Diastolic Pressure ناقص الـ LVEDP، يعني هو الـ pressure gradient الموجود وقت الـ relaxation. ولما يعمل tachycardia الـ diastole بيقصر أكثر من الـ systole، فبيقل الـ CPP وتزداد MVO2، وهاد بيسبّب supply-demand mismatch.
الفخ: أحسن خطأ إنه يختاروا MAP minus CVP لأن هاد الـ formula اللي يعرفوها لكل الـ organs، بس الـ coronary perfusion بيستخدم Aortic Diastolic Pressure ناقص LVEDP. والـ tachycardia ما بتحسّن CPP لأنها بتقصّر الـ diastole، ورفع LVEDP بيقلّل الـ gradient مش يزيده.

question:
A patient on a sodium nitroprusside infusion develops central cyanosis. Pulse
oximetry reads a persistent SpO₂ of 85%, which does not improve with 100%

oxygen. An arterial blood gas analysis, however, shows a PaO₂ of 25 kPa. What is
the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Severe hypoxaemia due to V/Q mismatch

englishExplanation:
Clinical Context:
This vignette presents the classic triad of methaemoglobinaemia: central cyanosis, a
'saturation gap' (low SpO₂ vs high PaO₂), and refractory hypoxaemia despite supplemental oxygen. While cyanide toxicity is the most common serious complication
of sodium nitroprusside (SNP), the clinical signs described here are pathognomonic
for methaemoglobinaemia.
Pathophysiology:
Normal haemoglobin contains iron in the ferrous (Fe² ⁺ ) state. Sodium nitroprusside
breakdown releases nitric oxide (NO), which can oxidise iron to the ferric (Fe³ ⁺ )
state, creating methaemoglobin. Ferric iron cannot bind oxygen. Furthermore,
methaemoglobin causes a conformational change in the remaining normal
haemoglobin tetramers (allosteric effect), shifting the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation
curve to the left and impairing oxygen unloading at the tissue level.
The Saturation Gap:
The discrepancy between SpO₂ and PaO₂ is the key diagnostic feature. PaO₂ measures dissolved oxygen in plasma, which remains normal or high (if on supplemental O₂) because methaemoglobin does not affect oxygen solubility. However, pulse
oximeters calculate saturation based on the ratio of light absorption at 660 nm (red)
and 940 nm (infrared). Methaemoglobin absorbs light at both wavelengths equally
(absorption coefficient ratio ~1.0). This ratio corresponds to an SpO₂ of approximately 85% on standard calibration curves. Consequently, as methaemoglobin levels rise, SpO₂ trends towards and becomes fixed at 85%, regardless of the true arterial saturation.
Differential Diagnosis: SNP Toxicity:

It is crucial to differentiate this from cyanide toxicity, the other major complication
of SNP. Cyanide toxicity causes histotoxic hypoxia (blocking mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase) leading to a high SvO₂ (bright red venous blood), profound lactic
acidosis, and a normal SpO₂. It does not typically cause cyanosis or a saturation
gap.
Clinical Pearl
The Saturation Gap is Diagnostic:
If a cyanotic patient has an SpO₂ of ~85% that doesn't improve with oxygen, and
their ABG shows a high PaO₂, you have diagnosed methaemoglobinaemia.
Chocolate-Brown Blood:
A classic bedside clue is that blood drawn from a patient with significant
methaemoglobinaemia will appear dark, 'chocolate-brown' and will not turn red
when exposed to air.
Confirm with Co-oximetry:
The diagnosis is confirmed by sending an arterial or venous blood gas sample for
co-oximetry. Unlike a standard ABG machine, a co-oximeter can measure the different species of haemoglobin (oxy-, deoxy-, carboxy-, and methaemoglobin) and will
report the exact percentage of methaemoglobin.
Treatment is Methylene Blue:
The first-line antidote is intravenous methylthioninium chloride (methylene blue)
at a dose of 1-2 mg/kg over 5 minutes. It acts as a cofactor for NADPHmethaemoglobin reductase, accelerating the reduction of ferric (Fe³ ⁺ ) iron back to
the ferrous (Fe² ⁺ ) state.
Caution in G6PD Deficiency:
Methylene blue should not be given to patients with known G6PD deficiency. In
these patients, methylene blue can act as an oxidising agent itself and can precipitate severe haemolysis.
Alternative Treatment in G6PD Deficiency:
In patients with G6PD deficiency where methylene blue is contraindicated, highdose intravenous ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) is the treatment of choice. While its action is slower, it provides a safe reduction pathway. Exchange transfusion is reserved for severe, refractory cases.
Cyanosis Thresholds:
Methaemoglobinaemia causes visible cyanosis at much lower concentrations (1.5
g/dL) than deoxygenated haemoglobin (5 g/dL). A patient may appear profoundly
cyanotic despite maintaining adequate oxygen delivery.
Mechanism of Tissue Hypoxia:

Tissue hypoxia in methaemoglobinaemia is twofold: firstly, the ferric iron cannot
bind oxygen (reducing capacity); secondly, the presence of methaemoglobin causes
a conformational change that increases the oxygen affinity of the remaining ferrous
haemoglobin (left shift), preventing oxygen unloading at the tissues.
Carboxyhaemoglobin Contrast:
Do not confuse the oximetry findings of methaemoglobinaemia with carbon monoxide poisoning. Carboxyhaemoglobin has light absorption characteristics similar to
oxyhaemoglobin at 660 nm, causing pulse oximeters to read falsely high (often
100%) despite severe hypoxia, whereas methaemoglobin causes a fixed reading of
~85%.
Other Common ICU Causes:
Beyond sodium nitroprusside, common ICU causes of acquired methaemoglobinaemia include local anaesthetics (specifically prilocaine and benzocaine), dapsone,
and inhaled nitric oxide.
Normal Reduction Pathways:
Under physiological conditions, small amounts of methaemoglobin are reduced by
the NADH-dependent cytochrome b5 reductase pathway. Methylene blue works by
activating a dormant alternative pathway (NADPH-dependent methaemoglobin reductase), which is why it is effective when the primary enzyme is overwhelmed.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: هاد التلت-stage الكلاسيكي: central cyanosis مع saturation gap، يعني SpO₂ 85% مع PaO₂ 25 kPa، وhypoxaemia ما بتتحسن مع 100% oxygen. السبب إنو sodium nitroprusside بيفكّ وبيطلع nitric oxide اللي بيعمل oxidise للـ iron بالـ hemoglobin من ferrous Fe2+ إلى ferric Fe3+، وهاد بيعمل methaemoglobin. الـ ferric iron ما بيعرف يمسك أكسجين، وكمان بيعمل conformational change بالـ oxyhaemoglobin curve وبيزحلقها لليسار، فبتضعف الـ unloading عند الـ tissues.
الفخ: cyanide toxicity هي أشهر complication خطرة عند sodium nitroprusside، فبيلخبطوا ويفتكروا إنو السبب. بس الـ saturation gap مع PaO₂ طبيعية أو عالية وما بتحسن مع الأكسجين، هاد علامة واضحة ومميزة لـ methaemoglobinaemia مش cyanide.

question:
A 65-year-old male with severe ARDS is on a ventilator with a tidal volume of 6
mL/kg and has poor lung compliance. The team wants to assess his fluid responsiveness. Which dynamic test is likely to be LEAST reliable in this specific
patient?

options.text: Passive leg raise (PLR) with a real-time cardiac output monitor.
Pulse pressure variation (PPV) or Stroke volume variation (SVV).
A fluid challenge of 250 mL of crystalloid.

correctAnswer: Pulse pressure variation (PPV) or Stroke volume variation (SVV).
englishExplanation:
Physiological Basis of PPV/SVV:
Pulse Pressure Variation (PPV) and Stroke Volume Variation (SVV) exploit the
heart-lung interaction during positive pressure ventilation. During mechanical inspiration, increased intrathoracic pressure transiently augments left ventricular
preload (by squeezing blood from pulmonary veins) while simultaneously impeding
right ventricular filling (by reducing venous return). During expiration, the opposite
occurs. In a preload-dependent patient operating on the steep portion of the FrankStarling curve, these cyclical preload changes produce large swings in stroke volume
and pulse pressure. A PPV or SVV >12–13% predicts fluid responsiveness with high
sensitivity and specificity. In a preload-independent patient (flat portion of the
curve), the same ventilatory swings produce minimal variation.
Limitations in ARDS:
PPV and SVV are validated only under strict conditions: sinus rhythm, closed chest,
no spontaneous breathing, and a tidal volume (Vt) of at least 8 mL/kg. In this patient, the low Vt (6 mL/kg) generates insufficient intrathoracic pressure swings to
challenge preload. Furthermore, poor lung compliance in ARDS means that applied
airway pressure is dissipated across the stiff lung parenchyma rather than being
transmitted to the pleural space and pericardium. This results in false-negative results, making PPV/SVV unreliable in this setting.
Static vs. Dynamic Parameters:
The question asks for the least reliable dynamic test. Central Venous Pressure
(CVP) is a static preload measure and is generally a poor predictor of fluid responsiveness. However, it is technically excluded from the category of 'dynamic tests'.
Among the dynamic options provided, PPV/SVV is the correct answer because its
physiological basis is disrupted by the patient's ventilator settings and lung
mechanics.
Reliable Alternatives in ARDS:
The Passive Leg Raise (PLR) and End-Expiratory Occlusion Test (EEOT) remain reliable in patients with low tidal volumes. PLR acts as a reversible 'autotransfusion'
of approximately 300 mL of venous blood and is valid even with arrhythmias or
spontaneous breathing. EEOT relies on the interruption of positive intrathoracic
pressure to transiently increase venous return and is particularly useful in prone patients where PLR is technically difficult.
Clinical Pearl
PPV/SVV Limitations in ARDS:
Low tidal volumes (less than 8 mL/kg) and reduced lung compliance in ARDS
dampen the cyclic changes in intrathoracic pressure required for PPV/SVV. This results in false negatives, where a fluid-responsive patient shows no variation.
Preferred Tests in ARDS:
Passive Leg Raise (PLR) and End-Expiratory Occlusion Test (EEOT) are the preferred functional hemodynamic monitoring tests for assessing fluid responsiveness
in ARDS patients, as they are independent of tidal volume magnitude.
Static Preload Indices:
Static parameters such as CVP and Global End-Diastolic Volume (GEDV) do not reliably predict fluid responsiveness. They reflect the patient's position on the FrankStarling curve (preload status) but not the slope of the curve (preload reserve).
Fluid Challenge Utility:
The ultimate test is to administer a fluid challenge and measure the response in cardiac output. However, this is irreversible. PLR and EEOT are valuable because they
predict the response to fluid without the risk of fluid overload.
Tidal Volume Challenge:
In patients ventilated with 6 mL/kg, transiently increasing tidal volume to 8 mL/kg
for 1 minute can unmask fluid responsiveness. An increase in PPV by greater than
3.5% (absolute) or PPV greater than 13% during the challenge predicts a positive
fluid response.
Airway Pressure Transmission:
For PPV/SVV to function, airway pressure must be transmitted to the pleural space
and pericardium. In 'stiff' lungs (low compliance), most pressure is dissipated
across the lung parenchyma, reducing the hemodynamic effect on the heart and
causing false negatives.
PLR Physiology:
A passive leg raise mobilises approximately 300 mL of blood from the splanchnic
bed and legs. It requires real-time cardiac output monitoring (e.g., arterial waveform analysis, echocardiography) to detect the transient increase in stroke volume.
EEOT Mechanism:
The End-Expiratory Occlusion Test (EEOT) involves a 15-second expiratory hold.
This interrupts the cyclic increase in intrathoracic pressure associated with mechanical ventilation, transiently increasing venous return and cardiac preload. An increase in cardiac output of 5% or more predicts fluid responsiveness.
Prone Positioning:
In prone ARDS patients, PLR is technically difficult or impossible to perform. EEOT
remains a valid and practical alternative for assessing fluid responsiveness in the
prone position.
Right Ventricular Failure:

PPV can be misleadingly high (false positive) in patients with right ventricular failure. In this setting, respiratory variations in arterial pressure may reflect changes in
RV afterload rather than LV preload dependence.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ PPV والـ SVV بيعتمدوا على الـ heart-lung interaction وقت الـ positive pressure ventilation: بالـ inspiration الـ intrathoracic pressure بتزيد فبتزاد الـ LV preload، وبنفس الوقت الـ RV filling بتقل. هاد الـ cyclic preload change بيسوي تغيرات كبيرة بالـ stroke volume والـ pulse pressure بس عند الـ preload-dependent patient. وبهاي الحالة Vt 6 mL/kg والـ poor compliance بيخلّوا الـ airway pressure ينبدد بالـ stiff lung وما يوصل للـ pleural space، فالـ result false negative.
الفخ: أحسن trap إنه يختاروا CVP أو fluid challenge، لأنهم بيسألوا عن fluid responsiveness مباشرة. بس الـ question بتدور على الـ dynamic test الأقل موثوقية، وPPV/SVV بتعمل بشكل صحيح بس مع Vt فوق 8 mL/kg وchest closed وsinus rhythm، وكل هالشروط مكسورة هنا.

question:
An intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) is inserted in a patient with cardiogenic
shock. To achieve optimal hemodynamic benefit, the balloon must inflate and deflate in sync with the cardiac cycle. When should the balloon be timed to inflate
and deflate?

options.text: Inflate at the start of systole; deflate at the end of systole.
Inflate at the end of diastole; deflate at the start of diastole.
Inflate at the dicrotic notch; deflate just before the start of systole.
Inflate with the P wave on the ECG; deflate with the T wave.
Inflate at the peak of the R wave; deflate at the start of the P wave.

correctAnswer: Inflate at the dicrotic notch; deflate just before the start of systole.
englishExplanation:
Physiological Principles:
The IABP functions via counterpulsation. Inflation occurs at the dicrotic notch
(aortic valve closure), marking the onset of diastole. This displaces blood proximally
and distally, raising the diastolic pressure (diastolic augmentation). Since the left
ventricle is perfused primarily during diastole, this augmentation significantly increases coronary perfusion pressure. Deflation occurs immediately prior to systole (end-diastole/presystolic). This creates a vacuum effect in the aorta, reducing

aortic end-diastolic pressure and thus reducing left ventricular afterload (isovolumetric contraction work) and myocardial oxygen demand.
Timing Triggers:
Timing is most commonly triggered by the arterial pressure waveform (dicrotic
notch) or the ECG. On the ECG, inflation is triggered during the T-wave (ventricular
repolarisation/diastole). Deflation is timed to occur just before the QRS complex
(end-diastole) to ensure the balloon is fully collapsed before isovolumetric contraction begins.
Clinical Pearl
Waveform Timing Rule:
"Inflate on the Notch, Deflate on the Upstroke" is the key mnemonic for timing
when using the arterial waveform as the trigger.
Augmentation Assessment:
Look for the "augmented diastolic pressure" on the arterial waveform. It should ideally be higher than the patient's native systolic pressure.
Afterload Reduction Assessment:
The assisted aortic end-diastolic pressure (BAEDP) must be lower than the unassisted patient aortic end-diastolic pressure (PAEDP). Consequently, the assisted
systolic pressure is usually lower than the unassisted systolic pressure.
Triggering Modes:
The IABP can be triggered by either the arterial pressure waveform (most common)
or the ECG. When using the ECG, inflation is timed to the middle of the T-wave, and
deflation is timed to occur just before the R-wave.
Absolute Contraindications:
The main absolute contraindications for an IABP are significant aortic regurgitation
(diastolic augmentation would worsen regurgitant flow) and aortic dissection.
Early Inflation Risks:
Inflation before the dicrotic notch (Early Inflation) is dangerous. It causes premature closure of the aortic valve, increases LVEDP, and increases wall
stress/afterload, potentially worsening cardiac failure.
Late Deflation Risks:
Deflation after the onset of systole (Late Deflation) is the most detrimental timing
error. The LV contracts against an inflated balloon, causing a massive increase in afterload and myocardial oxygen consumption.
Catheter Positioning:
The distal tip of the IABP should be positioned 2 cm distal to the origin of the left
subclavian artery. On CXR, this corresponds to the level of the aortic

knuckle/carina.
Helium Shuttle Gas:
Helium is used as the shuttle gas because of its low density (allows rapid
inflation/deflation cycling) and high solubility in blood (minimises embolus risk if
balloon rupture occurs).
Device Complications:
Complications include limb ischaemia (most common major complication), vascular injury (dissection, pseudoaneurysm), thrombocytopenia (mechanical destruction), and haemolysis. Daily monitoring of distal pulses and platelet count is
essential.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ IABP شغال بـ counterpulsation: الـ inflation بيصير عند الـ dicrotic notch يعني وقت إغلاق الـ aortic valve وبداية الـ diastole، وبيزاد الـ diastolic pressure، وبما إنو الـ LV بيتغذى بالـ diastole فالـ coronary perfusion بيزيد بشكل واضح. الـ deflation بيصير حالاً قبل الـ systole، وهاد بيعمل vacuum في الـ aorta فينزل الـ aortic end-diastolic pressure، الـ afterload بينقص والـ myocardial oxygen demand بينقص كمان.
الفخ: أحسن trap إنه يختاروا deflation بنهاية الـ systole، لأنهم بيفكروا إنو الـ balloon بينفخ مع systole. بس deflation لازم يصير حالاً قبل الـ systole عشان الـ balloon يكون مقفول قبل الـ isovolumetric contraction، والـ rule هي Inflate on the Notch, Deflate on the Upstroke.

question:
