question: A 65-year-old male presents to a rural emergency room with chest pain for one hour. The pain is substernal, dull, worse with exertion, and associated with nausea and diaphoresis. His past medical history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease. Home medications include insulin, atorvastatin, atenolol, aspirin, and warfarin. Of note, he was discharged from the hospital 6 weeks ago for an ischemic CVA. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse rate is 65/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 190/100 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. An ECG is performed and included below. After consultation with a cardiologist at the tertiary facility, it is decided to give thrombolytics. Which of the following is an absolute contraindication in this patient to administering thrombolytics?
englishExplanation:
Ischemic CVA
Expl anation
A. Anticoagulant use
Anticoagulant use is a relative contraindication to fibrinolytic use.
B. Chronic kidney disease
Chronic kidney disease is not a contraindication to fibrinolytic use.
C. Ischemic CVA
This patient presents with findings suggestive of an acute MI. Although PCI is the
preferred treatment of choice, some rural settings are not able to provide this means
of reperfusion to patients quickly enough and thrombolytics are subsequently given.
The thrombolytics Alteplase and Tenecteplase are typically given. There are important absolute and relative contraindications to be aware of before administering this
therapy as bleeding complications are a real concern. Absolute contraindications include a history of ICH, known AVM, known intracranial neoplasm, active bleeding,
history of ischemic stroke within 3 months (which this patient had), and suspected
aortic dissection or pericarditis.
For more information: <https://wikem.org/wiki/ThrombolyticsforSTEMI>
D. Uncontrolled hypertension
Severe uncontrolled BP (>180/110) is a relative contraindication to fibrinolytic use.

question: A 2-day-old neonate born at home via uncomplicated vaginal delivery is brought to the emergency department by his mother because he has had difficulty breathing for the past few hours. The mother received prenatal care, and the patient was otherwise healthy until today. The patient is pale and diaphoretic, and increased work of breathing is noted. Physical examination shows no murmurs on cardiac auscultation, but rales are noted in all lung fields. The abdomen is soft and non-tender. The liver edge is palpated 5 cm below the costal margin. Brachial pulses are bounding bilaterally, and femoral pulses are diminished and delayed. Chest x-ray study shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette and pulmonary vascular congestion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
englishExplanation:
Administer prostaglandin El
Expl anation
A. Administer prostaglandin El
This patient presents with signs and symptoms of acute heart failure. The timing of
two days postnatal is consistent with the timing of patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)
closure, making this concerning for a ductal-dependent congenital cardiac abnormality. In addition, the patient has delayed femoral pulses, which highly suggests
coarctation of the aorta. Coarctation of the aorta is difficult to diagnose prenatally
and may be missed even with normal prenatal screening. This patient should be
started immediately on a continuous prostaglandin El infusion to maintain the
PDA's patency. Echocardiography will confirm the diagnosis, and a surgical consult
should be obtained. With the use of prostaglandin and supportive measures, surgery
can usually be delayed until the patient is stabilized. In addition to prostaglandin,
inotropic support may be necessary to improve contractility in those with heart
failure.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430913/
B. Consult with a cardiothoracic surgeon

question: A 55-year-old male with a history of hypertension and chronic kidney disease is brought in by his family for altered mental status and vomiting. They report he had been complaining of a headache over the past day and, on the morning of presentation, started to display bizarre behavior. Vitals are as follows: HR 105/min, BP 230/140 mmHg, RR 16/min, Temp 98.6ºF (37ºC). The physical exam is significant for altered mental status but is otherwise unremarkable. The patient has no focal neurologic deficits. CT head is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial agent for the management of this patient's likely condition?
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
A. Aspirin
Nicardipine
This patient is presenting with a hypertensive emergency. While aspirin can be
given after intracranial hemorrhage is ruled out, the most appropriate initial agent
for the management is one that will address blood pressure control.
B. Nicardipine
Hypertensive emergency is defined as a markedly elevated blood pressure with evidence of acute cardiovascular, renal, or neurologic end-organ damage. Rapid reduction of blood pressure is achieved with a reduction of the mean arterial pressure
(MAP) by 25-30%. Excessive reduction of blood pressure should be avoided as it
may cause cerebral ischemia. The first-line agents for blood pressure reduction to
consider are nitroprusside, nicardipine, or labetolol. Nicardipine affects both coronary and cerebral circulations and is a pure arterial vasodilator that prevents tachycardia, bradycardia and decreased preload. It reliably reduces blood pressure and is
easy to titrate.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470371/'
C. Phentolamine
Phentolamine is useful in malignant hypertension due to cocaine as well as due to
tumors such as pheochromocytomas because it is an alpha-adrenergic antagonist.
D. Tissue-plasminogen activator (TPA)
This patient's presentation is most concerning for hypertensive encephalopathy
rather than stroke. Additionally, the degree of blood pressure elevation, in this case,
is a contraindication to thrombolytic therapy.

Nicardipine من الـ first-line agents مع nitroprusside و labetolol، وهو pure arterial vasodilator بيأثر على الـ coronary والـ cerebral circulations، وبيمنع tachycardia و bradycardia و decreased preload، وبيخفّض الضغط بشكل موثوق وسهل titration.
الفخ: الطلاب ممكن يختاروا aspirin لأن الـ CT head كان negative، بس Aspirin ما بيعالج الـ BP crisis وهنا مو موضوعه. السؤال سأل عن أول agent لتدبير ضغط الدم، فالـ answer هو nicardipine لأنه يوصل للـ MAP target بأمان.

question: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department via ambulance after his roommate called 911 because he had chest pain. The roommate says that the patient snorted cocaine just prior to the onset of pain. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F), pulse rate is 156/min, respirations are 27/min, and blood pressure is 210/150 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. The patient is diaphoretic, combative, and complaining of chest pain. He remains hypertensive after administration of intravenous lorazepam and sublingual nitroglycerin. Which of the following medications is most appropriate to administer next?
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
A. Esmolol
Phentolamine
This person is experiencing a hypertensive emergency due to sympathetic
toxicity/crisis from cocaine use. As this is related to excess alpha-I-mediated vasoconstriction, pure beta-blockers are contraindicated, as they may cause unopposed
alpha effects. Esmolol does not have any alpha-adrenergic blockade.
B. Fenoldopam
Fenoldopam is a peripheral dopamine-I receptor agonist that preserves renal blood
flow while functioning as an antihypertensive agent. It is a vasodilator but has little
to no alpha-adrenergic effects and can cause reflex tachycardia. It would not be useful in the setting of a hypertensive emergency due to sympathetic crisis.
C. Hydralazine
Hydralazine is frequently used for hypertensive urgency/emergency, although this
use is off-label. There is little evidence that it improves outcomes, has well-documented variations in blood pressure changes, and can cause hypotension even
hours after administration.
It is not effective in managing alpha-I-mediated vasoconstriction, which is the cause
of this patient's hypertensive emergency.
D. Phentolamine
This patient is experiencing a hypertensive emergency related to a sympathomimetic crisis. The significantly elevated blood pressure occurs in response to excessive alpha-I-mediated vasoconstriction. This can be caused by pheochromocytoma or sympathetic overdose (cocaine, mephedrone aka "bath salts," MDMA aka
"molly" or "ecstasy").
An alpha-I inhibitor, such as phentolamine, is the preferred agent to treat this hypertensive emergency. Nicardipine or clevidipine are additional treatment options,
as pure beta-blockers are contraindicated due to possible unopposed alpha effects.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430757/

question: A 65-year-old male with Marfan's syndrome presents with sudden onset chest pain that radiates to the back. On physical examination, he is hypertensive to 190/110 mmHg, tachycardic, and has a delayed radial-femoral pulse. Electrocardiogram is within normal limits. A CT chest angiography is performed and an image is shown. Treatment should be initiated with which of the following medications?
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
A. Diltiazem
Esmolol
This patient has an aortic dissection, and the treatment involves a short-acting betablocker titrated to a heart rate of less than 60 beats/min. In patients with contraindications to beta-blockade, a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
such as verapamil can be used for rate control.
B. Esmolol
This patient is presenting with an aortic dissection. Treatment involves esmolol or
labetalol titrated to a HR<60 beats/min. If HTN persists, nicardipine or nitroprusside should be added. Beta-blockade should precede vasodilators to prevent reflex
tachycardia. The goal is HR beats/min and SBP <120 mmHg within 60 min.
The most important treatment principle is rate reduction, followed by blood pressure reduction. As a beta blocker, esmolol effectively reduces the heart rate and is
easily titratable. Nitroprusside is preferred to nitroglycerin as it is a more potent arterial dilator, and it decreases afterload. However, nitroprusside should not be used
without first controlling the heart rate with beta-blockade since vasodilation alone
induces reflex activation of the sympathetic nervous system, leading to enhanced
ventricular contraction and increased aortic wall shear stress.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441963/
C. Nitroglycerin
This patient has an aortic dissection which should be first treated with a beta
blocker to slow the rate. Subsequently, nitroprusside is preferred to nitroglycerin as
it is a more potent reducer of blood pressure, and it decreases after load.
D. Nitroprusside
This patient has an aortic dissection which should be first treated with a beta

question: Which of the following best characterizes the rhythm on the attached EKG?
englishExplanation:
Third-degree AV block
Expl anation
A. Second-degree type I AV block (Wenckebach)
In a second-degree type I AV block (Wenckebach, where there is a progressive prolongation of the PR interval leading to a dropped P wave that is not followed by a
QRS complex.
B. Second-degree type II AV block (Mobitz 2)
In a second-degree type II AV block (Mobitz 2), every atrial impulse is not conducted to the ventricles. The condition is characterized by a consistent and fixed ratio of conducted to non-conducted beats. Typically, there is a "2:1" or "3:1" pattern,
meaning that every second or third atrial beat fails to conduct to the ventricles, resulting in a slower ventricular rate compared to the atrial rate. In this block, the P-R
interval is of consistent duration.
C. Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia is identified by a heart rate less than 60/min with regular P-P intervals that are equivalent to the R-R intervals. Also, the P-R intervals are
consistent.
D. Third-degree AV block
This EKG demonstrates third-degree AV block as the P waves and QRS complexes
are completely dissociated. Third-degree AV block, also known as complete heart
block, occurs when there is complete dissociation of electrical conduction between
the atria and ventricles. On an electrocardiogram, there will be regular P-P intervals, regular R-R intervals, no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes,
atrioventricular dissociation, and a slow ventricular rate.

![HIPPO-00535 source page 676](images/HIPPO-00535-Hipoo-p0676.jpg)

![HIPPO-00535 source page 677](images/HIPPO-00535-Hipoo-p0677.jpg)
arabicExplanation:
ليش: هاد ECG بيبيّن third-degree AV block يعني complete heart block، لأن في complete dissociation of electrical conduction بين الأطيار والبطينات. بتلاقي P waves و QRS complexes كل واحد لحاله بدون أي علاقة بينهم، مع P-P intervals منتظمة و R-R intervals منتظمة. هاد بيفرق عن Wenckebach و Mobitz 2 لأنهم بتبقوا فيها relationship بين الـ P والـ QRS، والـ conducted beats فيها نسبة ثابتة.
الفخ: الفخ إنك تختار second-degree type I أو Mobitz 2 لأنهم بتبقوا فيها ratio ثابت بين الـ conducted والـ non-conducted beats و PR interval ثابت. أما third-degree هو الوحيد اللي كل الـ P waves منفصلة عن الـ QRS.

question: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department via ambulance immediately after he had a syncopal episode. He says he was walking back to his dorm after working out at the campus fitness center when he felt light-headed and noticed his heart was racing. A bystander watched him lose consciousness and called 911. Electrocardiography is shown. Which of the following most likely caused the light-headedness and palpitations that this patient experienced prior to the syncopal episode?
englishExplanation:
Ventricular fibrillation
Expl anation
A. Atrial fibrillation
Atrial arrhythmias are more common in patients with Brugada pattern on electrocardiography when compared with the general population. However, ventricular arrhythmias are the most common arrhythmia that causes syncope and/or sudden
cardiac death. Only 10 to 30% of patients with Brugada syndrome have an atrial
arrhythmia.
B. Profound bradycardia
Certainly, bradycardia can be profound enough to cause syncope, but in this case,
the patient has a Brugada pattern electrocardiography, so it is prudent to assume
that he had a ventricular arrhythmia causing his syncopal episode. Ventricular arrhythmias are the most common arrhythmias that cause syncope and/or sudden
cardiac death in patients with Brugada syndrome.
C. Supraventricular tachycardia
Supraventricular tachycardia can be seen in young, healthy patients and can lead to
light-headedness and/or syncope. However, in this case, the patient has a Brugada
pattern on electrocardiography. Patients with this syndrome most commonly experience ventricular arrhythmias leading to syncope or sudden cardiac death.
D. Ventricular fibrillation
This patient has Brugada syndrome. He had a syncopal event, has a type I morphology seen in leads VI and V2, and has wide S waves in the inferior and lateral leads.
Brugada syndrome is an inherited, autosomal dominant condition, and symptoms
range from none to sudden cardiac death. Ventricular arrhythmia is most commonly the cause of syncope or sudden cardiac death, but atrial fibrillation and/or
supraventricular tachycardia can be seen.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519568/
Yealy D, Kosowsky J. Chapter 65. Dysrhythmias. In: Walls RM, Hockberger RS,
Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical Practice.
10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.

question: A 35-year-old male with a past medical history of hyperthyroidism presents to the emergency department with a chief complaint of profound weakness and inability to ambulate following a basketball game. Physical exam reveals extensive proximal muscle weakness and hyporeflexia. An ECG is most likely to demonstrate which of the following findings?
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
U waves
A. Epsilon waves
Epsilon waves are classically associated with arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia and are characterized by a notch in the terminal portion of the QRS in the
right precordial leads (VI-V3).
B. Osborne waves
Osborne waves are classically associated with hypothermia (although not pathognomonic) and are also known as prominent J waves (positive deflections at the
junction of the QRS and ST segment).
C. PR depression
PR depression is seen in pericarditis.
D. U waves
This patient is suffering from thyrotoxic periodic paralysis. This is a sporadic form
of hypokalemic periodic paralysis, which most commonly presents as sudden onset
weakness in the proximal muscles. It is reversible and can be treated with the replacement of potassium and the normalization of thyroid hormones. U waves are
evident on the ECG in the setting of hypokalemia.
Further information: https:/,/www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560670/
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريض عنده weakness مفاجئ بالـ proximal muscles بعد ما بلعب، ومعه hyperthyroidism، وهاد اسمه thyrotoxic periodic paralysis وهي sporadic form من hypokalemic periodic paralysis. المشكلة إن الـ potassium منخفض، والـ U waves بتظهر على الـ ECG بهالحالة. والحالة reversible وبيتعاملوا معاها بـ replacement of potassium ومع normalizing الـ thyroid hormones.
الفخ: الفخ إنك تختار peaked T waves أو PR depression، لأنهم بيطلعوا في hyperkalemia و pericarditis مش في hypokalemia. أما Epsilon waves فبتظهر في arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia كـ notch في آخر الـ QRS بالـ right precordial leads.

question: A 23-year-old male trauma patient on a mechanical ventilator suddenly deteriorates and becomes hypotensive and hypoxic. Physical exam reveals decreased breath sounds on the left, jugular venous distension, and tracheal deviation to the right. What is the most appropriate initial step in management?
englishExplanation:
Needle thoracostomy
Expl anation
A. Fluid bolus
This patient has a tension pneumothorax and requires emergent decompression. A
fluid bolus will not correct the hypotension.
B. Needle thoracostomy
This patient has the classic presentation of a tension pneumothorax, with tracheal
deviation, jugular venous distention, and decreased breath sounds. This is a life
threat that results when air is trapped in the pleural space under positive pressure,
displacing mediastinal structures and impairing cardiopulmonary function. It needs
early recognition and emergent management. Immediate treatment is with needle
decompression. ThlS is done with an angio-catheter at the second intercostal space
in the midclavicular line above the rib. Needle thoracostomy is followed by chest
tube placement.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559090/
C. Pericardiocentesis
This patient likely has a tension pneumothorax, presenting with tracheal deviation,
jugular venous distention, and decreased breath sounds. Cardiac tamponade
presents more classically as muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distention, and
hypotension (Beck's triad). Pericardiocentesis will not correct this patient's hemodynamic instability.
D. Thoracotomy
This question describes a case of tension pneumothorax. While resuscitative thoracotomy will treat tension pneumothorax, its indications are mainly for witnessed
prehospital/hospital cardiac arrest due to penetrating traumatic injuries. Treatment
for tension pneumothorax is with needle thoracostomy, followed by chest tube
placement. Thoracotomy is not indicated.

ليش: المريض على mechanical ventilator فجأة صار hypotension و hypoxemia، ومعاه decreased breath sounds على اليسار و jugular venous distension و tracheal deviation لليمين، وهاد triad كلاسيكي لتension pneumothorax. السبب إنو air trapped بالـ pleural space تحت positive pressure فـ displaces الـ mediastinum وبي impaired الـ cardiopulmonary function، وهاد life-threatening. لازم تعمل decompression فوري بـ needle thoracostomy بـ angio-catheter بالـ second intercostal space في الـ midclavicular line فوق الضلع، وبعدها بتحط chest tube.
الفخ: الفخ إنك تبدأ بـ fluid bolus لأن المريض hypotensive، بس السائل ما رح يصحّح الـ pressure داخل الصدر وبيضيّع وقت. الـ needle decompression هي أول خطوة وبيليها chest tube، فالـ thoracotomy مش أول خطوة.

question: A 33-year-old male is brought into the emergency department after capsizing his sailboat in cold water. Temperature is 85ºF (29.4ºC), pulse rate is 33/min, respirations are 33/min, and blood pressure is 68/40 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. Several attempts are made to establish peripheral venous access but they are unsuccessful. The patient requires a central line. Which of the following is the most appropriate site for central line placement?
englishExplanation:
Femoral vein
Expl anation
A. Femoral vein
In hypothermic patients, the myocardium is extremely irritable and high central
lines (internal jugular vein, subclavian) should be avoided as the guide wire can predispose to arrhythmia.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK545239/
B. Internal jugular vein
High lines (internal jugular, subclavian) are relatively contraindicated in hypothermia as the guide wire can irritate the myocardium and precipitate cardiac arrest.
C. Subclavian vein
High lines (internal jugular, subclavian) are relatively contraindicated in hypothermia as the guide wire can irritate the myocardium and precipitate cardiac arrest.
D. Supraclavicular vein
High lines (internal jugular, subclavian) are relatively contraindicated in hypothermia as the guide wire can irritate the myocardium and precipitate cardiac arrest. A
supraclavicular line also carries the risk of triggering an arrhythmia due to the guide
wire.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: هاد المريض عنده severe hypothermia، حرارته 29.4°C و pulse 33/min و blood pressure 68/40 يعني إنه badly shocked. في hypothermia الـ myocardium بيصير extremely irritable، والـ guide wire ممكن يسبّب arrhythmia إذا استخدمت line عالي مثل internal jugular vein أو subclavian vein. فـ femoral vein هي الأنسب لأنها بتتجنّب الـ high central lines.
الفخ: الفخ إنك تختار internal jugular vein أو subclavian vein لأنهم أكثر شيوعاً لإي central line. بس هنا الـ myocardium ما بيستحمل الـ guide wire، فـ femoral vein هي الاختيار الآمن.

question: You are called to evaluate a patient with sudden-onset chest pain and dyspnea. He was admitted yesterday for ST-elevation MI, and had undergone catheterization with stent placement. He appears diaphoretic with accessory muscle use. Physical exam reveals distant heart sounds. Temperature is 37.°C (98.6°F), pulse rate is 119/min, respirations are 31/min, and blood pressure is 86/63 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 91% on 2L via nasal cannula. What would be the expected finding on cardiac ultrasound?
englishExplanation:
Collapsed right ventricle
Expl anation
A. Collapsed left ventricle
This patient's distant heart sounds are concerning for pericardial tamponade. This
does not typically affect the left ventricle.
B. Collapsed right ventricle
This patient likely has cardiac tamponade due to a rupture of the free wall of the
ventricle. Ventricular wall rupture is a complication following myocardial infarction.
When the wall ruptures, patients develop hemopericardium and cardiac tamponade. Cardiac tamponade is seen on echocardiogram as a collapse of both the right
atrium and right ventricle.
Further information:
Mellemat, H and Tewelde, S, "Pericardiocentesis" in Roberts, James R, Catherine B.
Custalow, Todd W. Thomsen, Jerris R. Hedges. Roberts and Hedges' clinical procedures in emergency medicine and acute care, 7th edition, 2019.
C. Dilated left ventricle
This patient's distant heart sounds are concerning for pericardial tamponade. This
does not typically affect the left ventricle and should not cause dilation.
D. Dilated right ventricle
This patient's distant heart sounds are concerning for pericardial tamponade. This
should not cause dilation of the right ventricle. A pulmonary embolism may result
in a dilated RV.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريض كان عنده ST-elevation MI امبارح وخضع لـ catheterization مع stent placement، وبما نشأ عنده chest pain مفاجئ و dyspnea مع hypotension و distant heart sounds و tachycardia. هاد بيطرح cardiac tamponade بسبب rupture of the free wall of the ventricle، وهي complication معروفة بعد myocardial infarction. لما الجدار ينrupture بيصير hemopericardium و tamponade، وعلى الـ echocardiogram بتظهر collapse للـ right atrium والـ right ventricle مع بعض.
الفخ: الفخ إنك تختار collapsed left ventricle لأن الـ MI بيصيب الـ left ventricle، بس الـ tamponade بيضغط على الـ right side أولاً. الـ LV ممكن يتمدد مش ينهار، فاللي بينهار هو الـ right ventricle مع الـ right atrium.

question: A 25-year-old woman who underwent a total thyroidectomy two weeks ago presents with cramps in her hands and feet for the past 10 days. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse rate is 65/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 119/70 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 100%. Physical examination shows carpopedal spasms and hyperreflexia of deep tendon reflexes. Which of the following electrocardiographic findings is most consistent with her current electrolyte abnormality?
englishExplanation:
Prolonged QT interval
Expl anation
A. Flattening of T waves
Hypokalemia will often show the ECG finding of broad-flat T waves.
B. peaked T waves
This is a common ECG finding in patients with hyperkalemia.
C. Prolonged QT interval
This patient has hypocalcemia. A prolonged QT interval is the most common ECG
finding with hypocalcemia. Other signs and symptoms of this electrolyte abnormality may include extensive muscle cramping, convulsions, and positive Chvostek and
Trousseau slgns.
Reference: https://wwrw.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482465/
D. Shortened QT interval
This is the most common ECG finding in patients with hypercalcemia.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: القابلة عملت total thyroidectomy قبل أسبوعين، وهاي symptoms واضحة: carpopedal spasms مع hyperreflexia للـ deep tendon reflexes و muscle cramps باليدين والقدمين. هاي كل علامات hypocalcemia بسبب نقص الـ PTH بعد إزالة الـ thyroid gland. أكثر ECG finding في الـ hypocalcemia هو prolonged QT interval، وكمان الـ muscle cramps و convulsions ممكن تحصل، والـ Chvostek و Trousseau signs ممكن يطلعوا إيجابيين.
الفخ: الفخ إنك تختار peaked T waves أو flattening of T waves لأنهم بيطلعوا مع electrolyte abnormalities تانية. الـ peaked T waves بتظهر في hyperkalemia، والـ flattened broad T waves في hypokalemia، واللي بيخلي الـ QT يطول هو hypocalcemia.

question: Which of the following is the primary goal of performing thoracotomy in the emergency department?

options.text: Cross-clamp the aorta to prevent cerebral air embolism
Cross-clamp the descending aorta to improve upper extremity perfusion
Perform open cardiac massage to correct ventricular fibrillation

englishExplanation:
Release cardiac tamponade
Expl anation
A. Cross-clamp the aorta to prevent cerebral air embolism
While a goal of a resuscitative ED thoracotomy is to prevent and manage air embolism, this is done by placing the patient in the Trendelenburg position to minimize cerebral involvement and direct air emboli to less critical structures. Crossclamping the aorta is not a technique for preventing cerebral air embolism.
B. Cross-clamp the descending aorta to improve upper extremity
perfusion
Cross-clamping the descending thoracic aorta is a primary goal of ED thoracotomy
and is recommended if there is persistent hypotension despite pericardiotomy. This
is intended to improve cerebral and myocardial perfusion, not upper extremity
perfusion.
C. Perform open cardiac massage to correct ventricular fibrillation
Direct cardiac compressions with open massage is a primary goal of ED thoracotomy and is recommended to improve cardiac output. It is not used to correct ventricular fibrillation.
D. Release cardiac tamponade
A resuscitative ED thoracotomy is a procedure that is intended to temporize wounds
and stabilize a patient by direct control of intrathoracic injuries, decompression of
pericardial tamponade, and control of the aorta to prevent exsanguination. A pericardiotomy to release cardiac tamponade is one of the primary goals of ED thoracotomy. If cardiac tamponade is suspected or evident, a pericardiotomy should be
performed.
Further information: Jones, R and Rivers, E, "Resuscitative Thoracotomy" in
Roberts, James R, Catherine B. Custalow, Todd W. Thomsen, Jerris R. Hedges.
Roberts and Hedges' clinical procedures in emergency medicine and acute care, 7th
edition, 2019.
Page 1049 of 4185
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ resuscitative ED thoracotomy هدفه الأساسي إنك تتحكم مباشرة بالـ intrathoracic injuries، وتعمل decompression للـ pericardial tamponade، وتتحكم بالـ aorta عشان ما ينزف المريض. ولما تشك بـ cardiac tamponade أو تلاقيه evident، الـ pericardiotomy لتحرير الـ tamponade هدف أساسي من أهداف الـ thoracotomy. وبالإضافة لذلك بيتم الـ open cardiac compressions لتحسين الـ cardiac output، و cross-clamp للـ descending aorta إذا استمر hypotension رغم الـ pericardiotomy.
الفخ: الفخ إنك تختار perform open cardiac massage لأنو القلب متوقف، بس هاد الهدف لتحسين الـ cardiac output مش لتصحيح ventricular fibrillation. و cross-clamp الـ aorta ما بيعمل منع cerebral air embolism، هاد بيتم بـ Trendelenburg position.

question: A 55-year old female with a history of interstitial lung disease presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath. Physical exam demonstrates a thin female with telangiectasias on her face and hands. Additional skin findings on her hands are shown. She reports that when her hands get cold, the fingertips turn white. Your review of old serum lab testing reveals an abnormally positive serum ANA titer, for which she has never received follow-up. Which of the following other symptoms are most likely to be present in this patient?
englishExplanation:
Esophageal dysmotility
Expl anation
A. Erythema marginatum
This patient's exam and history is consistent with systemic sclerosis (formerly
CREST syndrome). Erythema marginatum is seen classically in rheumatic fever.
B. Erythema nodosum
This patient's exam and history are consistent with systemic sclerosis (formerly
CREST syndrome). Erythema nodosum is seen in many systemic disease processes,
such as sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, and coccidioidomycosis.
C. Esophageal dysmotility
This patient's exam and history is consistent with systemic sclerosis (formerly
known as CREST syndrome) with calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal
dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia. Systemic sclerosis is a form of scleroderma that can be further subdivided into limited systemic sclerosis
(CREST syndrome) or diffuse involvement based on clinical and lab features. 90%
of patients with systemic sclerosis are also ANA positive. The image demonstrates
sclerodactyly.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430875/
D. Tracheal stenosis
This patient's exam and history is consistent with systemic sclerosis. The localized
variant of systemic sclerosis (formerly called CREST syndrome) includes calcinosis,
Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasias.
90% are also ANA positive. The image demonstrates sclerodactyly. Tracheal stenosis is not associated with systemic sclerosis.

question: Which of the following cardiovascular abnormalities is most common among patients with systemic lupus erythematosus?
englishExplanation:
Pericarditis
Expl anation
A. Abdominal aortic dissection
Patients with an aortic dissection present with a "tearing" chest, abdominal, or back
pain. Risk factors include advanced age, connective tissue disease, hypertension,
aortic aneurysm, and atherosclerosis. While SLE may predispose to aonic dissection, pericarditis is more common and may occur in up to 66% of patients with this
diagnosis.
B. Acute coronary syndrome
Acute coronary syndrome includes myocardial infarction and unstable angina.
Patients will have angina that is either new onset, increasing in frequency or duration or angina that occurs at rest. Some common risk factors include increasing age,
family history, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, cigarette smoking, and obesity. Patients with SLE are at an increased risk for coronary artery disease, but it is
not as common as pericarditis.
C. Congestive heart failure
Impaired cardiac function can occur due to either diastolic dysfunction (impaired
ventricular filling), systolic dysfunction (impaired left ventricular ejection), or both.
Contributing factors include chronic hypertension, renal impairment, coronary
artery disease, and cardiomyopathies. In patients with SLE, myocarditis may lead to
congestive heart failure; pericarditis is more common and may occur in up to 66%
of patients with this diagnosis.
D. Pericarditis
Pericarditis is inflammation of the fibrous pericardial sac. Pericardial effusion may
also be present. Patients present with pleuritic chest pain that is worse when lying
supine. On examination, a pericardial friction rub may be heard. Associated ECG
findings include diffuse ST changes. Due to the inflammatory nature of SLE, pericarditis may occur in up to 66% of patients with this diagnosis. Pericarditis in patients with SLE usually follows the typical course without additional complications.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK535405/

Vasculitides. In: Walls RM, Hockberger RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's

Elsevier; 2023.

question: A 55-year-old female with a past medical history of IV drug abuse presents to the emergency department with severe right-sided flank pain and rash. The physical exam is significant for the rash shown below, as well as palpable purpura. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse rate is 70/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 170/97 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Urine is negative for infection. CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis reveals a perirenal hematoma and a possible intra-renal aneurysm. Which of the following conditions is most commonly associated with this disease?
englishExplanation:
Hepatitis B
Expl anation
A. Cryoglobulinemia
Cryoglobulinemia is associated with multiple myeloma and most commonly with
hepatitis C. The clumped proteins will obstruct vessels and cause necrosis. This
patient's aneurysm points to another disease process.
B. Hepatitis B
This patient's exam, particularly the intra-renal aneurysm and the livedo reticularis
rash, are consistent with polyarteritis nodosa (PAN). Up to 30% of cases of secondary PAN are associated with hepatitis B. Patients with associated hepatitis B infection can benefit from treatment with antivirals in addition to steroids.
Patients with PAN often have hypertension. Symptoms include fatigue, weight loss,
fevers, arthralgias, and skin lesions (erythematous nodules, palpable purpura,
livedo reticularis, and ulcerations) and most often affect the lower extremities but
can be diffuse.
PAN diagnosis is based on characteristic symptoms, exam findings, and lab results.
Diagnosis is then confirmed by biopsy when possible. If a biopsy site is not available, CTA can reveal renal, hepatic, or mesenteric microaneurysms which are also
diagnostic when combined with symptoms and exam findings. Treatment of PAN is
high-dose steroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg per day) over a month and tapered over 6-8
months.
Further information:

Vasculitides. In: Walls RM, Hockberger RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's
Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia:
Elsevier; 2023.
C. Human immunodeficiency virus
HIV should not predispose a patient to aneurysm formation.
D. Scleroderma
Page 1941 of 4185
Scleroderma classically causes skin thickening as well as Raynaud's phenomenon,
esophageal dysmotility, and organ dysfunction. It does not fit with this patient's
presentation.

question: A 70-year-old female with diabetes and hypertension presents to the emergency department with a chief complaint of left arm and left face numbness and weakness, and difficulty speaking. The symptoms lasted for approximately 45 minutes and then resolved. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse rate is 92/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 160/90 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. The neurological exam is normal. Her blood glucose is 285. EKG reveals atrial fibrillation. Upon admission, the patient has a carotid duplex which reveals right carotid stenosis of 65%. Which of the following interventions will most likely reduce this patient's immediate mortality?
englishExplanation:
Anticoagulation
Expl anation
A. Anticoagulation
The patient had a transient ischemic attack. Two interventions that reduce mortality
in patients with TIA are anticoagulation for patients with atrial fibrillation or LV
thrombus and carotid endarterectomy for carotid stenosis > 70%.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459143/
Papa L, Meurer WJ. Chapter 87. Stroke. In: Walls RM, Hockberger RS, Gausche-
Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical Practice. 10th ed.
Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
B. Blood glucose control
While long-term blood glucose control is important in decreasing morbidity and
mortality for this patient, emergent blood glucose control has not been shown to decrease the immediate morbidity of this patient.
C. Blood pressure control
While long-term blood pressure control is important in decreasing morbidity and
mortality for this patient, emergent blood pressure control has not been shown to
decrease the immediate morbidity of this patient.
D. Carotid endarterectomy
The patient only has 65% stenosis, thus anticoagulation is the better answer choice.

الفخ: الفخ إنك تختار carotid endarterectomy لأن الـ duplex طالع فيه 65% stenosis وكأنه السبب، بس الـ endarterectomy بتنفع بـ stenosis أكثر من 70% بس. الحجة للـ anticoagulation هنا هي الـ atrial fibrillation اللي طالعة بالـ EKG.

question: A 43-year-old patient presents with fatigue, decreased appetite, and persistent swelling of the face and extremities for the past month. They emigrated from central Asia in their teens and have a history of chronic hepatitis B infection in childhood. They have not had any recent colds or other infections. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse rate is 76/min, and blood pressure is 110/72 mmHg. Physical examination shows generalized edema. Heart sounds are regular without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. The abdomen is soft and non-tender. There is no shifting dullness or fluid wave. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Membranous glomerulonephritis
Expl anation
A. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Focal segmental glomerular sclerosis is one differential diagnosis of membranous
glomerulonephritis. It is most common in young African American men. Patients
may present with asymptomatic proteinuria or with symptoms of nephrotic syndrome including edema, proteinuria, and hypertension. It may be idiopathic or the
result of HIV infection or drug use.
B. IgA nephropathy
IgA nephropathy is the most common cause of nephritic syndrome worldwide and is
associated with upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infections. Patients commonly
present with acute gross hematuria and proteinuria. They may also have hyperten-
Sion and periorbital edema.
C. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is a chronic immune-mediated disease
that primarily affects children and young adults. It presents with varying severity
ranging from asymptomatic hematuria on urinalysis to gross hematuria, nephrotic
syndrome, or azotemia.
D. Membranous glomerulonephritis
Membranous glomerulonephritis is the most common cause of adult nephrotic syndrome. It can be idiopathic or associated with autoimmune disease, infectious disease, malignancy, or medications. In this case, it was likely triggered by this
patient's previous hepatitis B infection. Onset is slow; edema is the most common
presentation. Hypertension is unlikely early in the disease.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559169/
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريض عنده generalized edema مع fatigue و decreased appetite من شهر، ومعاه history of chronic hepatitis B من الطفولة و emigrated من central Asia. الـ membranous glomerulonephritis هو أكثر سبب لـ nephrotic syndrome عند الـ adults، والـ onset عنده slow والـ edema هو أكثر الـ presentations. هون غالباً الـ disease ارتبطت بـ hepatitis B السابقة، و FSGS و membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis بيبقوا ضمن الـ differential diagnosis، بس التربط مع hepatitis B هو اللي يرجّح الـ membranous glomerulonephritis.
الفخ: الفخ إنك تختار IgA nephropathy لأنه أشهر سبب لـ nephritic syndrome، بس الـ IgA بيجي مع URI و gross hematuria حادة، والمريض هاد ما عنده أي infection حديثة. والـ FSGS أكثر شيوعاً عند young African American men و idiopathic أو مع HIV أو drugs.

question: Which finding is included in the diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki disease?
englishExplanation: Kawasaki disease diagnostic criteria include fever ≥5 days and at least four of: bilateral nonpurulent conjunctival injection, inflammatory changes of lips/oral mucosa, erythema/swelling of hands or feet, nonvesicular rash, and cervical lymphadenopathy.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: معايير الـ Kawasaki disease بتطلب fever من 5 أيام أو أكثر، ومعها 4 على الأقل من علامات الخمسة. هاي العلامات هي bilateral nonpurulent conjunctival injection، inflammatory changes of the lips والـ oral mucosa، erythema أو swelling باليدين أو القدمين، nonvesicular rash، و cervical lymphadenopathy. فالـ cervical lymphadenopathy جزء أساسي من المعايير.
الفخ: الفخ إنك تختار fever for 3 days لأن الـ fever لازم تكون موجودة، بس 5 أيام على الأقل. والـ geographic tongue والـ ulcerating lesions باليدين مش من معايير Kawasaki، والمعايير بتحتاج 4 علامات إضافية فوق الـ fever.

question: A patient with sarcoidosis presents with bilateral lower-extremity edema and intermittent chest pain that has been gradually worsening over the last 2 weeks. Her ECG is shown below. What is the most likely electrolyte derangement?
englishExplanation:
This patient's ECG demonstrates a shortened QT interval, consistent with hypercalcemia. In sarcoidosis, there is uncontrolled synthesis of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 by macrophages that leads to resorption of calcium in the bone and increased absorption in the intestine. This can lead to hypercalcemia.

Review notes: ["visual_reference_no_image_attached_in_jsonl"]
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ ECG عندها بيبيّن shortened QT interval، وهاد هو الـ classic ECG finding مع hypercalcemia. السبب إنو في sarcoidosis في uncontrolled synthesis of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 من الـ macrophages، وهاد بيسبّب increased resorption of calcium من العظام و increased absorption من الأمعاء. فبيطلع عندها hypercalcemia، وهاد اللي بيخلّي الـ QT قصير مش طويل.
الفخ: الفخ إنك تختار hypocalcemia لأن الـ QT interval هو المحور، بس الـ hypocalcemia بتعمل QT طويل مش قصير. والـ hyperkalemia بتدي peaked T waves، والـ hypokalemia بتدي U waves، فمفيش منهم بيشرح الـ shortened QT.

question: A 7-year-old presents with fever and lethargy. The patient tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 infection 3 weeks ago and is unvaccinated. Examination reveals swollen, erythematous hands and feet as well as a diffuse rash. Laboratory testing revealed elevated CRP, troponin, BNP, and d-dimer as well as lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia. Bedside echocardiogram showed decreased left ventricular systolic function and a small pericardial effusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: This patient has features consistent with multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C), an inflammatory syndrome seen in children and adolescents associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection. It shares features with Kawasaki disease and can present with cardiovascular involvement and cytopenias.

الفخ: الفخ إنك تختار myocarditis لأن الـ troponin مرتفع والـ LV function نازلة، أو ARDS بسبب الـ dyspnea. بس MIS-C هي اللي بتجمع الـ fever مع الـ rash والـ extremity changes والـ cytopenias بعد infection بـ SARS-CoV-2.

question: A 58-year-old man with known severe coronary artery disease presents via am- bulance after a witnessed cardiac arrest. He has been intubated by EMS, and CPR is in progress. His end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO) drops from 20 mm Hg to 9 mm Hg during the course of 10 minutes; the waveform maintains a normal mor- phology. Bedside echocardiogram shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the most likely cause of the drop in EtCO?
englishExplanation: Monitoring of end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO) during cardiopulmonary ar- rest has become the standard of care in most emergency departments. EtCO may be used as a marker of perfusion during resuscitation of a patient in cardiac arrest. Near-normal EtCO levels (20 mm Hg) suggest that good chest compres- sions are being provided and that perfusion is adequate. EtCO should ideally be maintained above 10 mm Hg. A gradual decrease in EtCO may indicate that the person giving chest compressions is becoming fatigued and CPR should be provided by a different team member or an automated device. EtCO monitoring provides a real-time assessment of ventilation and perfu- sion in the setting of cardiac arrest, and it may also provide important prognostic information. Changes in EtCO during resuscitation may indicate issues with venti- lation, such as incorrect initial placement of the endotracheal tube or subsequent displacement of the endotracheal tube. Although colorimetric CO detectors may 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 change colors early in esophageal intubation, an adequate waveform will not be noted. A sudden decrease in CO with a poor waveform during resuscita- tion likely indicates displacement of the endotracheal tube. A sudden in- crease in EtCO may indicate a ROSC. An EtCO <10 mm Hg at the 20-min mark of resuscitation has been associated with a poor prognosis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Since no cardiac tamponade was noted on bedside echocardiogram, car- diac tamponade is not a likely cause of the gradual decrease of EtCO in this case. Cardiac tamponade can decrease EtCO by decreasing blood flow to the lungs. Displacement of the endotracheal tube would cause a sudden decrease in EtCO with concomitant loss of waveform. A gradual decrease in EtCO may be seen with expanding pneumothorax, which can be a complication of CPR. Significant internal hemorrhage is unlikely to be the cause in this patient with a witnessed cardiac arrest. In trauma, however, ongoing hemorrhage should be considered as a potential cause of decreasing EtCO.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: مراقبة الـ EtCO أثناء الـ CPR بقت standard of care، والـ EtCO بيستعمل كـ marker للـ perfusion وقت الـ resuscitation. قيمة قريبة من الـ normal زي 20 mm Hg بتدل إنو الـ chest compressions منيحة والـ perfusion adequate، والمفروض يضل فوق 10 mm Hg. النزول التدريجي بالـ EtCO والـ waveform لسا morphology طبيعي يعني إنو اللي بيعمل compressions تعب، فلازم تبدّل الـ compressor أو تستخدم جهاز آلي. والـ drop المفاجئ مع waveform ضعيف هو اللي بيعني displacement of the endotracheal tube، والـ ارتفاع بي indication على ROSC.
الفخ: الفخ إنك تختار displacement of the endotracheal tube لأن الـ EtCO نزل، بس الـ waveform بقى طبيعي. الـ tube displacement بيطلع مع waveform ضعيف بشكل مفاجئ، والـ drop التدريجي مع waveform سليم بيقول مشكلة بالـ compressions.

question: A 67-year-old woman presents with chest pain and dyspnea. Soon after arrival, she experiences a witnessed cardiac arrest. The ECG monitor shows the rhythm below. In addition to chest compressions, which resuscitative approach is the best next step? Credit: William J. Brady, MD, FACEP/copyright ACEP.

options.text: Electrical defibrillation and basic airway management
Invasive airway management and cardioactive medications
Invasive airway management and transcutaneous pacing

correctAnswer: Electrical defibrillation and basic airway management
englishExplanation: In cardiac arrest, the initial rhythm provides important information to guide man- agement. This patient's rhythm is ventricular fibrillation, which is a shockable rhythm. Electrical defibrillation is the most appropriate intervention and should be performed as early as possible after resuscitation is initiated. Chest compres- sions are, of course, a priority in early management. Studies have shown that basic airway management (eg, BVM) is appropriate while prioritizing com- pressions and defibrillation. The four cardiac arrest rhythm scenarios are: Ventricular fibrillation (VF) Pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT) Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) Asystole Two of the four — VF and pulseless VT — are considered shockable rhythms, meaning that electrical defibrillation is the most appropriate interven- tion and should be provided as early as possible after initiation of resuscitation. In VF and pulseless VT, electrical defibrillation and chest compressions are the priori- ties in early management. The nonshockable rhythms are PEA and asystole; electri- cal defibrillation is not indicated in these two rhythm scenarios. In all four cardiac arrest scenarios, appropriate chest compressions are indicated. Intravenous fluids, cardioactive medications, and airway management are additional priorities. If pos- sible, identification of the underlying or causative issue is important so that addi- tional therapy can be tailored to the situation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cardioactive medications should become a management priority only after maximizing chest compressions and defibrillation in patients with pulseless VF or VT. Transvenous pacing is unlikely to benefit the patient, is not indicated, and is a laborious procedure that cannot be easily done while chest com- pressions are ongoing. Additional therapies such as definitive airway management with orotracheal intuba- tion are important after the patient is stabilized but must not detract from the first steps in management — chest compressions and electrical defibrillation. Transcutaneous pacing is unlikely to benefit the patient and is not indicated. The priorities should be chest compressions, basic airway management, and debrillation. Key Points High-quality chest compressions and electrical defibrillation are very important in the treatment of cardiac arrest manifesting with pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. Invasive airway management and cardioactive medications can be important inter- ventions in all four cardiac arrest rhythm presentations but should not detract from chest compressions and defibrillation for ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ rhythm عندها على الـ monitor هو ventricular fibrillation، وهاد rhythm قابل للصدمة. الـ electrical defibrillation هو التداخل الأنسب وبيلزم ينعمل بأسرع وقت بعد ما يبدأ الـ resuscitation، مع الـ chest compressions كأولوية واضحة. والـ basic airway management مثل BVM كفاية لحما تنتظر الـ compressions والصدمة. أما PEA و asystole فهم rhythms مش قابلة للصدمة، فما في داعي لأي shock فيهما، والـ IV fluids والـ cardioactive medications والـ airway management أولويات إضافية.
الفخ: الفخ إنك تختار invasive airway management مع cardioactive medications، لأن الـ airway والـ drugs مهمين بس مش الأولوية. بالـ VF لازم تعمل shock أولاً مع الـ compressions، والـ cardioactive medications والـ invasive airway management بيجوا بعد هيك.

question: What is the appropriate treatment for pseudo–pulseless electrical activity?
englishExplanation: Pseudo-pulseless electrical activity (pseudo-PEA) is a condition of se- vere shock that should be treated with pressor agents and fluid resuscita- tion. A patient may appear to be in PEA with organized electrical activity on the monitor and an impalpable pulse. However, if the patient has a blood pressure so low their pulse is impalpable, they are not truly in cardiac arrest and, thus, not in PEA. Patients in pseudo-PEA must be identified because performing chest com- pressions on them may actually be detrimental. If chest compressions are performed asynchronously with the heart's intrinsic contractions, preload and car- diac output may be reduced. The best way to identify pseudo-PEA is by ultrasound or arterial line. If there are cardiac contractions or pulsations of the femoral artery on bedside ultrasound, chest compressions should not be performed. Instead, care should focus on increas- ing blood pressure with pressor support and fluid resuscitation. Pseudo-PEA may be encountered in any shock state, but it is most likely to be apparent in distributive shock, such as sepsis or anaphylaxis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cardioversion should be used for unstable tachydysrhythmias, such as supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, and ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. Intravenous epinephrine is given as bolus dos- ing during ACLS or as an infusion to increase blood pressure. Cardioversion should not be used for pseudo-PEA. Instead, pseudo-PEA should be treated with fluid re- suscitation and continuous infusion pressors. Chest compressions should not be used in pseudo-PEA. Compressions may reduce preload and cardiac output if they are asynchronous with intrinsic cardiac contractions. Pseudo-PEA should be treated with fluid resuscitation and continuous infusion pressors. Defibrillation is not a treatment for pseudo-PEA. Rather, it is reserved for ven- tricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Similarly, amio- darone is indicated for ventricular arrhythmias, not for PEA or pseudo-PEA. Instead, pseudo-PEA should be treated with fluid resuscitation and continuous in- fusion pressors.
arabicExplanation:

question: Which medication is recommended for managing refractory pediatric cardiac ar- rest due to ventricular fibrillation?
englishExplanation: According to PALS, amiodarone is recommended for use in refractory ven- tricular fibrillation following two unsuccessful defibrillation attempts and administration of epinephrine. The recommended initial dose of amio- darone is 5 mg/kg administered over 20-60 minutes, which can be repeated if needed up to two additional times (maximum dose is 15 mg/kg or 300 mg to- tal). Amiodarone is classified as a Vaughan-Williams class III antiarrhythmic, but in practice, it has broad antiarrhythmic properties, with effects on sodium, potassium, and calcium channels as well as beta blockade. Amiodarone is used for terminating ventricular arrhythmias in children and adults. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bupivacaine is a local anesthetic that is used frequently for nerve blocks due to its long duration of action. Bupivacaine is not routinely used as an antiar- rhythmic, and overdose can actually cause severe cardiotoxicity. It has no recom- mended role in PALS. The local anesthetic lidocaine, on the other hand, is recom- mended as an alternative agent to amiodarone. In this case, amiodarone is the most appropriate medication to treat refractory pediatric ventricular fibrillation. Flecainide is a Vaughan-Williams class Ic antiarrhythmic that is typi- cally used as a controller medication for supraventricular arrhythmias, such as supraventricular tachycardia and atrial fibrillation. Although flecainide is a potent antiarrhythmic, it is only available in oral form and, thus, has no role in the setting of cardiac arrest at any age. In this case, amiodarone is the most appropriate medication to treat refractory pediatric ventricular fibrillation. Procainamide is a Vaughan-Williams class Ia antiarrhythmic that is rec- ommended and used routinely for suppressing stable ventricular ar- rhythmias, such as ventricular tachycardia. However, procainamide does not have a recommended use in the management of pediatric cardiac arrest. In this case, amiodarone is the most appropriate medication to treat refractory pediatric ventricular fibrillation.

الفخ: الطلبة بيختاروا Bupivacaine لأنه drug بيوقف arrhythmias، بس هو local anesthetic بيستعمل للـ nerve blocks بسبب مدة تأثيره الطويلة. جرعة زيادة منه ممكن تسبّب cardiotoxicity شديدة، ومفيش له دور في PALS. البديل اللي PALS بتذكره هو Lidocaine.

question: A 3-year-old child with end-stage renal disease presents in pulseless electrical ac- tivity arrest. Which intervention is most likely to successfully resuscitate the patient? Credit: Copyright ACEP.
englishExplanation: This ECG is representative of the classic “sine wave” pattern of profound hy- perkalemia; in this case, it is severe enough to result in pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest. In addition to standard measures, such as CPR, PEA arrest due to presumed or known hyperkalemia should be treated aggressively with intravenous calcium, either in the gluconate or chloride form. The chloride form is preferred in cardiac arrest situations because it delivers three times the amount of calcium as calcium gluconate for the same volume. Although it carries a risk of ex- travasation injury, this is of lesser concern than controlling the life-threatening ef- fect of hyperkalemia. Hyperkalemia causes toxicity by reducing the passive gradient responsible for main- taining normal resting membrane potential, thereby raising the resting membrane potential. At higher potassium levels, this inhibits cardiac sodium channels (which are dependent on resting membrane potential to function properly) and ultimately slows depolarization. This is reflected most severely in the sine wave pattern, al- though it is essential to note that severe hyperkalemia can readily cause ven- tricular fibrillation or asystole and should be considered even in the ab- sence of classic ECG findings. Calcium antagonizes the effects of hyperkalemia by both antagonizing its effect on resting membrane potential and restoring sodium channel function. Incorrect Answer Explanations Amiodarone is appropriate as an adjunctive medication for the manage- ment of refractory pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fib- rillation, but it has no role in the management of PEA arrest with a wide-complex bradycardia. Furthermore, amiodarone use could be dangerous because of its wide receptor-blocking effects. This patient should be treated with empiric calcium chlo- ride because there is significant clinical concern for hyperkalemia-induced PEA arrest. Atropine is appropriate for the initial management of symptomatic bradycardia in children. However, this patient is presenting in PEA arrest with a wide-complex bradycardia, which is highly concerning for hyperkalemia, espe- cially given the patient's history of renal disease. Thus, atropine is not indicated in this situation, and the patient should be treated with calcium chloride. Procainamide is appropriate for managing stable ventricular arrhyth- mias, but it has no role in the management of PEA arrest with a wide-complex bradycardia. Giving procainamide in this circumstance could be dangerous because of its effect on cardiac sodium channels.

question: Which intervention has proven benefit for favorable neurologic outcomes in car- diac arrest?
englishExplanation: Chest compressions are the single most important intervention in car- diac arrest. Chest compressions attempt to provide perfusion to vital organs, in- cluding the brain, to improve neurologic outcomes. Guidelines were changed in 2010 to focus more on chest compressions and shorten the duration to initiation of chest compressions, moving from the ABC (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) model to the CAB (Circulation, Airway, Breathing) model. Chest compressions are so important that lay bystanders are advised to perform chest compressions in pre- sumed cardiac arrest because the benefit outweighs the potential harms, even if the patient is not actually in cardiac arrest. Guidelines recommend chest compressions at a depth of 2 in and a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. Incorrect Answer Explanations Amiodarone is an arrhythmic that can be utilized for ventricular tachyarrhyth- mias in cardiac arrest. Studies have shown that amiodarone is associated with in- creased survival to hospital admission but have not shown increased survival to hospital discharge or survival with favorable neurologic outcomes. Amiodarone can be considered for ventricular arrhythmias (pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ven- tricular fibrillation) at a dose of 300 mg IV. Epinephrine is one of the hallmarks of ACLS, although the evidence supporting im- proved neurologic outcomes is severely limited. Epinephrine is recommended by the American Heart Association at 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes. Some studies have shown increased rates of ROSC, survival to hospital admission, and hospital discharge. However, they have failed to show any improvement in neuro- logic outcomes. Intubation or advanced airway management is oftentimes pursued during cardiac arrest to prevent orogastric aspiration and improve ventilation. However, endotra- cheal intubation can be particularly difficult with ongoing CPR, which can lead to tube malposition. Furthermore, advanced airway management may interrupt valu- able chest compressions. Studies have not shown any survival benefit with favorable neurologic outcomes, and some nonrandomized studies have shown worse out- comes. If intubation occurs, continuous chest compressions should be done at a rate of 100 to 120 per minute without pauses for ventilation, while breaths should be delivered at 10 per minute or one every 6 seconds.

question: A 22-year-old man visiting the hospital suddenly collapses in the cafeteria. CPR is started immediately. An AED is applied, and a shock is delivered. The patient is in ventricular fibrillation on arrival to the emergency department. He is defib- rillated again, given epinephrine and amiodarone, and intubated. ACLS care is continued for another two rounds of CPR, defibrillation, and additional epineph- rine and amiodarone administration. The patient remains in ventricular fibrilla- tion. What should be done next?

options.text: Administer an additional 300 mg of amiodarone and prepare to give lidocaine
Change the vector orientation of the defibrillation pads and defibrillate again
Infuse 4 g of calcium gluconate intravenously over 15 minutes
Terminate resuscitative efforts because the patient is unlikely to survive

correctAnswer: Change the vector orientation of the defibrillation pads and defibrillate again
englishExplanation: This patient presents in refractory ventricular fibrillation (VF), or VF that is unresponsive to traditional ACLS care. Refractory VF can occur for multiple rea- sons, including coronary artery disease, ACS, and undiagnosed cardiac abnormali- ties, such as long QT syndrome and electrolyte abnormalities. Multiple strategies have been proposed to treat refractory VF and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT). One of the most discussed strategies is to change the way defibrillation is performed, such as changing the vector of the defibrillation. If the patient was initially defibrillated with pads in an anterior-posterior position, the position- ing may be changed to an anterior-lateral position and defibrillation tried again, or vice versa. Double sequential defibrillation, also known as dual sequential defibril- lation, has also shown benefit in refractory VT and VF. To perform double sequential defibrillation, place two sets of pads on the patient: one in an anterior- posterior position, and the second in an anterior-lateral position; ensure the pads are not touching one another. A variation of double sequential defibrillation in- volves placing both sets of pads next to each other in anterior-lateral positions. Some studies suggest using both defibrillators simultaneously; others suggest a short delay (<1 second) between defibrillation with each machine. Other treatments have also been proposed to treat refractory VT and VF. These treatments include magnesium when refractory arrhythmia is caused by prolonged QT and calcium in the setting of suspected hyperkalemia. Esmolol, a beta-blocker, has been shown to help terminate refractory VT and VF in small stud- ies. One study used a loading dose of 500 µg/kg of esmolol, followed by an infusion of up to 100 µg/kg/min. It has been suggested that esmolol confers benefit by block- ing the adrenergic or catecholamine storm produced in refractory VT and VF. There are also some data to support trying lidocaine if amiodarone has been ineffective. Incorrect Answer Explanations At this point, the patient has received two doses of amiodarone per the ACLS guide- lines. Giving an additional bolus of 300 mg is unlikely to have any effect. Administering a different antiarrhythmic such as lidocaine may have some benefit, but the recommendation is to change the vector orientation of the defibrillator pads first. Calcium should be administered in the setting of cardiac arrest if severe hypocalcemia or hyperkalemia is considered as a cause. In cardiac arrest, cal- cium is typically administered through bolus dosing of calcium chloride rather than slow infusion of calcium gluconate. Terminating resuscitation at this time is premature. This young patient had a witnessed in-hospital cardiac arrest and could still have a meaningful neurologic outcome. Additional treatment modalities should be tried first, such as changing the vector orientation of the defibrillator pads.

question: Which cardiac arrhythmia should prompt consideration of double sequential defibrillation?
englishExplanation: Double sequential defibrillation (also known as dual sequential defibrillation) has been studied for the treatment of refractory ventricular fibrillation (VF) and refractory pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT). Refractory VF can occur for multiple reasons, including coronary artery disease, ACS, and undiagnosed cardiac abnormalities, such as long QT syndrome and electrolyte abnormalities. There is a modest amount of evidence suggesting that double sequential defibrillation may be more successful at restoring a perfusing cardiac rhythm than continued attempts at single-set biphasic defibrillation. To perform double sequential defibrillation, place two sets of pads on the pa- tient: one in an anterior-posterior position, and the second in an anterior- lateral position; ensure the pads are not touching one another. A variation of double sequential defibrillation involves placing both sets of pads next to each other in anterior-lateral positions. Some studies suggest defibrillating with both defibril- lators simultaneously; others suggest a short delay (<1 second) between defibrilla- tion with each machine. Another treatment option for refractory VF or VT is to change the vector of the defibrillation. If the patient was initially being defibrillated with pads in an anterior- posterior position, this can be changed to pads in an anterior-lateral position and defibrillation tried again, or vice versa. Other treatments have also been proposed to treat refractory VT and VF. These treatments include magnesium (when refractory arrhythmia is caused by prolonged QT) and calcium (in the setting of suspected hy- perkalemia). Esmolol, a beta-blocker, has been shown to help terminate refractory VT and VF in small studies. One study used a loading dose of 500 µg/kg of esmolol, followed by an infusion of up to 100 µg/kg/min. It has been suggested that esmolol confers benefit by blocking the adrenergic or catecholamine storm produced in re- fractory VT and VF. There are also some data to support trying lidocaine if amio- darone has been ineffective. Incorrect Answer Explanations Defibrillation should not be used to treat supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). If SVT is unstable, synchronized cardioversion should be performed. If SVT is defibrillated instead of cardioverted, there is a risk of causing an R-on-T phenom- enon and inducing VF. Patients with unstable atrial fibrillation should have synchronized car- dioversion performed, not defibrillation. Defibrillation is reserved for VF and pulseless VT. VT with a pulse should be treated with synchronized cardioversion. This prevents an R-on-T phenomenon that may lead to VF. However, if a patient is in cardiac arrest and showing VT, defibrillation should be used. Refractory pulseless VT may be treated with double sequential defibrillation.

question: A 2-week-old girl presents via ambulance in shock. Which sign is most suggestive of a ductal dependent lesion from congenital heart disease?
englishExplanation: Shock or cyanosis occurring in the first 2 weeks of life is very alarming, and an undiagnosed congenital heart disease (CHD) should be strongly considered given that the ductus arteriosus is closing. Treatment with prostaglandins can be lifesaving. Other more common diseases such as septic shock must also be considered and treated as required in the critically ill neonate. With advances in imaging technology, CHD can be diagnosed in utero or in the newborn nursery. However, some disorders are not diagnosed until several weeks of life when the ductus arteriosus closes, and even then, the signs are subtle and easily missed. Common indicators of CHD are poor feeding with or without sweating, irritability, unexplained hypertension, hepatomegaly, and a pathologic murmur. On presentation, neonates with undiagnosed CHD often have mottled skin, cyanosis, and shock. If this is the case, especially if the in- fant is younger than 1 month of age, treatment with prostaglandins should be con- sidered as the culprit is likely a ductal dependent congenital heart lesion. Incorrect Answer Explanations Peripheral edema as a manifestation of heart failure is rare in infants. More common indicators of CHD are poor feeding with or without sweating, irritability, unexplained hypertension, hepatomegaly, and a pathologic murmur. The presentation described above with shock and central cyanosis is more consistent with a diagnosis of CHD. Murmurs are common in pediatric patients, present in more than 50% of newborns. Most of these patients have structurally normal hearts and have an "innocent" murmur, such as a grade 1 to 2 soft with normal split and normal periph- eral pulses. Two of the most common murmurs are: Peripheral pulmonary stenosis: a midsystolic high-pitched ejection murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border of the pulmonary area. The Still murmur: a low-pitched systolic ejection murmur heard best at the left lower sternal border and often described as musical. Stridor is audible breath sounds that typically originate from the ex- trathoracic airways. The presence of stridor indicates turbulent flow from a par- tial obstruction of the upper airways, glottis, or trachea. Congenital stridor presents at birth or within the first few weeks of life and is rarely life threatening. The most common causes include laryngomalacia, subglottic stenosis, bron- chogenic cysts, tracheomalacia, gastroesophageal reflux, and foreign body. Key Points Subtle indicators of congenital heart disease in neonates include poor feeding with or without sweating, unexplained hypertension, hepatomegaly, and a new patho- logic murmur. Signs of heart failure, such as edema, are uncommon in neonates. Shock and cyanosis in the first weeks of life strongly suggests a congenital heart dis- ease, and treatment with prostaglandins can be lifesaving.

question: A mother brings in her newborn son because she noticed he was working harder to breathe and the skin around his mouth looked blue. The baby was born 2 days earlier at home. On examination, he is awake and responsive but cyanotic. An ECG is obtained and shows a loss of right-sided forces and borderline left-axis deviation. What is the best choice for immediate pharmacotherapy?
englishExplanation:
This baby has signs of cardiac failure with resultant pulmonary edema, and the ECG shows a loss of right-sided forces and borderline left-axis devia- tion, which suggests tricuspid atresia as a cause of the cyanosis. Prostaglandin E (PGE) is a life-saving medication in this ductal-dependent cyanotic sce- nario and must be started as soon as possible. Dosing of the infusion is 0.05 mcg/kg per minute. Side effects of PGE1 include apnea, bradycardia, and hypoten- sion. Beyond initial care, the patient requires ICU admission and a cardiology con- 1 1 sultation. Treatment decisions are then made depending on the degree of cardiac defect and patient stability. Definitive repair with cardiothoracic surgery may be de- layed until the child grows and matures so that he is better prepared for the surgery. Incorrect Answer Explanations Atropine is used in pediatric resuscitation for bradycardia related to a vagal cause or as an antisialagogue. Prostaglandin, not atropine, is not used to keep the ductus arteriosus patent in ductal-dependent lesions, such as tricuspid atresia. Epinephrine, a staple medication in the resuscitation of critically ill patients, is not warranted in this case. This patient has clinical and ECG signs of a cyanotic car- diac defect, so the addition of epinephrine may cause cardiac instability and prompt worsening shunting of deoxygenated blood. A fluid bolus using normal saline is contraindicated in this clinical sce- nario. The child has signs of cardiac dysfunction and pulmonary edema, and adding fluid could worsen his condition.

question: A 4-day-old girl, born at home, presents with progressively worsening lethargy, pallor, diaphoresis, dyspnea, and discoloration of the legs that started 30 min- utes before presentation. She was previously noted to be acting normally and feeding well. Femoral pulses are absent. The right arm is pink and well perfused with palpable pulses. Telemetry monitoring shows sinus tachycardia. What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to treat this condition?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms consistent with a critical coarctation of the aorta dependent on the ductus arteriosus to maintain adequate systemic blood flow. Administration of alprostadil, a synthetic pros- taglandin E1, prevents closure of the ductus arteriosus and is necessary to stabilize patients in this situation prior to definitive procedural management. Other major “ductal-dependent lesions'' include hypoplastic left heart syndrome, pulmonary atresia with intact interventricular septum, transposition of the great arteries, tetralogy of Fallot, interrupted aortic arch, and criti- cal aortic and pulmonary stenosis. As the ductus arteriosus begins to close (usually within the first few days of life but up to 2 weeks after birth), perfusion through it becomes compromised, and the ductal-dependent abnormality rapidly becomes symptomatic. Unfortunately, presentation will vary between these pathologies, and most patients presenting to emergency departments in this situation will not have established diagnoses at the time of presentation. Any early newborn presenting with acute-onset respira- tory distress, difficulty or sweating with feeding, signs of shock (“grey baby”), or cyanosis (“blue baby”) without an identifiable alternative cause should be considered to have a possible ductal-dependent lesion. Differential blood pressure and pulse oximetry between “preductal” and “postductal” limbs is also strongly suggestive; the right arm is reliably “preductal,” whereas the legs are reliably “postductal.” Incorrect Answer Explanations Indomethacin is an NSAID that is classically used to close a patent duc- tus arteriosus. Consequently, use would close the ductus arteriosus faster rather than maintain it open. Administration of alprostadil (prostaglandin E1) is the cor- rect intervention in this case because it prevents the ductus arteriosus from closing. Milrinone is an inhibitor of phosphodiesterase-3 and is used as a positive in- otropic agent for patients with severe ventricular cardiac failure. Although a critically ill patient with congenital heart disease may also require this form of inotropic support, in this case, it is the sudden closure of the ductus arterio- sus that led to the patient's precipitous presentation. Consequently, administration of alprostadil (prostaglandin E1) is the correct intervention in this case because it prevents the ductus arteriosus from closing. Phenylephrine is given to increase systemic vascular resistance during an episode of shunting associated with tetralogy of Fallot, or a tet spell. It can diminish the right-to-left shunting and improve overall circulation. Phenylephrine has no role in the management of a closing ductus arteriosus di- rectly, although other vasopressors with inotropic activity, such as epinephrine, can be used as adjunctive therapy in certain circumstances. Administration of al- prostadil (prostaglandin E1) is the correct intervention in this case as it prevents the ductus arteriosus from closing.
