question: Which of the following echocardiographic findings is most consistent with Takotsubo syndrome?

options.text: Apical ballooning with regional wall motion abnormalities beyond a single coronary artery distribution
Asymmetric interventricular septal hypertrophy with intermittent left ventricular outflow tract obstruction
Biventricular dilation with globally reduced systolic function
Left ventricular dilation with reduced systolic function
Reduced ventricular cavity size and biatrial enlargement

correctAnswer: Apical ballooning with regional wall motion abnormalities beyond a single coronary artery distribution
englishExplanation:
Takotsubo syndrome is the preferred name for a clinical syndrome also known as Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, stress cardiomyopathy, and broken heart syndrome. It is characterized by acute, transient systolic and diastolic dysfunction of the left ventricle (LV) following physical or emotional stress. The exact pathogenesis has not been fully described, but it is thought to result from a sudden increase in circulating catecholamines that produce cardiomyocyte dysfunction. This dysfunction produces regional myocardial stunning and an urn-like shape of the LV that resembles an octopus trap used in Japan. A variety of causes and conditions have been described in relation to Takotsubo syndrome, including asthma, anaphylaxis, opioid withdrawal, seizures, sepsis, and gastrointestinal distress, though a comprehensive list is extensive.

The clinical presentation of Takotsubo syndrome often includes chest pain, dyspnea on exertion, and dizziness and is often concerning for acute coronary syndromes. ECG features often also suggest acute coronary syndrome, including ST elevation, sinus tachycardia, and QT prolongation. Point-of-care or formal echocardiography commonly shows ballooning of the apex with regional or segmental wall motion abnormalities that extend beyond the region of a single coronary artery distribution. Given that the initial presentation of Takotsubo syndrome is often indistinguishable from acute myocardial infarction, patients with concerning ST elevations should be treated accordingly, including with cardiac catheterization when appropriate. Patients who do not undergo catheterization should still be hospitalized for cardiac monitoring.



Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy appears on echocardiogram with asymmetric hypertrophy of the septum that may cause LV outflow tract obstruction (B).

An echocardiogram of dilated cardiomyopathy will show biventricular dilation and globally reduced systolic function (C) or LV dilation and reduced systolic function (D).

Restrictive cardiomyopathy is characterized on echocardiogram by reduced ventricular cavity size and atrial dilation (E).

Reveal Answer:

question: A 19-year-old man presents to the emergency department after passing out during soccer practice. A review of systems is negative except for occasional migraine headaches for which he takes naproxen as needed. Vital signs are within normal limits for his age. Physical exam is unremarkable. His ECG is shown above. Which of the following best explains these findings?
englishExplanation:
Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is a preexcitation syndrome caused by the presence of an accessory conduction pathway called the bundle of Kent. This pathway connects the atria to the ventricles. Conduction may occur simultaneously through the atrioventricular (AV) node and the accessory pathway or may bypass the AV node altogether and travel through the accessory pathway. Reentry through this accessory pathway results in tachydysrhythmias. Symptoms may include chest discomfort, lightheadedness, palpitations, syncope or near syncope, diaphoresis, or sudden cardiac death.

Electrocardiographic findings of WPW syndrome include a shortened PR interval (< 120 msec), a slurring of the initial QRS complex (delta wave), and a widened QRS complex. WPW in symptomatic patients may present with narrow or wide QRS complex tachycardia and may include atrial fibrillation. For hemodynamically stable patients with symptomatic WPW with narrow-complex tachycardia, vagal maneuvers may be attempted first, followed by adenosine. If adenosine fails, longer-acting AV nodal blockers such as beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers may be used. For refractory cases, procainamide is effective. When wide-complex tachycardia exists, medications that block the AV node should be avoided, including adenosine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and amiodarone. Unstable patients should receive synchronized cardioversion.



Ischemia from thrombosis (B) is less likely to occur in younger patients with few or no cardiac risk factors (e.g., hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, tobacco use). ECG characteristics of ischemia include hyperacute T waves, T wave inversions, and ST elevation or depression with reciprocal changes.

A myocardial channelopathy (C), such as Brugada syndrome, may cause syncope or sudden death in young, otherwise healthy individuals. These inherited disorders predispose individuals to fatal ventricular dysrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. ECG characteristics of Brugada syndrome include a coved ST segment with elevation > 2 mm followed by T wave inversion in leads V1–2 or a characteristic “saddleback” ST segment with elevation.

A tick-borne illness (D), such as Lyme disease, may produce varying degrees of AV block. This is the most common clinical feature of Lyme carditis.

Reveal Answer:
Ventricular tachycardia.

question: A 27-year-old man presents after a brief syncopal episode while sitting at a meeting at work. EMS was called and he has been awake and alert since leaving his office. He reports no current symptoms. Vital signs are unremarkable. His electrocardiogram is shown above. What pertinent finding would be most concerning in his family history?

options.text: Sudden cardiac death at age 40 years

correctAnswer: Sudden cardiac death at age 40 years
englishExplanation:
Brugada syndrome, first described in 1992, is an ECG abnormality that is associated with a high incidence of sudden cardiac death in patients with structurally normal hearts. It results from an inherited disorder of the sodium channels and is more common in male patients. The mean age of sudden death is 41 years. Diagnosis is dependent not only on the presence of the specific ECG abnormality but on the clinical scenario as well. Brugada sign is described as coved ST segment elevation > 2 mm in leads V1–V3 followed by a negative T wave. ECG changes may be transient. Patients with this ECG finding and one of the following clinical criteria, documented ventricular fibrillation or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, family history of sudden cardiac death under the age of 45 years, similar ECG finding in family members, inducible ventricular tachycardia with electrical stimulation, syncope or nocturnal agonal respiration, are at high risk for sudden cardiac death due to dysrhythmia. Definitive management is the placement of an automatically implanted cardiac defibrillator. Patients who are asymptomatic with Brugada sign on ECG but no clinical criteria for Brugada syndrome should be referred to a cardiologist for further evaluation.



Patients with Brugada syndrome are also at increased risk for atrial dysrhythmias, including atrial fibrillation (A). The presence of atrial fibrillation has been associated with increased disease severity and a higher incidence of ventricular fibrillation. However, a family history of atrial fibrillation alone would not increase the risk of Brugada syndrome.

Early coronary artery disease (B) is not linked to Brugada syndrome.

A family history of a hypercoagulable disorder (C) or known venous thromboembolism (VTE) in a family member increases a patient’s risk of developing VTE. ECG findings associated with a pulmonary embolism include sinus tachycardia, right ventricular strain, and a new incomplete right bundle branch block. This patient’s ECG is consistent with Brugada sign.

question: A 68-year-old man presents to the ED with acute abdominal and low back pain along with swelling of both legs over the past 2 days. He reports noticing a pulsatile abdominal mass over the last year but was never evaluated for it. Examination reveals a distended abdomen with a pulsatile midline mass, bilateral lower extremity edema, and prominent superficial abdominal wall veins. Which of the following additional findings would most strongly support the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Harsh midsystolic murmur radiating to the carotids

englishExplanation:
An arteriovenous (often aortocaval) fistula develops when periaortic inflammation causes the aorta to adhere to an adjacent vein, and pressure on the walls creates an abnormal communication. If blood also leaks into the retroperitoneum, the presentation mimics a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). More often, the aneurysm ruptures directly into the vena cava without external leakage, and the features of a large arteriovenous fistula predominate. These aneurysms are usually large, palpable in up to 90% of cases, and may produce a continuous abdominal bruit in about 75% and a palpable thrill in 25%. On physical examination, patients may have a wide pulse pressure, tachycardia, bounding peripheral pulses, and signs of volume overload such as hepatomegaly and lower extremity edema.

Blood shunting from artery to vein increases venous pressure, venous volume, and cardiac preload, often leading to high-output heart failure with dyspnea, jugular venous distention, and pulmonary edema. Elevated venous pressure can cause leg edema, cyanosis, and dilated superficial abdominal or leg veins. Distended veins in the bladder or rectum may rupture, causing hematuria or rectal bleeding. Because arterial blood is diverted into the venous system, the lower limbs may feel cool with weak pulses. Additional findings may include tachypnea, orthopnea, and a hyperdynamic precordium on palpation.

Kidney insufficiency is common, caused by reduced kidney perfusion from heart failure and increased kidney venous pressure. Hematuria is frequent in arteriovenous fistula but less common in other AAAs. Diagnosis relies on imaging, with CTA being essential to confirm the diagnosis.



Absent femoral pulses bilaterally (A) indicates acute arterial occlusion or severe aortoiliac disease that presents with extremity pain, not an arteriovenous shunt with preserved distal perfusion.

Free fluid on FAST exam (C) is suggestive of hemoperitoneum from aneurysm rupture into the peritoneal cavity. In an aortocaval fistula, bleeding occurs into the venous system rather than the free intraperitoneal space, so the FAST exam may be negative.

Harsh midsystolic murmur radiating to the carotids (D) is classic for aortic stenosis and unrelated to the abdominal vascular pathology described.

Pulsus paradoxus (E) is most often seen in cardiac tamponade, which presents with chest pain and dyspnea, not in aortocaval fistula.

Reveal Answer:

question: A 26-year-old man presents to the ED with a headache and chest pain. He reports no other medical conditions but smokes one pack of cigarettes and snorts cocaine daily. In the ED, his vital signs are a BP of 176/102 mm Hg, HR of 116 bpm, RR of 18/min, and SpO2 of 97% on room air. His ECG shows sinus tachycardia with evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy but no ischemia. Which of the following should be administered first to treat this patient’s symptoms?
englishExplanation:
Cocaine intoxication clinically presents as a sympathomimetic toxidrome that includes tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, chest pain, and mydriasis. Patients may also have hyperthermia and cardiac dysrhythmias. Cocaine exerts its effects by stimulating and blocking the reuptake of multiple neurotransmitters (dopamine, epinephrine, norepinephrine, and serotonin). Although many receptors are activated, the most profound effect is the adrenergic stimulation caused by norepinephrine and epinephrine, resulting in vasoconstriction, increased myocardial contractility, increased myocardial oxygen demand, and increased heart rate.

Cocaine-related chest pain ensues as a result of coronary vasospasm and ischemia due to increased myocardial oxygen demand. This chest pain is most effectively managed through benzodiazepines (i.e., diazepam), which will decrease the oxygen demand and sympathetic effects. Aspirin should be administered as well since cocaine induces platelet aggregation.



Haloperidol (B) is an antipsychotic that can be used to treat agitation that fails to respond to benzodiazepines. However, it can worsen hyperthermia and tachycardia because it has anticholinergic properties and so should be used in select patients with normal vital signs. There is no mention of this patient having significant agitation.

Heparin (C) should be administered if associated myocardial ischemia is present, which is not described in this case. Although chest pain in this setting is most directly attributable to coronary vasospasm, cocaine is prothrombotic and antifibrinolytic and causes platelet aggregation. Heparin may be indicated if the patient has concomitant coronary artery disease.

Metoprolol (D) and other beta-blockers are generally recommended to be avoided in cocaine-related chest pain due to the unopposed alpha stimulation that can lead to increased cardiac ischemia. While newer evidence suggests beta-blocker use is not associated with clinically significant hypertension, troponin elevation, or adverse events in patients presenting with acute cocaine toxicity, there is still a concern that it can lead to worsening vasoconstriction in patients with cocaine chest pain. Regardless, it would not be the first-line treatment option for cocaine-associated chest pain and hypertension.

Sodium bicarbonate (E) is used to treat wide-complex tachycardias associated with sodium channel blockage (such as with cocaine), but would have no role in the treatment of chest pain or hypertension.

One Step Further
Question:
True or false: Preexisting cardiovascular disease is a prerequisite for cocaine-related myocardial ischemia.

Reveal Answer:
False.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Cocaine Intoxication

Sympathomimetic toxidrome
Mydriasis
Hyperthermia
Hypertension
Tachycardia
Diaphoresis (unlike in anticholinergic overdose)
Seizures
Treatment
Benzodiazepines
Sodium bicarbonate for wide complex dysrhythmias
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريض عنده cocaine daily، و عنده tachycardia، hypertension، chest pain، مع headache. و الـ cocaine intoxication بيسبب sympathomimetic toxidrome لأنه بيزيد norepinephrine و epinephrine، فبيصير vasoconstriction و increased myocardial contractility و increased myocardial oxygen demand، و chest pain بتيجي من coronary vasospasm. و أكثر دوا فعّال ل chest pain هو benzodiazepines مثل diazepam لأنها بتقلل الـ oxygen demand والـ sympathetic effects.
الفخ: الخيار الغلط هو Haloperidol لأنه ممكن يزيد hyperthermia و tachycardia بسبب خصائصه anticholinergic، وهو مخصص للـ agitation اللي ما رد على الـ benzodiazepines. و heparin و metoprolol و sodium bicarbonate مو أول اختيار لهيك حالة.

question: A 55-year-old man presents to the ED following the sudden onset of squeezing substernal chest pain while shoveling snow. The pain has significantly improved since resting but is not fully resolved. He has a history of stent placement in the left anterior descending artery 2 years prior. His HR is 90 bpm, BP is 160/100 mm Hg, RR is 16/min, and SpO2 is 98%. An initial ECG shows T wave inversion in leads V2 and V3, which is unchanged compared to a previous ECG. It also shows 0.7 mm of ST depression in lead V1. He is admitted to the observation unit. Which of the following ECG findings, if present on reassessment, would be diagnostic of ongoing ischemia and potential development of non-ST elevation myocardial infarction?

options.text: 0.25 mm of ST depression in leads V2–V5
1.5 mm of ST elevation in leads V2–V3
New 1.5 mm T wave inversions in V4 and V5

correctAnswer: New 1.5 mm T wave inversions in V4 and V5
englishExplanation:
Non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) is a form of acute coronary syndrome. It is defined by the presence of > 0.5 mm of ST depression or of T wave inversions > 1 mm in two or more contiguous leads with elevation in cardiac biomarkers. It is essential for the emergency clinician to be able to recognize ECG changes that might suggest ongoing ischemia that requires further intervention before the troponin level results are available from lab testing.

The diagnosis of NSTEMI is frequently complicated by the presence of significant ECG abnormalities at baseline. Patients with chest pain and a history of cardiac disease with baseline ECG abnormalities often require admission or observation. Cardiac stress testing or invasive angiography is required in these patients to accurately assess the need for acute intervention.

Clinical decision tools, such as the HEART (history, ECG, age, risk factors, and troponin) score, are widely used for risk stratification in the setting of chest pain. Once new ECG changes develop, the emergency clinician should recognize the need for further cardiology evaluation and possible intervention.



An ST depression of 0.25 mm in two or more contiguous leads (A) is not sufficient for the diagnosis of NSTEMI. Rather, 0.5 mm of depression is required in two or more leads for the formal diagnosis.

1.5 mm of ST elevation in leads V2 and V3 (B) is not one of the diagnostic criteria for NSTEMI. While 1 mm of elevation is diagnostic of STEMI in most leads, this is not the case with leads V2 and V3. In these leads, 2.0 mm of elevation in men > 40 years, 2.5 mm in men < 40 years, and 1.5 mm in any woman would be diagnostic of STEMI.

Intermittent ventricular tachycardia (C) is not one of the formal diagnostic criteria for NSTEMI. However, it is a sign of myocardial irritability and could be related to developing or resolving myocardial ischemia.

One Step Further
Question:
What emergency department intervention is the most effective at reducing the morbidity and mortality of non-ST elevation myocardial infarction?

Reveal Answer:
Aspirin.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Non-ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI)

Sx: substernal chest pain that often radiates to left arm or jaw, dyspnea, nausea
Commonly presents with T wave inversions or ST segment depressions on ECG and elevated troponin
Medical therapy
Oxygen: indicated for SpO2 < 90%
Nitroglycerin: relieves ongoing chest pain, lowers BP
Morphine: relieves severe pain refractory to nitroglycerin
Beta-blockers: prevent recurrent ischemia and dysrhythmia
Antiplatelet agents: aspirin and P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g., prasugrel, ticagrelor, clopidogrel)
GPIIb/IIIa antagonists may be considered in certain patients (e.g., high-risk patients undergoing PCI)
Anticoagulation: in the acute setting (e.g., while hospitalized, until PCI is performed)
Lipid-lowering: high-intensity statin therapy lowers risk of death, recurrent MI, and stroke
ACE inhibitor or ARB: consider for certain patients (e.g., those with LVEF ≤ 40%, DM)
Treat underlying condition if NSTEMI is type 2
Revascularization strategy
Select reperfusion/management strategy (e.g., PCI, CABG) depending on factors such as symptoms, hemodynamic stability, troponin values, and risk of ischemic events (with consideration of risk scores like TIMI, GRACE)
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ NSTEMI بتتعرف على أساس ST depression أكبر من 0.5 mm أو T wave inversions أكبر من 1 mm في leads متجاورة، مع ارتفاع الـ cardiac biomarkers. و المريض عنده ألم صدر وتغييرات baseline بالـ ECG، فالـ clinician لازم يقدر يقرا التغيرات الجديدة حتى قبل ما تطلع نتيجة الـ troponin. و ظهور T wave inversion جديد في V4 و V5 بنسبة 1.5 mm يعني ischemia مستمرة ولازم ياخد cardiology evaluation و PCI محتمل.
الفخ: الخيار الغلط هو 0.25 mm ST depression في Leads V2–V5 لأن الحد المطلوب للتشخيص 0.5 mm في leads متجاورة. و ST elevation 1.5 mm في V2–V3 مش NSTEMI أصلاً، و VT المتقطع بدون أعراض بيشكل مشكلة مختلفة.

question: A 6-year-old girl presents to the ED pulseless and unresponsive. Paramedics initiated CPR and have given two shocks without effect. Intravenous access cannot be obtained and an intraosseous line is started. On arrival, the patient’s telemetry rhythm is seen above. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
englishExplanation:
Asystole is a rhythm in cardiac arrest that shows no electrical activity on an ECG. It can result from either intrinsic failure of the cardiac conduction system or be secondary to external factors such as hyperkalemia, hypothermia, hypoxia, or acidosis. The prognosis is grave for all patients with asystole, and in pediatric patients with out-of-hospital arrest, the mortality rate is 95%. The treatment in pediatric patients is standardized according to the Pediatric Advanced Life Support algorithm set forth by the AHA.

Initial management of cardiac arrest, in addition to oxygenation and chest compressions, is comprised primarily of defibrillation (for ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation only) and epinephrine. The initial defibrillation dose is 2 J/kg, followed by 4 J/kg, up to a maximum dose of 10 J/kg. Epinephrine can be given via IV or IO at 0.01 mg/kg ( 0.1 mL/kg of 1:10,000 concentration) or in patients without IV/IO access via endotracheal tube at 0.1 mg/kg (0.1 mL/kg of 1:1,000 concentration). Repeat dosing should occur every 3–5 minutes. However, these interventions may not be sufficient and a cause of asystole should also be sought since, without correction of the underlying disease process, it is unlikely that asystole will be reversed.





Epinephrine 0.1 mg/kg IO (1:10,000 concentration) (A) is the wrong dose.

Epinephrine 0.1 mg/kg IO (1:1,000 concentration) (B) is the correct concentration and dose for endotracheal tube administration, not IV/IO. Additionally, the IV/IO route is preferred when available.

Epinephrine 0.1 mL/kg IO (1:1,000 concentration) (D) is the wrong concentration.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the difference in treatment between asystole and pulseless electrical activity?

Reveal Answer:
No difference.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Epinephrine in Pediatric Advanced Life Support

There is no maximum total dose of epinephrine
Dose is 0.01 mg/kg or 0.1 mL/kg of the 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/mL) epinephrine solution given IV or IO
Repeat doses can be given every 3–5 minutes
If administration is required through the endotracheal tube, the dose is 0.1 mg/kg
After return of spontaneous circulation, epinephrine can be used as an IV drip at 0.1–1.0 mcg/kg/min, titrated to effect
Higher doses of epinephrine in the IV drip form cause hypertension, tachycardia, and excessive vasoconstriction
arabicExplanation:
ليش: البنت عمرها 6 سنين وصلت pulseless و unresponsive، و الـ telemetry بيبيّن asystole. و خوارزمية PALS بتقول إن الـ epinephrine بالـ IV أو IO هو 0.01 mg/kg، يعني 0.1 mL/kg من بتركيز 1:10,000، والجرعة تتكرر كل 3 إلى 5 دقائق. و الـ asystole ممكن تكون من hyperkalemia أو hypothermia أو hypoxia، فلازم تدوّر على السبب. و الـ defibrillation ب-dose 2 J/kg ثم 4 J/kg لحد 10 J/kg.
الفخ: الخيار الغلط هو Epinephrine 0.1 mg/kg IO لأن 0.1 mg/kg هي جرعة الـ 1:1,000 المستخدمة بالـ endotracheal tube مش بالـ IO. و 0.1 mL/kg من 1:1,000 بتبقى جرعة أكبر من 0.01 mg/kg.

question: A 72-year-old man with long-standing diabetes and chronic kidney disease presents to the ED with sudden-onset pain, pallor, and coolness of the left foot for the past 2 hours. Examination reveals diminished dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses on the left, delayed capillary refill, and decreased sensation in the toes. An ankle-brachial index is attempted. The reading on the affected side is 1.6. Which of the following best explains the measured index value?

options.text: Arterial calcification leading to noncompressible vessels
Extensive collateral circulation in the affected limb
Inability to perform the test in the setting of acute pain
Partial occlusion of the lower extremity vessels
Venous congestion masking arterial pressure changes

correctAnswer: Arterial calcification leading to noncompressible vessels
englishExplanation:
The ankle-brachial index (ABI) is a simple, noninvasive test that compares systolic blood pressure at the ankle with that at the brachial artery to evaluate lower extremity arterial perfusion. ABI ranges from 1.0 to 1.4, with values < 0.9 indicating peripheral arterial disease and values < 0.5 suggesting severe ischemia. However, in patients with diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, or advanced peripheral vascular disease, medial arterial calcification can stiffen vessel walls and lead to falsely elevated ABI values even in the presence of significant arterial occlusion, which can delay diagnosis. Toe-brachial index (TBI) measurement or pulse volume recordings can help in such cases, as digital arteries are less affected by calcification.

In the acute setting, ABI alone should not be relied upon because it may be misleading or time-consuming in unstable patients. Diagnosis should be driven by clinical features, including the classic six Ps of acute arterial occlusion (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, and poikilothermia). A careful vascular examination should include palpation of pulses, Doppler assessment, and comparison with the contralateral limb to detect asymmetry. Rapid recognition is essential to prevent irreversible ischemic injury.

Definitive confirmation is obtained through imaging, with duplex ultrasound being a rapid bedside option to assess flow and localize occlusion. CTA provides high-resolution visualization of the arterial tree and is preferred when surgical or endovascular intervention is being considered. In unstable patients or those with threatened limbs, imaging should be expedited, and treatment, such as anticoagulation, vascular surgery consultation, and possible urgent revascularization, should be initiated without delay.



Extensive collateral circulation (B) may preserve distal perfusion in chronic vessel occlusion, but it does not cause spuriously high ABI readings. ABI would usually be mildly reduced.

Pain (C) may limit cooperation but does not itself cause a falsely high ABI.

Partial vessel occlusion (D) could yield an ABI that is reduced but not severely low. However, this patient has symptoms highly suggestive of acute arterial occlusion (sudden pain, pallor, coolness, sensory loss). Noncompressible calcified arteries better explain a falsely elevated ABI in this setting than partial obstruction.

Venous congestion (E) affects some noninvasive flow measurements but has minimal impact on ABI calculations.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the dose of IV heparin in acute arterial occlusion?

Reveal Answer:
80 units/kg stat, then 18 units/kg/hr infusion.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Peripheral Artery Disease

Sx: pain in the affected extremity related to activity (intermittent claudication)
PE: cool extremity with absent or diminished pulses
Dx: ankle-brachial index (ABI) ≤ 0.9
If limb is threatened: contrast arteriography (gold standard)
Caused by atherosclerotic disease
Risk factors include smoking, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia
Tx options (depending on symptoms/severity) may include risk factor modification, supervised exercise therapy, pharmacologic therapy (e.g., cilostazol), revascularization (for limb-threatening ischemia)
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ ankle-brachial index يقارن ضغط الـ systolic عند الكاحل مع ضغط الـ brachial artery، والطبيعي منه بين 1.0 و1.4، وأقل من 0.9 يعني peripheral arterial disease. عند مريض diabetes mellitus أو chronic kidney disease بيصير medial arterial calcification بتقوّي جدران الـ vessels فبتخليها غير قابلة للانضغاط، وهاد بيخلي القراءة 1.6 عالية بشكل مضلل حتى لو في انقطاع شرياني كبير. عشان كذا بنقيس toe-brachial index أو pulse volume recordings لأن الـ digital arteries أقل تأثر بالـ calcification، والتشخيص لازم يعتمد على الفحص السريري والعلامات الكلاسيكية الستة.
الفخ: الخيار اللي الناس بتختاره هو partial occlusion of the lower extremity vessels لأن الرقم 1.6 سريع وبيوحي إن في Diseases وعائية، بس الـ calcification نفسه هو اللي رفع الرقم فوق الـ normal range. فرّق بين رقم مضلل وبين انسداد حقيقي بالـ clinical picture.

question: A 57-year-old man with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, and end-stage kidney disease, on dialysis via a left upper arm arteriovenous fistula, presents to the emergency department with 2 days of worsening shortness of breath, orthopnea, and lower extremity edema. Vital signs are HR 100 bpm, BP 150/90 mm Hg, RR 24/minute, and SpO2 92% on room air. He is afebrile. His extremities are warm and well perfused. Which of the following will help determine whether this patient is experiencing high-output or low-output heart failure?

options.text: Reflex bradycardia with transient fistula occlusion

correctAnswer: Reflex bradycardia with transient fistula occlusion
englishExplanation:
Heart failure is usually secondary to decreased cardiac output and high systemic vascular resistance (low-output heart failure). However, it can be due to decreased systemic vascular resistance leading to increased cardiac output and venous congestion from increased venous return to the heart (high-output heart failure). Etiologies of high-output heart failure include sepsis, hyperthyroidism, nutritional deficiencies, and arteriovenous fistulas. Symptoms of high-output heart failure have significant overlap with low-output heart failure. Both conditions will have signs and symptoms related to venous congestion, including lower extremity edema, tachypnea, dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, and pulmonary crackles, as well as jugular venous distension.

Characteristics that are unique to high-output heart failure are signs of increased cardiac output, including extremities that are warm and well-perfused, bounding pulses, and a hyperdynamic precordium, as well as any signs and symptoms associated with the etiology of the high-output heart failure. The diagnosis of high-output heart failure is clinical, based on the signs or symptoms described above. Additionally, in patients with high-output heart failure secondary to an arteriovenous fistula, transient occlusion (30 seconds) of the fistula will result in increased systemic vascular resistance, decreased cardiac output, reflex bradycardia, and raised arterial pressure. Echocardiography is useful, as it can show a dilated inferior vena cava and right ventricle suggestive of increased venous return secondary to low systemic vascular resistance. Treatment is supportive, including typical medical management of heart failure (diuretics, control of hypertension) as well as management of the etiology. A cardiology consult is indicated for consideration of right heart catheterization.



Decreased ejection fraction (EF) on echocardiography (A) indicates that < 55% of the left ventricular blood is ejected during systole and can be seen in both high- and low-output heart failure. Most patients with high-output heart failure have preserved EF. However, with persistent high-output heart failure, cardiac remodeling can result in a decreased EF. In low-output heart failure, decreased EF suggests systolic dysfunction, while preserved EF suggests diastolic filling dysfunction (restrictive cardiomyopathy, poor atrial kick).

Elevated brain natriuretic peptide (B) is secondary to hormone release from strained ventricular cells in the setting of increased ventricular filling pressures. In high-output heart failure, the right ventricle is often dilated due to increased venous return to the heart. In low-output heart failure, the left ventricle is often strained due to high systemic vascular resistance. Since elevated brain natriuretic peptide can be seen in both high- and low-output heart failure, it does not help differentiate the two.

Jugular venous distension (C) can be seen in both high- and low-output heart failure and is thus not useful for differentiation. In low-output heart failure, decreased forward movement of blood causes blood to back up through the pulmonary vasculature and then the systemic circulation, manifesting as jugular venous distention. In high-output heart failure, increased cardiac output results in increased venous return which itself can manifest with jugular venous distension.

One Step Further
Question:
What is a water hammer pulse?

Reveal Answer:
Bounding pulse with quick upstroke and downstroke.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
High-Output Cardiac Failure

High metabolic state, shunting
Risks: hyperthyroidism, AV fistulas, Paget disease, severe anemia, pregnancy
Tx: treat underlying condition
arabicExplanation:
ليش: هاد المريض عنده arteriovenous fistula، وهي من أسباب high-output heart failure لأن الـ fistula بتخلي الـ systemic vascular resistance ينزل فالـ venous return يزيد والـ cardiac output يرتفع. العلامات اللي بتميّز الحالة هي الأطراف الدافئة والحسنة التروية والـ bounding pulses والـ precordium الديناميكي. وبما إن كل الـ symptoms مشتركة مع low-output heart failure، لتأكيد التشخيص بنسد الـ fistula بشكل مؤقت حوالي 30 ثانية، وهاد بيزوّد الـ resistance ويخفّض الـ output وبيظهر reflex bradycardia.
الفخ: الخيار اللي الناس بتختاره هو decreased ejection fraction على echocardiography لأنه دايمًا associated مع heart failure. بس هاد بيتعارض مع الأطراف الدافئة والـ bounding pulses والـ precordium الديناميكي، وهذي علامات الـ high-output. الـ echo بيقدر يكون الـ ejection fraction طبيعي أو حتى مرتفع.

question: A 45-year-old man presents with chest pain. Which of the following features most strongly predicts acute coronary syndrome as the cause of his chest pain?

options.text: History of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and tobacco use

englishExplanation:
Chest pain is one of the most common presenting concerns in emergency departments. The causes of chest pain are varied and range from benign (e.g., muscle strain, costochondritis, pleurisy) to life-threatening (e.g., acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism). The emergency clinician's job is to carefully assess the patient with chest pain and rule out any life-threatening etiologies. As such, acute coronary syndrome must be considered in the differential of every patient presenting with chest pain. Acute coronary syndrome most commonly occurs when an atherosclerotic plaque is disrupted or eroded, resulting in platelet aggregation and thrombus formation at the site and diminished or absent flow within the affected vessel. Historical features are extremely important in helping categorize patients as low, moderate, or high risk for acute coronary syndrome, and performing a detailed history regarding chest pain character and associated symptoms is critical. Low-risk features include pleuritic, positional, reproducible, and sharp or stabbing pain. In addition, nonexertional pain and pain that is localized to a small inframammary area have a low likelihood of being cardiac in etiology. Some high-risk features include chest pressure (positive likelihood ratio [LR+] 1.52) and associated diaphoresis (LR+ 1.5). The highest risk features include pain similar to prior ischemic pain (LR+ 3.35), radiation to the right arm or shoulder (LR+ 2.31), radiation to both arms or shoulders (LR+ 2.58), and exertional pain (LR+ 2.81). Of the above choices, radiation to the right arm is the strongest predictor of a cardiac etiology of chest pain.



History of diabetes, hypertension, and tobacco use (A) are traditional cardiac risk factors that predict the lifetime risk of developing coronary artery disease. However, these risk factors are less helpful than historical features in predicting whether an acute presentation of chest pain is due to acute coronary syndrome. Pleuritic pain (B) is not a strong predictor of acute coronary syndrome. Pressure-like pain (C) is a high-risk feature but is less predictive of acute coronary syndrome than pain that radiates to the right arm.

One Step Further
Question:
Which groups of patients commonly have nonclassic presentations of acute coronary syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
Older patients, women, and patients with diabetes mellitus.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Chest Pain

Stable angina: chest discomfort precipitated by activity but symptoms abate after rest
Unstable angina: ischemic symptoms suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome with or without ECG changes indicative of ischemia
NSTEMI: troponin elevation, ECG typically with ST depressions
STEMI: troponin elevation, ECG shows ST segment elevation
Atypical chest pain:
Female patients, older population, those with diabetes
Nausea or vomiting
Epigastric pain
Weakness
Chest pain absent in 12.5% of MI cases
arabicExplanation:
ليش: لازم نعمل تاريخ دقيق لل pain لأن الـ acute coronary syndrome من أبداً ما تستبعد. الـ features منخفضة الخطورة زي الـ pleuritic والـ positional والـ reproducible والألم الحاد أو الطعني، وكذلك الألم غير المرتبط بالجهد أو المحصور بمساحة صغيرة تحت الثدي، كلّها بتقلل احتمال القلب. أما الـ high-risk features زي ضغط الصدر مع التعرّق فبتخلي احتمال الـ ischemia القلبية أعلى. والألم اللي بينتقل من الصدر للذراع هاد من علامات الـ myocardial ischemia، فعنده لازم تفكر بـ ACS وتعمل ECG و troponins متسلسلة.
الفخ: ناس كتير بتختار pleuritic pain لأنه بيتكلم عن ألم صدر، بس هاد من الـ low-risk features وبيميّزه إنه بيتغيّر مع التنفس والوضعية وبي reproduce عند الفحص. الـ pressure-like pain أحسن من الـ pleuritic، بس أقوى predictor هو الانتشار للذراع.

question: A 55-year-old woman with hypertension, diabetes, and obesity presents to the ED with a productive cough, dyspnea, and orthopnea. She has a T of 99.4°F (37.4°C), BP of 166/105 mm Hg, HR of 101 bpm, RR of 24/min, and SpO2 of 92% on room air, with S3 and crackles. Her chest X-ray is shown above. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Lab results are notable for a WBC count of 12,000 cells/µL, hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, and high-sensitivity troponin I of 0.2 ng/mL. Which therapy is indicated now?
englishExplanation:
The patient’s presentation is consistent with acute heart failure. Acute interventions for heart failure include nitrates, diuretics, and noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation. Therefore, furosemide is the best therapy at this time.

Heart failure is a clinical syndrome consisting of shortness of breath, exertional fatigue, and leg swelling due to diminished cardiac filling or pumping function that may be secondary to a variety of causes (e.g., myocardial infarction). Risk factors for acute heart failure include age > 65 years old, male sex, obesity, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and valvular heart disease.

There is no single historical feature, exam finding, or laboratory test that diagnoses acute heart failure with any degree of accuracy. However, the most sensitive symptom is dyspnea on exertion, and the most specific findings are orthopnea, peripheral edema, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Exam findings highly suggestive of acute heart failure include an S3 gallop, abdominojugular reflux, and jugular venous distension.

Natriuretic peptides, including B-type natriuretic peptide and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide, have high negative predictive value and are useful for ruling out heart failure when clinical uncertainty exists. Precipitants of acute heart failure include medication nonadherence, excess fluid or salt intake, kidney failure (including missed dialysis), substance abuse, poorly controlled hypertension, initiation of negative inotropes (e.g., calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers), initiation of salt-retaining medications (e.g., NSAIDs, steroids), and new antidysrhythmic medications.

Treatment of acute heart failure should be aimed at addressing oxygenation, ventilation, hemodynamics, and volume status. In the setting of hypertension, preload and afterload reduction therapy with nitrates (e.g., nitroglycerin), often followed by loop diuretics, is appropriate therapy for severe pulmonary edema.

IV furosemide should be dosed at 1–2.5 times the patient’s home oral dose, or 40–80 mg IV for diuretic-naive patients. Early administration of IV furosemide (within 60 minutes of ED arrival) has been associated with lower in-hospital mortality. Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation reduces work of breathing and improves oxygenation, with evidence supporting reduced intubation rates in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema.



Azithromycin (A) would be appropriate if pneumonia were the primary diagnosis. However, this patient’s presentation with orthopnea, S3 gallop, bilateral edema, and pulmonary edema on chest X-ray indicates heart failure as the primary process. While pneumonia may coexist as a precipitant, the immediate priority is decongestion with diuretics.

Dobutamine (B) is an inotrope indicated for cardiogenic shock with low cardiac output and hypotension. This patient is hypertensive (BP of 166/105 mm Hg), not hypotensive, making inotropic support unnecessary and potentially harmful. Inotropes are reserved for patients with evidence of hypoperfusion and low blood pressure.

Heparin (D) would be indicated if acute coronary syndrome (ACS) were suspected. While the high-sensitivity troponin I is mildly elevated (0.2 ng/mL), this is likely demand ischemia secondary to heart failure rather than primary ACS. The ECG shows only sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes, and the clinical presentation is more consistent with decompensated heart failure than acute myocardial infarction.

One Step Further
Question:
What ECG finding has the highest likelihood ratio for the diagnosis of heart failure?

Reveal Answer:
Atrial fibrillation.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Acute Decompensated Heart Failure

Sx: exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
PE: crackles, pitting edema, S3 heart sound
Labs: ↑ BNP
CXR: cardiomegaly, cephalization, Kerley B lines, effusions
Dx: ECHO (most useful study)
Tx
NIPPV: ↑ oxygenation, ↓ work of breathing, ↓ preload, afterload
Nitroglycerin: ↓ preload, afterload
Furosemide: diuresis
Hypotension without signs of shock: dobutamine (but may worsen hypotension)
Severe hypotension with signs of shock: norepinephrine (↑ systemic vascular resistance, ↑ HR, ↑ BP, ↑ myocardial oxygen demand)
arabicExplanation:
ليش: هاد المريض عنده acute heart failure واضحة، مع dyspnea و orthopnea و S3 و crackles و edema و tachycardia. لازم أول شي نسأل: هل في congestion؟ الـ orthopnea والـ peripheral edema والـ S3 gallop هي أكتر findings اختصاصية، والـ dyspnea على الجهد أكتر symptom حساسة. البنا نتعامل مع acute decompensation بnitrates و diuretics و NIPPV حسب الحاجة، وهنا furosemide هو العلاج الأنسب. وBNP وNT-proBNP عندهم قيمة تنبؤية سلبية عالية فبتساعد تستبعد الـ heart failure.
الفخ: ناس بتختار azithromycin لأن فيه cough و fever بسيطة و WBC 12,000، بس الـ S3 مع orthopnea و edema و crackles ما بتنفّس على pneumonia. وكمان dobutamine مش أول خطوة لأن ما في hypotension ولا shock، وهنا furosemide لتخفيف الـ congestion.

question: A 65-year-old man presents to the ED with shortness of breath, orthopnea, and pitting edema to the bilateral lower extremities. His ECG is shown above. What medication is he likely taking?
englishExplanation:
Digoxin is a medication made from the foxglove plant (Digitalis lanata). It works by increasing cardiac contractility and cardiac output and decreasing atrioventricular (AV) conduction, so it is useful in the treatment of patients with heart failure and atrial fibrillation. Digoxin inhibits the sodium-potassium-adenosine triphosphatase pumps, leading to increased intracellular sodium and extracellular potassium. This leads to changes in the sodium-calcium ion exchanger and a resultant increase in the amount of intracellular calcium available for stronger contractions, increasing stroke volume and cardiac output.

Digoxin effect is a commonly seen ECG finding in patients taking digoxin and is not a marker of digoxin toxicity. The digoxin effect presents as inverted or biphasic T waves, a shortened QT interval, and downsloping ST segment depression with a sagging or scooped appearance that has been referred to as a hockey stick, handlebar mustache, or Salvador Dali sign.

At usual doses, digoxin has minimal effect on electrolytes but can lead to life-threatening hyperkalemia in overdose or in patients with decreased excretion (e.g., kidney disease). High digoxin levels can produce many different dysrhythmias. Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia is not commonly seen but is highly suggestive of digoxin toxicity.

Symptoms of digoxin toxicity depend on the chronicity (acute or chronic) and include nausea, anorexia, vomiting, and changes in color vision (objects appearing yellow). Serum digoxin levels, kidney function, and electrolytes should be checked in all patients suspected of having digoxin toxicity. Definitive treatment is with digoxin-specific fragment antigen-binding antibodies.



Amiodarone (A) is a class III antidysrhythmic that is used for the treatment of ventricular and supraventricular dysrhythmias. Side effects include hypotension, bradycardia, and heart failure. ECG changes that can be seen with the use of amiodarone include bradycardia, AV block, and QT prolongation.

Diltiazem (C) is a class IV antidysrhythmic and calcium channel blocker. It works by slowing conduction through the AV node and causing a degree of suppression at the sinoatrial node. It is used to treat patients with supraventricular dysrhythmias. Diltiazem can lead to bradycardia and can lead to PR prolongation and severe bradycardia when taken in overdose.

Furosemide (D) is a loop diuretic that is often used in the treatment of congestive heart failure. Furosemide does not cause any ECG changes, but the electrolyte disturbances associated with its use may lead to ECG changes of hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalcemia. These include premature beats, junctional tachycardias, AV block, prolonged QT interval, and U waves.

Haloperidol (E) is a first-generation antipsychotic used in the treatment of various psychiatric conditions, most commonly schizophrenia, but it also has a role in the management of acute agitation and is often used in the ED for this reason. The most common ECG change seen is a prolonged QT interval, and the risk of this is higher with intravenous haloperidol versus oral.

One Step Further
Question:
What are some common plants that have cardiac glycoside properties and may cause symptoms similar to digoxin toxicity when ingested?

Reveal Answer:
Oleander, lily of the valley, and dogbane.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Digoxin Effect

Not a marker of toxicity, only indicates patient is taking digoxin
Downsloping ST depression with a characteristic slurred appearance (Salvador Dalí mustache)
Flattened, inverted, or biphasic T waves
Shortened QT interval
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريض عنده علامات classic لـ heart failure، والـ ECG اللي معروض بيحكي عن digoxin effect. الـ digoxin وDerived من نبتة foxglove، وبيرفع الـ contractility والـ cardiac output وبيقلل الـ AV conduction، فبمناسبة heart failure و atrial fibrillation. على الـ ECG بتظهر علامات معروفة اسمها digoxin effect، وهي T wave مقلوبة أو ثنائية الاتجاه، وQT interval قصير، و ST depression بشكل hockey stick أو تسمى Salvador Dali sign. وهاد الشي بيحكي إنه على الدواء، مش إنه عنده toxicity.
الفخ: الخيار اللي الناس بتختاره هو amiodarone لأنه دواء شائع لـ atrial fibrillation، بس الـ amiodarone بيعمل prolongation للـ QT، بينما digoxin effect بيقصّر الـ QT وبيعمل ST depression بشكل مقعّر. وكمان furosemide دوا heart failure بس ما بيطلع على الـ ECG.

question: Mycotic aneurysm is most commonly a complication of which of the following conditions?
englishExplanation:
The most common cause of mycotic aneurysm is septic emboli from endocarditis. Septic embolism refers to the phenomenon in which infections spread to other organs from a particular source via the bloodstream. The most common sources of septic emboli include bacterial endocarditis, septic thrombophlebitis, periodontal infections, and central venous catheter infections. High risk patients are those with chronic immunosuppression therapy, diabetes, obesity, kidney failure, malignancies, and intravenous drug use. Diagnosis of septic emboli should be considered in patients with high risk factors and with an infectious nidus presenting with septicemia. Early complications of septic emboli include ischemia from arterial occlusion. Late complications include seeding of the bacteria at the new location. For example, a mycotic aneurysm is an aneurysmal formation as a result of seeding of infection in an arterial wall. Mycotic aneurysms form over a long period of time and can thrombose. They can ultimately become a source of septic emboli themselves.



Disseminated tuberculosis (A) is not a typical source of mycotic aneurysm. Mycotic aneurysm is a misnomer since while mycotic infections are fungal in origin, the term mycotic aneurysm refers to bacterial infections. Therefore, they are not a complication of fungemia (C). While a periodontal abscess (D) can cause septic emboli, they do not typically cause mycotic aneurysms.

One Step Further
Question:
Septic emboli most commonly involve which organ system?

Reveal Answer:
Central nervous system.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Infected (Mycotic) Aneurysm

Most commonly due to Streptococcus viridans group, Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella spp
Fungal association is misnomer
True description of "mycotic aneurysm" is infected aneurysm resulting from bacterial endocarditis rather than infection of atherosclerotic vessels, infection of existing aneurysm, or post-traumatic infected pseudoaneurysm
Most often occurs at vessel bifurcations
Risks: endocarditis, advanced age, immunocompromised, trauma
Sx: painful, palpable, pulsatile mass with signs of infection (fever); back or abdominal pain if aorta involved
Dx: CTA
Tx: antibiotics, surgery vs endovascular treatment based on surgical risks
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ mycotic aneurysm بيصير لما البكتيريا تتزرع بجدار الـ artery وبيعملوا انتفاخ فيها، وبيجي غالباً من septic emboli مصدرها endocarditis. الـ endocarditis هو أكثر مصدر للـ septic emboli، مع septic thrombophlebitis و infections الـ periodontal و infections الكاتتر الوريدي المركزي. واسم الـ mycotic مضلل، لأن الـ mycotic infections ممكن تكون فطرية بس المصطلح هاد يعني infections بكتيرية. والمريض اللي عنده عوامل خطر زي immunosuppression و diabetes و obesity و kidney failure و malignancy و IV drug use لازم تفكر فيه.
الفخ: ناس بتختار fungemia لأن كلمة mycotic بتوحي بفطر، بس الـ mycotic aneurysm بالمصطلح هذا يعني بكتير وليس فطر، والـ fungemia مش مصدر شائع لهاد. وكمان periodontal abscess ممكن يسبب septic emboli، بس ما هو السبب المعتاد للـ mycotic aneurysm.

question: A 60-year-old man presents to the ED with chest pain. He has a medical history significant for coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus. He has had exertional chest pain that resolves with rest for the past 3 days. His pain today started 30 minutes ago while at rest and has been unrelenting. The patient’s rhythm strip is shown above. The hospital has a cardiac catheterization lab on standby 24 hours per day. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Heparinize followed by admission for urgent cardiac catheterization
Obtain complete blood count, metabolic panel, and cardiac troponins, and admit for provocative testing

englishExplanation:
Activation and emergent cardiac catheterization is the most appropriate step for this patient. The patients presentation and ECG findings are concerning for a posterior wall ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). A posterior STEMI is characterized by ST segment depression of at least 0.5 mm in leads V1 and V2. However, depression may also be seen in other leads. Typically ST elevation is commonly seen in the inferior leads concomitantly with the ST depression in V1–V3 as the posterior wall is typically supplied by the right coronary artery (most of the time) or by the left circumflex artery. ST elevation of approximately 1 mm in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF) or 2 mm in the precordial leads is concerning for an inferior wall or anterior and lateral wall infarction, respectively. Reciprocal depression is typically noted in leads opposite to the elevation.

Clinical features that are frequently reported include chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, lightheadedness, syncope, and palpitations. Primary percutaneous coronary intervention with stenting is the first-line and preferred therapy.



Heparinizing followed by admission for urgent cardiac catheterization (B) is appropriate for the treatment of a non-ST elevated myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). NSTEMI is one of several diagnoses on the spectrum of acute coronary syndrome. Patients will present with chest pain that is thought to be cardiac in nature. Patients may have atypical symptoms such as weakness, shortness of breath, dizziness, or fatigue. Women, patients with diabetes, and older patients are more likely to present with atypical symptoms. The patient's angina is usually unstable with it occurring at rest and lasting > 20 minutes, is new in onset, or increases in frequency, duration, or intensity compared to previous angina. ECG may show nonspecific changes or be normal. The ischemia must be severe enough to cause an elevation in troponin, as this is what ultimately makes the diagnosis of NSTEMI.

Initiating intravenous alteplase (C) is a treatment option for STEMI in the appropriate clinical scenario. Current recommendations suggest this is the preferred treatment option in patients with symptom onset within 12 hours and who cannot receive primary percutaneous coronary intervention within 120 minutes of first medical contact. Initiation of fibrinolytic therapy should be < 30 minutes from the time of presentation.

Obtaining CBC, metabolic panel, and cardiac troponins, and admitting for provocative testing (D) would be an appropriate treatment plan for unstable angina. Unstable angina is also on the continuum of acute coronary syndromes. Unstable angina classically is defined as angina at rest, lasting > 20 minutes in duration, new-onset angina that limits physical activity, or there is increasing angina that is more frequent, longer in duration, or occurs with less exertion than previous angina. The ECG in unstable angina is either nonspecific or shows no changes. The key difference between acute NSTEMI and unstable angina is the presence of detectable quantities of cardiac troponins suggesting more severe ischemia with NSTEMI. Elevated troponins may not be detectable for hours and thus both of these diagnoses may be indistinguishable initially.

One Step Further
Question:
What condition presents with T wave inversions in V1–V3 after the resolution of chest pain?

Reveal Answer:
Wellens syndrome, which is indicative of a high-grade stenosis of the left anterior descending artery.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)

Patient presents with substernal chest pain that radiates to the neck and arm
Lab tests will show elevated troponin I or troponin T and CK, ST segment elevations > 1 mm in two or more contiguous leads
In anterior leads (V2 and V3), ST segment elevation should be ≥ 1.5 mm in female patients, ≥ 2.0 mm in male patients ≥ 40 years, and ≥ 2.5 mm in male patients < 40 years
Treatment
Percutaneous coronary intervention: gold standard
Thrombolytic therapy
Aspirin
P2Y12 receptor blocker
Beta-blocker
Anticoagulation
Anterior wall ST elevation in leads V1 through V4
Inferior wall ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF
Lateral wall ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V5, and V6
Posterior wall ST depressions in leads V1 through V3 and elevations in leads V8 and V9
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريض عنده ألم صدر مستمر من 30 دقيقة أثناء الراحة بعد 3 أيام من exertional pain، ومعاه تاريخ CAD، وهاد بيوحي بـ ACS. الـ rhythm strip بيحكي عن posterior wall STEMI، و hallmark الـ posterior STEMI هو ST depression لا تقل عن 0.5 mm في الـ leads V1 وV2، مع ST elevation في الـ inferior leads II و III و aVF أو في الـ precordial leads. العلاج المفضل هو primary percutaneous coronary intervention مع stenting، ولأن الـ cath lab جاهز 24 ساعة لازم تناديهم فوراً.
الفخ: الخيار اللي الناس بتختاره هو heparinize followed by admission for urgent cardiac catheterization، بس هاد الإجراء المخصص لـ NSTEMI مش لـ STEMI. وكمان alteplase مش أول خيار لأن الـ cath lab متاح 24 ساعة والـ primary PCI أفضل من الـ thrombolytics.

question: A 15-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after fainting while playing basketball. He has no symptoms on arrival and appears well. His ECG is shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Check troponin levels and give aspirin
Give reassurance and recommend primary care follow-up

englishExplanation:
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) is caused by fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium. It presents on ECG with an epsilon wave, which is a small, positive deflection at the end of the QRS complex, with a prolonged S-wave upstroke and inverted T waves. However, the epsilon wave is only present in about half of cases. This patient has all three findings. It may be discovered incidentally or can present with ventricular dysrhythmias, syncope, palpitations, and sudden cardiac death. Dysrhythmias and cardiac arrest may be precipitated by physical exertion. Patients with symptomatic ARVC (syncope) should be admitted for a cardiac MRI and an implantable defibrillator.



Checking troponin levels and giving aspirin (B) would be the appropriate care of acute coronary syndrome (ACS). This patient does not have risk factors for ACS, and his ECG is consistent with ARVC.

Prescribing metoprolol (D) can be the appropriate treatment of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which presents with palpitations, syncope, and sudden cardiac death upon exertion in younger patients. The ECG may demonstrate large voltages with deep dagger-like Q waves in the inferior and lateral leads. The diagnosis can be supported with echocardiography. By reducing cardiac contractility with beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers, left ventricular outflow tract obstruction is reduced.

Reassurance and recommending primary care follow-up (C) would be appropriate management of vasovagal syncope, which presents with a prodrome of feeling warm and flushed, possible nausea and vomiting, followed by syncope with a rapid return to baseline. Patients will not have ECG changes in this condition.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the underlying pathophysiology of torsades de pointes?

Reveal Answer:
QT prolongation.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy

Autosomal dominant inheritance (most common)
Etiology: fibrofatty replacement of right ventricle myocardium
Clinical: syncope or sudden death from dysrhythmia
Dx: ECG shows epsilon wave (positive deflection buried in the terminal QRS complex), T wave inversion V1–V3, prolonged S wave upstroke
Tx: activity restrictions, beta-blockers to prevent dysrhythmia, implantable cardiac defibrillator
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الولد فجأة اتغمى أثناء sport، والـ ECG بتاعه فيه علامات ARVC: الـ epsilon wave، وهي انحراف صغير موجب بنهاية الـ QRS complex، مع prolongation في صعود الـ S wave و T waves مقلوبة. الـ epsilon wave موجودة بنص الحالات بس هون موجودة مع كل العلامات. الـ ARVC بيطلع مع ventricular dysrhythmias وإغماء وموت قلبي مفاجئ، والـ syncope مع exertion هاد أخطر شي. عشان كده لازم يندخّل بالمستشفى لعمل cardiac MRI، والـ ICD لازم ينحط.
الفخ: ناس بتختار reassurance لأن الولد كان well وطلع من الـ ED، بس إغماء مع effort هاد هيدفع لسبب قلبي خطر. وكمان metoprolol دوا hypertrophic cardiomyopathy اللي بيظهر بـ Q wave عميقة بشكل dagger في الـ inferior leads، وهاد مش توضيحاتنا.

question: An 11-year-old girl with anorexia and depression presents to the ED in cardiopulmonary arrest. A recently filled bottle of citalopram was found empty next to her with a suicide note. The family found her having seizure-like activity before calling emergency services. On arrival, CPR is in process using bag-mask ventilation and chest compressions. She already has intraosseous access. She has no pulse. The above rhythm is found. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
englishExplanation:
Torsades de pointes is a form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that is uncommon in children. Ventricular tachycardias in children are typically caused by prior cardiac surgery, myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, or a congenital or acquired cardiac electrical dysfunction. Torsades de pointes is most commonly caused by an acquired long QT syndrome. In children, this is typically caused by medications, electrolyte abnormalities, eating disorders, and bradydysrhythmias. The list of medications that can cause acquired long QT is extensive. Higher risk and commonly used medications include ondansetron, propofol, methadone, oxytocin, antipsychotics (including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors like citalopram), fluoroquinolones, macrolides, antimalarials, and amiodarone. Patients with torsades de pointes without a pulse should be treated with immediate defibrillation. Immediate treatment should follow the most recent American Heart Association pediatric cardiac arrest algorithm. Additional treatments include intravenous or intraosseous magnesium and overdrive pacing. Intravenous magnesium is indicated in children with torsades de pointes who do not respond to cardioversion. Overdrive pacing is not commonly used in children, and isoproterenol has been used instead to increase the heart rate.



Intravenous or intraosseous magnesium (A) is shown to be highly effective in treating torsades de pointes and should be administered as soon as possible. However, the longer a patient is in an abnormal rhythm causing hemodynamic instability, the more likely the patient is to develop asystole and be more difficult to restore circulation. Therefore, the priority in this patient is defibrillation.

Synchronized cardioversion (B) is the appropriate treatment for supraventricular tachycardia, atrial flutter, or stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.

While all patients in cardiopulmonary arrest could use a secure airway through endotracheal intubation (D), the timing of appropriate intubation is debated. In this patient, the priority is cardioversion, as the longer the delay to cardioversion, the less likely the chances of restoring spontaneous circulation.

One Step Further
Question:
Which formulation of ondansetron is less likely to cause acquired long QT syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
The oral formulation has a lower risk compared to the intravenous formulation.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Torsades de Pointes

ECG: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QT prolongation and QRS complex twisting around the isoelectric line
Most commonly caused by acquired or congenital long QT interval syndrome
Treatment
Unstable: immediate defibrillation
Stable: intravenous magnesium sulfate and discontinuation of the offending drug
arabicExplanation:
ليش: البنت عندها cardiac arrest والـ rhythm اللي معروض هو torsades de pointes، وهي polymorphic ventricular tachycardia نادرة عند الأطفال. أهم سبب لها هو acquired long QT syndrome، وهاد عند الأطفال بيجي من أدوية مثل citalopram والـ SSRIs، ومن اضطراب الأملاح ومن الـ eating disorders ومن الـ bradydysrhythmias. هي بلا pulse، فالعلاج هو immediate defibrillation حسب آخر بروتوكول AHA/cardiac arrest عند الأطفال. وبعدها بتضيف IV أو IO magnesium إذا ما استجابت.
الفخ: ناس بتختار administer intraosseous magnesium لأن torsades دايماً بتُعطى magnesium، بس هاد لمن ما تستجيب الـ cardioversion. والـ synchronized cardioversion للمريض اللي عنده pulse، أما هون بلا pulse فنعمل non-synchronized defibrillation.

question: A 56-year-old woman presents to the ED with right lower extremity pain and swelling. She is diagnosed with an acute femoral vein deep vein thrombosis. Under what circumstances would placement of an inferior vena cava filter be the treatment of choice in this patient?

options.text: History of breast cancer and on chemotherapy
Previous history of deep vein thrombosis

englishExplanation:
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) are two different forms of venous thromboembolism. Traditionally, the mainstay of treatment for both DVT and PE is with anticoagulation. However, there are absolute contraindications to anticoagulation that the clinician must take into account prior to initiating treatment. Absolute contraindications to anticoagulation include active bleeding into a site that is not easily compressible, severe current bleeding, recent high bleeding risk surgery, recent major trauma, and recent intracranial, spinal, or ocular hemorrhage.

In patients with a proximal DVT (such as in this patient with a femoral vein DVT) who have absolute contraindications to anticoagulation, an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter should be considered. IVC filters are not considered first-line treatment options because they are associated with complications, including thrombosis at the filter insertion site, guidewire entrapment, hemorrhage, device fracture, and device migration. Anticoagulation should be started as soon as possible, and the filter should be removed once it is clear that the anticoagulant therapy is tolerated.



A history of breast cancer (A) and a recent transatlantic flight (E) are risk factors for DVT. In these scenarios, the patient can be started on anticoagulation if there are no other contraindications.

Factor V Leiden (C) is a thrombophilic abnormality. This is not an absolute indication for an IVC filter but may result in lifelong anticoagulation if there is a history of recurrent DVT.

Previous history of DVT (D) by itself is also not an absolute indication for IVC filter placement. However, recurrent DVT, especially with a history of thrombophilic abnormality, may result in lifelong anticoagulation therapy.

One Step Further
Question:
When is it safe to stop administering enoxaparin to a patient with deep vein thrombosis on anticoagulation with enoxaparin and warfarin?

Reveal Answer:
When the INR is > 2 for 2 consecutive days.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)

Most commonly caused by stasis, hypercoagulable state, endothelial dysfunction (Virchow triad)
Risks: smoking, immobilization, surgery, oral contraceptive use
Central line placement in upper extremity DVT
Sx: unilateral extremity edema, extremity pain, tenderness, and warmth
PE: extremity swelling and pain, may show a positive Homans sign
Dx: made by ultrasound, gold standard is venography
D-dimer used in low-risk cases
Pretest probability by modified Wells score
Tx: anticoagulation
Warfarin is contraindicated in pregnancy
arabicExplanation:
ليش: عندها DVT في الـ femoral vein يعني proximal، والعلاج الأساسي للـ DVT و PE هو anticoagulation. المشكلة إن عندها intracranial bleeding قبل 7 أيام، وهاد contraindication مطلق للـ anticoagulation، ومعها النوع التاني وهو نزيف نشط مش قابل للضغط. ليش بعد هيك بنحط inferior vena cava filter؟ لأنه يمنع الـ emboli من الوصول للرئة. الـ filter مش أول خيار لأنه بيسبّب complications، ولازم نبدأ anticoagulation أول ما نقدر ونشيل الفلتر بعدين.
الفخ: ناس بتختار history of breast cancer أو recent transatlantic flight أو factor V Leiden، وهذي كلها risk factors بتخلي المريض يستاهل anticoagulation عادي. الـ IVC filter بيختلف: بنحطه بس لما يكون في contraindication مطلق للـ anticoagulation، لأن الفلتر نفسه بيسبّب thrombosis وكسر.

question: A 5-week-old boy with a history of a congenital heart defect is brought to the ED by his parents for an episode of cyanosis, shortness of breath, and agitation. While in the triage area, the boy’s SpO2 is noted to be 83%, and he is rushed back by the triage nurse when he has a brief episode of loss of consciousness. He is placed on a 100% oxygen nonrebreathing mask. He is now responsive but agitated and cyanotic. Physical exam reveals a systolic thrill and loud systolic ejection murmur at the left mid to lower sternal border. What is the most appropriate next step?
englishExplanation:
This boy is having a “tet spell,” a common episode in children with tetralogy of Fallot. Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic congenital heart defect in infants and is characterized by a large ventricular septal defect, right ventricular outflow obstruction (due to valvular or supravalvular pulmonic stenosis), an overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy.

Physical exam may reveal a systolic thrill, loud systolic ejection murmur at the left mid to lower sternal border, a single S2 aortic ejection click, and sometimes a continuous patent ductus arteriosus murmur. Depending on the amount of pulmonary stenosis and right ventricular outflow obstruction, right to left shunting may occur, resulting in cyanosis. If shunting is from left to right, with minimal right ventricular outflow obstruction, the child may be acyanotic. Some infants with tetralogy of Fallot have cyanosis at birth, but many also have episodes of cyanosis called tet spells.

Tet spells present with cyanosis, shortness of breath, agitation, and loss of consciousness. They are initially treated with simple maneuvers to increase pulmonary blood flow by increasing preload and promoting pulmonary vasodilation and by increasing afterload to reverse the right-to-left shunting. These are accomplished by placing the child on a 100% oxygen nonrebreather mask, flexing the knees to the chest to promote venous return and increase systemic vascular resistance, and calming the child by decreasing stimulation and placing the child in the parent’s arms. If necessary, the child may be given an intravenous fluid bolus (normal saline 5–10 mL/kg) to increase preload or morphine (0.1–0.2 mg/kg SC, IV, or IM).

The next lines of treatment include administration of sodium bicarbonate (2 mEq/kg) to treat acidosis and encourage pulmonary vasodilation, propranolol (0.2 mg/kg IV) to relieve infundibular spasm, or phenylephrine (2 to 10 micrograms/kg/min) to increase systemic vascular resistance. Ketamine may also be helpful with its sedative effects and its increase in systemic vascular resistance. Rapid-sequence intubation with neuromuscular blockade may be used as a last resort.



Endotracheal intubation (A) with neuromuscular blockade is a last resort if other simpler maneuvers do not successfully reverse a tet spell.

Stimulating the child (C) is contraindicated. Rather, calming the child and reducing stimulation are recommended.

Surgical intervention (D) or placement of devices through cardiac catheterization for correction of the congenital defect is not the first-line treatment in the ED. This is done around 6 months of age.

Reveal Answer:
Transposition of the great arteries (TGA).

question: Which of the following is considered a clinical risk factor with regard to the history, ECG, age, risk factors, and troponin score and pathway?

options.text: Family history of congestive heart failure

englishExplanation:
The history, ECG, age, risk factors, and troponin (HEART) score is a risk-stratification tool designed to identify ED patients who have a low risk for a major adverse cardiac event (MACE) in the ensuing 6 weeks following the index ED visit. It was developed as a means for rapid identification of such patients among ED patients in whom acute coronary sydrome (ACS) is considered so that they may be safely discharged for outpatient follow-up. It can be quickly calculated using data obtained in a standard ED evaluation for chest pain due to suspected ACS, including features from the HEART score. Each of these categories is scored from 0–2, and the total is summed to stratify the patient’s condition as low risk, intermediate risk, or high risk for MACE within the next 6 weeks.

There are several risk factors explicitly outlined within the HEART score, including hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, diabetes, tobacco smoking, and family history of coronary artery disease. A patient with one or two of such risk factors would receive a score of 1 within the R category, while three or more risk factors or the presence of known atherosclerotic disease is given a score of 2. A total score of 0–3 confers low risk and implies candidacy for discharge and outpatient follow-up, while 7–10 suggests high risk and warrants admission for urgent or emergent coronary evaluation and intervention. Intermediate scores (4–6) suggest an indication for observation and further evaluation. The HEART pathway is a clinical decision algorithm that expands upon the HEART score by using serial troponin testing, combined with the HEART score, to further risk stratify and determine appropriate patient dispositions. In this pathway, any patient with positive serial troponin testing should be admitted for inpatient cardiology evaluation, while those with low-risk HEART scores and negative troponin testing are appropriate for discharge. However, patients with intermediate- or high-risk HEART scores may be admitted to observation or inpatient units for provocative cardiac testing such as stress testing or advanced cardiac imaging.



Smoking tobacco, not cocaine (A), is the only substance use included in the HEART score calculation.

Family history of coronary artery disease is included in the HEART score, while family history of congestive heart failure (B) is not.

Inflammatory diseases such as lupus (E) and prior myopericarditis (D) are not included in the HEART score.

Reveal Answer:

question: A 63-year-old man with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency department for evaluation of a syncopal episode. He reports that he was walking his dog 1 hour ago when he suddenly lost consciousness. He then began experiencing sharp, central chest pain that radiated to his back. He is not having any shortness of breath. Physical exam reveals a man appearing uncomfortable with clear lung sounds, a regular heart rate and rhythm, and a faintly audible diastolic murmur. He is oriented to person, place, and time and has normal findings on neurologic exam. His BP is 80/45 mm Hg, HR is 105 bpm, RR is 18/min, and SpO2 is 95%. Due to his hypotension, you perform a rapid bedside cardiac ultrasound and see the image shown above. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
englishExplanation:
This patient has an acute aortic dissection causing a large pericardial effusion and likely cardiac tamponade. The most appropriate next step in management is rapid transfusion of blood products to bridge the patient to definitive surgical management and pericardiocentesis. While it is essential to consult cardiothoracic surgery concomitantly, controlled catheter drainage with a pigtail catheter can be performed to temporize the disease process and allow time to prepare for definitive operative care.

Acute aortic dissection occurs after a violation of the aortic wall allows blood to enter and dissect between the muscle layers, forming a false lumen. Aortic dissections may be classified by the Stanford system, wherein any involvement of the ascending aorta is a type A dissection, and involvement restricted to the descending aorta is a type B dissection. A proximal dissection involving the aortic root can result in a pericardial effusion leading to cardiac tamponade and is generally fatal. Classically, dissection presents with the abrupt onset of severe, tearing pain in the chest that radiates to the back. Syncope occurs approximately 10% of the time and is more common in type A dissections. Physical exam findings can be relatively normal but may include an aortic insufficiency murmur, a pulse deficit in radial or femoral arteries, neurologic symptoms, and hypertension. Hypotension may also occur, which makes the diagnosis more likely and worsens the prognosis. CT angiography is the diagnostic imaging test of choice, but bedside ultrasound may be used to rapidly identify an associated pericardial effusion. Transesophageal echocardiography is recommended to evaluate hemodynamically unstable patients but requires intubation and sedation, which is difficult in an unstable patient and should be done in consultation with cardiothoracic surgery. Emergent operative repair by a cardiothoracic surgeon is the only definitive treatment option for a patient with an acute type A dissection, and mortality increases by 1–2% every hour following the onset of symptoms.



The patient needs immediate cardiothoracic surgery consultation rather than cardiology consultation (A) to have surgical repair of his aortic dissection. Cardiology consultation would be more appropriate for a patient with an isolated pericardial effusion that is not caused by an acute dissection.

Endotracheal intubation (C) may eventually be required in this patient in the event of cardiac arrest. However, at this time, the emergent intervention is to prevent cardiac arrest with an infusion of blood products and slow drainage of the large pericardial effusion. This patient does not have respiratory compromise at this time, and endotracheal intubation may precipitate cardiac arrest.

An esmolol drip (D) is a recommended first-line agent for blood pressure and heart rate control in acute aortic dissection but not in a hemodynamically unstable patient. Hemodynamic goals include a heart rate of 60 bpm and systolic blood pressure < 120 mm Hg to reduce shearing forces on the aortic wall.

One Step Further
Question:
What percentage of emergency department patients without aortic dissection will have a pulse deficit of > 20 mm Hg between their arms?

Reveal Answer:
Approximately 20%.

CXR: widened mediastinum

Type A: involves ascending aorta
Type B: involves only descending aorta

question: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with chest pain. Her radiograph is seen above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Aortic coarctation is a narrowing (focal or long-segment) of the proximal aorta that is congenital and occurs in 0.03% of all births. The onset of symptoms can occur at any age, from neonatal to adulthood. Newborns typically present with heart failure as the ductus arteriosus closes, necessitating immediate treatment with prostaglandin E1. Diagnosis in later life is often precipitated by findings of hypertension, headaches, or leg claudication. Physical exam may reveal a heart murmur (e.g., gallop or mitral regurgitation), diminished lower extremity pulses, or a higher upper extremity systolic pressure than in the lower extremities. Transthoracic echocardiography is the initial test of choice in all patients. However, further evaluation with CT or MRI may be required when the echocardiogram is nondiagnostic. Aortic coarctation may also be seen on plain radiographs via the “3 sign” characterized by an indentation in the aortic arch. The fourth to eighth posterior ribs may also show notching owing to dilation of the intercostal arteries. The correction of aortic coarctation consists of surgical relief, angioplasty, or stenting. Even after correction, patients require frequent monitoring for complications such as aortic aneurysm and recurrence of coarctation. Left untreated, aortic coarctation can be fatal. Common causes of death include aortic rupture, heart failure, endocarditis, and intracranial hemorrhage.



Pneumonia (B) manifests on plain radiographs with opacification of the lung fields, not seen here.

Pneumothorax (C) can be identified by the loss of lung markings past the pleural edge, often seen first in the apices but not seen on this radiograph.

Rib fractures (D) may show discontinuity of the rib line or a linear lucency perpendicular to the rib. Plain radiographs are notoriously poor for evaluating rib fractures with a sensitivity as low as 50%.

Reveal Answer:
