question: Which of the following would be seen if an emergency department switched from regular troponin to a high-sensitivity troponin assay in the workup of acute coronary syndrome?

options.text: Improved negative predictive value, improved sensitivity
Improved negative predictive value, improved specificity

correctAnswer: Improved negative predictive value, improved sensitivity
englishExplanation:
Acute coronary syndrome is a primary concern in any patient presenting with chest pain. The typical workup of acute coronary syndrome involves an ECG, complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, serial troponins, and possibly a lipid panel. The high-sensitivity troponin assay is commonly used in the workup of acute coronary syndrome. It is more sensitive and less specific than a traditional troponin and thus is better at ruling out acute coronary syndrome that results in troponin elevation. It also has an improved negative predictive value. These attributes of a high-sensitivity troponin make it a good test for rapid and cost-effective evaluation of acute coronary syndrome in the emergency department. Moreover, an elevated high-sensitivity troponin is suggestive of a higher myocardial infarction and mortality rate.



Improved negative predictive value and improved specificity (B) is not true, as there is a reduced specificity at the expense of an increased sensitivity of this test. Improved sensitivity and improved specificity (C) is not usually a plausible change, as often increasing sensitivity will naturally reduce specificity. In some instances, a diagnostic test will have a higher sensitivity and specificity, such as an MRI as compared to a noncontrast CT scan in the workup of a stroke. Reduced sensitivity and improved specificity (D) is the opposite of what would be found with the use of high-sensitivity troponins.

question: A 65-year-old man with a medical history of coronary artery disease presents with chest pain and diaphoresis. His vital signs are a T of 98.5°F (36.9°C), BP of 180/110 mm Hg, HR of 100 bpm, RR of 20/min, and SpO2 of 92% on room air. He has a preexisting left bundle branch block. Which of the following ECG findings is an indication for emergent cardiac catheterization lab activation?

options.text: Concordant ST depression ≥ 1 mm in leads V4–V6
Concordant ST elevation ≥ 1 mm in lead III
Discordant ST depression ≥ 5 mm in leads V1–V3
Discordant ST elevation ≥ 1 mm in lead V2

correctAnswer: Concordant ST elevation ≥ 1 mm in lead III
englishExplanation:
The diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction (MI) in the presence of a left bundle branch block (LBBB) is a challenge, as altered ventricular depolarization produces changes that can mimic and obscure signs of ischemia. In a typical LBBB, deep S waves in the right precordial leads (V1–V3) are accompanied by discordant ST elevation and broad upright T waves. In the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5–V6), broad R waves are associated with discordant ST depression and T wave inversions. These changes follow the rule of appropriate discordance, which dictates the ST segment and T wave should be opposite in direction to the major vector of the QRS complex.

The Sgarbossa criteria were designed to improve the diagnosis of acute MI in the presence of an LBBB and can also be applied to ventricular paced rhythms. The original criteria are as follows: 1) concordant ST elevation ≥ 1 mm in any lead with a positive QRS complex, 2) concordant ST depression ≥ 1 mm in V1, V2, or V3, and 3) excessive discordant ST elevation ≥ 5 mm in leads with a negative QRS complex. The original criteria are specific (98%) but not sensitive (52%) for the diagnosis of acute MI and have since been modified to improve diagnostic accuracy. The modified Sgarbossa criteria redefine excessive discordant ST elevation as ≥ 25% of the depth of the preceding S wave, as opposed to ≥ 5 mm. Patients meeting any of the modified Sgarbossa criteria should undergo emergent cardiac catheterization. Importantly, the modified Sgarbossa criteria are only 91% sensitive for predicting acute MI and thus should not be used to exclude the diagnosis. When there is high clinical concern but a nondiagnostic ECG, then serial ECGs, cardiac enzymes, echocardiography, and the patient’s clinical status should be evaluated collectively to determine condition management.



Concordant ST depression ≥ 1 mm in leads V4–V6 (A) is not one of the Sgarbossa criteria. Concordant ST depression is only diagnostic of acute MI if present in leads V1, V2, or V3. To have discordant ST depression ≥ 5 mm in leads V1–V3 (C), the main vector of the QRS complex would need to be positive, which is not characteristic of an LBBB. Rather, it is concordant ST depression in these leads that is suggestive of acute MI. Discordant ST elevation ≥ 1 mm in lead V2 (D) does not indicate an acute MI. According to the modified Sgarbossa criteria, excessive discordant ST elevation is defined as ≥ 25% of the depth of the preceding S wave. Since the amplitude of the S wave is unknown in this case, it is not possible to determine if the ST elevation is excessive.

One Step Further

True or false: a new left bundle branch block in a patient with chest pain is an indication for emergent cardiac catheterization lab activation.

Reveal Answer:
False.

Concordant ST depression ≥ 1 mm in V1, V2, or V3
Excessive discordant ST elevation ≥ 25% of the depth of the preceding S wave

الفخ: ناس بتختار discordant ST elevation أو discordant ST depression لأنهم بيبانوا أوضح، بس في الـ LBBB هاد هو المتوقع طبيعي حسب الـ rule of appropriate discordance. الخطر بيبدأ لما الـ ST يطلع concordant مع الـ QRS، يعني بنفس الاتجاه.

question: A 67-year-old woman presents to the ED with intermittent lightheadedness and mild shortness of breath for the past 2 weeks. Each episode lasts a few hours and resolves with no clear aggravating or alleviating factors. The latest episode has persisted for at least 3 hours. Her vital signs are HR 148 bpm, BP 122/62 mm Hg, RR 16/min, and SpO2 98% on room air. ECG is shown. What is the most appropriate management?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response. This is noted on an ECG as a rapid irregular rhythm with RR intervals that have no repetitive pattern and no discernable P waves. The atrial rate is chaotic, and the ventricular rate is limited by the refractory period of the atrioventricular node, resulting in a rate of 150–170 bpm. Cardiac output is decreased due to both the loss of coordinated atrial contractions and the increased ventricular rate. Most patients with atrial fibrillation have underlying heart disease or hypertension. However, it can occur in the absence of heart disease or be due to noncardiac diseases such as hyperthyroidism.

Treatment of rapid atrial fibrillation is dependent on the patient’s hemodynamic stability and the duration of symptoms. This patient has likely been having paroxysmal rapid atrial fibrillation, as indicated by her intermittent symptoms over the preceding 2 weeks. Given this and her hemodynamic stability, rate control with a nodal blocking agent such as diltiazem or metoprolol is the initial treatment of choice.



Adenosine (A) is the pharmacologic treatment of choice for supraventricular tachycardia (also known as atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia [AVNRT]). The onset and resolution of AVNRT are typically abrupt. It occurs as a result of a reentry circuit within the atrioventricular node and presents with regular narrow-complex tachycardia at rates of 120–220 bpm.

Defibrillation (B) is indicated in cases of ventricular tachycardia without a pulse or ventricular fibrillation. Decreasing the length of time from arrest to defibrillation improves the chance of successful return of spontaneous circulation.

Synchronized cardioversion (D) is the treatment of choice for unstable tachydysrhythmias. It can also be used in hemodynamically stable patients with rapid atrial fibrillation who present with symptoms lasting < 48 hours. Atrial fibrillation that has been present for longer than that carries a risk of development of left atrial thrombi, which can become embolic with cardioversion.

One Step Further
Question:
When are nodal-blocking agents (e.g., diltiazem) contraindicated for rate control?

Reveal Answer:
In the setting of antidromic accessory pathway conduction, such as with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

Most common sustained dysrhythmia in adults

ECG: notable feature: no defined P waves
Labs: CBC, BMP, TSH, and free T4 (especially for first Afib)
Tx

Stable:
Acute: rate control (e.g., diltiazem, metoprolol)
Evaluate for long-term anticoagulation
Consider early rhythm control (within 1 year of diagnosis) in certain patients based on individualized factors (e.g., heart failure, symptoms)

Determine the need for anticoagulation by using CHA2DS2-VASc score

ليش: الـ ECG بيحكي عن atrial fibrillation مع rapid ventricular response، يعني إيقاع سريع غير منتظم ما في P waves واضحة. الـ atrial rate فوضوي والـ ventricular rate محدود بالـ refractory period للـ AV node فبيوصل 150 لـ 170 bpm، ومع loss of coordinated atrial contractions الـ cardiac output بينقص. ولأن symptoms بتتقطع على أسبوعين، هالمريضة عندها paroxysmal rapid AF وهي hemodynamically stable. فـ rate control بعقار بيعمل block للـ node مثل diltiazem أو metoprolol هو أول خيار، وبعدين بنقرر cardioversion حسب المدة.
الفخ: ناس بتختار adenosine لأنه دواء سريع بتهدّئ الـ tachycardia، بس adenosine للـ SVT أي AVNRT، وهاد إيقاع منتظم ببداية مفاجئة، بينما هون الإيقاع غير منتظم بدون P waves. والـ cardioversion الحل لو فيه hemodynamic instability، وهالمريضة مستقرة.

question: A 76-year-old man presents with weakness and dyspnea on exertion. His ECG is shown above. The patient’s blood pressure is 80/35 mm Hg. What management is indicated?
englishExplanation:
The patient presents with third degree heart block and requires placement of a transvenous pacemaker while awaiting placement of a permanent pacemaker. Third degree heart block or complete heart block is characterized by the absence of atrial impulse conduction. This is accompanied by a slow escape rhythm. If the escape rhythm is generated from above the bundle of His, the resulting QRS is narrow, and if it originates from below the bundle of His, it will be wide. The hallmark finding is atrioventricular dissociation or the absence of an electrocardiographic relationship between the atrial and ventricular activity. Treatment typically requires the placement of a pacemaker. Initially, transcutaneous pacing can be initiated, but a transvenous pacemaker should be placed as soon as possible.



Cardiology follow-up (A) can be arranged for patients with first degree and second degree type I heart blocks, which do not require emergent management. Intravenous fluids (B) are not indicated in this patient. Intravenous thrombolytics (C) are the treatment of choice for ST segment elevation myocardial infarction when percutaneous coronary intervention is not readily available.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
Lyme disease.

Rhythm will be

Notable feature: the independent beating of the atria and ventricles
Treatment
Asymptomatic: admission for cardiology evaluation
Symptomatic: atropine, isoproterenol, epinephrine, transcutaneous or transvenous pacing
Permanent: pacemaker
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ ECG بيحكي عن third degree heart block يعني complete heart block، وهاد مع hypotension شديد وضعف و dyspnea عند المجهود يعني حالة طارئة. hallmark الـ block ده هو atrioventricular dissociation يعني ما في أي علاقة بين الـ atrial activity والـ ventricular activity، وبيظهر معاه escape rhythm بطيء. العلاج الأساسي هون هو الـ pacemaker، وبما إن الـ BP عنده 80/35 بنبدأ transcutaneous pacing لو لازم وبنحط transvenous pacemaker بأسرع وقت ممكن لحين تجهيز permanent pacemaker.
الفخ: ناس بتختار cardiology follow-up لأن الـ first degree block بيحتاج متابعة بس، وهون في AV dissociation مع hypotension شديد. والـ IV fluids والـ thrombolytics ما بيعالجوا المشكلة لأن المشكلة في الـ electrical conduction وهون الحل هو الـ pacemaker.

question: A healthy 21-year-old man presents to the ED after a syncopal episode. The patient was walking to class when he felt a short duration of palpitations and syncopized. He reports previous episodes of palpitations that self-resolved and he has never sought medical attention for these symptoms. He is well appearing on exam with a normal cardiopulmonary exam and normal range vital signs. His triage ECG is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
englishExplanation:
This clinical scenario and ECG are consistent with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. This syndrome is most commonly seen in young (20–29-year-old) male patients. It is caused by an aberrant atrioventricular cardiac pathway that allows pre-excitation and bypass of the atrioventricular (AV) node. Bypass of the AV node allows faster propagation of electrical impulses and increases the risk of severe dysrhythmias. The diagnosis is made by ECG, with pathognomonic findings of a delta wave, a slurred upstroke of the QRS caused by depolarization from the accessory pathway, as well as a shortened PR interval.

The most common associated dysrhythmia is AV nodal reentrant tachycardia and these patients often present for palpitations or syncope. Patients with associated tachydysrhythmias require acute treatment in the ED (e.g., cardioversion for hemodynamically unstable patients; vagal maneuvers, adenosine, or procainamide for hemodynamically stable patients). The patient above, with delta waves and shortened PR interval but normal vital signs and mentation, would not require emergent treatment. Definitive treatment is utilized to prevent sudden cardiac arrest and symptomatic dysrhythmias and includes catheter-directed ablation or antidysrhythmics such as amiodarone if ablation is not an option.



Brugada syndrome (A) could present with a similar presentation, but ECG findings would show the saddle-back deformity or the coved-type ST segment in the anterior leads. This is due to a sodium channelopathy and is treated with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (B) can present with syncope in young adults but typically occurs with exertion. ECG findings would show left ventricular hypertrophy, left axis deviation, atrial enlargement, and abnormal Q waves.

Orthostatic syncope (C) would occur shortly after standing, typically without palpitations or ECG findings, and can be caused by dehydration, certain drugs, or autonomic instability.

One Step Further
Question:
What nonpharmacologic measures can be attempted to terminate supraventricular tachycardia?

Reveal Answer:
Vagal maneuvers such as forced expiration, Valsalva, cold water application, or carotid massage.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) Syndrome

Most commonly caused by an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) connecting atria to ventricles, bypassing AV node
ECG will show short PR interval, delta wave, wide QRS
Acute treatment
Orthodromic (narrow complex): vagal maneuvers, AV nodal blockers (adenosine, beta-blocker, calcium channel blocker)
Antidromic (wide complex): procainamide
Synchronized cardioversion for hemodynamically unstable patients
Definitive treatment is radiofrequency ablation
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الولد عنده syncope بعد palpitations وعمره 21 سنة، وهاد نمط كلاسيكي لpatient WPW. الـ ECG عنده فيه delta wave مع slurred upstroke للـ QRS complex و PR interval قصير، وهذي علامات pathognomonic للتشخيص. السبب مسار cardiac accessory بيشيل الـ AV node من الدائرة، فالـ electrical impulse بيوصل أسرع وبيزود خطر الـ dysrhythmias الخطيرة، وأكثرها شيوعاً AV nodal reentrant tachycardia. ولأنه hemodynamically stable و بدون symptoms حالياً مش محتاج تدخل عاجل، والعلاج النهائي catheter ablation أو amiodarone.
الفخ: ناس بتختار Brugada syndrome لأن عنده syncope وهو شاب، بس الـ Brugada بيطلع على الـ ECG كـ pseudo right bundle branch block مع ST elevation بنمط coved أو saddleback في V1-V3، بدون delta wave ولا PR قصير.

question: A 23-year-old man is admitted for a femur fracture. An admission ECG is shown above. What management is indicated?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s ECG shows a first-degree atrioventricular (AV) block, a normal variant finding in 2% of the population that requires no specific management. First-degree AV block is defined as prolonged conduction of atrial impulses. The PR interval is > 0.20 seconds (200 msec) and there is no loss of any atrial impulse. All impulses result in a ventricular response. Although it can be a normal variant, it can be seen in pathologic conditions like Lyme disease and should be followed up. However, no specific management is needed. Nodal depressing agents should be avoided or used with caution.



Atropine (A) is required for patients with symptomatic bradycardia.

Beta-blockers (B) are AV nodal blockers and should be used with caution in patients with first-degree AV blocks.

Transvenous pacing (D) is required for higher-degree AV blocks (second-degree type II and third-degree heart block).

One Step Further
Question:
How does carotid massage affect second-degree type I and type II heart blocks?

Reveal Answer:
Carotid massage will typically worsen second-degree type I block and improve second-degree type II block.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
First‐Degree Heart Block

Delayed AV node conduction
Associated with aging, digitalis, ischemia, inflammation, cardiomyopathies
Rhythm will be regular
PR interval will be > 0.20 s (200 msec) and constant
No specific treatment
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ ECG بيحكي عن first degree atrioventricular block، وهاد variant طبيعي عند حوالي 2% من الناس وما بيحتاج treatment محدد. التعريف إن الـ PR interval أكبر من 0.20 ثانية، بس ما في ولا atrial impulse ضايعة، وكل الـ impulses بتوصل للـ ventricle. فالمريض مستقر بدون symptoms، فالقرار reassurance مع متابعة، خاصة إذا بدك تفحص Lyme disease. بس لازم تتجنب nodal blocking agents لأنها بتزيد تأخير الـ AV node.
الفخ: ناس بتختار atropine أو transvenous pacing، بس هون الـ PR ثابت وما في ولا impulse ضايعة والمريض ما عنده bradycardia ولا symptoms. والـ transvenous pacing مخصص للـ second degree type II والثالث، والـ beta-blocker بيعمل block إضافي للـ node وهاد مش المطلوب.

question: A 65-year-old man with a history of hypertension and tobacco use presents to the emergency department for evaluation of dark stools. He reports that he has been having frequent dark, tarry stools for the last 24 hours. On arrival, he had a large, dark maroon, liquid stool. He has a history of abdominal aorta surgery but does not recall exactly what surgery he had. Physical exam reveals an ill-appearing, pale person with a well-healed midline surgical scar on the abdomen but no tenderness to palpation. His initial BP is 65/30 mm Hg, HR is 115 bpm, and T is 98.9°F (37.2°C). After a rapid transfusion of one unit of uncross-matched blood, the patient’s BP is 95/55 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Transfusion of a second unit of uncross-matched blood

englishExplanation:
This patient is experiencing life-threatening GI bleeding due to an aortoenteric fistula (AEF). He needs emergent vascular surgery consultation to repair the underlying cause of his bleeding, which is due to an abnormal connection between his previously repaired aortic aneurysm and the GI tract. AEFs can occur as a rare complication of prior aortic surgery, aortic aneurysms, postinfectious aortitis, trauma, and tumor invasion. This patient’s prior abdominal surgery and midline surgical scar indicate that he has had prior surgical repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). The third and fourth portions of the duodenum are the most common sites of AEFs. An AEF occurs in < 1.5% of patients with a prior endovascular repair or aortoiliac surgery. However, the incidence may be underestimated due to the high mortality rate associated with delayed or undiagnosed bleeds. Patients will often have a mild sentinel hemorrhage followed by massive hemorrhage with rapid exsanguination.

Approximately half of patients will have associated abdominal or back pain. If a patient has an unrepaired AAA, they may have a palpable pulsatile mass at any point in the midline abdomen. The classic triad of GI bleeding, abdominal pain, and a pulsatile abdominal mass occurs in < 15% of patients. To further complicate matters, the absence of bleeding does not exclude the presence of an AEF. Patients with a known AAA (repaired or unrepaired) presenting with massive bleeding and hemodynamic instability should be taken directly to the operating room for definitive diagnosis and repair. Bedside ultrasound may identify the presence of a AAA but will not identify an AEF. In hemodynamically stable patients, CT angiography is the noninvasive imaging modality of choice. Extravasation of contrast into the bowel lumen, ectopic gas adjacent to or within the aorta, focal bowel wall thickening, and discontinuity of the aortic wall are all CT findings that strongly correlate with the presence of an AEF. Additionally, any evidence of perigraft infection on CT should raise concern for the presence of an AEF. The mortality of an unrecognized fistula is 100%, while the mortality of a recognized fistula is 30%.



Abdominal ultrasound (A) is the appropriate imaging modality for surveillance of AAAs, but it is not the appropriate test for a patient with hypotension and GI bleeding due to an AEF. CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis is the preferred imaging study in a hemodynamically stable patient in whom the diagnosis of AEF is suspected. GI consultation (B) is typically appropriate in a patient with acute GI bleeding requiring a transfusion of blood products. However, in the case of a suspected AEF, vascular surgery consultation is more appropriate since they will be able to definitively manage the source of the patient’s bleeding. If an endoscopy were to be performed on a patient with a secondary AEF, aortic graft material may be seen protruding into the bowel lumen. The patient will likely require ongoing transfusion of blood products (C), but allowing for permissive hypotension, the patient is more stable with a systolic blood pressure > 80 mm Hg, and the priority at this point should be definitively managing the source of the bleeding. Given the risk for rapid loss of a large volume of blood, the patient may ultimately need a massive transfusion of blood products that should be readily available in the case of worsening hemodynamic status.

One Step Further
Question:
What sexually transmitted infection may be associated with postinfectious aortitis?

Reveal Answer:
Syphilis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Aortoenteric Fistula

Abnormal connection between aorta and GI tract
History of AAA, aortic repair, aortic graft replacement
Presents with rectal bleeding
PE: signs of shock, sepsis
Management includes blood transfusion or resuscitation and emergent surgical consultation
arabicExplanation:
ليش: Duk dar أسود tarry وبعدها large maroon liquid stool، ومعها hypotension وتسارع قلب، ومن عنده scar على الـ abdomen من عملية سابقة على الـ abdominal aorta. الـ aortoenteric fistula هي اتصال غير طبيعي بين الـ repaired aortic aneurysm والـ GI tract، وأشهر مكان فيها هو الـ third و fourth portions من الـ duodenum. غالباً بتبان كـ sentinel hemorrhage خفيف وبعدها نزيف هائل بزحيف. ولأن السبب ميكانيكي لازم يتصلح، بنطلب vascular surgery طوارئ ونكمّل transfusion والتقييم.
الفخ: ناس بتختار transfusion of a second unit of uncross-matched blood لأنها بتبي تحسّن الـ BP بسرعة، بس الـ transfusion دعم بس والسبب لازم يتصلح جراحياً. والـ abdominal ultrasound والـ GI consultation بيأخروا الوقت؛ الـ GI bleed مع aortoenteric fistula مش من الـ GI tract.

question: A 78 year-old-woman with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of shortness of breath. Four days earlier, she reported an episode of heartburn and nausea. On physical examination, she is tachycardic and hypotensive. She has inspiratory rales and a holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex with radiation to the left axilla. Her ECG reveals Q waves in II, III, and aVF. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Papillary muscle rupture is one of three catastrophic complications of acute myocardial infarction along with left ventricular wall rupture and interventricular septum rupture. It tends to occur several days following myocardial infarction. Papillary muscle rupture results in acute mitral regurgitation, pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock. Mitral regurgitation is recognized on physical exam by a new holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex with radiation to the left axilla. The only blood supply of the posteromedial papillary muscle comes from the posterior descending artery. Occlusion of this artery results in an inferior myocardial infarction (MI) pattern on ECG. This patient had symptoms of an MI 4 days ago and now has Q waves on ECG which are consistent with old inferior wall MI. Emergent surgical intervention is often necessary, with mitral valve repair or valve replacement along with percutaneous revascularization.



Aortic stenosis (A)presents on physical exam with a systolic ejection murmur heard best at the right second intercostal space with radiation to the carotids. Undiagnosed aortic stenosis is often discovered following a syncopal episode.

Cardiac tamponade (B)may present on physical exam as decreased or “muffled” heart sounds, jugular venous distension and hypotension. Low QRS voltage, tachycardia or electrical alternans may be seen on ECG.

Mitral valve prolapse (C) is often asymptomatic and is associated with a mid-systolic click heard best at the apex.

One Step Further
Question:
What is Beck triad?

Reveal Answer:
Muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distension, and hypotension.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Mitral Regurgitation

History
Acute: ischemic heart disease, endocarditis, MI, trauma
Chronic: rheumatic heart disease, degenerative mitral valve disease
Presentation
Acute Sx: dyspnea, pulmonary edema, cardiogenic edema
Chronic Sx: asymptomatic until CHF onset, S3
PE
Acute: unique, harsh, midsystolic murmur best heard at apex that radiates to the base or axilla
Chronic: blowing holosystolic murmur best heard at apex with radiation to axilla
Dx
Echocardiogram
Tx
Acute: nitroprusside, dobutamine, intra-aortic balloon pump, emergency surgery
Chronic: CHF Rx, valve repair or replacement
arabicExplanation:
ليش: قبل أربع أيام كان عنده episode لـ MI، والآن طلع عليه sudden dyspnea مع tachycardia و hypotension و holosystolic murmur at the apex بيطلع للـ left axilla، ومعه Q waves في II و III و aVF. هاد نمط inferior MI قديم. الـ posteromedial papillary muscle عندها مصدر واحد بس وهو الـ posterior descending artery، فسكوتها بتبطل تغذيتها وبتقطع فجأة وبتسبب acute mitral regurgitation مع pulmonary edema و cardiogenic shock. الـ papillary muscle rupture من complications الكارثية للـ acute MI بعد عدة أيام، وبيحتاج تدخل جراحي عاجل.
الفخ: ناس بتختار cardiac tamponade لأن في hypotension بعد MI، بس الـ tamponade بيبان ب decreased heart sounds و JVD و low QRS voltage، ومفيش murmur جديد. والـ aortic stenosis بيبان كـ systolic ejection murmur عند الـ right second intercostal space بيطلع للـ carotids، مو holosystolic.

question: A 70-year-old man with a medical history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation presents with left leg pain that started acutely 2 hours prior to arrival with no preceding trauma. His vital signs are unremarkable. On physical exam, the left lower extremity is cool to the touch, and there are no palpable posterior tibial or dorsalis pedis pulses. Strength and sensory exams are intact, and there is no swelling or focal tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient, who presents with acute onset of extremity pain, absent pulses, and a history of atrial fibrillation, most likely has an acute arterial occlusion due to an embolic event. Acute arterial occlusion results in an abrupt decrease in blood flow to an extremity and may result in acute limb ischemia and tissue loss. The most common cause is thrombosis at the site of an atherosclerotic plaque followed by embolic occlusion. Most emboli originate from the heart, with atrial fibrillation being the most common risk factor. Other etiologies include arterial dissection (spontaneous, iatrogenic, or traumatic), thrombosis of a peripheral arterial aneurysm, and vasospasm. Patient presentation varies based on the etiology and the presence of underlying peripheral arterial disease (PAD). Patients with preexisting PAD often have collateral circulation, allowing for residual perfusion to the extremity despite thrombotic occlusion. Symptoms may progress over hours to days and often include new or worsening claudication. Pain at rest in a patient with prior exertional symptoms is concerning for irreversible ischemia. Patients with an embolic etiology, especially if there is no preexisting vascular disease, present more dramatically with acute onset of severe pain and rapidly progressing symptoms. The signs and symptoms of acute limb ischemia can be remembered by the six Ps mnemonic: pain, pallor, poikilothermia, pulselessness, paresthesias, and paralysis. Pain is usually the first symptom, whereas sensory and motor changes are late findings indicative of limb-threatening ischemia. Patients with a thrombotic cause often have signs of PAD, including decreased or absent pulses on the contralateral limb, hair loss, and shiny skin. The lack of these findings suggests an embolic occlusion.

Acute arterial occlusion is a limb-threatening surgical emergency. All patients should be started on heparin, and vascular surgery should be consulted. Patients with limb-threatening ischemia (sensory or motor changes), regardless of the etiology, and all patients with suspected embolisms require emergent revascularization. Diagnostic imaging should not delay definitive management. The vascular surgeon will determine treatment, which may include catheter or open embolectomy, catheter-directed thrombolysis, angioplasty or stenting, and bypass grafting. If the diagnosis or etiology (thrombotic versus embolic) is unclear and there are no findings of limb-threatening ischemia, arterial ultrasound, CT angiography, or conventional angiography can help further evaluate the arterial anatomy prior to intervention. Thrombotic occlusion that is not acutely limb-threatening is often managed medically.



Compartment syndrome (B) can result in limb ischemia, as elevated compartment pressures cause decreased arterial flow. Patients with acute arterial occlusion can also develop compartment syndrome due to muscle breakdown and reperfusion injury. However, patients with primary compartment syndrome usually have significant extremity swelling and pain with muscle palpation and passive stretch. Deep vein thrombosis (C) rarely causes limb ischemia except in cases of extensive disease when venous pressures are high enough to cause decreased arterial perfusion, a syndrome known as phlegmasia cerulea dolens. Patients with phlegmasia cerulea dolens have marked asymmetric edema and mottling due to venous congestion, which is not present in this patient. Peripheral neuropathy (D) can cause extremity pain and mimic findings of chronic limb ischemia. However, it is less likely to start acutely, and unless there is underlying PAD, it should not present with pulselessness.

One Step Further
Question:
What does an ankle-brachial index > 1.4 indicate?

Reveal Answer:
Vascular calcification.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Wellens Syndrome

Highly specific for critical stenosis of the left anterior descending artery
ECG: deeply inverted or biphasic T waves in V2–3
May be pain-free
Normal or minimally elevated troponin
Tx: urgent percutaneous coronary intervention
arabicExplanation:
ليش: ألم مفاجئ في الرجل من ساعتين بدون أي trauma، مع رجل باردة وبلا posterior tibial ولا dorsalis pedis pulses، ومعه تاريخ atrial fibrillation. الـ AF أهم risk factor للـ emboli اللي بتنزل من القلب، وهاد بيسبّب acute arterial occlusion وقصور دم مفاجئ بالطرف. ولأنه ما عنده PAD سابق، ما عنده collateral circulation، فالعرض بيكون مفاجئ ودراماتيكي. الـ six Ps بتجمع العلامات: pain و pallor و pulselessness و paresthesia و paralysis و poikilothermia.
الفخ: ناس بتختار compartment syndrome لأن الطرف بيتألم، بس الـ compartment syndrome بيكون الـ compartment مشدود وبيوجع مع الـ passive stretch بعد trauma أو fracture، والطرف بيكون دافئ. والـ DVT بتدي تورّم ودفء مع نبضات سليمة، وهون الطرف بارد والنبضات غائبة.

question: A 22-year-old man presents to the ED with an expansive mood, increased energy, and aggression. His blood pressure is 177/118 mm Hg, heart rate is 110 bpm, and respiratory rate is 24/min. Physical exam shows hyperhidrosis and mydriasis. The patient is calmer after administration of benzodiazepines, but his blood pressure remains significantly elevated. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient’s hypertension?
englishExplanation:
Cocaine is a sympathomimetic that leads to symptoms of increased energy, aggression, tachycardia, hypertension, tremulousness, hyperhidrosis, and mydriasis. Typically, the management of cocaine intoxication involves observation, supportive therapy, and sedation, which can include the administration of benzodiazepines.

In patients presenting with hypertension, management can include blood pressure control, which typically requires administration of an alpha-blocker rather than a beta-blocker, secondary to the theoretical concern of precipitating a hypertensive crisis with the administration of a beta-blocker. Alpha-blocking medications include drugs such as phentolamine, which can be used as initial treatment of hypertension in these patients.



Hydralazine (A) can be used to treat hypertension, but it also carries the risk of causing a reflex tachycardia, which can be detrimental in those with cocaine intoxication. Hydralazine works as a direct-acting vasodilator that preferentially relaxes the smooth muscles of arteries, which can lead to a precipitous drop in blood pressure and tachycardia. Thus, it is not a preferred agent in this situation. Furthermore, hydralazine has a delayed and unpredictable blood pressure-lowering effect, and it can be difficult to titrate.

Nitroprusside (B) is a potent medication (also acting via nitric oxide) for lowering blood pressure. However, it carries a risk of causing a significant reflex tachycardia. It is typically administered after administration of a beta-blocker for this reason (though not in cocaine intoxication for the aforementioned reason).

Sodium bicarbonate (D) does not have any effect on blood pressure but is recommended in patients with QRS prolongation associated with cocaine intoxication.

One Step Further
Question:
What toxicity is associated with high doses of nitroprusside?

Reveal Answer:
Cyanide toxicity.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Sympathomimetic Toxidrome

Cocaine, amphetamines, stimulants: may be mixed with other agents
PE: hypertension, tachypnea, tachycardia, mydriasis, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, altered mental status, increased bowel sounds (anticholinergic toxicity is decreased bowel sounds)
Supportive care, benzodiazepines
Consider phentolamine for uncontrolled hypertension
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الولد عنده mood expansive و increased energy و aggression، ومعه hypertension و tachycardia و hyperhidrosis و mydriasis، وهاد كله stimulant effect متوقع من الـ cocaine. الـ cocaine sympathomimetic فبيحكّي على الـ hypertension مع tachycardia. بعد الـ benzodiazepines صار أهدأ بس الـ BP لسّا 177/118، فباقي لازم دوا للضغط. وبيستعمل alpha-blocker مثل phentolamine كأول خط لأن الـ beta-blocker خايف بيسبّب hypertensive crisis.
الفخ: ناس بتختار hydralazine لأنه vasodilator قوي، بس بيعمل reflex tachycardia وهاد ضار في cocaine intoxication، وبيسبب هبوط مفاجئ وغير متوقع في الـ BP. والـ beta-blocker بعد كمان مش الخيار، والـ answer هو الـ alpha-blocker.

question: A 16-year old boy presents to the emergency department after passing out. He collapsed without warning while sitting in class at school. A friend prevented him from hitting his head. There were no shaking movements or postictal period to suggest a seizure. He has had no ill symptoms but did feel palpitations and chest pain prior to his collapse. He reports plenty of intake during the day and has normal orthostatic vital signs. His father died unexpectedly in his sleep. His ECG is above. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Activity restrictions and outpatient cardiology follow-up
Outpatient Holter monitor placed in the ED

englishExplanation:
Brugada syndrome is usually caused by an autosomal dominant cardiac sodium channel disorder that can cause spontaneous ventricular fibrillation or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in otherwise well patients. It is more common in men and usually diagnosed in adulthood. Dysrhythmias from Brugada syndrome generally occur at night and these patients commonly have a pattern of nocturnal agonal respiration thought to be aborted cardiac dysrhythmias.

Cardiac dysrhythmia in patients with Brugada syndrome can be triggered by a fever, cocaine abuse, or overdose of a neuroleptic. Brugada syndrome is uncommonly diagnosed in children and many of these patients have a history of unexplained syncope.

A normal ECG does not rule out Brugada syndrome since the ECG findings can be transient. Stress testing, echocardiogram, and even cardiac MRI often reveal no abnormalities. When discovered, a Brugada ECG pattern appears as a pseudo-right bundle branch block with an ST segment elevation that descends with upward convexity into an inverted T wave (i.e., “coved type”) or ST segment elevation that begins to descend toward the baseline before rising again to an upright T-wave (i.e., “saddleback”). Symptomatic patients (e.g., syncope) with a Brugada pattern on their ECG are suspected to have a recent life-threatening cardiac dysrhythmia. As such they should be admitted to the hospital on continuous cardiac telemetry for consultation and workup by a cardiac electrophysiologist.



Activity restrictions and outpatient cardiology follow-up (A) is generally recommended for patients with syncope during exercise that have a normal ECG while in the emergency department.

An outpatient Holter monitor placed in the ED (C) is most appropriate for patients with frequent palpitations, syncope, near syncope, or dizziness, not those with suspected life-threatening dysrhythmia.

Reassurance and discharge (D) is most appropriate in patients with vasovagal syncope and a normal ECG, not for patients with Brugada syndrome.

One Step Further
Question:
Which psychiatric disorder is strongly associated with a Brugada pattern?

Reveal Answer:
Schizophrenia.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Brugada Syndrome

Autosomal dominant
Cardiac ion channel dysfunction associated with sudden cardiac arrest
Structurally normal heart
Diagnosis requires characteristic ECG and clinical findings
ECG with RBBB-like pattern
Type 1: coved ST elevation > 2 mm in ≥ 1 lead (V1–V3) followed by negative T wave (Brugada sign)
Type 2: saddleback ST elevation > 2 mm followed by upright or biphasic T wave
Type 3: coved or saddleback ST elevation < 2 mm
Type 2 and 3 changes are nondiagnostic and require further workup
Clinical
Vfib or Vtach
FH sudden cardiac death at < 45 years
Coved ST elevation in ECG of family members
Inducible Vtach
Syncope
Nocturnal agonal respiration
Treatment: ICD
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الولد فقد وعيه بدون warning، ومعه تاريخ عائلي قوي لأن أبوه مات فجأة وهو نايم. وكل علامات الـ Brugada syndrome موجودة: pseudo right bundle branch block على الـ ECG مع ST elevation بياخد شكل coved بينزل بانحناء علوي داخل T wave مقلوبة، أو شكل saddleback بينزل للـ baseline وبعدين يرجع. الـ Brugada بيحصل بسبب disorder في الـ cardiac sodium channel وبيسبب ventricular fibrillation أو polymorphic VT، وغالباً بالليل. والمريض اللي عنده syncope مع هاد الـ ECG pattern بيعتبر إنه مرّ على dysrhythmia خطير، فبيندخّل بالمستشفى على continuous telemetry.
الفخ: ناس بتختار reassurance and discharge أو outpatient Holter لأن الطفل بدا well، بس إغماء مع pattern الـ Brugada بيعني dysrhythmia خطير. والـ ECG العادي ما بيستبعد Brugada لأن الـ findings ممكن تكون مؤقتة، والـ Holter ما بيكفّي لمتابعة مريض بهاد الخطورة.

question: A 64-year-old woman presents to the ED with chest pain and dyspnea. The patient has a medical history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, and a recent diagnosis of breast cancer. She states her symptoms started abruptly 2 hours prior to arrival. She describes the chest pain as sharp, and her symptoms are worsened with deep inspiration. Vital signs are remarkable for HR 120 bpm, RR 28/min, BP 110/85 mm Hg, and SpO2 92%. Physical examination is unremarkable other than conversational dyspnea. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with T wave inversions in leads V2–V4. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Pulmonary embolism (PE) occurs when material, which is most commonly a thrombus, causes obstruction of the pulmonary trunk or one of its branches. A PE is classified into one of three categories. A massive PE, also called a hemodynamically unstable PE, results in a systolic blood pressure of < 90 mm Hg or a drop of ≥ 40 mm Hg in baseline systolic BP. Hemodynamically stable PEs are classified as submassive or low-risk. A submassive PE is defined as a PE that does not result in hypotension (or hypotension, if present, is fluid responsive) but does have right ventricular dysfunction, right ventricular dilation, elevated B-type natriuretic peptide (> 500 pg/mL), elevated troponin I (> 0.4 ng/mL), elevated troponin T (> 0.1 ng/mL), or new ECG changes (right bundle branch block, anteroseptal ST elevation or depression or anterolateral T wave inversion). A low-risk PE has no features of right heart strain and also does not have hemodynamic compromise. Risk factors for PE include coagulopathies (inherited or acquired), active cancer, recent surgery, hormonal therapies (estrogen), trauma, immobilization, and heavy cigarette smoking.

Clinical features for PE range from being asymptomatic to shock or sudden death. Most commonly, patients present with dyspnea, chest pain that can be pleuritic, cough, and features concerning for deep venous thrombosis. Hemoptysis is uncommon as is shock, dysrhythmia, or syncope. The recommended diagnostic approach for hemodynamically stable patients suspected of having a PE is to combine clinical and pretest probability assessment, D-dimer values (if appropriate), and diagnostic testing. An ECG should also be performed as part of the workup. There are no specific findings on ECG that suggest PE. However, signs of right heart strain may be present and suggest a submassive or massive PE. The classic S1Q3T3 is an ECG finding that may be present in a PE causing right heart strain. However, this pattern may be present in other causes of right heart strain such as severe pulmonary hypertension. Other ECG findings that have been shown to be more likely in patients with PE are both sinus tachycardia and T wave inversions in leads V2–V4. The pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria, or PERC, and the Wells criteria help stratify patients who are thought to be at risk for PE. Patients who are found to be low-risk and PERC-negative require no additional workup for PE. Patients who are PERC-positive but low-risk should be evaluated with the use of a D-dimer. Currently, if the D-dimer is < 500 ng/mL or less than the age-adjusted value (10 x age), then the patient requires no additional evaluation. However, if the D-dimer is greater than the thresholds noted above or the patient is moderate- or high-risk, then further evaluation with a CT angiogram of the chest or a ventilation-perfusion scan should be obtained. Patients found to be too unstable or unsafe to have advanced imaging performed should have a bedside echocardiogram and venous compression of the lower extremities to obtain a presumptive diagnosis. Treatment for PE starts with categorizing the patient into one of the three categories listed above. Patients found to be hemodynamically stable without contraindications to anticoagulation should be treated with anticoagulants as soon as possible.

Outpatient follow-up is imperative as these patients will require anticoagulation for typically 3 months but 6–12 months in specific cases. Currently, fibrinolytic therapy for submassive PE is not warranted on a routine basis but can be given on a case-by-case basis when the benefit outweighs the risk. The following situations for submassive PE may warrant the administration of fibrinolytic therapy: severe or worsening right ventricular strain, cardiopulmonary arrest due to PE with a BP > 90 mm Hg after resuscitation, extensive clot burden, or free-floating right atrial thrombus or ventricular thrombus. For patients found to be hemodynamically unstable and without contraindications to fibrinolytic therapy, the recommendation is to administer fibrinolytic therapy and then subsequently start anticoagulation. If thrombolysis is contraindicated or unsuccessful, embolectomy is an alternative therapy.



Non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (A) is on the continuum of acute coronary syndromes and resides between stable angina and ST elevation myocardial infarction. Unstable angina occurs when a patient starts experiencing angina at rest, which is usually > 20 minutes in duration, new onset of angina that markedly limits physical activity, or increasing angina that is more frequent, longer in duration, or occurs with less exertion than previous angina. Unstable angina and acute non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) differ primarily in whether the ischemia is severe enough to cause sufficient myocardial damage to release detectable quantities of a marker of myocardial injury measured with cardiac troponins. The ECG may be normal or have nonspecific findings.

ST elevation myocardial infarction (C) is characterized by ST segment elevation defined as approximately 1 mm in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF), 2 mm in the precordial leads, or 0.5 mm depression in leads V1 and V2 for a posterior MI. Reciprocal depression is typically noted in leads opposite to the elevation. Chest pain is the main symptom. However, atypical symptoms such as shortness of breath, weakness, lightheadedness, syncope, and palpitations are also frequently reported. Primary percutaneous coronary intervention with stenting is the first-line and preferred therapy. In this case, the ECG is not demonstrating changes consistent with an ST elevation myocardial infarction.

Wellens syndrome (D) represents a high-grade stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery. Its natural progression often leads to anterior wall myocardial infarction. Patients present classically with chest pain or pressure that resolves on its own before or during initial evaluation, or after the patient receives nitroglycerin or pain medications. The initial ECG may not demonstrate the classic finding as it will most often become evident when the patient becomes pain-free. Classically, Wellens sign is described as biphasic T wave inversion or deep symmetric T waves in leads V2–V4. ECG will be without Q waves, significant ST segment elevation, and normal precordial R wave progression. Cardiac enzymes are normal or minimally elevated. Medical management alone is not enough to stop the natural progression. Understanding and recognizing Wellens syndrome is of paramount importance as ST elevation may not be present and cardiac enzymes may also be negative. If a patient is diagnosed with unstable angina and subjected to a stress test for further cardiac evaluation, the patient may have sudden decompensation due to complete LAD occlusion and demonstrate an anterior ST elevated myocardial infarction. Treatment of patients with Wellens syndrome includes aspirin therapy, heparinization, and urgent cardiac catheterization to evaluate the need for angioplasty or coronary artery bypass surgery.

One Step Further
Question:
When is fibrinolytic therapy recommended for patients with a ST elevation myocardial infarction?

Reveal Answer:
In patients with symptom onset within 12 hours who cannot receive primary percutaneous coronary intervention within 120 minutes of first medical contact. Patients should have the infusion started within 30 minutes of arrival.

ECG: sinus tachycardia, nonspecific ST segment and T wave changes, RV strain, S1Q3T3 (classic finding)

Tx

ليش: pulmonary embolism بيصير لما مادة، وأغلبها thrombus، تسدّ الـ pulmonary trunk أو أحد فروعه. هالمريضة عندها active cancer وهاد عامل خطر معروف للـ PE. الألم chest pain حاد وبيزيد مع الشهيق مع dyspnea وtachycardia، والـ ECG فيه T wave inversions في V2–V4 وهي علامة RV strain. الـ hemoptysis والـ shock نادرين بهالـ PE، وهذا بيفرّقها عن MI.
الفخ: الطلاب بيختاروا non-ST elevation myocardial infarction لأن المريضة عندها coronary artery disease. بس الـ MI ألمه ضغط وثقل وبيزيد مع الجهد، مش sharp. وT wave inversions في V2–V4 ممكن تنبه على Wellens syndrome، بس Wellens بييجي بعد فترة بدون ألم ومعه preserved R waves.

question: A 66-year-old man presents to the emergency department in full cardiac arrest. Paramedics note that he was found unconscious at home in cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity. He has received three rounds of compressions and epinephrine twice. You confirm a lack of carotid pulse and see normal sinus rhythm with narrow QRS complexes on the cardiac monitor. Based on his presenting rhythm, which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s cardiac arrest?

options.text: Myocardial infarction with acute pump failure

englishExplanation:
Outcomes from cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity (PEA) have very poor outcomes. It has been proposed that outcomes could be improved if the differential diagnosis of PEA arrest could be focused to allow better cause-specific treatments than the cumbersome list of Hs and Ts (hypoxia, hydrogen ions, hypovolemia, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, hypokalemia, hyperkalemia, toxins, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, coronary thrombosis, pulmonary thromboembolism, trauma) that could cause PEA. As such, there is a new classification of PEA that is based on the initial electrocardiographic findings. Narrow-complex rhythms are usually secondary to mechanical causes and usually result in pseudo-PEA, a severe shock state in which the heart continues to pump but does not create a palpable pulse. Narrow-complex PEA is most often associated with mechanical problems causing right ventricular inflow or outflow obstruction, including cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, and pulmonary embolism. These etiologies are often identifiable on ultrasonography and are managed with aggressive fluid resuscitation as well as cause-specific treatments including pericardiocentesis, needle decompression, and thrombolysis, respectively. On the other hand, wide-complex PEA tends to be true electromechanical dissociation (i.e., true PEA) secondary to metabolic problems like hyperkalemia and sodium channel blocker toxicity, in addition to acute myocardial infarction with pump failure. Treatment for wide-complex PEA should include IV calcium chloride as well as sodium bicarbonate. While there is no outcome data to prove this theory, it does provide a good physiologic background to the difference between true- and pseudo-PEA and highlights the importance of early ultrasonography in the identification of the etiology of PEA arrest.



Hyperkalemia (A) causes a number of ECG abnormalities, progressing from peaked T waves to flattening of P waves, bradycardia, prolongation of the QRS complex, conduction blocks, and asystole. When severe hyperkalemia causes PEA arrest, the QRS complex is usually wide and it would be highly atypical to see normal sinus rhythm with a narrow QRS complex on the cardiac monitor. Treatment is with IV calcium chloride. Myocardial infarction with acute pump failure (B) is also more likely to cause true PEA with a wide complex secondary to disruption of the His-Purkinje system and a hypokinetic heart on ultrasound secondary to the infarction. Myocardial infarction typically will cause cardiac arrest with ventricular fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia. However, PEA can happen and has a very poor prognosis. Sodium channel blockade (D) will present with a widened QRS complex secondary to the flattening of phase zero of the cardiac action potential. It is treated with sodium bicarbonate to overcome the sodium channel blockade.

One Step Further
Question:
What bedside echocardiographic finding is classically seen with pseudo-PEA (i.e., narrow-complex PEA)?

Reveal Answer:
Hyperdynamic left ventricle.

High-quality CPR
Minimize interruptions
Epinephrine 1 mg every 3–5 minutes
Not shockable rhythm
The Hs and Ts

Hypovolemia
Hypothermia

ليش: المريض لقوه بــ pulseless electrical activity ومعه sinus rhythm بـ QRS complexes ضيق. الـ narrow-complex PEA بتكون عادة بسبب ميكانيكي، يعني انسداد inflow أو outflow للـ right ventricle، وهاد Possible cardiac tamponade أو tension pneumothorax أو pulmonary embolism. وكمان الـ PEA هاي أحياناً بتكون pseudo-PEA يعني صدمة شديدة والقلب لسا يضرب بس بدون pulse ملموس. والـ PE بتنعرف بـ ultrasound وبتنعالج بـ fluid resuscitation مع thrombolysis.
الفخ: الـ hyperkalemia والـ sodium channel blockade برضو بيسببوا arrest، بس هما بيسببوا wide-complex PEA يعني true electromechanical dissociation. وجود QRS ضيق بيوجّهك لمشكلة ميكانيكية، وهنا pulmonary embolism هو الاحتمال.

question: A 63-year-old man presents to the ED with chest pain, dyspnea, and syncope. He reports that he has been feeling well except for occasional dizziness and mildly decreased exercise tolerance. On physical examination, a systolic murmur is noted at the right second intercostal space which radiates to the carotids. Which of the following is the imaging modality of choice to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: CT of the chest with contrast

englishExplanation:
The classic triad of aortic stenosis is chest pain, dyspnea, and syncope. Typically, patients experience a long asymptomatic period followed by a stepwise onset of symptoms starting with dyspnea, ensued by chest pain, then syncope, and finally overt signs of heart failure. Decreased exercise tolerance and exertional dyspnea or dizziness may not be noticed or reported by the patient for some time prior to the onset of more ominous symptoms. Mortality increases significantly after the onset of symptoms.

Classic physical examination findings include a late-peaking systolic murmur at the right second intercostal space radiating to the carotids, a single or paradoxically split S2, an S4 gallop, and a diminished carotid pulse with a delayed upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus). Another important clinical finding is a narrowed pulse pressure, which may occur with or without hypotension.

Patients with aortic stenosis typically have diastolic dysfunction and depend on preload from atrial contraction to maintain cardiac output. It is important to remember that cardiac output can drop dramatically, especially if the patient is given nitroglycerin to treat chest pain or dyspnea. Nitrates, vasodilators, diuretics, beta-blockers, and calcium channel blockers are poorly tolerated in patients with symptomatic aortic stenosis and may cause significant and sudden hypotension. Positive-pressure ventilation may be necessary.

Transthoracic echocardiography confirms the diagnosis and determines the severity, and thus remains the first-line imaging modality of choice. Most patients with newly symptomatic aortic stenosis will require admission. Without surgery, nearly 50% of patients with classic symptoms die within one year. Any discharged patient should avoid all vigorous physical activity and be seen promptly by a cardiologist.



Cardiac magnetic resonance tomography (A), despite the limited availability in most centers, provides the gold-standard assessment of left ventricular volumes and ejection fraction, can quantify the aortic regurgitant volume and provide detailed assessment of the hypertrophic response, and is therefore an excellent imaging modality in aortic regurgitation. However, myocardial hypertrophic response is only weakly correlated with the hemodynamic severity of aortic stenosis and is less suited for its assessment.

A CT of the chest with contrast (B) may confirm a diagnosis of aortic dissection leading to acute aortic regurgitation, rapid onset dyspnea, and sudden-onset tearing chest or interscapular pain. Aortic regurgitation is associated with a high-pitched blowing diastolic murmur heard immediately after S2 in the second or third intercostal space at the left sternal border. Electrographically gated non-contrast CT can accurately quantify the calcium burden in aortic stenosis as an alternative measure of disease severity.

ECG (C) findings lack sensitivity and specificity in patients with aortic stenosis. The ECG usually demonstrates left ventricular hypertrophy, and a left or right bundle-branch block may be present.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common cause of aortic stenosis in the United States?

Reveal Answer:
Degenerative calcification.

الفخ: الـ ECG بيكشف علامات ثانوية بس ما بيثبّت درجة الـ stenosis، و CT chest مع contrast و cardiac MRI مش الفحص الأول لتأكيد الـ valve disease.

question: A 27-year-old man with no medical problems presents to the ED with fever and worsening weakness since past week. His temperature is 103°F (39.4°C), blood pressure is 95/48 mm Hg, heart rate is 127 bpm, respirations are 19/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Physical exam is notable for a holosystolic murmur heard best over the left lower sternal border, track marks on both of the patient’s forearms, and dry, flushed skin. The patient is given 2 L of IV fluids and his repeat blood pressure is 111/58 mm Hg and heart rate is 96 bpm. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms suggestive of bacterial endocarditis. Bacterial endocarditis presents with a fever and a new cardiac murmur typically in a patient with risk factors such as prosthetic valves or IV drug misuse. Findings in bacterial endocarditis can include petechiae, subungual hemorrhages, Osler nodes (tender subcutaneous nodules on the digits), Janeway lesions (nontender maculae on the palms and soles), Roth spots (retinal hemorrhages), embolic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, and CNS microabscesses. Other less specific findings include splenomegaly, gallops, dysrhythmias, pericardial rubs, and pleural friction rubs.

Any patient with a fever and a new cardiac murmur with risk factors should have blood cultures drawn and be assessed with an ultrasound searching for cardiac vegetations. After blood cultures are drawn, broad-spectrum antibiotics should be administered with possible regimens including vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam or vancomycin and gentamicin. Micafungin can be added empirically until a fungal etiology is also ruled out. Surgical removal of the vegetations may be necessary for source control of the infection.



Pericarditis (B) presents with chest pain worse when the patient is lying back and relieved when they sit up or lean forward, a pericardial friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation and PR depression on ECG.

Septic shock (C) presents with hypotension and tachycardia in the setting of infection that does not respond to fluid resuscitation. This patient responded to initial fluid resuscitation.

Sympathomimetic overdose (D)presents with adrenergic symptoms including hypertension, hyperthermia, dilated pupils, and diaphoresis. This patient presents with dry, flushed skin, likely secondary to dehydration.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient who uses IV drugs and has a new-onset early diastolic murmur, fever, and new-onset atrioventricular block?

Reveal Answer:
Perivalvular abscess (disrupts the conduction system).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Bacterial Endocarditis

Risk factors: injection drug use, valvular heart disease
Sx & syndromes:
Mild and nonspecific febrile illness - fever, rash, cough, and myalgias
Acute heart failure
Focal neurological deficit from septic cerebral embolus
Altered mental status
Axial spine pain from osteomyelitis
Pneumonia from septic pulmonary emboli
PE: fever, Roth spots, Osler nodes, murmur, Janeway lesions, anemia, nailbed hemorrhages, emboli (FROM JANE)
Dx: echocardiography and Duke criteria
Most commonly caused by:
IVDA: Staphylococcus aureus, tricuspid
Native valve: Staphylococcus aureus, viridans streptococci (most common in previously diseased), mitral
GI malignancy: Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis)
Tx: antibiotics
Dental prophylaxis indicated in some cases

ليش: عنده حمى 39.4 مع murmur جديد holosystolic، وهاد بالذات مع علامات IV drug use يعني track marks على الذراعين، وهاد عامل خطر معروف لـ bacterial endocarditis. الـ endocarditis بيسبب حمى مع murmur جديد، وبتظهر فيه علامات periphery زي petechiae وsubungual hemorrhages وOsler nodes وJaneway lesions. اللازم تاخد blood cultures وبعدها تعطي antibiotics واسعة المدى مثل vancomycin مع piperacillin-tazobactam أو gentamicin، وتعمل ultrasound تدور على vegetations، وقد تحتاج جراحة لإزالتها.
الفخ: الـ pericarditis بياخد ألم صدر worse عند الاستلقاء يتحسن عند الجلوس، مع friction rub وdiffuse ST elevation وPR depression. أما septic shock و sympathomimetic overdose ما بتشرحوا murmur جديد مع track marks.

question: A 61-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after several episodes of syncope. Her vital signs include a blood pressure of 136/88 mm Hg, heart rate of 58 bpm, respiratory rate of 20 breaths/minute, oxygen saturation of 97% on room air, and temperature of 99.1°F. Her rhythm strip is shown above. Which of the following heart blocks is present?

options.text: Second-degree Mobitz type I atrioventricular block
Second-degree Mobitz type II atrioventricular block

correctAnswer: Second-degree Mobitz type I atrioventricular block
englishExplanation:
The patient has a second-degree Mobitz type I atrioventricular (AV) block. A first-degree AV block refers to slowed conduction through the AV node, resulting in a prolonged PR interval, with preserved conduction of each sinus-generated impulse. In second-degree AV block, there is intermittent conduction through the AV node in which some atrial impulses are conducted through to the ventricles while others are blocked. There are two types of second-degree block: Mobitz type I and type II.

In second-degree Mobitz type I block, also referred to as Wenckebach, there is a progressive delay in each AV conduction until AV conduction is finally blocked. On electrocardiogram, this appears as progressive lengthening of each PR interval until a QRS complex is eventually dropped and the cycle repeats. Grouped beating, or clustering of QRS complexes separated by a pause from the dropped beat, is characteristic of second-degree type I AV block. Mobitz type I block is often transient, seen in association with inferior wall myocardial ischemia, medication toxicity, or cardiac surgery. Treatment is usually not necessary unless it is associated with a very slow rate with signs of hypoperfusion. In this case, atropine, which increases the rate of sinus node firing and conduction through the AV node, is usually effective.

The other type of second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II, is more ominous. Type II block is characterized by a constant PR interval with periodic nonconducted impulses, seen as an absence of a QRS complex. Because Mobitz type II blocks are associated with progression to third-degree, or complete heart block, patients should have transcutaneous pacer pads placed in anticipation of possible need. In third-degree AV block, there is no conduction through the AV node, and an escape pacemaker is responsible for the ventricular rate. On electrocardiogram, there is no association of P waves with QRS complexes, and the ventricular rate is 40–60 bpm, depending on whether a junctional or ventricular escape pacemaker takes over. Pacing is usually needed in a complete heart block.



First-degree AV block (A) shows a prolonged PR interval but no dropped beats.

Left anterior fascicular block (B) shows marked left axis deviation, qR pattern in lead aVL, and QRS duration < 120 ms.

Second-degree Mobitz type II AV block (D) is characterized by a constant PR interval with sporadic dropped beats.

Third-degree AV block (E) is characterized by no association between P waves and QRS complexes.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the definitive treatment for third-degree heart block?

Reveal Answer:
Internal pacemaker placement.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Second-Degree Heart Block (Mobitz I, Wenckebach)

Rhythm will be irregular
PR interval will be progressively lengthening
Notable feature: progressive lengthening of the PR interval until QRS complex fails to appear after a P wave (dropped beat)
arabicExplanation:
ليش: عندها syncope متكرر مع bradycardia بسيط و pulse rate 58. الـ second-degree Mobitz type I يعني تأخر تدريجي في الـ AV conduction لحد ما ينقطع بضة واحدة، وعلى الـ ECG بتشوف الـ PR interval بيطول بشكل تدريجي لحد ما QRS complex ين-drop وبعدين الدورة بتتكرر. هاد بيدي grouped beating، يعني تجمّع QRS complexes مع pause. والـ Mobitz I غالباً مؤقت ومرتبط بـ inferior wall ischemia أو toxicity دوا أو عملية قلب.
الفخ: الـ first-degree AV block بيرفع الـ PR بس كل P wave بتنزل، فما في QRS ضايع ولا bradycardia، وهاد ما بيفسّر الـ syncope.

question: Which of the following has been associated with a reduced rate of incessant or recurrent pericarditis in patients with a first episode of pericarditis?
englishExplanation:
The pericardium is a fibroelastic sac made up of visceral and parietal layers separated by a (potential) space, the pericardial cavity. In healthy individuals, the pericardial cavity contains 20 to 50 mL of an ultrafiltrate of plasma.

The therapy of acute pericarditis should be targeted as much as possible to the underlying etiology. In patients with an identified cause other than viral infection, specific therapy appropriate to the underlying disorder is indicated. However, in resource-rich countries, most cases of acute pericarditis in immunocompetent patients are due to viral infection or are idiopathic.

Because of the relatively benign course associated with the common causes of pericarditis (most cases), it is not necessary to search for the etiology in all patients. As such, most patients are treated for a presumptive viral cause with NSAIDs and colchicine.

Most patients have prompt resolution of symptoms without recurrent pericarditis when treated with NSAIDs alone. However, when used as an adjunct to NSAID therapy, colchicine reduces symptoms, decreases the rate of recurrent pericarditis, and is generally well tolerated.



Aspirin (A) is a first-line agent for symptom relief and inflammation control in acute pericarditis, but it has not been shown to independently reduce recurrence rates. It serves as background anti-inflammatory therapy to which colchicine is added.

Ibuprofen (C) is similarly used as first-line NSAID therapy for acute pericarditis symptoms but lacks evidence for preventing recurrence when used alone. Like aspirin, it is the foundation therapy that colchicine supplements to reduce recurrence.

Prednisone (D) is associated with an increased risk of recurrence and should be avoided in first-episode pericarditis. Corticosteroids are reserved only for patients who are refractory to or have contraindications to NSAIDs and colchicine.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the term to describe post-myocardial infarction pericarditis?

Reveal Answer:
Dressler syndrome.

Sx: pleuritic chest pain radiating to the back that is worse when lying back and improved when leaning forward
PE: tachycardia and pericardial friction rub, distant heart sounds

Tx: NSAIDs, colchicine, corticosteroids (in refractory cases, NSAID contraindication, or certain rheumatologic disease)
arabicExplanation:

question: A 17-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with his parents after a syncopal episode. The patient is adopted and does not know his biological parents. The patient was in gym class playing tennis when he suddenly lost consciousness. He does not remember anything from the event. His classmates stated he was unresponsive for 30 seconds. During this time, he demonstrated shaking of his upper and lower extremities. The patient remembers everything after waking up and reports no confusion. Physical exam and vital signs are unremarkable and unrevealing. His ECG is shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Consult to cardiology for automatic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement

correctAnswer: Consult to cardiology for automatic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement
englishExplanation:
Syncope is a sudden, brief loss of consciousness associated with a loss of postural tone from which recovery is spontaneous. Life-threatening conditions such as hypoglycemia, heat illness, anaphylaxis, cardiac dysrhythmia, or structural cardiac disease are rare but serious causes of syncope. Although these causes account for only 1–2% of syncope in children, they still warrant diagnostic consideration. Cardiac syncope is thought to present with sudden abrupt loss of consciousness without a prodrome and may be associated with chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath.

Brugada Syndrome is a genetic disorder of fast sodium channels causing a right bundle branch block pattern in leads V1–2 with pathognomonic J-point elevation and saddle-shaped or sloped ST segments. Sudden cardiac arrest may be the initial presentation in as many as one-third of patients. Patients may also present with an episode of syncope but palpitations or nocturnal agonal respirations have also been described. Automatic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (AICD) placement is recommended for patients who have survived sudden cardiac arrest or those with a history of syncope that is felt to be secondary to ventricular tachydysrhythmias.



Emergent cardiac catheterization (B) would be required for ST elevation myocardial infarction characterized by ST segment elevation of approximately 1 mm in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF), 2 mm in the precordial leads or 0.5 mm depression in leads V1 and V2 for a posterior myocardial infarction. Reciprocal depression is typically noted in leads opposite to the elevation. Chest pain is the main symptom. However, atypical symptoms such as shortness of breath, weakness, lightheadedness, syncope, and palpitations are also frequently reported.

Long QT syndrome is characterized by a QT interval of > 440 msec in men and > 460 msec in women, although some sources say > 460 msec in men and > 480 msec in women. This can be acquired or congenital and can lead to an increased risk of torsades de pointes. Acquired causes are commonly associated with medications (antidepressants, antidysrhythmics, antipsychotics, methadone, antibiotics, and ondansetron). Treatment for acquired prolonged QT syndrome involves removing the offending agent as well as close cardiac monitoring and treating associated dysrhythmias as needed. Beta-blockers, such as propranolol (C), are the mainstay of therapy for congenital causes.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a genetically determined heart muscle disease most often caused by mutations in one of several sarcomere genes. The mutation results in left ventricular hypertrophy, commonly of the septum, that results in left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Many patients have no or only minor symptoms. Thus, affected individuals are often diagnosed as a result of family screening, murmur on exam, or abnormal ECG. The abnormal ECG may show voltage criteria consistent with left ventricular hypertrophy or classically deep dagger Q waves in the lateral and inferior leads. On physical examination, patients may have a systolic murmur auscultated along the left sternal border. Patients who present with dyspnea, presyncope, or syncope on exertion, or who have a familial history of sudden cardiac death, warrant evaluation with a STAT echocardiogram (D) evaluating for left ventricular outflow tract obstruction secondary to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

One Step Further
Question:
How will a Valsalva maneuver alter the intensity of the murmur associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?

Reveal Answer:
Valsalva increases the intensity of the murmur.

Type 2 and 3 changes are nondiagnostic and require further workup

الفخ: الـ emergent cardiac catheterization lab بتطلب ST elevation myocardial infarction، وهاد ما موجود. الـ STAT echocardiogram ما بتغيّر إن الحالة cardiac arrest متوقع، وPropranolol لوحده ما بيعالج الخطر.

question: A 4-month-old previously healthy baby girl presents to the emergency department for irritability for the past 1 hour. The parents say she is refusing to eat, and they tried to lay her down for a nap, but she could not rest. The exam shows an afebrile, crying infant with HR of 233 bpm, RR of 60/min, BP of 83/52 mm Hg, T of 37.6°C, and SpO2 of 100%. The remainder of her exam is normal. In addition to obtaining an ECG, which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Chemical cardioversion followed by electrical cardioversion if needed
Sepsis workup to rule out occult infection
Vagal maneuvers followed by chemical cardioversion if needed

correctAnswer: Vagal maneuvers followed by chemical cardioversion if needed
englishExplanation:
Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) presents with nonspecific symptoms in infancy and can include rapid breathing, irritability, poor feeding, or failure to thrive. The diagnosis is confirmed based on the heart rate and characteristic ECG findings. Generally accepted heart rate cutoffs depend on age (children’s heart rate > 180 bpm, and infant’s heart rate > 200 bpm). The ECG will show a narrow complex, fast rhythm without appreciable P waves before the QRS complex. Most P waves will be buried in the QRS complexes, but sometimes, retrograde P waves (i.e., occurring after the QRS complex) can be seen.

Initial treatment depends on if the patient is hemodynamically stable or unstable. Treatment of unstable patients with signs of poor perfusion or hypotension should begin with synchronized electrical cardioversion (although adenosine can be used if an IV can be established rapidly). For children, the starting dose is 0.5–1 J/kg. If that is unsuccessful, the energy can be increased to 2 J/kg for all necessary repeated attempts. Treatment in a stable patient should start with vagal maneuvers. For infants, placing an ice pack over the face for 20–30 seconds may be sufficient. This activates the diving reflex, which is an effective way to increase vagal tone. If vagal maneuvers are unsuccessful, chemical cardioversion should be the next step. Adenosine is the agent of choice. Doses start at 0.1 mg/kg and must be pushed as a rapid infusion followed by a normal saline flush. If a second dose is needed, the dose is 0.2 mg/kg. As in adults, a maximum of three doses should be given. Management should also include a careful history and exam to rule out other sources of tachycardia, such as dehydration, sepsis, hyperthyroidism, and acute blood loss.



Pain can elevate the heart rate, but with exam findings showing no source of pain and a higher than expected heart rate, analgesia and ED observation (A) does not aid in treating the underlying pathology.

Chemical cardioversion followed by electrical cardioversion if needed (B) is a possible treatment for PSVT, but vagal maneuvers should be attempted first, especially in this infant who is not in extremis.

Providing reassurance and discharging home (C) should not be done with patients with abnormal vital signs without an appropriate workup.

A sepsis workup (D) is an important consideration in infants with unexplained tachycardia. Lab work, blood cultures, and urinalysis can be ordered if there is a concern for occult infection, but they are not required for all presentations of PSVT. Furthermore, this patient is afebrile and her symptoms are acute.

One Step Further
Question:
What are four risk factors associated with syncope that put a child at the highest risk for a cardiac cause?

Reveal Answer:
Mid-exertional syncope, syncope triggered by a loud noise or when swimming, absence of prodromal symptoms, and history of cardiac disease.

الفخ: الـ synchronized electrical cardioversion بتستخدم للمريض غير المستقر اللي عنده poor perfusion أو hypotension، مش لهالbaby. و chemical cardioversion من البداية قبل vagal maneuvers مش الترتيب الصح.

question: A 70-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance for the acute onset of severe right arm pain that woke him from sleep. He is unable to provide additional history due to pain. His HR is 140 bpm and irregular, BP is 180/120 mm Hg, and SpO2 is 94% on room air. Physical examination is significant for a cold and pale right upper extremity. Acoustic Doppler of the right upper extremity shows an absent pulse compared to a monophasic pulse in the left upper extremity. Point-of-care ultrasound reveals an irregularly irregular heartbeat but no other cardiac abnormalities. Which of the following is the best next step for this patient’s care?
englishExplanation:
Acute limb ischemia presents with the sudden onset of severe pain in one limb, usually in combination with an obvious perfusion deficit. Other components of the six Ps (pain, pallor, paralysis, pulse deficit, paresthesia, and poikilothermia) may also be present. Atraumatic acute limb ischemia is most commonly due to an embolus that arises from the atria in the setting of atrial fibrillation or thrombosis in a patient with severe peripheral arterial disease. Other etiologies of limb ischemia, such as venous occlusion and aortic dissection, are possible but rare, and patients typically do not present with the classic signs of limb ischemia in isolation. The first-line treatment for patients with acute limb ischemia includes a heparin bolus followed by an infusion. This therapy is traditionally performed even in patients for whom surgical or endovascular treatment is planned.



CT angiography (A) is typically performed after administering heparin to avoid delays in treatment. If aortic dissection or trauma is strongly suspected, angiography may occur before anticoagulation. An esmolol bolus (B) would be appropriate if this patient had an aortic dissection. The absence of chest pain, pericardial effusion, aortic root dilation on cardiac ultrasound, and any significant signs or symptoms outside of the affected limb is reassuring against a diagnosis of dissection. Vascular surgery consultation (C) is critical in all suspected cases of limb ischemia. However, initial treatment with heparin should not be delayed to obtain a consultation. Systemic thrombolytics (D) are not typically used for limb ischemia. In some cases, catheter-directed thrombolysis may be administered. Both systemic and local thrombolysis should only be initiated at the recommendation of a vascular surgeon.

One Step Further
Question:
What laboratory test is used to monitor anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin?

Reveal Answer:
The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT).
