question:
A 49-year-old man was admitted to the emergency department after a 
road traffic collision. His body mass index (BMI) was 42. His wife, who 
was a passenger in the car at the time, thinks he may have fallen asleep 
at the wheel. The possibility of obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea 
syndrome (OSAHS) is raised.
Which is true regarding OSAHS?

options.text: An Epworth sleepiness score of 5 implies significant sleepiness
Nocturia is a not a feature of OSAHS
A normal overnight oximetry will effectively exclude OSAHS
Smoking and alcohol consumption are associated with OSAHS
Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP) is recommended for the treatment of OSAHS

englishExplanation:
37. D.  Smoking and alcohol consumption are associated with OSAHS
The Epworth Sleepiness Scale consists of eight questions regarding the subjective likelihood of falling asleep in a given situation. A score of 10 or more implies excessive sleepiness.

RESPIRATORY | ANSWERS
90
90
Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP) is not recommended as a treatment for obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome (OSAHS).
Typically in patients with OSAHS the throat muscles relax as normal during stage 3–4 sleep (deep, 
refreshing sleep); the airway narrows to the point of either complete collapse (causing an apnoea) 
or becomes severely narrowed (causing an effortful hypopnoea); the effort to breathe against a 
closed or narrow airway eventually causes an arousal waking the patient up to stage 1–2 sleep 
(light, unrefreshing sleep); the muscle tone (and airway calibre) improves so air flow recommences 
with a loud gasp; the patient soon slips back into deep sleep, and the cycle continues. Disruption of 
deep sleep usually causes excessive daytime sleepiness.
When the patient’s airway is compromised their oxygen saturation (often) slowly falls by more 
than 4%, then rises suddenly back to baseline once arousal lightens sleep and muscle tone improves 
opening the airway. This change in saturation is not always seen (particularly in young, thin patients), 
so a normal oximetry study does not rule out OSAHS.
Usually, OSAHS is due to the normal throat muscle relaxation combined with excessive neck 
weight; sometimes, however, the throat muscles simply become excessively relaxed during deep 
sleep in a patient of normal weight. Alcohol exacerbates the reduction in throat muscle tone. 
Smoking can cause throat inflammation contributing to the narrowed airway. Nocturia, decreased 
libido, and irritability can all be features of OSAHS.
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Technology Appraisal 139. Continuous positive 
airway pressure for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome. March 2008. 
http://www.sleep-apnoea-trust.org.

question:
A 33-year-old woman, who was a Somalian refugee, was referred to the 
acute medical unit by her GP. She had a two-month history of worsening 
cough, fevers, night sweats, poor appetite, and malaise.
Her GP sent a sputum sample last week and checked her HIV status. 
The lab informed you that she was smear positive for acid and alcohol 
fast bacilli (AAFB) and was HIV positive.
What is true regarding her management?

options.text: Anti-tuberculosis treatment should be started before anti-retrovirals
She should be considered infectious until four weeks of anti-tuberculous treatment have
She should be started on a three-drug regimen of rifampicin, isoniazid, and ethambutol
She should stay in a side room until two sputum samples are negative for AAFB
A side room is only required if multi-drug resistant tuberculosis is suspected

englishExplanation:
38. A.  Anti-tuberculosis treatment should be started before anti-retrovirals
In this scenario it is very likely that the patient has tuberculosis (TB) (rather than an alternative 
mycobacteria); she comes from a high-risk demographic and has both symptoms and X-ray appearances consistent with TB. Further confirmatory early morning sputum samples should be sent off, 
and she should start on empirical TB treatment pending culture results (which may take up to eight 
weeks).
Standard treatment is a four-drug regimen: rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 
2 months, followed by a continuation phase of rifampicin and isoniazid for a further four months. 
These should be given as combination tablets to improve compliance and prevent resistance to individual drugs developing.
Rifater = Rifampicin + Isoniazid + Pyrazinamide
Rifinah = Rifampicin + Isoniazid
Patients who cough are considered infectious until completing two weeks of treatment.
If admitted, patients should be nursed in a side room with good ventilation and not allowed onto 
the open ward until three sputum samples are smear negative.
Starting anti-TB treatment takes precedence over anti-retrovirals. Pyridoxine 10 mg once daily may 
be added to her treatment regimen due to the increased risk of peripheral neuropathy with HIV 
and anti-TB medication. Starting anti-retrovirals first would increase the risk of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.
Ideally, patients with TB should be managed as an outpatient. Having TB is not a reason to admit. 
TB should be treated by a specialist physician (usually respiratory physician) with experience in 
managing TB.
Pozniak AL, Coyne KM, Mille RF et al. British HIV Association guidelines for the treatment of TB/HIV 
co-infection 2011. HIV Medicine 2011; 12: 517–524. doi: 10.1111/j.1468–1293.2011.00954.x

RESPIRATORY | ANSWERS
91

question:
A 61-year-old man with a recent diagnosis of mesothelioma was 
admitted to the acute medical unit with worsening breathlessness 
and severe chest pain. He lived alone. His exercise tolerance was 
approximately 100 metres. His daughter did his shopping for him, but he 
was otherwise independent.
His medication included morphine sulphate modified release 100 mg 
twice daily with morphine sulphate oral solution for breakthrough pain, 
diclofenac 50 mg three times daily, and paracetamol 1 g four times daily.
He had a moderate pleural effusion on his chest X-ray, and signs of 
ascites on examination.
Which is true?

options.text: Combination radiotherapy plus chemotherapy would have a slim chance of curing him
His ascites is not due to peritoneal metastases
An indwelling pleural catheter is not helpful to manage his effusion
Percutaneous cervical cordotomy at C1/C2 level is an option for pain management
Severe pain due to mesothelioma is uncommon

englishExplanation:
39. D.  Percutaneous cervical cordotomy at C1/C2 is an option for pain management
Primary peritoneal mesothelioma commonly causes ascites, abdominal metastases from pleural 
mesothelioma is a less common, but still seen, cause of ascites.
Unfortunately, severe chest pain is common. Mesothelioma commonly presents with chest pain and 
breathlessness either due to an associated (usually blood-stained) pleural effusion or due to encasement of the lung. An indwelling pleural catheter can be used to manage to the recurrent effusion. 
If the diagnosis is made by biopsy at thoracoscopy or Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) 
then a surgical pleurodesis or talc podrage may be undertaken at the same time.
For refractory pain a percutaneous cervical cordotomy at C1/C2 level which causes contralateral 
loss of pain sensation can be very effective.
No therapies currently offer a cure. Radiotherapy may be helpful for localized pain (e.g. from bone 
invasion). Combination chemotherapy may provide approximately three months’ survival advantage.
British Thoracic Society Standards of Care Committee. BTS statement on malignant mesothelioma in 
the UK. Thorax 2007; 62: ii1–ii19. doi: 10.1136/thx.2007.087619

question:
Researchers assessed the efficacy of varenicline, a licensed cigarette 
smoking cessation aid, in helping adult users of smokeless tobacco to 
quit. A randomized double-blind, placebo-controlled trial study design 
was used. Varenicline was administered at a dose of 1 mg twice daily for 
12 weeks. A total of 431 participants were recruited and randomized 
to varenicline (n = 213) or placebo (n = 218). All participants were 
offered brief behavioural support or counselling at the discretion of the 
investigators.
The primary endpoint was continuous abstinence from using smokeless 
tobacco for four weeks at the end of treatment (weeks 9–12). The rate 
of continuous abstinence was significantly higher in the varenicline 
group than for placebo (59% v 39%; relative risk 1.6, 95% confidence 
interval 1.32 to 1.87; P<0.001; number needed to treat five).*
What is the best interpretation of number needed to treat (NNT) of 
five for continuous abstinence at end of treatment in users of smokeless 
tobacco for varenicline compared with placebo?

options.text: Five users need to be treated with varenicline for one to experience an adverse side effect
Five users need to be treated with placebo for one to experience an adverse side effect
On average, five users need to be treated with varenicline for one person to be abstinent
On average, for every five users treated with varenicline one more would be abstinent at
On average, if five users were treated with varenicline then all of them would be abstinent

englishExplanation:
40. D.  On average, for every five users treated with varenicline one more would be abstinent at 
end of treatment than if those same people were treated with placebo
Number needed to treat (NNT) is constructed as a measure of the benefit from treatment with 
the intervention compared to the control for a clinical trial. NNT is sometimes referred to as number needed to treat to benefit (NNTB). In the trial above, the rate of abstinence was higher in the 
varenicline group than for the placebo group. The NNT of five reflects the benefit of treatment 
with varenicline compared with placebo. On average if five patients were treated with varenicline 
then one additional patient will benefit (i.e. be abstinent) at the end of treatment than if those same 
people had been treated with placebo (see Sedgwick & Joekes, 2014; Sedgwick, 2015a).
At the end of treatment, 59% of the varenicline treatment group achieved abstinence compared 
to 39% of the placebo group. Therefore, the varenicline group demonstrated an increase of 20% 
in abstinence compared to placebo. Hence, if 100 users of smokeless tobacco were treated with 
varenicline there would be 20 more achieving abstinence than if those same users had been treated 
with placebo. Hence, on average, five users need to be treated with varenicline for one more user 
to benefit than if those same five users had been treated with placebo. More generally, NNT is calculated as the reciprocal of the absolute risk difference between the treatment groups in the outcome of complete abstinence. In statistics, risk is an alternative name for probability or proportion. 
The risk difference between treatments was 0.20. Hence, NNT=1 ÷ 0.20=5.
When using NNT to describe the benefit of varenicline compared with placebo, it is important that 
the absolute rates of continuous abstinence for the varenicline and placebo groups are presented. In 
particular, an NNT of five could have been achieved with different trial results but so long as the difference between treatment groups in percentage continuous abstinence was 20% in favour of varenicline. However, if the rate of abstinence was 99% for the varenicline treatment group and 79% for the 
placebo group, it would no doubt have a different significance for the clinician and patient if the rate of 
abstinence was, for example, 29% for the varenicline treatment group and 9% for the placebo group.
NNT is a measure of the benefit of treatment with the intervention (varenicline) compared to 
control (placebo). If the intervention caused harm—for example, resulted in more side effects than 
placebo, or an inferior rate of abstinence—then the measure number needed to harm (NNH) 
would be used to reflect the harm caused by treatment (see Sedgwick, 2015b).
As a measure of the benefit of treatment, NNT is a comparative statement of the effectiveness 
of intervention (varenicline) with control (placebo) as described above. However, the comparator 
treatment is often not stated when interpreting NNT resulting in a misleading statement about the 
effectiveness of intervention. For example, the statement that ‘five users need to be treated with 
varenicline for one person to be abstinent at end of treatment’ implies for every five users treated 

RESPIRATORY | ANSWERS
92
92
with varenicline, one will benefit (achieve abstinence) and four will not. This is obviously an incorrect interpretation of NNT and the benefit of treatment with varenicline since at the end of the 
treatment, 59% of the varenicline treatment group had achieved abstinence; hence, approximately 
three out of five users of varenicline achieved abstinence.
Sedgwick P, Joekes K. Randomised controlled trials: evaluating and communicating treatment effects. 
BMJ 2014; 348: g1905.
Sedgwick P. Measuring the benefit of treatment: number needed to treat. BMJ 2015a; 350: h2206.
Sedgwick P. Measuring the detriment of treatment: number needed to harm. BMJ 2015b: 350: h2763.

question:
A 72-year-old man presented with a six-week history of fever, shortness 
of breath, night sweats, sinusitis, anorexia, muscle pains, and a weak 
left wrist. During initial investigations his GP had found persistent nonvisible haematuria and treated him with trimethoprim. Urine culture 
had been negative on three occasions.
On examination, his temperature was 37.8°C, his pulse was 105 beats 
per minute, and blood pressure 138/75 mmHg. His oxygen saturation 
was 90% on air. No cardiac murmurs were audible and there were no 
peripheral signs of infective endocarditis.
Investigations:
haemoglobin
87 g/L
(130–180)
white cell count
13.5 × 109/L
(4.0–11.0)
neutrophil count
11.9 × 109/L
(1.5–7.0)
lymphocyte count
1.5 × 109/L
(1.5–4.0)
platelet count
380 × 109/L
(150–400)
serum creatinine
335 μmol/L
(60–110)
serum C-reactive protein
135 mg/L
(<10)
urine microscopy: blood + +, no white cells; granular casts present
CXR showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates in an alveolar  
  filling pattern
Which non-invasive test is the best to support the likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
6. A.  ANCA titre
The symptoms and initial investigations suggest a small vessel vasculitis with renal, respiratory, and 
neuronal involvement such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)—formerly known as Wegener’s granulomatosis. This diagnosis would be supported by a positive cANCA on immunofluorescence and PR3 antigen on ELISA. The differential diagnosis includes microscopic polyangiitis, which 
would also be likely to demonstrate ANCA positivity (pANCA/MPO positive). The diagnosis 
would usually be confirmed with renal biopsy.
Anti-GBM disease is a cause of pulmonary–renal syndrome but does not typically present with neurological signs or symptoms.
Endocarditis can be associated with ANCA positivity and a similar picture of blood results; echocardiography is helpful if diagnostic uncertainty is raised by a subsequent positive blood culture, atypical ANCA or renal biopsy findings, or development of a new murmur.

question:
A 25-year-old woman returned from South Africa where she had been 
teaching orphaned children for the last year. She had been unwell for 
six weeks with fevers, night sweats, and a dry cough. She had become 
increasingly breathless over the last two weeks, which precipitated this 
admission.
On admission, she had a temperature of 37.9°C. There was dullness to 
percussion with absence of breath sounds at the right base. The rest of 
the clinical examination was unremarkable.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics were commenced after a diagnostic 
aspiration of her pleural effusion was performed, which led to 
symptomatic improvement.
Investigations:
chest X-ray showed a right pleural effusion
pleural aspirate: straw coloured fluid
protein 33 g/L
lactate dehydrogenase 1059 IU/L
cells: 1,000 lymphocytes
auramine stain: negative
gram stain: negative
day ten: mycobacterial growth in liquid culture
What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Arrange bronchoalveolar lavage before starting quadruple therapy for tuberculosis.
Await further identification before commencing treatment
Notify as tuberculosis but await culture sensitivities before commencing therapy
Start quadruple antituberculous therapy and notify as tuberculosis
Start quadruple antituberculous therapy but await culture confirmation of mycobacterium

englishExplanation:
7. D.  Start quadruple antituberculous therapy and notify as tuberculosis
This patient has primary pleural tuberculosis (TB) until proven otherwise. This occurs when a tuberculous focus in the periphery of the lung ruptures into the pleural space, and is most often seen in 
primary tuberculous infection.
Symptoms of TB typically include fever, night sweats, and weight loss, with additional symptoms 
according to the organ affected. Pulmonary TB occurs in about 80%, and a cough lasting for longer 
than three weeks that fails to respond to standard antibiotics with or without haemoptysis should 
arouse suspicion. Usually, the upper lobes are affected and there may be cavitation on chest X-ray.
Sites of infection in descending order of frequency:
● Pulmonary
● Pleural
● Adenopathy (localized/generalized)
● Genitourinary (17% white UK; 4% in Asian)
● Miliary or disseminated
● Bone and joint (10–15%)
● Abdominal (ileocecal and peritoneal)
● CNS (95% meningeal or tuberculoma)
● Pericardial
● Cutaneous TB or lupus vulgaris
● Cryptic disseminated TB
Any organ can be affected, and symptoms and onset may be indolent or dramatic.
Primary infection can be associated with a variety of hypersensitivity syndromes to TB proteins. 
Erythema nodosum is the most commonly encountered. More rarely the tuberculides including erythema induratum and phlyctenular conjunctivitis are associated with cryptic disease and 
resolve on TB therapy. PCR may be positive. They are usually associated with a strong cellular 
response.
Table 12.2  Table showing viral capsid antibody (VCA) IgM/IgG and Epstein–Barr nuclear antigen 
(EBNA) IgG along with interpretation of results.

This patient should be commenced on quadruple antituberculous chemotherapy with rifampicin, 
isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.
There is a statutory duty to notify the patient to the proper officer and there are specific enhanced 
surveillance TB notification forms which should be used.
Notification should be performed once the decision to treat tuberculosis is made. Culture confirmation is not a prerequisite. Bronchoalveolar lavage is not necessary now as there is a positive culture from pleural fluid, though it would have been an important initial investigation to increase the 
chance of positive yield, as only 60–80% of patients with tuberculosis have positive cultures.
She has been exposed to an area where there is multidrug resistant TB. Mycobacterial PCR can be 
used to help confirm mycobateria tuberculosis while awaiting further identification from culture. 
Gene probes can determine the presence of genes associated with rifampicin resistance, which although not 100% sensitive may give early warning of the possibility of multi-drug resistant (MDR) 
TB (the definition of MDR TB is resistance to both rifampicin and isoniazid). A Mantoux test or 
gamma interferon release assay measure the T cell mediated immune response to TB, and indicate 
exposure, but not necessarily active disease. The Mantoux cross-reacts with BCG, so may be positive in people who have been vaccinated. Interferon–Gamma Release Assays (IGRAs) do not react 
to BCG and are more specific to TB.
Culture can take up to eight weeks, though liquid broth techniques are typically positive within 
three weeks.
Standard TB chemotherapy involves quadruple therapy for the first two months. This ensures at 
least two active drugs within the regimen while sensitivities are awaited, avoiding inadvertent monotherapy (with the risk of further resistance) if there is resistance to one or more agents. After two 
months, the continuation phase of the regimen can be started, determined by antimicrobial sensitivities. If fully sensitive, mycobacteria tuberculosis is cultured then a further four months of isoniazid 
and rifampicin is given.
If there is resistance to one or more of the first-line drugs, alternative regimens should be given. 
MDR TB or extremely multi-drug resistant TB (XDR TB) should be discussed with experts in the 
management of resistant TB. It usually involves the additional use of an injectable agent for six 
months such as a quinolone, protionamide, or cycloserine. Duration of therapy can be two years or 
more, as these agents are not as powerful as first-line treatment, and close monitoring with directly 
observed therapy should be offered.
All patients with TB should be offered an HIV test. HIV greatly increases the risk of developing 
active TB compared with the non-HIV infected population. There is also a greater risk of death 
or complications if HIV remains undetected, which can be reduced by detection and treatment of 
the HIV.

question:
Regarding the therapeutic gas mixture Heliox, which of the following statements
is FALSE?

options.text: It is less dense than air, which reduces the work of breathing by promoting laminar flow through narrowed airways.
Its use is contraindicated in patients with severe hypoxemia because the maximum FiO₂ is limited.
It is typically supplied in mixtures such as 80% helium/20% oxygen or 70%
It has a higher density than atmospheric air, which helps to stent open airways.
It is most effective for conditions involving upper airway obstruction with turbulent airflow.

correctAnswer: It has a higher density than atmospheric air, which helps to stent open airways.
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Action:
This statement is false. The therapeutic benefit of Heliox derives from its low density (Helium is ~1/7th the density of Nitrogen). According to the Reynolds number
equation (Re = (Density × Velocity × Diameter) / Viscosity), the tendency for turbulent flow is directly proportional to gas density. By substituting nitrogen/oxygen
with helium, the Reynolds number is reduced, converting high-resistance turbulent
flow in narrowed upper airways into lower-resistance laminar flow. Heliox does not

provide positive pressure to 'stent' airways open unless explicitly combined with
CPAP or NIV.
Clinical Application:
Heliox is most effective in conditions of upper airway obstruction (e.g., post-extubation stridor, tracheal stenosis, extrinsic compression) where airflow is turbulent. Its
utility in distal airway obstruction (e.g., asthma/COPD) is debated because flow in
small airways is typically laminar (dependent on viscosity, not density) and the required FiO2 in severe exacerbations often precludes the use of a sufficient helium
concentration.
Clinical Pearl
Physical Properties:
Helium is approximately 1/7th the density of nitrogen. This low density is the primary physical property responsible for reducing resistance in turbulent flow
conditions.
Work of Breathing:
The primary clinical benefit is a reduction in the work of breathing during the acute
phase of airway obstruction, acting as a bridge therapy while definitive treatments
(e.g., steroids, adrenaline) take effect.
Indication: Upper Airway Obstruction:
Heliox is most effective for large, upper airway pathologies (e.g., post-extubation
stridor, tracheal stenosis, extrinsic compression) where high-velocity airflow creates
significant turbulence.
Hypoxemia Limitation:
To maintain the density benefit, the mixture must contain at least 60-70% helium.
This limits the maximum deliverable FiO2 to 0.3-0.4, making it unsuitable for patients with severe concurrent hypoxemia.
Vocal Frequency Shift:
A characteristic side effect is a high-pitched change in voice quality. Sound travels
faster through the lower-density gas, altering the resonant frequency of the vocal
tract.
Reynolds Number and Flow:
The Reynolds number (Re) predicts flow patterns; Re less than 2000 is typically
laminar, while Re greater than 4000 is turbulent. Since Re is directly proportional
to density, Heliox reduces Re, converting high-resistance turbulent flow into lowerresistance laminar flow.
Viscosity vs Density:

Helium is slightly more viscous than air. In distal airways where flow is already laminar (governed by Poiseuille's Law), resistance is proportional to viscosity.
Therefore, Heliox may theoretically increase resistance in the distal airways, explaining its lack of efficacy in pure distal obstruction (e.g., mild asthma).
Nebulisation Efficiency:
Heliox drives jet nebulisers poorly due to its low density, resulting in reduced
aerosol generation. To compensate, driving gas flow rates must be increased (often
to 10-12 L/min) compared to standard air/oxygen.
Ventilator Compatibility:
Standard ventilator flow sensors (hot-wire anemometers or differential pressure
pneumotachographs) are calibrated for air/oxygen. Using Heliox on incompatible
ventilators leads to inaccurate tidal volume monitoring (often over-reading delivered volume) unless a specific Heliox mode is activated.
Therapeutic Role:
Heliox is a temporising measure, not a curative treatment. It reduces the work of
breathing to prevent fatigue and intubation while definitive therapies (e.g., corticosteroids for oedema, antibiotics) take effect.

ليش: الجملة هاي غلط لأن فايدة الـ Heliox بتيجي من قلة كثافته، يعني كثافته تقريباً سبع من كثافة النيتروجين. لما بنخفف الكثافة، ميل التدفق المضطرب بيكفي وبيتحول لتدفق منتظم بقنوات الهواء الضيقة، وبيقلل مجهود التنفس بشكل كبير. بس الـ Heliox ما بيعطي ضغط موجب يسند القصبات إلا إذا اتحط مع الـ CPAP أو الـ NIV.
الفخ: كتير بيفكروا إنه الكثافة الأعلى إلها دور بسند القصبات، وبس هاد بالضبط هو الجملة الخاطئة بالموضوع، والحقيقة الكثافة الأقل هي سبب الفائدة وأهم استخدام إله باختناق الهواء العلوي.

question: A patient has a bloodstream infection with a Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC)-producing carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE). The organism is susceptible to meropenem-vaborbactam. What is the specific mechanism of the vaborbactam component?

options.text: It is a novel cephalosporin with a high affinity for the PBP2a protein.
It is a cyclic boronate-based, non-beta-lactam that inhibits KPC-class
It is a monobactam that is stable to all carbapenemases.
It is an efflux pump inhibitor that prevents the bacteria from pumping
It is a PBP2 enhancer that increases the binding of meropenem.

correctAnswer: It is a cyclic boronate-based, non-beta-lactam that inhibits KPC-class
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Action:
Vaborbactam is a first-in-class, non-beta-lactam beta-lactamase inhibitor based on
a cyclic boronic acid structure. It mimics the transition state of beta-lactam hydrolysis, forming a reversible covalent bond with the active site serine residue of the
beta-lactamase enzyme. This prevents the enzyme from hydrolysing the partner carbapenem (meropenem).
Spectrum of Activity:
Vaborbactam specifically targets Ambler Class A (e.g., KPC) and Class C (e.g.,
AmpC) serine beta-lactamases. Crucially, it does NOT inhibit Class B metallo-betalactamases (e.g., NDM, VIM) or Class D oxacillinases (e.g., OXA-48).
Clinical Application:
The combination is indicated for complicated urinary tract infections, hospital-acquired pneumonia, and bacteraemia caused by Enterobacterales where KPC-mediated resistance is suspected or confirmed.
Clinical Pearl
Mechanism of Action:
Vaborbactam is a cyclic boronic acid derivative that acts as a transition-state analogue, inhibiting serine beta-lactamases (Class A and C).
Reversibility:
Unlike suicide inhibitors (e.g., tazobactam, clavulanic acid) which are irreversible,
vaborbactam forms a reversible covalent bond with the enzyme's active site.
KPC Specificity:
Meropenem-vaborbactam is specifically designed to target KPC (Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase) producers, which are Ambler Class A enzymes.
The OXA-48 Gap:
Vaborbactam lacks activity against OXA-48-like enzymes (Class D), which are common in the UK and Europe. Ceftazidime-avibactam is the preferred agent for OXA48 producers.
Metallo-beta-lactamase Limitation:
Neither vaborbactam nor avibactam inhibits Class B metallo-beta-lactamases (e.g.,
NDM, VIM, IMP).
MBL Treatment Options:
Infections with metallo-beta-lactamases (MBLs) often require cefiderocol or the
combination of aztreonam plus ceftazidime-avibactam (aztreonam is stable to MBLs
but hydrolysed by other enzymes; avibactam protects it).
Renal Elimination:
Both meropenem and vaborbactam are renally excreted. Dosing must be adjusted in
renal impairment to avoid accumulation and potential neurotoxicity (seizures).
TANGO Trials:
The TANGO trials demonstrated that meropenem-vaborbactam was non-inferior to
piperacillin-tazobactam in UTIs and superior to 'best available therapy' for CRE
infections.
AmpC Activity:
Vaborbactam inhibits AmpC beta-lactamases, restoring meropenem activity against
derepressed Enterobacterales (e.g., Enterobacter cloacae).
Structural Mimicry:

The boronic acid moiety mimics the tetrahedral transition state of the beta-lactam
hydrolysis reaction, effectively trapping the enzyme.
Inhibitor Classification:
Vaborbactam is a boronate inhibitor. Avibactam and relebactam are diazabicyclooctane (DBO) inhibitors. Tazobactam, sulbactam, and clavulanate are beta-lactam
sulfones/clams.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ Vaborbactam مركّب مشتق من حمض البورون بحلقة ومش من عائلة الـ beta-lactam، وبيشتغل بمحاكاة الحالة الانتقالية لإنزيم الـ beta-lactamase. بيتكوّن معه رابطة تساهمية قابلة للارتداد بالـ active site، وهيك بيمنع الإنزيم من تحلل الـ meropenem. وبيستهدف بشكل خاص إنزيمات الصنف A مثل الـ KPC والصنف C مثل الـ AmpC.
الفخ: ما تختار إنه مثبط لمضخات الـ efflux أو إنه بيرفع ارتباط الـ meropenem بالـ PBP2a، لأن هدول بيوصفوا أدوية ثانية تمام، والـ Vaborbactam كيمياؤه مختلفة وما بيثبّط الـ metallo-beta-lactamases ولا إنزيمات الـ OXA-48.

question:
A 30-year-old man, who is a survivor of testicular cancer treated with a BEP
(Bleomycin, Etoposide, Cisplatin) regimen, requires an emergent laparotomy for
a bowel obstruction. What is the major anaesthetic and critical care concern for
this patient, related to his prior chemotherapy?

options.text: A high risk of seizures from imipenem.
A high risk of adrenal insufficiency.
A high risk of developing severe, irreversible pulmonary fibrosis when exposed
A high risk of malignant hyperthermia.
A high risk of profound nephrotoxicity from IV contrast.

correctAnswer: A high risk of developing severe, irreversible pulmonary fibrosis when exposed
englishExplanation:
The Bleomycin-Oxygen Interaction:
Bleomycin induces pulmonary toxicity via the production of superoxide free radicals, causing DNA strand breaks. The lungs are specifically vulnerable due to a deficiency of the inactivating enzyme bleomycin hydrolase. Exposure to high concentrations of inspired oxygen (FiO₂) facilitates further free radical production, acting as a 'second hit' that can precipitate fulminant pulmonary fibrosis or Acute
Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS).
Anaesthetic Management:
The classic teaching dictates minimizing FiO₂ to the lowest level necessary to maintain safe oxygenation (often targeting SpO₂ 88-92% or matching pre-operative
baseline). While recent evidence suggests the risk may be less absolute than historically thought, avoiding hyperoxia remains the standard of care. Fluid restriction is
also advocated to reduce the risk of pulmonary oedema in these susceptible lungs.
BEP Regimen Toxicities:
While Bleomycin affects the lungs, the other components of the BEP regimen have
distinct toxicities relevant to critical care:
•Cisplatin: Highly nephrotoxic (often causing hypomagnesaemia and
hypokalaemia), ototoxic, and neurotoxic. •Etoposide: primarily causes
myelosuppression.
Clinical Pearl

Oxygen Sensitivity:
Avoid hyperoxia. The historical 'Goldiner effect' suggests high FiO₂ precipitates
lung injury via free radical production. Aim for SpO₂ 88-92% or pre-operative baseline rather than 100%, provided tissue oxygenation is adequate.
Dose-Dependent Toxicity:
Toxicity is dose-dependent. A cumulative dose >400,000 units (400 mg) significantly increases the risk of pulmonary fibrosis, although idiosyncratic reactions can
occur at lower doses.
Cisplatin Nephrotoxicity:
The 'C' in BEP (Cisplatin) causes significant nephrotoxicity and electrolyte wasting
(specifically magnesium and potassium), which may complicate perioperative fluid
and electrolyte management.
Pulmonary Function Testing:
A reduction in the Diffusing Capacity of the Lungs for Carbon Monoxide (DLCO) is
the earliest and most sensitive pulmonary function test indicator of bleomycin
toxicity.
Fluid Management:
Patients with prior bleomycin exposure are prone to pulmonary oedema due to impaired lymphatic drainage and capillary leak. A judicious, restrictive fluid strategy is
recommended alongside oxygen limitation.
Mechanism of Toxicity:
Bleomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic that chelates iron and binds to DNA, leading
to single- and double-strand breaks via free radical production.
Enzymatic Deficiency:
The lungs and skin are preferentially targeted because they lack bleomycin hydrolase, the enzyme responsible for inactivating the drug.
Pulmonary Fibrosis Differentials:
Other drugs causing pulmonary fibrosis include amiodarone (phospholipidosis
mechanism), nitrofurantoin (hypersensitivity or oxidant stress), methotrexate (hypersensitivity pneumonitis), and busulfan.
Etoposide Toxicity:
The 'E' in BEP (Etoposide) is primarily associated with myelosuppression (leukopenia and thrombocytopenia), increasing infection and bleeding risk.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: دواء الـ Bleomycin بيتسبب سمية رئية عن طريق إنتاج جذور حرة فوق أكسجينية بتكسر خيوط الـ DNA، والرئتين حساسين خاصة لأنهم ناقصين إنزيم الـ bleomycin hydrolase. التعرض لتركيزات عالية من الأكسجين بيعمل ضربة ثانية ممكن تسبب تليّف رئي حاد أو ARDS. لهيك لازم نحافظ على أقل نسبة أكسجين كفاية مثل SpO2 من 88 ل92، ونقلل السوائل كمان.
الفخ: كتير بيخلطوا بين سمية الـ Bleomycin وبين سمية الـ Cisplatin اللي بتهجم الكلى والسمع، أو بينها وبين نوبات الـ malignant hyperthermia، بس هدول أدوية وأسباب ثانية وما إلها علاقة بالأكسجين.

question:
A 30-year-old healthcare worker from a country where BCG vaccination is routine requires screening for tuberculosis (TB). An Interferon Gamma Release
Assay (IGRA) is performed. Which of the following statements about the IGRA
test is correct?

options.text: A positive IGRA result reliably distinguishes between active TB disease and latent TB infection (LTBI).
The IGRA test is likely to be falsely positive due to the patient's prior BCG
The test measures the amount of interferon-gamma released by T-cells in response to antigens specific to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
A negative IGRA result definitively rules out active TB disease.
The IGRA test directly detects the presence of TB bacteria in the blood.

correctAnswer: The test measures the amount of interferon-gamma released by T-cells in response to antigens specific to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
englishExplanation:
Immunological Basis:
IGRA measures the in vitro release of interferon-gamma by patient T-cells in response to specific Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens. The key antigens utilized
are ESAT-6 (Early Secretory Antigen Target-6) and CFP-10 (Culture Filtrate
Protein-10). These proteins are encoded by the RD1 region of the M. tuberculosis
genome, which is deleted in M. bovis BCG and most environmental non-tuberculous
mycobacteria. Consequently, prior BCG vaccination does not cause false-positive results, making IGRA superior to the Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) in vaccinated
individuals.
Clinical Interpretation:
While highly specific, IGRA cannot distinguish between Latent TB Infection (LTBI)
and active TB disease; both states involve T-cell sensitization. Furthermore, a negative IGRA does not definitively rule out active TB, particularly in patients with profound immunosuppression (e.g., advanced HIV, anti-TNF therapy) who may be anergic and unable to mount an interferon response.

Cross-Reactivity Exceptions:
While IGRA does not cross-react with BCG or most non-tuberculous mycobacteria
(NTM), the RD1 region antigens (ESAT-6 and CFP-10) are present in
Mycobacterium kansasii, Mycobacterium szulgai, and Mycobacterium marinum.
Infection with these specific NTMs can result in a positive IGRA, representing a rare
but important cause of false positives for TB.
Clinical Pearl
BCG Specificity:
IGRA utilizes antigens (ESAT-6 and CFP-10) absent from the BCG vaccine strain.
Unlike the Tuberculin Skin Test (TST), IGRA specificity is unaffected by prior BCG
vaccination.
Differentiation Limitation:
A positive IGRA or TST only indicates TB infection. It requires clinical, radiographic, and microbiological evaluation to determine if the infection is active or
latent.
Sensitivity in Active Disease:
A negative IGRA does not exclude active TB, especially in a symptomatic or immunocompromised patient.
Measures Immune Memory:
IGRAs are a test of T-cell memory to TB antigens.
Preferred for LTBI Screening:
NICE NG33 recommends IGRA as the primary screening test for LTBI in adults
who have moved from high-incidence countries or have had BCG vaccination, replacing the two-step TST approach in many cohorts.
Indeterminate Results:
IGRA tests include a 'Mitogen' positive control tube. If T-cells fail to react to the mitogen (e.g., due to severe immunosuppression or lymphopenia), the result is
'Indeterminate', meaning the test is non-diagnostic rather than negative.
Window Period:
Like the TST, IGRA may be negative in the first 8 weeks following initial infection
(the window period) before cellular immunity is fully established.
Specific NTM Cross-Reactivity:
Although IGRA is highly specific for M. tuberculosis complex, false positives can occur with M. kansasii, M. szulgai, and M. marinum, as these organisms also express
ESAT-6 and CFP-10.
Sample Viability Requirements:

IGRA relies on the active secretion of interferon-gamma by living T-cells. Blood
samples require prompt processing or incubation (typically within 16 hours) to prevent lymphocyte death and false-negative or indeterminate results.
Test Components:
Standard IGRAs utilize three tubes: a 'Nil' tube (negative control to measure background interferon), a 'TB Antigen' tube (ESAT-6/CFP-10), and a 'Mitogen' tube
(positive control to confirm T-cell viability).
Methodological Variants:
Two main commercial assays exist: QuantiFERON-TB (uses ELISA to measure interferon concentration in whole blood) and T-SPOT.TB (uses ELISPOT to count the
number of interferon-secreting T-cells).

ليش: فحص الـ IGRA بيقاس فيه كمية الـ interferon-gamma اللي بتنطلق من خلايا الـ T عند التعرض لمستضدات خاصة بـ Mycobacterium tuberculosis مثل ESAT-6 وCFP-10. هاي البروتينات مش موجودة بجينوم الـ M. bovis BCG ولا بالنتايج البيئية، عشان هيك تطعيم الـ BCG ما بيسبب نتيجة كاذبة إيجابية، ولهيك الـ IGRA أفضل من الـ TST بمرضى تطعّموا سابقاً.
الفخ: ما تفتكر إنه النتيجة الإيجابية بتفرّق بين العدوى الكامنة والمرض النشط، ولا إنه السلباني بيستبعد المرض نهائياً، خصوصاً بمرضى الـ HIV المتقدمة أو اللي بياخدوا مضادات الـ TNF لأنهم ممكن يكونوا بحالة خمول مناعي.

question: In continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), the filtration fraction is typically kept below what percentage to minimize the risk of filter clotting?
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology:
Filtration Fraction (FF) represents the proportion of plasma water removed from
blood as it traverses the haemofilter. A high FF (>25%) causes significant haemoconcentration within the hollow fibres, increasing blood viscosity and promoting
protein deposition (concentration polarization) on the membrane surface. This is a
primary mechanical cause of premature filter clotting.
Calculation:
FF is calculated as the ratio of ultrafiltration rate (Q_UF) to plasma flow rate (Q_P).
FF = Q_UF / Q_P
Where Q_P = Q_Blood * (1 - Haematocrit).
In clinical practice, maintaining FF < 20-25% is the standard target to balance
clearance efficiency with filter patency.
Management:
If FF is elevated (>25%), it can be reduced by increasing the blood flow rate (Q_B),
decreasing the replacement fluid rate, or switching to/increasing the proportion of
pre-dilution replacement fluid.
Mechanism of Pre-dilution:
Pre-dilution involves adding replacement fluid to the blood before it enters the filter. This lowers the haematocrit and protein concentration of the blood entering the
hollow fibres, thereby reducing the effective filtration fraction and minimizing the
risk of clotting. However, this dilutes the solute concentration available for clearance, reducing the overall efficiency of the therapy compared to post-dilution.
Clinical Pearl
High FF Risks:
High filtration fractions cause intraluminal haemoconcentration and protein caking
on the membrane, directly leading to filter thrombosis.

Target FF < 25%:
Maintain Filtration Fraction (FF) < 20–25% in post-dilution CVVH to optimize filter patency.
How to Lower the FF:
To lower FF, increase the blood flow rate (Q_B) or decrease the convective volume
(replacement fluid rate).
Predilution:
Predilution replacement fluid dilutes blood entering the filter, reducing FF and clotting risk, but reduces solute clearance efficiency compared to post-dilution.
Filtration Fraction Formula:
Calculate FF using: FF (%) = [Q_Ultrafiltrate / (Q_Blood (1 - Haematocrit))] 100.
Blood Flow Dependency:
Post-dilution CVVH requires higher blood flow rates to support convective clearance without exceeding the 25% FF limit.
Haematocrit Impact:
A higher haematocrit reduces the plasma volume available for a given blood flow
rate. Therefore, patients with polycythaemia or those receiving red cell transfusions
may require higher blood flow rates or lower ultrafiltration rates to maintain a safe
filtration fraction.
Concentration Polarization:
This phenomenon occurs when retained solutes and proteins accumulate at the
membrane surface, forming a 'secondary membrane'. This increases resistance to
flow and is accelerated by high filtration fractions.
Clearance Efficiency:
Post-dilution is the most efficient mode for solute clearance because ultrafiltration
occurs at the undiluted plasma concentration. Pre-dilution reduces the concentration gradient, requiring higher fluid volumes to achieve the same solute removal.
Dilution Factor:
When using pre-dilution, the prescribed dose of dialysis/hemofiltration must be
corrected for the dilution effect. The dilution factor is calculated as Q_blood /
(Q_blood + Q_predilution).
arabicExplanation:

question: A flow-volume loop from a patient's spirometry test shows a 'coved' or 'scoopedout' appearance of the expiratory limb. This pattern is the classic hallmark of:

options.text: Obstructive lung disease (e.g., COPD or asthma)
Fixed upper airway obstruction (e.g., tracheal stenosis)
Variable extrathoracic obstruction (e.g., vocal cord paralysis)

correctAnswer: Obstructive lung disease (e.g., COPD or asthma)
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology of Obstructive Pattern:
In obstructive lung disease (e.g., COPD, asthma), pathophysiology involves increased airway resistance and, in COPD, loss of elastic recoil. During forced expiration, dynamic compression of the airways occurs earlier than normal. While Peak
Expiratory Flow (PEF) may be preserved or only mildly reduced, flow rates drop
precipitously as lung volume decreases. This creates the characteristic concave,
'coved', or 'scooped-out' appearance of the descending expiratory limb.
Comparison with Other Patterns:
Restrictive disease is characterized by a 'witch's hat' appearance: a tall, narrow loop
with a steep descending limb due to increased elastic recoil. Fixed upper airway obstruction causes flattening of both inspiratory and expiratory limbs (box shape).
Variable extrathoracic obstruction flattens the inspiratory limb, while variable intrathoracic obstruction flattens the expiratory limb.
Clinical Pearl

Obstructive Pattern Morphology:
The classic 'scooped-out' or concave descending expiratory limb indicates lower airway obstruction, driven by dynamic airway compression.
Restrictive Pattern Morphology:
Restrictive disease often presents as a 'witch's hat' shape: a tall, narrow loop with a
steep descending expiratory limb, reflecting increased elastic recoil and preserved
flow relative to the reduced lung volume.
Fixed Upper Airway Obstruction:
Flattening of both the inspiratory and expiratory limbs creates a rectangular or 'box'
shape, seen in conditions like tracheal stenosis or goitre.
Variable Extrathoracic Obstruction:
Flattening of the inspiratory limb (bottom of loop) occurs because negative intratracheal pressure during inspiration collapses the extrathoracic airway (e.g., vocal cord
paralysis).
Variable Intrathoracic Obstruction:
Flattening of the expiratory limb (top of loop) occurs because positive pleural pressure during forced expiration compresses the intrathoracic airway (e.g.,
tracheomalacia).
Neuromuscular Weakness Pattern:
Respiratory muscle weakness produces a small, rounded 'globular' loop with symmetrical reduction in both inspiratory and expiratory flows and volumes.
Saw-Tooth Pattern:
Rapid oscillations or a 'saw-tooth' appearance on the flow-volume loop typically indicate upper airway instability (e.g., obstructive sleep apnoea) or secretion
retention.
Equal Pressure Point (EPP) Migration:
In emphysema, loss of elastic recoil lowers alveolar pressure, causing the EPP to migrate distally into collapsible non-cartilaginous airways. This results in dynamic airway compression and the characteristic scooped appearance.
Effort Independence:
The descending limb of the expiratory loop is effort-independent. Once peak flow is
reached, increasing expiratory effort increases intrathoracic pressure, which compresses airways further and limits flow (Starling resistor effect).
FEF 25-75% Sensitivity:
Forced Expiratory Flow at 25-75% of vital capacity is the most sensitive indicator of
early small airway obstruction, often showing reduction before FEV1 changes.
Reversibility Criteria:

Significant bronchodilator reversibility is defined as an increase in FEV1 or FVC of
at least 12% AND 200 mL.
Mixed Defect Appearance:
Combined obstructive and restrictive disease (e.g., COPD plus pulmonary fibrosis)
shows a loop that is both narrow (reduced volume) and scooped (obstructive
morphology).
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الشكل المقعر أو المشطوف بطرف الزفير بيظهر بأمراض الانسداد مثل الـ COPD والربو، لأن مقاومة الهواء بتزيد وبيصير انضغاض ديناميكي مبكر للقصبات. النتيجة إن التدفق بيهوي بسرعة كل ما بتنزل حجم الرئة، فيظهر شكل النقر أو الـ scooped-out الكلاسيكي. وهاد بيميّزه عن التشبيه الصندوقي اللي بيمثل الانسداد الثابت للهواء العلوي.
الفخ: ما تاخذ شكل الـ witch's hat اللي بيمثل أمراض القيود، ولا تفتكر إنه تشويه الزفير بيعبر عن مشكلة بالهواء العلوي، لأن الانسداد الثابت بيسوي تسطيح للطرفين معاً مش نقر بس.

question:
A patient with a fungal infection is started on a conventional (deoxycholate) amphotericin B infusion. 30 minutes into the infusion, the patient develops high
fever, rigors, and chills. What is the mechanism of this "shake and bake"
reaction?

options.text: A direct neurotoxic effect of the drug.
The rapid lysis of fungal cells.
A direct, non-allergic stimulation of host immune cells, leading to a massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines.

correctAnswer: A direct, non-allergic stimulation of host immune cells, leading to a massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Reaction:
The classic "shake and bake" infusion-related reaction to conventional amphotericin
B deoxycholate is a non-allergic, cytokine-mediated response. The drug binds to
Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) and CD14 on host monocytes and macrophages. This interaction triggers the transcription and massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, specifically Tumour Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-alpha), Interleukin-1 (IL-1),
and Interleukin-6 (IL-6), alongside Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2). These mediators act
on the hypothalamus to elevate the thermoregulatory set-point, resulting in fever,
chills, and rigors.
Clinical Context:
This reaction typically occurs 1-3 hours after starting the infusion. While alarming,
it is distinct from IgE-mediated anaphylaxis (Type I hypersensitivity) and does not
usually require cessation of therapy if managed with premedication and slower infusion rates, unlike true anaphylaxis.
Clinical Pearl
Pre-medication is Key:
Pre-medication is standard practice for conventional amphotericin. The typical regimen includes Paracetamol 1g, an antihistamine (e.g., Chlorphenamine 10mg IV),
and often Hydrocortisone 25-50mg IV administered 30 minutes prior to the
infusion.

Pethidine for Rigors:
Pethidine (25-50 mg IV) is the specific pharmacological treatment for amphotericin-induced rigors that persist despite premedication. It acts on kappa-opioid
receptors to reduce the shivering threshold.
Lipid Formulations are Much Better:
The lipid-based formulations of amphotericin (liposomal, lipid complex) are associated with a dramatically lower incidence and severity of these infusion reactions, in
addition to their lower nephrotoxicity.
A "Test Dose" is Historical:
The old practice of giving a 1 mg "test dose" is no longer recommended as it does
not reliably predict severe reactions.
Saline Loading for Nephroprotection:
Amphotericin B causes afferent renal arteriolar vasoconstriction. Administering
500-1000 mL of 0.9% Sodium Chloride prior to the infusion (sodium loading) helps
mitigate the reduction in GFR and nephrotoxicity.
Electrolyte Wasting:
The drug increases distal tubular membrane permeability, leading to severe potassium and magnesium wasting. Daily monitoring and aggressive replacement of K+
and Mg2+ are mandatory during therapy.
Dosing Safety Alert:
Prescribing errors between formulations are fatal. Conventional Amphotericin B
(Fungizone) is dosed at 0.5-1.0 mg/kg/day. Liposomal Amphotericin B (AmBisome)
is dosed at 3-5 mg/kg/day. Administering a liposomal dose of the conventional drug
will cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias.
Mechanism of Action:
Amphotericin B is a polyene antifungal that binds to ergosterol in the fungal cell
membrane, forming pores that cause leakage of intracellular ions and cell death. It
has a higher affinity for ergosterol than human cholesterol, providing selectivity,
though some cholesterol binding still occurs and contributes to toxicity.
Distal Renal Tubular Acidosis:
The electrolyte wasting is caused by amphotericin-induced pore formation in the
distal tubule epithelium, creating a Type 1 (distal) Renal Tubular Acidosis. This
leads to hydrogen ion retention and severe potassium and magnesium wasting.

ليش: رد الفعل هون مش حساسية، الدواء بيرتبط بمستقبلات الـ TLR2 والـ CD14 على الخلايا البلعمية وبيطلق كمية ضخمة من السيتوكينات الالتهابية مثل TNF-alpha وIL-1 وIL-6. هدول المؤثرات بتشتغل على الوطاء وترفع نقطة ضبط حرارة الجسم، فتصير حمى ورжفة بعد ساعة لثلاث من بدء الحقن. والمعالجة المسبقة مثل Paracetamol وHydrocortisone مع إبطاء الحقن بتساعد كتير.
الفخ: ما تفتكر إنه حساسية من الصنف الأول بتستدعي إقلاع الدواء فوراً، ولا تفتكر إنه تفاعل بسيط بيتسبب بتحلل سريع لخلايا الفطريات، لأن الفعل هون على الجهاز المناعي مباشرة بدون أجسام مضادة من الـ IgE.

question: A patient on long-term sertraline is commenced on linezolid for a VRE wound infection. What is the PRIMARY pharmacological concern?

options.text: QTc prolongation from combined serotonergic and ion channel effects
Serotonin syndrome due to linezolid's reversible MAO inhibition combined with
Reduced linezolid efficacy due to CYP2D6 induction by sertraline
Bone marrow suppression from additive myelotoxicity
Hypertensive crisis from linezolid's irreversible MAO inhibition

correctAnswer: Serotonin syndrome due to linezolid's reversible MAO inhibition combined with
englishExplanation:
Why This Matters:
Linezolid is increasingly used in the ICU for VRE and MRSA infections. Its off-target activity as a reversible MAO inhibitor creates a clinically significant interaction
with all serotonergic drugs — an interaction that is frequently overlooked and can
be fatal if unrecognised.
Analysis of Each Option:
Option A — QTc prolongation:
INCORRECT as the primary concern. While some serotonergic drugs can affect QTc
(e.g., citalopram), the direct pharmacodynamic interaction between linezolid and
sertraline is serotonin syndrome via MAO inhibition + SERT blockade. QTc monitoring is not the primary concern with this combination.

Option B — Serotonin syndrome:
CORRECT. Linezolid inhibits MAO-A reversibly. MAO-A normally degrades serotonin in the synaptic cleft. Sertraline blocks the serotonin reuptake transporter
(SERT), increasing synaptic serotonin. Combined, these two mechanisms dramatically increase synaptic serotonin levels, risking serotonin syndrome.
Option C — CYP2D6 induction by sertraline:
INCORRECT. Sertraline is a CYP2D6 inhibitor (not inducer). More importantly,
linezolid is NOT primarily metabolised by CYP450 enzymes — it undergoes non-enzymatic oxidative morpholine ring opening. CYP-mediated interaction is not the
primary clinical concern here.
Option D — Additive myelotoxicity:
INCORRECT as the primary concern. Linezolid does cause dose-dependent myelosuppression (thrombocytopaenia, leucopaenia) through mitochondrial inhibition.
However, SSRIs do not cause bone marrow suppression, so additive myelotoxicity is
not relevant here.
Option E — Irreversible MAO inhibition → hypertensive crisis:
INCORRECT. Linezolid causes REVERSIBLE MAO inhibition — not irreversible.
Irreversible MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) cause hypertensive crises with
tyramine-containing foods. Linezolid's reversible inhibition does not carry the same
tyramine restriction requirement in short courses, though serotonin syndrome risk
with serotonergic drugs remains.
Management:
If linezolid is essential, sertraline should ideally be stopped 2 weeks before commencing (or as early as practically possible). Monitor closely for features of serotonin syndrome: clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, hyperthermia.
Clinical Pearl
Linezolid as a MAOI:
Linezolid inhibits monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A) in a reversible, non-selective
manner. This is an off-target effect from its oxazolidinone structure. It does not require dietary tyramine restrictions in short-term use, unlike irreversible MAOIs.
Serotonin Syndrome Triad:
The classic Hunter Criteria triad is: (1) neuromuscular excitability — clonus (especially inducible or ocular), hyperreflexia, tremor, myoclonus; (2) autonomic instability — hyperthermia, tachycardia, diaphoresis, hypertension; (3) altered mental
status — agitation, confusion.
Clonus is Key:

Inducible clonus (particularly at the ankle) is the most sensitive and specific single
finding for serotonin syndrome. Its presence in the context of serotonergic drug use
should prompt immediate clinical concern and drug cessation.
Hunter vs Sternbach Criteria:
The Hunter Criteria (sensitivity 84%, specificity 97%) outperform the older
Sternbach Criteria (sensitivity 75%, specificity 96%) for diagnosing serotonin syndrome. Hunter Criteria explicitly require clonus, hyperreflexia, or tremor for
diagnosis.
Differentiation from NMS:
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) and serotonin syndrome are frequently
confused. Key differences: onset (hours for SS, days–weeks for NMS), motor findings ('cogwheel/lead pipe' rigidity and bradyreflexia in NMS vs clonus and hyperreflexia in SS), and causative drug class (antipsychotics vs serotonergic agents).
Management:
Stop all serotonergic agents immediately. Benzodiazepines are first-line for agitation and seizure prevention. Cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist, 8 mg orally) can
be used as a serotonin antagonist. Severe hyperthermia (>41°C) requires sedation,
intubation, and active cooling.
ICU-Relevant Drug Combinations:
High-risk combinations in the ICU include: linezolid + SSRIs, linezolid + tramadol,
fentanyl (weak SERT inhibitor) + MAOIs, methadone + SSRIs, and methylene blue
(potent MAO inhibitor) + SSRIs. Methylene blue is used for methaemoglobinaemia
and this interaction is well-documented.
Irreversible MAOIs:
Phenelzine and tranylcypromine are irreversible MAO inhibitors. Their interaction
with tyramine-containing foods (aged cheese, cured meats) causes a hypertensive
crisis — not serotonin syndrome. This is a distinct mechanism from linezolid's reversible MAO inhibition.
Linezolid Myelotoxicity:
Separate from serotonin syndrome, linezolid causes dose- and duration-dependent
thrombocytopaenia, anaemia, and leucopaenia through mitochondrial ribosomal inhibition. FBC should be monitored weekly on linezolid; courses should not exceed
28 days without haematological review.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ linezolid بينثبط بعمق عن إنزيم الـ MAO-A، وبردو الـ sertraline بتسد ناقل إعادة امتصاص السيروتونين الـ SERT، والاثنين مع بعض بيرفعوا السيروتونين بالشق المشبكي بشكل كبير. لهيك الخطر الأساسي هو متلازمة السيروتونين مش أمراض القلب ولا خلل الإنزيمات. وكمان الـ linezolid ما بيتفسر بشكل أساسي عبر إنزيمات الـ CYP450.
الفخ: الطلاب غالباً بيختاروا مشكلة الـ QTc أو قصور النخاع، بس هدول مش المخاطرة الأساسية بهالجمع، والـ linezolid منثبط MAO قابل للعكس مش لا قابل للعكس، والمشكلة الأصلية هي السيروتونين.

question:
A patient with a severe TBI is being monitored with a cerebral microdialysis
catheter. The lab reports a lactate/pyruvate (L/P) ratio of 45. What is the most
likely interpretation of this finding?

options.text: It indicates a state of cerebral hyperemia.
It indicates a state of mitochondrial dysfunction or cerebral ischemia.
It suggests the presence of a non-convulsive seizure.
It is a marker of cerebral vasospasm.

correctAnswer: It indicates a state of mitochondrial dysfunction or cerebral ischemia.
englishExplanation:
Physiological Basis:
The lactate/pyruvate (L/P) ratio reflects the cytoplasmic redox state (NADH/NAD+
ratio). Under aerobic conditions, pyruvate enters the Krebs cycle. In anaerobic conditions or mitochondrial failure, pyruvate is converted to lactate, elevating the ratio.
Diagnostic Thresholds:
According to the International Microdialysis Forum consensus: Normal L/P ratio is
< 25. A ratio > 25 suggests metabolic burden, and > 40 indicates a severe metabolic
crisis.
Differentiating Causes:
A high L/P ratio (> 40) signifies energy failure but does not identify the cause. It
must be paired with Brain Tissue Oxygen (PbtO2) monitoring:
1. High L/P + Low PbtO2 (< 20 mmHg) = Ischemia (anaerobic metabolism).
2. High L/P + Normal/High PbtO2 = Mitochondrial Dysfunction (inability to utilize
oxygen).
Clinical Pearl
High L/P = Brain Energy Crisis:
This is the key interpretation. A ratio over 40 indicates a severe metabolic disturbance at the cellular level.
L/P Ratio Thresholds:
Normal L/P ratio is < 25. Values between 25-40 indicate metabolic distress. Values
> 40 confirm a severe metabolic crisis.
Pattern 1: True Ischemia:
Elevated L/P ratio (> 40) combined with low PbtO2 (< 20 mmHg) indicates classical ischemia where oxygen supply is insufficient for metabolic demand.
Pattern 2: Mitochondrial Dysfunction:
Elevated L/P ratio (> 40) combined with normal or elevated PbtO2 indicates mitochondrial failure (uncoupling), often seen in TBI even with adequate perfusion.
Aerobic Glycolysis (Hypermetabolism):

Elevated Lactate with a NORMAL L/P ratio (< 25) indicates hyperglycolysis (accelerated aerobic metabolism), which is often a compensatory mechanism and not necessarily harmful.
Neuroglycopenia:
Cerebral microdialysis glucose < 0.7 mmol/L is a critical marker of neuroglycopenia, which may occur independently of systemic blood glucose levels.
Glutamate as a Toxicity Marker:
Glutamate is the primary excitatory neurotransmitter. Sustained elevations (> 20
µmol/L) indicate excitotoxicity and impending cellular death.
Catheter Placement Matters:
Microdialysis is a regional monitor. The 'gold standard' placement is in the pericontusional penumbra (tissue at risk) rather than healthy tissue or the necrotic core.
Lactate vs L/P Ratio Specificity:
Do not confuse high lactate with metabolic crisis. High lactate alone can result from
hyperglycolysis (good prognosis). The L/P ratio is the specific discriminator: if the
ratio rises, the redox state has shifted to anaerobic metabolism or failure.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: النسبة بين اللاكتات والبيروفات بتعكس الحالة الأيضية بالخلية، ولما بتعدي 25 بصير في أزمة أيضية، وفوق 40 معناها أزمة طاقة خلوية حادة. هاي النسبة 45 بتشير إما لنقص أكسجة دماغية أو لخلل بقدرة الميتوكوندريا على استهلاك الأكسجين. وعشان نفرّق بين الحالتين لازم نشوف الـ PbtO2 معها: إذا منخفض معناها إقفار، وإذا طبيعي معناها خلل ميتوكوندري.
الفخ: ما تقول إنه طبيعي أو إنه علامة على ارتشاح الأوعية الدماغية أو نوبة صرع غير متشنجة، لأن النسبة فوق 40 بتشير لأزمة طاقة خلوية بالمخ بكل الحالات.

question:
A spirometry result shows a flow-volume loop that is tall and narrow, with a reduced total volume (FVC) but preserved or even supranormal flow rates for the
given lung volumes. The FEV₁/FVC ratio is high (>0.85). This 'witch's hat' appearance is classic for:

options.text: Restrictive lung disease (e.g., sarcoidosis or pulmonary fibrosis)

correctAnswer: Restrictive lung disease (e.g., sarcoidosis or pulmonary fibrosis)
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology of Restrictive Patterns:
This flow-volume loop pattern is characteristic of parenchymal restrictive lung disease (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis). The primary pathology is decreased lung compliance
('stiff lungs') leading to reduced Total Lung Capacity (TLC) and Functional Vital
Capacity (FVC).
Mechanism of the 'Witch's Hat':
The 'witch's hat' appearance results from the combination of reduced volume (narrow loop) and increased radial traction on airways. In parenchymal fibrosis, the increased elastic recoil keeps airways open and drives rapid expiration. Flow rates are

supranormal for the given lung volume, creating a tall, steep expiratory limb. The
FEV1/FVC ratio is typically preserved or elevated (>0.80-0.85).
Differential Diagnosis:
While both parenchymal and extraparenchymal causes (e.g., chest wall deformity,
neuromuscular weakness) cause restriction, the 'witch's hat' morphology is specific
to parenchymal disease due to high elastic recoil. Extraparenchymal restriction typically produces a 'miniature normal' loop where flow rates are reduced in proportion
to volume.
Clinical Pearl
Characteristic Morphology:
The 'witch's hat' appearance is pathognomonic for parenchymal restrictive disease.
It is defined by a narrow width (reduced volume) and a tall, steep expiratory limb
(preserved flow).
Spirometric Criteria:
In restriction, both FEV1 and FVC are reduced, but FVC is reduced proportionately
more. This results in a preserved or increased FEV1/FVC ratio (>0.75-0.80), unlike
the reduced ratio seen in obstruction.
High Elastic Recoil:
The stiff lungs 'snap back' quickly during expiration, which explains the high flow
rates relative to volume.
Causes of Restriction:
Distinguish parenchymal from extraparenchymal restriction. Parenchymal disease
(fibrosis) shows the tall 'witch's hat' due to high recoil. Extraparenchymal causes
(chest wall, neuromuscular) show a 'miniature normal' loop with normal recoil.
Full PFTs Needed:
Spirometry only suggests restriction. Definitive diagnosis requires static lung volumes demonstrating a Total Lung Capacity (TLC) below the 5th percentile of predicted (or <80% predicted).
Fixed vs Variable Obstruction:
Contrast the 'witch's hat' with upper airway obstruction patterns. Fixed obstruction
(tracheal stenosis) flattens both inspiratory and expiratory limbs (box shape).
Variable extrathoracic obstruction (vocal cord dysfunction) flattens primarily the
inspiratory limb.
Radial Traction Mechanism:
In pulmonary fibrosis, the fibrotic parenchyma exerts increased outward pull on the
airway walls (radial traction). This tethers the airways open, preventing the dynamic collapse seen in emphysema and allowing supranormal expiratory flow rates.

Gas Transfer (DLCO) Differentiation:
DLCO helps distinguish the cause of restriction. In parenchymal disease (fibrosis),
DLCO is reduced due to V/Q mismatch and membrane thickening. In extraparenchymal disease (chest wall deformity, neuromuscular), DLCO is typically normal when corrected for alveolar volume (KCO).
Obstructive Loop Morphology:
Contrast the convex 'witch's hat' with the concave 'scooped-out' expiratory limb of
asthma or COPD. The scooping reflects reduced flow rates at low lung volumes due
to loss of elastic recoil and early airway closure.
Compliance Definition:
Compliance is defined as the change in volume per unit change in pressure.
Restrictive diseases are characterised by low compliance (stiff lungs), requiring
greater pressure gradients to achieve the same tidal volume.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الشكل الطويل والضيق بمنحنى التدفق بيمثل أمراض القيود القلبية مثل الـ pulmonary fibrosis والـ sarcoidosis، لأن الرئة بتصير قاسية وقليلة الامتثال. السحب الشعيري الزايد بينفخ القصبات ويحفّز الزفير السريع، فيصير الحجم الكلي والـ FVC ناقصين بس التدفق بالنسبة للحجم عالي جداً. ولهيك نسبة الـ FEV1/FVC بترتفع فوق 0.85.
الفخ: ما تربط الشكل هاد بالـ emphysema ولا بالربو، لأن هدول بيعطوا منحنى مقرن أو مشطوف، ولا تفتكر إنه التشديد العضلي أو ضعف الأعصاب بيعمل نفس الشكل، لأن هدول بيعطوا منحنى طبيعي مصغّر.

question:
A patient with pneumonia develops a parapneumonic effusion. A diagnostic thoracentesis is performed. Which of the following pleural fluid analysis results is
the strongest indication for immediate insertion of an intercostal drain?

options.text: A clear, straw-colored fluid with a pH of 7.35.
A pleural fluid glucose of 5.5 mmol/L.
A pleural fluid LDH that is 0.4 times the upper limit of normal for serum.
A pleural fluid protein level of 20 g/L.

englishExplanation:
BTS Guideline Criteria:
According to the BTS Pleural Disease Guidelines, the specific indications for intercostal drain insertion in parapneumonic effusion are:
1. Frank pus or turbid fluid (empyema).
2. Presence of organisms identified by Gram stain or culture.
3. Pleural fluid pH < 7.20.
A pH < 7.20 indicates a complicated parapneumonic effusion driven by bacterial
metabolism producing acid. Without drainage, these effusions are unlikely to resolve with antibiotics alone and carry a high risk of loculation and fibrothorax.
Biochemical Analysis:
Pleural fluid glucose < 3.4 mmol/L is also a marker of complicated effusion, but pH
is the preferred primary marker for the decision to drain. Pleural fluid LDH is typically elevated (>1000 IU/L) in pleural infection, but absolute levels are less specific
for the immediate need for drainage compared to pH.
Handling of Samples:
Pleural fluid pH must be measured using a blood gas analyser. The use of litmus paper or pH meters is inaccurate and not recommended by BTS guidelines.
Pathophysiology of Pleural Acidosis:
In complicated parapneumonic effusions, the low pH results from increased metabolic activity of neutrophils and bacteria, which consume glucose and produce lactate and carbon dioxide. Concurrently, inflammation of the pleural membrane reduces the efflux of hydrogen ions from the pleural space. This acidic environment
impairs antibiotic efficacy (particularly aminoglycosides) and promotes fibrin deposition and loculation.
Clinical Pearl
Urgency of Acidosis:
A pleural fluid pH < 7.20 represents a medical emergency requiring prompt
drainage. Delay increases the risk of loculation, fibrothorax, and the need for surgical intervention.
Drainage Indications:

The definitive indications for intercostal drainage in parapneumonic effusion are:
frank pus/turbid fluid, positive Gram stain/culture, or pleural fluid pH < 7.20.
Ultrasound Guidance:
Thoracic ultrasound is mandatory prior to drainage to confirm the fluid pocket,
identify loculations, and reduce the risk of organ injury. It is superior to clinical examination and plain radiography for identifying septations.
Diagnostic Hierarchy:
Parapneumonic effusions are exudates by definition. If Light's criteria suggest a
transudate, alternative aetiologies (e.g., heart failure, cirrhosis) should be reconsidered unless the patient has been diuresed.
Intrapleural Therapy:
For loculated effusions failing simple drainage, combined intrapleural tPA and
DNase (as studied in the MIST-2 trial) significantly improves radiographic clearance and reduces the need for surgical referral compared to either agent alone.
Sample Handling:
Pleural fluid for pH analysis must be collected anaerobically in a heparinised syringe and analysed on a blood gas machine. Litmus paper and standard pH meters
are inaccurate and should not be used.
Simple vs Complicated Effusion:
A 'Simple' parapneumonic effusion is sterile, clear, with pH > 7.20, and typically resolves with antibiotics alone. A 'Complicated' effusion is defined by pH < 7.20, low
glucose (< 3.4 mmol/L), or positive bacteriology, necessitating drainage.
Mechanism of Low pH:
Pleural fluid acidosis is driven by bacterial and neutrophil metabolism producing
lactate and CO2, combined with loculation that prevents the efflux of hydrogen ions.
RAPID Score:
The RAPID score (Renal, Age, Purulence, Infection source, Dietary albumin) helps
stratify mortality risk in patients with pleural infection at presentation.
Antibiotic Penetration:
Most antibiotics (e.g., penicillins, cephalosporins) penetrate the pleural space well.
Aminoglycosides have poor activity in the acidic, hypoxic environment of an
empyema and should generally be avoided.

question:
An anaesthetist is setting the ventilator for a patient with severe COPD. The
patient's respiratory system has a resistance (R) of 20 cmH₂O/L/sec and a compliance (C) of 0.05 L/cmH₂O. What is the calculated time constant (τ) of the respiratory system?
englishExplanation:
Calculation:
The time constant (τ, tau) of the respiratory system is a measure of how quickly the
lungs fill and empty. It is calculated as the product of respiratory system resistance
(R) and compliance (C). The formula is τ = R × C. For this patient, τ = 20
cmH₂O/L/sec × 0.05 L/cmH₂O = 1.0 second.
Clinical Interpretation:
A time constant of 1.0 second is prolonged (normal intubated values are typically
0.5–0.7 seconds). This is characteristic of obstructive lung disease (high resistance)
or emphysema (high compliance). To ensure complete expiration and avoid dynamic hyperinflation (auto-PEEP), the expiratory time (Te) must be sufficient.
Since 95% of volume is exhaled in 3 time constants, this patient requires a Te of at
least 3.0 seconds.
Physiological Mechanism:
Expiration is a passive process driven by the elastic recoil of the lungs and chest
wall, opposed by airway resistance. This follows an exponential decay curve described by the equation V(t) = V0 * e^(-t/tau). This means that for every unit of
time 'tau' that passes, a fixed percentage of the remaining volume is exhaled. This
explains why patients with high resistance (large tau) require significantly longer
expiratory times to achieve the same degree of lung emptying as healthy patients.
Clinical Pearl
Tau = R × C:
This is a fundamental equation of respiratory mechanics.
Long Tau = Obstruction:
A long time constant (due to high resistance, as in asthma/COPD) means the patient is a "slow filler, slow emptier." They need a long expiratory time to avoid autoPEEP.
Short Tau = Restriction:
A short time constant (due to low compliance, as in ARDS/fibrosis) means the patient is a "fast filler, fast emptier." They can tolerate higher respiratory rates.
Setting the I:E Ratio:
Ventilator settings must respect tau. In ARDS (short tau), short expiratory time (Te)
allows higher rates. In COPD (long tau), extended Te is mandatory to prevent air
trapping, often requiring a lower respiratory rate or lower I:E ratio (e.g., 1:4).
Regional Variation:
Different parts of a diseased lung can have different regional time constants, leading
to V/Q mismatch.
The 3-Tau Rule:
Expiration follows an exponential decay curve. 1 time constant allows 63% exhalation, 2 allow 86.5%, 3 allow 95%, and 5 allow >99%. Clinical practice targets an expiratory time of at least 3 time constants to minimize intrinsic PEEP.
Units of Measurement:
Resistance is measured in cmH2O/L/sec. Compliance is measured in L/cmH2O.
Multiplying these cancels the pressure and volume units, leaving time in seconds.
Endotracheal Tube Resistance:
A significant component of resistance in intubated patients comes from the ETT itself. According to Poiseuille's Law, resistance is inversely proportional to the radius
to the power of 4. A smaller tube significantly increases resistance and therefore
prolongs the time constant.
Auto-PEEP Detection:
If expiratory time is less than 3 time constants, incomplete emptying occurs. This is
best detected on the ventilator flow-time scalar: the expiratory flow trace will not return to the zero baseline before the next inspiratory breath begins.

Frequency Dependence of Compliance:
In heterogeneous lungs (e.g., COPD), 'fast' alveoli (short tau) fill quickly, while
'slow' alveoli (long tau) fill slowly. As respiratory rate increases, slow units may not
have time to fill completely, causing the measured dynamic compliance to decrease
relative to static compliance.
Calculating Max Respiratory Rate:
To determine the maximum safe respiratory rate for a COPD patient, calculate the
required cycle time. If tau is 1.0s, required Te is 3.0s. If Ti is set to 1.0s, total cycle
time is 4.0s. Max RR = 60 / 4 = 15 breaths/min.

question:
Which of the following physiological changes is most characteristic of REM sleep
compared to NREM sleep?

options.text: A stable, slow heart rate and blood pressure.
An active, desynchronised EEG pattern similar to wakefulness.

correctAnswer: An active, desynchronised EEG pattern similar to wakefulness.
englishExplanation:
EEG Characteristics:
REM sleep is termed 'paradoxical sleep' because the EEG demonstrates low-amplitude, high-frequency, desynchronised beta-like waves, indistinguishable from the
awake state. This contrasts with the high-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves
seen in NREM Stage N3 (Slow Wave Sleep).
Autonomic Physiology:
NREM sleep is characterised by high vagal tone, resulting in a stable, slow heart
rate, regular rhythmic breathing, and reduced blood pressure. Conversely, REM
sleep features significant autonomic instability with fluctuating heart rate, blood
pressure, and respiratory rate due to phasic bursts of sympathetic activity.
Hormonal and Muscle Changes:
Growth hormone secretion peaks during NREM N3 (Slow Wave Sleep), not REM.
REM sleep is characterised by profound skeletal muscle atonia (excluding extraocular and diaphragm muscles) mediated by glycine inhibition of alpha-motor neurons
in the spinal cord.
Clinical Pearl
Paradoxical Sleep Definition:

REM sleep is defined by an active, awake-like EEG (desynchronised) occurring simultaneously with profound skeletal muscle atonia.
NREM Physiological Role:
Deep NREM sleep (slow-wave sleep) is associated with physical repair and growth
hormone release.
REM Cognitive Role:
REM sleep is thought to be critical for memory consolidation, learning, and emotional processing.
Autonomic Instability:
The variability in heart rate, blood pressure, and breathing during REM sleep can be
a period of risk for individuals with underlying cardiovascular disease.
Dreaming Physiology:
The vivid, story-like dreams we remember are almost exclusively from REM sleep.
Thermoregulation in REM:
Thermoregulatory responses (shivering and sweating) are suspended during REM
sleep, making the body poikilothermic; this is particularly relevant in critically ill
patients with environmental exposure.
Upper Airway Tone:
The muscle atonia of REM sleep affects the upper airway dilators (e.g., genioglossus), significantly increasing the risk of airway obstruction and apnoea, particularly
in patients with OSA or post-extubation.
Sedation and Sleep Architecture:
Common ICU sedatives (benzodiazepines, opioids, propofol) typically suppress both
REM and Slow Wave Sleep (N3), leading to non-restorative sleep and potential
'REM rebound' with vivid nightmares upon withdrawal.
Neural Control of REM:
Cholinergic neurons in the pontine tegmentum initiate REM sleep, while noradrenergic (locus coeruleus) and serotonergic (raphe nuclei) inputs inhibit it; this explains why antidepressants (SSRIs/SNRIs) often suppress REM sleep.
Sleep Spindles and K-Complexes:
These EEG features are characteristic of Stage N2 NREM sleep, which constitutes
the majority (45-55%) of total sleep time in adults.
Sleep Cycle Architecture:
A typical sleep cycle lasts 90-120 minutes, with the duration of REM sleep episodes
increasing in successive cycles throughout the night.
