question: A 47-year-old man with advanced cirrhosis presents with altered mental status, including lethargy, disorientation, and slurred speech. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse rate is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/87 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical examination shows tenderness to palpation of the abdomen and the presence of asterixis. Laboratory studies show evidence of chronic but stable liver disease and an elevated serum ammonia level. Administration of which of the following agents is most likely to have the greatest effect on improving this patient's mental status?
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
A. Bisacodyl
Lactulose
Bisacodyl (diphenylmethane) is a stimulant that increases intestinal motility by increasing peristaltic contractions. While this drug may decrease absorption of ammonia in the gut due to increased transit time, it is not considered a first-line treatment for hepatic encephalopathy.
B. Lactulose
This patient has signs and symptoms of hepatic encephalopathy, a reversible syndrome of altered mental status caused by impaired clearance of substances toxic to
the brain. Due to portal hypertension, blood flow is shunted away from the liver
which results in decreased clearance of neurotoxins. Ammonia is a major substance
that contributes to the development of hepatic encephalopathy. Ammonia is generated in the intestines by the breakdown of protein and urea by intestinal bacteria.
Lactulose is metabolized into fatty acids by the intestinal bacteria which lowers the
PH. The more acidic colon converts NH3 to NH4+, which is unabsorbable. Thus,
the NH4+ is excreted in the stool, thereby reducing the plasma levels of NH3.
Lactulose also works as a cathartic, and increases transit time thus limiting the ability of NH3 to be absorbed.
Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430869/
C. N-acetylcysteine
N-acetylcysteine is a drug used to prevent or lessen hepatic injury after an acetaminophen overdose. N-acetylcysteine substitutes glutathione, and binds the toxic
metabolite of acetaminophen, thus inactivating and detoxifying it. It would not be
useful in this scenario.
D. Spironolactone
Spironolactone competes with aldosterone receptor sites in the distal renal tubules,
thereby increasing sodium chloride and water excretion while conserving potassium
and hydrogen ions. This drug is used for the treatment of edema associated with
congestive heart failure, ascites due to cirrhosis of the liver, nephrotic syndrome,
hypertension, and other conditions. It is not a primary treatment for hepatic
encephalopathy.

question: A 55-year-old male with a history of gallstones presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain for the past 24 hrs. question: A 32-year-old woman who works in the toddler room of a daycare presents with four episodes of foul-smelling diarrhea over the past two weeks. She says the stools are greasy and float in the toilet water. The patient also has had fatigue, loss of appetite, weight loss, abdominal pain and cramping, and flatulence during this time. She takes no medications, and there is no history of recent antibiotic use or travel. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following laboratory studies is most likely to be abnormal?

options.text: Ova and parasite examination of the stool
Polymerase chain reaction for Clostridioides difficile toxin

correctAnswer: Ova and parasite examination of the stool
englishExplanation:
Ova and parasite examination of the stool
Expl anation
A. Fecal leukocytes
This patient has giardiasis. Fecal leukocytes are not found with this infection. The
presence of fecal leukocytes suggests colitis, which may be allergic, infectious, or
due to inflammatory bowel disease.
B. Ova and parasite examination of the stool
This patient has giardiasls, most likely contracted while changing diapers at the day
care center where she works. Foul-smelling, greasy stools that float are characteristic of Giardia species. Stool testing for ova and parasites performed on three separate specimens taken on different days result in a 90% identification rate of trophozoites or cysts. Ingestion of contaminated water while camping or traveling is another common source of Giardia infection.
Reference: https://mvw.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513239/
C. Polymerase chain reaction for Clostridioides difficile toxin
Stool samples can be tested by ELISA or PCR for C. difficile toxin; PCR is more sen-
Sitive and specific. This is a young patient who does not have a history of hospitalization or recent antibiotic use, making C. difficile infection unlikely.
D. Stool culture
Stool culture is not a reliable way to diagnose giardiasis, though it can be helpful for
excluding other causes of diarrhea. There are many types of culture media that are
specific to various bacterial causes of diarrhea, and a high index of suspicion for a
certain organism is useful in determining which culture medium to use.

question: Which of the following anatomical locations does Crohn’s disease most commonly affect?
englishExplanation:
Distal ileum
Expl anation
A. Distal ileum
Crohn's disease can occur in any part of the GI tract, mouth to anus. The distal
ileum is the most common location affected by Crohn's disease, occuring in up to
80% of patients. Thus, sigmoidoscopy should not be used in evaluation of these patients. Because bile salts are normally absorbed in the distal ileum, many patients
with Crohn's disease have a secretory diarrhea caused by passage of bile salts into
the colon. Vitamin B12 deficiency IS also common due to impaired absorption in the
ileum.
Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK436021/
B. Distal jejunum
While small bowel involvement is very common in Crohn's disease, it occurs more
often in the distal ileum.
C. Duodenal bulb
Gastroduodenal bulb is less common, occuring in around 10% of patients with
Crohn's disease. These patients may present with epigastric abdominal pain and
early satiety.
D. Sigmoid colon
The sigmoid colon is spared from disease in many patients with Crohn's disease.
Sigmoid colon involvement is much more common with ulcerative colitis, which
starts in the rectum and spreads proximally.

question: A 65-year-old male with no past medical history presents to the emergency department with left lower quadrant abdominal pain as well as a fever for three days. CT scan reveals left-sided diverticulitis without evidence of perforation or abscess. Vital signs are temperature of 37ºC (98.6ºF), heart rate is 85 bpm, respiratory rate is 19/min, blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient's condition?
englishExplanation:
Discharge home with oral antibiotics.
Expl anation
A. Discharge home with oral antibiotics.
This patient has uncomplicated diverticulitis and no significant medical co-morbidities. He can be managed at home with oral antibiotics, pain control, and a liquid
diet for 2-3 days. Diet can be slowly advanced thereafter.
The DINAMO trial, published in 2021, found that patients with uncomplicated
acute diverticulitls, whose symptoms were controlled in the emergency department,
could be managed without antibiotics. There were low rates of return visits and
complications in both the antibiotic treatment arm and the non-antibiotic treatment
arm of this study. There was no statistically significant difference in outcomes. Over
time, conservative treatment with bowel rest and pain control may be an option for
treating healthy patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis prior to initiating
antibiotics.
Further information: Mora-L6pez L, et al. Efficacy and Safety of Nonantibiotic
Outpatient Treatment in Mild Acute Diverticulitis (DINAMO-study): A Multicentre,
Randomised, Open-label, Noninferiority Trial. Ann Surg.
PMID:34183510
B. Hospital admission for IV antibiotics.
This patient is well appearing with normal vitals and the CT scan confirms no complications. He can be managed as an outpatient.
Inpatient treatment is recommended if the CT abdomen/pelvis shows complicated
diverticulitis (including micro-perforation) or if the patient has evidence of
sepsis/SIRS, severe abdominal pain/peritonitis, co-morbidities such as diabetes,
heart disease, liver disease, end-stage renal disease, immunocompromise, cannot
tolerate oral intake or has failed outpatient therapy.
C. Hospital admission for colonoscopy.
This patient is stable and has uncomplicated diverticulitis. Admission is not indicated. A colonoscopy could be considered 6-8 weeks after to evaluate the extent of
his disease and exclude underlying malignancy.

question: A 55-year-old woman presents, concerned she might have hepatitis C. She recently learned that a former boyfriend was diagnosed with hepatitis C. She is aware that he had a prior history of intravenous drug use. While dating, they had sexual intercourse without using condoms. The woman feels fine and has no chronic health problems. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial screening test to use in determining if this patient is a carrier of the hepatitis C virus?

options.text: Measurement of serum alanine aminotransferase levels
Measurement of serum aspartate aminotransferase levels

englishExplanation:
Enzyme immunoassay HCV antibody test
Expl anation
A. Enzyme immunoassay HCV antibody test
Testing for HCV infection begins with either a rapid or laboratory-conducted assay
for HCV antibody in the blood. A nonreactive result indicates no antibodies to HCV
were detected. A reactive result should be followed by confirmatory PCR testing,
which accurately identifies persons with chronic HCV infection.
Further information:
O'Mara SR, Wiesner L. Chapter 80. Hepatic Disorders. In: Tintinalli JE, Ma OJ,
Yealy DM, Meckler GD, Stapczynski JS, Cline DM, Thomas SH, eds. Tintinalli's
Emergency Medicine: A Comprehensive Study Guide, ge. New York, NY: McGraw-
Hill; 2020.
Haines EJ, Thompson H. Chapter 76. Liver and Biliary Tract Disorders. In: Walls
RM, Hockberger RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts
and Clinical Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
B. Hepatitis C RNA quantitative testing
Hepatitis C RNA quantitative testing measures the amount of hepatitis C virus in
the blood, and is sometimes referred to as the "viral load." This test is done before a
patient begins treatment for HCV, and it is used to monitor the patient's response to
treatment. It is not a screening test.
C. Measurement of serum alanine aminotransferase levels
Levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) increase when there is hepatocellular damage. While many patients with chronic HCV
infection have elevated liver transaminase levels, many patients with HCV will have
normal ALT and AST levels. Measuring levels of liver transaminases is an inaccurate, and inappropriate screening test for HCV infection.
D. Measurement of serum aspartate aminotransferase levels
Levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) increase when there is hepatocellular damage. While many patients with chronic HCV
infection have elevated liver transaminase levels, many patients with HCV will have
normal ALT and AST levels. Measuring levels of liver transaminases is an inaccurate, and inappropriate screening test for HCV infection.

question: A 35-year-old female presents to the emergency department with right upper quadrant pain and fever for 24 hours. Physical exam is significant for a positive Murphy's sign as well as scleral icterus. Serum lipase is normal. This patient likely has a gallstone causing obstruction in what part of the biliary tree?
englishExplanation:
Common bile duct
Expl anation
A. Common bile duct
This patient has signs and symptoms of cholangitis. Charcot triad
describes cholangitis as fever, right upper abdominal pain, and jaundice. The
Reynolds pentad adds altered mental status and sepsis. Choledocholithiasis is the
most common cause of cholangitis, with infection-causing stones in the common
bile duct leading to obstruction of the biliary system.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK558946/
B. Cystic duct
A cystic duct obstruction typically causes cholecystitis.
C. Hepatic duct
The hepatic duct is proximal to the gallbladder and thus is unlikely to be obstructed
by a gallstone.
D. Pancreatic duct
Gallstones are unlikely to obstruct the pancreatic duct.

question: A 55-year-old male with a history of diabetes, hypertension, and an abdominal aortic aneurysm repaired 7 years ago presents to the emergency department after a single episode of bloody emesis. He denies any abdominal pain, but reports vomiting approximately one-half of a cup of bright red blood. Physical exam reveals a well-appearing male and is unremarkable except for the rectal exam which demonstrates occult blood-positive stool. Initial hemoglobin is 11 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management of this patient?

options.text: CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis
Gastroenterology consult for elective outpatient endoscopy within the next several days
Nasogastric tube placement and gastric lavage

correctAnswer: CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis
englishExplanation:
CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis
Expl anation
A. CT angiography ofthe abdomen and pelvis
This patient's presentation, particularly with his history of aortic aneurysm repair,
is concerning for an aortoenteric fistula and a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is
indicated. This occurs most commonly after repair, but can also occur with primary
aortic aneurysms as well as in patients with aortic pathology due to syphilis and tuberculosis. It is caused by a fistula that forms between the aorta and the bowel. It
may present as a herald bleed, as in this case, and prompt diagnosis is important as
untreated mortality approaches 100%. CI' may demonstrate an actual thrombus and
will aid with surgical planning.
Further information:
Cowell CB. Chapter 72. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm. In: Walls RM, Hockberger RS,
Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical Practice.
10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
B. Gastroenterology consult for elective outpatient endoscopy within
the next several days
This patient's presentation, particularly with his history of aortic aneurysm repair,
is concerning for aortoenteric fistula. This requires emergent evaluation. Outpatient
endoscopy is not appropriate.
C. Gastroenterology consult for emergent endoscopy
This patient's presentation, particularly with his history of aortic aneurysm repair,
is concerning for aortoenteric fistula. Endoscopy is not the appropriate evaluation
for this disease process.
D. Nasogastric tube placement and gastric lavage
This patient's presentation, particularly with his history of aortic aneurysm repair,
is concerning for aortoenteric fistula. NG tube placement and lavage is unlikely to
provide any useful information and will be uncomfortable for the patient.

question: A 10-day-old ex-30-week premature infant presents with decreased oral intake, vomiting, and decreased activity. Vital signs are: HR 190/min, RR 55/min, BP 65/45 mmHg, and temperature 97.0F (36.1C). Physical exam reveals a lethargic child with a distended abdomen. There is no rebound or guarding. Abdominal x-ray is shown below. Which of the following is the likely cause of this patient’s presentation?

options.text: Ischemic necrosis of the intestinal mucosa with bacterial invasion and gas formation
Lack of innervation to a portion of the large intestine leading to obstruction
Small bowel twisting around the superior mesenteric artery
Telescoping of the bowel due to a lead point

correctAnswer: Ischemic necrosis of the intestinal mucosa with bacterial invasion and gas formation
englishExplanation:
Ischemic necrosis of the intestinal mucosa with bacterial invasion and gas
formation
Expl anation
A. Ischemic necrosis of the intestinal mucosa with bacterial invasion
and gas formation
This KUB shows findings suggestive of necrotizing enterocolitis. A supine abdominal x-ray is the mainstay of this diagnosis. Findings include: dilated bowel loops,
bowel wall edema with thumbprinting, pneumatosis intestinalis, and pneumoperitoneum (in severe disease).
Necrotizing enterocolitis occurs most commonly in premature infants. It is characterized by lethargy, increasing abdominal distension, poor PO intake and can
progress to sepsis and perforation.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11489407
B. Lack of innervation to a portion of the large intestine leading to
obstruction
Bowel obstruction due to lack of innervation is characteristic of Hirschprung's disease, which can progress to toxic megacolon.
C. Small bowel twisting around the superior mesenteric artery
Small bowel twisting around the superior mesenteric artery is the cause of malrotation with volvulus which is characterized by bilious vomiting.
D. Telescoping of the bowel due to a lead point
Telescoping of the bowel due to a lead point is the cause of intussusception.

question: A 22-year-old man with no significant medical history comes to the emergency department because he has a foreign body in his rectum. He says that he inserted a light bulb into his rectum 12 hours ago in response to a dare. He is uncomfortable but does not have significant pain. The patient believes the light bulb is still intact. On physical examination, the screw base of the light bulb can be visualized just past the dentate line in the distal portion of the rectal vault. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Observe the patient for self passage
Obtain a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
Refer for consultation with a surgeon

correctAnswer: Refer for consultation with a surgeon
englishExplanation:
Refer for consultation with a surgeon
Expl anation
A. Attempt bedside removal
The emergency department physician can attempt bedside removal of certain objects. However, surgery should be consulted for objects that are made of glass, have
sharp edges, or show signs of perforation. If a foreign body is removed at the bedside and then determined to be of size and shape that could cause perforation or injury, an x-ray and proctoscopic exam should be performed post-removal. In some
cases, patients are observed for 12 hours to ensure that no signs of perforation
develop.
B. Observe the patient for self passage
Anorectal foreign bodies should be removed. In the case of high-risk foreign bodies,
surgery should be consulted.
C. Obtain a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
A CT scan can be useful in the setting of a radiolucent object and in the detection of
perforation. However, if the object can be visualized on plain x-ray and there are no
signs of perforation by exam (fever, leukocytosis, abdominal pain, rectal bleeding,
peritoneal signs) or by x-ray, then a CT scan is usually not needed.
D. Refer for consultation with a surgeon
This patient is presenting with a high-risk rectal foreign body, and surgery should
be consulted for removal under general anesthesia. High-risk objects include those
that are made of glass, have sharp edges, or show signs of perforation.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557557/
Goodloe J, Soulek J. Chapter 51. Foreign Bodies. In: Walls RM, Hockberger RS,
Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical Practice.
10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.

question: A 29-year-old man comes to the emergency department because he has had epigastric pain and burning for the past several months. Review of the medical records shows multiple visits to his primary care clinic and the emergency department for recurrent peptic ulcer disease. Ulcers were confirmed on prior endoscopy, but a result of H. pylori testing was negative. Recent fasting gastrin level was elevated. Based on these findings, this patient is at risk for which of the following tumors?
englishExplanation:
Pituitary adenoma
Expl anation
A. Medullary thyroid carcinoma
This tumor occurs in patients with MEN type 2 and 3 and are not associated with
pancreatic tumors.
B. Mucosal neuromas
This tumor occurs in patient with MEN type 3. These are not associated with pancreatic tumors.
C. Pheochromocytoma
This tumor occurs in patients with MEN type 2 and 3 and are not associated with
pancreatic tumors.
D. Pituitary adenoma
This patient is presenting with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, likely from a pancreatic
gastrinoma. Pancreatic islet tumors are associated with multiple endocrine neopla-
Sia (MEN) type 1. Other tumors that occur in this autosomal dominant disease are
parathyroid hyperplasia and pituitary adenomas.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537344/

الفخ: الطلاب بختاروا pheochromocytoma أو medullary thyroid carcinoma بس لأنهم سمعوا إنهم مرتبطين بـ MEN. بس هدول الأورام موجودين بالـ MEN type 2 و 3 ومش مرتبطين بأورام البنكرياس، بعكس pituitary adenoma اللي بتيجي مع MEN type 1.

question: A 55-year-old male presents to the emergency department with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever. Physical exam reveals tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant and a positive Murphy’s sign. Crepitus is also noted in the abdominal wall near the right upper quadrant. Which of the following risk factors is most commonly associated with this disease process?
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
A. Cirrhosis
Diabetes mellitus
This patient's presentation is concerning for emphysematous cholecystitis. Cirrhosis
is not typically associated with this disease process.
B. Diabetes mellitus
This patient's exam is concerning for emphysematous cholecystitis caused by gasforming organisms such as Clostridium. Patients with emphysematous cholecystitis
may have crepitus of the right upper quadrant. Approximately one-third to one-half
of patients affected by this disease have diabetes. Morbidity and mortality are high,
as perforation is common. In these cases, the physical exam will be consistent with
cholecystitis but may demonstrate crepitus in the abdominal wall near the gallbladder. Ultrasound or CT scan may show air in the gallbladder wall. Treatment is
broad-spectrum antibiotics and cholecystectomy.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448099/
C. HIV infection
This patient's presentation is concerning for emphysematous cholecystitis. HIV infection is not typically associated with this disease process. HIV medications are
classically associated with pancreatitis.
D. Tobacco abuse
This patient's presentation is concerning for emphysematous cholecystitis. This is
not typically associated with tobacco use.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الصورة السريرية classic لـ emphysematous cholecystitis، واللي بتصير بسبب gas-forming organisms زي Clostridium، وعلامتها المميزة هي crepitus بجدار البطن حوالين الـ RUQ. الـ ultrasound أو الـ CT ممكن يبينوا هوا بجدار الـ gallbladder، والـ morbidity و mortality عالية لأن الـ perforation شائع. تقريباً ثلث إلى نصف المرضى المصابين بهذا المرض عندهم diabetes.
الفخ: الطلاب ممكن يختاروا cirrhosis بس لأنه فكروا بمشكلة بالكبد أو القناة الصفراوية. بس الـ cirrhosis مش مرتبط بهذه العملية المرضية، والمفتاح هو إنه الـ crepitus مع الـ diabetes هي الربط الصحيح للـ emphysematous cholecystitis.

question: A 25-year-old man who is otherwise healthy presents because of persistent, frequent bowel movements, intermittently with bloody mucus, for the past two weeks. He states that he has been having 2-3 bowel movements per day and often has the feeling of needing to empty his bowels. He denies any recent illnesses or foreign travel. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse rate is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/87 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical examination shows mild tenderness of the lower left abdominal quadrant without guarding or rebound. Which of the following is most likely based on this patient's history and physical exam findings?
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
Ulcerative colitis
A. Adenocarcinoma of the colon
Adenocarcinoma often presents with melena or non-grossly bloody stools along
with weight loss and night sweats.
B. Diverticultis
Diverticulitis is infection of the diverticula, outpouchings of the colon. It generally
presents with lower abd pain, fever and leukocytosis.
C. Ulcerative colitis
This patient is presenting with a history concerning for ulcerative colitis (UC). UC is
a chronic inflammatory and ulcerative disease arising in the colonic mucosa, most
often characterized by bloody diarrhea. Colonic involvement is usually left-sided,
and most often involves the rectosigmoid area. The bowel wall is symmetrically, and
uniformly involved from the rectum proximally. Fistulas and epithelioid granulomas do not occur. Extraintestinal symptoms, particularly arthritis, may also occur.
Patients with UC are also at increased risk for colon cancer.
Reference: https://w•ww.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459282/
D. Volvulus
Volvulus occurs when a loop of the intestine twists around itself, causing an obstruction. Volvulus can occur in the stomach, small intestine, and colon. It is most
common in the sigmoid colon. Symptoms can include abdominal pain, nausea and
vomiting, bloating, and constipation. In severe cases, volvulus can cause intestinal
obstruction, perforation of the intestine, and sepsis. This patient's history is more
concerning for inflammatory bowel disease.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريض عنده bloody diarrhea و tenesmus بدون حرارة أو leukocytosis، وهاد متوافق مع ulcerative colitis، وهي مرض التهابي مزمن بالـ colonic mucosa. الـ colonic involvement عادة بيكون بالأيسر وأكتر شي بالـ rectosigmoid area، والجدار يتأثر بشكل متماثل ومتساوي من الـ rectum لقدام. الـ fistulas والـ granulomas ما بتصير بهذا المرض، والمريض بيكون معرض لأعلى خطر للـ colon cancer.
الفخ: الطلاب بختاروا diverticulitis بس لأنه الألم بالـ lower left quadrant. بس الـ diverticulitis بتيجي مع fever و leukocytosis وبمريض أكبر بالعمر، وهون المريض شب صغير مع bloody mucus وبدون حرارة.

question: A 24-year-old male is being evaluated in the emergency department because of fever, vomiting, right lower quadrant abdominal pain, and diarrhea for the past two days. In addition to acute appendicitis, infection with which of the following organisms should be considered in the differential diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Yersinia species
Expl anation
A. Shigella species
Shigella classically presents with high fever, abdominal cramping and bloody mucoid diarrhea. Common complications associated with Shigella include: proctitis,
rectal prolapse, toxic megacolon, bowel obstruction, and colonic perforation (very
rare).
B. Vibrio cholerae
Vibrio cholerae classically presents with abdominal cramping and profuse watery
diarrhea with flecks of mucus (described as "rice water" stool) with nonbilious
vomiting.
C. Yersinia species
Classic Yersinia enterocolitica clinical manifestations include acute febrile gastroenteritis and pseudoappendicitis. Patients may present with classic symptoms of
appendicitis, including right lower quadrant abdominal pain, fever, vomiting as well
as elevated white blood count. Though patients with acute yersiniosis will also have
diarrhea. Diagnosis is made by stool culture in patients with GI symptoms.
Treatment is typically supportive with hydration. Aminoglycosides or TMP/SMX
may be used in cases of severe disease or if the patient is immunocompromised. It is
clinically challenging to differentiate appendicitis from pseudoappendicitis, even
with imaging, so some patients will be taken for surgery.
Further information:
DeKoning EP. Chapter 81. Acute Appendicitis. In: Tintinalli JE, Ma OJ, Yealy DM,
Meckler GD, Stapczynski JS, Cline DM, Thomas SH, eds. Tintinalli's Emergency
Medicine: A Comprehensive Study Guide, 9e. New York, NY: McGraw-Hill; 2020.
D. Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli
ETEC, "traveler's diarrhea," classically presents 4 days - 2 weeks after arrival to another country and is generally self-limited for 1-5 days. Classic symptoms include
malaise, anorexia, abdominal cramping, and profuse watery diarrhea.

question: A 45-year-old male comes to the emergency department with epigastric abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting for 18 hours. He has a history of chronic alcohol abuse. Physical exam reveals tenderness to palpation at the epigastrium with voluntary guarding. Laboratory analysis is as follows: white blood count 13,000 cells/mm3, hemoglobin 11 g/dL, hematocrit 33, platelet count 110,000/mm3, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 140 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 270 U/L, phosphatase (alkaline) 40 U/L, and serum lipase of 20 U/L. Bedside ultrasound is negative for gallstones or pericholecystic fluid. The abdominal x-ray is shown below. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient’s condition?
englishExplanation:
Analgesia and supportive care
Expl anation
A. Analgesia and supportive care
This patient's history as well as the radiograph showing calcifications in the pancreas is suggestive of chronic pancreatitis. Initial treatment is geared towards pain
control with analgesia and supportive care.
Further information: Singh VK, Yadav D, Garg PK. Diagnosis and Management of
Chronic Pancreatitis: A Review. JAMA. PMID: 31860051
B. Broad-spectrum antibiotics
Broad-spectrum antibiotics are not indicated for the treatment of chronic pancreatitis but may be indicated for superinfection in necrotizing pancreatitis.
C. ERCP for ductal drainage
If conservative management fails or if the patient has a pancreatic ductal obstruction, ERCP may be beneficial.
D. Surgical resection
Surgery is reserved for patients with persistent symptoms that do not respond to
conservative therapy including the cessation of alcohol use, analgesia and pancreatic enzyme supplementation.

question: A 27-year-old woman presents because of perianal itching and irritation for the past two weeks. She has tried the application of over-the-counter hemorrhoid creams without relief. She is sexually active and takes oral contraceptive pills. Physical examination of the perianal area shows multiple soft, moist cauliflower-like lesions. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism of this patient's condition?
englishExplanation:
Human papillomavirus
Expl anation
A. Haemophilus ducreyi
Haemophilus ducreyi is a fastidious Gram-negative coccobacillus causing the sexually transmitted infection, chancroid, a major cause of genital ulceration in developing countries characterized by painful sores on the genitalia.
B. Klebsiella granulomatis
Klebsiella granulomatis is a Gram-negative rod-shaped bacterium known to cause
the sexually transmitted infection, granuloma inguinale.
C. Human papillomavirus
Human papillomavirus (HPV) [>100 types] produces epithelial tumors of the skin
and mucous membranes.Condylomata acuminata (genital warts) are generally recognized as benign proliferations of the anogenital skin and mucosa resulting from
HPV infection.Despite the generally benign nature of these proliferations, certain
types of HPV can place patients at a high risk for anogenital cancer.Genital warts
are transmitted by sexual contact. Approximately two thirds of individuals who have
sexual contact with an infected partner develop genital warts.HPV types 16 and 18
have emerged as the high-risk types of HPV because they are responsible for most
high-grade intraepithelial lesions that may progress to carcinomas, particularly
those in the anogenital or mucosal category.
Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448132/
McKinzie J. Chapter 84. Sexually Transmitted Infectios. In: Walls RM, Hockberger
RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical
Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
D. Molluscum contagiosum virus
Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV) is a species of virus in the powirus family
which causes the disease, molluscum contagiosum. Molluscum can spread from one
person to another by sexual contact. Many, but not all, cases of molluscum in adults
are caused by sexual contact.The lesions are small, raised, and usually white, pink,
or flesh-colored with a dimple or pit in the center. They often have a pearly appearance and are usually smooth and firm.

question: A 55-year-old man comes to the emergency department because he has had upper abdominal pain radiating to his back for the past two months. He describes a burning pain that occasionally radiates into his chest, particularly when he lies down. Proton pump inhibitor therapy was initiated four weeks ago, but the patient continues to experience these symptoms. He has a history of tobacco use and daily alcohol consumption. Based on this patient’s symptoms and risk factors, which of the following tests is most likely to determine the diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
A. CT scan
Endoscopy
Given symptoms of GERD refractory to therapy, CT scan is not the test of choice for
establishing the diagnosis. However, CT scan would be of use if there was concern
for gastric perforation in the setting of severe peptic ulcer disease.
B. Endoscopy
Endoscopy is the preferred method of diagnosing complications of gastroesophageal
reflux disease (GERD). Because this patient has already been started on a proton
pump inhibitor without improvement of symptoms suggestive of GERD, endoscopy
would be the test of choice at this juncture.
Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441938/
C. Esophageal manometry
This diagnostic tool is used for diagnosing esophageal motility disorders such as
achalasia rather than establishing the diagnosis of GERD.
D. Urea Breath Test
This tests for H. pylori. Patients with an established diagnosis of peptic ulcer disease
should be tested for H. pylori however, in this case, the underlying cause of the
patient's symptoms is still unclear. He should therefore undergo an endoscopy. If it
is found that he has gastritis, a urea breath test would then be considered.

الفخ: الطلاب بختاروا CT scan بس لأنه فكروا بمشكلة بالبنكرياس أو الـ perforation بسبب الألم اللي بيوصل للظهر. بس الـ CT ما هو الاختبار المفضل لتشخيص الـ GERD، والـ endoscopy هو اللي بيشوف الـ mucosal complications.

question: A 26-year-old woman presents with an increased frequency of bowel movements and loose stools ever since her gallbladder was removed two months ago. She is also concerned because she is still experiencing mild, intermittent right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Her vital signs and physical exam are normal. Laboratory studies including liver function tests are normal. Right upper quadrant ultrasound reveals no signs of a retained stone or bile leak. The patient would like you to prescribe her the appropriate medication for her diarrhea. Which of the following is the next best step?

options.text: Explain to the patient that this is a normal finding after laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and no medical therapy is necessary

englishExplanation:
Treat the patient with cholestyramine
Expl anation
A. Explain to the patient that this is a normal finding after laparoscopic
cholecystectomy, and no medical therapy is necessary
Diarrhea after a cholecystectomy is often due to an increased concentration of bile
acids in the colon, which have a laxative effect. Often times, diarrhea resolves over
several weeks, but bile-acid sequestrants can be helpful in patients that have
chronic diarrhea, once other causes of diarrhea have been ruled out.
B. Prescribe a proton-pump inhibitor
This patient likely has post-cholecystectomy syndrome (PCS). VVhile a proton-pump
inhibitor would be recommended for symptoms of heartburn, it is not the therapeutic agent for diarrhea. Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant and is indicated in
the treatment of postprandial diarrhea, which is due to increased concentration of
bile acids in the colon.
C. Treat the patient with cholestyramine
This patient likely has post-cholecystectomy syndrome (PCS), which presents with a
constellation of symptoms that may include persistent right upper quadrant abdominal pain, fatty food intolerance, nausea, vomiting, heartburn, flatulence, indigestion, and diarrhea. Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant and is indicated in the
treatment of postprandial diarrhea, which is due to increased concentration of bile
acids in the colon.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK539902/
D. Treat the patient with loperamide
Loperamide is an antimotility agent, and while it may help to relieve her diarrhea, it
is not the best option, considering the cause of the patient's diarrhea.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريضة عندها diarrhea بعد الـ cholecystectomy ب شهرين، وهاد هو post-cholecystectomy syndrome، واللي بيصير بسبب زيادة تركيز الـ bile acids بالـ colon واللي إلها تأثير laxative. الـ cholestyramine هو bile acid sequestrant ومحدد بشكل واضح لعلاج الـ postprandial diarrhea الناتج عن هذه الزيادة. حتى إنه الـ diarrhea ممكن يتحسن لحاله بشوي أسابيع، بس الـ sequestrants بيستخدموا بالحالات المزمنة بعد ما نستبعد باقي أسباب الإسهال.
الفخ: الطلاب بختاروا إنه ما نعطي علاج لأنهم فكروا إنه نتيجة طبيعية بعد العملية. بس الـ cholestyramine يظل العلاج الصحيح للـ postprandial diarrhea المزمن، والـ loperamide ما بيعالج السبب الأساسي وهو الـ bile acids.

question: A 36-year-old man with cirrhosis is admitted to the ICU immediately after he comes to the emergency department because of bleeding esophageal varices. The patient is administered several blood transfusions before being stable enough to undergo a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) procedure. If this surgery is successful, this patient is at increased risk for which of the following complications during the first year post TIPS procedure?
englishExplanation:
Hepatic encephalopathy
Expl anation
A. Heart failure
Heart failure is not known to be a complication of TIPS procedure.
B. Hepatic encephalopathy
The incidence of hepatic encephalopathy following TIPS ranges anywhere from 5%
and 35% in the literature. This generally occurs anytime within the first year following the procedure. Treatment of post-TIPS encephalopathy is lactulose and is successful in 95% of cases. For persistent severe encephalopathy despite lactulose therapy, shunt occlusion should be considered.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513268/
C. Hepatorenal syndrome
Hepatorenal failure is not known to be a complication of TIPS procedure.
D. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is not known to be a complication of TIPS
procedure.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: بعد نجاح الـ TIPS procedure بيصير shunting للدم عشان يقلل ضغط الـ portal، بس هاد بيخلي مواد الـ ammonia توصل للدماغ وتسبب hepatic encephalopathy. الـ incidence بعد الـ TIPS بتتراوح بين 5% و 35% حسب الدراسات، وهاد بيصير بأي وقت خلال السنة الأولى بعد العملية. العلاج هو lactulose وبيشتغل بنسبة 95% من الحالات، وإذا استمرت الحالة الشديدة ممكن نفكر بإغلاق الـ shunt.
الفخ: الطلاب بختاروا spontaneous bacterial peritonitis أو hepatorenal syndrome بس لأنهم مضاعفات معروفة بالـ cirrhosis. بس اللي بيزحبط إنه السؤال عن المضاعفة بعد الـ TIPS بالتحديد، وهاد hepatic encephalopathy بسبب الـ shunting الجديد.

question: A 36-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because she had sudden onset of severe epigastric pain one hour ago. She has not had nausea or postprandial pain. Medical history includes epilepsy, intermittent abdominal pain, chronic back pain, and Helicobacter pylori infection 12 months ago. Currently, her only medications are phenytoin and ibuprofen. Physical examination shows conjunctival injection, dry mucous membranes, clear lung sounds, normal bowel sounds, and a diffusely tender abdomen. X-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ultrasonography of the right upper quadrant

englishExplanation:

The x-ray shows free air under the diaphragm, which is indicative of a perforation.

question: A 21-year-old man presents with vomiting and watery diarrhea for the past 24 hours. He says he has had cramping abdominal pain but no fever, chills, hematemesis, hematochezia, or recent history of antibiotic use. The patient was at a wedding 24 hours prior to symptom onset, and there are several other attendees with similar symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely pathogen?
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
Norovirus
A. Escherichia coli 0157:H7
E. coli 0157:H7 is a bacterial cause of diarrhea. It typically causes severe and bloody
diarrhea two to five days after ingestion of contaminated raw food such as dairy or
undercooked beef.
B. Giardia lamblia
Giardia lamblia is a parasitic cause of diarrhea after ingestion of contaminated food
or water. Its onset is seven to 14 days after exposure and can be linked to daycare
outbreaks or contaminated water sources while camping.
C. Norovirus
This patient has infectious watery diarrhea. Norovirus or Norwalk-like virus attributes to over one third of acute gastroenteritis cases in the United States. It is
transmitted through contaminated food from infected bowel or vomitus. Symptoms
begin 24 to 48 hours after exposure and resolve within 48 to 72 hours
spontaneously.
Further information:
Nguyen T, Akhtar S. Chapter 80. Gastroenteritis. In: Walls RM, Hockberger RS,
Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical Practice.
10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
D. Rotavirus
Rotavlrus typically causes severe, watery diarrhea and vomiting in children or
adults who are immunocompromised. Onset of symptoms is typically two days after
exposure.

الفخ: الطلاب بختاروا Rotavirus بس لأنه هو كمان سبب شائع للإسهال الفيروسي. بس الـ Rotavirus عادة عند الأطفال، بينما الـ Norovirus هو السبب الأول بالبالغين ومترافق مع outbreaks بأماكن مجتمعية زي الأعراس.

question: A 52-year-old man who is morbidly obese comes to the emergency department because he has had intermittent episodes of abdominal cramping, nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, and flushing during the past week. He says the episodes occur shortly after eating certain meals, and the symptoms slowly improve with time. Medical history includes diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, and obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Surgical history includes Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery one month ago and cholecystectomy eight years ago. Results of laboratory studies are within normal limits, and contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
englishExplanation:
Dietary modification
Expl anation
A. Dietary modification
This patient presents with dumping syndrome. Dumping syndrome is a common
complication following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery. There is early and late
dumping syndrome. Early dumping syndrome generally occurs approximately 15
minutes after a carbohydrate-rich meal when hyperosmolar chyme bypasses the pylorus and rapidly dumps into the jejunum causing a sudden influx of extracellular
fluid and subsequent autonomic response. Late dumping syndrome occurs two to
four hours after a meal, generally does not involve diarrhea, and is thought to be
secondary to hypoglycemia. Diagnosis is made clinically based on history, and the
mainstay of treatment is dietary modifications. Patients should be instructed to consume small, dry meals that are higher in fiber and lower in carbohydrates. They
should also be encouraged to separate their intake of solids and liquids by at least 15
minutes. In refractory cases, a pyloroplasty may be required. Admission is rarely
needed.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470542/
B. Endoscopy
Endoscopy is generally not needed to make the diagnosis of dumping syndrome.
However, if the diagnosis is unclear, an endoscopy may be performed as an outpatient. Stomal stenosis can mimic the symptoms of dumping syndrome; however, it
generally does not involve diarrhea and does not occur before two months
postoperatively.
C. Loperamide therapy
Dietary education and modification is the mainstay of treatment and should resolve
the diarrhea. Anti-diarrheal therapy is usually not warranted.
D. Testing of the stool
Testing of the stool may be performed if suspecting infectious or toxin-producing
etiologies (e.g. Giardia, worms, Clostridium difficile), however this vignette is describing dumping syndrome.

question: A 64-year-old male presents to the emergency department with throat pain and the sensation of food being stuck in his throat after eating a sandwich one hour prior. The patient is breathing comfortably and has no respiratory compromise. He is given IV glucagon, and after several minutes the obstruction passes. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge home with routine primary care
Discharge home with specialist referral for endoscopy

correctAnswer: Discharge home with specialist referral for endoscopy
englishExplanation:
Discharge home with specialist referral for endoscopy
Expl anation
A. Discharge home with routine primary care
This patient should have specialist followup to perform an upper endoscopic procedure to evaluate for treatable and malignant causes for upper GI partial obstruction.
B. Discharge home with specialist referral for endoscopy
This patient likely had a food impaction relieved by IV glucagon. Although this may
have been a simple obstruction, the possibility of an underlying stricture or mass
needs to be ruled out by esophagoscopy. The correct answer is discharging with a
specialist (GI) follow-up for endoscopy.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482131/
Goodloe J, Soulek J. Chapter 51. Foreign Bodies. In: Walls RM, Hockberger RS,
Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical Practice.
10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
C. Plain films of the neck
Soft tissue lateral x-ray of the neck is unlikely to give any pertinent information.
D. Upper GI series with contrast
This patient is presenting with food impaction, which has resolved. At this time,
there is no indication for emergent upper GI series.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريض كان عنده food impaction واللي انحلت بعد إعطاء IV glucagon، وهاد غالباً انسداد جزئي بالـ esophagus. حتى لو كان الانسداد بسيط، لازم نستبعد وجود stricture أو mass كامنة، ولذلك الإجابة الصحيحة هي الخروج مع إحالة لتخصص الـ GI لإجراء endoscopy. الـ esophagoscopy هو اللي بيكشف الأسباب القابلة للعلاج والأسباب الخبيثة للانسداد.
الفخ: الطلاب بختاروا discharge home with routine primary care بس لأنه انحل الانسداد والمريض بخير. بس هذا خطأ لأنه ما بيستبعد السبب الكامن وراء الانسداد، والـ endoscopy مع متابعة الـ specialist هو المطلوب.

question: A 45-year-old man comes to the emergency department because he has had progressive yellowing of his skin over the past week. He says he also has had weight loss and fatigue. Medical history includes no chronic disease conditions. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and jaundiced skin. The abdomen is nontender to palpation, and a palpable mass is noted in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. Laboratory studies show an elevation in alkaline phosphatase, alanine transaminase, aspartate aminotransferase, direct bilirubin, total bilirubin levels, amylase, and lipase levels. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial imaging study to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen

correctAnswer: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
Contrast-enhanced CI' scan of the abdomen
A. Abdominal ultrasonography
Ultrasonography would be appropriate if primary gallbladder disease was suspected
as causing this patient's symptoms. However, this patient is presenting with classic
symptoms of pancreatic cancer. Ultrasonography can assess biliary ductal dilatation
associated with a pancreatic mass, but it is limited in the visualization of a pancreatic mass.
B. Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen
This patient has painless jaundice with a Courvoisier sign (palpable, nontender gallbladder), which is suspicious of pancreatic cancer. Patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma usually present with painless jaundice (70%). This results from common
bile duct obstruction due to a mass of the pancreatic head. Multidetector computed
tomography (MDCT) with pancreatic protocol is the best imaging modality to diagnose pancreatic adenocarcinoma. MDCT with pancreatic protocol is the quickest
and most accurate imaging option in the emergency department.
Further information:
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK518996/
C. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the abdomen
Abdominal MRI with intravenous contrast is the best choice for the preoperative
evaluation of pancreatic cancer, assessing vascular invasion,
detecting metastatic hepatic disease. This is done if pancreatic cancer is highly suspected and initial CT scan is negative.
D. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography can detect the level of biliary or
pancreatic obstruction which would be helpful in the workup of this patient's jaundice but not in the initial diagnosis of a pancreatic mass.
Page 330 of 4185
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريض عنده painless jaundice مع palpable nontender mass بالـ RUQ وهاد Courvoisier sign، وهاد كلاسيكي لـ pancreatic cancer. الـ pancreatic adenocarcinoma بيجي بـ painless jaundice بنسبة 70% بسبب انسداد الـ common bile duct من كتلة برأس البنكرياس. الـ MDCT with pancreatic protocol هو أفضل وأسرع وأدق طريقة تصوير لتشخيص pancreatic adenocarcinoma بالـ emergency department.
الفخ: الطلاب بختاروا abdominal ultrasonography بس لأنه أول وأرخص فحص. بس الـ ultrasound بيثبت وجود dilation بالقنوات بس محدود بمشاهدة كتلة البنكرياس نفسها، والـ contrast-enhanced CT هو اللي ببين الكتلة بوضوح.

question: A 9-year-old girl is being treated in the emergency department for intractable nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea that she has had for the past three days. She weighs 30 kilograms. After an appropriate fluid bolus, maintenance intravenous fluid administration is planned. Which of the following is the most appropriate rate of fluid administration in this patient?
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
A. 100 cc/hr
70 cc/hr
The appropriate rate of maintenance fluid follows the 4:2:1 rule, 4mL/kg for ISt

question: A 66-year-old man comes to the emergency department because he has had intractable nausea and vomiting for the past two hours. He received his first cetuximab treatment yesterday for a recent diagnosis of colorectal cancer. He says he was given prophylactic antiemetics prior to infusion and remained compliant with the same regimen afterward. After initiating intravenous fluids, which of the following breakthrough treatments is most appropriate to relieve this patient's symptoms?
englishExplanation:
Olanzapine
Expl anation
A. Metoclopramide
Dopamine antagonists such as phenothiazines (e.g., metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) and butyrophenones (e.g., droperidol, haloperidol) were the original first-line
antiemetic therapies. Blocking dopamine receptors can lead to extrapyramidal reactions, disorientation, and sedation. 5-HT3 receptor antagonists have fewer adverse
events and dosing restrictions. Dopamine antagonists can be used for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting that is refractory to other treatments if olanzapine is already being used and patients are still experiencing symptoms.
B. Olanzapine
This patient has chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV). Cetuximab is
a low-emetic-risk intravenous chemotherapy. Both low and moderate-emetic-risk
antineoplastic agents (like cetuximab) are managed with a two-drug combination of
a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist and dexamethasone (with the only exception of specific
doses of carboplatin, which usually requires a three-drug combination.)
Breakthrough CINV is treated with a drug from a different class not used in the prophylactic regimen. Olanzapine is the drug of choice for patients who did not receive
olanzapine with their initial prophylactic regimen, in addition to continuing their
standard antiemetic regimen. Treatment-related sedation can be decreased with 5
mg versus 10 mg dosing. Alternative options include an NKI receptor antagonist,
lorazepam/alprazolam, a dopamine receptor antagonist, and cannabinoids
(dronabinol/nabilone).
Further information: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4573228/
C. Ondansetron and dexamethasone
This combination is the patient's prophylactic regimen for chemotherapy-induced
nausea and vomiting (CINV) due to his low-emetic-risk chemotherapy, cetuximab.
First-generation 5-HT3 receptor antagonists, such as ondansetron/palonosetron,
are the drugs of choice in preventing CINV. 5-HT3 receptor antagonists can treat
and prevent CINV by antagonizing 5-HT3 receptors on vagal nerve terminals
and/or in the chemoreceptor trigger zone. Corticosteroids work well when used
Page 1880 of 4185
alone to prevent nausea and vomiting due to low-emetic-risk chemotherapy and to
enhance the efficacy of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists when used together.
D. Palonosetron, aprepitant, and dexamethasone
The triple combination of palonosetron, aprepitant, and dexamethasone is a primary antiemetic prophylactic option for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting due to highly emetogenic cisplatin-based chemotherapy. Of note, high-emeticrisk chemotherapy-associated nausea and vomiting can also be managed with a
four-drug combination of an NKI receptor antagonist, a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist,
dexamethasone, and olanzapine.

الفخ: الطلاب بختاروا metoclopramide بس لأنه antiemetic معروف ومشهور. بس الـ dopamine antagonists زي metoclopramide بتحبط الـ dopamine receptors وممكن تعمل extrapyramidal reactions و sedation، والخيارات الأولى للـ breakthrough هي الـ olanzapine.

question: A 29-year-old gravida 1, para 1 woman at 34 weeks gestation presents with worsening abdominal pain over the past 12 hours. She says the pain is intermittent and colicky in the right upper quadrant and is associated with nausea. She denies diarrhea and vaginal or gastrointestinal bleeding symptoms. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse rate is 115/min, and blood pressure is 150/92 mmHg. On exam, the abdomen is mildly tender to palpation. No guarding or rebound is noted. She appears mildly jaundiced. Laboratory studies reveal: hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL; hematocrit 25%; platelet count 70,000/mm³; bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL; aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L; alanine aminotransferase 201 U/L; and lactate dehydrogenase 650 U/L. Urinalysis shows protein >300 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
HELLP syndrome
Expl anation
A. Cholecystitis
While this patient is experiencing intermittent colicky abdominal pain in the right
upper quadrant and has abnormal liver enzymes, the vignette described above is
more consistent with HELLP syndrome than cholecystitis. Cholecystitis does not
typically present with hemolysis and anemia. She is afebrile and pregnant, therefore
HELLP syndrome is the most likely etiology.
B. Choledocholithiasis
This patient is experiencing symptoms associated with choledocholithiasis including jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, and elevated liver enzymes.
Choledocholithiasis should be on a differential list and obtaining imaging would be
appropriate. However, she is pregnant with evidence of hypertension, hemolysis,
and thrombocytopenia which make HELLP syndrome more likely.
C. HELLP syndrome
This patient is exhibiting signs of HELLP syndrome; hemolysis, elevated liver enzyme levels, and low platelet count. This is a life-threatening condition that can occur during pregnancy with severe morbidity and mortality up to 25%. Treatment includes rapid stabilization of the mother and evaluation of the fetus. This is generally
felt to be a continuum of pre-eclampsia but can happen with or without previous
symptoms. It is generally recommended that these patients be transferred to a tertiary center with an available NICU. Blood pressure management and seizure prophylaxis are indicated. Delivery should be considered in patients close to term.
Blood transfusions and corticosteroids are other treatments.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560615/
D. Viral hepatitis
This patient does have elevated liver enzymes and increased bilirubin with jaundice
which can be appreciated in viral hepatitis. However, it is unlikely to present in this
manner. She is pregnant and therefore HELLP syndrome is the most likely reason
for her presentation.

question: A 24-year-old man presents with severe left-sided groin pain of 24 hours' dura- tion after lifting weights. He says that he has a lump in his groin that gets "worse" when he strains or lifts heavy objects but that he has always been able to "push it back in." His vital signs are BP 126/78, P 126, R 25, and T 38.4°C (101.2°F); SpO is 98% on room air. An abdominal examination reveals a 5-cm by 4-cm mass in the left inguinal area. The mass is firm and exquisitely tender to palpation with noted discoloration. What is the best next step in this patient's care?

options.text: Attempt manual reduction of the mass

englishExplanation: This patient's signs and symptoms (including severe pain, skin discoloration, and fever) suggest a strangulated inguinal hernia. This is a true surgical emer- gency, and immediate surgical consultation is warranted. Intravenous fluids, anal- gesia, antibiotics, and preoperative laboratory studies are also indicated. Strangulated hernias typically present with severe, exquisite pain at the hernia site with systemic signs of illness, including a toxic appearance, peritoneal findings, or sepsis. By definition, there is strangulation or vascular compromise of the tissue within the hernia. The history of a recurrent lump in the inguinal area that gets worse with straining or lifting heavy objects is suggestive of an inguinal hernia. Inguinal hernias are the most common type of hernia, occurring in about 75% of all hernias. They tend to be more common in male patients. Hernias can be re- ducible, incarcerated, or strangulated. A hernia is reducible if it is soft and can be 2 easily pushed back into the peritoneal cavity. An incarcerated hernia is firm, painful, and often nonreducible by direct pressure. Reduction of an incarcer- ated hernia should be attempted in the emergency department after ad- equate analgesia is provided; if the attempt is unsuccessful, general sur- gery should be consulted. After reduction of an incarcerated hernia, observation in the emergency department and serial abdominal examinations are reasonable. In contrast, when a patient exhibits signs of hernia strangulation, reduction should not be attempted in the emergency department. If the bowel is necrotic, there is a risk of sepsis; it should not be pushed back into the peritoneum because there is a likelihood of causing perforation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Admitting this patient to the hospital for serial examinations without taking any other action is inappropriate because a strangulated hernia is a surgical emergency. This patient requires immediate surgical consultation along with in- travenous fluids, analgesia, antibiotics, and preoperative laboratory studies. When a patient exhibits signs of hernia strangulation, which is an acute surgical emergency, reduction should not be attempted in the emer- gency department. If the bowel is necrotic, there is a risk of sepsis; it should not be pushed back into the peritoneum because there is a likelihood of causing perforation. Imaging, including plain x-rays of the abdomen, is of limited value in the management of a strangulated hernia. It delays definitive management, which is antibiotics and surgical repair, and it provides no information that will not be revealed during surgery.

question: A 65-year-old man presents with acute-onset abdominal pain after coughing. On examination, there is a balloon-like protrusion near the umbilicus that is mini- mally tender without skin changes. What is the best initial management?

options.text: Control pain and attempt manual reduction
Keep NPO and consult surgery immediately
Keep NPO and place nasogastric tube

correctAnswer: Control pain and attempt manual reduction
englishExplanation: This patient has an incarcerated hernia that should be reduced. To prepare for the reduction, the patient should be placed supine in Trendelenburg with an ice pack overlying the hernia. The patient should be given pain medication or procedural sedation to help with abdominal wall muscle relaxation, which will increase success of the reduction and make the patient more comfortable. To reduce the hernia, the outline of the abdominal wall defect should be palpated with the nondominant hand. Gentle, constant, inward pressure should be applied with the dominant hand at the base of the hernia. The smaller the defect, the more difficult the reduction will be and the higher the likelihood of strangula- tion. Reducible abdominal wall hernias without signs of bowel ischemia can be dis- charged with general surgery follow-up for elective surgical repair. Hernias that are unsuccessfully reduced and remain incarcerated require general surgery consultation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although patients with incarcerated or strangulated hernias should receive pain control, intravenous antibiotics are not generally indicated. Occasionally, patients with strangulated hernias may be given empiric antibiotics, but this patient presents with no signs or symptoms consistent with a strangulated hernia. This patient shows no evidence of strangulation and does not require emergent sur- gical consultation. If there is concern for strangulation, bedside reduction is contraindicated, and surgery should be consulted. Patients with strangulated hernias typically appear toxic and have systemic symptoms; the hernia may also have overlying skin changes. A normal lactate level test should not be used to rule out strangulation because it may be falsely normal. This patient has no signs or symptoms of a bowel obstruction, so a nasogastric (NG) tube is unnecessary. The placement of NG tubes is controversial even in pa- tients with bowel obstruction because it is a painful procedure and there is little re- search suggesting benefit of NG tube placement. Key Points Incarcerated hernias differ from strangulated hernias in that the hernia contents are not ischemic. Hernias that are unsuccessfully reduced and remain incarcerated require general surgery consultation. The smaller the fascial defect, the harder it will be to reduce the hernia and the higher risk for strangulation. Incarcerated hernias should be reduced with gentle, constant, inward pressure with the dominant hand placed at the base of the hernia.

question: Where do Spigelian hernias occur?

options.text: Anterior abdominal wall, adjacent to the semilunar line
Between the rectus abdominis muscles, at the level of the xiphoid
Between the rectus abdominis muscles, at the linea alba
Medial to the inferior epigastric vessels

correctAnswer: Anterior abdominal wall, adjacent to the semilunar line
englishExplanation: Spigelian hernias are slit-like defects in the anterior abdominal wall ad- jacent to the semilunar line. Most spigelian hernias occur in the lower ab- domen on the lateral edge of the rectus abdominis. They are rare compared to other types of hernia because they do not develop under abdominal layers of fat but be- tween fascia tissue that connects muscles. Because of this, the hernial defects tend to be smaller, which increases the risk of strangulation. Symptoms include abdominal pain, a bulge in the anterior abdominal wall, or symp- toms of incarceration or strangulation. Pain is often aggravated by maneu- vers that increase intra-abdominal pressure, similar to other ventral hernias. These hernias are less apparent on physical examination and are typically diagnosed on radiological studies such as CT scans. Spigelian hernias are surgi- cally repaired because of the high risk of strangulation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Epigastric hernias are typically located between the rectus abdominis at the level of the xiphoid. This type of hernia is caused by a preformed defect in the linea alba between the umbilicus and xiphoid. Most are asymptomatic, but symptoms may include nausea and abdominal pain in the epigastric region. Diastasis recti is located between the rectus abdominis at the linea alba. This is not a hernia, but a separation of the rectus muscles causing an increased dis- tance between the rectus abdominis muscles at the midline. It is common following pregnancy, but obesity and previous abdominal surgeries are also causes. The diag- nosis is made by history and physical examination. A midline abdominal bulge can be seen on abdominal examination, especially with Valsalva maneuvers. Direct inguinal hernias are typically located medial to the inferior epi- gastric vessels, specifically through the Hesselbach triangle. Direct in- guinal hernias are caused by weakness in the muscular layers, which may be due to several contributing factors including older age, smoking, increased intra-abdomi- nal pressure (eg, due to chronic cough or pregnancy), and connective tissue abnormalities.

question: Indirect inguinal hernias occur as a result of incomplete closure of which structure?
englishExplanation: Indirect inguinal hernias are most commonly caused by incomplete clo- sure of the processus vaginalis, an invagination of the parietal peritoneum that precedes testicular descent through the inguinal canal during embryogenesis. Indirect inguinal hernias protrude through the internal inguinal ring lateral to the epigastric vessels. Although most indirect inguinal hernias are congenital, they may also develop after long-term pressure on the processus vaginalis. This can be related to weakening or disruption of the abdominal wall tissues from smoking, old age, increased intraabdominal pressure, and connective tissue disorders. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although indirect inguinal hernias protrude through the internal inguinal ring, they are usually caused by an incomplete closure of the processus vaginalis. The deep (internal) inguinal ring is the entrance to the inguinal canal. It is bounded by the arched lower margin of the transversalis fascia (above and medially) and by the inferior epigastric vessels (below and medially). It contains the spermatic cord in males and the round ligament of the uterus in females. The functioning of the pubic symphysis is unrelated to indirect inguinal hernias. Pubic symphysis is the cartilaginous joint between the superior rami of the left and right pubis of the pelvis. The term sports hernia typically refers to ath- letes who may present with osteitis pubis, or inflammation of the pubic symphysis, which typically occur when athletes suddenly change direction, kick, or pivot. The superficial inguinal ring is uninvolved in indirect inguinal hernias. The superficial inguinal ring is the triangular opening within the aponeurosis of the external oblique that forms the exit of the inguinal canal, and it contains the ilioin- guinal nerve and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve. The deep inguinal ring is at the other end of the canal.

question: What is the appropriate technique used to completely reduce an inguinal hernia?

options.text: Place an ice pack on the area of swelling, and reassess after 20 minutes
Place the patient prone in Trendelenburg, and reassess after 20 minutes
Place the patient supine in Trendelenburg, and apply gentle, inward pressure
Place the patient supine in Trendelenburg, and apply intermittent, firm pressure

correctAnswer: Place the patient supine in Trendelenburg, and apply gentle, inward pressure
englishExplanation: Bedside reduction of an inguinal hernia is indicated when there is evi- dence of incarceration but no strangulation. To prepare for the reduction, the patient should be supine in Trendelenburg with an ice pack overlying the area of swelling. Pain control or procedural sedation is typically required to facilitate abdominal wall muscle relaxation. The outline of the abdominal wall de- fect should be palpated with the nondominant hand. Gentle, constant, inward pressure with the dominant hand should be applied. Constant pressure is neces- sary to prevent completely collapsing the lumen of the trapped small bowel, which will cause a ballooning effect. Patients with reducible hernias without signs of bowel ischemia can be discharged with a general surgery follow-up for elective repair. Incorrect Answer Explanations Placing an ice pack on the area of swelling may help reduce swelling. However, in order to fully reduce the hernia, manual pressure is typically required for reduction. The patient needs to be supine, rather than prone, to facilitate manual reduction. Having the patient prone is also an airway risk if any sort of procedural sedation is used to facilitate reduction. Constant and gentle pressure should be applied, instead of intermittent firm pres- sure. Intermittent firm pressure increases the likelihood of collapsing the intestinal lumen and causing strangulation, especially if the defect is small.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ bedside reduction لإلـ inguinal hernia بتصير لما يكون في incarceration بدون strangulation، ولازم نجهز المريض بوضعه supine بوضعية Trendelenburg مع ice pack فوق الانتفاخ. اللي بيصير إنه لازم مسكن أو procedural sedation عشان ترخي عضلات جدار البطن ويصير نجاح الردة أسهل. الردة بتصير بالضغط اللطيف والثابت للداخل بنبضة اليد المسيطرة مع تحسس حواف الـ defect باليد الثانية.
الفخ: الطلاب بختاروا intermittent firm pressure بس لأنه فكروا إنها أقوى فبتنجح. بس الضغط المتقطع والقوي بيزيد احتمال انسداد الـ lumen بالـ small bowel وبيمنع الفتق من الرجوع، والضغط الصحيح هو لطيف وثابت ومستمر.

question: What is associated with increased incidence of inguinal hernias in infants?
englishExplanation: Preterm birth increases the incidence of inguinal hernias, with the preva- lence being highest during infancy and declining with age. Between 25 and 35 weeks of gestation, each of the testis descends from its retroperitoneal, intra-abdominal lo- cation through the inguinal canal. The processus vaginalis obliterates, leaving no connection between the peritoneal cavity and the inguinal canal and scrotum. This is why 90% of pediatric inguinal hernias are diagnosed in boys. About 3% to 5% of healthy, full-term infants are born with an inguinal hernia, and in prema- ture infants, the incidence is up to 30%. Pediatric inguinal hernias are typically treated with surgery to prevent complications (eg, intestinal perforation, testicular atrophy, and ovarian damage). The contralateral inguinal canal is explored during surgery to detect a concomitant contralateral processus vaginalis defect. Incorrect Answer Explanations Delivery via cesarean section is not associated with an increased inci- dence of inguinal hernias in infants. It does, however, increase the risk of res- piratory distress syndrome. Oligohydramnios has no effect on the incidence of inguinal hernias in infants. Oligohydramnios refers to decreased amniotic fluid volume and is associ- ated with genitourinary tract abnormalities, fetal growth restriction, and chromoso- mal abnormalities. The most common cause of oligohydramnios is rupture of mem- branes, specifically preterm premature rupture of membranes. Increased incidence of inguinal hernias are unrelated to Turner syn- drome. It is the most common sex chromosomal abnormality found in girls, caused by one missing X chromosome, either partially or completely. Infants with Turner syndrome have increased risk of cardiovascular malformations, hearing loss, renal anomalies, ocular abnormalities, and neurocognitive deficits.

question: What is the most appropriate initial test for an otherwise healthy patient who presents with suspected esophageal candidiasis?
englishExplanation: Esophageal candidiasis is considered an AIDS-defining illness and is most commonly found in severely immunocompromised patients (eg, HIV-positive pa- tients, cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy, or those with hematologic abnor- malities and malignancies). Given the preponderance of HIV/AIDS–related cases, an otherwise healthy patient with suspected esophageal candidiasis should be ini- tially tested for HIV. After an HIV diagnosis has been ruled out or confirmed, an endoscopy with an esophageal biopsy can confirm the diagnosis of esophageal candidiasis. Esophageal candidiasis is most often caused by a Candida albicans infection of the esophagus and is strongly associated with coincidental thrush. Any patient who presents with thrush and odynophagia should be strongly suspected of hav- ing esophageal involvement. Esophageal candidiasis requires systemic antifun- gal treatment. Treatments, such as oral nystatin, clotrimazole, and miconazole, can be used to treat thrush alone but are ineffective for the treatment of esophageal can- didiasis. A 2- to 3-week course of oral fluconazole is a first-line treatment for esophageal candidiasis; other azoles, amphotericin B, and echinocandins (eg, micafungin) are generally reserved for fluconazole-resistant cases. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although severe retrosternal chest pain can occur with esophageal candidia- sis, a CT of the chest is not the best test to confirm the diagnosis. Suspected esophageal candidiasis is best confirmed by endoscopy with an esophageal biopsy, but this procedure is not required emergently. Although endoscopy with an esophageal biopsy is the gold standard for con- firmation of esophageal candidiasis, it is not required emergently. In fact, those with high clinical suspicion for esophageal candidiasis, such as AIDS pa- tients with odynophagia and coincidental thrush, can be empirically treated without an endoscopic diagnosis. Endoscopy is then reserved for those who do not improve after a few days on empiric antifungal medications. Endoscopy with an esophageal biopsy is the gold-standard test to diagnose esophageal candidiasis because a biopsy can show yeast and pseudohyphae invad- ing mucosal cells. Endoscopy and biopsy, however, are not required ini- tially or emergently.
