الفخ: الطلاب بختاروا esophageal biopsy أو endoscopy بس لأنه فكروا إنهم المطلوبين من الأول. بس هدول بيصيروا بعد ما نستبعد الـ HIV أولاً، والخزعة هي الخطوة المؤكدة بعد الفحص الأولى للـ HIV.

question: Which virus is a major cause of odynophagia in AIDS patients?
englishExplanation: Seriously immunocompromised patients — those with severe AIDS, transplant patients, and those on cytotoxic chemotherapy — are at high risk for cytomegalovirus (CMV), an AIDS-defining illness. CMV commonly affects the GI tract and can cause esophagitis, which often presents with odynophagia due to ulcers and erosions in the distal esophagus. CMV esophagitis is less common than candidal esophagitis, so patients with AIDS who present with esophagitis are often empirically treated with oral fluconazole for 2 to 3 weeks. If fluconazole treatment is unsuccessful, an endoscopy and biopsy should be used for definitive diagnosis. CMV is managed with intravenous ganciclovir for 3 to 6 weeks, along with the initi- ation or continuation of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Importantly, CMV retinitis is often present concurrently with CMV infection else- where; thus, screening for CMV retinitis is necessary prior to starting HAART. HAART initiation may cause immune reconstitution inflammatory syn- drome (IRIS) and produce blindness in patients with retinitis. Incorrect Answer Explanations EBV is a type of herpesvirus that is primarily associated with mononu- cleosis and a variety of lymphomas. EBV is a very rare cause of esophagitis, with CMV being more common. In HIV/AIDS patients, EBV is more often associated with oral hairy leukoplakia, which typically manifests as a painless white plaque on the tongue that cannot be scraped off. HHV-8 is associated with the development of Kaposi sarcoma in HIV/AIDS patients and is also considered an AIDS-defining illness. Kaposi sarcoma very rarely manifests in the GI tract and causes ulcera- tion. It is a much less common cause of odynophagia than CMV. HSV, however, is a common cause of esophagitis in HIV patients. HPV infections cause warts in various places on the body, and some strains are associated with cervical cancer. For an HIV patient, invasive cer- vical cancer is considered an AIDS-defining illness. However, HPV is a rare cause of esophagitis in HIV/AIDS patients and is much less common than CMV.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Cytomegalovirus، لأنه السبب الأهم للـ odynophagia عند مرضى AIDS. فاللي صار إنه المريض مناعيته منهارة، يعني عنده severe AIDS أو زرع عضو أو كيموثرابي cytotoxic، وهاد بيسبّب CMV infection بتمسّ الـ GI tract وتعمل esophagitis بقرحات وتآفات في الـ distal esophagus بتطلع odynophagia. وكمان هاد المرض بيعتبر AIDS-defining illness، وبيتعاملوا معه بـ IV ganciclovir لمدة 3 إلى 6 أسابيع مع HAART، ولازم يفحصوا للمريض عن CMV retinitis قبل ما يبدأ HAART لأن IRIS ممكن يسبّب عمى.
الفخ: EBV هو الاختيار الغلط الشائع، لأنو herpesvirus ارتبط بـ mononucleosis والـ lymphomas، وسبب نادر جداً للـ esophagitis، ومع مرضى HIV بيشوفوا عنده oral hairy leukoplakia بدون ألم. فلما تشوف esophagitis عند مريض AIDS، دوّر على CMV مش EBV.

question: What is first-line treatment for gastroesophageal reflux in the third trimester of pregnancy?
englishExplanation: Over-the-counter antacids are the first-line therapy for GERD during preg- nancy. These should be added for patients whose symptoms fail to im- prove with lifestyle modifications (eg, eating small meals, eliminating exacer- bating foods, elevating the head of the bed, and not eating within 3 hours of going to sleep). Antacids often provide immediate relief for patients. GERD is common in pregnancy due to loosening of the lower esophageal sphincter and delayed gastric emptying that result from pregnancy-related hormones. Typical symptoms include burning epigastric pain, which may radiate to the back or neck; pain when lying flat; and pain which is worsened by consuming particular foods (eg, acidic foods). Incorrect Answer Explanations H2-receptor antagonists (eg, cimetidine or ranitidine) are not first-line therapies for GERD during pregnancy. Although they are safe for use in preg- nancy, H2-receptor antagonists should be added after lifestyle modification and antacid use fail to provide relief. Proton pump inhibitors are used for severe, persistent GERD symptoms in pregnancy after H2-receptor antagonists and antacids have failed. Proton pump inhibitors are also safe in pregnancy and have not been shown to be teratogenic. Sucralfate is also not a first-line therapy for GERD during pregnancy. Sucralfate is a therapy used for GI ulcers. It creates a barrier against further damage from secreted gastric acid. Sucralfate is safe for use in pregnancy for patients who have persistent symptoms despite lifestyle modification and use of antacids and H2-re- ceptor antagonists.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Antacids، لأنها أول-line علاج للـ GERD وقت الحمل. فاللي صار إنه الـ GERD شائع بالحومل بسبب ارتخاء الـ lower esophageal sphincter وتأخر إفراغ المعدة بسبب هرمونات الحمل، وبيصير عند المريضة حرقة بمعدتها ممكن تنزل للظهر أو الرقبة وألم لحظة ما تنام ويزيد مع الأكل الحمضي. ولازم نبدأ بـ lifestyle modifications وهي وجبات صغيرة، وتجنّب الأكلات اللي بتزيد الأعراض، ورفع رأس السرير، وبلا أكل قبل 3 ساعات من النوم، وإذا ما تحسّن الوضع بنضيف antacids لأنها بتدي راحة فورية.
الفخ: H2-receptor antagonists مثل cimetidine و ranitidine بتيجي بالترتيب، و proton pump inhibitors بتستخدم بس لما الأعراض تبقى شديدة ومستمرة بعد ما H2 و antacids فشلوا، و sucralfate دواء للـ GI ulcers مش للـ reflux. يعني الترتيب مهم: antacids أولاً.

question: In an infant with vomiting after feeding and feeding irritability, which sign would support a diagnosis of GERD requiring medication or feeding changes?
englishExplanation: GERD in infants is characterized by frequent vomiting (reflux episodes) associated with complications such as esophagitis or poor weight gain. Feeding refusal and irritability (eg, back arching that occurs with feed- ing) are occasionally seen with GERD in infants. New vomiting beginning after 6 months of life or recurrent pneumonia are infrequently seen with GERD. Apnea or other acute changes in behavior (ie, brief resolved unexplained event [BRUE]) should not be attributed to reflux or GERD. Esophageal pH monitoring is occasionally performed and may assist in the diagnosis and management of GERD in infants. Management may include lifestyle changes or pharmacother- apy with a proton pump inhibitor. Gastroesophageal reflux is a normal physiologic process that affects many infants. It is characterized by frequent episodes of small volume regurgitation that occur after feeding. These patients are often described as “happy spitters.” Notably, other concerning findings that elevate the condition to GERD are absent. Incorrect Answer Explanations Frequent regurgitation is common in infants who are described as “happy spitters.” This is similarly termed gastroesophageal reflux but is consid- ered benign in the absence of symptoms that are concerning for GERD (eg, feed- ing refusal, poor weight gain, and irritability). Projectile vomiting that worsens over several days in the first 2 to 3 months of life should be concerning for pyloric stenosis and is not seen in patients with GERD. Patients with pyloric stenosis present with nonbilious projec- tile vomiting, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbances. Rectal bleeding should not be seen in infants with GERD. Blood in the stool of an infant with vomiting and colicky abdominal pain is suggestive of intus- susception, which typically affects children between the ages of 3 and 12 months. Bloody stools can also be seen in food protein-induced proctocolitis.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Poor weight gain، لأن الـ GERD بالرضّع بيصاحبه تكرار القيء مع مضاعفات حقيقية زي esophagitis أو تأخر واضح في زيادة الوزن. فاللي صار إنه الطفل يقيّ بعد الرضعة ويكون سريع الانزعاج وبيقوّس (back arching) وقت الرضاعة، هاد كله بيرفع الموضوع لـ GERD مش reflux طبيعي. والـ GERD ممكن يحتاج lifestyle changes أو proton pump inhibitor، وأحياناً بنعمل esophageal pH monitoring عشان نأكد.
الفخ: تكرار regurgitation بكميات صغيرة بعد الرضاعة هو reflux طبيعي عند الـ happy spitters، يعني لا إما فيه symptoms مزعجة. فلما تشوف baby happy spitter بلا تأخر وزن ولا رفض رضاعة، هاد reflux benign مش GERD.

question: A 60-year-old man with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presents for epigastric pain that radiates into the chest. Which feature would be most con- sistent with this pain being caused by gastroesophageal reflux?

options.text: Occurs predominantly at night after going to bed
Worsens with exertion and relieved with rest

correctAnswer: Occurs predominantly at night after going to bed
englishExplanation: GERD is a benign noncardiac cause of chest pain. GERD frequently presents with a burning or squeezing retrosternal pain that often occurs after meals and is relieved by antacids. It is common for this condition to present at night after going to bed. When patients lie flat, stomach contents push against the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) and can reflux into the esophagus, causing symptoms. Other associated symptoms may include sensa- tion of refluxed stomach contents, sour taste in the mouth, dysphagia, globus sensa- tion, hoarse voice, or chronic cough. Multiple substances are known to relax the LES, worsening reflux symptoms. These include alcohol, nicotine, and caffeine. It is important to evaluate patients for the presence of GI bleeding if a diagnosis of GERD is suspected. This should include asking the patient about the presence of hematemesis, black or tarry stools, or hematochezia. GERD should not cause GI bleeding. If bleeding is noted, this suggests another diagnosis such as peptic ulcer disease, esophagitis or esophageal erosion, Mallory-Weiss tear, esophageal varices, GI arteriovenous malformation, or diverticulosis, among others. It is also important to note that relief of symptoms from a “GI cocktail” in the emergency department is not diagnostic of GERD, and other diag- noses should still be considered as clinically indicated. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients experiencing melena should be evaluated for a more sinister diagnosis than GERD. GERD in and of itself should not cause significant GI bleeding. If there are signs and symptoms of GI bleeding, another diagnosis should be consid- ered, such as peptic ulcer disease, esophagitis or esophageal erosion, tumor, Mallory-Weiss tear, esophageal varices, GI arteriovenous malformation, or diverticulosis. Acid reflux symptoms may be associated with shortness of breath and are known to be a cause of chronic cough. However, epigastric pain radiating into the chest associated with shortness of breath in a patient with known hyper- tension and hyperlipidemia should raise concern that this pain may be cardiorespiratory in etiology. The presence of shortness of breath in this case should not reassure the clinician that the causative diagnosis is GERD. Epigastric pain into the chest that worsens with exertion and is relieved with rest in a patient with underlying hypertension and hyperlipidemia should be considered as cardiac angina until proven otherwise. GERD may worsen with exertion due to increased intra abdominal pressures that can oc- cur with exercise, causing increased pressure on the LES. However, this would be a diagnosis of exclusion after other diagnoses, particularly coronary artery disease, have been evaluated.

ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Occurs predominantly at night after going to bed، لأن الـ GERD سبب غيرcardiac شائع لألم الصدر. فاللي صار إنه المريض لما ينام مستوي، محتويات المعدة بتدفع على الـ lower esophageal sphincter وبتترجع للمريء، وهاد بيسبّب حرقة أو انضغاط خلف عظمة الصدر بتتحسن مع antacids وبتظهر بالليل بشكل خاص. وأعراض ثانية ممكن تجي معاه زي حموضة الفم أو dysphagia أو globus sensation أو بحّة أو cough، و alcohol و nicotine و caffeine بيرخوا الـ LES وب worsening للأعراض.
الفخ: stools سوداء وقارية معناها مش GERD، لأن الـ GERD ما بيسبّب نزيف، فإذا لقيتها دوّر على peptic ulcer disease أو esophagitis أو varices. واللي بيحس بألم worsens with exertion و relieved with rest لازم يفكّر بالقلب مش بالـ GERD.

question: What may be a complication of GERD?
englishExplanation: Esophageal strictures are a potential complication of GERD, resulting from the healing process related to erosive esophagitis. Esophageal strictures may result in progressive dysphagia to solids and, in some cases, to intermit- tent esophageal obstruction with food (ie, food impaction). Peptic strictures are often located at or near the gastroesophageal junction. Men, older patients, and those with a longer duration of GERD symptoms are all at higher risk for stricture formation. Patients with esophageal strictures may note gradually progressive dys- phagia to solids. This occurs several seconds after the initiation of swallowing, and patients have the sensation that food is stuck in the passage from the esophagus to the stomach. Symptoms usually develop after eating meat. Patients with peptic stricture alone may have a history of only heartburn and regurgitation, while pa- tients with esophageal cancer are likely to be older men who report weight loss. Incorrect Answer Explanations Metabolic acidosis is unassociated with GERD. Metabolic alkalosis may be seen with excessive use of antacids (eg, calcium carbonate) or baking soda (ie, sodium bicarbonate). Hypercalcemia may also be seen in overdoses of calcium carbonate. GERD is not a risk factor for head and neck cancers. Risk factors for head and neck cancers include tobacco and alcohol use, immunodeficiency, radi- ation, occupational exposures, and HPV infections. Chronic GERD in- creases the risk for adenocarcinoma of the esophagus. Water brash or hypersalivation is an uncommon symptom that may be associated with GERD. Dry mouth (ie, xerostomia) is not expected to result from GERD.

ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Food impaction، لأن esophageal strictures من complications الـ GERD. فاللي صار إنه الـ erosive esophagitis لما يتعافى بيسبّب تضيّق (stricture) في المريء، وهاد بيسبّب dysphagia تدريجي للأكل الصلب وأحياناً انسداد متقطع بالطعام يعني food impaction. والـ peptic strictures غالباً قريبة من الـ gastroesophageal junction، والخطر أعلى عند الرجال والكبار اللي عندهم GERD من زمان، والأعراض بتبان بعد أكل اللحم.
الفخ: metabolic acidosis مالها علاقة بالـ GERD؛ اللي بيصير مع GERD هو metabolic alkalosis من overuse للـ antacids مثل calcium carbonate أو baking soda، وأحياناً hypercalcemia. و GERD مش عامل خطر لسرطان الرأس والعنق، و اللي عنده وزن ناقص وكبار بيحكوا عن cancer مش stricture.

question: A patient presents with new-onset burning chest pain that occurs after meals. GERD is suspected. Which additional finding requires close follow-up with upper endoscopy?
englishExplanation: GERD is a diagnosis that may often be made clinically, and it is treated with empiric lifestyle and pharmacologic interventions. A number of risk factors for malignancy, including age older than 60 years, are indications for further workup including endoscopy. Other features suggestive of GI malignancy in- clude weight loss, anorexia, persistent vomiting, iron-deficiency anemia, GI bleeding, dysphagia, odynophagia, and GI cancer in a first-degree relative. GERD patients presenting with these symptoms should be referred to their primary physician or to gastroenterology for further evaluation. Additionally, screening for Barrett esophagus is necessary in patients with a 5- to 10-year his- tory of GERD plus these additional risk factors: age older than 50 years, male sex, white race, hiatal hernia, obesity, nocturnal reflux, tobacco use, and a first-degree relative with Barrett esophagus or adenocarcinoma. Incorrect Answer Explanations Being a member of the male sex, rather than the female sex, is a risk factor for progression to Barrett esophagus in patients with a greater than 5-year history of GERD. These patients require additional evaluation with upper endoscopy. Iron-deficiency anemia may be an early finding in GERD patients with GI malignancy. In the appropriate clinical context, it may prompt additional workup, including upper endoscopy. However, macrocytic anemia would be unex- pected in this context. Microcytic anemia would be an indication for early endoscopy. In a patient with GERD, metabolic alkalosis may result from overuse of antacids, such as calcium carbonate. In this context, hypercalcemia may be observed as well. Metabolic alkalosis is not a risk factor for malignancy and does not warrant close follow-up for endoscopy. A number of risk factors for malignancy (in- cluding age >60 years, not metabolic alkalosis) are indications for further workup including endoscopy.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Age older than 60 years، لأنه من عوامل الخطر اللي بتستدعي work-up إضافي بـ upper endoscopy عند مرضى GERD. والـ GERD غالباً بينعمل diagnosise سريري وبيتّعالج تجريبياً، بس إذا لقيت علامات زي وزن ناقص أو anorexia أو persistent vomiting أو iron-deficiency anemia أو GI bleeding أو dysphagia أو odynophagia أو حدا من عيلته عنده GI cancer، لازم تحوّله للـ primary physician أو gastroenterology. وكمان بنعمل screening للـ Barrett esophagus إذا عنده 5 إلى 10 سنة GERD مع عوامل زيادة.
الفخ: أنثى مش المشكلة، بالعكس الذكور هو عامل خطر للـ Barrett esophagus. و macrocytic anemia مش العلامة اللي بتستدعي endoscopy، الـ iron-deficiency anemia هي اللي بتستدعي endoscopy، و metabolic alkalosis بتظهر من overuse للـ antacids.

question: A 19-year-old man with a history of developmental delay is brought in by his mother after she saw him drink a small amount of household bleach. The patient denies any complaint, and the physical examination is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
englishExplanation: The appropriate management of asymptomatic accidental ingestion of a small amount of a low-concentration acidic or alkaline substance includes discharge with outpatient follow-up. Household bleach is the most common household al- kali. It has a sodium hypochlorite solution of 3% to 6% and a pH of 11; it is fairly dilute and only minimally corrosive to the esophagus. Household bleach ingestion rarely causes significant injury. Caustic alkali injuries can cause liquefaction necrosis, a process in which the hydroxide ion penetrates deep tis- sues and causes injury secondary to protein denaturation and lipid saponification. However, this is unlikely to occur in this patient, who ingested only a small quantity of household bleach. Incorrect Answer Explanations Certain agents are contraindicated in caustic ingestions. These include neu- tralizing agents, which release heat that can cause additional tissue injury. Ingestion of industrial-strength bleach or powdered hypochlorite solu- tion is much more likely to result in esophageal injury than ingestion of household bleach. Endoscopic evaluation is indicated in patients with these ingestions. Gastric decontamination with activated charcoal is relatively con- traindicated in caustic ingestions. Charcoal does not bind well to most caustics and can impair visualization if endoscopy is warranted.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Discharge home with outpatient follow-up، لأن التعرض العَرَضي لكميات صغيرة من مادة حمضية أو قلوية منخفضة التركيز ما بيسبّب إصابة كبيرة. فاللي صار إنه سرير المريء الخفيف (household bleach) هو أكثر alkali منزلي شيوعاً، وهو sodium hypochlorite بتركيز 3% إلى 6% و pH بحدود 11، أي ضعيف وم corrosive بشكل بسيط للـ esophageal wall. وكمان المريض ما عنده symptoms والفحص عنده طبيعي، و الـ ingestions الكاوية الكبيرة هي اللي بتعمل liquefaction necrosis.
الفخ: neutralizing agents ممنوعة لأنها بتطلق حرارة وبتزيد الإصابة، و gastric decontamination بـ activated charcoal شبه contraindicated لأنه ما بيلزق كويس مع caustics وبيعيّب الرؤية وقت endoscopy. أما industrial-strength bleach أو مسحوق hypochlorite فهاد اللي يستاهل endoscopy.

question: For a patient with dysphagia, which factor is most consistent with distal esophageal spasm?

options.text: Frequent episodes of gagging and coughing when eating
History of food “sticking” and retrosternal fullness with eating solids
Need for repeated swallows to complete swallowing
Needing to lift the neck or throw the shoulders back to complete swallowing

correctAnswer: History of food “sticking” and retrosternal fullness with eating solids
englishExplanation: Distal esophageal spasm (DES) is classically associated with dysphagia, a history of food “sticking,” and retrosternal fullness after eating, but retrosternal chest pain may also be present. Normally, food boluses are transported from the mouth to the stomach by peristaltic waves through the esophageal wall. Patients with DES have abnormal contractions in the distal esophagus that can lead to the improper transfer of a bolus (either solid or liquid) from the esophagus into the stomach, resulting in a characteristic “corkscrew” esophagus on barium esophagram. The underlying cause of this rare esophageal motility disorder is not well understood, but gastric acid exposure is a known secondary risk factor. Incorrect Answer Explanations Frequent episodes of gagging and coughing when eating are associated with oropharyngeal dysphagia. Reported “sticking” and retrosternal discom- fort after eating are much more consistent with distal esophageal spasm. Oropharyngeal dysphagia is characterized by abnormal transfer of a bo- lus from the pharynx to the esophagus. Unlike distal esophageal spasm, oropharyngeal dysphagia is very common and is associated with many different conditions, especially those causing neuromuscular weakness, such as stroke or brain injury. The need for repeated swallows to complete swallowing is more typical of patients with oropharyngeal dysphagia. Oropharyngeal dysphagia generally mani- fests as difficulty initiating a swallow and the sensation of residual food in the pharynx, which requires repeated swallows. These symptoms con- trast with distal esophageal spasm's characteristic “sticking” and retrosternal dis- comfort after eating. Needing to lift the neck or throw the shoulders back to complete swallowing is typi- cal of patients with achalasia. Achalasia is characterized by inadequate re- laxation of the lower esophageal sphincter and lack of peristalsis in the distal esophagus; a “bird beak” sign on barium esophagram demon- strates this pathology clearly. This abnormal relaxation results in solid and liq- uid dysphagia and regurgitation. Notably, these symptoms differ from the “sticking” and retrosternal discomfort after eating that characterize distal esophageal spasm.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي History of food “sticking” and retrosternal fullness with eating solids، لأن distal esophageal spasm كلاسيكياً بيجي مع dysphagia و food “sticking” و fullness خلف عظمة الصدر بعد الأكل، وأحياناً صدري وجع. واللي صار إنه في DES في انقباضات غير طبيعية بالجزء البعيد من المريء بتخلي الـ bolus ما ينزل صح للمعدة، وهاد بطلع corkscrew esophagus على barium esophagram. والسبب ما منضبط تماماً، بس تعرّض حمض المعدة عامل خطر ثانوي معروف.
الفخ: gagging وكحة وقت الأكل، والحاجة تبتلع عدة مرات، والحركة اللي ترفع الرقبة أو ترمي الكتفين لتبلع، هدول كلهم oropharyngeal dysphagia مش distal. فاللي بيوصف food “sticking” و retrosternal fullness بعد الأكل هو اللي بيميل لـ DES.

question: A 52-year-old man presents with severe chest pain radiating to his neck. It started acutely 2 hours earlier, has been unrelenting, and is worse with deep breathing and swallowing. According to his wife, he regularly smokes marijuana, has been vomiting multiple times today, and "threw up so hard he vomited blood." The patient confirms this, and his voice is notably hoarse. On examina- tion, he appears distressed due to pain, and his skin is sweaty. His vital signs are BP 174/89, P 112, R 24, and T 37.8°C (100°F); SpO is 98% on room air. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
englishExplanation: Boerhaave syndrome is a life-threatening, full-thickness perforation of the esophagus from a rapid rise in esophageal pressure. It can result from any straining valsalva maneuver or weakening of the esophageal mucosa (eg, forceful vomiting, coughing, heavy lifting, childbirth, foreign body or caustic in- gestion, esophagitis, cancer, or trauma). The patient's history of marijuana use with several episodes of vomiting is consistent with cannabinoid hypereme- sis syndrome. Boerhaave syndrome classically results in sudden, severe, and un- relenting chest pain that may radiate to the neck, back, shoulders, and abdomen. Thirty percent of patients develop emphysema in the mediastinal or cervical areas, resulting in crepitus on palpation or a Hamman crunch on auscultation. It is important to note that mediastinal emphysema can take time to develop; its absence does not necessarily rule out perforation. Although Boerhaave syndrome is often the cause of esophageal perforation, it is no longer the most common cause. In this era, iatrogenic causes are more common, resulting from upper endoscopy, esophageal dilatation, TEE, variceal treatment, and a variety of injuries. Incorrect Answer Explanations The presentation of Boerhaave syndrome can be clinically challenging and can mimic other conditions. Although acute myocardial infarction should be con- sidered in a patient who presents with chest pain, it is unlikely given the other as- pects of the complaint, including forceful vomiting and sudden onset of chest pain to the neck. This patient has a trigger for esophageal perforation with powerful emesis and evi- dence for laryngeal involvement. Although peptic ulcer disease can produce vomit- ing with bloody emesis, it usually has a relationship with food and body posi- tion. Perforation can be caused by an ulcer and can produce severe pain, but this would usually not ascend into the neck or shoulders. Pain from spontaneous pneumothorax is not associated with episodes of forceful vomiting. Perforation of the lower esophagus can cause a pneumotho- rax, but this would not be a primary presentation of a spontaneous pneumothorax.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Boerhaave syndrome، لأنه ثقب كامل السماكة في المريء بسبب ارتفاع سريع في ضغط المريء بعد vomitus عنيف. فاللي صار إنه المريض يستخدم marijuana وعنده episodes Vomiting كتير بما يتوافق مع cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome، وعنده sudden severe unrelenting chest pain بينزل للرقبة والظهر والكتف والبطن، وصوته hoarse. و 30% من الحالات بتعمل mediastinal emphysema أو cervical وتطلع crepitus أو Hamman crunch، بس غيابها ما بينفي perforation، وهاي اليوم مش أكثر أسباب perforation لأن iatrogenic أكثر.
الفخ: acute myocardial infarction بيجي بألم صدر، بس الميزة هون إن الـ vomiting العنيف والألم اللي ما بيخف والـ hoarseness بيشدوا على Boerhaave. والـ spontaneous pneumothorax بيسبّب ضيق نفس وألم، مش vomitus.

question: What is the most common cause of esophageal perforations?
englishExplanation: Today, esophageal perforations most commonly occur during medical procedures. They have been reported with upper endoscopy (most common), esophageal dilation, TEE, variceal treatment, intraoperative injury, and accidental esophageal intubation. Pain, fever, dyspnea, or crepitus within hours of esophageal instrumentation should be considered a sign of perforation unless proven otherwise. After an esophageal perforation occurs, saliva and gastric contents can enter the mediastinal, pleural, or peritoneal space, triggering a marked infectious and inflammatory response. Depending on the site of perfora- tion, patients may describe severe, unrelenting pain in the neck, chest, or abdomen with radiation to the back or shoulders. Fever, hypotension, tachycardia, and tachypnea are also common. A Hamman crunch can sometimes be heard on ex- amination. The diagnosis can often be established with CT of the neck and chest with intravenous contrast; if CT is negative but suspicion remains high, patients should undergo video esophagoscopy or esophagography with water-soluble con- trast. Management includes broad-spectrum antibiotics, emergent surgi- cal consultation, and supportive resuscitation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Boerhaave syndrome is a full-thickness esophageal rupture that occurs with suddenly elevated intraluminal esophageal pressure; forceful vomiting, cough- ing, heavy lifting, seizures, and childbirth can create sufficiently ele- vated pressure. Most ruptures occur in the distal esophagus. However, Boerhaave syndrome is no longer the most common cause of esophageal perforations. Foreign body ingestion can lead to an esophageal perforation; for example, esophageal perforations can occur secondary to injury caused by a swal- lowed pill, esophageal necrosis from button batteries, or injury caused by a sharp object. Foreign body ingestion, however, is a relatively rare cause of esophageal perforations. Traumatic injury of the esophagus is uncommon, and most cases are as- sociated with penetrating gunshot or stab wounds. Most traumatic esophageal perforations occur in the proximal and middle third of the esophagus; Boerhaave syndrome most commonly occurs in the distal esophagus.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Iatrogenic perforation، لأن perforations الـ esophageal اليوم بتكثر أثناء الإجراءات الطبية. فاللي صار إنه الـ upper endoscopy هو السبب الأكثر شيوعاً، وبعده esophageal dilation و TEE و variceal treatment و injury أثناء العملية و intubation بالغلط. وأي pain أو fever أو dyspnea أو crepitus خلال ساعات من الـ instrumentation لازم ينحسب perforation لحد ما يثبت العكس، والتشخيص غالباً بـ CT للرقبة والصدر مع contrast، ولو CT سلبية بكمّل esophagoscopy أو esophagography بمادة ذائبة بالماء، والعلاج antibiotics واسعة النطاق.
الفخ: Boerhaave بيحصل مع vomiting عنيف وارتفاع ضغط مفاجئ، أما foreign body ingestion أو traumatic perforation فهاد نادر مقارنة. فلما في procedure صار على المريء، الـ iatrogenic هي الافتراضي.

question: A mother brings in her 2-year-old son after she saw him put something in his mouth while he was playing. He has been in no distress since the event and is currently at baseline. X-rays are obtained and shown below. What is the appro- priate disposition? Credit: Copyright 2023 Dr. Yair Glick. Image courtesy of Dr. Yair Glick and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 52187. Used under license.

options.text: Admit him to the hospital for observation
Discharge home with outpatient follow-up in 3 to 5 days
Perform gastric lavage using a nasogastric tube

englishExplanation:
The object seen on the x-ray is a button battery in the esophagus, as indi- cated by the radiographic halo or double circle noted on the foreign body. Although coins and other objects are more commonly ingested, they usually require observation and supportive care. An ingested button battery or magnet, in contrast, may need to be removed in the emergency department if it is in the esoph- agus or more proximal; it can cause an external current that can result in hydroly- sis and erosion of the GI tract over time. A button battery that is lodged in the esophagus can cause erosion within a few hours and should be removed as soon as possible. Management otherwise depends on the age of the patient and the size of the button battery. The National Battery Ingestion Hotline can help in the decision- making process, 800-498-8666. Incorrect Answer Explanations Admission for observation is unlikely to be warranted because the child is in no distress. It is also not an appropriate treatment because the battery sim- ply needs to be removed; it can erode the upper GI tract rapidly. Discharge home with follow-up would be inappropriate for a button bat- tery in the esophagus. This needs to be removed to avoid erosion. Observation for 12 to 24 hours would be appropriate for an esophageal foreign body without red flags (eg, airway compromise, inability to swallow secretions, sharp ob- ject, button battery, magnet, or signs of obstruction) and if the ingested object did not have the potential to damage intestinal tissue. This is often the course of treat- ment when a child ingests a coin or dull-edged object. There is no advantage in ex- amining the stool in these cases; instead, close follow-up and immediate re-evalua- tion are indicated for any complaints of abdominal pain or vomiting. Gastric lavage has fallen out of favor with most toxicologists except in some cases of life-threatening toxic ingestions. It is never used in caustics or hydrocarbon ingestions.

Review notes: ["visual_reference_no_image_attached_in_jsonl"]
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Remove the foreign body endoscopically، لأن الأشعة بتبيّن button battery في المريء من خلال الـ double circle أو الـ halo. واللي صار إنه الباتري المعلق في المريء بيعمل تيار خارجي بيسبّب hydrolysis وerosion للـ GI tract، وبيقدر يعمل تآكل خلال ساعات قليلة، فلازم ينزع بأسرع وقت. والـ coins وأي objects تانية بتيجي أكثر بس غالباً بتحتاج observation و supportive care، وهاد الفرق.
الفخ: تاخذ الطفل admitted للمشاهدة أو تطلّعاه مع follow-up خطأ، لأن الباتري لازم ينزع مش بسنتابع، والطفل ما عنده أي distress. و gastric lavage بالـ NG tube مش إجابة أبداً.

question: Where do most esophageal foreign objects become lodged in pediatric patients?

options.text: Distal esophagus at the level of the gastroesophageal junction
Mid-esophagus at the level of the carina
Mid-esophagus at the level of the great vessels
Proximal esophagus at the level of the cricopharyngeus muscle

correctAnswer: Proximal esophagus at the level of the cricopharyngeus muscle
englishExplanation: Most pediatric foreign objects become lodged in the proximal esophagus at the level of the cricopharyngeus muscle due to the anatomical narrowing at this site. This is also referred to as the upper esophageal sphincter (UES). In adults, the majority of esophageal foreign bodies are lodged at the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). Other major areas of anatomic esophageal narrow- ing include at the intersection with the aortic arch and left mainstem bronchus as well as at the diaphragmatic hiatus that forms the lower esophageal sphincter. Pathologic narrowing, strictures, or other anatomic abnormalities can cause im- pactions at other levels but are much less common. Incorrect Answer Explanations Foreign body impaction can occur in the distal esophagus at the level of the lower esophageal sphincter. However, impaction at the gastroesophageal junction is less common in pediatric patients than in the proximal esophagus. Foreign body impaction can occur in the mid-esophagus at the level of the main- stem bronchi/carina. However, impaction at the mainstem bronchi/carina is less common than in the proximal esophagus. Foreign body impaction can occur in the mid-esophagus at the level of the aortic arch. However, impaction in the proximal esophagus is much more common.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Proximal esophagus at the level of the cricopharyngeus muscle، لأن أغلب الأغراض اللي بتبلعها الأطفال بتعلق في proximal esophagus بسبب التضيّق الموجود عند cricopharyngeus muscle، وهاد نفسه اسمه upper esophageal sphincter. أما بالبالغين فمعظم الأغراض بتعلق عند lower esophageal sphincter. والضيّقات التانية بنشوفها عند تقاطع المريء مع aortic arch و left mainstem bronchus وعند diaphragmatic hiatus، بس وجود stricture أو شذوذ تشريحي نادر.
الفخ: التعلق بالـ distal esophagus عند gastroesophageal junction هو الشائع في الكبار مش الأطفال، و mid-esophagus عند carina أو great vessels أقل شيوعاً. فإذا عرضك طفل، غالباً التعلق فوق.

question: An x-ray of a child with a suspected foreign body ingestion reveals a flat, circular object at the level of the thoracic inlet. Which factor can distinguish button bat- tery ingestion from coin ingestion?

options.text: Circular appearance on lateral chest x-ray

englishExplanation: Distinguishing button batteries lodged in the esophagus from coins is crucial. Button batteries are at high risk of causing rapid esophageal perforation, whereas coins are at much lower risk of serious injury. On an anteroposterior (AP) view of the chest, button batteries display the “double ring” sign, which looks like a circular object with a ring along the outer edge. Coins appear as a simple circular object without this ring. On a lateral x-ray, button batteries appear as a stack of two coins on top of each other, whereas a coin ap- pears as a single straight object. Incorrect Answer Explanations Given the anatomy of the tracheal rings, disk-shaped objects lodged in the tra- chea appear flat on AP x-rays and circular on lateral x-rays. Conversely, disk-shaped objects that are lodged in the esophagus appear circular on AP x-rays and flat on lateral x-rays. Given that both button batteries and coins are disk-shaped, orientation cannot distinguish between the two but can strongly suggest the anatomic location. Both button batteries and coins are radiopaque, so this feature cannot dif- ferentiate between the two. Thus, the double ring sign is among the most reliable signs to distinguish between these otherwise similar objects on x-ray. Button batteries and coins both come in a variety of sizes, so size cannot be used to distinguish between the two on x-ray. Instead, the double ring sign is among the most reliable x-ray findings to distinguish between these otherwise simi- lar objects.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Double ring sign، لأن التمييز بين button battery و coin على الأشعة مهم جداً. فاللي صار إنه الـ battery خطر سريع على esophageal perforation، والـ coin خطره أقل بكتير. على الـ AP view، الباتري بيبان كـ object دائري مع ring على الحافة الخارجية، وcoin بيبان دائرة بسيطة بدون هالحلقة. وعلى الـ lateral، الباتري بيبان mintain coin فوق coin، والـ coin بيبان object واحد مستقيم.
الفخ: الشكل على الـ lateral x-ray بيحدد المكان (trachea ولا esophagus) مش الباتري، و radiolucency ما تفيد لأن الاثنين radiopaque، وكمان الحجم ما بيفيد لأن الباتري والـ coin كليهما بأحجام متعددة. فعلياً الـ double ring sign هو أكتر علامة موثوقة.

question: What is the next best step for managing a confirmed button battery ingestion that is lodged in the proximal esophagus?
englishExplanation: Button batteries lodged in the esophagus require emergent removal be- cause they can cause mucosal injury, necrosis, and perforation within 6 hours of ingestion. If the battery is lodged within the esophagus, emergent con- sultation (and transfer, if necessary) for endoscopy is warranted to prevent serious injury. Other indications for endoscopy in esophageal foreign body management in- clude extremis, signs of esophageal perforation, the inability to handle secretions, or airway compromise. Ingested objects that require endoscopic removal in- clude button batteries, sharp or elongated objects, or multiple objects, especially multiple magnets. Any foreign body that has been present in the esophagus for over 24 hours also warrants endoscopic removal. Incorrect Answer Explanations Administration of intravenous glucagon can be considered for the man- agement of adults with distal esophageal food impaction. Glucagon works by relaxing the lower esophageal sphincter, allowing the object to pass. However, this therapy has a low overall success rate and can also cause vomiting, which can worsen the patient's clinical status. Glucagon is not indicated for pediatric proximal foreign bodies, especially button batteries. Administration of proteolytic enzymes, such as papain, is contraindi- cated in the management of any esophageal foreign body. Proteolytic en- zymes should not be used for button battery ingestions or food impactions because they have the potential to cause severe mucosal damage that can lead to esophageal perforation. Saline or other types of lavage are not indicated in the management of button batteries lodged within the esophagus. Complete esophageal obstruc- tion can lead to pooling of secretions, which can worsen with lavage. Button batter- ies, in particular, require emergent removal due to the high risk of esophageal mu- cosal injury.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Arrange for endoscopic removal، لأن الـ button battery اللي بالـ esophagus لازم تنزع بشكل عاجل، فممكن تسوي mucosal injury و necrosis و perforation خلال 6 ساعات من الـ ingestion. فاللي صار إنه الباتري علقت، لازم تعمل emergent consultation للـ endoscopy من غير تأخير، وهاد ينطبق كمان على objects حادة أو طويلة أو objects متعددة وخصوصاً magnets المتعددة، وأي object موجود بالـ esophagus أكثر من 24 ساعة لازم ينزع.
الفخ: intravenous glucagon ده للبالغين عند food impaction بالـ distal esophagus، ونجاحته ضعيف وبيعمل vomiting، ومش مناسب أبداً لطفل عنده button battery بالـ proximal. و proteolytic enzymes مثل papain ممنوعة مع أي foreign body.

question: A 7-year-old child presents with concern for ingestion of a foreign object. A plain x-ray shows a small button battery in the stomach. The child is playing without abdominal tenderness or respiratory distress. What is the next best step in man- agement of the options listed below?

options.text: Endoscopic removal of the foreign body

correctAnswer: Endoscopic removal of the foreign body
englishExplanation: Button batteries can cause severe damage to the GI tract and can cause ulceration or perforation of the esophagus and stomach. Once they have passed into the intestine or distally, though, asymptomatic patients typically can be man- aged expectantly with serial x-rays and monitoring to assess for passage from the stool. Most batteries in the intestine will pass without issues within a week. Although management continues to be controversial, most experts would agree that any esophageal button battery should be emergently removed. Many will also say that stomach button batteries should also be emergently removed; however, some sources recommend that patients with a button battery in the stomach with- out a magnet coningestion can follow-up in 24 hours, with repeat imaging in 24 to 48 hours. For batteries in the intestine and distal, management can be expectant if asymptomatic, or it can be managed with GI consultation and possible removal if the patient is younger (<5 years old) or large batteries. For symptomatic patients, emergent GI consultation and endoscopic removal can be considered. For asympto- matic patients with batteries distal to the stomach who are managed expectantly, patients should follow-up to assess for symptoms and undergo repeat ab- dominal x-rays in 10 to 14 days. Symptoms such as abdominal pain, vomit- ing, or signs of peritonitis or obstruction mandate immediate surgical consultation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Intravenous glucagon can be used in the management of distal esophageal food impactions in adults. It decreases the tone of the lower esophageal sphinc- ter. However, its overall success rates are low, and it can lead to nausea and vomit- ing, which is not recommended. Thus, glucagon is not indicated in the man- agement of foreign bodies within the stomach. Repeat abdominal x-rays for button batteries in the stomach should be completed in 24 to 48 hours, with a 24-hour GI follow-up ensured. These bat- teries have been known to cause mucosal damage and even perforation in the stom- ach. Thus, waiting 7 days for repeat testing and follow-up is too long. If the button battery is in the intestine, longer gap time between imaging is acceptable. Whole bowel irrigation can be considered in the management of patients who have ingested multiple small packets of drugs. However, this asymptomatic patient has a button battery in the stomach and can be managed expectantly.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Endoscopic removal of the foreign body، لأن الـ button battery بتسبب ضرر كبير بالـ GI tract وبتعمل ulceration أو perforation للمريء والمعدة. واللي صار إنه الباتري لسا بالمعدة فالنقاش حول إدارتها فيه خلاف، بس كثير من الخبراء بتنصح بإزالتها بشكل عاجل، وهاد هو الخيار الآمن. ولما الباتري تكون بعد الـ stomach والـ intestine والمريض بدون symptoms، وقتها بنتابعها expectantly مع serial x-rays ومتابعة نزولها مع الـ stool.
الفخ: تختاروا repeat x-ray بعد أسبوع على اعتبارها expectant management، بس هاد بس بينفع لو الباتري عدّت تجاوح الـ stomach والـ intestine والمريض بدون symptoms. هنا الباتري لسا بالمعدة، فالـ endoscopy هي الإجابة.

question: A patient presents with hematemesis after binge drinking alcohol. He reports ten episodes of nonbloody emesis prior to noticing “streaks of bright red blood.” He is hemodynamically stable, talking, and not actively vomiting on arrival. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

englishExplanation: Hematemesis following episodes of forceful vomiting and retching is concerning for Mallory-Weiss syndrome. Correct management for patients with suspected Mallory-Weiss syndrome and ongoing bleeding involves administration of a pro- ton pump inhibitor (PPI) for acid suppression and emergent endoscopy. If the patient is not actively bleeding, an endoscopy is not routinely performed. Mallory-Weiss syndrome results from a longitudinal, partial-thickness tear in the mucosa of the distal esophagus or proximal stomach due to increased intra-abdomi- nal pressure. Development of this syndrome is usually preceded by forceful vomit- ing or retching and is often associated with alcohol use. Most cases are mild, and bleeding spontaneously resolves. These patients are managed with PPI therapy alone following endoscopy. High-risk features for Mallory-Weiss syndrome include active bleeding on endoscopy, severe bleeding with hemodynamic instability or requiring transfusion, advanced age, multiple chronic comorbidities, and active anticoagulation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Mallory-Weiss syndrome is not an infectious process, so use of antibiotics would not be of added value. Management with a proton pump inhibitor is indicated for acid suppression in the setting of GI bleeding. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is unlikely to be of any benefit in the stable pa- tient with a suspected Mallory-Weiss tear. Gastroenterology consultation for endoscopy if actively bleeding is the management of choice, as it allows for di- rect visualization of the gastric mucosa and therapeutic intervention. Critically ill patients with massive GI hemorrhage may require rapid-se- quence intubation for airway protection due to significant risk of aspiration. This patient does not have any signs of massive hemoptysis or airway com- promise, so emergent intubation is not indicated.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Intravenous proton pump inhibitor therapy، لأن نزيف hematemesis بعد vomiting عنيف وretching بيرجّع لـ Mallory-Weiss syndrome. فاللي صار إنه فيه longitudinal partial-thickness tear في mucosa الـ distal esophagus أو proximal stomach بسبب ارتفاع intra-abdominal pressure، ومع alcohol. وكمان أغلب الحالات خفيفة والنزيف بيوقف لحاله، والـ management هو PPI للـ acid suppression مع emergent endoscopy، وبما إن المريض مو active bleeding فالـ endoscopy مش بشكل routinely.
الفخ: broad-spectrum antibiotics ما إلها لازمة لأن هاد مش infection، و CT للبطن والحوض ما بتفيد بمريض مستقر، و rapid-sequence intubation مش مطلوبة لأن المريض واقف يحكي ومش بيتقيّ. الـ PPI هي الفكرة.

question: Shortly after birth, a newborn is found to have a persistent cough, gagging, in- creased oral secretions, and respiratory distress. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: A tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) is an abnormal connection between the trachea and the esophagus, often causing newborns to aspirate and present clinically with cough, choking, and respiratory distress. There are several types of TEFs. They are characterized by anatomic location of the malformation and the presence or absence of an esophageal atresia (EA). EA prevents oral secretions and food from entering the stomach, so these infants have increased oral secretions and vomiting. The common classification of TEF and EA is as follows: Type A: EA without fistula Type B: EA with proximal TEF Type C: EA with distal TEF Type D: EA with proximal and distal TEF Type E: H-Type Fistula with no EA Incorrect Answer Explanations An esophageal web is a thin tissue that extends into the lumen of the esophagus. This newborn's presentation is inconsistent with an esophageal web because patients are usually asymptomatic. When they do experience symptoms, patients with esophageal webs will commonly present with intermittent dysphagia. Esophageal shortening is most commonly seen as a result of longstanding gastroe- sophageal reflux. Repeated reflux of stomach contents leads to inflammation, edema, and ultimately fibrosis of the esophagus. Congenital short esophagus is a rare condition associated with an intrathoracic stomach and hiatal hernia. These infants usually present with failure to thrive. Both congenital and ac- quired esophageal shortening require surgical repair. Tracheomalacia is a narrowing of the trachea during exhalation result- ing in stridor, cough, and respiratory distress. Although infants with tra- cheomalacia may have feeding difficulty, increased oral secretions are absent. Congenital tracheomalacia is due to cartilaginous defects in the trachea. Acquired tracheomalacia can be caused by inflammation due to recurrent infections, surgical complications, or external compression of the trachea from masses. Key Points Tracheoesophageal fistulas are rare. When present, tracheoesophageal fistulas typically occur with associated esophageal atresia. Newborns present with increased oral secretions, cough, choking, and respi- ratory distress. Congenital tracheomalacia is caused by a cartilaginous defect causing the trachea to partially collapse resulting in stridor, which is often positional. Acquired tracheomalacia can be caused by trauma, prolonged mechanical ventila- tion, or chronic infections and may require surgical repair depending upon the severity of symptoms.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Tracheoesophageal fistula، لأن الـ TEF وصلة شاذة بين الـ trachea والـ esophagus وبتخلي المواليد يستنشقوا ويسكبوا. فاللي صار إنه عند الطفل cough و choking و respiratory distress و increase في الـ oral secretions من أول أيام الحياة، وهذا presentation كلاسيكي. و الـ classification بيعتمد على مكان الـ malformation و presence أو absence الـ esophageal atresia، وEA بتخلي الـ secretions والطعام ما يوصلوا للمعدة فبتزيد.

question: Which diagnostic tool is most helpful in diagnosing H-type tracheoesophageal fistulas?

options.text: Chest x-ray following nasogastric tube placement
Upper GI fluoroscopy with water-soluble contrast

correctAnswer: Upper GI fluoroscopy with water-soluble contrast
englishExplanation: An upper GI fluoroscopy utilizes contrast to evaluate the esophagus, stom- ach, and duodenum and is the first-line diagnostic tool to evaluate for H-type tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF). An H-type TEF is associated with a patent esophagus; thus, it can be difficult to diagnose in a newborn because the clinical symptoms may be mild. Esophageal endoscopy and bronchoscopy can be instru- mental diagnostic tools when the defect is difficult to visualize. Because TEF and esophageal atresia (EA) are commonly associated with other ab- normalities like CHARGE syndrome (Coloboma, Heart defects, Atresia choanae, Retarded growth and development, Genital anomalies, and Ear anomalies and deafness) and VACTERL association (Vertebral anomalies, Anal atresia, Cardiac anomalies, TracheoEsophageal fistula, Radial or Renal anomalies, and Limb anom- alies), infants diagnosed with TEF and EA should undergo further evaluation in- cluding echocardiography and renal ultrasound. Incorrect Answer Explanations A barium swallow study is a fluoroscopy that can be used to evaluate for pha- ryngeal or esophageal abnormalities. Barium, a radiopaque contrast material, should be avoided when evaluating for TEF because the barium can cause pneu- monitis if aspirated. Barium swallow studies can be particularly useful in evaluating children with dysphagia. If the clinician suspects a TEF, a nasogastric (NG) tube can be inserted in the infant. An H-type TEF is unassociated with EA, and the NG tube will generally pass with ease, limiting its diagnostic utility. However, in patients with TEF asso- ciated with EA, the NG tube will typically stop advancing after 10 to 15 cm into the stomach. The NG tube will subsequently appear curled in the upper esophagus on chest x-ray. TEF can sometimes be visualized on prenatal ultrasound, but this is not a highly sensitive study. Maternal polyhydramnios and a small or absent fetal stomach bubble suggest TEF is present, at which point TEF can be confirmed by a fetal MRI.

question: Which initial task is critical in the preoperative management of infants with tra- cheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresia?

options.text: Place the infant in Trendelenburg position

englishExplanation: Patients with tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) often have additional con- genital anomalies, including congenital heart defects. Prior to surgery, it is imperative that these malformations are identified because specific anomalies (eg, right-sided aortic arch) may impact the surgical approach and are associated with higher morbidity. Furthermore, it is recommended that infants have laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy prior to surgical repair to further characterize anatomical abnormalities. TEF and esophageal atresia (EA) are often associated with CHARGE syndrome and VACTERL association. Infants with CHARGE syndrome have Colobomas, Heart defects, choanal Atresia, growth Retardation, and Genital and Ear abnormalities. VACTERL association includes Vertebral defects, anal Atresia, Cardiac defects, TEF, Renal abnormalities, and Limb anoma- lies. Infants with confirmed TEF and EA should be screened for these associated conditions. Incorrect Answer Explanations Infants with TEF should remain NPO (nothing by mouth) in preparation for surgical repair. A suction catheter should be placed in the esophageal pouch to con- tinuously clear any pooled secretions. A nasojejunostomy tube may pass into the je- junum in H-type TEF, but it would end in the esophageal pouch if EA is present. Trendelenberg positioning, with the head positioned lower than the feet, is contraindicated in patients with TEF and EA. Prior to surgery, the head of the bed should be elevated 30° to 45° for patients with TEF, which mini- mizes reflux and aspiration events. Because of the high risk for pulmonary aspira- tion, many experts also recommend prophylactic antibiotic treatment with ampi- cillin and gentamicin. Infants with TEF often develop respiratory distress, which requires prompt atten- tion. BVM ventilation should be avoided because it may cause gaseous distention. Alternatively, physicians should intubate patients, taking care to posi- tion the tip of the endotracheal tube distal to the fistula. Bronchoscopy can help with this. Gaseous distention increases the risk of hemodynamic compromise as a result of decreased venous return, and it can also lead to aspiration of stomach contents.

الفخ: nasojejunostomy feeds مش بديل، لأن الـ tube بيوصل للـ jejunum في H-type بس بيخلص بالـ esophageal pouch إذا فيه EA، والمفروض الطفل يضل NPO. و Trendelenburg position ممنوع لأنه بيزيد خطر aspiration.

question: Which chronic condition is most likely to develop after tracheoesophageal fistula repair?
englishExplanation: After the repair of a tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF), most patients ex- perience esophageal dysmotility and require additional therapy to aid in speech and swallowing. Patients are also at increased risk for GERD and esophagitis, and they should be treated with maximal proton pump inhibitor ther- apy. In adulthood, these patients are at increased risk for developing Barrett esoph- agus and, ultimately, esophageal cancer. Incorrect Answer Explanations Esophageal achalasia is a rare disorder affecting the esophagus in which nerve damage precludes normal peristalsis of the esophagus. The exact cause of achalasia is unknown, and its association with TEF repair is uncommon. Many of the symptoms of achalasia, such as regurgitation of food, heartburn, tran- sient chest pain, and nighttime cough, are similar to those symptoms seen in pa- tients with severe GERD. Patients who have had TEF repair commonly experience esophageal stricture, for which the treatment is esophageal dilatation. These stric- tures can be diagnosed by esophageal contrast studies and endoscopy. Presenting symptoms include recurrent respiratory infections, aspiration, cough, swallowing difficulties, and foreign body impaction. Esophageal varices are not a complication after TEF repair. Esophageal varices are dilated veins in the esophagus that result from portal hypertension. The elevated blood pressure in the portal venous system results in increased blood flow into the thin-walled esophageal vessels, causing swelling and increased risk for rup- ture. Esophageal varices are usually asymptomatic unless they rupture and bleed, at which time patients may present with hematemesis, hematochezia, or melena. Options for the treatment of ruptured varices include endoscopic sclerotherapy and endoscopic ligation of bleeding vessels. There are few case reports describing the rare development of TEF as a complication of these procedures.

question: What is the most common site of bleeding from varices in a patient with cirrhosis?
englishExplanation: The most common site of bleeding from varices is the distal esophagus. Whereas varices in the mid esophagus lie deep in the submucosa, varices in the distal esopha- gus near the gastroesophageal junction lie superficial and close to the surface. This superficial location increases the risk for bleeding. Other factors that increase the risk of bleeding include varices that are larger in diameter, certain appearance of varices (red wale marks or red streaks on the varices confer a higher risk), wors- ened liver function, and history of prior variceal bleeding. Incorrect Answer Explanations Varices in the gastric fundus are less common than varices in the distal esoph- agus. When bleeding from gastric varices occurs, it is more severe and has higher transfusion requirements than bleeding from esophageal varices. The proximal esophagus is not a common site of bleeding from varices. However, varices can occur at any point of the GI tract from the esophagus to the rectum. The rectum is not a common site of bleeding from varices. However, varices can occur at any point of the GI tract from the esophagus to the rectum.

question: What is the mechanism of action of octreotide treatment for variceal bleeding?
englishExplanation: In patients with GI bleeding from varices, octreotide decreases portal venous pressures and pressures in varices within seconds of administration. Octreotide has also been shown to achieve earlier hemostasis and decrease rates of rebleeding. However, there is no evidence to show that octreotide decreases mortality. Incorrect Answer Explanations Octreotide does not increase insulin release but rather suppresses it. This is the mechanism that supports its use for patients with hypoglycemia and sul- fonylurea usage. The suppression of insulin and other hormones may contribute to the ability of octreotide to regulate intestinal blood flow, which has been hypothe- sized to help decrease overall variceal pressures. Octreotide does not prevent infection in patients with variceal bleeding. Ceftriaxone is the medication that has been shown to prevent infection, reduce re- bleeding rates, and decrease rates of mortality in patients with variceal bleeding. Pantoprazole, rather than octreotide, is the medication that has been shown to decrease mucosal deterioration, which is one of reasons for its use in patients with GI bleeding from peptic ulcer disease. Pantoprazole also increases gastric pH, stabilizing clots on bleeding ulcers.

question: What is the most lethal complication of placing a Blakemore tube in a patient with bleeding from esophagogastric varices?
englishExplanation: The most lethal complication from Blakemore tube placement is esophageal perforation. This leads to mediastinitis and infection, with mortality rates of up to 50%. Esophageal perforation can occur if the gastric balloon is inflated above the diaphragm. Thus, an x-ray should be obtained prior to fully in- flating the gastric balloon to confirm its placement below the diaphragm. Additionally, esophageal perforation can occur if the esophageal balloon is inflated at exceedingly high pressures. The balloon should be inflated to pressures of 30 to 40 mm Hg. It is important to note that the Blakemore tube is placed as a tem- porizing measure as a bridge to definitive treatment, such as transjugular intrahep- atic portosystemic shunt. Incorrect Answer Explanations Airway obstruction will generally not occur since patients should be intubated prior to insertion of the Blakemore tube, but it can occur and can be substan- tially lethal. The Blakemore tube can be pulled out inadvertently, and the esophageal balloon can migrate into the oropharynx. This is another reason for pa- tients to be intubated prior to Blakemore tube placement. Aspiration pneumonia may occur from GI bleeding or other secretions exit- ing the esophagus and traveling into the tracheobronchial tree. Patients with GI bleeding and cirrhosis are also at increased risk of infections. However, this is not the most lethal complication of Blakemore tube insertion. Gastric perforation is not as likely to occur; the expansion of the gastric bal- loon to 250 mL is not enough to distend the stomach to the point of perforation. Additionally, the Blakemore tube has a rounded rubber tip that is unlikely to punc- ture through the stomach.

question: What is a late complication of esophageal cancer?
englishExplanation: Bronchoesophageal fistulas and tracheoesophageal fistulas result from direct erosion of an esophageal tumor through the esophageal wall into the mainstem bronchus or the trachea. The presentation varies, but it commonly in- volves frequent coughing and recurrent pneumonia. Dysphagia, iron defi- ciency anemia due to microscopic blood loss, weight loss, and retrosternal discom- fort are early complications of esophageal cancer. Esophageal cancer can be either squamous cell carcinoma (most common worldwide) or adenocarcinoma (most common in the United States). Known risk factors for developing esophageal squamous cell carcinoma include al- cohol use and smoking. Barrett esophagitis is a risk factor for esophageal adeno- carcinoma; the diagnosis is made by endoscopic biopsy of the esophageal mass. Metastasis of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma is most often to intrathoracic ar- eas, and esophageal adenocarcinoma most commonly metastasizes to intraabdomi- nal sites. GI cancers, such as esophageal cancers, gastric cancer, and pancreatic can- cer, have a high rate of associated clotting disorders. Incorrect Answer Explanations Dysphagia is an early complication of esophageal cancer. Patients may describe their solid food as “sticking.” Dysphagia may progress from solids to liquids over time. Iron deficiency anemia is a common early complication of esophageal cancer. Patients may have microscopic blood loss from the friable tumor site. However, it is rarely sufficient to develop melena or coffee ground emesis. Retrosternal discomfort, often described as burning, is an early complication of esophageal cancer. Because it is also a symptom of gastritis and GERD, patients with isolated retrosternal burning should be referred for outpatient endoscopy for further evaluation.

الفخ: dysphagia و iron deficiency anemia و retrosternal discomfort كلهم symptoms مبكرة للـ esophageal cancer مش متأخرة. فاللي جالك السعال المتكرر والـ pneumonia بعد ما كان البلع تمام، فكّر بالـ fistula.

question: What is the mechanism of lactulose in the management of hepatic encephalopathy?

options.text: Alters urine pH to increase urinary excretion of ammonia
Decreases absorption of ammonia through a laxative effect in the GI tract
Functions as an antibacterial agent in the gut to destroy ammonia-producing bacteria
Increases levels of endogenous zinc to aid in the metabolism of ammonia

correctAnswer: Decreases absorption of ammonia through a laxative effect in the GI tract
englishExplanation: Lactulose is a synthetic disaccharide that is a first-line treatment for hepatic en- cephalopathy (HE). It has several proposed mechanisms by which it reduces lev- els of circulating ammonia. First, lactulose acts as a hyperosmolar load in the GI system that is then readily broken down by colonic bacteria, yielding a laxative ef- fect that decreases systemic ammonia absorption. It also decreases the pH level of stool, trapping ammonia in the GI tract as ammonium for fecal ex- cretion. Finally, it is thought that lactulose directly stimulates colonic bacteria to absorb and break down ammonia. HE (also known as portosystemic encephalopathy) is seen in cirrhosis patients with toxin accumulation in the bloodstream due to impaired hepatic clearance. Ammonia is the most well-known toxin and is associated with the neuropsychiatric symptoms seen in HE. Impairments in cognitive and neuromuscular functioning are character- istic of HE and can range from subtle deficits to overt coma. Serum ammonia levels are usually elevated in HE but do not necessarily correlate to the degree of mental status change. Incorrect Answer Explanations Lactulose exhibits its primary effects in the GI tract, not the urinary system. However, lactulose does alter the pH in the intestines to trap ammonia in the form of ammonium in the stool. Lactulose is a synthetic disaccharide rather than an antibiotic. Second-line thera- peutics for HE include antibiotics (eg, neomycin, rifaximin, oral vancomycin) that destroy ammonia-producing bacteria in the gut. Zinc replacement is hypothesized to be useful in the management of HE, as zinc is an important nutrient needed in the metabolism of ammonia. However, this is not the mechanism of lactulose.

ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي Decreases absorption of ammonia through a laxative effect in the GI tract، لأن lactulose أول-line علاج للـ hepatic encephalopathy. فاللي صار إنه الـ lactulose بتعمل hyperosmolar load بالـ GI tract بتنكسر بـ colonic bacteria وبتعطي laxative effect بيقلل امتصاص الـ ammonia للدم، وكمان بتخفّض pH البراز فبتحبس الـ ammonia على شكل ammonium وبتطرحها مع الـ stool. وكمان بتتحفيز البكتيريا بالـ colon لتلتقط وتكسر الـ ammonia.
الفخ: lactulose تأثيرها بالـ GI tract مش بالـ urinary system، فلا تفكر إنها بتغيّر urine pH، وهي disaccharide اصطناعية مش antibiotic ما بتقتل بكتيريا. و endogenous zinc مالها أي علاقة بهاد.

question: A 45-year-old man presents with multiple episodes of bloody stool over the past 2 hours. His medical history includes hepatitis C with ascites, alcohol cirrhosis, and a recent endoscopy showing peptic ulcers. His vital signs are BP 66/45, P 134, R 24, and T 36.6°C (97.9°F); SpO is 93%. The physical examination is no- table for a nontender, distended, and firm abdomen and melena. After starting resuscitation with intravenous fluids and blood, what pharmacotherapy de- creases mortality?
englishExplanation: Cirrhosis patients who present with upper GI bleeding that is not attributed to varices should receive proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) in addition to prophylactic an- tibiotics. Of the choices available, only antibiotics have been shown to decrease mortality. Cirrhotic patients have a high risk of infection in the setting of GI bleed- ing. For either variceal bleeding or nonvariceal upper GI bleeding, cirrhotic patients should receive prophylactic antibiotics, ideally prior to endoscopy. Antibiotic pro- 2 phylaxis is associated with reduced mortality, decreased risk of bacterial infection, lowered risk of rebleeding, and shorter hospitalization. Standard antibiotic choices are ceftriaxone 1 g IV with transition to ciprofloxacin orally. The PPI of choice is pantoprazole 80-mg bolus IV, sometimes followed by an infusion of 8 mg/hr. Cirrhosis patients have an increased risk of translocation of gut bacteria in the set- ting of acute bleeding. The delivery of a PPI is aimed at increasing gastric pH to al- low for clot formation. It has been shown to reduce the need for surgical interven- tion and hospital length of stay, but has not been shown to decrease mortality. Incorrect Answer Explanations Erythromycin is a prokinetic used in GI bleeding primarily to improve visualization of endoscopy. It has not been shown to decrease mortality. Octreotide, a somatostatin analogue and splanchnic vasoconstrictor, is indicated for patients with variceal bleeding. This patient's recent endoscopy showed peptic ul- cers with no known varices, so splanchnic vasoconstrictors are not indicated. In pa- tients with varices and GI bleeding, octreotide has been shown to decrease rebleed- ing, but not mortality. Vasopressin is another vasoactive medication used to reduce splanchnic blood flow and portal hypertension. However, vasopressin has been largely replaced by octreotide for use in variceal bleeding because of other side ef- fects such as vasoconstriction in other organs (eg, cardiac, cerebral, limb). If any- thing, this may increase mortality in GI bleeding, not decrease it. Tranexamic acid (TXA) is an antifibrinolytic agent that has been used for many other bleeding situations. However, it has been studied for use in GI bleeding, and recent evidence suggests that TXA is not beneficial in GI bleeding, so it is not cur- rently recommended.

question: A 4-week-old Chinese girl presents with jaundice. Laboratory testing reveals a di- rect hyperbilirubinemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Biliary atresia is a disease of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts that leads to obstructive jaundice, cirrhosis, and death, if untreated. Obstructive jaundice causes a relative increase in direct bilirubin that results in di- rect (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia, which is a rare condition that is more common in individuals of Asian descent, particularly Asian females. Biliary atresia presents as new or persistent jaundice after 2 weeks of age, and the bilirubin profile reveals a predominance of direct (conjugated) bilirubin. Failure to thrive, signs of obstructive jaundice (acholic stools and dark brown urine), and hepatosplenomegaly can also be present. Nuclear medicine imaging is used to help determine whether obstruction exists, and percu- taneous transhepatic cholangiography is used to visualize the biliary tree with a con- trast medium and x-rays. Treatment for biliary atresia is surgical — the Kasai proce- dure (hepatoportoenterostomy). Early treatment, ideally before the infant is 2 months old, is the goal in children with biliary atresia. Delay in identification and treatment (after 3 months of age) leads to significantly worse outcomes in terms of both morbidity and mortality. Incorrect Answer Explanations Breast milk jaundice presents after the fifth day of life with indirect (un- conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia. The exact cause is unknown, but elevated bilirubin levels can be seen until the infant is 8 weeks old. The levels decrease with phototherapy and with temporary cessation of breastfeeding, although the latter is generally not recommended. Gilbert syndrome is a genetic defect, a liver dysfunction that results in ineffective processing of bilirubin. It leads to mild, intermittent jaundice and an indirect (un- conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia. Gilbert syndrome typically presents later in childhood or adolescence during periods of stress, fasting, or infection. Physiologic jaundice is due to an immature bilirubin conjugation system in the liver in the early neonatal period. This indirect (unconjugated) hyperbilirubine- mia typically presents before the fifth day of life and improves without treat- ment as the child's liver enzymes mature. Key Points Consider biliary atresia in children older than 2 weeks who present with new or per- sistent jaundice. Biliary atresia presents with a direct hyperbilirubinemia. Other more common forms of neonatal jaundice (eg, physiologic jaundice, breast- feeding jaundice, and breast milk jaundice) present with an indirect hyperbilirubinemia. Early identification and treatment of biliary atresia, ideally before the patient is 2 months old, lead to improved outcomes.
arabicExplanation:

question: What is the most common cause of medication-induced liver injury in the United States?
englishExplanation: Drug-induced liver injury is extremely common and can be caused by a wide variety of prescription and over-the-counter medications as well as herbs and supplements. Acetaminophen is the most common cause in the United States and drug-induced liver injury is the most common underlying cause of acute liver failure. These drug reactions are classified into two distinct groups. One is the predictable reaction, a dose-dependent hepatotoxicity. Acetaminophen is a classic example. The other is the idiosyncratic reaction, which is patient specific and not dose dependent. Isoniazid, amiodarone, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, and phenytoin are major examples. Clinically, drug-induced liver injury ranges from asymptomatic to frank liver failure with jaundice, malaise, vomiting, low grade fever, abdomi- nal pain, and encephalopathy. Laboratory results can show transamini- tis, hyperbilirubinemia, and elevated INR. Severe transaminitis with jaundice portends a poor prognosis. Emergency department management is largely restricted to reversible or treatable causes, such as acetaminophen or val- proic acid toxicity. Regardless of the source, nonessential medications should be held, and the patient should be admitted. Incorrect Answer Explanations Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid is a major cause of drug-induced liver in- jury; however, acetaminophen is a more common cause. The addition of a beta-lactamase inhibitor to a beta-lactam antibiotic dramatically increases the risk of liver injury. Ibuprofen, along with other NSAIDs, can cause hepatotoxicity but much less com- monly than acetaminophen. NSAIDs are more well known for causing acute kidney injury and peptic ulcers. Isoniazid is a classic example of an idiosyncratic hepatotoxin, and it fre- quently causes liver injury. The risk is higher when combined with rifampin. Although isoniazid is not commonly used in the United States, it is the most frequently used treatment for tuberculosis and, as a result, is a common cause of drug-induced liver injury worldwide.
arabicExplanation:

الفخ: الفخ إنك تختار amoxicillin-clavulanic acid أو Isoniazid لأنهم فعلاً من أسباب DILI، بس Acetaminophen أكثرهم شيوعاً. خلّيك تفرّق: Acetaminophen dose-dependent و predictable، بينما الباقي idiosyncratic و patient-specific.

question: A health care worker who was previously vaccinated against hepatitis B virus is exposed via needlestick to a patient who is HBsAg positive. The health care worker tests negative for HBsAb, his last tetanus vaccination was 4 years ago, and he has been regularly vaccinated. What is the recommended post-exposure prophylaxis?

options.text: Hepatitis B immune globulin and hepatitis B vaccination
Tetanus and hepatitis B immune globulin and hepatitis B vaccination

correctAnswer: Hepatitis B immune globulin and hepatitis B vaccination
englishExplanation: While the health care worker was previously vaccinated, he is no longer immune to hepatitis B because his HBsAb test is negative. Vaccination is required to boost long-term immunity. Hepatitis B immune globulin is also required, as it provides immediate anti-HBs antibodies and protects against infection for 3 to 6 months. Follow-up testing for anti-HBc and HBsAg should be performed 6 months after the exposure if the source patient was HBsAg positive or if their status was unknown. Incorrect Answer Explanations The health care worker was previously vaccinated against hepatitis B but tested neg- ative for HBsAb, which indicates that he is no longer immune. Hepatitis B immune globulin is appropriate for immediate immunity, but the health care worker also re- quires vaccination for long-term immunity, as the immune globulin will only pro- vide antibodies for 3 to 6 months. Although the health care worker was previously vaccinated against hepatitis B, he tested negative for HBsAb, so he is no longer immune. Hepatitis B vaccination is re- quired but will take time to boost immunity. Therefore, immune globulin must also be given to provide immediate immunity. The health care worker does not require administration of tetanus immune globu- lin, which is typically only given if the person has received fewer than three doses of tetanus toxoid. For those who have received more than three doses, and for wounds that are clean and minor, tetanus immune globulin is unnecessary. Tetanus immune globulin is only required for significant wounds, such as those contaminated with dirt, feces or saliva, for puncture wounds, or for someone who has received fewer than three doses of tetanus toxoid.
