الفخ: Azithromycin مو first-line للـ Giardia، وCiprofloxacin بيتّعمل للـ diarrhea بسبب Shigella أو Yersinia. وIodoquinol ما هو العلاج الأساسي. انتبه إن الـ answer لازم يكون single-dose oral therapy وهو tinidazole.

question: A 4-year-old girl is brought in because she has been "scratching her bottom all night." A cellophane tape test of her anus reveals ova on microscopy. What or- ganism is most likely causing this condition?
englishExplanation:
Nocturnal pruritus ani, or perianal itch, is a characteristic feature of Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) infestation. Pinworm is a common par- asite worldwide. It is frequently spread through fomites such as toys, clothing, and bedding material as well as by the fecal-oral route. Patients often scratch the area and then put their fingers in their mouths, resulting in autoinfestation. There are two ways to establish the diag- nosis: (1) by visualizing pale yellow adult worms approximately 1-cm long on the anal verge or (2) by touching transparent tape to the peri- anal region to collect ova, which can then be visualized by light mi- croscopy. Ova are rarely visible in stool. Pinworm infestation can be treated effec- tively with albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel pamoate. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ascaris lumbricoides, or roundworm, is contracted by fecal-oral con- tamination or by ingesting poorly cooked food. Diagnosis is established by the presence of characteristic ova in the stool; ova cannot be detected with cellophane tape testing. If a high worm load is present, a patient may excrete adult worms. Presentation can include significant and recurrent abdomi- nal pain. In severe cases, perforation and peritonitis are possible. Albendazole, mebendazole, and ivermectin are effective treatments. Necator americanus, a type of human hookworm, is a major cause of iron deficiency anemia worldwide. Diagnosis is established by the pres- ence of characteristic ova in the stool. As with roundworm infestation, ova cannot be found using cellophane tape testing. Ova mature in the soil into an infec- tive larva that then penetrates human skin, often through the feet. Albendazole and mebendazole are effective treatments. Trichuris trichiura, or whipworm, is another major worldwide cause of iron deficiency anemia. It is spread through fecal-oral contact, which leads to ingestion of ova. Diagnosis is established by stool examination. It is treated with albendazole or mebendazole.

question: Which clinical finding indicates an increased likelihood of appendicitis in a febrile prepubertal child who presents with acute abdominal pain?

options.text: Pain on jumping up and down
Pain on lying down fully supine

correctAnswer: Pain on jumping up and down
englishExplanation: Appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency in children. Determining whether a pediatric patient has pain with walking or jumping is an elegant method to assess abdominal pain: its presence indicates an increased likelihood of appendicitis. This is sometimes referred to as the “cough/hop” sign. A recent meta analysis found that the cough/hop sign had a positive likelihood ratio (LR+) of 7.64. Otherwise, when performing the physical examination of a pediatric patient with suspected appendicitis, the abdomen should be evaluated for tenderness, re- bound tenderness, guarding, and the "special signs" of peritoneal irrita- tion (McBurney sign, psoas sign, obturator sign, Rovsing sign). The physical exami- nation should include targeted evaluation for other diseases that commonly mimic appendicitis, so examinations of the lung and testes are warranted. Historical clues to the diagnosis include fever, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Diarrhea, anorexia, and pain with activity (walking, jumping, driving over speed bumps) can also be present. Fever and tachycardia are common, and tachypnea or respiratory distress can be found in perforated appendicitis. The differential diagno- sis of appendicitis in children is broad and includes diseases of the GI tract (gas- troenteritis, mesenteric adenitis, intussusception) and the genitourinary system (UTI, ectopic pregnancy, ovarian or testicular torsion), as well as systemic illnesses (pneumonia, DKA, vasculitis) and traumatic injuries. Appendicitis is characterized by obstruction of the appendiceal lumen, inflamma- tion, bacterial invasion, and ultimately appendiceal perforation. In children, appen- dicitis can progress rapidly from vague complaints to frank peritonitis. The classic presentation of nausea and periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant is found in only a minority of pediatric patients, reinforcing the im- portance of conducting a focused examination and ordering the correct diagnostic studies. Ultrasonography is the initial diagnostic test of choice in children with suspected appendicitis. It has the advantages of high sensitivity and specificity and no radiation exposure. If the ultrasound examination is nondiagnostic, serial exami- nations, repeat ultrasound, or CT is a reasonable choice. MRI is emerging in some centers as preferable to CT. Laboratory studies, including serum electrolytes, CBC count, and urinalysis, are commonly obtained in the appendicitis workup. No labo- ratory marker can reliably include or exclude the diagnosis. Patients with acute appendicitis should be NPO and undergo fluid resuscitation before being started on maintenance fluids. Pain medications, antiemetics, and antipyretics should all be used as needed. All children with acute appendicitis should be evalu- ated by a surgeon. Routine antibiotic use in nonperforated appendicitis is contro- versial and institution or surgeon dependent. But antibiotics should be given to pa- tients with perforated appendicitis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Pain on costovertebral percussion (CVA tenderness) is suggestive of pyelonephritis. Both pyelonephritis (upper urinary tract) and cystitis (lower uri- nary tract) are known mimics of appendicitis. Nephrolithiasis can also mimic appendicitis. Pain on lying down fully supine is suggestive of pericarditis. Pericarditis can be infectious or noninfectious. In most cases, an etiology is never found, al- though viral causes are suspected. The chest pain associated with pericarditis is of- ten described as being positional, with sitting up and leaning forward alleviating the pain and lying recumbent exacerbating the pain. Pain on swallowing solids is suggestive of pharyngitis. Pharyngitis can be bacterial or viral, and both streptococcal pharyngitis and viral upper respiratory dis- eases are known to mimic the abdominal pain of appendicitis. Viral URIs are thought to cause abdominal pain through swelling of the abdominal lymph nodes (mesenteric lymphadenitis). Why group A streptococcal pharyngitis causes abdomi- nal pain is unknown.

الفخ: الـ costovertebral percussion pain بتدل على مشكلة بالكلى مش بالـ appendix، والـ pain when lying supine والـ pain with swallowing solids ما إلها علاقة. الـ cough/hop sign هو الفحص اللي بيرجّح appendicitis.

question: A 12-day-old boy is brought in for evaluation of bloody stools and increased fussiness. He was born at 34 weeks' gestation by vaginal delivery with no compli- cations and a birth weight of 2 kg. On examination, a protuberant abdomen is noted; the stool is guaiac positive. An x-ray is obtained and shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Mary Jo Wagner, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation:
This x-ray demonstrates pneumatosis intestinalis, or air within the bowel wall. This is a hallmark finding of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), but up to one-third of patients with this condition do not have this finding. Necrotizing entero- colitis can be seen in premature and full-term neonates, usually within the first 1 to 2 weeks of life. Concerning clinical signs include a toxic appearance, lethargy or somnolence, a distended abdomen, and hematochezia. In general, emergency physicians should have a heightened suspicion for abdominal illness in the evaluation of any neonate or young infant presenting with decreased activity or failure to thrive. Incorrect Answer Explanations Gastroesophageal reflux, although common, is rarely a cause of abdominal pain and bloody stools in neonates. It is more commonly associated with vom- iting and possibly failure to thrive. Intussusception is an abdominal emergency that involves invagination of a section of bowel into the next section, with potential disruption of blood flow that could ul- timately lead to necrosis. The classic triad presentation is intermittent, colicky abdominal pain (followed by periods of sleepiness), emesis, and bloody stools, but this triad is present in less than half of those with the dis- ease. Intussusception rarely presents in children younger than 5 months or older than early school age. An x-ray may show a filling defect correspond- ing to the area of invaginated bowel. Volvulus is a surgical emergency; any bilious vomiting in a neonate warrants immediate evaluation. X-rays may not show signs of obstruction in this age group (eg, air or fluid levels, paucity of gas in the distal bowel). A high clinical suspi- cion might be confirmed with an upper GI series, which can then delineate the lo- cation of the volvulus.

question: A 64-year-old man presents with abdominal pain and tenesmus of 3 days' dura- tion. He recently underwent radiation treatment for prostate cancer. His vital signs include BP 126/66, P 88, R 16, and T 37.2°C (99°F). The physical examina- tion reveals a soft, nontender abdomen without guarding or rebound tenderness. The patient has discomfort on rectal examination, which produces brown stool that is guaiac positive; Hct is at baseline. What is the best next step in management?

options.text: Discharge with enemas and close follow-up
Order abdominal CT with rectal contrast

correctAnswer: Discharge with enemas and close follow-up
englishExplanation: This patient's history and clinical presentation are consistent with acute radiation proctocolitis. Supportive care for mild cases of acute radiation proctocolitis may include sucralfate retention enemas as first line or steroids (a hydrocortisone enema or foam) to decrease local inflammation and fiber stool softeners to de- crease diarrhea. The diagnosis of acute radiation proctocolitis is generally made based on the history, so further evaluation is not typically required. Acute radiation proctocolitis can result in severe disease requiring hospitalization for bowel rest and additional medical therapy; however, treatment is generally supportive. Bowel perforation can also occur and should be considered. Patients with a history of radi- ation therapy of the pelvis can also present with chronic radiation proctocolitis. This is a diagnosis of exclusion; chronic radiation proctocolitis generally presents within 2 years of therapy but can present at any time. Patients with acute proctitis are at greater risk for chronic disease. As with many cases in emergency medicine, close discussion with the patient's primary care physician or specialist is warranted when making a therapeutic and follow-up plan. Incorrect Answer Explanations Infectious causes should be considered, and stool testing may be considered. However, this patient does not have symptoms that suggest infection, so an- tibiotics are not required. The diagnosis of acute proctocolitis can generally be made clinically and does not require invasive testing. Instead, this patient should be discharged with steroid enemas, and close follow-up care should be arranged with his primary care physi- cian or a specialist. Complications such as perforation can be evaluated with CT and should certainly be considered. However, this patient's history and examination findings do not suggest additional complications; he can be treated with supportive care. Key Points Mild cases of acute radiation proctocolitis may be managed with supportive care and outpatient treatment. Consider infection and perforation when treating a patient with acute radiation proctocolitis; some patients have to be admitted for treatment. Chronic radiation proctocolitis is a diagnosis of exclusion.

question: Which finding is most concerning for impending bowel ischemia in a patient with a large bowel obstruction?
englishExplanation:
A normal cecal width is less than 9 cm. A cecal width greater than 12 cm should raise concern for bowel ischemia and possible bowel perfora- tion; other parts of the colon are considered dilated when they measure greater than 6 cm. As the obstruction progresses, the bowel dilates, leading to an increase in intraluminal pressure. When the intraluminal pressure approaches the systolic blood pressure, blood flow is compromised and ischemia develops. Ultimately, gangrene can lead to perforation, peritonitis, bacteremia, and sepsis. Other concerning examination findings include peritonitis, tachycardia, and hypotension. Laboratory markers that indicate high severity of disease include an elevated lactate level, high leukocytosis with a left shift, and signs of volume de- pletion or dehydration (including elevated Hct, BUN, and creatinine). Persistent lactic acidosis despite fluid resuscitation is concerning for bowel ischemia, and ele- vated lactic acid can represent volume depletion or bowel ischemia. Initial resusci- tation includes fluids and early surgical or gastroenterology consultation. Antibiotics should be given in cases of gangrene or perforation. Incorrect Answer Explanations An elevated lactate level (>2 mmol/L) should increase concern for bowel is- chemia and gut compromise, especially after adequate fluid resuscitation. A level of 1.2 is within normal limits for lactate and would not, by itself, indicate im- pending bowel ischemia. A fever is not diagnostic for the presence of bowel ischemia. The presence or a lack of fever would not be specific to bowel ischemia and perforation; however, the presence of one in the setting of abdominal pain should heighten sus- picion for gangrene and perforation and imaging should be considered. The presence of leukocytosis in conjunction with a left shift may suggest bowel ischemia and perforation. A WBC count of 9,000 cells/mm is not a significant elevation to help point to the presence of bowel ischemia. However, a WBC count over 20,000 cells/mm would be more suspicious for bowel gangrene, especially in the presence of a left shift.

question: What is the most common cause of large bowel obstruction?
englishExplanation: Colorectal cancer is the most common cause of large bowel obstruction. Other, less-common causes include volvulus, diverticular disease, fecal im- paction, strictures, hernias, and pseudo-obstruction. The typical presenta- tion of large bowel obstruction includes either acute or subacute abdominal pain and distension. In acute presentations, patients typically report paroxysmal crampy abdominal pain, distension, and obstipation; nausea and vomiting can also be present. In addition to abdominal pain, bloating, and distension, subacute presentations may be accompanied by a gradual onset of stool changes, weight loss, and rectal bleeding (especially if cancer is the cause of the obstruction). The diagno- sis can be determined with plain x-ray or abdominal CT scan. Incorrect Answer Explanations Adhesions are an uncommon cause of large bowel obstruction. However, adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction. Diverticular disease can lead to abscess formation, perforation, and large bowel ob- struction. However, diverticular disease is only responsible for approxi- mately 10% of cases of large bowel obstruction and is not the most common cause. Hernias are a known cause of small bowel obstructions. However, hernias are un- common in the setting of large bowel obstruction.

question: A 39-year-old man presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. His ab- domen is soft, largely distended, and diffusely tender. An abdominal x-ray is ob- tained and shown below. What is the best initial treatment for this condition? Credit: Copyright 2021 Dr. Varun Babu. Image courtesy of Dr. Varun Babu and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 83397. Used under license.
englishExplanation:
This patient has sigmoid volvulus, which should be treated with a flexible sigmoidoscopy. Sigmoid volvulus occurs when the sigmoid colon wraps around itself and its mesentery, resulting in a large bowel obstruction. This condition can be visualized on plain x-rays or CT as a dilated colon with the appearance of a bent in- ner tube. An association has been found between sigmoid volvulus and patients who reside in long-term care facilities as well as patients with neurologic and psy- chiatric conditions. Both gastroenterology and colorectal surgery should be consulted in cases of sigmoid volvulus. Although the initial treatment is decompression via flexible sigmoidoscopy with gastroenterology, many patients also receive an elective colon resection following the sigmoidoscopy to decrease the risk of recurrence. Surgery may also be indicated if the endoscopic decompression fails or if complica- tions such as perforation occur. Incorrect Answer Explanations Antibiotics are indicated when there are signs of bowel gangrene, perfo- ration, peritonitis, or sepsis. However, initial management should involve gas- troenterology consultation for endoscopic decompression via flexible sigmoidoscopy. Nasogastric tube placement and bowel rest are the treatments of choice for a small bowel obstruction due to adhesions. Nasogastric tube placement may be helpful for symptomatic control in patients with uncontrolled nausea and vomiting, but it will not provide reduction of the volvulus, which is re- quired for definitive treatment. Surgery is not a first-line treatment for sigmoid volvulus. However, it should be considered when sigmoid volvulus is complicated by peritonitis or perfo- ration and when endoscopic decompression through flexible sigmoidoscopy has failed. Resection is also often considered after the sigmoidoscopy on an elective basis to reduce the risk of resection.

question: A well-appearing 19-year-old man presents for evaluation of pain and swelling near his buttock that is worse with sitting. Visual inspection reveals a small fluc- tuant, erythematous mass near the midline at the superior edge of the gluteal cleft without surrounding erythema. What is the correct next step in management?

options.text: Elliptical surgical incision with clot removal
High-fiber diet and warm sitz baths after bowel movements
Longitudinal surgical incision lateral to the sacral midline

correctAnswer: Longitudinal surgical incision lateral to the sacral midline
englishExplanation: This patient has a pilonidal abscess, and the appropriate management of acute presentations is incision and drainage, with a longitudinal sur- gical incision lateral to the sacral midline. A pilonidal abscess is an acquired condition that results when an ingrown hair in the gluteal cleft induces a foreign body reaction. Subsequent bacterial growth in the trapped pore can lead to abscess formation. The diagnosis is made clinically based on the history and physical exami- nation, and, in general, labs and imaging are unnecessary. Antibiotics are indicated when surrounding cellulitis is present, and coverage should include skin flora and anaerobic organisms. Disease recurrence is common, and patients with sympto- matic disease should be referred for outpatient surgical follow-up for more defini- tive treatment. Incorrect Answer Explanations An elliptical incision with clot removal is part of the acute management of a thrombosed external hemorrhoid. Unlike a thrombosed hemorrhoid, a pilonidal abscess is managed with a longitudinal incision to allow for drainage of pus. An anal fissure, a painful superficial mucosal tear near the anal verge, is another common anorectal disorder. Supportive home measures for anal fissure in- clude a high-fiber diet and warm sitz baths to prevent stricture forma- tion. These measures would not be helpful in the acute management of a painful, infected pilonidal cyst. Meticulous hygiene and hair removal after resolution of an acute ab- scess may help prevent recurrence in patients with pilonidal disease. Limited data suggest that laser therapy may be superior to shaving or depilation. Although good hygiene is an important adjunct to the treatment of any infection, perianal hygiene and hair removal will do little to treat an acute pilonidal abscess.

question: What is the most common sign or symptom of an anal fissure?
englishExplanation: Patients with an anal fissure commonly describe acute pain with defeca- tion. They can also experience hours of persistent pain after develop- ment or exacerbation of an anal fissure, likely due to anal spasms. Pain related to an anal fissure eventually subsides between bowel movements, which helps distinguish this condition from other causes of rectal pain, such as throm- bosed external hemorrhoids. To compound the problem, fear of associated pain and bleeding can lead to stool holding, which worsens constipation and exacerbates fis- sures. Stool holding is often seen in pediatric patients. Parental guidance, dietary changes, and the use of assistive medical therapy, such as stool softeners, can relieve the cycle of chronic constipation. Physical examination of the anal area is necessary to confirm an anal fissure diagnosis, even when the patient provides the typical history of pain with defecation and seeing bright red blood on toilet paper. Separating the patient's buttocks to examine the area often makes the fissure visi- ble; having the patient bear down can also improve visualization. Most patients have only one fissure in the posterior midline; if patients have multiple fissures or fissures in positions other than the midline, causes other than trauma from passing hard stools should be considered. Treatment for anal fissures is usually supportive. Sitz baths, stool softeners, and a high-fiber diet can soothe and prevent further trauma to the area. Topical anesthetics, such as lidocaine gel, can temporarily reduce pain in the area, but they will not directly help healing. Topical nitroglycerin or nifedipine can reduce anal spasms, providing symptomatic relief and promot- ing healing of the torn mucosa. Unfortunately, a recent Cochrane database review concluded that medical therapy provides a cure rate for acute fissures that is only marginally better than a placebo. Surgical treatment options include lateral sphinc- terotomy and anal dilation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Dark, tarry, or melenic stools are seen primarily in patients with upper GI bleeding. Blood from sources in the stomach or the small intestine turns dark due to the oxidation of Hgb by intestinal enzymes. By contrast, patients with anal fissures commonly report small amounts of bright red blood on tis- sue paper or in the toilet. Anal fissures can be seen after frequent episodes of diarrhea, but they are most commonly caused by the trauma of passing hard stool. Some pa- tients report a history of neither diarrhea nor trauma from passing hard stool. Inflammatory bowel disease should be considered for patients with recurrent bloody diarrhea and persistent pain. Approximately 90% of anal fissures occur in the posterior midline. The etiology is unclear but may be related to reduced posterior anodermal blood flow compared to the lateral and anterior aspects of the anal canal. Anterior anal fissures are more common in women than in men. Lateral anal fissures or multiple fissures should prompt consideration of a secondary etiology, such as inflammatory bowel disease, granulomatous disease, malignancy, or an STI.

question: A patient presents with prolapsed internal hemorrhoids that cannot be reduced. What is the appropriate management?
englishExplanation: Internal hemorrhoids can be classified based on severity and clinical features (grade I to grade IV, increasing in severity). Grade IV hemorrhoids are nonre- ducible, can become edematous and ischemic, and may require surgical con- sultation for an emergent or urgent hemorrhoidectomy. Grade I hemorrhoids are nonprolapsed. Grade II hemorrhoids are prolapsed (usu- ally prolapsing after a bowel movement) but spontaneously reduce without any in- tervention. Grade III hemorrhoids are prolapsed but can be manually reduced. Hemorrhoids are vascular cushions within the anal canal that can become en- gorged. Since they are supplied by arterial blood, bleeding is typically described as bright red in color. Hemorrhoids that are above the dentate line are con- sidered internal hemorrhoids and are painless. External hemorrhoids occur below the dentate line and can be quite painful, particularly when thrombosed. Internal hemorrhoids may not be apparent on physical examination if they are non- prolapsed. Internal hemorrhoids cannot be readily palpated on digital examination and require anoscopy for visualization. By contrast, external hemorrhoids are easily visible on inspection of the anus. Management of most nonprolapsed internal hem- orrhoids and nonthrombosed external hemorrhoids includes the WASH regime: warm water, analgesics, stool softeners, and a high-fiber diet. Grade III hemor- rhoids require manual reduction in addition to the WASH regimen. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bedside incision and drainage may be indicated for a thrombosed external hemorrhoid. However, a prolapsed, nonreducible (grade IV) internal hemorrhoid requires an emergent surgical evaluation. Sitz baths and stool softeners, along with a high-fiber diet and analgesics, are indi- cated for nonprolapsed internal hemorrhoids and nonthrombosed external hemor- rhoids. This regimen is insufficient for a (grade IV) prolapsed, nonreducible internal hemorrhoid. Topical steroid therapy is often used for external hemorrhoids. However, a (grade IV) prolapsed, nonreducible internal hemorrhoid requires an emergent surgical consultation because of the risk of ischemia.

question: An 18-year-old patient presents with a several day history of fever and fatigue. They also have cervical lymphadenopathy, and tenderness is noted in the left up- per quadrant on abdominal examination. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
englishExplanation: The classic presentation of infectious mononucleosis (IM) is fever, lym- phadenopathy, pharyngitis, and fatigue, with a peak incidence in ages 15 to 24. Splenomegaly is seen in 50% to 60% of patients and generally re- solves after about 3 weeks. Malaise and headache are also often reported, and atypical lymphocytosis may be noted on laboratory evaluations. There are many clinical variants of IM, and some patients experience more limited symptomatology. Spontaneous or traumatic splenic rupture is a rare complication of IM. Urticarial, petechial, or maculopapular rash can occur, and various neurologic syn- dromes (including Guillain-Barré syndrome, cranial nerve palsies, meningoen- cephalitis, and transverse myelitis) are occasionally seen. The diagnosis of IM is made by the presence of heterophile antibodies in the ap- propriate clinical context using a mononucleosis spot test. Although heterophile an- tibodies are nonspecific, they are considered diagnostic in a patient with symptoms of IM. There is a 25% false-negative rate in the first week of infection. A patient with a negative mononucleosis spot test early in suspected IM should have repeat testing at a later date. Treatment is supportive with acetaminophen, NSAIDs, and hydration, and patients should be instructed to avoid contact sports or other activities that would put them at risk of splenic rupture. Incorrect Answer Explanations Hematologic malignancies are a cause of splenomegaly, but symptoms would not be expected to develop abruptly over days. IM is a more likely explanation for abrupt-onset viral symptoms associated with fevers. Portal hypertension can result from various processes and can contribute to the de- velopment of splenomegaly. However, causes of portal hypertension are more likely to be chronic in nature (eg, chronic alcohol use or nonalcoholic fatty liver disease) rather than acute, as in this case. The typical presentation of sarcoidosis includes cough, chest pain, and shortness of breath, which can be accompanied by fevers, weight loss, fatigue, and malaise. Symptom onset in sarcoidosis is gradual, and symptoms generally persist for months to a year before diagnosis, unlike IM (which is generally diagnosed within 1- 2 weeks of symptom onset).

question: A 19-year-old man presents with abdominal pain. He was recently diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis. His Hgb is 9.6 g/dL. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
englishExplanation: Splenomegaly is commonly seen in the setting of infectious mononucle- osis (IM), and splenic rupture is a complication that is thought to occur in 1 to 2 patients per 1,000 cases of IM. Approximately 50% of splenic rup- tures occur spontaneously, and they are more commonly seen in young men. A patient with splenic rupture would likely present with severe abdominal pain and falling Hgb. Splenic infarction is another rare complication of IM and would also present with abdominal pain. Management of splenic rupture associated with IM is similar to other causes of splenic injury. Conservative and supportive measures and splenic preserva- tion may be preferred when possible, but splenectomy may be required in some cases. Mortality from splenic rupture in IM is exceedingly rare. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute pancreatitis is a potential complication of IM, but it is much less common than splenic rupture. A recent review of the literature from 1966 to 2016 found 14 cases of pancreatitis and 37 cases of acalculous cholecystitis associ- ated with IM. Bleeding from a venous malformation could occur at any time and would not neces- sarily be associated with acute IM. Splenic rupture, however, is a known compli- cation of IM. Retroperitoneal hemorrhage would be an unexpected complication of IM. Subcapsular hemorrhage or capsular rupture and intraperitoneal hemorrhage would be more likely in the setting of IM and splenic rupture.

question: A 65-year-old man presents with several weeks of fatigue, malaise, early satiety, and weight loss. He has tender splenomegaly on examination, and laboratory studies show a WBC count of 80,000 cells/mm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: This patient presents with systemic symptoms, tender splenomegaly, and marked leukocytosis. Of the available options, leukemia, specifically chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), is the most likely answer. CML accounts for 15% to 20% of leukemias affecting adults, with a median age at onset of 50 and a slight male predominance. Exposure to ionizing radiation is a known risk factor. CML demonstrates a fluctuating clinical course. Many patients are asympto- matic at the time of diagnosis, with an abnormality incidentally discovered on rou- tine blood testing. Frequent findings at the time of diagnosis include anemia, splenomegaly, thrombocytosis, and a WBC count of 100,000 cells/mm. In general, a leukocytosis greater than 35,000 to 50,000 cells/mm should prompt consideration of hematologic malignancy. Incorrect Answer Explanations DRESS syndrome (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symp- toms) is characterized by a prodromal period (fever and malaise) follow- ing introduction of the causative medication and then a symmetric rash affecting the torso and extremities. Organ dysfunction and splenomegaly can be seen in the setting of DRESS syndrome, but this patient has no reported medication expo- sure or rash. Thus, DRESS syndrome is not the most likely diagnosis. Acute HIV infection generally begins to manifest 2 to 4 weeks after exposure and is characterized by fever, lymphadenopathy, sore throat, rash, myalgias, headache, splenomegaly, diarrhea, and weight loss. Acute HIV infection would not be expected to cause severe leukocytosis on initial laboratory testing. Polycythemia rubra vera is generally found incidentally in routine laboratory test- ing. However, early symptoms can include headache, dizziness, splenomegaly, early satiety, pruritus, and visual disturbance. Laboratory tests generally show elevated Hgb with normal or elevated leukocytes and platelets. By contrast, this patient presents with isolated severe leukocytosis, which is more consistent with a hematologic malignancy.

question: An 18-month-old boy with a history of sickle cell anemia presents with several days of weakness, pallor, and abdominal distension. He is tachycardic, and his abdomen is tender. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Splenic sequestration crisis is a feared complication in a young child with a history of sickle cell anemia (SCA). Crises are thought to result from sickled cells producing vascular congestion and obstruction within the spleen, resulting in sequestration and splenomegaly. This can result in a dangerous drop in circulating blood volume (Hgb), generally of at least 2 g/dL. Minor episodes of acute splenic sequestration can also occur in children with SCA and may resolve on their own. Together, episodes of splenic sequestration and other minor vaso-occlusive episodes contribute to fibrosis and auto-infarction of the spleen over time. Splenic sequestration crises may be the earliest manifestation of SCA in some children, generally occurring between 6 months and 5 years of age, at a median age of 1.4 years. Recurrence rates are higher in patients who have their first splenic sequestration crisis in the first year of life. Patients typically present with abrupt on- set of pallor, weakness, and tachycardia. They will demonstrate tender mas- sive splenomegaly on examination. Patients with SCA typically have spleens en- larged 1 to 2 cm below the costal margin, but during crises, much greater splenomegaly than is typical for them can manifest. Historically, mortality from splenic sequestration crisis was thought to be as high as 12% to 44%; however, more recent evidence suggests mortality is much lower, per- haps less than 1%. Acutely, patients are at risk for severe anemia and cardiovascular collapse. Treatment consists of intravenous fluids and blood transfusions to a goal Hct of about 35%. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute chest syndrome is a life-threatening complication of SCA that can present with fever, cough, tachypnea, chest pain, and wheezing. Patients generally show an abnormal infiltrate on chest x-ray. Acute chest syndrome would not be expected to cause pallor or tender splenomegaly. Aplastic crisis can present with abrupt-onset pallor and fatigue with a low reticulocyte count noted on laboratory evaluation. Unlike splenic sequestra- tion crisis, aplastic crisis would not be expected to present with abdominal fullness or tenderness. Mesenteric ischemia is an uncommon cause of severe abdominal pain in patients with SCA and would not be expected to cause pallor or tender splenomegaly. Splenic sequestration crisis is a more likely explanation for this patient's symptoms.

question: A patient presents with nausea, vomiting, flushing, palpitations, and colicky ab- dominal pain that occur shortly after eating. They underwent a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 2 months ago. The emergency department workup is reassuring. Upon discharge, what dietary modifications should be advised?

options.text: Eat smaller and more frequent meals

correctAnswer: Eat smaller and more frequent meals
englishExplanation: This patient's symptoms are consistent with early dumping syndrome, which results from the rapid emptying of gastric contents into the small bowel and resultant fluid shifts from the hyperosmolar contents. In the emergency department, early dump- ing syndrome is treated with supportive care and may require intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and electrolyte replacement; discharge counseling should focus on dietary modification, including smaller, more frequent meals. Symptoms of early dumping syndrome usually begin within 15 minutes of eating and can include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, colicky abdominal pain, and hypotension. The sympathetic nervous system also may be activated and cause tachycardia, palpitations, dizziness, and flushing. Late dumping syn- drome is a rarer complication of bariatric surgery that occurs 1 to 3 hours after meals. Rapid gastric emptying is thought to cause transient hyperglycemia, leading to increased insulin secretion. Once the intestinal contents are absorbed, this ele- vated insulin secretion causes hypoglycemia and sequelae. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bariatric patients with early dumping syndrome are advised to separate liquids and solids while eating to avoid exacerbating their symptoms. Patients with early dumping syndrome should avoid drinking during meals and up to 2 hours after meals. They should also be counseled to eat smaller, more frequent meals. Bariatric patients with early dumping syndrome should increase their complex carbohydrate intake and decrease their simple sugars and lac- tose. They should also be advised to increase their protein intake. They should be counseled to eat smaller, more frequent meals. Bariatric patients with early dumping syndrome should be advised to increase their dietary fiber intake, as it may delay the absorption of carbohy- drates in the small intestine. They should also be instructed to eat smaller and more frequent meals with more proteins and fewer simple sugars.

question: What is more consistent with gastric band slippage than gastric band overinfla- tion following laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding?

options.text: Failure to improve with band deflation

correctAnswer: Failure to improve with band deflation
englishExplanation: Gastric band slippage is one of the known complications of gastric band- ing that results from downward slippage of the band with resultant gastric pouch enlargement. Since the symptoms are caused by physical slippage of the band and not overinflation, deflating the band usually does not lead to clinical improvement. Symptoms of gastric band slippage include epigastric pain, re- flux, dysphagia, food intolerance, and vomiting. Gastric band slippage can be diagnosed with upper GI imaging, and emergency department management in- cludes intravenous fluid resuscitation and electrolyte replacement as needed. Surgical consultation and intervention are recommended to avoid complications, such as gastric ischemia, necrosis, and perforation. Gastric banding is the third most common bariatric surgery in the United States and involves the placement of an adjustable silicon band at the gas- tric cardia near the gastroesophageal junction. Gastric banding is a purely restric- tive modality that limits the amount of food that is consumed. Although gastric banding has the lowest mortality rate among bariatric procedures, it is associated with several complications, and almost 50% of patients require surgical revision or removal of the band. Gastric pouch dilation occurs in as many as 15% of patients undergoing la- paroscopic gastric banding procedures. Pouch dilation may result from an overly tight or improperly placed band or from excessive food intake. Symptoms of gastric pouch dilation overlap with gastric band slippage but should show improve- ment with deflation of the gastric band, a low-calorie diet, and small portion sizes for 4 to 6 weeks. The band can then be gradually reinflated. If the pouch does not return to its original size, surgical replacement or removal is indicated. Incorrect Answer Explanations Persistent epigastric pain may be experienced by patients with gastric band slippage or gastric pouch dilation. Clinical improvement with band de- flation is more consistent with gastric pouch dilation. Progressive food intolerance and dysphagia may be seen in both gastric pouch dilation and gastric band slippage. However, these symptoms should improve with band deflation if gastric pouch dilation is the underlying etiology. Patients with both gastric band slippage and gastric pouch dilation often present with recurrent reflux and vomiting. As the pouch dilation improves or resolves with band deflation, these symptoms should also improve.

question: Two weeks after a sleeve gastrectomy surgery, a patient presents with redness and warmth overlying the surgical site. What is the most likely organism to be identified from a culture of the surgical wound?
englishExplanation:
Surgical site infections occur in roughly 15% of bariatric surgery pa- tients, with a higher incidence in open procedures versus laparoscopic pro- cedures. Although surgical site infections may be polymicrobial, the most com- monly identified organisms are in the staphylococcal family. Surgical site infections most commonly occur within the first 2 to 3 weeks after surgery. The infection may remain superficial and only involve the skin, but it can also in- volve deeper subcutaneous or soft tissues or enter the abdominal cavity itself. Therapeutic interventions should focus on early recognition, antibiotics, and source control. Source control may involve opening the wound to allow drainage, abscess drainage, or further surgical intervention. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although Bacteroides fragilis is a known intra-abdominal pathogen that colonizes almost all human colons, it is much less likely to cause a surgical site infection. The most commonly identified organisms in surgical site infections are in the staphylococcal family. Escherichia coli is a common intra-abdominal pathogen that is known to cause surgical site infections, but E. coli is less common than staphy- lococcal species. Enterococcal species are also known to cause surgical site infections. Streptococcus pyogenes is a common cause of general cellulitis but is not one of the most common bacterial causes of surgical site infections. These infections are more commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase- negative staphylococcal species, Enterococcus species, and E. coli.

question: In the absence of a replacement gastrostomy tube of the same size, what should be placed through the longstanding stoma of a recently dislodged gastrostomy tube to maintain patency?

options.text: Foley catheter of the same French size as the gastrostomy tube
Foley catheter one French unit larger than the gastrostomy tube
Physician should place one finger in the stoma until a gastrostomy tube can be procured
Wire from a central venous catheter kit

correctAnswer: Foley catheter of the same French size as the gastrostomy tube
englishExplanation: In the event that a longstanding gastrostomy tube falls out, it is imperative to maintain patency of the gastrostomy tract so that the tract does not begin to narrow or close. Although an identical gastrostomy tube is a better long-term solution, the correct size may not be readily available. Foley catheters are usually readily available in multiple sizes. A Foley catheter of the same diame- ter may be placed quickly and safely in a mature tract to maintain patency and even provide nutrition when necessary. Gastrostomy tube complications are quite common; they include infection, bleed- ing, fistula formation, necrotizing fasciitis, and inadvertent tube re- moval. Accidental displacement is a very common complication, and if the tract is mature (approximately 4 weeks out from surgery) then replacement with a simi- lar gastrostomy tube or a Foley catheter of the same size is appropriate. If the tract is immature (<4 weeks from surgery), then a replacement tube should not be placed blindly in the emergency department because it may lead to false passage. When appropriate, the process to replace a gastrostomy tube is as follows: lubricate the replacement, place the tip with the ballon into the stoma, apply slow gentle pressure until the tube passes through the stoma, inflate the balloon, pull back gen- tly until there is traction against the skin, and then secure the tube, often using the attached bumper. If a bumper is unavailable, the tube can be taped or bandaged in place. Incorrect Answer Explanations There is no need to upsize the tract with a larger Foley catheter. A larger Foley catheter may be difficult to place, further traumatizing the tract. Instead either a similar gastrostomy tube or a Foley catheter of the same French size can be placed in the mature tract to keep it open. Depending on the size of the patient, the diameter of the gastrostomy tract, and the size of the physician's hands, it may be impossible to pass a finger through the tract. Attempting to force a finger into the tract may further traumatize it and lead to false passage. Moreover, it is unnecessary for a physician to stay in the room and maintain patency because they may need to place the tube itself. The wire from a central venous catheter would not maintain the diame- ter of the tract because the wire is too narrow. Additionally, the sharpness of the wire may lead to further damage or bleeding.

question: A 3-year-old presents with a displaced gastrojejunostomy (GJ) tube. The child's parent has the GJ tube with them; it appears intact. The parent has already placed a Foley catheter of the same diameter in the ostomy. What is the correct next step?

options.text: Consult the service that placed the tube for replacement
Replace Foley catheter with a gastrostomy tube of the same diameter
Replace with a clean GJ tube at bedside
Test the balloon(s) and replace the original GJ tube into the ostomy at bedside

correctAnswer: Consult the service that placed the tube for replacement
englishExplanation: A gastrojejunostomy (GJ) tube cannot be replaced without fluoroscopic or endoscopic guidance. There are multiple types of feeding tubes with which children may present. Because management differs by tube type, always ask the child's parents or try to ascertain which type of tube the patient has. A gastros- tomy tube can be replaced at the bedside if the tract is mature (approximately 4 weeks old), but GJ tubes cannot be replaced at the bedside even when ma- ture. Appropriately, the parents placed a Foley catheter into the gastric tract to maintain patency, but the GJ tube needs to be passed beyond the pylorus, which cannot be done blindly. Children usually have GJ tubes instead of just gastrostomy tubes. One port is used for feeding, and the other port is used for medications or venting. Ascertain why the patient has both ports because critical medications or nutrition may be specific to either. When needed, consider converting medications to intra- venous delivery while waiting for the consulting service to replace the tube. Incorrect Answer Explanations Replacing the Foley catheter with a gastrostomy tube may ultimately be decided as a temporary measure. However, this child had a GJ tube for a spe- cific reason and needs it replaced with a new GJ tube. Thus, consulting the service that placed the GJ tube is the best next step. Procuring an identical replacement is often the best course of action for a displaced gastrostomy tube, if able. However, a GJ tube should not be replaced at the bedside in the emergency department because it is usually impossible to advance the distal end through the pylorus. This should typically be done by the service that placed the tube or by interventional radiology. A GJ tube cannot be replaced correctly without fluoroscopic or endo- scopic guidance. Thus, replacement of even an intact GJ-tube is unlikely to be suc- cessful and should not be attempted.
arabicExplanation:

الفخ: الطلاب يختاروا تبديل الـ Foley بـ gastrostomy tube بنفس القطر أو إرجاع نفس GJ tube على السرير. الفرق إنه GJ tube ما بيدخل بدون توجيه fluoroscopic حتى لو المسار ناضج، بعكس gastrostomy tube العادي اللي ينبدل على السرير.

question: A patient with a long-standing history of alcoholic liver disease presents with an enlarging abdomen and gradually increasing shortness of breath. He is afebrile; the abdomen is distended but not tense or tender, and he has distended paraum- bilical veins. Which mechanism is causing his distended abdomen?

options.text: Adherence to a low-sodium, fluid-restricted diet, leading to renal fluid reabsorption
Increased permeability of the omentum vessels, causing plasma leakage
Replacement of hepatic tissue with fibrosis, causing portal vein hypertension
Thrombosis of the IVC with resulting venous obstruction

correctAnswer: Replacement of hepatic tissue with fibrosis, causing portal vein hypertension
englishExplanation: This patient likely has cirrhosis following long-standing alcoholic liver disease. Excessive, chronic ingestion of alcohol destroys hepatocytes by a variety of mecha- nisms, especially by the metabolization of alcohol into toxic degradation products. If the liver injury exceeds the rate of regeneration, fibrotic tissue replaces normal liver architecture, and liver function deteriorates. The most significant im- pact is on the portal venous system, where obstructed flow causes portal hyper- tension and increased hydrostatic pressure in the veins that drain the in- testines. This induces collateral flow from the vessels. In the stomach and esopha- gus, varices can form. Midgut collaterals are manifested as caput medusa, engorgement of the periumbili- cal veins radiating out from the umbilicus. Vessels in the hindgut can form hemor- rhoids as collaterals. The increased hydrostatic pressure pushes transudate out into the peritoneal space, leading to ascites. Portal hypertension from cirrhosis develops slowly, leaving time for collateral flow to form. Portal hyperten- sion from a portal vein thrombosis can develop very quickly and is manifested by primarily ascites without significant variceal vein development. Ascites from portal hypertension is best managed by relieving the obstructed flow directly, either through liver transplantation or a transjugular intrahepatic portal shunt. Before these procedures can be done, a patient is managed on a low-sodium, fluid-re- stricted diet and diuretics to minimize the fluid retention. Incorrect Answer Explanations A low-sodium, fluid-restricted diet minimizes fluid retention and reduces the progression of ascites. Replacement of hepatic tissue with fibrosis, causing por- tal vein hypertension, is the more likely cause of ascites. Intraperitoneal carcinomas, such as ovarian cancer, can seed the omentum and develop omental "caking." This can lead to an exudative leaking of plasma and the development of ascites. However, replacement of hepatic tissue with fibro- sis, causing portal vein hypertension, is the more likely cause of ascites in cirrhosis. Thrombosis of the IVC leads to bilateral lower-extremity edema, but likely not ascites. Portal vein thrombosis is associated with portal hypertension and ascites.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريض عنده cirrhosis من alcoholic liver disease طويل الأمد، والكحول المزمن يدمّر الـ hepatocytes وخصوصاً لما يتحول لمواد سامة. لما يصير الضرر أسرع من قدرة الكبد على التجدد، يحل النسيج الليفي (fibrosis) مكان بنية الكبد الطبيعية ويسوء عمل الكبد. أهم تأثير يكون على الجهاز البابي (portal venous system) اللي ينسد فيه الجريان فيسبب portal hypertension ويرفع الضغط الهيدروستاتيكي، وهذا يدفع السوائل للـ peritoneal space ويطلع ascites مع distended paraumbilical veins.
الفخ: كتير طلاب يختاروا thrombosis of the IVC بدل cirrhosis. الفرق إنه الانسداد في الوريد البابي أو الـ IVC عادة يصير بسرعة ويظهر بشكل ascites بدون أوردة جانبية واضحة، بعكس cirrhosis اللي يتطور ببطء وتتكوّن فيه collaterals زي caput medusa.

question: What is the best test to diagnose celiac disease?
englishExplanation: Patients with celiac disease often present with steatorrhea and flatulence, as well as signs and symptoms of malabsorption. Patients with recurrent diarrhea should be evaluated by a gastroenterologist and tested to rule out celiac disease and other bowel disorders. The preferred serologic test for celiac disease is tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A (tTG-IgA) antibody. The tTG-IgA test is 90% to 98% sensitive and 95% to 97% specific for celiac disease. Patients should also undergo an upper endoscopy with biopsy of the small bowel. There are many additional antibody assays that can be used in conjunction with tTG-IgA to determine if a patient has celiac disease. Treatment for celiac disease primarily involves removing gluten from the diet. If symptoms are unimproved after removal of gluten, prednisone or budesonide is recommended. In rare cases, children and adults with celiac disease can also present with celiac crisis (gliadin shock), which is often triggered by an im- mune stimulus (eg, infection, pregnancy, or surgery). In celiac crisis, patients develop severe diarrhea, which can be life-threatening. Incorrect Answer Explanations Anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA) are not associated with celiac disease, but they are associated with Crohn disease. ASCA are specific but not sensitive for diagnosing Crohn disease. HLA B27 is a human leukocyte antigen linked to spondyloarthritis and other autoimmune disorders, but not to celiac disease. There is thought to be a clinical link between HLA-DR3, DQ2, DQ8, and celiac disease. Perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA) are not as- sociated with celiac disease, but they are associated with ulcerative coli- tis (UC). pANCA are specific but not sensitive for diagnosing UC.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريض اللي عنده chronic diarrhea وعلامات سوء امتصاص لازم نفحصه عشان نستثني celiac disease. أحسن فحص مصلي هو tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A (tTG-IgA) antibody، لأنه حساسيته 90% لـ 98% وخصوصيته 95% لـ 97% لمرض celiac. بالإضافة لهذا لازم نعمل upper endoscopy مع biopsy للـ small bowel. والعلاج بالأساس هو إزالة الغلوتين من الأكل.
الفخ: الطلاب يوقعوا بمصيدة ASCA أو pANCA وينسوا إنهم لمرض Crohn والـ inflammatory bowel disease مش للـ celiac. وكمان HLA B27 مرتبط بالـ ankylosing spondylitis، فما إله علاقة بالـ celiac disease.

question: A 63-year-old man with a history of tobacco use and DVT on warfarin presents with intermittent, painless passage of bloody urine of 2 weeks' duration. His physical examination is unremarkable. A urinalysis reveals TNTC (too numerous to count) RBCs/hpf, 5 WBCs/hpf, negative nitrites, negative protein, and no bac- teria. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, WBC count 5.4 x 109/L, Hgb 13.8 g/dL, and INR 2.9. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is normal. What is the best next step in management?

options.text: Administer 10 mg of intravenous vitamin K to reverse anticoagulation
Prescribe a 7-day course of oral ciprofloxacin
Refer the patient to a urologist for cystoscopy
Tell the patient he has passed a stone and needs no treatment

correctAnswer: Refer the patient to a urologist for cystoscopy
englishExplanation: It is tempting to dismiss this patient's hematuria simply because he takes warfarin, but 80% of patients who have hematuria while taking anticoagulant drugs have some underlying pathology. This patient should be referred to urology for cystoscopy to evaluate for cancer of the urinary tract. Although the CT scan was normal, bladder cancer can be missed on CT, and the patient should have a cystoscopy. As little as 1 mL of blood in 1 L of urine can cause noticeable gross hematuria. More than 5 RBCs/hpf is considered significant and is an indication for further investigation. The most common causes of hematuria are kidney stones, carcinoma of the bladder or kidney, trauma, UTI, prostatic hypertro- phy, and glomerulonephritis. In men older than 40 years, carcinomas, espe- cially of the bladder, are the most common cause of hematuria. Risk factors for hematuria include smoking, workplace exposure, race (white), and family history. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient is not suffering from life-threatening hemorrhage or anemia, so immediate warfarin reversal with intravenous vitamin K is unneces- sary. Withholding warfarin temporarily, however, can be considered. An immunocompetent patient with a UTI would be expected to have dysuria, uri- nary urgency, or suprapubic abdominal discomfort. Additionally, a urinalysis would reveal the presence of WBCs, nitrites, or bacteria. This patient's presentation and workup are inconsistent with infection, so initiating antibiotics is inappropriate. Because this patient's hematuria is painless, urolithiasis is less likely. Given his age and medical history, carcinoma of the bladder is more likely and should be investigated.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريض عنده gross hematuria متقطع بدون ألم لمدة أسبوعين وهو مدخن وعلى warfarin، وهاد خطير لأنه 80% من اللي عندهم hematuria وهم على مضادات التخثر عندهم سبب مرضي كامن. عمره فوق 40، وهناك الـ carcinoma وخصوصاً bladder cancer هو أكثر سبب للـ hematuria بالرجال بهذا العمر. حتى لو الـ CT كان طبيعي، bladder cancer ممكن ينخفى عليه، فلازم نحوله لـ urology عشان cystoscopy.
الفخ: الطلاب يختاروا iv vitamin K أو مضاد حيوي أو يقولوا مرّ حصوة وما بدها علاج. الفرق إنه هون ما في نزيف مهدد للحياة ولا anemia ولا علامات UTI، والـ urinalysis نظيف من nitrites وبكتيريا، فالـ cystoscopy هي الخطوة الصحيحة.

question: A 54-year-old man presents with massive repeated hemoptysis. He produces 500 mL of bright red blood within 20 minutes of arrival. He has an irregular heart rate of 135; BP is 92/45. A stat portable chest x-ray is obtained and shown below. His wife says that he has atrial fibrillation and takes "something that starts with an 'X.'" In addition to considering reversal agents, what is the most appropriate next step in this patient's management? Credit: Timothy H. Kaufman, MD.

options.text: Immediately transfer to the operating room for emergent open thoracotomy
Intubate with a large endotracheal tube into the right mainstem bronchus
Position the patient on his right side with his head elevated

correctAnswer: Intubate with a large endotracheal tube into the right mainstem bronchus
englishExplanation:
The acute management of life-threatening pulmonary hemorrhage follows the same principle as any other resuscitation: airway, breathing, and circulation. This patient needs a definitive airway, and it should be established in a way that protects the remaining functional lung; the right lung can still ventilate and should be protected from blood pooling from the left lung hemorrhage. In this case, the best approach is a standard intubation, but the endotracheal (ET) tube should be pushed in deeply until it meets resistance. A single-lung intuba- tion of the right lung (the unaffected side in this case) is fairly easy to achieve with- out special equipment. Selectively intubating the left lung requires finesse and expe- rience and is made easier with the use of bronchoscopy. Without a bronchoscope, it is possible to maneuver the ET tube into the left mainstem bronchus by turning the tube 90 degrees to the left after passing the cords. Regardless, a large ET tube should be used in a patient with pulmonary hemorrhage so that a bronchoscope can be passed through it later for closer examination of the lung injury and possible sclerotic therapy of the bleeding vessel. Based on the history, the patient is most likely taking rivaroxaban, one of the novel anticoagulants. These medications do not require the frequent monitoring and adjustment necessary with warfarin use, but their function is not easily reversed; vitamin K has no role in their reversal. In addition to recently approved specific fab-fragment antidotes, there are some gen- eral therapies that can help the severely bleeding patient. Dabigatran has low pro- tein binding and can be removed via dialysis, or an activated prothrombin complex concentrate (factor VIII inhibitor bypass activity [FEIBA]) might help. The antico- agulation effect of rivaroxaban and apixaban can be lessened by the use of a pro- thrombin complex concentrate. Incorrect Answer Explanations An immediate, emergent open thoracotomy is an extreme measure with a high risk of death. Localized treatment of the bleeding vessel with a broncho- scope is a preferred approach. Regardless, the patient's airway must be secured and the anticoagulation reversed before a thoracotomy is possible. In theory, a patient with pulmonary hemorrhage should be placed with the bleeding side down (left in this case, not right) so that the blood pools in the “bad” lung and the “good” lung can continue to ventilate. This practice has not been validated by scientific study and might increase ventilation-perfusion mismatching. Intubation with a large endotracheal tube into the right mainstem bronchus is a bet- ter definitive management of the airway. CPAP is very effective in patients with ventilator failure such as those with COPD and congestive heart failure. However, it would be disastrous to attempt in a patient who is struggling to clear the blood from his airway. Intubation with a large endotracheal tube into the right mainstem bronchus is a better defini- tive management of the airway.

question: A 22-year-old man presents with months of intermittent lower abdominal cramping and bloody diarrhea that has worsened over the past week. He passed gross red blood this morning, has been dizzy, and "almost passed out twice." Abdominal examination is diffusely tender. Rectal examination reveals gross red blood on the examination glove, but no hemorrhoids were seen and the rectum was nontender. What is the most likely cause of the bleeding?
englishExplanation:
Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is the most likely cause of this patient's symp- toms. Classic presenting symptoms of IBD are abdominal pain, diarrhea, tenesmus, and bloody stools. IBD usually refers to two major disorders, Crohn disease and ul- cerative colitis. The crampy abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea are also consistent with the diagnosis of IBD, as would be tenesmus (feelings of cramping like having to defecate). Peak incidence of IBD is between the ages of 15 to 30, with another bimodal age of diagnosis around 50 to 80. There is a slight male preponder- ance for ulcerative colitis as well as a strong familial association with Crohn disease. Smoking is a risk factor for Crohn disease, but not for ulcerative colitis. Bleeding from IBD can be intermittent, and the symptoms can last for weeks prior to presen- tation. The diagnosis of IBD is generally confirmed with endoscopic evaluation. When clinically indicated, CT is the most useful imaging modality to evaluate for ex- traluminal complications in the emergency department. Incorrect Answer Explanations Colonic angiodysplasia is an acquired lesion, usually of the ascending colon and cecum, affecting patients older than 60 years. Although patients infrequently present with massive blood loss, they most often present with signs and symptoms of anemia and syncope due to intermittent episodes of bleeding. Bleeding from diverticula is unusual in this age group and is generally painless. Bleeding can be significant and is thought to be due to an erosion in the penetrating artery of the diverticulum. Hemorrhoids are the most commonly identified source of lower GI bleeding. Internal hemorrhoidal bleeding is usually associated with in- termittent, painless bleeding and can be found in patients of all ages. External hemorrhoids are usually painful and apparent on physical examination. Bleeding associated with hemorrhoids typically results in brown stool mixed with streaks of blood and blood after wiping, not the bloody diarrhea described by this patient. Furthermore, hemorrhoids generally do not cause abdominal pain, only localized rectal pain.

question:
A 40-year-old man presents with rectal pain. He denies fevers, chills, vomiting,
diarrhea, or abdominal pain.
Which factor by itself can help differentiate between the possible causes of rectal
pain?

options.text: History of pain with bowel movements

englishExplanation: It's important to ask about possible foreign body insertion in any patient with rectal pain since patients may hesitate to disclose that in their history. If not directly asked, the diagnosis of foreign body can be missed, as it may not be readily apparent on examination. This specific factor provides a clear clue to the cause of rectal pain that may be missed otherwise. Constipation, pain with bowel move- ments, and history of trauma can indicate more than one possible etiology and are not specific enough to differentiate possible causes of rectal pain.
arabicExplanation:

A 44-year-old man with an unknown medical history presents via ambulance for
being “altered.” Per EMS, the patient's sister called the police because the patient
had been missing work and not answering his phone for several days. EMS re-
ports there were several bottles of alcohol scattered around the house and the pa-
tient couldn't provide any further history. His vital signs are BP 89/60, P 114, R
20, and T 38.5°C (101.3°F); SpO  is 94% on room air. On examination, he is
jaundiced with spider angiomas and is oriented only to name. When questioned,
he responds only by shaking his head back and forth while muttering “no.” His
abdomen is distended with shifting dullness and mild generalized tenderness to
palpation. Some notable laboratory studies include:
WBC 19.4 x 10 /L
Blood glucose 54 mmol/L
Creatinine 2.9 mg/dL
AST 120 U/L
ALT 54 U/L
+ Anti-HAV IgG
- Anti-HAV IgM
+ Anti-HBs, - HBsAg, - Anti-HBc, - HBeAg
- HCV
Acetaminophen <5 mcg/mL
What is the most likely underlying medical condition that contributed to this
patient's presentation?

englishExplanation: The underlying problem in this patient's presentation is likely alcoholic cirrhosis. The brief history provided has some clues that are concerning for chronic alcohol use, including reports of bottles around the house and missed responsibilities (such as going to work) that are likely due to drinking. Additionally, his examination demonstrates some sequelae of chronic liver disease, including jaundice, abdominal ascites, and spider angiomas. The mild elevation of his transami- nases with an AST:ALT ratio of approximately 2:1 is also typical of chronic alcohol use.

question:
A 26-day-old boy who was born at term via spontaneous vaginal delivery at home
presents with constipation and two episodes of vomiting. The parents state that
he had his first bowel movement 2 days after he was born. He normally has three
to four small stools every day, until 3 days ago, when he stopped stooling alto-
gether. He is breastmilk fed only. He seemed more fussy today, and when he
vomited again, his parents became increasingly concerned. On examination, the
rectal vault is empty.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: In Hirschsprung disease, there is a failure of neural crest cell migration to the distal colon during fetal development. This results in abnormal inner- vation and poor motor function of the rectum, resulting in an empty rectal vault on digital examination. Hirschsprung disease presents with delayed meconium passage (typically >48 hours of life), stooling difficulties, bilious emesis, intestinal obstruction, or enterocolitis. If enterocolitis progresses to life- threatening toxic megacolon, patients may present lethargic, dehydrated, febrile, and with sepsis-like physiology, requiring intravenous antibiotics, hy- dration, and possible surgical management. Hirschsprung disease has a 4:1 male predominance and is associated with Down syndrome.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: بالـ Hirschsprung disease يفشل هجرة الـ neural crest cells للـ distal colon أثناء تكوّن الجنين، فيصير تعصيب غير طبيعي ووظيفة حركية ضعيفة بالـ rectum، ولهذا يكون الـ rectal vault فارغ عند الفحص الرقمي. عادة يظهر بتأخر مرور الـ meconium (أكثر من 48 ساعة من الولادة) وتعب بالتبرز وقيء صفراوي أو انسداد معوي. وهذا الطفل ما تبرز أول مرة إلا بعد يومين، ومعروف بغلبة الذكور بنسبة 4:1.
الفخ: الطلاب يختاروا intussusception أو infant botulism. الفرق إنه هذا الطفل 26 يوم، والـ intussusception بمثالي يصيب بين 6 و 36 شهر مع ألم متقطع وبراز جيلي، أما الـ rectal vault الفارغ مع تأخر الـ meconium فيرجّح Hirschsprung.

question:
A 40-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presents with abdominal
cramping and watery diarrhea that started 2 days ago during a family road trip to
the Grand Canyon. She has had four to five loose stools per day. Her son just re-
covered from 3 days of similar symptoms. Her vital signs include BP 142/80, P
90, R 18, and T 37.3°C (99.1°F). Abdominal examination is notable for mild dif-
fuse abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding. Skin turgor and capil-
lary refill are normal.
What is the most likely causative organism?
englishExplanation: Acute diarrheal illness (≤14 days) in immunocompetent hosts is most commonly infectious, short-lasting, and self-limited. Viral etiologies comprise the majority of all cases, with norovirus being the most com- mon overall since the introduction of routine rotavirus vaccination, accounting for 26% of diarrhea cases in the emergency department. Norovirus is transmissible via the fecal-oral route, with a 24 to 48 hour incubation period, and it read- ily spreads amongst close contacts, such as family members. The patient's mild case of watery diarrhea is characteristic of noninflammatory viral diarrheal illnesses and was likely acquired from her son. The presence of bloody or mucoid stools, 9/20/26, 1:17 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 34 of 974 fever, or tenesmus would be more consistent with an inflammatory or invasive diarrheal illness and would confer a higher probability of bacterial etiologies.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المرض الحاد بالإسهال لمدة أقل من 14 يوم عند شخص سليم المناعة عادة يكون معدياً وقصير وself-limited. الأسباب الفيروسية تشكّل أغلبية الحالات، والـ norovirus هو الأكثر شيوعاً بشكل عام من بعد إدخال تطعيم rotavirus الروتيني، ويشكّل 26% من حالات الإسهال بالطوارئ. الـ norovirus ينتقل بالطريق البرازي-الفموي بفترة حضانة 24 لـ 48 ساعة، وينتشر بسرعة بين المخالطين زي أفراد العائلة.
الفخ: الطلاب يختاروا Shigella أو Bacillus cereus. الفرق إنه الإسهال المائي الخفيف بدون دم أو مخاط وبدون حرارة عالية يمشي مع السبب الفيروسي، أما الشيجيلا فتسبب إسهال دموي التهابي مع حرارة، والـ son كان عنده نفس الأعراض قبله وهذا يرجّح الانتقال العائلي.

question:
A 28-year-old man with no medical history presents with abdominal pain that
started 2 hours ago after doing yard work at his home. The pain is severe, sharp,
and radiates to his back. His vital signs are BP 158/92, P 106, R 16, T 37.2°C
(99°F); SpO  is 98% on room air. His examination is notable for a rigid abdomen
with diffuse abdominal tenderness and a normal testicular examination. The pa-
tient has a comprehensive work-up including laboratory evaluation (CBC, com-
plete metabolic panel, serum lipase, urinalysis), an ECG, and a CT of the ab-
domen and pelvis with intravenous contrast, all of which fails to reveal an etiol-
ogy for the patient's symptoms.
What is the most appropriate next step in identifying the likely cause of the
patient's symptoms?
englishExplanation: Given the onset of the patient's symptoms after doing yard work, one must consider the diagnosis of black widow spider envenomation, which may be confirmed by identifying the site of envenomation on a skin examination. Skin examination may reveal a small puncture site surrounded by a circle of blanched tissue with a red perimeter (identified in 50% of cases), associated with local diaphoresis at the site of the wound (present in 20% of cases). Black widow envenomations can cause abdominal pain and muscle cramping that can closely mimic an acute surgical abdomen. Black widow envenomations can also mimic other severe disease processes such as myocardial infarc- tion, stroke, rabies, and tetanus. In the absence of a clear history or identifica- tion of the spider, these more severe etiologies must be ruled out depending on the presentation. Symptoms of black widow spider envenomations typically last 24 to 72 hours.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: البداية بعد شغل الحديقة وإثر heavy abdominal pain اللي تنتشر للظهر مع بطن متصلب، لازم نفكر بـ black widow spider envenomation. التشخيص يتأكد بإيجاد موقع اللسعة بالفحص الجلدي، واللي ممكن يبين نقطة صغيرة محاطة بحلقة نسيج شاحب مع حافة حمرا (بـ 50% من الحالات) مع تعرق موضعي بمكان الجرح (بـ 20%). هذا السم بيعمل أعراض تشبه البطن الجراحي الحاد مع تشنجات عضلية.
الفخ: الطلاب يطلبوا CT angiogram أو serum lactate بعد ما كل الفحوصات طلعت طبيعية. الفرق إنه الـ CT والتحاليل والـ ECG كلها ما بيّنت سبب، والأعراض المميزة لسم العنكبوت هي اللي بتوجّهنا، فالفحص الجلدي المتكرر والدقيق هو الخطوة الأهم لتأكيد التشخيص.

question:
A 35-year-old man with a history of sickle cell disease presents with penile pain.
He woke this morning with pain and tense swelling that has gradually worsened
over the past 4 hours. He had sex with his husband last night but didn't experi-
ence any discomfort at that time. His vital signs include BP 152/90, P 110, R 20,
and T 37.3°C (99.1°F). His examination is notable for a rigid and diffusely tender
penis without any visible lesions or urethral discharge.
Which test is most likely to confirm his diagnosis?

options.text: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast
Urethral cultures for gonorrhea and chlamydia

englishExplanation: This patient's presentation is highly concerning for priapism, which is defined as an erection extending beyond or entirely unrelated to sexual stimula- tion that lasts for ≥4 hours. Ischemic (low-flow) priapism is caused by impaired relaxation of cavernosal smooth muscle impairing venous out- flow functionally, resulting in compartment syndrome of the penis. Ischemic pri- apism is considered a urologic emergency. Tissue damage begins within 4 hours; 9/20/26, 1:17 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 62 of 974 if untreated, it leads to cellular necrosis, fibrosis, and permanent sexual dysfunc- tion. Timely differentiation from the far less dangerous nonischemic (high-flow) priapism is best accomplished by corporal aspiration and blood gas analysis, but color duplex ultrasonography of the penis may also be utilized.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: القصة قوية لـ priapism، واللي يعرّف كانتصاب يستمر لأكثر من 4 ساعات أو يكون بدون علاقة بالتحفيز الجنسي أصلاً. الـ ischemic (low-flow) priapism يصير بسبب خلل بارتخاء العضلات الملساء بالـ cavernosal واختلال تصريف الدم الوريدي، فيصير شي زي compartment syndrome بالقضيب. وهذه حالة طوارئ بولي، وضرر الأنسجة يبدأ خلال 4 ساعات. ولتأكيد التشخيص نعمل corporal blood gas analysis.
الفخ: الطلاب يختاروا urethral cultures أو retrograde urethrogram. الفرق إنه هون ما في إفرازات أو آفات أو أعراض سيلان، والـ corporal blood gas هو اللي يفرّق بين الـ ischemic والـ non-ischemic priapism، والمريض عنده sickle cell disease وهي من عوامل الخطورة المعروفة.

question:
A 20-year-old woman with a known 5-cm ovarian cyst presents with the acute
onset of left lower quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, she is extremely
tender in the left lower quadrant.
What is the best initial imaging modality for this patient?

options.text: Abdominal and pelvic CT with intravenous contrast
Abdominal and pelvic CT without intravenous contrast

englishExplanation: This patient's presentation is concerning for ovarian torsion, which is an uncom- mon diagnosis that should be evaluated with transvaginal ultrasound. Risk factors for ovarian torsion include ovarian enlargement, polycystic ovarian syndrome, fertility treatment, and pregnancy. Ovarian torsion most com- monly occurs in women of reproductive age but can also occur in children and post- menopausal women. It is most commonly diagnosed on the right ovary be- cause of the increased length of the utero-ovarian ligament and the loca- tion of the sigmoid colon on the left. 9/20/26, 1:17 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 76 of 974 Patients with ovarian torsion often present with the sudden-onset of severe uni- lateral lower abdominal pain along with nausea and vomiting; however, the pain may be gradual and intermittent. Patients may also endorse flank and groin discomfort. Patients are often tender on examination, and a mass may or may not be palpated. Transvaginal ultrasound is the study of choice, but it has some limitations because the ovary receives its blood supply from the ovarian and uterine arteries; thus, patients may have normal arterial blood flow but still be torsed. Torsion progresses from vascular congestion, engorgement, and edema to ischemia and infarction when arterial blood flow is interrupted. Treatment of ovarian torsion is surgical.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: القصة مثيرة للقلق لـ ovarian torsion، وهذه حالة غير شائعة لازم نقيّمها بالـ transvaginal ultrasound. من عوامل الخطورة تكبّر المبيض، والـ polycystic ovarian syndrome، وأدوية الخصوبة، والحمل. الـ ovarian torsion تصير غالباً بالنساء بسن الإنجاب، وتشخّص أكثر بالمبيض الأيمن بسبب طول الـ utero-ovarian ligament والموقع الأيسر للـ sigmoid colon.
الفخ: الطلاب يختاروا CT بالصبغة أو بدونه أو abdominal x-ray. الفرق إنه الـ transvaginal ultrasound هو اللي بيشوف المبيض والجريان الدموي فيه بسرعة وبدون إشعاع، والـ CT ما عليه حساسية كافية للـ torsion، والمريضة عندها cyst معروف حجمه 5 سم.

question: Which statement is true regarding Spigelian hernias?

options.text: Most cases have an unknown inciting event
Risk of strangulation is higher than with other common hernias
Ultrasound is the first-line imaging technique for diagnosis

correctAnswer: Risk of strangulation is higher than with other common hernias
englishExplanation: Risk of strangulation is highest with Spigelian hernias when compared to other common hernias. About 20% of these hernias present incarcer- ated, and up to 15% present strangulated. Although some patients present with swelling in the mid-to-lower abdomen lateral to the rectus muscle, other pa- tients do not have a palpable mass. This examination can be particularly difficult in obese patients. For patients with pain in the area concerning for a Spigelian hernia and a high index of suspicion for this diagnosis, imaging is an important adjunct to visualize the hernia anatomy.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: خطر الـ strangulation هو الأعلى بالـ Spigelian hernias مقارنة بباقي أنواع الفتق الشائعة. حوالي 20% من هذه الفتوق تجي incarcerated، وحتى 15% تجي strangulated. بعض المرضى يجيهم تورّم بالبطن الأوسط لتحت الجانب من العضلة المستقيمة، وفي مرضى ثانيين ما يكون عندهم كتلة محسوسة أصلاً، والفحص يكون صعب خصوصاً عند البدينين.
الفخ: الطلاب يختاروا إنه الـ ultrasound هو الفحص الأول أو إنه الـ Spigelian hernias شائعة. الفرق إنها نادرة وليست شائعة، والـ ultrasound مجرد إضافة مساعدة للتشخيص ومو الفحص الأول الأساسي، والخطر العالي للـ strangulation هو العبارة الصحيحة الوحيدة.

question:
A 19-year-old woman presents with 12 hours of abdominal pain that has steadily
worsened. She has a known intrauterine pregnancy at 10 weeks of gestation. Her
vital signs include BP 108/67, P 95, and T 34.7°C (94.5°F); SpO  is 97% on room
air. The pain is generalized and constant. She has had nausea and vomiting but
no diarrhea. She appears to be in moderate discomfort. On examination, the pa-
tient has tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant. She has a positive
psoas sign.
What is the preferred initial test to evaluate for appendicitis?
2

PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered

Page 82 of 974
englishExplanation: Graded compression ultrasonography is the preferred initial test to eval- uate the appendix in pregnant patients and in children. A thickened, noncompress- ible appendix larger than 6 mm in diameter is concerning for appendicitis. Ultrasound is generally available and less expensive than MRI. If an ultrasound is inconclusive, then MRI is recommended. Appendicitis is the most common nonobstetric surgical emergency in preg- nant patients. The diagnosis of appendicitis is complicated by anatomic changes that occur during pregnancy, and appendiceal rupture is more common in pregnant patients than nonpregnant patients.
