الفخ: طلاب كتير يختاروا hemiplegia مع dysarthria لأنه مشهد سكتة شائع، بس نزف الجسر بيعطي شلل كامل مع حدقات نقطية وفقدان النظر الأفقي، والتمييز إنه الحدقات النقطية إشارة مباشرة على نزف الجسر.

chapterTitle: Renal, Electrolyte, Acid–Base and Endocrine Emergencies
question:
A 42-year-old anxious woman presents to the ED with low back pain radiating down her left 
leg. She states that she has a history of a herniated disk but has never had advanced imaging or 
surgery. While the patient is lying supine, you lift her right leg to approximately 45 degrees, 
causing the patient to complain of pain radiating down her left leg below the knee. How do you 
interpret this result?

options.text: The patient probably has a vertebral compression fracture.
The patient has cauda equina syndrome.
The patient has a lumbar radiculopathy probably caused by a left-sided herniated disk.
The patient has crossed sensory nerve fibers resulting in paradoxical left-sided pain.

correctAnswer: The patient has a lumbar radiculopathy probably caused by a left-sided herniated disk.
englishExplanation:
The “crossed” straight leg raise (SLR) test is performed by raising the unaffected leg 
of a patient complaining of radicular low back pain while keeping the knee straight. The 
occurrence of pain radiating below the knee in the affected leg is nearly pathognomonic for a 
herniated disk with nerve root compression. Although the normal SLR test (performed on the 
affected leg) is more sensitive than the crossed SLR test, it has a low specificity. Therefore, many 
patients without true disk disease will have a positive SLR test. Pain which worsens when the 
ankle is dorsiflexed (Lasègue sign) may be a helpful adjunct to the initial examination. Of note, 
the SLR and crossed SLR tests are considered positive only if the patient complains of radicular 
pain radiating down the leg past the knee. The mere presence of back pain is considered a 
negative test.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: اختبار crossed straight leg raise بيصير برفع الرجل السليمة للمريض اللي بيشتكي من ألم قطني بجذور الأعصاب مع الحفاظ على الركبة ممدودة. حدوث ألم بيشع تحت الركبة بالرجل المصابة شبه pathognomonic لانزلاق غضروفي مع انضغاط جذر العصب. اختبار SLR العادي أكثر حساسية بس أقل نوعية، فكتير مرضى بدون مرض غضروفي حقيقي بيعطوا نتيجة موجبة. الألم اللي بيزيد لما نعمل dorsiflexion للكاحل (Lasègue sign) ممكن يساعد بالفحص الأولي. الاختبار يعتبر موجب بس إذا المريض بيشتكي ألم شعاعي تحت الركبة.
الفخ: طلاب كتير يختاروا cauda equina syndrome، بس هون الألم بمشي على مسار جذر عصب واحد، والتمييز إنه وجود ألم تحت الركبة مع انزلاق غضروفي بجذر واحد.

chapterTitle: Renal, Electrolyte, Acid–Base and Endocrine Emergencies
question: Which of the following corresponds to ischemia of the anterior circulation?

options.text: Hemiparesis and hemisensory loss of the left leg
Aphasia and hemiparesis of the right arm, leg, and face

englishExplanation:
The anterior circulation refers to the region of brain tissue served by the internal 
carotid arteries. Approximately 80% of cerebral blood flow is derived from the carotid arteries. 
This includes the anterior cerebral artery, the middle cerebral artery, and the ophthalmic artery 
(branch of the internal carotid artery just before joining the circle of Willis). Hemiparesis and 
hemisensory loss of the leg is a result of anterior cerebral artery ischemia. Transient monocular 
blindness (amaurosis fugax) is a result of ischemia in the ophthalmic artery. Aphasia and 
hemiparesis are due to ischemia in the middle cerebral artery. Ataxia and vertigo along with 
nausea and vomiting are caused by posterior circulation ischemia (to the cerebellum). The 
posterior circulation originates in the vertebral arteries (which originate from the subclavian 
arteries), which join to form the basilar artery and then bifurcate to form the two posterior 
cerebral arteries. This system supplies the remaining 20% of cerebral blood flow, delivering 
blood to the cerebellum and brainstem as well as to the visual occipital lobe and medial aspect 
of the temporal lobe.
arabicExplanation:

question: Which of the following is associated with carpal tunnel syndrome?
englishExplanation:
Carpal tunnel syndrome refers to median neuropathy due to compression at the 
wrist. Common conditions associated with carpal tunnel syndrome include diabetes, 
hypothyroidism, pregnancy, and rheumatoid arthritis. Findings include pain and paresthesias in 
the thumb, index, and long fingers. Phalen test (pain from holding the wrists flexed for 60 
seconds) is more sensitive than Tinel test (pain from tapping the volar wrist), but neither is 

reliable enough to exclude or prove the diagnosis and nerve conduction studies are the gold 
standard. Treatment involves wrist splinting, with surgery reserved for refractory cases.

A 30-year-old bodybuilder was visiting his mother on the acute 
medical unit when he developed acute severe right loin pain and visible 
haematuria. A renal stone was suspected. The busy urology registrar

What is the best choice of imaging to confirm renal calculi?
englishExplanation:
5. B.  Non-contrast helical CT urogram
Non-contrast helical CT urogram has the best diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity 95%) and is now considered the gold-standard investigation for renal colic. An intravenous urogram has a sensitivity of 
70–90% and may fail to detect radiolucent stones. Plain radiography has a sensitivity of 45–60% and 
ultrasonography a sensitivity of 37–64%. MR urography is a useful tool, often limited by time taken 
to scan and competing imaging priorities in the radiology department.

question:
A 68-year-old man with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on hemodialysis is admitted with a significant upper gastrointestinal bleed. Despite a normal platelet
count, PT, and aPTT, his bleeding persists. In addition to standard care, which
agent is administered specifically to improve platelet function in uremia?
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology:
Uraemic bleeding results from a qualitative platelet defect rather than thrombocytopenia. Uraemic toxins (e.g., guanidinosuccinic acid) interfere with the binding of
fibrinogen to the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor and von Willebrand Factor (vWF) to
the glycoprotein Ib receptor. This impairs platelet adhesion and aggregation.
Mechanism of Desmopressin (DDAVP):
Desmopressin (0.3 mcg/kg IV or SC) stimulates the release of pre-formed Factor
VIII and vWF from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies. This increases plasma levels
of these factors, enhancing platelet adhesion to the vessel wall despite the uraemic
environment. Onset is rapid (30-60 minutes).
Alternative Therapies:
Adequate dialysis is the definitive treatment. Cryoprecipitate (rich in
vWF/fibrinogen) is a second-line rescue therapy (onset 1 hour). Conjugated oestrogens are used for longer-term control (onset 6 hours, duration 14-21 days).
Tranexamic acid may be used as an adjunct but requires dose adjustment in renal
failure.

Clinical Pearl
Uraemia = Platelet Dysfunction:
Uraemic bleeding is characterised by a prolonged bleeding time despite a normal
platelet count, PT, and aPTT. The defect is qualitative (functional), involving impaired adhesion and aggregation.
DDAVP is First Line:
The effect of DDAVP is rapid (within 30-60 minutes) but transient (lasting 6-8
hours). It is ideal for an acute bleed or pre-procedural prophylaxis.
Tachyphylaxis:
Repeated doses of DDAVP become less effective (tachyphylaxis) as the endothelial
stores of vWF are depleted.
Dialysis Improves Platelet Function:
The definitive treatment for uraemic bleeding is adequate haemodialysis, which removes the uraemic toxins that impair platelet function.
Side Effects of DDAVP:
The main side effects are flushing, headache, and, importantly, hyponatraemia due
to its antidiuretic V2 receptor activity.
Role of Red Cells (Rheology):
Anaemia worsens uraemic bleeding because red blood cells physically push platelets
toward the vessel wall (margination). Transfusion to a haematocrit >30% can significantly improve bleeding time in uraemic patients.
Conjugated Oestrogens Timeline:
For recurrent or persistent bleeding, IV or oral conjugated oestrogens provide a sustained effect. Unlike DDAVP, the onset is delayed (6 hours) and peak effect occurs
at 5-7 days, but the benefit lasts for 2-3 weeks.
Cryoprecipitate as Rescue:
Cryoprecipitate (10 units) is reserved for life-threatening uraemic bleeding resistant
to DDAVP. It provides high concentrations of vWF, Factor VIII, and fibrinogen, acting within 1 hour.
Tranexamic Acid Risk:
In renal failure, tranexamic acid accumulates and crosses the blood-brain barrier,
significantly increasing the risk of seizures due to GABA inhibition. Dose reduction
is essential in patients with ESRD.
Mechanism of Oestrogens:
Oestrogens are thought to reduce the production of endothelial nitric oxide (NO)
and L-arginine, which are potent platelet inhibitors. This mechanism explains the
delayed onset of action compared to DDAVP.

question:
A critically ill patient has a complex infection. The team wants to use tigecycline
for its broad-spectrum coverage of MDR organisms. However, tigecycline has
three notable "holes" in its spectrum and should not be used to empirically cover
which group of pathogens?

options.text: Acinetobacter, ESBL E. coli, and Klebsiella

englishExplanation:
Mechanism and Spectrum:
Tigecycline is a glycylcycline antibiotic (a minocycline derivative) that inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit. It exhibits a very broad

spectrum of activity, covering Gram-positive organisms (including MRSA and
VRE), many MDR Gram-negatives (including ESBL-producers and Acinetobacter
baumannii), anaerobes, and atypical pathogens.
Intrinsic Resistance (The 3 Ps):
Despite its broad spectrum, Tigecycline has intrinsic gaps in coverage against the '3
Ps': Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Proteus species, and Providencia species. These organisms possess intrinsic efflux pumps (e.g., MexXY-OprM in Pseudomonas) that
render the drug ineffective.
Pharmacokinetic Limitations:
Tigecycline has a very large volume of distribution (>10 L/kg), resulting in high tissue concentrations but low serum concentrations. Consequently, it is not suitable
for treating bacteraemia or endocarditis.
Clinical Pearl
Intrinsic Resistance Spectrum:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Proteus species, and Providencia species are intrinsically
resistant to tigecycline due to constitutive expression of multidrug efflux pumps.
Pharmacokinetic Distribution:
Due to a large volume of distribution (>10 L/kg), serum levels are low despite high
tissue penetration. It is ineffective for primary bacteraemia and is not licensed for
ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) due to poor outcomes in clinical trials.
Mortality Signal:
MHRA and FDA warnings highlight an increased risk of all-cause mortality compared to other antibiotics. It should be reserved for situations where alternative
treatments are not suitable.
Bacteriostatic Activity:
Tigecycline is primarily a bacteriostatic agent, which limits its utility in severe, lifethreatening infections such as infective endocarditis or profound
immunosuppression.
Gastrointestinal Effects:
The most common adverse effects are severe nausea and vomiting, occurring in up
to 30% of patients, which may limit tolerability.
Hepatic Impairment:
No dose adjustment is required for mild-moderate hepatic impairment. However, in
severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C), the maintenance dose should be reduced
(e.g., 25 mg BD after the standard loading dose).
Hypofibrinogenaemia:

Tigecycline can cause significant hypofibrinogenaemia and prolonged PT/aPTT.
Coagulation profiles, specifically fibrinogen, should be monitored in critically ill
patients.
Mechanism of Action:
As a glycylcycline, tigecycline binds to the 30S ribosomal subunit with five times
higher affinity than minocycline, allowing it to overcome tetracycline resistance
mechanisms such as ribosomal protection and efflux.
Clostridioides difficile Sparing:
Unlike many broad-spectrum antibiotics, tigecycline demonstrates in vitro activity
against C. difficile and has a lower propensity to induce C. difficile infection.
Renal Pharmacokinetics:
No dosage adjustment is required in renal impairment or for patients receiving renal replacement therapy (haemodialysis or haemofiltration).
Pancreatitis Risk:
Acute pancreatitis is a rare but documented serious adverse effect associated with
tigecycline use, warranting discontinuation if suspected.
Standard Dosing:
The standard adult regimen is a 100 mg loading dose followed by 50 mg every 12
hours.

chapterTitle: Renal, Electrolyte, Acid–Base and Endocrine Emergencies
question:
A 58-year-old with alcoholic cirrhosis is diagnosed with hepatorenal syndrome acute kidney injury (HRS-AKI). What is the first-line medical therapy to reverse
the renal failure?
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology and First-Line Therapy:
Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI) is driven by severe splanchnic vasodilation leading to effective arterial hypovolemia, activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), and intense renal vasoconstriction. The cornerstone of therapy is to reverse this pathophysiology via splanchnic vasoconstriction and plasma
volume expansion. Terlipressin acts as a potent agonist at V1a receptors on vascular
smooth muscle cells in the splanchnic bed. When combined with intravenous albumin, it improves effective arterial blood volume and renal perfusion pressure, making it the definitive first-line medical therapy.
Administration Strategy:
Current BSG guidelines recommend administering Terlipressin by continuous intravenous infusion rather than bolus injection. Evidence suggests continuous infusion reduces the rate of adverse events (particularly respiratory failure and ischemic
complications) while maintaining efficacy. Albumin is typically dosed at 20-40g
daily after an initial loading phase.
Alternatives and Rescue:
Norepinephrine is an effective alternative vasoconstrictor, particularly for patients
already in the ICU with central access. Midodrine plus octreotide is significantly inferior and reserved for settings where terlipressin or norepinephrine are unavailable. TIPS (Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt) may be used in non-responders, while liver transplantation remains the only definitive cure.
Clinical Pearl
Combination Therapy Principle:

The cornerstone of HRS-AKI management is the combination of a splanchnic vasoconstrictor and intravenous albumin; neither agent is effective in isolation.
First-Line Vasoconstrictor:
Terlipressin has the strongest evidence base for reversing HRS-AKI and improving
renal function compared to other vasoconstrictors.
Alternative Vasoconstrictors:
Norepinephrine is the preferred alternative to terlipressin, particularly in the ICU.
Midodrine plus octreotide is significantly less effective and is a last-resort option.
Therapy is a Bridge:
Medical therapy for HRS is a bridge to the only definitive treatment, which is liver
transplantation.
Continuous Infusion Preference:
Administer Terlipressin via continuous IV infusion rather than bolus injection to reduce the risk of adverse events, specifically respiratory failure and ischemic
complications.
Diagnostic Volume Challenge:
Diagnosis of HRS-AKI requires excluding other causes and demonstrating a lack of
response to a 2-day volume expansion challenge with IV albumin (1 g/kg, max 100
g/day).
Adverse Effects Monitoring:
Terlipressin carries significant risks of ischemic events (cardiac, peripheral, mesenteric) and pulmonary edema; close monitoring of oxygen saturation and peripheral
perfusion is mandatory.
Terlipressin Mechanism:
Terlipressin is a prodrug converted to lysine-vasopressin. It acts as a specific V1a receptor agonist, causing splanchnic vasoconstriction which shifts blood volume to
the central circulation, increasing effective arterial blood volume.
Nomenclature Update:
The term 'HRS-AKI' has largely replaced the older 'Type 1 HRS' classification, aligning with the KDIGO AKI criteria. It is defined by an increase in serum creatinine of
≥26.5 micromol/L within 48 hours or ≥50% within 7 days.
Contraindications:
Terlipressin is relatively contraindicated in patients with severe ischemic heart disease or severe peripheral vascular disease due to its potent vasoconstrictive effects.

chapterTitle: Renal, Electrolyte, Acid–Base and Endocrine Emergencies
question: Which of the following is a potential metabolic complication of using regional citrate anticoagulation for Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy (CRRT)?
englishExplanation:
Metabolic Alkalosis Mechanism:
Metabolic alkalosis is a frequent complication of regional citrate anticoagulation
(RCA) when citrate metabolism is efficient. Citrate returned to the patient is metabolized (primarily in the liver and skeletal muscle) via the Krebs cycle. The metabolism of 1 mole of citrate generates 3 moles of bicarbonate. If the net citrate load exceeds the patient's acid generation, metabolic alkalosis develops. Management typically involves reducing the citrate dose (blood flow dependent) or reducing the bicarbonate concentration in the dialysis/replacement fluids.
Contrast with Citrate Toxicity:
Conversely, 'Citrate Toxicity' (accumulation) occurs when the body cannot metabolize the citrate load (e.g., severe liver failure or shock). This results in a High Anion
Gap Metabolic Acidosis (due to the unmeasured citrate anion) and systemic ionized
hypocalcemia, rather than alkalosis.
Clinical Pearl
Citrate is Metabolized to Bicarbonate:
1 mole of citrate → 3 moles of bicarbonate.
Metabolic Alkalosis Mechanism:
Metabolic alkalosis is the result of successful citrate metabolism, where the generated bicarbonate load exceeds the patient's buffering needs.
Citrate Toxicity:
Citrate accumulation (toxicity) manifests as a High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis
(HAGMA) due to the unmeasured citrate anion, accompanied by systemic ionized
hypocalcemia.
Calcium Ratio Monitoring:
A sign of citrate accumulation is a widening gap between the total calcium and ionized calcium. A Total Ca / Ionized Ca ratio > 2.5 is highly suggestive of
accumulation.
RCA is Preferred:
Despite potential complications, regional citrate anticoagulation is the preferred
method for CRRT in most ICUs due to a lower risk of bleeding compared to systemic heparin.
Mechanism of Action:
Citrate acts by chelating ionized calcium in the extracorporeal circuit. Calcium is a
necessary cofactor for clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X; removing it inhibits the coagulation cascade.
Hypomagnesemia Risk:

Citrate chelates magnesium as well as calcium. Significant magnesium loss occurs
across the hemofilter, frequently requiring active supplementation to prevent
arrhythmias.
Management of Alkalosis:
To correct RCA-induced metabolic alkalosis, decrease the citrate infusion rate (if
possible within flow ratios) or, more commonly, reduce the bicarbonate concentration in the replacement/dialysate fluid.
Hypernatremia Risk:
Trisodium citrate solutions impose a significant sodium load. Hypernatremia may
develop, necessitating the use of hyponatremic replacement fluids or adjustment of
the citrate solution.
Hypophosphatemia:
Standard citrate solutions do not contain phosphate, and CRRT clearance of phosphate is high. Significant hypophosphatemia is common and requires separate supplementation or phosphate-containing replacement fluids.
Circuit vs Systemic Targets:
RCA requires two distinct calcium targets: a low circuit ionized calcium (<0.35
mmol/L) to inhibit coagulation, and a normal systemic ionized calcium (1.1-1.3
mmol/L) to maintain physiological homeostasis.
Liver Failure Caution:
Severe liver failure impairs citrate metabolism (Krebs cycle), increasing the risk of
toxicity. While not an absolute contraindication, RCA requires vigilant monitoring
of the calcium ratio and acid-base status in these patients.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: القلاء الاستقلابي من مضاعفات الاستئناف الموضعي بالسترات المتكررة لما يكون أيض السترات فعالاً. السترات اللي بترجع للمريض بتتأيض بالكبد والعضلات الهيكلية عبر دورة Krebs، وكل مول من السترات بينتج 3 مول بيكربونات. إذا كان الحمل الصافي من السترات أكثر من إنتاج الحمض عند المريض بيصير قلاء استقلابي. الإدارة بتكون بتقليل جرعة السترات أو تقليل تركيز البيكربونات بسوائل الديال. بعكس ذلك سمية السترات، يعني تراكمها بفشل كبدي شديد أو shock، بتعمل حماض استقلابي بفجوة أنيونية عالية مع نقص كالسيوم متأين.
الفخ: طلاب كتير يختاروا حماض استقلابي، بس هاد يخص التراكم مش الأيض الفعال، والتمييز إنه نجاح أيض السترات يعطي قلاء.

chapterTitle: Renal, Electrolyte, Acid–Base and Endocrine Emergencies
question:
A 68-year-old patient with acute kidney injury is on continuous veno-venous
hemofiltration (CVVH). Which statement is most accurate regarding drug removal during this therapy?

options.text: Vancomycin is not removed due to its high molecular weight.
Digoxin is effectively removed due to its low protein binding.
Gentamicin will be significantly removed due to its low molecular weight and
Diazepam will be efficiently removed due to its low molecular weight.
Tricyclic antidepressants are effectively removed due to their low volume of

correctAnswer: Gentamicin will be significantly removed due to its low molecular weight and
englishExplanation:
Introduction:
Drug clearance by Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy (CRRT) is governed by
several key pharmacokinetic properties.
Pathophysiology of Clearance:
For a drug to be effectively removed by CVVH (hemofiltration/convection), it must
possess specific characteristics determining its Sieving Coefficient (Sc). The Sc is the
ratio of drug concentration in the ultrafiltrate to that in the plasma. Key factors include:
1. Low Molecular Weight (MW): Most drugs are <1500 Da, well below the cutoff of modern high-flux hemofilters (~30,000-50,000 Da).
2. Low Protein Binding: Only the unbound (free) fraction can pass through the
filter. High protein binding (>80%) significantly limits removal.

3. Small Volume of Distribution (Vd): Drugs sequestered in tissues (high Vd
>1 L/kg) have low plasma concentrations available for clearance, rendering RRT inefficient regardless of filter permeability.
Analysis of Options:
•Gentamicin (C): This aminoglycoside has a low MW (~480 Da), minimal protein
binding (<10%), and a small Vd (~0.25 L/kg). Its Sieving Coefficient is near 1.0,
meaning it is cleared at the same rate as the ultrafiltrate flow. This requires
significant dosing adjustment. Correct. •Vancomycin (A): Although larger (~1450
Da), it is well below the hemofilter cutoff. With moderate protein binding (~50%), it
has a Sieving Coefficient of ~0.7-0.8 and is significantly cleared by CVVH. Incorrect.
•Digoxin (B): Digoxin has a massive volume of distribution (>7 L/kg) due to
extensive tissue binding. Despite a small MW, the plasma load available for
clearance is negligible compared to total body stores. Incorrect. •Diazepam (D) &
TCAs (E): These agents are highly lipophilic with high protein binding (>95%) and
large volumes of distribution, making extracorporeal removal negligible. Incorrect.
Clinical Pearl
Characteristics Favoring Removal:
Characteristics favoring extracorporeal removal include small molecular weight
(<500 Da), low protein binding (<80%), small volume of distribution (<1 L/kg), and
high water solubility.
Volume of Distribution Impact:
A large volume of distribution (>1-2 L/kg) is the primary factor rendering a drug
non-dialyzable. Drugs like digoxin or tricyclic antidepressants are sequestered in
tissues, leaving low plasma concentrations available for clearance despite high
blood flow rates.
Convection versus Diffusion:
Convection (hemofiltration) relies on solvent drag and is more effective at removing
middle molecules (500-5000 Da) like vancomycin than diffusion (dialysis). Small
molecules are cleared efficiently by both modalities.
Protein Binding and Hypoalbuminaemia:
Only the unbound fraction of a drug is available for filtration. In hypoalbuminaemia, the unbound fraction of highly protein-bound drugs (e.g., phenytoin, midazolam) increases, potentially enhancing clearance and toxicity risk if not
monitored.
Sieving Coefficient Definition:
The Sieving Coefficient (Sc) quantifies membrane permeability to a solute, ranging
from 0 (impermeable, e.g., albumin) to 1 (freely permeable, e.g., urea, gentamicin).

Sc = Concentration in Ultrafiltrate / Concentration in Plasma.
Clearance Calculation:
In pure hemofiltration (CVVH), clearance of a non-protein-bound substance depends primarily on the ultrafiltration rate. Clearance (Cl) = Ultrafiltration Rate
(Quf) × Sieving Coefficient (Sc).
Filter Adsorption:
Certain drugs, particularly aminoglycosides and polymyxins (colistin), can bind reversibly to the hemofilter membrane (adsorption). This contributes to total clearance, especially early in the filter life, but saturates over time.
Rebound Phenomenon:
For drugs with a large volume of distribution, plasma levels may rebound significantly after stopping CRRT as the drug redistributes from tissues back into the intravascular space.
Vancomycin Clearance:
Vancomycin (MW ~1450 Da) is a middle molecule with moderate protein binding
(~50%). While too large for effective diffusive clearance with low-flux filters, it is effectively cleared by high-flux hemofiltration (convection), often necessitating therapeutic drug monitoring.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: تصفية الدواء بالـ CVVH بتعتمد خصائص حركية دوائية مهمة، ولازم الدواء يكون عنده وزن جزيئي منخفض، فمعظم الأدوية أقل من 1500 دالتون وهي تحت حد high-flux hemofilters البالغ 30000-50000 دالتون. لازم كذلك ارتباط بروتيني منخفض، لأن الجزء الحر بس بيمر، والارتباط أكثر من 80% بحد من الإزالة. ولازم حجم توزيع صغير، لأن الأدوية المتخزنة بالأنسجة بتراكيز بلازمية منخفضة فبتصير الإزالة غير فعالة. Gentamicin عنده وزن جزيئي حوالي 480 دالتون وارتباط بروتيني أقل من 10% وحجم توزيع 0.25 لتر/كغ، فمعامل النخل قريب من 1 وبينزال بشكل كبير.
الفخ: طلاب كتير يظنوا إنه vancomycin ما بينزال لحجمه الكبير، بس وزنه أقل بكثير من حد الفلتر وبينزال بمعامل نخل 0.7-0.8، والتمييز إنه gentamicin هو الأكثر تأثراً.

chapterTitle: Renal, Electrolyte, Acid–Base and Endocrine Emergencies
question:
A 50-year-old patient has acute kidney injury (AKI). Labs show a
BUN/Creatinine ratio of 12:1, fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) of 3.5%,
urine sodium of 45 mEq/L, and granular casts in the urine. What is the most
likely cause of the AKI?
englishExplanation:
Introduction:
The laboratory and urinalysis findings are classic for an intrinsic renal injury,
specifically ATN.
Pathophysiology:
Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN) is characterised by direct damage and death of the
renal tubular epithelial cells, usually due to ischaemia or nephrotoxins. The loss of
tubular integrity disrupts normal reabsorption and concentration mechanisms.

Interpreting the Labs:
•Loss of Reabsorptive Capacity: Damaged tubules cannot reabsorb sodium
effectively, leading to sodium wasting. This results in a high urine sodium (>40
mmol/L) and a high FeNa (>2%). •Loss of Concentrating Ability: Urine
osmolality drops towards plasma levels (~300 mOsm/kg) as the countercurrent
multiplier system fails. •Urea/Creatinine Relationship: In prerenal AKI, urea is
avidly reabsorbed with water, causing a disproportionate rise compared to
creatinine. In ATN, reabsorption fails, and both rise proportionately. •Urinalysis:
Sloughing of dead tubular epithelial cells forms 'muddy brown' granular casts, the
hallmark of ATN.
Clinical Pearl
FeNa is Key:
FeNa differentiates prerenal AKI (<1%) from ATN (>2%). In prerenal states, functioning tubules conserve sodium avidly. In ATN, damaged tubules waste sodium.
Look at the Urine Sediment:
The presence of 'muddy brown' granular casts is highly specific for ATN.
Phases of ATN:
ATN typically follows three phases: 1) Initiation (injury occurs), 2) Maintenance
(GFR nadir, oliguria, and uraemic symptoms lasting 1-2 weeks), and 3) Recovery
(tubular regeneration marked by polyuria and risk of hypokalaemia).
FeNa Caveats:
FeNa is invalid in patients receiving diuretics (which induce natriuresis).
Additionally, FeNa may be <1% in specific intrinsic causes like contrast nephropathy, rhabdomyolysis, and early sepsis.
FeUrea:
In patients on diuretics, Fractional Excretion of Urea (FeUrea) is superior to FeNa.
A FeUrea <35% suggests prerenal AKI, while >50% suggests ATN.
NICE NG148 Urinalysis Mandate:
NICE guidelines mandate urinalysis for all patients with AKI to exclude other
causes. Presence of blood and protein suggests glomerular pathology requiring urgent specialist referral.
Prerenal vs Intrinsic Biochemistry:
Prerenal AKI is characterised by Urine Na <20 mmol/L, Urine:Plasma Osmolality
>1.5, and disproportionately raised Serum Urea. Intrinsic AKI typically shows Urine
Na >40 mmol/L and Urine:Plasma Osmolality <1.1.
Urea:Creatinine Ratio:

In the UK (SI units), a Urea (mmol/L) to Creatinine (micromol/L) ratio helps differentiate causes. A ratio >0.1 (or >100 depending on scaling) suggests prerenal AKI
due to passive urea reabsorption. A lower ratio suggests intrinsic injury.
Pigment Nephropathy Exception:
Rhabdomyolysis and haemolysis can cause ATN with a low FeNa (<1%) due to intense renal vasoconstriction and tubular obstruction by pigment casts, mimicking
prerenal physiology initially.
Contrast-Induced Nephropathy:
Similar to pigment nephropathy, contrast-induced AKI often presents with a FeNa
<1% due to afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, despite being an intrinsic tubular
injury.
Postrenal Exclusion:
Renal ultrasound is the first-line investigation to exclude postrenal causes
(obstruction/hydronephrosis), especially in anuric patients or those with a history
of pelvic malignancy or stones.
Fluid Challenge Utility:
A fluid challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Rapid improvement in urine
output and biochemistry suggests prerenal aetiology; lack of response supports intrinsic ATN.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: النتائج المخبرية والتحليل البولي كلاسيكية لإصابة كلوية داخلية تحديداً ATN. الـ ATN بيتميز بتلف وموت مباشر للخلايا الظهارية الأنبوبية الكلوية عادة بسبب نقص التروية أو السموم، وفقدان سلامة الأنابيب بيعطل إعادة الامتصاص والتركيز الطبيعية. الأنابيب التالفة ما بتقدر تعيد امتصاص الصوديوم فبتضيع الصوديوم، فبيطلع صوديوم بالبول أعلى من 40 مليمول/لتر وFeNa أعلى من 2%. القدرة على التركيز بتنهار فبتقرب osmolality البول من البلازما حوالي 300. بالفشل الكلوي قبل الكلوي اليوريا بتنعاد امتصاصها مع الماء فترتفع أكثر من الكرياتينين، أما بالـ ATN فالاتنين بيرتفعوا بالتناسب. الـ casts الحبيبية الطينية بلون الطين هي سمة مميزة.
الفخ: طلاب كتير يختاروا Prerenal AKI، بس الـ FeNa فوق 2% والصوديوم العالي بنفيان الفشل قبل الكلوي، والتمييز إنه هاد تنخير أنبوبي حاد.

chapterTitle: Renal, Electrolyte, Acid–Base and Endocrine Emergencies
question: All of the following are clinical features of hypercalcemia, EXCEPT:
englishExplanation:
This statement is incorrect. Hypercalcemia characteristically shortens the QT interval on an ECG.
Pathophysiology of Symptoms:
High levels of extracellular calcium affect the function of multiple organ systems by
altering transmembrane electrical potentials and cellular signaling.
•Renal (A): Hypercalcemia impairs the kidney's ability to respond to ADH in the
collecting duct (a form of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), leading to polyuria and
secondary polydipsia. •Neurological (B): Calcium has a stabilizing effect on
neuronal membranes. Hypercalcemia raises the threshold for depolarization,
leading to decreased neuromuscular excitability. This manifests as lethargy,
weakness, confusion, and eventually coma. •Cardiac: Hypercalcemia accelerates
phase 2 (the plateau phase) of the cardiac action potential. This leads to a
shortened ST segment and therefore a shortened QT interval. It can also
cause bradycardia and AV block. A prolonged QT interval is a feature of
hypocalcemia. •Gastrointestinal (D): Hypercalcemia can cause constipation (by
decreasing smooth muscle motility) and is a recognized cause of acute pancreatitis.
•Vascular (E): Hypercalcemia can cause direct vasoconstriction and contribute to
hypertension.
Clinical Pearl
'Stones, Bones, Groans, and Moans':
The classic mnemonic for hypercalcemia symptoms: Stones (renal calculi), Bones
(pain/fractures), Groans (abdominal pain, pancreatitis, constipation), Moans

(psychiatric features), and Thrones (polyuria/constipation).
Short QT:
Remember the ECG finding: Hypercalcemia = Short QT. Hypocalcemia = Long
QT.
Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus:
The polyuria and dehydration caused by hypercalcemia-induced nephrogenic DI
can create a vicious cycle, worsening the hypercalcemia.
EKG Osborn Wave:
A 'J' wave or Osborn wave at the J-point can be seen in both hypercalcemia and
hypothermia.
First-Line Management:
Aggressive IV fluid rehydration (typically 0.9% sodium chloride) is the immediate
priority to restore intravascular volume and promote calciuresis, as most patients
are significantly volume depleted.
Diagnostic Hierarchy:
PTH measurement is the pivotal first step in differential diagnosis. Suppressed PTH
suggests malignancy or vitamin D excess, while normal/high PTH indicates primary
hyperparathyroidism or Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia (FHH).
Calcitonin vs. Bisphosphonates:
Calcitonin offers rapid calcium reduction (within hours) but exhibits tachyphylaxis
after 48 hours. Bisphosphonates (e.g., zoledronic acid) take 2-4 days to reach peak
effect but provide prolonged control.
Steroid Responsiveness:
Glucocorticoids are specifically effective for hypercalcemia mediated by 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (e.g., sarcoidosis, lymphoma) by inhibiting its conversion and intestinal calcium absorption.
Pancreatitis Relationship:
Hypercalcemia is a cause of acute pancreatitis (via secretory block and trypsinogen
activation). Conversely, hypocalcemia is a consequence of severe pancreatitis (due
to saponification of fat necrosis).
Corrected Calcium:
In hypoalbuminaemia, total calcium underestimates ionised calcium. The standard
correction formula is: Corrected Calcium = Measured Calcium + 0.02 * (40 Albumin [g/L]).
Refractory Management:
Denosumab (a RANKL inhibitor) is indicated for hypercalcemia of malignancy refractory to bisphosphonates. Renal replacement therapy with low-calcium dialysate

is reserved for severe symptomatic cases with renal failure or heart failure prohibiting fluid loading.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: فرط الكالسيوم بيقصر فترة QT على تخطيط القلب وليس بيطيلها، فإطالة QT ليست من صفاته. مستويات الكالسيوم العالية بالخارج خلوي بتأثر على أنظمة متعددة بتغيير الكمونات عبر الغشاء والإشارات الخلوية. كلوياً بيعطل استجابة الكلية لـ ADH بالأنبوبة الجامعة بشكل يشبه diabetes insipidus كلوي فيعمل polyuria وpolydipsia. عصبياً الكالسيوم بثبت أغشية الخلايا العصبية ويرفع عتبة إزالة الاستقطاب فيقل الاستثارية العصبية العضلية ويظهر خمول وضعف واختلاط وتغيب. قلبياً بيسرّع الطور الثاني من كمون الفعل فيقصر مقطع ST بالتالي يقصر فترة QT، ويمكن يسبب bradycardia وAV block. معدنياً ممكن يعمل pancreatitis وارتفاع ضغط.
الفخ: طلاب كتير يختاروا إطالة فترة QT كصفة لفرط الكالسيوم، بس إطالة QT هي سمة نقص الكالسيوم، والتمييز إنه فرط الكالسيوم يقصرها.

chapterTitle: Renal, Electrolyte, Acid–Base and Endocrine Emergencies
question:
A 45-year-old man with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and a pre-dialysis BUN
of 200 mg/dL (Urea ~71 mmol/L) undergoes his first-ever session of high-efficiency hemodialysis. Towards the end of the session, he develops a headache,
nausea, and then a generalized seizure. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Hypocalcemia from citrate in the dialysis circuit.

englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology:

Dialysis Disequilibrium Syndrome (DDS) is a form of iatrogenic cerebral oedema
caused by the rapid clearance of urea from the plasma during haemodialysis. In
chronic uraemia, brain cells accumulate idiogenic osmoles (organic osmolytes) to
maintain osmotic balance. During rapid dialysis, plasma urea drops significantly
faster than urea can be cleared from brain tissue due to the blood-brain barrier and
downregulated urea transporters (specifically UT-B). This creates a transient osmotic gradient that drives water into brain cells, leading to cerebral oedema and increased intracranial pressure.
Risk Factors:
High risk is associated with the first dialysis session, very high pre-dialysis urea
(>60 mmol/L), severe metabolic acidosis, extremes of age (paediatric/elderly), and
pre-existing neurological conditions.
Prevention:
The primary strategy is 'Start Low, Go Slow'. For the first session, limit blood flow
rates (Qb <200 mL/min), use a dialyser with a smaller surface area, reduce session
duration (e.g., 2 hours), and consider concurrent administration of mannitol or hypertonic saline to maintain plasma osmolality. Continuous Renal Replacement
Therapy (CRRT) is often preferred in the ICU setting for high-risk patients as it provides slower, more gradual solute clearance.
Analysis of Other Options:
Hypocalcaemia (A) from citrate toxicity typically presents with perioral paraesthesia, tetany, and hypotension rather than the headache-nausea-seizure progression
of DDS. Air embolism (B) usually causes sudden dyspnoea, chest pain, and cardiovascular collapse. Hypoglycaemia (D) can cause seizures but is less likely to be the
primary cause in this specific 'first session, high urea' context, especially if glucosecontaining dialysate is used. A hypertensive emergency (E) is a differential, but the
clinical picture described is the classic presentation of DDS.
Clinical Pearl
Primary Risk Factor:
The single most significant risk factor for DDS is a high pre-dialysis urea level (>60
mmol/L), particularly during the first-ever session of renal replacement therapy.
Pathophysiological Mechanism:
DDS results from a 'reverse urea effect'. Rapid plasma urea clearance creates an osmotic gradient because urea clearance from the CNS is rate-limited by the bloodbrain barrier and downregulated urea transporters (UT-B) in chronic uraemia.
Prescription Strategy:

Prevent DDS in high-risk patients by limiting urea reduction ratio (URR) to <30%
in the first session. Use low blood flow (150-200 mL/min), short duration (2 hours),
and concurrent flow dialysate.
Osmotic Agents:
Intravenous mannitol (1 g/kg) or hypertonic saline can be administered during the
dialysis session to mitigate the rapid drop in plasma osmolality and prevent cerebral
water shifts.
Differential Diagnosis:
Always exclude intracranial haemorrhage (subdural haematoma) in uraemic patients presenting with neurological deterioration, as uraemic platelet dysfunction
increases bleeding risk.
Clinical Presentation:
Symptoms range from mild (headache, nausea, restlessness, blurred vision) to severe (confusion, seizures, coma, and death from brainstem herniation).
Modality Selection:
Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy (CRRT) is preferred over Intermittent
Haemodialysis (IHD) in haemodynamically unstable patients or those at high risk
of DDS, as it allows for slower, more gradual solute clearance.
Dialysate Sodium:
Using a higher dialysate sodium concentration (sodium modelling) helps maintain
plasma tonicity during urea clearance, reducing the osmotic gradient driving water
into the brain.
Management of Established DDS:
Immediate cessation of dialysis is required if severe symptoms develop. Treatment
is supportive, focusing on airway protection and raising plasma osmolality with hypertonic saline or mannitol; anticonvulsants may be needed for seizures.
Chronic vs Acute Risk:
Patients with chronic kidney disease are at higher risk than those with acute kidney
injury because the chronic accumulation of idiogenic osmoles in brain tissue takes
time to develop, creating a larger potential gradient during rapid clearance.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: متلازمة اختلال الديال هي شكل من وذمة دماغية علاجية المنشأ بسبب التصفية السريعة لليوريا من البلازما خلال الديال الدموي. باليوريا المزمنة بتتراكم بالخلايا الدماغية osmoles عضوية للحفاظ على التوازن الأسموزي. خلال الديال السريع، يوريا البلازما بتنخفض أسرع من قدرة إزالتها من نسيج الدماغ بسبب الحاجز الدموي الدماغي وتنظيم ناقلات اليوريا UT-B، فبيتكوّن تدرج أسموزي مؤقت بيدفع الماء داخل الخلايا الدماغية ويسبب وذمة دماغية وارتفاع الضغط داخل القحف. عوامل الخطر تشمل أول جلسة ديال ويوريا قبل الديال أعلى من 60 مليمول/لتر وحماض استقلابي شديد. الوقاية هي البدء البطيء بجلسات قصيرة وتدفق أقل.
الفخ: طلاب كتير يختاروا نقص الكالسيوم من السترات، بس هاد يعطي أعراض عصبية عضلية مش نوبة صرع بعد أول جلسة، والتمييز إنه اليوريا العالية مع بداية أول ديال توجه للـ DDS.

chapterTitle: Renal, Electrolyte, Acid–Base and Endocrine Emergencies
question:
A patient has a severe, steroid-refractory cytokine release syndrome (CRS) after
CAR-T therapy. The team is deciding between anakinra and tocilizumab. What is
the key mechanistic difference between these two cytokine blockers?

options.text: Anakinra blocks the IL-6 receptor, while tocilizumab blocks the IL-1 receptor.
Anakinra blocks the IL-1 receptor, while tocilizumab blocks the IL-6 receptor.
Anakinra is a monoclonal antibody, while tocilizumab is a small molecule
Anakinra blocks TNF-alpha, while tocilizumab blocks all cytokines.
Both drugs block the IL-6 receptor, but tocilizumab is more potent.

correctAnswer: Anakinra blocks the IL-1 receptor, while tocilizumab blocks the IL-6 receptor.
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Action:
Tocilizumab is a humanised monoclonal antibody that binds to both soluble and
membrane-bound Interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptors, preventing IL-6 signal transduction. Anakinra is a recombinant form of the human Interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) that blocks the biological activity of IL-1 alpha and beta by competitively inhibiting their binding to the Interleukin-1 type I receptor (IL-1RI).
Clinical Context in CAR-T Toxicity:
IL-6 is the central driver of Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS), making tocilizumab
the first-line pharmacologic intervention for Grade 2+ CRS. IL-1 is a key upstream
regulator of IL-6 and is implicated in neurotoxicity (ICANS). Anakinra is typically
reserved for steroid-refractory CRS or for the management of ICANS, as it crosses
the blood-brain barrier more effectively than tocilizumab.
Clinical Pearl
Target Specificity:
Tocilizumab targets the IL-6 receptor (IL-6R), whereas Anakinra targets the IL-1 receptor (IL-1R). This mechanistic difference dictates their sequence in therapy:
Tocilizumab is first-line for CRS, while Anakinra is often reserved for refractory
cases or neurotoxicity.
ICANS Management:
Tocilizumab does not cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) effectively and may transiently increase serum IL-6 levels, potentially worsening neurotoxicity (ICANS).
Corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) are first-line for ICANS. Anakinra is increasingly used for steroid-refractory ICANS as it penetrates the BBB.
Anakinra Pharmacokinetics:
Anakinra has a very short half-life (~4-6 hours) and is often given as a continuous
IV infusion in the ICU, which is an advantage as it can be stopped quickly.
Tocilizumab Pharmacokinetics:
Tocilizumab has a long elimination half-life (11-13 days), meaning its blockade of
the IL-6 receptor persists long after administration. This contrasts with the short
half-life of anakinra.
Hyperinflammatory Syndromes:
Anakinra is also a first-line agent for other hyperinflammatory "cytokine storm"
syndromes, such as secondary HLH and Macrophage Activation Syndrome.
Siltuximab Alternative:
Siltuximab is a monoclonal antibody that binds directly to circulating IL-6 itself
(unlike tocilizumab which binds the receptor). It is considered in cases where

tocilizumab has failed or is contraindicated, though it is less commonly used in
standard first-line protocols.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: Tocilizumab هو جسم مضاد وحيد النسيلة بشري بيترابط مع مستقبلات interleukin-6 الذوابة والمتصلة بالغشاء ويمنع نقل الإشارة. Anakinra هو شكل مؤتلف من مضاد مستقبل interleukin-1 البشري ويثبط فعالية IL-1 alpha وbeta بتنافس على الارتباط بمستقبل interleukin-1 من النوع الأول. IL-6 هو المحرك المركزي لمتلازمة إطلاق السيتوكين، ولهيك tocilizumab هو التدخل الدوائي الأول للدرجة الثانية أو أعلى. IL-1 هو منظم أساسي في المنبع لـ IL-6 وبيرتبط بالسموم العصبية ICANS، وanakinra بيتحفظ للحالات المقاومة للستيروئيد أو للسموم العصبية لأنه بيعبر الحاجز الدموي الدماغي أكثر فعالية.
الفخ: طلاب كتير يخلطوا بين الهدفين، بس الصحيح إنه anakinra لمستقبل IL-1 وtocilizumab لمستقبل IL-6، والتمييز إنه tocilizumab ما بيعبر الحاجز الدماغي ويمكن يفاقم ICANS.

chapterTitle: Renal, Electrolyte, Acid–Base and Endocrine Emergencies
question: A 45-year-old female with a T5 spinal cord injury is experiencing autonomic dysreflexia with a BP of 180/110 mmHg. Triggers have been checked. Which medication is most appropriate for acute management of her hypertension?
englishExplanation:
Management Principles:
The management of hypertensive crisis in autonomic dysreflexia (AD) prioritises
non-pharmacological measures followed by rapid-acting, short-duration pharmacotherapy. According to the MASCIP (Multidisciplinary Association of Spinal Cord
Injury Professionals) guidelines, if systolic blood pressure remains >150 mmHg after sitting the patient up and removing triggers, pharmacological intervention is required. Sublingual Glyceryl Trinitrate (GTN) spray or tablets are the first-line choice
because they have a rapid onset, short duration, and can be easily terminated (spat
out or spray stopped) if hypotension occurs once the noxious stimulus is resolved.
Alternative Agents:
Nifedipine (immediate release, chewed) is a second-line alternative if GTN is ineffective or unavailable, but caution is required due to the risk of uncontrolled hypotension. Intravenous agents like hydralazine have a slower onset and longer halflife, making them less suitable for a condition where BP can plummet rapidly once
the trigger (e.g., blocked catheter) is fixed. Beta-blockers are generally contraindicated as monotherapy because AD often presents with reflex bradycardia due to vagal tone; blocking beta-receptors can leave alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and worsen hypertension or bradycardia.
Pathophysiology:
Autonomic dysreflexia is caused by a massive sympathetic discharge triggered by a
noxious stimulus below the level of injury (typically T6 or above). This sympathetic
outflow causes severe vasoconstriction in the splanchnic and peripheral vascular
beds below the lesion. The brain detects the resulting hypertension via baroreceptors and attempts to compensate by increasing vagal tone (causing bradycardia) and
inhibiting sympathetic outflow. However, the inhibitory signals cannot descend past
the spinal cord lesion, resulting in unopposed sympathetic hyperactivity below the
injury and parasympathetic dominance above.
Clinical Pearl

Sit Up, Loosen, and Check:
The first steps are always non-pharmacological: sit the patient up, loosen all tight
clothing, and check for bladder or bowel distension.
Fast-acting Vasodilators are Key:
If medication is needed, use a rapid and short-acting agent. Sublingual GTN (spray
or tablet) is the preferred first-line agent in UK guidelines. Nifedipine is an alternative. IV agents are reserved for refractory cases in a monitored setting.
Avoid Beta-Blockers:
Beta-blockers should generally be avoided as monotherapy. They can exacerbate the
reflex bradycardia and leave alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction unopposed, potentially worsening the hypertension.
Treat the Cause:
Remember that antihypertensive therapy is a temporizing measure. The definitive
treatment is to find and eliminate the noxious trigger.
Severe Complications:
Uncontrolled autonomic dysreflexia can lead to seizures, retinal haemorrhage, intracerebral haemorrhage, pulmonary oedema, and death.
The T6 Threshold:
Autonomic dysreflexia typically occurs in patients with spinal cord injuries at level
T6 or above. This level preserves the sympathetic outflow to the splanchnic vascular
bed, allowing for severe, unchecked vasoconstriction below the injury level.
Relative Hypertension:
Patients with high spinal cord injuries often have a low baseline blood pressure
(e.g., 90/60 mmHg). A reading of 120/80 mmHg may represent significant hypertension for them, and 180/110 mmHg constitutes a hypertensive crisis.
Symptom Asymmetry:
Classic presentation involves sympathetic overactivity below the lesion (pale, cool
skin, piloerection) and parasympathetic/withdrawal activity above the lesion (flushing, sweating, pounding headache, nasal congestion).
Common Triggers:
Bladder distension (e.g., blocked catheter) is the most common cause (approx.
85%), followed by bowel impaction and skin lesions (pressure ulcers, ingrown
toenails).
Mechanism of Bradycardia:
The hypertension triggers the carotid and aortic baroreceptors, stimulating increased vagal tone via the Vagus nerve (CN X), which remains intact. This causes

bradycardia, but the compensatory vasodilation signals cannot pass below the
spinal cord lesion.
Prophylactic Management:
Patients with recurrent episodes may require prophylactic alpha-blockers (e.g., doxazosin, terazosin) or botulinum toxin injections for detrusor overactivity.
Obstetric Considerations:
In pregnant women with SCI above T6, labour pain can trigger autonomic dysreflexia. Epidural anaesthesia is the most effective preventative measure during
labour.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: إدارة نوبة ارتفاع الضغط في خلل الاستقلال الذاتي بتفضل التدابير غير الدوائية أولاً ثم دواء سريع البدء وقصير المدة. حسب إرشادات MASCIP، إذا ضل الضغط الانقباضي أعلى من 150 مليمتر زئبق بعد رفع المريض ووضع جلوسه وإزالة المحرضات، لازم تدخل دوائي. نيتروغليسرين تحت اللسان هو الخيار الأول لأنه سريع البدء وقصير المدة ويمكن إيقافه بسهولة إذا هبط الضغط بعد حل المحرض. Nifedipine فوري المفعول خيار ثاني إذا لم يفعل GTN مع الحذر من هبوط الضغط غير المسيطر. الأدوية الوريدية مثل hydralazine أبطأ بدءاً وأطول عمراً ولا تناسب حالة قد يهبط فيها الضغط سريعاً. حاصرات بيتا ممنوعة لأنها تترك تقبض ألفا دون منافس وتزيد bradycardia.
الفخ: طلاب كتير يختاروا حاصر بيتا أو nifedipine، بس حاصرات بيتا تضر والتمييز إنه النيترات تحت اللسان أول خط بسبب سرعته وقابلية إيقافه.

chapterTitle: Renal, Electrolyte, Acid–Base and Endocrine Emergencies
question: Which of the following is NOT a recognized cause of hyperammonemia?

options.text: Inborn errors of the urea cycle
A large gastrointestinal haemorrhage in a patient with cirrhosis

englishExplanation:
Overview:
Hyperammonaemia results from an imbalance between ammonia production (gut
protein digestion, catabolism) and elimination (hepatic urea cycle, skeletal muscle
glutamine synthesis). Well-controlled primary hyperthyroidism does not significantly alter these pathways. While severe thyroid storm can theoretically induce hepatic dysfunction leading to elevated ammonia, a well-controlled state is not a recognized cause.
Mechanisms of Hyperammonemia in Options:
A) Urea Cycle Disorders: Primary defect in enzymes (e.g., ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency) prevents conversion of ammonia to urea.
B) Valproate Toxicity: Disrupts the urea cycle by inhibiting N-acetylglutamate
synthase (NAGS), the essential activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS
I), and by depleting carnitine (essential for fatty acid metabolism), leading to hyperammonaemia even in the absence of liver failure.
C) GI Haemorrhage: Provides a massive protein load to gut bacteria (increased
production) often in the context of impaired clearance (cirrhosis).
E) Severe Catabolism: Trauma, burns, or starvation lead to proteolysis and
amino acid breakdown, increasing the ammonia load.
Non-Hepatic Causes:
It is critical to recognize non-hepatic causes, particularly in patients with normal
liver function tests. These include drugs (valproate, carbamazepine), urease-producing urinary tract infections (e.g., Proteus, Klebsiella) in patients with urinary retention, and post-lung transplant hyperammonaemia (often associated with
Ureaplasma or Mycoplasma infections).
Clinical Pearl
Diagnostic Hierarchy:
In an adult with new-onset confusion and a high ammonia level, hepatic failure is
the primary differential diagnosis, whereas urea cycle disorders are more common
in neonates.
Neonatal Aetiology:
In a newborn presenting with lethargy and hyperammonaemia, a urea cycle defect
(inborn error of metabolism) should be the primary consideration.
GI Haemorrhage Pathophysiology:
In a cirrhotic patient, gastrointestinal haemorrhage precipitates encephalopathy via
two mechanisms: hypotension (reducing hepatic perfusion and clearance) and increased ammonia production from the breakdown of blood protein in the gut.
Valproate-Induced Hyperammonaemia:
Valproate-induced hyperammonaemia can occur with normal liver function tests
due to inhibition of N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS), which reduces CPS I activity, and carnitine depletion. Treatment involves L-carnitine supplementation.
Clinical Correlation:
The absolute serum ammonia level correlates poorly with the clinical severity
(grade) of hepatic encephalopathy; clinical assessment is the gold standard for
grading.
Urease-Producing Infections:
Urease-producing bacteria (e.g., Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella) causing urinary tract
infections, particularly in patients with urinary retention, can generate massive
amounts of ammonia, leading to encephalopathy even in the absence of liver
disease.
Pre-Analytical Sampling Errors:

Ammonia samples are prone to pre-analytical error. Delayed processing, haemolysis, or prolonged tourniquet time can result in falsely elevated levels. Samples must
be transported on ice and analysed immediately.
Late-Onset Urea Cycle Defects:
While typically paediatric, partial enzyme deficiencies (e.g., ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency) can present in adulthood during periods of metabolic stress
(post-partum, chemotherapy, high protein load).
Neurotoxicity Mechanism:
Ammonia crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to glutamine by astrocytes. Accumulation of glutamine acts as an osmole, drawing water into astrocytes
and causing cerebral oedema and intracranial hypertension.
Lactulose Mechanism:
Lactulose treats hepatic encephalopathy by acidifying the gut lumen. This converts
ammonia (NH_3) into ammonium (NH_4^+), which is not absorbed and is excreted (ion trapping), while also acting as a laxative to reduce nitrogenous load.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: ارتفاع الأمونيا بينجم عن اختلال التوازن بين إنتاجها من هضم بروتين الأمعاء والتقويض وإزالتها عبر دورة اليوريا الكبدية وتخليق الجلوتامين بالعضلات. فرط الدرقية الأولي المسيطر جيداً ما بيغير هالمسارات بشكل معتبر، وإذا صار فرط درقية شديد نظرياً ممكن يعمل خلل كبدي، بس الحالة المسيطر عليها ليست سبباً معترفاً به. نقص دورة اليوريا بيغير الإنزيمات زي نقص ornithine transcarbamylase فيمنع تحويل الأمونيا إلى يوريا. سمية valproate بتعطل دورة اليوريا بتثبيط N-acetylglutamate synthase واستنزاف الكارنيتين فيرتفع الأمونيا بدون فشل كبدي. النزف الهضمي الكبير بيحمل بروتيناً هائلاً للبكتيريا، والحروق والت trauma بيعملوا تقويضاً يزيد حمل الأمونيا.
الفخ: طلاب كتير يختاروا نزف هضمي أو سمية دوائية لأنها أسباب واضحة، بس المطلوب الاستثناء وهو فرط الدرقية المسيطر، والتمييز إنه غير معترف به كسبب.

chapterTitle: Renal, Electrolyte, Acid–Base and Endocrine Emergencies
question:
A 29-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation presents with sudden onset of fever,
chills, vomiting, and left flank pain. A urinalysis is positive for leukocyte esterase,
nitrites, and bacteria. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin and follow-up in 3 days.

englishExplanation:
Diagnosis and Risk Stratification:
This patient presents with the classic triad of fever, flank pain, and vomiting, indicative of acute pyelonephritis. In pregnancy, physiological changes (ureteral dilation,
urinary stasis) increase the risk of ascending infection. Pyelonephritis in pregnancy
is associated with significant maternal and fetal morbidity, including preterm
labour, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and sepsis. Consequently,
NICE CKS and RCOG guidelines mandate hospital admission for all pregnant
women with acute pyelonephritis.
Management Rationale:
Initial management requires intravenous antibiotics to ensure adequate tissue levels
and rapid bacterial clearance. Oral therapy is inappropriate for the acute phase due
to variable absorption (especially with vomiting) and the severity of the condition.
Intravenous cephalosporins (e.g., Ceftriaxone or Cefuroxime) are the standard of
care as they are effective against common uropathogens (Enterobacteriaceae) and
have a well-established safety profile in pregnancy.
Why other options are incorrect:
Nitrofurantoin (Option B) achieves therapeutic concentrations in the bladder but
poor tissue penetration in the renal parenchyma; it is indicated for cystitis but ineffective for pyelonephritis. Fluoroquinolones (Option E) are generally avoided in
pregnancy due to concerns regarding fetal cartilage development. Co-trimoxazole
(Option C) is avoided in the first trimester (folate antagonist) and at term (risk of
neonatal kernicterus), and oral administration is insufficient for initial pyelonephritis management.
Clinical Pearl
Pyelonephritis in Pregnancy = Admission + IV Antibiotics:
This is a firm rule. Do not treat these patients as outpatients.
Safe Antibiotics in Pregnancy:
Generally safe antibiotics include Beta-lactams (Penicillins, Cephalosporins),
Clindamycin, and Azithromycin.
Antibiotics to AVOID in Pregnancy ('FATT'):
Fluoroquinolones (cartilage toxicity), Aminoglycosides (ototoxicity/nephrotoxicity),
Tetracyclines (tooth discolouration/bone growth inhibition), and

Trimethoprim/Sulfonamides (folate antagonism in 1st trimester; kernicterus risk
with sulfonamides in 3rd trimester).
Treat Asymptomatic Bacteriuria:
Unlike in non-pregnant women, asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy must be
treated to prevent progression to pyelonephritis.
Common Pathogen is E. coli:
As with most UTIs, E. coli is the causative organism in the vast majority of cases.
Nitrofurantoin Tissue Penetration:
Nitrofurantoin is strictly a urinary antiseptic. It concentrates in the bladder but has
poor serum and renal tissue levels. Never use it for pyelonephritis or sepsis, regardless of pregnancy status.
Physiological Predisposition:
Progesterone causes smooth muscle relaxation leading to ureteral dilation and hypoperistalsis. Combined with mechanical compression by the gravid uterus (more
common on the right due to the sigmoid colon protecting the left), this creates urinary stasis, significantly increasing pyelonephritis risk.
Respiratory Complications:
Pregnant women with pyelonephritis are at increased risk of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) due to endotoxin-mediated alveolar capillary membrane injury. Monitor respiratory rate and oxygen saturation closely.
Post-Treatment Prophylaxis:
Recurrence is common; guidelines often recommend low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g., nitrofurantoin or cefalexin) for the remainder of the pregnancy after a
confirmed episode of pyelonephritis.
Imaging Modality of Choice:
Ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality to exclude obstruction (e.g.,
nephrolithiasis) or perinephric abscess, as it avoids ionising radiation.
Differential Diagnosis:
Important differentials include acute appendicitis (appendix may be displaced upwards by the gravid uterus), placental abruption (assess uterine tone and fetal heart
rate), and nephrolithiasis.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: هالحالة فيها ثلاثي التهاب الحويضة الحاد وهو حمى وألم خاصرة وقيء. بالحمل التغيرات الفسيولوجية من تمدد الحالب وركود البول بتزيد خطر العدوى الصاعدة. التهاب الحويضة بالحمل مرتبط باعتلال أمومي وجنيني معتبر يشمل الولادة المبكرة ومتلازمة ضيق التنفس الحادة والإنتان، ولهيك إرشادات NICE وRCOG بتفرض دخول المستشفى لكل حامل حتى لو بلا علامات إنتان. البدء لازم بمضادات حيوية وريدية لتأمين تراكيز نسيجية كافية وتصفية بكتيرية سريعة، والعلاج الفموي غير مناسب بالمرحلة الحادة بسبب الامتصاص المتغير خصوصاً مع القيء. السيفالوسبورينات الوريدية مثل ceftriaxone هي المعيار الذهبي لأنها فعالة على Enterobacteriaceae وآمنة بالحمل.
الفخ: طلاب كتير يختاروا nitrofurantoin أو مضاد حيوي فموي، بس nitrofurantoin بيعطي تركيز بالمثانة فقط ولا ينفع لالتهاب الحويضة، والتمييز إنه الحاجة لتراكيز وريدية بالparenchyma الكلوية.

chapterTitle: Renal, Electrolyte, Acid–Base and Endocrine Emergencies
question:
Which statement accurately describes a key advantage of using a Danis stent (a
removable self-expanding metal stent) over a Sengstaken-Blakemore tube for refractory esophageal variceal bleeding?

options.text: It is a permanent solution for portal hypertension.
It carries zero risk of oesophageal necrosis or perforation.
It allows for simultaneous endoscopic visualization through the stent lumen.
It can be left in place for a longer duration (up to 7 days), providing a more stable bridge to definitive therapy.
It is placed surgically via a thoracotomy.

correctAnswer: It can be left in place for a longer duration (up to 7 days), providing a more stable bridge to definitive therapy.
englishExplanation:
Bridging to Definitive Therapy:
The Danis stent (a self-expanding metal stent or SEMS) offers a significant temporal advantage over balloon tamponade. While balloon tamponade (e.g., SengstakenBlakemore) is typically limited to 24 hours (maximum 48 hours with periodic deflation) due to high risks of oesophageal pressure necrosis and aspiration, the Danis
stent can remain in situ for up to 7 days. This extended duration provides a stable
bridge to definitive therapy, such as Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt
(TIPS) or liver transplantation, allowing time for physiological stabilisation and logistical transfer to a specialist centre.
Physiological Advantages:
Unlike balloon tamponade, which completely obstructs the oesophagus, the Danis
stent maintains a patent oesophageal lumen. This allows the patient to swallow
saliva and oral fluids, significantly reducing the risk of aspiration pneumonia—a
major complication associated with balloon tamponade. Additionally, the stent does
not require external traction, improving patient comfort and reducing nursing requirements compared to the Sengstaken-Blakemore tube.

Anatomical Limitations:
The Danis stent is indicated specifically for refractory oesophageal variceal bleeding. It is ineffective for gastric varices (IGV/GOV2) as it does not provide compression to the gastric fundus. In contrast, a Sengstaken-Blakemore or Linton-Nachlas
tube can provide gastric compression. The stent works by exerting radial force
against the distal oesophageal wall, mechanically tamponading the varices while
preserving luminal patency.
Clinical Pearl
Bridge to TIPS:
The main advantage of the Danis stent over balloon tamponade is the extended duration of use (up to 7 days versus <24 hours), allowing for patient stabilisation and
transfer for TIPS.
Rescue Indication:
Like balloon tamponade, the Danis stent is a rescue therapy for variceal bleeding refractory to first-line endoscopic (banding/sclerotherapy) and medical
(vasopressors/antibiotics) treatment.
Device Removability:
The stent is designed with a retrieval loop at the proximal end, allowing for endoscopic removal once bleeding is controlled and definitive therapy is planned. It is
not biodegradable.
Migration Risk:
The most common complication is stent migration (either proximally or distally into
the stomach), which can lead to re-bleeding or obstruction. Migration rates are generally lower than the failure rates of balloon tamponade.
Aspiration Risk Reduction:
Unlike balloon tamponade, the Danis stent maintains oesophageal patency, allowing patients to swallow saliva and significantly reducing the risk of aspiration
pneumonia.
Anatomical Limitation:
The Danis stent is strictly for oesophageal varices. It provides no compression for
gastric varices; balloon tamponade (specifically Linton-Nachlas) or cyanoacrylate
glue remains indicated for gastric sources.
Bedside Deployment:
A unique feature of the Danis stent delivery system is that it can be deployed without fluoroscopy using a dedicated balloon inflation system, making it suitable for
bedside use in ICU, although endoscopic guidance is preferred when available.
No Traction Required:

Unlike the Sengstaken-Blakemore tube, which requires external traction (often using a bag of fluids or a tennis ball taped to the tube) to maintain placement, the
Danis stent is self-retaining due to radial force.
Airway Management:
While airway protection is often required for the variceal bleed itself, the Danis
stent does not mandate intubation solely for the device, whereas balloon tamponade
almost universally requires intubation to prevent aspiration of pooled secretions.
Mechanism of Action:
The stent exerts radial force against the distal oesophageal wall to mechanically
tamponade varices. This differs from the pneumatic compression of balloon
tamponade.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: داينز ستنت وهو دعامة معدنية ذاتية التوسع يعطي ميزة زمنية كبيرة على tamponade بالبالون. البالون مثل Sengstaken-Blakemore محدود عادة بـ 24 ساعة وبالحد الأقصى 48 ساعة مع تفريغ دوري بسبب خطر عالٍ من تنخر الضغط بالمريء والشفط. الستنت يمكن إنه يبقى بالمكان لمدة تصل إلى 7 أيام، وهذا يمنح جسراً مستقراً للعلاج النهائي مثل TIPS أو زراعة الكبد ويسمح بالاستقرار الفسيولوجي والنقل لمستشفى متخصص. كمان بيفضل patent lumen بالمريء فيبلع المريض لعابه وسوائله فيقل خطر ذات الرئة الشفطية. ما بيحتاج شداً خارجياً فبيرتاح المريض ويقل عبء التمريض.
الفخ: طلاب كتير يظنوا إنه يسمح بالرؤية بالمنظار من خلال تجويفه أو إنه علاج دائم، بس هاد غير صحيح، والتمييز إنه الميزة الحقيقية هي البقاء حتى 7 أيام كجسر للعلاج النهائي.

chapterTitle: Renal, Electrolyte, Acid–Base and Endocrine Emergencies
question:
A patient in the ICU has a baseline serum creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL. It has now
risen to 4.0 mg/dL. The patient has been anuric for the past 14 hours. According
to the KDIGO criteria, what stage of AKI does this represent?

options.text: This is now Chronic Kidney Disease

englishExplanation:
KDIGO Classification Analysis:
This patient qualifies for Stage 3 AKI through three distinct criteria defined by the
KDIGO guidelines (adopted by NICE):
1. Serum Creatinine (Relative): The increase from 106 µmol/L to 354 µmol/L represents a 3.3-fold rise. A rise of 3.0 times baseline or greater defines Stage 3.
2. Serum Creatinine (Absolute): An absolute serum creatinine of at least 353.6
µmol/L (4.0 mg/dL) classifies as Stage 3, provided there is an acute rise of at least
44 µmol/L (0.5 mg/dL).
3. Urine Output: Anuria for at least 12 hours is a specific criterion for Stage 3. Note
that for oliguria (<0.3 ml/kg/h), the duration required for Stage 3 is at least 24
hours.
Physiological Context: Creatinine Kinetics:
Serum creatinine is a delayed marker of kidney function. In the event of a sudden
and complete cessation of GFR (e.g., bilateral renal artery occlusion), creatinine
rises slowly as it accumulates in the body water—typically by 100–150 µmol/L per
day depending on muscle mass. This 'creatinine blind spot' means that urine output
is often a much earlier and more sensitive indicator of AKI than creatinine, as seen
in this case where anuria is already established.
Clinical Pearl
Stage 3 Has Multiple Triggers:
Stage 3 AKI can be defined by any of the following: a 3-fold rise in creatinine, an absolute creatinine of at least 353.6 µmol/L (4.0 mg/dL) with an acute rise, initiation
of renal replacement therapy, anuria for at least 12 hours, or oliguria (<0.3
ml/kg/h) for at least 24 hours.
Anuria is a Hard Sign:
Anuria for 12 hours is a very ominous sign and automatically qualifies as Stage 3
AKI.
Stage 3 = High Mortality:
Stage 3 AKI is associated with a very high mortality rate and a high likelihood of requiring renal replacement therapy.
AKI vs. CKD:

AKI is an acute process (hours to days). Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is defined as
an abnormality in kidney function or structure present for >3 months.
RRT as a Criterion:
The decision to start renal replacement therapy (RRT) for a complication of AKI
also automatically classifies the patient as Stage 3.
The Absolute Rise Caveat:
For the absolute creatinine threshold of 353.6 µmol/L (4.0 mg/dL) to qualify as
Stage 3, KDIGO specifies there must be an acute increase of at least 44 µmol/L (0.5
mg/dL) to distinguish it from stable CKD.
Urine Output Time Windows:
Urine output criteria are time-dependent: Stage 1 requires <0.5 ml/kg/h for 6–12
hours; Stage 2 requires <0.5 ml/kg/h for at least 12 hours; Stage 3 requires <0.3
ml/kg/h for at least 24 hours or anuria for at least 12 hours.
Creatinine Blind Spots:
Serum creatinine may underestimate AKI severity in patients with low muscle mass
(sarcopenia, elderly, amputees) or liver disease (reduced hepatic creatine synthesis).
In these groups, a 'normal' creatinine may actually represent significant renal
impairment.
Dilutional Masking:
Aggressive fluid resuscitation can dilute serum creatinine, potentially masking the
diagnosis or severity of AKI. A patient may have a stable creatinine concentration
despite a falling GFR if the volume of distribution has expanded significantly.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريض بيحقق المرحلة الثالثة بثلاث معايير من KDIGO. النسبة النسبية للكرياتينين ارتفعت من 106 مايكرومول/لتر إلى 354 مايكرومول/لتر أي 3.3 أضعاف، والارتفاع ثلاثة أضعاف أو أكثر عن الأساس يعرّف المرحلة الثالثة. المستوى المطلق للكرياتينين 353.6 مايكرومول/لتر أو أكثر أي 4.0 ملغ/دل يعتبر مرحلة ثالثة إذا معه ارتفاع حاد لا يقل عن 44 مايكرومول/لتر. قلة البول التامة أو انقطاعه لمدة 12 ساعة على الأقل معيار محدد للمرحلة الثالثة، بينما قلة البول أقل من 0.3 مل/كغ/ساعة تحتاج 24 ساعة للمرحلة نفسها. الكرياتينين مؤشر متأخر بينما إنتاج البول أسرع وأكثر حساسية.
