question: A 17-year-old girl comes to the emergency department because she has had worsening sore throat and fevers over the past six days. Today, she says she is unable to swallow due to significant pain. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse rate is 98/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/82 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. The patient's voice is muffled when speaking. Findings on oropharyngeal examination are shown. Which of the following is an advantage of point-of-care intraoral ultrasonography in guiding the management of this condition?

options.text: It decreases the need for intravenous antibiotic administration
It is more sensitive than a CT scan for making the diagnosis
It provides information about the patient's anatomy and the location of blood vessels

correctAnswer: It provides information about the patient's anatomy and the location of blood vessels
englishExplanation:
It provides information about the patient's anatomy and the location of blood
vessels
Expl anation
A. It decreases the need for intravenous antibiotic administration
This statement has not been shown to be true in the literature. Ultrasonography can
distinguish peritonsillar cellulitis from a peritonsillar abscess and aid in the incision
and drainage of an abscess. Regardless, both conditions require treatment with
antibiotics.
B. It is a painless procedure
Intraoral ultrasonography can be difficult to perform in young children or patients
with significant trismus due to discomfort and/or inability to open their mouth to
accommodate the intracavitary probe. In this case, transcutaneous ultrasonography
of the tonsil could be performed.
C. It is more sensitive than a CT scan for making the diagnosis
A CT scan is nearly 100% sensitive for identifying a peritonsillar abscess and any local complications. Disadvantages of CT scans include high cost, the waiting time to
obtain the test, the administration of iodinated contrast, and radiation exposure.
Consequently, intraoral and transcutaneous ultrasonography should be considered
in the evaluation of a patient with a suspected peritonsillar abscess.
The use of point-of-care ultrasonography (intraoral or transcutaneous) in the evaluation of presumed peritonsillar abscess has increased in popularity for these reasons: it is fast, inexpensive, and does not expose the patient to radiation.
D. It provides information about the patient's anatomy and the location
of blood vessels
Ultrasonography of the tonsils gives rich information about the patient's anatomy,
blood vessel location, and details about the abscess which can be helpful prior to
needle aspiration or incision and drainage.
There are virtually no contraindications for point-of-care ultrasonography in the
evaluation of a peritonsillar abscess, and it can be helpful in distinguishing peritonsillar abscess and peritonsillar cellulitis. These often present similarly.
Page 912 of 4185
Traditionally, blind needle aspiration or a CT scan has been used to distinguish the
two.

question: A 6-year-old male is brought in by his parents for shortness of breath and fever. Past medical history is significant only for no previous vaccinations as the parents do not believe vaccines are safe. Physical exam reveals an ill-appearing febrile child in distress who is sitting up and leaning forward with significant stridor. During the primary assessment, the child suffers a respiratory arrest. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial maneuver for this patient?
englishExplanation:
Bag valve mask ventilation
Expl anation
A. Bag valve mask ventilation
This patient is presenting with acute epiglottitis and has an upper airway obstruction. Bag valve mask can be used to try and overcome the obstruction. This may give
the providers time to obtain advanced airway equipment and specialist support.
Further information: Driver, B and Reardon, R, "Tracheal Intubation" in Roberts,

2019.
B. Rapid sequence intubation
This patient is presenting with acute epiglottitis and has an upper airway obstruction. While intubation can certainly be attempted, it is likely to be exceedingly difficult in the setting of obstruction. Bag valve mask can be used to try and overcome
the obstruction. This may give the providers time to obtain advanced airway equipment and specialist support.
C. Surgical airway
This patient is presenting with acute epiglottitis and has an upper airway obstruction. Bag valve mask can be used to try and overcome the obstruction. While a surgical airway may be required, bag valve mask may give the providers time to obtain
advanced airway equipment and specialist support. Further, remember that in
young children, cricothyrotomy cannot be performed and needle cricothyrotomy
will need to be performed instead.
D. Trans-tracheal jet ventilation
This patient is presenting with acute epiglottitis and has an upper airway obstruction. Bag valve mask can be used to try and overcome the obstruction. While needle
cricothyrotomy may be required, bag valve mask may give the providers time to obtain advanced airway equipment and specialist support and obviate the need for this
procedure.

question: The paramedics brought in a 52-year-old man from a trailer park. Per the report, the patient was found lying down inside the trailer and was last seen to be normal 3 days ago. Vital signs show BP 98/65 mmHg, HR 55/min, RR 9/min, Temp 96.8°F, and O₂ saturation 96% on room air. Physical exam is significant for bilateral pinpoint pupils. Upon foley insertion, amber-colored urine was obtained. Which of the following laboratory findings is most consistent with the urine finding?

options.text: Heme-negative urine dipstick, and large RBCs on urinalysis
Heme-negative urine dipstick, and no RBCs on urinalysis
Heme-positive urine dipstick, and large RBCs on urinalysis
Heme-positive urine dipstick, and no RBCs on urinalysis

correctAnswer: Heme-positive urine dipstick, and no RBCs on urinalysis
englishExplanation:
Heme-positive urine dipstick, and no RBCs on urinalysis
Expl anation
A. Heme-negative urine dipstick, and large RBCs on urinalysis
This patient likely has rhabdomyolysis due to prolonged immobilization.
Rhabdomyolysis classically presents with a urine dipstick detecting hemoglobin and
myoglobin as blood. The microscopic evaluation for RBCs is typically negative.
B. Heme-negative urine dipstick, and no RBCs on urinalysis
This patient was found down for a prolonged period and likely has rhabdomyolysis.
Rhabdo classically has heme-positive urine without RBCs.
C. Heme-positive urine dipstick, and large RBCs on urinalysis
This patient was found down for a prolonged period and likely has rhabdomyolysis.
Rhabdo classically has heme-positive urine without RBCs.
D. Heme-positive urine dipstick, and no RBCs on urinalysis
This patient's history is concerning for rhabdomyolysis as a potential complication
of prolonged immobilization. Rhabdomyolysis is characterized by muscle necrosis,
with the release of intracellular content into blood circulation. Myoglobin, a hemecontaining protein, is released from muscle cells and shows up as positive for the
heme test as the urine dipstick detects it as "blood". However, no or only a few red
blood cells are present on urinalysis.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448168/

question: A 10-year-old girl is brought in by her mother for evaluation after she is sent home from school for "pink eye." The patient also has pruritus. The mother says the family recently acquired a cat, and the patient has been playing with it frequently. Physical examination shows bilateral conjunctivitis with watery discharge. The patient most likely has which of the following?
englishExplanation:
Type I hypersensitivity
Expl anation
A. Type I hypersensitivity
Allergic conjunctivitis is a classic type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction.
Type I hypersensitivity reactions are an exaggerated immune response triggered by
the release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators in response to exposure
to an allergen. It is the most common form of hypersensitivity reaction and is associated with conditions such as allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, allergic
asthma, and anaphylaxis.
Further information:
Barksdale A, Ross W. Chapter 106. Allergy, Anaphylaxis, and Angioedema. In:
Walls RM, Hockberger RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine
Concepts and Clinical Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
B. Type II hypersensitivity
Allergic conjunctivitis is a classic type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction.
Type II is mediated by other antibodies (e.g. IgG).
C. Type III hypersensitivity
Allergic conjunctivitis is a classic type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction.
Type III involves immune complex deposition.
D. Type IV hypersensitivity
Allergic conjunctivitis is a classic type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction.
Type IV is mediated by T-cells.

question: A 41-year-old male with a history of HIV/AIDS presents with a progressively worsening headache for 1 week. He has never had headaches before and states he feels increasingly confused this week. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.9°F), pulse rate is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 145/87 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 100% on room air. Physical examination is grossly unremarkable, with a supple neck, intact neurologic exam, and no rashes. Head CT is shown. Last week's absolute CD4 count is 198/mL. While en route back from radiology, the patient has a 1-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure. After antiepileptics are administered, what is the next best step in the management of this patient?

options.text: Order MRI brain with and without contrast

englishExplanation:
Administer sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine
Expl anation
A. Administer sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine
This patient technically has a diagnosis of AIDS, given the CD4 count <200.
Additionally, this unenhanced CT demonstrates mass-occupying lesions in the basal
ganglia and hippocampus. The most common cause of mass-occupying lesions in
the brain in AIDS patients is toxoplasmosis (50%) and CNS lymphoma (30%).
Although the differential diagnosis for CNS lesions is quite broad in AIDS patients,
empiric antimicrobial therapy against toxoplasma should be initiated, given that the
classic presentation of toxoplasmosis encephalitis is headache, fever, and confusion.
Contrast-enhanced CT may demonstrate the classic ring-enhancing lesions.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441877/
B. Consult neurosurgery for brain biopsy
While the differential diagnosis of CNS lesions in AIDS patients are very broad, the
two most common CNS lesions are CNS toxoplasma and CNS lymphoma. While
brain biopsy may help differentiate the etiolow of this patient's mass lesion, empiric
antibiotic therapy is indicated while pending serology test results.
C. Order MRI brain with and without contrast
While an MRI brain is the next diagnostic imaging test to obtain to better characterize the CNS lesions, empiric antibiotics, including coverage for Toxoplasma, should
be administered while pending imaging tests.
D. Perform lumbar puncture
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in this patient, who has a mass-occupying le-
Sion and seizure.

question: A 2-year-old circumcised male is brought in by his parents after a 2-minute seizure 30 minutes prior to arrival. According to the parents, his whole body was shaking. Prior to the onset of his seizure, he had two days of nasal congestion, sore throat, and cough. On presentation, the child is alert and interactive. Initial vitals are significant for a temperature of 104ºF (40ºC). Physical exam is remarkable for rhinorrhea and mild erythema of the posterior pharynx. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admission, blood work, urinalysis, and chest radiograph
Admission, blood work, urinalysis, chest radiograph, and lumbar puncture
Reassurance and discharge home with close follow-up and return precautions.

correctAnswer: Reassurance and discharge home with close follow-up and return precautions.
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
Reassurance and discharge home with close follow-up and return
precautions.
A. Admission, blood work, urinalysis, and chest radiograph
This is a simple febrile seizure (single seizure, non-focal, less than 15 minutes). If
the child returns to baseline and has no other concerning symptoms for sepsis no
further workup is indicated. In complex febrile seizures (seizures lasting more than
15 minutes, focal seizures, or more than one seizure in 24 hrs) further testing should
be considered. Viral infections are the leading cause of febrile seizure and do not require admission and extensive workup.
B. Admission, blood work, urinalysis, chest radiograph, and lumbar
puncture
This is a simple febrile seizure (single seizure, non-focal, less than 15 minutes). If
the child returns to baseline and has no other concerning symptoms for sepsis no
further workup is indicated. In complex febrile seizures (seizures lasting more than
15 minutes, focal seizures, or more than one seizure in 24 hrs) further testing should
be considered. A lumbar puncture may or may not be indicated depending on the
clinical circumstances. Recent studies show the rate of bacterial meningitis is exceedingly low in otherwise well-appearing children with a febrile seizure.
C. Consult pediatric neurology
This is a simple febrile seizure (single seizure, non-focal, less than 15 minutes) and
is the result of the rise in body temperature. This is typically a benign, self-limited
condition and is generally not associated with long-term neurologic complications.
Neurology consultation is not needed in this situation.
D. Reassurance and discharge home with close follow-up and return
precautions.
This patient has an uncomplicated febrile seizure, and if he or she returns to baseline and is otherwise well-appearing, no further workup is indicated at this time.
Simple febrile seizures are single seizures, non-focal, and last less than 15 minutes.
Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448123/
Page 2320 of 4185

ليش: الطفل عنده تشنّج واحد عام non-focal استمر أقل من 15 دقيقة، ورجع لحالته الطبيعية بعد التشنج. هاد يطابق تعريف simple febrile seizure، والعدوى الفيروسية هي السبب الأكثر شيوعاً له. الـ simple febrile seizure ما يحتاج admission ولا فحوصات شاملة ولا lumbar puncture إذا الطفل رجع طبيعي وما في علامات sepsis. فالمطلوب فقط طمأنة الأهل وإخراج الطفل مع متابعة قريبة وتعليمات العودة.

question: A 3-year-old, previously healthy, fully vaccinated female is brought to your emergency department by ambulance after a witnessed seizure at home lasting approximately 6 minutes associated with tonic-clonic movements of the bilateral extremities. The paramedics report that the patient is back to baseline per her parents. She was also slightly tachycardic en route to the hospital, with a measured blood glucose of 105 mg/dL (5.83 mmol/l). Her vitals in the ER are BP 115/68 mmHg, P 135/min, RR 26/min, O₂Sat 98%, T104ºF (40ºC). On physical exam, the patient is noted to have a strong cry, no skin mottling, and no accessory muscle use or belly breathing. Her exam is normal except for rhinorrhea, a dry non-productive cough, and a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane on the right. You administer a 15 mg/kg/dose of acetaminophen, and a repeat temperature is 100F (37.8ºC). The child appears happy and is playing with her family in the room. What is the next best step in managing this patient?

options.text: Discharge home with antibiotics after a period of observation

correctAnswer: Discharge home with antibiotics after a period of observation
englishExplanation:
Discharge home with antibiotics after a period Of observation
Explanation
A. Discharge home with antibiotics after a period of observation
The patient's seizure meets all of the criteria for a simple febrile seizure. No additional workup is necessary for the patient's seizure other than what is indicated to
evaluate the cause of her fever. In this case, the patient's upper respiratory symptoms and acute otitis media make this the likely source of the patient's fever. The
criteria for simple febrile seizure are as follows: Age 6 months to 5 years, seizure
must be generalized (non-focal), single seizure in 24 hours, seizure must last less
than 15 minutes, normal neuro exam and with a return to baseline after a postictal
state.
Further information:
https:/,/www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448123/
B. Lumbar puncture
If the patient remained persistently altered, had multiple seizures, a focal neurologic deficit, or was without an obvious source for her fever, a lumbar puncture
should be considered.
C. Non-contrast head CI'
A non-contrast head CI' is not indicated in patients who meet the criteria for simple
febrile seizure.
D. Routine labs with blood cultures
Blood work is not routinely indicated in patients with simple febrile seizure, especiallywhen a source of fever is easily identified as is the case with this patient.

question: A 7-year-old fully vaccinated male is brought in by his mother with fever, vomiting, lethargy, and confusion that suddenly developed overnight. Two days prior, he went to the urgent care clinic with fever and right ear pain and was diagnosed with viral otitis media and discharged home. Shortly after arrival, he becomes obtunded and the decision is made to intubate for airway protection. Vital signs are: HR 160/min, RR 20/min, BP 100/60 mmHg, T 102.2ºF (39ºC). Physical examination reveals a lethargic child with a bulging tympanic membrane. What is the most appropriate sequence in management?

options.text: Blood cultures, IV antibiotics, CT Head, lumbar puncture
Blood cultures, lumbar puncture, IV antibiotics, vasopressors
CT Head, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, lumbar puncture
CT Head, lumbar Puncture, IV antibiotics, vasopressors

correctAnswer: Blood cultures, IV antibiotics, CT Head, lumbar puncture
englishExplanation:
Blood cultures, IV antibiotics, CT Head, lumbar puncture
Expl anation
A. Blood cultures, IV antibiotics, CT Head, lumbar puncture
Blood cultures and IV antibiotics should not be delayed for any reason if bacterial
meningitis is suspected. The indications for a CT head prior to LP in children in-
Clude coma, the presence of a CSF shunt, a history of hydrocephalus, recent CNS
trauma or neurosurgery, papilledema, or focal neurologic deficits. This patient is
obtunded and should receive a CI' prior to lumbar puncture.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470351/
B. Blood cultures, lumbar puncture, IV antibiotics, vasopressors
Besides delaying empiric antibiotic treatment, this option also forgoes a CT of the
head prior to the lumbar puncture. A CT of the head is indicated in this obtunded
patient.
C. CT Head, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, lumbar puncture
No delay in the initiation of empiric IV antibiotic treatment is appropriate in this
patient.
D. CT Head, lumbar Puncture, IV antibiotics, vasopressors
This child's clinical picture is very concerning for bacterial meningitis. He will need
a CT head prior to performing a lumbar puncture due to the risk of cerebral edema
and, consequently, herniation with the lumbar puncture. Empiric IV antibiotics,
however, should not be delayed in this case. The patient is septic but his blood pressure at this time is holding and vasopressors are not yet indicated.

الفخ: طلاب يختارون CT قبل الـ blood cultures، لكن يجب عدم تأخير الـ blood cultures والـ IV antibiotics مطلقاً في حال الشك بالتهاب السحائي البكتيري.

question: A 3-month-old female infant is brought in by her mother because she has not been feeding well for the past 24 hours. The patient has vomited both after feedings and between feedings four times since yesterday. The mother usually stays at home with the infant, but yesterday she went shopping and left her baby with her boyfriend. He says the baby did not "get into anything" but said, "Maybe she ate something that upset her stomach." The mother says the patient has not been as bright and alert as she normally is since she got sick. On examination, the patient is lethargic. Results of funduscopic examination are shown. Which of the following additional findings is most likely?

options.text: A laceration and swelling in the genital area
Crusty, oily patches on the scalp

englishExplanation:
Rib fractures
Expl anation
A. A laceration and swelling in the genital area
The presence of bruising, swelling, lacerations, or irritation in the genital region in
an infant, other than a typical diaper rash, raises a red flag for pediatric sexual
abuse. VVhile this is very concerning and should be properly worked up and reported to authorities as needed, this finding does not increase the concern for pediatric abusive head trauma. The presence of physical abuse does not also mean the
infant is being sexually abused as well, but both should be investigated further.
B. Crusty, oily patches on the scalp
Crusty, oily patches on the scalp describe the presence of cradle cap, which can be a
normal finding in a child this age and is not a sign of abuse. However, the presence
of bruising or other markings/wounds on the head in a nonambulatory child should
raise suspicion for physical abuse.
C. Firm, flat anterior fontanelle
In pediatric abusive head trauma, bulging fontanelles are commonly seen on examination. This is the result of fluid buildup in the brain from a subdural hematoma or
cerebral edema, which causes increased pressure inside the skull. A firm, flat anterior fontanelle would not be concerning for pediatric abusive head trauma.
D. Rib fractures
This baby most likely is a victim of pediatric abusive head trauma (also termed
shaken baby syndrome) due to the presence of retinal hemorrhages. A patient with
shaken baby syndrome can present with vomiting, poor feeding, decreased interaction, and lethargy. This history has a red flag with the boyfriend suggesting that the
child perhaps had eaten something which made her sick. A 3-month-old infant
should be exclusively formula or breastfed and is generally unable to eat any soft or
solid foods. A CT scan of the head, as well as a skeletal survey, should be performed.
Subdural hematomas are a common finding in pediatric abusive head trauma, as
well as rib and long bone fractures.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499836/

![HIPPO-01615 source page 2649](images/HIPPO-01615-Hipoo-p2649.jpg)

question: A 63-year-old Hispanic man with Alzheimer's disease is brought to the emergency department immediately after he fell at the nursing home where he resides. He has no history of frequent falls. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and multiple skin tears. Additional findings on physical examination are shown. X-ray studies show a spiral fracture of the humerus. Which of the following characteristics increases this patient's risk for this condition?
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
A. Age
Medical history
This patient is likely a victim of elder mlstreatment, the highest rates of which occur
in persons 80 years of age and older.
B. Ethnicity
African-Americans are the most common victims of elder abuse, neglect, psychological abuse, or exploitation, while Hispanics and other minorities are less likely to be
victims.
C. Gender
In reported cases, women are overrepresented as victims of all types of abuse except
abandonment.
D. Medical history
Dementia increases the risk of abuse, neglect, and financial exploitation. Although
pressure ulcers are a common condition and do not necessarily indicate neglect,
warning signs for abuse in this patient include spiral fractures of a long bone, dehydration, and skin tears without a history of frequent falls.
Further information: Lachs MS, Pillemer KA. Elder Abuse. N Eng J Med.

question: A 40-year-old male presents to the emergency department with recurrent nosebleeds. He has had 6 visits to the emergency department in the last month. He has been admitted multiple times with a full hematologic work-up that is negative. He is now requesting a repeat CT face and nasal biopsy, but the nosebleed resolves spontaneously. Further testing is not done, and immediately prior to discharge, the patient is caught digitally manipulating his nose. A factitious disorder is suspected. What is the type of manipulation and secondary gain typically seen in Munchausen’s syndrome?

options.text: Conscious manipulation for the sick-role incentive
Conscious manipulation of a proxy for prolonged contact with health care providers

correctAnswer: Conscious manipulation for the sick-role incentive
englishExplanation:
Conscious manipulation for the sick-role incentive
Explanation
A. Conscious manipulation for gainful incentive
This patient is not truly attempting to obtain gainful incentive but rather is trying to
assume the sick role. Munchausen syndrome involves conscious manipulation for
secondary gain of playing the "sick role". Malingering involves conscious manipulation for gainful incentive. Secondary gain may be difficult to determine but can in-
Clude a place to stay, food, drugs, or disability.
B. Conscious manipulation for the sick-role incentive
Munchausen syndrome involves conscious manipulation for the secondary gain of
playing the sick role". These patients subject themselves to unnecessary tests to secure the "sick rol.". Munchausen syndrome by proxy is rare and involves conscious
manipulation of a proxy (usually a child) for the secondary gain of prolonged contact with health care providers.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK518999/
C. Conscious manipulation of a proxy for prolonged contact with health
care providers
This patient is attempting to obtain secondary gain by assuming the sick role and
thus his presentation is consistent with Munchausen syndrome. Munchausen by
proxy involves manipulating a proxy, such as a child, in order for the proxy to assume the sick role.
D. Unintentional manipulation without secondary gain
This patient is attempting to obtain secondary gain by assuming the sick role.
Munchausen syndrome involves conscious manipulation for secondary gain of the
playing the "sick-role".

ليش: المريض عنده رعاف متكرر ودخل الطوارئ ست مرات خلال شهر، وكل الفحوصات الدموية سلبية، وطلب فحوصات غير ضرورية، وبعدها انكشف يعدّل أنفه بإصبعه. هالقصة توحي بـ factitious disorder، وتحديداً Munchausen syndrome. والـ Munchausen syndrome يعتمد على التلاعب الواعي conscious manipulation لتحقيق مكسب ثانوي هو لعب دور المريض sick role. هؤلاء المرضى يعرّضون أنفسهم لفحوصات غير لازمة للحصول على هذا الدور.
الفخ: طلاب يختارون Conscious manipulation for gainful incentive، لكن الـ Munchausen يعتمد على sick role، أما الحصول على مكسب مادي أو تعويض واضح فهو malingering.

question: A 5-year-old boy is brought in by his mother because he has had chest pain since he fell down their back steps and landed on his side earlier in the day. The patient points to the right posterior rib cage as the area where he has pain. This patient has never been evaluated in this hospital system before. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse rate is 118/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 80/56 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 99%. The patient appears nervous, is reluctant to talk, and avoids eye contact. The mother fidgets in her chair in the examination room. Physical examination shows linear bruises along the posterior ribs that appear to be in various stages of healing. The lungs are clear to auscultation, bilaterally. Abdominal examination shows mild tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant. X-ray studies of the chest and ribs show two posteromedial rib fractures along the right 7th and 8th ribs. When this finding is shared with the patient’s mother, she becomes anxious and wants to leave the clinic. In addition to treating the patient for his injury, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Avoid disclosure of this patient case to a third party

englishExplanation:
Notify Child Protective Services
Expl anation
A. Avoid disclosure of this patient case to a third party
HIPAA rules allow for disclosure of medical records surrounding concern for child
abuse.
B. Interrogate the patient's mother
There are no specific guidelines on interactions with parents in cases of suspected
child abuse; however, optimal treatment for this patient includes calm discussion
and working with his family to improve his health and safety, if possible.
C. Notify Child Protective Services
This patient's presentation and physical examination are suspicious for child
abuse. Medical providers are mandatory reporters of child abuse if this is suspected.
Reference:
https:/[publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/135/5/e20150356/33747/The-
Evaluation-of-Suspected-Child-Physical-Abuse
D. Obtain full-body x-ray studies
A full-body radiologic survey is often completed during a full evaluation of child
abuse by a medical team specializing in suspected child abuse cases. This evaluation
should be initiated by referral along with contacting Child Protective Services.

question: A previously healthy 5-month-old male infant is brought to the emergency department by his grandmother because he has had lethargy for the past two days. He had one episode of nonbloody, nonbilious emesis today. On physical examination, no external signs of head injury are noted but the patient’s right flank appears as shown. Which of the following additional findings is most likely on further evaluation of this patient?
englishExplanation:
Retinal hemorrhages
Expl anation
A. Blue-tinged sclera
This is a clinical feature of osteogenesis imperfecta (01), a rare inherited disorder
that must be differentiated from child abuse. Similar to children with inflicted
trauma, children with severe 01 can have multiple fractures, but should not have an
increased incidence of bruising.
B. Guaiac positive stool
The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in infants is intussusception,
which occasionally presents with bloody stools and However, there is no
association between intussusception and bruising, which is always abnormal in
nonambulatory infants.
C. Radial head subluxation
"Nursemaid's elbow ' is a common injury in children less than 3 years of age. It is
typically caused by pulling on a child's arm, but is not typically associated with
physical child abuse.
D. Retinal hemorrhages
This child is likely suffering from nonaccidental head trauma, a clinical entity that
often includes bilateral, extensive retinal hemorrhages. Bruising in any infant less
than 6 months of age is a red flag.

question: A 4-year-old male with a history of mastocytosis is brought in by his biological mother for nausea, vomiting, intermittent vision loss, seizures, and fevers at home. On exam the patient is playing on a tablet in no acute distress. Vital signs are within normal limits and the patient has an appropriate neurologic exam for his age. A complete blood count and basic metabolic panel are unremarkable, and the patient has no episodes of vomiting, nor seizures or vision loss while awaiting the results. The mother demands you recheck the labs and is adamant the patient needs an immediate CT scan of the head. What is the best step in management for this patient and family?

options.text: Admit patient and inform child protective services
Contact the patient's primary care physician

correctAnswer: Contact the patient's primary care physician
englishExplanation:
Contact the patient's primary care physician
Expl anation
A. Admit patient and inform child protective services
This patient is well-appearing and has no evidence of any physical abuse or effects
from medical abuse. It is important to confront what appears concerning for medical child abuse (formerly Munchausen's by proxy), but child protective services involvement at this time is premature.
B. Contact the patient's primary care physician
In cases of mild medical child abuse (formerly Munchausen's by proxy), where no
physical harm or consequences to the patient's health have yet manifested, the preferred initial approach is to attempt to corroborate information, and, in conjunction
with the patient's primary care physician, construct a plan for counseling and protection of the child patient. Although the mother is pushing for a CT, which would
expose the child to unnecessary radiation, there is no evidence she has taken any
physically harmful actions at this point in time.
Further information: Jenny C, Metz JB. Medical Child Abuse and Medical
Neglect. Pediatr Rev. PMID: 32005682
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK518999/
C. Contact the police immediately
At this time there is not evidence this patient is in imminent danger or criminal activity has taken place.
D. Order a CT head
The patient has no focal neurologic deficits and has had no witnessed neurologic
symptoms. At this time and given the peculiarity of the presentation, a CT head is
not indicated.

question: A 16-month-old boy is brought in by his mother for evaluation of an injured arm. The patient began to walk around 13 months of age, but his mother says he has really been getting better and faster at walking over the past few months. Which of the following examination findings is most likely to suggest that this patient is at an increased risk of harm in his home?

options.text: Multiple bruises in various stages of healing on the buttocks, posterior legs, upper arms, and ears
Multiple bruises in various stages of healing over the entire body and bleeding gums with any manipulation of the gums/oral mucosa
Multiple bruises in various stages of healing to the anterior lower legs, forearms, knees, and elbows
The patient has significant pain, is guarding, and will not flex or extend the elbow

correctAnswer: Multiple bruises in various stages of healing on the buttocks, posterior legs, upper arms, and ears
englishExplanation:
Multiple bruises in various stages of healing on the buttocks, posterior legs,
upper arms, and ears
Expl anation
A. Multiple bruises in various stages of healing on the buttocks,
posterior legs, upper arms, and ears
A toddler will commonly have bruising seen on the anterior portion of the body,
particularly the shins, forearms, elbows, and knees, especially when they are first
learning to walk and run. A toddler with bruising seen on protected areas, such as
the posterior thighs, ears, buttocks, genitals, or upper arms should cause suspicion
of child abuse.
Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470337/
B. Multiple bruises in various stages of healing over the entire body and
bleeding gums with any manipulation of the gums/oral mucosa
The presence of bleeding gums points to thrombocytopenia as a likely diagnosis and
is not a common finding in child abuse. Children with thrombocytopenia may also
have bruising in various stages of healing so a good history must be taken.
C. Multiple bruises in various stages of healing to the anterior lower
legs, forearms, knees, and elbows
Bruising to the anterior portions of the body, especially the knees, elbows, shins,
and forearms are common in toddlers who are learning to walk.
D. The patient has significant pain, is guarding, and will not flex or
extend the elbow
Swinging a young child around by an outstretched arm can cause a radial/ulnar
subluxation, or nursemaid's elbow, and is a common occurrence in childhood. This
injury can occur if the child is being spun around by their parents or siblings,
and/or if their arm is pulled quickly to get the child out of harm's way. A
nursemaid's elbow itself does not suggest child abuse.
Page 2766 of 4185
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الجواب الصح هو وجود كدمات متعددة بمراحل شفاء مختلفة على الـ buttocks والجزء الخلفي من الساقين والـ upper arms والـ ears. الطفل اللي بعمره سنة وثلاث شهور لما يبدأ يمشي بشكل طبيعي بتطلع عنده كدمات على الجزء الأمامي من الجسم، خصوصاً الـ shins والـ forearms والـ elbows والـ knees. أما الكدمات على المناطق المحمية زي الفخذ الخلفي والأذنين والمقعدة والأعضاء التناسلية فهي بتزيد الشك بإساءة معاملة الطفل. فهذا النمط من الكدمات هو اللي بيرفع احتمال تعرض الطفل للأذى في البيت.

question: A 3-year-old girl is brought in by her mother because of facial swelling for the past two days. She was seen one week prior for a viral upper respiratory tract infection which is largely resolved. Rapid strep testing was negative at that time. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse rate is 100/min, and blood pressure is 92/60 mmHg. On examination, there is bilateral periorbital edema. No rashes are present. Examination of a urine sample shows it to be foamy. Serum albumin is 2.0 g/dL (normal 3.4 to 5.5 g/dL). Which of the following findings on dipstick urinalysis is most likely to be seen in this patient?
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
Proteinuria
A. Bilirubinuria
Bilirubinuria is a sign of liver disease, and reflects elevated direct bilirubin in the
serum.
B. Hematuria
Hematuria has several causes, including glomerular disease, renal cell carcinoma,
malignant hypertension, nephrolithiasis, bladder cancer, and cystitis. Glomerular
disease should be suspected when there is hematuria with red cell casts, 'cola colored' urine, and proteinuria.
C. Ketonuria
Ketonuria is an indication that the body is breaking down fatty acids for energy.
This can be present in starvation, diabetic ketoacidosis, and hyperthyroidism.
D. Proteinuria
This patient has suspected nephrotic syndrome. Heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and lipiduria are the main characteristics of nephrotic syndrome. There
are many causes of nephrotic syndrome, including minimal-change nephropathy
(common cause in children), focal glomerulosclerosis, diabetes mellitus, and SLE.
Treatment involves a low salt diet, ACE inhibitor or ARB, and loop diuretics.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470444/

question: Which statement best describes the cough associated with pertussis in infants?

options.text: Intermittent, singular cough followed by a loud and distinct "whooping" sound
Paroxysmal, rapid cough associated with posttussive emesis
Productive cough associated with fever and respiratory failure
Seal-like barking cough associated with inspiratory stridor at rest

correctAnswer: Paroxysmal, rapid cough associated with posttussive emesis
englishExplanation: The characteristic cough of infantile pertussis is a paroxysmal, rapid cough associated with posttussive emesis and sometimes cyanosis. Classic pertussis is known to exist in three stages: the catarrhal stage, which presents like a URI; the paroxysmal phase, where the classic coughing spells, "whoop," and posttussive emesis are prevalent; and the convales- cent stage, when the symptoms start to subside. Although it is not com- pletely diagnostic, the presence of the characteristic cough can yield clues to the di- agnosis and can be helpful in selecting an empiric management plan. Even if a child appears relatively well, the risk of pertussis-associated apnea makes admission pru- dent; all children who are less than 6 months with presumed pertussis should be admitted, as pertussis in this age group can be particularly dangerous. Noticing a characteristic cough can lead to an appropriate admission for an infant who may otherwise be sent home, so it is important to maintain a high level of clinical suspicion in this age group. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although another name for pertussis is "whooping cough," the charac- teristic "whoop" is not typically seen in infants. If present, the child is usu- ally older than 2 or 3 years. It is thought that an infant's inspiratory effort is not strong enough to create the "whooping" sound. Pertussis coughs are also not typically intermittent and singular, but typically come in parox- ysms of coughs. A productive cough with fever and respiratory failure is more character- istic of severe bacterial pneumonia or bacterial tracheitis. A typical cough secondary to pertussis is nonproductive, and fevers are typically low-grade or nonexistent. However, a secondary bacterial pneumonia can be a complication of pertussis and should be considered in patients with a more severe symptom burden. A seal-like barking cough associated with inspiratory stridor at rest would be most consistent with moderate to severe croup. However, bacte- rial tracheitis can also present with a seal-like cough and stridor at rest.

question: A 3-month-old girl born at full term presents with failure to thrive, with a growth rate consistently falling below the second percentile. On presentation, she is afebrile with normal vital signs but appears lethargic. During the examination, she has a seizure. What is the most likely cause of the seizure?
englishExplanation: The most common cause of poor growth in infants is inadequate dietary intake. Overdilution of infant formula with water can cause significant hypona- tremia, particularly in infants with vomiting and diarrhea, which can cause altered mental status and seizures. A detailed history and physical examination can often indicate other causes of failure to thrive; for example, respiratory distress or cyanosis while feeding may indicate congenital heart disease. Other causes of failure to thrive include diseases that cause inadequate nutrient absorption (eg, GERD, protein allergies, inflammatory bowel disease) or increased me- tabolism (eg, infection, congenital syndromes). Additionally, neglect and in- gestions must always be considered in the differential diagnosis of poor growth. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although biliary atresia can cause poor growth in infants, patients with biliary atresia typically present with jaundice between the 3rd and 6th weeks of life. Caregivers may describe acholic stools and dark urine. Physical findings of bil- iary atresia may include ascites. The most common cause of poor growth in infants is inadequate dietary intake. Overdilution of infant formula with water can cause significant hyponatremia, leading to seizures. Hyperthyroidism is another possible cause of poor growth in infants, but it typically presents within the first 2 weeks of life as irritability. Examination findings, including hypertension, tachycardia, exophthalmos, and goi- ter, may also be present. The most common cause of poor growth in infants is inadequate dietary intake. Overdilution of infant formula with water can cause significant hyponatremia, leading to seizures. Maple syrup urine disease is an autosomal recessive disorder that can cause poor growth in infants. However, it typically becomes apparent soon after birth due to the characteristically sweet odor of the infant's urine. Other symptoms of maple syrup urine disease include poor feeding and lethargy. The most common cause of poor growth in infants is inadequate dietary intake. Overdilution of infant formula with water can cause significant hyponatremia, leading to seizures.

question: A 3-year-old boy fell from a shopping cart, hitting his head. There was no loss of consciousness, and his GCS score is 15. He has normal mental status and behav- ior and no signs of a basilar skull fracture. If the patient presents with vomiting, what is the recommended diagnostic approach according to the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) Pediatric Head Injury Prediction Rule?

options.text: No diagnostics required; the patient may be discharged
Observation or head CT are acceptable approaches

correctAnswer: Observation or head CT are acceptable approaches
englishExplanation:
The Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) Pediatric Head Injury Prediction Rule is an externally validated clinical decision tool that enables physicians to identify children at very low risk of clini- cally-important traumatic brain injuries (ciTBI) to avoid head CT. This patient is deemed moderate risk using this criteria based on the presentation of vomiting. Moderate risk patients may either undergo head CT or observation. There are two rules (one for age <2 and the other for ages 2-18) each utilizing six predictors to determine risk of a ciTBI. High-risk predictors are: GCS score ≤14, signs of basilar skull fracture or palpable skull fracture, or signs of altered mental status (eg, agitation, somnolence, repetitive questioning, or slow response to verbal communication). Moderate-risk predictors for children ages 2 to 18 are loss of consciousness, severe headache, vomiting, or severe mechanism (eg, rollover motor vehicle collision, patient ejection, death of another passenger, pedestrian or nonhelmeted bicyclist struck by a vehicle, fall >3 ft for chil- dren <2 y old or >5 ft for children ≥2 y old, or head struck with a high-impact ob- ject). For children <2 years old, occipital, parietal, or temporal scalp hematomas are included and vomiting is excluded as moderate-risk predictor variables. Patients with any high-risk predictors should undergo head CT. Those with no risk factors present do not need a head CT or period of observation. Those with moderate-risk findings, as in this case, may either undergo CT or a 4 to 6 hour period of observation. A several hour observation period is preferred, but the clinician may consider personal experience, parent preference, worsening signs or symptoms during observation period, age <3 months, and the presence of multiple versus isolated findings when deciding between observation and head CT in this circumstance. Incorrect Answer Explanations Head CT is recommended when any one of the high-risk predictors is present: GCS score<15, altered mental status, or signs of a basilar skull fracture. In the PECARN study, these were associated with a 4.3% incidence of clinically impor- tant TBI. Although subspecialty consultation should always be a viable option when expert advice is needed, neurosurgical consultation is not part of the PECARN de- cision rule. The PECARN rule is utilized to predict ciTBI, of which neurosurgical intervention is one. Other ciTBIs included in the rule are death, intubation, and hospital admission. Patients can be safely discharged if none of the PECARN risk predictors are present. If no predictors are present, the risk of ciTBI is <0.02% for age <2 and <0.05% for ages 2 to 18. This patient presented with vomiting, which is a mod- erate risk factor.

question: A previously healthy 3-month-old presents in cardiac arrest. The infant was intu- bated by EMS. On arrival, the infant is in asystole, cool to the touch, and noted to have livor mortis. What is the next best step?

options.text: Leave family alone with the infant

englishExplanation: Sudden unexpected infant deaths (SUIDs) must be reported to the office of the coroner or the medical examiner as soon as possible so that an in- vestigation can begin. Emergency clinicians should, in a manner sensitive to the patient's family, obtain a history that includes birth history; time the infant was last seen alive; when, where, by whom, and in what position the infant was found to be unresponsive; the sleeping environment; and history of any recent illnesses. Most jurisdictions have child death review teams, and this information may be helpful in their investigation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Since livor mortis is present, there is no indication to continue resuscita- tion. The emergency department clinician should pronounce the death. Bereaved families, if not present during the resuscitation, should be permitted to see and touch their child in the discreet presence of a staff member. Because the death of this infant was unexpected, an investigation into the death will be performed. Although the majority of unexplained infant deaths are not due to child abuse, abuse must always be considered. The family should be permitted to see and touch the infant in the discreet presence of an emer- gency department staff member, not by themselves. A careful physical examina- tion should be documented, particularly noting the presence of bruising or petechiae. Because the death of this infant was unexpected, an investigation into the death will be performed. Endotracheal and intravenous tubes and in- traosseous lines should be left in place until the patient has been examined by the coroner or the medical examiner. If the tubes and lines are distressing to the family, they may be cut and secured close to the skin to minimize their appearance.

question: What initial diagnostic study is indicated in the evaluation of an infant who expe- rienced a low-risk brief resolved unexplained event (BRUE)?
englishExplanation: A BRUE categorized as low-risk requires minimal diagnostic evaluation. After a full history and physical examination confirms no alternative diagnosis, a twelve-lead ECG may be performed. ECG may identify conditions such as long QT syndrome and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has replaced the older term “Apparent Life-Threatening Event” (ALTE) with the term “BRUE” in published guidelines regarding risk assessment and management. By definition, a BRUE occurs in an in- fant less than 1 year of age and is associated with one or more of the fol- lowing: an altered level of responsiveness, abnormal or absent breath- ing, change in muscle tone, or pallor or cyanosis. If there is an identified condition causing the event, or if the child has not completely returned to baseline with a normal appearance and vital signs, then the episode cannot be classified as a BRUE. Key measures in the management of infants who present after a low-risk BRUE include caregiver education and CPR training. These infants do not need hospitalization and may be safely discharged after a brief period of observation with close primary care follow-up. Immunization status is not factored in the risk stratification of BRUEs. However, underimmunized children are at risk for developing pertussis, symptoms of which are often insidious in onset. Before they develop the characteristic respiratory symptoms, infants with pertussis can have gagging and apnea that is consistent with a low-risk BRUE. For this reason, pertussis screening has been suggested as ac- ceptable testing to consider in this group. Incorrect Answer Explanations CBC could be considered in the screening of a BRUE with high-risk characteristics but is not indicated in low-risk BRUE. Infants who have high-risk characteristics of their BRUE should have additional evaluation, guided by a careful history and physical examination. A CBC can be obtained to evaluate for anemia or signs of infection. Previous studies have described an association be- tween BRUEs and anemia, although a clear causal relationship has not been established. Chest x-ray is not indicated for a low-risk BRUE. Current AAP guidelines suggest that chest x-rays in this clinical scenario increase healthcare costs, expose infants to unnecessary radiation, and increase caregiver anxiety. In a high-risk BRUE, a chest x-ray may be helpful if the infant has focal lung findings to suggest pneumonia. Additionally, if the child demonstrates URI symptoms, consider obtain- ing a viral respiratory panel. Viral testing may aid in diagnostic certainty and sug- gest an anticipated course of illness, but it rarely changes acute management. Gagging or choking during feeds can result in symptoms similar to BRUE. Isolated events are often benign and rarely require a swallow study. By defi- nition, if an event is suspected to be due to gastroesophageal reflux (GER), it is not a BRUE. Diagnostic tests, such as barium contrast studies, pH probes, and acid sup- pression therapy, are not indicated for infants who have experienced a low-risk BRUE. Parents should, however, be counseled on overfeeding, which increases the risk of GER and regurgitation.

englishExplanation: A full sepsis evaluation, including lumbar puncture and urinalysis, should be per- formed, and blood cultures should be ordered. Febrile newborns younger than 21 days remain at high risk of serious bacterial infection even when they appear well. englishExplanation: This presentation is concerning for coarctation of the aorta with a closing duc- tus arteriosus. Children born in hospitals are now routinely screened for coarcta- tion with pre- and post-ductal saturations, but the screening is not perfectly sensi- tive. Further workup for this concern would be blood pressures in all four extremi- ties in combination with pre- and post-ductal saturations. Any infant in distress should have sepsis on the differential diagnosis, but this patient's presentation war- rants further evaluation for coarctation. Echocardiography can confirm the diagno- sis. MRI and CT can also be used to confirm the diagnosis, evaluate the extent of coarctation, and help guide surgical planning. Neonates with severe heart failure or shock should be considered for coarcta- tion of the aorta. Presentation of this occurs when the patent ductus arteriosus closes. A differential cyanosis can be found where the oxygen saturation is lower in the lower extremities than the right arm. Thus, measuring blood pressure in all four extremities is important to aid in diagnosis.

question:
Musculoskeletal
A 5-year-old girl presents with a painless enlarging mass on her leg and possible
blood in the urine. She has no known medical issues and up-to-date vaccinations,
but her brother was diagnosed with cancer at a young age that presented with a
painful enlarging mass on the arm.
What is the most likely soft-tissue sarcoma to be diagnosed in this patient?
englishExplanation: Rhabdomyosarcomas are of soft-tissue origin and are the most common childhood soft-tissue sarcoma (approximately 4.5 cases per 1 million children and adolescents per year). The presentation of rhabdomyosarcoma is vari- able, as these may occur at any site. Most common presenting locations in- clude the head and neck region, the extremities, and within the genital and urinary systems. The majority of rhabdomyosarcomas present prior to age 7. Treatment for rhabdomyosarcoma (as well as other childhood malignancies) re- quires a multidisciplinary approach, including appropriate referrals to specialists such as pediatric oncology and other subspecialties depending on the site of involve- ment. There is an increased risk of rhabdomyosarcoma in patients who have first-degree relatives diagnosed with cancer (odds ratio 1.39), and that risk is further increased if the cancer was diagnosed before age 30 (odds ratio 2.37). 9/20/26, 1:18 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 744 of 974

الفخ: طلاب بختاروا Ewing sarcoma لأنه شافوا كتلة بالعظم وأخ مصاب بسرطان. بس الـ rhabdomyosarcoma هي sarcoma رخو الأنسجة وأكثر سرطان رخو شيوعاً بأعمار الأطفال، والـ Ewing sarcoma بيطلع من العظم وليس من الأنسجة الرخوة.

question:
Shared scenario:
A 22-year-old college student went to the health clinic complaining of a
fever over the last 5 days, fatigue, myalgias, and a bout of vomiting and
diarrhea. The clinic doctor diagnosed him with acute gastroenteritis and told
him to drink more fluids. Three days later, the student presents to the ED
complaining of constant substernal chest pain. He also feels short of breath.
His BP is 120/75 mm Hg, HR is 122 beats/minute, RR is 18 breaths/minute,

temperature is 100.9°F, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. An ECG
is performed revealing sinus tachycardia. A chest radiograph is
unremarkable. Laboratory tests are normal except for slightly elevated
WBC.

28.   Which test will help make the diagnosis in this patient?
englishExplanation:
28.  The answer is d. The patient has myocarditis. Flu-like complaints,
such as fatigue, myalgias, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and fever, are usually
the earliest symptoms and signs of myocarditis. Tachycardia is common
and can be disproportionate to the patient’s temperature (ie, HR faster
than what is expected). This may be the only clue that something more
serious than a simple viral illness exists. Approximately 12% of patients
also complain of chest pain. Given the inflammation of the myocardial
muscle, typically cardiac enzymes are elevated in these patients.
The ESR (a) is a nonspecific marker of inflammation. This test is
elevated when someone is acutely infected, but also in a host of
inflammatory conditions like the autoimmune diseases. Procalcitonin (b) is
used as a serum marker for occult infection. It has gained popularity in its
use as a screening test for sepsis of a bacterial nature. Like ESR, CRP (c) is
another nonspecific marker of inflammation. It will elevate in many
conditions and will not help the physician to narrow the diagnosis to a
specific organ system. LDH (e) is not a useful test in this case. LDH is often
used in the evaluation of patients for possible Pneumocystis jiroveci. It is
also helpful in identifying patients with hemolysis. Prior to the development
of better troponin and CK assays, LDH was used as a “cardiac enzyme” but
due to its lack of specificity for myocardium, it is no longer used.

![PreTest-5e-00028 source page 29](images/PreTest-5e-00028-PreTest-5e-p0029.jpg)

![PreTest-5e-00028 source page 51](images/PreTest-5e-00028-PreTest-5e-p0051.jpg)
arabicExplanation:

الفخ: كتير طلاب بيختاروا CRP أو ESR لأنهم مؤشرات التهاب. بس هدول مؤشرات التهاب غير نوعية وبترتفع في كتير حالات وما بيساعدوا نحصر التشخيص بجهاز معين، بعكس الـ Troponin اللي بيدل على تضرر عضلة القلب.

question:
Shared scenario:
A 14-day-old neonate presents with his parents with a 4-hour history of
fever. Parents report noticing that he “felt warm” and was having copious
nasal secretions while feeding. His rectal temperature at home was 102.3°F.
He was born via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery at term. The neonate
appears lethargic and has mottled extremities, but is hot to the touch. Vitals
include BP 74/48 mm Hg, HR 170 beats/minute, RR 40 breaths/minute, and
temperature 102.9°F.

182.   Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give a 20 cc/kg IV fluid bolus, administer broad-spectrum IV
Obtain blood cultures, administer broad-spectrum IM antibiotics, and
Give a 20 cc/kg IV fluid bolus, obtain blood and urine cultures,
Give a 20 cc/kg IV fluid bolus, obtain blood and urine cultures, obtain
Give a 20 cc/kg IV fluid bolus, obtain blood and urine cultures,

correctAnswer: Give a 20 cc/kg IV fluid bolus, obtain blood and urine cultures, obtain
englishExplanation:
182.  The answer is d. A febrile neonate is a child 28 days and younger
who presents with a fever. These neonates are at very high risk of serious
bacterial infections including UTI, pneumonia, meningitis, and bacteremia.
These neonates, therefore, need to receive a fluid bolus at 20 cc/kg and
broad-spectrum antibiotics to cover for the most common pathogens in
this age group (discussed later). The workup must also include blood and
urine cultures and an LP in order to obtain CSF for culture. These patients
then need to be admitted to the hospital for IV antibiotics and observation
until cultures have returned.
The other answer choices are incorrect for various reasons. Choice (a)
does not include blood, urine, or CSF cultures. Choice (b) does not include
urine or CSF culture and involves discharging the patient home. Choice (c)
does not include the LP with CSF culture. Choice (d) does not include LP
and CSF culture and involves discharging the patient home.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: هالرضيع عمره أربعة عشر يوم وعنده حرارة 102.3 مع خمول وترقّط بالأطراف، والرضيع بعمر 28 يوم أو أقل مع حرارة بكون بخطورة عالية جداً لعدوى بكتيرية خطيرة. وهالحالات لازم ياخدوا جرعة سوائل وريدية 20 cc/kg ومضادات حيوية وريدية واسعة الطيف تغطي الجراثيم الأكثر شيوعاً بهالعمر. وهاد التقييم لازم يشمل blood cultures و urine cultures و lumbar puncture للحصول على CSF للـ culture، وبعدها تنويم بالـ NICU للمضادات وعمل المراقبة لحد ما ترجع المزارع.
الفخ: كتير طلاب بختاروا الخيارات اللي فيها إخراج الطفل للبيت أو اللي بدون LP و CSF culture. بس أي خيار ما فيه سحب CSF بالـ LP ناقص، والأخطر إن في خيارات بترجع المولود للبيت، وهاد ما بيصير مع إنتان مولود بعمر 14 يوم.

question:
An 18-year-old woman is brought in by her roommate for confusion.
Over the last 24 hours, her roommate says the patient became progressively
confused, saying she was the president. On examination, she is somnolent,
but arouses to pain. She is not oriented to person, place, or time. Her initial
vital signs are BP 90/40, HR 120, temperature 101.1°F, and RR 20
breaths/minute. She has a flat, round, pinpoint rash on her abdomen that
does not blanch when pressed. After fluid resuscitation, what is the next
best step for this patient?

options.text: Call her parents for permission to treat
Admit the patient to the ICU

englishExplanation:
227.  The answer is d. This patient presents with signs and symptoms of
meningitis, as evidenced by altered mental status, fever, and a petechial
rash. Initial management is to stabilize the patient by attempting fluid
resuscitation. The next step should be blood cultures, antibiotics, and an LP,
typically in that order. Even delaying antibiotic initiation by 1 hour can
increase mortality by 3% to 7%. Therefore, antibiotics (d) would be the
correct first step out of the available answer choices.
This patient will need an LP, but since antibiotic delay can increase
mortality and it takes up to an hour for antibiotics to enter CSF and alter test
results, antibiotics should always be administered prior to obtaining an LP
(c). The patient will require hospitalization, most likely in the ICU (e), but
first needs further stabilization and treatment in the ED. Not only is this
patient 18, and allowed to make her own decisions, but in any emergent or
altered state, patients should be administered life-saving treatments and
thus, contacting her parents (a) is not immediately indicated. While a urine
drug screening (UDS) (b) may be obtained as part of the altered mental
status workup, in the setting of fever and hypotension, meningitis is much
more likely and therefore treating the infection is a higher priority at the
moment.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: البنت عمرها 18 سنة وعندها confusion متزايد مع somnolence وفيفر و hypotension و tachycardia، وطفح petechial ما بيختفي لما نضغط عليه على البطن. هالصورة بوجه لتشخيص meningitis. الخطوة الأولى إعادة الإرواء بالمحاليل الوريدية، وبعدها blood cultures ومضادات حيوية والـ LP، وعادة بهذا الترتيب. وتأخير المضاد الحيوي ساعة واحدة ممكن يزيد الوفيات بين 3% و 7%، ولأن المضاد بده لحد ساعة يدخل الـ CSF ويغير نتائج التحليل، فلازم نعطي المضاد الحيوي قبل الـ LP.
الفخ: طلاب كتير بيختاروا Perform a lumbar puncture أول شي لأنها أساس التشخيص. بس الـ LP بتأخر المضاد الحيوي وبتزيد الوفيات، والمضاد لازم يكون قبلها. وخيار الاتصال بالأهل غير مناسب لأنها 18 سنة والحالة إسعافية.

question:
A 2-year-old child presents to the ED with right elbow pain. She
reportedly “threw a tantrum” at naptime. Her father attempted to pick her
up out of the crib by the arm with her feet dangling. She later refused to use
her right arm and whimpers when anyone tries to move it passively. On
examination, there is no deformity, joint swelling, erythema, or
neurovascular compromise. The arm is held in slight flexion, pronated and
abducted. A radiograph of her elbow is shown in the figure. What is the
most appropriate next step?

(Reproduced with permission from Tarek Hanna, MD.)

options.text: Attempt to flex and supinate the forearm with slight pressure held at the
Apply traction to the wrist while pronating the arm and extending the
Apply an arm sling and refer for outpatient orthopedic referral
Order X-rays of the contralateral elbow for comparison

correctAnswer: Attempt to flex and supinate the forearm with slight pressure held at the
englishExplanation:
301.  The answer is a. The patient presents with nursemaid’s elbow, or
radial head subluxation due to immaturity of the annular ligament. This
injury is most commonly seen in toddlers as the annular ligament
strengthens over time. If there are no signs of joint effusion, the examiner
can flex and supinate the forearm with slight pressure held on the radial
head in an attempt to reduce the subluxation. The radial head should be
palpated and during the maneuver, a click noted by the examiner has been
shown to have a positive predictive value of over 90%. The child should
begin to use the arm within minutes of the reduction, and immobilization is
not needed for a first-time occurrence.
Pronation and extension of the forearm (b) is an incorrect method of
reduction. An orthopedic consult (c) would be unnecessary for a
nursemaid’s elbow injury. A sling (d) for immobilization is not required.
Reduction of a nursemaid’s elbow is both diagnostic and therapeutic. X-ray
images pre- and postreduction are not necessary unless there are signs of
joint effusion, bruising, or deformity. In pediatrics, contralateral imaging is
sometimes performed when there is diagnostic uncertainty between injury
and normal anatomic variation, but there is no role for contralateral
comparison (e) in this injury.

![PreTest-5e-00301 source page 355](images/PreTest-5e-00301-PreTest-5e-p0355.jpg)

![PreTest-5e-00301 source page 356](images/PreTest-5e-00301-PreTest-5e-p0356.jpg)

![PreTest-5e-00301 source page 378](images/PreTest-5e-00301-PreTest-5e-p0378.jpg)
arabicExplanation:
ليش: البنت عمرها سنتين وعندها ألم بالكوع بعد ما أبوها شالها من إيدها وهي معلقة بالهواء، وهي بتحمل الإيد مثنية و pronated و abducted، والـ radiograph ما فيه انتفاخ ولا تشوه. هالتشخيص nursemaid's elbow أو radial head subluxation بسبب عدم نضوج الـ annular ligament وهاد أكثر شي عند الأطفال الصغار. ولما ما يكون في علامات effusion، الخطوة هي محاولة ثني وسحب الـ forearm مع ضغط خفيف محتفظ به على الـ radial head لإرجاع الـ subluxation. الـ click اللي بحسه الفاحص عندها predictive value إيجابي فوق 90%، والطفل ببلش يستعمل إيده خلال دقائق.
الفخ: طلاب بختاروا Apply traction مع pronation و extension لأنهم سمعوا بمناورة ردّ، أو طلبوا استشارة orthopedics. بس التقنية الصح هي flexion مع supination والضغط على الـ radial head، والردّ بنفسه تشخيصي وعلاجي وما بده sling ولا صور.

question:
Shared scenario:
An 8-month-old infant is brought to the ED by her mother after she
reportedly rolled off of the couch. The mother left the infant on the couch
unattended for a few minutes. The mother heard a thud and then her
daughter was heard crying. She ran back into the room to find the baby
lying on the floor and crying. The mother immediately picked up the infant
and brought her to the ED for evaluation. On physical examination, the vital
signs include a BP of 76/50 mm Hg, HR of 140 beats/minute, RR of 26
breaths/minute, temperature of 36.8°F, and pulse oximetry of 98% on room
air. The infant is well nourished. She is moving all four extremities
spontaneously. There is soft tissue swelling in the region of the left lower
leg. A radiograph is obtained and shown in the figure.

302.   Based on the clinical scenario and radiograph, what is the most likely
diagnosis?

(Reproduced with permission from Tarek Hanna, MD.)
englishExplanation:
302.  The answer is b. A spiral fracture of the distal tibia is known by
the eponym Toddler’s fracture. It is a fracture commonly seen in
ambulatory children aged 1 to 3 years. The mechanism of injury usually
involves a trivial fall or a twisting mechanism on a planted foot. Spiral

fractures seen in nonambulatory children are highly suspicious for
nonaccidental trauma (child abuse).
Greenstick fractures (a) are seen in children because the bones are soft
and can bend resulting in incomplete fractures. X-rays demonstrate a “bow”
fracture in which the bone becomes curved in its longitudinal axis. The
outer cortex of the bone remains intact. The radiograph pictured
demonstrates a fracture (c) and is not within normal limits. The Salter
Harris classification is used to describe fractures involving the epiphyseal
plate (physis) or growth plate. A Salter Harris I fracture is a fracture
through the growth plate or physis. Diagnosis of this fracture is made
clinically as the radiographs are negative. A Salter Harris II fracture
involves the metaphysis and physis. A Salter Harris III fracture involves the
physis and epiphysis. A Salter Harris IV fracture (d) involves the physis,
metaphysic, and epiphysis. A Salter Harris V fracture (e) is a crush injury to
physis. This fracture appears as decreased space between the epiphysis and
diaphysis on radiograph.

![PreTest-5e-00302 source page 356](images/PreTest-5e-00302-PreTest-5e-p0356.jpg)

![PreTest-5e-00302 source page 357](images/PreTest-5e-00302-PreTest-5e-p0357.jpg)

![PreTest-5e-00302 source page 378](images/PreTest-5e-00302-PreTest-5e-p0378.jpg)

![PreTest-5e-00302 source page 379](images/PreTest-5e-00302-PreTest-5e-p0379.jpg)
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الرضيعة عمرها ثمانية شهور وطاحت عن الكنبة، والفحص بيبيّن انتفاخ بالأنسجة الرخوة بمنطقة الساق السفلية اليسرى، والـ radiograph بيبيّن كسر. والكسر اللي بالصورة هو spiral fracture بالـ distal tibia، والمعروف بـ Toddler's fracture. وهالنوع عادة بيشوف عند الأطفال اللي عم يمشوا بعمر سنة لثلاث سنين، والآلية عادة سقوط بسيط أو حركة لف على قدم ثابتة. لكن الـ spiral fracture عند طفل غير قادر على المشي بتزيد الشك الشديد بالـ nonaccidental trauma.
الفخ: كتير طلاب بختاروا Greenstick fracture أو Normal radiograph لأنه توقعهم كسر بسيط. بس الـ greenstick بيبيّن انحناء بالعظم مع بقاء القشرة الخارجية سليمة، وهنا في كسر واضح بالصورة، ومنها الـ Salter Harris ما بتوصف هالكسر.

question:
A 9-month-old boy is brought to the ED with a 2-day history of fever,
vomiting, and fussiness. The patient has had multiple episodes of emesis
that follow intense periods of fussiness after which the patient seems to
relax and go to sleep. He has had normal stooling. In between these
episodes, he has slightly decreased energy but otherwise seems well. Oral
intake is decreased and urine output has been decreased since the day of
symptom onset. Which of the following statements is true regarding this
condition?

options.text: The majority of patients present with vomiting, colicky abdominal pain,
Air enema is the therapeutic intervention of choice
Plain films of the abdomen usually confirm the diagnosis
Most of these have a “lead point” as the underlying pathologic cause

correctAnswer: Air enema is the therapeutic intervention of choice
englishExplanation:
353.  The answer is b. This is a classic story and presentation for
intussusception in which a part of intestine telescopes inside of another
resulting in ischemia that can lead to infarction of bowel. This is a true
gastrointestinal (GI) emergency. The most common type of
intussusception is ileo-colic and most commonly idiopathic in etiology.
Ileo-ileal and colo-colonic intussusceptions are possible though rare in
comparison. The most common age group is 3 to 12 months with greater
than 80% occurring within the first 2 years of life. Air enema is both
diagnostic and therapeutic and has been widely adopted as the
intervention of choice for these patients.
Although the classic triad consists of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting,
and currant jelly stools, fewer than 20% of patients will present with all of
these findings (a). Plain films cannot typically confirm or refute the
presence of intussusception, though air present in the cecum indicates no
ileo-colic intussusception (c). Radiographs are important, however, to
exclude the presence of free air before attempting an enema reduction.
From a diagnostic perspective, ultrasound has been employed and
demonstrated to have very high sensitivity for intussusception. Although
surgical consultation (d) is warranted before reduction for cases of
perforation identified with the air enema or unsuccessful reductions,
relatively few patients ultimately require surgical correction. There is a lead
point in a small minority of patients in the classic age range (e). The
incidence of pathologic lead points increases as the age of the patient
increases beyond the classic age group. Lead points can be hypertrophied
Peyer’s patches, a Meckel’s diverticulum, a polyp, or a tumor.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الرضيع عمره تسعة شهور وعنده حرارة واستفراغ ونوبات بكاء شديد متقطعة بيتبعها هدوء ونوم، وبين النوبات بيبدو بحالة جيدة نسبياً. هالقصة كلاسيكية للـ intussusception، حيث جزء من الأمعاء بيدخل جوة جزء تاني فيسبب نقص تروية وممكن infarction. النوع الأكثر شيوعاً هو ileo-colic وأغلب الحالات مجهولة السبب، وأكثر عمر الإصابة من 3 لـ 12 شهر. والـ Air enema هو التدخل العلاجي المفضل، وهو كمان تشخيصي وعلاجي بنفس الوقت، والصورة الشعاعية البسيطة مهمة لنستبعد وجود free air قبل المحاولة.
الفخ: طلاب بختاروا إن المرضى عادة بجيهم الثالوث الكامل أو إن الجراحة بتحتاج دائماً. بس أقل من 20% بجيهم الثالوث الكامل من colicky pain و vomiting و currant jelly stools، والجراحة بتحتاج بعد perforation أو فشل الردّ فقط.

question:
A 15-month-old girl is brought to the ED by emergency medical
services (EMS) secondary to seizure activity noted at home. The patient is
previously healthy child and her immunizations are up-to-date. She has had
no cough, congestion, vomiting, diarrhea, or rash. This afternoon, the
patient was being observed in the playroom when her eyes rolled back and
she began having generalized tonic-clonic activity that lasted for
approximately 2 minutes. When EMS arrived, the patient was in her
mother’s arms, tired but arousable, and in no apparent distress. On
examination, BP is 95/50 mm Hg, HR is 155 beats/minute, RR 32 is
breaths/minute, and temperature is 103.1°F. She has normal tympanic
membranes, oropharyngeal exam reveals several tiny erythematous and
vesicular appearing lesions in the posterior oropharynx, lungs and heart
examinations are normal, and abdomen is soft and nontender. Skin
examination is clear with brisk capillary refill. Over the course of your
evaluation, the patient becomes increasingly interactive and playful. Which
of the following is the most appropriate course of action for this patient?

options.text: Obtain complete blood count (CBC), blood culture, urinalysis, urine
Obtain blood and urine for culture, administer ceftriaxone, and
Reassure parents that this is a benign condition and that no further
Obtain routine blood work and head computed tomographic (CT) scan
Obtain head CT scan and perform LP secondary to fever and seizure to

correctAnswer: Reassure parents that this is a benign condition and that no further
englishExplanation:
358.  The answer is c. This patient had a simple febrile seizure.
Approximately, 2% to 5% of children will experience a febrile seizure
during their lifetimes. Febrile seizures occur between the ages of 3 months
and 5 years, are associated with fever, and are categorized as either simple
or complex. Simple febrile seizures are generalized and last less than 15
minutes typically at the start of an illness. Complex febrile seizures are
prolonged, recur within 24 hours, or are focal. The approach to a patient
with a febrile seizure is, for all intents and purposes, identical to that of the

same patient who has not had a seizure, so long as the seizure has stopped
by the time you are evaluating the patient. If the seizure continues, treat as
you would any other seizure with indicated medications (ie.,
benzodiazepines) with attention to the primary survey and correction of
hypoglycemia when present. Once the patient is stable, and the seizure has
abated, potential sources of the fever should be identified. This patient,
having a temperature of 103°F and lesions consistent with Coxsackie virus
infection on the posterior pharynx, does not need any testing. In
approximately half of all children with simple, febrile seizures, the source is
viral. In well-appearing children meeting the criteria for a simple febrile
seizure, minimal testing is necessary.
In the presence of an otherwise normal examination, other diagnostic
tests (a and b) are not indicated. CBC and blood cultures in otherwise wellappearing, fully immunized children of this age are no longer indicated to
evaluate for occult bacteremia. Neither a head CT scan nor a neurology
consultation (d) is warranted for a first-time febrile seizure. An LP to rule
out meningitis (e) is not indicated in this patient who has regained normal
mental status, appears well, and has no neurologic deficit.

question:
A 9-day-old boy is brought to the ED for fever and fussiness. He was
born full term. However, the delivery was complicated by premature
rupture of membranes (PROM) and the mother had a fever for which she
was treated with antibiotics before delivery. The baby did well in the
nursery, and has been at home and feeding without any difficulties until the
day of presentation when he became fussier, less interested in feeding, and
his parents noted an axillary temperature of 101.5°F. On presentation, his
HR is 160 beats/minute, RR is 48 breaths/minute, temperature is 102.4°F,
and pulse oximetry of 97% on room air. His anterior fontanelle is open and
flat, conjunctivae are clear, neck is supple without masses. His heart, lung,
and abdominal examinations are normal. The skin shows tiny (1-3 mm)
pustules with a surrounding rim of erythema on the patient’s trunk. No
vesicular lesions are noted. Which of the following is the most likely
organism responsible for this patient’s condition?
englishExplanation:
361.  The answer is c. This is a case of neonatal sepsis, an invasive
bacterial infection occurring during the first 90 days of life. The most
common causes of newborn sepsis are group B β-hemolytic Streptococcus
(GBS) and E. coli. Approximately, a third of women are carriers of GBS in

their vagina and exposure is through the birth canal. There is increased risk
with PROM that is thought to result in ascending infection. Increased
colony counts result in increased risk for neonatal sepsis and thus the
tendency to screen pregnant women and to treat at the time of delivery for
either screen-positive women or women with fever or PROM. Any neonate
younger than 4 weeks with fever higher than 100.3°F requires a full workup
to search for the source of infection. This workup includes a CBC, blood
culture, urinalysis and urine culture, and an LP for cell counts and culture.
One should consider sending the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for HSV culture
and polymerase chain reaction, particularly if there are any maternal risk
factors, suspicious skin lesions, or in any infant who is very ill. Empiric
antiviral therapy should also be administered in such cases pending test
results, as there is sufficient evidence now that neonates with HSV
meningitis may not have typical herpetic skin lesions. In this case, the
lesions on this patient’s trunk are most consistent with a benign newborn
rash called erythema toxicum neonatorum and are unrelated to the fever.
The other organisms listed are all known causes of neonatal sepsis. E.
coli (a) incidence is similar to GBS and is the most common of the enteric
pathogens that cause this condition. It is the most common cause of urinary
tract infections (UTIs) in infants, which can lead to bacteremia as well.
Listeria (b) is a commonly cited source of infection in neonatal sepsis but
with much lower incidence. Exposure is primarily from unprocessed meats
and unpasteurized produce. S. aureus (d) is an unlikely pathogen in an
immunocompetent patient of this age. HSV (e) is an important pathogen to
consider in neonatal sepsis. Obtaining the maternal history is important to
help diagnose this condition, though many patients who ultimately are
diagnosed with neonatal HSV have no known maternal history of vaginal
herpes.
