question: A man presents with difficulty walking and painful calves. He has a history of alcohol use disorder and ulcerative colitis, both untreated. He reports no history of chronic diarrhea. A blood toxicology screen is negative for alcohol and drugs of nonmedical use. His examination is significant for several neurologic findings, including altered proprioception, distal numbness, hyporeflexia, confusion, and nystagmus. Perioral and tongue examinations are unremarkable. Which of the following vitamin deficiencies is likely the cause of his symptoms?
englishExplanation:
Vitamin B1, thiamine, is necessary for energy, carbohydrate, lipid, and amino acid metabolism. It acts as a component of the coenzyme responsible for the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A. Thiamine is also essential for proper nerve and muscle function. Risk factors for deficiency include a diet high in refined sugars, alcohol use disorder, malnourishment, pancreatitis, liver disease, inflammatory bowel disease, bariatric surgery, kidney failure, chemotherapy, cancer, acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, hyperthyroidism, and chronic diarrhea.

Although uncommon in most resource-rich countries, thiamine deficiency still exists in present-day correctional facilities. Chronic thiamine deficiency can lead to beriberi, a condition marked by cardiac (wet beriberi) and nervous system (dry beriberi) abnormalities. Concerning dry beriberi symptoms include numbness, paresthesias, decreased proprioception, ataxia, hyporeflexia, painful calves, confusion, abnormal eye movements, nystagmus, vomiting, and partial paralysis.



Deficiency of vitamin B2 (riboflavin) (B) causes rash, cracked red skin in the corner of the mouth, light sensitivity, and a painful, smooth, purplish tongue.

Deficiency of vitamin B3 (niacin) (C) is called pellagra and is characterized by diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia.

Deficiency of vitamin C (ascorbic acid) (D) is called scurvy and results in anemia, abdominal pain, frequent infections, bleeding gums, loose teeth, bruising, poor wound healing, myalgia, headache, fatigue, and bone disorders.

Symptoms of vitamin D (calciferol) (E) deficiency vary with the severity and duration of the deficiency. Most patients with a vitamin D level > 12 ng/mL but < 20 ng/mL are asymptomatic. Prolonged severe vitamin D deficiency can lead to secondary hyperparathyroidism, phosphaturia, bone demineralization, and osteomalacia (in adults)

One Step Further

Which thiamine deficiency is classically referred to by the triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion?

Reveal Answer:
Wernicke encephalopathy (or disease).

question: A 44-year-old woman presents with dizziness. She states that the room spins to the right every time she turns her head quickly. These episodes last 3–5 seconds and resolve on their own. Which of the following additional findings is most likely to be present in this patient?

options.text: Horizontal nystagmus with the Dix-Hallpike maneuver
Reproduction of vertigo with tragal pressure
Resolution of symptoms with the Epley maneuver

correctAnswer: Resolution of symptoms with the Epley maneuver
englishExplanation:
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) occurs when otoliths that reside in the utricle of the inner ear are displaced into the posterior semicircular canal. When the head is turned rapidly, these otoliths move within the canal, and the patient feels the illusion of rotational motion. The otoliths typically settle within 3–5 seconds, leading to resolution of symptoms. To diagnose BPPV, the Dix-Hallpike maneuver is performed. The patient is placed in a sitting position on a bed or examination table. The patient's head is turned 45º and is laid supine quickly with his or her head hanging off the table. A positive test occurs when the nystagmus beats upward and torsionally with a reproduction of vertigo. This is repeated for both sides, with each repetition of the maneuver having decreased intensity and duration. A positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver indicates pathology in the posterior canal ipsilateral to the direction of the patient's head.

To treat BPPV, the Epley maneuver is performed. For example, if the patient has a positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver on the right, his or her head is rotated 45º to the right, and is laid supine quickly with his or her head hanging off the table. This is identical to the Dix-Hallpike test, except this position is held for 1–2 minutes. The patient's head is then rotated 90º to the left and is again held for 1–2 minutes. The patient is then instructed to lie on his or her left side, and the head is rotated to the left 90º. The patient will be looking at the floor at a 45º angle. After being held for 1–2 more minutes, the patient is moved back to the seated position. When performed correctly, the Epley maneuver has an 85% success rate.



The Dix-Hallpike maneuver elicits rotational and vertical nystagmus in the vast majority of patients with posterior canal dysfunction, not horizontal nystagmus (A).

Low frequency hearing loss (B) is typically seen in Ménière disease, which is caused by excess fluid in the endolymphatic duct of the inner ear. It is characterized by vertigo that lasts minutes to hours without specific triggers and is often accompanied by whooshing tinnitus. Treatment includes salt restriction, diuretics, and avoidance of alcohol, tobacco, and caffeine.

Reproduction of vertigo with tragal pressure (C), also known as Hennebert sign, is seen in superior canal dehiscence. Superior canal dehiscence occurs when the bone surrounding the superior semicircular canal erodes, causing communication into the intracranial fossa of the skull. Loud noises or abrupt changes in pressure cause vertigo that lasts minutes to hours. Diagnosis is made via high-resolution temporal bone CT, and treatment is surgical.

One Step Further
Question:
What is Tullio sign?

Reveal Answer:
Vertigo resulting from loud sounds, seen in superior canal dehiscence.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)

Presents with the sudden sensation of room spinning with positional changes of the head
Episodes last seconds to minutes
Most often caused by the presence of displaced otoconia within the semicircular canals
Posterior canal most commonly affected
Dx: Dix-Hallpike maneuver (posterior canal BPPV)
Tx: particle positioning maneuver (e.g., Epley maneuver)

question: A 62-year-old woman presents to the ED with episodes of dizziness beginning 3 days ago. She describes the events as spinning sensations made worse with position changes, and she reports multiple episodes lasting < 1 day. The dizziness is associated with hearing loss, tinnitus, nausea, and vomiting. On physical examination, horizontal nystagmus and decreased hearing on the left are present. The remainder of the ear and neurologic examination is within normal limits. A head CT and brain MRI are performed and are negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Ménière disease is characterized by episodic symptoms that include vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus, and a sense of fullness in the ear. Episodes can last from 20 minutes to 4 hours. Most cases involve one ear but may affect both ears over time. The exact cause is unknown but is thought to be due to excessive fluid in the inner ear (endolymphatic hydrops). The diagnosis is made after two episodes of vertigo, each lasting 20 minutes or longer (but no longer than 24 hours), hearing loss detected by audiometric examination (hearing test), and tinnitus or a feeling of fullness in the ear. There is no cure for Ménière disease, but symptomatic treatment options may include a low-salt diet, diuretic therapy, intratympanic injection of gentamicin or dexamethasone, and avoidance of caffeine, smoking, and alcohol. In chronic, severe, and disabling cases, surgery may be an option. Acute vertigo symptoms may be treated in the ED with benzodiazepines, such as diazepam, as it has sedative effects on the limbic system, thalamus, and hypothalamus. Antihistamines and antiemetics are also effective, such as meclizine, diphenhydramine, promethazine, and prochlorperazine.



An acoustic neuroma (A)causes a gradual onset and progressive worsening of hearing loss and tinnitus and may advance to neurologic signs such as ataxia. MRI is more sensitive than CT in detection and diagnosis. It can be treated by radiation and surgery.

Labyrinthitis (B) can be divided into three different subclasses: serous (most common), suppurative, and toxic (due to ototoxic medications). Each is associated with vertigo and hearing loss. Diagnosis is made by history and physical examination. Classically, labyrinthitis presents as a single, acute episode, contrasted with the multiple remitting and relapsing episodes seen in Ménière disease. Treatment is aimed at the underlying cause along with supportive care.

Vestibular neuritis (D) is associated with a sudden onset of severe vertigo increasing in intensity for hours then gradually subsiding over several days. Mild positional vertigo often lasts for weeks to months. It does not have any associated auditory symptoms. On examination, there may be spontaneous nystagmus toward the affected side. Treatment is supportive.

One Step Further
Question:
What cranial nerve transmits sound and equilibrium information?

Reveal Answer:
Cranial nerve VIII, the vestibulocochlear nerve.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Ménière Disease

Commonly presents with low-frequency hearing loss, episodic vertigo, fluctuating tinnitus or aural symptoms
Most often caused by too much inner ear endolymph and increased pressure within the inner ear
Dx: clinical
Tx options may include lifestyle changes (e.g., low-salt diet), pharmacologic therapy (e.g., diuretics, betahistine)

question: A 19-year-old man presents to the ED with fever, headache, and vision changes. On physical exam, you note unilateral lateral gaze palsy and periorbital edema. Vital signs are BP 100/60 mm Hg, HR 120 bpm, RR 20/min, and T 102.9°F (39.4°C). Which of the following is the most common preceding illness that progresses into this patient's most likely disease process?
englishExplanation:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with cavernous sinus thrombosis. Cavernous sinus thrombosis is usually a late complication of acute infectious sinusitis. It is more rarely caused by bacteremia or infections of the maxillary teeth. The cavernous sinuses are the most centrally located of the dural sinuses and lie on either side of the sella turcica and adjacent to the sphenoid sinus. Thus, cavernous sinus thrombosis is more commonly seen with sphenoid or ethmoid sinusitis. The internal carotid artery passes through the cavernous sinus. The third, fourth, sixth, and portions of the fifth cranial nerves also course through the sinus. This close proximity of veins, arteries, nerves, and paranasal sinuses accounts for the classic presentation of the disease. The clinical presentation is usually due to the venous obstruction as well as impairment of the cranial nerves that are near the cavernous sinus. Headache is the most common presenting symptom and is usually followed by fevers, periorbital edema, and cranial nerve signs. Lateral gaze palsy (isolated cranial nerve VI palsy) is most common as CN VI lies freely within the sinus, while the others course within the lateral walls of the sinus. As the infection tracks posteriorly, patients develop visual disturbances and proptosis. Periorbital edema and vision changes rapidly become bilateral due to the communicating veins bridging the cavernous sinuses. Cavernous sinus thrombosis should be considered in all patients with a headache and cranial nerve abnormalities.

Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a clinical diagnosis, although imaging is often used in cases of diagnostic uncertainty or to confirm the diagnosis. CT angiography is often used as a screening imaging study. However, a negative CT scan cannot rule out cavernous sinus thrombosis reliably when the clinical suspicion is high. MRI with MR venography (MRV) is the preferred imaging choice as the MRV will show the absence of venous flow in the affected cavernous sinus. Cavernous sinus thrombosis is generally a fulminant process with high rates of morbidity and mortality. Fortunately, the incidence of cavernous sinus thrombosis has decreased greatly with the advent of effective antimicrobial agents. Staphylococcus aureus accounts for approximately 70% of all infections. The clinician should also consider emergent otolaryngology consultation and admission to ICU level care for further care of these patients.



While bacterial meningitis (B), facial cellulitis (C), and periapical abscess (D) may all lead to cavernous sinus thrombosis, it is most commonly associated with direct extension of acute sinusitis.

One Step Further
Question:
What serious head and neck infection is classically preceded by a dental infection?

Reveal Answer:
Ludwig angina.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis

Life-threatening condition
Caused by infection, often S. aureus
Presentation: fever, periorbital edema, chemosis
CN VI dysfunction (lateral gaze palsy)
Dx: MRI, CT
Tx: antibiotics, heparin

ليش: هالمريض عنده علامات وأعراض بتتوافق مع الـ cavernous sinus thrombosis، واللي عادةً بيجي كمضاعفة متأخرة من عدوى الـ acute sinusitis. وبحالات أقل بيجي من bacteremia أو عدوى الأسنان في الـ maxillary، وأكتر شي بيتشوف مع الـ sphenoid أو ethmoid sinusitis لأنها قريبة من الـ cavernous sinuses. والعرض الأكثر شيوعاً هو الـ headache وبعدها الـ fever والـ periorbital edema وعلامات الأعصاب القحفية.
الفخ: الطلاب بيختاروا bacterial meningitis لأنها بتسبب fever و headache، بس وجود unilateral lateral gaze palsy والـ periorbital edema بيوجه نحو الـ cavernous sinus thrombosis واللي مصدرها الأكثر شيوعاً هو الـ acute sinusitis.

question: In evaluating a patient with nystagmus, you suspect the main cause is peripheral vestibular dysfunction. You decide to perform caloric testing. Which physical exam findings are expected in a patient with normal vestibular function?

options.text: Cold water in the left ear produces conjugate gaze to the left without nystagmus
Cold water in the right ear produces nystagmus to the left
Cold water in the right ear produces nystagmus to the right
Warm water in the left ear produces nystagmus to the right
Warm water in the right ear produces nystagmus to the left

correctAnswer: Cold water in the right ear produces nystagmus to the left
englishExplanation:
Any patient with nystagmus requires a complete neuro-ophthalmic examination, notably visual acuity, pupillary reaction to light, extraocular muscle function, confrontational testing, and measuring intraocular pressure. Certain specifics to look for in a patient with nystagmus include changes with gaze direction and dampening with fixation. It is also important to notice the fast phase direction and check for the presence of tinnitus, decreased hearing, vertigo, and torticollis. Another test commonly used in the evaluation of nystagmus is called caloric testing, in which the external auditory canals are irrigated with cold and warm water or air.

During caloric testing in a patient with nystagmus, the focus is on evaluating vestibular function and the integrity of the vestibulo-ocular reflex. The vestibulo-ocular reflex is a critical component of maintaining gaze stability during head movements by producing eye movements in the opposite direction to the head movement, allowing clear vision. Caloric testing involves irrigating the ear canal with warm or cold water or air, which creates a temperature gradient that stimulates the horizontal semicircular canal. This stimulation induces nystagmus, which is an involuntary eye movement, and the direction and amplitude of the nystagmus provide critical information on the asymmetry between the two vestibular systems.

When cold water is used, it mimics a head rotation to the opposite side. Warm water mimics a head rotation to the same side. Typically, warm irrigation causes nystagmus with the fast phase toward the irrigated ear, while cold irrigation causes it away from the irrigated ear. A helpful mnemonic describing the direction of expected fast-phase nystagmus during caloric testing is COWS, which stands for cold opposite side, warm same side. If this is not seen, consider vestibular dysfunction of the side being tested.



Cold water in the left ear producing conjugate gaze to the left without nystagmus (A) describes a normal response to caloric testing when a patient is in a coma, indicating intact brain stem function.

Cold water in the right ear producing nystagmus to the right (C) is an abnormal reaction. It normally produces nystagmus to the opposite side, not the same side.

Warm water in the left ear (D) or warm water in the right ear (E) normally produces nystagmus to the same side, not the opposite side.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the oculocephalic reflex (doll’s head phenomenon)?

Reveal Answer:
A normal reflex during which the eyes conjugately move in an opposite direction to head rotation, thus maintaining fixation on an object. If absent, consider a vestibular cause of nystagmus.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Caloric Reflex Testing

Test vestibulo-ocular reflex
Performed by infusing cold or warm water into external ear canal
Normal response
Nystagmus with fast component toward infused side with warm water or toward noninfused side with cold water
COWS: cold opposite, warm same
May induce nausea and vomiting
Abnormal test result suggests peripheral lesion or central vestibular disorder
Evaluation of coma
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ caloric testing بتعمل بغسل قناة الأذن الخارجية بماء بارد أو دافي أو هوا، وهذا بيخلي فرق بالحرارة يحفز الـ horizontal semicircular canal وبينتج عنه nystagmus. والهدف هو تقييم وظيفة الـ vestibular وعمل الـ vestibulo-ocular reflex اللي بحافظ على ثبات النظر أثناء حركة الراس. وبالوظيفة السليمة، الماء البارد بالأذن اليمنى بينتج nystagmus بيطلع نحو اليسار لأن الـ reflex بيعمل حركة عين بعكس اتجاه المحفز.
الفخ: الطلاب بيعكسوا الاتجاه ويختاروا إنه الماء البارد بالأذن اليمنى يعطي nystagmus نحو اليمين، بس القاعدة إنه الحلو الدافي بيعطي nystagmus نحو نفس الجهة والبارد نحو الجهة المعاكسة.

question: A 50-year-old woman presents with a sudden onset of dizziness, nausea, and vomiting for 1 day. She recently recovered from a bout of rhinosinusitis. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical exam reveals horizontal nystagmus and serous fluid behind the right tympanic membrane. When the examiner strikes a tuning fork and places it on the patient’s forehead, sound localizes to the left ear. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Labyrinthitis is a generally benign, self-limiting inflammation of the cochlear and vestibular apparatus. It may either be suppurative, caused by otitis media, mastoiditis, or meningitis, or serous, caused by an inflammatory response to a viral infection in close proximity. As such, serous labyrinthitis is typically preceded by a viral infection. Symptoms include rapid onset of severe vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and unilateral hearing loss, a distinguishing feature between labyrinthitis and vestibular neuritis. On physical exam, patients may have middle ear findings suggestive of a viral infection, such as serous fluid behind the tympanic membrane, and nystagmus, which may be unilateral, horizontal, or torsional. The Weber test is a physical exam test used to detect unilateral conductive and sensorineural hearing loss. It is conducted by striking a tuning fork and placing it on the middle of the patient’s forehead. Sound should localize to both ears equally in patients without sensorineural or conductive hearing loss. In patients with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, such as those with labyrinthitis, sound localizes to the unaffected ear. Sound localizes to the affected ear in patients with conductive hearing loss. The diagnosis of labyrinthitis is made clinically. Symptoms may last for days to weeks. Treatment includes corticosteroids and vestibular suppressants, such as benzodiazepines and antihistamines, particularly in the acute phase.



Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (A) presents as vertigo and nystagmus that is worse with head movement. It does not typically present with unilateral hearing loss. Endolymphatic hydrops (B), also known as Ménière disease, occurs due to increased endolymph in the cochlea and labyrinth of the ear. It presents similarly to labyrinthitis with unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo. Patients with Ménière disease typically have disease onset between the ages of 20–40 and have multiple episodes lasting on the order of hours. Lateral medullary syndrome (D), also known as Wallenberg syndrome, is caused by occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). Patients present with a constellation of symptoms in addition to vertigo and nystagmus, such as ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis), dysphagia, contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation to the body, and ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature to the face.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the nonpharmacologic treatment of benign paroxysmal peripheral vertigo?

Reveal Answer:
The Epley maneuver.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Labyrinthitis

Inflammatory process involving the inner ear membranous labyrinth
Sx: vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus
Vestibular neuritis + unilateral hearing loss = labyrinthitis
Can last days to 1 week
Risks: recent upper respiratory infection (most common)
Medications
Concurrent otitis media
PE: spontaneous horizontal nystagmus
Dx: clinical
Tx: corticosteroids, symptomatic care, vestibular rehabilitation
Remove any offending agents
Bacterial cause requires antibiotics and possibly surgical drainage
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ labyrinthitis هو التهاب حميد عادةً ومحدود ذاتياً بيصيب الـ cochlear و vestibular apparatus، وممكن يكون suppurative من الـ otitis media أو الـ mastoiditis أو الـ meningitis، أو serous من استجابة التهابية لعدوى فيروسية قريبة. والـ serous labyrinthitis بتسبقها عادةً عدوى فيروسية، والأعراض تشمل بداية سريعة لـ vertigo شديد مع nausea و vomiting وفقدان سمع من جهة وحدة، وهاد اللي بيفرقها عن الـ vestibular neuritis. وعلامات الأذن الوسطى زي سوائل مصلية خلف الـ tympanic membrane بتدعم التشخيص.
الفخ: الطلاب بيختاروا الـ endolymphatic hydrops لأنه بيربطوه بفقدان السمع بالـ Ménière، بس الـ labyrinthitis نوبتها حادة وحادة البداية بعد عدوى تنفسية والفرق الأساسي إنه فيها فقدان سمع مع التهاب أذن وسطى واضح.

question: A woman develops an acute attack of vertigo, nausea, and vomiting. You suspect viral labyrinthitis. Which of the following medications is the best choice for treating the vertigo?
englishExplanation:
Commonly a complication of otitis media, upper respiratory infection, or meningitis, labyrinthitis is an abnormality of the inner ear vestibular system, which consists of three semicircular canals, vestibule, utricle, and saccule. When the vestibular system is damaged, injured, or inflamed, balance deficits and vertigo arise. However, since an anatomic connection between the vestibular system and cochlea exists, tinnitus and decreased hearing also occur. The classic clinical picture of labyrinthitis is acute, profound, incapacitating vertigo, with nausea, vomiting, and nystagmus. Tinnitus and decreased hearing usually accompany the onset of vertigo. These symptoms resemble those of Meniere disease. However, in Meniere disease, symptoms are intermittent and possibly less severe. Furthermore, the pathology is different between the two conditions. Labyrinthitis is mainly due to inflammation, while an excess of inner ear fluid causes Meniere disease. Treatment of suspected viral labyrinthitis includes bed rest, hydration, antiemetics, and vestibular depressants. Treatment with corticosteroids during the acute period of vertigo has been shown to improve the recovery of peripheral vestibular function in patients with acute labyrinthitis.



Currently, the role of antiviral therapy, like acyclovir (A), in the treatment of labyrinthitis is not established. Studies to date do not show an improvement over placebo. Phentermine (B) is used as an appetite suppressant and plays no role in the treatment of labyrinthitis. Prochlorperazine (D), an antiemetic, is commonly used in the treatment of acute viral labyrinthitis. Its dopamine antagonism and anticholinergic effects help relieve nausea and vomiting but do not diminish the distressing sensation of vertigo.

One Step Further
Question:
Name two common viral causes of prenatal hearing loss?

Reveal Answer:
Rubella and cytomegalovirus.

Vestibular neuritis + unilateral hearing loss = labyrinthitis

Concurrent otitis media

Dx: clinical
Tx: corticosteroids, symptomatic care, vestibular rehabilitation
Remove any offending agents

arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ labyrinthitis بحسب المصدر هو خلل بالجهاز الدهليزي بالأذن الداخلية، واللي بيتكون من ثلاث قنوات هلالية والـ vestibule والـ utricle والـ saccule، ولما يتضرر أو يلتهب بيصير خلل بالتوازن و vertigo. وبيترافق مع tinnitus ونقص سمع لأن في اتصال تشريحي بين الجهاز الدهليزي والـ cochlea، والصورة الكلاسيكية هي vertigo شديد وحاد مع nausea و vomiting و nystagmus. والعلاج لحالة الـ viral labyrinthitis المفترضة بيتضمن راحة بالسرير والـ hydration والـ antiemetics والـ vestibular depressants.
الفخ: الطلاب بيختاروا acyclovir لأنه مضاد فيروسي، بس المصدر بيقول إنه دور مضادات الفيروسات غير مثبت بالعلاج، والـ corticosteroids بالمرحلة الحادة بتحسن استرجاع الوظيفة الدهليزية الطرفية.

question: A 57-year-old man with hypertension presents with the report of a floater in the right eye for the past 6 hours. He states that he has had increasing difficulty reading, as the cloudy area blocks his visual field. Additionally, he reports decreased vision in his right eye. Which of the following represents the appropriate management?

options.text: Administer timolol drops and urgently consult ophthalmology
Prescribe high-dose oral prednisone and refer to ophthalmology
Prescribe topical antibiotics and refer to ophthalmology
Refer patient to ophthalmology for further assessment

englishExplanation:
Posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) is an age-related separation of the vitreous gel from the retina caused by progressive vitreous degeneration and shrinkage. The prevalence increases with age, with additional risk factors including myopia, trauma, and intraocular inflammation. Pathophysiologically, aging causes collagen fibril aggregation and vitreous liquefaction, which, combined with weakened vitreoretinal adhesion, leads to posterior vitreous separation. While most cases are benign, tractional forces during acute vitreous detachment can cause full-thickness retinal tears in areas of strong vitreoretinal adhesion, and untreated retinal tears often progress to retinal detachment.

Patients typically present with monocular floaters and photopsias (brief peripheral flashes from retinal traction). High-risk features indicating possible retinal tear or detachment include decreased visual acuity, visual field defects, vitreous hemorrhage, and vitreous pigment (tobacco dust). Diagnosis is primarily clinical and made through dilated funduscopic examination, though optical coherence tomography can confirm PVD and identify vitreomacular traction. While most posterior chamber findings are identified via comprehensive ophthalmologic examination, point-of-care ocular ultrasound has gained increased popularity in the evaluation of the posterior chamber by emergency clinicians and may identify vitreous hemorrhage and vitreous or retinal detachment.

Emergency department management depends on risk stratification. Patients with decreased vision, visual field defects, vitreous hemorrhage, or vitreous pigment require emergent same-day ophthalmology consultation for comprehensive retinal examination and possible laser retinopexy or surgical repair. Patients with new-onset floaters or flashes but without high-risk features can be referred for outpatient ophthalmology evaluation within 1–2 weeks, with counseling to return immediately if vision worsens or visual field defects develop. Even when initial examination shows uncomplicated PVD, most delayed detachments occur beyond 6 weeks, making follow-up examination essential, especially in patients with vitreous hemorrhage, lattice degeneration, or fellow-eye history of retinal tear or detachment. Complications of untreated retinal detachment include progressive photoreceptor disruption, tissue necrosis, and permanent vision loss.



Timolol (A) is a beta-blocker used to reduce intraocular pressure in acute angle-closure glaucoma or other conditions with elevated intraocular pressure, not for PVD or retinal pathology.

Corticosteroids (C) are indicated for inflammatory ocular conditions such as posterior uveitis or optic neuritis, not for mechanical vitreoretinal pathology like PVD with potential retinal tear or detachment.

Topical antibiotics (D) treat bacterial conjunctivitis or corneal infections presenting with eye pain, discharge, and injection, not the painless floaters and vision changes characteristic of vitreoretinal pathology.

While appropriate for uncomplicated cases with floaters or flashes alone, this patient’s decreased vision represents a high-risk feature requiring emergent same-day evaluation rather than routine outpatient referral (E).

One Step Further
Question:
What percentage of patients with posterior vitreous detachment have a retinal detachment?

Reveal Answer:
14%.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Posterior Vitreous Detachment

Detachment of vitreous gel from retina
Precursor to retinal detachment occurring over weeks to months
Most common cause of retinal tears
Sx: floaters
Dx: ultrasound with hyperechoic floating membrane freely moving and NOT attached to the optic disc
Tx: ophthalmology evaluation
arabicExplanation:
ليش: هالمريض عنده floaters أحادية العين مع انخفاض حدة البصر وهذا يوحي بالـ posterior vitreous detachment، واللي هو انفصال مرتبط بالعمر للـ vitreous gel عن الـ retina بسبب تنكس وانكماش تدريجي. وبنسبة كبيرة الحالات حميدة، بس قوى الشد أثناء الانفصال الحاد ممكن تعمل تمزقات كاملة السماكة بالـ retina بمناطق الالتصاق القوي، والتمزقات غير المعالجة غالباً بتتطور لانفصال الشبكية. والعلامات عالية الخطورة اللي بتشير لتمزق أو انفصال هي نقص حدة البصر وعيوب المجال البصري ونزف الـ vitreous وصباغ الـ vitreous. والتشخيص بيتعمل بالـ dilated funduscopic exam.
الفخ: الطلاب بيختاروا مراجعة عادية للـ ophthalmology، بس وجود نقص حدة البصر ووجود انسداد بالمجال بيمثلوا علامات عالية الخطورة بتستدعي تقييم عيون إسعافي فوري.

question: A 78-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of painless vision loss in her right eye. She has a past medical history significant for hypertension, cerebral vascular accident, and atrial fibrillation. She is no longer on anticoagulation secondary to frequent falls. The patient states the symptoms started 40 minutes prior to arrival. Other than a right-sided mild headache she has no other complaints today. Vital signs are all unremarkable. Physical examination is remarkable for a heart exam that reveals an irregular rhythm with a regular rate and afferent pupillary defect on the right. She denies any temporal tenderness to palpation. Visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye and light perception only for the right eye. What additional historical or physical finding would you expect with this patient?

options.text: Cherry red macula on fundoscopic examination

correctAnswer: Cherry red macula on fundoscopic examination
englishExplanation:
Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) classically presents with a sudden onset of painless severe monocular vision loss. This is often associated with amaurosis fugax. If the occlusion occurs in the central artery, a patient will experience complete visual loss, whereas if the occlusion occurs in one of the arterial branches, then there will be sudden partial vision loss. Classically this presents with abrupt vision loss, with a large majority only being able to count fingers or have some light perception. An afferent pupillary defect and a cherry red spot (red macula) with surrounding opacification of the surrounding retina on fundoscopic evaluation may also be present. A thorough evaluation of an embolic source should be obtained, with the carotid arteries or heart being the most common sources of embolism. Temporal arteritis must be excluded as a diagnosis. The American Heart Association recommends that institutions develop protocols for the rapid evaluation of CRAO in a stroke center. There is a paucity of evidence regarding the best treatment for CRAO, but thrombolytics are reasonable within an appropriate time frame (< 4.5 hours). Other traditional treatments, digital orbital massage, acetazolamide, and timolol, have not proved beneficial.



Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (B) is a gaze abnormality that is characterized by impaired or weak adduction with horizontal eye movement of the affected eye as well as an abduction nystagmus of the opposite eye. This results from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, most commonly due to stroke or demyelination (multiple sclerosis). If the cause was due to multiple sclerosis, the patient would have painful, not painless, vision loss.

Jaw claudication (C) in a patient experiencing acute or subacute monocular vision loss is concerning for temporal arteritis, also known as giant cell arteritis. Temporal arteritis is a systemic vasculitis that can cause ischemic optic neuropathy. Patients classically are women older than 50 years of age. Associated symptoms are headache, jaw claudication, scalp or temporal tenderness, fatigue, sore throat, or anorexia. An afferent pupillary defect is often present, and fundoscopic examination may reveal flame hemorrhages. When suspected, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein (CRP) should be obtained, as both are typically elevated, with the CRP being the most sensitive of the two. Without a correct diagnosis or treatment, bilateral blindness can occur.

Central vein occlusion (D) causes acute, painless monocular vision loss similar to central retinal artery occlusion. Optic disc edema, retinal hemorrhages, and cotton-wool spots, also known as “blood and thunder,” will be present on optic examination. Vision loss is generally not as severe, with more blurring than complete vision loss compared to the arterial counterpart, and no immediate treatment is required other than discontinuing predisposing drugs (oral contraceptives or diuretics). Consultation with an ophthalmologist should be obtained.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the gold standard for diagnosing giant cell arteritis?

Reveal Answer:
Temporal artery biopsy.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Central Retinal Artery Occlusion

Sx: sudden, painless monocular vision loss
Funduscopy: retinal whitening, cherry-red spot, boxcar appearance (from segmental blood flow)
Tx: ocular emergency, evidence unclear regarding optimal therapy
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الـ central retinal artery occlusion بتجي كلاسيكياً بفقدان بصر وحيد العين شديد وغير مؤلم ومفاجئ، وممكن تترافق مع الـ amaurosis fugax. وإذا صار الانسداد بالشريان المركزي بيعاني المريض فقدان بصر كامل، وإذا صار بأحد الفروع بيصير فقدان جزئي مفاجئ، ومعظم الحالات بتقدر تعد الأصابع أو عندها إحساس ضوء بس. وكلاسيكياً بتشوف afferent pupillary defect و cherry red spot مع تعتيم الشبكة المحيطة بالـ fundoscopy.
الفخ: الطلاب بيختاروا retinal hemorrhages لأنهم بيربطوا بينها وبين ارتفاع الضغط، بس الخزعة الكلاسيكية للـ CRAO هي الـ cherry red macula والفحص بيتضمن كمان تقييم مصدر embolic من الشريان السباتي أو القلب.

question: A 45-year-old woman with a history of high blood pressure presents to the emergency department with vertigo. She developed sudden-onset vertigo associated with hearing loss in her left ear starting 2 hours ago. She notes having a “cold” a couple of weeks ago and has no ear pain at present. Which of the following physical exam findings is most consistent with a diagnosis of labyrinthitis in this patient?

options.text: Ability to hold gaze fixation with bilateral head thrust
Left eye gaze correction after uncovering the left eye
Rightward nystagmus when looking left or right

correctAnswer: Rightward nystagmus when looking left or right
englishExplanation:
Labyrinthitis is an inner ear disease characterized by inflammation of both branches of the eighth cranial nerve resulting in hearing loss and vertigo. In contrast, vestibular neuritis affects only the vestibular branch and thus causes vertigo without hearing loss. Labyrinthitis is most commonly due to a viral or postviral process, and common culprits include influenza, varicella, measles, mumps, and rubella. Bacterial causes are less common and can evoke labyrinthitis via mechanisms that are either serous or suppurative (e.g., meningitis and otitis media).

Symptoms are typically sudden onset with vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and hearing loss (tinnitus may also be present). The physical exam is immediately notable for unilateral horizontal nystagmus with fast beats away from the affected ear. The HINTS exam (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew) can aid in distinguishing peripheral and central vertigo in patients with at least one stroke risk factor and no history of recurrent vertigo. The presence of all three of the following findings is indicative of a peripheral cause: an abnormal head impulse test, normal nystagmus (e.g., unidirectional, horizontal, beating away from the affected side), and normal test of skew. The head impulse test is performed by instructing the patient to fix their gaze on the examiner while the examiner quickly turns the patient’s head to the left and right. The presence of a corrective saccade only when the head is turned to the affected side is abnormal and reassuring for a peripheral cause. The absence of nystagmus or the presence of unilateral and horizontal nystagmus is reassuring for a peripheral cause. Test of skew is achieved by instructing the patient to stare at the examiner’s nose and then covering and uncovering the eye on the affected side. If there is no skew or deviation of the eye seen upon uncovering the eye, this is considered normal and reassuring.

The treatment of labyrinthitis depends on the underlying etiology. Viral or postviral causes are largely self-limited and resolve in days to weeks. The use of steroids in viral labyrinthitis is unclear, with some studies showing benefits and others showing no effect. However, it should be noted that Ramsay Hunt syndrome (varicella zoster affecting cranial nerves V–IX) can present with a predominant eighth nerve palsy and requires treatment with steroids and antiviral medication. Bacterial causes should be treated with appropriate antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanic acid for otitis media). Symptomatic medications should target vertigo (e.g., meclizine or diazepam) as well as nausea (e.g., promethazine).



The ability to hold visual fixation with bilateral head thrust (A) is a normal head impulse test and is not consistent with a peripheral cause of vertigo. Labyrinthitis affects the vestibulo-ocular reflex when the head is turned to the affected side.

Left eye gaze correction after uncovering the left eye (B) is abnormal and indicative of a brainstem lesion. This is also referred to as vertical disconjugate gaze.

Left-sided ataxia (C) or ataxia of any kind is not associated with labyrinthitis. Patients may have an unsteady gait (listing toward the affected side), but there is no loss of coordination.

One Step Further
Question:
What further treatment can be recommended to patients with vertigo poorly controlled with medication?

Reveal Answer:
Vestibular rehabilitation.

Labyrinthitis

Inflammatory process involving the inner ear membranous labyrinth
Sx: vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus
Vestibular neuritis + unilateral hearing loss = labyrinthitis
Can last days to 1 week
Risks: recent upper respiratory infection (most common)
Medications
Concurrent otitis media
PE: spontaneous horizontal nystagmus
Dx: clinical
Tx: corticosteroids, symptomatic care, vestibular rehabilitation
Remove any offending agents
Bacterial cause requires antibiotics and possibly surgical drainage

question: A 48-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for 1 week of vertigo. The vertigo is nonpositional and episodic, typically lasting 1–2 hours per episode. She also notes nausea and a sensation of fullness and ringing in her left ear. She has a history of nephrotic syndrome and takes furosemide daily. She reports no headaches, fevers, ear pain, or ear drainage. Her cranial nerve exam is notable for diminished hearing on the left. Otoscopic examination of the ear is normal. There is no nystagmus. She has equal strength and sensation in all extremities. She is reluctant to ambulate due to her symptoms but is able to stand and walk without assistance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with the classic triad of symptoms associated with Ménière disease: hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo. The pathophysiology is poorly understood, but it is thought to be the result of increased endolymph in the labyrinthine system. Symptoms are usually unilateral but can be bilateral. The onset of vertigo is sudden and occurs in episodes that last between 20 minutes to several hours. Hearing loss is sensorineural and may persist between episodes of vertigo. There may also be associated nausea, vomiting, or aural fullness. Imaging is not required for the diagnosis of Ménière disease. However, the presence of any acute neurologic signs or symptoms should prompt evaluation for a central etiology of vertigo in the emergency department. Central causes of vertigo include cerebellar or brainstem stroke, cerebellar hemorrhage, and posterior circulation transient ischemic attack. The presence of focal weakness, persistent headache or neck pain, dysmetria, speech disturbance, acute hearing loss, visual deficits, spontaneous vertical nystagmus, or gait disturbance should prompt neuroimaging. Treatment of Ménière disease can include antihistamines, combination therapy with triamterene and hydrochlorothiazide, or calcium channel blockers. Patients with symptoms of Ménière disease should follow up with otolaryngology.



Benign paroxysmal peripheral vertigo (BPPV) (A) is the most common cause of vertigo and is due to dislodged otoconia in the semicircular canals. It presents as short episodes of vertigo and nystagmus that are < 2 minutes and worsened with positional change. The presence of vertical upward and rotary nystagmus with Dix-Hallpike testing confirms the diagnosis of BPPV. Treatment involves bedside maneuvers that reposition otoconia, such as the Epley maneuver.

Labyrinthitis (B) is a complication of otitis media, viral or bacterial. It may also present with vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus. However, it presents with constant, nonepisodic vertigo that can last several days. This patient’s symptoms are episodic, and she does not have signs or symptoms of an ear infection, which makes labyrinthitis unlikely.

Ototoxicity may be caused by various medications, including loop diuretics, aminoglycosides, and cytotoxic drugs. This patient is taking furosemide, a loop diuretic. Typically, ototoxicity will present with sensorineural hearing loss. While ototoxic medications can sometimes cause tinnitus, vertigo is rare, which makes a medication side effect (C) less likely.

Vestibular neuritis (E) is the second most common cause of vertigo. It presents as continuous vertigo that lasts for days but does not cause hearing loss or tinnitus, which makes it unlikely in this patient. Treatment is symptomatic, and it will spontaneously resolve within days to weeks.

One Step Further
Question:
Which bedside test can distinguish peripheral versus central causes of vertigo in patients with persistent vertigo and nystagmus?

Reveal Answer:
Head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew (HINTS) exam.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Ménière Disease

Commonly presents with low-frequency hearing loss, episodic vertigo, fluctuating tinnitus or aural symptoms
Most often caused by too much inner ear endolymph and increased pressure within the inner ear
Dx: clinical
Tx options may include lifestyle changes (e.g., low-salt diet), pharmacologic therapy (e.g., diuretics, betahistine)
arabicExplanation:

الفخ: الطلاب بيختاروا side effect من الـ furosemide لأنها مدرة بولي، بس أخذ الفيورسيمايد ما بيعمل نوبات متكررة معاها فقدان سمع و tinnitus وامتلاء بالأذن ولهيك التشخيص هو Ménière disease.

question: A 23-year-old woman presents to the ED with fever and headache. She was recently treated for sinusitis. However, her headache has since worsened. On physical exam, you note a unilateral lateral gaze palsy and periorbital edema. Which of the following is the most definitive diagnostic imaging study for this condition?
englishExplanation:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with cavernous sinus thrombosis. Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a clinical diagnosis, although imaging is often used in cases of diagnostic uncertainty or to confirm the diagnosis. CT angiography is often used as a screening imaging study. However, a negative CT scan cannot rule out cavernous sinus thrombosis reliably when the clinical suspicion is high. Magnetic resonance imaging with venography (MRV) is the preferred imaging choice as the MRV will show the absence of venous flow in the affected cavernous sinus.

Cavernous sinus thrombosis is usually a late complication of an infection of the paranasal sinuses. It is more rarely caused by bacteremia or infections of the maxillary teeth or other facial areas. The cavernous sinuses are the most centrally located of the dural sinuses and lie on either side of the sella turcica and adjacent to the sphenoid sinus. Thus, cavernous sinus thrombosis is more commonly seen with sphenoid or ethmoid sinusitis. The internal carotid artery passes through the cavernous sinus. The third, fourth, sixth, and portions of the fifth cranial nerves also course through the sinus. This close proximity of veins, arteries, nerves, and paranasal sinuses accounts for the classic presentation of cavernous sinus thrombosis.

The clinical presentation is usually due to the venous obstruction as well as impairment of the cranial nerves that are near the cavernous sinus. Headache is the most common presenting symptom and is usually followed by fevers, periorbital edema, and cranial nerve signs. Lateral gaze palsy due to an isolated cranial nerve VI palsy is usually seen first as CN VI lies freely within the sinus, while the others course within the lateral walls of the sinus. As the infection tracks posteriorly, patients develop visual disturbances and proptosis. Periorbital edema and vision changes rapidly become bilateral due to the communicating veins bridging the cavernous sinuses. Appearance of signs and symptoms in the contralateral eye is diagnostic of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Systemic signs indicative of sepsis are late findings. Cavernous sinus thrombosis should be considered in all patients with a headache and cranial nerve abnormalities.

Cavernous sinus thrombosis is generally a fulminant process with high rates of morbidity and mortality. Fortunately, the incidence of cavernous sinus thrombosis has decreased greatly with the advent of effective antimicrobial agents. Staphylococcus aureus accounts for most infections. Streptococcus pneumoniae, gram-negative bacilli, and anaerobes can also be seen. The generally accepted antibiotic regimen includes vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and metronidazole. Otolaryngology should be consulted, and the patient should be admitted to the ICU for further care.



While CT of the head (A) is often the first test used in patients with suspected cavernous sinus thrombosis, it is not the most definitive diagnostic test as it may miss cases usually caught by MRI with MR venography.

Invasive cerebral arteriography (B) would be the most definitive test for arterial blockage within the cerebral vasculature (although rarely done unless for interventional purposes), but does not image the venous system as well as the arterial system and is highly invasive.

Radiographs of the paranasal sinuses (D) may show air-fluid levels or opacification in sinusitis, but are not indicated in patients with cavernous sinus thrombosis.

One Step Further
Question:
What other serious neurologic condition is most often diagnosed using MRI with venography besides cavernous sinus thrombosis?

Reveal Answer:
Dural venous sinus thrombosis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis

Life-threatening condition
Caused by infection, often S. aureus
Presentation: fever, periorbital edema, chemosis
CN VI dysfunction (lateral gaze palsy)
Dx: MRI, CT
Tx: antibiotics, heparin
arabicExplanation:

الفخ: الطلاب بيختاروا الـ CT للراس لأنه الفحص الأسرع والأكثر توفراً، بس الـ CT السلبي ما بينفي التشخيص عند الشك العالي والـ MRV هو الأدق لإثبات غياب التدفق الوريدي.

question: A 30-year-old man with no significant medical history presents to the emergency department with dizziness. He reports that the symptoms were sudden in onset shortly after getting out of bed. You suspect vestibular neuritis. Using your hand, you cover one of the patient's eyes and quickly switch to covering the patient’s other eye while his gaze is on a fixed target. What would you expect to find if your suspicions are true?

options.text: A vertical corrective movement of the uncovered eye

englishExplanation:
The physical exam maneuver explained above is called the test of skew. You would expect a negative test of skew in a patient with vestibular neuritis, which is commonly caused by a viral or postviral inflammatory disorder affecting the vestibular portion of the eighth cranial nerve. Test of skew is part of a constellation of oculomotor exam maneuvers you can perform referred to as the head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew (HINTS) exam, and it is highly specific and sensitive for differentiating between central versus peripheral causes of persistent vertigo. In a patient with peripheral vertigo, you would expect no skew deviation on the exam.



Vertical corrective movements of the uncovered eye (A) would occur in patients with a central cause of vertigo. Skew deviation occurs in the presence of right-left imbalance in the otolith-ocular inputs, which causes vertical misalignment of the eyes. As the examiner alternates covering the patient’s eyes, a vertical (either up or down) corrective movement would be seen in the uncovered eye in a positive exam.

Direction-changing nystagmus (B) also suggests a central cause of vertigo and is not assessed during the test of skew.

Patients with peripheral vertigo may show improvement of symptoms (C) with a Dix-Hallpike maneuver, but this is not expected with skew deviation testing.

One Step Further
Question:
What diagnosis should be suspected in a young patient who had chiropractic manipulation of the neck and presents with acute onset headache, neck pain, vertigo, and ataxia?

Reveal Answer:
Cervical artery dissection.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Vestibular Neuritis

Viral or postviral inflammatory disorder of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)
Sx: acute vertigo associated with nausea, vomiting, gait impairment
PE: nystagmus, positive head impulse test, negative test of skew, fall toward on affected side
Tx: glucocorticoid taper ± antihistamines, antiemetics
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الاختبار المذكور هو test of skew، وفي المريض اللي عنده vestibular neuritis من أصل محيطي لازم تكون النتيجة سلبية، يعني ما في أي حركة عمودية للعين المكشوفة. السبب إن vestibular neuritis التهاب فيروسي أو بعد فيروسي يصيب الجزء الدهليزي من العصب القحفي الثامن. هالاختبار جزء من مجموعة HINTS اللي حساسة جداً ومحددة للتفريق بين أسباب الدوار المركزية والمحيطية.
الفخ: في ناس يختارون الحركة العمودية التصحيحية للعين المكشوفة، وهي تصير بالسبب المركزي للدوار مو المحيطي، وترتبط باختلال التوازن بين مدخلات otolith-ocular. فرّق بينهم إن المحيطي ما يعطي انحراف عمودي بالاختبار.

question: A 16-year-old girl presents to the ED with altered mental status. Her parents report that she became concerned about a headache 3 hours earlier and went to her room to lie down. When they checked on her 1 hour later, she was lethargic with slurred speech. On examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14, and she has right-sided lower facial drooping and decreased motor strength to the left upper and lower extremities. Her HR is 80 bpm, and her BP is 110/70 mm Hg. You learn that many members of the patient’s family have experienced thrombotic events. What is the mechanism behind this patient’s risk factor for these symptoms?
englishExplanation:
This patient likely has factor V Leiden, an inherited thrombophilia caused by a mutation to the factor V gene that leads to a factor V protein resistant to inactivation by activated protein C. Activated protein C is a natural anticoagulant. Therefore, resistance to its effect (or ineffective activated protein C activity) leads to increased activity of factor V and, thus, increased thrombin formation. Factor V Leiden puts patients at risk for venous and arterial thromboembolism, although the risk of arterial thromboembolism is much smaller than venous thromboembolism. Patients can present with superficial venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, cerebral vein thrombosis, myocardial infarction, or stroke. Factor V Leiden has been associated with stroke, especially in young people, young women, and those who smoke. Diagnosis is made via genetic testing.

The management of complications of factor V Leiden rests on treating the thromboembolic event. Treatment for stroke is dependent on the timing of symptom onset. In this case, thrombolytic agents, such as tissue plasminogen activator, could be considered in consultation with a neurologist. For hemodynamically stable patients presenting with venous thromboembolic events, low-molecular-weight heparin is usually the preferred initial treatment choice. The patient’s baseline platelet count, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, kidney function, and liver function should all be obtained before starting therapies, if possible.



Factor V Leiden is caused by resistance to the effects of activated protein C, not increased levels of protein C (A).

Increased protein C (B) and protein S (C) activity are not associated with an increased risk of venous and arterial thromboembolism.

One Step Further
Question:
Why is unfractionated heparin the preferred choice of anticoagulant for patients requiring surgical intervention?

Reveal Answer:
Unfractionated heparin has a shorter half-life than low-molecular-weight heparin.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Factor V Leiden

Autosomal dominant genetic disorder
Most common inherited hypercoagulability disorder
Most patients are heterozygous
Increased risk of venous thromboembolism
Risk increases with homozygosity or compound heterozygosity (carry another thrombophilia variant)
VTE risk reduction may include prophylactic anticoagulation for surgery and pregnancy, avoidance of exogenous estrogen
arabicExplanation:
ليش: المريضة عندها factor V Leiden، وهو thrombophilia وراثي بسبب طفرة بجين factor V تخلي البروتين مقاوم للتعطيل بواسطة activated protein C. ولأن activated protein C مضاد تخثر طبيعي، فالمقاومة له أو عدم فعالية activated protein C بتزيد نشاط factor V وبالتالي تكوين thrombin أكثر. هذا يرفع خطر الجلطات الوريدية والشريانية، وأحياناً يسبب جلطة بأوردة الدماغ أو سكتة عند الشباب خاصة المدخنين والنساء الصغيرات. التشخيص بالفحص الجيني.
الفخ: كتير طلاب يختارون زيادة نشاط أو مستويات protein C أو protein S، لكن المشكلة الأساسية هي مقاومة factor V للتعطيل وليس زيادة هالمضادات. تذكّر إن activated protein C هو الطبيعي المعطَّل، فالجواب هو عدم فعالية تأثيره.

question: A 39-year-old man with a history of acute myeloid leukemia presents to the ED with right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking. On physical exam, you note dense right-sided hemiplegia of the upper and lower extremities as well as expressive aphasia. Which of the following laboratory abnormalities would you also expect to find?
englishExplanation:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms associated with hyperviscosity syndrome. Hyperviscosity syndrome is defined as elevated serum viscosity that causes sludging, decreased microvascular perfusion, and vascular stasis. While hyperviscosity syndrome is most often due to elevated serum protein, it can also be caused by marked leukocytosis with > 100,000 cells/mm3 associated with diseases such as leukemias, most often when patients experience a blast crisis. Laboratory testing will reveal this significant leukocytosis. Signs and symptoms of hyperviscosity syndrome are primarily secondary to end-organ ischemia creating mimics of disease processes such as myocardial ischemia, stroke, pulmonary infarction, congestive heart failure, kidney failure, mucosal hemorrhages, or visual disturbances secondary to retinal ischemia. Management of hyperviscosity syndrome depends upon the etiology. Supportive care for any etiology includes intravenous fluid hydration and diuresis in tandem. Temporizing measures for patients with leukemias include leukapheresis, patients with elevated proteins require plasmapheresis, and patients with polycythemia vera require phlebotomy.



Anemia (A) is not associated with the presentation above.

Polycythemia (C) often refers to polycythemia vera. However, this patient is not showing signs or symptoms of polycythemia vera, such as headaches, hypertension, splenomegaly, and pruritus.

Thrombocytopenia (D) is not classically associated with the typical causes of hyperviscosity syndrome.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most appropriate treatment of polycythemia vera?

Reveal Answer:
Serial phlebotomy.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Hyperviscosity Syndrome

Sludging → ↓ perfusion
Causes: multiple myeloma, Waldenström macroglobulinemia, polycythemia vera, leukemias
↑ WBC, ↑ RBCs
Treatment in the setting of
Polycythemia vera: phlebotomy with IV fluids
Dysproteinemias: plasmapheresis
Blast transformations: leukapheresis
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الصورة هي hyperviscosity syndrome، يعني ارتفاع لزوجة المصل اللي يسبب تكدس الدم وتقليل تروية الشعيرات وركود وعائي. أكثر سبب ارتفاع بروتينات المصل، لكن ممكن كمان يكون بسبب leukocytosis شديد فوق 100,000 خلية مع اللوكيميا زي blast crisis. هالمريض عنده AML وأعراضه من نقص تروية الأعضاء اللي تتحاكي السكتة والنوبة القلبية والفشل الكلوي واضطرابات النظر. التحاليل راح تظهر هذا ال leukocytosis الكبير.
الفخ: في ناس يختارون polycythemia لأنها كمان ترفع اللزوجة، بس المريض ما عنده أعراض polycythemia vera زي الصداع وارتفاع الضغط. ركّز على قصة ال leukemia وأعراض نقص التروية العصبية لما تشوف خيارات فحص الدم.

question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the ED with dizziness and left upper extremity weakness. On physical examination, you note isolated 3/5 strength in the left upper extremity without other focal deficits. Her WBC count is 108,000/µL. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
englishExplanation:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms associated with hyperviscosity syndrome. Hyperviscosity syndrome is defined as elevated serum viscosity that causes sludging, decreased microvascular perfusion, and vascular stasis. The most common cause of hyperviscosity syndrome is elevated serum protein, most often secondary to Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia or less often due to multiple myeloma. The diagnosis of multiple myeloma is often made secondary to Bence-Jones proteins in the urine as well as an isolated elevation in a specific protein chain on serum or urine protein electrophoresis.

Hyperviscosity syndrome can also be caused by marked leukocytosis with > 100,000 cells/mm3, erythrocytosis, or hemoglobinopathies from diseases such as leukemia, polycythemia vera, or sickle cell disease, respectively. Signs and symptoms of hyperviscosity syndrome are primarily secondary to end-organ ischemia creating mimics of disease processes such as myocardial ischemia, stroke (as in this patient), pulmonary infarction, congestive heart failure, kidney failure, mucosal hemorrhages, or visual disturbances secondary to retinal ischemia. Ophthalmic examination will often reveal venous engorgement with “boxcar” segmentation. Laboratory studies will yield significant leukocytosis or hyperproteinemia, depending upon the etiology. Other abnormalities include elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and hypercalcemia. Management of hyperviscosity syndrome also depends upon the etiology. Supportive care for any etiology includes intravenous fluid hydration and diuresis in tandem. Temporizing measures for patients with leukemias are leukapheresis, for patients with elevated proteins is plasmapheresis, and for patients with polycythemia vera is phlebotomy.



Allopurinol (A) is an option if you suspect tumor lysis syndrome. However, this patient is not showing signs or symptoms of the characteristic electrolyte abnormalities associated with this disease process.

Furosemide (B) would be appropriate if you were worried about heart failure and volume overload. However, this patient’s presentation is more consistent with hyperviscosity syndrome.

Plasmapheresis (D) would be appropriate if the underlying etiology were hyperproteinemia, such as is seen with Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia or multiple myeloma. It would also be appropriate if the patient presented with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, which is comprised of fever, thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, kidney dysfunction, and altered mental status.

One Step Further
Question:
What are the typical laboratory findings associated with tumor lysis syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
Hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Hyperviscosity Syndrome

Sludging → ↓ perfusion
Causes: multiple myeloma, Waldenström macroglobulinemia, polycythemia vera, leukemias
↑ WBC, ↑ RBCs
Treatment in the setting of
Polycythemia vera: phlebotomy with IV fluids
Dysproteinemias: plasmapheresis
Blast transformations: leukapheresis
arabicExplanation:
ليش: هالمريضة عندها hyperviscosity syndrome بسبب WBC عالي جداً، والعلاج النهائي للوكيميا هو leukapheresis، وهو إجراء مؤقت يسحب الكريات البيضاء لتخفيف اللزوجة ونقص التروية. علاماتها مثل الدوخة والضعف بالطرف العلوي الأيسر ناتجة عن نقص تروية الأعضاء وتحاكي السكتة. بالمرضى اللي عندهم ارتفاع بروتينات المصل يكون plasmapheresis هو العلاج، أما polycythemia vera فالعلاج phlebotomy. الدعم يشمل سوائل وريديّة وإدرار البول بالمقابل.
الفخ: الطلاب يختارون plasmapheresis لأنه المشهور بهyperviscosity، بس هاي للحالة اللي سببها ارتفاع البروتين زي Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia أو multiple myeloma. ارجع لعدد الكريات البيضاء بالتحليل واعرف إن الجواب leukapheresis.

question: An 8-year-old boy who recently emigrated from Uganda presents to the ED with a facial mass that involves the jaw and orbit. He has ipsilateral lower facial numbness. Physical exam is shown above. Which of the following is this patient at risk of developing upon the initiation of treatment?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s rapidly growing jaw and orbital mass with facial numbness suggest endemic Burkitt lymphoma, common in regions like Uganda and linked to Epstein-Barr virus. It is a high-grade malignancy with rapid cell turnover, and initiating chemotherapy can lead to tumor lysis syndrome, marked by electrolyte imbalances and the risk of kidney failure due to massive tumor breakdown.

Burkitt lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. It has a rapid and aggressive clinical course with frequent bone marrow and central nervous system involvement. It is a medical emergency that requires immediate diagnostic and therapeutic intervention. Treatment is primarily with chemotherapy alone. Surgery and radiation therapy have no role in the treatment of Burkitt lymphoma.

Upon initiation of treatment, patients are at increased risk of tumor lysis syndrome with induction chemotherapy, so prophylactic allopurinol and aggressive hydration with urine alkalinization should be used to reduce this risk. Endemic Burkitt lymphoma most commonly involves the jaw and facial bones, including the orbit (> 50% of cases). Sporadic Burkitt lymphoma is less common and most often presents as abdominal tumors with bone marrow involvement. Common findings and symptoms in patients with Burkitt lymphoma include mandibular or maxillary mass, meningeal infiltration, cranial nerve involvement, headaches, vision changes, painless lymphadenopathy, bone marrow infiltration, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. Diagnosis is made by tissue biopsy.



Aplastic anemia (A) is more associated with medications, viruses, or autoimmune causes. It is not a typical complication of lymphoma treatment initiation.

Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (B) occurs after treatment of spirochetal infections like syphilis and is not related to chemotherapy or lymphoma.

Pulmonary fibrosis (C) may result from chronic exposure to certain drugs or autoimmune diseases but is not an acute concern in Burkitt lymphoma treatment.

One Step Further
Question:
What are the two most common infections that cause the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction upon initiation of antibiotics?

Reveal Answer:
Lyme disease and syphilis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Tumor Lysis Syndrome

Risks: more common in those with hematologic malignancy
1–5 days after chemotherapy
Can occur spontaneously with large tumor burden
Lab results: hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia
Tx: IVF + loop diuretic (washout), correct electrolyte abnormalities, dialysis (in severe cases)
Prevention: allopurinol, rasburicase
arabicExplanation:

question: A 33-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with irritability and anxiety. She states that whenever she goes to bed at night, she has an insatiable urge to move her legs and walk. When she ultimately walks and tries to go back to sleep, the urge returns. This evening, it has been happening for the past 7 hours and she is unable to sleep. Which of the following is most likely to also be found in this patient?
englishExplanation:
Restless leg syndrome typically presents with an uncomfortable sensation in the legs that is worse at night and when falling asleep. Patients often describe an urge to move their legs and walk around when trying to relax or go to bed. Common causes and associations with this condition include chronic kidney disease, diabetes, alcohol use, nicotine use, caffeine use, certain medications (such as steroids), multiple sclerosis, and Parkinson disease (or administration of other D2 blockers).

A common association with restless leg syndrome is low iron stores, as iron deficiency can precipitate restless leg syndrome. Iron is both a cofactor in the production of dopamine (a deficiency of which is associated with restless leg syndrome) and is required for hemoglobin production. Low iron levels can lead to microcytic and hypochromic anemia.

Treatment involves the administration of iron for serum ferritin < 75 mcg/L, as well as avoidance of exacerbating agents for restless leg syndrome. Dopamine agonists may be considered, but they are not a preferred initial agent due to concerns for symptom augmentation with longer term use.



Folate deficiency (A) presents with megaloblastic anemia and is common in those with alcohol use disorder. It has not been linked to restless leg syndrome.

Hereditary spherocytosis (B) presents secondary to a defect in ankyrin or spectrin and presents with anemia, an elevated mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, and cells that lack central pallor. IV immunoglobulin therapy or splenectomy can reduce hemolysis, and these patients will require folate supplementation.

Sideroblastic anemia (D) can occur secondary to an aminolevulinic acid synthase defect (which requires vitamin B6 as a cofactor) or in lead poisoning secondary to inhibition of ferrochelatase. As a result, iron is not incorporated into hemoglobin, and it accumulates in immature red blood cells. The diagnosis can be confirmed with a Prussian blue stain.

One Step Further
Question:
Besides restless leg syndrome, what other movement disorder can be exacerbated by iron deficiency?

Reveal Answer:
Parkinson disease.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Restless Legs Syndrome (Willis-Ekbom Disease)

Subjective urge to move legs, often accompanied by an uncomfortable sensation
Consequences include delayed sleep onset, sleep fragmentation, daytime sleepiness, significant distress, and impairment in functioning
Polysomnography demonstrates periodic leg movements in > 80%
Underlying pathology related to disturbances in dopaminergic system and iron metabolism
Management
Behavioral modifications
Symptoms may worsen with certain medications (antidepressants, antihistamines, dopamine receptor antagonists)
Remove offending agents when possible
Oral iron supplementation recommended if low ferritin levels (adults < 75 ng/mL, children < 50 ng/mL)
Pharmacotherapy for chronic Sx with gabapentinoid medications
Dopamine agonists are not a preferred initial agent due to concerns for symptom augmentation with long term use

question: Which of the following infections should be ruled out by pretreatment screening before initiating treatment with a tumor necrosis factor-alpha inhibitor?
englishExplanation:
Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha inhibitors have become cornerstone therapies for treating chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, plaque psoriasis, and inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. TNF-alpha is a proinflammatory cytokine central to the immune response, playing a key role in the activation of macrophages, recruitment of neutrophils and monocytes, and formation and maintenance of granulomas, which are critical for containing infections like tuberculosis.

Infliximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody composed of both human and murine components, and it binds to both soluble and transmembrane forms of TNF-alpha, neutralizing its biological activity. By suppressing TNF-alpha, infliximab and other TNF-alpha inhibitors effectively reduce inflammation and halt disease progression. However, this immunosuppression presents at the cost of impaired host defense, especially against intracellular pathogens that are controlled by granulomatous responses. This includes Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Histoplasmosis, and other opportunistic fungal infections.

Because of this, all patients should be screened for latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI), using a tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay, before initiating TNF-alpha inhibitors. If positive, appropriate treatment for LTBI should be started before initiating biologic therapy. Additionally, screening for hepatitis B and C is recommended, as reactivation of chronic viral hepatitis can occur under immunosuppression.

Other contraindications or cautions include active or chronic infections, such as untreated herpes zoster, invasive fungal infections, and nonhealing infected skin ulcers. TNF-alpha inhibitors are also generally avoided in patients with moderate to severe heart failure (class III/IV) due to an observed increased risk of worsening cardiac function. Patients should be monitored closely for signs of infection throughout treatment, and live vaccines should be avoided during therapy due to the immunosuppressive effects.



Hepatitis A virus (A) causes acute, self-limited hepatitis and is not associated with reactivation risk or chronic carriage, making pretreatment screening unnecessary.

Legionella (B) is a cause of atypical pneumonia and does not persist in a latent form, so screening before immunosuppressive therapy is not relevant.

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (C) can cause skin and soft tissue infections, but is not a latent infection requiring pretreatment evaluation in patients starting TNF-alpha inhibitors.

One Step Further
Question:
Where is Histoplasmosis capsulatum endemic, necessitating screening questions to assess the risk of underlying fungal infection before starting patients on immunosuppressive therapy, such as a TNF-alpha inhibitor?

Reveal Answer:
The Midwest.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF)-Alpha Inhibitors

Adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab pegol, golimumab
Used for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases: rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease, plaque psoriasis
Mechanism of action: TNF-alpha is a key cytokine in inflammation, involved in macrophage activation, neutrophil/monocyte recruitment, and granuloma formation
These inhibitors are chimeric monoclonal antibodies that neutralize both soluble and membrane-bound TNF-alpha
Infection risk: immunosuppression increases susceptibility to intracellular pathogens, especially Mycobacterium tuberculosis and fungal infections like histoplasmosis
Pretreatment screening: TB, hepatitis B and C
Cautions
Active or chronic infections (e.g., untreated zoster, invasive fungal infections, infected ulcers)
Moderate to severe heart failure due to worsening outcomes
Live vaccines are contraindicated during treatment

الفخ: طلاب يختارون hepatitis A أو Legionella لأنهم أسباب شائعة للعدوى، لكن الفحص الإلزامي قبل TNF-alpha inhibitors هو ال tuberculosis لأنها المكبوحة بال granulomas. لا تنسى كمان العدوى الفطرية الانتهازية.

question: An 85-year-old man presents to the ED with gait disturbance and memory loss over a period of months. He finally came to the hospital when he developed urinary incontinence. What syndrome does this constellation of symptoms describe?
englishExplanation:
Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) is a potentially reversible cause of dementia and is characterized by the triad of gait disturbance, memory loss, and incontinence. NPH results from cerebrospinal fluid buildup in the ventricles, leading to increased intracranial pressure with edema of the periventricular white matter and corona radiata. The periventricular white matter contains the sacral motor nerve fibers that produce gait instability, and when compressed, incontinence ensues.



Alzheimer disease (A) presents with progressive dementia but does not include motor abnormalities. However, it is important to remember that many older patients have more than one diagnosis at the time of presentation. Lewy body dementia (B) is characterized by progressive dementia with visual hallucinations, cognitive fluctuations, and parkinsonism. Wernicke syndrome (D) is a manifestation of thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency. This is usually secondary to alcohol misuse and manifests with the triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and impaired memory. In contrast to NPH, urinary incontinence or frequency are absent. The treatment is thiamine.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the characteristic finding on lumbar puncture for normal pressure hydrocephalus?

Reveal Answer:
Normal opening pressure.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus

CSF buildup in ventricles
LP often shows opening pressure within normal limits
Urinary incontinence, gait disturbance (ataxia), dementia
Potentially reversible by placement of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt

الفخ: الطلاب يختارون Alzheimer disease لأنها أشهر سبب للخرف، بس ما فيها اضطرابات حركية ولا سلس بول. أما Wernicke syndrome فتثلاثيها شلل العين وترنّح وضعف ذاكرة بدون سلس بول.

question: A 2-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a prolonged first-time seizure. He has been seizing for 30 minutes and has received rectal diazepam and two doses of intravenous midazolam at appropriate doses by EMS. His point-of-care glucose is 92 mg/dL. The patient continues to seize on arrival. You are informed that an empty pill bottle of isoniazid was found at home. Which of the following is the most appropriate next medication to administer?
englishExplanation:
Isoniazid is a common antituberculosis drug that is related to niacin (i.e., vitamin B3) and pyridoxine (i.e., vitamin B6), an overdose of which causes a functional pyridoxine and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) deficiency. GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter, a deficiency of which causes seizures. Seizures usually start between 30 and 120 minutes after a severe isoniazid ingestion, with less severe ingestions presenting as altered mental status. Management of status epilepticus due to an isoniazid ingestion is both pyridoxine and benzodiazepines. This will replete the functional deficiency of pyridoxine. Pyridoxine is relatively benign, will not cause harm in patients with status epilepticus due to other causes, and is the only medication that will stop status epilepticus due to an isoniazid ingestion. Complications of an isoniazid ingestion are typically due to prolonged seizure activity and can progress to anoxic brain injury.



Fosphenytoin (A), levetiracetam (B), and phenobarbital (C) are appropriate in patients with status epilepticus but will not stop seizures due to isoniazid ingestion. Phenobarbital may be used if pyridoxine is not immediately available, but it is unlikely to stop the seizure and is associated with adverse side effects.

One Step Further
Question:
What are the adverse effects of a chronic isoniazid ingestion?

Reveal Answer:
Hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Isoniazid (INH) Toxicity

At therapeutic doses, side effects include neuropathy and liver injury
AST or ALT > 3x upper limit of normal: consider discontinuing or temporarily holding INH
In overdose, ↓ B6 (pyridoxine) → ↓ GABA → refractory seizures with anion gap metabolic acidosis and protracted coma
Antidote: B6 (pyridoxine)
