question:
A 45-year-old dance instructor presented via her GP with a diagnosis of 
possible transient ischaemic attack. She described blurred vision lasting 
minutes on three occasions and tingling in her right hand and left hand. 
This was made worse by her dancing exercise. The patient had also 
noticed that her balance had been affected on a few occasions and she 
was concerned about her job.
Examination revealed normal neurology.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
11. D.  Multiple sclerosis
This history is a typical example of Uhthoff’s phenomenon where neurological symptoms are exacerbated by increases in body temperature, typically during exercise or in a hot bath. It is typically 
associated with multiple sclerosis (MS).
MS can present initially with either transient neurological symptoms or slowly progressive neurological deficits. Eighty-five percent of MS presents in the relapsing remitting form. Patients develop 
neurological deficits which typically evolve over the course of a few hours or days and persist for a 
few days or weeks and then resolve.
The inflammation in MS can occur anywhere in the brain or spinal cord. Typical first neurological 
symptoms of MS include ataxia, monocular visual loss secondary to optic neuritis, diplopia, paraparesis, and sensory disturbance. It is important to note that a diagnosis of MS should not be made 
after a single episode of CNS inflammation leading to transient neurological symptoms. In this situation, the term ‘clinically isolated syndrome’ (CIS) is used.
Symptoms may only be apparent or exacerbated when the body temperature rises such as in a hot 
bath, during an infection, or, as in this case, during exercise (Uhthoff’s phenomenon). There may 
also be a positive sensory disturbance along the spine on flexion of the neck (Lhermitte’s sign). 
However, this can be present in other pathologies affecting the cervical spinal cord.
Useful investigations include an MRI of the brain and spinal cord, lumbar puncture, and evoked potentials. The MRI brain is important for both diagnosis of MS and prognosis after CIS. The MRI typically reveals ovoid high-signal lesions on T2 images with a predilection for the periventricular deep 
cerebral white matter, corpus callosum, cerebellum, and spinal cord. In the context of CIS, if there is 
only a solitary characteristic inflammatory lesion then the lifetime risk of MS for that patient is 20%, 
whereas if there are multiple lesions then it is 80%. CSF examination should be essentially normal 
apart from the presence of oligoclonal bands (90%). The presence of oligoclonal bands is not of 
prognostic value in CIS or MS and can be seen in other CNS inflammatory conditions. Lesions within 
the optic nerves and spinal cord are often poorly seen on MRI but the presence of demyelination in 
these areas can be detected by finding delay on visual or sensory-evoked potentials respectively.
The diagnosis of relapsing remitting MS requires more than one inflammatory event separated clinically in both time and anatomical location with some supportive investigations such as typical lesions 
on MRI, neurophysiological evidence of demyelination, and the presence of oligoclonal bands in the 
CSF. Alternatively, there may be progressive neurological deficits with these supportive features in 
the case of primary progressive disease.
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Clinical Guideline 186. Multiple sclerosis in adults: 
management 2014.

seizure. Sodium bicarbonate should be given as an initial bolus followed by an infusion. Phenytoin 
is contraindicated, as it is a sodium channel blocker and thus may cause cardiac arrhythmia and seizure by exacerbating sodium channel blockade.
Tricyclic poisoning
Although seen less often in overdose, all tricyclic antidepressants are very toxic in overdose acting 
on a wide range of receptors including muscarinic, gaba, alpha, and histamine causing an anticholinergic picture. Importantly, though, they cause sodium channel blockade leading to cardiac symptoms, often termed the quinidine action as seen with class I antiarrhythmics.
Patients should be observed for a minimum of six hours for symptoms and discharged only when 
symptom-free. Overdose of 10 mg/kg or more can produce life-threatening toxicity and symptoms 
may take up to 24 hours to appear due to delayed absorption. See Table 13.3.

Treatment is supportive, maintain airway, support ventilation if required, correct hypotension, 
and manage delirium with benzodiazepines. Sodium bicarbonate is required if indicated, as previously outlined. The therapeutic target is correction of hypotension and the prolonged QRS. 
Blood pH should be maintained at 7.5 to 7.55; this may require a repeat bolus and follow-up 
infusion.
Seizures should be treated with benzodiazepines and not phenytoin, as this is also a sodium channel 
blocker. Torsade de pointes can be treated with magnesium sulphate but other antiarrythmic drugs 
should be avoided. Patients with who do not respond to emergency and supportive treatment will 
require critical care.

See Table 13.4 for anticholinergic toxidrome.

366
366
Sodium bicarbonate
Sodium bicarbonate has two principle indications in the management of the poisoned patient:
1.	Cardiotoxicity in sodium channel blockade, for example, with tricyclic antidepressants and 
type 1 antiarrhythmics.
2.	Enhanced elimination in salicylate poisoning.
It has three main mechanisms:
	
i.	Provides a large sodium load overcoming sodium channel blockade while buffering acidosis 
with bicarbonate ions.
	
ii.	Elevates blood pH, which prevents shift of ionized drugs to the central nervous system 
(CNS), e.g. aspirin, and aids sodium channel function.
	
iii.	Urinary alkalization, increasing the amount of ionized salicylate in the renal tubules preventing 
reuptake of salicylate or ‘ion trapping’.
Absorption and distribution
While rate of absorption does not affect the amount of drug absorbed, it does influence the time 
to peak plasma levels and hence the time to maximal expected symptoms of poisoning. Factors 
influencing absorption in overdose include drug preparation and gastrointestinal motility (anticholinergic drugs, alcohol, opiates). These factors must be considered when risk-assessing the patient.
Distribution will influence the final plasma concentration. Small molecular weight, non-ionized, 
lipid-soluble drugs distribute widely and have a large apparent volume of distribution. These drugs 
also have a long half-life of elimination and, therefore, prolonged toxicity. Dialysis is not an effective 
method of elimination for these drugs, a good example being tricylcic antidepressants.

the management of tricyclic antidepressant overdose. Emergency Medicine Journal 2011; 28: 347–368.

chronic kidney disease has deteriorated resulting in a build up of active opiate and benzodiazepine 
metabolites. Her symptoms are principally central nervous system and respiratory depression suggesting opiates and or benzodiazepine toxicity. Despite remaining well saturated, she has significant

respiratory depression and hypercapnia, which also contributes to reduced consciousness. Symptoms 
and signs can be clouded by the actions of other drugs; for example, pupil size should be pinpoint but 
the presence of two serotonergic drugs (tramadol and citalopram) may antagonize the opiate effect.
Naloxone is a very effective opiate receptor antagonist and quickly reverses opiate side effects. 
Patients who have a history of long-term use are at risk of withdrawal if aggressive reversal is given 
so doses should be carefully titrated to effect. The half-life of naloxone is 60–90 minutes—shorter 
than opiates—so an infusion may be required.
Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist but should not be used in polypharmacy toxicity, chronic 
benzodiazpine use, underlying seizure disorder, or risk of seizure. The half-life of flumazenil is 40–80 
minutes.
Opiate/opioid toxicity
Common in the drug-abusing population but must also be considered in any patient receiving opiates presenting with symptoms consistent with an opioid toxidrome; classically respiratory depression, miosis, and central nervous system (CNS) depression. As previously discussed, naloxone is the 
antidote but consideration must be given to the half-life of elimination of the opioid in use.
There are some opioids which require special consideration.
Tramadol
Structurally related to venlafaxine, tramadol rarely causes classical opioid toxicity. Its toxic effects 
are related to its serotonergic actions and hence seizures, tachycardia, and delirium are often seen. 
This should be treated as per a serotonin-type poisoning. Other opiates with serotonergic effects 
include fentanyl and pethidine.
Dextropropoxyphene
No longer licensed but still used in a small number of long-term users. Dextroproxyphene is 
the opioid combined with paracetamol in co-proxamol. It is associated with seizure and cardiac 
arrhythmia.
Methadone
A very long-acting opioid used in drug-addiction treatment. The toxic effects may last 24 hours and 
patients are at particular risk of respiratory arrest once they fall asleep, even if they appear to have 
been well while awake. A long period of observation should be considered. These patients are also 
at risk of acute withdrawal if high doses of naloxone are given by bolus.
Monitoring in opioid toxicity
Caution should be taken when monitoring patients with opioid toxicity. Pulse oximetry readings are 
used as a surrogate marker for ventilation, but patients on high-flow oxygen may remain oxygenated 
with significant respiratory and central nervous system depression. Respiratory monitoring must 
include respiratory rate; ideally, patients should be monitored off oxygen. Patients who become 
hypoxic should have immediate review and treatment with oxygen while being reassessed. The 
treatment for respiratory depression in opioid overdose is naloxone, not oxygen.
Factors in risk assessment
Aside from substance, quantity, and timing, other factors must be considered when risk-assessing a 
poisoned patient. Most drugs undergo hepatic metabolism to inactive metabolites; factors reducing 
this capacity, such as chronic liver disease, will delay the clearance of such drugs and increase the 
period of toxicity. Chronic heart failure may reduce hepatic blood flow, having a similar effect. Inactive metabolites are usually excreted via the kidneys but active metabolites (e.g. opiates and benzodiazepines) and unchanged drugs (e.g. digoxin, lithium) are also excreted. Reduction in glomerular 
filtration rate will reduce this capacity.

368
368
The elderly are generally at higher risk of adverse drug effects because of reduced glomerular filtration and polypharmacy. Hepatic metabolism does decline but the significance of this is variable 
between individuals probably depending on many other factors such as genetic variation. The very 
young are at increased risk because of a higher blood–brain barrier permeability, lower glomerular 
filtration rate, and immature enzyme systems.
Changes in physiology during pregnancy influence metabolism. Pregnant women have a higher cardiac 
output, and thus hepatic flow, and a higher glomerular filtration rate. This increases the rate of drug 
clearance and may result in sub-therapeutic levels. Lower plasma protein concentrations result in more 
unbound and, therefore, active drugs when the drug is usually highly protein bound, e.g. phenytoin.

4. C.  Digoxin-specific FAB fragments 400 mg intravenous infusion
Yew berries contain a cardiac glycoside, which is similar to digoxin, and is also bound effectively by 
digoxin-specific FAB fragments. The indications for digoxin specific FAB fragments are:
● serum potassium >6 mmol/L
● life-threatening arrhythmia
● cardiovascular compromise (including cardiac arrest)
Calcium chloride should not be given as it may precipitate arrhythmias and cause further deterioration. Sodium bicarbonate and insulin/dextrose may be given for hyperkalaemia if digoxin-specific 
FAB fragments are not immediately available. Atropine can be used for a compromised bradycardia.
Cardiac glycosides
There are cardiac glycosides present in several plants in the UK including foxglove, lily of the valley, and yew. In Australasia, the common source is oleander, which is a very popular hedge plant. 
All of these glycosides can cause a digoxin-like toxicity which can be very successfully treated with 
digoxin-specific FAB fragments. The digoxin assay can be used to detect plant cardiac glycosides 
and, although levels are less accurate and do not correlate well with toxicity, they give some indication of the amount ingested.
Cardiac glycosides inhibit Na+/K+ pump resulting in an increase in intracellular calcium, decreased 
sympathetic stimulus, and increased vagal stimulus. This results in increased ventricular automaticity, 
AV conduction block, and bradycardia.
In digoxin ingestion, peak plasma concentration is at around six hours. Cardiac glycosides have a large 
volume of distribution, thus haemodialysis is not effective. They are mostly excreted unchanged by 
the kidneys; renal impairment significantly increases the half-life of elimination. See Table 13.5.
Cardiac glycosides commonly cause metabolic disturbance, with hyperkalaemia and hypercalcaemia 
being very common in acute poisoning. Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia are often seen in

question:
A 76-year-old man attended the acute medical unit with a nontraumatic swelling to his knee. He felt well, was afebrile, and had a cool, 
non-erythematous right knee with a restricted but reasonable range of 
movement, which was only mildly painful. One week ago, he attended 
the hospital with new onset atrial fibrillation and was discharged to 
the community team who had been overseeing an induction course 
of warfarin. He was advised to take 2 mg warfarin once daily. His INR 
after three days was 2.8 (<1.4) and today it is >10. He took no other 
medication, drank alcohol rarely, and was a non-smoker. He was very 
clear that he took ‘one small tablet’ each night.
Which of the following is the cause of his excessively raised INR?
englishExplanation:
6. B.  Cytochrome P450 enzyme polymorphism
Warfarin is a substrate of cytochrome P450 2C9 (CYP2C9) of which there are several polymorphisms. Two in particular 2C9*2 and 2C9*3 have 12% and 5% of the normal activity resepctively. Approximately 2–3% of patients carry this polymorphism and these patients display excessive sensitivity 
to warfarin.
Vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR) reduces vitamin K epoxide back to vitamin K hydroxyquinone 
to allow it to activate coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X. Warfarin inhibits this enzyme to reduce 
the amount of active clotting factors available. Polymorphism of the VKOR enzyme produces an 
enzyme that is less inhibited by warfarin and resistance to anticoagulation.
ATP-binding cassette transporter proteins may have a role in reducing bioavailability of warfarin. Nacetyltransferase and enterohepatic circulation do not influence warfarin metabolism or activity.
The treatment of warfarin overdose depends on whether the patient requires therapeutic warfarin 
or not. In patients not normally on warfarin and without evidence of any bleeding, 10 mg of vitamin 
K should be given orally if they have ingested more than 0.25 mg/kg or the INR is greater than 4.0. 
This can be increased to 20 mg in large overdose. If there is a coagulopathy then INR should be 
measured six-hourly until it has normalized; repeat doses of vitamin K may be required. In patients 
without bleeding but who require warfarin for therapeutic reasons, more caution is required as aggressive reversal can lead to problems achieving therapeutic anticoagulation. Advice can be sought 
from a haematologist but generally if the INR is excessively raised, i.e. >8, a small dose of vitamin K 
(1–2 mg orally or 0.5–1 mg intravenously) should be given to lower the INR to a more acceptable 
level. Again, INR should be monitored regularly until at a therapeutic level.
Any patient with active or life-threatening haemorrhage should have urgent correction of the coagulopathy with prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma. Dosing advice will be 
available from a haematologist.
Vitamin K is a very effective antidote. Although warfarin prevents the activation of vitamin Kdependent clotting factors, the production of those factors is unaffected and the plasma levels are 
normal. Vitamin K works very quickly to activate these dormant factors, as they will take effect 
within an hour or two (although peak effect will be later).
Pharmacogenetics
Genetic variation significantly influences an individual’s drug metabolism. This may result in faster or 
slower metabolism of an active drug or potentially faster or slower conversion of a pro-drug to an 
active substance. A rare but very important example of this would be suxamethonium, a depolarizing paralysing agent that is usually rapidly metabolized to inactive substances by plasma pseudocholinesterase. Autosomal recessive inheritance of an abnormal pseudocholinesterase can result in 
paralysis for hours or days rather than minutes.

POISONING AND PHARMACOLOGY | ANSWERS
371
Ethylene glycol and methanol themselves cause a relatively mild CNS effect, presenting with a 
picture of mild intoxication possibly without the odour of alcohol. However, the metabolites are 
particularly toxic and result in rapid deterioration. Methanol ingestion results in CNS toxicity, retinal 
Acetylation of drugs varies greatly on a racial basis. Individuals can be classified as slow or fast acetylators, within European populations 40% are fast acetylators compared with 90% of Japanese. Slow 
acetylation may result in increased drug side effects such as peripheral neuropathy with isoniazid.
Expression of cytochrome P450 isoenzymes also varies greatly. Individuals can be classified as extensive, ultra-rapid, intermediate, and poor metabolizers. The significant effects of this variation 
are seen in poor metabolizers (PM) and ultra-rapid metabolizers (UM). With PM, sustained plasma 
levels are seen leading to an increase in side effects of the drug. The opposite occurs in UM, where 
drug response is sub-therapeutic at standard doses. Again, when a pro-drug is activated by CYP 
P450, therapeutic effect may be lost if the individual expresses the PM phenotype. A good example 
of this is the lack of analgesic effect some patients experience with codeine.
Ultimately, any enzyme, receptor, or transport protein may be affected by genetic variation, all of 
which will influence the therapeutic effect and side effect profile of a drug.
Pirmohamed M. Cytochrome P450 enzyme polymorphisms and adverse drug reactions. Toxicology 
2003; 192: 23–32.
Hall AM. Warfarin: a case history in pharmacogenetics. Heart 2005; 91: 563–564.
Royal Society of Medicine. Personalised Medicines: hopes and realities. September 2005.

question:
A 45 year-old man was referred to the acute medical unit by his 
GP because of a delayed presentation of therapeutic excess use of 
paracetamol. He had been trying to relieve dental pain from an abscess. 
He weighed 80 kg and had taken approximately 16 × 500 mg tablets of 
paracetamol in a 24-hour period. The last time he ingested paracetamol 
was 36 hours ago. He felt well and had no abdominal pain and no clinical 
signs of jaundice. No blood sampling had been done yet. Despite his 
dental pain, he had been able to eat normally and he had no other 
medical conditions and was taking no other medication.
On examination, he was apyrexial with a pulse of 86 beats per minute 
and blood pressure 110/68 mmHg. His respiratory rate was 14 breaths 
per minute and his oxygen saturation was 98% on room air.
Investigations:
ECG: normal sinus rhythm
What are the most appropriate next steps in management?

options.text: Explain that the risk of hepatotoxicity is low and offer methionine orally
Measure serum electrolytes, creatinine, bicarbonate, paracetamol, liver functions tests, and
Measure serum paracetamol level, liver function tests, and INR and assess the need for
Reassure him and discharge with advice to avoid paracetamol for 48 hours
Start n-acetylcysteine and measure serum electrolytes, creatinine, bicarbonate,

englishExplanation:
8. C.  Measure serum paracetamol level, liver function tests, and INR and assess the need for treatment with the results
Single-overdose ingestions are assessed based on a time/plasma level graph which previously used 
a high-risk and normal-risk curve. This is no longer the case as the National Poisons Information 
Service (NPIS) paracetamol-overdose guidelines were changed in September 2012. All patients are 
now assessed on a single-time/dose curve and the NPIS no longer recommends the consideration 
factors such as starvation and enzyme inducing drugs in treatment decisions.
Uncontrolled dental pain often triggers unintentional excess therapeutic use. Patients who have 
ingested greater than 150 mg/kg in a 24-hour period should receive a course of n-acetylcysteine. 
Patients who have ingested 75–150 mg/kg can be assessed clinically. Any patients with symptoms or signs of hepatotoxicity, such as abdominal pain, vomiting, hepatic tenderness, or jaundice 
should have immediate treatment. In the absence of these features take a venous blood sample for 

POISONING AND PHARMACOLOGY | ANSWERS
373
measurement of paracetamol concentration, U&Es, bicarbonate, creatinine, ALT, and INR. If there 
is detectable paracetamol greater than 24 hours post last ingestion, raised ALT (more than twice 
normal limits), or increased INR at any time, then treatment should be given. In obese patients, 
dose and n-acetylcysteine calculations should use a maximum of 110 kg.
Paracetamol overdose
Paracetamol is the commonest agent seen in overdose in the UK accounting for 40–50% of selfpoisoning presentations.
At recommended doses, 90% of paracetamol is conjugated with glucuronide and sulphates, 5% 
is excreted renally, and 5% is metabolized to the highly toxic N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine 
(NAPQI) by cytochrome P450 isoenzymes. This process is increased by cytochrome P450-inducing 
drugs. Normally, NAPQI conjugates with glutathione but in overdose more NAPQI is produced as 
the conjugative pathways are saturated. This quickly depletes the liver of glutathione leaving unconjugated NAPQI to cause hepatocellular injury.
N-acetylcysteine
The recommended regime of n-acetylcysteine (Parvolex®) is an extremely effective antidote. It is most 
effective when given within the first eight hours but continues to be of benefit up to 24 hours post 
ingestion. N-acetylcysteine acts as a glutathione donor increasing the capacity to conjugate NAPQI 
and preventing hepatocellular injury. It is also possible that it acts by sulphation of paracetamol.
Reactions to n-acetylcysteine are common, seen in up to 20% of patients receiving it. The typical 
features are flushing, urticaria, tachycardia, hypotension, and wheeze. The reaction is not an allergic reaction but a dose-dependent direct histaminergic response. If it occurs, the infusion should 
be stopped and the patient given an antihistamine and a steroid if it is significant. Hypotension can 
be corrected with fluids and bronchospasm with nebulized salbutamol. Severe reactions are very 
rare but can require anaphylaxis treatment and critical-care support. The reaction will usually settle 
within 15–30 minutes at which point the infusion can be recommenced and a slower rate. Evidence 
does not support slowing down the rate of loading to reduce the incidence of reaction although the 
recent guideline changes include loading over one hour rather than 15 minutes. Previous reactions 
are not a contraindication to n-acetylcysteine unless the reaction was severe.
Oral methionine is an alternative antidote in paracetamol overdose; however, it is poorly tolerated 
and is not effective beyond eight hours. It can be considered in patients who refuse intravenous treatment or admission; however, NPIS now recommends oral use of n-acetylcysteine in those patients.
Liver-unit referral
The Kings College criteria are a prognostic tool for patients with acute liver failure (ALF). The criteria for ALF secondary to paracetamol overdose are: pH <7.30 or
INR >6.5 (PT >100 s) and serum creatinine >300 micromol/L (>3.4 mg/dL) in patients with grade 
3 or 4 hepatic encephalopathy.
Bailey et al. Management of anaphylactoid reactions to intravenous n-acetylecysteine. Annals of Emergency Medicine 1998; 31: 710–715.
Kerr et al. The Australasian Clinical Toxicology Investigators Collaboration randomized trial of different loading infusion rates of n-acetylcysteine. Annals of Emergency Medicine 2005; 45: 402–408.
UK National Poisons Information Service. Guideline for paracetamol poisoning. Commissioned by 
Public Health England.  http://www.toxbase.org

months ago. The partner informed staff that she had previously been 
treated at a psychiatric inpatient facility for a severe depressive illness 
three years ago, but was currently not under mental health services.
On admission, she appeared to be intoxicated, with a fluctuating GCS 
of 12–14. Her temperature was 37.5°C, pulse was 90 beats per minute, 
blood pressure was 110/72 mmHg and her oxygen saturation was 98% 
breathing air. Capillary blood glucose concentration was 4.2 mmol/L. 
There were no other abnormalities on physical examination.
Initial acute medical management of the polypharmacy overdose 
included intravenous acetylcysteine. The nursing staff reported that 
she intermittently kept verbalizing that she wanted to be left alone and 
not to have any treatment but further history from the patient was not 
possible.
Medico-legally, how could you proceed if you wanted to implement the 
acute medical management plan?

options.text: The patient has capacity but override her wishes under the Mental Capacity Act 2005
The patient has capacity but override her wishes under the Mental Health Act 1983
The patient lacks capacity and act in her best interests under the Mental Capacity Act 2005
The patient lacks capacity and act in her best interests under the Mental Health Act 1983
Under common law, as you have a duty of care to the patient

englishExplanation:
7. C.  The patient lacks capacity and act in her best interests under the Mental Capacity Act 2005
Mental Capacity Act 2005
The Mental Capacity Act states that a person lacks capacity if they are unable to make a specific 
decision, at a specific time, because of an impairment of, or disturbance, in the functioning of mind 
or brain.
Assessing capacity
To be able to make a decision, a person should be able to:
● Understand the decision to be made and the information provided about the decision. 
The consequences of making a decision must be included in the information given.

PSYCHIATRY | ANSWERS
416
416
● Retain the information—a person should be able to retain the information given for long 
enough to make the decision. If information can only be retained for short periods of time, it 
should not automatically be assumed that the person lacks capacity. Notebooks, for example, 
could be used to record information which may help a person to retain it.
● Use that information in making the decision—a person should be able to weigh up the pros 
and cons of making the decision.
● Communicate their decision—if a person cannot communicate their decision—for example, if 
they are in a coma—the Act specifies that they should be treated as if they lack capacity. You 
should make all efforts to help the person communicate their decision before deciding they cannot.
You will need to assess a person’s capacity regularly, particularly when a care plan is being developed or reviewed.
Fluctuating capacity
Some patients are intermittently or temporarily unable to make a decision for themselves. It may be 
possible to wait until the patient has capacity or, where this is not the case, patients must be treated 
in accordance with their best interests or according to consent given by someone authorized to act 
on the patient’s behalf—someone with parental responsibility in the case of a minor, or a person 
with a personal welfare lasting power of attorney (LPA).
Advanced decisions
Adults with the capacity to do so can make decisions about how they want to be treated if they 
later lose their capacity. An advance decision to refuse treatment (ADRT) is legally binding in England and Wales under the terms of the Mental Capacity Act 2005. It must specify the treatments 
being refused, and in what circumstances, and may be made verbally or in writing. If, however, the 
refusal relates to life-sustaining treatment, the decision must be in writing, signed, and witnessed. It 
must also clearly state that the refusal stands even if it will place the individual’s life at risk.

question:
Which of the following statements regarding decontamination, disinfection, and
sterilization in the ICU is NOT true?

options.text: Decontamination is a broad term that includes cleaning and disinfection.
Sterilisation is a process that destroys all microbial life, including bacterial
Disinfection eliminates all forms of microbial life, including bacterial spores.
Sterilisation is required for instruments that enter sterile body tissues.
Disinfection is appropriate for non-critical items that contact intact skin.

correctAnswer: Disinfection eliminates all forms of microbial life, including bacterial spores.
englishExplanation:
Definitions:
Sterilisation is a validated process used to render an object free from all forms of viable microorganisms, including bacterial spores and viruses. Disinfection is a
process that reduces the number of viable microorganisms to a level previously
specified as appropriate for its intended purpose but does not necessarily inactivate
bacterial spores. Therefore, the statement that disinfection eliminates all forms of
microbial life including spores is false.
Spaulding Classification:
The Spaulding classification determines the level of decontamination required
based on infection risk:
• Critical (enters sterile tissue/vascular system): Requires sterilisation (e.g., surgical
instruments, CVCs).
• Semi-critical (contacts mucous membranes/non-intact skin): Requires high-level
disinfection or sterilisation (e.g., laryngoscopes, bronchoscopes).
• Non-critical (contacts intact skin): Requires low/intermediate disinfection (e.g.,
BP cuffs, stethoscopes).

Decontamination Cycle:
Decontamination is the combination of processes—including cleaning, disinfection,
and/or sterilisation—used to render a reusable medical device safe for further use.
Cleaning is the essential first step; organic matter prevents effective disinfection or
sterilisation.
Mechanisms of Action:
Sterilisation and disinfection methods target specific microbial survival pathways.
Steam sterilisation (autoclaving) denatures essential proteins and enzymes through
moist heat. Chemical agents like glutaraldehyde act as alkylating agents, cross-linking proteins and nucleic acids. Chlorhexidine disrupts cell membranes and precipitates cytoplasm. Understanding these mechanisms explains why spores (with
durable coats and dehydrated cores) are resistant to agents that only disrupt membranes (like alcohols) but susceptible to extreme heat or strong alkylating agents.
Clinical Pearl
Sterilisation Kills Spores:
This is the defining difference. Sterilisation is an absolute term; an item is either
sterile or it is not.
Disinfection Does Not Guarantee Spore-Free:
Disinfection exists on a spectrum (low, intermediate, high-level), but none of these
levels guarantees the complete elimination of all bacterial spores.
Spaulding Classification:
Medical devices are categorised by risk: Critical items (entering sterile tissue) require sterilisation; Semi-critical items (mucous membranes) require high-level disinfection; Non-critical items (intact skin) require low-level disinfection.
Autoclaving:
Steam sterilisation (autoclaving) is the most common, efficient, and reliable method
of sterilisation used in hospitals.
Prions:
Special sterilisation procedures are required to inactivate prions (e.g., from
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease), which are highly resistant to standard sterilisation
methods.
Cleaning is Prerequisite:
You cannot sterilise or disinfect a dirty instrument. Organic matter (blood, pus) inactivates disinfectants and shields microorganisms from sterilisation processes.
Thorough cleaning must always precede disinfection or sterilisation.
C. difficile and Spores:

Alcohol-based hand rubs and many standard disinfectants are ineffective against
Clostridioides difficile spores. Physical removal with soap and water and environmental cleaning with chlorine-releasing agents (e.g., hypochlorite) are required.
Single-Use Devices:
Devices marked with the ISO symbol (a number 2 in a crossed-through circle) are
not validated for reprocessing. Re-use transfers legal liability for device failure or
infection transmission to the clinician or organisation.
Thermal Disinfection:
Automated washer-disinfectors use moist heat (e.g., 90°C for >1 minute) to achieve
high-level disinfection without chemicals. This is quantified by the A0 concept
(time-temperature relationship).
Ethylene Oxide:
A gas sterilisation method used for heat-sensitive equipment. It acts as an alkylating
agent but requires long aeration times due to toxicity and flammability risks.
Chlorhexidine Residual Activity:
Unlike povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine binds to the stratum corneum (keratin), providing persistent antimicrobial activity for hours after application. This makes it superior for CVC insertion sites.
Filtration Sterilisation:
Used for heat-sensitive liquids (e.g., drugs) or gases. A 0.22-micron filter physically
removes bacteria and fungi but may not remove small viruses or mycoplasma.
Hydrogen Peroxide Vapour:
An automated room decontamination method used for terminal cleaning (e.g., after
MDR organisms). It is an oxidising agent that degrades to oxygen and water, leaving
no toxic residue.

الفخ: كتير طلاب يختاروا عبارة الـ Spaulding أو إن الـ sterilisation مطلوبة للأدوات اللي تدخل الأنسجة المعقمة، لأنهم يظنوها False. الفرق إن تعريف الـ disinfection لا يشمل القضاء على الأبواغ، وهذا هو الخطأ الحقيقي.

question:
An 82-year-old woman with a history of untreated hypothyroidism is found unresponsive. She is bradycardic (HR 40 bpm), hypotensive (BP 75/50 mmHg),
and hypothermic (33°C). She requires intubation for a GCS of 5. An ECG shows
sinus bradycardia with low voltage QRS and prolonged QT interval. Which of the
following is the most critical initial pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Aggressive external warming with a forced-air blanket.
An intravenous bolus of 3% hypertonic saline to correct hyponatremia.
An intravenous loading dose of hydrocortisone.
An intravenous loading dose of levothyroxine (T4).

correctAnswer: An intravenous loading dose of hydrocortisone.
englishExplanation:
Adrenal Protection (The 'Steroids First' Rule):
Administration of thyroid hormone increases basal metabolic rate and accelerates
the hepatic metabolism of cortisol. In patients with autoimmune thyroid disease
(who may have co-existing Addison's disease/Schmidt's syndrome) or pituitary failure, this sudden increase in demand without adequate adrenal reserve can precipitate a fatal adrenal crisis. UK guidelines (Society for Endocrinology) mandate empiric hydrocortisone (e.g., 50-100 mg IV) prior to or simultaneously with thyroid
hormone replacement.
Thyroid Hormone Replacement:
While Levothyroxine (T4) is the definitive treatment, peripheral conversion of T4 to
T3 is impaired in critical illness. Consequently, many guidelines suggest a combination of IV T4 (loading dose 300-500 mcg) and IV Liothyronine (T3) (loading dose
10-20 mcg), provided cardiac monitoring is in place.
Rewarming and Resuscitation:
Aggressive active external rewarming (e.g., forced-air blankets set to high) causes
peripheral vasodilation. In a volume-depleted, vasoconstricted patient with myocardial depression, this leads to 'rewarming shock' and cardiovascular collapse. Passive
rewarming (insulating blankets) is preferred initially until haemodynamic stability
is assured.
Clinical Pearl
Steroids Before T4:
This is an unmissable, critical safety step in managing myxoedema coma. The standard dose is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV.
The Clinical Triad:
The classic presentation is Altered Mental Status, Hypothermia, and a Precipitating
Event (e.g., infection, surgery) in a patient with hypothyroidism.
Passive, Not Active, Rewarming:
Avoid aggressive active external rewarming. Rapid peripheral vasodilation in the
setting of myocardial depression and hypovolemia precipitates 'rewarming shock'.
Use passive rewarming measures initially.
IV T4 + T3:

The ideal hormone replacement regimen is controversial, but many guidelines recommend a loading dose of both IV levothyroxine (T4) and IV liothyronine (T3), as
the peripheral conversion of T4 to the active T3 is impaired in critical illness.
Non-Pitting Oedema:
The term "myxoedema" refers to the characteristic deposition of mucopolysaccharides (glycosaminoglycans) in the dermis, leading to doughy, non-pitting oedema.
Hyponatraemia Mechanism:
Hyponatraemia in myxoedema coma is driven by impaired free water excretion (decreased GFR) and elevated ADH levels. It typically resolves with thyroid hormone
replacement; hypertonic saline is reserved for severe neurological manifestations.
Precipitating Factors:
Myxoedema coma rarely occurs spontaneously. Actively search for the 'I's: Infection
(sepsis), Infarction (MI/Stroke), Iatrogenic (sedatives/opioids), or Iodine
deficiency/excess.
ECG Features:
Classic ECG findings include sinus bradycardia, low voltage QRS complexes, and QT
prolongation. The latter predisposes patients to Torsades de Pointes, necessitating
careful electrolyte monitoring.
Airway Challenges:
Intubation can be difficult due to macroglossia and laryngeal myxoedema (mucopolysaccharide infiltration). Anticipate a difficult airway and have advanced airway equipment available.
Refractory Hypotension:
Hypotension may not respond to vasopressors alone because hypothyroidism
causes downregulation of adrenergic receptors. Haemodynamic stability often requires thyroid hormone replacement alongside volume and vasopressors.
Schmidt's Syndrome:
Also known as Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 2, this is the co-occurrence of Addison's disease, autoimmune thyroid disease, and Type 1 diabetes. This
association underpins the mandatory use of steroids before T4.
Gastric Atony:
Severe hypothyroidism causes gastric atony and ileus. This renders oral medication
absorption unreliable, mandating the intravenous route for initial resuscitation
drugs.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: إعطاء الهرمون الدرقي بيزيد معدل الأيض القاعدي ويسرّع استقلاب الكورتيزول بالكبد، ومريض قد يكون عنده Addison مع أمراض الدرق المناعية أو فشل pituitary. هذا الارتفاع المفاجئ بالطلب من دون احتياطي كظري كافي ممكن يعمل adrenal crisis قاتل، فالقواعد البريطانية توصي بإعطاء hydrocortisone تجريبي 50 إلى 100 mg IV قبل أو مع الهرمون الدرقي. والـ rewarming الخارجي الحماسي ممكن يعمل rewarming shock بسبب توسع الأوعية عند مريض ناقص الحجم.
الفخ: كتير طلاب يختاروا الـ levothyroxine لأنه العلاج التعريفي لـ myxoedema coma. الفرق إن قاعدة الأمان الأساسية هي الـ steroids قبل T4، لأن إعطاء الهرمون وحده ممكن يفجّر adrenal crisis قاتل.

question:
A 19-year-old takes a large intentional overdose of colchicine. 12 hours later, she
presents with severe nausea, vomiting, and profuse watery diarrhea. What is the
most feared, life-threatening complication that typically occurs in the second
phase (24-72 hours) of colchicine toxicity?

options.text: Profound bone marrow suppression and multi-organ failure leading to cardiogenic shock.
A hyperfibrinolytic state causing uncontrollable haemorrhage.

correctAnswer: Profound bone marrow suppression and multi-organ failure leading to cardiogenic shock.
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology:
Colchicine binds to tubulin, inhibiting microtubule polymerisation and arresting
cell division in metaphase. This disrupts cellular function in tissues with high
turnover rates (GI tract, bone marrow) and impairs intracellular transport in nondividing cells (myocardium, neurons).

Clinical Phases:
Toxicity typically follows three phases:
1. Phase 1 (0-24 hours): Severe gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting,
profuse cholera-like diarrhoea), abdominal pain, and hypovolaemia. Peripheral
leukocytosis is common due to demargination and stress response.
2. Phase 2 (24-72 hours): Multi-organ failure. Features include bone marrow
suppression (pancytopenia), direct cardiotoxicity (reduced contractility, arrhythmias), mixed shock (cardiogenic/distributive), metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis,
and renal failure. This is the period of highest mortality.
3. Phase 3 (>7 days): Recovery phase (if the patient survives), characterised by
rebound leukocytosis and transient alopecia.
Management Principles:
Treatment is supportive. Aggressive fluid resuscitation is required for Phase 1
losses. Early administration of activated charcoal is recommended (within 1 hour, or
longer if extended release) and multiple-dose activated charcoal (MDAC) may be
considered due to enterohepatic circulation, though evidence is mixed. G-CSF is
used for severe neutropenia. Extracorporeal elimination (dialysis/haemofiltration)
is ineffective due to the large volume of distribution.
Clinical Pearl
Mechanism of Action:
Colchicine arrests mitosis in metaphase by binding to tubulin. This mechanism underpins the delayed onset of bone marrow suppression and mucosal injury, as these
tissues have high turnover rates.
Small Therapeutic Window:
Colchicine has a very narrow therapeutic index. An ingestion of >0.5 mg/kg is potentially fatal.
No Specific Antidote:
No specific antidote exists (colchicine-specific Fab fragments are
experimental/unavailable). Haemodialysis and haemofiltration are ineffective due
to high protein binding and large volume of distribution (Vd > 2 L/kg).
Drug Interactions:
Colchicine is a substrate for CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein. Co-administration with
potent inhibitors (like clarithromycin or cyclosporine) can dramatically increase
colchicine levels and precipitate toxicity even at therapeutic doses.
Sepsis Mimicry:
The multi-organ failure phase with fever, hypotension, and pancytopenia can be indistinguishable from severe septic shock. A thorough history is essential to

differentiate.
Phase 3 Alopecia:
Patients surviving the initial multi-organ failure often develop transient alopecia
starting around day 10, signaling the recovery phase (Phase 3).
Enterohepatic Circulation:
Colchicine undergoes significant enterohepatic circulation. While evidence is limited, Multiple-Dose Activated Charcoal (MDAC) is sometimes considered in severe
early presentations to interrupt this cycle.
Biphasic Leukocyte Response:
Leukocytosis is common in Phase 1 due to demargination and stress response. This
is followed by profound leukopenia and pancytopenia in Phase 2 due to bone marrow suppression (mitotic arrest).
Neuromyopathy Presentation:
Colchicine can cause a direct neuromyopathy characterised by proximal weakness,
distal sensory loss, and areflexia. This may be confused with Critical Illness
Polyneuropathy or Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Cardiovascular Collapse Mechanism:
Shock in Phase 2 is mixed: hypovolaemic (from GI losses), distributive (vasoplegia
similar to sepsis), and cardiogenic (direct myocardial depression). This makes
haemodynamic management particularly challenging.

الفخ: طلاب كتير يختاروا الهيموراج بسبب الـ hyperfibrinolytic state أو الـ neuropathy بسبب سميته العصبية. الفرق إن المرحلة الثانية تتميز بتثبيط نقي العظم وفشل أعضاء متعدد وصدمة قلبية، وهي اللي تحدد الوفيات.

question:
A patient with a massive propranolol overdose has a QRS duration of 170 ms. In
addition to standard supportive care, what is the rationale for administering intravenous sodium bicarbonate in this specific overdose?

options.text: To correct the associated metabolic acidosis.
To overcome the drug's membrane-stabilizing activity (sodium channel
To enhance the renal excretion of the drug.

correctAnswer: To overcome the drug's membrane-stabilizing activity (sodium channel
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Action:
Propranolol possesses potent membrane-stabilizing activity (MSA), functioning as a
Class I antiarrhythmic by blocking cardiac fast sodium channels. In massive overdose, this results in QRS prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias, mimicking tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) toxicity. Sodium bicarbonate acts via two mechanisms:
1) Increasing extracellular sodium concentration to competitively overcome channel
blockade, and 2) Alkalinizing the serum (target pH 7.45-7.55), which decreases the
fraction of ionized drug available to bind sodium channels.
Clinical Pearl
'Propranolol is a TCA in Disguise':
In overdose, you must treat it as both a beta-blocker and a sodium channel blocker.
Wide QRS is the Indication:
Per TOXBASE, sodium bicarbonate (50-100 mL of 8.4%) is indicated if the QRS duration exceeds 120 ms or if there are arrhythmias associated with QRS widening.
A Multi-modal Antidote Approach:
Severe propranolol toxicity often requires simultaneous therapies: Glucagon (bypass beta-receptors), High-Dose Insulin Euglycaemic Therapy (HIET) for inotropy,

Sodium Bicarbonate for QRS widening, and Intralipid for cardiac arrest or refractory shock.
Seizures:
The lipophilicity and MSA of propranolol also mean it readily enters the CNS and
can cause seizures, another feature that mimics TCA overdose.
Not All Beta-Blockers are the Same:
Beta-blocker toxicity varies by agent: Propranolol causes sodium channel blockade
(wide QRS); Sotalol causes potassium channel blockade (long QT/Torsades);
Atenolol/Bisoprolol primarily cause bradycardia and hypotension without significant conduction interval widening.
Monitoring Bicarbonate Therapy:
When using sodium bicarbonate for QRS narrowing, aim for a serum pH of 7.457.55. Monitor for hypernatremia and hypokalemia, which are common complications of aggressive bicarbonate loading.
Lipophilicity Matters:
Propranolol is highly lipophilic with a large volume of distribution, making it resistant to haemodialysis. In contrast, hydrophilic beta-blockers like atenolol and sotalol are readily dialysable.
Glucagon Mechanism:
Glucagon acts by stimulating adenylate cyclase via a non-adrenergic receptor pathway, increasing intracellular cAMP and calcium influx to improve inotropy even in
the presence of complete beta-blockade.
High-Dose Insulin Mechanism:
High-Dose Insulin Euglycaemic Therapy (HIET) functions as a positive inotrope by
facilitating myocardial glucose uptake (providing essential metabolic substrate during stress) and modulating intracellular calcium handling.
Intralipid Mechanism:
Intravenous lipid emulsion acts primarily as a 'lipid sink', sequestering lipophilic
drugs like propranolol from the plasma to reduce tissue concentration. It also provides free fatty acids as a high-efficiency energy substrate for the myocardium.
ECG Manifestations:
Beyond QRS widening, propranolol toxicity may cause sinus bradycardia, AV block,
and QT prolongation (though less common than with sotalol). The QRS widening is
the specific marker for sodium channel toxicity.

question:
A patient on a stable dose of the SSRI sertraline for depression develops MRSA
bacteremia and is started on linezolid. Two days later, the patient becomes agitated, confused, and develops shivering, hyperreflexia, and a temperature of
39°C. This presentation is most likely due to which pharmacological property of
linezolid?

options.text: Its inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis.
Its action as a weak, reversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI).
Its displacement of sertraline from plasma proteins.

correctAnswer: Its action as a weak, reversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI).
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Interaction:
Linezolid is an oxazolidinone antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis.
Crucially, it also possesses non-selective, weak monoamine oxidase inhibitor
(MAOI) activity. When co-administered with serotonergic agents like SSRIs (sertraline), it prevents the breakdown of serotonin while the SSRI inhibits reuptake. This
dual mechanism leads to excessive intrasynaptic serotonin accumulation and
toxicity.
Clinical Diagnosis:
The patient presents with the classic triad of Serotonin Syndrome: altered mental
status (agitation, confusion), autonomic instability (hyperthermia), and neuromuscular hyperactivity (hyperreflexia, shivering). The presence of hyperreflexia and
shivering specifically points to serotonin toxicity rather than other causes of sepsis
or delirium.
Differential Diagnosis:
It is vital to distinguish Serotonin Syndrome from Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
(NMS). Serotonin Syndrome is characterized by hyperreflexia and clonus (neuromuscular hyperactivity). In contrast, NMS presents with 'lead-pipe' rigidity and
bradyreflexia/hyporeflexia.
Clinical Pearl
MAOI Mechanism:
Linezolid possesses reversible, non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibition properties. This activity is unrelated to its antibacterial mechanism but is sufficient to precipitate serotonin toxicity when combined with other serotonergic agents.
Serotonergic Drug Interactions:
Avoid combining linezolid with SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, triptans, and specific opioids
(fentanyl, tramadol, pethidine, methadone, dextromethorphan). These agents increase intrasynaptic serotonin.
Hunter Criteria for Diagnosis:
The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria are the gold standard for diagnosis. Key features include spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus with agitation, or ocular clonus

with agitation. Hyperreflexia and tremor are also major components.
Management:
The first and most important step is to stop all serotonergic agents. Supportive care
is the mainstay of treatment. In severe cases, the serotonin antagonist cyproheptadine may be used.
Differential: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome:
Differentiation is primarily based on neuromuscular tone and time course.
Serotonin Syndrome presents with hyperreflexia and clonus (lower limbs > upper
limbs) and has a rapid onset (<24 hours). NMS presents with lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, and a slower onset (days to weeks).
SSRI Washout Periods:
To eliminate interaction risk, SSRIs should ideally be withdrawn 2 weeks prior to
starting an MAOI (5 weeks for fluoxetine due to its long half-life). In acute sepsis requiring linezolid, this is rarely possible, necessitating careful risk-benefit assessment or alternative antibiotics.
Antibacterial Mechanism:
Linezolid inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 23S rRNA of the 50S
ribosomal subunit. This is distinct from beta-lactams (cell wall synthesis inhibitors)
or aminoglycosides (30S subunit inhibitors).
Safe Opioid Alternatives:
Phenylpiperidine opioids (fentanyl, pethidine, tramadol, methadone) inhibit serotonin reuptake and are high-risk in combination with MAOIs. Morphine, oxycodone, and hydromorphone do not significantly affect serotonin reuptake and are
safer alternatives.
Mitochondrial Toxicity:
Prolonged linezolid use (>2 weeks) can cause mitochondrial protein synthesis inhibition due to similarity between bacterial and mitochondrial ribosomes. This manifests as lactic acidosis, thrombocytopenia, and peripheral neuropathy.

question:
What is the primary molecular mechanism responsible for the hypermetabolic
crisis seen in Malignant Hyperthermia?

options.text: A gain-of-function mutation in the ryanodine receptor (RYR1)
Downregulation of the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca² ⁺ -ATPase (SERCA)
Overproduction of ATP leading to excess heat generation
Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria

correctAnswer: A gain-of-function mutation in the ryanodine receptor (RYR1)
englishExplanation:
Introduction:
The core of Malignant Hyperthermia pathophysiology lies in abnormal intracellular
calcium handling within skeletal muscle.
Pathophysiology:
The ryanodine receptor (RYR1) functions as the primary calcium release channel on
the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR). In MH-susceptible individuals, mutations in the

RYR1 gene (or rarely the CACNA1S gene) cause the channel to remain open excessively when exposed to volatile anaesthetics or suxamethonium. This 'gain-of-function' leads to massive, sustained calcium efflux into the myoplasm. High intracellular calcium drives continuous actin-myosin cross-bridging (rigidity) and stimulates
metabolic activity. The cell consumes vast amounts of ATP to fuel contraction and
drive the SERCA pump's attempt to re-sequester calcium. This hypermetabolic state
depletes ATP and oxygen while generating immense amounts of CO2, lactate, and
heat.
Analysis of Options:
While sodium channels (A) are involved in action potential propagation, they are
not the site of the MH defect. The SERCA pump (C) is functionally normal but overwhelmed; it works intensely to re-sequester calcium, consuming ATP. The crisis involves massive ATP consumption and depletion, not overproduction (D).
Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation (E) (seen in dinitrophenol poisoning)
causes heat generation but is not the primary mechanism in MH, where mitochondria remain coupled but are driven to maximal activity.
Clinical Pearl
Genetic Basis:
MH is an autosomal dominant disorder, meaning a patient with a susceptible parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the trait. A thorough family history of anaesthetic problems or sudden death during surgery is crucial.
Calcium's Role:
Think of MH as a 'calcium channelopathy' of skeletal muscle. The uncontrolled release of this key intracellular messenger is the final common pathway that initiates
the entire hypermetabolic crisis.
Metabolic Signature:
The profound increase in metabolism results in a mixed respiratory and metabolic
acidosis. The respiratory component comes from massive CO₂ production, and the
metabolic component from lactic acid production due to inadequate oxygen delivery
to hyperactive muscles.
Muscle-Specific:
The defect is specific to skeletal muscle. Cardiac and smooth muscle are generally
not affected because they utilize different isoforms of the ryanodine receptor (RYR2
in the heart) and have different calcium handling mechanisms.
Safe Anaesthesia:
For known MH-susceptible patients, a 'trigger-free' anaesthetic is required. This
mandates Total Intravenous Anaesthesia (TIVA) with propofol or regional anaesthesia. Volatile agents and suxamethonium are strictly contraindicated. Non-depolarising muscle relaxants (e.g., rocuronium) are safe.
Dantrolene Mechanism:
Dantrolene is the specific antidote for MH. It acts as a direct antagonist at the RYR1
receptor, inhibiting calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and halting the
hypermetabolic cascade.
Diagnostic Hierarchy:
An unexplained rise in end-tidal CO₂ (ETCO₂) is the most sensitive and earliest sign
of an MH crisis. Hyperthermia is frequently a late sign; waiting for a temperature
rise significantly increases mortality.
Disease Associations:
Patients with Central Core Disease, Multi-minicore Disease, and King-Denborough
syndrome have a high prevalence of RYR1 mutations and must be managed as MHsusceptible.
Dantrolene Dosing:
The initial dantrolene dose is 2.5 mg/kg IV push, repeated every 5-10 minutes until
symptoms subside or a cumulative dose of 10 mg/kg is reached. Early administration is the single most important factor in survival.
Recrudescence Risk:
Recurrence of symptoms (recrudescence) occurs in up to 25% of cases within 24
hours. Patients require extended ICU monitoring and often continued dantrolene
maintenance (1 mg/kg every 4-6 hours).
Diagnostic Gold Standard:
The In Vitro Contracture Test (IVCT) on a fresh muscle biopsy remains the gold
standard for diagnosis. Genetic testing is specific but has low sensitivity (many
causative mutations are yet unidentified), so a negative genetic test does not rule
out susceptibility.
Masseter Muscle Rigidity:
Masseter muscle rigidity (MMR), defined as jaw muscle spasm preventing mouth
opening after suxamethonium, is a warning sign. If MMR occurs, the procedure
should ideally be halted, or anaesthesia continued with non-triggering agents under
close monitoring for MH signs.
Differential Diagnosis:
Differentials include Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (caused by dopamine antagonists, evolves over days rather than minutes), Serotonin Syndrome (characterised
by hyperreflexia and clonus rather than lead-pipe rigidity), and Thyroid Storm (precipitated by stress in thyrotoxic patients).
arabicExplanation:
ليش: أساس pathophysiology الـ malignant hyperthermia هو خلل في التعامل مع الكالسيوم داخل العضلة الهيكلية. مستقبل الـ ryanodine RYR1 هو قناة إطلاق الكالسيوم الأساسية على الشبكة الساركوبلازمية، وعند الأشخاص المؤهلين وراثياً بتبقى القناة مفتوحة بشكل مفرط عند التعرض للمخدرات المتطايرة أو suxamethonium. هذه الـ gain-of-function mutation تعمل تدفق كالسيوم هائل ومستمر للـ myoplasm، فيصير تيبس عضلي واستهلاك ضخم للـ ATP مع إنتاج كثير من الحرارة وثاني أكسيد الكربون.
الفخ: بعض الطلاب يختاروا إنه فك ارتباط الفسفرة التأكسدية بالميتوكوندريا لأنه يسبب حرارة. الفرق إن هذا يخص تسمم dinitrophenol، أما الـ malignant hyperthermia سببه طفرة gain-of-function بقناة RYR1.

question:
A 28-year-old woman presents with agitation, diaphoresis, a temperature of
38.5°C, and ocular clonus after starting an antidepressant and St. John's Wort.
After discontinuing the offending agents, what is the most specific pharmacological treatment for moderate to severe serotonin syndrome?
englishExplanation:
Introduction:
The management of Serotonin Syndrome is primarily supportive, but a specific antidote exists for more severe cases.
Physiology of Management:
The absolute first step is to discontinue all serotonergic agents. For mild
cases, this along with supportive care is often sufficient. For moderate to severe
symptoms, management targets the clinical effects. Benzodiazepines are the cornerstone of initial pharmacological treatment to reduce agitation and neuromuscular hyperactivity. Cyproheptadine is the specific pharmacological antidote recommended by TOXBASE for moderate-to-severe cases. It acts as a potent 5-HT2A receptor antagonist, directly counteracting the serotonin excess. It is only available in
oral/NG formulations.
Analysis of Options:
Diazepam (E) is first-line for symptom control (agitation/rigidity) but is not a specific antagonist. Bromocriptine (A) is a dopamine agonist used for Neuroleptic
Malignant Syndrome (NMS). Dantrolene (C) is indicated for Malignant
Hyperthermia and is not recommended for Serotonin Syndrome (TOXBASE).
Labetalol (D) may be used for autonomic control but does not treat the underlying
pathology.
Clinical Pearl
Benzodiazepines First:
In any agitated patient with serotonin syndrome, benzodiazepines are the first-line
medication. They provide sedation and control the life-threatening autonomic and
neuromuscular hyperactivity.
Cyproheptadine Use:
Cyproheptadine is available only for oral or nasogastric administration. TOXBASE
recommends an initial loading dose of 12 mg, followed by 2 mg every 2 hours if
symptoms persist. It is indicated when benzodiazepines and supportive care fail to
control symptoms.
Cooling is Vital:
For patients with significant hyperthermia (>39°C), aggressive external cooling is
essential. This may require sedation and even paralysis and intubation in severe
cases to halt endogenous heat production from muscle activity.
Avoid Dopamine Antagonists:
Avoid typical antipsychotics (e.g., Haloperidol) for agitation as they inhibit heat dissipation and can mimic/worsen Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS), complicating the diagnosis. While Chlorpromazine has 5-HT2A antagonist properties, it
can cause severe hypotension and is generally reserved for specialist use when
Cyproheptadine is ineffective or unavailable.
Resolution Timeline:
With discontinuation of the offending agent and supportive care, symptoms of
Serotonin Syndrome usually resolve within 24-48 hours, although it may be longer
for drugs with long half-lives like fluoxetine.
Hunter Criteria Specificity:

The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria are more sensitive and specific than the
older Sternbach criteria. Diagnosis requires a serotonergic agent plus one of: spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus with agitation/diaphoresis, ocular clonus with
agitation/diaphoresis, tremor with hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with temperature
>38°C and ocular/inducible clonus.
Neuromuscular Gradient:
Neuromuscular findings in Serotonin Syndrome typically exhibit a gradient where
lower limb hyperreflexia and clonus are more pronounced than in the upper limbs.
This distinguishes it from NMS, which presents with generalized 'lead-pipe' rigidity.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: إدارة الـ serotonin syndrome أول خطوة فيها إيقاف كل الأدوية السيروتونينية، والحالات الخفيفة عادة تكفيها الرعاية الدعمية. أما الحالات المتوسطة لشديدة فالـ benzodiazepines هي حجر الأساس لتقليل الهيجان والنشاط العصبي العضلي. والـ cyproheptadine هو الترياق النوعي الموصى به من TOXBASE للحالات المتوسطة لشديدة، لأنه مضاد قوي لمستقبل 5-HT2A ويتعاكس مباشرة مع زيادة السيروتونين، بس متوفر فقط بصيغة فموية أو أنبوب معدة.
الفخ: كتير طلاب يختاروا الـ dantrolene لأنه الترياق المعروف للـ hyperthermia، أو الـ bromocriptine لأنه يستخدم بالـ NMS. الفرق إن الترياق النوعي للـ serotonin syndrome هو الـ cyproheptadine، أما الـ dantrolene فمخصص للـ malignant hyperthermia.

question:
Which of the following statements regarding multiple-dose activated charcoal
(MDAC) is FALSE?

options.text: MDAC is indicated for toxins like theophylline that undergo enterohepatic
The mechanism of 'gut dialysis' involves the drug diffusing from the intestinal
MDAC is absolutely contraindicated in a patient with a decreased level of consciousness unless their airway is protected.
MDAC is highly effective for enhancing the elimination of iron.
Bowel obstruction is a major contraindication to the use of MDAC.

correctAnswer: MDAC is highly effective for enhancing the elimination of iron.
englishExplanation:
Analysis of the False Statement:
Activated charcoal acts by adsorbing substances onto its large surface area. It poorly
adsorbs small, charged ions, metals, and alcohols. Specifically, it does not bind iron,
lithium, borates, cyanide, ethanol, ethylene glycol, or methanol. Therefore, MDAC is
ineffective for iron elimination. The primary decontamination method for significant iron ingestion is Whole Bowel Irrigation (WBI), and the specific antidote is
deferoxamine.
Mechanism of MDAC:
MDAC enhances elimination via two mechanisms: 1) Interruption of enterohepatic
circulation (binding drug excreted in bile), and 2) 'Gut Dialysis' (creating a concentration gradient that draws drug from the splanchnic circulation back into the gut
lumen).
UK Indications for MDAC:
According to TOXBASE, MDAC should be considered for life-threatening ingestions
of: Carbamazepine, Dapsone, Phenobarbital, Quinine, and Theophylline. It may also
be considered for Salicylates, though urinary alkalinisation is the priority.
Contraindications:
Absolute contraindications include bowel obstruction, ileus, and an unprotected airway in a patient with reduced consciousness (GCS < 15). Aspiration of charcoal can
cause severe pneumonitis.
Clinical Pearl
Indications for MDAC:
Remember the mnemonic for drugs where MDAC is effective: 'These Pills Cause
Dark Stools' (Theophylline, Phenobarbital, Carbamazepine, Dapsone, Salicylates).
Airway Safety:
MDAC should only be administered to patients who can reliably protect their airway
or are intubated. Aspiration of charcoal causes severe pneumonitis and can be fatal.
Substances Not Adsorbed:
Activated charcoal does not bind metals (iron, lithium), alcohols (ethanol,
methanol, ethylene glycol), corrosives (acids, alkalis), or hydrocarbons. It is ineffective for poisonings involving these agents.
Iron Toxicity Management:
Since charcoal is ineffective, gastrointestinal decontamination for significant iron
ingestion involves Whole Bowel Irrigation (WBI) with polyethylene glycol. Systemic
toxicity is treated with the chelating agent deferoxamine.
Mechanism of Action:
Activated charcoal adsorbs toxins via van der Waals forces onto its massive surface
area (approx. 1000 square metres per gram). This prevents absorption from the GI
tract.
Gut Dialysis Phenomenon:
For drugs with small volumes of distribution and low protein binding, MDAC maintains a low intraluminal concentration of free drug. This creates a concentration

gradient promoting diffusion of drug from splanchnic capillaries back into the gut
lumen.
Enterohepatic Circulation:
MDAC interrupts the enterohepatic cycle by binding drug metabolites excreted in
bile, preventing their reabsorption. This is a key mechanism for carbamazepine
elimination.
Dosing Regimen:
A typical MDAC regimen involves an initial dose of 50g followed by smaller doses
(e.g., 25g) every 2-4 hours. Treatment usually continues until clinical improvement
or serum levels fall.
Laxative Co-administration:
Cathartics (e.g., sorbitol) may be given with the first dose of charcoal to prevent
constipation but should generally be avoided with subsequent doses to prevent severe diarrhoea and electrolyte disturbances.
Complications of MDAC:
Risks include bowel obstruction, bezoar formation, and aspiration. Bowel sounds
should be monitored, and treatment withheld if ileus develops.
Theophylline Elimination:
MDAC significantly reduces the half-life of theophylline. However, for severe toxicity (seizures, arrhythmias, or extreme levels), haemodialysis is the definitive extracorporeal treatment.

الفخ: كتير طلاب يختاروا إنه ممنوع بانسداد الأمعاء أو مع مجرى هوائي غير محمي لأنه يظنوها False. لكن هذول مضبوطين، والخطأ الحقيقي هو الادعاء إن الـ MDAC فعال بالحديد لأنه أساساً ما بيربط المعادن.

question:
Sugammadex is a selective relaxant binding agent renowned for its unique mechanism. For which of the following neuromuscular blocking agents does it have
the highest binding affinity?
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Action and Affinity:
Sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin designed to encapsulate steroidal
neuromuscular blocking agents in a 1:1 ratio. It has the highest binding affinity (Ka)
for Rocuronium (~2.5 x 10^7 M^-1), followed by Vecuronium (~1.0 x 10^7 M^-1),
and then Pancuronium (~2.6 x 10^6 M^-1). While the affinity for Vecuronium is
lower than for Rocuronium, it is sufficient for effective reversal. Sugammadex has
no affinity for benzylisoquinolinium agents (atracurium, cisatracurium, mivacurium) as their molecular structure does not fit within the cyclodextrin ring.
Clinical Pearl
Rocuronium > Vecuronium >> Pancuronium:
This is the order of binding affinity for steroidal muscle relaxants.
Zero Affinity for Benzylisoquinoliniums:
Sugammadex is completely ineffective for reversing atracurium, cisatracurium, or
mivacurium.
Mechanism of Encapsulation:
Sugammadex forms a tight 1:1 complex with steroidal neuromuscular blocking
agents through encapsulation, effectively removing the drug from the neuromuscular junction down a concentration gradient.
Implications for RSI:
The ability to rapidly and reliably reverse a profound rocuronium block has made
the combination of rocuronium and sugammadex an alternative to suxamethonium
for rapid sequence induction (RSI).

Benzylisoquinolinium Reversal:
For benzylisoquinolinium agents, reversal is achieved with an acetylcholinesterase
inhibitor like neostigmine.
Contraceptive Interaction:
Sugammadex can bind progesterone, reducing the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. Patients should be advised to treat the administration as equivalent to one
missed pill and use additional precautions for 7 days.
Dosing Weight:
Sugammadex dosing is calculated based on Total Body Weight (TBW), even in
obese patients, unlike Rocuronium which is often dosed on Ideal Body Weight
(IBW).
Renal Elimination:
The sugammadex-rocuronium complex is excreted unchanged by the kidneys. Use
is not recommended in patients with severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30 mL/min)
due to prolonged clearance.
Adverse Effects:
Significant bradycardia and cardiac arrest have been reported within minutes of administration; co-administration of anticholinergics may be required if bradycardia
occurs. Hypersensitivity reactions (including anaphylaxis) can also occur.
Re-administration of NMBA:
If neuromuscular blockade is required within 24 hours of sugammadex administration, a benzylisoquinolinium agent should be used. If rocuronium or vecuronium
must be used, a waiting period is required (e.g., 24 hours for standard doses) or
higher doses may be necessary depending on the time elapsed.

الفخ: كتير طلاب يختاروا الفيكورونيوم لأنه ستيرويدي كذلك ويُعكس بالسوغاماديكس، بس ألفته أقل من النوروكورونيوم، والأتراكوريوم أو السيسأتراكوريوم فخ تاني لأنه ما ينعكس نهائياً.

question:
Which of the following is UNLIKELY to be a manifestation of theophylline
toxicity?
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology:
Theophylline toxicity involves adenosine receptor antagonism and phosphodiesterase inhibition, leading to increased intracellular cAMP and a massive release of
endogenous catecholamines. This results in a profound sympathomimetic surge.
Clinical Manifestations:
Gastrointestinal symptoms such as severe nausea and vomiting are almost universal
and typically the earliest signs. Cardiovascular instability is characterized by sinus
tachycardia, supraventricular arrhythmias (including atrial fibrillation and SVT),
and hypotension driven by beta-2 mediated peripheral vasodilation. Neurological
toxicity manifests as agitation, coarse tremors, and hyperreflexia, progressing to
generalized tonic-clonic seizures which are often resistant to standard
anticonvulsants.
Metabolic Profile:
A hallmark of theophylline toxicity is severe hypokalemia caused by beta-2 receptor
stimulation driving potassium intracellularly. Other metabolic features include hyperglycemia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia, and lactic acidosis.
Hyperkalemia is not a feature of pure theophylline toxicity.
Clinical Pearl
Theophylline Toxicity = Sympathetic Overdrive:
The clinical picture is one of massive catecholamine release.
Refractory Hypokalemia:
Hypokalemia results from intracellular shift driven by catecholamines rather than
total body depletion. Aggressive replacement is required to prevent arrhythmias,
but rebound hyperkalemia can occur once toxicity resolves.
Seizure Refractoriness:
Seizures are a major cause of morbidity and are often refractory to standard benzodiazepine therapy. They may require aggressive management with barbiturates,
propofol, or general anaesthesia.
Role of Beta-Blockers:
Hypotension in theophylline toxicity is primarily due to beta-2 mediated vasodilation. Non-selective beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol) or beta-1 selective agents can
paradoxically improve blood pressure by reversing this vasodilation and controlling
tachycardia, though caution is required in asthmatics.
Haemodialysis/Haemoperfusion:
Haemodialysis is the preferred method for extracorporeal elimination in severe toxicity (seizures, shock, rising levels despite MDAC). While haemoperfusion has

higher clearance rates, it is rarely available and associated with more complications.
Multiple-Dose Activated Charcoal (MDAC):
MDAC is the mainstay of elimination enhancement, interrupting enterohepatic circulation and promoting 'gastrointestinal dialysis' of theophylline across the gut wall.
Metabolic Acidosis:
Lactic acidosis is a common finding, resulting from both beta-adrenergic stimulation of glycolysis and tissue hypoperfusion.
Chronic vs Acute Toxicity:
Chronic toxicity occurs at lower serum concentrations than acute toxicity and
presents more insidiously, often with seizures or arrhythmias as the first sign in elderly patients.
Adenosine Resistance:
Theophylline is a competitive antagonist at adenosine receptors. Consequently,
supraventricular tachycardias induced by toxicity are typically resistant to therapeutic doses of adenosine.
Vomiting Mechanism:
Vomiting is multifactorial, resulting from both direct gastric irritation and central
stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone. This often limits the effective administration of oral activated charcoal, necessitating antiemetic cover.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: تسمم الثيوفيلين يعمل عبر تثبيط مستقبلات الأدينوزين وتثبيط الفوسفودايستراز، فترتفع الـ cAMP داخل الخلايا وينطلق كم هائل من الكاتيكولامينات الداخلية. هذا الاندفاع السمبثاوي المفرط بيجيب غثيان وقيء شديدين مبكرين، وتسارع جيبي واضطرابات فوق بطينية وهبوط ضغط من توسع الأوعية الطرفي. عصبياً بيصير هياج ورجفة وخفق منعكسات شديد يتطور لتشنجات معممة. أما الاستقلابي فالعلامة المميزة هي نقص البوتاسيوم الشديد، لأن تحفيز مستقبلات بيتا-٢ يدفع البوتاسيوم لداخل الخلايا، وموجود كذلك فرط سكر وخلايا دموية منخفضة المغنيسيوم والفوسفات وحماض لاكتيكي.
الفخ: طلاب كتير يختاروا فرط البوتاسيوم لأنه شائع في التسممات القلبية، بس في الثيوفيلين النقص هو القاعدة، فتذكّر أن الثيوفيلين = نقص بوتاسيوم وفرط سكر.

question:
A 40-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with confusion and
ataxia after ingesting windshield washer fluid. His blood gas shows a severe
HAGMA and a high osmolar gap. He also complains of blurred vision. Which
substance is responsible for his symptoms?
englishExplanation:
Diagnosis:
The combination of the source of ingestion (windshield washer fluid), the clinical
symptoms (confusion, blurred vision), and the laboratory findings (HAGMA, osmolar gap) is classic for methanol poisoning.
Pathophysiology Review:
Source: Methanol is the primary toxic component in windshield washer fluid, deicing products, and industrial solvents.
Mechanism:
Methanol is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde, and subsequently to formic acid. Formic acid inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase,
causing histotoxic hypoxia and severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA).
Clinical Features:
Visual disturbances are pathognomonic, ranging from blurred vision to a "snowstorm" appearance and eventual blindness due to optic neuropathy.
Analysis of Options:
•Ethylene glycol (A): Found in antifreeze. Metabolised to glycolic and oxalic acid.
Causes acute kidney injury (calcium oxalate deposition) and cranial nerve palsies,
but not the classic visual loss of methanol. •Propylene glycol (C): A solvent in IV
medications (e.g., lorazepam). Can cause HAGMA and an osmolar gap in high doses
but lacks specific visual toxicity. •Isopropanol (E): Found in rubbing alcohol.
Metabolised to acetone (D). Causes a high osmolar gap and ketosis but no
metabolic acidosis. It causes haemorrhagic gastritis and CNS depression, not visual
loss. •Acetone (D): A metabolite of isopropanol; not a primary ingestant causing
this presentation.
Clinical Pearl
Common Toxic Sources:
Antifreeze typically contains ethylene glycol. Windshield washer fluid typically contains methanol. Rubbing alcohol typically contains isopropanol. High-dose IV lorazepam infusions can cause propylene glycol toxicity.
Methanol Ocular Toxicity:
Visual complaints (blurred vision, photophobia, "snowstorm" field) in the context of
a high anion gap metabolic acidosis are pathognomonic for methanol poisoning, resulting from formic acid toxicity to the optic nerve.
Isopropanol Characteristics:

Isopropanol is the only common toxic alcohol that causes a high osmolar gap and
ketosis (due to its metabolite acetone) without a metabolic acidosis.
Acetone Breath:
The acetone produced from isopropanol metabolism can sometimes give the
patient's breath a characteristic 'fruity' or nail-polish remover odour.
Gap Evolution:
Toxic alcohol ingestion presents with a high osmolar gap early (due to the parent alcohol). As metabolism proceeds, the osmolar gap decreases and the anion gap increases (due to acidic metabolite accumulation).
Extracorporeal Elimination Criteria:
Indications for haemodialysis in toxic alcohol poisoning include: refractory metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.0), visual impairment (methanol), renal failure (ethylene glycol), or serum concentration > 500 mg/L.
Fomepizole Mechanism:
Fomepizole acts as a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH), preventing the conversion of parent alcohols (methanol/ethylene glycol) into their toxic
metabolites (formic acid/glycolic acid). It has an affinity for ADH approximately
8000 times higher than that of ethanol.
Therapeutic Cofactors:
Adjunctive therapy involves cofactors to enhance non-toxic metabolic pathways:
folinic acid (or folic acid) for methanol to accelerate formate breakdown, and
thiamine/pyridoxine for ethylene glycol to divert glyoxylate metabolism.
Methanol CNS Findings:
In addition to ocular toxicity, severe methanol poisoning can cause bilateral putaminal haemorrhage or necrosis, which may be visible on CT or MRI brain imaging.
Osmolar Gap Calculation:
The osmolar gap is the difference between measured osmolality and calculated osmolarity. Calculated osmolarity = 2 x [Na] + [Urea] + [Glucose]. A gap > 10
mOsm/kg suggests the presence of unmeasured osmotically active substances.
Ethylene Glycol Urinalysis:
Ethylene glycol ingestion leads to the formation of calcium oxalate crystals in the
urine, which may appear as envelope-shaped (dihydrate) or dumbbell-shaped
(monohydrate) crystals on microscopy.
