الفخ: الطالب بيختار نزف هضمي وقيء أو pancytopenia أو حروق جلدية وتساقط شعر كأنها أسوأ مؤشر موت. الفرق: التدمير بالـCV والـCNS هو اللي تقريباً مميت مباشرة وبيدمج بالـminutes، والأعراض الهضمية أبطأ.

question: You receive a satellite call from Denali (Mount McKinley) base camp station (altitude 2200 meters) for a 45-year-old male with a chief complaint of headache, nausea, and vomiting. These symptoms started shortly after the man was dropped off via helicopter. He is afebrile with unremarkable vital signs and a normal neurologic exam. In addition to descent, what is the most appropriate therapy?
englishExplanation:
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
Expl anation
A. Benzodiazepine therapy
This patient's symptoms are most conslstent with acute mountain sickness.
Appropriate treatments include carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, NSAIDs, oxygen,
and, if necessary, in severe cases descent.
B. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
This patient's history is most consistent with acute mountain sickness, which typically occurs at altitudes of higher than 2000m (6500ft). Acetazolamide is used to
treat acute mountain sickness because it induces a metabolic acidosis. This, in turn,
triggers compensatory hyperventilation, which can speed acclimatization. It can be
used as a treatment for acute mountain sickness or as prophylaxis. Other treatments
include dexamethasone, NSAIDS, and in severe cases, descent. AMS should be distinguished from High Altitude Cerebral Edema, which typically occurs at higher altitudes ( >4500m (14000ft) and has more pronounced neurologic symptoms, including ataxia (early finding), lethargy, altered mental status, and seizures.
Further information: Swenson ER. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and high altitude
sickness.

While acetazolamide is a diuretic that can be helpful for acute mountain sickness, it
is not a potassium-sparing diuretic.
D. Thiazide diuretic
While acetazolamide is a diuretic that can be helpful for acute mountain sickness, it
is not a thiazide diuretic.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الأعراض مع patient أُسقط بالهليكوبتر عند ٢٢٠٠ متر ومعاهم صداع وقيء وغثيان بدون حرارة ودون فحص عصبي غير طبيعي، بتتconsistent مع acute mountain sickness، وهي بتصيب عادة فوق ٢٠٠٠ متر. الـAcetazolamide مثبط لـcarbonic anhydrase وبيسبب metabolic acidosis، وهاد بيشغّل compensatory hyperventilation وبيسرّع الـacclimatization، وبيُستخدم كعلاج وكـprophylaxis. وخيارات ثانية زي dexamethasone وNSAIDs والنزول في الحالات الشديدة.

question: A group of hikers is approximately five minutes from a mountainside emergency clinic when one of them calls the clinic to say that a lightning storm overtook them and some of them have sustained injuries. The emergency clinic physician goes to the scene and finds four hikers. One is sitting against a tree, holding pressure on a forehead laceration. Another is pacing around the scene with visible burns to the right forearm and cannot hear instructions. The other two hikers are both lying on the ground: one is breathing and only moving his arms, and the other is not breathing and is pulseless. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Attempt to calm the agitated patient
Begin cardiopulmonary resuscitation on the pulseless patient
Help the bleeding patient hold pressure
Perform an evaluation of the supine breathing patient while using spinal precautions

correctAnswer: Begin cardiopulmonary resuscitation on the pulseless patient
englishExplanation:
Begin cardiopulmonary resuscitation on the pulseless patient
Expl anation
A. Attempt to calm the agitated patient
Although an agitated patient can be distracting when confronted with a multiple-casualty scenario, attempting to calm the agitated patient is not a priority in this situation. CPR should be promptly performed on the cardiac arrest patient. The most
common injury associated with lightning strikes is tympanic membrane rupture,
which could explain why this patient is hard of hearing. Burns are also common
with lightning injuries and can occur from direct electrical injury, superheating of
metals in contact with the body, or from vaporization of sweat or water on the skin
surface.
B. Begin cardiopulmonary resuscitation on the pulseless patient
The correct answer is prompt cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) of the cardiac
arrest patient. Lightning strike victims should be managed with "reverse triage,"
and patients not spontaneously breathing or pulseless should be addressed first.
Lightning's high current and voltage cause a massive cardiac depolarization, similar
to a single direct current defibrillation. The return of spontaneous circulation is
more likely than cardiac arrest in the general population. Prolonged apnea may occur even with cardiac activity due to the stunning of the medulla's respiratory center, and airway support may be necessary.
Further information: Leer-Greenberg B, Bakhsh A. When Lightning Strikes. EMRA.
http://www.emra.org/emresident/article/when-lightning-strikes/.
C. Help the bleeding patient hold pressure
It is common for lightning strikes to cause secondary traumatic injury, either from
being thrown by the shock wave or from flying objects. This patient has evidence of
head trauma but is sitting up and holding pressure on the laceration. Given the location of the laceration, this person is unlikely to exsanguinate. Although there is a
risk of intracranial injury, this individual is well enough to be sitting up and holding
pressure. Management of the bleeding is not a priority in this reverse triage
situation.
D. Perform an evaluation of the supine breathing patient while using
spinal precautions
Page 1302 of 4185
This patient appears to be unable to move his lower body. Keraunoparalysis is a rare
transient paralysis that occurs with electrical injury and typically affects lower limbs
and may last several hours. It may mimic spinal cord injuries. Thus spinal precautions should be maintained until advanced imaging can be performed. Given that
this patient is not in extremis, CPR should be prioritized.

question: A 35-year-old intoxicated male is witnessed to fall out of a boat into the ocean and is fully submerged for 7 minutes. He is in full cardiopulmonary arrest when he is pulled out of the water and CPR is initiated immediately. Which of the following is a poor prognostic indicator?
englishExplanation:
>5 minutes of submersion time
Expl anation
A. minutes of submersion time
The poorest prognostic indicator of submersion injury of the choices provided is
minutes of submersion time. Other poor prognostic indicators are: age < 3 years,
delayed initiation of CPR, need for prolonged CPR, acidosis, GCS 3, and warm water
drowning.
Further information: Szpilman D, Bierens JJLM, Handley AJ, et al. Drowning. New
Eng
Med.
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmra1013317
Schmidt A, Sempsrott J. Drowning In The Adult Population: Emergency
Department Resuscitation and Treatment. Emerg Med Pract.
https : / ,/www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26301918
B. Age years
Age less than 3, not greater than 3, is a poor prognostic indicator In drowning
victims.
C. Early initiation of CPR
Early initiation of CPR is a favorable, not poor, prognostic indicator
D. Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis, is a poor prognostic indicator as it suggests prolonged down time and accumulation of lactic acid.

question: A 30-year-old female presents with swelling and cramping in her left hand. She reports putting on a pair of gardening gloves when she suddenly felt pain in her hand and possibly saw a spider fall out of the glove. On exam, she is in moderate distress secondary to pain. Skin examination reveals a central punctum with some mild surrounding erythema. The patient complains of significant muscle spasms. What is the mechanism of action of the toxin found in this spider’s venom?

options.text: Hemolytic toxin causing disseminated intravascular coagulation
Necrotoxin inducing local skin breakdown and necrosis

englishExplanation:
Neurotoxin causing release of neurotransmitters
Expl anation
A. Enterotoxin causing neuromuscular junction blockade
This patient is likely suffering from a black widow envenomation. This does not
block the neuromuscular junction.
B. Hemolytic toxin causing disseminated intravascular coagulation
DIC is not a common result of black widow envenomation.
C. Necrotoxin inducing local skin breakdown and necrosis
Necrosis is more commonly seen in brown recluse bites and is not characteristic of
black widow spider bites.
D. Neurotoxin causing release of neurotransmitters
This patient likely suffered a bite from a black widow spider (Latrodectus) which
produces a neurotoxin that acts on the pre-synaptic membrane to release acetylcholine and norepinephrine. This induces diffuse muscle cramping, pain,
vomiting, and sweating.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499987/
Curtis A, Erickson T. Chapter 53. Venomous Animal Injuries. In: Walls RM,
Hockberger RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and
Clinical Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: سم الأرملة السوداء (Latrodectus) يحتوي على سم عصبي مسبق المشبكي بيحرر أستيل كولين ونورأدرينالين، وهذا يسبب تشنجات عضلية منتشرة وألم شديد وإقياء وتعرق، وهي الأعراض اللي ظهرت على المريضة.
الفخ: الطالب بيغلط ويختار سم نخراني زي العنكبوت البني، لكن الأرملة السوداء ما بتسبب نخر جلدي، والأعراض عصبية بحتة.

question: A patient is bitten on the hand by a snake in the deserts of central Nevada. Over the next several hours, his hand becomes severely swollen and painful. He presents to the emergency department the next morning with a severely swollen forearm with all compartments tense to the touch with radial and ulnar pulses difficult to palpate. What is the appropriate treatment at this time?

options.text: Antibiotics and surgical debridement of envenomation site

englishExplanation:
Antivenom, labs and supportive care
Expl anation
A. Antibiotics and surgical debridement of envenomation site
Surgical debridement of snake bite sites is rarely indicated. This patient has compartment syndrome and requires treatment.
B. Antivenom, labs and supportive care
This patient likely was envenomated by a rattlesnake based on geography. The cytotoxm of Crotolids causes swelling, pain, and cell lysis, with the treatment being appropriate quantities of the Crotalid antivenom. If the bite is on an extremity, the
swelling can mimic compartment syndrome, but fasciotomies should not be done
unless severe swelling persists after extensive antivenom treatment. Tourniquets
and debridement are not indicated.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK431065/
Curtis A, Erickson T. Chapter 53. Venomous Animal Injuries. In: Walls RM,
Hockberger RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and
Clinical Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
C. Surgical fasciotomy for compartment syndrome
Fasciotomy is not indicated in compartment syndrome due to a snake envenomation unless it is refractory to antivenom treatment.
D. Tourniquet to upper arm
Tourniquets are not indicated in snake envenomations, particularly if there is a concern for compartment syndrome.

question: A 33-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because he has had foot pain radiating up his leg since he hiked in Arizona earlier in the day. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows an area of erythema on the dorsum of the right foot and an apparent puncture site. Tapping on the area produces paresthesia in the foot. No other myoclonic jerking, excess salivation, or abnormal eye movements are noted. Cranial nerves are intact, and the Glasgow Coma Scale score is 15/15. In addition to observing this patient in the emergency department for the next few hours, which of the following is the best next step in treatment?
englishExplanation:
Analgesics
Expl anation
A. Analgesics
This patient has most likely experienced a scorpion envenomation. The most common species causing scorpion stings in the United States is Centruroides exilicauda.
The tap test, which includes tapping at the site of the sting to see if there is increased pain or paresthesia, confirms a Centruroides exilicauda sting.
Treatment is based on the classification of severity. (This patient has a Class II
envenomation).
The severity of the envenomation is classified as follows:
Class I - Local pain/paresthesia.
Class II - Local pain/paresthesia and pain proximal to the site.
Class III - Local pain/paresthesia and either cranial nerve dysfunction. (increased
oral secretions, abnormal tongue movements, nystagmus, blurred vision) or skeletal
muscle dysfunction (myoclonic jerking).
Class IV - Both central nervous dysfunction and skeletal muscle dysfunction. It can
lead to hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, pulmonary edema, and organ failure.
Class 1/11 envenomations are treated with analgesics and require close observation
for several hours to monitor for progression.
Class III is treated with analgesics, benzodiazepines, and antivenom.
Class IV is treated with antivenom and close monitoring, as the patient may need
intubation and cardiopulmonary support.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430928/
Curtis A, Erickson T. Chapter 53. Venomous Animal Injuries. In: Walls RM,
Hockberger RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and
Clinical Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
B. Antihistamines
This patient has experienced a scorpion envenomation. Antihistamines will not
manage this sting.
C. Antivenom
Antivenom is not needed for a Class II envenomation.
Page 1316 of 4185
D. Benzodiazepines
Benzodiazepines are helpful for managing associated anxiety or skeletal muscle dysfunction, which this patient does not have.

الفخ: الطالب بيستعجل ويعطي مضاد سم أو بنزوديازيبينات، لكن هاد محجوز للحالات الشديدة (درجة ٣-٤) اللي فيها علامات عصبية مركزية.

question: A 33-year-old female is brought into the base camp medical tent (altitude of 5,380 m (17,600 ft)) for headache and unsteady gait. Vital signs are: HR 110/min, RR 20/min, BP 116/82 mmHg, O₂ 91% RA, T 98.6ºF. Physical exam is remarkable for an altered female with ataxia. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive management of this patient's condition?
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
Descent
A. Acetazolamide
Acetazolamide and other carbonic anhydrase inhibitors can be used to prevent or
treat acute mountain sickness. This patient is presenting with hard neurologic signs
(altered and ataxia) concerning for high altitude cerebral edema (HACE). The definitive treatment for this condition is descent.
B. Descent
This patient is presenting with hard neurologic signs (altered mental status and
ataxia) concerning for high altitude cerebral edema (HACE). Descent is the primary
treatment. If descent is not possible, hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) with an inflatable pressure bag (e.g., Gamow bag) or chamber is an alternative. Additional
treatment measures include supplemental oxygen and dexamethasone.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430916/
C. Nifedipine
Nifedipine and other calcium channel blockers are used primarily for high-altitude
pulmonary edema, not high-altitude cerebral edema.
D. Sildenafil
Phosphodiesterase inhibitors such as sildenafil are useful primarily for high altitude
pulmonary edema, not high altitude cerebral edema.

الفخ: الطالب بيفكر بالأسيتازولاميد أو النيفيديبين للوقاية أو العلاج، لكن مع علامات عصبية واضحة، النزول هو الخيار الوحيد المنقذ للحياة.

question: An 11-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because she has burning, throbbing pain, swelling, and linear red marks over a large area of her leg after she swam in the ocean. An image of her leg is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply meat tenderizer to the affected area
Immerse the area in cold water

englishExplanation:
Irrigate with seawater
Expl anation
A. Administer antivenom
Generally, antivenom is not recommended for jellyfish envenomation. However,
consider antivenom for box jellyfish if the patient has severe envenomation symptoms that might include: headache, weakness, hypotension, cramping, myalgia,
nausea/vomiting, respiratory depression, arrhythmia, and seizures.
B. Apply meat tenderizer to the affected area
Contrary to popular belief, meat tenderizer is not beneficial, nor is urine. Local irrigation with 5% acetic acid is recommended for certain species, including those
found in Australia and the Indo-Pacific.
C. Immerse the area in cold water
Hot water immersion is recommended if tolerated, as some jellyfish have a specific
heat labile venom. Cold water does not provide this advantage.
D. Irrigate with seawater
This child is presenting after jellyfish envenomation. Jellyfish have stinging, venomcontaining nematocysts located primarily on their tentacles. Upon activation by a
stimulus, nematocysts release a sharp, hollow tube through a harpoon-like mechanism. This delivers venom into subcutaneous tissues. The severity of envenomation
is determined by the amount of direct skin exposure to the animal. Local reactions
include: immediate pain, pruritis, burning, and erythemic eruption in the pattern of
contact ("tentacle prints"). Local reactions usually resolve in days to weeks.
Systemic symptoms might occur after a significant envenomation with headache,
weakness, hypotension, cramping, myalgia, nausea/vomiting, respiratoty depres-
Sion, arrhythmia, and seizures.
The initial treatment is to irrigate with salt water after tentacle removal, which can
help to remove nematocysts. Do not rinse with fresh water, as the isotonic solution
makes nematocysts fire.
Further information:
Devlin JJ and Knoop KJ. Marine Trauma and Envenomation. In: Tintinalli JE, Ma
OJ, Yealy DM, Meckler GD, Stapczynski JS, Cline DM, Thomas SH, eds. Tintinalli's
Page 1331 of 4185
Emergency Medicine: A Comprehensive Study Guide, 9e. New York, NY: McGraw-
Hill; 2020:1333-1337.
Curtis A, Erickson T. Chapter 53. Venomous Animal Injuries. In: Walls RM,
Hockberger RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and
Clinical Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.

question: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department via ambulance from his home, where he was accidentally shocked while installing a new light fixture. The shock occured in his right hand, and a small first-degree burn is noted on the hand. The patient does not have chest pain or dizziness, and he did not experience an associated loss of consciousness. Electrocardiography shows no abnormalities, and urinalysis shows no myoglobinuria. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

options.text: Admit to the hospital with telemetry monitoring
Repeat electrocardiography and measure troponin in two hours

englishExplanation:
Discharge to home
Expl anation
A. Admit to the hospital with telemetry monitoring
Admission to the hospital is not necessary after sustaining a minor electrical injury
from a low-volt power source unless there are changes on electrocardiography, arrhythmia, evidence of rhabdomyolysis, or a history of loss of consciousness. If the
patient had sustained an electrical injury from a high-volt power source such as a
power line or lightning, admission would be appropriate.
B. Discharge to home
This patient sustained an electrical injury from exposure to a low-voltage power
outlet. Patients who are mildly symptomatic after a low voltage injury (e.g., small
burn) should undergo electrocardiography and urinalysis. If normal, they may be
discharged to home. Low voltage is defined as <600 volts. Most home power outlets
are 120 volts, although some appliances may be higher.
Further reading: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448087/
C. Repeat electrocardiography and measure troponin in two hours
Serial troponins and electrocardiography are recommended for high-voltage electrical injuries but are not needed with low-voltage shocks without chest pain, loss of
consciousness, or arrhythmia.
D. Transfer to a burn center
This burn does not necessitate transfer to a burn unit. Routine first aid and consideration of tetanus immunization are appropriate prior to discharge.

question: A 33-year-old female presents to the emergency department with toe pain after skiing. She is concerned that she may have frostbite. She complains of a burning, pruritic pain in her toes. Examination reveals red plaques, as shown in the figure. If rewarming and drying the foot does not relieve the patient’s symptoms, which of the following is the next most appropriate treatment?
englishExplanation:
Nifedipine
Expl anation
A. Colchicine
This patient most likely has chilblains. While effective for gout, colchicine is not a
recommended treatment for this condition.
B. Indomethacin
This patient most likely has chilblains. While effective for gout and other inflammatory conditions, indomethacin is not a recommended treatment for chilblains.
C. Nifedipine
This patient most likely has chilblains which is also referred to as pernio. This is an
inflammatory injury occurring after exposure to cold. The injury is superficial and
generally self-resolving. Lesions commonly appear within 24 hours of cold exposure
and typically resolve within a few weeks. Lesions can blister or ulcerate, and patients often report symptoms of burning, tenderness, or pruritus. Treatment is supportive, with rewarming and drying the extremity recommended. Nifedipine is an
option for severe cases.
Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK549842/
D. Surgical debridement
This patient most likely has chilblains which does not require debridement.

question: A patient is brought into an emergency room after recently completing a half marathon. He is complaining of diffuse muscle cramps and nausea. Vital signs are normal except for a heart rate of 105/min. What is the most likely etiology of his muscle cramps?
englishExplanation:
Electrolyte depletion
Expl anation
A. Electrolyte depletion
The patient is suffering from heat cramps. Cramping is caused by exertion and is
also known as exercise-associated muscle cramps (FAMCs). This condition is due to
a relative deficiency of sodium, potassium, chloride, or magnesium. Exertion-related cramping can occur with exercise in both cold and warm temperatures. It is
not necessarily related to elevated body temperature. The treatment is oral rehydration and stretching. The literature has shown that oral and IV rehydration are
equivalent for the treatment of heat illness.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK553117/
B. Muscle breakdown
While rhabdomyolysis is certainly a consideration in this patient, the history is
more suggestive of heat cramps. These are caused by electrolyte and fluid depletion.
C. Severe hypovolemia
Hypovolemia may contribute to heat cramps, however, the primary cause is electrolyte disturbances, classically seen in endurance athletes due to fluid replacement
with hypotonic fluid (water) rather than electrolyte solutions.
D. Vasodilation
This patient is presenting with heat cramps which are not caused by vasodilation.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: العداء بعد نصف ماراثون مع تشنجات عضلية منتشرة وغثيان، السبب هو استنزاف الكهارل (صوديوم، بوتاسيوم، كلور، مغنيسيوم) من التعرق المطول. التشنجات المرتبطة بالجهد (EAMCs) تحصل حتى في درجات حرارة باردة، والعلاج ترطيب فموي وتمديد.
الفخ: الطالب بظنها انحلال عضلي أو جفاف شديد أو توسع وعائي، لكن العلامات الحيوية مستقرة والتشنجات نموذجية لنقص الكهارل مش لل rabdo.

question: A local fisherman presents to a tropical emergency department in Fiji after having been bitten by a sea snake. The patient feels well but knows of the danger of such bites. Of those listed, what is the most worrisome toxic effect of the venom of this snake?
englishExplanation:
Respiratory depression
Expl anation
A. Anaphylaxis
Sea snake envenomation does not classically cause anaphylaxis. This is more common in Hymenoptera envenomations
B. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
DIC is not a common complication of sea snake envenomation. This is more commonly seen in rattlesnake envenomations.
C. Respiratory depression
Sea snakes are of the Elapidae family whose venom contains a potent neurotoxin.
The symptoms can involve severe rhabdomyolysis. More concerning is the potential
for an early tetany followed by a late flaccid paralysis leading to respiratory cessation. Treatment is with an Elapidae antivenom.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK532973/
Curtis A, Erickson T. Chapter 53. Venomous Animal Injuries. In: Walls RM,
Hockberger RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and
Clinical Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
D. Seizure
Seizure is not a common complication from sea snake envenomation.
arabicExplanation:
ليش: سم أفعى البحر (Elapidae) يحتوي على سم عصبي قوي بيسبب شلل رخو متأخر بيودي لوقف التنفس. الرابيدوميوليز الشديد ممكن يحصل، لكن الكارثة الحقيقية هي الشلل التنفسي اللي بيحتاج تنبيب وتهوية ميكانيكية.
الفخ: الطالب بيفكر بالحساسية المفرطة أو DIC، لكن سم الأفاعي البحرية عصبي بحت، والصعوبة التنفسية هي السبب الرئيسي للوفاة مش الحساسية.

question: A 39-year-old male presents to the emergency department after having stepped on an animal while wading near the shore in the ocean. He has a smaller stinger protruding from his calf. He brought in a picture of the animal, as shown. In addition to stinger removal, what is the proper treatment at this time?

options.text: Wound left open, hot water immersion

correctAnswer: Wound left open, hot water immersion
englishExplanation:
Wound left open, hot water immersion
Expl anation
A. Wound closure, antivenom
Patients suffering from stingray attacks will often have a barb in the skin with a significant wound. The stinger should be removed but the wound irrigated and left
open. The toxin is heat labile, and symptoms may be improved with hot water immersion. Antivenom is not indicated.
B. Wound closure, cold water immersion
The standard treatment for stingray injuries is hot water immersion. Stingray
venom is heat-labile and inactivated by heat. Water should be heated to a temperature that will not result in burns.
C. Wound left open, antivenom
Antivenom is not indicated for stingray envenomation. The management includes
hot water immersion, as stingray venom is heat-labile and can be inactivated by
heat.
D. Wound left open, hot water immersion
Patients suffering from stingray envenomation will often have a barb in the skin
with a significant wound. The stinger should be removed, but the wound should be
irrigated and left open. The toxin is heat labile, and symptoms may be improved
with hot water immersion. Antivenom is not indicated.
Further information:
Curtis A, Erickson T. Chapter 53. Venomous Animal Injuries. In: Walls RM,
Hockberger RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and
Clinical Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.

question: A 45-year-old intoxicated homeless man presents with multiple bites to his right foot while foraging in the forests of North Carolina. He reports seeing a "red, yellow, and black" snake. His leg has multiple small puncture wounds on his right foot. He has some mild decreased sensation around the wounds. Ptosis is also noted on neurologic examination. Otherwise, the exam is normal, and he does not report any other symptoms. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer Centuroides antivenom and admit to ward
Administer Crotalid antivenom and admit to ward
Clean the wound and discharge with good wound care instructions and PMD followup in 24 hours for wound check
Immobilize the extremity, provide wound care, and admit to ICU

correctAnswer: Immobilize the extremity, provide wound care, and admit to ICU
englishExplanation:
Immobilize the extremity, provide wound care, and admit to ICU
Expl anation
A. Administer Centuroides antivenom and admit to ward
Centuroides is a scorpion genus that includes the classic Centuroides exilicauda
"Arizona bark scorpion," found classically in the southwest United States Sonoran
desert. Antivenin does exist, but this would not be the appropriate medication to administer to this patient.
B. Administer Crotalid antivenom and admit to ward
Crotalinae is a family of snakes, including rattlesnakes (Americas) and pit vipers
(Asia/Americas). Rattlesnake bites are the leading cause of snakebite injuries in
North America. Rattlesnake envenomations generally are primarily hemotoxic,
causing necrosis and coagulopathy. The snake described in the question stem is a
coral snake, so administering crotalid antivenom is inappropriate.
C. Clean the wound and discharge with good wound care instructions
and PMD followup in 24 hours for wound check
This would be inappropriate, given that the patient may have suffered coral snake
envenomation with a potential for delayed neurotoxicity.
D. Immobilize the extremity, provide wound care, and admit to ICU
This patient has been bitten by a coral snake. These snakes are brightly colored and
are commonly found in the southeastern and southwestern United States. The
venom of coral snakes is a highly potent neurotoxin, and the neurotoxic effects and
respiratory insufficiency may be delayed up to 12 hours. These patients usually have
a minimal local reaction but may develop severe neurotoxic symptoms, including
fasciculations, diplopia, bulbar palsies, and eventual respiratory paralysis.
Currently, there is a limited supply of antivenom for Elapid envenomation, as production ceased in the US in 2006. The local Poison Control Center should be contacted if antivenom treatment is indicated. All patients require admission for
observation.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519031/
Curtis A, Erickson T. Chapter 53. Venomous Animal Injuries. In: Walls RM,
Hockberger RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and
Clinical Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.

question: A lactrodectus (black widow) envenomation can mimic which of the following clinical scenarios?

options.text: Diabetic foot ulcer with necrotizing wound
Encephalitis with altered mental status and fever
Peritonitis with abdominal wall rigidity and pain

correctAnswer: Peritonitis with abdominal wall rigidity and pain
englishExplanation:
Peritonitis with abdominal wall rigidity and pain
Expl anation
A. Botulism toxicity with flaccid paralysis
Black widow spider envenomation causes spasms and pain, not paralysis.
B. Diabetic foot ulcer with necrotizing wound
Black widow spider envenomation causes spasms and pain but should not cause
necrotizing wounds. Brown recluse envenomation can cause wounds that appear to
be diabetic foot ulcers.
C. Encephalitis with altered mental status and fever
Black widow spider envenomation causes spasms and pain but should not cause altered mental status.
D. Peritonitis with abdominal wall rigidity and pain
Lactrodectus (black widow) spider envenomation involves a neurotoxin that releases norepinephrine and acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions. Within minutes of being bitten, the area near the wound may become painful, red, and swollen.
There is also a classic appearance of local diaphoresis within an area of central
clearing. Neuromuscular symptoms, including muscle pain and cramping, usually
occur within an hour. Abdominal pain is also a commonly reported symptom, with
cases where the abdominal wall muscle spasm has been mistaken for peritonitis,
with patients receiving a laparotomy negative for intra-abdominal pathology.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499987/
Curtis A, Erickson T. Chapter 53. Venomous Animal Injuries. In: Walls RM,
Hockberger RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and
Clinical Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.

الفخ: الطالب بيفكر بالتسمم الوشيقي (شلل رخو) أو قرحة قدم سكري نخرية أو التهاب دماغ، لكن الأرملة السوداء بتسبب تشنجات مش شلل، وما بتخلي جروح نخرية.

question: You are treating an 18-year-old patient for heat stroke. His original vital signs upon presentation were BP 94/51 mmHg, P 144/min, RR 24/min, O₂Sat 97%RA, T 106.2ºF (41.2ºC). You apply ice packs to the patient's axilla and groin but have no facilities for cold water immersion. After 3 liters of normal saline IV and 15 minutes of cooling, his vitals are BP 80/44 mmHg, P 158/min, RR 24/min, O₂Sat 96%RA, T 105.5F (40.8ºC), and the patient's mental status begins to deteriorate. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
englishExplanation:
Initiate evaporative cooling
Expl anation
A. Administer acetaminophen rectal
This patient is suffering from heat stroke which is not a hypothalamus problem but
rather secondary to exposure. Acetaminophen is not likely to have any effect.
B. Administer midazolam for sedation
This patient is already hypotensive, which will likely be worsened by midazolam.
Further, he is not agitated; sedation is not necessary.
C. Initiate evaporative cooling
The patient has exertional heat stroke. Cooling measures and IV fluids have been
initiated, but the patient has become hypotensive with continued severe hyperthermia. The definitive treatment is continued cooling measures, specifically evaporative cooling. IV fluids should be continued, but rapid and effective cooling measures
are the most important treatment to prevent morbidity and mortality and resolution
of the hypotension. Mild to moderate hypotension is common and should resolve
with rewarming. Early vasopressors may result in arrhythmia induction, and the
subsequent peripheral vasoconstriction may further delay cooling efforts and
worsen the patient's clinical condition. Acetaminophen has no part in treating this
hyperthermia as it is environmental and not central in origin and may cause worsening liver injury and morbidity later in the clinical course.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK553117/
D. Initiate vasopressors
Vasopressors may be an attractive choice in treatment as the patient is hypotensive
despite IV fluid. Still, the subsequent peripheral vasoconstriction may further delay
cooling efforts and worsen the patient's clinical condition.

question: A 42-year-old male from Louisiana presents with the chief complaint of a wound to his left forearm. He reports he first noticed a small, painless red lesion on his arm three days previous after picking up wood from a lumbar yard. He believes he may have been bitten by a spider. Vital signs are: BP 120/80 mmHg, P 65/min, RR 16/min, T 99.0ºF (37.2ºC). Skin examination reveals a 3 cm erythematous lesion with blisters and a central area of ulceration on his left forearm. Which of the following is the best choice in management?

options.text: IV antibiotics and admission for observation
Local wound care and dapsone therapy
Local wound care and surgical referral

correctAnswer: Local wound care and surgical referral
englishExplanation:
Local wound care and surgical referral
Expl anation
A. IV antibiotics and admission for observation
Antibiotics are not required in brown recluse bites unless there is evidence of see
ondary infection. This case can be managed as an outpatient with a surgical referral.
B. Local wound care and dapsone therapy
While local wound care and tetanus administration is indicated in this case, antibi-
Otics are only necessary if there is associated cellulitis.
The evidence does not support the use of dapsone.
C. Local wound care and surgical referral
The patient has a bite from a brown recluse spider (Loxosceles), and correct management involves local wound care and tetanus administration if there is evidence
of ulceration. Antibiotics are not required unless there is evidence of secondary infection. Surgical referral is indicated if ulceration is present for possible delayed debridement (2-3 weeks post-bite).
Further information:
https:/,/www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537045/
Curtis A, Erickson T. Chapter 53. Venomous Animal Injuries. In: Walls RM,
Hockberger RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and
Clinical Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
D. Oral antibiotics and discharge home
Antibiotics are not required in brown recluse bites unless there is evidence of see
ondary infection

question: A 4-year-old girl is brought in by ambulance after being bitten by fire ants 20 minutes ago. The mother states that she heard her daughter screaming while playing in the backyard and found numerous ants covering her body. Within several minutes, she began having intractable vomiting and diarrhea. The girl states that her body itches and burns. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.1°F), pulse rate is 140/min, respirations are 35/min, blood pressure is 70/50 mmHg, and O2 saturation of 99% on room air. Examination of both emesis and stool do not show any blood. Physical examination shows multiple scattered wheals on the body surface. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. The abdomen is soft, and non-tender. Parenteral administration of which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
englishExplanation:
Epinephrine
Expl anation
A. Antivenom
Hymenoptera envenomation unfortunately does not have an antivenom.
B. Diphenhydramine
This patient is manifesting anaphylaxis (GI symptoms + dermatologic manifestation), and epinephrine is indicated, not just symptomatic antihistamines.
C. Epinephrine
Hymenoptera stings have antigen cross-over between similar species, which include
sawflies, bees, wasps, and fire ants. Individuals with anaphylaxis to one
Hymenoptera species will likely have a similar reaction to another. Fire ants are
wingless Hymenoptera. Criteria for anaphylaxis include: 1) acute onset
dermatologic/mucosal reaction (generalized hives, pruritus or flushing, swollen
lips-tongue-uvula) + respiratory compromise or hypotension; 2) acutely at least 2 of
the following, in the setting of likely allergen (skin/mucosal involvement; respiratory compromise; hypotension; GI symptoms); OR 3) hypotension in the setting of
known allergen. This patient meets the second criteria for anaphylaxis and should
receive epinephrine next.
Further information:
Curtis A, Erickson T. Chapter 53. Venomous Animal Injuries. In: Walls RM,
Hockberger RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and
Clinical Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
D. Methylprednisolone
This patient is presenting with anaphylaxis and epinephrine is indicated, not just
supportive therapy.

question: A 55-year-old homeless male presents with bilateral foot pain. The past few days have been rainy and cold, and the patient states that he has been sleeping on the street and has not changed his clothes. On exam, his feet are erythematous, macerated, and edematous, with occasional bullae. In addition to treating his current condition, what is the most appropriate recommendation to prevent a similar problem in the future?
englishExplanation:
Dry socks
Expl anation
A. Active and frequent rewarming
This patient likely has trench foot. While warming is important, frequently getting
wet/cold and rewarming can worsen this. The most important treatment is keeping
the wounds dry.
B. Dry socks
This patient is suffering from trench foot, aka immersion foot. This condition is
caused by prolonged exposure to a cold temperature that is above freezing and
damp. This leads to vasoconstriction, ischemia, and eventually gangrene. Advanced
trench foot often involves blisters and open sores, which can lead to fungal infections. The most important treatment is prevention by keeping the feet dry. Topical
barriers are an adjunctive treatment that may be used for patients who have hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating) as a contributory cause.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482364/
C. Topical antifungal
This patient has trench foot which is an exposure injury, not a fungal infection.
D. Zinc oxide
Zinc oxide is used to treat burns and as a barrier cream but is not part of the management of trench foot.

ليش: المريض مشرد مع رجلين مبللتين وباردين لأيام، طورت قدم خندق (trench foot): احمرار، تطرية، وذمة، فقاعات. أهم وقاية وعلاج: جوارب جافة وتغييرها باستمرار. القدم الرطبة الباردة بتسبب تضيق وعائي وإقفار ينتهي بالغرغرينا.
الفخ: الطالب بيفكر بإعادة تدفئة متكررة أو مضادات فطرية أو أكسيد الزنك، لكن التدفئة المتكررة بتخرب أكثر، والوقاية بالحفاظ على الجفاف هي الأساس.

question: Which of the following factors is the best predictor of survivability in a patient who sustained a hypothermic submersion injury?

options.text: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation initiated with five rescue breaths
Resuscitation continued until core temperature reaches 32.0 to 35.0°C (93.0 to 95.0°F)
Submersion for less than five minutes
The submersion injury occurring in ≤6.0°C water temperature

correctAnswer: Submersion for less than five minutes
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
Submersion for less than five minutes
A. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation initiated with five rescue breaths
Current recommendations state that rescue breaths should begin as soon as possible, but this is not the most predictive factor in surviving a hypothermic submersion
injury. Some recommendations suggest starting CPR with five rescue breaths instead of two prior to initiating chest compressions. Ventilation is the most important initial treatment of drowning. The greatest morbidity and mortality associated
with nonfatal drowning is due to cerebral hypoxia. Therefore, the priority in resuscitation must address and correct hypoxia rapidly.
Of note, hypothermic patients rescued from the water should initially have their
pulse checked for 30 seconds. Their pulse may be weak but still present, and starting CPR on an (albeit weak) organized rhythm can put the patient into a fatal arrhythmia. Gentle positioning/movement of a hypothermic patient is necessary in
order to prevent the induction of dysrhythmia.
B. Resuscitation continued until core temperature reaches 32.0 to
35.00C (93.0 to 95.00F)
It is true resuscitative efforts should be continued until the patient's core temperature reaches 32.0 to 35.00C (93.0 to 95.00F) and asystole has been present for 220
minutes; however, it is not the best predictor for survivability in hypothermic submersion injuries.
C. Submersion for less than five minutes
Cold water submersion may decrease metabolic demands and activate the diving reflex in drowning victims. The diving reflex is a primitive reflex that stimulates the
vagus nerve to shunt blood from the periphery to the brain and cardiac tissue, resulting in bradycardia and decreased metabolic demand which sustains mean arterial pressure and decreases cardiac output.
Although there have been reports of cold water drowning and success with prolonged resuscitation, the duration of submersion is the most critical factor in determining a "good" outcome, which is defined by survival and neurologic function. It is
well documented that a submersion injury lasting less than five minutes is the best
predictor for survivability and neurologic outcomes.
Page 1412 of 4185
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430833/
PMID: 28613583
D. The submersion injury occurring in s6.00c water temperature
While prolonged resuscitative efforts can be successful in submersion injuries in
s6.00C water temperature, it is not the best predictor of survivability. Studies vary
widely regarding whether or not cold water s6.00C is neuroprotective. Considering
the variable data and what we know about the diving reflex, most experts agree that
prolonged resuscitations should be attempted when drowning occurs in s6.00C water, or hypothermia may have preceded asphyxia, especially in children.

الفخ: الطالب بيركز على درجة حرارة الماء البارد جداً أو CPR المبكر، لكن حتى في ماء مثلج، لو الغمر طال أكثر من ٥ دقايق، فرصة النجاة بتقل بشكل دراماتيكي.

question: A 45-year-old fisherman and owner of a wholesale aquarium business presents with multiple superficial, painful lesions on his hands. He is otherwise well appearing. He is afebrile with stable vital signs and denies other symptoms. Physical exam is shown below. Which of the following is the best medical treatment to resolve this patient's likely condition?
englishExplanation:
Clarithromycin PO
Expl anation
A. Acyclovir PO
This patient has Mycobacterium marinum characterized by ulcerations on areas exposed to contaminated water. Herpetic whitlow classically is a herpes simplex virus
rash presenting with painful vesicular lesions to the fingers, most commonly contracted by dentists or medical providers exposed to oral secretions. Most cases are
self-limited, although antivirals may be indicated in immunocompromised/severely
infected patients. Surgical debridement/lancing should be avoided to prevent
superinfection.
B. Ciprofloxacin PO
This patient has Mycobacterium marinum characterized by ulcerations on areas exposed to contaminated water. Vibrio vulnificus causes blistering dermatitis, and
generally also presents with abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, and other symptoms. Vibrio septicemia is associated with: 1) consumption of raw/undercooked
seafood, classically raw oysters, or 2) inoculation of Vibrio into open skin wounds
when exposed to warm Vibrio-infested seawater. Antibiotic treatment for vibrio
septicemia consists of doxycycline and third-generation cephalosporin IV. For minor cutaneous wound infections due to Vibrio in otherwise healthy adults, oral
doxycycline or an oral fluoroquinolone generally suffices.
C. Clarithromycin PO
This patient has Mycobacterium marinum or "Fish tank granuloma/Aquarium
Granuloma," characterized by ulcerations on areas exposed to contaminated water.
Generally, treatment for superficial skin involvement in an immunocompetent patient is monotherapy with clarithromycin, doxycycline, or TMP-SMX.
Immunocompromised patients or those with more severe disease may need dual
therapy with clarithromycin and rifampin.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441883/
D. Itraconazole PO
Sporotrichosis ("rose gardener's disease") is a soil fungal infection that classically
appears as a painless papule on the finger/hand/arm at the site of inoculation and
Page 1420 of 4185
spreads proximally via lymphatics. The papule enlarges and develops into a pustule
that ulcerates. Itraconazole is the initial drug of choice for cutaneous sporotrichosis.

![HIPPO-00069 source page 1418](images/HIPPO-00069-Hipoo-p1418.jpg)

![HIPPO-00069 source page 1419](images/HIPPO-00069-Hipoo-p1419.jpg)

![HIPPO-00069 source page 1420](images/HIPPO-00069-Hipoo-p1420.jpg)

![HIPPO-00069 source page 1421](images/HIPPO-00069-Hipoo-p1421.jpg)

الفخ: الطالب بيفكر في سيبروفلوكساسين لـ Vibrio أو أسيكلوفير للهربس أو إيتراكونازول للفطريات، لكن القرحات المزمنة في متعاملين مع أحواض سمك = M. marinum = كلاريثروميسين.

question: A 16-year-old high school football player is brought to an ED for acting bizarrely during practice and then passing out. It is mid-August in Mississippi, and the team has been running double practices. The patient remains altered and lethargic in the ED. His temperature is 106.5ºF (41.4ºC), and he is warm and diaphoretic. Cooling measures for the treatment of heat stroke are initiated. Five minutes after implementing ice packs, spraying the patient with tepid water with a fan blowing across his bare skin, and administering chilled normal saline IV, the patient begins to shiver rigorously. His temperature is now 103.6F (39.8ºC). What should you do?

options.text: Discontinue cooling measures because he is within a safe temperature range

englishExplanation:
Administer lorazepam IV
Expl anation
A. Administer acetaminophen PO/PR
This patient likely has exertional heat stroke. Because this is due to external heat exposure, not a hypothalamus-mediated fever, acetaminophen is unlikely to help.
B. Administer lorazepam IV
The clinical scenario in this question describes exertional heat stroke, but the cooling measures have caused the patient to shiver, which is counteractive to cooling efforts through additional heat production. Shivering can be controlled by the cautious administration of benzodiazepines to allow for continued cooling without
causing worsening hypotension. Acetaminophen has no part in treating this hyperthermia as heat stroke is environmental and not central in origin and may cause
worsening liver injury and morbidity later in the clinical course. Cooling measures,
specifically evaporative cooling, should continue as this patient is still dangerously
hyperthermic. The goal temperature to prevent morbidity and mortality in exertional heat stroke is 102 OF (38.90C). Cooling measures should be ceased at this
temperature to avoid over-cooling and hypothermia.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459311/
C. Discontinue cooling measures because he is within a safe
temperature range
The goal temperature to prevent morbiditiy and mortality in exertional heat stroke
is 102.0F (38.90C).
D. Paralyze and intubate the patient
While this patient's shivering is likely slowing down his cooling, paralysis is not indicated at this time as there are other less extreme measures to control these symptoms and he has no other indication for intubation.

question: A 28-year-old man with no significant medical history comes to the emergency department immediately after sustaining burns to his skin after he fell into a fire pit. Physical examination shows third-degree burns circumferentially to the abdomen as well as anterior thighs, posterior forearms, and bilateral hands. An estimate of 35% full-thickness burns is made, and a 5.7 L infusion is planned for the first eight hours based on the Parkland formula. This patient is at increased risk of developing which of the following complications?
englishExplanation:

Expl anation

Critically ill burn patients receiving large amounts of fluid resuscitation are at the

to abdominal compartment syndrome.
Further information: Kollias S, et al. Abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS) in a

This is an otherwise young, healthy individual without any heart disease, who is at

from fluid resuscitation.

question: A 3-year-old girl presents with acute foot pain that started while she was walking barefoot in the backyard. Her vital signs are BP 90/palp, P 176, R 36, and T 38.1°C (100.6°F); SpO is 97% on room air. On examination, she appears restless and ataxic; excessive oral secretions, jerking muscular movements, and rapid wander- ing eye movements are noted. No abnormality is seen on her foot. Envenomation by which creature is most consistent with this presentation?
englishExplanation: The presentation of a child in severe pain associated with excessive oral secre- tions, muscular jerking, and wandering eye movements is classic for se- vere envenomation by a bark scorpion (Centruroides). The venom is pri- marily neurologically excitatory, leading to activation of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. The most common presentation is localized pain or paresthesia. Systemic toxicity is rare but is most common in young children. Skeletal muscular dysfunction with jerking muscle movements, cranial nerve dysfunction, hypersalivation, and ataxia and opsoclonus (rapid multi- vectorial involuntary conjugate eye movements) are seen in severe cases. Without an- tivenom treatment, symptoms can last 24 to 48 hours. Management is supportive, with airway control, pain control, and sedation as needed. Antivenom is currently available in the United States and has proven efficacy, but it is very expensive and should be considered only in severe envenomations. Incorrect Answer Explanations The main toxic component of the venom from a black widow spider (Latrodectus species) is alpha-latrotoxin. It causes the release of neurotransmitters, predominantly acetylcholine and norepinephrine. The release of acetylcholine can cause severe local- ized and occasional systemic myalgias. Localized diaphoresis might occasionally be seen near the bite site. Norepinephrine release can cause hypertension and tachy- cardia. Although patients might be very uncomfortable and restless due to the pres- ence of pain, ataxia, excessive oral secretions, jerking muscular movements, and rapid, wandering eye movements are not expected manifestations of black widow spi- der envenomation. The systemic toxicity described in this case is not a manifestation of envenomation from the Loxosceles species, of which the brown recluse spider is the most notori- ous in the United States. Most bites do not cause any significant problem, but the de- velopment of a necrotic skin wound is rare but possible. Children are at risk for hemolysis, the most feared but extremely rare systemic complication. A significant portion of rattlesnake (Crotalus) bites are "dry," and no local or sys- temic effects occur. If signs of envenomation occur after a rattlesnake bite, manifesta- tions are typically local tissue damage (swelling, muscle necrosis) and potentially hematologic abnormalities (thrombocytopenia and/or hypofibrinogenemia). Unlike scorpion stings and most spider bites, evidence of skin puncture (fang marks) is expected. Neuromuscular abnormalities such as myokymia (movement of individ- ual muscle fibers) and fasciculations are occasionally seen after envenomation by rat- tlesnakes, and cranial nerve dysfunction, respiratory paralysis, and weakness can be seen with the Mojave rattlesnake. Key Points The most common symptom in bark scorpion envenomation is localized pain, but se- vere symptoms (eg, ataxia, cranial nerve dysfunction, hypersalivation, muscle jerk- ing, and unusual eye movements) can develop in children. Black widow spider bite envenomation causes localized pain and diaphoresis that can spread systemically. North American rattlesnake envenomation causes pain and edema and can have se- vere hematotoxic effects.

question: A child sustained an insect bite to his eyelid. What additional condition is likely to develop?
englishExplanation: Preseptal cellulitis is an infection of structures anterior to the orbital septum of the eye. It can develop after insect bites or direct trauma to the face or eyelid. Preseptal cellulitis occurs most commonly in children, who present with pain, redness, and swelling of the eyelid. It is important to distinguish preseptal cellulitis from the more severe orbital cellulitis. Common features of orbital cellulitis that are absent in pre- septal cellulitis include painful limitation of extraocular movements, ophthalmople- gia, and proptosis. In younger children, it can be difficult to obtain a full ophthalmic examination, so CT imaging may be required to differentiate between the two diag- noses. Preseptal cellulitis can be treated effectively with oral antibiotics targeting Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae, which are the most common bacterial pathogens. Incorrect Answer Explanations Adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis is associated with URIs and is unlikely to result from local eyelid trauma. Adenovirus is highly contagious and typically causes conjunctivi- tis, coryza, pharyngitis, and adenopathy in the setting of a febrile illness. Keratoconjunctivitis is a more severe eye infection than conjunctivitis because kerati- tis denotes inflammation of the cornea. Patients experience a foreign body sensation, photophobia, blurred vision, tearing, and pain. Treatment measures include support- ive measures, symptomatic treatment with artificial tears, and topical antihistamines. Affected patients should be evaluated by an ophthalmologist, who can also determine if ophthalmic corticosteroids should be administered. Dacrocystitis does not result from local trauma to the eyelid. Rather, it results from an obstruction in the nasolacrimal duct causing inflammation of the nasolacrimal sac. The nasolacrimal duct can be congenitally obstructed or the obstruction can de- velop as a result of trauma or surgery to the nasolacrimal duct, medications, or neo- plasms. Once obstructed, tears become stagnant, creating a nidus for infection and inflammation. Affected individuals present with redness, swelling, and tenderness of the medial canthus, which may extend to the nasal bridge. Patients should be treated with antibiotics to cover gram-positive organisms because Staphylococcus and Streptococcus are the most common bacterial etiologies. Endophthalmitis is inflammation of the intraocular fluid that results from direct in- jury to the eye itself, not the eyelid. This inflammation is usually coupled with infec- tion. Patients present with a hypopyon (ie, an accumulation of WBCs in the anterior chamber), eye pain, redness, photophobia, and decreased visual acuity. Endophthalmitis is an ophthalmologic emergency and should be treated immediately with empiric intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime to avoid complete vision loss.

question: What is the appropriate treatment for stingray envenomation?
englishExplanation: Stingray envenomation should initially be treated with hot water immer- sion. Stingray venom is heat labile, and its effects can be reversed or lessened by immersion in hot (not scalding) water. Further analgesic efforts, including local anesthetic injection, may be required if hot water immersion is insufficient. Other marine envenomations that may benefit from hot water immersion include those from many jellyfish and various fish (eg, catfish, lionfish, stonefish, and weever- fish). Antibiotic prophylaxis remains controversial. Careful attention should be made to manage the hot water carefully, as burning of the skin can occur if not closely monitored. Stingrays have a whip-like tail that contains a spine surrounded by venom. Envenomation typically occurs when the stingray is threatened, often in the context of being stepped on. When the body of a stingray is stepped on, it re- flexively whips its tail and often envenomates the dorsal aspect of the offending foot. Potential complications include anatomic injury from the spine, effects of the venom, and infections. In most cases, the major manifestation of exposure is local- ized severe pain from the venom itself. Systemic effects are possible but uncommon. Local skin changes can occur, and occasionally, the broken spine or foreign debris can be embedded in the wound. In rare cases, deep stingray wounds may cause pen- etrating trauma and require surgical exploration. Incorrect Answer Explanations Immersing the body part in acetic acid (eg, vinegar) is not indicated for the treatment of stingray envenomation. Topical application of acetic acid appears to be beneficial in decreasing stinging nematocyst discharge for many (but not all) Cnidaria species, commonly referred to as jellyfish. In certain species, acetic acid application can increase nematocyst discharge. Geographic location can help guide whether to use acetic acid. In the United States, one is more likely to encounter a species that acetic acid application may cause nematocyst discharge, so ocean wa- ter can be used instead to aid in tentacle removal. In the Indo-Pacific region (where one is more likely to encounter a species that acetic acid application may de- crease nematocyst discharge), acetic acid use is appropriate. Cold water immersion is not indicated for analgesia in stingray enveno- mation. Stingray venom is heat labile, and its effects can be reversed or lessened by immersion in hot (not scalding) water. Further analgesic efforts, including local anesthetic injection, may be required if hot water immersion is insufficient. Currently, there is no antivenom for stingray envenomation. However, there is an antivenom for stonefish envenomation, which typically occurs on the bottom of the foot; significant swelling and erythema at the site of envenomation are typical.

question: A 20-year-old man presents 1 hour after being bitten on the hand by his pet rat- tlesnake. He feels nauseated, describes a metallic taste, and has pain at and around the bite site. His vital signs are normal. A CBC reveals a platelet count of 45,000/mm. What is appropriate initial management?

options.text: Place a tourniquet on the arm

englishExplanation: Antivenom is indicated in patients suffering from moderate to severe toxicity fol- lowing Crotalid envenomation. Patients should be evaluated for local tissue ef- fects, signs of systemic toxicity, and coagulopathy and bleeding. The pa- tient is suffering local effects (arm swelling and pain), systemic symptoms (metallic taste and nausea) and coagulopathy (thrombocytopenia); thus, he should be adminis- tered antivenom with the goal of halting the progression of swelling and reversing the thrombocytopenia. The patient should also receive four to six vials of Crotalidae poly- valent immune Fab or ten vials of Crotalidae immune equine F(ab)2. Doses may be repeated if effects of envenomation are not controlled following the first dose. Incorrect Answer Explanations Prophylactic antibiotics are unnecessary with rattlesnake envenomation because in- fections are rare. Antibiotics are reserved for later management if clinical symp- toms and signs suggest an infection. Thrombocytopenia or decreased fibrinogen may occur with rattlesnake en- venomation. Both are initially best treated with antivenom administration, not blood 3 products. Blood products may be used later if there is failure to respond to antivenom administration. There is no role for the placement of tourniquets that decrease arterial flow in the management of rattlesnake bites; ischemia and worse outcomes would be expected. Constriction bands that diminish lymphatic flow that could po- tentially decrease systemic envenomation are no longer recommended for North American rattlesnake bites. Despite severe soft tissue swelling, true compartment syndrome is uncommon, so a fasciotomy is rarely indicated.

question: Which characteristic distinguishes hybrid honeybees from North American honeybees?

options.text: Single bee able to sting multiple times
Venom more likely to cause anaphylaxis

englishExplanation: Hybrid or African-derived honeybees, known previously as “killer” bees or Africanized honeybees, are hybrids of African honeybees that escaped from labo- ratories in Brazil and are currently present in most of the southern regions of the United States. The primary distinction between Africanized bees and the more com- mon North American variety is that the Africanized bees are much more aggres- sive. With a perceived threat, often to the hive, many more bees respond than would those of the North American variety. As a result, a person can sustain a massive num- ber of stings that can lead to rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury. Hospital admission is appropriate for patients who have a large number of stings. Hybrid honeybees is a more neutral term that is not racially charged. Incorrect Answer Explanations The venom potencies of Africanized “killer” bees and North American honeybees are thought to be equivalent. The danger lies in the Africanized bees' lower threshold for provocation, heightened response, and resulting increased number of bees that will sting. Both Africanized bees and North American honeybees are capable of only one sting. When they sting, the barbed stinger apparatus is dislodged from the bee's ab- domen, and the bee eviscerates itself. Vespids such as wasps, hornets, and yellow jackets have the ability to withdraw the stinger and sting multiple times. Bumblebees can also sting more than once. The risk of anaphylaxis is not higher from the sting of an Africanized bee sting than from a North American bee, nor is it related to the number of stings. Although ana- phylaxis is the major systemic threat to an individual from most bee stings, in the case of a massive number of stings from an Africanized bee, systemic toxicity re- sults from a direct venom effect.

question: An otherwise healthy 30-year-old man is brought in because he lost consciousness and developed hemiplegia after surfacing from a dive. He was using compressed gas and made a rapid ascent. What is the definitive treatment approach for the un- derlying condition?

options.text: Administer oxygen and intravenous fluid and monitor
Determine treatment based on brain imaging results
Instruct the patient to perform the Valsalva maneuver

englishExplanation: This patient has a classic presentation of cerebral air embolism, the onset of cerebral symptoms immediately or soon after surfacing after a rapid or uncontrolled ascent. The primary treatment for cerebral air embolism is recompression with hyperbaric oxygen. Administration of 100% oxygen and intravenous fluid is appropriate while arranging the definitive treatment. Cerebral air embolism occurs when air bubbles either transfer from the low pressure venous side via intracardiac (such as via the presence of a patent foramen ovale) or pulmonary ar- teriovenous shunts to the arterial side or develop spontaneously on the arterial side and embolize to the brain. Typically this occurs in the setting of pulmonary baro- trauma from a too-rapid ascent. Incorrect Answer Explanations Administration of 100% oxygen and intravenous fluid with the goal of in- creasing tissue perfusion is appropriate while arranging for hyperbaric oxygen therapy. However, the patient has already manifested classic symptoms of cerebral air embolism and should receive definitive treatment rather than be moni- tored for symptom resolution. Since this patient has a classic presentation of cerebral air embolism and requires hy- perbaric oxygen treatment, initial brain imaging is unnecessary and should not delay definitive treatment. It would be extremely unlikely that a patient who presents in this classic fashion would have an intracranial hemorrhage or other etiol- ogy that would warrant initial brain imaging. There is no role for a Valsalva maneuver in the treatment of cerebral air embolus. In fact, performing a Valsalva maneuver while breathing compressed gas during a rapid ascent (as can happen during breath-holding, coughing, or vomiting) can lead to pulmonary barotrauma and cause a cerebral air embolus. Performing a Valsalva maneuver during descent is often done to “clear the ears” (equalize the pressure between the inner ear and outer ear canal). Continuing descent without adequate equalization can lead to barotitis, also known as ear squeeze, characterized by a range of manifestations that can include ear pain, hemo- tympanum, vertigo, and tympanic membrane perforation. Key Points The definitive treatment for cerebral air embolism is hyperbaric oxygen. The classic presentation of cerebral air embolism is the presence of cerebral symp- toms that occur immediately or soon after surfacing from a rapid or uncontrolled ascent.

question: An otherwise healthy 35-year-old patient suffers a myocardial infarction after a deep sea diving trip. What is the most likely underlying etiology of this complication?
englishExplanation: Ascent while deep water diving must be done carefully to prevent the uncommon complication of arterial gas embolism. In this patient's case, myocardial infarc- tion is likely from an embolus lodged in a coronary artery. Pulmonary baro- trauma can occur while deep sea diving. Rapidly ascending without exhaling can lead to expansion of gas in the lungs and alveolar rupture. Tearing of pul- monary veins can also occur, which can cause air to return to the left heart and em- bolize through the arterial system. Incorrect Answer Explanations Flash pulmonary edema can occur from acute heart failure secondary to myocardial infarction, but it would not be the etiology of an acute myocardial infarction while deep sea diving. Pulmonary edema, however, is a complication of ascending al- titudes while mountain climbing (ie, high-altitude pulmonary edema). In the setting of shock, hypovolemia leads to hypotension, which strains the heart and elevates troponins. However, this patient's history is inconsistent with a myocar- dial infarction induced by severe hypovolemia or hypotension. A pulmonary embolism can be a complication of an underlying condition that predisposes a person to an air embolism while deep sea diving, but it is not the etiol- ogy of an air embolism. Pulmonary embolisms can elevate cardiac enzymes due to right heart strain.

question: A patient presents with intense muscle aches, chest pain, and shortness of breath after returning by plane from a diving trip in Hawaii. What is a reasonable first step to treat this condition?

options.text: Place the patient in a hyperbaric chamber
Place the patient in the prone position

englishExplanation: When an arterial air embolism from deep water diving is suspected, the patient should immediately be positioned in supine and given 100% oxygen. These two measures can decrease air bubble size by displacing nitrogen and help- ing to resorb the embolus. This patient likely developed decompression sick- ness from flying after deep water diving. Decompression sickness and its associated musculoskeletal pain occur when nitrogen comes out of solution and forms bub- bles in the venous circulation. If these bubbles reach the arterial circulation through a patent foramen ovale, the patient can suffer a stroke or myocardial infarction. Incorrect Answer Explanations Anticoagulation has been used as therapy for arterial air embolisms, but its evidence is minimal. For a patient in critical condition, anticoagulation can be initiated after the patient is placed in supine and given 100% supplemental oxygen. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is a treatment for air embolisms related to deep water diving, but it is not the first step in treatment. Placing a patient in a hyperbaric cham- ber depends on the patient's acuity and stability. When an arterial embolism is suspected, the patient should be placed in the supine — not the prone — position immediately. When a venous embolism is suspected, the patient should be placed in the left lateral decubitus position, also known as Durant maneuver.

question: Which condition mandates consultation for emergent hyperbaric oxygen therapy in the setting of decompression sickness?
englishExplanation: The presence of any potentially life- or function-threatening signs or symp- toms in the setting of decompression sickness (DCS) is an indication for hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) therapy. This includes any focal inner ear or other neurologic manifestations, such as vertigo, ataxia, seizures, motor weakness, sensory changes, and bowel or bladder changes. These are known as “type II” DCS symptoms. Other type II symptoms include cardiopulmonary (chest pain, dyspnea, or “the chokes”), vascular, and abdominal symptoms; these should also be treated with HBO therapy. Less severe symptoms, such as musculoskeletal pain, rash, and local swelling, are known as “type I” DCS symptoms. Type I symptoms are managed conser- vatively with high-flow oxygen, intravenous fluids, and pain or symptom control. HBO therapy is effective for type I DCS symptoms as well, and it should be considered for more severe cases or those not improving with conservative manage- ment. Note that type I DCS symptoms may be more prominent than subtle type II symptoms. Thus, it is essential to perform a full and detailed history and physi- cal examination to determine if type II symptoms are present. DCS occurs after the transition from an area of higher pressure to an area of lower pressure as gasses dissolved in the plasma at higher pressure bubble out in the lower-pressure environment. Although DCS is classically associated with rapid ascent while diving, it can also occur after rapid movement from other higher- pressure environments to areas of lower pressure, such as leaving a caisson or pressurized mine, space walking, or rapid ascent to high altitude. Incorrect Answer Explanations In the absence of other concerning neurologic signs or symptoms, headache is considered a type I DCS symptom that does not, in itself, re- quire HBO therapy, although it will likely respond well to recompression. Type I DCS symptoms should be treated with supplemental oxygen, pain or symptom con- trol, and rehydration with intravenous fluids; HBO therapy can be considered but is not strictly indicated. Vertigo due to DCS, however, should be treated with HBO therapy. Joint pain is a classic manifestation of type I DCS known as the “bends.” Joint pain is considered the most common manifestation of DCS, and it can be treated akin to other type I DCS symptoms (ie, HBO therapy can be considered but is not strictly indicated). Vertigo from DCS, however, should be treated with HBO therapy. Skin rash is another classic manifestation of type I DCS known as cutis marmorata or “the skin bends.” DCS skin rash generally presents with areas of mottled (and often pruritic) painful skin, and it occurs in areas with higher fat concentrations (eg, the abdomen, thighs, buttocks, upper arms, and breast area). According to the Divers Alert Network, approximately 20% of patients with “the skin bends” also have neurologic symptoms. Thus, all those with cutis marmorata should be screened thoroughly for even mild neurologic abnormalities. Patients who present with isolated skin findings should be treated like other type I DCS patients: HBO therapy can be considered but is not strictly indicated. DCS-asso- ciated vertigo, however, should be treated with HBO therapy.

question: A 40-year-old man presents after sustaining a brief shock to his right index finger while fixing an electrical outlet in his kitchen. He denies loss of consciousness and other symptoms. The physical examination and ECG are normal. What is the most appropriate disposition plan?

options.text: Admit for telemetry and serial examinations of the right arm
Discharge home with precautions to return if he has increased pain
Observe for 6 hours with telemetry and serial examinations then determine disposition
Order CBC, chemistry, CK, and coagulation studies then determine disposition

correctAnswer: Discharge home with precautions to return if he has increased pain
englishExplanation: This patient had a low-voltage exposure with no loss of consciousness. Since he has normal physical examination and ECG findings, the appropriate disposi- tion is to provide reassurance and discharge him home with return pre- cautions. The voltage a patient is exposed to and the corresponding current that is transmitted are the major determinants of what complications might ensue. A home electrical outlet, which this patient was exposed to, is low voltage (United States 120 volts; Australia and Europe 240 volts). Low-voltage exposures, de- pending on the time of exposure and current path, are capable of induc- ing both immediate (burn injuries, dysrhythmias, respiratory arrest) and delayed (compartment syndrome) injuries. However, if there is no evi- dence of immediate complications, delayed complications are extremely unlikely. Patients exposed to higher voltages (>600 volts), on the other hand, are at risk for significant complications even in the absence of presenting complications. They should undergo laboratory testing (CBC, chemistry, CK, INR), telemetry, and serial examinations, particularly looking for the development of compartment syn- drome and rhabdomyolysis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Admission is not needed. This patient was exposed to low voltage from a home elec- trical outlet, had no loss of consciousness, and had normal examination and ECG findings. It is extremely unlikely that he will develop subsequent complications, such as compartment syndrome, dysrhythmias, or rhabdomyolysis. Had the same pa- tient sustained an exposure to more than 600 volts, admission for contin- uous telemetry and serial arm examinations would be appropriate. Emergency department observation is unnecessary based on the low-voltage expo- sure and the lack of worrisome findings. It is extremely unlikely that he will develop compartment syndrome, dysrhythmias, or rhabdomyolysis. Laboratory testing is unnecessary in this case because the voltage exposure was only 120 volts, he did not lose consciousness, and he has a normal ECG and no related ab- normalities on physical examination. Under different circumstances, such as exposure to more than 600 volts, laboratory testing would be indicated. Key Points Home electrical outlets are low voltage, and asymptomatic patients who have been shocked by them aren't likely to develop major complications. High-voltage exposures are a different story; exposure to more than 600 volts can lead to delayed complications — compartment syndrome, dysrhythmias, and rhabdomyolysis.

question: A 4-year-old boy presents after sticking a fork into a home electrical outlet with his right hand and getting shocked. There was no loss of consciousness. His right el- bow was on the ground at the time. Although he cried initially, he has remained asymptomatic. Physical examination reveals two extremely small first-degree burns on his right hand and elbow. A 12-lead ECG is normal. What is the appropri- ate management?

options.text: Admit to a monitored bed for 24 hours
Admit to a nonmonitored bed for serial peripheral vascular examinations
Observe in the emergency department for 6 hours; if no dysrhythmias occur, dis- charge home

englishExplanation:
This patient can be safely discharged home. He has suffered an electrical shock from a low-voltage source (<1,000 volts). A home electrical outlet supplies 120 to 240 volts. He has no transthoracic exposure, no loss of consciousness, and a physical examination that is notable for only small superficial burns. If the path of electricity was transthoracic or unknown (unlike this case), an ECG should be ob- tained. However, if the patient has a normal ECG and is asymptomatic, admis- sion is not indicated as later dysrhythmias do not occur after low-voltage injuries. Incorrect Answer Explanations Since the shock was from a low-voltage source and it did not transmit across the heart, there is no risk for cardiac injury. If the current was transthoracic and the patient was either symptomatic or had a new abnormal finding on ECG, then continued monitoring is indicated. Electrical shocks from low-voltage sources are very unlikely to cause sig- nificant vascular injury. Combined with the unremarkable physical examination, serial peripheral vascular examinations are not needed. Serial evaluations for vascu- lar injury would be indicated for anyone who has a shock from a high-voltage source (>1,000 volts), even with an initially benign examination. Since the shock was from a low-voltage source and it did not transmit across the heart, there is no risk for cardiac injury; thus, the patient can be safely discharged. The required length of monitoring if the patient was at risk for cardiac in- jury is not well described, but overnight monitoring is a reasonable approach.
