question: In the setting of a hyphema, which condition is most likely to require additional medication to aid in clotting to decrease the risk of developing increased intraocu- lar pressure?
englishExplanation: Hemophilia A is characterized by a lack factor VIII, which is required for clotting, and bleeding events in these patients are directly related to deficiency of plasma factor levels. Treatment of bleeding events in hemophilia A requires adminis- tration of factor VIII based on the severity of bleeding and the desired increase of fac- tor level. Patients with hemophilia A are at significant risk for hyphema. Ocular bleeding is considered to be severe and can lead to vision loss, so factor VIII should be administered to attain a desired factor level increase of 100% in hemo- philia A patients with hyphema. A typical initial dose is 50 units/kg, which will likely require repeat dosing every 8 to 24 hours. Incorrect Answer Explanations Factor V Leiden is a mutation of factor V of the clotting cascade which leads to clotting events. Hyphema in the setting of Factor V Leiden does not require specific reversal to avoid complications associated with hyphema, such as increased intraocular pressure. Increased intraocular pressure due to hyphema in a patient with Factor V Leiden should be treated in the same way as in other patients: with topical beta-blockers and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. Patients with systemic hypertension and hyphema do not require specific administration of medication to decrease risk of increased intraocular pressure related to their systemic hypertension. They would require treatment of the hyphema with the same medications as in other patients, including topical cycloplegics, anti- cholinergics, and glucocorticoids as well as oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and topical beta-blockers in the setting of increased intraocular pressure. Patients with sickle cell disease are at increased risk for spontaneous hy- phema. Additional medication is not needed for these patients to assist in clotting, but the approach to these patients may differ if they have sickle cell disease or sickle cell trait. Hyphema in a patient with sickle cell that does not involve increased intraocular pressure should be treated in the same way as in other patients: with cycloplegics and topical glucocorticoids. Sickle cell patients with elevated intraocular pressure in the setting of hyphema should not receive carbonic anhydrase inhibitors or mannitol due to the risk for increased sickling. Furthermore, it is important to note that this population is at risk of rebleeding, so the sickle cell status of the patient should be known.

question: A 54-year-old man presents with eye pain. A focused physical examination is per- formed, and the following finding is noted. What is the best next step in management? Credit: Yoko Okunuki, Junichi Sakai, Takeshi Kezuka, and Hiroshi Goto (CC BY 4.0; via Wikimedia Commons)

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees

correctAnswer: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees
englishExplanation: Hyphema is an accumulation of blood in the anterior chamber of the eye. Once hyphema is identified, it is important to raise the head of the bed as soon as possible; raising the head of the bed to 45 degrees can prevent occlusion of the trabecular meshwork by promoting layering of suspended RBCs inferiorly by gravity. Trauma is the most common cause of hyphema, but it can also occur sponta- neously in conditions such as hemophilia and sickle cell disease and in patients on anticoagulation therapy. One of the most common complications of hyphema is in- creased intraocular pressure. Incorrect Answer Explanations The treatment of hyphema in the emergency department consists of interventions de- signed to prevent rebleeding and intraocular hypertension. Treatments used to achieve these aims include cycloplegics, miotics, corticosteroids, and an- tifibrinolytic agents. Interventions should be directed by an ophthalmologist who is able to closely follow-up with the patient for serial examinations to ensure no re- bleeding, infection, or corneal perforation occurs in the setting of topical steroids. Although consultation with an ophthalmologist is crucial, elevation of the head of the bed is a simple intervention that should precede contact with an ophthalmologist. Measuring intraocular pressure is a component of a routine ophthalmic workup, but an open globe must be excluded prior to measuring intraocular pres- sure with tonometry in the setting of trauma. Intraocular hypertension (defined as pressure >21 mm Hg) occurs in more than 30% of cases after a hyphema but may not occur for several days after the injury, necessitating close follow-up during the first week. Although intraocular pressure measurement is crucial, elevation of the head of the bed is a simple intervention that should precede a focused physical exam- ination with tonometry. Hyphema is most commonly encountered as a consequence of blunt trauma. Associated findings can include orbital wall fractures, globe rupture, eyelid laceration, corneal abrasion, lens dislocation or subluxation, and corneal foreign bod- ies. In addition to a slit-lamp examination, a focused ophthalmic examination should evaluate for the presence of globe rupture; inspect the eyelids, lashes, lacrimal ducts, and cornea; and assess pupillary response, visual acuity, extraocular movements, and visual fields. Restricted upgaze or lateral gaze can suggest a blow-out fracture with entrapment. Diagnosis requires CT of the facial bones. Although CT of the facial bones may be required to rule out concomitant injuries, elevating the head of the bed in the presence of hyphema is a simple intervention that should occur prior to obtain- ing facial bone CT.

question: A 50-year-old man with a history of ulcerative colitis presents with an atraumatic red and painful right eye associated with blurred vision, watery discharge, and photophobia that began 2 days earlier. His visual acuity is slightly decreased in the right eye but normal in the left eye. Pain with a consensual light reflex is present. Flare and ciliary flush are noted on slit-lamp examination, but the intraocular pressure is within normal limits. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: ARZTSAMUI/Shutterstock.com.
englishExplanation: A painful consensual light reflex in the presence of a red eye is highly sug- gestive of iritis (anterior uveitis). The uvea consists of the middle layer of the eye (iris, ciliary body, and choroid); when the anterior portion of the uvea is inflamed, it involves the iris and ciliary body — a condition commonly called iritis. Inflammation of the anterior uvea and spasm of the ciliary body result in the patient's symptoms, including eye pain, blurred vision, tearing, and con- sensual photophobia. Minor trauma and chronic inflammatory condi- tions, such as ulcerative colitis and systemic infections, are often associ- ated with iritis. Visual inspection often reveals circumcorneal redness of the eye, particularly at the limbus (junction of the cornea and the sclera), which is known as “ciliary flush.” Slit-lamp examination reveals cells (leuko- cytes in the anterior chamber giving the appearance of dust in a beam of light) and flare (hazy appearance to the anterior chamber due to protein accumulation) and of- ten shows synechiae (adhesions between the lens and the papillary margin of the iris). In some cases, decreased intraocular pressure (IOP) may also be present. Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist is recommended in cases of suspected iritis be- cause patients need a full, dilated eye examination within 24 hours to ascertain if the inflammation involves the posterior uvea. Causes of iritis include infections (eg, herpes, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, syphilis), systemic inflammatory conditions (eg, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, sarcoidosis, multiple sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus), drugs (eg, bisphosphonates, fluoroquinolones), or other causes such as lym- phoma. Treatment of noninfectious iritis involves anticholinergic dilating prepara- tions (which help prevent synechiae formation but are contraindicated if acute nar- row-angle glaucoma is suspected), topical steroids (which reduce the inflammatory response), and oral analgesics (which help reduce ocular pain). Infectious cases of iri- tis should be treated with the appropriate agent (eg, antiviral medication for herpes or cytomegalovirus infections) with the help of an ophthalmology consultation. Incorrect Answer Explanations The hallmark of glaucoma is elevated IOP, which this patient does not have. Patients with acute narrow-angle glaucoma experience ocular redness, blurry vi- sion, mild-to-moderate pain, nausea, vomiting, and the perception of “halos” forming around objects. Corneal clouding is often present, IOP is elevated, and the affected pupil is mid-dilated. Acute narrow-angle glau- coma should be managed with pilocarpine, timolol, and hyperosmotic agents. Definitive treatment is surgical iridotomy. Patients with corneal abrasions often complain of acute discomfort, pho- tophobia, watery discharge, and foreign body sensation. Ciliary injection is usually present, and fluorescein staining reveals an epithelial defect. Simple corneal abrasions should not present with cells and flare on slit-lamp exami- nation, which rather suggests the anterior chamber inflammation of iritis. Additionally, a painful consensual light reflex should not be seen with corneal abrasions. Patients with scleritis present with severe orbital discomfort that is often bilateral. Redness is most apparent at the sclera, not the limbus. Nodular patches of the sclera and scleral edema are usually present, as are tearing and photophobia. Scleritis is often associated with systemic disease or infection. Treatment can involve oral analgesics and high-dose steroids, but emergent ophthal- mologic consultation is imperative.

question: Which topical medication should be avoided in patients with iritis?
englishExplanation: Pilocarpine is a muscarinic cholinergic agonist used to induce miosis. Miotics should be avoided in iritis because they may increase inflammation and the risk of posterior synechiae formation. Iritis is caused by inflammation of the iris and surrounding structures found along the anterior portion of the uvea. It is also known as anterior uveitis, which can include inflammation of the nearby ciliary body (iridocyclitis) in addition to the iris. Inflammation of the vitreous humor is known as intermediate uveitis; inflammation of structures posterior to the lens, such as the choroid and retina, is termed posterior uveitis. Iritis is the most common form of uveitis. Patients present with photophobia, ciliary flush or diffuse conjunc- tival injection, and decreased vision. Incorrect Answer Explanations Atropine is a long-acting cycloplegic agent that is in the same family of medications as homatropine, scopolamine, and cyclopentolate. Cycloplegic agents are frequently used to treat anterior uveitis by decreasing ciliary muscle spasm in order to relieve pain, keeping the pupils mobile in order to prevent synechiae formation, and preventing further protein leakage (flare). Cyclopentolate is a short-acting cycloplegic agent that is in the same family of medications as homatropine, scopolamine, and atropine. Cycloplegic agents are fre- quently used to treat anterior uveitis by decreasing ciliary muscle spasm to re- lieve pain, keeping the pupils mobile in order to prevent synechiae formation, and preventing further protein leakage (flare). Prednisolone is a topical corticosteroid that is used to treat anterior uveitis. Topical corticosteroids are the drugs of choice in the treatment of noninfec- tious iritis. Ophthalmic corticosteroids decrease inflammation in the anterior chamber.

question: An otherwise healthy 22-year-old man presents with redness, pain, blurred vision, and photophobia of the left eye with minimal tearing that has worsened over the past 2 weeks. He also endorses a 1-month history of low back pain and hip pain that is worse at night and improves with exercise. On examination, his left pupil appears constricted, and conjunctival injection is concentrated around the limbus. What is the most likely cause of his ophthalmic complaints?
englishExplanation: Anterior uveitis (or iritis) is associated with systemic inflammatory diseases such as seronegative spondyloarthropathies (eg, ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, Behçet's disease, and psoriatic arthritis). Patients with ankylosing spondylitis have a frequency of uveitis of approximately 25% to 30%. Uveitis may be the first presentation of an underlying spondyloarthropathy and should prompt consideration for follow-up and further testing. Although activity and severity of uveitis is not associated with spondyloarthropathy, 50% of patients with recurrent iri- tis have spondyloarthropathy. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients with acute angle-closure glaucoma have conjunctival injection, ocular pain, blurred vision, and photophobia. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is typically unilat- eral, and discharge is minimal. Although it may appear similar to uveitis due to the preceding similarities, pain with acute angle-closure glaucoma is typically severe and can be associated with a headache and vomiting, unlike uveitis. Additionally, the pupil in acute angle-closure glaucoma is typically fixed and mid- dilated; in iritis, the pupil is constricted and poorly responsive to light. Infectious conjunctivitis can be viral or bacterial and is a common cause of red eye. Although conjunctivitis can be unilateral, it is not uncommon for the disease to spread bilaterally due to the transmission that results from patients rubbing their eyes. Conjunctivitis produces mild discomfort, and vision is unaffected. Although conjunctivitis causes a red eye similar to iritis, conjunctivitis is usually painless. Infectious keratitis causes inflammation of the cornea and is typically associated with viruses, but keratitis can also be caused by bacteria, fungi, and parasites. Keratitis can be associated with conjunctivitis, but it is more painful and causes blurred vision. If keratitis is associated with a secondary anterior uveitis, a con- stricted pupil will be observed, but keratitis alone is associated with a normal pupillary size and response.

question: What approach is contraindicated for a first-time presentation of demyelinating optic neuritis?
englishExplanation: Oral steroids have been found to have a higher 2-year and 10-year recurrence risk of optic neuritis in either eye when compared to intravenous corticosteroid use; therefore, oral steroids are contraindicated as a treatment for demyelinat- ing optic neuritis without prior intravenous steroid therapy. Intravenous steroids have been found to accelerate the recovery of visual function in selected pa- tients with demyelinating optic neuritis; however, long-term visual outcomes are similar in patients who receive no intravenous corticosteroids. Optic neuritis is an inflammation of the optic nerve that causes monocu- lar vision loss. The most common etiology is demyelination, but others include parainfectious causes associated with viral syndromes (eg, measles, mumps, rubella, chickenpox, whooping cough; and following vaccination); infectious causes (eg, cat- scratch disease, Lyme disease, syphilis, cryptococcal meningitis, and varicella-zoster virus); and noninfectious causes (eg, sarcoidosis and autoimmune disorders). Incorrect Answer Explanations Interferon beta is a cytokine administered weekly via intramuscular injection. It has immunomodulatory effects on the progression of multiple sclerosis. Patients with a diagnosis of optic neuritis and evidence of white-matter lesions on brain MRI with first attack — which is suggestive of multiple sclerosis — can benefit from treatment with interferon beta. Intravenous methylprednisolone is strongly recommended in patients with optic neuritis and abnormal brain MRI that is suggestive of underlying multiple scle- rosis. Intravenous corticosteroids have been found to relieve pain, increase the rate of visual recovery (but not long-term outcome), and decrease the risk of developing multiple sclerosis within 2 years after symptom onset. Without treatment, the prognosis of optic neuritis is excellent, with vision im- proving within a few weeks. Improvement continues over months, with 90% of pa- tients achieving 20/40 visual acuity or better at 1 year. Subtle changes to color vision and a mild relative afferent pupillary defect may persist. question: A 57-year-old man presents with difficulty seeing out of his right eye over the past 3 hours. He denies ocular trauma, eye pain, and headaches. This presentation is more consistent with retinal detachment. A central retinal vein occlusion presents with a monocular vision loss that is typically painless. On ophthalmoscopic examination, the classic finding is a “blood-and-thunder” fundus. These patients require further evaluation by ophthal- mology. question: From which artery does an embolus originate that leads to central retinal artery occlusion?
englishExplanation: The internal carotid artery (ICA) branches include the ophthalmic artery, which supplies the central retinal artery. Therefore, plaque rupture from the in- ternal carotid artery can lead to thrombosis of the central retinal artery, which is a terminal artery. The ICA also branches into other intracranial vasculature, including the anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery. An embolus from the ICA can occlude any of these vessels, causing a cerebrovascular accident (CVA). In a patient who presents with a central retinal artery occlusion or CVA, it is important to evalu- ate the ICA and carotids with additional imaging studies, such as carotid Dopplers, MRI, or CT angiography of the head and neck. This imaging assesses vessel narrowing and extracranial carotid atherosclerosis for possible endarterectomy or stenting to prevent further CVAs. Incorrect Answer Explanations The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) originates from the internal carotid artery. The branches of the ACA do not supply the ophthalmic artery; therefore, an embolus from this vessel cannot occlude the central retinal artery. The basilar artery originates from the vertebral arteries. Its branches include the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, pontine arteries, and superior cerebellar artery. It does not supply the central retinal artery. The middle cerebral artery originates from the internal carotid artery. Its branches include the lenticulostriate arteries and superior and inferior trunks. These branches do not supply the ophthalmic artery; therefore, an embolus from this vessel cannot occlude the central retinal artery.

question: For which nasal foreign body is a topical vasoconstricting agent such as oxymeta- zoline contraindicated in toddlers?
englishExplanation: Removal of a button battery from a toddler's nose is an emergent procedure (within 4-8 hours) because the battery can cause alkaline necrosis of the nasal septum. However, the use of a topical nasal vasoconstricting agent such as oxymetazoline to make removal easier is contraindicated; the presence of an ion charge from the nasal drops can cause electrolysis and result in a severe alkaline burn. Otherwise, vaso- constricting agents are recommended for the management of many nasal foreign bodies. Vasoconstriction has the advantage of potentially minimizing bleeding during or after the removal procedure and of decreasing local edema around the foreign body to ease removal. Incorrect Answer Explanations Even if the sponge absorbs some of the vasoconstricting agent when it is applied, a vasoconstricting agent can still reduce the nasal mucosal swelling and de- crease the bleeding and trauma associated with removal of the foreign body. Hard plastic toy beads are often difficult to grasp, and using a vasoconstricting agent can decrease local edema to make removal easier. Magnets, particularly those across the nasal septum, can be quite destructive. Removal can be accomplished by using the handle of bayonet forceps to attract one of the magnets away from the septum. A topical nasal vasoconstricting agent is often useful, not contraindicated, in this setting. Key Points Topical nasal vasoconstricting agents are helpful for the removal of most nasal for- eign bodies. Topical nasal vasoconstricting agents or any other electrolyte liquid should not be used when the foreign body is a button battery.

question: A 38-year-old woman with a history of asthma and eczema presents with nasal congestion of 1 week's duration. Over the past few days, she has had persistent sneezing, rhinorrhea, and nasal stuffiness. Examination reveals inflamed nasal turbinates and slight erythema in the oropharynx. There is no tenderness to palpa- tion of her sinuses and no fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with symptoms consistent with allergic rhinitis, a diag- nosis that is primarily clinical. Patients with allergic rhinitis tend to have other atopic medical conditions, such as asthma and eczema. Treatment involves remov- ing any precipitating allergens, such as pollen or pets. Allergic rhinitis is treated with nasal inhaled steroid sprays, saline nasal rinses, and oral antihistamine. For more severe cases, inhaled or systemic steroids might be indicated. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient has no sinus tenderness, facial pain, or fever and has not had symptoms for more than 10 days, so bacterial sinusitis is unlikely. The use of antibiotics in sinusitis is controversial, as there is mixed evidence that it improves outcomes. Nasal foreign body is unlikely since the patient is an adult. With a nasal foreign body, symptoms are more likely to be unilateral. Treatment for nasal foreign body is removal, either emergently if there are signs of airway compromise or electively in the emergency department or by an ENT specialist. Button batteries in the nose must be removed immediately. This patient has no fever, cough, sore throat, or myalgias, so a URI is unlikely at this time. Most URIs are viral and require only supportive therapy.

question: A patient presents with 5 days of acute nasal congestion, purulent nasal discharge, and facial pain that worsens with leaning forward. What is the best initial treatment?
englishExplanation: This patient has acute rhinosinusitis (ARS), which is a common disease process seen in the emergency department. Most of the cases of ARS are actually acute viral rhinosinusitis (AVRS), whereas only about 2% of these infections represent acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS). AVRS and many cases of ABRS are self limited, and the initial focus of treatment should be symptomatic care, which includes nasal saline irrigation, over-the-counter analgesics and antipyretics, and intranasal steroids. Other symptomatic treatments with less evidence include in- tranasal ipratropium, intranasal saline spray, oral decongestants, oral antihis- tamines, and nasal oxymetazoline. The diagnosis is typically clinical, with patients presenting with two or more of the following: nasal congestion, facial pain or pressure, anosmia, or purulent nasal discharge. Additionally, fever, tooth pain, maxillary pain, and increase in symptoms with leaning forward may be reported. Complications of ABRS include pe- riorbital sinusitis, orbital sinusitis, Potts puffy tumor (osteomyelitis of the frontal bone), intracranial abscess, or meningitis. Physicians should make sure to do a thor- ough history and physical examination to make sure none of these complications, al- though rare, exist. ABRS can be initially treated symptomatically in an immunocompetent host. Recommendations vary, but one recommendation is to provide symptomatic treatment as above for 7 days; if the patient is not improving, then start antibi- otics. Others argue for a wait-and-see antibiotic prescription. A general thought is to reserve antibiotics for patients with purulent nasal discharge and symp- toms for more than 7 to 10 days. The antibiotics of choice are amoxicillin, amox- icillin-clavulanate, or doxycycline if the patient is allergic to penicillin. If the patient is at high risk for Pseudomonas, then high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate is recommended. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although nasal oxymetazoline can provide symptomatic relief of nasal congestion due to ARS, it is not the first-line treatment recommended — nasal saline irrigation is. Nasal oxymetazoline is also not recommended for use beyond 3 days as it can lead to rebound congestion or dependence. First-line therapy for ARS includes nasal saline irrigation, analgesics, antipyretics, and nasal steroids. Patients can also use oral decongestants, nasal decongestants, and oral antihistamines. Although oral amoxicillin is the correct treatment for a patient who has prolonged ABRS requiring antibiotic therapy, most patients with ARS do not need antibi- otics, as ARS is most often viral in nature or self limiting. Oral antibiotics are not the correct treatment for someone who has only had symptoms for 5 days. Most recom- mendations state to initially treat ARS patients with symptomatic therapy as above, and if symptoms persist for more than 7 to 10 days, then treat with antibiotics. Macrolides, such as azithromycin, are not a recommended treatment for ABRS anymore due to the high resistance against Streptococcus pneumoniae. If one were to treat with antibiotics, the first-line therapy would be amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate.

question: What clinical finding distinguishes an aphthous ulcer from herpes labialis?

options.text: Aphthous ulcers are >1 cm, while the lesions from herpes labialis tend to be <0.3 cm
Aphthous ulcers are frequently associated with signs of systemic illness
Aphthous ulcers are painless, while herpes labialis lesions are painful
Aphthous ulcers generally occur on the nonkeratinized mucosa inside the mouth

correctAnswer: Aphthous ulcers generally occur on the nonkeratinized mucosa inside the mouth
englishExplanation:
Aphthous ulcers, commonly called “canker sores,” are multifactorial, noninfectious, inflammatory lesions that generally form on nonkera- tinized oral tissue. Typical locations include the buccal mucosa, soft palate, and floor of the mouth, including underneath the tongue. By contrast, herpes labialis le- sions — caused by HSV-1 and commonly called “cold sores” — occur predominantly on the keratinized oral tissue outside of the lips and around the mouth. When they do occur intraorally, these lesions generally appear on keratinized tissue, primarily the hard palate and tightly bound oral gingiva. Both types of lesion are recurrent and of- ten provoked by stress, illness, or trauma. However, the early disease progression is distinct. Aphthous ulcers first appear as erythematous, painful macules that evolve into ulcers, whereas herpes labialis is characterized by small painful vesicles that eventually rupture and coalesce into larger ulcers. In terms of appearance, both lesions are characterized by an exudative, yellowish ulcera- tion surrounded by an erythematous border, but their shape tends to differ. Because herpetic lesions are often formed by several vesicles, the outline tends to be irregular. Aphthous ulcers are generally oval-shaped and stand-alone in appearance. Both lesions tend to self-resolve in 1 to 2 weeks. Treatment is supportive and in- cludes general oral hygiene and pain control using 2% viscous lidocaine or an over- the-counter, swish-and-spit anesthetic. Topical steroids such as dexamethasone oint- ment can expedite healing for aphthous ulcers, whereas treatment for herpes labialis can include antiviral medication such as acyclovir or valacyclovir. Incorrect Answer Explanations Lesion size is an unreliable way to differentiate between these common oral afflic- tions. Aphthous ulcers tend to be between 3 and 5 mm, and although complex aphthous ulcers can be larger, they are comparatively rare. The individual vesicles of herpes labialis tend to be small, but they commonly coalesce into one large irregular ulceration. Aphthous ulcers generally occur on the nonkeratinized mu- cosa inside the mouth, while herpes labialis lesions occur predominantly on the kera- tinized oral tissue outside of the lips and around the mouth. Aphthous ulcers are rarely associated with signs of systemic illness. In fact, symptoms such as fever, malaise, and arthralgias should prompt further investigation for the presence of an autoimmune or systemic disease. Aphthous ulcers generally oc- cur on the nonkeratinized mucosa inside the mouth, while herpes labialis lesions oc- cur predominantly on the keratinized oral tissue outside of the lips and around the mouth. Both aphthous ulcers and herpes labialis lesions are quite painful. Therefore, pain is an unreliable way to differentiate between the two oral afflictions. Aphthous ulcers generally occur on the nonkeratinized mucosa inside the mouth, while herpes labialis lesions occur predominantly on the keratinized oral tissue out- side of the lips and around the mouth. Key Points Aphthous ulcers and herpes labialis can be differentiated based on location: Aphthous ulcers are intraoral and found on nonkeratinized mucosal surfaces, while herpes labialis predominantly occurs periorally on keratinized surfaces. When found intraorally, herpes labialis typically occurs on the keratinized tissue of the hard palate and oral gingiva. Aphthous ulcers tend to be round or oval-shaped and are well circumscribed, while the ulcerations of herpes labialis are irregularly shaped and formed by multiple vesicles. Aphthous ulcers are treated with oral hygiene, topical anesthetics, and topical steroid ointments.

question: A 5-year-old girl presents after a fall. An examination reveals tenderness but no movement of the upper left central incisor. Minimal blood is noted around the su- perior aspect of the tooth, but no other oral lacerations are noted and the tooth is otherwise intact. What is part of the appropriate management for this injury?

options.text: Dental resin bridging of affected tooth to another stable tooth
Emergent dental consultation in the emergency department
Extraction of the tooth in the emergency department
Soft diet and follow-up with a pediatric dentist in 48 to 72 hours

correctAnswer: Soft diet and follow-up with a pediatric dentist in 48 to 72 hours
englishExplanation: Most pediatric dental injuries are minor and rarely require significant intervention. In this case, there is tenderness but no movement of an intact tooth and some bleeding to the sulcus, which is consistent with a dental concussion. No emergent evaluation is needed, and a soft diet with follow-up is the best approach. The peri- odontal ligament is the soft tissue that maintains the tooth in position, and it can be easily injured with trauma. Thus, it is important for emergency physicians to be fa- miliar with the different traumatic injuries that can occur to the periodontal liga- ment. Concussion refers to injury without increased mobility or displacement of the tooth but with pain to percussion. Subluxation occurs with injury to the periodontal ligament or other supportive tissues, with increased movement of the tooth but with no displacement. Intrusion indicates dentition that is displaced into the bony socket; there can be associated bony injury to the socket. Lateral luxation occurs with dental displacement from the socket in a lateral direction. Extrusion indicates dentition that is partially displaced out of the bony socket. Avulsion occurs with den- tition that is completely displaced out of its socket. When managing pediatric dental trauma, it is also important to determine primary versus secondary teeth. Most chil- dren don't start losing primary teeth until age 6 or 7, then they have a mix of primary and permanent teeth until about age 13. Incorrect Answer Explanations A dental resin bridge is used to anchor a subluxed tooth into position, but its use is reserved for affixing a permanent tooth. Since this child is 5, all of her teeth are primary teeth. Additionally, this tooth is not mobile and does not necessitate a bridge, even if it was a permanent tooth. Emergent dental consultation is not required for this case due to the nature of the in- jury. The tooth is in position without significant luxation and is a primary tooth. Although an emergent consultation is not needed, urgent dental follow-up is advised. Extraction should only be considered in the setting of dental trauma with a primary tooth that is severely luxated but not avulsed. Extraction may be per- formed by a dental specialist if warranted, but this is rarely performed in the emer- gency department. Key Points Pediatric dental concussion warrants dental follow-up but not an emergency consultation. When treating a pediatric patient who has a dental concussion, tell the parents to put the child on a soft diet and follow up with a dentist.

question: A 50-year-old man presents with fever and odynophagia. A physical examination reveals throat swelling, tongue elevation and swelling, and trismus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Ludwig angina is a severe inflammation caused by infection of both sides of the floor of the mouth. It results in massive swelling of the tongue, which can lead to airway obstruction and difficulty swallowing. The cheek can also be swollen and firm because this disease may be an extension of a dental abscess, poor dental care, or recent lower-molar extraction. Classic signs include fever, malaise, and drooling. Physical examination will reveal tender and “woody'' induration in the sub- mandibular space, which results in tongue elevation. Trismus is typically ab- sent initially, but it will be present as the disease progresses to the parapharyngeal re- gions. The patient should be positioned upright; if indicated, fiberoptic intubation should be used to manage the airway, and care should be taken to avoid induc- ing laryngospasm or complete airway obstruction with the airway manipulation. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics should be given to cover polymicro- bial and anaerobic bacteria. A CT scan may confirm the diagnosis in stable patients. All patients should be admitted for intravenous antibiotics, surgical source control, and consultation with ENT. Incorrect Answer Explanations Epiglottitis occurs more often in adults than children because childhood im- munization against Haemophilus influenzae type B is becoming more widespread. Adults with epiglottitis usually present with 2 to 3 days of worsening throat pain, fever, and pain on swallowing. However, the swelling from epiglottitis occurs lower in the airway than with Ludwig angina, making tongue swelling a distinguish- ing factor favoring Ludwig angina. The presentation of exudative pharyngitis includes fever, sore throat, pharyngeal exu- dates, and tender cervical adenopathy. However, the tongue's swelling and elevation in this case differentiates Ludwig angina from pharyngitis. Peritonsillar abscess presents with sore throat, fever, and a “hot potato” voice. Distinguishing features include asymmetry of the tonsillar pillars, uvular deviation, and trismus. Although trismus can be present with peritonsillar abscess and Ludwig angina, peritonsillar abscesses are not commonly associated with tongue swelling or elevation. Trismus is also present late in the course of Ludwig angina.

question: A 32-year-old man presents with fever, sore throat, and neck pain. His vital signs are BP 107/60, P 130, R 25, and T 38°C (100.4°F); SpO is 94% on room air. On examination, tense edema and erythema overlying the patient's neck and edema to the floor of the mouth are noted. The patient is spitting secretions into a basin. What is the most important next step?

options.text: Obtain a CT scan of the neck

englishExplanation: Ludwig angina is a polymicrobial infection of the submental, sublingual, and sub- mandibular spaces. Infection can progress rapidly and cause airway compro- mise by posterior displacement of the tongue. Late signs of airway compromise in- clude stridor, an inability to manage secretions, and cyanosis; therefore, early de- finitive airway management is key. As these intubations can be difficult, con- sider alternatives to traditional rapid sequence intubation, such as awake fiberoptic intubation. A tracheostomy may be necessary if intubation fails. 2 Incorrect Answer Explanations Antibiotic administration for patients with Ludwig angina is a critical component in care; however, definitive airway management should take precedence be- cause it may take over 1 week for resolution of edema with antibiotic therapy. Additionally, antibiotics should be given intravenously. Although most cases may be managed with close observation and intravenous antibiotics, the patient in this scenario has signs of a compromised airway with an inability to tolerate secretions. Although airway management, including adequate preoxygenation, is critical in pa- tients with Ludwig angina, BiPAP is unlikely to be beneficial. In these patients, airway compromise is likely due to posterior displacement of the tongue, ren- dering BiPAP ineffective. Obtaining a CT scan of the neck can be helpful in situations where the diagnosis of Ludwig angina is equivocal; however, patients can have difficulty breathing when supine. Definitive airway management should take precedence in patients with a clinical diagnosis of Ludwig angina.

question: A 45-year-old man presents with right submandibular swelling over the past week. He denies trauma and says the pain is worse when he eats. There are no signs of overlying erythema, and he has no other symptoms. The physical examination re- veals a firm submandibular gland with no drainage; attempts to milk the gland do not remove the mass. What is the appropriate disposition?

options.text: Discharge the patient on oral antibiotics
Instruct him to use analgesics and sialogogues
Obtain a CT scan of the face
Perform incision and drainage of the mass

correctAnswer: Instruct him to use analgesics and sialogogues
englishExplanation: This patient has symptoms consistent with sialolithiasis, which occurs when a sali- vary gland stone gets stuck in the salivary duct. The obstruction most commonly oc- curs in the submandibular gland (80%), followed by the parotid gland. Salivary gland stones are almost always unilateral in presentation and usually consist of calcium carbonate or calcium phosphate. They are most likely to be symptomatic in middle- aged men. Sometimes, the stone can be milked out of the duct, which resolves the symptoms. If not, as long as the patient does not have any signs of an underlying in- fection with the obstruction, the only therapy needed in the emergency department is analgesia and sialogogues (like lemon drops) to help promote passage of the stone. If the stone does not pass, the patient should follow up with an ENT specialist. Incorrect Answer Explanations Without any signs of infection, antibiotics are not indicated. Passage of the stone will resolve the symptoms. Analgesia and sialogogues are the most appropriate emer- gency department therapy. The diagnosis is made based primarily on clinical examination. CT of the face, along with emergent ENT consultation, is needed only if there is suspicion for an abscess. This patient is afebrile and has no other clinical signs of an overlying infection. Analgesia and sialogogues are the most appropriate emergency department therapy. Since there are no signs of an abscess, incision and drainage is not indicated. If a pa- tient with salivary gland stones does have an abscess, ENT consultation is prudent to determine the next treatment steps. Analgesia and sialogogues are the most appropri- ate emergency department therapy. Key Points Sialolithiasis most commonly presents in middle-aged men in the submandibular gland. Assuming no other signs of infection, initial treatment is to promote passage of the obstructing stone using sialogogues. If there are signs of overlying infection, antibiotics and close ENT follow-up are indicated.

question: A 52-year-old woman presents with unilateral facial swelling that has been present for the past week without fever or systemic symptoms. She says she has had a "bad tooth" for about a month but has been unable to see a dentist. She is immunocom- petent, and she has no trismus. What is the next step in treatment?

options.text: Perform local aspiration of the swelling

englishExplanation: This patient has a periodontal infection that has extended into the buccal space without evidence of systemic infection. The initial treatment is oral an- tibiotics. Penicillin VK, amoxicillin/clavulanate, clindamycin, and doxy- cycline may be appropriate antibiotic choices. Chlorhexidine gluconate 0.12% rinse is an alternative, but it is expensive and not always covered by insurance. The underlying etiology of the patient's symptoms is usually dental caries and poor dental hygiene, so a follow-up appointment with a dentist is indicated. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although this patient may eventually require a tooth extraction, this rarely needs to be performed in the emergency department. Most dentists prefer that the patient start a course of antibiotics before extraction. Instead, this patient should be started on a course of oral antibiotics and referred to a dentist.

question: A patient presents with an abrupt onset of fever, sore throat, agitation, stridor, and drooling. A portable lateral neck x-ray is suspicious for epiglottitis. What is the next best step in management?
englishExplanation: Epiglottitis can present acutely, with rapidly progressive symptoms. It typically presents with fever, sore throat, and drooling. It can progress to sig- nificant airway compromise and obstruction within hours. Signs and symptoms of impending complete airway obstruction are stridor, tripod or sniffing posture, agi- tation, restlessness, or marked respiratory distress (eg, retractions). If these clinical features are present, emergency assistance should be called, with securing the airway (ie, intubation) as the priority. This procedure should ideally be performed by the most experienced operator in a controlled setting (ie, the operating room), with the most advanced airway equipment available. Preparations should be made for an emergency surgical airway. If clinical signs of impending com- plete obstruction are present, direct visualization by laryngoscopy should not be at- tempted unless attempting to secure the airway, and imaging should be deferred. Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), Streptococcus pneumoniae, group A Streptococcus, and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common organ- isms that can cause epiglottitis. With the development of the vaccination for Hib, epiglottitis is now more commonly seen in adults than in children. Antibiotic cover- age should include an anti-staphylococcal agent and a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin. Steroids may be given to mitigate airway edema. Incorrect Answer Explanations CT imaging can exacerbate symptoms of epiglottitis. Because the patient must lie supine, it may precipitate respiratory distress and airway obstruction. The diagnosis of epiglottitis is typically confirmed by lateral x-rays or by the gold stan- dard, direct laryngoscopy. Lateral neck x-rays can show an enlarged epiglottis (usu- ally >8 mm in adults), or thickened aryepiglottic folds. If there are clinical signs of impending airway obstruction, imaging should be deferred. Diagnostic laryngoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosing epiglottitis. However, in patients with impending respiratory obstruction, the focus should be on securing a definitive airway. Fiberoptic intubation is often used for definitive airway management; however, operators should use intubation equipment that they are comfortable with, and which gives them the best chance at a successful first-pass intubation. Supraglottic airways, such as laryngeal mask airways, should never be placed in patients with epiglottitis. These devices are ineffective because the air- way obstruction is below the level of the supraglottic airway. Fiberoptic intubation is preferred, if available. Preparations should be made for a surgical airway.

question: Which pharmacologic option is the most appropriate antimicrobial coverage for acute infectious epiglottitis in an immunocompromised patient?
englishExplanation: Epiglottitis is classically caused by bacterial pathogens. Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) remains an important bacterial cause of infectious epiglottitis, despite a rapid decline in cases among vaccinated children. Other important bacteria include Staphylococcus aureus (including methicillin-resistant strains), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, and group A Streptococcus. In the immuno- compromised patient, it is important to provide coverage with broad-spectrum an- tibiotics tailored to cover Pseudomonas, and antifungals for Candida spp. should be considered as well. It is suggested that all immunocompromised patients with in- fectious epiglottitis receive a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin and an anti-staphylococcal agent (eg, vancomycin). Antibiotic treatment for infectious epiglottitis is typically continued for 7 to 10 days but can be extended in immunocompromised patients. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ampicillin-sulbactam is a beta-lactam antibiotic. It covers both gram-negative and gram-positive organisms, but does not cover MRSA and should not be the sole antibiotic of choice in immunocompromised patients with epiglottitis. The combination of cefazolin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is typi- cally used to treat cellulitis and soft tissue infections, not epiglottitis. Cefazolin is a first-generation cephalosporin, so it should not be used in immuno- compromised patients with epiglottitis. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a folate synthesis inhibitor that has antimicrobial activity against MRSA. Clindamycin is a lincosamide antibiotic that is typically used in skin and soft tissue infections. It provides antimicrobial coverage against S. aureus and MRSA. However, it should not be used as the sole antibiotic treatment in immunocompro- mised patients with epiglottitis.

question: A 6-year-old boy is brought in with a 3-day history of URI symptoms, including congestion, a fever that had been low grade, and a nonproductive cough. The mother says his temperature was 40.5°C (104.9°F) today. On examination, the boy is lethargic but arousable, and stridor is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: The most likely diagnosis in this case is bacterial tracheitis, a secondary bacterial infection following a viral URI; high fever and a toxic appear- ance are commonly associated with the airway symptoms. Other names for this disease process are membranous laryngotracheobronchitis, pseudomembranous croup, and bacterial croup. It is relatively uncommon (4-8/1,000,000 children), and the average patient age is between 5 and 8 years. The most common pathogen in bac- terial tracheitis is Staphylococcus aureus, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Streptococcus pyogenes, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. If bacterial tracheitis is suspected, emergent ENT consultation is warranted because mortality rates can be as high as 20%. Bronchoscopy is the diagnostic method of choice, and intubation under controlled circumstances might be needed to control a tenuous airway. Given the narrowing of the airway, a smaller-than-anticipated endotracheal tube might be needed. Given the copious drainage from the larynx, intubation might require advanced airway techniques and tried-and-true classics like looking for air bubbles. Emergency department man- agement also includes initiation of antibiotic therapy. The initial antibiotic choice is ampicillin-sulbactam combined with clindamycin and a third-generation cephalosporin. Vancomycin should be added if MRSA is a concern. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bronchiolitis is a lower respiratory tract infection that is usually caused by RSV and is most commonly seen in children younger than 2 years. Children with bronchiolitis do not usually present with stridor or lethargy, but they do tend to have more nasal con- gestion, cough, and wheezing. Bacterial tracheitis is suggested by the high fever and a toxic appearance with associated airway symptoms. Pneumonia does not tend to present with stridor. If in doubt, a chest x-ray can differ- entiate between the two since air-space disease on radiography and the absence of stridor suggest pneumonia. Bacterial tracheitis is suggested by the high fever and a toxic appearance with associated airway symptoms. Viral laryngotracheobronchitis, or croup, tends to present in slightly younger patients (6 months to 3 years), whereas bacterial tracheitis can present across a broader age range. Patients with croup also tend to have a less toxic appearance than with bacte- rial tracheitis. A barky or brassy cough is the classic sign of croup. Bacterial tra- cheitis is suggested by the high fever and a toxic appearance with associ- ated airway symptoms.

question: A 63-year-old woman presents with bleeding from a tracheostomy site. She under- went the procedure 10 days ago as part of her treatment for esophageal cancer. She is acutely short of breath, appears in extremis, and has significant hemoptysis. What is the most likely source of the bleeding?
englishExplanation: Erosion into the tracheoinnominate artery can cause life-threatening hemor- rhage. This is a rare complication after tracheostomy, but when it does occur, it is most common 1 to 3 weeks after the procedure. Immediate treatment should in- clude direct pressure and hyperinflation of the tracheostomy tube cuff with gentle tube traction, which provides direct internal pressure to the bleeding artery. An urgent consultation from ENT or thoracic surgery is necessary to ar- range definitive treatment. If bleeding is not controlled with the actions described, then an endotracheal tube should be placed below the bleeding innominate artery with the assistance of a flexi- ble nasopharyngoscope or bronchoscopy and advanced past the tracheostomy tube while withdrawing the tracheostomy tube. An endotracheal tube placed in this man- ner can be used to ventilate the patient, reduce aspiration of blood, and allow the physician to apply internal digital pressure to the artery while the patient is trans- ferred to the operating room for arterial repair by an ENT or thoracic surgeon. Non– life-threatening bleeding after a tracheostomy can be treated by removing the tube and applying silver nitrate or pressure with moist gauze. Incorrect Answer Explanations Portal hypertension resulting in dilation of the esophageal veins can cause life-threatening bleeding if they rupture, but it is not associated with a re- cent tracheostomy tube placement. Bleeding secondary to esophageal varices can be fatal and requires aggressive airway management, emergent GI consultation, and temporizing measures that might include placement of Sengstaken-Blakemore or Minnesota tubes for balloon tamponade. This patient's malignancy does increase her risk for a pulmonary embolism, and the hypoxia is a worrisome sign. However, her recent tracheostomy increases her risk for tracheoinnominate artery fistula formation, which can present with hemoptysis (a seemingly minor sentinel bleed) or severe hemorrhage. A tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) is a communication between the tra- chea and esophagus that can be the result of a congenital malformation. It also can be an acquired condition, such as in the case of a tracheostomy-associated TEF. Secondary to a tracheostomy tube placement, TEF can be caused by erosion from an overinflated cuff or direct trauma from the procedure itself. It is best diag- nosed with bronchoscopy.

question: Replacing a dislodged tracheostomy tube within the first week after cannulation carries the greatest risk of what complication?
englishExplanation: Dislodgement of a tracheostomy tube within the first week after place- ment is a medical emergency. The stoma is still considered immature within 1 week after cannulation, and manipulation carries the risk of creating a false lu- men. Replacement of a dislodged tracheostomy tube within the first week after can- nulation should be performed under direct visualization with fiber optics. Replacement should not be delayed, as the stoma can narrow within hours. If endo- scopic placement is unavailable, endotracheal intubation may be indicated. Incorrect Answer Explanations Hemorrhage is a significant complication after tracheostomy placement. Even minor bleeding can indicate a sentinel bleed, and tracheoinnominate artery fis- tula needs to be ruled out. However, this is not a significant risk after early dislodge- ment of a tracheostomy tube. Obstruction is a common early and late complication with tracheostomy. It is com- monly caused by increased mucus production, granulation tissue, dried secretions, or blood. However, the greatest risk of replacing a dislodged tracheostomy tube with an immature stoma remains the creation of a false lumen. Pneumothorax is a complication after initial tracheostomy placement that occurs in approximately 2% of procedures. When a tracheostomy tube with an immature stoma is dislodged, the greatest risk of replacement is creating a false lumen, so the procedure should be performed with fiber optics.

question: A 32-year-old man presents with a sore throat, muffled voice, and fever. He was diagnosed 1 week ago with streptococcal pharyngitis, but he did not fill the antibi- otics he was prescribed. Examination of the posterior oropharynx shows erythe- matous and enlarged tonsils with exudates and a right-sided fullness with uvular deviation to the left. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms consistent with a peritonsillar ab- scess (PTA). PTA typically presents with significant sore throat, fever, muf- fling of the voice, pain, increased difficulty swallowing, and peritonsillar fullness on examination, often with uvular deviation to the contralateral side. Patients may also have drooling and difficulty breathing depending on the ab- scess size. PTAs are often caused by mixed pathogens, with Group A Streptococcus being the most common organism. PTA is often considered a complication of un- treated streptococcal pharyngitis, although it can also develop even if treatment is initiated appropriately. Most often, diagnosis of PTA is clinical. Examination findings are particularly helpful, including peritonsillar region fullness with uvular deviation. Imaging is not usually required. Treatment of PTA involves draining the ab- scess and administration of antibiotics. This can be done in the emer- gency department, and emergency physicians should be comfortable per- forming this procedure. Drainage of the abscess is typically done using an 18G needle on a syringe into the ab- scess after topical anesthesia and drawing back. A guard should be used to cover the needle so that no more than 1 cm is exposed. This will help prevent inadvertent insertion of the needle into the carotid artery. There is also risk of bleeding and aspiration with this procedure. A scalpel can also be used to open the abscess with a guard in place. However, this is less often practiced by emergency physicians due to increased risk and less familiarity and is more likely to be employed by ENT. If the procedure cannot be done safely at the bedside (ie, uncooperative pediatric pa- tient needing sedation or impending airway compromise), ENT should be involved for potential operative management. Medication treatment of a PTA includes antibiotics active against Group A Streptococcus, such as amoxicillin- clavulanate or clindamycin. Steroids, such as a single dose of dexametha- sone, should be given, as they seem to improve symptoms in the setting of a PTA. Incorrect Answer Explanations Mononucleosis can often be confused with streptococcal pharyngitis. The posterior oropharynx examination will be similar. However, the findings on examination suggest an abscess has formed and this is inconsistent with typical mononucleosis. There can be secondary bacterial superinfection leading to devel- opment of a PTA, although this is not as common in mononucleosis as it is in strepto- coccal pharyngitis. Retropharyngeal abscess (RPA) should be considered in patients with fever, neck pain, and difficulty swallowing with voice changes. These symptoms will also often be seen with a PTA. However, unlike a PTA, an RPA will not usually present with peritonsillar swelling and uvular deviation. The abscess in an RPA is more posteriorly and inferiorly located. Uvular angioedema should be considered when there is swelling to the uvula and may or may not include other findings of angioedema, such as tongue and lip swelling. Uvular angioedema will not present with findings of tonsillitis, and the uvula will typically be midline and swollen.

A 16-year-old girl with no significant past medical history presents with a 2-day
history of redness, pain, and swelling of her right auricle. She had a high chon-

englishExplanation: Auricular perichondritis is an infectious and inflammatory condition of the soft tissue over the cartilaginous auricle and pinna of the external ear. It can occur fol- lowing major or minor ear trauma, such as scratching, piercings, or burns, although in some cases there is no history of preceding trauma. It classically presents as a red, warm, swollen, tender pinna and auricle that spares the lobule (earlobe) and tragus of the ear. In some cases, there is an underlying abscess. The most common microorganism implicated in suppurative perichondritis is Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It is important not to miss this diagnosis and to treat with appropriate antimicrobials and abscess drainage; as misdiagno- 2 9/20/26, 1:17 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 311 of 974 sis and inadequate infection control can lead to progression of the infection with liquefaction and necrosis of the cartilage and permanent disfigurement of the ear. Because of emerging resistance patterns, consultation with local antibiograms is indicated to guide antibiotic selection. Other less common bacterial pathogens implicated in perichondritis include Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Proteus species.

patient complains of a right-sided headache and decreased hearing from his right

of the otoscopic examination is shown.
What is the most likely skull fracture finding on CT imaging of the head?
Credit: Fidan V, Ozcan K, Karaca F/CC BY 2.0.
englishExplanation: The physical examination finding shown is hemotympanum, an accumulation of blood behind the tympanic membrane, which lends a dark hue to the tympanic membrane and often develops within hours of an injury. When hemotympanum is noted on physical examination, a basilar skull fracture needs to be considered and further evaluation undertaken. Because basilar skull frac- 2 9/20/26, 1:17 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 316 of 974 tures commonly involve the petrous ridge of the temporal bone, hearing loss is a common presenting symptom and can be conductive or sensorineural based on the location of the fracture. Additionally, the hemotympanum itself can cause acute hearing loss (hypoacusis or anacusis). Otic capsule involvement strongly influences the severity of hearing impairment and prognostication for hear- ing loss. Other clinical examination findings that are highly suggestive of a clinically significant head injury include periorbital ecchymosis, retroauricular ecchy- mosis, and clear rhinorrhea or otorrhea.

A 72-year-old woman with a past medical history of diabetes complains of
drainage and pain from her right ear for the past 3 weeks. She was prescribed
topical fluoroquinolone drops 2 weeks ago with interval worsening of symptoms.
The patient states she has attempted to clean her ear with a cotton-tipped swab
but that she continues to wipe copious pus away from her ear canal. She also re-
ports slightly decreased hearing in the affected ear. The patient appears uncom-
fortable and complains of severe pain in the ear. She also states her face feels
weaker on the affected side. Examination of her right ear reveals purulent
drainage that obscures visualization of the tympanic membrane as well as promi-
nence of the right ear compared with the left.
What is the best next step in management?

options.text: Administer insulin, intravenous fluids, and neomycin-polymyxin B-hydrocorti-
Order CT imaging of the head, arrange for outpatient ENT referral, and pre-
Order CT imaging of the head, consult ENT urgently, and admit for intravenous
Place an ear wick and prescribe topical fluoroquinolone drops and oral

correctAnswer: Administer insulin, intravenous fluids, and neomycin-polymyxin B-hydrocorti-
englishExplanation: Malignant otitis externa is a serious infection that can advance to cause temporal bone and skull base osteomyelitis if untreated. These infections can extend into the sagittal sinus and cause septic thrombosis as well as meningitis and intracranial abscesses. Patients may have already failed topi- cal antibiotic therapy for uncomplicated otitis externa; this should further raise the suspicion for malignant otitis externa. Patients who appear systemically ill should be treated for sepsis with broad-spectrum coverage. Clinical di- agnostic features include severe otalgia, profuse otorrhea, debris and granulation tissue in the external auditory canal, aural fullness, positive 9/20/26, 1:17 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 323 of 974 x-ray imaging, cranial nerve palsies, and the risk factors of diabetes and age older than 65 years. Although nuclear scan was once considered gold-standard imaging, CT imaging with contrast should be obtained to determine the extent of local infection. Fluoroquinolones have been employed both for Pseudomonas coverage and bone penetration. In the setting of fluoroquinolone resistance, other an- tipseudomonal agents such as ceftazidime or piperacillin-tazobactam should be used. Topical antibiotic drops should be avoided because they can interfere with obtaining an accurate wound culture. Most patients with malignant otitis externa also have diabetes, and addressing hyperglycemia should be part of the treatment.

A previously healthy 4-year-old boy presents with fever, ear pain, and facial
swelling. His vital signs are BP 92/64, P 136, R 28, and T 38.3°C (100.9°F); SpO
98% on room air. He has been on amoxicillin for acute otitis media for 6 days.
Tonight, he began looking very tired, drinking less than usual, and had a fever.
HEENT examination is remarkable for a bulging left tympanic membrane, poste-
rior auricular swelling, erythema, and tenderness. He has no stridor, trismus,
drooling, submandibular fullness, or fluctuance anterior to his ear. His physical
examination is otherwise unremarkable.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: 2 9/20/26, 1:17 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 325 of 974 This patient has multiple features that are concerning for acute mastoiditis. Mastoiditis is an infrequent but severe complication of acute otitis me- dia (AOM). Prior to the widespread usage of antibiotics, mastoiditis was more fre- quently seen, but since the 1950s, it has tapered off in incidence due to antibiotic therapy for AOM. The recognition of mastoiditis and differentiation between mastoiditis and uncom- plicated AOM is a crucial task for emergency physicians evaluating pediatric pa- tients. Mastoiditis often presents with signs of AOM (eg, bulging tym- panic membrane, fever, and ear pain) in addition to systemic signs of infection, posterior auricular swelling, fluctuance, tenderness, and au- ricular proptosis. Posterior auricular swelling and tenderness are fairly sensitive for mastoiditis and are present in 85% and 81% of patients with mastoiditis, respec- tively. Systemic signs and symptoms are also common but less sensitive, present in 76% of patients.

creased vision, and photophobia after being struck in the eye with a baseball. His
visual acuity is 20/20 in the right and 20/100 in the left eye. His intraocular

englishExplanation: This patient has iritis, which accounts for 90% of uveitis cases. In trau- matic iritis, blunt injury to the eye leads to cell death and a subsequent inflamma- tory reaction in the anterior chamber. Cell and flare refers to the WBCs (cell) and proteinaceous material (flare) that leak onto the corneal endothelium. This can form keratic precipitates (as seen in the image above) or collect in the dependent portion of the anterior chamber to form a hypopyon. Topical cycloplegics such as cyclopentolate or scopolamine should be used in the emergency de- partment setting to prevent adhesions to the lens, stop further protein leakage, and treat pain caused by spasms of the ciliary body and pupil. Aside from pain, other symptoms include photophobia, decreased visual acuity, and the presence of floaters. Ophthalmology follow-up should be ob- tained within 24 to 48 hours of emergency department presentation.

A 32-year-old woman presents after a low-speed motor vehicle collision. She was
the restrained driver of a sports utility vehicle. The airbags did not deploy, there
was no glass broken in the vehicle, and no compartment intrusion. There was no
loss of consciousness. The patient was ambulatory at the scene. On arrival, she
complains of right-sided facial pain and pain with attempting to move her right
eye. She says that she hit her right cheek on the steering wheel. She states her vi-
sion is normal and denies pain elsewhere or other injuries. She does not wear
contacts or glasses.
Her vital signs are BP 140/90, P 86, R 18, and T 36.8°C (98.2°F); SpO  is 100%
on room air. Her right inferior orbital region is noted to be swollen and tender.

equal and reactive to light bilaterally. Visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally. She has

are normal, and the anterior chamber is clear. On lid eversion, no foreign bodies

globe rupture. Intraocular pressure is 16 mm Hg. There are no other signs of

An or- bital wall fracture should be considered in the differential diagnosis of a patient presenting with localized pain, vision changes, or difficulty with extraocular movements after trauma. CT is the diagnostic study of choice for evaluation for orbital fracture. CT can also be helpful in determining the cause of limitations to eye movement and vision changes associated with orbital fractures.

A 29-year-old man presents after a high-speed motor vehicle collision where he
hit his left orbital region on the steering wheel. He complains of eye pain and vi-
sion loss in his left eye. He denies pain elsewhere or other injuries. He does not
wear contacts or glasses.
His vital signs are stable. There is swelling and tenderness of the left orbital re-
gion. His left eye is noted to be proptotic, hard to the touch, and there is an unre-
active dilated pupil. The right eye is normal. He is unable to discern any letters
on the Snellen chart with his left eye. Right eye visual acuity is 20/20. On fluo-
rescein examination, there is no evidence of globe rupture. Intraocular pressure
is 40 mm Hg. The rest of the physical examination is normal.
What is the next step in management?

options.text: Administer timolol drops to the left eye
Place an eye shield over the left eye

englishExplanation: This patient has orbital compartment syndrome, likely secondary to a retrob- ulbar hematoma, and requires emergent lateral canthotomy and cantholy- sis to prevent permanent vision loss. Retrobulbar hematomas form behind the eye within the confines of the orbit, and patients can present with eye pain, propto- sis, difficulty moving the eye, and decreased visual acuity. Retrobulbar hematomas can exert pressure on the eye itself, causing orbital compartment syn- drome. Orbital compartment syndrome is characterized by severely de- creased visual acuity (or vision loss) and increased intraocular pressure (>30 mm Hg). Patients with orbital compartment syndrome often have a dilated unreactive pupil and an afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressure should not be checked if there is any suspicion for globe rupture. Lateral cantho- tomy must not be delayed for imaging in patients with suspected orbital com- partment syndrome, as irreversible vision loss can occur within 60 to 120 minutes.

A 29-year-old man presents after a high-speed motor vehicle collision with or-
bital compartment syndrome, likely secondary to a retrobulbar hematoma. A lat-
eral canthotomy is performed. As the procedure is begun, the patient becomes
unresponsive. He is in a narrow-complex bradycardia on telemetry. Notable vital
signs include BP 78/42 and P 28. His glucose is 110. A faint radial pulse is palpa-
ble. He is given atropine IV, and his mental status subsequently normalizes.
Repeat vital signs are BP 132/88, P 92, R 18, and T 36.8°C (98.2°F); SpO  is
100% on room air. Repeat intraocular pressure is 18 mm Hg.
What was responsible for the patient's syncope?
englishExplanation: Pressure on the periorbital soft tissues and traction on the extraocular muscles can trigger bradycardia due to the oculocardiac reflex, which results in a vagal response that causes sinus bradycardia or junctional rhythm. Bradycardia from the oculocardiac reflex can be profound and result in syncope or even death. The oculocardiac reflex can occur during procedural ma- nipulation of the periorbital soft tissues and extraocular muscles, or it may occur spontaneously secondary to pressure on the periorbital soft tissues from edema and/or retrobulbar hematomas. It is also caused by pressure on the globe or trac- tion on the extraocular muscles. Atropine can increase heart rate by inhibit- ing the vagal response in the oculocardiac reflex.

A 60-year-old woman complains of fever and bilateral periorbital pain. Her ex-
amination shows bilateral periorbital edema with proptosis and restricted ex-
traocular movements. An urgent CT scan is performed (shown).
Which cranial nerve finding is most commonly associated with her diagnosis?
9/20/26, 1:17 AM
PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered

Page 386 of 974
Credit: Copyright 2025 Associate Professor Frank Gaillard. Image courtesy of
Associate Professor Frank Gaillard and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 5025. Used under
license.
englishExplanation: The patient has cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST). CST is a rare, usually infectious thrombosis of the cavernous sinus. Most cases of CST arise due to the contiguous spread of infections in the central part of the face, such as sinusitis, den- tal infections, or cellulitis. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen. Rarely, CST is caused by compression of the cavernous sinus from head trauma or a tumor. The diagnosis of CST carries high morbidity and mortality because of its proximity to important structures including the in- ternal carotid artery, the sympathetic plexus, the abducens nerve (cra- nial nerve VI), the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III), the trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV), and the ophthalmic and maxillary branches of the trigeminal nerve (V1 and V2). Of these structures, the internal carotid, sympathetic plexus, and abducens nerve lie within the lumen of the cavernous sinus and are at highest risk of compression from CST. Thus, cranial nerve VI is the most common as- sociated neuropathy, with failure of the lateral rectus muscle resulting in limited eye abduction. Often, CST progresses to complete ophthalmople- gia. Other common physical examination findings in CST include fever, altered mental status, periorbital edema and erythema, and proptosis.

minutes prior to arrival while cleaning wax out of his right ear using a clean Q-

A 6-year-old boy presents with several weeks of scalp itchiness, circular patches
of hair loss, broken hair shafts, and palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. The
child is otherwise well appearing, has normal vital signs, and has no other health
conditions.
What condition may develop in association with this patient's diagnosis?
englishExplanation: A kerion is a severe inflammatory subtype of tinea capitis that most com- monly arises from the dermatophyte genera Trichophyton and Microsporum. In 9/20/26, 1:17 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 403 of 974 contrast to uncomplicated tinea capitis, permanent alopecia and scar- ring can result. Prepubescent children are particularly susceptible because of their low levels of sebum production, which allows for colonization by dermato- phytes. Kerions can be confused with abscess and cellulitis because of the presence of painful pustules and drainage in addition to alopecia and erythema. The gold standard for diagnosis of tinea capitis is a fungal culture, al- though this testing can be impractical in an emergency department setting. Major criteria suggestive of kerion include tenderness to palpation, alopecia, pustules and purulent drainage, and scaling of the scalp. Minor criteria include associated lymphadenopathy, plaques, erythema, itching, and demarcated borders of the lesion.

felt a sudden pop. Subsequently, she noted severe pain anterior to the ear bilater-

has no edema, erythema, or exudates.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: This patient's presentation is consistent with an anterior temporomandibular joint (TMJ) dislocation. This is the most common type of TMJ dislocation, and patients frequently present with trismus and malocclusion immediately af- ter an inciting event (commonly yawning, singing, eating, or, as with this pa- tient, laughing). It is caused by excessive anterior movement of the mandibular condyle, which results in the condyle becoming lodged in the anterior aspect of the TMJ articular eminence. If there is antecedent trauma to the mandible (eg, if a pa- tient falls and strikes their face or is assaulted in the face), imaging to evaluate for the presence of a mandibular fracture is mandatory. Imaging should be strongly considered in nontraumatic presentations as well, unless it would un- reasonably delay reduction.

englishExplanation: This patient's presentation is strongly suggestive of aphthous stomatitis (also re- ferred to as canker sores). Aphthous stomatitis is an entity that is thought to affect up to 20% of the population at one point in their lives. It typically manifests as painful, solitary ulcerative lesions on the oral mucosa less than 1 cm in diameter (commonly 3-5 mm). The etiology is not well defined, but it is believed 9/20/26, 1:17 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 426 of 974 that factors such as stress, local trauma, certain medications, certain vita- min deficiencies, and genetic predisposition all play a role. These ulcers are self limited and resolve spontaneously within 10 to 14 days in most patients. The singular ulcer in the image represents a manifestation of so-called simple aph- thosis, in which the lesions are limited to the oral mucosa. In patients with le- sions that are large (typically >1 cm in diameter) and present in both oral and genitourinary mucosa (complex aphthosis), other diagnoses need to be entertained, including systemic vasculitides such as Behçet syndrome.

of progressive facial swelling that began while he was eating lunch with his fam-
ily. On arrival, his vital signs are BP 80/40, P 115, R 30, and T 37.0°C (98.6°F);
SpO  is 95% on room air. On examination, he appears anxious and has a swollen
tongue and rapid breathing.
What treatment is most appropriate?
englishExplanation: This patient's dramatic presentation is consistent with anaphylaxis. Anaphylaxis is a type I hypersensitivity reaction and typically involves two or more organ systems. In this patient, there is evidence of cutaneous symptoms (an- gioedema, hives), respiratory involvement (tachypnea), and cardiovascular involve- ment (hypotension). In the large majority of patients, symptoms peak within 30 to 60 minutes after onset. Intramuscular epinephrine 1:1,000 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) every 5 to 15 minutes is the treatment of choice and should be given empirically in patients with suspected anaphylaxis.

A 72-year-old man with a history of diabetes and benign prostatic hyperplasia
presents with 6 days of progressively worsening neck pain. He denies recent falls
or trauma to the neck. He recalls having a Foley catheter placed for difficulty uri-
nating several weeks ago, which he says was complicated by a urine infection for
which he completed a course of antibiotics. His vital signs are BP 148/96, P 92, R
12, and T 37.5°C (99.5°F); SpO  is 98% on room air. There are no overlying skin
changes on his neck, but tapping in the midline of the neck at approximately the
C6 level elicits significant pain. His physical examination findings are otherwise
unremarkable. A bedside ultrasound reveals a post-void residual volume of 50
mL. The initial laboratory workup results include a comprehensive metabolic
panel within normal limits, a WBC count of 10,500 cells/mm  with a normal dif-
ferential, an ESR of 106 mm/hr, and a CRP level of 59 mg/L.
What is the preferred imaging modality to diagnose this clinical entity?

options.text: CT imaging of the spine with and without contrast
MRI of the spine with and without contrast
Plain film imaging of the spine

correctAnswer: MRI of the spine with and without contrast
englishExplanation: This patient has a history, examination findings, and initial laboratory workup that is highly suggestive of discitis and/or vertebral osteomyelitis (spondylodiscitis). Discitis is an infection of the intervertebral disc tissue. When infection encompasses the nearby vertebral bodies (vertebral osteomyelitis), the combined entity is called spondylodiscitis. Although there is a bimodal dis- tribution of disease burden, most affected patients are aged 50 to 70 years, with a lower incidence in patients younger than 20 years. Affected men outnumber women with a ratio of approximately 2:1. Fever is often absent in these pa- tients, with an estimated prevalence of 35% on initial evaluation. The patient's history of immunocompromise due to diabetes mellitus constitutes a risk factor (as well as a poor prognostic factor). This infectious process affects the lumbar spine most commonly, followed by the thoracic spine and fi- nally the cervical spine. The most common etiology is hematogenous spread from bacteremia; in this patient, this is likely related to his antecedent UTI follow- ing Foley catheter placement. The preferred imaging modality is MRI with and without gadolinium contrast, which has the best balance of availability, specificity (92.5%-97%), and sensitivity (93%-96%).
