A 37-year-old man presents with 12 hours of gradual, involuntary twisting mo-
tions of his neck after turning his head while watching television. His symptoms
are worsened by trying to straighten his neck and mildly improved by placing his
hand on the spasm. He states he recently increased one of his medications.
Which medical problems in this patient's history may be the precipitant of his
presentation?
englishExplanation: This patient has cervical dystonia, also known as spasmodic torticollis, the most common form of focal dystonia. Dystonia is defined as abnormal postur- ing, twisting, and repetitive movements caused by the involuntary contrac- tions of agonist and antagonist muscle groups. Dystonia can be inherited or ac- quired. Acquired dystonia is typically caused by TBI, drug side effects, or neurologic diseases. Drug-acquired dystonia (dystonic reactions) are commonly associated with dopamine-receptor blocking drugs, dopamine agonists, calcium channel blockers, and antiepileptic drugs. In particular, drugs that alter the ratio of dopamine to acetylcholine receptors in the basal ganglia are associ- ated with a high risk of acute dystonia. Although first-generation antipsy- chotics are commonly associated with dystonia, second-generation an- tipsychotics, SSRIs, and antiemetics are also strongly associated with dystonia. In particular, some studies have suggested that the risk of acute dystonia is highest when SSRI use is combined with other antidepressants or antipsychotics. About one-third of acutely psychotic patients will likely have a drug-in- duced movement disorder within the first few days of starting an an- tipsychotic, with men between the ages of 18 and 35 years being at the highest risk.

A 56-year-old man with a history of diabetes and hypertension presents stating
his voice sounds funny. He reports having a tooth extraction 2 days prior. He has
no allergies to medications. His vital signs are BP 156/92, P 106, R 12, and T
38.8°C (101.8°F); SpO  is 99% on room air. He denies any recent history of
drooling. His physical examination is notable for the finding of an edematous
and erythematous neck, which is tender to palpation. His voice sounds abnormal,
and he seems to have difficulty articulating certain consonants.
What is the correct antimicrobial therapy for this patient?
englishExplanation: This patient's presentation is highly concerning for a submandibular space in- fection, also known as Ludwig angina. The immediate priority is to en- sure that the patient's airway is uncompromised, given the unpredictable and notably nonlinear nature of associated edema in the oropharynx, which can re- sult in sudden asphyxiation. These patients require admission to the ICU and administration of intravenous antibiotics. Submandibular space infections are often associated with recent dental procedures and have a polymicro- bial source, including oral anaerobes (ie, Peptoniphilus sp., Fusobacteria sp.), viridans group streptococci, and Streptococcus pyogenes (also known as group A Streptococcus). Moreover, in patients with risk factors for immunosup- pression (such as this patient, who has a history of diabetes), aerobic gram-negative bacteria as well as Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) can all be part of the infectious microbiota. The combination of vancomycin and meropenem is the best choice in this situation. Alternatives to meropenem in immunocompromised patients include piperacillin-tazobactam, imipenem, or ce- fepime, and metronidazole.

The patient should be placed in a high-visibility area of the emer- gency department with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and intravenous access. question:
A 22-year-old man calls the ED from a local bar. He was punched in
the face 10 minutes ago and is holding his front incisor tooth in his hand.
He wants to know what the best way is to preserve the tooth while coming
to the ED. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to give the
caller?

options.text: Place the tooth in a napkin, and bring it to the ED
Place the tooth in a glass of water, and bring it to the ED
Place the tooth in a glass of beer, and bring it to the ED
Pour some water over the tooth, and place it back into the socket
Place the tooth in a glass of milk, and bring it to the ED

correctAnswer: Pour some water over the tooth, and place it back into the socket
englishExplanation:
109.  The answer is d. The patient has an avulsed tooth, which is a dental
emergency. Avulsed permanent teeth require prompt intervention. The best
environment for an avulsed tooth is its own socket. Reimplantation is
most successful if the tooth is returned to its socket within 30 minutes of
the avulsion. A 1% chance of successful replantation is lost for every
minute that the tooth is outside of its socket. The tooth should only be
handled by the crown to prevent disruption of the root. If the patient cannot
replant the tooth, he or she should keep the tooth under his or her tongue or
in the buccal pouch so that it is bathed in saliva. If that cannot be achieved,
then the tooth can be placed in a cup of milk (e) or in saline. The best
transport solution is Hank solution, which is a buffered chemical solution.
However, it is typically unavailable in this setting.
The worst option is to transport the tooth in a dry medium, such as a
napkin (a). Water and beer (b and c) are less than ideal. Saliva, milk, or
saline are better liquid transport mediums.

question:
A 37-year-old man presents to the ED with complaints of 2 days of a
sore throat and subjective fever at home. He denies cough or vomiting. His
BP is 130/75 mm Hg, HR is 85 beats/minute, RR is 14 breaths/minute, and
temperature is 101°F. He has diffuse tonsillar swelling and bilateral
exudates. His cervical lymph nodes are enlarged and tender bilaterally.
Which of the following is the next best step in management?

options.text: Administer penicillin and discharge the patient without further testing
Perform a rapid antigen test; if negative, confirm with a throat culture
Perform a rapid antigen test; if negative, administer penicillin and
Perform a rapid antigen test; if positive, administer penicillin and
Discharge the patient without treatment or further testing

correctAnswer: Administer penicillin and discharge the patient without further testing
englishExplanation:
172.  The answer is a. The patient has a modified Centor score of 4
(history of fever, tender adenopathy, no cough, exudates, age 15-45 years)
(see following figure). The Centor criteria are used for predicting
streptococcal pharyngitis and whether or not to treat the patient with
antibiotics. Because of his high score, it is likely that the patient has group
A β-hemolytic streptococcal infection and that he should receive empiric
antibiotics. In addition, he should be treated symptomatically with fluids,
topical anesthetics, and acetaminophen or ibuprofen.
Patients with a Centor criterion of 2 or 3 should have a rapid antigen
test and a throat culture performed. If the rapid antigen test is negative, a
confirmatory throat culture may be sent (b), but antibiotics (c) should not be
initiated. If the rapid antigen test is positive, patients should be treated with
an antibiotic (d). A patient with many predictive signs and symptoms
should be treated with antibiotics rather than discharged (e).

question:
A 28-year-old mechanic with no past medical history presents to the
ED after a small amount of battery acid was splashed in his right eye. He is
complaining of extreme pain and tearing from his eye. Which of the
following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Check the pH of the tears

englishExplanation:
471.  The answer is d. Chemical injuries to the eye must be immediately
irrigated with a minimum of 1 to 2 L of normal saline as soon as they
arrive in the ED. Topical anesthesia and the use of a Morgan lens (a special
device to provide large volume irrigation to the eye) can help facilitate this
procedure.
Irreversible eye damage can occur if irrigation is held for physical
examination and visual acuity testing (b). Checking the pH of the tears (c)
helps determine the effectiveness of irrigation, but should be checked after
irrigation has begun. When the ocular pH returns to 7.5 to 8.0, irrigation can
be stopped and a complete eye examination should be performed.
Remember to check visual acuity and pay special attention to corneal
clouding or corneal epithelial defects. Patients with epithelial defects or
corneal clouding should receive an ophthalmic antibiotic (e). Patients
without corneal or anterior chamber involvement only need erythromycin
ointment. The ophthalmologist (a) should be notified, after initial
stabilization, of all patients with chemical injury to the eye and follow-up
should be arranged within 12 to 24 hours.

question:
A 45-year-old man presents to the ED with intense bilateral eye pain,
tearing, and foreign body sensation. He denies any trauma, past medical

history, or contact lens use. He works as a pipe-fitter and uses a welder
regularly. His physical examination is significant for bilateral decreased
visual acuity and injected conjunctiva. Fluorescein staining reveals diffuse
punctuate corneal lesions with a discrete inferior border. His pupils are
equal, round, and reactive to light. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
472.  The answer is c. This patient has UV keratitis, also known as
welder’s flash or photokeratitis, which is a radiation burn on the cornea
from exposure to a UV-ray-containing light source. The pathophysiology
is desquamation of the corneal epithelium due to inflammation from UV
exposure, thus exposing corneal nerve endings. UV keratitis can result from
unprotected exposure to the welder’s arc, sun, snow, artificial sun lamps,
and tanning booths. Patients usually present 6 to 12-hours postexposure
complaining of eye pain, blepharospasm, tearing, photophobia, and foreign
body sensation. Physical examination reveals an injected eye with
decreased visual acuity. Corneal examination reveals punctuate lesions that
are clearly demarcated by a protective covering, such as the inferior
conjunctiva. Treatment consists of oral analgesics and lubricant antibiotic
ointments. Cycloplegics and topical analgesic agents are not currently
recommended for outpatient care. Treatment is guided to assist in the quick,
natural healing capacity of the cornea, in which the patient should feel

better in a couple of days. Follow-up examination with eye exam in 1 to 2
days should be arranged.
A superimposed corneal abrasion (a) is possible however does not
manifest as bilateral punctate lesions. Traumatic iritis (b) usually occurs
following blunt trauma and manifests with consensual photophobia and eye
pain. Physical examination reveals ciliary flush, cells, and flare in the
anterior chamber, and a sluggish pupil. A corneal foreign body (d) usually
follows a traumatic injury in which the patient can recall something getting
into the eye. Corneal foreign bodies can be visualized under slit lamp
examination and may present with an associated abrasion or ulceration. The
history and physical examination are not consistent with bacterial
conjunctivitis (e), which manifests as thick purulent discharge, conjunctival
inflammation, and irritation.

question: A 3-year-old boy presents after swallowing a quarter. He now feels it is stuck. Which location is an obstruction most likely to occur at?
englishExplanation:
Swallowed foreign bodies in pediatrics most commonly obstruct at the level of C6, the cricopharyngeus muscle, one of the four natural areas of luminal narrowing in the esophagus. The cricopharyngeus is the muscle of the upper esophageal sphincter. Depending on the type of material, a plain radiograph may not reveal the object, particularly with food bolus obstructions. Pediatric patients often swallow objects like coins, and it may be difficult to ascertain whether a coin is in the trachea or esophagus. On a soft tissue X-ray, a coin located in the esophagus appears in the coronal plane, en face, as opposed to appearing sagitally when in the trachea.

Most foreign bodies under 2 cm by 5 cm will pass spontaneously through the GI tract. If the patient is without severe symptoms, foreign bodies less than this size are observed for 24 hours, as only 10–20% require endoscopic removal. Under 1% of cases will necessitate surgical removal. Pediatric patients account for > 75% of esophageal foreign bodies. Other risk factors include psychiatric diseases, no teeth, incarceration, and underlying structural abnormalities of the esophagus (rings, strictures, diverticula, malignancy).



The aortic arch (A) at the level of T4 is the second most common location for foreign body obstruction in the esophagus.

The gastroesophageal junction (C) at T11 is the third most common location for obstruction.

The pylorus (D), located in the region of the lower thoracic spine, is beyond the esophagus, and once a foreign body passes through the lower esophageal sphincter into the stomach, it usually continues through the gastrointestinal tract without incident.

The tracheal bifurcation (E) at T6 is the fourth most common site of obstruction, particularly as the left mainstem bronchus pushes against the esophagus.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
Button batteries, sharp objects, and multiple magnets.

question: A 14-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a bug in his ear, acute in onset, approximately 20 minutes ago. The bug is easily visualized in the left external ear canal. It is removed with alligator forceps. On repeat inspection, an insect wing is left in the ear canal. Irrigation successfully removes the wing. On reinspection, the irrigation caused a small amount of redness to the canal without bleeding and there are no other findings. The tympanic membrane is intact. What is the appropriate treatment for this patient?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin twice per day for 10 days
Topical 2% acetic acid solution every 6 hours for 7 days

englishExplanation:
Foreign bodies found in the external ear canal is a common concern among children and young adults who present to the emergency department. Small children have a tendency to place small objects such as beads, pebbles, small toys, and food into the ear. Older children and young adults are more likely to have insects crawl into the external ear canal. When an insect crawls into an ear, the patient quickly becomes aware of the disturbance and generally goes immediately to the emergency department. The bug is frequently still alive and moving.

There are several tools available to remove foreign bodies in the ear including cerumen loops and scoops, right-angle hooks, and alligator forceps. Foreign bodies that are difficult to remove with these tools can sometimes be flushed out of the ear canal with butterfly tubing or a small catheter that is pushed past the foreign body so that irrigation will push the foreign body outward. Suctioning can also help to remove these foreign bodies. Depending on how painful the foreign body is and how cooperative the patient is, topical lidocaine solution may be needed to drown live insects and provide a small amount of topical anesthesia. Uncooperative patients and small children may require minor anxiolytics or sedation to be able to remove the foreign body. Other solutions that can be used to kill an insect before removal include mineral oil or ethanol.

After removal, it is important to inspect the canal for debris and remove it all, especially debris from an insect. If small parts are left inside the external ear canal, irrigation can help remove these small particles. However, irrigation should not be used if the tympanic membrane appears to be perforated. Once all foreign bodies and debris have been removed, the clinician can make decisions regarding further treatment. Tiny abrasions and redness will heal on their own and do not require further treatment. Patients who had live foreign bodies in the ear do not necessarily require further treatment after removal. Topical antibiotics should be considered when there has been serious cutaneous damage or when there appears to be a local inflammatory reaction from organic material that was left in place for a long time.



Oral amoxicillin twice per day for 10 days (B) or another antibiotic is generally not needed after a foreign body has been removed from the external ear canal. Oral antibiotics are only indicated for the treatment of middle ear infections such as otitis media.

Topical 2% acetic acid solution every 6 hours for 7 days (C) can be used in patients with suspected otitis externa or inflammation of the external ear canal. However, this patient does not have evidence of significant canal inflammation or otitis external.

Similarly, topical ofloxacin daily for 7 days (D) can also be used for cases of severe inflammation or otitis externa, but this patient does not have evidence of such an infection.

One Step Further
Question:

Reveal Answer:
Button batteries, penetrating foreign bodies such as a pencil or a bobby pin, and foreign bodies with evidence of injury to the tympanic membrane or middle ear.

Removal requires a cooperative or restrained patient
Irrigation is contraindicated if tympanic membrane may be violated

Prior to removal, any live insects should be killed with alcohol, mineral oil, or lidocaine
Otitis externa prophylaxis with ototopical antibiotics is indicated if the external auditory canal or tympanic membrane has been excoriated during the foreign body removal

question: Which ocular physical exam finding is suggestive of endophthalmitis?
englishExplanation:
Endophthalmitis is an infection within the eye, typically with involvement of the vitreous or aqueous humor. The infection can be caused by either bacteria or fungi, but not by viruses or parasites. Most cases are a result of inoculation by trauma, surgery, or extension from a corneal infection (keratitis). Seeding may also occur secondary to bacteremia or fungemia. The majority of cases are caused by bacteria and will present in an acute fashion. This is a vision-threatening condition that requires prompt diagnosis and treatment.

Acute post-cataract endophthalmitis is the most common form and in the United States is almost always due to bacteria. The majority of cases will present within 1 week of the surgery but can present up to 6 weeks after surgery. Clinical features include a 12- to 24-hour history of decreasing vision and eye discomfort. Otherwise, patients will typically feel well and be afebrile. Physical exam findings will be confined to the affected eye and may include conjunctival injection or chemosis (although these may be postoperative changes), decreased visual acuity, and a hypopyon, which is described as a layering of white blood cells in the anterior chamber.

The diagnosis of endophthalmitis is made clinically and is confirmed by aqueous or vitreous culture. However, negative cultures cannot exclude the diagnosis. Therefore, treatment is still indicated if suspicion remains high. Treatment of endophthalmitis requires prompt ophthalmologist consultation. Endophthalmitis requires intravitreal antibiotics with the addition of systemic antibiotics. Vancomycin and ceftazidime or amikacin are the preferred intravitreal antibiotics.



Corneal ulceration (A) can be a cause of endophthalmitis due to trauma or a worsening corneal abrasion. However, a corneal ulcer alone is not suggestive of endophthalmitis.

Hyphema (B) is a collection of blood in the anterior chamber and is a result of trauma or can be spontaneous. A hyphema would not be expected in endophthalmitis.

Seidel sign (D), also known as the waterfall sign, occurs during ocular evaluation with fluorescein. It signifies a globe rupture and occurs as a result of aqueous humor leaking from the globe defect.

One Step Further
Question:
A teardrop pupil on pupillary exam is concerning for what disease process?

Reveal Answer:
Globe rupture. This finding along with a Seidel sign are both concerning for globe rupture and warrant further evaluation and treatment by an ophthalmologist.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Endophthalmitis

Bacterial or fungal infection of the vitreous or aqueous humor
Most commonly caused by exogenous sources (e.g., from eye surgery, intravitreal injections, ocular trauma)
Tx depends on various factors such as underlying cause and may include intravitreal antibiotics, surgery

question: Which of the following is most suggestive of optic neuritis versus other causes of vision loss?

options.text: Gradually worsening upper quadrant vision loss

englishExplanation:
Optic neuritis has many possible causes, including infection, autoimmune conditions, vitamin B12 deficiency, and diabetes. The most common cause is multiple sclerosis (MS). Optic neuritis presents as painful vision loss with a central scotoma and dyschromatopsia (loss of color, red vision in particular). Patients often notice that colors appear washed out or less vivid than normal. MS symptoms may be worsened with exposure to heat or exercise (Uhthoff phenomenon). The diagnosis of optic neuritis can be supported with an MRI with and without contrast, which will not only support this diagnosis but also determine if MS is present. Treatment is centered on high-dose intravenous steroids.



Gradually worsening upper quadrant vision loss (A) described as a curtain coming down over the eye is indicative of retinal detachment. It may progress slowly, but in some cases, it can occur suddenly. Ultrasound will reveal a hyperechoic retina that moves back and forth with eye movement.

Painless vision loss (C) may describe conditions such as central retinal vein occlusion (blood and thunder findings on funduscopy) or central retinal artery occlusion on funduscopy with retinal pallor (D) that shows a distinct cherry red spot at the fovea. The cherry red spot occurs due to the occlusion of the central retinal artery, leading to ischemia of the retina except at the fovea, where the choroidal circulation provides some blood flow, making it appear relatively red against the pale retina.

One Step Further

What is a Marcus Gunn pupil?

Reveal Answer:
An afferent pupillary defect that is detected with the swinging flashlight test.

Sx: acute monocular vision loss, pain worse with eye movements, loss of color (red) vision, and transient worsening of vision with increased body temperature (Uhthoff phenomenon)
Dx: made clinically
Bedside US might be helpful, MRI will confirm demyelination
Tx: IV methylprednisolone

question: A 52-year-old man presents for evaluation of mouth pain. The patient reports worsening pain along his upper teeth for several days. Today, he developed a subjective fever and sought evaluation. Physical examination demonstrates a gray pseudomembrane covering edematous interdental papillae. When scraped and removed, the underlying tissue bleeds. What is the patient’s diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (ANUG) is an invasive bacterial infection of the periodontal tissue. Characteristically, the physical examination will demonstrate pain and edematous papilla between the teeth. The papilla also become ulcerated and their traditional pointed edges become blunted. A gray pseudomembrane that bleeds when removed may also develop. Patients may develop systemic signs of fever, malaise, and local lymphadenopathy. Treatment includes acute management with local debridement, chlorhexidine rinses, and analgesics. Dramatic resolution usually occurs within 48 hr. If a patient is febrile, antibiotics (e.g., penicillin, clindamycin, metronidazole) may be important adjunctive therapy.



Diphtheria (B) is a bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium diptheriae. The infection is uncommon given widespread immunization. An infected person will have a fever, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy. A classic gray membrane may form in the posterior pharynx in up to half of patients.

A periapical abscess (C) is a localized abscess in the gingiva adjacent to the apex of a tooth. These are typically treated with incision and drainage.

Vincent angina (D) is a potential complication of ANUG in which the infection spreads into the fauces and tonsils.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the treatment for diphtheria?

Reveal Answer:
Equine serum diphtheria anti-toxin plus erythromycin (although penicillin is an acceptable alternative).

question: A person who has used tobacco and alcohol long term presents with 3 months of a white patch on the floor of their mouth. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Oral leukoplakia is a premalignant white patch or plaque that may eventually progress to an ulcer or mass. It is a premalignant oral lesion. The biggest risk factors are tobacco and alcohol use. If oral leukoplakia persists for > 2 weeks, biopsy and treatment are required. These precancerous lesions are typically surgically removed with cryotherapy and laser ablation. Oral hairy leukoplakia is associated with HIV/AIDS. Unlike oral candidiasis (thrush), the white plaques of oral leukoplakia cannot be scraped off.



Leukocytosis (A) and leukopenia (C) refer to an increased and decreased number of white blood cells in the blood, respectively.

Leukomalacia (B) may refer to brain white-matter necrosis, which occurs near the lateral ventricles in infants.

One Step Further
Question:
What benign oral condition is characterized by multiple areas of erythema on the tongue surrounded by well-demarcated plaques?

Reveal Answer:
Benign migratory glossitis, or geographic tongue.

question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment regimen for a 67-year-old man with acute otitis media with no evidence of middle ear effusion or systemic infection on exam?

options.text: Placement of an ofloxacin-moistened wick for 3 days with otolaryngology follow-up

englishExplanation:
Otitis media is defined broadly as inflammation of the middle ear and is further differentiated into acute otitis media (AOM) and otitis media with effusion. AOM is characterized by the presence of a middle ear effusion with signs of concomitant active infection, such as erythema of the tympanic membrane and otalgia. Conversely, otitis media with effusion has signs of effusion on exam without evidence of active infection and, in adults, is commonly associated with significant comorbidities, including head and neck cancers, sinusitis, and lymphoid hyperplasia. While primarily a condition of childhood and infancy, AOM can also affect adults, though much less frequently. The predominant causative pathogens in adults are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

The clinical syndrome of AOM is similar in adults and children, often including unilateral otalgia with or without fever. However, adults commonly do not experience the preceding upper respiratory infection that children frequently do. There is variable incidence of associated otorrhea, hearing loss, and vestibular symptoms (i.e., tinnitus, vertigo). Objectively, the tympanic membrane often appears erythematous and bulging or retracted but may have a yellow or white appearance due to suppurative inflammation behind it.

While no specific treatment guidelines exist for AOM in adults, the recommended first-line antibiotic treatment options generally include either amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate in simple cases without evidence of intracranial complications or systemic infectious signs to suggest sepsis. However, patients who are at high risk of complications or systemic disease due to immune compromise, advanced age, recent hospitalization, or antibiotic use should be treated initially with amoxicillin-clavulanate rather than amoxicillin alone. This patient’s age of 67 years serves as an indication to treat initially with amoxicillin-clavulanate. Inadequately treated AOM in adults may be complicated by tympanic membrane perforation, acute mastoiditis, intracranial infection (e.g., subdural empyema), and lateral sinus thrombosis.



While observation (A) is recommended for healthy children who are > 6 months old and meet other mild disease criteria, this method has not been evaluated in adults.

In rare cases of otitis externa in which ear canal edema is so prominent as to limit delivery of topical antibiotics, an antibiotic-moistened wick can be placed for 2–3 days (C) until symptoms improve, but this strategy is not appropriate for AOM.

Topical antibiotics such as ofloxacin (D) or polymyxin B-neomycin-hydrocortisone (E) are not indicated in the treatment of AOM, as systemic antibiotic therapy is required to penetrate the middle ear.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common intracranial complication of chronic otitis media and mastoiditis?

Reveal Answer:
Meningitis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Acute Otitis Media in Adults

Similar presentation and treatment as children with some key differences
OM with effusion is differentiated from OM without effusion
OM with effusion is associated with other significant pathology (sinusitis, nasopharyngeal lymphoid hyperplasia, head and neck tumors)
Most common causative organisms: S. pneumoniae, H. influenza, S. aureus, P. aeruginosa
Sx: otalgia with or without fever and typically no viral prodrome
PE: TM may be red, yellow, or white, retracted or bulging, and decreased mobility of TM
Tx: amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate
OM with effusion is treated for 3 weeks
For recurrent infections, refer to ENT

question: A 4-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a muffled voice and fever. On physical exam, he is stridulous at rest. Vital signs are a BP of 90/60 mm Hg, HR of 135 bpm, RR of 36/min, and T of 103.1°F (39.5°C). Which of the following is the most likely position of comfort for this patient?
englishExplanation:
This child is exhibiting signs and symptoms of epiglottitis. Typical symptoms include rapid onset of fever, dysphagia, dysphonia, and stridor. Children will often present in the tripod position and should not be disrupted or removed from their position of comfort. Diagnosis of epiglottitis is often clinical, but if the diagnosis is not clear, a lateral soft tissue X-ray of the neck may be obtained and classically reveals a thumbprint sign. X-rays should be done at the bedside, given the risk of losing the patient’s airway in radiology. Historically, this was most commonly caused by Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib). Following the advent of the Hib vaccine, the incidence has decreased, but this bacteria still remains an important cause, especially in unvaccinated or incompletely immunized children. Other important causes include Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus species.

Management of epiglottitis should focus on close airway monitoring, keeping the patient in a position of comfort, and scheduling consultations with otolaryngology and anesthesia. Definitive airway management should preferably be performed in the operating room. Intravenous antibiotics, which should include a third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime or ceftriaxone) and an antistaphylococcal agent (vancomycin), should be initiated after securing the airway so as not to agitate the child and cause airway compromise.



The fetal (A) position is the most common position of comfort for patients with peritoneal irritation.

Left lateral decubitus (B) is commonly a position of comfort to a patient with a mainstem bronchus foreign body on the left to better aerate their right lung.

Supine (C) positioning is a position of comfort for many patients with nausea or diseases with symptoms worsened by movement, such as vertigo.

One Step Further

What finding would be expected on a left lateral decubitus X-ray of the chest in a patient with a foreign body in the left mainstem bronchus?

Reveal Answer:
Hyperinflation of the left lung.

Epiglottitis

Most commonly caused by H. influenzae (decrease since Hib vaccine), Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species
Sx: rapid onset of fever, muffled voice, dysphagia, respiratory distress
PE: sore throat, stridor, leaning forward, drooling, red swollen epiglottis on direct visualization
Imaging: enlarged epiglottis (thumbprint sign) on lateral neck X-ray
Tx: airway management and IV antibiotics (third-generation cephalosporin AND antistaphylococcal)

question: A 29-year-old woman presents to the ED for a left eye problem. Her visual acuity, extraocular movements, and intraocular pressures are normal. There are no findings of orbital cellulitis or ocular trauma on examination. Which of the following is most consistent with the diagnosis of chalazion?

options.text: Nontender nodule on upper lid margin
Tender pustule at lower lid margin
Warm, fluctuant nodule below medial lower lid

correctAnswer: Nontender nodule on upper lid margin
englishExplanation:
A chalazion is a painless, sterile inflammatory condition of the eyelid oil glands. It can be deep, involving the meibomian glands, or superficial, involving the sebaceous glands, and it can be acute or chronic. They present as a nontender nodule on the upper lid margin but may involve the lower lid and may be recurrent. Because they are sterile, noninfectious nodules, chalazia do not usually cause pain. Management involves thorough eye and vision examinations to rule out other ocular inflammatory or infectious conditions and warm compresses. There is no indication for needle aspiration, incision and drainage, or antibiotics in the emergency setting. Referral to an ophthalmologist in 1–2 weeks may be indicated, depending on the size of the lesion. Corticosteroid injections into the lesion or incision and drainage can be deferred for outpatient management.



A hordeolum is a tender pustule at the lower lid margin (B).

Dacryocystitis is an acute infection of the lacrimal duct and presents as a warm, fluctuant nodule below the medial lower lid (C).

A pterygium is an area of wing-shaped corneal fibrosis (D) due to wind or dust overexposure or other chronic eye irritation.

What is pus in the anterior chamber called?

Reveal Answer:
Hypopyon.

Most commonly caused by obstruction of meibomian glands
Tx: warm compresses

question: A 40-year-old healthy man presents to the emergency department with eyelid swelling for 2 days. Examination is significant for a small pustule on the right lower medial eyelid margin near the eyelash follicle, without eye discharge or injection. The patient’s extraocular movement, pupillary reaction, and visual acuity are all within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
A hordeolum is a common, painful, acute purulent inflammation of the eyelid margin caused by bacterial infection and obstruction of sebaceous glands. The condition affects all age groups and can be classified as external or internal. External hordeola (styes) result from infection of the glands of Zeis or Moll associated with eyelash follicles, while internal hordeola involve the meibomian glands in the tarsal plate. The most common causative organism is Staphylococcus aureus, though recurrent hordeola are common and may be associated with Demodex mite infestation, particularly in adults in their 20s. The condition is typically self-limited, with spontaneous drainage and resolution occurring within approximately 1 week in many cases.

Hordeola present as well-defined, tender masses at the lid margin with acute onset of pain, erythema, and localized swelling. External hordeola characteristically demonstrate a pustule at the eyelid margin near an eyelash follicle, while internal hordeola may point toward the conjunctival surface. The key distinguishing feature from a chalazion is the clinical presentation, as hordeola are acute, painful, and purulent, whereas chalazia are chronic, painless, firm, nodular masses located in the midportion of the eyelid. Chalazia develop over weeks to months and lack the acute inflammatory signs of hordeola. Diagnosis is clinical, based on the lesion’s characteristic appearance and location. Vision, extraocular movements, and pupillary reactions remain within normal limits, helping differentiate hordeola from more serious conditions like orbital cellulitis.

Emergency department management of hordeola centers on conservative measures, as most cases resolve spontaneously. The mainstay of treatment includes warm compresses applied to the eyelid for 10–15 minutes several times daily to promote spontaneous drainage. Despite frequent prescription in emergency and acute care settings, antibiotics do not improve resolution rates and are generally unnecessary for uncomplicated hordeola. Lid hygiene and scrubs may provide symptomatic relief. Incision and drainage may be considered for lesions that are refractory to conservative management. Potential complications include spread of infection to adjacent glands and tissues, development into generalized eyelid cellulitis, and progression to a chronic chalazion if the internal hordeolum remains unresolved. Recurrence is very common, and patients with frequent recurrences should be evaluated for Demodex infestation through eyelash epilation and microscopy.



Blepharitis (A) is a chronic bilateral inflammation of the eyelid margins characterized by crusting, scaling, and erythema along the entire lid margin rather than a discrete pustular lesion. Patients typically present with burning, itching, and foreign body sensation, chronically affecting both eyes.

A chalazion (B) is a chronic, painless, firm nodular mass in the midportion of the eyelid (not at the margin) caused by lipogranulomatous inflammation from meibomian gland obstruction. Unlike the acute, painful pustule described in this case, chalazia develop gradually over weeks and lack purulent drainage.

Orbital cellulitis (D) is a severe infection posterior to the orbital septum that presents with proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, pain with extraocular movements, and often vision changes. This patient’s extraocular movements, pupillary reactions, and visual acuity are within normal limits and thus effectively exclude orbital cellulitis.

Preseptal cellulitis (E) presents with diffuse eyelid swelling, erythema, and warmth without a discrete pustular lesion. While extraocular movements and vision remain normal (distinguishing it from orbital cellulitis), the swelling is more extensive and involves the entire eyelid rather than a localized pustule at the lid margin.

Reveal Answer:
Decreased visual acuity or intraocular pressure > 40 mm Hg due to retrobulbar process (e.g., hematoma or infection).

Most commonly caused by bacterial infection (staphylococcal species)
Treatment is warm compresses ± topical antibiotics
Differentiate from a chalazion (typically painless, often subacute presentation)

question: What is the most frequently isolated organism in acute suppurative parotitis?
englishExplanation:
Acute suppurative parotitis, which occurs when decreased salivation or stasis results in the migration of oral bacteria to the gland, presents with facial erythema, swelling, and tenderness over the parotid gland. Patients are typically older adults with a history of recent surgery or hospitalization, dehydration, or anticholinergic medication use.

Although polymicrobial in etiology, Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequently isolated pathogen. Other organisms may include viridans streptococci, gram-negative bacteria such as Escherichia coli and Eikenella, and anaerobes such as Bacteroides. Pseudomonas may be present in patients who are hospitalized.



Although Bacteroides fragilis (A), Escherichia coli (B), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (C), and viridans streptococci (E) may be present in acute suppurative parotitis, they are not the most frequently isolated pathogen.

question: A 46-year-old man with a history of diabetes and HIV infection presents to the emergency department with 2 days of nasal congestion, right ear pain, and yellow drainage from the ear. He takes metformin and antiretroviral therapy. He has not had recent fevers, headaches, or vision changes. His vital signs are within normal limits. The right ear canal appears erythematous and edematous with a purulent exudate. He has pain with manipulation of the pinna. The surrounding area is unaffected. Evaluation of the right tympanic membrane is limited due to canal edema. What is the most appropriate treatment?
englishExplanation:
Otitis externa is an infection of the external auditory canal incited by damage to the epithelium, a loss of protective wax, or an accumulation of moisture. Common microbial etiologies include Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus species, Streptococcus species, Enterobacter species, Proteus mirabilis, and fungal species (e.g., Aspergillus and Candida species). The diagnosis is based on the clinical findings of canal erythema and edema and the variable presence of purulence and debris. Patients will likely have ear pruritus and ear pain exacerbated by manipulation of the pinna. A topical antipseudomonal antibiotic (e.g., polymyxin B with neomycin and hydrocortisone, ofloxacin, and ciprofloxacin with hydrocortisone) is the first-line choice of therapy. If there is a history of immunosuppression, a history of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, or extension beyond the ear canal, additional oral antibiotics are indicated. Intravenous antibiotics are indicated if there is suspected malignant otitis externa (i.e., infection of the external auditory canal and temporal bone). Oral regimens may consist of an oral fluoroquinolone (e.g., ciprofloxacin). Complications of otitis externa include mastoiditis, osteomyelitis, and intracranial extension, which are related to the contiguous spread of infection. Fever, severe canal edema, intense pain, and lymphadenopathy should prompt evaluation for an underlying complication.



Intravenous cefepime (A) and intravenous meropenem (B) offer systemic parenteral therapy in the treatment of Pseudomonas infections, which could be considered for patients with malignant otitis externa who cannot otherwise take oral medications or who appear systemically ill. This patient’s vital signs are within normal limits and he has not tried oral therapy already to suggest a lack of improvement that requires IV therapy.

Oral acyclovir (C) is appropriate in the treatment of Ramsay Hunt syndrome, also termed herpes zoster oticus. This syndrome is caused by a varicella-zoster virus infection of the facial nerve, manifesting with unilateral peripheral nerve palsy and an erythematous vesicular rash of the ear canal or auricle.

Oral amoxicillin (D) is appropriate in the treatment of otitis media, which clinically appears as ear pain, fever, middle ear effusion, and variable degrees of tympanic membrane bulging, impaired movement, otorrhea, or an air-fluid level.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:

Tx: topical antimicrobials with or without steroids

Tx: fluoroquinolone (often IV therapy needed)

question: A 20-year-old man with human immunodeficiency virus presents with severe oral pain and gingival bleeding. Oral examination is shown above. There is no facial edema, erythema, or fever. What is the best next step in management?

options.text: Discharge home with chlorhexidine, penicillin, and dental referral

correctAnswer: Discharge home with chlorhexidine, penicillin, and dental referral
englishExplanation:
Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (ANUG) is a periodontal infection in which bacteria invade normal oral tissue. It is characterized by painful, edematous interdental papillae. While the interdental papillae are normally pointed, in ANUG there is blunting and ulceration. There may also be a pseudomembrane covering the gingiva which, if removed, reveals bleeding, ulcerated tissue. It is most frequently noted around the anterior incisors and posterior molars. Patients may also have fetid breath, lymphadenopathy, malaise, and fever. Risk factors for developing ANUG include a compromised immune system (e.g., HIV), poor oral care, stress, smoking, and malnutrition. Treatment consists of analgesics, systemic antibiotics (e.g., clindamycin or penicillin), and chlorhexidine rinses. Dental referral is also essential as these patients require thorough debridement and close follow-up.



Admission for intravenous clindamycin (A) is not indicated as patients typically respond well to outpatient care.

Discharge home with cephalexin (B) does not provide complete treatment as the patient should also have close dental follow-up.

Discharge home with nystatin (D) is indicated in cases of oral thrush, which is not present in this patient.

question: A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance for difficulty breathing. He cannot provide additional history. Stridor is audible from across the room. Physical examination shows intercostal retractions, significant swelling beneath the jaw, and palpable fluctuance. On oral examination, only the soft palate is visible. The patient cannot open his mouth more than one finger width. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial method for airway control in this patient?
englishExplanation:
Ludwig angina occurs when a bacterial infection in or near the sublingual space pushes the soft tissue structures of the inferior and anterior oropharynx into the airway. Due to the minimal amount of space present, rapid progression to airway compromise may occur even with the initiation of empiric antibiotics and frequent airway reassessments. Advanced cases of Ludwig angina can be recognized by the presence of stridor, increased work of breathing, or intolerance of oral secretions. In these patients, endotracheal intubation should not be attempted, even with video assistance or hyperangulated blades. The standard of care is intubation in an operating room setting, following preparation for tracheostomy. In the emergency department setting, the usage of a nasal fiberoptic scope to assess the severity of airway obstruction, followed by attempted nasal intubation, is recommended if otolaryngology assistance is not available. Planning for failure of the primary airway plan is critical. The patient should be marked and locally anesthetized for possible tracheostomy before attempting intubation.



Blind oral intubation (A) should not be attempted in the setting of Ludwig angina, even with the assistance of a bougie. The risk of inducing laryngospasm or worsening airway edema is dramatically elevated by airway inflammation. A cricothyrotomy (B) is an appropriate backup option for this patient if nasal intubation fails. The site should be marked and anesthetized before attempting intubation. All forms of oral intubation (D) are contraindicated in the setting of severe Ludwig angina. The anatomic location of the swelling will prevent visualization of the larynx if the swelling is severe enough to cause airway compromise. The proper use of a laryngeal mask airway (E) requires significant space in the supraglottic area in order to seal properly. Severe airway edema prevents the effective use of laryngeal mask airways.

What is the most common primary source of infection in Ludwig angina?

Reveal Answer:
Dental infections.

PE: tongue elevation, brawny edema under the chin, dysphagia, dysphonia, drooling
Dx: clinical, CT
Tx: fiberoptic or awake intubation, IV antibiotics, ENT consultation

question: An 8-year-old boy develops progressive eye redness and swelling, as shown above. Which of the following is the most important initial feature differentiating orbital cellulitis from preseptal cellulitis?
englishExplanation:
Orbital cellulitis is a sight-threatening emergency involving infection of the soft tissues posterior to the orbital septum, most commonly affecting children and young adults. However, preseptal cellulitis (anterior to the orbital septum) is far more common, accounting for 90–95% of periocular infections in pediatric populations. The pathogenesis typically involves direct extension from adjacent paranasal sinuses, particularly the ethmoid sinuses. Other etiologies include dental abscesses, trauma, postsurgical complications, and hematogenous seeding. Common bacterial pathogens include Staphylococcus species, Streptococcus species, Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Bacteroides species, and other gram-negative organisms.

Clinical presentation differs markedly between the two conditions, as orbital cellulitis presents with fever, proptosis, painful eye movements, ophthalmoplegia, chemosis, and potential vision loss. Patients are typically more systemically ill with significantly elevated inflammatory markers. In contrast, preseptal cellulitis manifests with eyelid erythema, warmth, tenderness, and swelling without globe involvement, no pain with eye movements, and generally low-grade fever. Diagnosis in the emergency department requires a focused eye examination assessing visual acuity, extraocular movements, pupillary responses, proptosis, and intraocular pressure. While orbital cellulitis is primarily a clinical diagnosis, CT of the brain and orbits with contrast is critical to evaluate for complications, including subperiosteal abscess, orbital abscess, and intracranial extension. MRI may be performed when CT is nondiagnostic.

Emergency department treatment requires immediate hospitalization, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and ophthalmology consultation. Recommended antibiotic regimens include vancomycin (to cover methicillin-resistant S. aureus and penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae) combined with ceftriaxone, ampicillin-sulbactam, or piperacillin-tazobactam, with consideration for anaerobic coverage (e.g., metronidazole), given the polymicrobial nature of sinogenic infections. The use of corticosteroids remains controversial, and surgical intervention is indicated for patients with subperiosteal or orbital abscesses who do not improve within 24–48 hours of IV antibiotics and those with signs of progression or orbital compartment syndrome. Complications can be devastating and include permanent vision loss from optic neuritis, central retinal artery occlusion, and exposure keratopathy, as well as life-threatening intracranial extension causing cavernous sinus thrombosis, CNS infections (e.g., abscess, meningitis), and osteomyelitis.



While an afferent pupillary defect (A) can occur in severe orbital cellulitis with optic nerve involvement, it represents a late complication rather than an initial differentiating feature and indicates advanced disease requiring urgent intervention.

Purulent discharge (C) can occur in both preseptal and orbital cellulitis and is not a reliable differentiating feature. It may result from associated conjunctivitis in preseptal cellulitis or from the primary infection in either condition.

Scleral injection (D) can be present in both conditions and is not specific for orbital cellulitis, though chemosis (conjunctival edema) is more characteristic of orbital involvement.

While vision loss (E) is a serious complication of orbital cellulitis, it represents advanced disease rather than an initial differentiating feature. Pain with eye movement is a more sensitive early clinical sign that should prompt immediate evaluation.

Reveal Answer:
Acute dacryocystitisi.

question: A 12-year-old girl presents with sudden-onset right-sided facial swelling associated with a foul taste in her mouth. Physical exam reveals an underweight teenage girl. She has difficulty opening her mouth. The oropharynx is clear without swelling or exudates. There is swelling and tenderness to the right preauricular space, extending beyond the angle of the mandible. Temperature is 39.7°C, blood pressure is 114/64 mm Hg, and heart rate is 134 bpm. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation is consistent with acute bacterial parotitis. Risk factors for parotitis include old age, sialoliths, neoplasms, Sjögren syndrome, and HIV. Bacterial parotitis is rare in older children and adolescents but can occur more often in those with anorexia and bulimia. This patient’s fever is an indicator of severe infection that is unlikely to respond to oral antibiotics. Other indicators include leukocytosis and significant comorbidity (e.g., immunosuppressed). Additionally, the patient’s degree of swelling is concerning for possible extension into the deeper structures of the neck. Notable complications of parotitis include airway compromise, Lemierre syndrome, and facial nerve palsy.

Bacterial causes are often polymicrobial, with Staphylococcus aureus, viridans group streptococci, and Eikenella corrodens comprising commonly cultured pathogens. The antibiotic choice must cover Staphylococcus with consideration for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) coverage if the patient has any risk factors (e.g., prior MRSA infection or nursing home resident). Ampicillin-sulbactam is available in IV formulation, has broad spectrum coverage, and is the first-line therapy for bacterial parotitis.



Amoxicillin-clavulanate (A) and cephalexin (C) are appropriate first-line oral antibiotics for patients without signs of severe infection (e.g., fever, leukocytosis, and significant comorbidity).

Moxifloxacin (D) is available in IV formulation and has anti-staphylococcal and broad-spectrum coverage. However, it is not the first line for parotitis and is contraindicated in pediatric patients due to tendinopathy.

Reveal Answer:

question: What is the most common infectious etiology of conjunctivitis in adults?
englishExplanation:
Viral conjunctivitis is the most common type of conjunctivitis in adults and is most often caused by adenovirus. Patients present with symptoms of redness, watery or mucoserous discharge, and irritation. It is typically bilateral (but may initially affect only one eye), and there is often a preceding or concomitant upper respiratory illness. Physical examination findings include preauricular lymphadenopathy, diffuse conjunctival injection, and enlarged follicles on the inferior palpebral conjunctiva. Visual acuity, examination of the cornea and anterior chamber, and intraocular pressures are normal.

Treatment consists of supportive care with cool compresses. Some patients may get relief from an over-the-counter topical antihistamine or ocular decongestant, but this treats only the symptoms and not the cause. Topical antibiotics are reserved for those patients in whom the etiology is unclear or if there is concern for a superimposed bacterial infection.



Enterovirus (B) may also cause viral conjunctivitis but is less frequently implicated than adenovirus.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa (C) is a concerning cause of bacterial conjunctivitis in patients who wear contact lenses.

Staphylococcus aureus (D) and Streptococcus pneumoniae (E) are common causes of bacterial conjunctivitis, but neither are responsible for the majority of cases overall.

question: A 29-year-old man with a history of sickle cell disease presents to the emergency department with a painful eye. He reports the pain started without incident and has been worsening. He decided to seek medical care when his coworkers noticed that his eye looked different, as seen above. On exam, his intraocular pressure is 22 mm Hg in the affected eye and 17 mm Hg in the unaffected eye. Ophthalmology has been called to evaluate. What management is contraindicated in this patient’s care?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s exam is consistent with a hyphema likely caused by his underlying sickle cell disease. A hyphema is a spontaneous or post-traumatic collection of blood in the anterior chamber. Diagnosis is clinical. Notably, the layering of blood may not be apparent on exam until the patient sits upright, as the blood commonly layers posteriorly while supine or reclined. Unless associated with other sequelae of direct ocular trauma, most hyphemas have a good prognosis. Risk factors for permanent vision loss include sickle cell disease, coagulopathies, and large-volume hyphemas. Patients commonly present after direct ocular trauma or with medical comorbidities that are at risk for spontaneous hyphemas. They may describe eye pressure or pain (due to increased intraocular pressure) or change in vision, especially with accommodation. The mainstay of treatment is the management of the underlying cause and control of intraocular pressure. Common medications used to manage elevations in intraocular pressure include topical timolol and acetazolamide. Notably, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, such as acetazolamide, are contraindicated in patients with sickle cell disease and hyphemas, as they may worsen sickling and further inhibit outflow via the trabecular meshwork. All patients with hyphemas should be evaluated by an ophthalmologist to assess the risk of rebleeding, which can lead to permanent vision loss.



Treatment of hyphemas centers around intraocular pressure control. This may be obtained by head of bed elevation (A) to prevent the settling of blood clots and subsequent occlusion of the trabecular meshwork, and topical timolol (D), which decreases the secretion of aqueous humor.

Topical prednisolone (C) may be associated with a lower risk of rebleeding but does not directly alter intraocular pressure. None of these treatments are contraindicated if the patient has sickle cell disease.

question: A 42-year-old plumber presents after splashing drain cleaner into his eye. He irrigated his eye with water for 30 minutes at the job site and then came directly to the emergency department. What is the next step in management?

options.text: Check ocular pH and continue irrigating the eye until the pH remains neutral
Discharge home with erythromycin ointment if visual acuity is normal
Use phenylephrine drops for cycloplegia to help alleviate patient discomfort

correctAnswer: Check ocular pH and continue irrigating the eye until the pH remains neutral
englishExplanation:
Chemical burns to the eye are an ocular emergency and require swift treatment to limit the extent of injury. Exposure to alkaline substances, such as drain cleaners, ammonia, lye, and bleach, causes liquefactive necrosis that can penetrate and dissolve tissues until removed. These burns tend to be deeper and more catastrophic than acid burns, which cause coagulation necrosis that limits the depth of penetration. Immediate treatment includes copious irrigation for at least 30 minutes, ideally at the scene prior to transfer to the hospital. The pH should be checked and irrigation should continue until the pH remains neutral 30 minutes after the last irrigation. Ophthalmology consultation is indicated for all chemical burns.



Alkali burns can result in increased intraocular pressure (A). However, the first line of treatment is continued irrigation until a neutral pH is obtained, not checking the intraocular pressure.

Discharging home (C) is not recommended until the eye has been adequately irrigated and a full eye examination is completed.

Cycloplegic drops are indicated once irrigation is complete, but phenylephrine (D) should not be used as it can result in worsening ischemia of the limbus due to constriction of the blood vessels.

Using pH paper dipped into the inferior conjunctival fornix.

question: Which of the following commonly causes artifactual widening of the retropharyngeal space on lateral neck X-rays?
englishExplanation:
The retropharyngeal space is a potential space located posterior to the pharynx and anterior to the cervical spine. It is best evaluated on lateral neck X-rays. Widening of this space can indicate serious pathology such as retropharyngeal abscess, hematoma, or malignancy. However, several technical and physiologic factors can lead to false, or artifactual, widening. Emergency clinicians should recognize these factors to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary interventions.

Neck flexion during imaging is the most common cause of artifactual widening of the retropharyngeal space. When the neck is flexed, the soft tissues posterior to the pharynx are compressed and appear thicker on X-rays. This positioning alters the normal anatomic relationships and exaggerates the prevertebral soft tissue shadow, mimicking pathology. Proper technique requires the neck to be in a neutral or slightly extended position to accurately assess the retropharyngeal space.

Other factors that may influence the appearance of the retropharyngeal space include the phase of respiration and patient cooperation. Imaging during expiration, crying in pediatric patients, or poor inspiratory effort can also falsely increase the apparent thickness of the prevertebral soft tissues. Therefore, X-rays should ideally be obtained during quiet inspiration with the patient calm and properly positioned.

In the ED, accurate interpretation of lateral neck X-rays is critical, particularly when evaluating for deep neck space infections. Misinterpretation due to positioning artifacts can lead to unnecessary CT, antibiotic use, or surgical consultation. Conversely, failure to recognize true widening may delay the diagnosis of life-threatening conditions, such as retropharyngeal abscess or expanding hematoma, which can compromise the airway.



A cervical spine fracture (A) may be associated with prevertebral soft tissue swelling due to hematoma, which represents true, not artifactual, widening. This is a concerning and clinically significant finding rather than a benign imaging artifact. Therefore, this option does not represent a common cause of false widening and should prompt further evaluation.

Deep inspiration (B) actually helps reduce the apparent thickness of the retropharyngeal space by expanding the airway and surrounding soft tissues. X-rays are ideally obtained during inspiration for this reason. Therefore, deep inspiration does not cause artifactual widening and instead improves diagnostic accuracy.

Esophageal dilation (C) is not a typical cause of retropharyngeal space widening on plain X-rays. The esophagus lies posterior to the trachea and does not significantly alter the prevertebral soft tissue contour in a way that mimics retropharyngeal pathology. This finding would be better evaluated with other imaging modalities if clinically suspected.

While supine positioning (E) can slightly affect soft tissue appearance, it is not a primary or common cause of significant artifactual widening of the retropharyngeal space. Positioning of the neck, specifically flexion versus extension, plays a much larger role. Supine films may be less ideal than upright films, but they do not typically produce the marked widening seen with neck flexion.

question: A 21-year-old man presents for evaluation of a sore throat with a fever for 2 days. On examination, his oropharynx is erythematous with enlarged tonsils and bilateral exudates. In addition to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which of the following has been shown to produce the greatest reduction in pain?
englishExplanation:
Dexamethasone administered in a single dose of 0.6 mg/kg up to a maximum of 10 mg is associated with a reduction of pain and duration of pain in patients with moderate to severe pharyngitis. The medication is available orally or parenterally and has the same effectiveness in either form. The mainstay of therapy for patients with pharyngitis is treatment with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents.



Acetaminophen (A) is an appropriate analgesic to use in the treatment of pharyngitis. However, this medication has no underlying anti-inflammatory properties and will not address the underlying cause of pain.

Intravenous hydration (C) is sometimes administered to patients who report decreased intake due to their throat pain but will likely not impact their degree of pain directly.

Penicillin (D) is often prescribed for patients with exudative pharyngitis. However, data do not suggest any significant impact on pain or duration of pain as a result of the administration of antibiotics. Additionally, many antibiotics carry the risk of allergic reaction or side effects like diarrhea which should be considered before their administration. In children, antibiotics are usually administered as a preventive measure against the development of rheumatic heart disease from streptococcal infections.

question: A 45-year-old man presents to the ED for right eye pain and photophobia after being hit in the right eye with a glass bottle 2 days ago. On exam, visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally, and a ciliary flush is noted in the right eye. On fluorescein staining, there are no corneal abrasions, and the Seidel test is negative. Intraocular pressure is measured as 15 mm Hg on the right and 13 mm Hg on the left. There is both direct and consensual photophobia. By what mechanism does the first-line treatment work to reduce the patient’s eye pain?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with signs and symptoms consistent with traumatic iritis, which is a subtype of anterior uveitis localized to the iris and typically caused by blunt trauma. Eye trauma causes direct injury to the iris as well as an inflammatory reaction that causes increased eye pain within the first few days of injury. Symptoms include ocular pain, photophobia secondary to pupillary constriction, and decreased visual acuity if inflammatory cells enter the anterior chamber. The examination can show anterior cells and flare and increased intraocular pressure, depending on the severity of inflammation. More severe trauma can cause adhesions (i.e., synechiae) to form between the iris and anterior lens, which can inhibit aqueous outflow from the posterior chamber and lead to secondary glaucoma. Consensual photophobia is common and refers to pain in the injured eye with light shined in the uninjured eye, and results from pupillary constriction as opposed to a direct sensitivity to light itself.

First-line treatment of traumatic iritis is cycloplegics, including cyclopentolate and scopolamine. Cycloplegics paralyze the ciliary muscles, resulting in pupillary dilation and a decrease in the pupillary spasms and accommodation that cause pain. Cycloplegics also prevent synechiae formation, which decreases the risk of secondary glaucoma. Topical steroids can be added to cycloplegics to decrease intraocular inflammation but should be avoided with corneal defects and are best prescribed in consultation with an ophthalmologist.



Decreases intraocular inflammation (A) is the mechanism by which topical steroid drops work. Topical steroids can be used to treat traumatic iritis but should be avoided if there are any corneal defects, as this could increase the risk of infection. Topical steroids are second-line medications and can be added to cycloplegics, often after consulting with ophthalmology. In this patient with mild symptoms and no changes in visual acuity, steroids may be unnecessary.

Prevents synechiae formation (C) is a secondary effect of cycloplegics and can decrease the risk of glaucoma secondary to trauma, but it does not directly reduce the pain the patient is currently having. This patient’s pain, as indicated by consensual photophobia, is secondary to pupillary constriction, and the mechanism by which cycloplegics reduce this pain is ciliary muscle paralysis.

Reduces aqueous humor production (D) is the mechanism by which timolol drops work in the treatment of glaucoma. Since traumatic iritis can cause glaucoma if circumferential synechiae block the outflow of aqueous humor, timolol drops can be useful in some cases of traumatic iritis, but would not be the first line and would not directly reduce this patient’s pain.

One Step Further
Question:
What toxidrome would be caused by a systemic overdose of cycloplegics?

question: A 19-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for ear pain. She had her tragus pierced a few days ago. Shortly after, she began having increased pain at her piercing site. Her physical exam reveals a tender tragus with erythema covering both the tragus and surrounding auricle. She reports pain when moving her auricle in any direction. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient’s condition?

options.text: Oral cephalexin and removal of the piercing
Oral ciprofloxacin and removal of the piercing
Topical hydrocortisone cream and removal of the piercing
Warm compresses and salt water soaks around the piercing

correctAnswer: Oral ciprofloxacin and removal of the piercing
englishExplanation:
This patient has acute perichondritis, an infection of the connective tissue surrounding the cartilaginous tissue of the ear. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common microbe responsible for this infection. Risk factors include any trauma or skin breakdown over the helix or tragus, especially with indwelling material like ear piercings. Diagnosis is clinical, but if an abscess is present, wound cultures should be taken after incision and drainage to ensure appropriate sensitivities. Given the poor blood supply to cartilage, prolonged courses of antibiotics may be required. Despite treatment, auricle necrosis, auricle deformity, and permanent cartilage damage may occur. Treatment is with immediate removal of any foreign bodies (e.g., earrings), antipseudomonal antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin), and close follow-up to ensure adequate improvement. Some sources also recommend adding topical antibiotics to cover Staphylococcus aureus.



Oral cephalexin (A), while a common antibiotic used in uncomplicated cellulitis, does not have the pseudomonal coverage required in the treatment of perichondritis.

Patients may present with evidence of contact dermatitis after piercings due to an unknown nickel allergy. The lesions typically appear as erythematous flaking or blistering with or without pruritus. Treatment is with avoidance of the allergen and topical steroids (C).

Warm compresses and salt water soaks (D) are common post-piercing recommendations to aid in the comfort and prevention of infection but have no role in active infection treatment.

One Step Further

What beta-hemolytic Streptococcus infection presents similarly to perichondritis?

Reveal Answer:
Erysipelas can present with the Milian sign or evidence of an overlying skin infection involving the pinna.

Perichondritis

Infection of connective tissue and cartilage of the ear
Pseudomonas aeruginosa most common organism
Risks: trauma, burns, skin breakdown, piercing
Sx: redness, pain, erythema to pinna and cartilaginous portion of ear, spares lobule
Sometimes associated with abscess
Tx: consider I&D, obtain wound culture
Antipseudomonal antibiotics (e.g., levofloxacin)
Otolaryngology follow-up

question: A 43-year-old man presents to the ED for a diffuse headache for the last 3 days and pain in the left ear. He has no medical history and takes no daily medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals an erythematous tympanic membrane on the left with point tenderness along the bony prominence posterior to the left ear. Neurologic examination reveals no focal findings. A CT scan is shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment step in the management of this patient’s condition?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and discharge with outpatient otolaryngology referral

englishExplanation:
This patient has clinical and radiographic features of acute mastoiditis, which is the most common suppurative complication of otitis media and represents infection of the mastoid air cells with destruction of the bony trabeculae and coalescence of the cells. While most commonly associated with otitis media, mastoiditis can also occur as a complication of hematologic malignancies, mononucleosis, and temporal bone sarcoma. Its incidence has decreased in the era of modern antibiotics, and it is typically caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, though Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Fusobacterium necrophorum may also be involved, particularly in patients who have recently received antibiotics.

The most frequent clinical features of mastoiditis are fever, otalgia, headache, and erythema. Tenderness over the mastoid process posterior to the ear is a classic finding, and the tympanic membrane is commonly erythematous and bulging such as in acute otitis media. There are no specific diagnostic criteria for mastoiditis, but it can be diagnosed on clinical evaluation alone and does not require CT imaging. However, patients with symptoms that suggest potential intracranial extension should undergo imaging to confirm the diagnosis and rule out complications such as a brain abscess and subdural empyema. Localized tenderness over the mastoid does not suggest intracranial extension in itself, but this patient’s more diffuse headache warrants imaging to evaluate for such complications.

Patients with suspected or confirmed mastoiditis require parenteral antibiotics as a first step in treatment. There is some variation in the recommended first-line antibiotic (particularly among children versus adults), with vancomycin as a common first-line agent. Some references list ceftriaxone as a first-line option, but it is important to consider the likelihood of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), as infection rates have been rising and this organism is more likely to be associated with mastoiditis in adult patients. Patients with recent antibiotic exposure should be treated with an antipseudomonal antibiotic such as piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime along with vancomycin. Consultation with otolaryngology should be ordered in the emergency department or otherwise early in the hospital course, as surgical management is often necessary and specialist involvement aids in the management of associated complications.

LEARNING TIP: When deciding the best treatment for acute mastoiditis, it is important to remember that the treatment in children differs slightly from the treatment in adults. Mastoiditis is much more common in children and rare in adults. In adults, it is more often related to chronic suppurative otitis media. While beta-lactam/beta-lactamase combination therapy may be a first-line treatment in children, this is not the case in adults. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus must be a strong consideration as a cause of mastoiditis in adults.



Ampicillin-sulbactam (A) is not a first-line agent for mastoiditis in adults, and there is no evidence of intracranial complications on CT to warrant neurosurgical involvement.

IV cefazolin (B) is not the most appropriate choice for treating acute mastoiditis, as it does not provide adequate coverage for the typical organisms associated with this condition. Cefazolin primarily targets gram-positive organisms and is effective against Streptococcus species and methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, but it lacks activity against MRSA, some gram-negative pathogens, and anaerobes.

Ketorolac plus neurology evaluation (C) would not provide any antibiotic coverage or involve the appropriate specialty needed for definitive care for this patient with mastoiditis.

Amoxicillin-clavulanate is a commonly used oral antibiotic for otolaryngologic infections, but this patient requires inpatient IV antibiotics and urgent otolaryngology evaluation rather than oral antibiotics and outpatient follow-up (E).

One Step Further

What dose of vancomycin should be given for acute mastoiditis in children?

Reveal Answer:
15 mg/kg.

Sx: fever, otalgia, and retroauricular swelling and tenderness
PE: erythema and protrusion of the external ear
Dx: clinical, CT can confirm the diagnosis
Tx: admission and IV antibiotics

question: An 18-year-old man presents to the emergency department with throat pain. He is in obvious discomfort and has difficulty speaking. Vital signs include a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F), heart rate of 110 bpm, and blood pressure of 100/70 mm Hg. During the exam, you notice that his tongue protrudes from his mouth. You also note trismus, neck fullness, and stridor. What is the most likely source of this infection?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with Ludwig angina, which most commonly arises from an odontogenic infection. Ludwig angina is a rapidly expanding infection of the submandibular space and is potentially life-threatening as it can compromise the airway. The submandibular space spans from the floor of the mouth to the hyoid bone. Ludwig angina usually begins with a mild infection, often from a periapical abscess that spreads into the submandibular space. Patients present with fevers, chills, pain, and trismus. If the swelling is advanced, they may also develop neck swelling, tongue protrusion, drooling, and stridor. Treatment involves IV antibiotics and surgery to address the source of the infection. Additionally, management in the emergency department should include aggressive protection of the airway, which may involve early intubation.



Cellulitis (A), otitis media (C), and pharyngitis (D) are all common infections of the head and neck and can potentially spread to the submandibular space. However, given the proximity, odontogenic infections are the leading cause of Ludwig angina.

One Step Further
Question:
What two spaces is the submandibular space divided into?

Reveal Answer:
Sublingual and submylohyoid spaces.

Rapid Review

Aggressive, rapidly spreading cellulitis of bilateral submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces
Risks: dental infections (molars), immunodeficiency, diabetes
PE: tongue elevation, brawny edema under the chin, dysphagia, dysphonia, drooling
Dx: clinical, CT
Tx: fiberoptic or awake intubation, IV antibiotics, ENT consultation
