question: A 55-year-old man with a tracheostomy placed 2 weeks ago presents to the ED with bleeding from the tracheostomy. His T is 97°F (36.1°C), BP is 125/80 mm Hg, HR is 102 bpm, RR is 15/min, and SpO2 is 97% on room air. Brisk bleeding is noted from the stoma. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Direct pressure through the stoma internally and externally

correctAnswer: Direct pressure through the stoma internally and externally
englishExplanation:
Tracheoinnominate fistula (TIF) is a rapidly fatal diagnosis. It occurs after a tracheostomy in which a fistula develops between the stoma and the innominate artery. TIF is caused by erosion of the tracheal wall. Prolonged pressure from the tracheostomy tube or cuff can lead to erosion of the tracheal wall, eventually reaching the innominate artery. This is more likely with high cuff pressures, low tracheostomy placement, prolonged tracheostomy, surgical trauma (accidental injury to the innominate artery during tracheostomy placement), and infection. Local infection can weaken the tissue between the trachea and the artery, facilitating the formation of a fistula. TIF represents a severe complication arising from tracheostomy, typically manifesting within the initial 4 weeks postprocedure, though it may develop at any subsequent point. The associated mortality with TIF is high.

Rapid bleeding from the tracheostomy site may be noted, including pulsatile bleeding. When this diagnosis is suspected, immediate management may include hyperinflating the cuff and applying pressure internally and externally to the innominate artery to prevent further bleeding. While the clinician does this, otolaryngology should emergently be consulted for further care and treatment in the operating room.



Administration of tranexamic acid (A) helps reduce bleeding by preventing the breakdown of blood clots. Although beneficial in various bleeding scenarios, it may not provide the immediate control necessary for active, brisk bleeding from a tracheostomy site. Although it may help this patient, local compression is likely to be more effective for rapid control of the bleeding and preventing further decompensation.

Cauterization with silver nitrate (B) might be appropriate for a small, punctate bleed that is clearly visualized and is not arterial. This patient’s bleeding is too rapid and concerning to use silver nitrate.

Suctioning the tracheostomy tube (D) can help maintain airway patency by removing blood from the airway, but it does not address stopping the source of the bleeding. It is an important supportive measure but should not be the primary or initial step in managing active bleeding from a stoma.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
Bacterial tracheitis.

question: A 19-year-old woman presents with pain in her mouth. She underwent an extraction of an impacted molar 3 days before the onset of her pain. Her pain had been improving. However, it began worsening acutely today. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Iodoform gauze packing moistened with oil of clove

correctAnswer: Iodoform gauze packing moistened with oil of clove
englishExplanation:
This patient likely has a dry socket, also known as acute alveolar osteitis. Patients undergo dental extraction and after the procedure, a hemostatic blood clot forms in the socket. Pain is common for 24 hours post-procedure and then improves. When the healing blood clot is lost from the socket, the patient develops acute, severe pain. Most commonly, it occurs 3–4 days after the extraction and is associated with a foul odor. Pain is related to local inflammation and osteitis (inflammation of exposed bone). Treatment includes packing the open socket with iodoform gauze. The gauze is saturated with either a medicated dental paste or eugenol (oil of cloves). Patients will require analgesia and may benefit from a nerve block.



Dilute hydrogen peroxide rinses (A) will not provide benefit in this situation. One goal is to maintain the seal of the socket through packing or dental sealing. Rinsing with hydrogen peroxide will interfere with this. Rinsing with dilute hydrogen peroxide is part of the treatment for acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis.

Incision and drainage (B) is not indicated for the treatment of dry socket. There is no abscess collection and nothing to drain. The pain is caused by the dislodgement of the blood clot with subsequent inflammation.

A root canal (D) includes opening the pulp chamber of a tooth, removing the pulp, and irrigating and sterilizing the canal in which the pulp sits. This is performed to remove diseased pulp tissue and requires the presence of a tooth. Since the entire tooth has been removed prior to the development of dry socket, this technique does not apply.

One Step Further

What is expected on physical examination of dry socket?

Reveal Answer:
Exposed bone and no clot in the extraction site.

PE: inflammation and local osteitis with a clean extraction site
Treatment is via packing socket with iodoform gauze and eugenol oil

question: A 49-year-old man with diabetes is transferred from an outside hospital for facial swelling. He has had a fever and odynophagia after a recent tooth extraction. On physical examination, he has swelling and erythema in the submental space. A CT of the neck demonstrates soft tissue stranding of the submental and submylohyoid space with a developing phlegmon. When he returns from CT, his voice is muffled, and he is having difficulty tolerating his secretions. Which of the following is the best next intervention at this time?
englishExplanation:
Ludwig angina is a potentially life-threatening, rapidly progressive, infection of the three mandibular spaces: the submental, sublingual, and submandibular spaces. These spaces track down into the mediastinum and communicate directly with the parapharyngeal space, which makes airway compromise a concerning complication. All three spaces must be involved bilaterally for the infection to be considered Ludwig angina. The most common cause of Ludwig angina is odontogenic from an infected mandibular molar.

Patients often present with elevation of the tongue, tense induration of the submandibular tissue, trismus, drooling, stridor, dysphagia, and dyspnea. The diagnosis can be made clinically, but if able to be obtained, a CT scan of the soft tissues of the neck with IV contrast may show an abscess, phlegmon, or subcutaneous air from gas-producing organisms. Broad-spectrum antibiotics covering gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms should be given. Early orotracheal intubation is essential for securing the airway, as airway compromise may progress rapidly. Emergent surgical or ENT consultation is indicated while preparing for airway management.



Bedside incision and drainage (A) is not appropriate for managing Ludwig angina due to concerns about airway compromise. Antibiotics alone are often sufficient, but if surgical intervention is required, it should be done in the operating room with otolaryngology or oromaxillofacial surgery.

Because Ludwig angina is primarily odontogenic, patients may need to have their infected teeth extracted. Although a dentistry consultation (B) may eventually be needed, securing the airway and administering IV antibiotics should not be delayed.

Soft tissue ultrasound (D) may demonstrate cellulitis changes or focal abscess, but performing it may delay appropriate management such as airway intervention. Clinicians should not rely on ultrasound findings to make management decisions.

Reveal Answer:

question: A 43-year-old man with a history of HIV on antiretroviral therapy presents to the emergency department with concerns about a muffled voice and intermittent stridor that began when he awoke today. Last week he underwent the drainage of a periapical abscess and extraction of the associated molar. Yesterday he developed a sore throat, odynophagia, and neck pain. His physical exam is notable for faint stridor, a muffled voice, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, 1+ tonsils without exudates bilaterally, and no tenderness of the floor of the mouth. What imaging modality is indicated to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Computed tomography of the neck soft tissues
Magnetic resonance imaging of the neck soft tissues
Radiography of the lateral neck soft tissue
Ultrasonography of the neck soft tissues

correctAnswer: Computed tomography of the neck soft tissues
englishExplanation:
A retropharyngeal abscess is a collection of purulent material within the retropharyngeal potential space that lies anterior to the prevertebral fascia and posterior to the pharynx. This space extends caudally from the base of the skull to the level of the carina. Patients with recent intraoral procedures, trauma, foreign body, immunocompromised state, or extension from odontogenic infection are at a higher risk. They may present with odynophagia, dysphagia, neck pain, lymphadenopathy, vocal changes (e.g., muffled voice), and even stridor that leads to respiratory distress. Contrast CT of the soft tissues of the neck is the most sensitive testing modality for determining the diagnosis of retropharyngeal abscess. Imaging hallmarks include a ring-enhancing fluid collection in the retropharyngeal space, though more subtle or earlier findings include fat stranding, reactive edema, fluid tracking between tissue planes, and even mass effect. Early otolaryngology consultation for surgical intervention is key. Most infections are polymicrobial and often involve Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and anaerobes, which can be covered by empiric antimicrobial regimens such as piperacillin-tazobactam, ampicillin-sulbactam, and clindamycin plus metronidazole. Vancomycin or linezolid may be added for patients at risk for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. The progression of infection can lead to extension into the mediastinum, airway mass effect and compromise, and aspiration secondary to abscess rupture.



Barium esophagography (A) is helpful in the characterization of dysphagia, as it may reveal a diagnosis such as an esophageal stricture, an esophageal diverticulum, or achalasia, but it is less sensitive in characterizing retropharyngeal and prevertebral tissue. MRI (C) provides greater detail but is unnecessary given the increased resources required when there is widespread availability of computed tomography. Radiography (D) may demonstrate thickening and anterior displacement of the retropharyngeal wall, leading to prevertebral widening. This modality is less sensitive for characterizing the size and impact on nearby structures, which are critical to know with a suspected retropharyngeal abscess. Ultrasonography (E) is insufficient for characterizing deeper structures of the neck. This modality would be helpful for identifying superficial areas of soft tissue swelling, such as a cutaneous abscess or phlegmon, and in cases of suspected lymphadenitis.

One Step Further
Question:
What diagnosis should be suspected in a patient with a recent upper respiratory infection, fever, unilateral neck swelling and pain, and variable cranial nerve deficits (e.g., abducens nerve palsy)?

Reveal Answer:
Lemierre syndrome.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Retropharyngeal Abscess

Risks: trauma or URI
Most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, group A Streptococcus, respiratory anaerobes, foreign body
Sx: fever, sore throat, dysphagia, neck pain
PE: trismus, stridor, nuchal rigidity, muffled voice, cri du canard (duck quack)
Toxic-appearing child, 3–5 years old
X-ray: widened retropharyngeal (prevertebral) space twice the size of the vertebral body
Dx: CT imaging, if patient is stable

question: A 54-year-old man presents to the emergency department for sudden onset of flashes in his left eye. There is no associated pain. His ocular ultrasound is shown above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation and ultrasound are most consistent with retinal detachment. Retinal detachment may present with monocular flashes, floaters, a curtain in the visual field, or loss of visual acuity. It is typically diagnosed with dilated ophthalmoscope exam but may also be detected with point-of-care ultrasound. Ocular ultrasound will demonstrate the hyperechoic retinal membrane within the vitreous, which will move with ocular movements. It adheres to the optic disc, as seen in the image above. Retinal detachment requires urgent evaluation by a retina specialist.



Intraocular foreign body (A) is typically associated with eye pain or discomfort. Some foreign bodies may be visualized on ultrasound, depending on their echogenicity. This patient’s presentation is not consistent with a foreign body. Vitreous hemorrhage (D) commonly causes floaters and produces a snow globe appearance on ultrasound, with multiple echoes within the posterior chamber of the vitreous. Posterior vitreous detachment (B) appears as a swaying linear structure in the posterior chamber on ultrasound. In contrast with retinal detachment, it is not tethered to the optic disc.

question: A 60-year-old woman with a history of diabetes mellitus presents to the ED with severe left ear pain and low-grade fever. Examination of her auditory canal is shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
englishExplanation:
Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa is a life-threatening invasive infection of the external auditory canal and can spread to involve the base of the skull. Malignant otitis externa is overwhelmingly seen in older patients with diabetes mellitus. The most common contributing organism is Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which has been implicated in most cases. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative organism capable of growing in distilled water. A patient with suspected malignant otitis externa may have a history of ear irrigation. Clinical manifestations include otalgia and otorrhea. The pain is generally more severe than that found in simple otitis externa, although the two may be difficult to distinguish, especially early on in the disease process. The classic physical exam finding is granulation tissue in the inferior portion of the external auditory canal.

As the infection progresses, osteomyelitis of the skull base and temporomandibular joint can develop. Disease progression to osteomyelitis can manifest as cranial nerve deficits, with the facial nerve being the most likely to be affected. Other central nervous system complications include meningitis, brain abscess, and dural sinus thrombophlebitis. The diagnosis of malignant otitis externa is based on clinical, laboratory, and radiographic findings. A markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein can support the diagnosis and is the most characteristic lab abnormality.

Computed tomography showing bone erosion and soft tissue changes in the subtemporal region may strongly suggest the diagnosis. The recommended treatment for malignant otitis externa is ciprofloxacin 400 mg intravenously every 8 hours, although mild cases can be treated with oral therapy. Other antipseudomonal antibiotics such as cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, and ceftazidime are also appropriate.



Cephalexin (A) is a beta-lactam antibiotic used to treat gram-positive bacterial infections.

Clindamycin (C) is a bacteriostatic antibiotic that is used to treat gram-positive and anaerobic bacterial infections.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (D) and vancomycin (E) are used to treat gram-positive bacterial infection secondary to methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can also cover some gram-negative and protozoa. None of these antibiotics have activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

question: Which of the following is the most common etiology of external otitis?
englishExplanation:
The most common cause of otitis externa is infection due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. The pain from otitis externa is caused by inflammation and edema of the ear canal skin, which is normally adherent to the bone and cartilage of the auditory canal. The inflammatory reaction can be caused by bacteria, fungi, or contact dermatitis. Cerumen protects the canal by forming an acidic coat that helps prevent infection. Factors that predispose to otitis externa include the absence of cerumen, often from excessive cleaning by the patient, water that macerates the skin of the auditory canal and raises the pH, and trauma to the skin of the auditory canal from foreign bodies or the use of cotton swabs. Treatment includes suction and gentle warm irrigation of the canal. Treatment with a 2% acetic acid solution or an alternative drying medication can be administered. A topical antibiotic drop with a steroid is the first-line therapy (neomycin/polymyxin/hydrocortisone). Use the suspension rather than the solution if the tympanic membrane is ruptured.



Fungal infections compose < 10% of external otitis cases. The most common fungi are Aspergillus niger (A) and Candida (B) species and they are more prevalent in tropical climates.

Moraxella catarrhalis (C) is a common contributor to otitis media but is not often implicated in otitis externa.

question: A parent brings her healthy 2-year-old girl to the ED with a concern of ear pain. On physical exam, you visualize a live insect in the left external auditory canal. What is the best way to care for this child?

options.text: Irrigation of the ear with alcohol or mineral oil to kill the insect; forceps removal; ototopical antibiotics only if there is excoriation of the external auditory canal
Irrigation of the ear with tap water to kill the insect; irrigation removal; ototopical antiobiotics to prevent otitis externa
Removal of the insect with curette; ototopical antibiotics only if there is excoriation of the external auditory canal
Removal of the insect with forceps; ototopical antibiotics for prevention of otitis externa

correctAnswer: Irrigation of the ear with alcohol or mineral oil to kill the insect; forceps removal; ototopical antibiotics only if there is excoriation of the external auditory canal
englishExplanation:
The most common foreign body (FB) concern in the ED is the foreign body in the external auditory canal (EAC). These FBs cause relatively little pain and can go for quite some time without being noted. Stones, paper, beads, food, and insects are some of the most common substances that are found in patients’ ears. When discovered, the FB should be removed, but this requires either cooperation, physical restraint, or chemical restraint of the patient. Most objects do not cause direct injury to the EAC, so if they are not removed in the ED, patients can be referred to the otolaryngologist for elective evacuation. FBs may be removed using a curette, alligator forceps, or irrigation with an IV catheter and a 20 cc syringe. Irrigation is contraindicated if there is suspicion that the tympanic membrane may have been violated. Irrigation is also contraindicated if the FB is organic material such as food. Live insects should be killed first with alcohol or mineral oil, followed by any type of removal. Prophylactic ototopical antibiotics for otitis externa are required if there has been an excoriation of the EAC during the FB removal.



Irrigation of the ear with tap water (B) is contraindicated for soft objects, organic matter, or seeds, since it may lead to swelling of the object. Ototopic antibiotic prophylaxis is only indicated if the EAC has been excoriated during the removal of the FB.

Removal of the insect with curette (C) or forceps (D) and without killing it first can cause severe pain and alarming symptoms to the patient secondary to insect movement on the exquisitely sensitive tympanic membrane and medial EAC.

question: Which of the following findings on examination is most concerning for a diagnosis of orbital cellulitis as opposed to preseptal cellulitis?
englishExplanation:
Orbital cellulitis (infection of the orbital fat and ocular muscles) and preseptal cellulitis (infection of the eyelid) often present similarly, but it is critical for the emergency clinician to differentiate these conditions. While preseptal cellulitis is generally benign and can be treated outpatient, orbital cellulitis is a rapidly progressive vision-threatening condition. Both often spread from local upper respiratory infections, leading to bacterial inoculation. In orbital cellulitis, most commonly paranasal sinusitis erodes the thin lamina papyracea. Trauma or surgery can also predispose patients to secondary infection. While patients with both orbital and preseptal cellulitis can have fever, eyelid swelling, and leukocytosis, patients with orbital cellulitis will typically have visual symptoms including ophthalmoplegia, diplopia, limitation of extraocular movement, proptosis, or abnormal pupillary response due to swelling and inflammation of the optic nerve and extraocular muscles posterior to the eye. The presenc of any of the above symptoms should prompt rapid administration of intravenous antibiotics to cover Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci, as these are the most commonly isolated pathogens, as well as emergent ophthalmology consult. Intravenous vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin or piperacillin-tazobactam is most often used as empiric therapy. Facial computerized tomography can be used in equivocal cases to help with diagnosis as well as to rule out abscess.



Eyelid swelling with erythema (A) is a hallmark finding of preseptal cellulitis. In cases of isolated preseptal cellulitis, the orbit is not involved and only the eyelid is infected, leading to these superficial findings.

Numbness of the forehead (B) would be caused by impingement of cranial nerve V1 (ophthalmic nerve), which passes through the cavernous sinus, and would more likely be affected in cavernous sinus thrombosis or infection instead of orbital pathology.

Preceding rhinosinusitis (D) may be seen in both orbital cellulitis and preseptal cellulitis and cannot reliably distinguish the two etiologies.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
Cranial nerves III, IV, VI, and the maxillary and ophthalmic branches of cranial nerve V.

question: Which of the following is the best management of corneal abrasions once the diagnosis is made?

options.text: Oral antibiotics and an eye patch

englishExplanation:
Corneal abrasions are common ophthalmic injuries, often resulting from trauma, foreign body exposure, or improper contact lens use. Risk factors include occupational hazards (e.g., construction work), contact lens wear, and dry eye syndromes. Patients typically present with severe eye pain, tearing, foreign body sensation, photophobia, and mild visual disturbances. Diagnosis is confirmed using fluorescein staining, which highlights epithelial defects under cobalt blue light.

The best management for corneal abrasions is topical antibiotics and pain control. Topical antibiotics, such as erythromycin ointment or trimethoprim-polymyxin B drops, help prevent secondary bacterial infection, particularly in individuals with a high risk, such as contact lens wearers (who require antipseudomonal coverage like fluoroquinolones). Pain control can be achieved with oral NSAIDs or topical cycloplegics, and patients should be counseled to avoid rubbing their eyes and to return for worsening symptoms. Small, uncomplicated abrasions typically heal within 24–48 hours without sequelae.



Corticosteroids (A) delay epithelial healing and increase the risk of corneal ulceration and secondary infection, particularly from fungal or bacterial sources. They are contraindicated in managing corneal abrasions unless directed by an ophthalmologist.

Oral antibiotics (B) are not required for corneal abrasions unless there is a risk of significant infection (e.g., associated eyelid trauma with cellulitis). Additionally, eye patching is no longer recommended, as it does not speed up healing and may increase infection risk by creating a warm, moist environment conducive to bacterial growth.

While topical anesthetics (C) (e.g., proparacaine, tetracaine) provide immediate pain relief, they generally should not be prescribed for home use. If used excessively, repeated application can delay corneal healing, impair protective reflexes, and increase the risk of corneal melt and ulceration. These drops are useful for diagnostic purposes in the emergency department but should not be given for long-term outpatient treatment.

Ophthalmology consultation (E) is unnecessary for nearly all corneal abrasions. If there is concern for significant ulceration or deeper pathology, ophthalmology may be needed.

question: A 24-year-old man presents to the ED due to a sore throat. Physical examination shows the findings above. Which of the following describes the appropriate procedural technique for the treatment of this patient’s condition?

options.text: Attach a 3.5 inch spinal needle to a 10 mL syringe and aspirate
Cut the distal 1 cm of an 18-gauge IV catheter and aspirate via the needle attached to a 10 mL syringe
Use a bare No. 11 blade to make a curvilinear incision 2 cm deep and 3 cm long
Use a bare No. 11 blade to make a vertical incision 2 cm deep and 2 cm long

correctAnswer: Cut the distal 1 cm of an 18-gauge IV catheter and aspirate via the needle attached to a 10 mL syringe
englishExplanation:
Peritonsillar abscess (PTA) refers to a purulent infection contained between the tonsillar capsule, superior constrictor muscle, and the palatopharyngeus muscle. It is thought to develop due to the contiguous spread of adjacent infection from within the tonsil itself or mucous glands within the superior tonsillar pole. Typical clinical manifestations include sore throat, fever, dysphagia or odynophagia, trismus, and changes in voice. Unilateral tonsillar swelling with uvular deviation represents additional objective data and is usually a clinical finding that helps secure the diagnosis. The diagnosis is usually apparent from clinical data alone, but imaging (e.g., CT, intraoral ultrasound) may be needed when the diagnosis is uncertain.

Treatment for a PTA consists of abscess drainage and antibiotics, with needle aspiration (18- or 20-gauge) and incision and drainage (I&D) considered first-line strategies, depending on clinician preference and clinical circumstances. However, needle aspiration is often simpler to perform and causes less pain. Thus, it is preferred by many emergency clinicians. With either method, care must be taken to avoid damage to surrounding tissues and structures, as the carotid artery and jugular vein lie posterolateral to the tonsils and may be injured.

One strategy to reduce the risk of vascular injury is to cut the distal 1 cm off of an IV catheter and replace it over the needle before aspirating with a 10-mL syringe attached to the needle. This allows the catheter itself to serve as a protective sheath, preventing overly deep advancement of the needle. When performing I&D, a No. 11 blade should be used to make a stab incision of approximately 0.5 cm in depth. The blade can be similarly protected by wrapping tape around the scalpel while leaving the distal 0.5 cm exposed.

After drainage of a PTA, all patients should receive antimicrobial therapy. Cultures should be sent at the time of drainage, but common causative agents include Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus (including methicillin-resistant strains). Amoxicillin-clavulante and clindamycin are appropriate agents in regions with low rates of methicillin resistance, while ampicillin-sulbactam and clindamycin are IV options. However, methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) should be empirically covered (e.g., vancomycin, linezolid) in patients with systemic illness (e.g., sepsis) or when MRSA is suspected based on patient characteristics or local prevalence. Although strong evidence is lacking, glucocorticoids are commonly used to reduce inflammation and hasten symptom relief, with minimal side effects.



Simply attaching a spinal needle to a syringe and aspirating (A) provides no safeguard against overly deep needle penetration and would increase the risk of vascular injury. Some protective measure against this (e.g., cutting the IV catheter) should be implemented when possible.

While a No. 11 blade is appropriate when performing I&D of a PTA, incisions at a depth of 2 cm (C, D) risk injury to the neck vasculature, and using a bare blade increases the risk of overpenetration. Depth should be limited to 0.5 cm by wrapping tape around the scalpel to prevent potential complications.

question: Which of the following findings on ocular ultrasound is most consistent with a vitreous hemorrhage?

options.text: Biconvex mass in the posterior chamber that moves independently of eye movements
Echogenic opacity in the most posterior aspect of the posterior chamber
Hyperechoic opacities scattered through the vitreous

correctAnswer: Hyperechoic opacities scattered through the vitreous
englishExplanation:
Vitreous hemorrhage can occur spontaneously or in the setting of trauma. On ocular ultrasound, it will be seen as a hyperechoic material in the posterior chamber and vitreous. Depending on the extent and age of the bleed, it can have different appearances. Early on, it is characterized by small dots or mobile opacities in the middle portion of the posterior chamber that can be found in a whirlpool-type pattern. Over time, the hemorrhage can become more echogenic and form membranes that can be confused with a retinal detachment. Unlike a retinal detachment, which moves with eye movements, the echogenic membrane associated with vitreous hemorrhage will remain horizontal with eye movement.



Distortion of the normal shape of the globe, decreased globe size, buckling of the sclera, and anterior chamber collapse (A) can be seen with globe rupture.

A lens dislocation is seen as a biconvex mass in the posterior chamber that moves independently of eye movements (B).

Retinal detachments are typically seen as an echogenic opacity or membrane in the most posterior aspect of the posterior chamber (C) adjacent to the optic disk, whereas vitreous hemorrhage is typically seen in the midportion of the posterior chamber.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
< 5 mm.

Posterior vitreous detachment: thin, hyperechoic membrane off the posterior surface of the globe that is NOT tethered to the optic nerve, very mobile
Vitreous hemorrhage: swirling echogenic material in the posterior chamber with eye movement (washing machine sign)
Central retinal artery occlusion: diminished or absent flow of the CRA with color Doppler mode
Lens dislocation: hyperechoic convex shape in vitreous chamber detached from normal anterior position
Retrobulbar hematoma: anechoic lucency just posterior to the globe
Optic nerve pathology (papilledema): measure the optic nerve 3 mm posterior to the retina
Width > 5 mm is considered abnormal

question: A 16-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of difficulty breathing. The history and physical is consistent with a spontaneous pneumothorax, which you confirm by a chest X-ray. You decide to place a thoracostomy tube, as the pneumothorax is large and the patient is in severe distress. You insert the tube at the fifth intercostal space along the midaxillary line. Which direction should you direct the tube during the procedure?
englishExplanation:
A thoracostomy tube (i.e., chest tube) is indicated in patients who require drainage of the pleural space to allow for lung inflation. This is most common in patients with a large pneumothorax, a hemothorax, or large pleural effusion. There are no absolute contraindications during a life-threatening event such as a tension pneumothorax, but anticoagulation or coagulopathy can cause significant bleeding and complicate the procedure.

The standard approach is under sterile technique at the mid- or anterior axillary line in the fifth intercostal space. The procedure is painful, even with appropriate local analgesia, and additional sedation may be required for awake patients. A 1–2 cm incision is made, and a tunnel is bluntly dissected using a Kelly clamp. Care should be taken to avoid the neurovascular bundle beneath each rib. Inserting a finger can confirm proper placement inside the thorax before the tube is inserted with the Kelly clamp. The thoracostomy tube should be inserted posteriorly and superiorly for best fluid drainage if it is being inserted for trauma or hemothorax. The thoracostomy tube should be inserted anteriorly and superiorly for best air drainage if inserting the tube for a pneumothorax alone. The tube should be sutured in place and attached to a one-way Heimlich valve or water seal device to allow continuous removal of air or fluid. Alternative methods using a Seldinger technique with smaller bore tubes or using a pigtail catheter may be appropriate in certain circumstances. An additional technique using an anterior approach at the second intercostal space in the midclavicular line is described as more comfortable and may be acceptable to drain a pneumothorax when seen clearly on X-ray and when a smaller catheter can be used.



Inserting the tube inferiorly such as anteriorly and inferiorly (A) or posteriorly and inferiorly (C) risks insertion into the mediastinum or lung parenchyma and can result in significant injury. In a case when the tube is inserted into the lung fissure, it should be removed and replaced as necessary, as it is unlikely to provide the intended drainage.

Inserting a thoracostomy tube posteriorly and superiorly (D) is appropriate positioning but is best for drainage of fluid. Placement anteriorly and superiorly is best for drainage of air, as in this patient.

One Step Further

Rapid lung re-expansion can result in what complication?

Reveal Answer:
Re-expansion pulmonary edema.

Primary is without underlying lung disease
Secondary is with underlying lung disease
Sx: acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain
PE: decreased breath sounds, decreased fremitus, hyperresonance to percussion
Dx
Upright CXR: absence of lung markings along lung periphery
Pleural U/S: absence of lung sliding
Tx
Small ≤ 2–3 cm (or < 25% pleural space), no respiratory compromise: observation with oxygen administration

question: A 60-year-old man presents to the emergency department for 1 week of vision changes that have been progressing. He notes that he is seeing cobwebs float around his left eye and that they persist when he takes off his glasses. Visual acuity is 20/40 on the right and 20/70 on the left. Ocular ultrasound of his left eye shows a serpiginous line within the globe extending across the posterior globe from 4 to 9 o'clock. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Posterior vitreous detachment is the most common cause of retinal tears. The vitreous is a gel-like structure in the posterior eye, overlying the retina. Pockets of liquid can penetrate through the vitreous, causing the vitreous to detach from the retina. If the tear encounters an area of strong vitreoretinal adhesions, the tear can penetrate deeper and cause a retinal detachment. Risk factors for vitreous detachment include trauma, ocular surgery, and myopia, which is associated with > 50% of nontraumatic detachments. Symptoms include cobweb-like floaters from the vitreoretinal separation and pinpoint flashes of light resulting from mechanical depolarization of retinal axons secondary to the vitreous tugging on the retina. Ocular ultrasound is a sensitive bedside test for vitreous and retinal detachments and can be used as an adjunct to funduscopy. Ultrasound findings of both vitreous and retinal detachments demonstrate a serpiginous structure within the globe that can often be differentiated by the involvement of the optic nerve. A vitreous detachment can cross over the optic nerve, while retinal detachment will never cross the optic nerve since it is made of nerve fibers, which converge into the optic nerve. Treatment of vitreous detachment by an ophthalmologist may include only reassurance, but they do require urgent referral for a complete retinal exam to rule out occult retinal tears.



Intraocular foreign body (A) can present with floater(s) within the globe but should not have a serpiginous structure attached to the posterior globe. Patients also typically have a history of ocular trauma.

Retinal detachment (B) on ocular ultrasound would show a similar serpiginous structure within the globe. However, it would not cross the optic nerve, as discussed above. Retinal detachments are an emergency, as the progression of the detachment can result in full vision loss. Patients should have an urgent referral to ophthalmology for further evaluation and retinal reattachment. If the macula is still attached, an ophthalmology referral should be emergent to try to prevent the spread to the macula. The macula is located lateral to the optic nerve, in the direct line of sight, and can be found by drawing a straight line from the pupil, through the lens, to the retina.

Vitreous hemorrhage (D) can be associated with retinal detachment when a full-thickness retinal tear causes disruption of blood vessels or is isolated. It presents with flashes and floaters like that of a retinal detachment and a shower of black spots associated with the hemorrhage. On ultrasound, hemorrhage may be seen as swirling within the globe. Urgent referral to ophthalmology is indicated.

One Step Further
Question:
How can you increase the sensitivity of ultrasound for the diagnosis of vitreous hemorrhage?

Reveal Answer:
Increase the gain.

Detachment of vitreous gel from retina
Precursor to retinal detachment occurring over weeks to months
Most common cause of retinal tears
Sx: floaters
Dx: ultrasound with hyperechoic floating membrane freely moving and NOT attached to the optic disc
Tx: ophthalmology evaluation

question: A 35-year-old man presents with right eye pain after drilling at his construction site 5 hours earlier. You note a metallic foreign body at the 3 o’clock position on the cornea and remove it using a 27-gauge needle. A rust ring is visible on the cornea. When is the most appropriate time to attempt rust ring removal?

options.text: 1 hour after development of the rust ring
24 to 48 hours after development of the rust ring
4 to 6 hours after development of the rust ring
5 to 7 days after development of the rust ring

correctAnswer: 24 to 48 hours after development of the rust ring
englishExplanation:
The best time to remove a rust ring is 24 to 48 hours after development to allow for clearer delineation between healthy tissue and retained rust.

Immediate removal attempts can lead to increased trauma to the cornea, as the rust may still be embedded within edematous or inflamed tissue. Waiting also enhances visualization for more precise removal, often using a corneal burr or fine-needle under slit lamp magnification. However, care must be taken not to delay removal excessively, as prolonged retention can increase the risk of corneal staining, persistent inflammation, or infectious keratitis. The procedure should always be followed by application of topical antibiotics and close follow-up to monitor for complications.



1 hour after the development of the rust ring (A) does not allow enough time for the rust to separate from viable tissue, increasing the risk of damaging the cornea during removal.

4 to 6 hours after development of the rust ring (C) still falls within a premature window when the rust is often too embedded and difficult to fully extract without causing additional injury.

5 to 7 days after the development of the rust ring (D) allows excessive time for the rust to incite inflammation or scarring, potentially worsening the outcome and leading to complications like persistent corneal staining or infection.

One Step Further
Question:
Can an MRI be used to identify intraocular foreign bodies?

Reveal Answer:
If the foreign body is metallic, an MRI is contraindicated because it can dislodge the foreign body and damage surrounding tissue.

Rapid Review

Apply topical anesthesia
Use cotton-tipped applicator, needle with the slit lamp, or Alger brush to dislodge

question: A 17-year-old student presents to the ED with unilateral hearing loss. Vital signs include a blood pressure of 110/72 mm Hg, heart rate of 60 bpm, respiratory rate of 14/min, oxygen saturation of 99% on room air, and a temperature of 36.7°C (98.1°F). Weber and Rinne testing supports conductive hearing loss of the left ear. Otoscopic examination reveals a waxy-appearing polyp situated behind a normal-appearing tympanic membrane. There is no purulent discharge or tympanic perforation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Cholesteatoma is an abnormal growth of keratinizing squamous epithelium in the middle ear or mastoid process, most commonly affecting adolescents and adults < 65 years. Despite its name, it is unrelated to cholesterol or gallbladder pathology. This lesion results from chronic inflammation, negative middle ear pressure, or eustachian tube dysfunction, which leads to the retraction of the tympanic membrane and accumulation of keratin debris. The condition can be congenital, arising from embryonic epithelial remnants located medial to an intact tympanic membrane, or acquired, which is far more common and typically results from chronic otitis media or repeated infections, often starting at the pars flaccida of the tympanic membrane.

Patients present with progressive conductive hearing loss, which is the most common symptom due to ossicular chain erosion. Other associated symptoms may include a sensation of fullness in the ear, tinnitus, vertigo, imbalance, and in more advanced cases, facial nerve weakness or paralysis. Otoscopic examination may reveal a pearly white, waxy mass or debris behind a retracted tympanic membrane or a foul-smelling, white-pasty otorrhea if the tympanic membrane is perforated. Chronic inflammation may also produce polyps or granulation tissue in the middle ear, making the condition easily mistaken for chronic suppurative otitis media.

Cholesteatomas are locally invasive and can erode surrounding structures, including the ossicles, facial nerve canal, labyrinth, and even the cranial vault, potentially leading to life-threatening complications such as meningitis, brain abscess, or lateral sinus thrombosis. Therefore, early diagnosis is essential. Imaging with high-resolution CT of the temporal bone may be used to assess the extent of disease. Definitive treatment is surgical, involving microscopic excision via tympanomastoidectomy to fully remove the lesion, reconstruct damaged structures, and prevent recurrence. Long-term follow-up is often necessary due to the risk of regrowth.



Acoustic neuromas (A) present with sensorineural, not conductive, hearing loss. Furthermore, these masses occur in the inner ear and temporal bone on the vestibular nerve and would not likely be viewable during an otoscopic examination.

Otitis media (C) presents with otalgia, hearing loss, fever, and tympanic membrane abnormalities like erythema, bulging, or cloudiness. Although retrotympanic masses can result from chronic suppurative middle ear infections, current infection is unlikely in this patient.

Otosclerosis (D) involves abnormal bone growth of the footplate of the stapes and can cause conductive hearing loss, but it would not present with a polyp on otoscopic examination.

Squamous cell carcinoma (E) is an epithelial cell malignancy that typically occurs on the external, not the middle, ear due to prolonged sun exposure. It has an ulcerated, erythematous appearance with or without bleeding.

One Step Further
Question:
What are the complications of untreated cholesteatoma?

Reveal Answer:
Facial nerve palsies and erosion of the ossicles with subsequent deafness and vertigo.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Cholesteatoma

Acquired: history of chronic ear infections or tympanostomy tubes
Congenital: no prior history of chronic ear infections
Sx: painless otorrhea, new-onset hearing loss
PE: white mass behind the tympanic membrane, deep retraction pockets
Treatment is tympanomastoid surgery
Complications: permanent hearing loss, CN palsy, vertigo, infection

question: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department by ambulance with massive hemorrhage from his cuffed tracheostomy that was placed 15 days ago. Which of the following is the best next step?

options.text: Remove the tracheostomy tube and manually compress the anterior trachea
Replace the tracheostomy tube with a cuffed endotracheal tube

englishExplanation:
There are a number of causes of bleeding from a tracheostomy, including granulation tissue, tracheal irritation or infection, or erosion into nearby vessels including thyroid vessels and the innominate artery. Bleeding from a tracheoinnominate artery fistula is rare but can be life-threatening. Tracheoinnominate artery fistulas usually present between 1 and 3 weeks after tracheostomy, and massive hemorrhage can be preceded by smaller sentinel bleeds, which should be taken seriously.

The first step in managing a tracheoinnominate artery fistula is hyperinflating the tracheostomy cuff in an attempt to tamponade the bleeding while preparing for definitive operative repair. Direct digital pressure into the sternal notch can also help compress the innominate artery. If bleeding is not controlled with cuff hyperinflation, the tracheostomy tube can be slowly withdrawn while putting pressure on the anterior trachea.

The next step is to replace the tracheostomy with an endotracheal tube with the cuff below the fistula to prevent aspiration. This can be done by intubating orally or directly through the stoma. Intubating over a bronchoscopy may assist in getting the cuff past the innominate artery. After an endotracheal tube is placed, a finger placed into the trachea can provide direct anterior pressure against the manubrium or a thumb in the sternal notch to control hemorrhage. This position should be maintained while transporting the patient to the operating room. If the tracheostomy tube is uncuffed, it should be removed immediately and replaced with a cuffed endotracheal tube, and the hemorrhage should be controlled with direct digital pressure.



Removing the tracheostomy tube and manually compressing the anterior trachea (B) is an important step in the management of hemorrhage from a tracheoinnominate artery fistula but should not be the first step in care. The tracheostomy cuff should be hyperinflated first, as it does not require removal of the tube, so it can be done more quickly while also preventing aspiration. Only if this step fails to control hemorrhage should the tracheostomy tube be removed for manual compression. Even then, endotracheal intubation should be attempted prior to digital compression, as it will prevent aspiration and be nearly impossible once a finger is in the trachea. Direct digital compression can be applied externally at the sternal notch and can be done immediately while the cuff is being hyperinflated.

Replacing the tracheostomy tube with a cuffed endotracheal tube (C) should be done to control the airway and prevent aspiration if the tracheostomy tube must be removed if hyperinflation is not successful or if the current tracheostomy tube is uncuffed.

Suctioning the tracheostomy (D) has no role in the management of massive hemorrhage from a tracheostomy, which can be life-threatening and requires immediate steps to control bleeding.

One Step Further
Question:
How much air should be used to hyperinflate the tracheostomy cuff?

Reveal Answer:
Up to 50 mL of air, but bleeding can be controlled with 10–35 mL depending on the size of the cuff.

الفخ: الخيار B (Remove the tracheostomy tube and manually compress the anterior trachea) غير صحيح لأنه لا يتناول الحالة بطريقة مناسبة أو قد يسبب ضرراً. الخيار C (Replace the tracheostomy tube with a cuffed endotracheal tube) غير صحيح لأنه لا يتناول الحالة بطريقة مناسبة أو قد يسبب ضرراً. الخيار D (Suction the tracheostomy) غير صحيح لأنه لا يتناول الحالة بطريقة مناسبة أو قد يسبب ضرراً.

question: A 43-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with acute-onset headache and right eye pain. On examination, you notice she has a cloudy cornea with a fixed midposition pupil. She is stating that, in addition to pain, she is also starting to see halos form around lights. Which of the following mechanisms is the main cause of this condition?

options.text: A sudden increase in blood pressure
Accumulation of fluid in the retrobulbar space

englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with acute angle-closure glaucoma, a vision-threatening emergency. The main cause of acute angle-closure glaucoma is obstruction of aqueous humor outflow, usually by the lens or the iris obstructing the trabecular meshwork, which prevents the flow of aqueous humor from the posterior chamber to the anterior chamber. Patients usually present with eye pain, a fixed midposition pupil, conjunctival injection, a hazy-appearing cornea, and elevated intraocular pressures. An acute attack is usually precipitated by pupillary dilation, which increases the contact between the iris and the lens. As the flow of aqueous humor is blocked, increased pressure from the posterior chamber will cause the iris to bow forward, which can worsen the obstruction, leading to further increases in pressure. This increase in pressure will eventually cause corneal edema, which often leads to a hazy appearance on physical exam and can sometimes cause visual disturbances in patients. Initial management of acute angle-closure glaucoma is aimed at rapidly decreasing intraocular pressure by blocking the production of aqueous humor (topical beta-blocker, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors), facilitating drainage of aqueous humor (topical alpha agonist), and reducing the volume of vitreous humor (mannitol).



A sudden increase in blood pressure (A) is the most common cause of subconjunctival hemorrhages, which can also be caused by sneezing, vomiting, or laughing. However, it is not a common cause of acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Accumulation of fluid in the retrobulbar space (B) can cause eye pain as well as increased intraocular pressures, leading to vision loss, but is usually precipitated by trauma. Patients usually also have proptosis on exam.

Tissue damage to the lens (D) is the main mechanism for developing cataracts, usually due to chronic ultraviolet exposure or systemic diseases such as diabetes.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the normal range of intraocular pressures?

Reveal Answer:
10–20 mm Hg.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma

Sx: acute unilateral pain and vision loss, headache, vomiting, seeing halos around lights
Clinical: can occur in the setting of significant hyphema
PE: cloudy cornea and fixed mid-dilated pupil
Dx: increased IOP on tonometry

question: A previously healthy 14-year-old boy presents to the ED with a 5-day history of sore throat, fever, and increasing right-sided neck pain with swelling. He reports difficulty swallowing. Physical examination reveals T of 39.2°C (102.6°F), tachycardia, right-sided tonsillar swelling without exudates, tender right cervical lymphadenopathy, and a firm, tender swelling along the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. A contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrates thrombosis of the right internal jugular vein with surrounding inflammatory changes. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and obtain blood cultures
Obtain a throat culture and start empiric amoxicillin
Start outpatient oral antibiotics and discharge home with close follow-up

correctAnswer: Administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and obtain blood cultures
englishExplanation:
Lemierre syndrome is a rare but life-threatening septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein, usually caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum, an anaerobic gram-negative bacterium. It typically follows an oropharyngeal infection, such as pharyngitis or peritonsillar abscess, and most commonly affects adolescents and young adults. The hallmark of the condition is an internal jugular vein thrombus with associated systemic sepsis and potential septic emboli, often affecting the lungs.

Diagnosis is based on clinical suspicion in a patient with recent pharyngitis, persistent fever despite antibiotics, neck pain or swelling, and radiographic evidence of internal jugular vein thrombosis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck is the imaging modality of choice to confirm the diagnosis. Early initiation of broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering anaerobic organisms, including beta-lactam and beta-lactamase inhibitors (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam) or carbapenems, is crucial. Blood cultures should be obtained to guide antibiotic therapy. In severe cases, anticoagulation or surgical intervention may be considered, though these remain controversial.

Complications of Lemierre syndrome include septic emboli, most commonly to the lungs, leading to cavitary pneumonia or empyema. Other potential complications include septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, and, in rare cases, multiorgan failure. Early recognition and aggressive treatment are critical to improving outcomes, making immediate IV antibiotic therapy the best next step in care.



While corticosteroids (B) may reduce airway swelling in some infectious causes of pharyngitis or epiglottitis, they are not the primary treatment for Lemierre syndrome. This condition is driven by septic thrombophlebitis, requiring antimicrobial therapy. Steroids alone would not address the underlying infection and could potentially worsen outcomes if they suppress the immune response.

Obtaining a throat culture and starting empiric amoxicillin (C) would be best for streptococcal pharyngitis, a common cause of sore throat in adolescents. The presence of neck swelling, prolonged fever, and internal jugular vein thrombosis suggests Lemierre syndrome in this patient. Amoxicillin would not provide adequate coverage for Fusobacterium necrophorum and other anaerobic bacteria responsible for the condition, leading to worsening infection and potential complications.

While peritonsillar or retropharyngeal abscesses can present similarly to Lemierre syndrome, the lack of a discrete abscess on imaging and the presence of internal jugular vein thrombosis make incision and drainage (D) an inappropriate treatment choice. Incision and drainage may be necessary if an abscess is present but is not the primary treatment for Lemierre syndrome, which requires systemic IV antibiotic therapy.

Given the severity of Lemierre syndrome, outpatient oral antibiotics (E) are insufficient. The condition carries a high risk of systemic sepsis and complications, necessitating IV antibiotic therapy and hospital admission for close monitoring. Delayed treatment can result in life-threatening complications such as septic emboli to the lungs or other organs.

Reveal Answer:

Dx: CT of the neck, blood culture

Complications: persistent bacteremia, septic pulmonary emboli

question: A 4-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with unequal pupils. There is no history of trauma, eye redness, eye pain, headaches, vision changes, or photophobia. The patient is well-appearing without ptosis and has normal extraocular movements, but his right pupil is about 2 mm larger than the left pupil. In bright and dim light the difference in pupil size is the same. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Patients with unequal pupils must be examined in bright and dim light to determine which pupil is abnormal. An abnormally miotic (small) pupil will have a greater difference in size compared with the normal pupil when examined in dim light because the small pupil is unable to dilate appropriately. An abnormally mydriatic (large) pupil will have a greater difference when examined in bright light because the large pupil is unable to constrict appropriately. Pupils that are equally different in bright and dim light are the result of physiologic anisocoria. Physiologic anisocoria is a congenital difference in the size of pupils that has not always been noticed previously. Old photographs can be useful to verify chronicity.



An Adie pupil and cranial nerve III palsy result in an abnormally mydriatic pupil. An Adie pupil (A) is caused by parasympathetic denervation of the pupillary sphincter muscle. It is usually associated with trauma or viral illness and deep tendon hyporeflexia on exam. Cranial nerve III palsy (B) generally presents with double vision, ptosis, and weakness in adduction, elevation, and depression with the affected eye resting downward and outward. It is frequently partial and, depending on the cause of the palsy, can be painful (e.g., an adult with a subarachnoid hemorrhage or aneurysm) or painless (e.g., midbrain lesion).

Horner syndrome (D) results in an abnormally miotic pupil. Congenital Horner syndrome should be suspected in children with anisocoria and heterochromia (asymmetrically colored pupils). It is often associated with diplopia, vertigo, ataxia, weakness, and, in children, impaired facial flushing.

question: A 9-year-old boy without significant medical history presents to the ED with his parents for evaluation of chest pain. He has been reporting constant left-sided chest pain for 1 week that worsens in the afternoons. On exam, his pain is reproduced when his hands are placed behind his head while extending his neck and placing posterior traction on his outward elbows. Which additional piece of history or physical exam finding is most consistent with this patient's most likely diagnosis?

options.text: An ability to pull the ribs forward intermittently
Frequently wears his backpack on one shoulder

correctAnswer: Frequently wears his backpack on one shoulder
englishExplanation:
This patient's symptoms are most consistent with costochondritis, a poorly studied costosternal pain syndrome that is characterized by a specific constellation of symptoms and physical exam findings. It is the most common cause of pediatric chest pain. Diagnosis is reliant on a history not consistent with other causes of chest pain and a physical exam as noted below. In school-aged children and adults, wearing heavy bags on only one shoulder may precipitate this condition. Other common causes of costochondritis include recent viral illness and cough. Patients commonly present with multiple tender costosternal junctions. The physical exam maneuver described above is known as the crowing rooster maneuver. It has been argued to indicate this diagnosis over other causes of chest pain. The patient's hands are placed behind their head with their neck in extension. Their pain is reproduced with posterior traction of both of their abducted elbows. Treatment involves eliminating exacerbating factors, using nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, and continuing normal activity. The course of costochondritis can last ≥ 6 months.



An ability to pull the ribs forward (A) refers to slipping rib syndrome, which involves the eighth through tenth ribs and is due to weakening of the fibrous tissue. The ribs rub together, leading to pain. Patients often describe a popping or clicking sensation on exam, which is not evident in this patient.

Costochondritis is not associated with major trauma (C) or specific sports, like baseball (D).

One Step Further

What ribs have been found to be involved more often in costochondritis—the upper or the lower ribs?

Reveal Answer:
The upper ribs.

Rule out life-threatening pathology
Tx: ice or heat, pain control, exercise and PT

question:
A 65-year-old male presents to the emergency department with severe right eye pain and proptosis following blunt
trauma to the face. On examination, you note a tense, swollen eyelid with limited eye movement and decreased visual acuity. The intraocular pressure is 51 mm Hg.
Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Perform immediate lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis
Order an urgent CT scan of the orbits
Apply ice packs to reduce swelling

correctAnswer: Perform immediate lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis
englishExplanation:
Perform immediate lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis
Explanation
The patient's symptoms (severe eye pain, proptosis, tense eyelid, limited eye movement, and decreased visual acuity)
strongly suggest an orbital compartment syndrome. When this syndrome is suspected, this procedure should be performed immediately in the emergency department without waiting for specialist consultation or imaging studies.
Signs of orbital compartment syndrome include:
Markedly elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) with or without a decrease in the visual acuity of the affected eye
Proptosis
Tight orbit
Relative afferent pupillary defect
Intraocular vascular changes
Decreased extraocular movements
How to perform lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis:
Step 1: Identify the lateral canthus. Cleanse the area with antiseptic and anaesthetise with 1 ml of 1% Lidocaine
(preferable with adrenaline)
Step 2: Crush the lateral canthus with the forceps for 1 to 2 minutes to reduce incisional bleeding. Then, cut through
the crushed tissue with tenotomy scissors to perform the canthotomy.
Step 3: Perform the inferior cantholysis
Step 4: Perform superior cantholysis if there is no improvement after canthotomy and inferior cantholysis

A 28-year-old snowboarder presents to the Emergency Department complaining of severe eye pain, tearing, and
photophobia after spending the day on the ski slopes without protective eyewear. IOP is 18mm Hg bilaterally.
Extraocular movements are unrestricted with no diplopia. There is no discharge from the eye.

englishExplanation:

Explanation

can also develop after welding.
Photokeratitis presents with symptoms of eye pain, tearing, photophobia, and a gritty sensation in the eyes. It typically develops 6-12 hours after UV exposure.

squash game. On examination, you note a collection of blood in the anterior chamber of the eye. Seidels test is negative. IOP is 19mmHg.

englishExplanation:
Topical cycloplegics and steroids
Explanation
In cases of traumatic hyphema, the initial management focuses on reducing pain, preventing further bleeding, and
controlling intraocular pressure. Topical cycloplegics help relieve pain and prevent pupillary movement, which can
exacerbate bleeding. Topical corticosteroids (systemic for severe cases) may reduce associated inflammation.
A majority of hyphemas will resolve with medical management alone. Approximately 5 percent of patients with traumatic hyphema require surgery.

question:
A 45-year-old patient presents to the Emergency Department with a 3 cm laceration on the forehead, just above the
medial aspect of the eyebrow. You decide to perform a supratrochlear nerve block for anaesthesia.
Which of the following statements is correct regarding the technique for this procedure?

options.text: The needle should be inserted at a 90-degree angle to the skin surface
The injection site is the superomedial border of the orbit
A volume of 10 ml of local anaesthetic is typically required
The supratrochlear artery should be visible or palpable as a landmark
The anaesthetic is injected in a fan-like distribution laterally

correctAnswer: The injection site is the superomedial border of the orbit
englishExplanation:
The injection site is the superomedial border of the orbit
Explanation
The injection site is the superomedial border of the orbit—this is the most accurate anatomical landmark for this
nerve block. It can also be given in conjunction with a supraorbital block to provide complete anaesthesia to the forehead (often with a single injection). 1-2 mls is usually sufficient.

question:
A 35-year-old male is brought to the emergency department following a high-speed motor vehicle collision. On examination, the patient has significant facial swelling, a flattened midface, and malocclusion. There is also evidence
of CSF rhinorrhoea.
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Le Fort III fracture
Explanation
This type of fracture, also known as craniofacial disjunction, involves the separation of the facial bones from the cranial base.
It is characterised by a flattened midface and significant facial swelling and often presents with CSF rhinorrhoea due
to the involvement of the cribriform plate. The presence of malocclusion further supports this diagnosis, as it indicates a disruption of the normal dental alignment.

question:
A 28-year-old patient presents to the Emergency Department with a history of ear pain and discharge for the past
24 hours following a swimming session. On examination, you notice a small perforation in the tympanic
membrane.
Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment for this patient?
englishExplanation:
Topical ciprofloxacin drops
Explanation

For a ruptured tympanic membrane (TM) with suspected bacterial infection, topical fluoroquinolone drops (such as
ciprofloxacin) are the first-line treatment. They provide high local antibiotic concentrations with minimal systemic
absorption and are effective against common pathogens causing otitis externa and media.
Unlike neomycin/gentamicin-containing drops, they are not ototoxic.

question:
A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a sudden onset of unilateral hearing loss in his
right ear that started 12 hours ago. He denies any pain, vertigo, or tinnitus. On examination, his right external auditory canal and tympanic membrane appear normal.
Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: MRI of the internal auditory canal

englishExplanation:
Oral corticosteroids
Explanation
This patient's presentation is consistent with Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL), defined as a rapid onset
of hearing loss of at least 30 dB in three contiguous frequencies occurring over 72 hours or less. The initial management for SSNHL is prompt administration of oral corticosteroids, ideally within 14 days of symptom onset.

However, there is little evidence for any benefit of oral or intratympanic steroid treatment, and patients should be referred to ENT for audiometry.

question:
A 45-year-old male presents to the Emergency Department with a swollen and painful left ear following a rugby
match. On examination, you notice a fluctuant swelling on the anterior surface of the pinna.
What is the most likely consequence if this condition is left untreated?
englishExplanation:
Avascular necrosis of cartilage
Explanation
Untreated pinna haematoma can lead to separation of the perichondrium from the underlying cartilage. This separation disrupts the blood supply to the cartilage, resulting in avascular necrosis. If left untreated, the cartilage may die
and become necrotic, leading to a permanent deformity of the ear known as "cauliflower ear."

question:

loss in her left ear. She reports feeling unsteady and has difficulty walking.

question:
A 23-year-old hockey player presents with pain and 
swelling around his jaw on the left side. This was preceded by 3 days of fever, malaise, and body aches. Several of his teammates have similar symptoms. What 
complications are associated with this illness?
englishExplanation:
13.  The answer is A. (Chapter 243) This patient presents 
with a classic presentation for mumps, or viral parotitis. 
The course typically progresses from a 3- to 5-day viral 
prodrome, followed by unilateral and then bilateral swelling of the parotid gland. It can cause outbreaks given it is 
transmitted by airborne droplets. Parotitis is most commonly caused by the paramyxovirus, and less commonly 
by influenza, parainfluenza, coxsackie, echovirus, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, or human immunodeficiency virus. Twenty to 30% of men will also suffer from 
associated orchitis. Other complications include mastitis, 
pancreatitis, aseptic meningitis, sensorineural hearing 
loss, myocarditis, polyarthritis, hemolytic anemia, and 
thrombocytopenia. It is not known to cause renal failure. 
Sialolithiasis and salivary duct stricture can result in bacterial parotitis, which has a more acute-onset and associated red, tender skin overlying the gland.

The patient is seated; the provider places thumbs

mandible, with a subsequent “wrist flip” motion, which

also attempts to push the condyle downward and backward. The gag reflex method entails simply inducing the 
gag response in the patient with a tongue blade or other

question:
A 64-year-old man presents with a nosebleed that he 
has been unable to control at home with direct pressure. Which of the following would be an acceptable 
FIRST STEP in controlling the bleeding?

options.text: Apply silver nitrate chemical cauterization to the
Clear the nose, apply oxymetazoline, and hold
Clear the nose, then use electrical cautery applied
Pack the nose with a commercially available balloon or nasal tampon/sponge

correctAnswer: Clear the nose, apply oxymetazoline, and hold
englishExplanation:
17.  The answer is B. (Chapter 244) When a patient presents with epistaxis, the first step in controlling the bleeding 
is to clear the nose and apply a vasoconstrictor, like oxymetazoline or phenylephrine topically, then hold steady 
direct pressure on the nose for 10 to 15 minutes. If this has 
failed, additional interventions may be attempted, such as 
chemical cautery with silver nitrate. Silver nitrate cautery 
must be performed in a dry field and to only one side of 
the septum to avoid perforation. If the above methods have 
failed, a trial of application of thrombogenic foam or gel 
should be attempted. If all of this has failed, nasal packing 
with a commercially available balloon, nasal tampon or 
sponge or layered ribbon gauze is a viable option. Electrical cautery is reserved for otolaryngology and should not 
be performed in the emergency department due to risk of 
perforation of the septum.

question:
Which of the following statements about nasal septal 
hematoma is MOST ACCURATE?

options.text: After incision and drainage, nasal packing should
Incision and drainage should be performed
Incision and drainage will help avoid ischemic
Infection of nasal septal hematoma is self-limited

correctAnswer: Incision and drainage will help avoid ischemic
englishExplanation:
20.  The answer is C. (Chapter 244) Nasal septal hematoma is a complication of nasal fractures. The vascular 
supply of the septal cartilage runs through the perichondrium, so when a hematoma lifts this off of the cartilage, 
the blood flow is obstructed, resulting in ischemic necrosis. As such, an urgent incision and drainage is indicated, 
and this should be performed in the emergency department at the time of injury. A week later is too long. Left 
untreated, the patient runs the risk of developing to ischemic necrosis and resultant saddle deformity. An infected 
septal hematoma can spread to local structures resulting 
in osteomyelitis, meningitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, 
or meningeal abscess. After careful incision and drainage 
with sterile technique, the bilateral nares should be packed 
to avoid reaccumulation of fluid.

correct placement of the anesthetic medication?
englishExplanation:
23.  The answer is C. (Chapter 245) To perform a successful inferior alveolar nerve block, have the patient open 
his/her mouth with the provider retracting the check away 
from the patient’s dentition to relax the musculature. Palpation of the coronoid notch can aid in the needle direction. The physician should direct the needle from the

a sufficient location. If the injection is given too low, the 
sphenomandibular ligament will impede delivery of the 
anesthetic to the inferior alveolar nerve.

minimum of four square knots should be placed to allow

question:
What percentage of posttonsillectomy bleeding 
requires surgical intervention?
englishExplanation:
30.  The answer is D.  (Chapter 246) Posttonsillectomy 
bleeding rates range from <1% to 15%. Half of these will 
require surgical intervention, so it is important to involve 
the otolaryngologist as soon as possible. Bleeding is most 
common in adults aged 21 to 30 and more than 70 and can 
occur many days after the procedure. In fact, the most serious hemorrhage occurs 5 to 10 days post operation. This 
bleeding can result in airway obstruction, hemorrhagic 
shock, and death, so prompt treatment is essential. While 
awaiting otolaryngologist arrival, the emergency physician can control hemorrhage with direct pressure using a 
tonsillar pack or 4 × 4 gauze on a long clamp, moistened 
with thrombin or lidocaine with epinephrine. Cauterization with silver nitrate can also be performed if the site 
of bleeding can be identified, after appropriate anesthesia. 
If using a pack, be sure to secure the pack with a suture 
taped to the patient’s cheek to prevent aspiration. Nebulized epinephrine or tranexamic acid is another option for 
controlling bleeding.

question:
A 27-year-old male presents with a rash (Fig. 9-2). The patient states that his wife first 
noticed a single spot on his back approximately 10 days ago. He denies fever or pain and 
complains only of mild pruritus. Over the last few days, many new “spots” have cropped up on 
his back and trunk. On examination, you note that the lesions have a fine scale around the 
border and seem to be arranged along the skin lines of the back. Which of the following is the 
most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient has pityriasis rosea, which is a common, self-limited rash that is thought 
to be of viral etiology. It most commonly occurs between the ages of 10 and 35 with a mean age 
of 23. Approximately 20% to 50% of patients present with a “herald patch,” a single, 2- to 10-cm 
salmonpink plaque with a fine silvery scale that rings the border of the lesion. Many patients 
believe they have ringworm, and the lesion may commonly be mistaken for ringworm before 
the development of additional lesions (KOH testing can rule this out). Approximately 1 to 2 

weeks after the herald patch, multiple additional 1- to 2-cm round and oval lesions develop on 
the trunk. The longitudinal axis of the oval lesions runs along the skin lines of the back and the 
overall pattern may resemble the branches of a pine tree. For this reason, pityriasis is often said 
to have a “Christmas tree” distribution. No treatment is necessary and the lesions resolve within 
2 to 3 months, although ultraviolet B (UVB) phototherapy will hasten resolution and decrease 
pruritus.

question:
A 34-year-old female presents with an infection. You decide to prescribe penicillin. She 
states that she is allergic to penicillin but cannot recall the reaction and has never been skin 

tested. You consider switching to a cephalosporin. Which of the following is the best estimate 
for cross-reactivity in this patient?
englishExplanation:
Patients with reported penicillin allergies rarely have true immune-mediated allergic 
reactions. Most simply have one of a variety of adverse medication effects. The historically 
quoted cross-reactivity rate between cephalosporins and penicillins of 10% is likely flawed. Early 
studies demonstrating this 10% rate occurred at a time when penicillin impurities were present 
during cephalosporin production in laboratories. Furthermore, most second-, third-, and 
fourth-generation cephalosporins have a penicillin cross-reactivity rate no greater than other 
antibiotics. Current estimates of cross-reactivity in patients with reported penicillin allergies are 
<1%, and some experts argue that it is far less than 1%. Patients with confirmed true allergic 
reactions to penicillin still have a <5% cross-reactivity rate. Patients who report a 
non-anaphylactic allergy to penicillin can safely receive a cephalosporin if watched briefly in the 
ED for adverse events.

question:
A 36-year-old man presented to the outpatient clinic with a six-week 
history of right-knee pain and swelling. He played football regularly, but 
could not recall sustaining an injury. The knee was constantly painful 
and occasionally felt like it was going to ‘give way’, although it had never 
actually done so. He had a seven-year history of plaque psoriasis.
On examination, there was a moderate warm effusion of the right knee, 
with flexion limited to 0–70°. McMurray’s test was negative.
What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Colourflow ultrasound scan of the knee
Contrast MR scan of the knee

englishExplanation:
7. B.  Contrast MR scan of the knee
The key differential diagnoses are psoriatic arthritis (PsA) and mechanical knee pain. Synovial 
fluid analysis may suggest inflammatory disease such as PsA, but is not specific. The history of 
problems is likely to be too short for x-rays to show changes of PsA and will not be helpful with 
mechanical knee pain. Isotope bone scans may show inflammatory changes, but these would not 
be specific, and some inflammatory change may be seen after injuries. Ultrasound scans may show 
some changes of PsA, such as synovitis, enthesitis, and tenosynovitis, but will miss other changes 
of PsA such as bone marrow oedema, and will not help with mechanical knee pain. Contrast 
(gadolinium)-enhanced MR scans will differentiate between PsA and mechanical knee pain, readily 
showing the pathology in either condition. This technique is a significant advance in the diagnosis 
of a variety of inflammatory joint diseases, including PsA and other sero-negative arthritides, as 
well as rheumatoid arthritis.
