question:
A 28-year-old woman from India presented to the dermatology 
department with a rash consisting of several reddish macules on her 
face, trunk, and limbs. Some were hypopigmented. Over the previous 
six months, she had become aware of reduced sensation in both hands 
and her right foot, and had a trophic ulcer on her right foot. She was 
noted to have thickened greater auricular and ulnar nerves, reduced 
sensation to light touch in a glove and stocking distribution beyond the 
palmar crease on her right hand and fingertips on the left, and the right 
forefoot. Some of the macules were noted to be anaesthetic.
What can be said of the likely diagnosis in this lady?

options.text: It is likely that she caught this from a nine-banded armadillo
The neuropathy would be expected to recover with antibiotic therapy
Steroids can be a useful adjunct to treatment

englishExplanation:
17. E.  Steroids can be a useful adjunct to treatment
This patient has leprosy, a chronic granulomatous condition of skin and nerves, caused by infection 
with mycobacterium leprae.
There are few conditions which give rise to enlarged peripheral nerves, and the combination of this 
together with evidence of nerve damage, and hypopigmented anaesthetic macules makes leprosy 
the most likely diagnosis in this setting. The presence of mycobacteria in slit-skin smears together 
with these features is diagnostic, though not all cases have easily visible mycobacteria, especially 
patients with paucibacillary disease.
Mycobateria leprae grows very slowly. It has a doubling time of 12 days. It has fastidious growth 
requirements, and has never been cultured in vitro. Laboratory culture is possible in vivo in the footpad of laboratory mice, and can infect nine-banded armadillos in the wild, though humans are the 
main reservoir of infection.
Leprosy is a disease of humans. It is not very contagious, and is probably spread by nasal secretions 
of patients who have multibacillary disease. Incidence of leprosy in household contacts of cases of 
multibacillary disease is up to ten times that of the local population.
The clinical manifestations of leprosy are on a spectrum ranging from multibacillary to paucibacillary disease, depending on the cell mediated immune response generated within the patient. A strong cell-mediated response is associated with tuberculoid leprosy, or paucibacillary 
disease. There is asymmetric involvement of peripheral nerves (only one nerve is usually affected) and a few macules, which are anaesthetic. Biopsy demonstrates epithelioid granulomas 
with neural involvement, and absent to scanty bacteria seen on Ziehl–Nielsen or Wade–Fite 
staining.
At the other end of the spectrum, lepromatous or multibacillary disease is associated with a poor 
cell-mediated response, large numbers of symmetrically distributed macules, symmetric nerve infiltration, and widespread infiltration of the skin. Macules may not be anaesthetic, but the patient is 
likely to have symmetric predominantly sensory loss on testing. Infiltration of the skin on the face 
and loss of eyebrows may give the characteristic leonine facies.
Patients with lepromatous disease may also have complications in other organs including the eyes, 
testes, lymph nodes, kidneys, and bones. Management of leprosy not only involves treating the 
infection, which is curable with multi-drug therapy, but also management of its complications and 
sequelae, and support to reduce stigma.
Treatment is according to WHO multi-drug-based therapy, based on whether the patient has multibacillary or paucibacillary disease. Treatment for paucibacillary disease consists of dapsone 100 mg 
daily combined with rifampicin 600 mg monthly for six months. Multibacillary disease is treated for 
1–2 years with a combination of daily dapsone 100 mg and clofazimine 50 mg daily, and a 300 mg 
dose once per month, together with monthly rifampicin 600 mg.
Patients can shift in their immunological status, before during and after treatment. This can give rise 
to acute symptoms, or lepra reactions. If a patient is ‘upgrading’ towards the tuberculoid end of the 
spectrum this is known as a type 1 reaction. This can result in sudden inflammatory infiltration of 
skin and or nerves, leading to acute damage. Treatment of this reaction involves the use of steroids 
to reduce inflammation and aim to preserve nerve function, alongside the antimicrobial management of the leprosy. Lepra reactions resulting from a shift towards the lepromatous end of the 
spectrum are known as type 2 reactions, which include erythema nodosum leprosum. These can 
also be treated with steroids. Sometimes, additional anti-inflammatory agents are needed, including 
thalidomide. As in paucibacillary disease, multi-drug treatment for leprosy is continued alongside 
treatment for the reaction.

5. D.  Tumour Breslow thickness
The most accessible prognosticator is the Breslow thickness. This is a measure of invasion of the 
melanoma. If the melanoma is limited to within the epidermis without breaching the basement 
membrane zone, then the tumour is classified as in situ, with a Breslow thickness of zero and there 
is an excellent prognosis. Once invasive, prognosis is gauged at 1 mm steps of invasion up to 4 
mm. With no invasion, as long as the histology has been correctly reported, the prognosis is 100% 
five-year survival. This drops to >90% survival at 1 mm, around 80% survival at 2 mm and 70–80% 
survival with 3 mm thickness depending on associated ulceration. An ulcerated melanoma with >4 
mm thickness results in a five-year survival prognosis for the patient of about 50%. Tumour ulceration is taken as a further element in the prognosis, but is secondary to the thickness of the tumour. 
Diameter of a pigmented lesion is used in both the ABCDE and Glasgow seven-point scale systems 
for identifying a pigmented lesion of greater risk of being a melanoma, but it has no bearing on 
prognostication of a melanoma once it is diagnosed. No form of imaging or node sampling would 
be appropriate at this point, until the Breslow thickness is established. The presence of widespread 
adenopathy is likely to represent dermatopathic adenopathy related to the exacerbation of eczema.

question:
A patient in the ICU has a bloodstream infection. The team is considering starting an echinocandin (e.g., caspofungin). While this drug class has excellent
Candida and Aspergillus activity, it has no clinically useful activity against which
two major fungal pathogens?

options.text: Cryptococcus neoformans and the Zygomycetes (e.g., Mucor).

correctAnswer: Cryptococcus neoformans and the Zygomycetes (e.g., Mucor).
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Resistance:

Echinocandins (caspofungin, anidulafungin, micafungin) act by non-competitively
inhibiting the synthesis of (1,3)-beta-D-glucan, a major structural component of the
fungal cell wall. This leads to osmotic instability and cell lysis. Their spectrum is
strictly defined by the presence of this target. Cryptococcus neoformans is intrinsically resistant because its cell wall is composed primarily of alpha-glucan and chitin,
with very little beta-glucan, which is further shielded by its polysaccharide capsule.
Similarly, the Mucorales (Zygomycetes) lack (1,3)-beta-D-glucan, relying instead on
chitosan and chitin for structural integrity, rendering echinocandins ineffective.
Clinical Pearl
Intrinsic Resistance:
Echinocandins lack activity against Cryptococcus neoformans and Mucorales
(Zygomycetes) because these fungi possess minimal (1,3)-beta-D-glucan in their cell
walls, rendering the drug target absent.
Primary Indication:
This is their primary use in the ICU. They are first-line for most invasive Candida
infections, as they cover fluconazole-resistant C. glabrata and C. krusei.
CNS Penetration:
A major pharmacokinetic limitation is their large molecular size and high protein
binding (>99%), which prevents them from crossing the blood-brain barrier effectively. They are not suitable for fungal meningitis.
Renal Pharmacokinetics:
They are hepatically metabolised (caspofungin, micafungin) or undergo chemical
degradation (anidulafungin) and do not require dose adjustment in renal failure or
haemofiltration.
Candida parapsilosis Sensitivity:
Candida parapsilosis demonstrates intrinsically higher MICs to echinocandins due
to a naturally occurring amino acid change in the Fks1p subunit. While echinocandins are still often effective, fluconazole is preferred if susceptibility is confirmed.
Fungicidal vs Fungistatic:
Echinocandins are fungicidal against Candida species (cell wall disruption leads to
osmotic instability) but only fungistatic against Aspergillus species (active at hyphal
tips and branching points).
Safety Profile:
They have a favourable safety profile with few side effects compared to amphotericin or azoles because their target, (1,3)-beta-D-glucan synthase, is not present in
mammalian cells.
Pneumocystis Nuance:

Echinocandins have activity against the cyst form of Pneumocystis jirovecii (which
contains beta-glucan) but not the trophic form. They are not effective as monotherapy for PCP, but this activity distinguishes them from the total lack of effect on
Cryptococcus.

question:
A patient with Crohn's disease is being screened prior to starting therapy with the
TNF-alpha inhibitor infliximab. In addition to screening for latent TB, which viral serology is mandatory to check due to a high risk of fulminant reactivation?

options.text: Hepatitis B Surface Antigen (HBsAg) and Core Antibody (anti-HBc)

correctAnswer: Hepatitis B Surface Antigen (HBsAg) and Core Antibody (anti-HBc)
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology of Reactivation:
TNF-alpha promotes viral clearance and inhibits HBV replication in hepatocytes.
Inhibition of TNF-alpha disrupts this immune control, allowing rapid viral replication. This can lead to fulminant hepatitis, hepatic failure, and death, particularly in
patients with chronic infection (HBsAg positive) or resolved infection (HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive) where covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) persists in
the liver.
UK Guideline Requirements (BSG 2019):
The British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) guidelines on IBD mandate a full viral screening panel prior to commencing biologic therapy. This includes Hepatitis B
(HBsAg and anti-HBc), Hepatitis C (HCV Ab), HIV, and VZV (varicella zoster).
While HCV is screened, HBV is the specific agent associated with a high risk of fulminant reactivation requiring pre-emptive prophylaxis.
Management Strategy:
1. HBsAg Positive: High risk. Requires prophylactic nucleos(t)ide analogues (e.g.,
entecavir or tenofovir) starting 2-4 weeks before immunosuppression and continuing for 6-12 months after cessation.
2. HBsAg Negative / anti-HBc Positive: Moderate risk (occult carrier).
Requires monitoring of HBV DNA and ALT every 1-3 months, or prophylaxis if
high-risk factors are present (though prophylaxis is more strongly indicated with Bcell depleting agents like rituximab).
Clinical Pearl
Mandatory Screening Targets:
Before initiating TNF-alpha inhibitors, mandatory screening must exclude latent
Tuberculosis (CXR + IGRA) and Hepatitis B (HBsAg + anti-HBc). Missed screening
can lead to fatal reactivation syndromes.
Core Antibody Significance:

Screening must include both the surface antigen (for active infection) and the core
antibody (for past, resolved infection), as both groups are at risk of reactivation.
Prophylactic Antiviral Therapy:
HBsAg positive patients require prophylactic antiviral therapy (entecavir or tenofovir) commencing 2-4 weeks prior to biologic initiation and continuing for at least
6-12 months after discontinuation.
Risk with B-Cell Depletion:
The risk of HBV reactivation is even higher with B-cell depleting therapies like
rituximab.
Comprehensive Viral Screen:
BSG guidelines mandate screening for HBV, HCV, HIV, and VZV (chickenpox) prior
to biologic therapy. This identifies chronic infections and opportunities for vaccination (e.g., VZV) before immunosuppression.
Occult Hepatitis B:
Patients who are HBsAg negative but anti-HBc positive have 'resolved' or 'occult' infection. They retain viral cccDNA in hepatocytes and are at risk of reactivation (reverse seroconversion) during potent immunosuppression.
Pre-Therapy Vaccination:
Screening identifies seronegative patients who should be vaccinated against HBV
and VZV before starting therapy. Live vaccines (VZV) are contraindicated once immunosuppression begins.
Antiviral Selection:
Entecavir and tenofovir are the preferred prophylactic agents due to their high barrier to resistance; lamivudine is generally avoided due to high rates of drug resistance with long-term use.

question:
A 37-year-old man presents with myalgias and tea-colored urine after an intense
workout. His CK is 8,000 U/L. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous fluids to maintain a brisk urine output.
Administer diuretics to force a diuresis.
Admit for observation and electrolyte monitoring only.

correctAnswer: Administer intravenous fluids to maintain a brisk urine output.
englishExplanation:
Initial Management:
The primary goal in rhabdomyolysis is the prevention of Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)
caused by haem pigment nephropathy. The mainstay of treatment is aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation to maintain a high urine output (typically targeted at 13 mL/kg/hr or 200-300 mL/hr) until myoglobinuria resolves. This dilutes intratubular myoglobin and increases tubular flow, preventing cast formation.
Fluid Choice:
Balanced crystalloids (e.g., Hartmann's/Plasmalyte) or 0.9% sodium chloride are
appropriate. While 0.9% saline was traditionally preferred to avoid potassium load,
balanced crystalloids are increasingly used to prevent hyperchloraemic metabolic
acidosis, provided hyperkalaemia is not severe.
Adjunctive Therapies:
Sodium bicarbonate and mannitol are controversial. Meta-analyses have failed to
demonstrate a clear benefit of bicarbonate over saline alone for preventing AKI in
rhabdomyolysis. It is generally reserved for correcting severe metabolic acidosis or
managing hyperkalaemia. Diuretics (loop diuretics) should only be considered if the
patient remains oliguric despite adequate volume resuscitation and exclusion of
obstruction.
Pathophysiology of Injury:
Myoglobin induces renal injury via three primary mechanisms: renal vasoconstriction due to nitric oxide scavenging; intratubular obstruction from precipitation with
Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin), which is favoured by acidic urine pH; and direct tubular toxicity from oxidative injury caused by the haem moiety.
Clinical Pearl
Rhabdo = Fluids:
Aggressive volume expansion is the single most important intervention to prevent
pigment nephropathy. Delay in resuscitation significantly increases AKI risk.
Urine Output Targets:
Titrate IV fluids to achieve a urine output of 1-3 mL/kg/hr (or >200 mL/hr) until
CK levels decline and urine clears.
Electrolyte Disturbances:
Expect the 'dead cell' triad: Hyperkalaemia, Hyperphosphataemia, and
Hyperuricaemia. Hypocalcaemia occurs early (deposition in muscle);
Hypercalcaemia may occur late (recovery phase).

Hypocalcaemia Management:
Do not treat early hypocalcaemia unless the patient is symptomatic (tetany,
seizures) or has severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. Exogenous calcium can
increase muscle damage and precipitate calcium phosphate crystals.
Compartment Syndrome:
Always assess for compartment syndrome, especially in unconscious patients or
those with traumatic rhabdomyolysis. Pain out of proportion to injury or tense compartments requires urgent surgical consultation.
Urinary Alkalinisation:
Routine alkalinisation of urine with sodium bicarbonate is not supported by highquality evidence and is not recommended in UK guidelines unless treating severe
metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.1) or hyperkalaemia.
CK Kinetics:
Creatine Kinase (CK) typically rises within 12 hours of injury, peaks at 1-3 days, and
declines 3-5 days after cessation of muscle injury. A failure to decrease suggests ongoing muscle damage or compartment syndrome.
Myoglobin vs CK Clearance:
Myoglobin has a short half-life (2-3 hours) and clears rapidly, meaning urine colour
may normalise while CK (half-life ~36 hours) continues to rise. A falling CK indicates cessation of muscle injury, whereas persistent elevation suggests ongoing
myolysis.
Tamm-Horsfall Protein Interaction:
Myoglobin precipitates with Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin) in the distal
tubule to form obstructive casts. This reaction is pH-dependent and is enhanced in
acidic urine, providing the physiological rationale for alkalinisation despite the lack
of definitive clinical evidence.

question:
A patient is day 10 post-allogeneic stem cell transplant for leukemia. They develop a new fever, a non-pruritic maculopapular rash, and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Labs show rising inflammatory markers. What is this syndrome,
which can be difficult to distinguish from sepsis or acute GVHD, called?
englishExplanation:
Definition & Pathophysiology:
Engraftment Syndrome (ES) is a systemic inflammatory condition characterised by
non-infectious fever and capillary leak. It occurs during the phase of neutrophil recovery (typically days 7-21 post-transplant) when regenerating granulocytes release
pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha). This cytokine storm increases
endothelial permeability, leading to the hallmark non-cardiogenic pulmonary
oedema.
Diagnostic Criteria (Spitzer):
Diagnosis is clinical, often using the Spitzer Criteria. Major criteria include: 1) Noninfectious fever, 2) Skin rash (maculopapular, affecting >25% BSA), and 3) Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Minor criteria include weight gain, hepatic dysfunction, or transient encephalopathy. Diagnosis requires all three major criteria, or
fever plus one major and one minor criterion.
Management:
It is a diagnosis of exclusion; sepsis must be ruled out. Once suspected, the mainstay of treatment is intravenous corticosteroids (e.g., Methylprednisolone 1
mg/kg/day), which typically yields a rapid resolution of symptoms within 24-48
hours.
Clinical Pearl
Diagnostic Timing:
The key diagnostic clue is the timing. The syndrome occurs concurrently with the
first signs of neutrophil engraftment (ANC > 0.5 x 10^9/L), typically 7-21 days posttransplant.
Diagnostic Approach:
It is critical to first rule out infection as the cause of the fever and systemic inflammation, as the presentation mimics sepsis.
Corticosteroid Therapy:
First-line treatment is IV corticosteroids (typically methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg).
Response is usually dramatic and rapid (within 24-48 hours), helping to distinguish
it retrospectively from sepsis or other causes.
Pathophysiological Mechanism:
The core pathophysiology is a capillary leak syndrome driven by cytokine release,
leading to weight gain, effusions, and pulmonary oedema.
Transplant Type Association:

While classically described in autologous transplants, Engraftment Syndrome is a
well-recognised complication of allogeneic HSCT, particularly with peripheral blood
stem cell sources.
Spitzer Diagnostic Criteria:
The classic triad for the Spitzer Diagnostic Criteria consists of Non-infectious Fever
+ Rash + Pulmonary Oedema occurring within 96 hours of engraftment.
Differential Diagnosis: VOD/SOS:
Distinguish from Veno-occlusive Disease (VOD/SOS) by the clinical features: VOD
presents with painful hepatomegaly, weight gain, and hyperbilirubinaemia, whereas
Engraftment Syndrome is dominated by fever, rash, and pulmonary symptoms.
G-CSF Association:
The use of Granulocyte-Colony Stimulating Factor (G-CSF) is a known risk factor
and may precipitate or worsen the syndrome; withholding G-CSF is a standard part
of initial management.
Differential Diagnosis: Acute GVHD:
Distinguishing Engraftment Syndrome from hyperacute Graft-versus-Host Disease
(GVHD) is challenging; however, GVHD typically presents with more prominent
gastrointestinal symptoms (diarrhoea) and liver dysfunction compared to the pulmonary dominance of Engraftment Syndrome.
Biomarkers:
C-reactive protein (CRP) is universally elevated in Engraftment Syndrome.
Procalcitonin may also be raised without infection, limiting its utility as a discriminator between this syndrome and sepsis.
Renal Impairment:
Renal dysfunction is a minor criterion in the Spitzer classification and results from
intravascular depletion and cytokine-mediated tubular injury.

question: A 72-year-old patient with Stage 3 Chronic Kidney Disease (eGFR 45 mL/min) is diagnosed with Candida esophagitis. The physician prescribes oral fluconazole. What adjustment to the standard dosing regimen is required?

options.text: The dose should be increased to overcome renal resistance.
The dose should be reduced (typically by 50%) after a standard loading dose.
The drug should be switched to IV administration.
The drug is contraindicated and an alternative agent must be chosen.

correctAnswer: The dose should be reduced (typically by 50%) after a standard loading dose.
englishExplanation:
**Pharmacokinetics:**
   - Fluconazole's clearance is highly dependent on renal function.
   - Unlike most other azoles, fluconazole is primarily excreted unchanged in the urine (>80%).
   - Therefore, its clearance is directly proportional to creatinine clearance.
  **Dosing in Renal Impairment:**
   - In patients with renal impairment (CrCl < 50 mL/min), the dose must be reduced to prevent accumulation.
   - UK guidelines (BNF, Renal Drug Handbook) recommend administering the standard loading dose on day 1, followed by a 50% reduction in the daily maintenance dose.
   - The loading dose is not reduced because the volume of distribution (Vd) remains unchanged in renal failure; only the maintenance dose is adjusted to match the reduced clearance.
   - Patients on regular haemodialysis should receive the full standard dose after each dialysis session.
  **Excellent Bioavailability:**
   - Oral and IV doses of fluconazole are equivalent (1:1).
  **A Potent CYP Inhibitor:**
   - Fluconazole is a strong inhibitor of CYP2C9 and CYP2C19, and a moderate inhibitor of CYP3A4.
   - This significantly increases levels of warfarin (INR monitoring required), phenytoin, and tacrolimus.
  **Intrinsic Resistance Profile:**
   - Candida krusei is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole.
   - Candida glabrata often demonstrates dose-dependent susceptibility (S-DD) or resistance; high-dose fluconazole or an echinocandin is preferred for these species.
  **QT Interval Prolongation:**
   - Like other azoles, fluconazole can prolong the QT interval.
   - Caution is required when co-prescribing with other QT-prolonging agents (e.g., macrolides, antipsychotics, amiodarone).
  **CNS Penetration:**
   - Fluconazole achieves excellent CSF penetration (approx.
   - 70-80% of plasma levels), making it the azole of choice for Cryptococcal meningitis and CNS Candida infections.
  **Mechanism of Action:**
   - Fluconazole inhibits the fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme 14-alpha-demethylase.
   - This prevents the conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol, an essential component of the fungal cell membrane.
  **Urinary Tract Candidiasis:**
   - Because fluconazole is excreted unchanged in the urine, it achieves high urinary concentrations.
   - This makes it the drug of choice for susceptible Candida cystitis, unlike echinocandins which have poor urinary penetration.
  **Echinocandin Comparison:**
   - Echinocandins (e.g., anidulafungin, micafungin) are not renally cleared and require no dose adjustment in renal failure.
   - They are preferred for critically ill patients with unknown species or renal instability until sensitivities are confirmed.
  **Hepatotoxicity Monitoring:**
   - Although less hepatotoxic than older azoles, fluconazole can cause reversible transaminitis.
   - Liver function tests should be monitored during prolonged therapy.

question: A patient with severe psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis is treated with ustekinumab. What is the specific molecular target of this monoclonal antibody?

options.text: It targets the p40 subunit, thereby blocking both Interleukin-12 and Interleukin-23.
It is an IL-1 receptor antagonist.

correctAnswer: It targets the p40 subunit, thereby blocking both Interleukin-12 and Interleukin-23.
englishExplanation:
**Mechanism of Action:**
   - Ustekinumab is a fully human IgG1κ monoclonal antibody that targets the p40 protein subunit shared by both interleukin-12 (IL-12) and interleukin-23 (IL-23).
   - IL-12 is a heterodimer of p35 and p40 subunits, while IL-23 is a heterodimer of p19 and p40 subunits.
   - By binding to the p40 subunit, ustekinumab prevents these cytokines from binding to the IL-12Rβ1 receptor on the surface of immune cells (T-cells and NK cells).
   - This blockade inhibits the downstream Th1 (driven by IL-12) and Th17 (driven by IL-23) inflammatory pathways.
  **Clinical Relevance:**
   - Inhibition of the IL-12/23 pathway is effective in immune-mediated diseases such as plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis.
   - It offers an alternative mechanism of action for patients who have failed TNF-alpha inhibitors.
  **IL-12/23 Blocker:**
   - Ustekinumab is defined by its dual blockade of IL-12 and IL-23 via the shared p40 subunit, distinguishing it from selective IL-23 inhibitors (e.g., guselkumab) which target the p19 subunit.
  **Uses:**
   - Licensed indications include moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis.
  **Infection Screening:**
   - Prior to initiation, patients must be screened for tuberculosis (latent TB), Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C, as biologic therapy can reactivate latent infections.
  **Vaccination Safety:**
   - Live vaccines (e.g., MMR, Yellow Fever, BCG) are contraindicated during treatment with ustekinumab.
   - Non-live vaccines (e.g., Influenza, Pneumococcal) are safe but may have reduced immunogenicity.
  **Nomenclature Decoding:**
   - The suffix '-kinumab' denotes an interleukin-targeting monoclonal antibody.
   - The pre fix 'uste-' is unique to the drug, and '-u-' indicates a fully human source (under older nomenclature conventions).
  **Dosing Considerations:**
   - For psoriasis, dosing is often weight-stratified (e.g., 45 mg for ≤100 kg, 90 mg for >100 kg).
   - In Crohn's/UC, an initial IV loading dose is typically followed by subcutaneous maintenance.
  **Pharmacokinetics:**
   - Ustekinumab has a long half-life ranging from 15 to 45 days.
   - This allows for infre quent maintenance dosing intervals, typically every 12 weeks for psoriasis and every 8-12 weeks for Crohn's disease.
  **Perioperative Management:**
   - Due to infection risk, elective surgery is generally scheduled at the end of a dosing interval (when drug levels are lowest).
   - Treatment is restarted post-operatively only after wound healing is satisfactory and there is no evidence of infection.
  **Rare Neurological Adverse Effects:**
   - Although rare, cases of Reversible Posterior Leukoencephalopathy Syndrome (RPLS) have been reported with ustekinumab.
   - Clinicians should be vigilant for symptoms such as headache, seizures, confusion, and visual disturbances.
  **Selective IL-23 Inhibitors:**
   - Newer agents like guselkumab and risankizumab target the p19 subunit specifically.
   - This selectively inhibits IL-23 without affecting the IL-12 pathway, theoretically preserving Th1-mediated immunity against intracellular pathogens and tumours.

question: A woman at 34 weeks gestation presents with intense itching, particularly on her palms and soles, which is worse at night. There is no visible rash. Liver function tests show a significantly elevated total bile acid level. Which of the following statements about Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy (ICP) is TRUE?

options.text: The pruritus is typically associated with a polymorphic skin rash.
The condition is benign and poses no significant risk to the fetus.
Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) is the first-line medical treatment and is considered safe in pregnancy.
The condition is chronic and usually persists for months after delivery.
Serum bile acid levels are a poor diagnostic marker for ICP.

correctAnswer: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) is the first-line medical treatment and is considered safe in pregnancy.
englishExplanation:
**Diagnosis and Presentation:**
   - Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy (ICP) typically presents in the third trimester with pruritus affecting the palms and soles, worse at night, without a primary rash (excoriations may be seen).
   - Diagnosis is confirmed by unexplained pruritus and elevated total bile acids (>19 µmol/L).
  **Management and UDCA:**
   - Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) is the standard first-line pharmacological treatment and is considered safe in pregnancy.
   - Mechanistically, UDCA is a hydrophilic bile acid that displaces toxic hydrophobic bile acids from the hepatocyte pool and stimulates biliary secretion via post-transcriptional upregulation of transporters.
   - While widely prescribed, RCOG guidelines highlight evidence from the PITCHES trial showing UDCA does not significantly improve itch or reduce adverse perinatal outcomes (stillbirth, preterm birth) compared to placebo.
   - It is still offered, but patients should be informed of the limited evidence for clinical benefit.
  **Risk Stratification:**
   - ICP is not benign (Option B is false).
   - It is associated with spontaneous preterm birth, meconium staining, and stillbirth.
   - The risk of stillbirth rises significantly when serum bile acids exceed 100 µmol/L (Option E is false).
   - Delivery timing is guided by these levels.
  **Course:**
   - The condition resolves rapidly after delivery, typically within 48 hours to a few weeks (Option D is false).
   - Persistent abnormalities suggest underlying chronic liver disease.
  **Itch Without Rash:**
   - This combination in the third trimester of pregnancy is ICP until proven otherwise.
  **Palms and Soles:**
   - The itching classically involves the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, although it can become generalized.
  **Bile Acids Drive Risk:**
   - Fetal risk correlates with maternal bile acid concentrations.
   - Peak bile acids >100 µmol/L are associated with a significant increase in stillbirth risk, guiding the decision for earlier delivery (often 35-36 weeks).
  **UDCA for Treatment:**
   - UDCA is the primary pharmacological agent used to lower bile acids and is safe in pregnancy.
   - However, RCOG guidelines note that it does not clinically improve pruritus or reduce stillbirth risk (PITCHES trial).
  **Plan for Delivery:**
   - Delivery timing is risk-stratified: consider planned birth at 35-36 weeks for severe ICP (bile acids >100 µmol/L) and 38-39 weeks for mild-moderate cases (<100 µmol/L).
  **Postpartum Resolution:**
   - Pruritus typically resolves within days of delivery.
   - Liver function tests should be re checked at least 4 weeks postpartum to ensure normalization; persistence suggests underlying hepatobiliary disease.
  **Vitamin K Supplementation:**
   - Routine Vitamin K is not recommended, but it should be offered to women with ICP who have prolonged prothrombin time or evidence of steatorrhea due to fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption.
  **Mechanism of Fetal Toxicity:**
   - The mechanism of stillbirth in ICP is thought to be sudden fetal arrhythmia or placental vasospasm caused by high levels of toxic bile acids crossing the placenta.
   - This explains why fetal monitoring (CTG) is often not predictive of sudden outcomes.
  **Differential Diagnosis:**
   - Key differentials include Polymorphic Eruption of Pregnancy (PEP, formerly PUPPP), which presents with a rash (striae-sparing), and Pemphigoid Gestationis (autoimmune blistering disease).
   - ICP is distinct due to the absence of a primary rash.

question: A 5-year-old male is brought to the emergency department for evaluation of a facial rash. The patient has no past medical history and is otherwise well. The physical exam is significant for the facial lesions shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Expl anation
A. Impetigo
Impetigo
This patient's exam, particularly the "honey-colored crust" is consistent with impetigo. Impetigo begins as a vesicle or a pustule on an erythematous base and then
coalesces and ruptures producing the stereotypical honey-colored crust.
It is most common in children 2-5 years old and is highly contagious. The most
common pathogen responsible for impetigo is S. aureus, accounting for over 2/3 of
cases. Group A beta-hemolytic Strep is the second most common etiology.
Treatment is with topical mupirocin unless it is diffuse or severe, in which case systemic antibiotics should be used.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430974/
B. Irritant cheilitis
Irritant cheilitis, often known as lip licker's cheilitis is an erythematous and scaling
rash of the lip. It does not spare the Vermillion border.
C. Perioral dermatitis
Perioral dermatitis is an inflammatory skin condition around the mouth and
presents as erythematous papules and pustules or scaly patches. The Vermillion
border is spared.
D. Seborrheic dermatitis
Lesions of seborrheic dermatitis occur in areas rich in sebaceous glands such as the
scalp and face. The rash presents as salmon-colored papules and/or plaques with a
fine scale and yellow crust.
In adults, if the face is involved, lesions typically present as blepharitis or are found
in the malar region, nasolabial/alar folds, center of the forehead, eyebrows, postauricular area, and external ear canal. Infants are more affected by seborrheic dermatitis than children with cradle cap, diaper region, and skin creases of the neck
and axillae.

question: A 6-year-old male with no past medical history presents with a painful raised scalp rash. This patient is presenting with a kerion due to a tinea capitis infection. This is due

This patient is presenting with a kerion due to a tinea capitis infection. This is due

This patient is presenting with a kerion due to a tinea capitis infection. Tinea capitis

question: A 16-year-old boy is brought in by his mother for a skin rash he has had for a week. He states it started as a round, itchy patch on his chest. It became scaly as he scratched it and began to clear, leaving only a raised, pink border where the original lesion began, as demonstrated in the attached image. He denies fever or cough. What is the most appropriate step in management?

Topical clotrimazole
Expl anation
A. Doxycycline
The history and rash pictured are most consistent with tinea corporis. Doxycycline
is commonly used to treat rashes due to rickettsial infection, such as Lyme disease.
B. Topical clotrimazole
The pruritic, centrally clearing spot with a residual, raised border is most consistent
with a tinea corporis, or ringworm infection. The treatment for tinea infection is
topical antifungals, usually topical azoles.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK544360/

Topical corticosteroids can temporarily relieve pruritis but may worsen fungal infections and should be avoided if tinea is suspected
D. Topical nystatin
Localized tinea corporis commonly responds to topical therapy. However, nystatin
topical is not effective for tinea corporis.

question: A 5-year-old female presents to the emergency department with a pruritic rash. Her next door neighbor reportedly has the same problem. Expl anation

Oral ivermectin, while not the appropriate first-line therapy, is not contraindicated

This patient is presenting with scabies, suggested by her linear excoriations and

Treatment Guidelines, 2021. MMVVR Recomm Rep. Published
2021 Jul 23. PMID: 34292926

Ivermectin 1% lotion is a treatment option for scabies and is not contraindicated in
children.
D. Topical permethrin
This patient is presenting with scabies, suggested by her linear excoriations and
close contact with similar symptoms. Given its efficacy and safety, topical permethrin is the preferred therapy for children and is not contraindicated.

Isolation from unaffected individuals; spray home with pediculicide

clothing

bedding and clothing

Acantholysis is often called 'Nikolsky's sign', and occurs when superficial layers of
the epidermis separate from the deep layers when rubbed laterally by a finger or
cotton swab. This finding is unique to pemphigus vulgaris, and is not found in other
blistering diseases, such as erythema multiforme, bullous impetigo, drug eruptions,
contact dermatitis, dermatitis herpetiformis, or bullous pemphigoid.

As explained in the correct answer, there are a large variety of diseases that may
manifest with the presence of bullae.

Of the blistering diseases mentioned, autoimmune disease is more commonly associated with bullous pemphigoid and dermatitis herpetiformis.
D. Presence of lesions on oral mucosa
This is often the first place that bullae are seen in cases of pemphigus vulgaris, but is
not a distinguishing feature.

question: A 33-year-old female presents with fever, diffuse rash, and muscle aches. The patient has a history of epilepsy and was recently started on a new anti-epileptic medication. englishExplanation:
Positive nikolsky sign
Expl anation
A. Erythema migrans
Erythema migrans is characteristically seen in Lyme disease.
B. Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum (EN) is a benign condition of palpable painful nodules, classically on the shins. It is associated with many systemic diseases, such as sarcoidosis,
coccidioidomycosis, and inflammatory bowel disease.

Nikolsky sign is a skin finding in which the top layers of the skin slip away from the
lower layers when rubbed. This patient's presentation IS concerning for toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). TEN can occur after starting new medications. Anti-epileptics
are classically associated with this disease. This disease is characterized by skin
sloughing, and patients can end up with significant desquamation. Death is typically
from sepsis and/or organ failure. These patients should be admitted to an ICU for
close monitoring. The treatment is supportive care.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK574530/
D. Presence of pastia's lines
Pastia's lines are present in scarlet fever

question: A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department complaining of hip and back pain and stiffness for the past 4 months which gradually improves throughout the day with exercise. Radiographs of the hips and back reveal progressive fusion of the lumbar vertebrae and fusion of the sacroiliac joints. Which of the following is the most commonly associated extra-articular condition seen with this patient's suspected diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Inflammatory bowel disease
Expl anation
A. Conjunctivitis
Ankylosing spondylitis can also commonly present with acute anterior uveitis, but
not conjunctivitis. Conjunctivitis is a common extra-articular symptom of reactive
arthritis along with urethritis.
B. Inflammatory bowel disease
This patient's presentation and radiographic findings are most consistent with
ankylosing spondylitis, an inflammatory spine disease. It is characterized by
sacroiliitis and spinal fusion. It is more common in males and is usually diagnosed
before the age of 40. Imaging will show a "bamboo spine" and fused sacroiliac
joints. It is also associated with a positive HLA-B27. The most common extra-articular manifestation is inflammatory bowel disease in almost 50% of patients, followed by uveitis in approximately 30%.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470173/
Hudson K, Agrait-Gonzalez M. Chapter 102. Arthritis. In: Walls RM, Hockberger
RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical
Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
C. Psoriasis
Approximately 10% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis also have psoriasis, but
the most common extra-articular manifestation is inflammatory bowel disease. This
is present in almost 50% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis.
D. Urethritis
Urethritis is an extra-articular symptom of reactive arthritis,
not ankylosing
spondylitis.

question: A patient presents with multiple firm, painless, elliptical-shaped purple macules on his face, groin, and legs. He is HIV positive but does not take medications. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Kaposi sarcoma is an AIDS-related vascular tumor caused by HHV-8 in- fection. Kaposi sarcoma has a characteristic appearance of elliptical-shaped le- sions along skin tension lines. Lesions can be macules, papules, or nodules. They are painless and nonpruritic, and they are most commonly found on the face, geni- talia, and lower extremities. Due to vascularity, lesions may vary in color from pink to brown and can be mistaken for ecchymosis or purpura; a biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis. Kaposi sarcoma is considered an AIDS-defining illness and is associated with CD4 cell counts less than 200. Although cutaneous manifestations are most common, vis- ceral involvement is possible. The oral, GI, and respiratory systems are the most affected noncutaneous sites. With advancements in antiretroviral therapy, the inci- dence of Kaposi sarcoma has greatly decreased. Treatment consists of antiretrovi- ral therapy for active HIV infection. Local chemotherapy can be provided intrale- sionally for limited disease, but more extensive cases require systemic chemotherapy. Incorrect Answer Explanations HSV can cause oral and genital lesions, particularly in immunocompromised patients. These lesions are typically painful and described as clusters of vesi- cles on an erythematous base. HSV is diagnosed clinically and treated with an- tiviral therapy, such as acyclovir or valacyclovir. Molluscum contagiosum is a contagious infection caused by the poxvirus. Although it is common in children, infections in adults should raise suspicion for an underlying immunocompromised state. Lesions are painless and described as flesh-colored domes with an umbilicated center. Treatment is self-limited, and hygiene is imperative to reduce spread. Syphilis is an STI caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum. Primary syphilis presents as a painless genital ulcer. Secondary syphilis features systemic symp- toms along with widespread erythematous macules and papules, predominantly on the palms and soles. Penicillin should be used to treat both primary and sec- ondary syphilis.

question: The following lesion is noticed during the physical examination of a patient. What is associated with an increased risk of developing this condition? Credit: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
englishExplanation:
The lesion depicted is melanoma, identifiable by its Asymmetry, irregular Border, varying Colors, large Diameter, and Evolving appearance and symptoms (ABCDE mnemonic); this mnemonic helps to identify lesions that are concerning for melanoma based on appearance. Along with family history, one of the most significant risk factors in the development of melanoma is ultraviolet light (UV) exposure, which is thought to contribute to 90% of melanoma cases in the United States. This includes UV light emitted by tanning beds, which can be fifteen times stronger than the midday sun. Due to this associa- tion, the WHO has labelled UV-emitting tanning devices a carcinogen to skin, similar to tobacco for lung cancer. It is thought that intense intermittent exposure, as occurs in tanning beds or with direct sun exposure that leads to severe sunburn, holds greater risk. As little as one sunburn with blisters in childhood doubles risk of devel- oping melanoma, although there is a cumulative effect as well. Additional risk factors include total number of nevi (birthmarks or moles on the skin), hair color (blond, red), skin color (white, fair), eye color (blue, green), older age, and immunosuppression. Melanoma is the most lethal form of skin cancer, the third most common cancer among men and women ages 20 to 39, the fifth most common cancer in men of all age groups, the sixth most common cancer in women of all age groups in the United States, and the only cancer that is rising in incidence, having doubled in the last few decades. Prevention (ie, patient education to limit UV exposure), early detec- tion, and referral are key to survival — early disease is curable while metastatic dis- ease carries a dismal 5-year survival rate of only 16%. Incorrect Answer Explanations Chronic arsenic exposure from ingesting contaminated water, seafood, or medications has been linked to basal cell carcinoma, which is the most common form of skin cancer. The nodular form makes up approximately 80 percent of cases and is typically characterized by a pink or flesh-colored papule, usually on the face, that has a pearly or translucent quality. It may often be described as having a "rolled" border, where the periphery is more raised than the middle. This picture shows a melanoma, and one of the most significant risk factors in the de- velopment of melanoma is UV exposure. Although there is no known link between smoking and melanoma, a statistically significant association has been identified between smoking and risk for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. These lesions also tend to (but not al- ways) appear on sun-exposed areas of fair-skinned people and range from an erythe- matous, well-demarcated, scaly patch or plaque of an in situ lesion to the firm hyper- keratotic papules, plaques, or nodules of well-differentiated invasive disease to fleshy, granulomatous papules or nodules without keratosis if poorly differentiated. This pic- ture shows a melanoma, and one of the most significant risk factors in the develop- ment of melanoma is UV exposure. Unprotected intercourse is a risk factor for STIs, several of which have associated skin manifestations. Early lesions of Kaposi sarcoma, which is associated with HIV/AIDS, may be mistaken as skin cancer nevi and often have vary- ing colors similar to melanoma. This picture shows a melanoma, and one of the most significant risk factors in the development of melanoma is UV exposure.

question: While examining a 39-year-old woman, a flat, irregularly shaped brown and black 3-mm lesion is noted on her left arm. She states it has evolved there over the past year and occasionally bleeds. Which characteristic of the lesion is the most impor- tant factor for survival for localized disease? Credit: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
englishExplanation:
Melanoma is classified into four stages at diagnosis, starting with localized disease as the primary stage (I/II), followed by regional metastasis (stage III) and distant metastasis (stage IV). For localized stage I or II cutaneous melanoma, tumor thickness or depth (known as the Breslow index) is the single most im- portant prognostic factor for survival; survival decreases with increasing Breslow thickness. For stage III disease, the amount of regional lymph node in- volvement is the main predictor of prognosis. In stage IV disease, the site, number, and surgical resectability of metastasis, as well as LDH level, all play a role in progno- sis. Common sites of metastasis are brain, lung, bone, and soft tissues. The 5-year survival rate for stage IV disease is poor, making early detection crucial. The ABCDE mnemonic is a sensitive, although nonspecific, tool that can be used to identify characteristics in moles that are concerning for melanoma: Asymmetry (if the mole could be folded in half, the right side would not match the left side); Border irregularity (the edges appear irregular, jagged, or crusty, rather than smooth and consistent throughout); Color variation (the pres- ence of more than one color, especially black, white or blue); Diameter greater than 5 mm (while larger moles raise suspicion, smaller moles can still be melanoma); and Evolution (any changes to the size, shape, or color; new symptoms such as bleeding or itching; or any new lesions in adulthood). It is not necessary to have all of the above signs, and any suspicious lesion should be referred to dermatol- ogy. The “ugly duckling” sign is also useful — any pigmented lesion that is different from the other's on an individual is very suspicious. Incorrect Answer Explanations Mole diameter greater than 5 mm is a criterion in the ABCDE mnemonic for identify- ing lesions concerning for melanoma, but diameter itself does not play a role in prog- nosis or staging. Similar to an iceberg, a lesion may be deeper than it appears; lesions smaller than 5 mm can certainly be melanoma, and not all lesions greater than 5 mm are melanoma. Thus, it is important to also look for the other features of the ABCDE mnemonic or the “ugly duckling” sign as well. For localized melanoma, tumor thickness or depth is the most important prognostic factor for survival. Increasing patient age does appear to be an independent prognostic fac- tor with respect to overall survival rates, but it is not as significant as tumor thick- ness for prognostication of localized disease. Theories for this suggest that age is as- sociated with declining host immune defense mechanisms. Older patients also tend to have thicker primary tumors and a higher proportion of ulcerated melanomas (an- other prognostic factor). Men older than 60 years have the highest mortality rates from melanoma. Although gender does appear to play a role in survival rates, it is not as significant as tumor thickness. Better survival rates in women have been re- ported in a large number of studies, even after adjustment for tumor thickness and anatomic site.

question: While examining an otherwise healthy 32-year-old African American man, a dark brown 4-mm band is noted on the great toenail, with an area of pigmentation of the lateral nail fold and some nail dystrophy. He does not recall any trauma, there is no nail deformity, and the findings are only on a single toe. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: This patient most likely has acral lentiginous melanoma, which is present on palmar, plantar, or subungual surfaces (ie, subungual melanoma) and fulfills many criteria for diagnosis in appearance, size, and extension to the nail fold. Levit et al. identified a variation of the ABCDE(F) mnemonic to be used to identify characteris- tics concerning for subungual melanoma: Age (peaks at age 50-70); Band of brown or black color, Breadth greater than 3 mm, Border (irregular or blurred); Change in the band; Digit involved (great toe or thumb have highest frequency); Extension of pigment to the proximal or lateral nail fold (Hutchinson sign, pathognomonic) or free edge of nail plate; and Family history of melanoma. It is unnecessary to have all of the above signs, and any suspicious lesion should be referred. Melanoma has sev- eral subtypes, including acral lentiginous which makes up less than 5% of cases and is the most common type in African American patients. Subungual melanoma has a poor prognosis if not identified early and often requires digit ampu- tation for cure. Incorrect Answer Explanations Melanonychia occurs with melanin in the nail plate, causing a brown or black discoloration in bands (longitudinal or transverse) that can affect the whole nail plate as well. Longitudinal melanonychia has many causes that are usually benign, including drugs, fungal infections, inflammatory conditions, trauma, and systemic disorders. Longitudinal melanonychia can also occur normally in darker-skinned people (is commonly seen in African Americans) and is known as ethnic melanonychia. It usually occurs in more than one nail and is only rarely as- sociated with nail dystrophy, as opposed to the acral lentiginous melanoma described in this case. Onychomycosis is a chronic fungal infection of the toenails or fingernails that typically begins with whitish, yellowish, or brownish discoloration of a distal corner of a nail. Rarely, onychomycosis may be from a fungus that produces melanin, causing a brown to black discoloration of the nail plate in various patterns. Fungal melanonychia typically involves two to five nails and tends to be less than 3 mm in width, which differs from melanoma. Subungual hematoma is blood that is trapped under the nail after trauma. It can have a very similar appearance to subungual melanoma, which often causes a delay in diagnosis. Traumatic longitudinal melanonychia typically involves one nail and tends to be less than 3 mm in width. This patient did not have a history of trauma, and subungual melanoma must be considered in all cases of presumed subungual hematoma that are not healing.

question: What is the most common cause of a unilateral neck mass in older adults?
englishExplanation: In older patients, 75% of neck masses are neoplastic. The most common cause of a unilateral neck mass in an adult is squamous cell carcinoma of the up- per aerodigestive tract, metastatic to cervical lymph nodes. Other common neo- plasms are tumors of the parotid or submandibular gland, thyroid gland, and lym- phoma. Neoplastic lymph nodes are firm and can become fixed or nonmobile. Adults with a history of smoking or heavy alcohol consumption are at high risk for neoplasm. The first approach to a unilateral neck mass in older adults is to determine if it is likely infectious based on history and physical examination findings. Infection is less common but can be treated with oral antibiotics. If there are obvious signs of infec- tion (eg, warmth, erythema, tenderness to palpation, fever, and recent upper respira- tory or dental infection), then treatment for likely infection can be considered with close follow-up in 2 weeks; if not resolved, then a malignancy workup must be per- formed. Findings suggestive of malignancy rather than infection include duration of >2 weeks, size >1.5 cm, firm texture, fixed or nonmobile, and nontender. Unless infection is obvious, unilateral neck masses in older adults should be referred for close outpatient workup of malignancy. Incorrect Answer Explanations Most neck masses in adolescents and young adults are caused by infec- tion. Mononucleosis can present with cervical lymphadenopathy, malaise, and pharyngitis. Neoplastic causes are more common in older adults. Parotitis is an acute infection of the parotid gland. Acute suppurative paroti- tis is caused by an acute bacterial infection of the parotid gland, usually associated with decreased salivary flow. This presents with unilateral facial pain and swelling. Viral parotitis (mumps) presents with unilateral or bilateral parotid swelling. This is most common in children younger than 15. Thyroid disorders can present with enlargement of the thyroid gland (goiter). This usually presents as an anterior neck mass (more so than unilat- eral), although the enlarged gland may be asymmetric. This enlargement is a chronic condition that tends to be slower in onset than squamous cell carcinoma.

question: In a geriatric patient with a history of decubitus pressure ulcer, what finding sug- gests progression of the ulcer to a deeper soft tissue infection?
englishExplanation: In the setting of a decubitus pressure ulcer, progression from a superficial infection to a spreading soft tissue infection may be characterized by spreading ery- thema, warmth, induration, tenderness, increased purulent drainage, foul smell, frank tissue necrosis, and systemic symptoms (eg, fevers and malaise). Pressure ulcers are a common occurrence in older patients, the critically ill, and patients with a spinal cord injury or other neuromuscular disease. Healing and recovery may be enhanced by local wound care, antiseptics, and improved nutrition. Pressure ulcers result from compromised tissue when it is compressed between a bony prominence and an external surface for a prolonged pe- riod of time. Healing and blood flow are impaired, and bacterial contamination may occur. Many patients live with pressure ulcers for very long periods of time, al- though they can cause pain and morbidity and decrease quality of life. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bacterial colonization is typical of chronic superficial decubitus ulcers and does not indicate progression to a surrounding soft tissue infection. Bacteria in pressure ulcers may be skin flora or can represent bacterial spread from contact with the surrounding environment. Colonization results from factors such as impaired tis- sue healing and bacterial biofilms. Poorly healing tissue is characteristic of superficial pressure ulcers and does not indicate an acute progression to a pathologic soft tissue infection. Poorly healing tissue may result from a combination of factors, including poor blood supply, compression between a bony prominence and another surface, malnutrition, expo- sure to moisture and feces, and sensory loss. Serous drainage (exudate), which is usually clear in color, is commonly seen in chronic superficial pressure ulcers. Purulence and markedly increased drainage can be signs of acute infectious progression.

question: A woman with a history of multiple sclerosis presents for evaluation of a new pres- sure ulcer. Her vital signs are normal, and her symptoms are limited to pain at the site. On examination, she has a 2-cm stage 2 sacral ulcer with moderate yellow ex- udate and no surrounding erythema or warmth. What is the best next step in management?
englishExplanation: This patient has a stage 2 sacral ulcer without evidence of associated invasive in- fection. The initial treatment is wound care and application of a dressing to cover the area and keep it moist, such as saline gauze or hydrocolloid dressing. Basic principles of wound care for decubitus pressure ulcers include debridement of superficial necrotic tissue, application of moist dressing, nutritional support, and pressure relief. Some wounds may be amenable to hyperbaric oxygen therapy. In 2016, the National Pressure Injury Advisory Panel (NPIAP) suggested using the terminology "pressure injury" instead of "pressure ulcer." Current guidelines recom- mend staging of pressure injury as follows: Stage 1: nonblanchable erythema of intact skin Stage 2: partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis Stage 3: full-thickness skin loss Stage 4: full-thickness skin and tissue loss with exposed deeper structures Unstageable: full-thickness loss obscured by slough or eschar Deep tissue pressure injury: persistent nonblanchable deep red, maroon, or pur- ple discoloration. Local wound care is generally recommended for stages 1 to 2, while surgical inter- vention may be needed for stages 3 to 4. Although some sources recommend the use of silver sulfadiazine, it has generally fallen out of favor. The following agents should not be used because they may impair wound healing: peroxide, chlorhexidine gluconate, and iodine-containing products. If there is no clinical improvement with excellent wound care, tissue biopsy and culture or evaluation for underlying osteomyelitis may be required. Incorrect Answer Explanations Admission for antibiotics may be required in the setting of an acute soft tissue infec- tion or osteomyelitis. However, this patient does not provide history or have examination findings that are consistent with an acute invasive infectious process. This patient does not present with a history or examination findings that would sug- gest invasive infection (eg, osteomyelitis). MRI and bone biopsy may be neces- sary to rule out osteomyelitis in patients who present with markers of an acute infectious process (eg, fevers, myalgias, spreading warmth or redness, visi- ble bone, elevated inflammatory markers, or sepsis physiology). Surgical consultation for debridement is unnecessary for stage 1 and 2 sacral pressure ulcers. A small amount of necrotic tissue may be debrided during routine wound care, but it is not necessary for this to be performed in the operating room or by a surgical service.

question: A patient has a sacral decubitus ulcer and systemic symptoms. What is the imaging modality of choice to exclude osteomyelitis?
englishExplanation: In a patient with a sacral pressure ulcer and suspected osteomyelitis, MRI has a high sensitivity and negative predictive value for osteomyelitis. MRI is the imaging modality of choice, superior to plain x-ray, for the exclusion of os- teomyelitis. In patients with decubitus pressure ulcers, osteomyelitis should be suspected in the presence of exposed bone, recurrent soft tissue infec- tions, systemic symptoms, elevated inflammatory markers, and failure of a chronic wound to heal with appropriate care. Although suggestive, exposed bone does not always indicate the presence of osteomyelitis. Clinical suspicion is in- adequate for the diagnosis of osteomyelitis, and advanced imaging should be per- formed to evaluate for bony involvement. Bone biopsy is the definitive test for an osteomyelitis diagnosis. MRI is the imaging study of choice for determining the extent of cortical and marrow involvement, and it may be useful in evaluating soft tissue involvement and ischemic complications. MRI is particularly useful early in the disease when plain x-ray has poor sensitivity (22% to 75%) for osteomyelitis. Plain x-ray is also less sensitive dur- ing the first 2 weeks following infection — as many as 80% of patients will have a nor- mal plain x-ray during this time. Bone marrow signal abnormalities detected by MRI can occur in a variety of pathologic processes, including contusion, fracture, post- surgery, neoplasm, and Charcot arthropathy. The correct diagnosis is established by clinical context. Incorrect Answer Explanations CT is more useful than plain x-ray in assessing cortical irregularity, periosteal reac- tion, and soft tissue involvement. However, CT is unable to discern marrow edema, so it cannot be used to rule out early osteomyelitis. Image quality is also significantly compromised in the setting of surgical hardware. Plain x-ray is a reasonable screening modality, particularly in ruling out other pathol- ogy. However, the sensitivity of plain x-ray for osteomyelitis is estimated at 22% to 75%, so it should not be used to rule out osteomyelitis in the appropriate clinical context. Ultrasound is of limited utility in the diagnosis and exclusion of os- teomyelitis because it has very poor penetration of bone. Soft tissue and pe- riosteal reactions may be visualized, heightening clinical suspicion. However, ultra- sonography cannot be used to rule out osteomyelitis.

question: Which treatment should be avoided in patients who present with venous stasis dermatitis and ulcers and associated complications?
englishExplanation: Topical antibiotic cream is not recommended in the treatment of venous stasis dermatitis and ulcers because it can complicate the clinical picture, as many topically applied antibiotic creams and ointments can cause aller- gic contact dermatitis. Treatment of venous stasis dermatitis and ulcers primarily aims to relieve symptoms and allow healing. Compression therapy and eleva- tion of the lower extremities are the mainstays of treatment. Oral antibi- otics can be used to help treat superinfected venous stasis ulcers, as evidenced by in- creased warmth, pain, lymphangina, and fever. Oral antihistamines are useful in the treatment of pruritus, which is often associated with chronic venous stasis disease. Topical steroid creams, especially those with low potency, may be useful in the short term to improve erythema, pruritus, and scaling. Incorrect Answer Explanations Oral antibiotics play a role in the treatment of venous stasis ulcers that are superinfected by bacteria. Oral antibiotics have no role in routine prophylaxis or healing of venous stasis ulcers, but they are not contraindicated. Oral antihistamines are useful in the treatment of chronic venous stasis disease and in assisting with the routine healing of ulcers by preventing pruritus and controlling symptoms. While they do not directly promote healing of ulcers, oral antihistamines help prevent superinfection due to scratching. Topical steroid creams are useful in the treatment of chronic venous sta- sis ulcers and dermatitis, particularly in relieving scaling, erythema, and pruritus. While they do not directly promote healing of ulcers, topical steroid creams are helpful in preventing superinfection due to scratching.

question: In what anatomical location are venous stasis ulcers most likely to be found?

options.text: On the distal toes of the foot
Plantar foot surface at the pressure points

englishExplanation: Causes of lower-extremity ulcers include venous stasis disease, diabetic or other neuropathy, and arterial ischemia. The anatomic location of the ulcers may offer clinical insight into the cause. Venous stasis ulcers are most commonly found just superior to the medial or lateral malleoli due to venous insuffi- ciency and reflux in the veins. They are often shallow with irregular borders with overlying exudate. By contrast, neuropathic ulcers are usually found on the plantar surface of the feet at the pressure points or in areas of prior injury due to failure to perceive the tissue damage. Ulcerations due to arterial ischemia are usu- ally found at the distal portion of the toes and result from tissue necrosis due to poor perfusion. Ulcers can also occur over an area of prior injury or infection. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ulcers on the distal toes are most commonly associated with arterial ischemia due to tissue necrosis from poor perfusion. These ulcers often have a “punched- out” appearance. Ulcers may develop over prior areas of infection, particularly infections due to Staphylococcus or Streptococcus. However, these are not venous stasis ulcers. The clinical appearance is related to the causative organism. Ulcers on the plantar pressure point surfaces of the foot are often related to neuropathy and less commonly associated with venous stasis. Because neuropathy decreases neurologic sensation, they are often painless. They can have a “punched- out” appearance with a thick rim of callus.

question: Which skin sensation abnormality is most commonly associated with venous stasis disease?
englishExplanation: Most patients with chronic venous stasis disease experience pruritus. Pruritus results from dry, scaly skin associated with venous stasis dermatitis. Since excoriation can result in infections of the skin, attempting to control pruritus is important in the symptomatic treatment of these patients. Venous stasis disease is caused by venous hypertension in the lower extremities. Multiple things can cause this disease, including venous valvular incompetence that results in reflux, venous obstruction, and venous thrombosis. Venous stasis disease is highly associated with older female patients with a family history of the disease. Smoking, obesity, and a history of DVT are also associated with the development of venous stasis disease. Incorrect Answer Explanations Allodynia is pain due to a stimulus that does not normally provoke a pain response. Patients exhibiting allodynia may feel pain due to light touch or other minimal skin contact. Allodynia is not associated with venous stasis disease. Hypoesthesia is a reduced sense of touch or sensation. It is a common side effect of medical conditions such as decompression sickness or beriberi. Hypoesthesia is not associated with venous stasis disease. Paresthesia is a painless sensation of burning or prickling that often oc- curs in the extremities. It suggests a sensory nervous system abnormality and is commonly seen in peripheral neuropathies, including diabetic neuropathy. Risk factors for neuropathies may overlap with those for venous stasis disease.

question: An 87-year-old man with a history of diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presents with a painful wound to the medial aspect of the left ankle (see image) that he first noticed 2 months ago. It seems to improve with elevation. He denies fevers, chills, and wound drainage. He had a similar episode about a year ago that has resolved. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Casa nayafana/Shutterstock.com.
englishExplanation: Venous stasis ulcers are the most common cause of chronic lower-ex- tremity ulcers. Risk factors include old age, obesity, trauma, and a history of DVT. On physical examination, the wound appears irregular and shallow over a bony prominence. Associated symptoms include edema and varicosities. The prognosis is worse with large ulcers and prolonged duration. Venous stasis ulcers can recur and persist. Treatment is typically conservative with compression therapy, elevation, and aspirin. Surgical management is indicated in large or prolonged ulcers refractory to conservative treatment. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cellulitis is due to inflammatory reactions triggered by cells within the skin itself that are invaded by bacteria. The skin is typically warm, tender, and erythema- tous without a line of demarcation. Symptoms develop gradually over a few weeks. Treatment includes antibiotics and monitoring of infection resolution. Diabetic foot ulcers result from prolonged pressure on areas that may not have sensation due to neuropathy. Often found on the plantar aspects of the feet, they are rarely painful until deep or infected. Treatment can include reduc- ing pressure to the area or surgical skin grafting. Peripheral vascular disease is associated with cardiac disease or stroke, leading to tissue ischemia. Patients may present with claudication and ulcers that are deep and round with sharply demarcated borders. Diminished pedal pulses and cool limbs may also be present due to a lack of arterial circulation. Treatment in- cludes antiplatelet medications.

question: A 65-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes presents with a large wound to the bottom of her great toe that has been worsening for months. The wound is deep, with exposed bone and purulent drainage without surrounding erythema. There is a monophasic Doppler signal from the dorsalis pedis artery. The rest of the foot and ankle examination is normal. What complication has this patient likely developed secondary to the ulceration?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with what is likely an arterial insufficiency ulcer that has progressed to osteomyelitis, given the presence of a purulent infection involv- ing exposed bone. Arterial insufficiency ulcerations are seen in the setting of peripheral arterial disease, a known complication of poorly controlled diabetes. Typically, they begin with a skin injury that does not heal due to poor cir- culation. The wound will likely progress into an ulceration that is at risk of infection. Infection will lead to progressive tissue destruction and can often involve the bone, causing osteomyelitis. These patients are also at increased risk of other asso- ciated infections and complications, including cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis, neuropathic osteoarthropathy (Charcot foot), and gangrene. Osteomyelitis should be suspected in deep ulceration wounds in which the bone is visible or in which a probe inserted into the wound contacts bone. Osteomyelitis is typically a polymicrobial infection. Imaging can be obtained in situations where the clinical examination is inconclusive for osteomyelitis. X-rays can be useful as an initial screening test, although the overall sensitivity for os- teomyelitis on x-ray is low. Additional x-ray findings can be helpful in treating the patient and evaluating for other complications, such as the presence of a foreign body or soft tissue gas. MRI is the preferred imaging modality, but it is less readily available, particularly from the emergency department. Treatment of os- teomyelitis includes broad-spectrum antibiotics; local wound care, with debridement; and interventions focused on improving vascular flow, including blood glucose con- trol and revascularization procedures. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cellulitis is a known complication that can develop from any wound. In this case, the patient does not have surrounding erythema and, outside of poor circulation, the foot examination is normal. Hence, cellulitis is less likely occurring in this case. Dry gangrene is a complication of peripheral arterial disease. Dry gangrene will present with necrotic black tissue and usually has a clear demarcation between healthy and diseased tissue. This is not currently present in this pa- tient, although she is at risk of developing this in the future. Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency, identified by the presence of a rapidly spreading infection along the fascial planes. This usually is seen clinically by se- vere pain in the extremity, swelling, crepitus on palpation, and soft tissue gas on imaging. This patient is not showing signs of this. However, this condition can develop from infected ulcerations. If necrotizing fasciitis is suspect, broad-spec- trum antibiotics should be administered, and surgery should be consulted immediately.

question: What is the first-line therapy for an infant with atopic dermatitis?
englishExplanation: Nonpharmacologic therapy, such as emollient ointments, is the first-line treatment for an infant with atopic dermatitis. Atopic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory condition with associated pruritus. In infants and toddlers, it most of- ten presents with a pruritic, red, crusted lesion on the extensor surfaces of the limbs, trunk, face, or scalp. It is often associated with a family history of atopy, such as eczema, asthma, or other allergic conditions. A primary pathophysiologic cause of atopic dermatitis is epidermal barrier dysfunc- tion, specifically in the stratum corneum. An altered stratum corneum may result in increased permeability and water loss. Thus, emollient ointments or thick creams are recommended to be applied at least twice a day for patients with atopic dermatitis as first-line therapy. Other therapies, such as topical corticosteroids, may be useful in infants who do not respond to conservative measures. Incorrect Answer Explanations IL-4/IL-13 receptor alpha antagonists, such as dupilumab, have been shown to help atopic dermatitis. However, dupilumab is only approved for patients older than 2 years. Emollient ointments are first-line therapy in infants younger than 2. Oral corticosteroids may improve an acute exacerbation of atopic dermatitis, but they are not recommended for long-term therapy. Additionally, they are not rec- ommended for use in infants for this purpose. Emollient ointments are first-line therapy in infants younger than 2. Topical calcineurin inhibitors, such as tacrolimus ointment, may be useful in the treatment of atopic dermatitis. However, it is only approved for patients older than 2 years. Emollient ointments are first-line therapy in infants younger than 2.

question: A patient presents with an isolated wrist rash after wearing a new bracelet. The rash is streaky with linear papules on an erythematous base confined to the af- fected area. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
englishExplanation: Type IV hypersensitivity reactions (delayed type) cause contact dermatitis, which is the rash affecting this patient. Type IV hypersensitivity reactions involve CD4+ T lymphocytes, which recognize antigens 48 to 72 hours after exposure and trigger a cell-mediated immune response. This differs from other hypersensi- tivity reactions that are primarily associated with antibodies. Contact dermatitis is an inflammatory reaction of the skin that presents after expo- sure to an irritant, such as jewelry, latex, or articles of clothing. Poison ivy exposure is another well-known example of this condition. Contact dermatitis is diagnosed clini- cally, and an examination typically reveals streaky, pruritic lesions on an ery- thematous base in the area that was exposed to the irritant. Eruptions may appear immediately after exposure or up to several days later. Management consists of removing the irritating agent and applying low-dose topical corticos- teroid creams. Antihistamines can be used as an adjunct for associated pruritus. Incorrect Answer Explanations A type I hypersensitivity reaction is an immediate IgE-mediated reaction that results in mast cell activation. Some common examples include anaphylaxis and angioedema. A type II hypersensitivity reaction is an antibody-mediated cytotoxic reaction that results in activation of the complement system. Hemolytic disease of the newborn and Goodpasture syndrome are examples of type II hypersensi- tivity reactions. A type III hypersensitivity reaction occurs when antigen-antibody complexes de- posit in tissues and activate the complement system. Examples include post- streptococcal glomerulonephritis and rheumatoid arthritis.

question: According to current Infectious Disease Society of America (IDSA) guidelines, what is an indication for systemic antibiotics in the setting of a skin abscess?

options.text: Mild infection with no surrounding cellulitis

englishExplanation: According to the 2014 IDSA guidelines for skin and soft tissue infections, purulent skin and soft tissue infections (abscesses) respond well to isolated incision and drainage. Needle aspiration has been shown to be inadequate, even under ul- trasound guidance. Indications for systemic antibiotics, either orally or parenter- ally, after incision and drainage include patients with immunosuppression, fail- ure to resolve with incision and drainage, or signs of systemic infection, such as meeting systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria. Extremes of age or recurrent abscesses can also be considered for systemic an- tibiotic therapy. Most skin abscesses in the United States are caused by MRSA, and antibiotics given should cover this organism. Incorrect Answer Explanations First lifetime abscess is not an indication for systemic antibiotics. Recurrent ab- scesses may be considered for antibiotics in the interest of decolonization. Signs or symptoms of systemic infection are the most common indication for sys- temic antibiotics for abscess. Although patients who are immunocompromised may have an indication for systemic antibiotics in the setting of abscess, it is unlikely that a medical history of hyperten- sion would cause immunosuppression. Patients with other medical comorbidities re- quiring immunosuppressive medications may be considered for systemic an- tibiotics in the setting of abscess. Mild infection without surrounding cellulitis will generally respond well to incision and drainage alone.
