question: A 42-year-old man presents with right hand warmth and erythema after he cut his skin with a kitchen knife last evening. The cut is noted over the dorsum of the hand with 6 cm of surrounding erythema and warmth. The patient has no pain with movement of his fingers or hand. What is the best disposition for this patient?

options.text: Admit for incision and drainage of the area
Discharge with oral antibiotics and reevaluation in 2 weeks

englishExplanation: Superficial hand cellulitis without an abscess may progress rapidly to deeper space infections. Observation in the hospital for rapid spreading of the in- fection is the best option. Other feasible options include outpatient oral antibi- otics with reevaluation within 48 hours or admission for intravenous an- tibiotics. Per the 2014 Infectious Diseases Society of America practice guidelines for antibiotics, coverage should be directed initially against Streptococci species. Coverage for MRSA may be appropriate in patients in whom the source of infection is penetrating trauma or who have high risk for or history of MRSA. Risk factors for MRSA include systemic symptoms, intravenous drug use, or evidence of MRSA infection elsewhere. Incorrect Answer Explanations Admission to the hospital for incision and drainage of the area is not indicated for this patient. This patient lacks symptoms suggestive of deep-space hand infection, which include pain with motion of the fingers and tendon sheaths, severe throbbing pain, and loss of hand function. Discharge home with oral antibiotics may be appropriate for patients with mild hand cellulitis. However, reevaluation within 48 hours is recommended for patients who are discharged with oral antibiotics. This is only appropriate for reliable pa- tients; they should be instructed to return immediately if symptoms worsen. Discharge home with topical antibiotic ointment would be inappropriate for this pa- tient. Topical antibiotics are appropriate treatment for impetigo, and topical acyclovir is appropriate for herpetic whitlow; however, topical agents have no utility in cellulitis.

question: What is the ideal duration of oral antibiotic therapy for uncomplicated cellulitis in a patient with no significant comorbidities?
englishExplanation: Recent recommendations from the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) and American College of Physicians (ACP) now suggest 5 to 6 days of oral antibi- otics for the treatment of uncomplicated cellulitis. Antibiotic choice should be directed initially against Streptococci species; first-generation cephalosporin antibiotics are a reasonable choice. Coverage for MRSA may be appropriate in pa- tients in whom the source of infection is penetrating trauma or who have high risk for or history of MRSA. Risk factors for MRSA include systemic symptoms, intravenous drug use, or evidence of MRSA infection elsewhere. A 5-day treatment course is also recommended by ACP for antibiotics in COPD exacerbation, bronchitis, and commu- nity-acquired pneumonia. Incorrect Answer Explanations A 3-day treatment of oral antibiotics is inadequate for cellulitis. Three days is the recommended length of treatment with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for an uncomplicated UTI (cystitis) in women. A 5-day treatment of nitrofuran- toin continues to be recommended for a UTI. A 10-day doxycycline treatment is recommended for early suspected Lyme disease with a single erythema migrans. This duration of treatment is unlikely to be necessary for uncomplicated cellulitis. A 14-day treatment with B-lactam antibiotics is the recommended course of treatment for pyelonephritis, not uncomplicated cellulitis. There is in- sufficient evidence to recommend a shorter course of antibiotics for pyelonephritis at this time, but this duration of treatment is unlikely to be necessary for uncomplicated cellulitis.

question: A 35-year-old patient with no comorbidities presents with erythema and warmth of the medial left lower leg. Ultrasound images are shown below. What is the most appropriate treatment? Credit: Copyright 2022 Dr. Hadiel Kaiyasah. Image courtesy of Dr. Hadiel Kaiyasah and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 46177. Used under license.

options.text: Enzymatic wound debridement of the area
Incision and drainage of the area

englishExplanation:
The ultrasound images above demonstrate the classic “cobblestoning” appearance found in cellulitis. Cobblestoning is seen on ultrasound due to edema in the tissues in areas of cellulitis. With the associated case description, the most likely diag- nosis is uncomplicated cellulitis. Recent recommendations from the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) and American College of Physicians (ACP) now suggest 5 to 6 days of oral antibiotics for treatment of uncomplicated cel- lulitis. The antibiotic choice should be directed initially against Streptococci species; first-generation cephalosporin antibiotics are a reasonable choice. Coverage for MRSA may be appropriate in patients in whom the source of infection is penetrat- ing trauma, have purulence associated with the cellulitis, or who have high risk for or history of MRSA. Risk factors for MRSA include systemic symptoms, intravenous drug use, or evidence of MRSA infection elsewhere. This ultrasound image demon- strates cobblestoning, not a discrete abscess pocket that would necessitate incision and drainage. Antibiotics are the appropriate treatment for uncomplicated cellulitis. Intravenous vancomycin is not the recommended empiric treatment for uncompli- cated cellulitis. Empiric treatment should initially be directed at Streptococci species and MSSA, unless the patient has purulence or a clear risk factor for MRSA. Vancomycin would be used as part of a broader spec- trum of antibiotics, not as monotherapy.

question: A 52-year-old man presents with redness to his forearm. The patient states that he was nipped by a dog 3 days ago and noticed redness starting 2 days ago. The dog's vaccinations are up to date. What is the best initial outpatient antibiotic choice for this patient?
englishExplanation: Cellulitis related to dog bites may be caused by Pasteurella multocida, skin flora, or anaerobic bacteria. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the antibiotic of choice because it is effective against all of those microbiologic agents as a monotherapy. Alternative regimens may include an antibiotic with Pasteurella species coverage (eg, levofloxacin, doxycycline, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) plus antibiotics with anaerobic coverage (eg, clindamycin or metronidazole). Monotherapy with moxifloxacin (which covers Pasteurella species and anaerobic bacteria) may be useful, but there is currently insufficient evidence to recommend this therapy. Duration of therapy continues to be guided by clinical re- sponse. Patients with cellulitis resulting from animal bites should be reevaluated frequently, and antibiotic therapy should be extended as appropriate. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cephalexin does not cover Pasteurella species, which are a common cause of cellulitis related to animal bites. Cephalexin also has poor anaerobic cover- age. Cephalexin is an appropriate regimen for uncomplicated cellulitis not re- lated to animal bites. Clindamycin does not cover Pasteurella species, which are a common cause of cellulitis related to animal bites. Clindamycin does have good anaerobic coverage. In animal bites, clindamycin may be useful in combination antibiotic therapy with antibiotics that have Pasteurella species coverage. Clindamycin may also be used as an alternative regimen for uncomplicated cellulitis not related to animal bites. Levofloxacin does cover Pasteurella species, which are a common cause of cellulitis related to animal bites. However, levofloxacin does not have good anaerobic coverage, a second common cause of cellulitis. Thus, levofloxacin may be useful in combination antibiotic therapy with antibiotics with good anaerobic cov- erage for patients with animal bites.

question: What is the most effective pharmacotherapy to decrease toxin production associ- ated with a necrotizing soft tissue skin infection?
englishExplanation: Clindamycin provides antimicrobial coverage for streptococcal and staphylococcal infections. Because toxin production is one of the key components that contributes to the extensive tissue damage in necrotizing skin and soft tissue in- fections, clindamycin should be added to the primary antibiotic regimen for gram-positive infections. Clindamycin mitigates toxin production and limits the destructive nature of necrotizing infections, even with bacteria that are re- sistant to its antimicrobial effects. Up to 75% of the time, necrotizing soft tissue infec- tions are caused by polymicrobial sources of gram-positive and gram-negative bacte- ria and anaerobes. These infections are most common in patients who have significant comorbidities, such as alcoholism, diabetes, recent trauma, and intravenous drug abuse. They often have subtle clinical presentations; pain out of proportion to the examination should be a major red flag when evaluating a patient with any soft tissue skin infection. Signs of necrotizing fasciitis include skin bullae, discoloration, crepitus, fever, and systemic toxicity. Although an- tibiotics, resuscitation, and imaging are important components of overall manage- ment, the standard of care is early surgical consultation for exploration and debridement. Necrotizing skin and soft tissue infections have mortality rates up to 35%, and if debridement is delayed beyond 24 hours, the mortality rate in- creases markedly. Incorrect Answer Explanations Amikacin, an aminoglycoside antibiotic, provides strong coverage against gram-negative bacteria, including Pseudomonas, Enterobacter, and Escherichia coli. Amikacin, however, is insufficient to treat necrotizing soft tissue infections due to their polymicrobial nature. Amikacin is rarely used in isolation; it targets the bacteria itself and does not affect toxin production. Providing early and strong broad-spectrum antibiotics is necessary to help reduce the spread of these rapidly progressing infections. Used alone, piperacillin-tazobactam provides appropriate broad-spectrum coverage for aggressive gram-negative microbes and some gram-positive bacteria. It does not, however, reduce toxin production, as clindamycin does when added to the antibiotic regimen. Vancomycin provides appropriate broad-spectrum gram-positive cover- age. However, it does not reduce toxin production without the addition of clin- damycin. Providing early and strong broad-spectrum antibiotics is necessary to help reduce the spread of these rapidly progressing infections.

question: An obese adolescent boy presents with balanitis. In addition to STI screening, for what other comorbidity should the patient be screened?
englishExplanation: Balanitis, or cellulitis of the glans penis, may be caused by a number of things. One common cause is Candida albicans, particularly in infants with diaper dermatitis or adolescents with diabetes mellitus. Occasionally, fungal balanitis can be the present- ing complaint for new-onset diabetes in at-risk adolescents. Candidal balanitis is treated with topical antifungal creams. Other possible causes of balanitis include trauma, fixed drug eruptions, STIs, Group A Streptococcus, and irritant contact dermatitis. Treatment should be oriented to the presumed cause, which can usually be elicited from the history and physical examina- tion but may require Gram staining and culture of discharge. Incorrect Answer Explanations Crohn disease may be associated with erythema nodosum (ie, raised, tender, red or violet nodules) on the extensor surfaces of the extremities. Although patients with Crohn disease may be placed on immunomodulatory therapy that can put them at risk for candidal balanitis, it is not a presenting complaint for Crohn disease. Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA) may be associated with a macular salmon-pink rash. Although patients with JRA may be placed on immunomodulatory therapy that can put them at risk for developing candidal balanitis, it is not a presenting complaint for JRA. Moderate persistent asthma may be associated with atopic dermatitis, a chronic pru- ritic inflammatory condition that is also associated with allergies. Although patients with asthma may be placed on chronic steroid therapy that can put them at risk for developing candidal balanitis, it is not a presenting complaint for asthma.

question: Which skin disease requires treatment with an oral medication?
englishExplanation: Tinea is a fungal infection caused by dermatophytes that affects the keratinous lay- ers of the skin. The rash is characteristically red, circular (like a ring), and itchy. Tinea infections are named according to their locations — tinea corporis is "ringworm of the body," tinea cruris is "jock itch," and tinea pedis is "athlete's foot." Tinea capitis, "ringworm of the scalp," is different from the other tinea infections in that it involves both skin and hair shafts. Due to hair shaft involvement, tinea capitis requires oral medication, rather than topical treatment. The oral agents used include terbinafine (for 4 to 6 weeks) in children older than 4 years and griseofulvin (for 6 to 8 weeks). Checking baseline blood tests (liver function tests) prior to griseofulvin treatment is no longer recommended. Incorrect Answer Explanations Tinea corporis, most commonly caused by Trichophyton rubrum, and fungal skin in- fections other than tinea capitis are treated with topical antifungal agents, in- cluding butenafine and terbinafine. Tinea cruris, or jock itch, is most commonly seen in males and is treated with topical antifungal agents. Successful treatment often takes about 2 weeks and is then con- tinued for 1 week after resolution of the lesions. Tinea pedis, or athlete's foot, is also treated with topical antifungal medication. Due to the issues of absorption, many clinicians recommend treating tinea pedis with a prolonged course (4 to 8 weeks) of topical antifungal therapy with terbinafine.

question: A 52-year-old undomiciled man presents with an itchy rash on his hands and groin. A physical examination shows linear maculopapular excoriations in the in- terdigital spaces bilaterally. What is the most appropriate topical treatment?
englishExplanation: This patient has a pruritic rash that is localized to the interdigital spaces and groin, which is highly suggestive of scabies. Scabies, which is caused by a skin infestation of the mite Sarcoptes scabiei, is treated with topical permethrin cream 5% that is washed off after 8 to 14 hours. Permethrin is an insecticide that disrupts the sodium channels in the parasite's cell membranes, ultimately leading to cell death. Treatment may be repeated in 1 week if symptoms persist after ini- tial dosing. Additionally, all clothing and bedding should be washed in hot water with detergent, and close contacts should be monitored for similar symptoms and treated as needed. Oral ivermectin can be used as an alternative first-line agent or if topi- cal therapy with permethrin fails. Oral therapy is also recommended for large out- breaks in high-risk settings where topical administration may not be feasible (eg, nursing homes, prisons, homeless shelters). Scabies is transmitted through direct person-to-person contact, including sex- ual activity. Features of scabies include eruptions of linear burrows, papules, and pustules in the interdigital spaces, groin, axilla, and periumbilical region. Intense pruritus results from a type IV hypersensitivity reaction to the mite and is clas- sically worse at night. Although a microscopic evaluation of skin scrapings will show visible mites, scabies can be diagnosed clinically. Incorrect Answer Explanations Clotrimazole is an antifungal medication with topical preparations that can treat tinea infections of the skin. It is not a treatment for scabies, however. Lindane is an insecticide that was once commonly used for scabies, but it is no longer considered a first-line agent due to its higher side effect profile. Lindane toxicity affects the CNS and can result in seizures and possibly death. Selenium sulfide shampoo is a chemical compound used to treat sebor- rheic dermatitis and pityriasis versicolor. It is frequently used in the manage- ment of dandruff, but it is not a treatment for scabies.

question: A teenage patient presents for STI screening. They should be advised that what preventative measure is most protective against HPV-associated cancer?
englishExplanation: When administered correctly, the HPV vaccine has been shown to pre- vent approximately 90% of all cancers due to HPV. Since HPV vaccines were first recommended, cases of precancerous cervical changes in young women and gen- ital warts in teenagers and young adults have decreased. It is recommended that ado- lescents receive two doses of HPV vaccine, 6 to 12 months apart. This is usually ad- ministered at age 11 or 12, but can be given as early as 9 years old. If an individual has not received the complete HPV immunization series by the age of 15, three doses of the vaccine are recommended. The vaccine can be given up to age 45 but is generally not recommended for individuals older than 26 years. The vaccine is very safe, and the most common side effect that patients encounter, if any, is local pain and irritation at the injection site. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cervical conization is a treatment option if abnormal cervical cells are present; however, it is not a prophylactic measure to prevent these pre- cancerous changes from occurring. Almost all cervical cancer is caused by HPV, but people infected with high-risk strains are often asymptomatic. If precancerous cells are noted on screening tests, options for treatment target eradicating the cells. Conization and loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) can be used to remove the abnormal cells. Alternatively, the cells can be frozen off with cryotherapy or burned off with laser therapy. Although condom use should certainly be encouraged, patients can still transmit HPV via oral sex. HPV vaccination is a more effective prevention measure. Additionally, during vaginal and anal sex, condoms leave areas of skin exposed, which can subse- quently transmit infection. Sexually transmitted strains of HPV can be categorized as either low- or high-risk. Low-risk strains of the virus may cause oral or anogenital warts but are otherwise generally benign. Infections with high-risk strains can cause cancers of the vagina, vulva, cervix, oropharynx, penis, and anus. The HPV vaccine helps to protect against infections from both types. Antivirals are not indicated in the treatment of HPV infections, as there is no cure. Additionally, prophylactic antivirals targeting HPV do not prevent occurrence of anogenital warts, nor do they prevent cancer. The sexually transmitted HPV strains that cause genital warts rarely cause cancer, and the associated genital warts will often resolve on their own.

question: What is the expected time to resolution for molluscum contagiosum in a 16- month-old?
englishExplanation: Molluscum contagiosum is a self-limited viral illness. Reports of how long the le- sions (mollusca) can last vary from 3 to 6 months, 6 to 9 months, or 6 to 12 months, with some cases measured in years. Generally, lesions resolve in 6 to 9 months. They are characteristically small and raised; pink, white, or flesh colored; and dome shaped, with a depression or dimple in the middle. They appear pearly or waxy and are smooth and firm. In some patients, the rash is pruritic. Molluscum contagiosum infection is common in young children (1 to 4 years old) and, as is evident from the name, easily spread through autoinoculation. Because the virus lives on the epidermis, it is contagious as long as the child has lesions. Children can spread it to other parts of their own body and to others who touch or share cloth- ing, towels, or other fomites. Because there is no recommended emergency depart- ment treatment for molluscum contagiosum to clear the lesions, minimize spread, or shorten the duration of illness, instructions should focus on preventing transmission. The child should avoid picking at the lesions, and good handwashing should be en- couraged. Covering the lesions with clothing or bandages also helps prevent spread- ing, as does not sharing personal items. In typical cases, the rash is made up of 10 to 20 lesions, but immunocompromised patients may develop hundreds of lesions. Dermatologists and primary care physicians sometimes treat cases that are disturb- ing to patients or family members. Incorrect Answer Explanations The duration of other viral exanthems that present in childhood, including measles and rubella, can be measured in days. Since molluscum contagiosum lesions typi- cally last much longer, setting appropriate expectations based on the correct diagno- sis is an important part of the patient education passed on in the discharge instructions. Rashes associated with varicella and fifth disease, which are likely familiar to par- ents, can last from days to weeks. Since molluscum contagiosum lesions last much longer, communicating correct information is important. Otherwise, parents may be- come upset when the lesions persist, which can lead to the unnecessary and pre- ventable use of medical resources. Although most resources indicate that mollusca can persist for up to 3 to 4 years, these cases are atypical. Telling parents that the rash could last that long creates un- necessary discouragement. Instead, parents are better served with accurate informa- tion and reassurance that the illness is self-limited, although prolonged. Key Points Molluscum contagiosum is a self-limited viral illness. The lesions of molluscum contagiosum typically resolve in 6 to 9 months. Education about the condition and instructions on how to prevent molluscum conta- giosum from spreading are important in setting expectations for parents.

question: What is the correct first-line treatment for Pediculosis capitis (ie, head lice)?
englishExplanation: Topical permethrin (1%) is one of the less expensive and more readily available pedi- culicides, and it is the first-line in treatment of head lice. Permethrin works by modi- fying voltage-gated sodium channels and ultimately serving as a neurotoxin that kills lice. Topical permethrin is the most widely used and widely studied pediculicide in the United States; however, the clinician should familiarize themselves with local re- sistance patterns, as a “knock-down resistance mutation” is leading to increasing per- methrin resistance worldwide. Topical permethrin is administered to freshly-cleaned hair, left on for 10 minutes, and then rinsed off. After application, the hair should not be shampooed for 24 to 48 hours. A repeat application is recommended 9 to 10 days after initial application if live lice are seen in the interim. Wet combing, which is a method for mechanical re- moval of lice, can be used in cases where pediculicide therapy is not desired or con- traindicated (eg, a child ≤2 months old). The head louse is 2 to 3 mm long and grayish white in color. The female lives 3 to 4 weeks and lays her eggs at the base of the hair shaft, about 2 mm from the scalp. A typical affected scalp will have fewer than 10 live lice. Lice are most commonly spread by head-to-head contact. Contrary to popular thought, infestation secondary to con- tact with pillows, hair brushes, and helmets is less common. Because the diagnosis of head lice is associated with a great stigma, clinicians should reassure those with head lice that head lice do not represent poor hygiene and do not spread any significant diseases. Incorrect Answer Explanations Anti-itch medications, such as cetirizine, may help with itching but will not cure lice. Notably, pruritus results from sensitization to the saliva that the head louse injects into the scalp when it feeds. Sensitization may take 4 to 6 weeks, so in a patient with- out a prior infestation, itching may not be present early in course of infestation. In a patient without prior infestation, the onset of itching may be delayed until sensitiza- tion occurs after 4 to 6 weeks. Oral ivermectin is reserved for patients that fail first- and second-line treatments; ad- ditionally, oral ivermectin is not recommended in patients <15 kg. The clinician should be aware that common causes of treatment failure are poor adherence to ap- plication recommendations and continued contact with other affected individuals. If these factors have been ruled out, the next step is to switch to an alternative topical pediculicide. If that fails, oral ivermectin is third-line. Combination therapy with topical permethrin and oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxa- zole is thought to have higher success rates than use of permethrin alone. However, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole carries risk for rare adverse effects, including neu- tropenia, hemolysis, renal impairment, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Additionally, the use of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole alone has a lower success rate in treatment of head lice; dual therapy should be used only in resistant cases.

question: Which medication is recommended for the symptomatic treatment of pityriasis rosea in an adolescent patient?
englishExplanation: Pityriasis rosea is a benign and self-limited viral exanthem associated with herpesviruses 6 and 7. Treatment is symptomatic and includes topical admin- istration of a topical corticosteroid in the medium potency group such as triam- cinolone or hydrocortisone to relieve itching. Topical anti-itch creams with pramox- ine or menthol can also be helpful, as can oral antihistamines. Sunlight, or ultra- violet-B exposure, has been used to decrease symptoms after the initial stage. Pityriasis rosea can be a reactivation of a latent virus. The rash appears as small el- liptical papules or plaques, classically on the trunk along the skin cleav- age lines, that create the characteristic “Christmas tree” pattern. Often, a larger ovoid papule called a herald lesion or herald patch appears up to 3 weeks be- fore the systemic rash. The rash often appears on the extremities and occasionally on the face, hands, and feet, but rarely, in the mouth. For severe cases, oral acyclovir or phototherapy can be attempted, but these are not recommended for routine use. Incorrect Answer Explanations Pityriasis rosea is a benign, self-limited illness that does not require treatment with antibiotics such as amoxicillin. The use of other antibiotics, including erythromycin, has been studied, but there have been no definitive results to indicate this treatment. Oral steroids are not indicated in the treatment of pityriasis rosea. Topical steroid creams or ointment such as triamcinolone are beneficial to relieve itching. Antifungal medications such as terbinafine are not indicated in the treat- ment of pityriasis rosea, but they are often prescribed, especially if only the her- ald patch is seen. This lesion is generally 3 cm or larger, with a distinctive scaly plaque-like edge, similar to and possibly mistaken for ringworm.

question: A 5-year-old boy presents for evaluation of "welts that he gets all over his body." His mother says that the welts come and go in red, itchy patches and that he has had them for about 1 week. What is the typical course of illness?

options.text: The child will become critically ill without epinephrine
The child will soon begin to develop joint swelling
The rash may continue for another month
The rash will resolve and will not likely return

correctAnswer: The rash may continue for another month
englishExplanation: In this case, the mother's description of the rash matches the characteristic appear- ance of acute urticaria — pruritic, urticarial, intermittent wheals on multi- ple parts of the body. It is common in children and can last as long as 6 weeks, so a likely progression is that it will continue like this for another month. Urticaria has many triggers, including foods (particularly nuts and shellfish); medications (acetylsalicylic acid, ibuprofen, and antibiotics — especially penicillin and sulfa); in- sect stings or bites; physical stimuli such as pressure, cold, heat, exercise, or sun exposure; latex exposure; blood transfusions; bacterial infections; viral infections; pet dander; pollen; and plants, such as poison oak and poison ivy. In most cases, however, the inciting agent or etiology cannot be deter- mined. The condition most likely associated with urticaria is eczema. In mild cases like this one, a simple antihistamine such as diphenhydramine is the typical treatment. Incorrect Answer Explanations Epinephrine is indicated in the setting of anaphylaxis or airway compromise. There is no role for prophylactic epinephrine, and inappropriately administering epi- nephrine to an asymptomatic child will not prevent future pruritic episodes. Adults who develop chronic urticaria lasting more than 6 weeks may have an autoim- mune component, as seen in systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid arthritis. Children are much more likely to develop acute urticaria, which does not have this association. Although the rash will likely resolve at some point within 6 weeks of onset, its com- plete resolution at any one point does not suggest that there will be no future episodes of pruritic urticaria. It is common for the urticaria rash to come and go.

question: A 4-month-old with a history of recurrent croup presents with progressively wors- ening noisy breathing. On examination, a 5-cm bluish purple “birthmark” is noted in a beard distribution. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: This patient has a cutaneous infantile hemangioma (IH), which is a soft, mobile, vas- cular tumor with a bluish hue. IHs are the most common pediatric vascular tumor. Cutaneous IHs located in the cervicofacial, mandibular, or “beard” distribution (ie, chin and anterior neck) increase a child's risk for airway IHs; in fact, 50% of children with airway IHs have concomitant cutaneous IHs. Airway IHs are usually located in the subglottic region (generally the narrowest part of the pediatric airway) and can cause hoarseness, progressive stridor, or biphasic stridor that clinicians may confuse for croup; however, airway IHs often do not re- spond to racemic epinephrine (the treatment for stridor in croup). Based on the patient's age and the location of their cutaneous IH, the most likely cause of stridor is an airway IH. Airway IH is one of the life-threatening ways IHs can present. Other life-threatening IHs include liver lesions that cause high output cardiac failure, hy- pothyroidism, or bleeding from ulcerated IH. Incorrect Answer Explanations Juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis is characterized by papilloma-like lesions on the vocal cords. Although juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis could cause stridor in an in- fant this age, it is less likely in the presence of a cutaneous hemangioma, as 50% of patients with airway IHs have cutaneous IHs. Juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis typi- cally presents during infancy. It can manifest as persistent hoarseness (>6 weeks) or stridor that does not respond to racemic epinephrine. Juvenile laryngeal papillo- matosis is most often caused by HPV (thought to be vertically transmitted from in- fected mothers during birth). Laryngomalacia is characterized by flaccid supralaryngeal tissues that collapse and cause a distinctive saccade sound with inspiration. Although laryngomalacia could cause stridor in an infant this age, it is less likely the diagnosis in this patient, as a cu- taneous IH in a beard distribution increases the likelihood that the child has an air- way IH. In laryngomalacia, stridor worsens in the supine position with head and neck flexed. Most cases resolve by 12 to 24 months, but 20% of cases warrant surgical intervention. Laryngotracheitis (croup) is common in children aged 6 months to 3 years. This child's age and cutaneous findings make croup less likely, as a cutaneous IH in a beard distribution increases the likelihood that a child with stridor has an airway IH. Croup is acute and associated with URI symptoms or fever. Recurrent croup, croup that does not respond to racemic epinephrine, or croup outside of the standard age range warrants ENT referral.

question: A patient presents with a soft, mobile, 2-cm, painless subcutaneous nodule on her back. The overlying skin appears normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: The diagnosis of a lipoma can often be made clinically; lipomas are rubbery, round, ovaloid, or multilobed collections of fat cells localized to subcutaneous tissue, and they are most commonly located on the trunk, neck, arms, and axillae. Lipomas are the most common benign skin tumor. They vary in size from 1 cm to >10 cm. Lipomas typically grow to a certain size, then persist at that size. If the diagnosis is unclear, ultrasound can be used to distinguish a lipoma from other lesions, such as epidermoid cysts or ganglion cysts. Treatment includes observation or surgical exci- sion if they become symptomatic or bothersome. Incorrect Answer Explanations Dermoid cysts are congenital subcutaneous nodules found in infants and young chil- dren. The location of this lesion makes it very unlikely to be a dermoid cyst. The most common locations of dermoid cysts include the anterior fontanelle, submental re- gion, and lateral forehead near the eyebrow. Dermoid cysts are filled with epidermal and dermal tissues and can be found along embryonic fusion lines on the face, scalp, and spine. Dermoid sinuses (usually marked by a tuft of hair) can create a connection between dermoid cysts and the surface of the skin, and it may communicate with the CNS, increasing risk for meningitis. This nodule is subcutaneous and does not demonstrate a central punctum; thus, it is unlikely to be an epidermoid cyst. Epidermoid cysts are a capsule filled with keratin debris. They are firm, skin-colored, freely mobile nodules that often have a central punctum and are commonly located on the central trunk and face. Epidermoid cysts can occur as a result of trauma or simply from a plugged follicle. They are at risk for getting secondarily infected. Surgical removal of the entire capsule is standard of care. Because this nodule is located on the patient's back, it is unlikely to be a pilar cyst. Pilar cysts are hard spheres composed of keratin debris. They are dome-shaped and originate from the hair follicle, so they are most commonly located in the dermis or subcutis of the scalp. Pilar cysts do not have a punctum and are firmer than epider- moid cysts. Treatment includes complete removal of the cyst lining, as simple inci- sion and drainage will often lead to recurrence.

question: A 50-year-old patient is diagnosed with a 2-cm, painless lipoma. What is the most appropriate next step?
englishExplanation: Lipomas are diagnosed clinically and should be observed for a year for changes in size or character; they do not necessitate any intervention unless a patient has pain, is concerned about cosmesis, or if the diagnosis is unclear. Large lipomas (>5 cm) can be treated with lipolytic agents, liposuction, or excision. Lipomas are encapsulated, subcutaneous fatty tumors. They are the most common benign tumor of the skin. Lipomas are most common on the trunk or upper extremi- ties and can be round, ovaloid, or multilobulated. Painful lesions in these regions in an adolescent or young adult should raise suspicion for angiolipomas, which are more common in this age group and are often excised due to pain. Incorrect Answer Explanations Biopsy is indicated if a lipoma is >5 cm, painful, demonstrates rapid growth, appears atypical, or feels firm to touch. Biopsy would not be indicated in a 2-cm, painless lesion. Lipomas can be excised if a patient suffers from discomfort or prefers to do so for cosmetic reasons, but it is not necessary, as lipomas are benign. Most lipomas should be first managed with observation. This diagnosis of lipoma can usually be made clinically based on location, palpation, and absence of tenderness. In this situation, ultrasound is unnecessary. However, if the diagnosis is unclear, an ultrasound can differentiate lipoma from an epidermoid cyst or ganglion cyst.

question: A 35-year-old woman presents with a "huge clot" in her mouth 1 week after being accidentally hit by one of her children. She is 6 months pregnant but has no preg- nancy-related complaints. She says the lesion does not hurt but bleeds easily if ir- ritated. The physical examination reveals minor oozing. What is the diagnosis? Credit: Diann Krywko, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation: Pyogenic granuloma is the commonly used term for the vascular lesion depicted in this case. In pregnant patients, it might be referred to as granuloma gravidarum. Neither name is accurate, however, as this benign collection of capillaries is not granulomatous, purulent, or infective; lobular capillary he- mangioma is a better term. It develops as a result of minor skin (or in this case, mu- cosal) trauma in about one third of patients and occurs most commonly in children, pregnant women, and younger adults. Usually found on the hands or other ex- tremities, its appearance is usually shiny and bright red; the lesion bleeds easily and briskly when touched. In fact, bleeding is usually the impetus for seeking care in the emergency department. Suggested interventions to treat the bleeding include pressure, suturing, and silver nitrate (although not on the face). In pregnant patients, this type of hemangioma can resolve spontaneously after delivery. For this reason, unless the lesion is actively bleeding, conservative management and waiting until the postpartum period are prudent. In general, patients should be re- ferred for biopsy and histology to evaluate for other more serious causes, and for de- finitive treatment. Follow-up depends on the area of the body affected, either surgery or dermatology for skin lesions or dentist/oral surgeon for oral lesions. Recurrence rate can be as high as 40% if nonsurgical means are used for removal. Incorrect Answer Explanations Gingivitis presents as more diffuse irritation of the gingiva. A focal lesion such as this is not consistent with gingivitis and is more consistent with a pyogenic granuloma. Melanomas can be discolored, but they tend to be brown and are not as large as this lesion is. The “ABCDE Checklist” is a tool for remembering the diagnos- tic criteria of a melanoma: Asymmetry, Border, Color, Diameter/Difference, Elevation/Evolving. A periodontal abscess is a pus-filled cavity. This lesion is vascular, not an ab- scess, and is consistent with pyogenic granuloma.

question: What is a risk factor for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS)?
englishExplanation: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is caused by the hematoge- nous spread of exfoliative toxins produced by Staphylococcus aureus. Although this disorder most commonly occurs in young children, cases in older chil- dren and adults do occur, particularly when a patient has a serious underlying illness such as kidney disease. Increased incidence in the setting of kidney disease is be- lieved to be a result of diminished excretion of exotoxins. Additional risk factors that lead to elevated levels of circulating exotoxin include immunodefi- ciency and overwhelming staphylococcal infection. In addition to antibiotics (usually penicillins), treatment of SSSS should include analgesic medication, appropriate fluid replacement, and gentle wound care. Tight dressings and adhesives should be avoided, as these can worsen bullae formation and desquamation. Patients are typically admitted for initial inpa- tient management, although discharge on oral antibiotics after a short hospitalization may be appropriate if the patient responds to intravenous treatment. For severe cases of SSSS, admission to a burn unit or ICU may be required. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although SSSS is most common in children, this disorder typically occurs in in- dividuals younger than 6, with a peak incidence at ages 2 to 3. Increased suscep- tibility in young children may be attributable to decreased circulating antibodies that neutralize exfoliative toxins produced by S. aureus as well as decreased rates of renal excretion of the formed toxins. SSSS is more common in Caucasian children. Thus, Black race is not considered a risk factor. Peak incidence of SSSS occurs in summer and fall months. Thus, S. aureus infection in the winter is not a risk factor. Key Points Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome occurs most commonly in children younger than 6. Risk for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is increased by elevated levels of circu- lating Staphylococcus aureus exfoliative toxins, which may occur from decreased ex- cretion (eg, kidney disease) or factors contributing to more severe infection (eg, im- munodeficiency, diabetes mellitus). Incidence of staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome exhibits seasonal variation, with the disorder occurring more frequently in the summer and fall months.

question: By what route does Staphylococcus aureus mediate skin damage in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS)?

options.text: Inflammatory mediator release in cell apoptosis

englishExplanation: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is caused by the hematoge- nous spread of exfoliative toxins produced by Staphylococcus aureus. Exfoliative toxins spread from a distant site of infection (eg, pharyngitis, cellulitis, otitis media) to the skin, resulting in erythema, bullae, and sub- sequent characteristic desquamation. Bullae are formed by exfoliative toxins A and B, which cleave desmoglein 1 in the upper epidermis, causing bullae formation and superficial desquamation. A positive Nikolsky sign demonstrated by skin sloughing with gentle mechanical pressure will be present on physical examination. Notably, the source of S. aureus infection may not be readily apparent at the time of symptom development in SSSS. This disorder is most common in young children. Incorrect Answer Explanations The release of inflammatory mediators following p53-mediated apoptosis of ker- atinocytes contributes to the pain and erythema in skin damaged by ultraviolet B light, also known as sunburn. This process does not occur in SSSS. SSSS results from the hematogenous spread of exfoliative toxins and oc- curs following infection at a site distant to rash formation. Like SSSS, bul- lous impetigo also occurs from exfoliative toxins produced by S. aureus. The exfolia- tive toxins are believed to be the same in both disorders. The lesions produced in bullous impetigo, however, occur from localized infection as opposed to hematogenous spread. Immune system activation is implicated in several skin disorders that overlap with SSSS in clinical presentation, including staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome and Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS-TEN). Damage in SSSS, however, occurs from the direct interaction between outer skin pro- teins and hematogenous exfoliative toxins and does not involve immune system activation. Key Points Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome occurs following S. aureus infection at a dis- tant site as opposed to a localized skin infection. Exfoliative toxins involved in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome are transported to sites of skin involvement via hematogenous spread. Skin lesions in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome are caused by the direct interac- tion of exfoliative toxins with connective proteins (eg, desmoglein 1) in the upper epidermis.

question: Which life-threatening skin disorder has mucocutaneous involvement, a positive Nikolsky sign, and full-thickness skin sloughing involving approximately 8% of to- tal body surface area?
englishExplanation:
Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) is a life-threatening dermatologic condition de- scribed as a diffuse rash with target lesions that progress to blisters and bullae. SJS involves the hands, soles, and mucous membranes with full-thickness skin necrosis affecting less than 10% of the total body surface area (BSA). SJS is often caused by a drug reaction, although infection and malignancy have also been implicated. SJS was once described as part of a continuum of dermatologic condi- tions starting with erythema multiforme (EM), progressing to SJS, and culminating in toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). However, EM is now believed to be distinct from SJS and TEN. SJS is defined as skin detachment of <10% BSA, whereas TEN is more se- vere, defined as >30% BSA skin detachment. Another entity, SJS/TEN overlap, is defined as skin detachment of 10% to 30% BSA. Treatment for SJS requires hospitalization in an ICU or burn unit for optimal administration of flu- ids and electrolytes, control of pain and infection, and cessation of the offending agent. Incorrect Answer Explanations Erythema multiforme (EM) is a discrete rash known best for its target le- sion appearance. It is associated with several culprits: infections (HSV), drugs (sulfa and other antibiotics, anticonvulsants), autoimmune diseases, and idiopathic etiologies. There are two classifications of EM: minor and major. EM minor is a self-limited rash that mostly involves the extremities and has no pro- dromal symptoms or mucous membrane involvement. Outpatient treatment and sup- portive care are usually adequate. EM major is more severe, starting with a pro- dromal viral illness and progressing to a rash that involves the palms, soles, and mu- cous membranes. Treatment typically includes observation to ensure the disease does not progress further. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS), also known as Ritter dis- ease or dermatitis exfoliativa neonatorum, is a diffuse, tender, scarlatini- form erythematous rash. It causes skin blisters and sloughing (positive Nikolsky sign), but the mucous membranes are spared. It is most often seen in infants and has a low mortality rate of less than 5%. Although SSSS is rare in adults, it has a much higher mortality rate when it does occur in adults. An exfoliative toxin in cer- tain strains of Staphylococcus aureus causes SSSS. Both SSSS and bullous im- petigo are blistering skin diseases caused by the staphylococcal exfolia- tive toxin. In bullous impetigo, the exfoliative toxins are restricted to the area of in- fection, and bacteria can be cultured from the blister contents. In SSSS, the exfolia- tive toxins spread hematogenously, causing epidermal damage at distant sites; the bullous materials are sterile. Treatment consists of supportive care (fluids and pain control) and eradication of the primary infection. Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), also known as Lyell disease, is a life- threatening dermatologic condition characterized by a diffuse, erythema- tous macular rash that coalesces to form bullae; necrosis develops, and the epidermis separates from the dermis. SJS and TEN are thought to be part of a spectrum of disease. SJS is the less severe form, with <10% BSA of skin detach- ment; TEN is more severe, with >30% BSA skin detachment. SJS/TEN overlap en- compasses 10% to 30% BSA of skin detachment. Mucosal involvement and positive Nikolsky sign are both present. In TEN, symptoms first affect the eyes, then spread caudally to the thorax and upper extremities, and finally progress to the lower body, involving more than 30% of BSA. TEN is most commonly drug-induced (sulfa, penicillin, and NSAIDs are implicated) but has also been associated with infection, malignancy, and vaccines. People with AIDS who are taking sulfa prophylaxis have a thousand-fold higher risk of developing TEN. Patients with TEN are treated in an ICU or burn unit. Administration of the offending agent is stopped, and fluids, electrolytes, and pain and infection control are provided. To date, no spe- cific therapy has proven effective. Despite hospitalization and aggressive resuscita- tion, the mortality rate in patients with TEN remains high secondary to sepsis and multisystem organ failure. Key Points Stevens-Johnsons syndrome is a life-threatening condition. Characteristics of Stevens-Johnson syndrome include diffuse rash, target lesion, bul- lae, involvement of hands or soles and mucous membranes, full-thickness necrosis, less than 30% total body surface area.

question: What is characteristic of Henoch-Schönlein purpura?

options.text: Flat red rash that spreads from the face to the trunk in areas of pressure or minor traumas
Maculopapular rash in the distal joints that spreads centrally
Lower-extremity rash that appears in crops

correctAnswer: Lower-extremity rash that appears in crops
englishExplanation: Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP) is a small-vessel vasculitis typically seen in children who present with symptoms including rash, abdominal pain, joint pain, and hematuria after a URI. The rash typically begins as sym- metrical maculopapular lesions on the buttocks and lower extremities that appear in crops and then become palpable purpuric lesions. Supportive treatment is usually all that is needed for HSP, and it is usually self-limit- ing over 3 to 4 weeks. Patients requiring hospitalization are those with uncontrollable pain, renal insufficiency, GI bleeding, changes in mental status, or dehydration. Skin necrosis is very rare with HSP. Incorrect Answer Explanations A red, flat red rash that starts on the face and spreads down to the neck, trunk, arms, and legs that coalesces over time is classic for the rash of measles (rubeola). Measles is an acute viral respiratory illness that is very conta- gious. It is classically described by the three C's: cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. Other symptoms of measles include fever, barky cough, erythematous eyes, rhinor- rhea, and fatigue. Vascular occlusion can cause areas of purpura with necrosis in patients taking warfarin. Warfarin-induced skin necrosis can occur early in warfarin therapy, as a transient hypercoagulable state may be present. A blanching maculopapular rash that begins over the distal joints, spreads centrally, and progresses into petechiae more classically de- scribes the rash of Rocky Mountain spotted fever. The rash in HSP is classi- cally found in dependent areas, such as in the lower extremities and buttocks; how- ever, it can be found in the trunk and extremities in children that are unable to walk. Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) may occur in children following a viral infec- tion. Thrombocytopenia usually causes purpura or petechiae in areas of pressure or minor trauma, such as along the waist from the underwear band or the ante- rior shins from bumping into things. Skin necrosis can sometimes occur with this condition.

question: How are purpura best described?

options.text: Any skin eruption resulting from extravasated blood
Fluid-filled circumscribed lesion larger than 0.5 cm in diameter
Nonpalpable circumscribed area of skin color change
Superficial, elevated, solid lesion smaller than 0.5 cm in diameter

correctAnswer: Any skin eruption resulting from extravasated blood
englishExplanation: Knowledge of how to accurately identify and describe skin lesions is required in order to correctly diagnose dermatologic conditions. Purpura describes any skin erup- tion resulting from extravasated blood, including petechiae (<3 mm). Purpuric lesions may be caused by minor trauma (eg, bruises) or may be the harbin- ger of life-threatening illness (eg, purpura fulminans). Purpura can be various shades of color that are consistent with hemorrhage. Since the blood is extravascular, a defining characteristic of purpura is that the lesions do not blanch; this is in contrast to many blanchable erythematous lesions resulting from blood vessel vasodilation in which the mobile intravascular RBCs move with compression. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bullae are fluid-filled circumscribed lesions that are larger than 1 cm in diameter. Bullae are filled with watery, clear fluid. The differential diagnosis of bul- lae includes infection, drug reactions, contact dermatitis, sunburn, and rheumato- logic disease, among others. Macules are nonpalpable circumscribed areas of skin color change that are less than 1 cm in size; patches are greater than 1 cm in size. The differential diagnosis of macules includes infectious disease, drug reactions, rheumatologic dis- ease, and melanoma, among others. Macules may be benign (nevi or Mongolian spots). A papule is a superficial, elevated, solid lesion that is smaller than 0.5 cm in diameter. Papules may be isolated (as seen in warts and neoplastic disease, in- cluding basal cell and squamous cell carcinomas) or be part of a larger papular erup- tion (as seen in acne, drug eruptions, and molluscum contagiosum, among others).

question: A 6-year-old patient who was recently treated for streptococcal pharyngitis presents with a temperature of 38.2°C (100.8°F), a purpuric rash on the legs and buttocks, lymphadenopathy, and bilateral ankle pain. The remainder of the exami- nation results are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: This patient likely has hypersensitivity vasculitis due to a beta-lactam an- tibiotic. Hypersensitivity vasculitis (also known as serum sickness or serum sick- ness–like reaction) is characterized by small vessel inflammation. It manifests as palpable purpura (usually in the lower extremities), urticaria, fever, arthritis/arthralgia, malaise, and lymphadenopathy. Symptoms usually de- velop 7 to 10 days after antigen exposure. After cessation of the inciting drug, symp- toms usually resolve over days to weeks. Platelets and coagulation labs should be nor- mal, but mild leukocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), and low complement levels (C3 or C4) may be seen. A biopsy in hypersensitivity vasculitis would demonstrate leukocytoclastic vasculitis but would not show IgA deposition. A similar condition on the differential is IgA vasculitis (also known as Henoch- Schönlein purpura [HSP]). Like hypersensitivity vasculitis, IgA vasculitis is a leukocytoclastic vasculitis of the small vessels. It can manifest as palpable purpura (without thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy), arthritis/arthralgia, abdomi- nal pain, or kidney disease, but these findings are not always present. Streptococcal infection can be a trigger for HSP. The arthritis and arthralgia usually manifest in the joints of the lower extremities. A diagnosis of IgA vasculitis can generally be made clinically. Platelet and coagulation studies, if performed, are normal. Urinalysis should be performed to evaluate for proteinuria. Patients with IgA vas- culitis can generally be treated with NSAIDs and supportive care. They must be monitored closely in the outpatient setting for evidence of IgA nephritis. Although a skin biopsy in both hypersensitivity vasculitis and IgA vasculitis would demonstrate leukocytoclastic vasculitis, a biopsy in hypersensitivity vasculitis would not show IgA deposition. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) should be considered in a patient with a rash 2 to 4 weeks after a group A streptococcal infection. However, this pa- tient does not meet the diagnostic criteria for ARF. Additionally, the child received a course of antibiotics, which decreases the risk of ARF. ARF occurs 1 to 5 weeks after group A streptococcal pharyngitis and is generally characterized by chorea, carditis, arthritis, subcutaneous nodules, and erythema marginatum. To be diagnosed with ARF, a child must either meet two major criteria or one major criterion and two mi- nor criteria. The major criteria are arthritis, carditis/valvulitis, CNS involvement, subcutaneous nodules, and erythema marginatum. The minor criteria are arthralgia; fever; prolonged PR interval on ECG; and elevated acute phase reactants, CRP, and ESR. Child abuse should always be on the differential in a child who presents with purpura or ecchymotic lesions. However, the presence of a low-grade fever, recent antibiotic use, and diffuse skin and joint findings in this patient make traumatic bruising from child abuse unlikely. The TEN-4-FACES tool can help clinicians stratify risk in chil- dren with bruising. This tool reminds clinicians that bruising is most concerning for child abuse when noted on a child's torso, ear, or neck; in children younger than 4 years (especially ≤5 months); or when a frenulum tear or a facial or patterned bruise is noted. Lyme disease can lead to fever, myalgias, arthralgias, and a rash, typically targetoid (known as erythema migrans). This rash is not usually characterized by pur- pura, but rather, targetoid in nature. Lyme disease is caused by the bacteria borrelia burgdorferi, typically spread from exposure to a tick bite. Lyme disease can sometimes manifest with unknown exposure to a tick bite. Lyme disease should not present after streptococcal pharyngitis and antibiotics. In fact, amoxicillin is one of the antibiotics (likely given in this case) used to treat Lyme disease. Other antibiotics used for Lyme disease include doxycycline and cefuroxime.

question: Which finding distinguishes poison ivy dermatitis from phytophotodermatitis?
englishExplanation: Poison ivy dermatitis is characterized by intense pruritus. Phytophotodermatitis can be intensely painful, but is not pruritic. Poison ivy dermatitis is a type IV hypersen- sitivity reaction to the protein urushiol, which is present in poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac. Approximately 70% of people are sensitized to these plants. Dermatitis occurs after direct exposure to the protein, which is released by damaged plants. Treatment includes supportive care, topical corticosteroids for mild reac- tions, and oral corticosteroids for severe reactions. Phytophotodermatitis is a phototoxic reaction that occurs after topical exposures to certain plant-derived substances, including celery, parsnip, parsley, lemons, and limes. This condition is frequently seen in gardeners, children, and food-industry workers. Skin manifestations are similar to those of poison ivy dermatitis, with the exception of being isolated to sun-exposed areas. Treatment includes sun avoid- ance, broad-spectrum sunscreen, supportive measures, and topical or oral steroids for more severe reactions. When compared to poison ivy dermatitis, phytophotoder- matitis carries an increased risk of prolonged hyperpigmentation (months to years) of affected areas. Incorrect Answer Explanations Both conditions manifest multiple hours after exposure, so the delay would not dif- ferentiate between the two. Because it is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction, poison ivy dermatitis generally manifests 4 to 96 hours after exposure. Phytophotodermatitis generally manifests 24 hours after sun exposure. Both poison ivy dermatitis and phytophotodermatitis manifest as papules, plaques, or bullae in a linear, patterned distribution. One distinguishing factor in appearance is that phytophotodermatitis should only manifest on sun-exposed regions of the skin. Poison ivy dermatitis will occur on the areas of the skin that were exposed to the plant, or more specifically, the urushiol. Both conditions are caused by exposures to plants. Poison ivy dermatitis is caused by exposure to poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac, as urushiol protein in all three cross-reacts. Phytophotodermatitis can be caused by fig, St. John's wort, and many herbs and vegetables.

question: A 3-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with worms in her vagina. Her parent says that while changing the girl’s diaper earlier in the day, she noticed approximately four small white worms in the vaginal area. She wiped them away and applied diaper cream. However, the worms have returned and the parent is distressed. The child has been well otherwise. She is playful and interactive, with normal vital signs. On exam, she has small white worms crawling near her anus without other findings. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
englishExplanation:
This story and physical exam are consistent with pinworms, or Enterobius vermicularis. Pinworms are one of the most common nematode infections in the world and the most common in the United States. The intestinal parasite is transmitted by the fecal-oral route and is often acquired from contaminated bedding and toys where people are living in crowded conditions. The worms are most often found in children. Enterobius vermicularis eggs are ingested and hatch into larvae in the small intestine. The larvae migrate to the large intestine where they mature and meet. Gravid adult females travel to the perianal region at night to lay eggs, which cause the most common symptom of intense anal itching. The eggs become infective within a short period of time and get deposited on clothes, sheets, and under fingernails. Finger sucking and nail biting lead to autoinfection. Eggs can be visualized with the tape test. Tape is pressed against the perianal region and then placed on a glass slide to visualize the eggs under a microscope. The diagnosis is often made by visual inspection of the anal area where mobile white, pin-shaped worms are seen. Worms and eggs are generally not passed in the stool. Effective treatment is with a single dose of albendazole or mebendazole, and then a repeat dose in 2 weeks. Treatment of the entire household is warranted, and families should be instructed to wash all clothing and bedding and improve hygiene practices such as clipping fingernails, washing hands, and taking more frequent baths.



Intravenous ciprofloxacin (A) is indicated for patients with bacterial diarrhea. This patient does not have diarrhea, and ciprofloxacin does not treat parasitic infections.

Oral metronidazole (C) is the recommended therapy for protozoan infections, most commonly Giardia lamblia. Protozoan infections typically present with diarrhea and bloating. This patient is not presenting with symptoms of giardiasis.

Topical clotrimazole (D) is used to treat fungal infections, such as diaper rash, but is not indicated for the treatment of pinworms.

Reveal Answer:

question: A 7-year-old boy presents to the ED with bilateral elbow, knee, and abdominal pain. Physical exam reveals the above. Which of the following is the pathophysiology underlying this disease process?
englishExplanation:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms of immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV), formerly known as Henoch-Schönlein purpura. IgA vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis that occurs primarily in children. It presents with the classic triad of purpura, arthritis, and abdominal pain. Signs and symptoms include palpable purpura of the lower extremities and buttocks (dependent areas), colicky abdominal pain, bloody stool, arthritis of the wrists, elbows, and knees, scrotal edema, gross hematuria (rare), and hypertension secondary to kidney involvement.

Diagnosis is largely clinical. However, laboratory tests, such as a CBC, BMP, INR, and a urinalysis should be performed to rule out other diagnoses. Kidney impairment is the most serious complication of IgAV and is in up to 50% of patients. In contrast to other diseases that present with purpura, the platelet count will be normal or high. Coagulation studies, such as an INR, will be normal. A urinalysis may reveal hematuria and proteinuria. Management is supportive. Most patients have spontaneous resolution of symptoms in 4–6 weeks. Patients with IgAV should be admitted if there is severe arthritis, evidence of intussusception, or any sign of kidney involvement, including significant hypertension, elevated creatinine, or significant proteinuria.



Autoimmune platelet destruction (A) is the cause of immune thrombocytopenia, which presents with isolated thrombocytopenia.

Deficiency in ADAMTS13 (B), which is a metalloprotease, is the cause of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). TTP presents with thrombocytopenia, fever, kidney impairment, altered mental status, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.

Hereditary decrease in factor VIII (C) is the cause of hemophilia A, a bleeding disorder. These patients will often have an elevated PTT and spontaneous bleeding depending upon the severity of the disease process. It is an X-linked recessive disorder.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the appropriate treatment for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura?

Reveal Answer:
Plasmapheresis.

Sx: rash that begins on buttocks and lower extremities, abdominal pain, arthralgia, hematuria, proteinuria
PE: pink papules → raised purpura → ecchymosis that is not painful
Tx: supportive care
Complications: nephropathy (ESKD more common in adults), intussusception (more common in children)

The patient is irritable on arrival and reports no other symptoms and wants to leave. His T is 97.6°F (36.4°C), BP is 121/81 mm Hg, HR is 81 bpm, RR is 17/min, and SpO2 is 99% on room air. Physical exam is notable for the finding above. The patient has a history of hives when receiving penicillin. Which of the following is the most appropriate management after cleansing and exploring the wound and ensuring no foreign bodies are present on X-ray?
englishExplanation:
Bite injuries increase the risk of infection. In particular, human bites are polymicrobial and may cause infection with Staphylococcus aureus, viridans streptococci, Eikenella corrodens, Bacteroides, and Peptostreptococcus. Initial management of a human bite focuses on thorough irrigation and examination of the wound, which helps reduce the risk of subsequent infection. The patient's tetanus vaccination status should be updated if it has been > 10 years since the last vaccination. Imaging is also indicated to rule out the presence of a foreign body.

Patients with a human bite should receive prophylactic antibiotic treatment. The preferred first-line agent is amoxicillin-clavulanate. Other appropriate antibiotic regimens in patients who are allergic to penicillin include doxycycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole or clindamycin as second-line treatment options. Treatment duration is 3–5 days. Patients with infected wounds or systemic symptoms or those requiring surgical debridement may be treated with IV antibiotics, with ampicillin-sulbactam as the preferred first-line treatment.



Ceftriaxone, metronidazole, and hospital admission (A) may be an appropriate treatment regimen for a human bite in patients with systemic symptoms or those requiring surgical debridement due to deep injuries or seeded infection. Admission is not necessary for all bite injuries.

Cephalexin and discharge (B) is appropriate management of an uncomplicated cellulitis that presents with warmth, erythema, and tenderness of the skin. It does not offer sufficient coverage for a human bite that includes the organism Eikenella corrodens.

Ciprofloxacin plus clindamycin is an appropriate antibiotic regimen for treating a human bite in a patient allergic to penicillin. However, ciprofloxacin monotherapy (C) would be insufficient. When choosing to use these antibiotics, it is essential to remember that fluoroquinolones are associated with numerous side effects, including tendon rupture, aortic injury, and delirium in older patients. Clindamycin carries an increased risk of antibiotic-associated diarrhea and Clostridioides difficile infection.

One Step Further
Question:
In what location are bite wounds typically sutured closed for an improved cosmetic outcome?

Reveal Answer:
The face.

Human Bites

Polymicrobial (Eikenella corrodens)
Hand wounds: irrigate and leave open
Fight bites: associated boxer fracture of fourth or fifth metacarpal
Tx: Abx for all (amoxicillin-clavulanate)
IV Abx and surgical debridement may be needed for deep space infection, open joint, tendon involvement, necrotizing infection

question: A 65-year-old man with hypertension presents to the emergency department for a progressive skin nodule on his face for several months. Examination reveals a 1 cm skin-colored lesion with raised pearly margins and visible vessels on his left cheek. He reports no other associated symptoms or lesions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Basal cell carcinoma is the most common of the nonmelanotic skin cancers, present in older patients on sun-exposed areas such as the head, neck, and scalp. It will typically begin as a small raised lesion with smooth pearly edges that will progress in size and may show telangiectatic vessels. Other risk factors include immunosuppression and ionizing radiation. There is no acute treatment for basal cell carcinoma in the emergency department. However, patients should receive short interval follow-up with dermatology and will likely require a biopsy for definitive treatment. In general, basal cell carcinoma has low metastatic potential, but lesions on the lips, ears, and nose carry a higher risk.



Kerion (B) is a fungal infection caused by Trichophyton spp that presents with painful, raised, purulent scalp lesions leading to hair loss in the affected area. Kerions should be treated with oral griseofulvin.

Melanoma (C) is a malignant growth of melanocytes commonly seen in middle-aged patients. They appear as rapidly enlarging pigmented lesions with irregular borders, and treatment involves dermatology referral for definitive diagnosis and care.

Squamous cell carcinoma (D) is the second most common nonmelanotic skin cancer, presenting with ulcerated papules on the head and neck and in chronic wounds. Patients with these lesions should also be referred for dermatology follow-up.

One Step Further
Question:
What skin lesion commonly precedes squamous cell carcinoma?

Reveal Answer:
Actinic keratosis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Basal Cell Carcinoma

Most common type of skin cancer
Sx: painless, slow-growing lesion
Subtypes include nodular (most common), superficial, morpheaform
Nodular: pearly papule with rolled borders or telangiectasia on face, ears, neck
Superficial: slightly scaly plaque on trunk
Dx: clinical exam, dermoscopy, shave, punch, or excisional biopsy
Tx options include surgical excision for lesions with a low recurrence risk, Mohs micrographic surgery for lesions with a high recurrence risk
Prevention includes sunscreen, UV light protection

question: An 80-year-old woman with a medical history of Parkinson disease presents with a rash. For several weeks, she has had a pruritic, erythematous rash involving her chest, abdomen, and arms. She was recently seen at urgent care, where she was diagnosed with urticaria and prescribed antihistamines. Over the last several days, she has developed large blisters and continues to have significant itching. She has not had any new exposures and has no systemic symptoms. Her vital signs are unremarkable. On physical exam, the patient has multiple tense bullae scattered across her trunk, axillae, and the flexural surfaces of her arms. There is no mucous membrane involvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This older patient, who presents with pruritic, tense bullae preceded by an urticaria-like rash, most likely has bullous pemphigoid. Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune blistering disease characterized by tense subepithelial blisters due to autoantibody deposition at the epithelial basement membrane. Autoantibodies target two hemidesmosomal proteins, bullous pemphigoid antigen 180 and bullous pemphigoid antigen 230. Bullous pemphigoid is largely a disease found in older patients, with most presenting between ages 60–75. Observational data suggest an association with several chronic neurological conditions, including multiple sclerosis, dementia, and Parkinson disease, but no causal relationship has been proven. Prior to the development of blisters, there is often a prodromal phase characterized by pruritic eczematous patches or urticaria-like plaques. The classic lesion of bullous pemphigoid is a tense fluid-filled bulla on an erythematous base that is often intensely pruritic. As the bullae rupture, a crusted erosion is left behind that heals without scarring. It is most commonly distributed on the trunk, flexural surfaces of the arms, groin, and axillae, though some patients have a localized form affecting a specific body region, such as the anogenital area or lower legs. Approximately 10–30% of patients will have mucous membrane involvement, most frequently in the oral cavity.

The diagnosis is made through the combination of clinical findings, serum autoantibody testing, and examination of tissue via routine histopathology and direct immunofluorescence. Mild disease is treated with high-potency topical steroids. Moderate to severe disease often requires a prolonged systemic steroid taper, with the possibility of adding a steroid-sparing agent such as doxycycline combined with niacinamide, dapsone, methotrexate, or mycophenolate.



Contact dermatitis (B) presents with pruritic, erythematous, scaly plaques and is caused by exposure to an irritant or allergen. While severe cases of contact dermatitis may involve blistering, large tense bullae are not common. Additionally, this patient has no new exposures to likely contact allergens. Pemphigus vulgaris (C) is a chronic blistering condition characterized by flaccid blisters that easily erode, as opposed to the tense blisters of bullous pemphigoid. Nearly all patients with pemphigus vulgaris have mucous membrane involvement. Patients with Stevens-Johnson syndrome (D) are ill appearing and have mucosal involvement. Cutaneous blisters are painful and flaccid, leading to generalized skin sloughing.

One Step Further
Question:
What cancer treatment has been associated with drug-induced bullous pemphigoid?

Reveal Answer:
Immune checkpoint inhibitors.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Bullous Pemphigoid

Autoimmune blistering condition
Most common in patients aged > 60 years
Sx and findings: intensely pruritic lesions → large, tense blisters or bullae → rupture w/ formation of erosion/crust
PE: tense and firm blisters that do not extend with lateral pressure
Nikolsky sign negative: absence of slippage of the epidermis from the dermis when slight rubbing pressure is applied to the skin
Tx options: wound care, corticosteroids, doxycycline, immunosuppressants

question: A 4-year-old boy presents to the ED with diffuse joint pain and swelling. On physical exam, you note the above findings. Which of the following is a complication of this disease process?
englishExplanation:
Immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV), formerly known as Henoch-Schönlein purpura, is a small-vessel vasculitis that occurs primarily in children. It presents with the classic triad of purpura, arthritis, and abdominal pain. Signs and symptoms of IgAV include palpable purpura of the lower extremities and buttocks (dependent areas), colicky abdominal pain, scrotal edema, gross hematuria (rare), hypertension secondary to kidney involvement, and arthritis of the wrists, elbows, and knees. The colicky abdominal pain in IgAV can be related to ileoileal intussusception and requires an abdominal ultrasound to identify.

Diagnosis of IgAV is clinical, but laboratory testing, including a CBC, BMP, coagulation studies, and a urinalysis, should be performed. Kidney impairment is the most serious complication of IgAV and occurs in up to 40% of patients. The serum creatinine may be elevated, and there may be evidence of proteinuria and hematuria. Management of IgAV is supportive. Most patients have spontaneous resolution of symptoms in 4–6 weeks. If ileoileal intussusception is present, barium or air enema should be performed to reduce the intussusception. Patients with IgAV should be admitted if there is severe arthritis causing difficulty with ambulation, evidence of intussusception, or any sign of kidney involvement, including hypertension, elevated creatinine, and significant proteinuria.



Hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis (A) is associated with pyloric stenosis and is secondary to recurrent projectile nonbilious vomiting.

In Meckel diverticulum, ectopic gastric tissue can erode into the intestinal mucosa, causing potentially massive and painless gastrointestinal bleeding (C). While bloody stools can be seen in patients with IgAV, this is secondary to intussusception and resultant ischemia and is generally painful.

Toxic megacolon (D) is associated with long-standing constipation secondary to Hirschsprung disease. It occurs when massive dilation of the colon proximal to the aganglionic segment occurs, leading to bloody stool, fever, and a high risk of colonic perforation.

One Step Further

What is the most common presentation for patients with malrotation and midgut volvulus?

Reveal Answer:
Bilious emesis.

IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis most common in children 3–15 years old
10% of cases occur in adults
Risk factors: history of recent URI
Sx: rash that begins on buttocks and lower extremities, abdominal pain, arthralgia, hematuria, proteinuria
PE: pink papules → raised purpura → ecchymosis that is not painful
Tx: supportive care
Complications: nephropathy (ESKD more common in adults), intussusception (more common in children)

question: A 54-year-old man with diabetes presents with severe leg pain. The pain has worsened over the last two days with increased swelling of the calf. He has no chest pain or shortness of breath. Vital signs are: T 101.8°F, BP 98/62, HR 118, RR 18. Physical examination is notable for erythema of the calf, severe tenderness, and crepitus. You initiate IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: CT scan with intravenous contrast of the lower extremity
Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremity
Measurement of serum lactate and CPK

englishExplanation:
Necrotizing fasciitis is an infection of the subcutaneous tissue that spreads rapidly across the fascial planes and is often fatal even with aggressive treatment. Risk factors for necrotizing infections include diabetes, vascular insufficiency, and immunosuppression. Classically, patients have pain out of proportion to examination. Later findings include diffuse swelling, erythema, induration, and crepitus. The gold standard for diagnosis is direct visualization in the operating room by a surgeon. Surgeons may elect to perform a bedside biopsy prior to full exploration. Management includes aggressive IV hydration, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and surgical debridement.



CT scan with intravenous contrast of the lower extremity (A) may demonstrate findings suggestive of a necrotizing infection including subcutaneous gas, stranding along the fascial planes, or fluid collection. However, the negative predictive value of CT scan has not been quantified and is not yet considered the gold standard. Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremity (B) may be helpful in identifying venous thrombosis as a cause of edema and fullness of the leg. Additionally, sonography may visualize an area of deep fluid collection and may demonstrate artifact from a significant amount of subcutaneous air, if present. Measurement of serum lactate and CPK (C) is helpful when positive but not sensitive enough to rule out the diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis. The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) incorporates other laboratory markers (CRP, WBC, hemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose) into a decision-rule, however, it lacks sufficient sensitivity in larger studies.

What is the name of necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum?

Reveal Answer:
Fournier gangrene.
