question: A 78-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a chief concern about a new rash. The patient has a medical history of rheumatoid arthritis, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus. He states the rash started 3 days ago with a red lesion that was pruritic. Yesterday, he noticed this lesion had transformed into a 5 mm blister. Today, he states the lesion has increased in size to approximately 1.5 cm, and there are now several other new lesions. There is associated pruritus which he states is quite severe. He’s otherwise feeling well and has no other symptoms. Vital signs are within normal limits. His physical examination reveals several tense fluid-filled bullae and blisters on bilateral upper extremities. Traction on the skin does not produce any extension of the bullae or blisters. There are no other lesions or concerning findings on physical examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune disorder that causes blistering and formation of bullae. This disorder is caused by immunoglobulins and complement deposition within the epidermal basement membrane. This deposition is ultimately what leads to the presentation of blister and bullae formation. Classically this occurs in older patients, usually over the age of 60. This is a chronic disorder and is known for fluctuating exacerbations and remissions. Clinical features may include a prodromal phase that precedes the formation of blisters. This prodromal phase is characterized by pruritic eczematous, papular, or urticarial-like skin lesions. This may be the only clinical feature a patient develops, whereas others develop 1–3 cm bulla. The bullae are tense with an erythematous, urticarial, or noninflammatory base. Pruritus is commonly associated with the bullae and can be quite severe. Extension of the blister with skin traction (Nikolsky sign) is not present. This, along with how tense the blister is, helps differentiate bullous pemphigoid from pemphigus vulgaris.

Diagnosis is made by both clinical and laboratory findings. Although clinical findings may suggest the diagnosis, other disease processes can present similarly. Thus, laboratory confirmation is needed. Skin biopsy from the edge of an intact blister or serum testing evaluating for basement membrane antibodies helps confirm the diagnosis. Treatment consists of both topical and systemic glucocorticoids, with topical being first-line. When the disease process is extensive or if topical treatment is not practical, feasible, or fails, systemic treatments should be administered.



Pemphigus vulgaris (B)is a life-threatening blistering disease that is characterized by acantholysis secondary to the binding of circulating IgG to epithelial cells. It is the most common form of pemphigus but still remains a rare disorder. Flaccid bullae that extend with skin traction are classic characteristics that help differentiate the disease process from other blistering diseases. The average age of onset is between 40 and 60 years and both men and women are equally affected. Clinical features include flaccid bullae or blisters that will almost always have mucosal involvement. In fact, the oral cavity represents the most common initial site of disease. The blisters rupture easily resulting in painful erosions. The diagnosis is made by clinical, histologic, and serological findings.

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (C)is caused by certain strains of Staphylococcus aureus that release an exfoliating toxin that results in impaired cell adhesion, blistering, and superficial denuding of the skin. It most commonly occurs in infants and young children. Patients classically present in the first week of life and are febrile and irritable with diffuse blanching erythema that is often around the mouth. Flaccid blisters occur 1–2 days after initial presentation. The diagnosis is based on clinical presentation which includes a positive Nikolsky sign and skin biopsy. Treatment consists of intravenous penicillinase-resistant penicillin (nafcillin or oxacillin) or vancomycin in areas with a high prevalence of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis (D) is a severe mucocutaneous reaction that is most commonly triggered by medications and is characterized by extensive necrosis and detachment of the epidermis. Toxic epidermal necrolysis is on a continuum with Stevens-Johnson syndrome with the latter being diagnosed when < 10% of the total body surface area is involved. When > 30% of the body surface area is involved, toxic epidermal necrolysis is diagnosed. Medications such as allopurinol, anticonvulsants, lamotrigine, sulfonamide antimicrobials, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital are the medications that most commonly trigger the reaction. Clinical features include a prodromal phase which includes a fever and influenza-like symptoms that occur 1–3 days before the onset of cutaneous lesions. These lesions are classically erythematous macules with purpuric centers that are ill-defined and often coalesce. Mucosal involvement occurs in the majority of patients. Nikolsky sign is often present on examination. Diagnosis is made by clinical features noted above with a suggestive history of drug exposure. A skin biopsy should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis.

One Step Further
Question:
What infectious organism is responsible for cases of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis?

Reveal Answer:
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the second most common cause behind medications, particularly in children.

Rapid Review

Autoimmune blistering condition
Most common in patients aged > 60 years
Sx and findings: intensely pruritic lesions → large, tense blisters or bullae → rupture w/ formation of erosion/crust
PE: tense and firm blisters that do not extend with lateral pressure
Nikolsky sign negative: absence of slippage of the epidermis from the dermis when slight rubbing pressure is applied to the skin
Tx options: wound care, corticosteroids, doxycycline, immunosuppressants

الفخ: الخيار B (Pemphigus vulgaris) غير صحيح لأنه لا يتناول الحالة بطريقة مناسبة أو قد يسبب ضرراً. الخيار C (Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome) غير صحيح لأنه لا يتناول الحالة بطريقة مناسبة أو قد يسبب ضرراً. الخيار D (Toxic epidermal necrolysis) غير صحيح لأنه لا يتناول الحالة بطريقة مناسبة أو قد يسبب ضرراً.

question: A 34-year-old man presents to the emergency department with pain in his left ankle and leg. He indicates that today he was cleaning his house when he suddenly noticed redness, swelling, and pain in his left ankle. He reports no injury or known insect bite. Since the onset of symptoms 2 hours ago, his pain has worsened significantly, and the redness has now spread up to his knee. Vital signs show HR 118 bpm, BP 127/89 mm Hg, RR 12/min, and T 37.9℃. On examination, his left ankle is erythematous, swollen, and exquisitely tender to the touch. The redness extends up to his left knee but is less painful there. No induration, fluctuance, or crepitus is found. He continues to report severe pain in the leg despite intravenous hydromorphone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Skin and soft tissue infections can be mild conditions such as cellulitis, abscess, and fungal infections to more severe infections such as necrotizing fasciitis and toxic shock syndrome. The source of a skin infection may not always be evident, but many infections arise from a break in the skin such as a cut, injection, or abrasion. Hematogenous seeding from another infected site is another possible source. Most skin infections present with erythema, warmth, and some induration. Important clinical features that are present in this patient with a skin infection include rapidly advancing erythema, systemic toxicity detected in an elevated heart rate, and severe pain that is out of proportion to physical exam findings. These aspects all suggest that this patient most likely has necrotizing fasciitis.

Necrotizing fasciitis is an aggressive infection of the subcutaneous tissue that spreads rapidly along the fascial planes. Typical bacterial isolates include group A beta-hemolytic streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus, enterococci, and anaerobes such as Bacteroides and Clostridium. Most cases are polymicrobial. Necrotizing fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis and should be suspected in patients such as the one in this question. Other signs of necrotizing fasciitis include altered mental status, hemorrhage, blistering, and crepitus. Crepitance describes skin that feels crackly, and it suggests underlying subcutaneous emphysema from gas-forming organisms. Crepitus is diagnostic but not required for a diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis.



An abscess (A) occurs when bacteria accumulate below the epidermis and draw neutrophils and cytokines to the site, which promotes the development of purulence. The overlying epidermis prevents drainage and eventually, a painful, red mass is seen. It is often tender and warm. The fluid collection under the epidermis is described as fluctuant. The patient in this question does not have a painful, red, fluctuant mass.

Cellulitis (B)is an inflammatory condition of the skin and subcutaneous tissue that is the result of a bacterial infection. It may be purulent or nonpurulent. The cardinal and typical feature of cellulitis is confluent inflammation due to increased blood flow. Induration can be found and simply means a hardening of the skin as it becomes engorged with interstitial fluid and takes on the appearance of an orange peel. The patient in this question, at the very least, has cellulitis, but his physical exam findings, pain out of proportion to exam, and the rapidity of his worsening redness should lead the clinician toward a diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis.

Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (D) is a severe, toxin-mediated syndrome that rapidly progresses to shock, with multiorgan failure and, eventually, death. The syndrome is caused by group A streptococci, often in the setting of a severe soft tissue infection. Patients may have viral symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, myalgias, and chills. High fever with tachycardia and hypotension are typical and altered mental status is common. A diffuse rash can be present in a minority of patients. Although this patient has a more serious infection than typical cellulitis, he is not presenting with shock at this time and his rash is localized rather than confluent.

question: A 33-year-old woman presents to the ED with the lesions seen above. She began taking an antibiotic for her urinary tract infection 2 days prior to noting the lesions. Which of the following signs and symptoms would also be expected in this patient?
englishExplanation:
The lesions are due to erythema nodosum, an inflammatory reaction between the dermis and adjacent adipose tissue. It is thought to be a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to various infections, drugs, or a systemic disease. Sulfonamides, oral contraceptives, penicillins, and phenytoin are often implicated. The patient is likely taking sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim for her UTI. A variety of infections and systemic disorders such as streptococcal infections (most common infection), sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, lymphoma, and leukemia are associated with erythema nodosum.

The hallmark lesions of erythema nodosum are tender erythematous subcutaneous nodules that have a blue hue as they resolve. Symmetrical pretibial involvement is most common, although the extensor surfaces of the forearm, thigh, and trunk may also be affected. Patients may have just the nodules or may have systemic symptoms, including fever and malaise. Arthralgias are seen in 90% of patients at some time during the disease course and have been known to persist for up to 2 years after resolution. The skin eruption can last up to 8 weeks.

Treatment is mainly supportive with the identification of the underlying disorder. NSAIDs may be useful in controlling the arthralgias.



Extensor, not flexor (B), surfaces are usually involved in patients with erythema nodosum.

Mucous membranes (C) are not involved as in other disorders such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis.

The skin lesions of erythema nodosum are tender, not nontender (D).

question: A 6-year-old boy presents for evaluation of a rash beginning 3 days ago that has progressed to cover his bilateral lower extremities and buttocks. His parent says the boy has no medical conditions and is fully immunized. A review of systems is positive for a recent sore throat, abdominal pain, and joint pain that resolved last week. Vital signs are within normal limits. On physical exam, the patient has a nonblanching, palpable rash on both legs. What abdominal complication is most commonly associated with the suspected diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV), formerly called Henoch-Schönlein purpura, is the most common systemic vasculitis in children. It is primarily a childhood disease and typically affects children 3–15 years old. The pathogenesis of IgAV is an immune-mediated vasculitis that is associated with IgA deposition thought to occur after a recent upper respiratory infection. Clinical manifestations include palpable purpura without thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy, arthralgias or arthritis, abdominal pain, and kidney involvement.

Features develop over a course of days to weeks and vary in the order of their presentation, with purpura and joint pain commonly presenting first. Intussusception is the most common gastrointestinal complication and occurs secondary to a lead point that is caused by edema and hemorrhage. The diagnosis is typically made clinically and is straightforward when purpura without thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy is present along with two of the other three features (arthritis or arthralgias, abdominal pain, and kidney disease). However, the classic rash may be absent in up to 25% of patients, making the diagnosis harder to determine.

The treatment for IgAV is primarily supportive, as the majority of patients will recover spontaneously. Pain should be treated with acetaminophen or NSAIDs, with corticosteroids being reserved for cases that are severe and refractory to the treatments above. Close consultation with a nephrologist should occur if kidney involvement is present. Hospitalization is warranted for patients with the inability to maintain adequate hydration with oral intake, severe abdominal pain, significant gastrointestinal bleeding, changes in mental status, severe joint involvement limiting ambulation or self-care, or kidney insufficiency (elevated creatinine), hypertension, or nephrotic syndrome.



Appendicitis (A)presents with right lower quadrant pain that classically follows nonspecific periumbilical pain. Patients have severe tenderness with associated rebound tenderness and guarding. Although appendicitis should be considered in patients of all ages presenting with abdominal pain, it is not the most common complication for IgAV.

Malrotation (C)occurs secondary to the failure of the superior mesenteric artery to rotate completely during embryology. This results in bilious vomiting with associated abdominal distention, tenderness, and, at times, peritonitis. Patients may also demonstrate hemodynamic compromise in severe cases. Presentation most commonly occurs in patients < 1 year old, with a vast majority occurring in patients < 5 years old. Malrotation is not a complication of IgAV.

Pancreatitis (D) is an uncommon complication of IgAV.

Reveal Answer:

question: A 60-year-old man with a history of tobacco use presents to the ED with the finding shown above. He is retired from working as a professional winemaker. He reports no fevers, chills, or rapid weight loss. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common cancer in humans and is caused by exposure to ultraviolet light, particularly the ultraviolet B spectrum. It is more common in older patients, but its incidence in patients < 50 is increasing. Light-skinned individuals are more at risk, as darker skin is inherently protected from photodamage by melanin. BCC occurs on sun-exposed areas, most commonly on the head and neck, but may appear anywhere. Characteristic lesions may appear translucent or ulcerated with telangiectasias and a rolled or pearly border. Diagnosis is by interpretation of punch biopsy or shave biopsy. Treatment options include surgical excision, Mohs microsurgery, electrodesiccation and curettage, and irradiation.



Endocarditis (B) may present with skin or nail findings related to disseminated bacterial infection such as petechiae from septic emboli, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, microabscesses, and purpura.

A Lisch nodule (C) is a pigmented iris hamartoma seen in patients with type I neurofibromatosis. They are usually yellow-brown, oval, or round papules that do not affect vision.

Melanoma (D) lesions are characteristically asymmetric with irregular borders and irregular pigmentation, and they frequently change color, size, or shape over time.

Reveal Answer:

question: A patient presents to the ED for evaluation of a skin lesion. Just beneath the midline of the left clavicle, there is a symmetric 1 cm skin-colored nodule, mobile when palpated, and with a central punctum. The lesion has been present for several years. Over the course of a week, the lesion has become increasingly painful, with scant surrounding erythema and fluctuance in the lesion itself. Which of the following is the best initial step in management for this lesion?
englishExplanation:
Epidermoid cysts (commonly called sebaceous cysts) result from the accumulation of keratin-rich material within a dermis-like cyst wall. A diagnosis of epidermoid cysts is typically made in the presence of a discrete nodule with a central punctum that is mobile on palpation. The diagnosis can be complicated by localized infection or inflammation, which can occur spontaneously and involve a substantial amount of surrounding tissue.

Fluctuance of an epidermoid cyst should prompt incision and drainage. Antibiotics are not necessary if the patient has good access to follow-up, as cyst contents are often sterile. In the absence of fluctuance, drainage is not required, and injection of steroids into the lesion is sufficient. Injections consist of triamcinolone and are typically performed in the outpatient setting.



Excision (A) of an epidermoid cyst is typically performed in the outpatient setting by a dermatologist. Lesions should not be excised when inflamed, as there is a greater risk of secondary infection and poor wound healing.

Local steroid injection (C) is not appropriate in the setting of fluctuance.

Oral antibiotics (D) are unlikely to be helpful, as most cysts are sterile, even in the presence of inflammation.

Oral NSAIDs (E) may speed the resolution of inflammation but are not a replacement for a local steroid injection or incision and drainage.

question: A 34-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis develops a tender rash as pictured above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient has erythema nodosum, an inflammatory and immunologic reaction of the subcutaneous fat that most commonly affects women ages 15–30 years. The rash presents with numerous tender subcutaneous nodules that are most commonly seen in the pretibial areas of bilateral lower legs but may also be seen in the arms. Lesions are initially bright red and slightly elevated but become less raised and yellow or violet, resembling bruises, as they resolve over 1–2 weeks. The disease is self-limited, but complete resolution of the rash may take 3–6 months due to recurrent new lesions. Other common symptoms include fever and arthralgias. The most common cause, especially in children, is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction after a strep infection. In adults, it may also be seen as a result of inflammatory bowel disease, sarcoidosis, malignancy, or a reaction to drugs, such as oral contraceptives, sulfonamides, penicillins, or immunizations. Treatment is symptomatic and aimed at the underlying cause.



Erythema marginatum (A) involves migratory pink annular lesions with sharp margins that affect the trunk and sometimes the limbs. They often appear and disappear within hours, similar to urticaria. It is one of the major Jones criteria for diagnosing acute rheumatic fever. Similar to erythema nodosum, it occurs after an acute streptococcal infection.

Erythema migrans (B) is an expanding red annular lesion with central clearing at the site of a tick bite that can grow up to 10 cm in size. It is seen in Lyme disease. There can be multiple lesions due to hematogenous spread of infection.

Erythema multiforme (C) involves many fixed lesions that evolve into target lesions over 1–2 days. Areas affected may include oral mucosa, palms, and soles. Similar to erythema nodosum, erythema multiforme has many possible causes. However, inflammatory bowel disease is more commonly known to cause erythema nodosum.

question: A 2-week-old female patient is brought to the emergency department for a red lesion that has been increasing in size over the last week. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of the lesion pictured above?
englishExplanation:
The picture above shows an infantile hemangioma, a type of vascular tumor and the most common tumor of infancy. Most hemangiomas are not present at birth but become evident in the first days to weeks of life. Hemangiomas are characterized by a phase of proliferation in the first year of life with growth in the size of the lesion followed by a phase of involution, marked by gradual regression of the lesion. Diagnosis is typically clinical, though in more ambiguous cases biopsy may be done for confirmation. While the majority of hemangiomas are uncomplicated and self-limited, ulceration, bleeding, or infection may occur. Hemangiomas that involve the airway may result in airway compromise and should be considered in children with cervicofacial mandibular distribution of hemangiomas that develop hoarseness or stridor.



The majority of infantile hemangiomas are self-limited and resolve by 9 years of age. As such, incision and drainage (A), surgical consultation (C), and topical silver nitrate (D) would not be indicated.

question: A 7-day-old boy presents with umbilical cord discharge and redness. The infant was born at home via an uncomplicated delivery, has been eating well, and is afebrile. Examination is significant for normal vital signs for age and an erythematous cord stump with 1 centimeter of surrounding erythema and purulent discharge. Which of the following is the appropriate management of this infant's condition?

options.text: Admission for empiric treatment with vancomycin
Discharge with topical mupirocin to the umbilicus
Wound culture and inpatient treatment with intravenous vancomycin and gentamicin

correctAnswer: Wound culture and inpatient treatment with intravenous vancomycin and gentamicin
englishExplanation:
This infant’s clinical presentation is most consistent with a diagnosis of omphalitis. Omphalitis is an infection of the umbilicus, umbilical stump, and surrounding tissues seen in neonates. It is a rare condition but has a high mortality rate. Additionally, it must be differentiated from normal cord separation that may have cord discharge but will not have surrounding erythema. Patients commonly present with purulent discharge and local erythema and induration of the surrounding skin. More severe cases may present with fever, diffuse abdominal erythema, and poor feeding, which should be concerning for sepsis or more advanced spread. Localized omphalitis can easily spread through the umbilical vein, leading to portal vein thrombosis as well as intra-abdominal spread causing peritonitis or necrotizing fasciitis.

Risk factors include male sex, home birth (or other nonsterile birth), prolonged labor, and prolonged rupture of membranes. Most cases are polymicrobial in nature, including Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, as well as gram-negative bacteria such as Escherichia coli. Given this, initial treatment should include wound culture and inpatient treatment with intravenous vancomycin and gentamicin. Wound culture can be helpful due to the wide variety of potential pathogens, including anaerobes. Additionally, patients with systemic signs such as fever or poor feeding should have blood cultures and cerebrospinal fluid cultures obtained to rule out sepsis.



Admission for empiric treatment with vancomycin (A) is incorrect as it does not include gram-negative coverage and also does not include a wound culture to help direct care. Discharging with oral amoxicillin (B) is incorrect as these patients should be admitted for parenteral antibiotics given the severity of the infection and their young age. Discharging with topical mupirocin (C) is also not correct, as neither discharge planning nor topical treatment would be adequate care.

question: A 47-year-old man with diabetes presents to the emergency department with a dusky right leg with foul-smelling hemorrhagic bullae and palpable crepitus. In addition to immediate surgical consultation, which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?
englishExplanation:
This patient has signs and symptoms concerning for a severe, necrotizing soft tissue infection which requires broad-spectrum antibiotics. These infections are most commonly polymicrobial, including gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic species. Therefore, the combination of intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam is appropriate antimicrobial coverage. Clindamycin should also be administered for its antitoxin effects. Risk factors for necrotizing soft tissue infections include diabetes mellitus, advanced age, heart disease, alcohol use disorder, peripheral vascular disease, human immunodeficiency virus, intravenous drug use, and chronic skin infections. Either direct invasion from direct skin trauma (e.g., surgical incision, insect bite) or hematogenous spread are common mechanisms of infection. Patients are usually systemically ill and require aggressive fluid resuscitation, antimicrobial coverage, and early surgical consultation.



Neither combination of ceftriaxone and doxycycline (A) nor levofloxacin and tobramycin (B) would provide sufficient anaerobic coverage to treat necrotizing soft tissue infections. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and cephalexin (C) would not provide sufficient gram-negative or anaerobic coverage.

question: A 3-week-old term girl presents with a rash that has been present since birth. She is eating well, has regained her birth weight, and is making normal wet and dirty diapers. She has had no fevers. There is no family history of asthma or eczema. Her parents are concerned because her rash has worsened over the last week. Your exam shows a well appearing, alert infant with vital signs within normal limits for age and the above rash. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Salmon-colored greasy patches with yellow scale characterize seborrheic dermatitis (i.e., cradle cap) that occurs most commonly on the scalp but can also be found in the diaper area and axillae. The rash seems more upsetting to the parents than the infants, as they otherwise are asymptomatic and healthy. The rash can appear severe, especially when it develops into dark red patches in the diaper area and trunk. It usually clears without treatment within 2–3 months but can last 8–9 months. For seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, removing dry, flaky skin with a soft brush after using oil or petrolatum can improve the appearance and help with the anxiety of the parents. While conservative treatment is recommended, the rash can be improved with topical corticosteroids or ketoconazole cream in severe cases.



Acropustulosis of infancy (A) is an uncommon, benign, chronic, and recurrent pustular rash on the palms and soles of infants, although it can involve the scalp. However, unlike the flaky lesions found in this patient, the lesions appear pustular.

Atopic dermatitis (B) can appear much like seborrheic dermatitis initially but usually has a waxing and waning course and a family history of atopy.

Erythema toxicum (C) is an extremely common benign rash with blotchy macules and papules usually clustered over the face, trunk, and proximal extremities that fade over 5–7 days but can recur for several weeks. It is flea-bitten, not flaky, in appearance.

question: A patient in the ED has a presumptive diagnosis of toxic epidermal necrolysis after taking trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
englishExplanation:
Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are a spectrum of the same disease process, which is an immune complex-mediated hypersensitivity reaction. In SJS, a less severe form of TEN, < 10% of the body surface area (BSA) is involved. TEN includes patients with > 30% BSA involvement, and there is an SJS/TEN overlap in patients with 10–30% BSA involvement. TEN is most often caused by medications such as sulfa antibiotics, allopurinol, lamotrigine, certain anticonvulsants, and NSAIDs.

TEN most often begins with prodromal symptoms such as malaise, myalgias, sore throat, fevers, anorexia, and conjunctivitis. Dermatologic manifestations most often start on the face and thorax before spreading to the rest of the body. Lesions progress from coalescing macules to purpuric spots and flaccid bullae. Nikolsky sign is positive, which is seen when slight pressure is applied to the skin and there is slippage of the epidermis from the dermis. This leads to large areas of raw, exposed dermis. Mucous membrane involvement is common, and conjunctival involvement may lead to permanent blindness.

Treatment involves discontinuation of the offending agent. Patients with TEN require hospitalization in an ICU or burn unit. The airway should be closely monitored, as the disease process can involve the respiratory mucosa and lead to sloughing of the airway lining. The mainstay of treatment is supportive care, including fluid hydration, electrolyte replacement, wound care, pain control, and infection prevention.



Data surrounding the use of intravenous immune globulin (A) are limited and conflicting. No high-quality evidence supporting its use exists and a significant survival benefit has not been found.

The use of systemic corticosteroids (C) has not been studied and remains controversial. Early observational studies indicate a higher frequency of complications, including infection and increased mortality. Therefore, at this time, corticosteroids are not recommended.

The only therapy that has been well studied in TEN is thalidomide (D). Treatment with thalidomide was studied in a randomized, placebo-controlled trial but was stopped early because of increased mortality. Thalidomide is actually contraindicated for use in TEN, as it was found to make the condition worse.

Reveal Answer:

question: A previously healthy 6-month-old female infant presents to the emergency department with a rash in the diaper area. The rash is erythematous, macular, and located all over the diaper area, sparing the folds of the groin. The infant’s vital signs are within the normal ranges, and she appears well. Which of the following topical medications is the first-line treatment for this condition?
englishExplanation:
This infant is presenting with contact dermatitis in the diaper area. Contact dermatitis is a type of skin inflammation that occurs when the skin comes into direct contact with an irritant or allergen. Contact dermatitis is divided into two types: irritant, such as seen in this patient, and allergic. Allergic contact dermatitis differs in that the symptoms are often delayed for several days after exposure. This type is also rare in infants due to their impaired ability to react to allergens.

Symptoms of irritant contact dermatitis can include pruritus, erythema, edema, vesicles, and crusting lesions. Examination will often show a sharp demarcation between involved and uninvolved skin, along with a distribution that can potentially be traced back to a specific exposure. The mainstay of treatment involves the elimination and avoidance of the suspected irritant. Thick emollients and barrier creams such as zinc oxide or vaseline may be helpful for the relief of symptoms. In more severe cases, topical corticosteroids may be required. Most cases will resolve with these initial therapies, but chronic exposure to an irritant may result in lichenification, fissures, scaling, excoriations, and hyperpigmentation.



Topical corticosteroids (A) may eventually be required but are not the first-line treatment for this condition.

Mupirocin (B) is used to treat mild bacterial infections of the skin.

Nystatin ointment (C) is used to treat fungal infections. These can be differentiated from diaper contact dermatitis by the presence of satellite lesions and primary involvement of the skin folds.

Reveal Answer:

question: A 38-year-old woman presents with a pruritic rash that has developed over the past several weeks. Physical exam reveals well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with a silver scale located on both elbows. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with psoriasis, a chronic inflammatory skin disease that can develop at any age. Its rash appears as well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with a silver scale and they are usually symmetrically distributed. The most common sites of involvement include the scalp, extensor elbows, knees, and gluteal cleft. However, the hands, feet, trunk, or nails may also be involved. The rash may be localized or diffuse. Diagnosis is often suspected based on clinical presentation but may be confirmed by skin biopsy. Localized disease may be treated with topical betamethasone or other high-potency topical corticosteroids. Alternative treatments include vitamin D analogs, tar, and topical retinoids. More severe disease may be treated with phototherapy, systemic retinoids, methotrexate, or biologic immune modifying agents. This patient has limited, localized psoriasis, so topical corticosteroids are a reasonable treatment option.



Oral cephalexin (A) has no role in the treatment of psoriasis, as it is immune-mediated, rather than bacterial, in etiology.

Topical diphenhydramine (C) has no role in the treatment of psoriasis.

Topical mupirocin (D) is an antibiotic and not indicated because psoriasis is not a bacterial illness.

question: An 80-year-old man presents to the ED with a pruritic and painful rash. He has a prior history of psoriasis, but states this does not seem to be related. Physical exam is shown above. Nikolsky sign is negative. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism by which the most likely disease process occurs?

options.text: IgE cross-linking on mast cells or basophils
IgG autoantibodies against the basement membrane
T lymphocyte delayed activation and reaction to antigen

correctAnswer: IgG autoantibodies against the basement membrane
englishExplanation:
This patient is exhibiting symptoms and physical exam findings consistent with bullous pemphigoid, a chronic bullous disease that involves IgG autoantibodies against the basement membrane (subepidermal). It is the most common bullous disease and is classically seen in adults > 60 years. It may be caused by repeated skin trauma and the presence of other inflammatory skin conditions such as psoriasis. However, it is often idiopathic.

Signs and symptoms include a pruritic rash that evolves into tender, tense bullae occurring most often over the legs, forearms, and axillae. Mucosal involvement is uncommon. Nikolsky sign is negative. Diagnosis is by needle biopsy to discriminate from pemphigus vulgaris. However, it may be differentiated clinically based on the differences between the two, as pemphigus vulgaris includes oral involvement, flaccid bullae, and a positive Nikolsky sign, while bullous pemphigoid does not.

Management includes wound care, steroids and doxycycline, and sometimes the addition of dapsone and immunomodulators such as azathioprine, cyclosporine, and methotrexate. This disease process often improves and relapses spontaneously. Mortality, though rare, is most commonly caused by sepsis. Overall, bullous pemphigoid has a relatively good prognosis when compared to pemphigus vulgaris.



IgE cross-linking on mast cells or basophils (A) is the mechanism by which type I hypersensitivity reactions or anaphylaxis occur.

IgG autoantibodies against the desmosomes (C) is an example of type II or cytotoxic hypersensitivity reactions and is the mechanism by which pemphigus vulgaris occurs.

T lymphocyte delayed activation and reaction to antigen (D) is the mechanism by which type IV or delayed hypersensitivity reactions occur. An example of this is the tuberculin skin test.

Reveal Answer:

question: A 67-year-old farmer presents to the emergency department with concerns about a skin lesion. His exam is shown above. He has not seen a clinician in over 20 years but has no concerns otherwise. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Basal cell carcinoma presents with a pearly papule with or without telangiectasias that typically occurs on sun-exposed areas such as the upper lip. Risk factors include advanced age, smoking, immunosuppression, albinism, xeroderma pigmentosum, and sun exposure (such as with outdoor careers like farming). Though basal cell carcinoma is not an emergency, patients must be referred to outpatient dermatology for a biopsy and possible surgical excision of the malignant lesion. Patients should be advised to wear sun-protective gear and initiate cessation of any risk factors such as smoking.



Actinic keratosis (A) is a precursor lesion to squamous cell carcinoma and presents with scaly lesions in sun-exposed areas. Melanoma (C) presents with a hyperpigmented skin lesion that has an irregular border with a dark color and uneven pigmentation across the lesion. Sun exposure is a key risk factor. Squamous cell carcinoma (D) would present in an older patient with a scaly or ulcerated lesion and can be associated with numbness in the area from invasion of the local nerves. It is more common in sun-exposed areas and people who smoke.

question: A 14-year-old boy presents to the ED with intense pruritus in his groin, axillae, and between his fingers after returning home from a 4-week summer camp 1 week ago. He reports several other campers had similar symptoms. On exam, you note excoriations in the inguinal region and axillae, surrounding scattered erythematous papules. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
englishExplanation:
This patient has scabies, a pruritic dermatitis caused by cutaneous infection with the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. Scabies is spread by skin-to-skin contact and should be considered in patients with generalized pruritus, especially when exposure to others with similar symptoms is reported. The rash of scabies involves papules, which are often excoriated. Burrows are pathognomonic but not uniformly present. Unless previously infected, pruritus generally takes 3–6 weeks to develop because symptoms are due to delayed (type IV) sensitivity reaction. The pruritus is classically worse at night and affects the web spaces of the fingers, flexor aspect of the wrists, axillae, groin, nipples, and the periumbilical region. Except in cases involving an immunocompromised host, the scalp and face are generally spared.

Diagnosis is clinical but can be confirmed by placing scrapings collected with a #15 blade scalpel in mineral oil for microscopic examination. The treatment of choice for primary scabies infection is the application of topical scabicidal agents, with repeat application in 7 days. The treatment of choice is permethrin 5% lotion. Individuals affected by scabies should avoid skin-to-skin contact with others. Patients with typical scabies may return to school or work 24 hours after the first treatment.



Topical ketoconazole (A) is an antifungal agent used to treat topical dermatophytes (e.g., tinea) and is ineffective against scabies.

Lindane (B) was once a common treatment for scabies but is associated with significant potential for toxic manifestations, especially seizures. Because of this, it is no longer used to treat scabies.

Prednisone (D) can be used as adjunctive therapy to reduce associated pruritus but will not eradicate the condition.

question: Which of the following would be consistent with a diagnosis of staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome?

options.text: History of antibiotic use prior to the onset of symptoms
Sparing of the intraoral mucous membranes

correctAnswer: Sparing of the intraoral mucous membranes
englishExplanation:
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) primarily affects infants and young children and is caused by exotoxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus. Patients develop tender erythroderma, often noted initially around the mouth, which then becomes widespread with extensive bullae formation and eventual exfoliation. While the lips may be involved, intraoral mucous membrane involvement is not seen. Patients are often febrile and irritable and there may be a history of preceding upper respiratory symptoms. Nikolsky sign, slipping of the epidermis away from the underlying dermis when gentle lateral pressure is applied, is positive. Diagnosis is made clinically and confirmed with wound culture. Treatment includes antibiotics active against S. aureus, such as cephalexin or dicloxacillin. Infants with extensive involvement may need to be admitted for fluid resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics.



A history of antibiotic use prior to the onset of symptoms (A) would be more consistent with a diagnosis of Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. Most of these cases are secondary to a hypersensitivity reaction to medication, which causes separation of the epidermis and dermis resulting in widespread bullous formation and exfoliation. Mucous membrane involvement is prominent.

Honey-colored crusted lesions (B) are seen in impetigo. Also common in young children and the result of infection with S. aureus, patients present with papules and vesicles that break open and form adherent honey-colored crusts.

Nikolsky sign (C) is positive in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.

question: A 54-year-old woman presents to the ED with a painful rash. She experienced severe mouth sores and pain with swallowing for the past week and then developed this rash. Physical exam is shown above. Nikolsky sign is positive. Which of the following is the most common precipitating factor for the development of this rash?

options.text: A diet high in garlic, leeks, and onions

englishExplanation:
Pemphigus vulgaris is a rare, potentially life-threatening autoimmune blistering disorder that primarily affects middle-aged and older adults. The disease is characterized by the development of painful, flaccid bullae and erosions on the skin and mucous membranes, especially in the oral cavity. One of the hallmark signs on physical examination is a positive Nikolsky sign, in which gentle lateral pressure on the skin causes epidermal shearing. The condition arises when IgG autoantibodies target desmoglein-3 and sometimes desmoglein-1, two cadherin-type proteins involved in keratinocyte adhesion in the epidermis. The strongest and most consistent precipitating factor is genetic susceptibility, particularly in individuals with specific HLA genotypes such as HLA-DR4 and HLA-DR14, which are more prevalent in those of Ashkenazi Jewish descent and people from the Mediterranean region.

The acute care clinician plays a key role in recognizing pemphigus vulgaris based on clinical features, particularly the combination of painful mucosal ulcerations, superficial erosions, flaccid bullae, and a positive Nikolsky sign. ED management includes wound care, supportive treatment (e.g., fluids and pain control), and urgent dermatologic consultation. Although definitive diagnosis requires skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence showing IgG and C3 in a net-like pattern around keratinocytes, clinical suspicion should prompt early treatment initiation. Systemic corticosteroids are the first-line treatment, with immunosuppressive agents such as rituximab or azathioprine often added in consultation with dermatology. Infections, fluid loss, and sepsis are common complications due to skin barrier compromise.



Garlic, leeks, and onions (A) are foods that contain thiol compounds, which have been speculated to exacerbate pemphigus in some reports. However, the evidence is anecdotal and weak. There is no solid epidemiological support for this being a common or consistent trigger.

Black fly bites (B) are associated with onchocerciasis (river blindness), a parasitic disease with a dermatologic component. There is possibly a connection between black fly bites and pemphigus foliaceus, a cutaneous-only form of pemphigus. However, there is no connection between insect bites and pemphigus vulgaris. The rash of onchocerciasis differs significantly, and it does not involve mucosal ulcerations or a positive Nikolsky sign. Thus, the clinical features in this case are inconsistent with insect bite-related dermatologic disease.

Ultraviolet (UV) exposure (D) can exacerbate certain autoimmune blistering conditions, such as bullous pemphigoid or porphyria cutanea tarda, but it is not a common or established inciting factor for pemphigus vulgaris. While UV light may exacerbate preexisting lesions in susceptible individuals, it is not considered a primary precipitating factor in disease development.

While penicillamine (E) is a known drug that can induce pemphigus-like eruptions, such drug-induced pemphigus is much less common than genetically mediated disease. Drug-induced cases tend to resolve with cessation of the offending agent, and they represent a minority of total pemphigus vulgaris cases. Therefore, while penicillamine is relevant in the differential diagnosis, it is not the most common precipitating factor.

Dx: confirmed by biopsy
Tx: high-dose steroids, supportive care
Other options may include immunosuppressives, IV immunoglobulins, immunoadsorption, rituximab
Complications: dehydration, secondary infection, thromboembolism (can have high mortality without treatment)

question: A 68-year-old woman presents with a rash. She initially noticed pruritic red papules over her trunk and extremities 2 weeks ago, which then progressed to tense bullae. She reports no new medications or exposures. Her rash is shown in the picture above. Nikolsky sign is negative. What is the likely etiology of her rash?
englishExplanation:
Bullous pemphigoid is a disease that primarily affects patients between ages 60 and 80 years old. It is an autoimmune disorder that involves autoantibody-mediated damage to the epithelial basement membrane zone. Patients present with a prodrome of a pruritic erythematous urticarial or papular rash followed weeks later by the development of tense bullae atop normal or erythematous skin. The bullae can rupture leaving moist, erythematous erosions and crusting. Nikolsky sign, slipping of the epidermis away from the underlying dermis when gentle lateral pressure is applied, is absent. The lesions can be numerous and widespread but do not typically affect the mucous membranes. Treatment includes topical steroid ointment for localized disease. Oral prednisone is indicated in widespread disease. Lesions heal without scarring. Patients often have a chronic, relapsing course.



Bullous pemphigoid is not secondary to a bacterial (B), fungal (C), or viral (D) infection.

One Step Further
Question:
How does pemphigus vulgaris differ from bullous pemphigoid in presentation?

Reveal Answer:
Patients with pemphigus vulgaris are often younger with painful, flaccid bullae that may involve the mucous membranes and are Nikolsky sign positive.

PE: tense and firm blisters that do not extend with lateral pressure

question: A 25-year-old woman with no medical history presents with an irregularly shaped, dark patch of skin on the sole of her foot. She says that she has had it for about a year and it has become larger. It measures about 8 mm in diameter and is irregular. It is not tender. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Melanoma is a cutaneous malignancy that is responsible for the most deaths of any skin cancer. Fortunately, melanoma is less common and only accounts for 4–5% of skin cancers. Melanoma tends to appear on the lower extremities of women and the head, neck, and trunk of men. Its typical appearance is that of an irregularly shaped and pigmented lesion > 6 millimeters in diameter that increases in size. Risk factors for melanoma include fair skin, history of dysplastic nevi, multiple nevi (> 50), prior history or family history of melanoma, immunocompromised state, and xeroderma pigmentosum.



Basal cell carcinoma (A) is the most common skin cancer. It is most common among men and found in sun-exposed areas of the head and neck. The typical appearance is a pearly papule with well-defined borders and telangiectasias. Kaposi sarcoma (B)is associated with an immunocompromised state, typically HIV. Patients present with painless, raised, brown-black or purple papules or nodules. They are most commonly found on the face, chest, genitals, and oral cavity. Spider nevi (D) are typically found in patients with liver disease. They are found on the upper chest and shoulders and have the appearance of red, branching capillaries. They do blanch on palpating.

question: Which of the following skin cancers is seen above?
englishExplanation:
Basal cell carcinoma is due to a malignant transformation of epithelial cells and usually occurs in sun-exposed areas such as the forehead and nose. It is slow-growing. It is often described as a small pearly nodule with telangiectatic vessels. It may develop a central ulcer with a “rolled” raised edge.

Signs and symptoms include a painless, slowly enlarging lesion that may bleed with minor trauma or fail to heal. Patients may report a “pimple” or sore that persists for months, crusts over, and recurs. Pigmented variants can appear brown or black and may be mistaken for melanoma. Morpheaform (sclerosing) subtypes present as flat, scar-like plaques with ill-defined borders.

Diagnosis is confirmed by skin biopsy, with shave biopsy or punch biopsy being the most common methods. Dermoscopy can aid clinical evaluation by revealing characteristic features such as telangectasis, ovoid nests, and leaf-like structures. Histopathology shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artifact from surrounding stroma.

Treatment depends on tumor size, location, subtype, and patient factors. Surgical excision with clear margins is the gold standard for most lesions. Mohs micrographic surgery is preferred for high-risk tumors (aggressive histologic subtypes, recurrent lesions, or tumors in cosmetically sensitive areas such as the face).

Other options include electrodesiccation and curettage for low-risk superficial tumors, topical therapies (imiquimod, 5-fluorouracil) for superficial basal cell carcinoma, cryotherapy for select small low-risk lesions, and radiation therapy for patients who are not surgical candidates or as adjuvant therapy.



Kaposi sarcoma (B) is a multisystem vascular neoplasm characterized by mucocutaneous violaceous lesions (often mistaken for ecchymosis), usually associated with acquired immune deficiency syndromes (e.g., AIDS). These lesions can occur anywhere on the body.

Melanoma (C) results from the malignant transformation of melanocytes related to sun exposure. Early identification is critical because this is a rapidly growing neoplasm. Cutaneous features concerning for melanoma include recent change (in size, shape, and color), irregular borders, irregular pigmentation, and areas of pigment regression.

Squamous cell carcinoma (D) has a greater malignant potential than basal cell has. It also occurs in sun-exposed areas and is often described as an ulcerated nodule or a superficial skin or lip erosion. Telangiectasia is uncommon. Patients sometimes describe it as a “cut that won’t heal that bleeds easily.”

question: A 2-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a fever and irritability for 1 day. Her parent reports decreased oral intake today. The girl has some congestion and says her mouth hurts. Vital signs include a T of 38.7℃ (101.7℉), HR of 140 bpm, and RR of 20/min. You notice one small ulcer on her left inner cheek and another on the left side of her tongue. What is the most likely cause of this syndrome?
englishExplanation:
This patient is likely presenting with either herpangina or hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). Clinical syndromes are characterized by an oral enanthem and a maculopapular or vesicular rash to hands and feet. Most cases occur in children under 5 years of age. The most common cause of HFMD is coxsackievirus. The virus is usually transmitted person to person through either the fecal-oral route or through contact with oral or respiratory secretions.

Enterovirus A71 is more common in the Asian-Pacific regions, but coxsackievirus is more common overall. Diagnosis is made clinically. Laboratory studies are not required. Complications of herpangina and HFMD are rare. Treatment is supportive with ibuprofen, acetaminophen, and oral hydration. No specific antiviral exists for treatment.



Echovirus (B) is another cause of herpangina and HFMD, but it is not as common as coxsackievirus, particularly in the United States.

Primary herpes simplex virus (C) gingivostomatitis consists of erythema and edema of the gingiva with clusters of vesicles. The gums are friable and usually bleed easily. The rash in this question is not characteristic of herpes gingivostomatitis.

Varicella-zoster virus (D) is responsible for chickenpox, which presents as a diffuse vesicular rash in children, but it is not responsible for oral lesions.

question: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a tender and swollen area on her lateral thigh. She has had swelling there for several years, but over the last 3 days, the swelling has increased and the area has become red and painful. On examination, she appears well with normal vital signs. On her lateral right thigh, there is a round, tender area of swelling and redness with central fluctuance. What is the best way to minimize the recurrence of this entity?

options.text: Create a large incision and recommend repeated incision and drainage with frequent packing changes for several days
Give intravenous antibiotics until complete resolution
Inject triamcinolone acetonide after incision and drainage

englishExplanation:
Epidermoid cysts, improperly called sebaceous cysts, are the most common cutaneous cysts. They can occur anywhere on the body and usually present as nodules with a central punctum. The cyst wall contains stratified squamous epithelium, and the cavity is filled with keratinous material. The cysts can remain dormant for several years, and there is not a good way to know which cysts are at risk for inflammation and abscess formation. Cysts are infected with bacteria when they become larger, painful, and erythematous. Fluctuant cysts require incision and drainage. To treat the abscess, anesthesia should be injected around the lesion rather than into it to avoid rupturing the cyst wall. Then a small incision with a number 11 blade or a 4 mm punch should be performed. The cyst contents can be expressed with lateral pressure, and hopefully, the cyst wall will be released from the surrounding tissues and can be extracted through the incision. The best way to prevent recurrence is to completely remove the cyst wall. Unfortunately, this can be difficult for severely inflamed and infected cysts. If needed, the patient should be referred for follow-up care and removal of the cyst wall when the inflammation has improved.



Creating a large incision and recommending repeated incision and drainage with frequent packing changes for several days (B) would not necessarily prevent the recurrence of this cyst. A larger incision is likely to rupture the cyst wall, making it much more difficult to remove.

Giving intravenous antibiotics until complete resolution (C) is not necessary. When inflamed, many of these cysts do not require any antibiotic therapy for resolution. Antibiotics are only recommended for severe surrounding cellulitis or those that do not respond to drainage alone.

Injection of triamcinolone acetonide after incision and drainage (D) would not be appropriate. Mildly inflamed, uninfected epidermoid cysts may resolve on their own. Injection of triamcinolone acetonide may hasten the resolution of the inflammation and prevent infection, but the patient in this question has a fluctuant lesion, which suggests abscess formation requiring more than triamcinolone acetonide injection, and triamcinolone will not prevent recurrence.

Reveal Answer:

question: An 18-year-old woman presents with an itchy rash that began 1 month ago when she noticed a large patch on her neck. After about a week, it developed into the more diffuse papulosquamous rash that she presents with now. You inform the patient that the rash will last 8–12 weeks and then prescribe cetirizine. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Pityriasis rosea is a common acute eruption that usually affects children and young adults. The cause is unknown. It is characterized by the formation of an initial herald patch, followed by the development of a diffuse papulosquamous rash. This condition is difficult to identify until the appearance of characteristic, smaller, secondary lesions that follow the Langer lines. The rash of pityriasis rosea typically lasts 8–12 weeks, with complete resolution in most patients.

An important goal of treatment is to control pruritus, which may be severe. Zinc oxide, calamine lotion, topical steroids, and oral antihistamines are usually helpful. Systemic steroids are generally not recommended. Patients should be reassured about the self-limited nature of pityriasis rosea. Persistence of the rash or pruritus beyond 12 weeks should prompt reevaluation of the original diagnosis, consideration of biopsy to confirm the diagnosis, and questioning the patient again about the use of medications that may cause a rash similar to that of pityriasis rosea.



Findings of contact dermatitis (A) can include erythema, vesicles, bullae, exudates, and crusting from the breaking of blisters, swelling, and scaling. Taking a careful history and patch testing are often the key to diagnosis.

In scabies (C), patients present with a pruritic rash that is often worse at night. Skin findings include papules, nodules, burrows, and vesiculopustules. The distribution includes the interdigital spaces, wrists, ankles, waist, groin, and axillae. Pruritic nodules around the axillae or umbilicus or on the penis and scrotum are highly suggestive of scabies.

Tinea corporis (D) is a fungal skin infection characterized by red, itchy, and often ring-shaped lesions on the body. More lesions can develop, but they are typically similar in morphology.

Tinea versicolor (E) presents with hypopigmented, pink to brown macules and patches on the trunk with fine scale. Versicolor means varied colors, and this tinea tends to be white, pink, and brown. Tinea versicolor is found on the back, chest, abdomen, and upper arms, often in a cape-like distribution.

question: An 8-year-old girl presents with a 4-day history of progressive rash accompanied by fever. The rash (shown above) started on the face with subsequent spread to the torso, followed by involvement of the extremities. The highest temperature over the past 24 hours is 102.3°F (39.1°C). No other symptoms are noted. She was diagnosed with partial seizures 3 weeks ago and was started on oxcarbazepine. Which of the following is associated with this rash?
englishExplanation:
These clinical features are consistent with drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome (DIHS), also known as drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS). This is considered a T cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction and is associated with specific human leukocyte antigen polymorphisms. Reactivation of herpes viral infection (human herpesvirus 6, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus) is also believed to play a role in many cases of DIHS. Skin findings begin as a maculopapular eruption progressing to coalescing plaques that are symmetrically distributed on the torso and extremities. The pattern of spread is from head to toe. Facial edema is common. Mucosal involvement can occur in half of cases but is generally mild. Generalized lymphadenopathy is common. Eosinophilia occurs in 82–95% of cases. Solid organ involvement is seen in up to 90% of cases, and liver involvement is seen most commonly. Elevations of liver transaminases up to 10 times the upper limit of normal are seen in half of those with liver involvement, although progression to liver failure is rare. Kidney involvement as acute interstitial nephritis occurs in up to one-third of patients. Pulmonary and cardiac involvement occur less commonly.



Anemia (A) is generally not seen in DIHS. Neutrophilia, contrasted with neutropenia (C), is seen in most patients. Thrombocytosis (D) is not commonly described in DIHS, although thrombocytopenia is occasionally seen.

One Step Further

What are the most common medications associated with drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
Anticonvulsant medications, with aromatic anticonvulsants (carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) being most often implicated.

question: An 82-year-old woman who uses a wheelchair and has a history of dementia presents from a skilled nursing facility with low back pain. Her vital signs are within normal limits. On physical examination, there is an erythematous area overlying the sacrum with full-thickness skin loss and visible subcutaneous fat. Which of the following is the correct staging of this patient’s pressure-induced skin injury?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with a history and physical examination consistent with a stage 3 pressure-induced skin ulcer. Pathogenesis involves external forces to the skin in combination with host-specific factors. Risk factors include immobility, malnutrition, decreased skin perfusion, and neurological disorders that lead to sensory loss such as delirium, dementia, spinal cord injury, and neuropathy. Thus, pressure-induced skin injuries are common in patients who reside in long-term care facilities and hospitals. Injuries are classified in stages based on erythema, thickness, and visualized subcutaneous fat, tendon, joint, bone, or eschar. Stage 3 pressure-induced skin ulcers are full-thickness injuries with subcutaneous fat visible. Treatment involves continued wound care, pain control, and monitoring for infection and progression of disease.



Stage 1 (A) pressure-induced injury is classified as an intact area of nonblanching erythema that lasts for > 1 hour after relief of external pressure.

Stage 2 (B) pressure-induced injury is a partial-thickness disruption of the dermis.

Stage 4 (D) pressure-induced injury is a full-thickness loss of tissue with visible muscle, tendon, joint, or bone.

question: A 78-year-old man presents to the ED with a worsening rash. He underwent a liver transplant 11 years ago and has taken tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone consistently since the surgery. He reports a good quality of life after his transplant. He avoids alcohol and manages stress by taking frequent fishing trips. The lesions as shown above are scattered and crusty and located primarily on his head. He reports that they have been present for several months but have recently changed in appearance. Which of the following is this patient at risk of developing?
englishExplanation:
This patient has actinic keratoses, which are a precursor for squamous cell carcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma is a malignancy of epidermal keratinocytes. It is usually caused by ultraviolet light exposure, and those with fair skin are at highest risk. Other causes of squamous cell carcinoma include human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, arsenic exposure, and immunocompromised status (such as patients with histories of taking immunosuppressive medications for solid organ transplants).

These lesions most commonly arise on sun-exposed areas, particularly the lip, ear, head, and neck. They appear as a well-defined red or brown thickened patch. Diagnosis is by biopsy, which will show malignant transformation of keratinocytes. Lesions > 2 cm in diameter and > 4 mm deep have a high risk of metastases. Treatment is with 5-fluorouracil ointment, cryosurgery, or full surgical excision.



Basal cell carcinoma (A) is a malignancy arising from the basal layer of the epidermis or follicular structures. It usually appears as a nonhealing, ulcerated wound with raised borders. It does not arise from actinic keratoses.

Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (B) is a rare type of cancer that affects the skin and originates from T lymphocytes. Immunosuppression (as in the case above) is a risk factor for the development of this condition. However, actinic keratoses, as depicted above, are not precursors for this condition.

Kaposi sarcoma (C) is a tumor caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) and is classically seen in patients with HIV as an AIDS-defining illness when the CD4 count decreases to a low enough level.

Malignant melanoma (D) classically presents as a darkly pigmented lesion in sun-exposed areas with irregular borders. It does not arise from actinic keratoses.

One Step Further

True or false: generally, dermatologists and experts recommend using a broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of at least 50 or higher.

Reveal Answer:
False. The recommendation is an SPF of 30 or higher.

question: Which of the following is most commonly associated with erythema nodosum?
englishExplanation:
Erythema nodosum, thought to be a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to a systemic disease or medication, is a vasculitis involving the venules and veins of the skin. It affects young adults primarily in their second to fourth decades, with women affected almost four times as often as men. A prodrome of nonspecific symptoms, including fever, malaise, and myalgias, is followed by the development of subcutaneous nodules, primarily on the anterior tibial surfaces. Lesions may also be seen on the forearms, trunk, and thigh. The nodules are often erythematous, well-circumscribed, and very tender. While many cases are found to be idiopathic, the most commonly implicated disease is a preceding streptococcal infection. Patients may give a history consistent with preceding streptococcal infection (e.g., fever and sore throat), and an antistreptolysin O titer should be checked. Treatment includes symptomatic care with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications.



Inflammatory bowel disease (A), particularly Crohn disease, has been implicated in cases of erythema nodosum but not as commonly as streptococcal infection.

Patients with sarcoidosis (B) are at increased risk for developing erythema nodosum, but this is not as common of a preceding illness as a streptococcal infection.

Tuberculosis (D) has also been associated with the development of erythema nodosum, but preceding streptococcal infection is more common.

question: A 27-year-old man with AIDS has the rash shown in the picture above. What type of isolation is required if he is admitted?
englishExplanation:
Varicella-zoster virus (human herpesvirus 3) is the causative agent in both chickenpox and shingles. Herpes zoster, shown in this patient, occurs from reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus that has been dormant in a dorsal root nerve ganglion since an episode of chickenpox. Most reoccurrences occur in older (> 55 years) and immunocompromised patients. Prior to the onset of rash, patients experience tingling or hyperesthesia in the dermatome. Painful, vesicular lesions then appear on the skin along the distribution of the dermatome. Patients are considered infectious from 5 days before the appearance of the rash until 5 days after the appearance of the vesicles. If the patient is immunocompromised with localized herpes zoster, standard precautions plus airborne (negative pressure room) and contact precautions should be followed until disseminated infection is ruled out.



Droplet precautions (B) are indicated for viruses with larger respiratory particles. These precautions include a mask worn when entering a patient’s room. One of the most common indications for droplet precautions is influenza.

Positive pressure (C) precautions involve positive air pressure such that the air inside the patient’s room is forced out of the room into the surrounding environment. This type of isolation is sometimes used in patients with neutropenia.

Standard precautions (D) are universal for every patient in the hospital setting and are not unique to any particular disease entity.

Reveal Answer:
A recent Cochrane review does not support this practice.

question: A 62-year-old man presents with right-sided chest pain for 4 days. The pain is unilateral and of a deep burning and stabbing quality. He uses tobacco daily and reports a long-term history of COPD, which is managed with tiotropium 18 mcg dry powder per capsule inhaled once daily and albuterol 90 mcg/actuation inhaled once or twice every 2–4 hours as needed. Vital signs today are a BP of 121/91 mm Hg, HR of 98 bpm, RR of 15/min, and T of 98.5°F (36.9ºC). Cardiac exam reveals a regular rate and rhythm. On pulmonary exam, there is a slightly prolonged expiratory time. Physical exam of the chest reveals a normal anteroposterior diameter with a light pink vesicular dermatitis on the right side. An ECG is performed and shown above. What management should be initiated?

options.text: Cephalexin 500 mg PO four times daily
Nitroglycerin 0.6 mg SL as a single dose

englishExplanation:
This patient presents with herpes zoster (shingles) and should have appropriate pain control started, such as acetaminophen. Herpes zoster results from the reactivation of dormant varicella-zoster virus developing in patients with a history of chickenpox. Risk factors for the development of herpes zoster include advanced age, immunocompromised status, and chronic lung or kidney disease.

Typically, pain in a dermatomal distribution precedes the eruption of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in the same dermatome. The vesicles are cloudy at first and progress to crust formation later in the course. The pain associated with the disease is often severe and debilitating. Patients may not initially see a dermatitis and may report unilateral deep burning or stabbing chest pain. If no obvious rash is initially present, a chest X-ray or ECG may be performed to rule out cardiovascular concerns, both of which are typically unremarkable in patients with herpes zoster.

The mainstay of treatment is pain control and oral antiviral medications, depending on the timing of symptom onset and comorbidities. Orally administered corticosteroids were commonly recommended in the treatment of herpes zoster, but given recent clinical trials showing variable results, they are not typically recommended.



Antibiotics such as cephalexin (B) are only indicated if there is a superinfection of the lesions.

Antihistamines such as fexofenadine (C) have not been shown to hasten the rate of healing or aid in symptom relief in patients with varicella-zoster.

Nitroglycerin (D) is used for patients with anginal chest pain or pain associated with acute coronary syndrome.

Corticosteroids such as prednisone (E) have not been proven to be beneficial, although when combined with antivirals, such as valacyclovir, they may help with pain reduction.

question: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a rash that started as pruritic lesions that progressed to tense blisters. Physical exam is notable for the skin lesions shown above that do not slough when lateral pressure is applied to them. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with findings suggestive of bullous pemphigoid, an autoimmune blistering disorder that is more often found in those > 60 years. Bullous pemphigoid presents initially with pruritic eczematous, papular, or urticarial-like skin lesions. These skin lesions can subsequently progress to the classical tense bulla with a thick covering that does not slough when pressure is applied to them (a negative Nikolsky sign). This is in contrast to pemphigus vulgaris, which presents with flaccid blisters that slough or extend easily when pressure is applied to them. The lesions are typically highly pruritic and can ultimately rupture leaving erosions and crusts that eventually heal. The diagnosis is made clinically. However, a biopsy can confirm the diagnosis. The treatment of bullous pemphigoid is initially topical steroids. Systemic steroids or doxycycline might be required for widespread disease.



Dermatitis herpetiformis (B) presents with highly pruritic grouped papules and vesicles that appear similar to a herpes infection. This condition is commonly seen in celiac disease, which presents with diarrhea and weight loss secondary to exposure to gluten-containing foods.

Pemphigus foliaceus (C) presents similarly to pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that rupture easily when pressure is applied to them. It can be differentiated from pemphigus vulgaris by its typical absence of mucosal lesions.

Pemphigus vulgaris (D) presents with flaccid bullae that rupture easily when pressure is applied to them with lesions that can be found in the oral mucosa. The treatment of pemphigus vulgaris is systemic steroids.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
IgA deficiency (leading to repeat infections of the mucosal surfaces).

question: A 15-year-old boy presents with an itchy rash to the groin. The rash is scaly and has a reddish-brown color. It does not fluoresce under a wood lamp. What is the pathogen responsible for this condition?
englishExplanation:
This patient has tinea cruris, otherwise known as jock itch. It is caused by a dermatophyte, most commonly Trichophyton rubrum. Infection occurs at the epidermal layer and results in inflammation and hyperplasia of the skin that produces areas of scaly skin with dermatitis. Tinea cruris does not fluoresce under a wood lamp. question: A 67-year-old man presents to the ED with 2 days of myalgias, headache, and low-grade fever. Today, he noticed the lesion on his nose, as shown above. What is the next step in management?
englishExplanation:
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus, a potentially sight-threatening infection, is caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus in the trigeminal ganglion. Patients often present with a prodrome of fever, headache, malaise, and hypesthesia in the affected eye and forehead, followed by a vesicular rash along the trigeminal dermatome. Vesicular lesions on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) are associated with a high risk of herpes zoster ophthalmicus as this area is innervated by the nasociliary branch of the trigeminal nerve, which also innervates the globe. Ophthalmologic examination is a crucial step in this patient’s evaluation as early diagnosis of ocular involvement is critical in preventing the progression of infection and loss of vision. Findings can include hyperemic conjunctivitis, episcleritis, and punctate keratitis. Emergent ophthalmologic consultation is indicated when the diagnosis is suspected. Treatment includes oral antiviral agents.



Discharging with acyclovir (A) is the appropriate treatment for uncomplicated herpes zoster involving a trunk or extremity dermatome.

Treatment with prednisone (B) is controversial. Studies have not shown a clear benefit with the addition of prednisone to antiviral medications when treating herpes zoster. Systemic steroids are also associated with potential complications, such as hyperglycemia and secondary bacterial infection.

A lumbar puncture (D) is indicated in those cases in which patients with evidence of herpes zoster have symptoms concerning for meningeal involvement.

Reveal Answer:

question: A 73-year-old man presents with a painful wound on his lower leg. An image of the wound is provided above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Venous stasis ulcers are a condition caused by chronic venous insufficiency. Damaged venous valves in conditions such as phlebitis and varicose veins are the most common causes of chronic venous insufficiency. This can then lead to stasis of venous blood flow, which causes edema and stasis dermatitis. Early stasis dermatitis is characterized by an orange-like skin hyperpigmentation and dependent edema. The skin may also become dry, tight, and hairless. Locations commonly involved in stasis dermatitis are the medial distal and pretibial areas of the legs. Chronic stasis dermatitis leads to worsening edema and, eventually, ulceration. The most common sites of venous stasis ulcers are the bilateral malleoli and the medial aspect of the calf. Symptoms include pain, cramping, leg heaviness, and fatigue. Diagnosis is made clinically. Treatment is limb elevation, compression stockings, and local wound care. Cases complicated by a secondary bacterial infection should be treated with antibiotics.



Arterial ulcers (A) are most often caused by chronic changes due to peripheral artery disease. Ulceration is typically very painful and often occurs at pressure points such as the base of the heel and the toe joints.

Diabetes-related ulcers (B) usually result from minor trauma that goes unnoticed due to underlying neuropathy. Over time, ulcerations form in pressure points such as the plantar metatarsal heads and heel.

Pressure ulcers (C) are caused by prolonged periods of external force on the skin. They are most common among patients who are hospitalized or reside in a long-term facility with underlying risk factors such as immobility, dementia, and diabetes mellitus. Ulceration may occur anywhere on the body, predominantly in pressure points such as the sacrum, coccyx, heels, or hips.
