question: A 3-year-old boy presents with his parent to the emergency department with right arm pain. The parent reports that they were pulling the patient out of the pool when he developed arm pain. On examination, the patient is not using his right arm and is holding it in a flexed position. The patient appears well, and there is no notable swelling or ecchymosis. However, the patient cries every time you attempt to manipulate the arm. What is the appropriate next step in care?

options.text: Place the patient in a long arm splint
Place the patient in a sling

englishExplanation:
This patient presents with a radial head subluxation, also known as a pulled elbow. Radial head subluxations are common elbow injuries in young children and often occur from axial traction on a pronated forearm with the elbow in extension. As a result, many parents will report pulling of the arm, swinging, falling, or twisting of the arm as the initial event that caused the injury. The patient will often present by holding the affected elbow close to the body, either in full extension or flexed with the forearm in pronation. The child often shows no distress unless the extremity is manipulated. Swelling or ecchymosis around the elbow is rare unless an underlying fracture exists.

Management of radial head subluxation involves reduction in the emergency department, preferably using the hyperpronation method. This method involves supporting the patient’s elbow and placing mild pressure on the radial head while hyperpronating the forearm. The supination and flexion method can also be used. In this method, the elbow is supported, and the forearm is fully supinated and the elbow is fully flexed in one motion. Patients usually have immediate resolution of their pain with a successful reduction. They can be discharged from the emergency department without additional imaging, immobilization, activity restriction, or specific follow-up instructions.



Calling Child Protective Services (B) would be inappropriate at this time. While it is always important to be thorough when treating children with acute injuries, the mechanism of action reported by the parent supports the injury.

Placing the patient in a long arm splint (C) would be incorrect, as patients do not need immobilization for a radial head subluxation after successful reduction. A long arm splint would be appropriate if the patient had a concomitant elbow fracture.

Placing the patient in a sling (D) would also be unnecessary, as patients do not need additional immobilization if the subluxation is appropriately reduced.

One Step Further
Question:
Which ligament is displaced in a radial head subluxation?

Reveal Answer:
The annular ligament.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pulled Elbow (Radial Head Subluxation)

Child 1–4 years old
Most commonly caused by longitudinal traction on a pronated forearm while the elbow is extended
History of being pulled up by the wrist
PE: the affected arm is held close to the body in a flexed and pronated position
Tx
Hyperpronation method: apply pressure to the radial head and hyperpronating the forearm
Supination-flexion method: supinate and fully flex the elbow while applying pressure to the radial head and pulling with gentle traction

question: A man presents to the emergency department after an altercation at the bar. He appears intoxicated and is belligerent with staff. He will not provide any history except that his jaw hurts and his teeth feel “weird.” Police officers who accompany him report that he sustained multiple blows to the face and fell to the ground. The patient has difficulty opening his mouth but is able to range open 3–4 cm wide. His oral exam shows malalignment of his upper and lower teeth with step-off. What injury is most consistent with this patient’s clinical presentation?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents after facial trauma with mandibular pain, difficulty moving the jaw, and malalignment of his upper and lower teeth, all consistent with mandibular fracture. Mandibular fractures generally occur as a sequela of facial trauma. Multiple concurrent mandibular fractures are common, occurring around 60% of the time. Diagnosis can be suggested by clinical exam, with palpable or visual step-offs, loss of sensation or jaw movement (from disruption of the inferior alveolar nerve), and severe trismus. A tongue blade test can also be employed, in which a patient is instructed to bite a tongue blade with the affected side and lever the blade against their teeth to attempt to break it. The ability to break the tongue blade has a sensitivity of > 95% for ruling out an ipsilateral fracture and can be used to rule out patients with low-risk injuries. The tongue blade test is relatively nonspecific (68%) and a definitive diagnosis should be made with a CT scan or panoramic radiography of the jaw. Treatment is often surgical, with patients requiring 6–8 weeks for recovery.



Dental root fracture (A) is another common injury associated with facial trauma. Root fracture would be suspected if the patient had only one offset tooth. However, this patient has a linear shift of the left lower teeth with a step-off and severe jaw pain, which is more consistent with a mandibular fracture.

Facial nerve injury (B) can present with loss of the superficial facial muscles, but the muscles of mastication are generally spared. The facial nerve is less commonly injured in mandibular fractures.

Temporomandibular joint dislocation (D) can also present with jaw pain and trismus, but this patient has a dental step-off, which indicates a more substantial injury.

One Step Further
Question:
What nerve innervates the main muscles of mastication?

Reveal Answer:
The V3 branch of the trigeminal nerve. This is the only branch that carries motor fibers.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Mandible Fracture

Likely due to trauma
Most commonly in condyle, angle, or body of mandible
Sx: pain, swelling, facial asymmetry, bruising
Dx: X-rays, panoramic X-ray
CT is best
Tx: bandage and analgesics, open fracture needs antibiotics, update tetanus
Plastics, OMFS, ENT referral or consultation depending on injury
Monitor airway

الفخ: الطالب يختار Dental root fracture خطأً بدلاً من C، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: A 23-year-old woman is brought to the ED via EMS following a motor vehicle collision. Vital signs are a T of 36.4°C (97.5°F), BP of 80/42 mm Hg, HR of 114 bpm, RR of 22/min, and SpO2 of 98% on room air. Physical examination shows a gravid uterus with abdominal tenderness and dark red vaginal bleeding. The uterine fundus is 2 cm below the costal margin, and the fetal head is palpable on the abdominal wall. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Trauma occurs in up to 8% of pregnancies via both intentional and unintentional mechanisms and most commonly results from interpersonal violence, motor vehicle collisions, and falls. It is a leading cause of maternal death and can be further complicated by several obstetric conditions, including spontaneous abortion, prelabor rupture of membranes, placental abruption, uterine rupture, and preterm birth. All female individuals of reproductive age presenting with traumatic injuries should be screened for pregnancy, given that some are unaware of pregnancy at the time of presentation.

Given that this patient has a gravid uterus and vaginal bleeding, obstetric complications of trauma should be suspected. Uterine rupture is a rare obstetric consequence of trauma that most commonly occurs due to pelvic fractures sustained in motor vehicle collisions, injuring the uterine wall. It can also occur in the setting of stab wounds or gunshot wounds, but this is much less common. Uterine rupture should be suspected in pregnant patients with traumatic injuries who present with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding, with further suspicion in cases of maternal shock and palpable fetal parts through the abdominal wall. After initial resuscitation, treatment specifically for the uterine injury may involve simple repair of the injury or hysterectomy, depending on the extent of the injuries and the importance of future reproductive potential for the patient.



Obstetric complications from trauma can be difficult to differentiate from injuries to intra-abdominal organs, but hollow viscus perforation (A) presents with classic peritonitic signs (e.g., distention, guarding, rigidity) rather than palpable fetal parts and vaginal bleeding.

Placenta previa (B) may become apparent in the setting of trauma in pregnancy but most commonly presents with painless vaginal bleeding in the third trimester.

Third-trimester vaginal bleeding and abdominopelvic pain following trauma raise suspicion for placental abruption (C), but fetal parts palpable through the abdominal wall is much more suspicious for uterine rupture.

Trauma can cause prelabor rupture of membranes (D), but this will usually display as the discharge of painless, nonbloody fluid through the vagina rather than abdominal pain with bleeding.

One Step Further
Question:
What test is used to identify fetomaternal hemorrhage?

Reveal Answer:
Kleihauer-Betke test.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Uterine Rupture

Risks: multiple C-sections, uterine scar, prostaglandin use, trauma
Sx: sudden severe uterine pain + vaginal bleeding
PE: hemorrhagic shock, easily palpable fetal anatomy
EFM: FHR abnormalities
Tx: emergent C-section

الفخ: الطالب يختار Hollow viscus perforation خطأً بدلاً من E، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department after being struck in the face during a fight in his college dorm. He has a nasal bridge deformity with a blue, grape-like mass protruding from the left nasal septum. The remainder of his exam is atraumatic. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in managing this patient's injury?
englishExplanation:
This patient has a nasal septal hematoma which should be treated promptly with bedside incision and evacuation of the clot to prevent damage to the underlying cartilage. Careful inspection of the nose should be performed during the secondary trauma survey to assess for this, as it is easily missed if the index of suspicion is not high. It appears as a blue or purple mass against the nasal septum. It may be associated with other signs of facial trauma, including a nasal bridge deformity, periorbital ecchymosis, midface instability or facial lacerations. If a septal hematoma is suspected but not apparent on exam, inserting a gloved small finger and palpating along the septum may be indicated. There are no absolute contraindications to incising a septal hematoma. If left untreated, pressure necrosis of the nasal septum is likely to occur, resulting in collapse of the cartilaginous structures and a saddle nose deformity. Other complications include abscess formation and septal perforation. Septal hematomas should be incised and the hematoma evacuated completely. Needle aspiration is inadequate to fully remove the clot. If bilateral hematomas are present, both require incision and drainage with special care to avoid a through-and-through septal perforation. Prompt otolaryngology follow-up should be arranged.



Discharge home with otolaryngology follow-up (B) without incision and evacuation of a nasal septal hematoma is inappropriate care.

Emergency operative exploration (C) is unnecessary for uncomplicated, isolated nasal septal hematomas. Patients may be discharged home with appropriate follow-up after successful incision and drainage in the ED.

Nasal packing and empiric antibiotics (D) are appropriate once the septal hematoma has been incised and evacuated, but not as a surrogate to draining the hematoma.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common acute complication of a nasal septal hematoma?

Reveal Answer:
Septal abscess.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Septal Hematoma

Etiology: facial trauma
PE: purple-bluish swelling of septum
Tx: drainage followed by packing
Complications: septal abscess or avascular necrosis of septum → saddle nose
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي A لأن Bedside incision and evacuation This patient has a nasal septal hematoma which should be treated promptly with bedside incision and evacuation of the cl  فهذه النقاط تؤكد اختيارها.
الفخ: الطالب يختار Discharge home with otolaryngology follow-up خطأً بدلاً من A، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: A patient who weighs 225 kg (496 lb) fell onto their shoulder during an altercation. The X-ray is shown above. What is the diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Posterior shoulder dislocation is an uncommon but critical diagnosis to recognize in the emergency department. The mechanism typically involves a posteriorly directed force or internal rotation of the arm during trauma, seizures, or electrical injuries. In this case, the patient’s fall onto their shoulder likely caused a posteriorly directed force, leading to the dislocation.

Radiographically, posterior shoulder dislocations are best identified on anteroposterior, axillary lateral, and trans-scapula (Y) X-rays by the lightbulb sign (a rounded, internally rotated humeral head), the rim sign (widened joint space), or loss of the normal overlap between the humeral head and the glenoid. The X-ray above demonstrates these classic findings. Prompt diagnosis is essential, as delayed recognition can lead to complications such as chronic instability or avascular necrosis of the humeral head.

Treatment typically involves closed reduction under sedation or with adequate analgesia and relaxation, followed by sling immobilization and outpatient physical therapy. In cases of significant soft tissue injury or recurrent dislocations, surgical intervention may be required.



Acromioclavicular (AC) joint separations (A) occur from direct trauma to the shoulder, often from a fall onto the lateral aspect. Patients have tenderness and a visible deformity at the AC joint. X-rays reveal widening or elevation of the distal clavicle relative to the acromion. This patient’s X-ray lacks evidence of AC joint misalignment and instead shows features consistent with posterior dislocation.

Anterior shoulder dislocations (B) are the most common type of shoulder dislocation and usually occur with forced abduction and external arm rotation. Clinically, patients exhibit a squared-off shoulder appearance with the humeral head palpable anteriorly. X-ray findings include subcoracoid positioning of the humeral head. These findings are absent in this case, as the X-ray demonstrates posterior displacement with internal rotation of the humeral head.

Proximal humerus fractures (D) typically present with focal tenderness, swelling, and ecchymosis over the proximal arm and shoulder. On X-ray, the humeral head may appear fragmented or malaligned, but the characteristic signs of dislocation, such as the lightbulb sign or joint space widening, are absent. This patient’s X-ray lacks fracture lines or displacement consistent with a proximal humerus fracture.

Scapular fractures (E) are uncommon and typically result from high-energy trauma, such as motor vehicle collisions. Pain and tenderness are localized to the scapula, and X-rays reveal cortical disruptions in the scapular body or processes. This patient’s X-ray does not demonstrate scapular abnormalities and instead shows a dislocated humeral head posteriorly.

One Step Further
Question:
What kind of injury causes a patient to have the arm locked overhead in 110–160° of abduction?

Reveal Answer:
Inferior glenohumeral dislocation (luxatio erecta).

Rapid Review

Posterior Shoulder Dislocation

Injury from posteriorly directed force when the arm is in adduction and internal rotation
PE: arm adducted, internally rotated
Dx: check the Y view

Complications: injuries to labrum and rotator cuff
Can be a missed diagnosis leading to chronic shoulder instability and avascular necrosis

question: A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a single vehicle collision at 70 mph. He was an unrestrained driver, lost control of his car, and hit a tree. There was extensive front-end damage to his car. He has chest pain and difficulty breathing. On exam, he has equal lung sounds bilaterally with no tracheal deviation. He has tenderness over the anterior chest wall with surrounding ecchymosis. What imaging is the preferred method for diagnosing a sternal fracture in this patient?
englishExplanation:
Sternal fractures can be associated with anterior chest trauma, most commonly from the chest wall hitting a steering wheel or bicycle handlebars. Restrained passengers are more likely than unrestrained passengers to present with a sternal fracture. Symptoms include anterior chest pain, sternal tenderness, ecchymosis, and swelling. A CT scan of the chest remains the preferred method for diagnosing a sternal fracture. The use of intravenous contrast will also identify injuries to surrounding internal structures. It is estimated that up to 94% of sternal fractures are only visible on chest CT. Once the diagnosis is made, further care involves pain control and treatment of associated injuries. Those who develop respiratory compromise from the injury or who have nonunion may require operative intervention.



Sternal fractures may be diagnosed on plain chest X-ray (A), but sensitivity is limited. It is estimated that a chest X-ray misses the diagnosis in up to 50% of cases.

Ultrasound (C) may be more sensitive and specific than plain X-ray, but it is operator dependent. In the hands of a skilled ultrasonographer, sensitivity and specificity for identifying sternal fractures may be as high as 89% and 95%, respectively.

While nondisplaced sternum fractures may be seen on lateral view sternum X-rays (D), they have the same rate of misdiagnosis as plain chest radiographs.

One Step Further
Question:
What thoracic injuries are most likely to be associated with sternal fractures?

Reveal Answer:
Rib fractures, pulmonary contusions, spinal fractures, retrosternal hematomas, pneumothorax, hemothorax, hemopericardium, cardiac contusion, and great vessel injuries.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Sternal Fracture

PE: tenderness over palpation of the chest
Dx: CXR (lateral), CT, ultrasound
Obtain additional workup: ECG, troponin, cardiac monitoring
If workup negative and no significant comorbidities, can be discharged with return precautions

الفخ: الطالب يختار Chest X-ray خطأً بدلاً من B، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: Which of the following physical exam findings is most suggestive of a Le Fort III fracture?
englishExplanation:
Le Fort fractures involve the maxillary bone and surrounding midface structures and are classified as type I, II, or III based on the fracture pattern. All Le Fort fractures result in mobility of the maxilla, including the hard palate, due to separation of the maxilla from the cranial base.

Le Fort I fractures are confined to the lower midface, whereas Le Fort II and especially Le Fort III fractures may involve disruption of the cribriform plate and be associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

The presence of CSF rhinorrhea raises concern for ascending infection such as meningitis and may warrant further imaging with maxillofacial CT and potentially beta-2 transferrin testing to confirm the diagnosis. Prompt recognition is critical for both diagnosis and appropriate surgical consultation.



Infraorbital anesthesia (B) involving the ipsilateral cheek and lip is associated with inferior orbital wall (orbital floor) fractures due to injury of the infraorbital nerve.

Limited upward gaze (C) may also occur with orbital floor fractures due to entrapment of the inferior rectus and inferior oblique muscles.

Mobility of the mandible (D) can occur with mandibular fractures. Le Fort fractures involve the midface, not the mandible.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common facial fracture?

Reveal Answer:
Isolated nasal bone fracture.

Rapid Review
Le Fort Fracture

I: transverse fracture that separates maxilla from pterygoid and nasal septum
II: maxilla and palate fractured
III: craniofacial dissociation
II and III: CSF rhinorrhea

الفخ: الطالب يختار Infraorbital anesthesia خطأً بدلاً من A، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: A 28-year-old man presents with intractable pain underneath his cast 5 days after sustaining a tibia and fibula fracture of his left leg. He reports that he was seen at his orthopedic surgeon’s office yesterday for the same pain and was given another prescription for stronger pain medicines after an exam. A new cast was applied before discharge, and he is supposed to follow up in 6 days. However, he insists that the pain medicine is not helping him at all. Physical examination after cast removal reveals paresthesias of the skin between the first two toes and intense pain with passive flexion of the toe. The anterior aspect of his lower leg feels tense and tender. What is the most important next step in management?

options.text: Application of ice and elevation of the extremity
Discharge with outpatient orthopedic follow-up if delta pressure is ≤ 30 mm Hg
Emergent consultation with an orthopedic surgeon

correctAnswer: Emergent consultation with an orthopedic surgeon
englishExplanation:
Acute compartment syndrome is a condition of elevated intramuscular pressures within the confined space of the compartments created by fascia and bone, which results in tissue ischemia and ultimately infarction and irreversible tissue damage. Acute compartment syndrome is a life- and limb-threatening complication of fractures, crush injuries, burns, vascular injuries, intense exercise, infiltration of intraosseous or other lines, or pressure from casts, splints, and pneumatic garments. About three-quarters of cases are associated with fractures, particularly fractures of the tibia. In children, supracondylar fractures of the elbow are at the highest risk for the development of compartment syndrome.

The most commonly involved spaces are the flexor compartment in the forearm and the anterior compartment of the lower leg. Normal compartment pressure is between 10 and 12 mm Hg. It is generally thought that tissue pressures > 20 mm Hg lead to a clinically significant reduction of blood flow and oxygenation of the tissues inside the affected compartment. Patients may present with acute compartment syndrome within 2 hours of injury or up to 6 days later and classically present with pain out of proportion to physical exam findings. For this reason, increasing analgesic requirements may sometimes be the only clue to developing compartment syndrome. If objective signs are present, tenseness of externally palpable compartments may be the earliest and most objective finding. Passive stretching of involved muscle groups produces intense pain, as does manual compression of an affected compartment. Active movement is likely to be painful as well, while the nerves passing through the affected compartment may be compromised and produce paresthesias. Paresis and muscle weakness are late findings. Pulses are usually maintained unless the presentation is particularly late. Hence, some of the classic five Ps of pain, paresthesias, pallor, pulselessness, and paresis more accurately reflect the late results of acute arterial obstruction and are not always helpful in the diagnosis of acute compartment syndrome before the occurrence of irreversible damage.

The key to the management of acute compartment syndrome is early consideration of the diagnosis and emergent consultation with orthopedic surgery as the diagnosis can be made based on the history and physical exam. Direct measurement of compartment pressure can be done to confirm the diagnosis in equivocal cases but should not delay consultation. There are several systems available for measurement. One is the handheld pressure tonometer. When measuring, obtain at least two measurements and measure adjacent compartments as well. Traditionally, pressures over 30–50 mm Hg were thought to be indications for fasciotomy. However, a better determination may be to take the patient’s diastolic blood pressure (DBP) into account and calculate the delta pressure, which is obtained by subtracting the intracompartmental pressure from the DBP. The reasoning is that a patient with hypotension is less tolerant of elevated compartment pressures as opposed to a normo- or even hypertensive patient. A delta pressure ≤ 30 mm Hg is regarded as concerning and indicative of needing fasciotomy. The affected compartment must also be taken into consideration, since some, such as the ones in the hand, are less tolerant of elevated pressures than others. With a late diagnosis, muscle and nerve damage may be irreversible. Chronic pain and contractures may be observed in such cases.



Application of ice and elevation of the extremity (A) is commonly regarded as part of the first management steps for an acute sprain or fracture, particularly in the prehospital setting. However, the application of ice should be avoided in this case since it may further compromise microvascular flow. Discharge with outpatient orthopedic follow-up if delta pressure is ≤ 30 mm Hg (B) would be inappropriate as this patient has clear signs and symptoms of acute compartment syndrome and a delta pressure ≤ 30 mm Hg confirms the diagnosis. Even if this patient had a normal delta pressure, this patient's signs and symptoms alone should prompt orthopedic surgery consultation in the emergency department. A radiograph of the extremity (D) will not help establish the diagnosis of compartment syndrome in this patient with a known fracture.

One Step Further
Question:
Compartment syndrome of the deep posterior compartment of the lower leg will lead to which passive movement producing intense pain?

Reveal Answer:
Toe extension.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Compartment Syndrome

Most commonly caused by tibia fracture
Most common sites: forearm, lower leg
PE: paresthesias, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis, and pain out of proportion to exam (6 Ps)
Pain (severe) is usually the first symptom
Dx: if delta pressure < 30 mm Hg (diastolic pressure – direct pressure)
Tx: fasciotomy

الفخ: الطالب يختار Application of ice and elevation of the extremity خطأً بدلاً من C، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: A 12-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after an assault at school. He is alert and is able to report that he was stabbed in the abdomen with a knife. Vital signs show HR 80 bpm, RR of 14/min, BP 124/76 mm Hg, and SpO2 of 98% on room air. He has a single stab wound just below the umbilicus without other injuries. His abdomen is soft and nondistended without guarding or rebound. An upright X-ray shows no pneumoperitoneum. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the evaluation and management of this patient's condition?
englishExplanation:
Penetrating abdominal trauma in children, while less common than blunt trauma, remains a significant source of morbidity and mortality, particularly in urban settings. The rate of pediatric penetrating trauma has been increasing in some regions, with gunshot wounds and stabbings being the most common mechanisms. The majority of pediatric penetrating trauma patients are male, with a median age of 14 years, and Black and Hispanic children are disproportionately affected. The pathogenesis depends on the mechanism, as stab wounds cause injury along a relatively predictable, low-energy tract, whereas gunshot wounds produce more extensive tissue damage through cavitation and irregular trajectories, resulting in a higher rate of hollow viscus injury. The most commonly injured organs include the small bowel, liver, and spleen, with anterior abdominal wall and junctional zone injuries associated with higher morbidity.

Children with penetrating abdominal trauma present with an external wound and variable degrees of abdominal pain, tenderness, guarding, and signs of peritonitis, depending on the depth and organs involved. The initial evaluation should follow standard ATLS principles, beginning with the primary survey with assessment of hemodynamic stability, followed by the secondary survey. Indications for immediate laparotomy include hemodynamic instability, peritonitis, evisceration, impalement, hematemesis, blood per rectum, or enteric matter in the wound. Historically, digital rectal examination has been recommended to identify hematochezia, but more recent evidence has suggested very limited utility, and it should be reserved for patients with increased clinical suspicion for bowel injury (e.g., wounds near the rectum, altered mental status requiring intubation). In hemodynamically stable patients without these signs, a selective approach is recommended. For anterior abdominal stab wounds, local wound exploration (LWE) is the recommended first step to assess for fascial penetration. Patients in whom peritoneal violation is confirmed or suspected based on LWE should be admitted for serial abdominal examinations, laboratory monitoring, and CT imaging as indicated. In pediatrics specifically, routine CT is not recommended given the lower rate of significant intra-abdominal injury and the desire to minimize radiation exposure.

Emergency department treatment begins with identification of an unstable airway, breathing, or circulation and resuscitation as needed. Once hemodynamic stability is confirmed and indications for laparotomy are excluded, LWE is performed under local anesthesia, often requiring extension of the wound for adequate visualization. Prophylactic antibiotics are recommended when peritoneal violation is suspected, and laparotomy is indicated if the patient develops peritoneal signs, hemodynamic instability, or a hemoglobin drop > 2 g/dL without other explanation. Complications of penetrating abdominal trauma include wound infection, intra-abdominal abscess, necrotizing fasciitis, diffuse suppurative peritonitis, and sepsis, with hollow viscus injury carrying the highest risk of infectious complications.



While CT of the abdomen (A) is a valuable adjunct in penetrating trauma, it has poor sensitivity for identifying injuries requiring laparotomy in stab wounds and is inferior to serial physical examination in pediatric patients. In pediatric patients specifically, routine CT is not recommended due to the lower rate of significant intra-abdominal injury and the goal of minimizing radiation exposure, and it is more appropriate for back and flank wounds or gunshot wounds in which trajectory assessment is needed.

Premature discharge (B) without at least confirming that the anterior fascia is intact (via LWEE) would be inappropriate, as superficial appearance can be misleading.

Immediate exploratory laparotomy (C) is indicated for hemodynamic instability, peritonitis, evisceration, or impalement. This patient is hemodynamically stable with a soft, nontender abdomen and no peritoneal signs, making routine laparotomy unnecessary.

question: Which of the following radiographic findings is most consistent with pseudosubluxation of C2 on C3 in a 4-year-old who presents to the ED after a ground-level fall?

options.text: Anterior displacement of the posterior vertebral body line of C2 relative to C3 by > 4.5 mm
Disruption of the smooth, continuous curve of the posterior cervical line
Presence of a Mach band at the C2–C3 interspace
Smooth, gentle anterior displacement of C2 on C3 with the anterior aspect of the spinous process of C2 aligned with or posterior to that of C3
Widening of the predental space > 5 mm

correctAnswer: Smooth, gentle anterior displacement of C2 on C3 with the anterior aspect of the spinous process of C2 aligned with or posterior to that of C3
englishExplanation:
Pseudosubluxation of C2 on C3, also known as physiologic anterior subluxation, is a common finding in young children, particularly those < 8 years old. It occurs due to the relative hypermobility and ligamentous laxity of the pediatric cervical spine, combined with the incompletely developed cervical musculature. Radiographically, this manifests as anterior displacement of the C2 vertebral body on C3. However, a key distinguishing feature from true subluxation is the alignment of the spinous processes. In pseudosubluxation, the anterior aspect of the spinous process of C2 will typically be aligned with or posterior to the anterior aspect of the spinous process of C3. This is because the posterior ligaments remain intact, preventing significant displacement.

To differentiate pseudosubluxation from true cervical spine injury, several radiographic parameters are crucial. The anterior displacement of C2 on C3 in pseudosubluxation is generally < 2 mm. The Swischuk line, a smooth curve drawn connecting the anterior aspect of the posterior arch of C1 to the anterior aspect of the posterior arch of C3, should remain intact. Widening of the predental space (the space between the anterior arch of C1 and the odontoid process of C2) > 5 mm in children suggests atlantoaxial instability, not pseudosubluxation. The presence of a Mach band, an optical illusion caused by overlapping structures, is not a direct indicator of pseudosubluxation or instability at C2–C3.

In the emergency department, the primary goal is to rule out true injury. A careful clinical examination, including assessment for focal neurological deficits, neck tenderness, and mechanism of injury, is paramount. If clinical suspicion for injury is low and radiographic findings are consistent with pseudosubluxation (< 2 mm anterior displacement of C2 on C3 with normal spinous process alignment and intact Swischuk line), and the patient is neurologically intact, further imaging or intervention is usually not required. However, any concerning clinical findings or radiographic abnormalities warrant further investigation with advanced imaging (e.g., CT scan) and consultation with a specialist.



Anterior displacement of the posterior vertebral body line of C2 relative to C3 by > 4.5 mm (A) is concerning for true subluxation or ligamentous injury and warrants further investigation with advanced imaging. This degree of displacement is beyond the typical range for physiologic pseudosubluxation.

Disruption of the smooth, continuous curve of the posterior cervical line (B) (Swischuk line) suggests posterior ligamentous injury or true subluxation and necessitates further evaluation to rule out cervical spine instability. Swischuk line should remain smooth and continuous in cases of pseudosubluxation.

A Mach band (C) is an optical illusion that can occur at interfaces of different densities on radiographs. It is not a specific finding related to pseudosubluxation or cervical spine instability and can be seen in normal radiographs.

A predental space > 5 mm (E) in children indicates potential atlantoaxial instability, often due to ligamentous injury or underlying conditions. This finding is not characteristic of pseudosubluxation at the C2–C3 level.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
A stable avulsion fracture of the spinous process.

question: Which injury pattern comprises a tripod fracture?

options.text: Lateral orbit, orbital floor, and maxilla
Nasal bridge, maxilla, and orbital floor

englishExplanation:
A zygomaticomaxillary complex (tripod) fracture involves fractures of the lateral orbit, zygoma, and maxilla. Despite being referred to as a tripod fracture, the term is somewhat inaccurate because a fourth suture is often involved: the sphenozygomatic suture, located between the sphenoid and zygomatic bones. This fracture typically results from a direct blow to the face, such as from trauma during sports, motor vehicle collisions, or assaults.

On physical examination, patients often present with tenderness, swelling, and ecchymosis around the affected area, which can make detailed assessment challenging. Malocclusion of the upper teeth is also common due to the involvement of the maxilla, causing misalignment of the dental arches. This misalignment can affect the patient’s bite and jaw function.

Another key feature of a zygomaticomaxillary fracture is potential involvement of the infraorbital nerve, which can be disrupted by the fracture. This nerve innervates the maxillary teeth, the upper lip, and the cheek. When damaged, patients may report numbness or paresthesia (tingling) in these areas, which is a common finding in these fractures.

Tripod fractures usually require operative stabilization to prevent long-term complications. If left untreated, the fractured zygoma can sink posteriorly and inferiorly due to the loss of structural support, leading to significant facial asymmetry and cosmetic deformities. Additionally, the fracture can affect the function of the eye and cheek muscles, leading to difficulty with eye movement or diplopia (double vision) if the orbit is involved. Due to the complexity of the injury and the risk of long-term functional and cosmetic issues, early recognition and operative repair, typically involving open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), are critical. CT imaging is the gold standard for diagnosing the extent of the fracture and planning the surgical approach.



Lateral orbit, orbital floor, and maxilla (A) can be involved in facial fractures, this pattern does not describe a classic tripod fracture, as it does not involve the zygoma, which is crucial in the tripod fracture.

Lateral, medial, and posterior malleolus (C) describes a trimalleolar fracture, which is an injury to the ankle that involves the lateral, medial, and posterior malleoli, not a facial injury.

Nasal bridge, maxilla, and orbital floor (D) involves the nasal bones and the orbit but does not represent the classic tripod fracture pattern, which must include the zygoma.

question: A 35-year-old man is stabbed in the neck after a fight and brought to the ED. His vital signs are within normal limits. Exam is notable for a slow leak of blood from the wound, which is not pulsatile. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: MRI of the neck with contrast

englishExplanation:
Penetrating neck trauma can be a serious injury, as patients can have aerodigestive and vascular injuries. Management is based on the patient’s clinical status and hard and soft signs of injury. While sources can vary on the list of specific hard signs of injury, some include active pulsatile bleeding, expanding hematoma, bruits or thrill over the injury, shock unresponsive to initial fluid therapy, and absent or asymmetric pulses indicating possible arterial disruption. Soft signs are less definitive and include stable hematoma, minor hemorrhage, hypotension in the field, and neurological deficits that may suggest vascular impairment. When hard signs of injury are present, especially alongside hemodynamic instability, patients are typically taken directly to the operating room without undergoing imaging. This patient is hemodynamically stable and has no hard signs of injury since he has slow venous bleeding. For this reason, performing a CTA of the neck is appropriate. CTA is the preferred imaging modality to assess for underlying tissue and artery injury in penetrating neck trauma in stable patients without hard signs of vascular injury.



Bedside exploration (A) would be appropriate for a minor wound to perhaps look for a foreign body. However, penetrating trauma to the neck in a stable patient requires a CTA to assess for possible missed arterial injury.

MRI of the neck with contrast (C) would be a slow, time-consuming, and unnecessary imaging study. It might be a more accurate test to assess for suspected malignancy or infectious collections.

Transferring to the operating room (D) is not necessary at this time in a stable patient with no hard signs of injury. If hard signs were to arise, then emergent transfer would be warranted.

question: A 17-year-old boy presents to the ED with a gunshot wound to the right flank. Vital signs include a BP of 75/48 mm Hg, HR of 133 bpm, RR of 32/min, and SpO2 of 93%. The patient is intubated, and packed red blood cells are administered with minimal improvement. A bedside FAST examination is negative. Physical examination reveals a single wound to the right flank. What management should be pursued?
englishExplanation:
The patient presents with a gunshot wound to the abdomen and hemodynamic instability, mandating an exploratory laparotomy. The diagnostic workup and management of gunshot wounds are complicated in patients with hemodynamic stability. However, management in an unstable patient with a penetrating injury is more straightforward. Initial stabilization should start with the airway, breathing, and circulation. Volume resuscitation should be administered in the form of packed red blood cells. The patient should be exposed to search for all wounds as gunshot wounds can often be missed in the axilla and groin if the patient is not systematically examined. A FAST examination should be performed as it may rapidly reveal the presence of intraperitoneal blood. Regardless of the FAST examination findings, patients with gunshot wounds to the abdomen require exploratory laparotomy if they are hemodynamically unstable or have peritoneal signs, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, intraperitoneal air, evidence of diaphragmatic injury, or signs of evisceration.



A CT scan of the abdomen (A) may reveal the exact location of the injury but will delay care in this hemodynamically unstable patient.

Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) (B) was widely used prior to the FAST examination to identify intra-abdominal bleeding after trauma. However, in this patient, DPL findings would not change management.

Observation and repeat FAST examination (C) can be performed in select patients with penetrating injuries if they do not have any of the previously mentioned hard signs requiring immediate operative care.

One Step Further

What findings constitute a positive diagnostic peritoneal lavage?

Reveal Answer:
Aspiration of > 10 mL of blood or any bile, feces, or urine, or lavage fluid with > 100,000 RBC/µL, > 500 WBC/µL, or the presence of amylase in the aspirated fluid.

question: A 25-year-old man is a restrained passenger in a head-on motor vehicle collision. He reports left hip and knee pain. Radiographs are unremarkable. Exam shows no apparent joint effusion, intact extensor mechanism, and intact pulses, but there is gross laxity of left knee internal ligaments. What complication of this injury is this patient most likely to be experiencing?

options.text: Diminished plantar flexion of the foot

englishExplanation:
This patient has a knee dislocation with spontaneous reduction prior to presentation. It most commonly occurs following motor vehicle collisions or contact sports injuries but may also occur in less violent trauma such as a fall in patients who have morbid obesity. Because of severe ligamentous damage, spontaneous reduction occurs about half the time. A spontaneously reduced knee dislocation should be suspected in any patient who presents after trauma with a grossly unstable knee. The most common nerve injury is a peroneal nerve injury, which causes paresthesia of the dorsal aspect of the foot and diminished dorsiflexion of the foot, i.e., “foot drop.” Popliteal artery injury is also common and can be present even with normal distal pulses. Vessel patency should be evaluated with ankle-brachial index or with CT angiography of the lower extremity. Proximal tibial fractures are also seen in these cases and may be missed on plain films. A knee with complete disruption of all major ligaments and the joint capsule may exhibit less swelling and pain than when there is less severe injury with partial disruption and a tense hemarthrosis. Treatment involves posterior splint immobilization in 15° of flexion and immediate consult to orthopedics, and possibly vascular surgery.



Diminished extension of the knee (B) is seen when there is a rupture of the quadriceps mechanism, which can involve the quadriceps or patellar tendon, a patellar fracture, or an avulsion of the tibial tuberosity. However, this patient is described as having an intact knee extensor mechanism.

Diminished plantar flexion of the foot (C) is seen in cases of tibial nerve injury, which is less common than peroneal nerve injury in cases of knee dislocation.

Hemarthrosis of the knee (D) can be seen in knee dislocations or in any injury involving internal knee ligamentous or meniscal injuries. However, this patient is described as having no apparent joint effusion. A torn anterior cruciate ligament accounts for about 75% of all knee hemarthroses.

question: A 19-year-old man presents for evaluation after an altercation. He reports that the night prior to evaluation, he was punched multiple times in the face and then thrown to the ground. There was no loss of consciousness. He reports pain in the entire midface region and nose. Physical examination demonstrates tenderness on palpation of nasal bones with soft tissue swelling. There is no crepitus. When you grasp the upper teeth and rock them, the maxilla and nasal structures move as a unit, but the orbits do not move. What is the patient’s diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s physical examination is consistent with a Le Fort II fracture, which is a bilateral fracture forming the shape of a pyramid. The injury includes fractures of the nasal bridge, maxilla, lacrimal bones, orbital floor, and rim. When grabbing the upper teeth, the entire region moves as a unit. Treatment is surgical.



A Le Fort I (A) fracture is a transverse fracture that extends above the roots of the teeth and through the maxilla. It may be either unilateral or bilateral. In this case, when the upper teeth are grabbed, the maxilla may move. The patient may also report malocclusion on biting.

Le Fort III (C) fractures are complex fractures that separate the skull from the face. The fractures extend from the bridge of the nose through the orbital walls (medial, lateral, and floor) and finally into the zygomatic arch. This results in craniofacial disjunction.

Le Fort IV (D) fractures are similar to Le Fort III fractures but also include the frontal bone.

A CSF leak may occur because the fracture may involve the base of the sphenoid.

question: A 70-year-old man presents after a fall down 12 stairs at home. He reports a headache. There is a large parietal scalp hematoma. His noncontrast computed tomography scan of the head is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely source of bleeding?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s imaging and physical examination are consistent with a traumatic acute subdural hematoma. A subdural hematoma is a collection of blood between the dura and the arachnoid mater. Subdural hematomas occur when there is a rupture of the bridging veins from the movement of the brain relative to the skull, such as that seen with acceleration-deceleration injuries. Subdural hematomas may be acute, subacute, or chronic.

Subdural hematomas occur most commonly in individuals with brain atrophy, such as older patients and those with alcohol use disorder or previous traumatic brain injury. This results in blood filling the potential space between the dura and arachnoid. Acute subdural hematomas are characteristically seen after a traumatic head injury. The use of antithrombotic agents such as warfarin and aspirin also increases the risk of subdural hematoma.

Patients typically present with a headache, mental status changes, seizures, or focal deficits. Subdural hematoma is diagnosed on noncontrast CT of the head and appears as a crescent-shaped hematoma that may cross suture lines.

Management of subdural hematomas includes neurosurgical consultation for possible surgical evacuation. However, small subdural hematomas may be closely observed with serial noncontrast CT scans of the head. Indications for emergent surgery in a patient with a subdural hematoma include neurologic deterioration and > 5 mm of midline shift on CT imaging.



The internal carotid artery (B) is a major artery supplying blood to the brain. Damage to the internal carotid artery can lead to large-scale ischemic stroke or intracranial bleeding, but it does not cause the slow venous bleeding associated with subdural hematomas.

Meningeal veins (C) course through the dura mater, while bridging veins drain the underlying neural tissue and puncture through the dura mater, making these more prone to shearing and causing a subdural hematoma than meningeal veins.

The middle meningeal artery (D) is the vessel most commonly injured in epidural hematomas, not subdural hematomas.

The superior sagittal sinus (E) is where the meningeal veins and bridging veins drain. It is typically not involved in causing a subdural hematoma.

question: A 27-year-old man is involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He has a contusion to his anterior chest wall. He reports chest discomfort, and his ECG demonstrates non-specific ST and T wave changes. His troponin level is mildly elevated. Which of the following sequela is most likely to occur within 2 weeks of injury?
englishExplanation:
This patient likely has a myocardial contusion. This is a difficult diagnosis to make because of somewhat unclear diagnostic criteria. The only true mechanism by which the diagnosis can be made is histologically. It occurs in cases of severe blunt chest trauma. It is postulated that the heart is contused from compression between the sternum and the vertebra or an elevated diaphragm. In most cases, the contused myocardium heals spontaneously. More than 50% of cases develop a pericardial effusion approximately 2 weeks after the injury. Rarely, the contusion can lead to necrosis of the ventricular wall, causing either ventricular rupture or aneurysm. Most patients with a myocardial contusion have external chest wall trauma. The most sensitive sign is sinus tachycardia, although this carries a very low specificity due to the fact that most severe trauma patients will have this. The role of cardiac enzyme testing is not clear, although some recent evidence does suggest a higher risk of cardiac complications in patients with an elevated troponin level. ECG evaluation is most commonly nonspecific without any pathognomonic changes for a cardiac contusion.



An impaired ejection fraction (A) is possible immediately after the injury if the contusion is severe. On echocardiography, the area of contusion appears similar to an area of infarction with limited motion.

Myocardial rupture (B) is a very rare complication of myocardial contusion. In the area of contusion, a hematoma forms. With reabsorption of the hematoma, an area of necrosis forms, which can ultimately rupture. This occurs around 2 weeks after the injury but is very rare and much less common than a pericardial effusion.

Several cases of severe dysrhythmia (D) have occurred up to 12 hours after the injury. Less significant dysrhythmias have been reported up to 72 hours after the injury.

What medications should a patient with a cardiac contusion receive?

Reveal Answer:
Analgesia (there are no cardiac specific medications).

question: A 6-year-old girl presents to a rural ED (90 miles from the next nearest city) with a head injury after falling from a play structure on a playground. Initially, she got up and continued to play but subsequently reported head pain. While being monitored in the ED, she develops persistent vomiting. Her head CT scan is above. Which of the following is the most appropriate step to care for this patient?

options.text: Air transfer to a facility with pediatric neurosurgery
Ground transfer to a pediatric trauma center
Monitor for oral tolerance after a concussion

correctAnswer: Air transfer to a facility with pediatric neurosurgery
englishExplanation:
There is good data that well-appearing children do not need cross-sectional head imaging after a minor closed head injury unless they have altered mental status or signs of a basilar skull fracture. Those who are well-appearing and back to their baseline but had any loss of consciousness, vomiting, severe headache, or a severe mechanism can also usually be closely monitored for 4–6 hours instead of obtaining cross-sectional imaging. If children worsen during their monitoring period of 4–6 hours, like in this patient, cross-sectional imaging should be rapidly obtained. The above CT scan shows a convex area of bleeding, which suggests the unusual presence of an arterial intracranial bleed (i.e., epidural hematoma).

Epidural hematomas are one of the major reasons for this monitoring period in children after a head injury. While they are extremely rare, even mild trauma in young children can cause one. Most children with an epidural hematoma present with a high-risk mechanism, such as a fall from > 10 feet, a motor vehicle collision, or a direct blow to the temporal region. The classic presentation of an epidural hematoma is an initial loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval until the arterial bleed causes an increase in intracranial pressure and a rapid coma. This lucid interval is typically 4–6 hours, the same duration as the monitoring period for children.

Definitive treatment for an epidural hematoma is with emergent neurosurgical intervention. Administering hypertonic saline and mannitol, elevating the head of the bed, and inducing hyperventilation (if intubated) are encouraged but are temporizing measures only. Any delay in surgical intervention will result in permanent neurologic injury or death, while patients who receive prompt treatment will usually have good outcomes. As such, rural facilities caring for a child with an epidural hematoma should transport them to a facility with a pediatric neurosurgeon by the most rapid method available, which in this case is air transfer.



Contacting child protective services (B) with concern for child abuse is important when abuse is suspected. Intracranial bleeding from child abuse is typically a subdural hematoma, whereas epidural hematomas, like in this patient, are more likely to be accidental, especially in the setting of known trauma.

Ground transfer to a pediatric trauma center (C) is most appropriate in the case of a patient with an epidural hematoma when the two hospitals are within the same city and transport by ground is as fast as or faster than by air.

If the CT scan results had been normal, monitoring for oral tolerance after a concussion (D) would be appropriate.

Reveal Answer:

question: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department after hitting his tooth on a pipe while doing home repairs. Physical exam reveals the finding above. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Smooth the edge with a file and refer for follow-up with a dentist
Smooth the edge with a file, apply calcium hydroxide paste, and refer for follow-up with a dentist within 1 week

englishExplanation:
Dental trauma can lead to fractures of the tooth. When there is dental trauma, it is first important to perform a thorough trauma exam to ensure no other injuries are present. A tooth fracture can be diagnosed clinically. An Ellis class III fracture presents when a fracture goes through the enamel and dentin and enters the pulp. A small red or pink area will be noted on exam (this is the pulp) along with exposure of the dentin, which is yellowish in color. An Ellis class III fracture threatens the tooth's viability. Management requires analgesia and an urgent dental consult for a pulpotomy to prevent infection. Calcium hydroxide paste can be used to cover the area if the patient can see a dentist in a timely fashion. Early care is important in an Ellis class III fracture for improved tooth survival.



Amoxicillin-clavulanate and dental follow-up tomorrow (A) is not appropriate management of any type of tooth fracture. There is no clear evidence that antibiotic prophylaxis is helpful in the case of dental fracture, though it is sometimes used.

Smoothing the edge with a file and referring for follow-up with a dentist (C) is appropriate management of an Ellis class I fracture. This fracture type only involves the enamel. Smoothing the surface can reduce the risk of caries in the future.

Smoothing the edge with a file, applying calcium hydroxide paste, and referring for follow-up with a dentist in 1 week (D) is appropriate management of an Ellis class II fracture, which presents with dental pain, temperature and air sensitivity, and exposure of the yellow dentin layer.

question: Considering adult facial bony anatomy, which of the following facial bones is LEAST likely and MOST likely to be fractured in the setting of facial trauma?

options.text: Frontal bone is least likely and nasal bone is most likely
Mandible is least likely and maxilla is most likely
Maxilla is least likely and zygoma is most likely
Zygoma is least likely and orbital bones are most likely

correctAnswer: Frontal bone is least likely and nasal bone is most likely
englishExplanation:
Nasal bone fractures account for almost half of all facial fracture injuries. Assaults and sports injuries cause the majority of these injuries. The nose is easily exposed to trauma as it is the most anterior and prominent feature of the face. The frontal sinus is protected by a thick cortical bone and is typically more resistant to fracture than other facial bones. Frontal sinus fractures occur only with high impact traumas such as motor vehicle collisions, assaults with weapons, and industrial incidents. Because of the high energy required to fracture the frontal sinus bone, it is rare to find an isolated fracture without other underlying intracranial pathology. Taking this information into consideration, the facial bone LEAST likely to fracture is the frontal sinus bone, and the facial bone MOST likely to fracture is the nasal bone.



Mandible fractures are more common in higher impact injuries such as motor vehicle collisions, sports injuries, and interpersonal violence. Most fractures occur at the angle of the mandible or the mandibular condyle. A decent blow to the face during a fight is enough to fracture the mandible, making it more likely to break than the frontal bone. Hence, the mandible is least likely, and the maxilla is most likely (B) is incorrect.

Fractures of the maxilla are often the result of high energy blunt force from motor vehicle collisions and falls. Because of its relationship with the orbital bones, nasal cavity, and oral cavity, maxilla fractures can be life threatening and disfiguring. Zygomatic fractures typically occur secondary to motor vehicle collisions. Due to the thickness of the bone, isolated zygomatic fractures are uncommon. Taken together this information means that the maxilla is LEAST likely and zygoma is MOST likely (C) is incorrect.

Orbital fractures commonly occur in men in the third decade of life secondary to motor vehicle collisions or interpersonal violence. Orbital fractures typically do not occur in isolation as the orbits are set back in the facial structure. The weakest portions of the orbit, and therefore the most frequently fractured, include the orbital floor bones, the maxilla, and the lamina papyracea. A direct blow to the eye frequently causes a blowout fracture of the orbital bones. However, this fracturing likely helps to prevent globe rupture. It is easier to fracture the orbital bones (D) than many other facial bones, but nasal fractures are still more likely than orbital fractures.

question: An animal laboratory worker presents with paresthesias on his forearm. While at work 2 days ago, he was bitten on the arm by a monkey. Physical examination does not reveal any abnormalities other than the bite mark on his forearm. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent to administer?
englishExplanation:
Primate bites are rare outside of research and zoo settings in the United States. Bites by primates are highly infectious, although infecting bacterial organisms are not well identified. Monkeys carry Cercopithecine herpesvirus 1, also called Herpesvirus simiae or more simply, B virus, which is fatal to humans if not treated early. Treatment is with acyclovir. Humans can develop infections after bites or scratches. Following an incubation period of 2 days to 5 weeks, symptoms begin with paresthesias and subsequent development of vesicles. Untreated infection may lead to encephalitis and coma. Treatment with intravenous acyclovir improves survival, especially when started early.



Bacterial infections may develop after an animal bite but most commonly manifest as cellulitis. In this clinical scenario, the physical examination does not reveal evidence of cellulitis 2 days after the bite, and the symptoms of paresthesias should guide the clinician to be concerned about B virus. While it is prudent to prophylactically treat human and monkey bites with antibiotics after the event, this patient's physical examination does not suggest a developing infection. Ampicillin (B) is a penicillin-based antibiotic that provides gram-positive coverage. However, it is ineffective against B virus.

Fluconazole (C) is an anti-fungal agent that may be used in topical candidal infections or vaginal yeast infections.

Vancomycin (D) is frequently used as an antibacterial agent for skin infections and has excellent activity against Streptococcus and Staphylococcus, particularly methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

One Step Further

Should a primate bite be sutured?

Reveal Answer:
Primate bites, along with cat bites, typically should not be sutured, unlike dog bites, which can be repaired if they are uncomplicated.

question: Which of the following neurovascular structures is most likely to be injured with a tibiofemoral dislocation?
englishExplanation:
Dislocation of the tibiofemoral joint is considered a potentially limb-threatening injury. It is often the result of high-energy trauma, such as a motor vehicle collision, but may also occur with more minor mechanisms such as falling and sports-related injuries. The majority of dislocations are anterior (i.e., the tibia is anteriorly displaced relative to the femoral condyles) and result from hyperextension of the knee. While many dislocations are clinically apparent on examination with abnormal positioning of the knee, ecchymosis, and hemarthrosis, a significant number of dislocations spontaneously reduce prior to presentation, making diagnosis more difficult.

Injury to the popliteal artery is the most severe complication associated with knee dislocations and can be catastrophic if missed. Signs of vascular injury include pallor, diminished or absent pulses, paresthesias, and paralysis. All patients with a knee dislocation should undergo vascular assessment (e.g., CT angiography or ankle-brachial index with observation for serial exams) even if the physical exam is unremarkable. While the popliteal artery is the most common vascular injury associated with a knee dislocation, injury to the peroneal nerve is the most frequently encountered neurologic injury, affecting up to 40% of patients. Symptoms would include decreased sensation to the dorsum of the foot and weakness with dorsiflexion at the ankle. In addition to frequent neurovascular injuries, tibiofemoral dislocations are associated with significant ligamentous injury.



The femoral artery (A) is not typically injured with a knee dislocation, as it terminates proximal to the knee.

The posterior tibial artery (C) and the posterior tibial nerve (D) may be injured with a knee dislocation but are less common. Signs of injury to the posterior tibial nerve include decreased plantar sensation and weakness with plantar flexion of the foot.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the ankle-brachial index (ABI)?

Reveal Answer:
The ratio of the systolic blood pressure at the ankle compared to the systolic brachial pressure. An ABI < 0.9 is considered abnormal.

question: A previously healthy 8-year-old boy presents after he sustained an injury to his arm while playing with his twin sibling on the playground. An X-ray is seen above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Pediatric bones tend to bow rather than break when a force is applied to them. A torus fracture, also known as a buckle or cortical fracture, typically results in bulging or buckling of the periosteum secondary to compressive forces. These fractures are usually of the metaphysis and result in minimal visual deformity. There is usually soft tissue swelling and point tenderness at the site of injury. It is essential to review the cortical margins on the radiograph for any asymmetry, bulging, or deviation, which can be a subtle clue to diagnosing a torus fracture. The treatment is similar to other stable fractures and includes splinting in a position of function and close orthopedic follow-up.



A corner fracture (A), also known as a bucket handle fracture, is associated with child abuse. These fractures result from a mechanism of pulling, twisting, or shaking of the limb that causes rapid acceleration-deceleration with a resultant epiphyseal-metaphyseal chip fracture. Greenstick fractures (B) are incomplete fractures that result in cortical disruption on only one side of the bone. These fractures may result in angulation and they may require reduction. Scaphoid fractures (C) are the most common fractured carpal bone and are associated with snuffbox tenderness on physical exam. Failure to identify and splint a scaphoid fracture can lead to avascular necrosis.

question: What is an expected X-ray finding in a patient with a Maisonneuve fracture?

options.text: Fracture at the base of the fifth metatarsal

englishExplanation:
A Maisonneuve fracture involves a specific injury pattern that includes a proximal fibular fracture, deltoid ligament disruption, and disruption of the syndesmosis between the tibia and fibula. It typically results from a high-energy rotational injury to the ankle. The injury mechanism is often a pronation-external rotation force, leading to an unstable ankle injury involving medial malleolar injury or deltoid ligament disruption.

On an X-ray, a proximal fibular fracture is the expected finding in a Maisonneuve fracture. While the primary area of pain may be the ankle, the injury extends up the fibula, often unnoticed unless examined appropriately. Tenderness or swelling over the proximal fibula should raise suspicion for this fracture. Additionally, the widening of the medial clear space seen on an ankle X-ray results from the syndesmotic injury and ligamentous instability caused by the rotational forces.

Diagnosing a Maisonneuve fracture requires careful clinical evaluation and imaging of the entire lower leg, including the ankle and the proximal fibula. Definitive treatment typically involves surgical intervention to stabilize the syndesmosis, especially if the injury is unstable. This may include fixation of the syndesmosis and, at times, fixation of the fibula. In the meantime, a long leg posterior splint suffices for stabilization. Early recognition and management are crucial to prevent chronic instability and arthritis of the ankle joint.



A Jones fracture is a fracture of the base of the fifth metatarsal (A), usually caused by an acute inversion injury. It occurs in the midfoot, and while it can be associated with ankle injuries, it is anatomically distinct from the Maisonneuve fracture. The Maisonneuve fracture involves the fibula and the syndesmosis.

A lateral malleolus fracture (B) is a break in the distal fibula. While lateral malleolus fractures are common in ankle injuries, they do not occur in the setting of a Maisonneuve fracture. The Maisonneuve fracture can be associated with a medial malleolus fracture in addition to disruption of the deltoid ligament. However, the key to diagnosing a Maisonneuve fracture is identifying a proximal fibular fracture, not a lateral malleolus fracture, which occurs more distally.

A posterior malleolus fracture (C) involves the posterior part of the distal tibia, often associated with ankle fractures and ligamentous injuries. However, in the case of a Maisonneuve fracture, the injury pattern is more specifically related to the proximal fibula and syndesmosis rather than the posterior tibia. Though both can be seen in complex ankle injuries, the posterior malleolus is not the characteristic finding.

A tibial plateau fracture (E) involves the proximal tibia and is commonly caused by high-energy trauma, such as motor vehicle collisions or falls from a height. This type of fracture is located above the knee, far from the ankle joint, and is not associated with the injury mechanism of a Maisonneuve fracture.

One Step Further
Question:
Which nerve can be injured and lead to neuropraxia after a Maisonneuve fracture?

Reveal Answer:
Peroneal nerve.

question: You are evaluating a 19-year-old man who presents to the ED for a burn. Based on the American Burn Association’s criteria, which of the following would necessitate transfer of this patient to a burn center?

options.text: Full-thickness burn of 5% total body surface area
Partial-thickness burn of 8% total body surface area
Superficial burn of 25% total body surface area

correctAnswer: Full-thickness burn of 5% total body surface area
englishExplanation:
Burns are classified based on the depth of tissue damage, percent of body surface area affected, and source of the burn (chemical, thermal, electrical, radiation). Superficial (first-degree) burns involve only the epidermis and appear as reddened, intact, nonblistered skin. Partial-thickness burns are deeper and involve the dermis. They can be further classified into superficial or deep partial burns. They may blister and are very painful. Full-thickness burns (third- and fourth-degree) extend into the subcutaneous tissues and into muscle, fascia, and bone. Because of the depth of injury and associated nerve damage, full-thickness burns are usually not painful. The American Burn Association has developed criteria for the disposition of burn patients. These are guidelines and should never discourage a clinician from admitting or transferring a patient when they feel it is clinically indicated. Full-thickness burns in patients of any age require transfer to a burn center.



Adults with partial-thickness burns < 10% (C), superficial burns (D) of any extent, and patients with diet-controlled diabetes (B) do not require transfer to a burn center. However, patients with burns and significant comorbidities may require transfer to a burn center.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
Patients with significant comorbidities and or immunosuppression, lack of resources (transportation, finances, shelter), and those at the extremes of age.

question: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the ED by her coach after she was knocked over by an opposing team member during a soccer game. A video of the event shows the patient being struck in the lateral knee while pivoting to kick the soccer ball. She reports pain with weight-bearing and the feeling that her knee is going to give out on her. On exam, there is tenderness on the lateral aspect of the affected knee. Laxity is noted on anterior drawer and Lachman testing. There is also pain in the joint with varus testing. The remaining physical exam and knee testing are negative. X-ray of the knee shows an avulsion fracture near the lateral tibial plateau. Which ligamentous injury is most common with this type of fracture?
englishExplanation:
A Segond fracture is an avulsion fracture of the lateral tibial plateau. The mechanism of injury is excessive internal rotational force with varus stress in a flexed knee. This fracture involves the insertion site of the lateral capsular ligament and is often accompanied by anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries. Exam findings for ACL tears include pain, swelling, and limited range of motion of the affected knee. The patient may have instability in the joint or the feeling that it may give out. Additionally, anterior drawer, Lachman, and pivot shift testing will be positive.

The anterior drawer test is performed with the patient lying supine with their leg flexed 90 degrees. The examiner stabilizes the lower leg and pulls the tibia anteriorly. The Lachman test is similar to the anterior drawer test and differs only in positioning. The patient lies supine with their leg flexed 20–30 degrees. The examiner stabilizes the thigh and attempts to move the tibia forward relative to the femur. The test is positive when increased anterior movement of the tibia occurs compared to the femur. The Lachman test is considered more sensitive and reliable for partial ACL tears than the anterior drawer test. In the pivot shift test, the patient lies on their back with the knee extended. The examiner bends the knee while applying valgus force with slight external rotation to the tibia. An abnormal clicking sound or sudden reduction of the tibia indicates an ACL abnormality. Diagnosis is confirmed through imaging, which may suggest tears based on the location of fracture sites. However, definitive testing like MRI may be required.

Treatment of Segond fractures is dependent upon the severity of knee instability. It ranges from conservative treatment with rest, ice, compression, elevation, and physical therapy for less severe injuries to surgical intervention for more severe tears. Orthopedic surgery consultation or referral is recommended.



The lateral collateral ligament (LCL) (B) is often injured during hyperextension with a varus stress. LCL injuries are less common because the contralateral leg usually provides some protection. They are also more stable than medial collateral ligament injuries. The collateral ligament stress test will be positive with LCL injuries. This test involves the patient lying supine while the examiner applies valgus and varus stress to the joint at 0 degrees and again at 30 degrees. Positive findings for LCL injury will be observed with the knee in the flexed position. The examiner will feel a widening over the lateral aspect of the joint line during varus stress, which was not described in this case.

The mechanism for medial collateral ligament (C) injury is often valgus stress resulting from a direct blow to the lateral aspect of the knee. This injury is also assessed with the collateral ligament stress test. Positive findings are also seen during flexion, but in this case, the test is positive when widening of the medial joint line is felt during valgus stress to the joint.

Posterior cruciate ligament (D) injury results from a posterior force on a flexed knee. Examples include dashboard injuries or falling directly onto a flexed knee. Instability of the knee joint is often not noticed immediately. The posterior drawer and the posterior sag signs are the clinical tests of choice for assessing these injuries. The posterior drawer sign is performed with the patient lying supine and the knee flexed 90 degrees. The examiner holds the foot and applies a backward force to the tibia. Movement of the tibia > 5 mm posteriorly is indicative of injury. The posterior sag sign test is performed with the patient supine and a pillow placed under the thigh with the knee flexed 45 or 90 degrees. The examiner observes the tibia. Any posterior sagging backward is considered positive, which is not seen in this case.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
With the patient seated, the leg may be passively elevated at the ankle into full extension, causing the tibia to fall backward relative to the femur.
