question: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department after being involved in a motor vehicle collision. He was an unrestrained driver traveling highway speeds when he hit a tree head on. He is awake and alert but reports intense right leg pain. Vital signs are a BP of 135/70 mm Hg, HR of 95 bpm, RR of 16/min, and SpO2 of 98% on room air. Physical exam reveals the right leg to be shortened and internally rotated. X-ray confirms a posterior hip dislocation. Which of the following is the most common injury associated with a traumatic posterior hip dislocation?

options.text: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

englishExplanation:
Hip dislocations are true orthopedic emergencies. Because of the considerable force required to cause these injuries, patients often have other injuries, and a thorough physical exam is required. Up to 70% of patients with a hip dislocation have an associated fracture of the acetabulum. The force required to dislocate a pediatric hip is less than that of an adult because the acetabulum is not completely developed. Because of this, minor trauma can dislocate the hip in a young child, and in school-aged children, athletic injuries are the most common cause of traumatic hip dislocation. In the teenage years and beyond, motor vehicle collisions are the predominant cause.

Posterior hip dislocations are almost always the result of motor vehicle collisions. A seated vehicle occupant typically has the hip adducted, flexed, and internally rotated at the time of impact. The force is transmitted through the femoral shaft to the femoral head as the knee strikes the dashboard, and the femoral shaft dislocates posteriorly. These dislocations account for 80–90% of hip dislocations. Anterior hip dislocations are seen in 10–15% of patients and include pubic, obturator, and iliac crest dislocations. Less commonly, central and inferior dislocations can occur.

Patients with posterior hip dislocations typically hold the hip flexed, adducted, and internally rotated, and the leg generally appears shortened. In contrast, patients with anterior hip dislocations hold the hip in abduction, slight flexion, and external rotation, and the leg may appear lengthened. The neurovascular exam should focus on the sciatic nerve and femoral vessels. The most common associated injury is an acetabular fracture, but sciatic nerve palsy occurs in approximately 10% of patients with hip dislocations. Most commonly, the peroneal nerve is involved, as manifested by weakness of the extensor hallucis longus, weakness of dorsiflexion, and numbness over the dorsum of the foot.

An anteroposterior pelvis X-ray should be obtained in all trauma patients and will identify most hip dislocations. A lateral view of the hip is recommended if a dislocation is noted. Associated fractures are important to diagnose because they (especially acetabular fractures) may impede attempts at closed reduction.

Reduction of hip dislocations should be performed within 6 hours. The incidence of avascular necrosis (AVN), traumatic arthritis, and permanent sciatic nerve palsy increase exponentially with the length of time the hip remains dislocated. Up to 15% of patients with hip dislocations develop AVN. Other risk factors for development of AVN include total dislocation time, severity of the injury, number of reduction attempts, and underlying comorbid conditions.

In the case of simple dislocations, closed reduction should be attempted in the ED, typically with the use of procedural sedation. The Allis technique is the most commonly used technique for reducing posterior hip dislocations. The patient is placed in a supine position with the pelvis stabilized by an assistant. The knee of the affected extremity is flexed, and steady traction is applied in line with the deformity. The hip is slowly brought to 90° of flexion while applying upward traction. The assistant then pushes the greater trochanter forward toward the acetabulum. Other techniques often used are the Stimson, Whistler, and Captain Morgan techniques. If closed reduction is unsuccessful, the patient should be taken to the operating room for open or closed reduction under general anesthesia.

After reduction, postreduction anteroposterior pelvis X-rays should be obtained to verify adequacy of reduction. Most patients with a native hip dislocation will require admission to the hospital for serial exams and orthopedic surgery evaluation.



AVN of the femoral head (B) is the most severe complication seen with hip dislocations. The incidence of AVN of the femoral head occurs in 5% of patients who undergo prompt reduction, but increases to 50% if reduced > 6 hours after injury.

Femoral artery injury (C) is a rare complication of anterior hip dislocations. If any arterial injury is suspected, immediate reduction should be performed along with vascular surgery consultation. More than 85% of the bleeding associated with pelvic fractures is venous in nature.

Sciatic nerve injury (D) affects 10% of patients. The risk of sciatic nerve involvement is also time dependent, and the incidence of permanent nerve palsy increases with delay in reduction.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the incidence of late osteoarthritis after traumatic hip dislocations?

Reveal Answer:
Up to 20% of simple dislocations will develop late osteoarthritis, but this can be much higher for more complex dislocations.

Posterior more common than anterior
PE
Posterior: internally rotated, sciatic nerve injury
Anterior: externally rotated, femoral artery, vein, nerve injury
Tx: emergent reduction under conscious sedation
Complications: avascular necrosis of the femoral head

question: A 33-year-old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant presents to the ED after a motor vehicle collision. The patient was a restrained driver who was rear-ended at a moderate speed. She says that her abdomen did not hit the steering wheel. She reports mild abdominal cramps. Vital signs are within normal limits. There is no abdominal tenderness to palpation, and no vaginal bleeding is noted. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admit for fetal and uterine monitoring
Consult OB/GYN for emergent cesarean section
Obtain a CT scan of her abdomen

correctAnswer: Admit for fetal and uterine monitoring
englishExplanation:
This patient is at risk for placental abruption (abruptio placentae), which can occur after trauma to the abdomen in a pregnant patient. Patients often present with vaginal bleeding, abdominal or back pain, and uterine contractions. However, some patients present with only mild abdominal pain or preterm labor. The uterus is thought to change shape when subjected to strong acceleration-deceleration forces or direct trauma, which can cause shear stress at the uteroplacental interface, resulting in placental abruption.

The importance of fetal and uterine monitoring lies in their negative predictive value for predicting placental abruption. Although the amount of time the patient needs to be monitored is controversial, general recommendations suggest monitoring for 4–6 hours.



Although the patient has a viable pregnancy, consulting OB/GYN for an emergent cesarean section (B) is not necessary, as the extent of the injury has not been identified and no indications for emergency cesarean section are currently present.

While obtaining a CT scan (C) can be appropriate in the traumatic setting to assess for injuries, this patient’s exam does not warrant a scan.

Transvaginal ultrasound (D) examination is of limited usefulness in diagnosing placental abruption and has a high false negative rate.

One Step Further
Question:
A perimortem cesarean section should be performed within how many minutes after a witnessed cardiac arrest in a woman with a viable pregnancy?

Reveal Answer:
4 minutes.

Risk factors: prior Hx, hypertension, trauma, cocaine and methamphetamine use, cigarette smoking
Painful vaginal bleeding
Most often during the third trimester
Lab results: hypofibrinogenemia occurs with severe abruption
Tx: fetal monitoring, hemodynamic stabilization, delivery for maternal or fetal instability at any gestational age
Mother stable and category I FHR
< 32 weeks magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection
< 34 weeks antenatal steroids
34–36 weeks: consider antenatal steroids
> 36 weeks: delivery

الفخ: الطالب يختار Consult OB/GYN for emergent cesarean section خطأً بدلاً من A، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: A 29-year-old man presents to the ED with pain during chewing after being hit in the face by a basketball. On physical exam, you note significant swelling over the left inferior and lateral face and misalignment of the inferior premolars. Which of the following is the gold standard diagnostic imaging test in patients with this injury?

options.text: Computed tomographic angiography of the head
Computed tomographic scan of the maxillofacial bones

correctAnswer: Computed tomographic scan of the maxillofacial bones
englishExplanation:
This patient has signs and symptoms consistent with a mandibular fracture. Plain mandibular X-rays and panoramic radiographs are screening tests for mandibular fractures. However, a CT scan of the facial bones is the gold standard diagnostic test. The tongue blade test is a way of detecting even subtle mandibular fractures. The patient bites the blade while the examiner attempts to break it. The inability to stabilize the blade is an indication that the patient may have a mandibular fracture and should undergo imaging. The mandible is the second most commonly fractured facial bone behind the nasal bone. Signs and symptoms of a mandibular fracture include trismus, tooth misalignment, malocclusion of the bite, intraoral lacerations, and missing teeth. The most common fracture locations include the mandibular condyle, body of the mandible, and angle of the mandible. Management depends on location and whether the fracture is open or closed. Open fractures require IV antibiotics, such as penicillin or clindamycin, and hospital admission. Patients with closed fractures may be discharged with dental follow-up. The patient should be given adequate oral analgesics and instructed to observe a soft diet and chew on the nonfractured side. Many fractures will require open reduction and internal fixation but do not require admission initially if not open fractures.



CT angiography of the head (A) is an excellent study for the evaluation of vascular injury in a patient with skull base fractures or high cervical spine fractures.

Panorex of the mandible (C) and plain mandibular X-ray (D) are good screening tests for mandibular fracture. However, these are not the gold standard, as they can miss more subtle fractures that lead to long-term morbidity.

One Step Further
Question:
For what pathology is a panorex of the mandible an excellent evaluation?

Reveal Answer:
Mandibular dislocation.

Likely due to trauma
Most commonly in condyle, angle, or body of mandible
Sx: pain, swelling, facial asymmetry, bruising
Dx: X-rays, panoramic X-ray
CT is best
Tx: bandage and analgesics, open fracture needs antibiotics, update tetanus
Plastics, OMFS, ENT referral or consultation depending on injury
Monitor airway

الفخ: الطالب يختار Computed tomographic angiography of the head خطأً بدلاً من B، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: A 33-year-old man presents to the ED with severe knee pain after a hard landing with a parachute. He reports he felt a popping sensation and is now unable to bear weight on that leg. He reports no other injuries. Physical examination reveals significant swelling, hematoma, and tenderness on the affected side. The patient is unable to extend the knee. A plain radiograph of the affected knee is shown above. Which of the following is the recommended treatment for the suspected condition?

options.text: Administration of a corticosteroid injection and physical therapy referral
Emergent orthopedic consult for surgical intervention with open reduction and internal fixation
Immobilization with a knee immobilizer in full extension and urgent referral to orthopedic surgery
Orthopedic consult for arthroscopic knee surgery to repair the ligament

correctAnswer: Immobilization with a knee immobilizer in full extension and urgent referral to orthopedic surgery
englishExplanation:
Traumatic injury to the patella tendon requires significant force, most commonly due to sudden quadriceps contraction after a jump or fall with the knee in a flexed position of > 60°. Risk factors include conditions that lead to a weakening of the collagen structure, including previous injuries, corticosteroid injections, and systemic illnesses such as diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis.

Commonly, the patient will present with severe pain, swelling, and inability to actively extend the knee or maintain a passively extended knee against gravity. A complete patellar tendon rupture on the lateral radiograph will classically show a high-riding patella (patella alta). Sometimes, incomplete tears are challenging to diagnose, so an MRI may be needed. The treatment of a complete tear from the ED is immobilization with a knee immobilizer in full extension and urgent referral to orthopedic surgery (generally within 1 week). Patients should also be non-weight-bearing and be provided with crutches. Delayed diagnosis of a patellar tendon rupture may lead to significant retraction of the patella proximally and subsequent development of quadriceps contractures or adhesions. Surgical intervention is required to reattach complete tendon ruptures, and repair should be performed soon after injury for the best recovery.



Administration of a corticosteroid injection and physical therapy referral (A) is inappropriate for acute tendon ruptures. Corticosteroid injections are generally contraindicated in acute ruptures as they can further weaken tendon structures and impair healing. Physical therapy alone would be insufficient to address the structural damage from a complete rupture, and without surgical intervention, the patient would likely experience persistent functional impairment and weakness in knee extension.

Surgical intervention with open reduction and internal fixation (B) is incorrect because this technique is typically used for fractures, not tendon ruptures. Open reduction and internal fixation is primarily performed to stabilize bone fractures using plates, screws, or rods, not for repairing tendon injuries. Patellar tendon repair involves reattaching the tendon to its anatomic position rather than fixing a bony fracture. Furthermore, an emergent orthopedic consult is not necessary for these injuries. An urgent referral is adequate as long as the patient is placed in a knee immobilizer, made non-weight-bearing, and can see orthopedics within 1 week.

Arthroscopic knee surgery to repair the ligament (D) is typically not the preferred approach for treating patellar tendon ruptures. These ruptures generally require an open surgical repair for direct visualization and reattachment of the tendon to the patella. Arthroscopic procedures are more suitable for intra-articular injuries such as meniscal tears or ligamentous injuries, where minimally invasive techniques can provide adequate access and repair.

One Step Further

True or false: quadriceps tendon ruptures are more frequent than patellar tendon rupture in patients > 40 years.

Reveal Answer:
True.

Sx: pain, swelling, and bruising over anterior knee
PE: unable to extend knee, palpable defect
Dx: patella alta on X-ray
Tx: knee immobilizer in extension, non-weight-bearing, urgent referral to orthopedics for surgical repair of complete tears

question: A 46-year-old woman with a history of major depressive disorder and myocardial infarction status post drug-eluting stent 12 days ago presents to the ED after a motor vehicle collision. She was intubated in the field and immediately transported to the hospital. Her home medications include aspirin, clopidogrel, and sertraline. A head CT shows a subdural hemorrhage. Vital signs are BP 179/69 mm Hg, HR 90 bpm, T 37.4°C (99.3°F), and RR 18/min. Other notable lab results include hemoglobin 10 g/dL and platelets 190,000/µL. Electrolytes are within normal limits. What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Continue aspirin and clopidogrel due to recent stent placement
Rapidly lower systolic blood pressure to 130–140 mm Hg and hold antiplatelet agents
Transfuse platelets and immediately take the patient to surgery

correctAnswer: Rapidly lower systolic blood pressure to 130–140 mm Hg and hold antiplatelet agents
englishExplanation:
Subdural hemorrhage (SDH) is a common neurosurgical diagnosis, especially in adults, with incidence rising due to aging and increased use of antithrombotic agents. The pathophysiology involves rupture of bridging veins, often exacerbated by cerebral atrophy, trauma, and coagulopathy. Antiplatelet therapy and selective serotonin receptor inhibitors like sertraline further increase bleeding risk, as seen in this patient.

Clinically, SDH presents with altered mental status, headache, and focal deficits. Exam findings may include decreased consciousness and neurologic deficits. Intubation in the field suggests severe injury. Diagnosis is confirmed by noncontrast head CT, which is the gold standard for acute intracranial hemorrhage. Laboratory assessment should include CBC, coagulation studies, and evaluation for anemia, which is associated with poor outcomes.

Emergency management prioritizes rapid blood pressure control to a systolic target of 130–140 mm Hg to minimize hematoma expansion, discontinuation of antiplatelet agents to reduce further bleeding, and urgent neurosurgical and cardiology consultation to balance the risk of stent thrombosis versus hemorrhagic progression. Multidisciplinary input is essential given the recent stent placement and high risk for both cardiac and neurologic complications.



Although administration of four-factor prothrombin concentrate (A) has been shown to reduce hematoma expansion in patients with warfarin- or direct oral anticoagulant-related intracranial bleeding, it does not benefit bleeding related to antiplatelet agents.

Continuing aspirin and clopidogrel (B) in the acute setting of intracranial hemorrhage increases the risk of hematoma expansion and poor outcomes. Antiplatelet agents should be held, with multidisciplinary assessment for timing of resumption.

Platelet transfusion and immediate surgery (D) are not indicated unless there is evidence of herniation or rapid deterioration. Routine platelet transfusion for antiplatelet-associated SDH is not supported by guidelines and may increase adverse events.

One Step Further
Question:
True or false: andexanet alfa is approved by the FDA for the reversal of oral factor Xa inhibitors in individuals with intracranial hemorrhage.

Reveal Answer:
True.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Subdural Hematoma

Caused by tearing of the bridging veins between arachnoid and dura
Risks: traumatic head injury, advancing age, anticoagulant use, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia
Sx: acute or subacute neurologic Sx, headache, mental status changes, seizures, or focal deficits
Dx: crescent-shaped hematoma on noncontrast CT
Tx: neurosurgical consultation, blood pressure control, reversal of anticoagulation

question: A 9-year-old girl presents after twisting her ankle while roller-skating. Her radiograph is shown above. What type of fracture is shown?
englishExplanation:
The Salter-Harris classification of fractures is used to describe fracture patterns in children with open growth plates (physis). It is helpful in describing the severity of the fracture prognostically related to the growth plate. In the image shown, the fracture line extends through the physis and into the metaphysis. This is the most common type of Salter-Harris fracture, a type II fracture. It is helpful to remember the mnemonic using the word Salter.





Salter-Harris I (A) fractures involve the area of hypertrophic cartilage involved in bone formation. This may cause elements of the physis to separate from the metaphysis. However, these injuries may have normal radiographs. In patients with focal tenderness over the physis, splinting or a supportive boot is recommended until follow-up radiography is obtained.

Salter-Harris III (C) fractures extend through the physis and into the epiphysis.

Salter Harris IV (D) fractures extend from the articular surface of the bone, through the epiphysis, across the physis, and into the metaphysis. Salter Harris V fractures disrupt the germinal matrix of the bone and compress the physis. These carry a poor prognosis related to bone growth.

One Step Further
Question:
What fracture in children occurs secondary to increased elasticity of the bones?

Reveal Answer:
Greenstick fracture.

SALTER mnemonic
I: slipped epiphysis
II: fracture above physis, most common
III: fracture below physis
IV: fracture through physis
V: erasure of the growth plate
Management

III: nonoperative versus surgery depends on stability of the joint, refer to ortho
IV–V: surgery required
Negative radiographs do not rule out a Salter I fracture

question: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision, reporting chest and back pain. His vital signs are significant for a blood pressure of 85/50 mm Hg, heart rate of 115 bpm, and oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. Exam reveals ecchymosis of the left anterior chest wall, no crepitus, but diminished breath sounds on the left hemithorax, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation is consistent with tension pneumothorax, a clinical diagnosis that requires immediate intervention. In a traumatic injury, a pneumothorax can be formed and allow air into the extrapleural thorax. This will lead to a rise in intrathoracic pressure during every inspiratory cycle and ultimately impairs venous return to the heart, causing obstructive shock. Rapid assessment and diagnosis are critical in these patients to normalize the intrathoracic pressure. These patients will present with diminished breath sounds, distended neck veins, hypotension, and tracheal deviation. Diagnosis should be made clinically in patients with hypotension and diminished breath sounds unilaterally. In most cases, this will follow chest trauma or positive pressure ventilation. Treatment requires needle or finger thoracostomy of the affected side at either the fourth or fifth anterior axillary line or the second intercostal midclavicular space in adults. This should be performed prior to imaging studies, as delays in treatment allow for worsening obstructive shock and can ultimately lead to cardiac arrest. Needle and finger decompression converts this to an open pneumothorax and will need to be followed by tube thoracostomy once the patient is stabilized. Patients with a persistent pneumothorax following tube thoracostomy should be evaluated for a possible bronchial injury.



Diagnosis and treatment of tension pneumothorax should be made clinically, and treatment should not be delayed for imaging studies, including a bedside chest X-ray (A).

Bilateral tube thoracostomy (B) is not indicated in this patient, as there is no obvious defect with the right lung, and thoracostomy on the left side should be performed first. Needle or finger thoracostomy is fast and will reverse the obstructive shock.

Rapid sequence intubation (D) is not needed in this patient who appears to be protecting his airway and phonating normally, given his normal mental status. Additionally, positive pressure will likely worsen the tension pneumothorax.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the ultrasound finding in a patient with a pneumothorax?

Reveal Answer:
A lack of lung sliding and movement artifact.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Tension Pneumothorax

Often history of chest trauma
PE: diminished or absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation away from the side of the injury, hypotension, jugular venous distension
Dx: made clinically
Tx: needle decompression of the chest in the fourth or fifth intercostal space in the anterior or midaxillary line or second intercostal space in the midclavicular line, followed by chest tube insertion
Finger thoracostomy followed by chest tube insertion may be faster

ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي C لأن Needle thoracostomy This patient’s presentation is consistent with tension pneumothorax, a clinical diagnosis that requires immediate interv  فهذه النقاط تؤكد اختيارها.
الفخ: الطالب يختار Bedside chest X-ray خطأً بدلاً من C، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: A 28-year-old man presents by EMS after being the restrained driver in a high-speed motor vehicle collision. On examination, he is noted to have malocclusion. When the forehead is held stationary and the upper teeth are grasped, there is movement of the nasal complex, but the orbit and lateral face do not appear to move. What type of Le Fort fracture is most likely?
englishExplanation:
The Le Fort fractures are midface fractures that involve either complete or partial detachment of the maxilla from the skull. They are classified by their location and the bones involved in the fracture pattern using the Le Fort classification system.

Le Fort I fractures involve a transverse fracture line through the maxilla above the roots of the teeth, separating the maxilla from the pterygoid plate and the nasal septum and detaching the hard palate from the skull.

A Le Fort II fracture is a pyramidal fracture pattern that includes the nasal bridge, maxilla, lacrimal bones, orbital floor, and orbital rim. In this fracture pattern, the entire nasal complex will move when the maxilla is rocked with the forehead held steady.

A Le Fort III fracture, also known as craniofacial dislocation, is characterized by a fracture line that travels transversely through the midface at the level of the nasal bridge and extends through the zygomatic arches.

Maxillofacial CT is the imaging modality of choice for the diagnosis of midface fractures. Management is surgical.



A Le Fort I (A) fracture is a horizontal fracture separating the maxilla from the nasal floor and is also called a floating palate.

A Le Fort III (C) fracture is also referred to as craniofacial disjunction or floating face. It involves the separation of the entire midface from the skull base.

The Le Fort classification system of midface fractures is comprised of three different types of fracture patterns. A Le Fort IV (D) fracture does not exist.

One Step Further
Question:
What part of the face is movable in a Le Fort I fracture?

Reveal Answer:
Maxilla (the upper teeth).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review

I: transverse fracture that separates maxilla from pterygoid and nasal septum
II: maxilla and palate fractured
III: craniofacial dissociation
II and III: CSF rhinorrhea

ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي B لأن Le Fort II The Le Fort fractures are midface fractures that involve either complete or partial detachment of the maxilla from the s  فهذه النقاط تؤكد اختيارها.
الفخ: الطالب يختار Le Fort I خطأً بدلاً من B، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: A 30-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after an accidental exposure to white phosphorus on her left arm. She washed the area with copious amounts of water prior to arrival. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in care?
englishExplanation:
White phosphorus is an incendiary and ignites when exposed to air. It is used in fireworks as well as in the formulation of insecticides and fertilizers. Burns from white phosphorus are classically ongoing and slow to heal. As long as it is exposed to air it will continue to burn, thus, copious irrigation and submersion in water or normal saline are necessary. White phosphorus fluoresces, so Wood lamp examination may aid in identifying residual chemicals on tissues during medical assessment. When phosphorus is absorbed systemically, this becomes a medical emergency necessitating early aggressive management. Physiologic effects include electrolyte abnormalities (e.g., hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia), kidney failure, and hepatotoxicity. Burns may appear minor, but patients should be transferred to the nearest burn center and admitted for monitoring. Clinicians should wear protective clothing and avoid direct contact with contaminated skin, clothing, and body fluids.



Copper sulfate detoxification (A) is contraindicated for white phosphorus burns because it leads to hemolysis and portends a greater mortality risk to patients.

Discharging home with analgesia (B) is inappropriate management of white phosphorus burns. Patients need admission for supportive care and monitoring. Copious irrigation is paramount to rid tissue of any exposed substance.

Therefore, it is not recommended to prevent further water exposure (C) in patients exposed to white phosphorus.

One Step Further
Question:
What category of chemicals causes burns by cellular membrane disruption?

Reveal Answer:
Organic solvents.

Initial Tx: decontamination of clothing and skin
Acid: coagulation necrosis
Tx: copious hydrotherapy (neutralization may be worse)
Alkali: liquefactive necrosis
Burns tend to penetrate deeper into tissue layers than acidic burns and are associated with greater morbidity
Tx: copious hydrotherapy (neutralization may be worse)
Elemental: lithium, potassium, sodium exposure
Hydrotherapy is contraindicated because of the exothermic reaction upon contact with water
Phenol (carbolic acid) also should not be irrigated with water
Tx: brush off or apply mineral oil

الفخ: الطالب يختار Copper sulfate detoxification خطأً بدلاً من D، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: A 47-year-old man is thrown violently against the steering wheel of his truck during a motor vehicle collision. On arrival at the ED, the patient reports severe chest pain. His BP is 60/40 mm Hg, and his RR is 40/min. Which of the following will best indicate a tension pneumothorax as the cause of this patient’s hypotension rather than cardiac tamponade?
englishExplanation:
The life-threatening injuries that occur with blunt chest trauma include massive hemothorax, tension pneumothorax, and cardiac tamponade. It is critical to be able to clinically differentiate these conditions and identify the cause of this patient’s hypotension to prevent cardiopulmonary collapse. There are many similarities on exam seen with a tension pneumothorax and cardiac tamponade, but one major difference is that a tension pneumothorax is associated with decreased breath sounds on the side of the injury. The breath sounds in patients with cardiac tamponade should be present and clear. Ultrasound can further support the diagnosis and would demonstrate an absence of pleural sliding in a tension pneumothorax (though this is a clinical diagnosis) versus an echogenic rim of fluid in tamponade.



Electrical alternans on ECG (B) suggests a diagnosis of cardiac tamponade. Electrical alternans is defined by the changing amplitude or morphology of the QRS complex in a single lead every other beat. Although this is pathognomonic, it is rarely seen. There are no characteristic ECG changes seen in patients with a tension pneumothorax. Additionally, this patient requires immediate intervention, and an ECG is a time-consuming procedure. Elevated jugular venous pressure (C) is present in both cardiac tamponade and tension pneumothorax. However, in severely hypotensive patients, it may be absent with either condition. Pulsus paradoxus (D) is defined as a drop of > 10 mm Hg in systolic blood pressure with spontaneous inspiration. This is seen in patients with cardiac tamponade and those with chronic pulmonary disease. It is not characteristic of tension pneumothorax.

One Step Further
Question:
Why does a tension pneumothorax cause hypotension?

Reveal Answer:
Progressive mediastinal shift and increased intrathoracic pressure impedes venous blood return to the heart, causing a marked decrease in preload.

Dx: made clinically
Tx: needle decompression of the chest in the fourth or fifth intercostal space in the anterior or midaxillary line or second intercostal space in the midclavicular line, followed by chest tube insertion
Finger thoracostomy followed by chest tube insertion may be faster

question: A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department after an assault in which he was strangled with a cord. On arrival, he has a hoarse voice and notable stridor with a small bleeding wound over his anterior neck. The patient is intubated. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to further evaluate this patient’s likely underlying injury?

options.text: CT and CTA of the neck
MRI of the neck with and without contrast

correctAnswer: CT and CTA of the neck
englishExplanation:
Tracheal injuries usually result from direct trauma to the trachea from blunt trauma, such as a clothesline injury, strangulation, and hanging. They are rare, accounting for < 1% of all trauma cases, and often result from direct blunt force in motor vehicle collisions. Hard signs of tracheal injury can include stridor, hemoptysis, dysphonia, visible air or bubbling in a wound, and airway obstruction, each indicating a potentially life-threatening condition that requires immediate intervention. Soft signs, which suggest a need for further evaluation but are less immediately dire, include hoarseness, neck tenderness, subcutaneous emphysema, cervical ecchymosis or hematoma, tracheal deviation or cartilaginous step-off, laryngeal edema or hematoma, and restricted vocal cord mobility. These signs are crucial for diagnosing tracheal injuries and determining the severity and appropriate response.

Management first involves securing the airway (if needed). Immediate airway management might be necessary. Options include awake fiberoptic-guided intubation and emergency tracheostomy if standard intubation fails. Next, CT imaging is the optimal diagnostic test of choice. Given that blunt trauma to the neck can also involve the vasculature, a CTA should be included when obtaining a CT of the neck. Patients with a tracheal injury will require admission and otolaryngology consultation. Conservative management might be sufficient for minor injuries, while severe cases require surgical intervention.



Local wound exploration (B) would not be the best method of assessing for a tracheal injury, especially in this patient with what seems to be a minor puncture injury yet with hoarseness and stridor. Exploration may further damage underlying structures.

MRI of the neck with and without contrast (C) may accurately assess for soft tissue injuries but is a time-consuming test and is less appropriate than CT imaging.

Ultrasound of the neck (D) may demonstrate tracheal injury but is not the most appropriate test for assessing potential tracheal injury. Ultrasound imaging would need further confirmation of findings with a CT scan and would not accurately assess for arterial injury either.

Reveal Answer:
Pain with tongue movement or rotation of the head.

question: An 84-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a witnessed fall by nursing home staff. The patient was reaching up to turn on the fan in his room when he lost his balance and fell forward, landing directly on his chin. The patient is alert and talking but has weakness and loss of sensation and temperature perception in both upper extremities. What is the most likely lesion?
englishExplanation:
The most common incomplete spinal cord lesion is central cord syndrome. This results from a hyperextension injury of the neck and is often seen in patients with degenerative arthritis. In this syndrome, hyperextension of the neck causes the ligamentum flavum to buckle, which concusses the central cord. This injury often damages the spinothalamic and pyramidal tracts as well. Exam findings include weakness and the loss of pain and temperature sensation, which are greater in the upper extremities than the lower extremities.

CT scan is the gold standard for the emergent evaluation of acute spine trauma. However, it does not provide a detailed evaluation of the spinal cord or surrounding soft tissues. MRI provides a more comprehensive assessment of these structures and should be considered after initial trauma resuscitation. Initial management involves emergent stabilization of the patient, cervical spine immobilization, and neurosurgical intervention. Surgery may be required to stabilize the cervical spinal column and decompress the spinal cord. More than half of patients will regain bowel and bladder function and the ability to ambulate. Function in the upper extremities varies depending on the severity of the initial injury and the extent of neurologic recovery.



Brown-Séquard syndrome (A) occurs when there is damage to one side of the spinal column. This results in a combination of motor weakness, loss of proprioception and vibration sense on the same side as the injury, and pain and temperature sensation loss on the opposite side. This patient has bilateral weakness with loss of pain and temperature sensation in the upper extremities, which is inconsistent with Brown-Séquard syndrome.

A complete spinal cord injury (C) results in a total loss of sensory and motor function below the level of the injury. This patient has both motor function and sensation in the lower extremities and thus does not fit the criteria for a complete spinal cord injury.

Posterior cord syndrome (D) involves injury to the posterior columns of the spinal cord bilaterally. This results in gait ataxia and touch, vibration, and proprioception abnormalities. Motor function, pain, and temperature sensation are typically unaffected. This patient has alterations in motor function and pain and temperature sensation, which are not consistent with posterior cord syndrome.

One Step Further
Question:
What five elements comprise the National Emergency X-Radiography Utilization Study (NEXUS) criteria for cervical spine imaging?

Reveal Answer:
No midline spinal tenderness, no focal neurologic deficits, normal alertness, no intoxication present, and no painful distracting injury.

question: An 18-year-old boy presents to the ED with partial-thickness burns to his entire back and right arm. The patient weighs 70 kg. How much crystalloid solution is required in the first 24 hours, based on the Parkland formula?
englishExplanation:
Following a burn injury, the patient has profound shifts in intravascular fluids. Several formulas exist for the determination of fluid resuscitation needs. However, the Parkland formula is the most well known and widely applied. The Parkland formula provides an estimate of the initial fluid needs of the severely burned patient. The fluid requirement (lactated Ringer solution) is calculated for the first 24 hours after the burn occurs. One-half of this fluid is administered over the first 8 hours. The second half is administered over the following 16 hours.

Parkland Formula

Fluid required = 4 mL x body weight (kg) x % total body surface area of burn (excluding superficial burns)

In this patient, who weighs 70 kg and has approximately 27% total body surface area burns, the amount of fluid needed in the first 24 hours of care is 7,560 mL. This is an estimate. The clinician should monitor the adequacy of fluid resuscitation by following vital signs and urine output. The goal urine output is 30 mL/hr in adults and 1–2 mL/kg/hr in children.



Of 1,260 mL (A), 10,080 mL (B), and 5,040 mL (C), none follow the Parkland formula.

One Step Further
Question:
What happens to cardiac output immediately following a severe burn injury?

Reveal Answer:
Cardiac output decreases. This is one reason why significant fluid resuscitation is needed.

question: A 6-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with her parents after falling from a tree onto her ankle. Her X-ray is shown above. What type of fracture does this patient have?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s X-ray is consistent with a Salter-Harris type III fracture. This patient’s fracture is distal (lower) to the growth plate and thus is a type III fracture. Salter-Harris fractures are more common than sprains and strains in childhood, with type II being the most common. This is due to children’s cartilaginous growth zones being weaker than their adjacent ligaments and bones. Thus, a patient with continued bony joint pain near the growth plate after conservative management for a sprain should be imaged and treated as a Salter-Harris type I injury if imaging is normal. Types I and II can be treated conservatively with splinting and close orthopedic follow-up. Type III fractures require an orthopedic consultation, as these may lead to limb growth disruption and should be followed closely. Types IV and V, while less common, almost always lead to limb length discrepancies and require surgical fixation to ensure anatomical alignment.



Salter-Harris type I (A) is when the injury causes a mild epiphyseal slip. An X-ray will appear normal, but if there is distinct pain overlying the growth plate, patients should be treated with splinting and close orthopedic follow-up.

Salter-Harris type II (B) is when the fracture extends through the growth plate and metaphysis. Treatment is similar to Salter-Harris type I and has excellent prognosis.

Salter-Harris type IV (D) is when the fracture extends through the growth plate, metaphysis, and epiphysis. Treatment is with surgical correction and patients are at high risk for limb length discrepancies.

One Step Further
Question:
Salter-Harris type V injuries are most common in what joints?

Reveal Answer:
Ankles and knees.

question: An 82-year-old woman with osteoporosis falls against her kitchen table. She presents with acute right shoulder pain, proximal right upper extremity edema, and near-absent active shoulder joint range of motion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Obtain a passive range of motion measurement

englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms consistent with a proximal humerus fracture. Proximal humerus fractures are most commonly seen in older patients. The most common type of fracture occurs at the surgical neck, which is the epiphyseal-diaphyseal junction, just inferior to both tuberosities. Patients present with shoulder pain that is worse with movement, limited motion of the shoulder, the arm resting in an adducted position against their sides, swelling, and ecchymosis.

As with any suspected fracture, it is imperative to assess distal neurovascular supply with motor, sensory, and pulse examination. Complications from shoulder injuries include injury to the axillary nerve, the brachial plexus, and vascular structures, such as the axillary artery. Prompt identification of neurovascular compromise and intervention can limit long-term complications.



Passive range of motion measurements (A) will most likely be noncontributory and difficult to obtain and may exacerbate the injury.

Radiographs (B) should be obtained after the clinician is assured that no acute neurovascular compromise is present.

The Hawkins test (D), which usually follows Neer testing of the shoulder, is used to evaluate subacromial impingement in the setting of rotator cuff syndrome or tear. The results of this test are most likely noncontributory, given this presentation, and may exacerbate the injury.

Referral to orthopedic surgery (E) is appropriate for management of proximal humeral fractures. However, consultation should occur after a focused physical exam confirms distal perfusion and neurologic integrity and radiographs confirm a fracture.

One Step Further
Question:
Which three rotator cuff muscles insert on the greater tuberosity?

Reveal Answer:
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor.

question: A previously healthy 12-year-old girl presents to the emergency department after she was accidentally hit in the left eye by a ball during soccer practice. No loss of consciousness was reported. Her parents state that she is acting normally. The patient’s only concern at this time is pain and blurry vision in her left eye. On examination, her vital signs are within the normal ranges. There is injection of the left eye surrounding the cornea, and the pupil is round and reactive with worsening pain during the examination. The remainder of her examination is normal. Which of the following represents the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms consistent with traumatic iritis, inflammation within the anterior chamber of the eye following blunt trauma. Typical symptoms include eye pain, redness, photophobia, and visual changes. On examination, there may be injection surrounding the cornea, which is referred to as a ciliary flush. Treatment typically involves cycloplegic eye drops and topical steroids. If left untreated, traumatic iritis can lead to glaucoma or vision loss. Thus, if suspected, this diagnosis should be discussed with an ophthalmologist to ensure proper evaluation with a slit lamp and close follow-up until resolution.



Anterior uveitis (A) refers to inflammation of the iris and ciliary body that occurs in the absence of trauma.

Hyphema (B) is bleeding within the anterior chamber secondary to trauma. This should be noticeable on a good eye exam and is not mentioned in this case.

Traumatic globe rupture (C) will often present with vision loss and pupillary defect.

One Step Further
Question:
What does a teardrop-shaped pupil in the setting of ocular trauma represent?

Reveal Answer:
Globe rupture, with the narrowest point of the teardrop pointing toward the defect.

question: A 19-year-old man is brought to the ED after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. Bystanders report that he briefly lost consciousness, was alert for a short period, and then became increasingly somnolent. On arrival, his Glasgow Coma Scale score is 6, and his left pupil is dilated and nonreactive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Epidural hematomas account for approximately 1–2% of all traumatic brain injuries but are more common in young adults and adolescents, who have less brain atrophy and a more rigid dura mater. The classic mechanism involves blunt trauma to the side of the head, especially involving the pterion, the thinnest region of the skull. Clinical features include headache, vomiting, decreased consciousness, and focal neurologic signs like anisocoria or hemiparesis. A lucid interval, though classically taught, is present in only about 20–30% of cases.

This patient has a classic presentation of an epidural hematoma with traumatic head injury, followed by a lucid interval and subsequent neurologic deterioration, often with ipsilateral fixed and dilated pupil due to uncal herniation. Epidural hematomas typically result from trauma to the temporal bone, leading to laceration of the middle meningeal artery. Blood collects between the inner skull and the dura mater, forming a biconvex (lentiform) hyperdensity on CT that does not cross suture lines. The expanding hematoma increases intracranial pressure and may cause brain herniation, coma, and death if not rapidly treated.

In the ED, prompt diagnosis is made with a noncontrast head CT, which typically shows a lens-shaped, hyperdense collection. Management involves emergent neurosurgical consultation for craniotomy and evacuation, along with airway protection and management of elevated intracranial pressure (e.g., head elevation, mannitol, hypertonic saline).



Cerebral contusions (A) are parenchymal injuries due to blunt trauma, often affecting the frontal and temporal lobes. Symptoms may be similar, but they do not cause a lucid interval, mass effect, or pupil asymmetry unless very large. CT shows areas of intraparenchymal hemorrhage rather than a discrete extra-axial collection.

Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) (B) results from shearing forces in high-speed trauma and typically presents with persistent coma without a lucid interval. CT findings are often normal or show punctate hemorrhages at the gray-white junction. The presentation here of initial lucidity followed by deterioration and signs of uncal herniation is inconsistent with DAI.

Subarachnoid hemorrhages (D) typically present with a sudden, severe thunderclap headache or can be related to head trauma, but they are not classically associated with a trauma-induced transient loss of consciousness followed by deterioration. Furthermore, this patient's dilated, nonreactive pupil is more consistent with an epidural hematoma than with a traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage. CT would show blood in the basal cisterns and sulci.

Subdural hematomas (E) result from tearing of bridging veins, typically from acceleration-deceleration injuries. They present insidiously, often in older adults, and appear as crescent-shaped hyperdensities on CT that can cross suture lines. The described lucid interval and temporal trauma are more consistent with an epidural hematoma.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the Cushing reflex?

Reveal Answer:
A late sign of increased intracranial pressure characterized by a triad of hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations.

CT will show a biconvex lens-shaped opacity
Treatment is emergent evacuation

question: A 23-year-old man presents with chest pain after a motor vehicle collision. The patient’s chest struck the steering wheel. He has no other concerns or injuries. Chest X-ray is unremarkable. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with anterior ST depressions. Troponin is positive at 3.50 mg/dL. What management is indicated?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with a myocardial contusion and should have an echocardiogram performed to look for any cardiac damage. Myocardial contusion describes a nebulous condition. It can occur through several mechanisms including a direct blow to the chest and compressive force over a prolonged period of time. Histologically, the disorder has similar findings to those seen after acute myocardial infarction. The majority of contusions heal spontaneously but small pericardial effusions may develop. Delayed rupture after resorption of a hematoma is a feared but rare complication. Patients with myocardial contusion will present after trauma with external signs of trauma and typically have other concomitant thoracic lesions (pulmonary contusion, pneumothorax, hemothorax). Patients will typically have tachycardia (up to 70%). ECG may show dysrhythmia or ST changes but may also be normal. Although myocardial contusion has a very low rate of cardiac complications and it is not effective to admit all patients for a workup, in the presence of ECG changes and elevated biomarkers, observation and echocardiography is a reasonable approach. An echocardiogram can be used to diagnose pericardial effusion, thrombi formation, and valvular disruption.



Cardiac catheterization (A) is not necessary after a myocardial contusion, as coronary artery obstruction is not part of the pathophysiology. The patient should not be discharged home (B) without an echocardiogram. Pericardiocentesis (D) is only necessary in the presence of a large pericardial effusion or one causing cardiac tamponade.

One Step Further
Question:
What is commotio cordis?

Reveal Answer:
Commotio cordis is blunt cardiac trauma from a direct blow to the heart that results in a dysrhythmia, hypotension, and loss of consciousness.

Associated with dysrhythmias (SVT, VF) and rarely myocardial infarction

PE: visible evidence of chest trauma
Workup: ECG, troponins, FAST

question: Parents bring their 2-year-old son into the emergency department after the child tripped over a ball while chasing his sibling across the living room. The child is reporting mild shin discomfort. Radiographs obtained show the above findings. There are no other signs of trauma on exam. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Place in a controlled ankle movement boot

correctAnswer: Place in a controlled ankle movement boot
englishExplanation:
The patient is presenting with a nondisplaced spiral fracture of the tibia, also known as a toddler fracture. These fractures usually occur between the ages of 9 months and 3 years, when children are first learning to walk. The mechanism of action frequently involves twisting of the leg during a fall and is a low-energy fracture. These fractures are often subtle and hard to identify on plain radiographs. At times, these fractures may not appear at all on radiographs initially and can take up to seven days before they become apparent. For initial treatment of these fractures, the patient should be immobilized in a controlled ankle movement boot or a long or short leg cast and instructed to follow up with an orthopedist within a week. Some studies show patients immobilized with a controlled ankle movement boot will have similar outcomes without the risks involved with casting, such as skin breakdown and longer duration of immobilization.



Calling child protective services (A) would be inappropriate at this time. A toddler fracture is a common fracture type in children, and the mechanism presented above is consistent with radiographic findings. Whenever children present with trauma, a thorough physical exam should be performed, but there are no signs of trauma in the above vignette. Measuring lower extremity compartment pressures (B) would be incorrect. Although significant lower extremity fractures involving the tibia can lead to compartment syndrome, a toddler fracture is a low-energy injury that involves a small nondisplaced tibial fracture, which is not usually associated with compartment syndrome. Recommending weight-bearing as tolerated (D) is incorrect. These patients should be immobilized and referred for outpatient orthopedic follow up.

Question:
How many compartments are in the lower leg?

Reveal Answer:
Four.

question: A 37-year-old man presents to the ED after being robbed. He was hit in the left eye 2 hours ago and now has severe left eye pain and blurry vision. His ocular exam reveals an afferent pupillary defect on the left. His right eye appears normal with an intraocular pressure of 16 mm Hg. His left eye has periorbital ecchymosis, proptosis, conjunctival injection, and an intraocular pressure of 25 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
A retrobulbar hematoma is the build-up of blood within the retrobulbar compartment of the eye. These hematomas are caused by shearing of the vessels within the retrobulbar compartment. While most commonly due to direct trauma, other causes like Valsalva maneuvers, arteriovenous malformations, and coagulopathies may be seen. This condition is strongly associated with vision loss. Therefore, ophthalmologic consultation and definitive treatment should be started immediately.

Patients commonly present after a known traumatic event with eye pain, blurry vision, afferent pupillary defects, and proptosis. While the diagnosis is often made clinically, computed tomography of the orbits can be used to help identify the extent of the bleeding and to clarify a diagnosis. Treatment includes evaluation for and reversal of coagulopathies, close intraocular pressure monitoring, and emergent ophthalmologic consultation. Significant retrobulbar bleeding may lead to orbital compartment syndrome and the need for emergent lateral canthotomy. Any patient with clinical findings consistent with a retrobulbar hematoma should be immediately prepped for lateral canthotomy while another staff member contacts ophthalmology for an emergent consult.



Blowout fractures of the orbit (A) are associated with abnormal posterior displacement of the eye, not proptosis. In addition, findings of ocular muscle entrapment may be seen on exam.

Post-traumatic glaucoma (B) presents similarly to nontraumatic glaucoma and is not associated with proptosis. It commonly presents as acute monocular vision loss and severe pain after localized trauma to that eye. Findings of elevated intraocular pressure are required for diagnosis.

Traumatic iritis (D) is not associated with proptosis or increased intraocular pressures. It commonly presents hours to days after local ocular trauma and is due to ciliary body spasms. Patients report pain worsening with light and will have consensual photophobia on exam.

One Step Further
Question:
How do retrobulbar hematomas appear on sonography?

Reveal Answer:
As a posterior globe echolucency (black).

question: Which of the following patients has the highest risk of a cervical spine injury, according to the 2024 Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network cervical spine imaging guidelines?

options.text: A 10-year-old child with arm numbness after a fall from a gymnastics beam
A 16-year-old child with repetitive questioning and vomiting after a closed head injury while playing football
A 6-month-old child with a depressed parietal skull fracture after being dropped
A 6-year-old child with midline neck pain after being restrained in a motor vehicle collision

correctAnswer: A 10-year-old child with arm numbness after a fall from a gymnastics beam
englishExplanation:
In 2024, the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) created and validated risk factors for cervical spine injury in children after blunt trauma. The four high-risk factors for a cervical spine injury include a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 3–8; being unresponsive on the alert, verbal, pain, unresponsive scale; having abnormal airway, breathing, or circulation; and focal neurological deficits, including paraesthesia, numbness, or weakness. These patients should have a computed tomography scan to evaluate for a cervical spine injury.

Five risk factors were also found to be not insignificant. Patients with these risk factors should be considered for imaging, but their risk is significantly lower than if they had the above four risk factors. A GCS score of 9–14, substantial torso injury, substantial head injury, posterior midline neck tenderness, and verbal or pain level on the alert, verbal, pain, unresponsive scale are risk factors that put children at a lower yet not negligible risk of having a cervical spine injury. The article recommends starting with a plain X-ray in these patients. Individuals without any of these findings can be safely cleared clinically.

Of the answer choices, the patient with arm numbness after a fall from a gymnastics beam is considered the highest risk and should have advanced cross-sectional imaging of her cervical spine.



Mild altered mental status (B) alone, a substantial head injury (C), and midline neck pain (D) are lower risk factors for a cervical spine injury than focal neurologic deficits.

One Step Further

What blunt mechanisms of injury might not be covered by the 2024 PECARN cervical spine imaging guidelines?

Reveal Answer:
Strangulation and hanging.

question: A 51-year-old woman presents to the ED with left wrist pain after a fall while walking on the pavement. She has pain and tenderness about the volar aspect of the wrist and palm of the hand. She has decreased grip strength and numbness in her thumb, index, and long fingers. Her X-ray is shown above. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

options.text: Foreign body removal and splint application
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and activity modification

englishExplanation:
This patient has a lunate dislocation, an orthopedic emergency. It is usually caused by a high-energy injury, such as a fall onto an outstretched hand. Normally, the distal radius, lunate, and capitate line up vertically on a lateral X-ray of the wrist. In a lunate dislocation, the lunate bone is displaced in a volar direction and may create a palpable fullness of the volar wrist. It appears tilted and displaced, like a spilled teacup sign on X-ray. A lateral X-ray is the single most important image to obtain.

Immediate orthopedic consultation is indicated, especially if neurological deficits are present. Attempted reduction in the ED can be pursued, but operative fixation is often required after closed reduction, even if successful. Complications include acute carpal tunnel syndrome and post-traumatic arthritis.



Foreign body removal (A) is not indicated as the patient has a carpal bone dislocation rather than a foreign body.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and activity modification (B) is appropriate for mild soft tissue injuries or tendinopathies but is inadequate for a lunate dislocation. The patient’s neurovascular compromise and abnormal carpal alignment require emergent orthopedic evaluation and likely surgical repair.

An oncology referral (C) is not necessary as the patient’s injury is directly due to trauma without underlying malignancy.

What is Kienböck disease of the lunate?

Reveal Answer:
Chronic, progressive collapse of the lunate, possibly related to undiagnosed fractures of the lunate, repetitive trauma, or abnormal biomechanical loading patterns at the radiocarpal joint.

question: Which one of the following is an indication for exploratory thoracotomy in the setting of a traumatic hemothorax in an adult patient?

options.text: 1,000 mL of output after initial tube insertion
120 mL/hr of continuous output for 5 hours
250 mL/hr of continuous output for 3 hours

correctAnswer: 250 mL/hr of continuous output for 3 hours
englishExplanation:
According to accepted surgical criteria, persistent chest tube output ≥ 200 mL/hr for three consecutive hours is an indication for urgent thoracotomy in the setting of traumatic hemothorax. Thus, an output of 250 mL/hr for 3 hours indicates ongoing intrathoracic bleeding that is unlikely to resolve spontaneously and carries the risk of progressive hemodynamic compromise or retained hemothorax, indicating the need for thoracotomy.

Guidelines also indicate that immediate output > 1,500 mL, > 20 mL/kg during initial drainage, or bleeding > 7 mL/kg/hr are additional absolute indications for surgical intervention, along with radiographic evidence of increasing hemothorax or clinical decompensation despite resuscitation.



1,000 mL of output after initial tube insertion (A) is not an absolute indication for thoracotomy. The classic threshold is ≥ 1,500 mL immediately upon chest tube placement, which represents massive hemothorax. Less than this should be monitored with serial output and clinical assessment.

120 mL/hr of continuous output for 5 hours (B) yields 600 mL over 5 hours, which is below the hourly threshold that typically prompts surgical intervention. Continued monitoring and supportive care would be appropriate unless clinical signs deteriorate.

6 mL/kg/hr of persistent bleeding (D) does not meet the threshold of > 7 mL/kg/hr used for body-weight-based indications. Unless the patient is small enough that 6 mL/kg/hr exceeds other volume thresholds, this alone does not justify surgical intervention.

question: A pelvic X-ray in a trauma patient shows cephalad displacement of the hemipelvis with disruption of the sacroiliac joint and diastasis of the pubic symphysis. Which injury pattern describes this fracture, according to the Young-Burgess classification?
englishExplanation:
Young-Burgess classification of pelvic fractures is a system used to categorize pelvic ring fractures based on the mechanism of injury and direction of compressive forces. It is widely used in trauma and emergency medicine because it helps predict associated injuries, pelvic stability, and the risk of severe hemorrhage to guide management. There are three primary injury patterns: vertical shear (VS), lateral compression (LC), and anterior-posterior compression (APC), as well as a fourth combined mechanism (CM).

VS injuries occur when the hemipelvis is displaced either superiorly (vertically) or posteriorly due to longitudinal forces to the pelvic ring. Anterior forces can result in widening of the pubic symphysis or may result in unilateral or bilateral rami fractures. Posterior forces will cause fractures through the sacroiliac (SI) joint, iliac wing, or sacrum. The fracture pattern includes vertical displacement of the hemipelvis and disruption of the SI joint and the sacrotuberous, sacrospinous, and posterior SI ligaments. This pattern of injury is both rotationally and vertically unstable. VS injuries have a high risk of hemorrhagic shock and multiorgan injury and require surgical stabilization.

LC injuries are caused by side impact forces that compress the pelvis laterally and are often associated with head, thoracic, and abdominal trauma. LC type I injuries involve sacral compression fractures with ipsilateral pubic rami fractures. This injury is considered a relatively stable pelvic fracture and is the most common pelvic fracture pattern. LC type II injuries involve compressive fractures to the iliac wing (crescent) posteriorly. They are rotationally unstable but stable vertically. LC type III patterns are caused by extreme lateral forces that create LC type I or II fractures with a contralateral open book injury. These fractures are highly unstable and have a high risk for severe hemorrhage.

APC injuries are caused by frontal impact forces and have a higher risk of vascular injury compared to LC patterns due to widening of the pelvic ring. APC type I injuries are associated with minor external rotation that causes widening of the pubic symphysis < 2.5 cm with SI joint widening anteriorly. These are mostly stable because the posterior ligaments remain intact. APC type II injuries are the result of increased external rotational forces. The fracture pattern includes pubic symphysis diastasis > 2.5 cm and opening of the anterior SI joint due to disruption of the anterior SI ligament with intact posterior SI ligaments. This type of pelvic fracture is rotationally unstable but vertically stable and has a significant risk of hemorrhage. APC type III injuries are caused by severe external rotational forces that completely disrupt the pelvic ring. The fracture pattern is the same as that of APC II injuries, with the addition of the complete disruption of the SI joint ligaments. This leads to both rotational and vertical pelvic instability. This type of pelvic fracture has the highest risk of hemorrhagic shock due to vascular injuries.

CM injuries are those that involve two or more Young-Burgess injury patterns and are often seen in high-energy traumas like motor vehicle collisions or multi-impact traumas. As CM may involve any combination of LC, APC, or VS injuries, this fracture pattern commonly includes bilateral injuries, which result in a highly unstable pelvis. They are associated with head, intrathoracic, and intra-abdominal injuries and confer a higher mortality rate compared to the other individual categories. These are the most severe pelvic fractures in the Young-Burgess classification system.



APC type II (A) is defined as widening of the pubic symphysis and opening of the anterior SI joint with intact posterior SI ligaments, which does not describe the fracture in the X-ray.

LC type I (B) is a sacral fracture with ipsilateral pubic rami fractures without widening of the pubic symphysis. This is not described in the X-ray.

LC type III (C) injury pattern is either a unilateral sacral or crescent fracture with a contralateral open book injury. This does not describe the X-ray findings.

question: A 24-year-old man presents to the ED after being struck in the right side of the head with a blunt object. He has hemotympanum and mastoid ecchymosis on the right. A CT of the head demonstrates a fracture of the petrous portion of the temporal bone. Which of the following structures is most likely to be affected by this injury?
englishExplanation:
A basilar skull fracture involves at least one of the five bones that make up the skull base, which include the cribriform plate (ethmoid bone), orbital plate (frontal bone), petrous and squamous portions of the temporal bone, sphenoid, and occipital bones. Temporal bone fractures can result in a myriad of complications due to the structures that lie within the petrous segment, including the middle ear structures that contain the organs of hearing (e.g., ossicles, semicircular canals, or vestibulocochlear nerve), internal carotid artery, facial nerve branches, and venous structures.

The stapedius muscle is another structure that lies within this territory and is at risk for injury. It originates at the pyramidal eminence of the mastoid wall of the temporal bone and attaches to the neck of the stapes bone. It receives its innervation from a branch of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII). It contracts in response to loud noises and pulls the stapes posteriorly to prevent excessive oscillation. The middle meningeal artery is at risk for damage with temporal bone trauma, and damage to this vessel can lead to an epidural hematoma. The classic presentation of an epidural hematoma is a person with head trauma who experiences an initial loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval. This period of neurologic recovery is falsely reassuring and is often followed by clinical deterioration.

On initial physical exam, patients with basilar skull fractures may have clear rhinorrhea or otorrhea secondary to a CSF leak, or hemotympanum, which is blood behind the tympanic membrane. Retroauricular or mastoid ecchymosis (Battle sign), and periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes) are later findings that occur 1–3 days following the trauma.

Most patients with basilar skull fractures require admission to the hospital for further monitoring. If intracranial bleeding is present, neurosurgical services should be consulted. Most CSF leaks resolve on their own without any complications, but if the leak lasts > 7 days, patients have an increased risk for meningitis and neurosurgical consultation and antibiotic therapy should be considered.



The middle cerebral artery (MCA) (A) does not lie within the petrous portion of the temporal bone but is an intracerebral vessel. Because the MCA is an intracerebral vessel, it is not often injured by skull fractures. Thrombotic events involving the MCA can lead to an acute ischemic stroke with paralysis and sensory deficits in the contralateral face, arm, and leg.

The trochlear nerve (C) is also referred to as cranial nerve IV and has the longest intracranial course of any cranial nerve. It innervates the superior oblique muscle, which is responsible for intorsion of the eye. The trochlear nerve does not run through the petrous portion of the temporal bone, so injuries to this nerve would not be expected in these fractures. Patients with injuries to the trochlear nerve present with fourth cranial nerve palsies and report binocular vertical diplopia or tilting of objects, blurred vision, difficulty focusing, or dizziness and may adopt an unconscious head tilt.

The vertebral artery (D) enters the skull through the foramen magnum of the occipital bone and does not lie within or travel through the petrous portion of the temporal bone. Injuries to the vertebral arteries can be caused by trauma, connective tissue disease, and hypertension and can lead to ischemic strokes.

Reveal Answer:
Temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical.

question: A 19-year-old man presents for evaluation after a fall. The patient was rollerblading and fell backward onto the pavement. There was no loss of consciousness, and his only concern is a headache. On physical examination, the patient has a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. There is no scalp hematoma. His cervical spine is nontender. On inspection of the ear canal, you see blood behind the tympanic membrane. What injury is associated with this physical exam finding?
englishExplanation:
This patient's physical examination demonstrates hemotympanum, which is blood behind the tympanic membrane. This finding is associated with a basilar skull fracture, which is a linear fracture often through the temporal bone causing bleeding in the middle ear. Patients with this finding need a CT scan of the brain, with attention paid to the temporal bone area. Basilar skull fractures may be associated with dural tears, which may be a portal of entry for infection.



A depressed skull fracture (B) would be noticeable on the external calvarium and not lead to findings in the middle ear. These may be palpated on physical examination or may just be associated with a scalp hematoma overlying the fracture site.

Intracerebral contusions (C) occur from direct trauma to the head and are an area of bleeding within the brain parenchyma. Multiple contusions may occur as a result of the coup-contrecoup mechanism. Contusions may also occur under the site of a depressed skull fracture.

Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage (D) is the most common abnormality seen on CT scan after head injuries. Isolated traumatic subarachnoid injuries tend to have good outcomes. Although, severe cases of hemorrhage may lead to cerebral vasospasm.

question: A 24-year-old intramural football player presents with sudden-onset pain in the right foot after pivoting quickly to catch the ball during practice this evening. He has had no prior injury to the area. On exam, there is tenderness to palpation over the right lateral forefoot. He is not able to ambulate due to the pain. X-ray shows an acute transverse fracture at the base of the fifth metatarsal near the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction. What is the most appropriate treatment for this fracture?

options.text: Air cast, weight-bearing as tolerated, and specialty follow-up in 1–2 weeks
Crutches, walking boot, and specialty follow-up in 1–2 weeks
Elastic wrap and primary care follow-up in 1–2 weeks
Postoperative shoe, weight-bearing as tolerated, and primary care follow-up in 1–2 weeks

correctAnswer: Crutches, walking boot, and specialty follow-up in 1–2 weeks
englishExplanation:
A Jones fracture is a fracture involving the base of the fifth metatarsal of the foot near the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction. Acute Jones fractures result from lateral and medial forces on the base of the fifth metatarsal during plantar flexion, typically when an athlete pivots with the heel off the ground as with football, soccer, or basketball. These fractures involve the intermetatarsal zone, often involving the proximal diaphysis of the bone and extend toward the intermetatarsal joint of the fourth and fifth metatarsals. Due to their location and blood supply, they are at a higher risk of nonunion. The risk of nonunion requires close specialty referral either to orthopedic surgery or podiatric medicine for all highly active people and athletes. Displaced fractures can require surgical intervention, especially those fractures that have ≥ 2 mm of displacement.

X-ray is the imaging modality of choice for a Jones fracture. Initial treatment includes crutches and a walking boot, although some patients may require non-weight-bearing status due to pain. Historically, these fractures were treated with prolonged immobilization, but newer recommendations show that most patients heal well with some weightbearing as tolerated. Referral to a specialist is recommended within 1–2 weeks. High-level athletes may benefit from surgical intervention because surgery decreases recovery time and has a lower nonunion rate than nonsurgical interventions. Nonoperative management includes a controlled ankle movement (CAM) walking boot for 4–8 weeks with physical therapy.

Recently, there has been better delineation of the location of a Jones fracture (zone 2 of the metatarsal) versus a proximal stress fracture (zone 3 of the metatarsal). The two are close together and can be challenging to differentiate on X-ray. Stress fractures are the result of chronic microtrauma and occur less frequently than acute fractures. They may present with chronic but increasing pain after an acute injury. Clinicians may incorrectly consider these types of fractures as acute. Thus, a history of chronic pain in the area will help to distinguish between acute and stress fractures. Management of stress fractures is similar to a Jones fracture and includes a CAM boot or posterior splint for 2 weeks, followed by physical therapy. Resumption of physical activities should be delayed until ambulating pain free, and activity should be advanced at the specialist's recommendations. Persistent pain or nonunion after 3–6 months is an indication for surgery.



Air cast, weight-bearing as tolerated, and specialty follow-up in 1–2 weeks (A) is not an appropriate treatment for an acute Jones fracture. An air cast provides no support to the lateral foot or fifth metatarsal. This patient cannot ambulate, so weight-bearing as tolerated is not an appropriate initial treatment.

Elastic wrap and primary care follow-up (C) would be appropriate management for an injury with no pain on ambulation and no fracture on imaging or for a pseudo-Jones avulsion injury. In this case, the patient has an acute Jones fracture with pain and an inability to ambulate.

Postoperative shoe, weight-bearing as tolerated, and primary care follow-up in 1–2 weeks (D) may be an appropriate treatment for a pseudo-Jones injury or a proximal shaft fracture but is not the best treatment in this case.

question: Which of the following eyelid lacerations requires an emergent ophthalmology consult?

options.text: Eyelid laceration accompanied by a corneal abrasion
Eyelid laceration accompanied by a subarachnoid hemorrhage
Eyelid laceration that has visible fat protruding
Eyelid laceration that is 1 cm caused by a dog bite

correctAnswer: Eyelid laceration that has visible fat protruding
englishExplanation:
A patient with an eyelid laceration with visible fat protrusion requires an emergent consultation with an ophthalmologist. The presence of fat in an eyelid laceration suggests that the orbital septum has been violated, which allows for orbital fat to protrude through the laceration. Orbital septum violation puts the patient at high risk for levator muscle damage and orbital injury. Patients with levator muscle damage often present with limited elevation of the upper eyelid. A CT scan of the orbits should be performed to assess the extent of orbital injury, and repair should be performed by an ophthalmologist or plastic surgeon.



Although an eyelid laceration accompanied by a corneal abrasion (A) or subarachnoid hemorrhage (B) may indicate trauma, they do not always require consultation with an ophthalmologist. As long as significant injury to the globe has been ruled out, simple eyelid lacerations can be repaired in the ED without consultation with a specialist.

Eyelid lacerations caused by dog bites (C) can prove to be problematic, and should prompt physicians to initiate prophylactic antibiotic therapy, but should not affect management of simple eyelid lacerations.
