question: A 4-year-old girl presents to the ED after falling from a barstool onto a tile floor 1 hour ago. She had no loss of consciousness or vomiting. She is very playful and interactive on exam without any bruising behind the ears or around the eyes. Her ear exam finding is shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Monitor in the ED for 3 more hours

englishExplanation:
An ear examination is an important part of an evaluation of a child with a closed head injury because the most common sign of a basilar skull fracture in children is hemotympanum. Basilar skull fractures in children are strongly associated with intracranial injury, many of which have significant morbidity and mortality and may include apnea and altered mental status on presentation. Other presentations include a CSF leak seen as otorrhea or rhinorrhea, bleeding into the mastoid air cells seen as retroauricular bruising (i.e., Battle sign), and bleeding from a cribriform plate fracture seen as periorbital bruising (i.e., raccoon eyes).

Basilar skull fractures are commonly associated with cranial nerve VI, VII, or VIII impairment and present as an inability to abduct an eye, facial weakness or numbness, and hearing loss. Hearing loss is very common, which can be from cranial nerve dysfunction, hemotympanum, tympanic membrane perforation, or ossicular injury. Children may also express dizziness or vertigo.

A CT scan of the brain should be performed in children with physical exam findings of a basilar skull fracture to evaluate for intracranial injury. A basilar skull fracture may be difficult to see on a CT scan, so children with exam findings but a normal CT should still be presumed to have a basilar skull fracture. Treatment is as directed by a pediatric neurosurgeon or otolaryngologist. Bacterial meningitis is a late complication of a CSF leak from a basilar skull fracture, but prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended.



Amoxicillin (A) is the appropriate treatment for a child with uncomplicated otitis media, not hemotympanum.

Monitoring for worsening (C) is a common practice in children with a head injury from a significant mechanism or those with loss of consciousness or vomiting but who appear well, but it does not replace a CT scan in children with signs of a basilar skull fracture.

Reassurance and discharge (D) would be appropriate for this patient should the signs of a basilar skull fracture be missing.

Ensuring vaccinations are up to date.

question: Which of the following radiographic signs supports the diagnosis of a Galeazzi fracture?
englishExplanation:
Galeazzi fractures are relatively uncommon injuries that occur more frequently in adults than children, with an average patient age of 34 years. The typical mechanism involves forceful axial loading and torsion of the forearm, commonly from a fall onto an outstretched hand. The injury results from ligamentous disruption at the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ), including the triangular fibrocartilage complex and interosseous membrane. In pediatrics, a Galeazzi-equivalent fracture may occur, involving a distal radial fracture with distal ulnar physeal separation rather than true DRUJ dislocation.

Patients present with forearm and wrist pain following trauma, with visible deformity, swelling, and tenderness over the distal radius and wrist. Diagnosis is established through radiographic evaluation with anteroposterior and lateral views of the forearm and wrist. However, underdiagnosis is common because DRUJ disruption may be subtle or overlooked. Radiographic signs suggesting DRUJ injury include radial shortening, fracture within 7.5 cm of the lunate facet, and the presence of ulnar styloid fracture, with ulnar styloid fracture carrying the highest predictive value for DRUJ injury.

Initial management includes analgesia, neurovascular assessment, and splinting with prompt orthopedic consultation. Children may be successfully treated with closed reduction and long-arm cast immobilization. However, in adults, nonsurgical treatment fails in a significant majority of cases due to deforming forces on the distal radius and DRUJ instability. Thus, open reduction and internal fixation of the radius is the preferred treatment in adults. Complications from misdiagnosis or inadequate management include DRUJ instability, malunion, limited forearm range of motion, chronic wrist pain, and post-traumatic osteoarthritis.



A midshaft ulna fracture (B) is a component of a Monteggia fracture, not a Galeazzi fracture. A Monteggia fracture consists of an ulnar shaft fracture with radial head dislocation, which is the opposite pattern from Galeazzi.

Radial head dislocation (C) is the hallmark finding of a Monteggia fracture, not a Galeazzi fracture. The Galeazzi injury involves the wrist joint (DRUJ) rather than the elbow.

While radial head fractures (D) can occur with elbow trauma, they are not associated with Galeazzi fractures. A Galeazzi fracture involves the radial shaft or diaphysis, not the radial head, and the associated joint injury is at the wrist (DRUJ), not the elbow.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common ulna fracture?

Reveal Answer:
The midshaft ulna fracture, often occurring due to a nightstick-type injury mechanism.

Rapid Review

question: A 23-year-old man with a history of morbid obesity presents to the ED after injuring his left index finger 3 hours ago while injecting sealant with a high-pressure nozzle. He is in severe pain and intravenous access cannot be obtained due to his habitus. Exam shows his left index finger is similar in size to other digits, with a nonbleeding 0.5 cm laceration on the lateral middle phalanx. He refuses range of motion testing due to pain but is neurovascularly intact distal to the injury. Which of the following is contraindicated in this patient?

options.text: Passive and active range of motion testing

englishExplanation:
This patient has sustained a high-pressure injection injury. The most common cause of high-pressure injection injuries is with trigger-activated tools (e.g., portable epinephrine pens), and they usually occur in the nondominant hand. Diagnosis is primarily made clinically. Radiographs may supplement the diagnosis as they often show the dissemination of fluid or air beneath the injury and across fascial planes. Fractures are not uncommon, due to the high localized pressure. Upon arrival, the patient’s high-pressure injection injury commonly seems innocuous. However, underlying ischemia may be ongoing. As little as 6 hours of delay to treatment increases the already high amputation rates of 30–48%. Patients will present with a history of high-pressure injection tool use and delayed onset of a myriad of symptoms such as pain, swelling, discoloration, and neurologic deficits.

Treatment depends on the composition of the injection injury. If only water is injected, most patients can be observed for signs and symptoms of ischemia and compartment syndrome. For epinephrine auto-injector injuries, ischemia and pain result and can be treated with either subcutaneous phentolamine or close observation. Digital blocks for pain control can increase the pressure within the injured finger leading to further neurovascular compromise. Therefore, they are contraindicated in these injuries. For any other compositions, treatment includes immediate hand surgery consultation, parenteral pain control, elevation of the extremity, intravenous antibiotics with skin flora coverage, and radiographs. Notably, imaging and further workup should not delay immediate hand surgery evaluation and likely emergent operative debridement.



As noted above, treatment of high-pressure injection injuries includes elevation of the extremity (B) to help reduce swelling and further increases in intra-digital pressure and intravenous ceftriaxone (C) or another antibiotic that covers skin flora.

A full physical exam, including passive and active range of motion testing (D), despite the pain, should be done to exclude tendinous injuries.

One Step Further
Question:
Which treatment for epinephrine auto-injector injuries has better outcomes - subcutaneous phentolamine or close observation?

Reveal Answer:
There is no clear evidence for either having better outcome rates.

Complications: infection, amputation

question: Which of the following appropriately describes neurogenic shock?

options.text: Cool, clammy distal extremities; sinus tachycardia; decreased preload
Cool, clammy distal extremities; sinus tachycardia; increased preload
Warm, dry distal extremities; normal sinus rhythm; decreased preload
Warm, dry distal extremities; sinus tachycardia; decreased preload

correctAnswer: Warm, dry distal extremities; normal sinus rhythm; decreased preload
englishExplanation:
Neurogenic shock is a type of distributive shock that occurs with a central nervous system or spinal cord injury. It occurs in < 20% of patients with spinal cord injuries and is secondary to a loss of peripheral sympathetic innervation resulting in vasodilation. If the injury occurs through the T1–T4 cord levels, loss of sympathetic innervation to the heart leaves unopposed vagal stimulation, resulting in bradycardia or absence of reflex tachycardia. Therefore, in general, patients with neurogenic shock are warm, peripherally vasodilated, and hypotensive with a relative bradycardia and decreased preload. Treatment of neurogenic shock focuses on fixing any underlying hypovolemia with either blood products (in the setting of hemorrhage) or fluids (if fluid depleted). If IV fluids are not adequate to maintain organ perfusion, positive inotropic or vasopressor agents may be beneficial adjuncts to improve cardiac output and raise perfusion pressure. The recommendation is to maintain a higher MAP than in other traumatic injuries, with pressures close to 85–90 mm Hg.



Cool, clammy distal extremities; sinus tachycardia; decreased preload (A) is the description of hypovolemic shock. Cool, clammy distal extremities; sinus tachycardia; increased preload (B) is the description of cardiogenic shock. Warm, dry distal extremities; sinus tachycardia; decreased preload (D) is the description of septic shock, which is another form of distributive shock. The key difference between the two types is the relative bradycardia that is seen in neurogenic shock.

One Step Further
Question:
True or false: neurogenic shock and spinal shock are two words used to describe the same thing.

Reveal Answer:
False. Spinal shock is the temporary loss or depression of spinal reflex activity that occurs below a complete or incomplete spinal cord injury.

Hypotension, poikilothermia, bradycardia
Airway support, fluids, atropine, vasopressors
Spinal

Neurologic deficits without hemodynamic changes

question: A 17-year-old girl presents to the ED with bilateral eye pain. The patient woke up with pain and photophobia. She notes that yesterday she was skiing at a resort in Colorado and forgot to wear her ski goggles but did apply sunscreen to her face. She initially thought the pain might be some dust or something irritating her eyes, but the pain continues to intensify. On exam, her pupillary reflexes and cranial nerves are intact. Her visual acuity is 20/40 bilaterally, and she has no history of vision correction. She has conjunctival injection, and an example of a fluorescein stain of her eye is shown in the image above. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with bilateral eye pain and conjunctival injection after skiing at high altitude without goggles, most consistent with ultraviolet keratitis, the most common cause of radiation damage to the eye. The epithelial layer of the cornea absorbs the majority of ultraviolet radiation, and prolonged exposure can cause desquamation of the epithelium. Tanning beds, welding torches, and sun exposure (including ultraviolet rays reflected off of snow, snow blindness) are risk factors if patients do not wear appropriate eye protection. Similar to cutaneous sunburn, pain develops between 8 and 12 hours after exposure. Patients may have conjunctival injection, photophobia, and decreased visual acuity. Fluorescein dye shows diffuse punctate corneal uptake and can help rule out corneal abrasion. Patients are generally treated supportively, with oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain and lubricating eye drops or ointments. Topical antibiotics are often administered but have no proven benefit.



Contact dermatitis (A) could present with conjunctival or facial irritation after a new exposure (such as sunscreen). However, this patient has decreased visual acuity and diffuse fluorescein uptake on exam, which is more consistent with ultraviolet keratitis.

Corneal abrasions (B) could also cause intense discomfort, and skiing without goggles would be a risk factor. However, corneal abrasions are generally rapid in onset and unilateral. This patient also has no distinct areas of fluorescein uptake on exam.

Disciform keratitis (C) is an ocular reactivation of herpes simplex virus that manifests itself in pain, decreased visual acuity, and a distinct disciform distribution of keratic precipitates. It is usually unilateral and gradual in onset.

One Step Further
Question:
How long do the symptoms of ultraviolet keratitis generally last?

Reveal Answer:
Between 48 and 72 hours.

question: Which of the following tests is the most sensitive physical examination maneuver to identify an injury to the anterior cruciate ligament?
englishExplanation:
The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is one of the four major ligaments of the knee (anterior cruciate, posterior cruciate, medial collateral, and lateral collateral). It provides anterior stability to the knee joint and is the most commonly injured ligament of the knee. A tear results from deceleration, hyperextension, or marked internal rotation of the tibia on the femur. Most ACL tears occur during sporting activities such as skiing, football, soccer, and basketball. Clinically, there is usually rapid development of hemarthroses, causing significant swelling. Almost half of individuals report feeling or hearing a pop, which is the most reliable indicator. There is usually instability of the knee or a wobbly feeling.

The Lachman test is the most sensitive test (approximately 98% sensitivity) for an ACL tear. This is performed by placing the knee in 20–30° of flexion with the leg slightly externally rotated. One hand is placed behind the tibia with the thumb on the tibial tuberosity, and one hand is placed on the thigh while the examiner pulls the tibia anteriorly. In a patient with an intact ACL, a firm end point should be elicited. With a positive test, the examiner feels a soft end point at the end of the motion, indicating an ACL tear.

X-rays are often performed in acute knee injuries but are not helpful in making a diagnosis of an ACL tear. However, they may be helpful in ruling out other associated injuries or causes of knee pain. A Segond fracture is an avulsion fracture of the lateral tibial condyle that is indicative of disruption of the lateral capsule and associated ACL injury. MRI is rarely necessary to make a diagnosis. Rest, ice, crutches, immobilization, and NSAIDs are common initial treatment options. Patients should be referred to orthopedic surgery. Management options are often surgical, but nonoperative management can be pursued depending on the patient’s age, functional status, and medical comorbidities.



While the anterior drawer test (A) is used to assess the integrity of the ACL, it is less sensitive than the Lachman test with a sensitivity of approximately 48%. The anterior drawer test can be affected by hamstring muscle tension and may not reveal subtle laxity present in ACL injuries.

McMurray test (C) is used to identify meniscal tears. It is performed with the patient lying supine on a stretcher, at which time the examiner flexes the foot and extends the knee while internally and externally rotating the tibia on the femur. A clicking indicates a positive test.

The Thompson test (D) is performed to evaluate the integrity of the Achilles tendon. With the patient lying prone, the calf is squeezed, which causes plantar flexion of the ankle joint. If flexion does not occur with the squeezing, the Achilles tendon is injured.

Valgus stress (E) applied to the knee joint assesses the integrity of the medial aspect of the joint, including the medial collateral ligament.

One Step Further
Question:
What structures of the knee make up the unhappy triad?

Reveal Answer:
Anterior cruciate ligament, medial collateral ligament, and medial meniscus.

Reports pop and swelling
Clinical tests: Lachman test (most sensitive), anterior drawer test, pivot shift test
Imaging modality of choice: MRI (highly sensitive and specific)
Treatment is nonemergent surgical intervention

الفخ: الطالب يختار Anterior drawer test خطأً بدلاً من B، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: A 5-year-old boy presents to the ED after being struck by a car. A FAST exam is performed with one of the images shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of the findings shown? What does the ultrasound image shown above, obtained on a 5-year-old boy who presented after being struck by a motorized vehicle, show?
englishExplanation:
Blunt abdominal trauma (BAT) is the most common form of trauma in children, with motor vehicle collisions being the leading mechanism, though non-accidental trauma is the leading cause in children ≤4 years old. The spleen is the most commonly injured solid organ, followed by the liver and the kidney.

The pathogenesis of intra-abdominal hemorrhage in pediatric blunt trauma involves direct force transmission to solid organs (spleen, liver, kidney), which causes parenchymal disruption and bleeding into the peritoneal cavity. Children are particularly vulnerable because of their relatively larger solid organs, thinner abdominal wall, and less protective musculature and fat compared to adults.

Clinically, children with intra-abdominal hemorrhage may present with abdominal pain, tenderness, distension, and abdominal wall ecchymosis (e.g., seatbelt sign). Hemodynamic instability may be present, though many initially appear stable, as children have robust compensatory mechanisms that maintain hemodynamics longer, even with significant blood loss. The FAST exam is a rapid bedside ultrasound that evaluates four windows (subxiphoid/cardiac, right upper quadrant/Morison's pouch, left upper quadrant/splenorenal recess, and suprapubic/pelvis) for free fluid. The eFAST expands this to include views of both lungs to evaluate for pneumothorax. While still used in children, it is poorly sensitive and less reliable than in adults and is not appropriate to rule out intra-abdominal injury. However, a positive FAST exam in an unstable child may obviate the need for CT and prompt direct operative intervention.

Treatment in the ED follows ATLS principles beginning with the primary survey, IV access, fluid resuscitation, and blood product administration as needed. The vast majority of pediatric solid organ injuries are managed nonoperatively with observation, with intervention (e.g., laparotomy, angiography) needed in rare cases. Indications for operative intervention include hemodynamic instability unresponsive to resuscitation with a positive FAST, peritonitis, or hollow viscus injury. Transfusion of >40 mL/kg of blood products is strongly associated with the need for intervention or death. Complications include delayed hemorrhage, missed injuries (especially hollow viscous, pancreas), and the risks of unnecessary CT radiation exposure in the pediatric population.



While ascites (A) can appear as anechoic fluid in Morison's pouch, in the acute setting of a pediatric trauma patient struck by a car, free fluid is presumed to represent hemoperitoneum, not iatrogenic ascites from fluid resuscitation. This would be an unlikely finding this early in the clinical course.

The gallbladder (C) is an anechoic fluid-filled structure, but it is located anteriorly within the gallbladder fossa on the visceral surface of the liver, not in the hepatorenal recess posteriorly between the liver and kidney. A band-like collection in Morison's pouch is anatomically distinct from the gallbladder. [1-2]

Pericardial effusion (D) is assessed on the subxiphoid (cardiac) view of the FAST exam, not the right upper quadrant/hepatorenal view. Pericardial fluid appears as an anechoic stripe surrounding the heart, not in Morison's pouch.

While perihepatic fat (E) can occasionally create echogenic or hypoechoic artifacts near the liver, it does not produce a discrete anechoic band-like collection in the hepatorenal recess. Free fluid in Morison's pouch collects with sharp angles in the most gravity-dependent areas, distinguishing it from fat or edge artifact.

One Step Further
Question:
Where in the left upper quadrant is fluid most commonly seen on a positive FAST exam?

Reveal Answer:
Between the spleen and the diaphragm.

Stable patient + positive FAST → CT
Unstable patient + negative FAST → repeat FAST or DPL
Unstable patient + positive FAST → laparotomy
eFAST adds pulmonary evaluation

الفخ: الطالب يختار Ascites from fluid resuscitation خطأً بدلاً من B، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: An 8-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after he jumped on the bed and fell onto his hands. It was witnessed by his parent, who reports he began crying immediately and did not hit his head. The patient only has arm pain. An X-ray of his forearm is shown above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s X-ray is consistent with a torus fracture. They are most commonly seen in children’s extremities secondary to an axial loading force. This axial loading force leads to buckling of the cortex and underlying periosteum. They may appear subtle on plain radiography. However, more advanced imaging (e.g., computed tomography) is not indicated purely for the evaluation of torus fractures. Patients commonly present with point tenderness over the fracture site with or without overlying swelling. A firm ridge across the fracture line may be palpable, but lack of this does not preclude the diagnosis. The injured extremity should be splinted, and the patient should be given close follow-up within 1 week. In cases of distal radius torus fractures, follow-up can be made with the pediatrician alone. Otherwise, orthopedic follow-up should be recommended.



Greenstick fractures (A) are characterized by cortical rupture on one side with an intact cortex on the other side. The bone will be bowed away from the disrupted cortex.

Plastic deformation injuries (B) result from trauma that is forceful enough to create a bend in the bone without causing any cortical disruption.

Salter-Harris type I fracture (C) is a transverse fracture through the physis. Radiographs may appear normal, but patients will have point tenderness over the growth plate.

One Step Further
Question:
What is another name for a torus fracture?

Reveal Answer:
Buckle fracture.

question: A 17-year-old boy presents with dizziness, nausea, and headache after falling off a trampoline this evening. He thinks he lost consciousness for a second but otherwise was awake shortly after the incident. He vomited once after the fall but has not since. There are no focal findings on neurologic examination, and he is ambulatory. After 6 hours of observation, he remains neurologically intact, has not had further vomiting, and appears well. What are the most appropriate disposition recommendations to give this patient?

options.text: No sports activity but may return to other activities immediately
Outpatient cognitive and physical rest for 1 week, with a gradual return to physical activity
Outpatient cognitive and physical rest for 24–48 hours, with gradual return to physical activity

correctAnswer: Outpatient cognitive and physical rest for 24–48 hours, with gradual return to physical activity
englishExplanation:
The term concussion is often used synonymously with mild traumatic brain injury, but, more specifically, it describes a pathophysiological state resulting in symptoms and signs experienced by patients after a mild traumatic brain injury. A concussion typically results in short-lived impairment of neurologic function after a direct blow to the head or face that spontaneously resolves. Clinical signs and symptoms of a concussion reflect a functional disturbance rather than structural injury to the brain. No abnormalities are seen on neuroimaging. The incidence of concussion is highest among boys playing collision sports, such as rugby, football, hockey, and lacrosse. In girls, those who participate in soccer, lacrosse, and hockey have the highest incidence of concussion. Children with a concussion may manifest headaches, confusion or disorientation, difficulties with memory, inattentiveness, slow speech, dizziness, gait abnormalities, vomiting, and emotional lability. Patients may or may not have experienced loss of consciousness.

A diagnosis of concussion is determined clinically based on the mechanism of injury, symptoms, and examination findings. Management of concussion includes removal from competitive sports, restriction of physical activity, and neurocognitive rest. Observational studies have suggested that strict physical rest for more than a few days after a concussion may prolong symptoms. Therefore, the recommendation is brief cognitive rest for 24–48 hours after concussion, followed by a gradual return to noncontact physical activity. Patients with worsening or persistent symptoms for > 21 days should be referred for specialty evaluation. Patients with persistent neurological symptoms in the acute setting (e.g., drowsiness, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score < 15, persistent vomiting) should be admitted for observation. Potential long-term complications related to repeated concussions include permanent changes in mood, behavior, cognition, somatic symptoms, and, in severe cases, dementia or Parkinsonian-like symptoms.



Inpatient admission for 24-hour observation (A) would only be recommended for patients with immediate complications from a head injury, including those with a GCS < 15, seizures, recurrent vomiting, or abnormalities on CT imaging.

All patients should have a period of cognitive rest for at least 24–48 hours before returning to normal activities (B).

Outpatient cognitive and physical rest for 1 week with a gradual return to physical activity (C) is not recommended as these adolescents become deconditioned and a prolonged period of rest does not improve outcomes.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
Decisional capacity.

question: What function is significantly impaired by rupture of the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon?

options.text: Flexion at the distal interphalangeal joint
Flexion at the proximal interphalangeal joint

correctAnswer: Flexion at the proximal interphalangeal joint
englishExplanation:
Injuries to the flexor tendons in the hand are typically the result of lacerations, but closed traumatic disruption (e.g., avulsion fractures) can also occur. Careful examination of the hand with specific knowledge about the function of various tendons is essential, as presentations can be subtle.

The flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and travels distally through the anterior compartment of the forearm. At the wrist, four tendons come off the muscle and travel through the carpal tunnel. The tendons insert at the proximal aspect of the middle phalanx of each of the four fingers. The flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon passes deep to the split of the distal FDS tendon and inserts at the base of the distal phalanx. The primary function of the FDS is flexion at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint, but it also assists with flexion at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint. On examination, the patient should be asked to flex at the PIP joint against resistance while the other three fingers are held in extension.

Injuries to flexor tendons should be referred to a hand specialist for definitive care. If one is not immediately available, open wounds should be irrigated and approximated, the hand should be splinted in partial flexion at the MCP, PIP, and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, and the patient should be referred for urgent outpatient care.



The FDP is primarily responsible for flexion at the DIP joint (A), but the FDS is responsible for PIP flexion.

The FDS and FDP together assist with flexion at the MCP joint (B), but rupture of the FDS would not significantly impair MCP joint flexion.

The pincer function (D) also requires an intact FDP in the finger. To test the function of the FDP, the patient should attempt to flex the DIP joint against resistance while holding the MCP and PIP joints in extension.

Thumb flexion (E) is controlled by the flexor pollicis longus, not the FDS.

Reveal Answer:
The median nerve.

question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after being burned while an adult was lighting a bonfire with gasoline. He weighs 20 kg, has 10% full-thickness burns, 10% partial-thickness burns, and 10% superficial burns. How much IV lactated Ringer should the patient receive in the first 8 hours after injury according to the Parkland formula?
englishExplanation:
Resuscitation of a patient with severe burns is similar to any other resuscitation, focusing on the airway, breathing, and circulation. Early intubation should be performed in patients with signs of pharyngeal or airway swelling. Other concerning signs include full-thickness burns, large (> 15%) partial-thickness burns, burns to the face or genitals, chemical burns to the eyes, circumferential burns, significant burns to the hands or feet, and electrical burns with loss of consciousness or entrance and exit wounds. Clinicians should also be aware that an estimated 10–20% of children’s burns result from nonaccidental trauma. Determining the percentage of burned body surface area is challenging in children due to their different proportions, so an appropriate diagram should be used instead of the adult rule of nines. Formulas such as the Parkland formula and the Galveston formula should be used to determine the amount of fluid needed for resuscitation. Areas of superficial burns should not be included in the calculation of the total area burned for these formulas. For the Parkland formula, 4 mL/kg/% of body surface area burned should be given over 24 hours, with the first half given in 8 hours after the burn. So for our patient, 4 mL × 20 kg × 20% body surface area is 1,600 mL, and half of that, or 800 mL, should be given in the first 8 hours.



If the patient had 30% body surface area of full- and partial-thickness burns, 1,200 mL (A) would be appropriate. Remember that areas of superficial burns should not be included in the formula calculations. This patient should receive 1,600 mL (B) of fluid in 24 hours. If this patient had 30% body surface area burned, 2,400 mL (C) is the amount of fluid they should receive in 24 hours.

One Step Further

What additional fluid should be added to the Parkland formula for patients < 30 kg?

Reveal Answer:
Regular maintenance fluid with 5% dextrose.

الفخ: الطالب يختار 1,200 mL خطأً بدلاً من D، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: A 22-year-old man presents to the ED after injuring his lower leg while playing soccer. He is found to have a comminuted tibia fracture on X-ray. He reports progressively worsening severe pain in the calf. He continues to scream in pain despite repeated doses of hydromorphone. On examination, he is afebrile with a heart rate of 110 bpm and blood pressure of 117/63 mm Hg. There is swelling of the midcalf with intact distal pulses and weakness with dorsiflexion of the foot. Based on your clinical suspicion, compartment pressure is measured and found to be 36 mm Hg. What is the delta pressure of the compartment?
englishExplanation:
Occurring in the presence of increased pressure within a nonexpandable space, compartment syndrome results in decreased venous blood flow, worsening congestion, and eventual arterial compromise if left untreated. Most often associated with long bone fractures, compartment syndrome can also occur in the setting of soft tissue injury, crush injuries, and spontaneous hemorrhage. Clinically, patients present with pain out of proportion to the injury, pain with passive stretching of the muscles in the compartment, and paresthesias.

Pallor and loss of pulses are late and ominous findings. While compartment syndrome is diagnosed clinically, measurement of the pressure within the compartment can provide confirmation of the diagnosis. While compartment pressures < 30 mm Hg generally do not cause compartment syndrome, tolerance to tissue ischemia varies between individuals. Because of this, many sources advocate using the delta pressure (diastolic blood pressure - compartment pressure) as a more reliable indicator of compartment syndrome. A delta pressure < 30 mm Hg indicates the need for a fasciotomy. In this patient, the delta pressure is 63 - 36, or 27 mm Hg.



The delta pressure is calculated by subtracting the direct pressure of the compartment from the diastolic blood pressure. In this case, the delta pressure is 27 mm Hg, not 35 mm Hg (B).

The systolic pressure minus the diastolic pressure (i.e., 54 mm Hg (C)) is not correct. Likewise, the systolic pressure minus the direct compartment pressure (i.e., 81 mm Hg (D)) is also not correct. While a single elevated pressure is concerning, rising or persistently elevated pressures are superior to a single measurement when confirming the diagnosis.

What sensory finding is consistent with compartment syndrome in the anterior compartment of the lower leg?

Reveal Answer:
Decreased sensation between the first and second toes.

Most common sites: forearm, lower leg
PE: paresthesias, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis, and pain out of proportion to exam (6 Ps)
Pain (severe) is usually the first symptom

question: A 74-year-old man presents after a fall 2 hours ago. He reports midline cervical spine pain, with tenderness from C1 to C6. He has full strength in all extremities, intact sensation, and normal reflexes. CT of the cervical spine demonstrates a fracture. Which of the following cervical spine injuries represents a stable fracture pattern in this neurologically intact patient?
englishExplanation:
Vertebral compression fractures are generally considered stable cervical spine injuries when they occur in isolation without involving the posterior column or ligamentous complexes. These injuries typically result from axial loading combined with flexion, leading to a loss of anterior vertebral body height, while the posterior vertebral wall and posterior elements remain intact. Because the patient presents 2 hours after a fall with midline cervical spine tenderness but remains entirely neurologically intact, demonstrating full strength in all extremities, intact sensation, and normal reflexes, the clinical picture aligns with a stable mechanical column. On imaging, preferably CT, a stable compression fracture involves < 40% loss of anterior vertebral height and lacks any translation or angulation that would suggest a multicolumn disruption.

Management for an isolated, stable vertebral compression fracture in a neurologically intact patient primarily focuses on conservative therapy rather than urgent surgical stabilization. Initial treatment consists of pain control, a short course of rigid or semi-rigid cervical orthosis collar immobilization for comfort, and close outpatient follow-up with serial plain radiographs to ensure proper healing and alignment without progressive collapse. Because the posterior ligamentous complex remains undamaged, the inherent structural integrity of the spinal column prevents translation or subluxation during physiological movement.



Bilateral C2 pedicle fractures (A) often occur from trauma while the neck is in extension and can lead to subluxation of C2 on C3, which is unstable.

Flexion teardrop fractures (B) occur with the neck in flexion at the time of injury, leading to a wedge-shaped fracture fragment of the anterior inferior vertebral body. This often disrupts the anterior and posterior ligaments, which makes these injuries unstable and often associated with neurologic injury.

A Jefferson fracture (C) pattern involves the anterior and posterior arches of C1, leading to disruption of the transverse ligament, which can widen the predental space and is considered unstable.

Posterior atlantoaxial dislocation (D) is a rare, high-energy injury involving disruption of the articulation between C1 and C2 with posterior displacement of the atlas. This injury pattern requires destruction of the transverse atlantal ligament, tectorial membrane, and anterior longitudinal ligament, among other stabilizing structures. The extensive ligamentous disruption makes this injury inherently unstable, carrying a high risk of neurovascular complications.

One Step Further

Are oblique spinous process fractures stable?

Reveal Answer:
Yes, these are known as clay shoveler’s fractures.

Bilateral facet dislocation: anterior dislocation ≥ 50% of vertebral body, hyperflexion
Odontoid fracture (types II and III): high cervical pain radiating to the occiput
Hangman fracture: C2, extreme hyperextension
Teardrop fracture: anterior displacement of wedge-shaped fragment, hyperflexion
Other unstable fractures: atlanto-occipital dislocation (anterior and posterior), flexion-distraction injury
Imaging decision: NEXUS criteria or Canadian C-Spine Rule

question: Which of the following periorbital wounds should be repaired by oculoplastics rather than the emergency clinician?

options.text: A wound 5 mm from the medial canthus
A wound that is 25 mm across the lid without crossing the margin
Any wound involving the outer surface of the eyelid

correctAnswer: A wound 5 mm from the medial canthus
englishExplanation:
Eyelid lacerations require a careful and thorough examination to ensure that no sensitive structures have been injured. A careful examination for orbit injury, lacrimal duct injury, and deep muscle involvement is crucial. Indications for oculoplastics consultation for repair include the following: lacrimal duct injury, lid margin involvement (specifically > 1 mm), wounds < 8 mm from medial canthus, through-and-through lacerations, associated ptosis, involvement of deep muscle structures, and injuries that penetrate the tarsal plate. When any of the above features are present, oculoplastics should be consulted, tetanus vaccination status should be updated, and the wound should be irrigated and debris removed.



While > 1 mm deep wounds require oculoplastics, a 0.7 mm deep wound (A) would not.

A wound that is 25 mm across the lid without crossing the margin (C) can be repaired by the emergency clinician and does not necessarily require oculoplastics unless other structures are involved.

Wounds involving the inner aspect of the eyelid, not the outer surface (D), should be repaired by oculoplastics.

question: What is often the only clinical finding of pericardial tamponade after penetrating trauma?
englishExplanation:
Cardiac tamponade is defined as the accumulation of fluid in the pericardium under pressure. In the setting of trauma, most injuries are from guns or knives. Of the two, guns are less likely to cause tamponade since the pericardial defect is usually larger and more irregular and hence does not seal itself, making exsanguinating hemorrhage more common. Blunt mechanisms rarely lead to cardiac tamponade. The study of choice is the focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) examination. Without the availability of bedside sonography, cardiac tamponade can be deceptively challenging to diagnose due to the body’s various compensatory mechanisms. Sinus tachycardia is often the only clinical finding of pericardial tamponade. The classic combination of muffled heart sounds, hypotension, and distended neck veins is called the Beck triad and is present in < 10% of cases. Hypotension is an ominous sign reflecting decompensation or systemic hypovolemia from other injuries. Kussmaul sign (an increase in jugular venous distension with inspiration) and pulsus paradoxus (fall in systolic blood pressure with inspiration) may be found in moderate to severe tamponade, but these are unreliable signs. Narrowing of the pulse pressure is not sensitive, but if found, it should provide suspicion for tamponade until proven otherwise. If cardiac tamponade is identified on the FAST exam, perform a pericardiocentesis if the patient is hemodynamically unstable, especially if in a rural setting. A pericardiocentesis in the setting of trauma is a temporizing measure that needs to be followed by a thoracotomy in the operating room. Unstable patients who will not survive transfer to the OR, especially those who lose their vital signs in the emergency department after penetrating chest trauma, are candidates for an immediate ED thoracotomy.



Muffled heart sounds (A) are part of the Beck triad of classic findings of pericardial tamponade but are present in < 10% of cases.

Narrowed pulse pressure (B) points to cardiac tamponade until proven otherwise in the right clinical setting. However, it is not a sensitive sign.

Widened pulse pressure (D) is not usually encountered in the setting of pericardial tamponade.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
Approximately 65 mL.

question: An 87-year-old woman presents to the ED with facial pain after tripping and striking her face on her bedpost. On physical exam, you note the findings shown above. Which of the following radiographic signs is associated with this injury?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with signs and symptoms consistent with an orbital blowout fracture, a condition commonly caused by direct trauma to the orbit, resulting in a fracture of the orbital floor. Orbital blowout fractures occur when increased intraorbital pressure from trauma forces orbital contents through the thin floor of the orbit into the maxillary sinus. This type of injury requires a thorough ophthalmologic evaluation, including visual acuity testing and fluorescein staining, to assess for serious globe injuries, such as corneal abrasions, globe rupture, or retinal detachment.

Imaging studies are essential for confirming the diagnosis. Plain X-rays may show a teardrop sign, which is the radiographic appearance of periorbital fat or the inferior rectus muscle herniating into the maxillary sinus. However, CT imaging of the orbits is more definitive and provides detailed visualization of the fracture, including the extent of muscle or fat entrapment. This imaging is especially important if surgical repair is anticipated.

Patients with orbital blowout fractures often present with diplopia, particularly with upward gaze, which is a hallmark sign of inferior rectus muscle entrapment. The muscle can become trapped between the fractured bony segments of the orbital floor, leading to restriction of eye movement. Diplopia due to muscle entrapment may also be accompanied by enophthalmos, or sunken appearance of the eye, if the fracture results in displacement of orbital contents.

A common complication of orbital blowout fractures is infraorbital nerve palsy or neuropraxia, which occurs due to damage to the infraorbital nerve as it passes through the orbital floor. This can result in paresthesia or numbness of the upper lip, maxillary teeth, and cheek.

Management of orbital blowout fractures includes pain control with analgesics and prophylactic antibiotics if there is evidence of sinus involvement or disruption to reduce the risk of infection. The patient should have close follow-up with an ophthalmologist. If inferior rectus entrapment is present, urgent referral to an ophthalmologist within 24-48 hours is required, as operative management may be necessary to release the entrapped muscle and prevent permanent motility deficits or vision impairment. Additionally, patients should avoid activities that could increase intraocular pressure, such as nose blowing or heavy lifting, to prevent further herniation or complications.



The Hampton hump (A) is the pathognomonic but rarely seen wedge-shaped infarct seen on chest X-ray in patients with pulmonary embolism.

The lightbulb sign (B) is the classic radiographic appearance of a posterior shoulder dislocation.

The steeple sign (C) is the classic radiographic appearance of the subglottic stenosis seen with croup on neck X-ray.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
Lightning strike or seizure.

question: Which of the following fractures is most commonly nonoperative in adults?
englishExplanation:
Most patients with a radial head fracture will not require operative management. Radial head fractures are typically caused by indirect trauma (e.g., a fall on an outstretched hand). There are four types of radial head fractures, ranging from the more common type I (nondisplaced fracture) and type II (marginal fracture with minimal displacement) to the rarer type III (comminuted fracture) and type IV (fracture with dislocation). Type I and II injuries are usually treated with a sling and range of motion exercises. It is important to fully test the patient’s range of motion. If the range of motion is limited by pain, the joint should be injected with an anesthetic agent (lidocaine, bupivacaine) and tested again. Continued limited range of motion in spite of pain control suggests the presence of entrapped fragments, and orthopedic surgery may be required.



A Galeazzi (A) involves a midshaft radial fracture with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint. This is an unstable fracture that requires surgical repair.

A Lisfranc injury (B) often results in a fracture and dislocation and is usually treated surgically. Osteoarthritis and chronic pain can develop with untreated injuries.

A Monteggia (C) fracture of the forearm involves a fracture of the proximal ulna and dislocation of the radial head. There are poor outcomes associated with nonsurgical management.

Most tibial plateau fractures (E) also require surgery for acceptable functional outcomes.

question: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department after being T-boned on his motorcycle by a semitruck traveling at a high rate of speed. He was helmeted and had a protective jacket on. He is hypotensive and tachycardic on arrival and has normal saline hanging provided by EMS. A pelvic binder is applied, and a bedside X-ray of the pelvis shows a complex fracture of the left iliac wing and the left sacral ala with widening of the pubic symphysis. The FAST exam is negative for free fluid. He remains hypotensive and tachycardic. What is the most appropriate next step in the treatment of this patient?

options.text: General surgery consult for emergent operative care

englishExplanation:
Patients with hemorrhagic shock and pelvic fractures have a mortality rate of nearly 50%. Acute hemorrhage dramatically increases mortality associated with pelvic fractures. Over 75% of deaths in these patients are the result of uncontrolled hemorrhage. Treatment of hemorrhage in these patients includes resuscitation with early transfusion, stabilization with a pelvic binder, identification of the source of bleeding, controlling the bleeding with angiography versus pelvic packing during laparotomy, and preventing hypothermia.

Treatment with fluids and blood products is essential. However, treatment with fluids alone may contribute to ongoing bleeding and dilution of clotting factors. Advanced trauma life support (ATLS) guidelines recommend 1 L isotonic fluid bolus in all patients with shock. Blood should be administered if the patient is refractory to the initial fluid bolus. Emergent transfusion should not be delayed for type and crossmatch analysis. ATLS recommends a 1:1:1 transfusion ratio of plasma, platelets, and packed red blood cells. Massive transfusion protocols should be activated for patients with severe hemorrhagic shock.

In addition to blood transfusions, early mechanical stabilization with a pelvic binder reduces the fracture and can potentially decrease blood loss in the pelvic space. This decreases the amount of blood products required and is associated with improved survival rates.

Up to one-third of major pelvic injuries are associated with intra-abdominal injuries as well. However, unnecessary laparotomy in a hemodynamically unstable patient with pelvic fractures without abdominal injury has a higher mortality rate. Thus, it is imperative to determine whether hemorrhage is the result of pelvic injuries or an injury within the abdominal cavity. Patients with persistent hypotension are too unstable to identify the source of bleeding with CT scanning. The recommended modality for identifying bleeding in these patients is a bedside FAST exam. A positive FAST exam is an indicator to proceed with laparotomy before angiography. Hemorrhagic shock with a negative FAST exam suggests that the source of hypotension is within the pelvis. In these cases, angiography is recommended before laparotomy. This method of hemorrhage control is highly effective and < 10% of patients undergoing embolization rebleed. Complications may include gluteal muscle necrosis, femoral pseudoaneurysm, ischemia to the lower extremity, and rhabdomyolysis.



Additional fluid resuscitation (A) is not recommended and may dilute clotting factors and worsen bleeding.

General surgery for emergent operative care (C) is also not recommended for this patient. In a hypotensive patient with an open-book pelvic fracture and a negative FAST exam, immediate blood administration should be initiated while determining the next step in their care. If the patient remains hypotensive despite fluids and blood administration, the patient should be considered for more invasive treatments.

Initiation of vasopressors (D) is not a part of the management of hemorrhage in an open-book pelvic fracture. There are no human studies to support the use of vasopressors in the treatment of hemorrhagic shock in trauma patients. Vasopressor therapy use may be harmful. Treatment of hemorrhage in these patients includes appropriate resuscitative measures with intravenous fluid bolus and blood administration, with definitive management through embolization.

One Step Further

What are the three distinct regions of the abdomen that are critical in assessing when caring for a trauma patient?

Reveal Answer:
The peritoneal cavity, retroperitoneal space, and pelvic cavity.

question: A 29-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision. He is initially stabilized, and his blood pressure is 137/68 mm Hg, heart rate is 110 bpm, respiratory rate is 24/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. A CT scan is performed and demonstrates an intraluminal filling defect with an abnormal aortic contour. Which of the following is the best next treatment for this patient?
englishExplanation:
Aortic disruption can occur after blunt injury to the chest, such as in a motor vehicle collision. The acceleration-deceleration injury can damage the aorta, causing an intimal tear (type I disruption), intramural hematoma (type II), pseudoaneurysm (type III), or rupture (type IV). Chest radiography may demonstrate a widened mediastinum or abnormal aortic contour, and CT imaging can show an intraluminal filling defect (such as a dissection or extravasation of contrast). The care of a patient should be based on the severity of the injury and hemodynamic stability. Essentially all type II–IV injuries require operative repair, with type IV injuries typically presenting with severe hemodynamic instability requiring emergency surgery. Less severe injuries and hemodynamically stable patients can initially be treated with anti-impulse therapy with a goal of a systolic blood pressure < 100 mm Hg and a heart rate around 60 bpm. By reducing the heart rate and blood pressure, further aortic injury can be reduced, and if transection has occurred, blood loss can be reduced. An ideal initial medication is esmolol, which is a beta-blocker with fast titratability.



Diltiazem (A) is an appropriate initial rate control agent for aortic disruption if there is a contraindication to a beta-blocker, such as in severe COPD or asthma with an acute flare, in which beta-blockade could cause further bronchoconstriction.

Hydralazine (C) is a vasodilator that can increase aortic wall shear stress. It would also cause a reflex tachycardia if given first.

Nitroprusside (D) or nitroglycerin could be added to this patient’s blood pressure regimen if esmolol alone could not achieve a systolic blood pressure of 100 mm Hg. These medications would be started after esmolol to avoid a reflex tachycardia.

Reveal Answer:
Labetalol.

question: A 33-year-old man fell from a tree while cutting limbs. He sustained significant perineal and genital trauma. Disruption of which of the following structures indicates a testicular rupture?
englishExplanation:
The common mechanisms of blunt genitourinary traumas are falls, assaults, motor vehicle-related injuries, and sports-related injuries. Penetrating injuries are usually due to stab wounds or gunshot wounds. Timely diagnosis and appropriate management are aimed at minimizing or preventing kidney dysfunction, urinary incontinence, and sexual dysfunction. A detailed history should be obtained to determine the time and mechanism of injury. The external genitalia, perineum, and gluteal folds should be thoroughly checked. Blood found on the pants or underwear is an important finding that may suggest genitourinary trauma. A digital rectal examination should be performed to inspect for blood, sphincter tone, or prostate abnormalities (e.g., bogginess or “high riding” prostate). External genital trauma may include penile fractures, scrotal lacerations or avulsions, testicular rupture, or testicular dislocation. A rupture has occurred if the tunica albuginea, the thick fibrous capsule that envelops each testis, is disrupted. The tunica vaginalis fills with blood and forms a hematocele. Diagnosis of testicular trauma is best evaluated with color Doppler ultrasonography. In addition to parenteral analgesia and appropriate tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics (when indicated), urology should be consulted for testicular blunt or penetrating trauma. Testicular ruptures require immediate repair.



Buck fascia (A) is one of many membranous tissue layers that define the male genitourinary system. It is the deep fascial layer of the penis and does not envelop the testes.

The tunica vaginalis (C) is a potential space that remains intact in testicular rupture. It fills with blood and forms a hematocele.

The integrity of the vas deferens (D) does not define testicular rupture as it is external to the testes.

One Step Further

What is the most common cause of ureteral trauma?

Reveal Answer:
Intraoperative, iatrogenic injury (approximately 80% of ureteral injuries).

question: A 7-year-old boy presents to the ED with wrist pain after a fall off of the monkey bars at school. He reports no head injury or other pain from the fall. He has tenderness and swelling over the ulnar area. An X-ray shows a small fracture line through the metaphysis that extends into the physis. What is the diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
The Salter-Harris classification system is typically used to describe pediatric physeal fractures. Fractures are graded I–V. The severity of the injury and its associated complications generally increase with each increase in grade. A common mnemonic to remember Salter-Harris fracture grades is:

S: Straight across - type I - through the physis

A: Above (proximal) - type II - through the physis and metaphysis

L: Lower (distal) - type III - through the physis and epiphysis

T: Through - type IV - through the epiphysis, physis, and metaphysis

ER: Erasure - type V - a crush injury of the physis

A Salter-Harris II fracture is the most common type, extending through the physis and into the metaphysis. Treatment of this fracture depends on the degree of displacement and neurovascular status. Patients with open fractures should always receive IV antibiotics and immediate orthopedic surgery consultation. For a displaced, closed, Salter-Harris II fracture, reduction should be performed in the ED and a volar or sugar tong splint placed for immobilization. Splinting alone is adequate for nondisplaced fractures. All patients with Salter-Harris II fractures should be referred to orthopedic surgery for evaluation within 7 days.



A Salter-Harris I fracture (A) is a fracture through the physis only. It causes the epiphysis to separate from the metaphysis, and it may not be apparent on X-ray.

A Salter-Harris III fracture (C) is a fracture through the physis and epiphysis.

A Salter-Harris IV fracture (D) is a fracture through the epiphysis, physis, and metaphysis.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the name of a fracture of the distal third of the radius with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint?

Reveal Answer:
Galeazzi fracture.

III: fracture below physis
IV: fracture through physis
V: erasure of the growth plate
Management
I–II: nonoperative

IV–V: surgery required
Negative radiographs do not rule out a Salter I fracture

question: A 21-year-old man presents after a motor vehicle collision. His vital signs are HR of 133 bpm, BP of 75/43 mm Hg, and SpO2 of 97% on room air. An e-FAST exam is shown above. What management should be pursued?

options.text: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
Transfer to operating room for exploratory laparotomy

correctAnswer: Transfer to operating room for exploratory laparotomy
englishExplanation:
Ultrasound evaluation should be performed as part of the initial examination and resuscitation of the trauma patient, and this is referred to as the FAST exam. The FAST examination uses ultrasound to look for the presence or absence of free fluid in four different anatomic locations: the pericardium, the hepatorenal space (Morison pouch), the splenorenal space, and the suprapubic region (around the bladder). On ultrasound, free fluid appears anechoic (dark or black). The FAST examination can be rapidly performed and has a high sensitivity and specificity for free intra-abdominal fluid. The eFAST examination adds thoracic views to evaluate for pneumothorax.

In a patient with blunt abdominal trauma, a patient with positive findings on a FAST exam can proceed down two management pathways, depending on hemodynamic stability. The hemodynamically stable patient may be taken for CT scan for further evaluation of injuries. However, the hemodynamically unstable patient should immediately be transferred to the operating room for an exploratory laparotomy.



This patient is presenting with tachycardia and hypotension consistent with hemorrhagic shock. A CT scan (A) should not be performed in hemodynamically unstable patients with hemoperitoneum.

Diagnostic peritoneal aspiration (B) was widely used prior to the advent of ultrasound but now is only useful in specific situations, particularly when the FAST is equivocal.

Interventional radiology (C) may be indicated in patients with presumed bleeding from pelvic injuries but should not delay operative management in patients with clear intra-abdominal bleeding.

One Step Further
Question:
What eFAST findings indicate a pneumothorax is present?

Reveal Answer:
Absence of lung sliding and a lung point sign (lung sliding and absence of lung sliding in the same space, representing the edge of a pneumothorax).

Unstable patient + positive FAST → laparotomy
eFAST adds pulmonary evaluation

question: A 4-year-old girl presents to the ED with her parents, holding her left arm after falling from her bicycle. She has left elbow swelling with limited range of motion due to pain. Her radial pulse is intact and there is no open bony deformity. Plain films of the left upper extremity are pending. Which of the following findings is consistent with a Salter-Harris type III fracture?
englishExplanation:
Pediatric injuries involving the physis (growth plate) are characterized using the Salter-Harris classification. This classification describes the fracture line relative to the physis. Injuries of the physis may affect normal bone growth and development, so orthopedic intervention may be necessary depending on the severity of the fracture type. Salter-Harris type I fractures occur when the epiphysis slips off the metaphysis with no associated fracture fragment. Type I injuries rarely affect skeletal development. Salter-Harris type II injuries extend into the metaphysis and are the most common of the Salter-Harris injuries. Salter-Harris type III injuries extend into the epiphysis. Salter-Harris type IV injuries involve the metaphysis, the physis, and the epiphysis. Salter-Harris type V injuries result from axial loading mechanisms and crush the epiphysis. These may be radiographically silent but often impact normal bony development.



Fractures with dislocations (B) may not involve the growth plate and are not part of the Salter-Harris classification.

Intra-articular compaction (C) is seen in Salter-Harris type V injuries.

Metaphyseal extension (D) is seen in Salter-Harris type II injuries.

One Step Further
Question:
What pediatric fractures are concerning for nonaccidental trauma?

Reveal Answer:
Long bone shaft fractures in a nonambulatory child, metaphyseal corner (or “bucket handle”) fractures, sternal fractures, posterior rib fractures, occipital bone fractures, or skull fractures crossing suture lines.

question: What collection of clinical signs is most indicative of retroperitoneal bleeding in a trauma patient?

options.text: Grey Turner, Cullen, and Fox signs

correctAnswer: Grey Turner, Cullen, and Fox signs
englishExplanation:
Retroperitoneal bleeding due to trauma may be difficult to diagnose because the retroperitoneal space is deep and not easily accessible on physical exam. Nonspecific signs such as hypotension, tachycardia, and other signs of shock without an obvious source should raise suspicion. Additional findings such as pallor, diaphoresis, and alterations in mentation may also point to significant blood loss.

Certain exam findings can further suggest retroperitoneal hemorrhage:

Grey Turner sign: ecchymosis over the flank

Bryant sign: scrotal ecchymosis

Fox sign: proximal thigh ecchymosis

Cullen sign: periumbilical ecchymosis

Seatbelt sign: ecchymosis across the abdomen

Pelvic instability: often associated with vascular injury

While these signs lack sensitivity and specificity and are not pathognomonic for retroperitoneal bleeding, their presence should raise the clinician’s suspicion for such bleeding. Conversely, their absence does not negate the possibility of retroperitoneal bleeding, making imaging critical for accurate diagnosis.



The Ballance sign is left lower quadrant dullness from coagulated blood from a splenic injury, the Kehr sign is left shoulder pain from diaphragmatic irritation seen in splenic rupture, and the Bryant sign is scrotal ecchymosis associated with pelvic fractures and retroperitoneal hematomas. While the Bryant (A) sign may be seen with retroperitoneal bleeding, the Ballance and Kehr signs are not.

The Mittendorf (C) sign is a whitish opacity seen on the lens of the eye and is indicative of persistent fetal vasculature, and the Hennebert sign is the induction of vertigo and nystagmus when pressure is applied to the external auditory canal as seen with otosclerosis. Neither of these signs is seen with retroperitoneal bleeding.

The Rosenbach sign is tremors in the outstretched fingers or eyelids and is an indicator of hyperthyroidism. The Bassler sign is tenderness over the McBurney point and is suggestive of acute appendicitis rather than hemorrhage. The Carnett (D) sign is worsening abdominal pain with tensed muscles indicative of abdominal wall pain. None of these signs are associated with retroperitoneal hemorrhage.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the role of the rectal exam in the trauma patient?

Reveal Answer:
As part of the neurologic exam (anal sphincter tone) for patients with neurologic deficits suggestive of spinal cord injury.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Retroperitoneal Trauma and Bleeding

Sx: hematuria, back pain, abdominal pain
PE: Grey Turner sign, Cullen sign
Dx: CT imaging required for diagnosis
Ultrasound is poor at evaluating retroperitoneal injuries
Tx: depends on injury, situation, and hemodynamic stability
Observation and serial exams, endovascular repair, surgery

الفخ: الطالب يختار Ballance, Bryant, and Kehr signs خطأً بدلاً من B، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: A 50-year-old woman presents to the ED as the restrained driver in a head-on motor vehicle collision. She was intubated at the scene due to increased work of breathing and gasping respirations. On physical examination, she is found to have significant bruising of the anterior abdominal and an unstable pelvis. Her chest X-ray is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s respiratory failure?
englishExplanation:
The X-ray above demonstrates diaphragmatic rupture leading to the migration of intra-abdominal contents into the thorax. Diaphragmatic injuries are most commonly due to penetrating trauma. Injuries to the diaphragm resulting from blunt trauma are rare and most commonly result from a rapid and significant increase in intra-abdominal pressure, classically caused by sudden compression of the abdomen. This is most typically seen in patients with central obesity who experience trauma resulting in a collision with the driving column or airbags.

Diaphragmatic injuries are most commonly seen on the left side of the chest, with the presence of the liver acting as a protective barrier on the right side of the diaphragm and abdomen. Morbidity and mortality associated with diaphragmatic injuries result from the migration of intra-abdominal contents into the chest, leading to decreased lung expansion or incarceration and subsequent necrosis of the bowel segment. Management of injuries to the diaphragm is surgical.



Bronchial rupture (A) is associated with pneumomediastinum, and physical examination may show crepitus from the presence of subcutaneous emphysema. The X-ray shown above does not show any evidence of pneumomediastinum.

Flail chest (C) occurs due to segmental fracturing of the anterior or lateral segments of three or more consecutive ribs, leading to the presence of a flail segment of ribs. This results in chest wall collapse during inspiration, secondary to the negative intrathoracic pressure in the inspiratory phase of the respiratory cycle. No rib fractures are evident in the image above.

Tension pneumothorax (D) results from an expanding pneumothorax that leads to mediastinal shift. This results in compression of the heart, causing impaired diastolic filling and leading to the classic findings of hypotension and jugular venous distention.

One Step Further
Question:
What type of fractures are associated with diaphragmatic injuries?

Reveal Answer:
Pelvic fractures.

CXR: NGT curled in chest (limited sensitivity)
CT of the abdomen and pelvis, laparoscopy
Associated injuries
Injury to liver, spleen, bowel, or kidney
Rupture of lungs or thoracic aorta

question: A 24-year-old man presents to the ED after being stabbed in the left mid-chest. Bedside ultrasound is shown above. Which of the following is a characteristic exam finding associated with this disease process?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with pericardial tamponade. Pericardial tamponade is defined as a collection of fluid or air that creates external cardiac pressure, resulting in decreased ventricular filling and hemodynamic compromise. Rapid pericardial fluid accumulation leads to elevated intrapericardial pressure and myocardial compression. The rate of accumulation rather than the volume is responsible for hemodynamic instability. Lower right-sided heart pressures result in evidence of compressive effects on the right heart first. Signs and symptoms of pericardial tamponade include Beck triad of hypotension, jugular venous distension, and diminished heart sounds. Pulsus paradoxus is also commonly present, which is an exaggerated decrease in systolic blood pressure of > 10 mm Hg with inspiration. Kussmaul sign may also be present, which is paradoxical jugular venous distention with inspiration. The ECG can show signs of diffuse ST segment elevation or electrical alternans. Chest radiography may show cardiomegaly. Echocardiogram is the diagnostic study of choice for the diagnosis of pericardial effusion and tamponade, demonstrating collapse of the right ventricle in early diastole. Management in the setting of trauma is emergent operative intervention, but if surgery is delayed, pericardiocentesis should be performed if hemodynamic compromise is present. However, this is often unsuccessful in patients with hemorrhagic tamponade. Definitive treatment is surgical with a pericardial window or thoracotomy. Intravenous fluid resuscitation may be trialed in patients with hypovolemia but should be avoided in those with euvolemia or hypervolemia. Positive pressure ventilation is contraindicated as it will further decrease venous return.



Hyperresonance to percussion (B) is a hallmark of tension pneumothorax. Sternal crepitus (C) is often seen in patients with a sternal fracture and should raise suspicion for myocardial contusion or pneumomediastinum. Tracheal deviation (D) is also seen in patients with tension pneumothorax and is an indication for needle decompression.

One Step Further
Question:
What are common nontraumatic cause of pericardial tamponade?

Reveal Answer:
Malignancy, infection, idiopathic, iatrogenic, post myocardial infarction, and uremia.

PE: muffled heart sounds, JVD, hypotension (Beck triad), pulsus paradoxus
ECG: low-voltage QRS, electrical alternans
Echocardiography
Diastolic collapse of RV (less sensitive but very specific)
Early systolic collapse of RA (sensitive and specific)
Plethoric IVC (sensitive)
Tx: pericardiocentesis or pericardial window

question: What is the most frequently injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma?
englishExplanation:
Blunt abdominal trauma, most frequently due to motor vehicle collisions, is regularly encountered in the emergency department and can result in significant morbidity and mortality. Multiple mechanisms exist by which the abdominal organs can be injured, including rupture of hollow viscus organs due to a sudden rise in intra-abdominal pressure from external compressive forces, crushing of organs due to blunt forces on the abdominal wall, and lacerations at the point of attachment to the abdominal wall or the organ itself due to shearing forces created by sudden deceleration. The spleen and liver are the most commonly injured organs in blunt abdominal trauma, and in many cases, the spleen is the only organ injured.



The aorta (A) is less frequently injured in blunt abdominal trauma than both the spleen and the liver.

The colon (B) and small intestine (C) can be injured in blunt abdominal trauma but much less frequently than the spleen and liver. When hollow viscus injury does occur, it is often due to compression of the bowel between a lap belt and the vertebral column, resulting in a contusion or perforation of the intestines.

One Step Further
Question:
What are the most common intra-abdominal seat belt injuries?

Reveal Answer:
Mesenteric laceration and jejunum injury.

question: A 63-year-old man presents with right arm pain after a fall. His X-ray is shown above. What structure is commonly injured with this fracture?
englishExplanation:
Radial nerve injury is the most common nerve injury seen after humeral shaft fractures. These fractures usually occur from a direct blow to the arm and can be seen in falls and motor vehicle collisions. Patients present with severe pain, arm swelling, and decreased range of motion. The arm can be shortened or rotated in a complete fracture depending on the location of the injury. A complete neurovascular exam should be performed as with all fractures and dislocations. The radial nerve may be injured during humeral fracture in up to 20% of patients. The injury is usually a neuropraxia and resolves spontaneously in most patients. However, this recovery can take months. Humeral fractures rarely need specific reduction maneuvers for treatment. They should be placed in a coaptation splint and a sling. Gravity alone is typically successful in fracture reduction.



The axillary nerve (A) may be injured during glenohumeral dislocations. The median nerve (B) may be injured during posterior elbow dislocations. Anterior elbow dislocations can be associated with ulnar nerve injury (D).

One Step Further
Question:
When should a hanging cast be placed in a humerus fracture as opposed to a sugar tong splint?

Reveal Answer:
A hanging cast is used for humerus fractures that are grossly displaced or comminuted.

Most common cause of traumatic radial nerve injury

Sensory loss in the radial nerve distribution (dorsum of hand)
Can cause brachial artery injury

question: Which of the following tests for function of the median nerve?

options.text: Abduction of the index finger against resistance
Extension of the wrist against resistance
Pincer function of the thumb and index finger
Sensation of the dorsum of the first webspace

correctAnswer: Pincer function of the thumb and index finger
englishExplanation:
The median nerve, which is derived from the medial and lateral cords of the brachial plexus, contains nerve roots from C5–T1. In the forearm, it becomes the anterior interosseous nerve, which supplies the deep muscles of the anterior forearm, and the palmar cutaneous nerve, which innervates the skin of the lateral aspect of the palm. It then crosses through the carpal tunnel terminating as the recurrent branch, responsible for innervating the thenar muscles, and the palmar digital branch. The palmar digital branch innervates the palmar surface and fingertips of the thumb, index, and middle digits, as well as the lateral two lumbrical muscles. Motor function of the median nerve can be tested by having the patient make an OK sign (pincer function of the thumb and index finger) or oppose the thumb and fifth finger. Sensation at the volar tip of the index finger confirms sensory function of the median nerve.



The ulnar nerve is responsible for abduction of the index finger against resistance (A).

Extension of the wrist against resistance (B) and sensation of the dorsum of the first webspace (D) is a function of the radial nerve.

Sensation of the lateral forearm (E) is provided by the musculocutaneous nerve, which stems from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus. It contains fibers from the nerve roots C5, C6, and C7.

One Step Further
Question:
In what part of the hand is the ulnar nerve responsible for sensation?

Reveal Answer:
The palmar and dorsal surfaces of the fifth digit and the medial aspect of the fourth digit.

question: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department for right eye pain. He was seen in the emergency department 2 days ago for facial trauma leading to right orbital and sinus fractures without impingement. He was given antibiotics for his sinus fractures. His slit lamp exam and fluorescein exam at that time were normal. He has not yet followed up with a specialist. He reports acute-onset right eye pain when he woke up this morning that worsens when he looks at his phone. During examination, he shields both of his eyes from the light. Otherwise, he has intact extraocular motions without pain and has mild right-sided sinus tenderness. His slit lamp examination is shown above. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Computed tomography scan of the orbits
Intravenous vancomycin and emergent ophthalmology consultation

englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation is consistent with traumatic iritis or ciliary nerve irritation and ciliary muscle spasms due to blunt trauma. Most patients report delayed pain after blunt trauma to their eye. Diagnosis is clinical. Patients commonly present with visual changes and eye pain that worsens with light. Physical exam commonly reveals consensual photophobia and flares and cells on slit lamp exam. Visual changes are due to an underlying ciliary spasm leading to inappropriate accommodation of the pupils. Consensual photophobia is due to pain with consensual tightening of the pupil against the spasming ciliary muscles of the injured eye. The mainstay of treatment is purely symptom control. Tropicamide or homatropine drops are the most commonly prescribed treatments, as they are cycloplegics and mydriatics. Steroid drops may improve the surrounding inflammation but are also associated with delayed healing of corneal abrasions, if present, due to blunt trauma. All patients should be closely followed by an ophthalmologist to ensure proper healing.



Computed tomography scan of the orbits (A) may be useful for the evaluation of a retrobulbar hematoma or orbital bone injuries after blunt ocular trauma. This patient already had a scan with the injuries listed above. He has not had recurrent trauma since the incident, and his exam is more consistent with traumatic iritis.

Erythromycin ointment and ophthalmology follow-up (B) is the mainstay of treatment for corneal abrasions. However, this patient had a normal fluorescein exam after the injury.

Intravenous vancomycin and emergent ophthalmologic consultation (C) is the mainstay of treatment for endophthalmitis, an infection of the interior of the eye. This is due to direct penetrating trauma to the eye. Endophthalmitis leads to severe pain and loss of vision and may lead to a hypopyon, layering of white blood cells in the anterior chamber, on slit lamp examination.

One Step Further
Question:
Will tetracaine improve the pain of traumatic iritis?

Reveal Answer:
No, as it does not affect the ciliary muscle spasms.
