question: A 57-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after falling from a tree while trimming branches. The patient reports that prior to landing she grabbed onto a branch with her right hand, but lost her grasp and then fell to the ground. Upon arrival, the patient’s arm is held in the position shown above. Physical examination is notable for numbness along the patient’s right deltoid, a nontender humerus, intact radial and ulnar pulses, and the inability to move her right arm from above her head. Which of the following techniques is the appropriate management of this condition?
englishExplanation:
Luxatio erecta (inferior shoulder dislocation) is the rarest type of glenohumeral dislocation, representing only 0.5% of all shoulder dislocations. The mechanism of injury is typically a high-energy axial load applied directly to the shoulder joint, or a forceful hyperabduction of the arm, such as a person suddenly grasping an object above their head while falling, as in the case with this patient. On examination, the classic appearance of an inferiorly dislocated shoulder is an arm locked in marked abduction with the forearm flexed and pronated. Thorough evaluation of the extremity is vital, as luxatio erecta carries the highest risk of neurovascular, fracture, and soft tissue injury of any shoulder dislocation.

Axillary nerve injuries are noted in up to 60% of cases, as seen with this patient reporting numbness along her deltoid, though most resolve after successful reduction. Up to one-third of patients have concomitant humeral fractures, approximately 10% sustain rotator cuff tears, and 3% develop axillary artery injuries. In cases of humeral neck or shaft fractures or vascular compromise, open reduction should be pursued to hasten repair of arterial injuries and reduce the risk of avascular necrosis, as closed reduction of an inferiorly dislocated shoulder with a fractured proximal humerus can worsen existing displacement.

When closed reduction is indicated, traction-countertraction is the preferred method, which involves overhead traction in the longitudinal tract of the abducted arm with simultaneous cephalad pressure on the humeral head by one provider, and countertraction directed toward the patient’s feet with a sheet wrapped around the shoulder by another provider. A second approach, called the “two-step” maneuver, would also be an appropriate technique for closed reduction. This involves first converting the inferior dislocation to an anterior one by applying stabilizing pressure to the medial epicondyle of the elbow, and then pushing on the humeral shaft and rotating the humeral head from an inferior to anterior location, followed by reduction of the anterior dislocation.



The Allis maneuver (A) is a method for reducing posterior hip dislocations involving one provider providing pelvis stabilization and another holding the extremity with the knee flexed and applying in-line longitudinal traction with the femur while gently adducting and flexing the hip until reduction is achieved.

Scapular manipulation (B) involves rotation of the scapula with medial and inferior traction with concurrent downward traction on the injured arm to allow the humeral head to relocate into the glenoid. This technique is used for anterior shoulder dislocations and is not a useful maneuver for luxatio erecta.

Similarly, the Stimson technique (C) is also utilized for anterior shoulder dislocations and involves a prone patient hanging the injured arm off of the stretcher with a 10–15 lb weight attached to the arm, with reduction taking approximately thirty minutes to achieve.

Reveal Answer:
An internally rotated humeral head resembling a light bulb, seen on AP X-ray with posterior shoulder dislocations.

question: An 18-year-old hurdler tripped and fell, contacting the running track through his hyperextended left wrist. He presents to the ED with dorsolateral wrist pain, erythema, edema, and anatomic snuffbox tenderness. Initial anteroposterior, lateral, and oblique radiographs are negative for fracture. He is splinted and discharged. Which of the following should be recommended on his discharge paperwork?

options.text: MRI in 4 weeks if pain persists
Primary care medical clearance examination for upcoming orthopedic surgery

englishExplanation:
A fall onto an outstretched hand injury (outstretched refers to wrist hyperextension) is a common cause of scaphoid fracture, which represents the most common fractured carpal bone. The most common fracture site on the scaphoid is the waist. Since the blood supply to the scaphoid enters distally, any fracture or displacement > 1 mm is worrisome for complications of osteonecrosis and nonunion.

A scaphoid fracture should be suspected any time there is snuffbox tenderness. Wrist and scaphoid X-rays may be negative in the setting of acute fracture. Therefore, patients with snuffbox tenderness or suspicion of scaphoid fracture should be placed in a thumb spica splint with repeat radiographs or MRI in 10–14 days.



Bone scans (A) are sensitive for detecting occult fractures but are not the first-line follow-up since they expose patients to radiation, and repeat radiographs in 2 weeks are usually sufficient.

Waiting 4 weeks for repeat MRI (B) or plain radiographs is too long. Repeat imaging should occur within 10–14 days.

It is unknown if a true fracture is present at this time, so surgery (C) would not be arranged at discharge.

This wrist erythema and edema are related to trauma and not to an underlying rheumatologic condition (E).

Reveal Answer:
The more proximal the fracture, the greater the likelihood of osteonecrosis.

question: A 27-year-old man presents to the ED after a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which he was the unrestrained driver and his abdomen struck the steering wheel. Which of the following is most likely injured in this patient?
englishExplanation:
One of the most common organs injured in blunt abdominal trauma is the spleen. The liver and spleen are the most commonly injured organs in the setting of a motor vehicle collision in which the patient hits the steering wheel. An injury to the spleen can cause bleeding, leading to hypotension, tachycardia, and a positive FAST exam that demonstrates free intraperitoneal fluid. However, the most common physical exam finding is abdominal tenderness with referred left shoulder pain. This is a specific finding in a splenic injury.

Any hemodynamically unstable patient presenting with abdominal pain and a positive FAST exam should be taken to the operating room for exploration and to stop the bleeding. Radiography that demonstrates left-sided lower rib fractures should increase suspicion of a splenic laceration. In uncertain cases of a visceral injury in a hemodynamically stable patient, an abdominal CT scan can further characterize potential injuries and helps plan operative care. Conditions that can predispose the spleen to rupture include infectious mononucleosis, which causes splenic enlargement, increasing the risk of injury with even minor abdominal trauma.



Colon (A) injury presents with abdominal pain and peritoneal signs with infection from colonic flora. The colon is less likely to be injured with blunt trauma and more likely to be injured with penetrating trauma.

The pancreas (B) can be injured in blunt abdominal trauma but is not nearly as commonly injured as the spleen and liver.

Small intestine (C) is less likely to be injured in blunt abdominal trauma. However, blunt abdominal trauma can cause pathologies such as a duodenal hematoma, which would present with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and obstruction of the duodenum on a CT scan.

One Step Further
Question:
What physical exam findings can suggest urethral injury in a trauma patient?

Reveal Answer:
Blood at the urethral meatus.

question: A 35-year-old woman presents with a left ring finger injury after being kicked in the fingertips while sparring. On exam, the patient is unable to straighten the distal joint of the affected finger. The fingertip remains flexed when the fingers of the left hand are extended. There is pain and swelling around the distal interphalangeal joint. Which specific complication can be prevented if this injury is recognized early?
englishExplanation:
The exam findings are indicative of mallet finger, an injury to the extensor tendon of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. Improper or delayed treatment may lead to the complication of swan-neck deformity. This results in a permanent abnormal flexion of the DIP and involves the central slip. Symptoms often include pain, decreased grip strength, and difficulty with fine motor tasks. Conservative approaches may involve splinting and exercises to strengthen surrounding muscles. Immobilization of the DIP in full extension or 5–15 degrees of hyperextension is recommended. An aluminum splint can be applied, or a custom-made splint may be used. The metal ring splints are generally not recommended due to patient discomfort. In more severe cases or cases that are refractory to conservative measures, surgical intervention may be required. Given the high incidence of complications from mallet finger, referral to hand surgery is recommended.



Boutonniere deformity (A) involves flexion of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint and hyperextension of the DIP, not hyperflexion of the DIP. This is the result of a rupture to the insertion of the extensor expansion into the base of the phalanx. Dupuytren contracture (B) is a progressive thickening of the palmar fascia of the hand, leading to contracture of the fingers. While post-traumatic arthritis (C) may be a common complication from any injury, it is not specific to injuries of the extensor tendon of the distal interphalangeal joint of the finger.

One Step Further
Question:
What medications have been found to cause tendinopathy or tendon rupture?

Reveal Answer:
While rare, fluoroquinolones, high-dose or prolonged use of corticosteroids, and statins may cause tendinopathy or tendon rupture.

question: A 23-year-old woman presents to the ED for bilateral eye pain. She was sitting by a fire for a few hours after a full day of skiing when she noticed gradually worsening bilateral eye pain, tearing, and photophobia. An example of her fluorescein exam is shown above. What is this patient’s most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Radiation burn, or ultraviolet keratitis, is characterized by diffuse corneal injury due to the direct effects of ultraviolet radiation. The classic fluorescein exam finding is diffuse punctate uptake due to the ultraviolet light causing corneal epithelial damage. Risk factors include snow sports, welding, and tanning bed use in patients who do not use or improperly use eye protection. Diagnosis is made with a fluorescein exam. Patients commonly have a delayed onset, of up to 10 hours, of symptoms from initial injury. Symptoms include bilateral eye pain, photophobia, and tearing. Physical exam may reveal conjunctival injection and decreased visual acuity. Treatment is with ophthalmic antibiotics and cycloplegics, although the benefit of antibiotics is weak. Patients should have ophthalmology follow-up within 24 hours if their symptoms have not resolved. Ultraviolet keratitis often resolves within 24 hours.



Herpes keratitis (A) presents on fluorescein exam with dendritic lesions with or without the classic clear vesicles on the eyelid or conjunctiva. It is treated with a topical antiviral, like trifluridine, cycloplegics, and an emergent ophthalmologic evaluation.

Smoke irritation (C) will commonly present with bilateral conjunctival injection and a normal fluorescein exam. Avoidance of the source of irritation is the first-line treatment.

Thermal burns (D) more commonly present as eyelid injuries due to the Bell phenomenon. If there is a thermal burn to the globe, patients most commonly present with superficial corneal lesions that are treated as corneal abrasions.

One Step Further
Question:
What is Bell phenomenon?

Reveal Answer:
The defense mechanism for the eyes in which they move outward and upward while closing the eyelids to avoid injury.

PE: fluorescein staining will show multiple punctate lesions
Tx: topical NSAIDs or oral pain medication with or without antibiotics, cycloplegics

question: A 26-year-old woman is brought to the ED after a motor vehicle collision, and she has a large hematoma on her forehead and a tourniquet on her left arm to slow an arterial bleed. She has a blood pressure of 87/52 mm Hg and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7. What is the best initial fluid resuscitation strategy in this patient?

options.text: Crystalloid infusion and packed red blood cells to restore normal blood pressure
Crystalloid infusion and packed red blood cells with permissive hypotension
Crystalloid infusion to restore normal blood pressure, up to 6 L

correctAnswer: Crystalloid infusion and packed red blood cells to restore normal blood pressure
englishExplanation:
This patient has hemorrhagic shock from an arterial bleed and has signs concerning for intracranial hemorrhage (blunt trauma to the forehead and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7). Fluid resuscitation is a critical and time-sensitive intervention in hemorrhagic shock. Although crystalloid products are often used initially, hemorrhagic shock should be treated with blood transfusion. Permissive hypotension can be an acceptable strategy in the case of isolated hemorrhage but is contraindicated in the setting of severe head trauma. Intracranial hemorrhage increases intracranial pressure. If mean arterial pressure is decreased while intracranial pressure is increased, cerebral perfusion pressure may diminish dramatically leading to irreversible brain damage.



Colloids (A), such as albumin, are not superior to crystalloids for resuscitation in hemorrhage and should be avoided because of their relative expense.

Permissive hypotension (C) is contraindicated in those with suspected intracranial hemorrhage.

Crystalloids (D), such as normal saline or Ringer lactate, can be used initially for resuscitation in hemorrhagic shock, but blood is the preferred resuscitative product. As a general rule, patients with hemorrhagic shock should receive no more than 2 L of crystalloid before blood products are also administered.

One Step Further
Question:
Which type of intracranial hemorrhage increases intracranial pressure most rapidly?

Reveal Answer:
Epidural hematoma results from a high pressure arterial bleed and can rapidly increase intracranial pressure.

Class IV: negligible urine output, confusion
Hypotension is a late finding in pediatrics
Shock index: HR / SBP
> 0.7 is an indicator of hemorrhagic shock
> 0.9 is an indicator for needing transfusion

question: A 15-year-old girl presents to the ED with a gunshot wound to the upper right chest. She is confused and agitated but cooperative with instructions. Her heart rate is 165 bpm, blood pressure is 88/52 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 84% with a nonrebreather facemask. She has diminished lung sounds on the right and is struggling to breathe. Two large bore intravenous lines are being placed, and uncrossmatched whole blood is hung. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in this patient's care?

options.text: Endotracheal intubation with etomidate and rocuronium
Thoracostomy tube placement on the right

correctAnswer: Thoracostomy tube placement on the right
englishExplanation:
The advanced trauma life support (ATLS) system was designed by the American College of Surgeons to standardize the care of trauma patients. The primary survey has historically been a rapid evaluation of the airway, breathing, circulation, and disability, and ends with exposure of the patient. This assessment is considered the ABCs of trauma, each step occurring in rapid succession with the goal of completing a primary survey within moments of the patient’s arrival. A change adopted in 2025 by the ATLS system is the xABCDE approach, which involves first finding and controlling catastrophic hemorrhage (e.g., with the application of a tourniquet or compression) to prevent exsanguination before evaluating the airway.

Previous training emphasized securing an airway with an endotracheal tube as soon as possible in hemodynamically unstable patients. Newer training encourages running processes in parallel with goal endpoints of endotracheal intubation, venous access, and stabilizing hemodynamics. Medically optimizing a patient for endotracheal intubation can reduce the risk of hemodynamic collapse and enhance success rates by improving intubation conditions. This patient is showing signs of severe hypovolemic shock and is at risk of cardiovascular collapse from loss of sympathetic tone or worsening hypoxia, both of which could occur with immediate rapid sequence intubation.

This patient has diminished lung sounds on the right, and the placement of a thoracostomy tube on the right is both diagnostic and therapeutic for either pneumothorax or hemothorax. Most patients will need some amount of sedation to tolerate a thoracostomy tube, so delayed sequence intubation using ketamine is most appropriate. This would also allow bag-mask ventilation in this confused patient. The thoracostomy tube would result in lung reexpansion and should improve oxygenation. This and the addition of a blood transfusion could normalize her hemodynamics for endotracheal intubation. This would allow the patient to tolerate a longer period of apnea during intubation without cardiopulmonary collapse.



Patients who are somewhat aware are less likely to tolerate bag-mask ventilation (A), and while this may improve the hypoxia, it is less likely to optimize moving toward endotracheal intubation when done without sedation.

Directly moving to rapid sequence endotracheal intubation (B) before optimizing hemodynamics will give a shorter period of time to perform the intubation without cardiopulmonary collapse.

An eFAST exam (C) would confirm the diagnosis of either a pneumothorax or a hemothorax, but a thoracostomy tube would also treat the problem and could improve hemodynamics.

One Step Further
Question:
Which intervention during endotracheal intubation is best known to prolong apnea time without hypoxia?

Reveal Answer:
Apneic oxygenation.

question: A 54-year-old man who takes an anticoagulant for a relatively recent deep vein thrombosis presents for evaluation of back pain that began after lifting weights at the gym today. He has been unable to ambulate due to profound lower extremity weakness. On examination, his cranial nerves are intact. He exhibits intact strength against an opposed force in his bilateral upper extremities proximally and distally. He is unable to flex or extend at the hips, knees, or ankles. He has diminished pain sensation below the umbilicus with intact position sense in his bilateral lower extremities. What is the likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Anterior cord syndrome can arise from a hyperflexion injury that causes contusion of the anterior spinal cord and can be related to hematoma formation, which could be a risk in this patient taking an anticoagulant. The spinothalamic tracts responsible for pain and temperature sensation and corticospinal tracts responsible for motor function are the anterior most cord structures often affected. Injury to these tracts leads to bilateral motor weakness and reduced sensation below the level of the injury. Sensation to vibration, position, and light touch remains intact. Magnetic resonance imaging of the entire spine can aid in the diagnosis. Prompt evaluation for surgical correction should be considered to evaluate for a reversible underlying cause (e.g., fracture fragment compressing the spinal cord).



Cauda equina syndrome (B) involves lower extremity weakness, impaired bowel and bladder function (e.g., urinary retention, bowel or bladder incontinence), perianal anesthesia, diminished rectal tone, and hyporeflexia in the lower extremities, which can result from nerve root injury below L2. This patient’s injury appears to be higher than L2.

Central cord syndrome (C) manifests with loss of pain and temperature sensation and with bilateral upper extremity weakness that is more prominent than lower extremity weakness.

Conus medullaris syndrome (D) shares clinical findings seen in cauda equina syndrome but involves the spinal cord at the level of L2 and affects upper motor neurons to cause hyperreflexia of the lower extremities.

One Step Further
Question:
Occlusion of what artery can lead to anterior cord syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
Anterior spinal artery.

question: A 23-year-old man presents to the ED after falling from a 10 ft ladder. On examination, he has an open, displaced tibia fracture with 1 cm overlying laceration and minimal active bleeding. Which of the following antibiotics is most appropriate for initial prophylaxis?
englishExplanation:
A fracture that communicates with the skin surface is defined as an open fracture and represents a true time-dependent orthopedic emergency because of the risk of osteomyelitis. The high morbidity associated with bone infection requires rapid initiation of treatment, including early parenteral antibiotics, coverage of the wound with a moist sterile dressing, and urgent surgical washout and debridement.

Open fractures are commonly described using the Gustilo-Anderson classification, which stratifies injuries based on wound size, degree of contamination, soft tissue damage, and the presence of vascular injury.

Initial ED management focuses on hemorrhage control with a sterile pressure dressing after removal of gross debris, splinting of the extremity without reduction unless vascular compromise is present, and irrigation with saline, followed by coverage with saline-soaked dressings.

Antibiotic strategies include cefazolin for all open fractures, with gentamicin added for higher-grade injuries, while broad-spectrum beta-lactams such as ceftriaxone or piperacillin-tazobactam may provide equivalent coverage.

In cases involving farm injuries or potential fecal contamination, additional coverage with penicillin or ampicillin is recommended to address clostridial organisms.

Open distal tuft fractures of the fingers and toes are an important exception, as these injuries commonly result from crush mechanisms with an overlying skin wound and can usually be managed by the emergency clinician alone. Vigorous irrigation and debridement are sufficient treatment for these injuries when digital arterial flow is intact, and infections of the distal tuft are uncommon.



Doxycycline (B) has activity against atypical organisms and some gram-positive and gram-negative pathogens. However, it is not the first-line antibiotic for prophylaxis in open fractures. It lacks consistent coverage of Staphylococcus aureus and does not provide the same efficacy as cefazolin in this clinical context. Doxycyline may be used as part of a regimen for specific indications such as marine injuries or when unusual pathogens are suspected, but it is not for routine open fracture prophylaxis.

Gentamicin (C) is an aminoglycoside used for coverage of gram-negative organisms. It is not appropriate as monotherapy for open fracture prophylaxis. In type III open fractures (extensive soft tissue damage, high contamination), gentamicin is used in addition to cefazolin. For this patient with a type I open fracture, cefazolin alone is sufficient.

Penicillin (D) is reserved for specific situations, such as prophylaxis against Clostridium perfringens in farm-related injuries or when anaerobic contamination is a concern. It is not the appropriate first-line agent for prophylaxis in a routine open tibial fracture without gross contamination. As monotherapy, it would inadequately cover the most common skin flora implicated in infection.

One Step Further
Question:
What is unhappy triad of knee?

Reveal Answer:
Rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament, tear of the medial collateral ligament, and injury to the medial meniscus.

الفخ: الطالب يختار Doxycycline خطأً بدلاً من A، ويجب التفريق بينهما بدقة.

question: A 33-year-old man presents to the ED after getting punched in the eye in a bar fight. On physical exam, his affected eye does not look upward with upward gaze. CT imaging is seen above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient has entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle on exam, and the CT scan shows a left orbital blowout fracture with disruption of the orbital floor and herniation of orbital contents into the maxillary sinus. Orbital wall fractures are often suspected based on clinical examination and confirmed via CT scan. Approximately one-third of blowout fractures coincide with ocular injuries, such as abrasion, traumatic iritis, hyphema, lens dislocation or subluxation, retinal tear, or detachment. Thus, a thorough eye examination is essential. The most common sites for orbital blowout fractures are the inferior wall (maxillary sinus) and the medial wall (ethmoid sinus via the lamina papyracea). Medial wall fractures may lead to subcutaneous emphysema, which can worsen with sneezing or nose blowing.

Fractures of the inferior wall may trap the inferior rectus muscle, resulting in restricted upward gaze and diplopia. Other physical exam findings suggestive of this condition include enophthalmos, crepitus, and possible paresthesias inferior to the orbit (from infraorbital nerve injury). Other injuries, including ocular injuries such as an open globe, may be present. The diagnosis can be supported with a CT scan. Treatment may involve antibiotics, plastic surgery or otolaryngology consultation, sinus precautions, and possible surgical repair, though this can often occur outpatient at a later time. Surgery is generally indicated if there is muscle entrapment that affects ocular mobility and causes diplopia or significant cosmetic deformity. The timing of surgery is crucial and often performed within 2 weeks from injury to prevent fibrosis of the entrapped muscle. Patients with blowout fractures and normal initial eye exams should be referred to an ophthalmologist for a dilated exam to exclude any undetected retinal issues.



Le Fort fractures (A) are broken up into several types. These are complex fractures that involve the maxilla and surrounding facial bones but typically do not specifically impact eye movement unless there is extensive damage.

An open globe (B) is possible and should be worked up in patients with eye trauma. A teardrop-shaped pupil and Seidel sign on fluorescein stain may be seen on exam. While serious and needing immediate care, it does not usually cause restricted eye movement without other visible signs of globe injury like severe eye pain and visual loss.

Retrobulbar hematoma (D) is also possible in the setting of an orbital floor fracture. It would present with eye pain, proptosis (rather than enophthalmos), reduced visual acuity, and elevated intraocular pressure. It typically would not selectively affect upward gaze without other signs of elevated eye pressure.

One Step Further

What type of facial fracture presents with craniofacial disjunction and shifting of the entire face when pressure is applied to the palate?

Reveal Answer:
Le Fort fracture type III.

PE: inferior rectus entrapment, enophthalmos
Dx: CT will show teardrop sign
Tx: decongestants, refraining from nose blowing, specialist referral (antibiotics are controversial)

question: A patient presents with epistaxis following blunt trauma to the nose. Which of the following characterizations of an intra-nasal mass is most suggestive of a nasal septal hematoma?

options.text: Complete blockage of the nasal cavity
No change in the size of the swelling with oxymetazoline
Presence of associated nasal bone fracture

correctAnswer: No change in the size of the swelling with oxymetazoline
englishExplanation:
In any situation of nasal trauma, the examiner must inspect the inside of the nares for a septal hematoma. A septal hematoma looks like a large purple mass extending from the septum. In the setting of blunt trauma, submucosal blood vessels are torn and blood accumulates between the perichondrium and the cartilage of the septum leading to the hematoma. Within days, the hematoma can become infected and drainage is indicated. Additionally, the pressure of the hematoma on the septum may lead to necrosis and septal perforation. On physical examination, it is often difficult to distinguish between soft tissue edema as a result of blunt trauma or an actual hematoma. A septal hematoma should not change size with the administration of oxymetazoline.



Typically, a septal hematoma does not have a bright red discoloration (A) but is more purple in color due to the accumulation of blood under the perichondrium.

Both regular soft tissue swelling as well as a hematoma may cause complete blockage of the nasal cavity (B), so this cannot be used as a discriminatory criterion.

While septal hematomas are often associated with the presence of an associated nasal bone fracture (D), it is common to have significant soft tissue swelling without the development of a hematoma.

What are two complications of a nasal septal hematoma?

Reveal Answer:
Abscess and saddle nose deformity.

question: A 30-year-old man presents with altered mental status after being struck in the head with a line drive while playing baseball. A computed tomography image is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely source of bleeding in this patient?
englishExplanation:
An epidural hematoma occurs due to accumulation of blood in the potential space between the dura mater and the skull. The most common primary mechanism of injury is blunt trauma to the temporal or temporoparietal area that causes a skull fracture and disruption of the middle meningeal artery. The classic progression of disease involves blunt head trauma that results in a loss of consciousness or altered mental status, followed by a period of lucidity and subsequent rapid neurologic deterioration. Diagnosis of an epidural hematoma is made via computed tomography, showing a hyperechoic biconvex-shaped hemorrhage in the temporal region that does not cross suture lines. This is in contrast to a subdural hematoma, which is crescent-shaped, may cross suture lines, and may occur anywhere in the brain. Patients with epidural hematomas are at risk for rapid herniation due to high-pressured arterial bleeding from the middle meningeal artery. Ideal treatment is neurosurgical evacuation. However, Burr hole placement in the emergency department is indicated in patients with midline shift, unequal pupils, a Glasgow Coma Scale score < 8, and anticipation of extended time to treatment by a neurosurgeon. Temporizing measures to reduce intracranial pressure (elevation of the head of the bed to 30°, mannitol, and hypertonic saline), maintenance of cerebral perfusion, prevention of cerebral vasoconstriction, and seizure prophylaxis (phenytoin, fosphenytoin) are also indicated.



Disruption of an arteriovenous malformation (A) is one of the mechanisms of subarachnoid hemorrhage in addition to the rupture of a cerebral aneurysm. Shearing of bridging veins (B) is the mechanism causing a subdural hematoma. Inflammation of the temporal artery (D) is the pathogenesis behind temporal arteritis, also known as giant cell arteritis.

One Step Further
Question:
What is xanthochromia?

Reveal Answer:
Yellowish cerebrospinal fluid most commonly seen in patients after a subarachnoid hemorrhage.

question: An 11-year-old girl presents after getting hit in the eye with a golf ball. She reports right eye pain and decreased vision. Examination reveals moderate periorbital swelling, conjunctival hemorrhage, and a teardrop-shaped pupil. Visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye, and she has light perception only in the right eye. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Eye shield, CT scan of the orbit, and emergent ophthalmology consultation
Measure intraocular pressure and emergent ophthalmology consultation
Ocular ultrasound and emergent ophthalmology consultation
Timolol drops, intravenous acetazolamide, and emergent ophthalmology consultation

correctAnswer: Eye shield, CT scan of the orbit, and emergent ophthalmology consultation
englishExplanation:
This patient has a ruptured globe resulting from direct trauma to the eye. Blunt trauma to the eye causes a sudden elevation in intraocular pressure, leading to scleral rupture. Patients will present with ocular pain and decreased vision. Examination often reveals chemosis or subconjunctival hemorrhage overlying the scleral defect. If rupture occurs at the limbus, an irregularly shaped (teardrop) pupil may be seen.

Management of suspected globe rupture involves protection of the eye (optimally with a curved eye shield that does not touch the globe), CT scan of the orbit, 30-degree head-of-bed elevation, and emergent ophthalmology consultation. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics should be administered, as well, to reduce the development of endophthalmitis. Historically, succinylcholine was contraindicated as a paralytic agent if the patient required intubation because it was believed that increasing intraocular pressure could lead to ocular extrusion. Recent studies have demonstrated a lack of increased poor outcomes with succinylcholine.



Although a decreased intraocular pressure (< 10 mm Hg) supports the diagnosis of a globe rupture, tonometry (B) should not be performed in patients with a high suspicion of a globe rupture, as any increase in pressure can worsen the defect or lead to extrusion of intraocular materials.

Ocular ultrasound (C) should be avoided for the same reason as avoiding tonometry as it will increase ocular pressure and cause extrusion of intraocular material..

Timolol drops and acetazolamide (D) are two treatments directed at reducing intraocular pressure in acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Reveal Answer:
The presence of a stream of fluorescein dye (after application) secondary to globe rupture.

IOP measurement contraindicated

question: A healthy 33-year-old woman who has no medical history and does not take any medications presents to the ED due to concern for facial asymmetry in her forehead. She noticed this following a motor vehicle collision she was involved in several months prior. Following her collision, she was thoroughly evaluated with CT brain, facial bones, and cervical spine, all of which resulted without acute injuries. She was ultimately discharged from the ED after having a large forehead and scalp laceration repaired in the trauma bay. Assuming her new facial asymmetry is a direct result of her recent traumatic injury, which of the following is most likely responsible for her concern?

options.text: Facial muscle paralysis following traumatic injury
Failure to identify a galeal defect
Laceration to a distal branch of the trigeminal nerve

correctAnswer: Failure to identify a galeal defect
englishExplanation:
When evaluating scalp lacerations, care must be taken to perform a thorough wound exploration to identify defects of the galea. Failure to identify a galeal defect can result in facial asymmetry and deformities in facial expression. The galea is a thick fibrous layer just superficial to the periosteum and deep to the skin and connective tissue. It is the anchoring structure for the frontalis muscle. If the frontalis muscle loses its anchoring point, contraction can result in visible asymmetry. Furthermore, galeal repair after laceration prevents the spread of deep infection as well as subgaleal hematomas.

The galea should be repaired if the lesion is > 0.5 cm and can be done so in a simple interrupted fashion with your choice of absorbable sutures sized 3.0 or 4.0. Most scalp lacerations require repair, as the scalp is highly vascular, and closure may be required to prevent bleeding. Frontal scalp lacerations (covered by hair) in young men are considered cosmetic, as men are likely to bald later in life.



Though facial muscle paralysis following traumatic injury (A) is possible, this is less likely in this clinical scenario. The insulting injury is located on the scalp and forehead, not near the maxilla or ear, where one would expect the facial nerve. Given the location of the wound, only a small distal branch of the facial nerve could potentially be affected, which would be less likely to result in facial asymmetry.

In a woman who is not on anticoagulation, delayed intracranial hemorrhage is exceedingly unlikely. Furthermore, an indolent epidural hematoma (C) does not occur, as they are classically caused by the middle meningeal artery.

Though laceration of a distal branch of the trigeminal nerve (D) is theoretically possible, this would result in sensory deficit rather than muscular atrophy.

What is a technique of laceration repair unique to the scalp?

Reveal Answer:
Hair apposition, which is performed by taking a bundle of hair on each side of the wound, twisting the hair, and gluing the twisted hair to hold the laceration closed.

question: A 33-year-old man presents with a partial thickness burn to his forearm from a grease fire. Which of the following topical agents has been shown to delay wound healing?
englishExplanation:
Burn injuries result in approximately 450,000 patients seeking medical attention in the United States each year, with 10% of these patients requiring hospitalization. Burn severity is subdivided into four categories: superficial (first-degree), partial thickness (second-degree), full thickness (third-degree), and fourth-degree. First-degree burns are characterized by injury to the epidermis alone and appear erythematous with extreme tenderness to palpation. Second-degree burns are also very painful and are further divided into superficial partial-thickness burns (blanching erythema and exhibiting weeping or blisters) and deep partial-thickness burns (white or yellow coloration and dry). Third-degree or full thickness burns are black or white in coloration, nonblanching, feel leathery and dry, and exhibit loss of sensation. Fourth-degree burns extend to the bone.

Circumferential burns resulting in neurovascular compromise require escharotomy. Airway management is paramount in burn patients. Airway compromise can result in the immediate term from inhalation injury, leading to airway edema or lung injury, but can also present in a delayed fashion owing to airway edema from large volume resuscitation. Airway edema should be evaluated via laryngoscopy, and patients with edematous airways should receive awake intubation. Inhalation injury is suggested by large total body surface area (TBSA) burns, carbonaceous sputum, and facial burns. Patients with suspected inhalation injury should also be evaluated for carbon monoxide poisoning, which is treated with 100% oxygen via a nonrebreather mask.

Fluid resuscitation should be initiated for burns ≥ 20% TBSA using guidelines such as the Parkland formula with a goal urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/hr. Superficial epidermal burns require no dressing and can be treated with topical therapy such as aloe vera. Partial- and full-thickness burns should be cleaned with antiseptic and covered with antimicrobial dressings such as bacitracin. Silver sulfadiazine has been shown to delay wound healing and is no longer routinely recommended. Tetanus should be updated if the patient has not been immunized in the last 5 years. Criteria for referral to a burn center include partial-thickness burns > 10% TBSA, any full-thickness burn, and burns to the face, hands, feet, major joints, or genitals.



Bacitracin (A) does not penetrate eschar but otherwise has no negative effects on wound healing.

Bismuth tribromophenate (B) has good antimicrobial properties and no negative wound healing effects.

Mafenide acetate (C) can result in metabolic acidosis but has no negative effect on wound healing.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
Deep partial-thickness and full-thickness burns.

question: A 22-year-old woman presents to the ED with abdominal pain after tripping and falling down five stairs. She struck the left side of her abdomen during the fall. She is 31 weeks pregnant. Her laboratory testing results include blood type A and Rh status negative. Which of the following is the next step in treatment?

options.text: Anti-D immune globulin 300 mcg intramuscular injection
Two units of type O blood transfusion

correctAnswer: Anti-D immune globulin 300 mcg intramuscular injection
englishExplanation:
Trauma is the cause of the majority of maternal deaths during pregnancy. Approximately 5–10% of women experience some form of trauma during their pregnancy, with the majority occurring during the third trimester. The best care for the fetus is caring appropriately for the mother. Maternal Rh status needs to be determined and anti-D immune globulin should be administered if indicated. Given that this patient is Rh negative, she will require anti-D immune globulin 300 mcg intramuscular injection since she sustained direct abdominal trauma and is at risk for maternal-fetal hemorrhage. If untreated, this could lead to Rh sensitization and fetal hydrops. If there is evidence of, or concern for, significant maternal-fetal hemorrhage, the Kleihauer-Betke test can be performed. Positive testing may indicate severe trauma and significant maternal-fetal hemorrhage, requiring additional anti-D immune globulin as the standard dose clears only 15 mL of fetal red blood cells. Additional monitoring should include assessing fetal heart rate with Doppler and placing the patient on fetal cardiotocographic monitoring if the fetus is > 20 weeks gestation. These patients should be monitored for a minimum of 4 hours before discharge home if no injuries are identified, maternal vital signs remain stable, and cardiotocographic tracing is unremarkable.



Betamethasone 12 mg IM (B) is the appropriate therapy for preterm labor to encourage fetal lung maturation before delivery. It is given twice, 24 hours apart.

Nifedipine 20 mg PO (C) is a tocolytic that will help ease uterine contractions in preterm labor to attempt to delay delivery.

Two units of type O blood transfusion (D) would be appropriate if the patient exhibited unstable vital signs or evidence of significant hemorrhage. However, this is not indicated in this patient.

Reveal Answer:
Terbutaline.

question: An 18-year-old college pitcher presents to the ED after being struck in the eye by a baseball. He has severe eye pain and proptosis of the right eye. Visual acuity is 20/25 on the left and hand waving on the right. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Obtain computed tomography of the orbits

englishExplanation:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms of a retrobulbar hematoma, a condition in which blood accumulates behind the eye (globe), leading to orbital compartment syndrome. The expanding hematoma increases pressure on critical structures such as the optic nerve, globe, and central retinal artery, causing ischemia. Retrobulbar hematoma is most commonly caused by trauma, as in this case, and can lead to irreversible vision loss if not addressed promptly.

Signs and symptoms of a retrobulbar hematoma include severe pain, vision loss (such as this patient’s vision limited to hand waving), proptosis (protrusion of the globe), afferent pupillary defect, and ophthalmoplegia (paralysis or limited movement of the extraocular muscles). There may also be evidence of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), further supporting the diagnosis.

Diagnosis is primarily clinical, given the combination of proptosis, vision loss, and pain following trauma. Although CT of the orbits can be obtained to confirm the diagnosis or assess for associated fractures, definitive treatment should not be delayed if the diagnosis is clear. The key to preventing permanent vision loss is to promptly relieve orbital pressure. This is done through an emergent lateral canthotomy and cantholysis, a procedure that releases the pressure within the orbit.

The goal is to relieve orbital pressure and restore blood flow to the optic nerve and globe. Improvement in proptosis and ocular tension should be observed immediately after the procedure. If the globe remains tense or if vision does not improve, further intervention may be required. Throughout the process, ophthalmology should be consulted immediately to manage ongoing care and potential complications. Vision loss can become permanent after 90 to 120 minutes of ischemia, so rapid recognition and intervention are essential. Lateral canthotomy is a sight-saving procedure that buys time while awaiting specialized care.



Acetazolamide (A) can reduce IOP in conditions like acute angle-closure glaucoma, but it is not the best treatment for orbital compartment syndrome, in which surgical decompression is required urgently. IOP-lowering agents should be administered to temporarily reduce compartment pressure until surgical decompression can be performed. These agents include intravenous carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, topical beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, and in some cases, intravenous mannitol at a dose of 1 to 2 g/kg. Once ischemia and vision loss occur, timely canthotomy becomes critical.

While measuring IOP (B) could help confirm the diagnosis of increased pressure within the eye, immediate intervention (lateral canthotomy) is prioritized over diagnostic testing in a situation with such obvious signs of orbital compartment syndrome and impending vision loss.

A CT scan (C) can help visualize fractures or hematomas, but in a patient with clear signs of orbital compartment syndrome, imaging should not delay the necessary emergent treatment (lateral canthotomy) to prevent permanent vision loss.

Reveal Answer:

question: A patient presents to the emergency department after a skiing collision and is diagnosed with a fibular head fracture. Which of the following findings on neurovascular examination would most likely be seen with this injury?

options.text: Decreased sensation between the first and second toes
Weakness with plantar flexion of the ankle

correctAnswer: Decreased sensation between the first and second toes
englishExplanation:
Many orthopedic injuries may also cause nerve or vascular injuries due to the close proximity of these structures and the force required to break bones. A thorough neurovascular examination should be performed to evaluate strength, sensation, and blood flow of the major muscles and nerves distal to any suspected injury. Knowledge of anatomy and function can also help assess which nerves are most at risk, given a suspected or known fracture. The common peroneal nerve courses around the fibular head prior to bifurcating into the superficial and deep peroneal nerves. It is susceptible to injury here from fibular head fractures as well as from excess pressure with casting or during operative procedures. These branches of the peroneal nerve continue to the foot, where the deep peroneal nerve provides sensation between the first and second toes and motor function to the tibialis anterior (dorsiflexion and inversion of the ankle) and extensor hallucis longus (extension of the great toe). The superficial peroneal nerve innervates the peroneus longus, which aids in ankle eversion and provides sensory innervation to much of the dorsum of the foot. Fractures with neurovascular compromise should be emergently reduced and referred to orthopedics.



The tibial nerve provides sensation to the calf (B) after passing through the popliteal fossa and is unlikely to be affected by a fibular head fracture.

A weakened dorsalis pedis pulse (C) would more likely be seen after injury to the tibia or knee. The popliteal artery passes through the popliteal fossa and then gives rise to the anterior tibial artery, which ultimately becomes the dorsalis pedis artery.

Weakness with plantar flexion of the ankle (D) would be caused by injury to the tibial nerve, which also passes through the popliteal fossa. Injuries to all of these structures may be seen with knee dislocations.

Reveal Answer:
Popliteal artery via the tibioperoneal trunk.

question: A 33-year-old man presents to a community emergency department reporting severe pain in his left hand after spilling an unknown liquid on himself while at work, where he transports waste products at a semiconductor fabrication plant. After irrigating the affected area with water, he notified his supervisor about the incident and was instructed to go to the hospital due to “very harmful chemicals” in the liquid. Physical exam is notable for injuries to the patient’s left hand pictured above and is otherwise unremarkable. Which of the following electrolyte disturbances is consistent with systemic toxicity related to this chemical exposure?
englishExplanation:
Used primarily for industrial purposes such as glass etching, metal cleaning, and semiconductor production, hydrofluoric acid is a highly potent inorganic acid, capable of producing lethal systemic toxicity from even trace exposure. Aside from the corrosive effect of direct skin exposure that results in burns from free hydrogen ions, the fluoride ions penetrate deeper into the tissue, forming insoluble salts with calcium and magnesium and rapidly dissociating soluble salts with other cations, which leads to deeper tissue destruction. Without treatment, hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia result from the consumptive process initiated by free fluoride ions, along with hyperkalemia, which is initiated by the efflux of potassium from cells initiated by hypocalcemia. Along with intravascular volume losses from the tissue destruction, mortality is attributable to the resultant electrolyte abnormalities and the directly cardiotoxic effect of fluoride ions, which trigger cardiac dysrhythmias, the primary cause of death from hydrofluoric acid exposure. Immediate decontamination is vital, along with the administration of topical calcium gluconate gel to exposed areas, which forms complexes with free fluoride ions prior to deeper tissue penetration. If pain persists, or if there is a delay in presentation with severe tissue destruction prior to evaluation, intravascular calcium gluconate should also be administered either intra-arterially through the brachial artery or intravenously with the use of a Bier block.



Hydrofluoric acid toxicity does not result in hypercalcemia, hypermagnesemia, and hypokalemia (A), hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and hyperkalemia (B), or hypocalcemia, hypermagnesemia, and hypokalemia (C), as systemic fluoride consumes calcium and magnesium that lowers these levels and secondarily causes hyperkalemia through intracellular shifting brought about by hypocalcemia.

One Step Further
Question:
Burns from which chemicals should not be treated with immediate water irrigation?

Reveal Answer:
Dry lime (creates calcium hydroxide with water, a liquefactive alkali), elemental metals (produce strong exothermic reactions with water creating hydrogen gas), and phenol (not water soluble). Substances should be manually removed before irrigation is initiated.

question: A 3-year-old boy presents after biting through a television power cord 20 minutes prior to arrival. The parents note that the child cried immediately and did not lose consciousness. He has since been acting normally and is tolerating oral fluids. On physical exam, there is an eschar over the left oral commissure without bleeding. There are no other burns to the tongue or oropharynx. What is the most serious complication of this injury?
englishExplanation:
Electrical burns in children most commonly involve the lips, mouth, and tongue. These injuries typically result after a child, usually under the age of 3, chews or sucks on an electrical cord. Electrolyte-rich saliva conducts electricity to the mucous membranes, which have a high risk of thermal injury due to their relatively low resistance. The oral commissure is the most common site for an oral burn after electrical injury. Oral commissure burns usually appear gray or white and are typically painless due to underlying nerve injury. Initial evaluation of any patient with facial burns requires careful inspection of the mouth and oropharynx for signs of airway involvement. The presence of soot in the mouth, singed nasal hairs, wheezing, voice changes, or respiratory distress should heighten the suspicion for airway burns and prompt consideration for early endotracheal intubation.

Patients with isolated oral commissure burns do not usually require workup or admission to the hospital. Emergency management includes providing tetanus vaccination for those who are unvaccinated, arranging expedited follow-up with an oral or plastic surgeon, and educating parents about the most serious potential complication of delayed bleeding. Bleeding from an oral commissure wound is rare in the immediate setting, as the blood vessels are cauterized by thermal injury. However, as the eschar sloughs, there can be massive bleeding from the labial artery, usually within the first 2 weeks of injury. In the event of bleeding, parents should be instructed to apply direct compression of the commissure with two fingers and to seek immediate emergency care. Patients with oral commissure burns often require reconstructive surgery or splinting to ensure adequate cosmetic and functional outcomes, but this is not done emergently.



Cardiac dysrhythmias (A) are uncommon after household electrical injuries. Standard household current in the United States is 110 V. Cardiac dysrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, and other sequelae of electrical injuries are typically observed after high voltage injuries, defined by a current > 1,000 V. Patients with low voltage injuries who have no cardiac symptoms, who had no loss of consciousness, and who have a normal screening ECG are considered low-risk for dysrhythmias and do not require prolonged monitoring on telemetry. Additionally, oral commissure burns result from a local arc of electrical current that does not typically reach the myocardium. While infection (C) is possible after any burn, it is not immediately life-threatening. Delayed labial artery bleeding can lead to exsanguination and death and is the most important complication to educate parents about prior to discharge. Microstomia (D), or decreased mouth size from perioral contracture, is a potential complication of oral commissure burns that can lead to morbidity, but it is not immediately life-threatening.

Reveal Answer:
False.

question: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after falling from a roof. She reports tingling in her fingers and toes. She is immobilized in a cervical collar. An image of her vertebra is seen above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
A Jefferson fracture is a burst fracture of the lateral masses of C1. It is caused by axial loading or a vertical compression force that is transmitted through the occipital condyles and causes displacement of the lateral masses from their articulation with the facets of the axis (C2). The anterior and posterior arches of C1 are often fractured as well. This is an unstable cervical spine fracture. On X-ray, the lateral masses can be viewed as laterally displaced from the atlantoaxial unit. Further imaging should be obtained to evaluate for other spinal injuries, especially in the presence of neurological deficits.



A hangman fracture (A) is caused by extreme hyperextension and creates fractures of the bilateral pedicles of C2. It is also an unstable injury. Odontoid fractures (C) can occur from a variety of mechanisms, including shearing force or extreme flexion. Type I odontoid fractures are stable; types II and III are unstable. Teardrop fractures (D) are unstable and may occur at any vertebral level, although the cervical spine is the most common location. They result from extreme flexion that causes an anterior displacement of a wedge-shaped vertebral body fragment that resembles a teardrop.

question: A 30-year-old man presents to the ED after a high-speed single-vehicle collision in which he swerved to miss a deer and hit a bridge head-on. He appears in acute distress and has asymmetric radial pulses and chest wall ecchymosis. A chest X-ray is obtained and shows a widened mediastinum. Which of the following is the most common location for this type of injury?
englishExplanation:
Blunt aortic injury usually occurs when high-energy compression, shearing, or torsional forces are applied to the chest. Common mechanisms include fall from a height greater than 10 feet and motor vehicle collisions at speeds greater than 30 miles per hour. In motor vehicle collisions in which there is front-end impact, the chest impacts the steering wheel, allowing inertia to carry the intrathoracic contents forward. However, the aorta is anatomically fixed at the left subclavian artery origin by the ligamentum arteriosum. This causes the proximal descending aorta to decelerate with the chest wall while the ascending aorta is mobile and continues forward at impact. This can cause aortic rupture or tears in the intima or media, creating dissection or pseudoaneurysm formation that may predispose to aortic rupture. The aorta may also become compressed between the sternum and the vertebral bodies, increasing intraluminal pressure and causing rupture. Aortic rupture is usually rapidly fatal, and many patients do not survive to ED evaluation.

Patients with blunt aortic injury may be asymptomatic or have minimal symptoms such as back pain, chest pain, or dyspnea. However, these injuries may be clinically occult, and providers should consider aortic trauma in any patient with high-energy mechanisms. Clinical clues that might suggest blunt aortic injury include asymmetric pulses or blood pressures in extremities, hypotension, interscapular murmurs or bruits, palpable rib fractures, flail chest, chest wall contusions (e.g., seat belt markings), or expanding thoracic outlet hematoma. Mediastinal widening on chest radiography is suggestive of great vessel injury. CT angiography is the diagnostic modality of choice to evaluate for aortic injury. Trauma or vascular surgery consultation is needed upon initial suspicion or at diagnosis.



Ascending aortic injuries and traumatic rupture at the aortic root (A) are less common than tears at the ligamentum arteriosum and are almost always fatal.

The brachiocephalic artery origin (B) and right subclavian artery origin (D) are not tethered, therefore, they are not as common as the left subclavian artery origin for aortic injuries.

question: A 33-year-old man presents to the ED after a fall from a bicycle. He reports left shoulder pain and has a visible deformity. A chest radiograph confirms a clavicle fracture. Which of the following is an indication for surgical repair of this patient’s fracture?

options.text: Comminuted fracture without skin tenting, significant displacement, or neurovascular compromise
Midshaft fracture with > 2 cm of shortening
Nondisplaced midshaft fracture with pain during overhead motion

correctAnswer: Midshaft fracture with > 2 cm of shortening
englishExplanation:
Clavicle fractures are common injuries, particularly in younger adults and athletes, accounting for approximately 2–5% of all fractures and almost half of shoulder girdle fractures. The majority occur in the midshaft, typically from direct trauma such as a fall onto the shoulder or an outstretched hand. Midshaft fractures often present with visible deformity, pain with arm movement, and localized swelling. Most cases can be managed nonoperatively with a sling and outpatient orthopedic follow-up. However, there are certain features that suggest a higher risk of nonunion or functional impairment, prompting consideration for surgical management.

Surgical repair, typically with open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), is indicated for specific patterns of midshaft fractures. One major indication is > 1.8–2 cm of shortening or displacement. Such fractures are associated with a higher risk of malunion and long-term functional deficits, including strength loss and reduced shoulder endurance. Other surgical indications include open fractures, skin tenting (suggesting impending skin compromise), neurovascular injury, severely comminuted and displaced fractures, and a floating shoulder (clavicle fracture with scapular neck fracture). ORIF improves union rates, restores anatomic alignment, and typically results in better cosmetic and functional outcomes in select patients.



Although comminution is a risk factor for nonunion, isolated comminution without skin tenting, significant displacement, neurovascular injury, or skin compromise (A) does not by itself necessitate surgical repair. In the absence of significant shortening, open fracture, or other complications, conservative management remains appropriate.

Most nondisplaced distal third fractures (C) are treated conservatively. While certain distal third fracture types (Neer type II or V) are at higher risk of nonunion and may warrant surgery, this requires displacement or ligamentous instability. The key descriptor here is “nondisplaced,” which strongly favors nonsurgical management.

Pain with motion is common in clavicle fractures, especially early after injury. A nondisplaced midshaft fracture without other risk features (shortening, displacement, skin compromise) is typically treated conservatively. Functional symptoms alone, such as pain during overhead motion (D), especially in the acute setting, are not a surgical indication. Thus, this patient needs to have other factors describing the fracture that would necessitate surgical care, rather than pain alone.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder).

question: A 34-year-old woman presents to the emergency department in cardiac arrest with high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation underway. Emergency medical personnel report that she is currently 27 weeks pregnant. Which of the following is the most common cause of death in this patient population?
englishExplanation:
Trauma is the cause of most maternal deaths during pregnancy. Approximately 5–10% of women experience some form of trauma during their pregnancy, with the majority occurring during the third trimester. Motor vehicle collisions are the most common, followed by domestic violence and accidental falls. Signs and symptoms of trauma during pregnancy include vaginal bleeding, which may be a sign of placental abruption, premature rupture of membranes, uterine contractions or tenderness, and absent or decreased fetal movement. Uterine tenderness and pain are much more common than true abdominal pain in traumatic injuries in pregnant patients, as peritoneal stretching results in decreased nerve density per area during pregnancy.

Diagnosis of injuries includes the characteristic trauma panel of laboratory testing and consideration of imaging in a manner similar to nonpregnant patients, with the risk-benefit analysis of radiation exposure taken into consideration. The best care for the fetus is caring appropriately for the mother. Additionally, maternal Rh status needs to be determined and Rhogam administered if indicated. If there is evidence of, or concern for, significant maternal-fetal hemorrhage, the Kleihauer-Betke test can be performed to further assess. Positive testing may indicate severe trauma and significant maternal-fetal hemorrhage, requiring additional Rhogam as the standard dose clears only 15 mL of fetal red blood cells. Additional monitoring should include assessing fetal heart rate with Doppler and placing the patient on fetal cardiotocographic monitoring if the fetus is > 20 weeks gestation. These patients should be monitored for a minimum of 4 hours prior to discharge home if no injuries are identified, maternal vital signs remain stable, and cardiotocographic tracing is unremarkable. If the patient remains in cardiac arrest, a perimortem cesarean section may be considered.



Infection (A) and suicide (B) are possible, albeit less common, causes of maternal death during pregnancy.

Vaginal bleeding (D) is a rare cause of maternal death during pregnancy.

question: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the ED by her parent, who reports she placed her finger in a wall electrical socket. In the ED, the child is easily consolable but holds her right index finger in the air. Visual inspection reveals localized erythema at the distal tip but good capillary refill. There are no other signs of trauma. Which diagnostic test should be performed next?
englishExplanation:
There are two basic types of electrical current: alternating (AC) and direct (DC). This child sustained a low-voltage (< 1,000 volts) electrical injury from an unprotected wall socket. In the United States, household wiring has 120 volts of alternating current with a frequency of 60 Hz. Alternating current causes continuous tetanic muscle contraction between 8 and 22 mA that does not allow the individual to release the electrical source. This child sustained a superficial thermal burn and most likely did not become part of the circuit, given that there are no clear entry or exit wounds. However, patients sustaining such an injury still warrant an ECG and cardiac monitoring in the ED. The most common ECG abnormality is sinus tachycardia and nonspecific ST-T wave changes that resolve spontaneously. Atrial or ventricular ectopy, fibrillation, interval prolongations, or blocks may also be seen. Asystole and ventricular fibrillation are more commonly seen in higher-voltage exposures.



Although a urinalysis (D) to screen for myoglobin and a basic metabolic panel (A) to check kidney function might be performed, it is not necessary given the nature of this child’s injury. Creatine phosphokinase and serial cardiac-specific troponins may be obtained if significant skeletal muscle or cardiomyocyte damage is suspected.

A chest radiograph (B) will provide no useful information, given the clinical exam.

Reveal Answer:
Nerves.

question: A 36-year-old man presents to the emergency department with ankle pain. He states that he was jumping to grab a ball when he was playing basketball and felt a “pop” at the back of his ankle. On exam, he has a positive Thompson test. What is the most appropriate next step in care?

options.text: Apply a splint with the ankle in slight plantarflexion
Obtain CT angiography of the extremity to rule out vascular compromise
Place the patient in a controlled ankle movement boot

correctAnswer: Apply a splint with the ankle in slight plantarflexion
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with an Achilles tendon rupture. These usually occur when sudden forces are exerted on the Achilles tendon. They often occur during strenuous activities that involve rapid acceleration or pivoting on a foot. Many patients will report feeling a pop or feel like they were struck at the back of their ankle. Patients often present with significant pain, and a defect is often easily identified and palpated. However, a small percentage of patients may present without pain or significant difficulty ambulating. Certain tests, such as the Thompson test, can help provide a more accurate means for diagnosing Achilles tendon ruptures on exam.

For this test, the patient lies prone with their knee flexed at 90°. The examiner squeezes the patient’s calf muscles which should cause contraction of an intact Achilles tendon, leading to plantar flexion. If the tendon is completely ruptured, no plantar flexion would be seen, leading to a positive finding. MRI may help differentiate the extent of the tear and could potentially differentiate between partial and complete tears, but this can be performed in the outpatient setting.

Initial care of Achilles tendon ruptures consists of conservative management, analgesics (anti-inflammatories), and immobilization with the ankle in slight plantarflexion. All patients should be discharged with close follow-up with orthopedic surgery, as many of these patients will be treated operatively.



Consulting orthopedic surgery in the emergency department (B) would be inappropriate, as an isolated Achilles tendon rupture is not an indication for emergency surgery.

Obtaining CT angiography of the extremity to rule out vascular compromise (C) is also inappropriate, as most Achilles tendon injuries caused by running and jumping are not significant enough to lead to vascular injury. Assessment for such should start with a physical exam, not imaging.

Placing the patient in a controlled ankle movement boot (D) would still allow some movement in the ankle. These patients should be immobilized in slight plantarflexion and placed in non-weight-bearing status when discharged from the emergency department.

Reveal Answer:

question: A 24-year-old man presents to the ED after electrocution while at work. He has experienced muscle spasms, cramping, and pain since the episode. His T is 97°F (36.1°C), BP is 125/80 mm Hg, HR is 112 bpm, RR is 19/min, and SpO2 is 100% on room air. Physical examination reveals diffuse muscle tenderness. Laboratory values are notable for a potassium of 6.0 mEq/L, calcium of 6.8 mEq/L, creatinine of 1.9 mg/dL, and phosphorus of 5.1 mg/dL, while other results are still pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

options.text: Ringer lactate bolus and sodium bicarbonate ampule

englishExplanation:
Electrical injuries can be life-threatening and can cause deep injury to underlying tissues and cardiac dysrhythmias. One possible complication of electrical injury is rhabdomyolysis, which occurs when skeletal muscle breakdown causes the release of intracellular contents. Laboratory findings suggestive of rhabdomyolysis include a creatine kinase over five times the upper limit of normal, hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, and hyperphosphatemia. Acute kidney injury is a possible complication of rhabdomyolysis and is caused by myoglobin accumulation.

The best treatment and prevention of acute kidney injury in rhabdomyolysis is fluid administration to ensure adequate urinary output. Start administering IV normal saline at 1 L/hr or other appropriate fluid to maintain urine output. Continue aggressive IV rehydration for the next 24–72 hours. One approach is to quickly correct the fluid deficit using IV crystalloids, followed by an infusion rate of 4 mL/kg/h, aiming to maintain a urine output of at least 3–4 mL/kg/h. Alternatively, target a urine output of 200–300 mL/hr. Electrolyte derangements should be addressed, as they are common in this condition.



Furosemide (A) might be an appropriate treatment for hyperkalemia. However, it could potentially worsen kidney function without proper hydration. To prevent kidney injury and hyperkalemia, giving IV fluids first is more appropriate and will likely prevent the need for loop diuretic administration.

A nephrology consult to initiate dialysis (B) would be warranted in a patient with acute kidney failure with an emergent need for dialysis, such as hyperkalemia, acidosis, or fluid overload. It is generally more appropriate after initial measures to stabilize electrolyte imbalances have failed and after reassessing kidney function following initial treatment.

Ringer lactate and sodium bicarbonate (D) would not be the best treatment. While some older sources might recommend sodium bicarbonate treatment for severe rhabdomyolysis, more recent evidence does not suggest a benefit to bicarbonate administration. IV crystalloid alone is preferred to manage fluid balance and facilitate kidney excretion of myoglobin.

Reveal Answer:
Positive for blood but a urinalysis without red blood cells (from cross-reactivity with myoglobin on urine dipstick).

question: A 5-year-old girl was playing on the playground after school when she accidentally collided with another child. She immediately developed pain and swelling around her nose, and there was some bleeding from the left nare that stopped on its own. She is now reluctant to touch or move her nose. On exam, there is tenderness over the nasal bridge with associated soft tissue swelling. No obvious septal deviation or septal hematoma is present. She is able to breathe out of both nares, and no other injuries are noted. What is the appropriate treatment plan for this child?

options.text: Conscious sedation and reduction of the nasal bone fracture
CT scan of the face and orbits
Motrin, ice, and specialty follow-up in 3 days
Supportive care with family clinician follow-up in 10 days

correctAnswer: Motrin, ice, and specialty follow-up in 3 days
englishExplanation:
Due to the anterior position and structure of the nasal bridge, it is more commonly injured with facial trauma. Epistaxis frequently accompanies nasal injuries. Palpation of the nose for tenderness and crepitus should be performed. Each nare should be held closed to ensure the patient is able to breathe from either side. The septum should be examined for the presence of a septal hematoma. A filter test may be performed if CSF rhinorrhea is suspected.

If the nose is acceptably straight, the patient is able to breathe out of both nares, there is no CSF rhinorrhea or septal hematoma, and epistaxis is controlled, then no further emergent evaluation is necessary. When the swelling over the nasal bridge makes determining the appearance difficult, an outpatient referral for specialty follow-up is recommended in 3–5 days. In children, there may be premature closure of sutures and uneven growth. Therefore, specialty consultation should be obtained within 3 days of the injury. Imaging for suspected isolated nasal bone fractures has little clinical value and should only be obtained when other fractures are suspected.



This case is an example of a simple, uncomplicated nasal bone fracture. CT scan of the face and orbits (B) is only required when additional injuries are suspected and is not indicated in this case.

The patient has no nasal deviation or septal hematoma and can breathe out of both nares. Thus, there is no indication for conscious sedation and reduction of the nasal bone fracture (A).

While supportive care is indicated for pain and swelling control, follow-up with a specialist in 3 days and not a family clinician in 10 days (D) is recommended due to the risk of premature closure of the nasal bone sutures and uneven growth.

One Step Further
Question:
What is a Le Fort III fracture?

Reveal Answer:
A Le Fort III fracture is a craniofacial dissociation that involves a horizontal fracture line extending through the orbits, separating the entire midface from the skull.

question: A 38-year-old man presents to the ED after a motor vehicle collision. He is in respiratory distress with asymmetrical chest expansion. He has breath sounds bilaterally and ecchymosis over the left chest wall. The patient is tachypneic, and his oxygen saturation is 84%. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment for this patient?

options.text: Immediate surgical intervention for rib fixation

englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation, with asymmetrical chest expansion, respiratory distress, and low oxygen saturation, is concerning for severe chest wall injury, such as flail chest. Flail chest occurs when multiple contiguous ribs are fractured in two or more places, creating a segment in the chest wall that has no bony attachment to the thoracic cage. This segment will move paradoxically with respiration compared to the rest of the chest wall. This abnormal movement disrupts normal respiratory mechanics and may lead to impairment in ventilation and respiratory compromise.

The primary goal in the management of flail chest is to ensure adequate oxygenation, ventilation, pain control, and surgical stabilization. Oxygen administration may be required to maintain saturation > 90%. Nasal cannula, a nonrebreather mask, and in more severe cases, noninvasive positive pressure ventilation may be required. In extreme cases when patients cannot maintain oxygen saturation or are inadequately ventilating, intubation and mechanical ventilation may be necessary to ensure adequate oxygenation.

Pain management is important for adequate ventilation and may prevent atelectasis and pneumonia. Analgesia may be best obtained with intravenous opioids, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories, and paravertebral or epidural nerve blocks. Adequate pain control will allow for improved respiratory effort, improved deep breathing to prevent atelectasis, and improved secretion clearance. Careful monitoring of respiratory function is necessary with opioid use to prevent worsening respiratory depression.

Consultation with a trauma surgeon is necessary for all patients with flail chest. Emergent surgical plating is considered in cases when there is severe flail chest with significant chest wall instability. Early surgical intervention has been associated with fewer complications, improved functional and cosmetic results, and improved recovery. Other indications for delayed surgical intervention include patients with respiratory failure despite appropriate medical management, failure to wean off the ventilator, and intractable pain.

This patient is in acute respiratory distress. The paradoxical movements associated with flail chest lead to the inability to generate appropriate tidal volume, which leads to poor ventilation and oxygenation. The immediate management should be intubation with mechanical ventilation to compensate for the loss of chest wall integrity by ensuring the lungs can expand fully with each breath, promoting adequate gas exchange.



Chest tube placement (A) is indicated for pneumothorax or hemothorax, not flail chest. This patient has bilateral breath sounds, which points away from these diagnoses. The primary issue in flail chest is the abnormal movement of the chest wall, altering respiratory mechanics, rather than fluid or air collections that would require evacuation.

Immediate surgical intervention for rib fixation (B) is not a first-line treatment for flail chest. While it may be considered in severe, unstable cases, it is typically reserved for patients with extensive rib fractures that do not improve with standard treatments. This patient is in acute distress, and his airway needs to be addressed before any other interventions. Immediate management should focus on airway support and ventilation.

Needle decompression (D) is used for tension pneumothorax, not flail chest. This procedure involves relieving pressure in the chest due to trapped air in the pleural cavity, but it does not address the respiratory compromise caused by flail chest, in which the chest wall movement is compromised.
