question: An 82-year-old woman presents with right hip pain after a fall. An X-ray is shown above, confirming the diagnosis. The clinician has decided to perform a fascia iliaca compartment block. Between which two muscles should the block be performed?

options.text: Rectus femoris and vastus lateralis muscles

englishExplanation:
This patient has an intertrochanteric fracture, a type of proximal femur fracture. Other types of femoral fractures include femoral neck, greater trochanter, and subtrochanteric fractures. Patients with proximal femoral or hip fractures are often made nonweightbearing and require pain control until surgical repair. In the past, these patients would be treated with multiple as-needed opioid doses for extended periods of time, depending on operating room availability. In older adults, frequent opioid dosing is associated with an increased risk of delirium, constipation, nausea, vomiting, apnea, and other serious adverse effects. An alternative to as-needed opioid administration is an ultrasound-guided compartment block, which provides long-term analgesia with minimal risk and adverse effects. Some options for a compartment block include the fascia iliaca compartment block and the pericapsular nerve group block. General equipment needed for a fascia iliaca compartment block includes an ultrasound machine with a high-frequency linear probe, sterile equipment (such as probe cover, gloves, wipes, and towels to set a sterile field), saline flushes, a 25-gauge needle with a small syringe (i.e., 3 mL), 20- or 22-gauge spinal needle with a large syringe (i.e., 60 mL), and a local anesthetic. Bupivacaine 0.5% is commonly used at a dose of 2 mg/kg. Other options include lidocaine, mepivacaine, and ropivacaine. Dexamethasone 10 mg (preservative-free, if available) may be added to extend the duration of analgesia.

Using a high-frequency linear ultrasound probe, identify the femoral vessels in a transverse orientation, which from medial to lateral are the femoral vein, femoral artery, and femoral nerve. Once identified, slide the ultrasound probe laterally, away from the femoral nerve. Visualize a superficial muscle (the sartorius muscle) and a deeper muscle (the iliacus muscle). Between the two muscles, there will be a hyperechoic linear structure that is the fascia iliaca. The area just beneath the fascia iliaca is the target for a fascia iliaca compartment block. Once landmarks are identified, inject a small amount of local anesthetic superficially using a 25-gauge needle and small syringe, creating a skin wheal. Then, using an in-plane approach, insert the spinal needle and visualize the entirety of the needle (hyperechoic on ultrasound) in real-time as it is passed just under the fascia iliaca. Piercing the fascia iliaca should produce a “pop” that is felt by the operator. Once in position, aspirate to ensure the needle is not in a vessel, and inject the entirety of the contents. The iliacus muscle should separate from the fascia iliaca, as the anesthetic, which is visualized as hypoechoic on ultrasound, accumulates in the desired location. If the superficial sartorius muscle separates from the fascia iliaca, this means the needle did not pierce the fascia iliaca and should be advanced. To facilitate proper placement, tubing may be attached to the spinal needle such that a second operator can inject the anesthetic while the primary operator is stabilizing the needle in place. As the anesthetic spreads medially and laterally, it reaches the femoral nerve and lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, which innervates the surroundings of the hip and proximal femur, thereby providing adequate analgesia for hip and proximal femur fractures.



Iliacus and psoas major muscles (A), psoas major and sartorius muscles (C), and rectus femoris and vastus lateralis muscles (D) are incorrect. The fascia iliaca lies between the sartorius and iliacus muscles. The psoas major muscle extends from the lumbar region to the pelvis and femur. It is located medially to the iliacus muscle. The rectus femoris muscle extends from the pelvis to the knee. It is located laterally to the sartorius muscle. The vastus lateralis is lateral to the sartorius muscle and the rectus femoris. The pericapsular nerve group block is performed between the iliacus and psoas major muscles. However, this clinician wants to perform a fascia iliacus compartment block.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the toxic dose of bupivacaine?

Reveal Answer:
> 2.5 mg/kg without epinephrine (175 mg maximum) or > 3 mg/kg with epinephrine (225 mg maximum).

question: Which of the following is the most common nerve injury associated with anterior shoulder dislocation and reduction?
englishExplanation:
The shoulder is the most commonly dislocated large joint, with anterior dislocations accounting for the vast majority of cases. Dislocations occur primarily in two patient groups: men in their 20–30s and women in their 60s. Most dislocations are the result of a fall onto an elevated, externally rotated, and abducted arm. Nearly all anterior dislocations result in the humeral head in the subcoracoid or subglenoid position. On presentation, patients will be holding the affected arm in slight abduction and external rotation, and there will be a “squared-off” appearance of the shoulder with anterior fullness. A detailed neurovascular exam prior to any reduction attempts is imperative, as nearly half of patients may have some degree of nerve dysfunction.

There are numerous techniques available for shoulder reduction, some of which do not require procedural sedation. Following attempted or successful reduction of the joint, a repeat neurovascular exam should be done. The axillary nerve is the most commonly injured nerve, both as a result of the dislocation itself and with the reduction of the joint. Injury to the axillary nerve can be detected by testing for sensation of the lateral shoulder and strength testing of the deltoid and teres minor muscles, the latter of which may be difficult in the acute setting. The majority of these injuries resolve without intervention.



A brachial plexus injury (B) can occur with traction of the brachial plexus resulting from the downward pressure of the shoulder while the neck is pushed laterally away from the side of the injury. This is a common injury in football or rugby but can also occur during childbirth.

The musculocutaneous nerve (C) provides motor function to the muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm and sensation to the lateral forearm.

A radial nerve injury (D) can occur in the setting of a midshaft humerus fracture and results in a wrist drop. None of these injuries are commonly associated with anterior shoulder dislocation or reduction.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the significance of a Bankart lesion?

Reveal Answer:
It is a predisposing factor for recurrent shoulder dislocations.

Rapid Review

Anterior Shoulder Dislocation

Most commonly caused by trauma from a fall or forceful throwing motion
PE: arm abducted and externally rotated, positive apprehension test result
Diagnosis is made by anteroposterior and axillary shoulder X-rays
Humeral head displaced inferiorly and medially
Complications: axillary nerve damage, Bankart lesion (glenoid labrum disruption), Hill-Sachs deformity (cortical depression in the humeral head)

question: Which of the following best indicates a need for knee radiography based on the Ottawa Knee Rule in a patient with an acute knee injury?

options.text: The patient has a history of prior anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction
The patient is unable to actively flex the knee to 90°
The patient reports generalized knee pain without point tenderness
The patient reports pain while walking but can bear weight

correctAnswer: The patient is unable to actively flex the knee to 90°
englishExplanation:
The Ottawa Knee Rule is a clinical tool developed to identify patients with acute knee injuries who are at risk for fracture and thus require radiographic imaging. The rule recommends obtaining a knee radiograph if any of the following criteria are met: age ≥ 55 years, isolated patellar tenderness, tenderness at the head of the fibula, inability to flex the knee to 90°, or inability to bear weight both immediately and in the ED (defined as taking four steps). Thus, the inability to flex the knee to 90° is a clear indication for radiography per the rule, as it raises concern for underlying fracture or joint injury.

Knee injuries are frequently encountered in the emergency setting, particularly in active individuals and older adults. Mechanisms of injury often include falls, direct blows, or twisting motions. Common injuries range from contusions and ligamentous sprains to fractures of the patella, tibial plateau, or femoral condyles. Risk factors for more serious injuries include older age, osteoporosis, and high-energy trauma. Patients typically present with pain, swelling, reduced range of motion, and difficulty bearing weight. The Ottawa Knee Rule has high sensitivity (approaching 100%) for detecting clinically significant fractures, allowing clinicians to avoid unnecessary imaging in low-risk patients.

Management in the emergency department begins with assessing for serious injury. When the Ottawa Knee Rule criteria are not met, imaging can often be deferred. Treatment for minor injuries includes NSAIDs, rest, ice, and supportive devices such as knee braces or crutches. More severe injuries or fractures require orthopedic consultation and possibly immobilization. Missed injuries can result in chronic pain, instability, or functional limitations, so early identification of red flags, guided by validated tools like the Ottawa Knee Rule, is critical.



A history of previous knee surgery, like anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (A), does not, by itself, meet the Ottawa Knee Rule criteria. Unless the patient also meets one of the five specified criteria (e.g., unable to flex to 90°, cannot bear weight), radiography is not required based on this rule.

Age ≥ 55 years is one of the criteria for imaging under the Ottawa Knee Rule. A 43-year-old patient (B) without any of the other risk criteria (no fibular head or patellar tenderness, full range of motion, can bear weight) does not meet the threshold for radiography.

Generalized knee pain without point tenderness (D) or nonspecific tenderness is not one of the Ottawa Knee Rule criteria. The rule specifically identifies isolated patellar tenderness and fibular head tenderness as red flags. Generalized pain without inability to bear weight or flex the knee does not warrant imaging.

Finally, according to the Ottawa Knee Rule, patients who are able to bear weight (E) (defined as four steps both immediately and in the ED) and have no focal bony tenderness do not require imaging. Mild pain while walking is not an indication for radiography in isolation.

One Step Further
Question:
What are hard signs of vascular injury after a severe knee injury?

Reveal Answer:
Hard signs of vascular compromise after a knee injury include absent pedal pulses, cool mottled foot, expanding popliteal hematoma, or popliteal hemorrhage.

Ottawa Knee Rule

Obtain knee radiographs for
Age ≥ 55 years
Isolated patella tenderness
Isolated fibula head tenderness
Inability to flex knee 90°
Inability to bear weight (four steps) immediately after injury AND in ED

question: A 50-year-old man presents to the ED with hand weakness. He works as a carpenter and recently noticed difficulty gripping his tools. On physical exam, he is unable to completely extend the interphalangeal joints of the ring and small finger in his right hand. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured?
englishExplanation:
Ulnar neuropathy can occur secondary to overuse injuries as the result of repetitive blunt trauma. The ulnar nerve courses over the flexor retinaculum as it moves into the hand through the ulnar canal. The roof of the ulnar canal is made up of the superficial palmar carpal ligament. The floor consists of the deeper flexor retinaculum and hypothenar muscles. The pisohamate ligament forms the medial border, and the hook of the hamate defines the lateral boundary of the ulnar canal. Injury to the ulnar nerve at the level of the wrist results in an ulnar claw hand. The partial or complete denervation of the third and fourth lumbricals, which flex the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, results in hyperextension of the MCP joints. The lumbricals are involved in the extension of the interphalangeal joints of the fingers, and denervation will lead to flexion of the interphalangeal joints. The resulting MCP extension and interphalangeal joint flexion results in a claw deformity.



The median (A) nerve can be injured from repetitive blunt trauma as it moves through the carpal tunnel. Carpal tunnel syndrome is the most common upper extremity mononeuropathy. Classic symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome are pain and paresthesias of the first three digits and the radial side of the fourth digit. Involvement of the thenar eminence muscle group leads to weakness of thumb abduction and opposition.

A common site of radial (B) nerve injury is at the level of the spiral groove at the midportion of the humerus. Patients will present with weakness of wrist extensors, leading to wrist drop. Patients will also have weakness of the finger extensors, triceps, and brachioradialis.

The recurrent branch of the median nerve (C) courses distal to the flexor retinaculum and innervates the intrinsic muscles of the thumb. In contrast to carpal tunnel syndrome, injury to the recurrent branch of the median nerve is rare and often difficult to diagnose.

One Step Further
Question:
Fracture of what carpal bone is associated with ulnar nerve injury?

Reveal Answer:
Hamate. The ulnar nerve courses under the hook of the hamate and fractures can lead to ulnar injury.

question:
A 28-year-old rock climber presents to the Emergency Department following a fall onto an outstretched hand from
3 meters height. They report pain and swelling in their right wrist.
On examination:
Tender in the anatomical snuffbox
Pain on axial loading of the thumb
Decreased range of motion of the wrist
Swelling over the dorsal aspect of the wrist
Watson's test is positive
No obvious deformity
Intact neurovascular status
No other injuries noted
Which clinical finding is most specific for a scaphoid fracture in this patient?

options.text: Pain on axial loading of the thumb
Decreased range of motion of the wrist
Swelling over the dorsal aspect of the wrist

correctAnswer: Pain on axial loading of the thumb
englishExplanation:
Pain on axial loading of the thumb
Explanation
Pain on axial loading of the thumb has a specificity of 97% for scaphoid fracture. This test involves compressing the
thumb along its longitudinal axis while the wrist is in slight extension. The force is transmitted through the thumb
metacarpal to the trapezium and then to the scaphoid, making it a highly specific test for scaphoid pathology. The
high specificity means that a positive test strongly suggests a true scaphoid injury.

Explanation for incorrect answers:
A) Pain in anatomical snuffbox—While this test is sensitive (90%), it has lower specificity (40%). Many other wrist injuries, including simple soft tissue injuries, can cause snuffbox tenderness.
B) Watson's test - This test primarily assesses scapholunate instability rather than acute scaphoid fracture. A positive
test here might suggest associated ligamentous injury, but it isn't specific for fracture.
D) Decreased range of motion—This is a nonspecific finding that occurs in many wrist pathologies, including sprains,
tendinitis, and other carpal injuries.
E) Dorsal swelling - This is another nonspecific finding that can occur with any wrist trauma and doesn't specifically
indicate scaphoid involvement.

question: Which of the following statements about joint pathology is true?

options.text: Viscosity of synovial fluid increases in inflammatory or infectious arthritis.
Osteoarthritis (OA) classically affects the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal
A cardiac rub in the setting of arthralgias suggests systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

correctAnswer: A cardiac rub in the setting of arthralgias suggests systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
englishExplanation:
Viscosity decreases with any inflammatory process of the joint because of decreased 
hyaluronic acid, which is the main contributor to synovial fluid viscosity. RA classically affects the 

metaphalangeal and PIP joints of the hand, whereas OA affects the first carpometacarpal joint 
as well as the PIP and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints. SLE may cause inflammation of serosal

question: The pictured deformity in Figure below occurs in:
englishExplanation:
This is the swan neck deformity. It is caused by hyperextension at the proximal 
interphalangeal (PIP) joint and flexion at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. The DIP joint 
flexion occurs due to elongation or rupture of the extensor tendon attachment to the distal 
phalanx (i.e., similar to a mallet injury). Left untreated, PIP hyperextension occurs as a 
consequence of the distal mallet deformity. However, the deformity can begin in the PIP joint as 
well due to synovitis of the volar capsule resulting in PIP hyperextension. In the latter case, DIP 
flexion occurs as a secondary effect. Both the swan neck and boutonniere deformities are 
common in rheumatoid arthritis.

question:
A 41-year-old female with fibromyalgia syndrome presents with an acute flare of her pain. 
Her only daily medication is gabapentin, and she takes acetaminophen as needed for pain. Her 
vital signs are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy to add to 
acetaminophen for pain?
englishExplanation:
Tramadol is a useful adjunct to acetaminophen for treatment of fibromyalgia. It has 
been shown to decrease pain better than acetaminophen alone. It should be used in caution in 
patients who are on a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, as it may theoretically increase the 
risk of serotonin syndrome. Without a history of chronic opiate use and opioid tolerance, 
starting oxycodone therapy from the ED is not the best possible management for the patient’s 
health. Aspirin should no longer be used as first-line analgesic therapy for any condition. 
Furthermore, no anti-inflammatories (including all NSAIDs and steroids) work effectively in 
fibromyalgia pain management as the primary pathophysiology is not inflammatory—rather, it is 
pain hypersensitivity.

question: Which of the following is characteristic of gout but not pseudogout?

options.text: Crystal formation is the primary pathophysiology.
Dietary modifications can prevent acute attacks.
The knee and the ankle can be involved.
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is usually elevated in acute attacks.

correctAnswer: Dietary modifications can prevent acute attacks.
englishExplanation:
Gout occurs due to uric acid crystal accumulation in the joints. Mechanisms include 
uric acid overproduction and undersecretion as well as exogenous precursor ingestion of dietary 

purines converted to uric acid by xanthine oxidase. High purine foods include mussels, organ 
meats, salty fish (sardines, herrings, etc.), alcohol, and poultry. Pseudogout occurs due to 
synovial deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals. There are no dietary modifications that 
will aid in preventing pseudogout flares. Although the most common joint affected in gout is the 
first metatarsophalangeal, the knee and the ankle can also be affected. The knee is the number 
one joint to be affected in pseudogout, followed by the wrist and the ankle. ESR is elevated in 
most acute attacks of both diseases. NSAID therapy is first-line for acute attacks of both.

is most at risk for developing which of the following?
englishExplanation:
Reactive arthritis is the name which is now given to arthritis, urethritis, and 
conjunctivitis that occurs after an infection (thus, “reactive”) and which was formerly called 
Reiter syndrome. It is a reactive arthritis that occurs following C. trachomatis infection of the 
genitourinary tract or Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, or Yersinia infection of the 
gastrointestinal (GI) tract. It is part of a group of arthritides known as the seronegative 
spondyloarthropathies. This group includes ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive 
arthritis, and the arthropathy of inflammatory bowel disease. They are grouped because of their 
common involvement of the sacroiliac joint, lack of rheumatoid factor, and presence of the 
HLA-B27 genetic marker. Reiter syndrome is most common in young men aged 15 to 35 and 
occurs 2 to 6 weeks after an episode of urethritis or dysentery. The classic triad is arthritis, 
urethritis, and conjunctivitis. The arthropathy in reactive arthritis is an enthesopathy, which 
refers to pathology at the site of ligament or tendon insertion to bone. It most commonly 
involves the lower extremities, particularly the Achilles tendon (“lover’s heel”).

question: Which of the following is true regarding patients with temporal (or giant cell) arteritis?

options.text: The most specific finding is jaw claudication.
Permanent visual loss occurs in 50% of patients.
Treatment with corticosteroids should be withheld until there is biopsy-proven disease.
Vertigo is the most sensitive clinical finding.
The peak age of onset is 40 years.

correctAnswer: The most specific finding is jaw claudication.
englishExplanation:
Temporal arteritis (or giant cell arteritis) is a large vessel vasculitis that primarily 
affects branches of the carotid artery. The disease is rare before the age of 50, and incidence 
peaks in the seventh decade. The most sensitive finding is a new headache, whereas the most 
specific finding is jaw claudication. However, the disease often presents vaguely with systemic 
symptoms such as a fever of unknown origin, fatigue, malaise, and anorexia. The diagnosis 
should be considered in any older person with fever of unknown origin. Scalp pain is a more 
specific finding than headache, particularly when localized over the temporal artery. Vertigo is 
not a manifestation of the disease. Permanent visual loss occurs in only 15% of patients and is 
usually preceded by the development of blurring, diplopia, or amaurosis fugax. Corticosteroids 
are the treatment of choice and should never be withheld if the diagnosis is seriously 
considered. Multiple studies have demonstrated that treatment with steroids does not affect 
the accuracy of biopsy if performed within a few weeks.

question: Which of the following is true regarding rheumatoid arthritis (RA)?

options.text: The distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints are commonly affected.
Arthritis is commonly polyarticular and asymmetric.
Fifteen percent of patients will have a negative rheumatoid factor (RF).
The disease is equally common in women and in men.
Arthritic involvement of the spine is uncommon in RA.

correctAnswer: Fifteen percent of patients will have a negative rheumatoid factor (RF).
englishExplanation:
The DIP joints are never affected in RA, which provides a useful means of 
differentiating the disease from osteoarthritis. The arthritis of RA is typically polyarticular and 
symmetric, particularly affecting the hands (metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal 
joints), wrists, and elbows. The disease is twice as common in women and peaks in the fourth to 
sixth decade. Two thirds of patients with RA develop cervical spine disease, although thoracic 
and lumbar disease is uncommon. The disease most commonly involves the occipitoatlantoaxial 
junction, and anterior atlantoaxial subluxation may occur. RFs are autoantibodies directed at the 
crystallizable fragment (Fc) of human immunoglobulin molecules. The exact incidence of RF 
depends on the assay used and the threshold titer used to separate positive from negative 
results. In general, roughly 15% of patients with RA will be seronegative (RF within the normal 
range), and those patients tend to have milder disease.

extending up to the forearm, and had noticed that his hand occasionally 
felt cold and turned white and then blue. He had been dropping objects 
at work, where he was a toolmaker. He was a left-handed non-smoker.

englishExplanation:
2. E.  Nerve-conduction studies
The diagnosis is carpal tunnel syndrome—a condition due to an entrapment neuropathy affecting 
the median nerve in the carpal tunnel in the wrist.
It is most prevalent among middle-aged women, and is associated with a variety of conditions: 
wrist injuries (e.g. Colles’ fractures); rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory arthritides 
(which may cause synovitis or tenosynovitis of the wrist); diabetes mellitus; thyroid disease (especially hypothyroidism); peri-menopausal state; renal dialysis; acromegaly; and amyloidosis. Repetitive activities and professions involving vibrating tools may also increase the risk of carpal tunnel 
syndrome.
Although often bilateral, it may be unilateral, usually involving the dominant hand. Symptoms include 
numbness, tingling, pain (which may extend proximally as far as the elbow), and weakness. Autonomic symptoms (colour and temperature changes) may lead to the clinical picture being confused 
with Raynaud’s phenomenon, which may also lead to symptoms of pain and numbness after significant vasospasm.
Examination reveals a variety of possible abnormalities: muscle weakness and wasting (especially 
abductor and flexor pollicis brevis); sensory change (affecting the palmar aspect of the thumb, 
index, middle, and radial aspect of the ring finger); and positive provocation tests of the median 
nerve in the carpal tunnel (Tinel’s and Phalen’s).
Nerve-conduction studies show typical changes of slowing of conduction in the median nerve 
within the carpal tunnel. Other conditions which can sometimes be mistaken for carpal tunnel syndrome include thoracic outlet syndrome, cervical spondylosis/disc disease, and peripheral neuropathies (e.g. due to diabetes).

and two episodes of amaurosis fugax within the previous 48 hours. He 
had a history of hypertension and smoked ten cigarettes per day, with a 
40-pack-year smoking history.

moderate temporal scalp tenderness, and mild bilateral expiratory 
wheeze.

options.text: Intramuscular methylprednisolone 120 mg for three days
Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g for three days
Oral dexamethasone 8 mg twice a day

englishExplanation:
5. B.  Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g for three days
The diagnosis is giant cell arteritis (GCA). The combination of a new unilateral temporal headache, 
constitutional symptoms, an abnormal temporal artery, scalp tenderness, and transient visual disturbance in a man over 50 years old would be compatible with a diagnosis of complicated GCA. Other 
possible symptoms include scalp pain, fevers, symptoms of polymyalgia rheumatica, chest/throat 
pain, and jaw/tongue claudication. Additional signs include visual field/pupillary defects, retinal abnormalities (pallor, haemorrhages, arterial occlusion), upper cranial nerve palsies, and abnormalities 
in the upper limb pulses.
5% of patients with GCA do not demonstrate an inflammatory response. A temporal artery biopsy 
(TAB) should be considered, but treatment should not be delayed whilst waiting for a biopsy, especially with visual symptoms. TAB is only positive in approximately 70% of patients even without 
steroids, due to the nature of the ‘skip’ lesions in the artery. Steroids will affect the results of the 
TAB, but results may remain positive for several weeks.
The British Society for Rheumatology (BSR) Guidelines on the treatment of GCA recommend that 
complicated GCA (i.e. where visual loss is impending or threatened) treatment should be 500 mg–1 
g intravenous methylprednisolone for three days and then oral prednisolone 60 mg per day. Where 
visual loss has occurred, the starting dose of prednisolone is 60 mg per day. In uncomplicated GCA, 
the starting dose of prednisolone is 40–60 mg per day.
Dasgupta B, Borg F, Hassan N et al. BSR and BHPR Guidelines for the management of giant cell arteritis. British Society for Rheumatology. 2010.

22. B.  Parvovirus B19 arthritis
The most likely diagnosis is parvovirus B19 arthritis. Parvovirus B19 infection has also been called 
‘erythema infectiosum’ or ‘Fifth disease’. It is a single-stranded DNA virus. Parvovirus B19 infection 
is very common, often occurring in outbreaks, especially in settings such as schools and nurseries; 
non-immune adults who work in such settings are particularly susceptible to infection.
Typical symptoms of the infection include fever, malaise, headache, myalgia, nausea, and coryzal 
symptoms, which typically begin five to seven days after initial infection. Approximately one week 
later, the classical ‘slapped cheek’ rash appears; this is, however, uncommon in adults, which can 
often lead to under-diagnosis. Parvovirus infection may, especially in adults, be asymptomatic. Complications of the infection include arthritis and, more rarely, myocarditis, vasculitis, and meningoencephalitis. Parvovirus infections can precipitate significant haematological complications in those 
with pre-existing disease (e.g. haemoglobinopathies).

an acute symmetrical arthritis affecting the small joints of the hands and feet. It will typically last for 
one to three weeks, but in a small number of people may be prolonged, lasting for months; there 
are, however, no long-term sequelae. Parvovirus arthritis may cause an occasional, transient false 
positive rheumatoid factor result, reflecting the immune response to the viral infection.
Treatment is according to symptoms: simple analgesia, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs 
(NSAIDs) and, occasionally, low-dose corticosteroids have all been used.

question:
A 65-year-old Peruvian woman was visiting her daughter in London. 
She had a grand mal seizure and was brought to the emergency 
department. On arrival, she was complaining of right hip pain.
Investigations:
Figure 12.1  X-ray right hip.
What can you tell the daughter about this condition?

options.text: Her mother acquired this by ingesting food contaminated with human urine
Serological tests are not useful in diagnosis
She is likely to require lifelong anticonvulsants even with definitive treatment
Steroids should be avoided in treating this condition
The intermediate host is the pig

englishExplanation:
9. E.  The intermediate host is the pig
She has neurocysticercosis. This is the second-commonest cause of epilepsy worldwide, with TB as 
the first. It is caused by the tissue stage of Taenia solium or the ‘pork tapeworm’, and acquired by 
ingestion of ova in food contaminated by infected human faeces.
Taenia solium is actually a human tapeworm, with the pig as an intermediate host. The tapeworm 
inhabits the human gut, and is contracted by ingestion of undercooked pork, in which the intermediate stage encysts. On reaching the human gut the cyst develops and matures into an adult 
tapeworm, and eggs or segments are passed in faeces.
If humans ingest these eggs they can, like the pig, become an intermediate host. Eggs hatch within 
the gastrointestinal tract and pass into the bloodstream, and encyst in skeletal muscle, bone, eye or 
brain, persisting for many years. On dying they can elicit an acute inflammatory response, leading to 
acute symptoms. The most common presentation is with epilepsy. Other complications include hydrocephalus, focal neurological signs, psychiatric disease, encephalopathy, and cognitive impairment.
Diagnosis may be made by identifying characteristic lesions on MRI or CT. Plain radiographs may 
show rice-grain shaped calcified cysts in skeletal muscle, as in this case. Serology may be of help. 
Often the diagnosis is clinical.
Anticonvulsants and steroids are important in reducing acute symptoms, before and during antihelminthic therapy with praziquantel 50mg/kg for 15 days, albendazole 15 mg/kg daily for 15 to 30 
days (or a 10-day course with both agents). This is avoided if there is active encephalopathy for fear 
of exacerbating the inflammatory response on killing the cysts. Steroids reduce the inflammatory 
response in this situation during antihelminthic therapy.
Surgical excision of intraventricular cysts should also be considered.
O’Dempsey T. ‘Intestinal cestode infections (tapeworms) including cysticercosis’, Lecture notes: tropical medicine. Edited by Beeching N, Gill G. 7th edn. Wiley-Blackwell. 2014.

question:
A 29-year-old woman on an orthopaedic ward complained of pain 
following surgery to repair a complex fracture of her right ankle. She 
was given tramadol and within an hour she became sweaty and agitated. 
She had a past medical history of bulimia nervosa and was taking 
fluoxetine 60 mg daily, mirtazepine 30 mg at night, and diazepam 5 mg 
three times daily as required.
On examination, her temperature was 38.2°C, her pulse was 102 beats 
per minute and regular, and her blood pressure was 164/92 mmHg. 
Neurological examination revealed mydriasis, tremor, hyperreflexia, 
and increased tone in all limbs but greatest in the lower extremities 
and clonus induced by rapid dorsiflexion of the left ankle. Additional 
examination findings included normal skin colour and hyperactive bowel 
sounds.
Which medication should not be discontinued?
englishExplanation:
1. A.  Diazepam
The patient is presenting with classical symptoms of serotonin syndrome—a potentially lifethreatening syndrome often missed by clinicians. Management should include discontinuing serotonergic drugs, which would include all options apart from diazepam. Indeed, benzodiazepines are 
recommended for the control of agitation in serotonin syndrome and have been found to improve 
survival in animal models of serotonin syndrome, perhaps through a blunting of the hyperadrenergic state.
The serotonin syndrome
Serotonergic neurons in the central nervous system (CNS) assist in the regulation of wakefulness, 
affective behaviour, appetite, thermoregulation, sexual behaviour, nociception, and motor tone. 
The peripheral serotonergic system helps regulate vascular tone and gastrointestinal motility. The 
serotonin syndrome is a predictable consequence of excessive serotonergic agonism in the central 
and peripheral nervous systems. It usually occurs in overdoses of serotonergic drugs or when serotonergic medications are used in combination, although it can occur in patients taking therapeutic 
doses of serotonergic medications. A large number of medications are associated with the serotonin syndrome, including monoamine oxidase inhibitors, selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors 
(SSRIs) and other antidepressants, opiate analgesics, antiemetics, the ‘mood stabilizers’ valproate 
and lithium, antihistamines, over-the-counter cough and cold remedy dextromethorphan, and the 
herbal products tryptophan and St John’s Wort. Illicit substances associated with the serotonin syndrome include amphetamines, MDMA (‘ecstasy’), and LSD.
Its clinical manifestations range from mild to life-threatening. Mild cases involving only restlessness 
or tremor and sweating may be easily missed. With increasing severity, there is increasing vital sign 
and neuromuscular abnormalities. In life-threatening cases, patients may have severe hypertension, 
tachycardia, agitated delirium, convulsions, muscular rigidity, and core temperatures of more than 
41.0°C. No investigations confirm the diagnosis and it must be made on the patient’s history and 
examination. The history should include a full inquiry into all prescribed and over-the-counter medications and illicit substances. The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria state that in the presence of a 
serotonergic agent, serotonin syndrome is diagnosed if any of the following are present:
● Tremor and hyperreflexia
● Spontaneous clonus
● Increased muscle tone, temperature >38.0°C, and either ocular clonus or inducible clonus
● Inducible or ocular clonus and either agitation or diaphoresis
The differential diagnosis includes anticholinergic poisoning, malignant hyperthermia, and the neuroleptic malignant syndrome, but clinical differences help to differentiate between each condition, as 
illustrated in Table 16.1.

PSYCHIATRY | ANSWERS
411
Management includes discontinuation of serotonergic drugs, provision of supportive therapy, control of agitation with benzodiazepines, and consideration of serotonin 2A antagonist administration. 
Cyproheptadine, an antihistamine, is a potent 5-HT2A blocker at higher doses (12–32 mg in a 24hour period) and case-series evidence supports its use in moderate to severe cases. Bromocriptine 
and dantrolene use should be avoided. Bromocriptine can precipitate serotonin syndrome and dantrolene is ineffective in animal studies of serotonin syndrome.
Bienvenu OJ, Neufeld KJ, Needham DM. Treatment of four psychiatric emergencies in the intensive care unit. Critical Care 
Medicine 2012; 40: 2662–2670.
Boyer EW, Shannon M. The serotonin syndrome. N Engl J Med 2005; 352: 1112–1120.
Taylor D, Paton C, Kapur S. The Maudesley prescribing guidelines in psychiatry. 11th edn. Chichester: Wiley-Blackwell, 2012.

question:
A 70-year-old man with hypertension is prescribed a course of levofloxacin for a
community-acquired pneumonia. He presents two days later with acute, tearing
chest pain. A CT scan confirms a Type A aortic dissection. This is a rare but
recognised complication of which antibiotic class?
englishExplanation:
Association and Risk:
Systemic fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) are associated with a small but significant increased risk of aortic aneurysm and dissection.
The MHRA advises that these drugs should only be used in patients at risk of aortic
aneurysm (e.g., elderly, hypertension, pre-existing aneurysm) after careful benefitrisk assessment and consideration of other therapeutic options.
Pathophysiology of Toxicity:
The mechanism of connective tissue toxicity involves the upregulation of matrix
metalloproteinases (MMPs), specifically MMP-2 and MMP-9, and the downregulation of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs). This imbalance leads to the
degradation of collagen types I and III, compromising the structural integrity of the
aortic wall and tendons (particularly the Achilles tendon).
Antibiotic Mechanism of Action:
Fluoroquinolones are bactericidal agents that inhibit bacterial DNA replication by
targeting DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV. This mechanism is
distinct from the off-target effect on mammalian collagen that leads to the connective tissue complications described above.

Clinical Pearl
Aortopathy Association:
Systemic fluoroquinolone use is associated with a significantly increased risk of aortic aneurysm and dissection, particularly in older patients. This risk is mediated by
collagen degradation.
QTc Prolongation:
Fluoroquinolones, particularly moxifloxacin and levofloxacin, block the potassium
HERG channel, prolonging the QTc interval and increasing the risk of Torsades de
Pointes.
Neuropathy:
Peripheral neuropathy associated with fluoroquinolones can be acute in onset, severe, and potentially permanent. Treatment should be discontinued immediately if
symptoms arise.
Regulatory Restrictions:
The MHRA advises avoiding fluoroquinolones in patients with a history of aneurysm, family history of aneurysm, or risk factors (e.g., Marfan syndrome, EhlersDanlos, elderly) unless no other appropriate antibiotics are available.
Tendon Rupture Mechanism:
The same collagen degradation mechanism (MMP upregulation) causing aortopathy
leads to tendinopathy and tendon rupture, most commonly affecting the Achilles
tendon. This risk is increased by concomitant steroid use.
Safety Counselling:
Patients prescribed fluoroquinolones must be advised to seek immediate emergency
care if they experience sudden severe abdominal, chest, or back pain (suggestive of
dissection) or joint pain/swelling.
Seizure Threshold:
Fluoroquinolones inhibit GABA-A receptors and can lower the seizure threshold,
particularly in patients with epilepsy or those taking NSAIDs concurrently.
Dysglycaemia:
These agents can cause both hypoglycaemia (especially in diabetics on sulphonylureas) and hyperglycaemia, necessitating careful glucose monitoring in at-risk
patients.
Clostridioides difficile Risk:
Fluoroquinolones are classified as '4C' antibiotics (along with Clindamycin, Coamoxiclav, and Cephalosporins), carrying a high risk of inducing Clostridioides difficile infection.
Myasthenia Gravis Caution:

Fluoroquinolones possess neuromuscular blocking activity and can exacerbate muscle weakness in patients with myasthenia gravis. They should be avoided in this
population.
Absorption Interactions:
Oral bioavailability is significantly reduced by chelation with multivalent cations.
Administration should be separated from antacids, iron, calcium, magnesium, or
enteral feeds by at least 2-4 hours.
Moxifloxacin Pharmacokinetics:
Unlike ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin, moxifloxacin is primarily metabolised by the
liver and does not require renal dose adjustment. However, it achieves low urinary
concentrations and is unsuitable for treating urinary tract infections.

question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is treated with abatacept. This drug is a fusion protein that consists of the extracellular domain of CTLA-4 and the Fc portion of human IgG. What is its mechanism of action?

options.text: It blocks the de novo purine synthesis pathway.
It prevents the "Signal 2" co-stimulation of T-cells by binding to CD80/86 on

correctAnswer: It prevents the "Signal 2" co-stimulation of T-cells by binding to CD80/86 on
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Action:
Abatacept is a selective T-cell co-stimulation modulator. It is a soluble fusion protein comprising the extracellular domain of human CTLA-4 and the modified Fc
portion of human IgG1. It binds with high affinity to CD80 (B7-1) and CD86 (B7-2)
on antigen-presenting cells (APCs).
Physiology of T-Cell Activation:
Full T-cell activation requires two signals. Signal 1 is the specific binding of the Tcell receptor (TCR) to the antigen-MHC complex. Signal 2 is a co-stimulatory signal,
primarily mediated by CD28 on the T-cell binding to CD80/86 on the APC. Without
Signal 2, T-cells become anergic or undergo apoptosis. CTLA-4 is a natural negative
regulator that binds CD80/86 with higher affinity than CD28, displacing it to inhibit activation. Abatacept mimics this natural 'brake,' sequestering CD80/86 and
preventing Signal 2.
Distinction from Other Biologics:
Unlike rituximab (anti-CD20, B-cell depletion), tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist), or infliximab (anti-TNF alpha), abatacept specifically targets the co-stimulation pathway upstream of cytokine release.
Clinical Pearl
A 'Signal 2' Blocker:
T-cell activation requires antigen recognition (Signal 1) and co-stimulation (Signal
2). Abatacept blocks Signal 2 by binding CD80/86 on APCs, preventing their interaction with CD28 on T-cells, leading to anergy.
Checkpoint Inhibition Contrast:
The cancer immunotherapy drug ipilimumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits
CTLA-4. By blocking this inhibitory receptor, it removes the 'brake' on T-cells to enhance anti-tumour immunity. This is the physiological opposite of abatacept, which
mimics CTLA-4 to suppress immunity.
Infection Risk:
As a potent immunosuppressant, abatacept increases the risk of opportunistic infections, TB reactivation, and viral hepatitis. Screening for latent TB and Hepatitis B/C
is mandatory prior to initiation.
False Hyperglycaemia (Maltose):
The intravenous formulation of abatacept contains maltose. This can react with
GDH-PQQ based glucometers to produce falsely elevated blood glucose readings, a
critical safety issue in diabetic ICU patients.
COPD Caution:

Abatacept is associated with an increased frequency of adverse respiratory events
and COPD exacerbations. It should be used with caution in patients with significant
chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
Vaccination Timing:
Live vaccines are contraindicated during treatment and for 3 months after discontinuation due to the risk of disseminated infection. Pneumococcal and influenza
vaccinations (inactivated) are recommended prior to starting therapy.
Belatacept Distinction:
Belatacept is a second-generation CTLA-4-Ig with higher affinity for CD80/86 than
abatacept. It is primarily used in renal transplantation to avoid calcineurin inhibitor
toxicity, whereas abatacept is used in autoimmune disease.
Combination Therapy Contraindication:
Abatacept should not be combined with TNF-alpha inhibitors (e.g., adalimumab) or
other biologic DMARDs due to a significantly increased risk of serious infection
without added clinical benefit.
Sepsis Management:
In patients admitted with sepsis, abatacept must be withheld. The half-life is approximately 13-16 days, meaning immunosuppressive effects persist for weeks after
the last dose, potentially complicating source control and recovery.
Administration Routes and Maltose:
Abatacept is available as both intravenous infusion (weight-based) and subcutaneous injection (fixed dose). Crucially, only the IV formulation contains maltose;
the subcutaneous formulation does not interfere with GDH-PQQ glucometers.

question:
A 65-year-old female post-orthopedic surgery is on heparin. Her platelet count
drops from 250 to 90 x 10⁹/L. She has no active bleeding. What is the most appropriate *initial* step in the diagnostic process?

options.text: Continue heparin and monitor platelet count

englishExplanation:
Introduction:
When faced with thrombocytopenia in a heparin-exposed patient, the first step is to
formally assess the clinical likelihood of HIT before proceeding with testing or treatment changes.
Rationale for Pre-test Probability:
HIT antibody tests (like the ELISA) are very sensitive but not specific, meaning they
can have false positives. Ordering these tests indiscriminately on every patient with
thrombocytopenia leads to over-diagnosis and unnecessary, potentially harmful,
changes in anticoagulation. Therefore, a clinical decision rule is needed to determine which patients warrant testing.
The 4Ts Score:
The 4Ts score is the standard tool endorsed by the British Society for
Haematology (BSH) to calculate the pre-test probability of HIT. It assesses four
domains:

•Thrombocytopenia: Degree of fall (>50% is 2 points). •Timing: Onset relative to
heparin start (Days 5-10 is typical). •Thrombosis: New thrombosis or skin necrosis.
•oTher causes: Likelihood of alternative explanations (e.g., sepsis, drugs).
Management Based on Score:
Management is dictated by the score:
•Low Probability (0-3): HIT is very unlikely (<1%). Continue heparin and
investigate other causes. •Intermediate (4-5) or High (6-8) Probability: Stop
heparin immediately. Send HIT screen (immunological assay). Start non-heparin
anticoagulation (e.g., Argatroban, Danaparoid, or Fondaparinux/DOACs depending
on local policy and renal function) while awaiting results. Do not wait for lab
confirmation to stop heparin.
Pathophysiology:
HIT is an immune-mediated disorder caused by IgG antibodies against the platelet
factor 4 (PF4)-heparin complex. These immune complexes bind to Fc-gamma-RIIa
receptors on platelets, causing intense platelet activation, aggregation, and the release of pro-thrombotic microparticles. This results in a consumptive thrombocytopenia alongside a paradoxical hypercoagulable state due to thrombin generation.
Clinical Pearl
Clinical Risk Stratification:
Always calculate the 4Ts score before stopping heparin or ordering HIT lab tests.
This prevents unnecessary interventions in low-probability cases.
Post-Surgical Thrombocytopenia:
A mild drop in platelet count is very common after major surgery (like orthopaedics) due to haemodilution, consumption, and inflammation. This is an important 'oTher cause' to consider in the 4Ts score.
Management of High Probability Cases:
If the 4Ts score is intermediate or high, you should treat the patient as if they have
HIT (stop heparin, start alternative) while you await the results of the laboratory
tests.
Role of Bone Marrow Biopsy:
A bone marrow biopsy has no role in the diagnosis of HIT, which is a peripheral
consumptive process.
Platelet Transfusion Contraindications:
Avoid prophylactic platelet transfusions in HIT. Transfusing platelets can theoretically fuel the thrombotic process by providing more antigen target, though this is
debated. Reserve for life-threatening bleeding only.
Vitamin K Antagonists Risks:

Do not start Vitamin K Antagonists (warfarin) until the platelet count has recovered
(>150 x 10⁹/L). Early initiation can cause venous limb gangrene and skin necrosis
due to rapid Protein C depletion.
Direct Oral Anticoagulants:
Recent BSH guidance supports the use of DOACs (e.g., rivaroxaban) as initial treatment for clinically stable HIT patients without life-threatening thrombosis, offering
an oral alternative to parenteral argatroban or danaparoid.
Rapid Onset Presentation:
While typical HIT occurs 5-10 days after exposure, 'Rapid Onset' HIT can occur
within 24 hours if the patient has received heparin in the previous 100 days (circulating antibodies persist).
Diagnostic Assays:
Immunological assays (e.g., PF4-ELISA) have high sensitivity but low specificity.
Functional assays (e.g., Serotonin Release Assay or HIPA) are the gold standard
with high specificity but are technically demanding and often require referral to
specialist centres.
Pathophysiological Mechanism:
HIT is caused by IgG antibodies binding to PF4-heparin complexes. This complex
activates platelets via Fc-gamma-RIIa receptors, leading to thrombin generation. It
is distinct from non-immune heparin-associated thrombocytopenia (Type I HIT),
which is a benign, transient, non-immune interaction causing mild
thrombocytopenia.

question:
Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of co-trimoxazole
(trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)?

options.text: It inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis.
It inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosome.
It causes sequential blockade of two steps in the bacterial folic acid synthesis
It disrupts the bacterial cell membrane.

correctAnswer: It causes sequential blockade of two steps in the bacterial folic acid synthesis
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Action:
Co-trimoxazole demonstrates synergistic antimicrobial action through sequential
blockade of folate synthesis. Bacteria, unlike humans, must synthesize de novo folic
acid essential for DNA production. Sulfamethoxazole is a structural analogue of
para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) and competitively inhibits dihydropteroate synthase. Trimethoprim inhibits the downstream enzyme dihydrofolate reductase
(DHFR). This dual blockade results in bactericidal activity, whereas the individual
components are typically bacteriostatic.
Spectrum of Activity:
Co-trimoxazole has a broad spectrum covering Gram-positive (including some
MRSA) and Gram-negative organisms. It is the treatment of choice for
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP), Nocardia species, and
Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (a relevant ICU pathogen often resistant to
carbapenems).
Clinical Pearl
Sequential Blockade of Folate Synthesis:
This is the core mechanism of TMP-SMX.
Basis for Selective Toxicity:
Humans lack dihydropteroate synthase (utilizing dietary folate instead) and have a
dihydrofolate reductase isoenzyme with very low affinity for trimethoprim compared to the bacterial enzyme, minimizing toxicity to host cells.
Enzyme Targets:

Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase; Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase.
ICU Drug of Choice:
Co-trimoxazole is the first-line therapy for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
(PJP), Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, and Nocardia infections.
Pseudo-Renal Failure:
Trimethoprim inhibits the tubular secretion of creatinine, causing an isolated rise in
serum creatinine without a genuine decrease in GFR. This must be distinguished
from true nephrotoxicity (interstitial nephritis) caused by sulfonamides.
Hyperkalemia Risk:
Trimethoprim is structurally similar to the potassium-sparing diuretic amiloride. It
blocks sodium channels in the distal tubule, leading to hyperkalemia, particularly in
renal impairment or when combined with ACE inhibitors/spironolactone.
Haematological Toxicity:
Long-term or high-dose use (e.g., PJP treatment) can cause bone marrow suppression (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, megaloblastic anaemia) due to folate antagonism. Folinic acid may be co-administered to mitigate this.
Fluid Load in PJP Treatment:
Intravenous formulations require significant dilution to prevent precipitation (standard dilution is 1 ampoule per 125ml, though concentration can be increased to 1
ampoule per 75ml in central lines). The high doses required for PJP treatment result in a substantial obligatory fluid load, which can be problematic in ARDS.
Warfarin Interaction:
Co-trimoxazole significantly potentiates the effect of warfarin by inhibiting CYP2C9,
the enzyme responsible for metabolising the more active S-enantiomer of warfarin.
Close INR monitoring is essential.
Hypoglycaemia Risk:
Sulfamethoxazole is structurally similar to sulfonylureas and can stimulate pancreatic insulin release, leading to hypoglycaemia, particularly in patients with renal impairment or those on concurrent sulfonylureas.
Dermatological Emergencies:
Sulfonamides are a classic cause of severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs), including Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN).
Any sign of a blistering rash warrants immediate cessation.
Pharmacokinetic Ratio:
The fixed-dose combination is formulated in a 1:5 ratio (e.g., 80mg trimethoprim to
400mg sulfamethoxazole) to achieve the optimal synergistic plasma concentration

ratio of approximately 1:20, reflecting their different volumes of distribution.

question:
Compared with vancomycin monotherapy, the combination of vancomycin with
piperacillin-tazobactam is associated with which renal outcome?

options.text: Reduced risk of AKI due to synergistic bactericidal effect reducing infection
No significant difference in AKI incidence when AUC-guided vancomycin monitoring is used
Significantly increased risk of AKI, particularly in the first 48–72 hours of
Increased AKI risk only in patients with pre-existing CKD
Higher AKI risk only when vancomycin trough levels exceed 20 mg/L

correctAnswer: Significantly increased risk of AKI, particularly in the first 48–72 hours of
englishExplanation:
Why This Matters:
Vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam is one of the most commonly prescribed empirical antibiotic combinations in the ICU. The significantly increased nephrotoxicity risk compared to vancomycin + meropenem is a high-yield clinical pharmacology topic and directly impacts antibiotic prescribing decisions in critically ill
patients.
Analysis of Each Option:
Option A — Reduced AKI risk from faster infection clearance:
INCORRECT. While faster bacterial killing might theoretically reduce sepsis-related
AKI, this does not outweigh the direct pharmacokinetic nephrotoxicity interaction.
Multiple large studies consistently demonstrate increased AKI with VPT regardless
of clinical response.
Option B — No difference with AUC-guided monitoring:
INCORRECT. This is a common misconception. The 2022 ASHP/IDSA/SIDP
guidelines specifically acknowledge that the nephrotoxicity excess with VPT persists
even with AUC-guided vancomycin dosing (target AUC/MIC 400–600 mg·h/L).
The mechanism is independent of overall vancomycin exposure levels.
Option C — Significantly increased AKI risk, first 48–72 hours:
CORRECT. Multiple meta-analyses demonstrate a 3- to 4-fold increased AKI risk
with vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam vs vancomycin alone or vancomycin +
meropenem. AKI typically manifests within the first 48–72 hours of combination
therapy.
Option D — Only in pre-existing CKD:
INCORRECT. While pre-existing CKD does increase risk further, the nephrotoxicity
interaction occurs even in patients with normal baseline renal function. Risk stratification should not limit concern only to CKD patients.

Option E — Only when trough >20 mg/L:
INCORRECT. The OAT-mediated nephrotoxicity interaction occurs through a pharmacokinetic mechanism independent of vancomycin trough levels. Even therapeutic
trough levels do not protect against the interaction.
Mechanism:
Piperacillin-tazobactam competitively inhibits OAT1/OAT3 on the proximal tubular
basolateral membrane. These transporters normally secrete vancomycin into the
tubular lumen. Their inhibition traps vancomycin within tubular cells, causing oxidative mitochondrial injury.
Clinical Pearl
Magnitude of Risk:
Multiple meta-analyses and observational studies consistently demonstrate a 3- to
4-fold increased risk of AKI with vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam (VPT) compared to vancomycin monotherapy or vancomycin + meropenem, even when controlling for baseline renal function.
Mechanism — OAT Inhibition:
Piperacillin-tazobactam competitively inhibits organic anion transporters (OAT1
and OAT3) on the proximal tubular basolateral membrane. These transporters normally excrete vancomycin from blood into the tubular lumen. Inhibition traps vancomycin within tubular cells, increasing intracellular concentration and oxidative
mitochondrial injury.
Persists with AUC Monitoring:
Critically, the nephrotoxicity excess persists even with AUC-guided vancomycin
monitoring (target AUC/MIC 400–600). The 2022 ASHP/IDSA/SIDP guidelines
specifically acknowledge this and recommend considering an alternative beta-lactam when glycopeptide cover is required.
Vancomycin + Meropenem as Alternative:
The combination of vancomycin + meropenem does not carry the same OAT-mediated nephrotoxicity interaction. When broad Gram-positive and Gram-negative
cover is both required, vancomycin + meropenem is the preferred combination over
vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam.
Early AKI Detection:
AKI from VPT typically manifests within the first 48–72 hours of therapy. Serial
creatinine monitoring should be performed at least every 24–48 hours in patients
receiving this combination, particularly those with pre-existing renal impairment,
haemodynamic instability, or concurrent nephrotoxins.
Piperacillin-Tazobactam Alone is Not Nephrotoxic:

Piperacillin-tazobactam monotherapy does not cause significant AKI. The nephrotoxicity is specifically a pharmacokinetic drug-drug interaction mediated through
shared tubular transporters — not an intrinsic property of piperacillin-tazobactam
itself.
Risk Stratification:
Patients at highest risk of VPT-associated AKI: pre-existing CKD, baseline creatinine >100 µmol/L, concurrent vasopressors, concurrent aminoglycosides, haemodynamic instability, or age >65 years.
Clinical Consequence:
AKI in critically ill patients is independently associated with increased ICU length of
stay, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and mortality. Avoiding preventable drugrelated AKI should be a priority in antimicrobial stewardship programmes.
Nephroprotective Antibiotic Switch:
If vancomycin combination therapy is required and pip/taz-associated nephrotoxicity is a concern, substituting meropenem for piperacillin-tazobactam eliminates the
OAT1/OAT3-mediated interaction. This is not de-escalation (meropenem has
broader Gram-negative coverage including ESBLs and AmpC producers) but a deliberate switch to reduce tubular toxicity while maintaining empirical breadth.

question:
A 70-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis has anaemia. Labs: low serum
iron, low TIBC, high ferritin, low transferrin saturation. Which statement is NOT
true?

options.text: The anaemia is likely due to chronic inflammation.
The anaemia can be normocytic or microcytic.
Total Iron-Binding Capacity (TIBC) is usually low or normal.

englishExplanation:
Correct Answer Analysis:
This statement is incorrect (and therefore the correct answer). A normal or high ferritin level is a defining characteristic of the anaemia of chronic disease (ACD). In
contrast, a low ferritin level is pathognomonic for iron deficiency anaemia.
Pathophysiology Review:
ACD is driven by inflammation-mediated changes in iron homeostasis, orchestrated
by the hormone hepcidin. Hepcidin traps iron within the reticuloendothelial system (macrophages). This means that while circulating iron is low, the body's iron
stores are replete or overloaded. Ferritin is the main intracellular iron storage protein. Therefore, in ACD, ferritin levels will be normal or high. Ferritin is also an
acute-phase reactant, so the underlying inflammatory condition (like rheumatoid
arthritis) will independently cause it to be elevated.
Analysis of Other Options:
•(A) Correct. The chronic inflammation of rheumatoid arthritis is the trigger. •(B)
Incorrect. Ferritin is high. A low ferritin would indicate true iron deficiency. •(C)
Correct. Transferrin saturation (Serum Iron / TIBC) will be low because the
numerator (iron) is low and the denominator (TIBC) is also low or normal. •(D)
Correct. ACD is classically a normocytic anaemia, but can become microcytic over
time. •(E) Correct. TIBC (representing transferrin) is low or normal in response to
inflammation.
Clinical Pearl
ACD = High Ferritin, Low TIBC:

The hallmark pattern of Anaemia of Chronic Disease is: Low Serum Iron,
Low/Normal TIBC, High/Normal Ferritin. This contrasts with Iron Deficiency
Anaemia: Low Serum Iron, High TIBC, Low Ferritin.
Inflammation is the Cause:
ACD is seen in any chronic inflammatory state: autoimmune diseases (RA, lupus),
chronic infections (TB, HIV), chronic kidney disease, and cancer.
Hepcidin is the Mediator:
Think of hepcidin as the 'jailer' that locks iron up inside macrophages, making it unavailable for red blood cell production.
Functional Iron Deficiency:
ACD represents 'functional' iron deficiency (iron sequestration) rather than absolute deficiency. Oral iron is often ineffective due to hepcidin-mediated downregulation of ferroportin in the gut, which blocks absorption.
Soluble Transferrin Receptor (sTfR) Utility:
sTfR is a key discriminator when ferritin is equivocal. In pure ACD, sTfR is normal
(erythropoiesis is suppressed). In Iron Deficiency (or mixed ACD/IDA), sTfR is elevated as erythroid precursors upregulate receptors to scavenge iron.
Zinc Protoporphyrin (ZPP):
ZPP levels rise in iron deficiency (zinc replaces missing iron in heme) and lead poisoning, but are generally normal in early ACD, offering another diagnostic clue.
Ferroportin Internalisation:
The molecular mechanism of hepcidin involves binding to ferroportin, the sole cellular iron exporter. This complex is internalised and degraded, blocking iron release
from enterocytes (absorption) and macrophages (recycling).
Interleukin-6 Driver:
Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is the primary inflammatory cytokine responsible for stimulating hepatocyte synthesis of hepcidin. This links the inflammatory response directly
to iron sequestration.
Reticulocyte Haemoglobin Content:
Reticulocyte haemoglobin content (CHr or Ret-He) is a valuable real-time indicator
of iron availability for erythropoiesis. Unlike ferritin, it is not an acute-phase reactant and can help identify functional iron deficiency.
Oral Iron Resistance:
Because hepcidin downregulates gut ferroportin, patients with ACD are often resistant to oral iron therapy. If iron supplementation is indicated (e.g., in mixed deficiency), intravenous iron is typically required to bypass the gut block.
Differentiation Index:

The sTfR/log(ferritin) index is a calculated value that improves diagnostic accuracy
when distinguishing between pure ACD and ACD with co-existing iron deficiency
anaemia.

question:
A patient with lupus nephritis is treated with mycophenolate mofetil. What is the
specific mechanism of action of this immunosuppressive agent?

options.text: It is a calcineurin inhibitor that blocks the production of IL-2.
It is a prodrug of 6-mercaptopurine that inhibits purine synthesis.
It is a reversible inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), a
It is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that depletes B-cells.
It is a potent inhibitor of the TNF-alpha cytokine.

correctAnswer: It is a reversible inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), a
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Action:

Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is a prodrug that is rapidly hydrolysed to its active
metabolite, mycophenolic acid (MPA). MPA is a potent, reversible, non-competitive
inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH). IMPDH is the ratelimiting enzyme in the 'de novo' synthesis of guanosine nucleotides.
Selectivity for Lymphocytes:
T-cells and B-cells are critically dependent on the 'de novo' pathway for the generation of purines required for proliferation. Unlike other cell types, lymphocytes lack
the 'salvage' pathway (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase pathway)
to recycle purines. Consequently, MMF selectively inhibits lymphocyte proliferation
and antibody formation while largely sparing other rapidly dividing cells.
Clinical Application:
In Lupus Nephritis, MMF is recommended by NICE (NG222) and KDIGO as a firstline option for both induction therapy (often comparable to cyclophosphamide but
with less gonadal toxicity) and maintenance therapy.
Clinical Pearl
Lymphocyte-Specific:
Lymphocytes lack the purine salvage pathway, making them exclusively dependent
on de novo synthesis. This explains MMF's high specificity for T and B cells compared to other antimetabolites.
Aza vs. MMF:
MMF has largely replaced azathioprine in solid organ transplantation due to its superior efficacy and different side-effect profile.
GI Side Effects are Dose-Limiting:
Gastrointestinal toxicity (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea) is the most common doselimiting side effect. Enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium may improve tolerability
in some patients.
Teratogenic:
MMF is a potent teratogen associated with first-trimester pregnancy loss and congenital malformations. Effective contraception is mandatory before, during, and for
6 weeks after stopping therapy.
Infection Risk Profile:
MMF is particularly associated with viral reactivation, notably Cytomegalovirus
(CMV) and Herpes Zoster, more so than azathioprine. In the ICU, consider CMV tissue invasion in patients on MMF presenting with unexplained colitis or
pneumonitis.
Haematological Toxicity:

Bone marrow suppression is a major concern, primarily manifesting as neutropenia.
Regular FBC monitoring is essential, and dose reduction or interruption is required
if the absolute neutrophil count falls significantly (typically <1.3 x 10^9/L).
Lupus Nephritis Guidelines (NICE NG222):
For active proliferative lupus nephritis, MMF is a first-line induction agent (alongside corticosteroids). It is preferred over cyclophosphamide in patients concerned
about fertility, as it lacks the gonadotoxicity associated with alkylating agents.
Enterohepatic Recirculation:
MMF undergoes significant enterohepatic recycling. The inactive metabolite
(MPAG) is excreted in bile, converted back to active MPA by gut flora, and reabsorbed. This causes a secondary plasma peak 6–12 hours post-dose.
Isoform Specificity:
MMF preferentially inhibits the Type II isoform of IMPDH, which is significantly
upregulated in activated lymphocytes. Resting cells rely more on the Type I isoform,
further enhancing the drug's selectivity for active immune responses.
Drug Interactions:
Drugs that interfere with enterohepatic recirculation (e.g., cholestyramine, activated
charcoal) can significantly lower MMF exposure. Proton pump inhibitors may also
reduce absorption of MMF (less so with enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium).
Bioavailability:
MMF has excellent oral bioavailability (>90%) and the conversion from intravenous
to oral dosing is typically 1:1, facilitating early step-down from IV therapy in the
ICU.

question:
A 55-year-old kidney transplant recipient on a stable dose of azathioprine is
started on allopurinol for gout. Two weeks later, he presents with fever and pancytopenia. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A drug-drug interaction leading to severe azathioprine toxicity.
A drug-drug interaction leading to subtherapeutic azathioprine levels and graft
The development of a post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder.

correctAnswer: A drug-drug interaction leading to severe azathioprine toxicity.
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Interaction:
Azathioprine is a prodrug converted to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP). 6-MP is
metabolised via three pathways: methylation by TPMT (inactive), oxidation by
Xanthine Oxidase (inactive), or conversion to 6-thioguanine nucleotides (6-TGN,
active/cytotoxic). Allopurinol is a potent Xanthine Oxidase inhibitor. By blocking
the inactivation pathway, it shunts metabolism towards the production of cytotoxic
6-TGNs, causing severe myelosuppression.
Management:
Immediate cessation of the offending agent and supportive care for
pancytopenia/sepsis is required. If concurrent use is clinically essential, the BNF
advises reducing the azathioprine dose to one-quarter of the usual dose.
Alternative Agents:
Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is metabolised by glucuronidation and does not interact with xanthine oxidase inhibitors, making it a safer alternative in patients requiring allopurinol.
Clinical Pearl
Allopurinol + Azathioprine = Severe Myelosuppression:
This is a critical drug interaction to remember. The same applies to allopurinol and
6-mercaptopurine.
The Enzyme is Xanthine Oxidase:
Xanthine oxidase is responsible for the catabolism (inactivation) of 6-mercaptopurine. Its inhibition by allopurinol shunts metabolism towards the active, cytotoxic
thioguanine nucleotides.
Dose Reduction is Mandatory:
If co-prescription is unavoidable, the BNF mandates reducing the azathioprine dose
to one-quarter (25%) of the original dose.
Febuxostat has the Same Interaction:

Febuxostat is a potent non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor. The BNF advises
avoiding concomitant use with azathioprine entirely due to the risk of severe
toxicity.
TPMT Genotyping:
Another key factor in azathioprine metabolism is the enzyme TPMT. Patients with
low or absent TPMT activity are also at very high risk of myelosuppression.
Mycophenolate is Safe:
Mycophenolate mofetil does not utilize the xanthine oxidase pathway for metabolism. It can be safely co-administered with allopurinol without dose adjustment.
NUDT15 Polymorphism:
In addition to TPMT, NUDT15 gene variants are a significant cause of thiopurineinduced leukopenia, particularly in patients of East Asian ancestry.

question:
Which group of pulmonary hypertension (PH) is characterized by conditions like
idiopathic PH, inherited PH, and scleroderma-related PH?
englishExplanation:
WHO Classification:
The World Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension (WSPH) classifies PH into five
groups based on pathophysiology:
* Group 1 (Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension - PAH): Characterized by precapillary PH due to primary pulmonary vascular disease. Includes idiopathic, heritable (BMPR2), drug/toxin-induced, and PAH associated with connective tissue diseases (Systemic Sclerosis/Scleroderma is the most common), HIV, portal hypertension, and congenital heart disease.
* Group 2: PH due to left heart disease (HFpEF, HFrEF, valvular disease). This is
the most common cause of PH.
* Group 3: PH due to lung diseases and/or hypoxia (COPD, ILD, OSA).
* Group 4: PH due to pulmonary artery obstructions (Chronic Thromboembolic
Pulmonary Hypertension - CTEPH).
* Group 5: PH with unclear and/or multifactorial mechanisms (e.g., Sarcoidosis,
haematological disorders).
Haemodynamic Definition:
Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (Group 1) is haemodynamically defined by the
presence of pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension. Current guidelines define this as
a mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) > 20 mmHg, a pulmonary artery wedge
pressure (PAWP) ≤ 15 mmHg, and a pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) > 2
Wood Units. This distinguishes it from post-capillary PH (Group 2), where the
PAWP is > 15 mmHg.
Pathophysiology of Group 1:
The core pathology in Group 1 PAH is a vasculopathy affecting the small pulmonary
arterioles. This involves vasoconstriction, smooth muscle proliferation, endothelial
dysfunction, and thrombosis in situ. Key molecular pathways involved include overexpression of endothelin-1 (vasoconstrictor), downregulation of prostacyclin (vasodilator), and reduced nitric oxide availability. These three pathways are the targets for current specific PAH therapies.
Clinical Pearl
Group 1 = PAH:

Group 1 is synonymous with Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension. This is the group for
which targeted vasodilator therapies are primarily indicated.
Scleroderma is a Key Association:
Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma) is the connective tissue disease most strongly associated with Group 1 PAH. Screening with annual echocardiography is recommended for these patients.
Pre-Capillary by Definition:
Group 1 PAH is defined haemodynamically as pre-capillary PH: mPAP > 20 mmHg,
PAWP ≤ 15 mmHg, and PVR > 2 Wood Units according to ESC/ERS guidelines.
Treatment is Specialized:
The management of Group 1 PAH is complex and involves targeted therapies acting
on the endothelin, nitric oxide, and prostacyclin pathways.
CTEPH is an Important Differential:
Group 4 (CTEPH) is an important differential for any patient with pre-capillary PH,
as it is potentially curable with a surgical procedure (pulmonary
thromboendarterectomy).
Group 2 Distinction:
Group 2 (Left Heart Disease) is distinguished from Group 1 by a post-capillary
haemodynamic profile (PAWP > 15 mmHg). Pulmonary vasodilators are generally
contraindicated in Group 2 as they may precipitate pulmonary oedema.
Vasoreactivity Testing:
Acute vasoreactivity testing is mandatory in idiopathic, heritable, and drug-induced
PAH to identify the small subset of patients who may respond to high-dose calcium
channel blockers.
Genetics of PAH:
BMPR2 mutations are the most common genetic cause of heritable PAH.
Penetrance is incomplete (approximately 20%), meaning not all carriers develop the
disease.
Drug-Induced PAH:
Specific drugs associated with Group 1 PAH include anorexigens (e.g., fenfluramine), methamphetamines, and tyrosine kinase inhibitors like dasatinib.
Pulmonary Veno-Occlusive Disease (PVOD):
PVOD is a rare subgroup of Group 1 PAH characterized by obstruction of pulmonary
venules. Standard PAH vasodilators can precipitate life-threatening pulmonary
oedema in these patients and should be used with extreme caution.
Prognostic Importance of RV Function:

Right ventricular function is the primary determinant of survival in PAH.
Progressive RV failure, rather than the absolute level of pulmonary pressure, dictates the clinical outcome.

الفخ: الخيار Group 2 قد يبدو مناسباً ظاهرياً لكنه لا يتوافق مع المعايير السريرية المطلوبة هنا.

question: A 50-year-old on methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis is prescribed erythromycin. How might this affect her methotrexate levels?

options.text: Erythromycin will have no effect on methotrexate levels.
Erythromycin will accelerate the renal clearance of methotrexate.
Erythromycin will convert methotrexate into an inactive metabolite.

englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Interaction:
Methotrexate is primarily excreted unchanged by the kidneys via glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion. Erythromycin inhibits organic anion transporters
(OAT1/OAT3) and P-glycoprotein (P-gp) in the renal tubules. This inhibition reduces the renal clearance of methotrexate, leading to accumulation and increased
toxicity. While erythromycin is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor, methotrexate undergoes
negligible hepatic metabolism, making the CYP mechanism irrelevant in this specific interaction.
Clinical Consequences of Toxicity:
The accumulation of methotrexate primarily affects rapidly dividing cells. In the
ICU, this presents as severe bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia, neutropenic
sepsis), mucositis (stomatitis, GI ulceration, diarrhoea), and potentially acute hepatotoxicity or pneumonitis. Because methotrexate is excreted 80-90% unchanged by
the kidneys, any concurrent acute kidney injury creates a vicious cycle of accumulation and worsening toxicity.
Clinical Pearl
Macrolides Can Increase Methotrexate Levels:
Macrolides inhibit renal organic anion transporters (OATs) and P-glycoprotein, reducing methotrexate clearance. This interaction can precipitate severe toxicity even
in patients on stable long-term doses.
Methotrexate Toxicity is Serious:
High levels can cause life-threatening bone marrow suppression, mucositis, and
multi-organ failure.
Other Drugs that Increase MTX:
Other drugs that can increase methotrexate levels by reducing its renal clearance include NSAIDs, penicillins, and proton pump inhibitors.
Mechanism of Action:
Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), preventing the conversion
of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate. This depletes the intracellular pool of reduced
folates required for purine and thymidylate synthesis, halting DNA replication.
Rescue Therapy Mechanism:
Folinic acid (leucovorin) is the specific antidote for methotrexate toxicity. It is a reduced folate that bypasses the DHFR block, allowing DNA synthesis to resume.
Folic acid is ineffective for acute rescue as it requires DHFR for activation.

Trimethoprim Contraindication:
Trimethoprim is an absolute contraindication in patients taking methotrexate. Both
drugs inhibit DHFR; co-prescription causes synergistic folate antagonism leading to
severe, rapid-onset bone marrow suppression and pancytopenia.
Third-Spacing Pharmacokinetics:
Methotrexate accumulates in 'third spaces' such as pleural effusions and ascites.
These reservoirs slowly release the drug back into the circulation, prolonging the
terminal half-life and increasing systemic toxicity risk.
NSAID Interaction Mechanism:
NSAIDs increase methotrexate toxicity via two mechanisms: inhibition of renal
prostaglandin synthesis (reducing afferent arteriolar flow and GFR) and direct competition for secretion by organic anion transporters in the proximal tubule.
Methotrexate Pneumonitis:
This is a hypersensitivity reaction that can occur at any dose and is not strictly dosedependent. It presents with dyspnoea, dry cough, and fever. It is distinct from the
dose-dependent bone marrow suppression.
Glucarpidase Role:
In cases of severe methotrexate toxicity with renal failure (delayed elimination),
glucarpidase can be used. It is a recombinant enzyme that hydrolyses extracellular
methotrexate into inactive metabolites (DAMPA and glutamate), providing an alternative clearance pathway.
Urine Alkalinisation:
Methotrexate and its metabolites can precipitate in renal tubules in acidic urine.
Maintaining high urine flow and alkalinisation (pH > 7.0) increases solubility and
prevents crystalluria-induced AKI.
