question:
A 30-year-old woman with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) presents with
high fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia. Laboratory tests show a ferritin of 8,000 µg/L. You suspect Macrophage Activation Syndrome (MAS).
Which of the following laboratory findings is most specific for the T-cell activation seen in HLH/MAS?

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate showing evidence of hemophagocytosis.
Elevated serum ferritin levels above 5,000 µg/L.

englishExplanation:
Diagnosis:
The question is assessing understanding of laboratory findings that are indicative of
Macrophage Activation Syndrome (MAS), a condition associated with
Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). The correct answer is elevated soluble CD25 (sIL-2R) levels, which indicates T-cell activation.
Pathophysiology:
Macrophage Activation Syndrome is a severe, potentially life-threatening condition
characterized by excessive activation and proliferation of macrophages and T-cells.
In MAS, there is a dysregulation of immune responses leading to excessive cytokine
release, also known as a "cytokine storm." T-cells, when activated, express the alpha
chain of the IL-2 receptor, known as CD25. Soluble CD25 (sIL-2R) reflects the level
of T-cell activation in the body because its levels increase when it is shed from activated T-cells into the bloodstream.
Why C is Correct:
Elevated soluble CD25 (sIL-2R) levels are specifically associated with T-cell activation, making it a critical marker in the context of HLH/MAS. In this case, the
patient's clinical presentation including high fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia, along with elevated ferritin, suggests MAS, hence measuring sIL-2R levels
helps in confirming significant T-cell activation characteristic of HLH/MAS.
Key Distinguishing Feature:
While several laboratory findings may indicate MAS or support a diagnosis of HLH,
elevated sIL-2R is directly linked to T-cell activation, which is a core feature of the
syndrome. This marker not only assists in diagnosis but also correlates with disease
activity, making it distinct from other laboratory parameters that may reflect secondary changes or other complications.
Why Not the Others:
A: Bone marrow aspirate showing evidence of hemophagocytosis is important for
diagnosis but is not specific for T-cell activation; it can also occur in a variety of
other conditions.
B: Elevated serum ferritin levels above 5,000 µg/L, though suggestive, is not specific for T-cell activation as high ferritin can occur in several inflammatory conditions.

D: Hypertriglyceridemia and hypofibrinogenemia are indicative of systemic inflammation and liver involvement but do not specifically indicate T-cell activation.
E: Elevated liver enzymes (AST/ALT) and LDH are reflective of systemic inflammation and organ dysfunction and are not specific to T-cell activation.
Clinical Pearl
HLH Pathophysiology:
HLH is characterised by uncontrolled immune activation with macrophage and cytotoxic T-cell hyperactivity, leading to a cytokine storm.
sCD25 Significance:
sCD25 (soluble IL-2 receptor alpha-chain) is shed by activated T-cells and directly
reflects the degree of pathological T-cell activation in HLH.
Ferritin Threshold:
Ferritin >10,000 mcg/L is strongly suggestive of HLH but not pathognomonic - it
can also rise in sepsis, liver failure, and other inflammatory states.
HLH-2004 Criteria:
Diagnosis requires 5 of 8 features: fever, splenomegaly, 2+ cytopenias,
hypertriglyceridaemia/hypofibrinogenaemia, haemophagocytosis, low NK activity,
sCD25 >=2400 U/mL, ferritin >=500 mcg/L.
Hypertriglyceridaemia Mechanism:
Cytokines (particularly TNF-alpha and IL-1) inhibit lipoprotein lipase activity, causing hypertriglyceridaemia.
Hypofibrinogenaemia:
Hypofibrinogenaemia reflects consumptive coagulopathy driven by macrophage activation and DIC - a marker of disease severity.
Haemophagocytosis Caveat:
Bone marrow haemophagocytosis lacks specificity (also seen in sepsis) and may be
absent early in HLH - it is not required for diagnosis.
Secondary HLH Triggers:
Secondary HLH most commonly occurs in SLE, lymphoma, EBV infection, and sepsis - always identify and treat the underlying trigger.
The H-Score:
The H-Score is a validated clinical tool used to estimate the probability of reactive
haemophagocytic syndrome (secondary HLH/MAS). It incorporates nine parameters: temperature, organomegaly (hepatomegaly, splenomegaly), number of cytopenias, triglycerides, fibrinogen, ferritin, AST, immunosuppressed status, and evidence of haemophagocytosis on bone marrow aspirate. Scores are weighted and

summed - a score >169 carries >93% probability of HLH. Unlike the HLH-2004 diagnostic criteria, the H-Score was specifically developed and validated for
secondary/reactive HLH in adults and is increasingly used as the primary bedside
diagnostic tool in ICU practice. An online calculator is freely available at
mdcalc.com.

question:
A 25-year-old male presents with severe muscle pain and dark urine after a
marathon. Labs show very high CK, myoglobinuria, and hyperkalemia. Which
electrolyte abnormality is *not* typically seen in the acute phase of this
condition?
englishExplanation:
Introduction:
The condition described is rhabdomyolysis. The electrolyte disturbances are a direct
result of the release of intracellular contents from necrotic muscle cells.
Pathophysiology:
Skeletal muscle cells are rich in potassium, phosphate, and various enzymes (like
CK). When the muscle cell membrane is damaged, these contents leak out into the
circulation.
•Hyperkalaemia (A): The release of large amounts of intracellular potassium can
cause acute, life-threatening hyperkalaemia. •Hyperphosphataemia (B):
Phosphate is also released from the damaged muscle, causing hyperphosphataemia.
•Hypocalcaemia (C): In the acute injury phase, the high levels of phosphate
released precipitate with serum calcium. Furthermore, calcium is sequestered into
the injured muscle tissue due to increased sarcolemmal permeability. This
combination leads to hypocalcaemia. •Hyponatraemia (E): This is often seen
due to the shift of extracellular fluid and sodium into the injured muscle cells (thirdspacing).
Conclusion:
Hypercalcaemia (D) is not seen in the acute phase. It can, however, occur as a
late complication during the recovery phase (diuretic phase), as the calcium that
was deposited in the muscle is mobilised back into the circulation.
Clinical Pearl
Acute Phase = Low Calcium:
In the initial phase of rhabdomyolysis, expect hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia,
and hypocalcaemia.
Recovery Phase = High Calcium:
Hypercalcaemia is a late finding (recovery/diuretic phase), caused by the mobilisation of calcium previously sequestered in muscle tissue and rebound
hyperparathyroidism.
CK is the Marker:
A massively elevated Creatine Kinase (CK) level (often >5,000 to >100,000 IU/L) is
the hallmark laboratory finding.
Kidney Injury Mechanisms:
Rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI involves three mechanisms: renal vasoconstriction
(hypovolaemia/haem scavenging NO), tubular obstruction (myoglobin casts), and

direct tubular toxicity (haem-induced oxidative stress).
Fluid Resuscitation:
Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation is the cornerstone of treatment. Aim for a high
urine output (e.g., 200-300 mL/hr) until myoglobinuria clears.
Bicarbonate and Mannitol Controversy:
Routine use of sodium bicarbonate or mannitol is not supported by high-quality evidence. They may be considered in specific cases (e.g., severe acidosis or failure to
achieve diuresis) but are secondary to crystalloid resuscitation.
Compartment Syndrome Risk:
Monitor for compartment syndrome, particularly in traumatic rhabdomyolysis or
unconscious patients. Intracompartmental pressures >30 mmHg may require
fasciotomy.
Urinalysis Discrepancy:
Myoglobin causes a positive dipstick for blood (haem pigment) but microscopy
shows few or no red blood cells. This dissociation is a key diagnostic clue.
Hyperuricaemia Mechanism:
Breakdown of muscle cell nuclei releases purines, leading to hyperuricaemia. This
contributes to tubular obstruction via uric acid crystal formation.
ECG Monitoring:
Continuous cardiac monitoring is essential due to the rapid rise in potassium. Look
for peaked T waves, PR prolongation, and QRS widening.
Renal Replacement Therapy:
Early RRT may be required for refractory hyperkalaemia, severe metabolic acidosis,
or fluid overload, rather than waiting for conventional uraemic indications.
Etiological Categories:
Causes are broadly traumatic (crush injury, compartment syndrome) or non-traumatic (exertion, heat stroke, drugs like statins/cocaine, seizures, infections).

question:
A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presents with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. A bronchoscopy is performed, and the sequential BAL
returns become progressively bloodier. This is diagnostic of Diffuse Alveolar

Hemorrhage (DAH). What is the first-line treatment for this life-threatening autoimmune emergency?
englishExplanation:
First-Line Management:
The immediate first-line treatment for Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage (DAH) secondary to SLE is high-dose intravenous corticosteroids (typically methylprednisolone 500mg-1g daily for 3 days). This targets the underlying immune-mediated
pulmonary capillaritis. While infection must be excluded or covered empirically, delaying steroid therapy in active autoimmune DAH carries a high mortality risk.
Adjunctive and Escalation Therapies:
Following steroid initiation, induction immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide
or rituximab is standard for severe SLE manifestations. Plasma exchange (PLEX) is
reserved for specific indications such as concurrent Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic
Purpura (TTP), Catastrophic Antiphospholipid Syndrome (CAPS), or anti-GBM disease, though some centres use it for refractory SLE-DAH. Tranexamic acid may be
used as a nebulised adjunct but does not treat the underlying cause.
Clinical Pearl
'Progressively Bloodier BAL':
This is the pathognomonic finding on bronchoscopy that confirms DAH.
A Pulmonary-Renal Emergency:
DAH often occurs as part of a 'pulmonary-renal syndrome,' with a concurrent
rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
The 'Big Three' Causes:
The three main immunological causes of DAH to remember are ANCA-associated
vasculitis (GPA, MPA), Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture's syndrome), and Systemic
Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
'Steroids First, Ask Questions Later':
In patients with known autoimmune disease presenting with life-threatening DAH,
high-dose steroids should be initiated immediately. Empirical broad-spectrum antimicrobials are co-administered until infection is definitively excluded, as sepsis
can mimic or precipitate DAH.
The KCO Paradox:
An elevated gas transfer (TLCO/KCO) is a hallmark of acute alveolar haemorrhage.
The presence of intra-alveolar haemoglobin binds carbon monoxide avidly, resulting in a supranormal KCO, often >120-140% predicted, unlike other causes of alveolar shadowing.
Hemosiderin-Laden Macrophages:

While sequential bloody BAL is diagnostic of acute bleeding, the presence of
hemosiderin-laden macrophages on cytology indicates subacute or chronic haemorrhage (appearing >48 hours after onset).
Lupus-Specific Associations:
DAH in SLE is rare (<5% of cases) but carries a high mortality (~50%). It is frequently associated with active lupus nephritis; urinalysis is mandatory to identify
red cell casts or proteinuria indicative of pulmonary-renal syndrome.
Infection Mimics:
In immunosuppressed SLE patients, opportunistic infections such as
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonitis or Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP)
can present with similar bilateral infiltrates and hypoxaemia. CMV PCR and PJP
immunofluorescence on BAL fluid are essential investigations.
Nebulised Tranexamic Acid:
Nebulised tranexamic acid (typically 250-500 mg) can be used as a local haemostatic adjunct in DAH. It aims to inhibit alveolar fibrinolysis without the systemic
thrombotic risks associated with high-dose IV administration.
Urinalysis Importance:
Urinalysis is a critical bedside test in suspected DAH. The presence of dysmorphic
red blood cells or red cell casts suggests active glomerulonephritis, strongly supporting a diagnosis of pulmonary-renal syndrome (e.g., vasculitis or SLE) rather
than isolated pulmonary pathology.
Plasma Exchange Indications:
While not first-line for SLE-DAH generally, plasma exchange is the primary treatment for Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture's) to remove pathogenic antibodies. In
SLE, it is reserved for refractory cases or when there is concurrent Thrombotic
Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) or Catastrophic Antiphospholipid Syndrome
(CAPS).
Macrophage Activation Syndrome:
Patients with severe SLE flares are at risk of Macrophage Activation Syndrome
(MAS), a form of secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). Features
include persistent fever, hyperferritinaemia, pancytopenia, and liver dysfunction,
requiring aggressive immunosuppression.

question: A 55-year-old ICU patient with late-onset HAP has cultures positive for MRSA. The patient has moderate renal impairment and a documented history of an anaphylactic reaction to vancomycin. What is the most appropriate antibiotic therapy?

options.text: Administer vancomycin with a slow infusion and pre-treat with antihistamines.
Linezolid 600 mg IV twice a day.

correctAnswer: Linezolid 600 mg IV twice a day.
englishExplanation:
**Management of MRSA Pneumonia:**
   - Linezolid is the preferred agent for MRSA pneumonia when vancomycin is contraindicated.
   - It demonstrates superior penetration into the epithelial lining fluid (ELF) of the lung compared to glycopeptides.
   - UK guidelines recommend linezolid or vancomycin (with variable positioning depending on local stewardship) for confirmed MRSA pneumonia, but linezolid is the clear choice here due to the patient's allergy profile.
  **Contraindications and Safety:**
   - A history of anaphylaxis (IgE-mediated Type 1 hypersensitivity) is an absolute contraindication to vancomycin.
   - This must be distinguished from 'Red Man Syndrome' (non-immunological histamine release), which is managed by slowing the infusion.
   - Daptomycin is contraindicated in pneumonia as it is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant, leading to therapeutic failure.
  **Renal Considerations:**
   - The patient has moderate renal impairment.
   - Linezolid requires no dose adjustment for renal failure, making it pharmacokinetically favorable.
   - Conversely, Ceftaroline (Option E) is active against MRSA but requires dose reduction in moderate renal impairment (CrCl 30-50 ml/min) and has less established evidence for HAP compared to linezolid.
  **Linezolid Lung Penetration:**
   - Linezolid is the preferred alternative to vancomycin for MRSA pneumonia due to superior epithelial lining fluid (ELF) penetration and 100% oral bioavailability, facilitating IV-to-oral switch.
  **Daptomycin Contraindication:**
   - Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant, resulting in therapeutic failure in pneumonia; it is indicated for MRSA bacteraemia and right-sided endocarditis.
  **Linezolid Adverse Effects:**
   - Prolonged linezolid therapy (>14 days) risks dose-dependent myelosuppression (particularly thrombocytopenia), optic/peripheral neuropathy, and lactic acidosis.
   - Weekly FBC monitoring is mandatory.
  **Linezolid Renal Pharmacokinetics:**
   - Linezolid requires no dose adjustment in renal failure.
   - In contrast, vancomycin, te icoplanin, and ceftaroline all require dose modification based on creatinine clearance or therapeutic drug monitoring.
  **Vancomycin Infusion Reaction:**
   - Vancomycin infusion reaction (formerly 'Red Man Syndrome') is a common, non-allergic histamine release reaction caused by rapid infusion.
   - It is distinct from true IgE mediated anaphylaxis.
  **Linezolid Drug Interactions:**
   - Linezolid is a reversible, non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI).
   - Co-administration with SSRIs, tricyclics, or opioids (e.g., pethidine, fentanyl) increases the risk of serotonin syndrome.
  **Linezolid Mechanism of Action:**
   - Linezolid is an oxazolidinone that inhibits the initiation of bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 23S ribosomal RNA of the 50S subunit, preventing the formation of the 70S initiation complex.
  **Ceftaroline Pharmacology:**
   - Ceftaroline is a fifth-generation cephalosporin with activity against MRSA due to its high affinity for penicillin-binding protein 2a (PBP2a), which mediates methicillin resistance.
  **Mitochondrial Toxicity Mechanism:**
   - The mechanism of linezolid-induced lactic acidosis and myelosuppression is the inhibition of mitochondrial protein synthesis, which structurally resembles bacterial protein synthesis.
  **Teicoplanin in Pneumonia:**
   - While teicoplanin is active against MRSA, it has variable lung penetration and requires aggressive loading doses.
   - It is generally considered a second-line alternative to linezolid or vancomycin for HAP.

question: A patient in the ICU with MRSA ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is not improving on vancomycin. The team is considering switching to an alternative agent. Which of the following antibiotics is a poor choice for treating pneumonia specifically because it is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant?
englishExplanation:
**Mechanism of Action:**
   - Daptomycin is a cyclic lipopeptide antibiotic that exerts bactericidal activity by inserting into bacterial cell membranes in a calcium-dependent manner, causing rapid depolarization and potassium efflux.
   - However, it is contraindicated in pneumonia because it binds with high affinity to the dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine component of pulmonary surfactant.
   - This sequestration inactivates the drug within the alveolar space, preventing it from achieving adequate minimum inhibitory concentrations (MIC) despite therapeutic serum levels.
  **Clinical Context:**
   - For MRSA ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) where vancomycin is ineffective or contraindicated, Linezolid is the preferred alternative in UK practice (NICE NG191).
   - Unlike vancomycin, which has variable lung penetration (ELF:plasma ratio ~0.4–0.5), Linezolid possesses excellent lung tissue penetration with an ELF:plasma ratio of ~4.0, ensuring high concentrations at the site of infection.
  **Pharmacology of Alternatives:**
   - Linezolid is an oxazolidinone that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit, preventing the formation of the initiation complex.
   - Ceftaroline is a fifth-generation cephalosporin that retains activity against MRSA by binding to penicillin-binding protein 2a (PBP2a), which has low affinity for other beta-lactams.
  **Surfactant Inactivation:**
   - Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant via high-affinity binding to di palmitoylphosphatidylcholine.
   - It should never be used for the treatment of pneumonia, regardless of the organism's susceptibility profile.
  **Linezolid Pharmacokinetics:**
   - Linezolid is the primary alternative to glycopeptides for MRSA pneumonia due to superior lung tissue penetration.
   - It achieves epithelial lining fluid (ELF) concentrations approximately 4-fold higher than plasma concentrations.
  **Daptomycin Myotoxicity:**
   - Daptomycin is associated with skeletal muscle toxicity ranging from myalgia to rhabdomyolysis.
   - Weekly monitoring of Creatine Kinase (CK) is mandatory during therapy, increasing to more frequent monitoring in patients with renal impairment or concomitant statin use.
  **Toxin Suppression Strategy:**
   - In severe, necrotizing MRSA pneumonia caused by Panton-Valentine Leukocidin (PVL) toxin-producing strains, protein synthesis inhibitors like clindamycin or linezolid are recommended to suppress toxin production.
  **Linezolid Adverse Effects:**
   - Linezolid use is limited by duration-dependent bone marrow suppression (particularly thrombocytopenia after 10-14 days) and mitochondrial toxicity (lactic acidosis, optic neuropathy) associated with prolonged courses.
  **Drug Interactions:**
   - Linezolid is a weak, reversible non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI).
   - Caution is required when co-administering with serotonergic agents (SSRIs, TCAs, fentanyl) to avoid serotonin syndrome.
  **Ceftaroline Mechanism:**
   - Ceftaroline is a fifth-generation cephalosporin with anti-MRSA activity mediated by binding to PBP2a.
   - Unlike daptomycin, it is not inactivated by surfactant and can be considered for MRSA pneumonia, particularly as salvage therapy.
  **Vancomycin Lung Penetration:**
   - Vancomycin is a large hydrophilic molecule with relatively poor lung tissue penetration (ELF:plasma ratio ~0.4–0.5).
   - Achieving therapeutic levels in the lung often requires aggressive serum trough targets (15–20 mg/L), increasing the risk of nephrotoxicity.
  **Renal Dosing Considerations:**
   - Daptomycin requires dosing interval adjustment in severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 ml/min) to prevent accumulation and myotoxicity.
   - Linezolid does not require dose adjustment in renal failure, although its metabolites may accumulate.

الفخ: الخيار Linezolid قد يبدو مناسباً ظاهرياً لكنه لا يتوافق مع المعايير السريرية المطلوبة هنا.

question: A patient with an infected prosthetic joint has been on linezolid for 6 weeks. They now complain of painful tingling in their feet and blurred vision. These symptoms are most likely due to which mechanism of linezolid toxicity?

options.text: Disruption of bacterial folic acid synthesis

englishExplanation:
**Mechanism of Toxicity:**
   - Linezolid acts by binding to the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit of the bacterial ribosome, preventing the formation of the 70S initiation complex.
   - Human mitochondrial ribosomes share significant structural homology with bacterial ribosomes.
   - Consequently, linezolid can cross-react and inhibit mitochondrial protein synthesis.
   - This mitochondrial dysfunction manifests clinically as lactic acidosis, myelosuppression (particularly thrombocytopenia), and neuropathies (peripheral and optic).
   - These effects are typically associated with prolonged courses (>28 days).
  **Clinical Implications:**
   - Peripheral neuropathy is often a 'glove and stocking' sensory distribution and may be irreversible.
   - Optic neuropathy presents as decreased visual acuity, blurred vision, or loss of colour vision and warrants immediate cessation of the drug.
   - Lactic acidosis is a direct consequence of disrupted mitochondrial respiration.
  **Pharmacological Classification:**
   - Linezolid is a synthetic oxazolidinone antibiotic.
   - Its unique mechanism of action— binding to the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit to prevent formation of the 70S initiation complex—means it lacks cross-resistance with other protein synthesis inhibitors like macrolides, lincosamides, or tetracyclines.
  **Mitochondrial Pathophysiology:**
   - Inhibition of mitochondrial protein synthesis is the unifying mechanism for the major long-term side effects of linezolid, including lactic acidosis and neuropathy.
  **Duration-Dependent Toxicity:**
   - The risk of mitochondrial toxicities increases significantly with treatment duration, especially when the course exceeds 28 days.
  **Haematological Monitoring:**
   - Weekly full blood counts are recommended for all patients.
   - Thrombocytopenia is the most common haematological toxicity, typically occurring after 10-14 days of therapy.
  **Neuropathy Prognosis:**
   - Linezolid should be discontinued promptly if new neurologic or visual symptoms develop.
   - Peripheral neuropathy may be irreversible even after drug cessation.
  **Lactic Acidosis:**
   - A rare but serious complication of linezolid, also related to mitochondrial dysfunction.
  **Serotonin Syndrome Risk:**
   - Linezolid is a reversible, non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI).
   - Co-administration with SSRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, 5-HT3 antagonists (e.g., ondansetron), or pethidine carries a risk of serotonin syndrome.
  **Tyramine Interaction:**
   - Due to MAO inhibition, patients should avoid tyramine-rich foods (e.g., mature cheese, yeast extracts, fermented soy) to prevent hypertensive crises, although this interaction is generally weaker than with irreversible MAOIs.
  **Visual Monitoring:**
   - Patients receiving linezolid for >28 days require formal visual function monitoring.
   - Any report of visual changes mandates immediate ophthalmic assessment.
  **Bioavailability:**
   - Linezolid has approximately 100% oral bioavailability, allowing for a 1:1 conversion from intravenous to oral dosing without dose adjustment.
   - This facilitates early discharge or OPAT.
  **Renal Impairment:**
   - No dose adjustment is required in renal failure.
   - However, the two primary metabolites may accumulate in patients with severe renal impairment, the clinical significance of which is unknown.
  **Spectrum of Activity:**
   - Linezolid is active against Gram-positive bacteria, including Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Vancomycin-Resistant Enterococci (VRE).
   - It is bacteriostatic against enterococci and staphylococci, but bactericidal against streptococci.

question: Imipenem is co-formulated with cilastatin primarily for which reason?

options.text: To enhance CNS penetration of imipenem
To broaden the spectrum against Pseudomonas aeruginosa
To prevent hydrolysis of imipenem by renal dehydropeptidase-I
To reduce the risk of Clostridioides difficile colitis
To improve oral bioavailability of imipenem

correctAnswer: To prevent hydrolysis of imipenem by renal dehydropeptidase-I
englishExplanation:
**Why This Matters:**
   - Understanding the imipenem/cilastatin combination is a classic pharmacology question in critical care.
   - Cilastatin has no antimicrobial activity — its sole purpose is pharmacokinetic protection.
   - This concept frequently appears in FFICM and critical care pharmacology assessments.
  **Analysis of Each Option:**
   - Option A — CNS penetration: INCORRECT.
   - Cilastatin does not improve CNS penetration.
   - Imipenem actually has poorer CNS penetration compared to meropenem and carries a significantly higher seizure risk, particularly in patients with CNS pathology or renal impairment.
   - Meropenem is the preferred carbapenem for CNS infections.
   - Option B — Pseudomonas spectrum: INCORRECT.
   - Cilastatin does not alter antimicrobial spectrum.
  **Key Distinction:**
   - Meropenem and ertapenem are structurally modified to resist DHP-I hydrolysis — they do not require cilastatin.
   - Meropenem also carries a lower seizure risk than imipenem, making it preferred for CNS infections and patients with epilepsy.
  **DHP-I Hydrolysis:**
   - Imipenem is uniquely susceptible to hydrolysis by renal dehydropeptidase-I (DHP-I) on the brush border of proximal tubular cells.
   - Without cilastatin, imipenem is cleaved to nephrotoxic metabolites and loses >70% of urinary activity.
  **Cilastatin is NOT an Antibiotic:**
   - Cilastatin has no intrinsic antibacterial activity.
   - It is a selective competitive inhibitor of DHP-I that exists solely to protect imipenem from degradation in the renal tubule.
   - It also attenuates imipenem-related nephrotoxicity independently.
  **Meropenem Stability:**
   - Meropenem is structurally modified at the 1-beta position to resist DHP-I hydrolysis.
   - It does not require cilastatin co-administration.
   - Ertapenem shares this stability.
  **Seizure Risk:**
   - Imipenem carries a significantly higher risk of seizures compared to meropenem, particularly in patients with CNS pathology, prior seizure history, or renal impairment (which raises imipenem plasma levels).
   - Meropenem is the preferred carbapenem for CNS infections.
  **Spectrum Difference:**
   - Ertapenem lacks activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter species — despite being a carbapenem.
   - Imipenem and meropenem retain pseudomonal cover.
   - This distinction is frequently tested in critical care pharmacology.
  **ESBL Coverage:**
   - Carbapenems are the treatment of choice for extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacterales.
   - They are stable to hydrolysis by ESBLs (Class A) but are inactivated by carbapenemases (KPC, NDM, OXA-48).
  **Carbapenem-Resistant Organisms:**
   - Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) are classified as Priority 1 Critical pathogens by the WHO.
   - Treatment options are limited: ceftazidime-avibactam (for KPC/OXA-48), aztreonam-avibactam (for NDM), or colistin-based regimens.
  **Renal Dose Adjustment:**
   - Both imipenem and meropenem require dose reduction in significant renal impairment.
   - Imipenem particularly accumulates in AKI, further increasing seizure risk.
   - Meropenem extended-infusion dosing (over 3 hours) optimises time-dependent killing against resistant organisms.
  **MRSA Coverage:**
   - No carbapenem has activity against MRSA.
   - If MRSA is a concern in a critically ill patient requiring broad-spectrum cover, a glycopeptide (vancomycin) or lipopeptide (daptomycin) must be added.

question: A 65-year-old man with MRSA endocarditis is being treated with a high-dose (10 mg/kg) daptomycin infusion. Which laboratory test must be monitored weekly to screen for this drug's most significant dose-dependent toxicity?
englishExplanation:
**Mechanism of Toxicity:**
   - Daptomycin is a cyclic lipopeptide that inserts into bacterial cell membranes, causing rapid depolarisation.
   - However, it can also interact with mammalian skeletal muscle membranes, leading to myopathy and potential rhabdomyolysis.
   - This toxicity is dose dependent, with risks increasing significantly at doses >8 mg/kg/day and in patients with renal impairment.
  **Monitoring Guidelines:**
   - The BNF and SPC mandate baseline Creatine Kinase (CK) measurement for all patients.
   - During therapy, CK must be monitored weekly.
   - More frequent monitoring (e.g., every 2-3 days) is indicated in patients with renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min), those taking concomitant myotoxic drugs (e.g., statins, fibrates, ciclosporin), or those with baseline CK elevation (>5x ULN).
  **Management of Toxicity:**
   - If patients develop unexplained muscle pain/weakness and CK >1000 U/L (approx.
   - 5x ULN), or if they are asymptomatic but CK >2000 U/L (approx.
   - 10x ULN), daptomycin should be discontinued immediately.
  **Skeletal Muscle Toxicity:**
   - All patients on daptomycin require a baseline CK measurement and weekly monitoring during therapy to screen for myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.
  **Statin Interaction:**
   - The risk of myopathy increases when daptomycin is co-administered with HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins).
   - UK guidelines advise considering the temporary suspension of statins and fibrates during daptomycin therapy.
  **Pulmonary Inactivation:**
   - Daptomycin must never be used to treat pneumonia as it is bound and inactivated by pulmonary surfactant, rendering it ineffective in the alveolar space.
  **Pharmacodynamics:**
   - Daptomycin exhibits concentration-dependent killing.
   - It is dosed as a single large daily dose to maximise the Cmax/MIC ratio (Peak/MIC), which is the PK/PD index predictive of efficacy.
  **Renal Dosing Strategy:**
   - Daptomycin requires dose adjustment in severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min).
   - The strategy involves maintaining the dose magnitude (to preserve Cmax) but extending the interval to every 48 hours (to prevent accumulation).
  **Eosinophilic Pneumonia:**
   - A rare but serious adverse effect is eosinophilic pneumonia, typically presenting 2-4 weeks after initiation with fever, dyspnoea, and hypoxic respiratory failure.
   - Diagnosis requires bronchoalveolar lavage showing >25% eosinophils.
  **Coagulation Assay Interference:**
   - Daptomycin can cause a false prolongation of PT and INR due to an interaction with the phospholipid reagents used in the laboratory assay.
   - This is an artifact and does not represent true anticoagulation.
  **Licensed Indications:**
   - Daptomycin is licensed for complicated skin and soft tissue infections (cSSTI), right sided infective endocarditis (RIE) due to Staphylococcus aureus, and associated bacteraemia.
   - It is not licensed for left-sided endocarditis, though often used off-label.
  **Mechanism of Action:**
   - Daptomycin binds to bacterial membranes in a calcium-dependent process, causing oligomerisation and channel formation.
   - This leads to rapid potassium efflux, membranedepolarisation, and inhibition of DNA/RNA synthesis without cell lysis (limiting endotoxin release).
  **Dosing Weight:**
   - Daptomycin should be dosed based on Total Body Weight (TBW), even in obese patients.
   - This contrasts with hydrophilic antibiotics like aminoglycosides which often use adjusted body weight.

question: A 35-year-old man comes to the emergency department 6 hours after he cut his foot while surfing in the ocean. He is otherwise healthy, and his immunizations are up-to-date. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse rate is 95/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/87 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical examination shows a 3-cm laceration to the sole. Some associated erythema is noted extending up the calf with hemorrhagic bullae. X-ray study of the leg shows no abnormalities, and bedside exploration shows no foreign bodies. Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic therapy?
englishExplanation:
Ceftazidime and doxycycline
Expl anation
A. Ceftazidime and doxycycline
Soft-tissue infections following salt or brackish water exposure must be treated aggressively with coverage for V. vulnificus because they can rapidly progress to
necrosis and sepsis. Skin lesions should be cultured and stained. The CDC recommends combination therapy with intravenous ceftazidime and a tetracycline (e.g.
doxycycline). V. vulnificus is a lethal disease with an overall mortality rate of approximately 35%•
Further information: Kam Cheong Wong et al, Antibiotic use for Vibrio infections:
important insights from surveillance data, BMC Infect Dis. 2015; 15: 226.
B. Levofloxacin and vancomycin
This patient's history is concerning for Vibrio infection. Vancomycin is indicated for
possible methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection.
C. Levofloxacin or doxycycline
Mild wound infections in patients who do not have significant comorbidities may
generally respond well to oral antibiotics (such as doxycycline or a fluoroquinolone).
In this patient's case, with fever, tachycardia, and hemorrhagic bullae, broader antibiotic therapy is necessary.
D. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus an aminoglycoside
Since doxycycline and fluoroquinolones are sometimes contraindicated in children,
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus an aminoglycoside is the preferred alternative

question: A 9-year-old boy is brought in by his mother because he has had lesions on the posterior aspect of his knees for the past four months. A photograph of the lesions is shown. Which of the following is considered the first-line treatment for this condition?
englishExplanation:
Topical steroids
Expl anation
A. Lukewarm baths
Lukewarm baths are the first-line treatment for nummular dermatitis. Nummular
dermatitis is an inflammatory skin condition with multiple pruritic coin-shaped lesions, most commonly on the extremities. Treatment focuses on lifestyle changes to
reduce exposures to skin irritants, such as bathing in lukewarm water, using gentle,
hypoallergenic cleansers and detergents, and moisturizing. Topical corticosteroids
can also be helpful.
B. Phototherapy
Phototherapy is a second-line treatment in the management of severe atopic dermatitis that is uncontrolled on topical treatments. It can be used in combination
with emollients and topical corticosteroids. Multiple treatments are usually necessary. Adverse effects include an increased risk of skin cancer.
C. Topical steroids
Atopic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that causes severe dryness and pruritus. Topical corticosteroids with emollients are considered the firstline treatment. Emollients should be used multiple times a day. Corticosteroid potency depends on the severity of disease, the patient's age, and the location of the
rash.
Further information: https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dermatologicdisorders/dermatitis/atopic-dermatitis-eczema;
https : / /www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448071/
D. Zinc oxide ointment
This is the first-line treatment for diaper dermatitis. Zinc oxide ointment is a barrier
agent that prevents moisture and chemicals from touching the skin.

question: A 33-year-old gardener with no past medical history presents with a nodular rash that started on the dorsum of her hand and now appears to be tracking up her arm. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse rate is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/87 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. On physical exam, she has several painless papulonodular, erythematous lesions the size of a quarter on the dorsum of her hand that tracks proximally up the dorsal aspect of her arm. Laboratory studies are unremarkable. What is the next best step in managing this patient?
englishExplanation:
Itraconazole
Expl anation
A. Amphotericin B
Amphotericin B is recommended for disseminated, life-threatening or visceral
sporotrichosis not simple lymphocutaneous and cutaneous sporotrichosis.
B. Azithromycin
Azithromycin is used to treat cat scratch disease caused by Bartonella henselae
which can result in subacute regional lymphadenitis. It can cause solitary or regional lymphadenopathy similar to sporotrichosis. Patients who are gardeners or
work in landscaping are at high risk for transmission. Lesions rarely resolve without
antibiotic treatment.
C. Cephalexin
Sporotrichosis is a fungus and is, therefore, not susceptible to cephalexin.
D. Itraconazole
Painless papulonodular, erythematous lesions on the hand of a patient who works
as a farm worker, landscaper, or rose gardener should immediately raise concerns
for the fungal infection, sporotrichosis. These infections can be divided into cutaneous, pulmonary, and disseminated syndromes. The cutaneous syndrome arises
from minor trauma of the skin, which is common in rose gardeners. The initial lesions are red and papulonodular. They may be smooth or verrucous and involve the
lymphatics. Itraconazole is the treatment of choice for patients with lymphocutaneous and cutaneous sporotrichosis.

question: A 76-year-old female, retired postal worker, presents with worsening knee pain over the past 4 months. She says both of her knees hurt and are stiff in the morning but start to improve after 30 minutes. She has increased pain during the day with activity which improves with rest. She denies a history of knee injury, surgery, or trauma. Medical history includes obesity and gastrointestinal bleed in her 40s. Vital signs are normal. Exam reveals crepitus bilaterally without erythema or edema. Knee x-rays show joint space narrowing and medial osteophytes. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial drug therapy?
englishExplanation:
Acetaminophen
Expl anation
A. Acetaminophen
This patient is presenting with knee pain secondary to osteoarthritis.
Acetaminophen is the preferred analgesic for mild to moderate osteoarthritis, especially in patients with a history' of gastrointestinal bleed. Weight loss will also be important for this patient. Studies have shown a 3- to 6-fold decrease in the load on
the knee with every pound lost.
Further information:
Hudson K, Agrait-Gonzalez M. Chapter 102. Arthritis. In: Walls RIVI, Hockberger
RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical
Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
B. Methotrexate
Methotrexate is a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug, which is a class of medications used to treat rheumatoid arthritis. This patient has osteoarthritis, not rheumatoid arthritis.
C. NSAIDs
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen are used by
many patients with mild to moderate osteoarthritis, but it is a medication to use
with caution in patients with a history of a gastrointestinal bleed such as this patient. Acetaminophen is a more appropriate choice.
D. Oral corticosteroids
Oral corticosteroids should not be used in patients with a history of gastrointestinal
bleed such as this patient. Intraarticular corticosteroid injections may be an effective treatment option for acute pain due to osteoarthritis but have a variable response and carries its own set of risks. Acetaminophen is a more appropriate initial
treatment.

question: A 32-year-old professional pianist comes to the emergency department because he has had worsening numbness in his hands over the past month. He says his symptoms are worse at night. Physical examination shows decreased grip strength bilaterally as well as numbness and tingling in the median nerve distribution that are reproduced with the test shown. After this patient's initial condition is treated, it is most appropriate for him to be screened by his primary care physician for which of the following endocrine abnormalities?
englishExplanation:
Hypothyroidism
Expl anation
A. Addison disease
Addison disease, or adrenal insufficiency, involves the loss of mineralocorticoid and
glucocorticoid production by the adrenal glands. Clinical manifestations include
malaise, exertional fatigue, weight loss, weakness, hypotension, and hyperpigmentation. Patients can also present in an acute adrenal crisis, with nausea and vomiting, confusion, coma, and shock. Treatment involves corticosteroid replacement
therapy.
B. Decreased testosterone
Decreased testosterone can lead to symptoms of decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, decreased sperm count, reduced muscle mass, loss of axillary/pubic hair, hot
flashes, depressed mood, and poor concentration. Carpal tunnel syndrome and similar symptoms are not associated with decreased testosterone levels.
C. Hyperparathyroidism
Most patients with hyperparathyroidism are asymptomatic, with elevated calcium
levels noted on laboratory testing. The phrase 'bones, stones, abdominal groans,
and psychic groans" has been used to describe symptoms of hypercalcemia: bone
pain, kidney stones, abdominal pain, and psychosis or depression.
D. Hypothyroidism
This patient is presenting with carpal tunnel syndrome and has a positive Phalen
test. A positive Phalen test is characterized by the reproduction of symptoms that
patients with carpal tunnel syndrome typically present with such as paresthesia
(burning, tingling, numbness) in the distribution of the median nerve.
Carpal tunnel syndrome affects patients with comorbid hypothyroidism at a higher
rate than the general population and may be correlated with poorly controlled hypothyroidism. Other risk factors for carpal tunnel syndrome include obesity, female
gender, connective tissue disease, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes mellitus, and pregnancy. Patients will have pain and numbness in the median nerve distribution,
which includes digits one through three and half of the fourth digit. Treatment can
involve splinting, corticosteroid injections, and surgical decompression.

question: A 60-year-old man presents because he had sudden onset of left knee pain and swelling one day ago. He has not sustained any trauma to the knee. Pseudogout
This patient has pseudogout as evidenced by the presence of calcium pyrophosphate

This patient has pseudogout as evidenced by the presence of calcium pyrophosphate
crystals on microscopy. Diagnosis of osteoarthritis is made radiologically.
Arthrocentesis is useful to rule out other conditions and will not show inflammation
in synovial fluid.
C. Pseudogout
The image shows the presence of calcium pyrophosphate crystals which is diagnostic for pseudogout. Calcium pyrophosphate crystals are rhomboid in shape and positively birefringent under a polarizing filter. The knee and wrist are the most commonly affected joints.

RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical

This patient has pseudogout as evidenced by the presence of calcium pyrophosphate
crystals on microscopy. Synovial fluid analysis shows an elevated white blood cell
count consistent with inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis.

question: A 67-year-old male presents with worsening low back pain for 3 weeks. He states that the pain is mild to moderate, located in his lower lumbar area and radiating down both of his legs to his feet with intermittent numbness and tingling in both legs. He states the pain is worse with walking or prolonged standing during the day and improved at night or with sitting down or leaning forward. He denies trauma, recent illness, drug use, incontinence, or saddle anesthesia. His neurologic exam, including lower extremity strength, sensation, reflexes, and coordination are unremarkable. The ankle-brachial index is 0.95 bilaterally. The straight leg raise test is negative. Lumbosacral x-rays are read as "no acute process; mild-to-moderate degenerative changes." What is the modality of choice for diagnosing this patient's likely condition?
englishExplanation:
MR lumbar spine
Expl anation
A. CT angiography of lower extremities
CT angiography of the lower extremities is the diagnostic modality of choice for
cases of vascular claudication. While this patient has exertional pain, the ankle
brachial index (ABI) is 0.9 bilaterally, which is normal, making vascular claudication unlikely.
B. Electromyography
Electromyography (EMG) or nerve conduction studies are not required for the diagnosis Of lumbar spinal stenosis, and is more commonly ordered in cases of
neuropathy/ myopathy.
C. MR lumbar spine
This patient is presenting with classic history and physical exam findings for lumbar
spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication). Mechanical compression/increased intrathecal pressure compressing the nerve roots is the proposed underlying mechanism, where an erect/extended position narrows the lumbar canal, whereas
sitting/hip flexion widens the lumbar canal. Low back pain is generally mild-moderate, associated most commonly with bilateral leg pain accompanied by
numbness/tingling. Neurologic examination in the early stages of lumbar spinal
stenosis is often normal. The key diagnostic distinction of neurogenic claudication is
from vascular claudication, which is characterized by diminished extremity pulses.
Magnetic resonance imaging is the modality of choice for the diagnosis of lumbar
spinal stenosis. CT myelography is an alternate in patients for whom MRI is
contraindicated.
Further information: https://w•ww.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK531493/
D. Ultrasound abdomen
While abdominal aortic aneurysm is part of the differential diagnosis for an elderly
patient with low back pain and certainly ultrasound screening is a quick and effective method to exclude this diagnosis as an etiology, this patient's history and presentation is more consistent with lumbar spinal stenosis and neurogenic
claudication.

question: A 45-year-old man who was recently started on hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension presents because he woke up with exquisite left great toe pain. Physical examination shows an erythematous and swollen left first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint with a greatly decreased range of motion secondary to pain. Which of the following results from diagnostic testing would best confirm the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Joint fluid analysis revealing negatively birefringent crystals
Joint fluid analysis revealing positively birefringent crystals

correctAnswer: Joint fluid analysis revealing negatively birefringent crystals
englishExplanation:
Joint fluid analysis revealing negatively birefringent crystals
Expl anation
A. Increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate
An increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is common in an acute gout attack, but can also be elevated in other causes of an acute, inflamed foot, such as septic arthritis or cellulitis.
B. Joint fluid analysis revealing negatively birefringent crystals
Joint fluid analysis showing negatively birefringent crystals is the diagnostic test of
choice for gout as it is both sensitive and specific for gout. These crystals are needleshaped and composed of monosodium urate. The high serum uric acid, elevated
ESR, and radiographic findings would certainly increase your suspicion of gout, but
these are not the best tests.
Further information:
Hudson K, Agrait-Gonzalez M. Chapter 102. Arthritis. In: Walls RM, Hockberger
RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical
Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
C. Joint fluid analysis revealing positively birefringent crystals
This finding would suggest pseudogout, which on synovial fluid analysis shows positively birefringent, rhomboid-shaped, calcium pyrophosphate crystals. The knee is
the most common site of pseudogout attacks, while the majority of cases of acute
urate gout occur in the first MTP joint.
D. Serum uric acid of 8.0 mg/dL
Uric acid measurement alone cannot make the diagnosis of gout, though a value
greater than 8.0 mg/dL can raise suspicion. In fact, at the time of an attack, many
patients have normal uric acid levels.

question: A 33-year-old male with a history of testicular cancer status post orchiectomy and chemotherapy, now in remission for almost one year, is brought in by ambulance with acute onset low back pain for 2 hours. He was driving over a speed bump in his parking garage when he felt excruciating back pain. His pain is in the middle of his back and radiates to his buttocks. He is not taking any medications and denies drug use. Vital signs are within normal limits. His abdomen is benign, and his genital exam is unremarkable except for an absent left testis. He has tenderness to percussion of his T12-L1 midline. You note 4/5 strength to bilateral lower extremities with decreased light touch sensation in L4/L5/S1 distributions bilaterally, as well as in the perineum. Knee reflexes are bilaterally 3+. The lumbosacral x-ray series is read as mild to moderate degenerative disc disease. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?

options.text: Admit to observation for pain control and serial exams
Order MRI spine and consult neurosurgery
Order serum alpha-fetal protein and beta-hCG
Order serum erythrocyte sedimentation rate, blood cultures and antibiotics

correctAnswer: Order MRI spine and consult neurosurgery
englishExplanation:
Order MRI spine and consult neurosurgery
Expl anation
A. Admit to observation for pain control and serial exams
While this patient will require admission, cauda equina syndrome is a surgical
emergency that requires MRI and neurosurgical consultation.
B. Order MRI spine and consult neurosurgery
This patient has several red flags concerning for cauda equina syndrome, including
a history of presumably metastatic testicular cancer as well as an abnormal neurologic exam. Emergent neurosurgical consultation should be placed pending MRI.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537200/
C. Order serum alpha-fetal protein and beta-hCG
While serum tumor markers may be part of the workup to confirm the presence of
active testicular cancer, this is not an emergent test and is not the next best step in
the management of cauda equina syndrome.
D. Order serum erythrocyte sedimentation rate, blood cultures and
antibiotics
Although this patient has received chemotherapy, it was one year ago and there are
no additional risk factors to suggest occult spinal infection.

question: A 65-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of pain and swelling in his right knee joint that began one day ago. He denies fever or a history of trauma but states that he has hyperparathyroidism. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse rate is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/87 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 100% on room air. Physical examination shows erythema, edema, tenderness, and warmth of the right knee joint. There is pain with range of motion of the affected knee. X-ray study of the right knee is shown. Arthrocentesis is planned. Which of the following findings on synovial fluid analysis confirms the suspected diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped crystals
Expl anation
A. Elevated white blood cell count
While total white blood cell count in synovial fluid during an acute attack can range
from 10,000-50,000 cells per mm3 (90% of which are neutrophils), this finding
alone does not confirm the presence of pseudogout. Rather, this finding simply
demonstrates an inflammatory synovial fluid.
B. Gram staining shows no organisms
In calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate deposition disease, no organisms should be
identified on Gram staining of synovial fluid. Although this finding helps to exclude
an infectious etiology, this finding alone does not confirm the suspected diagnosis.
C. Normal glucose level
In calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate deposition disease, synovial glucose levels are
usually normal. However, this finding alone does not confirm the suspected
diagnosis.
D. Positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped crystals
This patient most likely has pseudogout, calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD)
crystal deposition disease, which involves intra-articular and/or extra-articular deposition of CPPD crystals. The x-ray shows chondrocalcinosis, which is typical of
pseudogout. Acute, subacute, or chronic arthritis can occur, usually in the knee or
other large peripheral joints. Acute attacks can be similar to gout but usually not as
severe. Patients may be asymptomatic between attacks or have continuous lowgrade symptoms in multiple joints, similar to rheumatoid arthritis or osteoarthritis.
Diagnosis of CPPD crystal deposition disease is established by identifying rhomboid- ('classic') or rod-shaped crystals in synovial fluid. These crystals are usually
weakly or strongly positively birefringent, using compensated polarized light
microscopy.

RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical
Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.

question: A 34-year-old transgender woman who works as a medical transcriptionist seeks evaluation for pain in her right wrist and hand for the past six months. Over the past month, the pain has been more consistent and has also been associated with numbness in her hand. The pain is worse at night; shaking her hand helps alleviate the pain. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse rate is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/87 mmHg. Which of the following additional physical examination findings is most likely to be present?

options.text: Decreased sensation in the fourth and fifth fingers
Pain and swelling over the radial styloid
Pain when the patient makes a fist over the thumb while ulnarly deviating the wrist.
Wrist pain when the patient presses her palms together with the elbows flexed to ninety degrees.

correctAnswer: Wrist pain when the patient presses her palms together with the elbows flexed to ninety degrees.
englishExplanation:
Wrist pain when the patient presses her palms together with the elbows flexed
to ninety degrees.
Expl anation
A. Decreased sensation in the fourth and fifth fingers
Decreased sensation in this distribution suggests ulnar nerve entrapment.
B. Pain and swelling over the radial styloid
Pain and swelling over the radial styloid is consistent with deQuervain
tenosynovitis.
C. Pain when the patient makes a fist over the thumb while ulnarly
deviating the wrist.
This describes Finkelstein test for deQuervain tenosynovitis.
D. Wrist pain when the patient presses her palms together with the
elbows flexed to ninety degrees.
This patient has suspected carpal tunnel syndrome. This maneuver describes the reverse Phalen test which, if positive, suggests compression of the median nerve in the
carpal tunnel.

question: A 38-year-old woman presents with a complaint of muscle pain and progressive muscle weakness for the past six months. Her weakness has made it more difficult for her to brush her hair and climb the stairs in her home. She denies difficulty swallowing or shortness of breath. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.3°F), pulse rate is 73/min, respirations are 17/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mmHg. On physical examination, there is no tenderness to palpation of any major muscle groups, but there is marked proximal weakness involving her shoulder and pelvic girdle musculature. No rash is seen. Which of the following is the first-line treatment for the suspected disease?
englishExplanation:
Prednisone
Expl anation
A. Cyclosporine
This patient is presenting with polymyositis. First-line treatment for polymyositis is
corticosteroids, which can help reduce inflammation and improve muscle strength.
Immune-modulators (methotrexate, azathioprine, cyclosporine) are second-line options in those patients who either do not respond to steroids or develop severe adverse effects due to steroids usage.
B. IVIG
This patient is presenting with polymyositis. First-line treatment for polymyositis is
corticosteroids, which can help reduce inflammation and improve muscle strength.
Immune-modulators (methotrexate, azathioprine, cyclosporme) are second-line options in those patients who either do not respond to steroids or develop severe adverse effects due to steroids usage. Intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG) can be
used in the setting of chronic refractory polymyositis.
C. Methotrexate
This patient is presenting with polymyositis. First-line treatment for polymyositis is
corticosteroids, which can help reduce inflammation and improve muscle strength.
Immune-modulators (methotrexate, azathioprine, cyclosporine) are second-line options in those patients who either do not respond to steroids or develop severe adverse effects due to steroids usage.
D. Prednisone
This patient is presenting with polymyositis. Polymyositis is an autoimmune idiopathic inflammatory myopathy. The typical presentation is the gradual onset of
symmetric weakness of the proximal muscles, including those in the hips, shoulders, neck, and upper arms. The weakness may cause difficulty standing up from a
seated position, climbing stairs, or lifting objects. In some cases, weakness of the
muscles involved in swallowing or breathing may occur. Other symptoms that may
be present in polymyositis include fatigue, fever, weight loss, and joint pain. The diagnosis is based on a combination of clinical evaluation, laboratory studies, and
muscle biopsy. Typical labs include a CPK level up to 50 times the normal range and
positive antinuclear and myositis antibodies.

agents may also be used in some cases.

question: A 21-year-old male college student presents for acute onset low back pain while playing ultimate frisbee that morning. He jumped up to catch the frisbee but missed and landed on his lower back/buttocks, immediately feeling pain in his lower back. The pain is sharp and radiates down to his left lateral thigh. He denies any past medical history and denies other injuries. His back examination reveals no midline tenderness or mild tenderness to his left upper buttock. There is a small contusion along the left lower back. Left straight leg raise is positive, and the right cross straight leg raise is negative. His neurologic exam is unremarkable: with normal strength, sensation, reflexes, pulses, and lower extremity range of motion. Pain is improved with ibuprofen, and his gait is slightly antalgic. Lumbar spine x-ray is negative for fracture. Which of the following is the best management in this patient, in addition to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs?
englishExplanation:
Supportive care
Expl anation
A. Back brace
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms suggestive of a lumbar radiculopathy, however he has no red flags for cord compression such as bowel or bladder
incontinence or bilateral lower extremity symptoms. Treatment is supportive. Back
braces are unlikely to be useful for radicular pain.
B. Glucocorticoid
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms suggestive of a lumbar radiculopathy, however he has no red flags for cord compression such as bowel or bladder
incontinence or bilateral lower extremity symptoms. Treatment is supportive.
Glucocorticoids are not indicated for this young otherwise healthy patient.
C. MRI Lumbar spine
This patient presents with signs and symptoms suggestive of lumbar radiculopathy,
however, he has no red flags for cord compression, such as bowel or bladder incontinence or bilateral lower extremity symptoms. Treatment is supportive. This patient has no red flags for cord compression or cauda equina syndrome. There is no
indication for MRI at this time.
D. Supportive care
This patient is presenting with acute uncomplicated musculoskeletal low back pain.
Given the patient's clinical improvement with pain medication, discharge with appropriate aftercare instructions and supportive care is indicated at this time. There
are no red flags indicating further diagnostic workup (such as MRI) or emergent
surgical intervention at this time. Bed rest should NOT be advised to patients;
rather, return to activity as tolerated should be recommended to expedite recovery.
Short-term NSAIDs or acetaminophen is first-line therapy, barring contraindications. Evidence for adjunctive therapies, such as glucocorticoids and muscle relaxants, is controversial. Several society guidelines recommend against the use of glucocorticoids. Opioids are occasionally prescribed for breakthrough severe pain as
needed.

question: A 40-year-old man who works as a construction worker comes to the office because of right wrist pain that has worsened over the last six weeks. He states that the pain is worse with certain tasks and at night when he is sleeping. Additionally, the first three digits of his hand occasionally feel numb. On physical examination, his grip strength is slightly decreased on the right, but there is no atrophy of the intrinsic muscles of the hand. Body mass index is 32 kg/m². Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse rate is 80/min, respirations are 17/min, and blood pressure is 128/87 mmHg. question: A 43-year-old male, with a history of diabetes and alcohol abuse, presents for progressively worsening low back pain over the past week. He is status-post L4-L5 discectomy 2 months ago. The patient reports a remote history of intravenous drug use when questioned but denies recent use. He further denies trauma, numbness or weakness, bowel/bladder incontinence, or saddle anesthesia. He denies night sweats or weight loss. Temperature is 100.4ºF (38ºC), otherwise, vital signs are normal. Exam reveals mild L4 and L5 midline tenderness to palpation without overlying skin changes, his rectal tone is normal, patient ambulates with an antalgic gait, otherwise abdominal and neurologic exams are unremarkable. Lumbosacral X-rays show no significant change from the most recent post-operative X-ray. Pain is slightly improved with parenteral morphine. Which of the following risk factors places this patient at highest risk for his condition?
englishExplanation:
Intravenous drug abuse
Expl anation
A. Alcohol abuse
Alcohol abuse is a risk factor for spinal epidural abscess but not the most common
cause.
B. Diabetes
Diabetes is the most commonly associated medical comorbidity implicated in spinal
epidural abscess but intravenous drug abuse places the patient at higher risk for
spinal epidural abscess than diabetes alone.
C. Intravenous drug abuse
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms consistent with spinal epidural
abscess (SEA) which is an infection of the central nervous system. SFA typically
presents with midline back pain, fever, and neurologic deficits. There are 3 mechanisms of SEA: entry into the epidural space from a contiguous infection (e.g., psoas
muscle abscess, osteomyelitis, skin infection), hematogenous spread, and direct inoculation (e.g., steroid injection, surgery, nerve block)
The most common risk factor is intravenous drug abuse. Other risk factors: recent
spine surgery/procedure, cancer, indwelling vascular catheter, immunosuppression,
diabetes, alcohol abuse, and renal failure. Staphylococcus aureus: most common
causative organism
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441890/
D. Recent spinal surgery
Direct instrumentation such as acupuncture, paraspinal or epidural injection, lumbar puncture, and central nervous system surgery increases the risk of spinal epidural abscess but intravenous drug abuse puts the patient at higher risk.

question: A 58-year-old man comes to the emergency department because he has had worsening knee pain and “buckling” over the past six months. He says he has knee stiffness in the morning that begins to improve after 30 minutes. The pain is worse with activity and improves with rest. The patient has no history of knee injury, surgery, or trauma. Medical history includes metabolic syndrome and uncontrolled asthma requiring frequent corticosteroid tapers. He has a 30—pack-year history of smoking cigarettes. Body mass index is 32 kg/m². Physical examination shows crepitus bilaterally with no erythema or edema. X-ray studies of the knee show joint space narrowing and medial osteophytes. Which of the following is the greatest risk factor for this patient's current condition?
englishExplanation:
Increased body mass index
Expl anation
A. History of cigarette smoking
Cigarette smoking increases a person's risk of developing rheumatoid arthritis, not
osteoarthritis. In fact, multiple studies have found an inverse association between
the risk of knee osteoarthritis and smoking.
B. History of corticosteroid use
Corticosteroid use increases the risk of osteoporosis, not osteoarthritis.
C. Increased body mass index
This patient has osteoarthritis (OA). His obesity is one of the most important risk
factors for both the development and progression of OA. Body weight affects
weight-bearing joints like the knee and hip, and obese patients present with more
severe joint degeneration and the need for joint replacement. Studies have shown
that patients with a body mass index kg/m2 were 6.8 times more likely to develop knee OA than those with a normal body mass index.
Weight loss is an important nonpharmacologic intervention in treating OA in obese
patients. Every pound lost can decrease the load across the knee three- to six-fold.
Physical therapy combining aerobic and resistance training can help facilitate
weight loss, increased strength, reduced pain, and increased mobility. Bracing and
pharmacotherapy with oral, topical, and/or intra-articular options are additional
treatment modalities.
Further information:
Hudson K, Agrait-Gonzalez M. Chapter 102. Arthritis. In: Walls RM, Hockberger
RS, Gausche-Hill M, et al. Rosen's Emergency Medicine Concepts and Clinical
Practice. 10th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2023.
D. Male gender
Most types of arthritis are more common in females, including osteoarthritis as well
as rheumatoid arthritis. The exception being gouty arthritis, which is more common
in males.

question: A 47-year-old man who is a truck driver presents with pain and swelling in his right elbow. This pain has steadily increased over the last two weeks and has made it quite uncomfortable for him to drive his truck. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse rate is 80/min, respirations are 17/min, and blood pressure is 126/84 mmHg. Physical examination shows an area of focal swelling directly overlying the olecranon process that is tender to palpation. The area of swelling is not warm to the touch or erythematous, and his range of motion is intact. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient's condition?
englishExplanation:
Rest and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications
Expl anation
A. Aspiration of bursal fluid
Aspiration of the bursal fluid is not a first-line treatment, as oftentimes the fluid
rapidly returns. Aspiration also introduces an area for bacteria to enter and can
cause infection. Aspiration can be done for diagnostic purposes as well, to look for
infection or crystal-forming disease.
B. Bursectomy
Bursectomy, or surgical excision of the bursa, is the last-resort treatment for persistent, chronic bursitis, with a thick capsule.
C. Corticosteroid injection
Corticosteroid injection is a controversial treatment for olecranon bursitis. It is
commonly done second-line, after failure of NSAIDs, rest, and shielding, and can
result in more rapid resolution of symptoms. However, with the olecranon bursa being so superficially located, skin atrophy, infection, and chronic local pain can
occur.
D. Rest and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications
This patient is presenting with a classic case of olecranon bursitis: a swelling of the
tissue of the bursa caused by repetitive micro trauma to the elbow. Rest,ice, and
NSAIDs are the initial treatments of choice, along with shielding from continued
trauma. If patients are non-responsive to these conservative therapies, the next step
is the aspiration of the bursal fluid, and eventually surgery if episodes are recurrent.
Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470291/

question: A 45-year-old woman presents because she has had pain in the right lateral hip for the past two weeks. She says the pain is sharp with direct pressure, such as lying on her right side or standing for a long time. She has no history of joint catching, clicking, or instability. The patient has no known injury, although she started running two months ago and is currently running three days a week, five miles per day. She has tried taking ibuprofen 600 mg every eight hours, which helps but does not completely resolve the pain. Vital signs are normal The patient appears comfortable in a seated position and has a normal body habitus. On physical examination, no gait abnormalities are noted. Strength and range of motion are within normal limits in the right hip. Results of the FABER test is negative. and piriformis stretch test are negative. Direct pressure over the lateral hip reproduces the pain. Which of the following best explains this patient's symptoms and physical exam findings?
englishExplanation:
Trochanteric bursitis
Expl anation
A. Hip labral tear
A labral tear often presents as sharp pain with weight bearing but often includes a
clicking or catching sensation inside the hip joint. Patients with labral tears have a
positive FABER test.
The FABER test is performed with the patient lying flat on their back on an examination table with the affected leg flexed at the hip and knee. The examiner places
the ankle of the affected leg on the opposite knee, and then gently presses down on
the affected knee, applying a downward force toward the table. The examiner then
moves the affected hip into abduction and external rotation while keeping the knee
in a flexed position. assessing the patient's pain response and range of motion. If the
patient experiences pain or restriction of movement during the test, this may indicate a labral tear. The test is thought to be positive if there is pain in the groin, hip
joint, or lateral thigh area.
B. Meralgia paresthetica
Meralgia paresthetica presents most commonly in pregnant or obese patients as
paresthesia or hyperesthesia of the anterior thigh.
C. Piriformis syndrome
Piriformis syndrome presents with buttock pain and posterior thigh symptoms such
as sciatica-type pain. On physical examination, the patient may have a positive piriformis stretch test. This test involves the patient lying on their back with their legs
straight and then crossing the affected leg over the other leg so that the ankle rests
on the opposite knee. The examiner gently pushes down on the affected knee while
stabilizing the opposite hip. If the patient experiences pain in the buttock region or
down the leg, this may indicate piriformis syndrome.
D. Trochanteric bursitis
Trochanteric bursitis is most commonly described as lateral hip pain localized to the
greater trochanter and is most common in runners and middle-aged women. The
symptoms may include pain and tenderness on the outside of the hip, pain that radiates down the leg (especially along the outer thigh), stiffness and difficulty moving
the hip, and pain that worsens with activities that involve the hip. Treatment for
Page 2089 of 4185
trochanteric bursitis includes rest, ice, physical therapy, NSAIDs, corticosteroid injections, and in severe cases, surgical removal of the bursa.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK538503/

question: A 45-year-old female security officer presents with pain in her right heel for the past 2 weeks. The pain is exacerbated when she takes the first few steps out of bed in the morning and with increased activity. She says she recently started a new running program to train for her first 5K race. She denies recent trauma. Exam reveals tenderness to palpation of the anteromedial aspect of the plantar surface of the right heel. Which of the following additional findings on physical examination is most likely?

options.text: Pain with medial and lateral calcaneal compression
Pain with palpation of the posterior calcaneus
Pain with passive dorsiflexion of the foot
Pain with percussion over the tarsal tunnel

correctAnswer: Pain with passive dorsiflexion of the foot
englishExplanation:
Pain with passive dorsiflexion of the foot
Expl anation
A. Pain with medial and lateral calcaneal compression
Pain with medial and lateral calcaneal compression suggests a pathology such as a
calcaneal stress fracture, particularly if there has been a history of trauma. An individual who is suspected of having a stress fracture should be placed in a walking
boot for four to six weeks.
B. Pain with palpation of the posterior calcaneus
Pain with palpation of the posterior calcaneus suggests Achilles tendonitis or retrocalcaneal bursitis. Individuals with plantar fasciitis typically identify the medial aspect of the anterior calcaneus as the primary source of pain and note that the pain
tends to improve with rest and worsen significantly with the first steps of motion.
C. Pain with passive dorsiflexion of the foot
This patient has suspected plantar fasciitis. Pain with passive dorsiflexion of the
foot, or the windlass test, is an expected finding in the physical exam of an individual with plantar fasciitis, a condition caused by degeneration and irritation at the insertion of the plantar fascia at the medial calcaneal tuberosity. It is typically selflimited and can be treated conservatively with rest, ice, splints, shoe inserts, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and corticosteroids.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK431073/
D. Pain with percussion over the tarsal tunnel
Tarsal tunnel syndrome is the resulting neuropathy from compression of the posterior tibial nerve which runs posterior to the medial malleolus. Patients often present
with paresthesia and pain in the affected foot. Individuals who have plantar fasciitis
will not report pain with percussion over the tarsal tunnel.

question: A 41-year-old male recent field worker immigrant from El Salvador presents with acute onset low back pain for 4 hours. He was lifting a crate of fruit when he felt a sharp pain in his lower back radiating down his right posterior leg to the ankle. He has been unable to ambulate, secondary to severe pain. He denies any past medical history and does not abuse drugs. He states he has been having a mild, chronic cough for years, unintentional weight loss of 10 lbs over the past month, and fevers at night. On examination, the abdomen is benign, and you note midline point tenderness to L1 with no overlying skin changes. Neurologic exam demonstrates full strength and sensation to bilateral lower extremities. A post-void residual results 10 cc. Lumbosacral x-ray series demonstrates osteoporotic L1 vertebral endplates with loss of L1-L2 intervertebral disc space height. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?

options.text: Order blood cultures, then ceftriaxone and vancomycin

Expl anation
A. Consult neurosurgery
While neurosurgery ultimately may need to be consulted, the patient is neurologically stable and the next best step is to order an MRI to determine the extent of
spinal osteomyelitis secondary to tuberculosis.
B. Discharge home with supportive care
This patient has concerning features for spinal osteomyelitis secondary to tuberculosis and should not be discharged home with only supportive care.
C. Order MRI spine
This patient has risk factors for osteomyelitis as a cause of his acute onset low back
pain: constitutional symptoms, recent immigration, and plain radiograph findings
of vertebral endplate abnormalities suggestive of spinal tuberculosis. An MRI is indicated to better delineate the extent of osteomyelitis prior to initiating likely tuberculosis antibiotics.

question: A 5-year-old boy presents to the emergency department due to limping on his left leg which has worsened over the past 3 weeks. There is no history of trauma, no recent illness and he has no medical history. All vital signs are normal. Examination of his left knee and abdomen is normal. He has mild discomfort with hip range of motion and mildly restricted abduction. X-ray is included below. What is the initial management for this condition?

options.text: Admission and orthopedic consultation for femoral osteotomy
NSAIDs, protective weight bearing, and orthopedic referral

correctAnswer: NSAIDs, protective weight bearing, and orthopedic referral
englishExplanation:
NSAIDs, protective weight bearing, and orthopedic referral
Expl anation
A. Admission and orthopedic consultation for femoral osteotomy
Surgery may be needed if conservative management is not sufficient. Typically this
is indicated in children older than 8 years old and who have loss of of the lateral pillar height.
B. Admission for broad-spectrum antibiotics
This child has Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, not septic arthritis. Antibiotics are not
indicated in the treatment of this condition.
C. MRI hip and orthopedic referral
MRI hip is not necessary if the disease is seen on plain film (AP Pelvis and/or frog
leg lateral). If the plain films are normal, which can occur early in the disease
process, and the physician has a high degree of suspicion, MRI can be ordered to
evaluate for Legg-Calve-Perthes disease.
D. NSAIDs, protective weight bearing, and orthopedic referral
This child has Legg-Calve-perthes disease or avascular necrosis of the capital
femoral epiphysis of the femoral head. While the cause is unknown, it is seen more
commonly in males than females and in children ages 3-12 years old (most present
between 5-7 years old). The insidious development of a limp will prompt most evaluations. physical exam may show antalgic gait, discomfort with rotation of the hip
and decreased internal rotation and abduction of the hip. There will be a lack of systemic symptoms such a fever. Plain films are used for initial evaluation, although

question: A 55-year-old male with a history of hypertension and diabetes presents to the emergency department with a painful, swollen right knee. He denies any recent trauma but does endorse intermittent subjective fevers over the past 24 hours. Arthrocentesis demonstrates a WBC count of 120,000/mm3 as well as rhomboid-shaped crystals. options.text: Admission to the hospital and orthopedics consult for possible septic arthritis

A repeat arthrocentesis is unlikely to change management in this patient.
