question: A 72-year-old female, with a history of osteoporosis, presents with acute onset low back pain after an accidental ground-level fall this morning. She was walking across the kitchen and slipped on some water, landing directly on her buttocks. Her back pain is diffuse across her lower back and radiates to her right lateral thigh. She denies numbness or weakness. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical exam is unremarkable, except for mild bilateral low lumbar paraspinal tenderness. Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory and opioid medication mildly improve the pain. The patient walks gingerly with an antalgic gait. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
englishExplanation:
CT lumbar spine
Expl anation
A. CT lumbar spine
CT imaging to evaluate for compression fracture is indicated in elderly patients as
well as patients with a history of osteoporosis who present with acute back pain after a mechanical ground-level fall or minor trauma. CT is the best imaging modality
for evaluating spinal fractures.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK547673/
B. Discharge home with supportive care
This patient has 2 historical red flags (age years and trauma in the setting of osteoporosis) that indicate the need for CT imagmg.
C. Lumbosacral x-ray
While x-rays can be obtained and possibly show a fracture, CT is considered the best
imaging modality in elderly patients and those with a history of osteoporosis.
D. MRI lumbar spine
MRI is best utilized to evaluate for disc and ligamentous injury, not bony fracture. If
the patient had signs or symptoms of cord compression and/or an abnormal neurological exam, MRI would be indicated.

question: A 1-year-old patient is brought into the emergency department by their family for a swollen right hand. Vital signs are within normal limits, and the patient is afebrile. The mother denies a history of trauma. On exam, the hand is noted to be red and diffusely swollen. The mother notes there was one prior episode that presented similarly four months ago that resolved after a month. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Acute dactylitis
Expl anation
A. Acute dactylitis
Acute dactylitis is the most common presenting symptom for patients with sickle
cell disease. It most commonly occurs in patients 6-18 months of age and represents
bone infarction. It is not an infection.
Children with dactylitis have swollen, tender, and warm feet or hands. There may be
pain, fever, and reduced movement. Episodes typically resolve within a month but
may be recurrent. The mainstay of therapy is analgesics and hydration.
Further information: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK526064/
B. Cellulitis
This patient's sickle cell disease is more suggestive of a process involving the bone
than the soft tissue.
C. Osteomyelitis
This patient has no infectious symptoms and the acute onset argues against
osteomyelitis.
D. Septic joint
This patient has no infectious symptoms and no specific joint pain.

question: A 78-year-old woman presents because she has had progressive difficulty with combing her hair due to stiffness in her shoulders for the past four months. The stiffness occurs in the morning and lasts greater than 30 minutes. She also feels discomfort in the muscles of her shoulders and neck. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.3°F), pulse rate is 72/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 120/72 mmHg. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 102 mm/hr. Which of the following medications is the most appropriate first-line therapy?
englishExplanation:
Prednisone
Expl anation
A. Duloxetine
Duloxetine is a selective serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SSNRI)
antidepressant used to treat depression and anxiety. It can also be used in the management of fibromyalgia. This patient is presenting with proximal muscle weakness
in the absence of other systemic symptoms. Her symptoms and lab results indicate
that she has polymyalgia rheumatica.
B. Naproxen
While naproxen may relieve the discomfort of polymyalgia rheumatica, low-dose
prednisone is the first-line therapy.
C. Prednisone
This patient likely has polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). This is a disorder that typically affects people over the age of 50 and causes pain and stiffness in the shoulders,
neck, and hips. PMR often causes pain and stiffness in the muscles of the shoulders,
neck, and hips. The pain is typically worse in the morning or after periods of inactivity. Low-dose corticosteroids are the first-line management. Other treatment options include NSAIDs and methotrexate.
Further information: https://wikem.org/wiki/Polymyalgia_rheumatica
D. Pregabalin
Pregabalin is an anticonvulsant that the Federal Drug Administration approved for
fibromyalgia. Fibromyalgia is characterized by diffuse muscle pain, as opposed to
proximal muscle weakness, and is associated with extreme fatigue and sleep
disturbances. Pregabalin is not a treatment for polymyalgia rheumatica, which is
what this patient has.

question: A 32-year-old woman, who is being treated successfully for systemic lupus erythematosus, presents after having a miscarriage. Which of the following tests should be ordered to assess this patient's risk for further miscarriage or blood clots?
englishExplanation:
Serum anti-phospholipid antibodies
Expl anation
A. Chromosome studies
Karyotyping can be done in couples experiencing frequent miscarriages to detect
chromosomal abnormalities. Karyotyping can also be done on the aborted embryo
or fetus. However, this is only typically done if all other testing, including antiphosopholipid antibody testing, is normal.
B. Complete blood count
While a complete blood count can show thrombocytopenia in patients with antiphospholipid syndrome, this is not a sensitive or specific finding.
C. Serum albumin levels
This is not a helpful test in determining the future risk of blood clot and miscarriage
in a patient suspected of having antiphospholipid syndrome.
D. Serum anti-phospholipid antibodies
Patients with SLE are at increased risk for developing antiphospholipid syndrome
(APLS), which may cause blood clots or recurrent miscarriages. Thrombus formation can be arterial or venous, and can involve the heart, lungs, and skin. Recurrent
miscarriages are common. Serum anti-phospholipid antibodies are the best test to
indicate the presence of this condition.

question: Which imaging modality is preferred in the diagnosis of avascular necrosis of bone?
englishExplanation: MRI is up to 100% sensitive in the diagnosis of avascular necrosis of bone and is considered the gold standard imaging modality in the diagnosis of this disease process. Avascular necrosis may be associated with trauma and, in that set- ting, is most common in the proximal femur, proximal humerus, scaphoid, or talus. This condition, also known as osteonecrosis, may also be associated with nontrau- matic causes in patients with underlying medical conditions such as sickle cell dis- ease, Gaucher disease, a history of decompression disease or radiation treatments, and glucocorticoid use. Incorrect Answer Explanations MRI is preferred over CT, given the risks of radiation associated with CT and the sensitivity of MRI. However, CT may be used to demonstrate subchon- dral fractures, which can affect the prognosis in the setting of osteonecrosis. Plain x-rays have low sensitivity in the diagnosis of avascular necrosis, es- pecially early in the disease process. However, it is reasonable to begin with x-rays to assess for pathognomonic signs of the disease process or other pathology that could explain the patient's symptoms. Radionuclide bone scanning has low sensitivity in the diagnosis of avas- cular necrosis. This modality may be helpful in patients with contraindications to other imaging types.

question: A fracture of what portion of the scaphoid bone places a patient at the highest risk of avascular necrosis?

options.text: Distal pole because the arterial supply enters the distal scaphoid
Distal pole because the arterial supply enters the proximal scaphoid
Proximal pole because the arterial supply enters the distal scaphoid
Proximal pole because the arterial supply enters the proximal scaphoid

correctAnswer: Proximal pole because the arterial supply enters the distal scaphoid
englishExplanation: Proximal fractures of the scaphoid are at the greatest risk of avascular necrosis and must be referred to an orthopedic surgeon. The vascular supply en- ters the bone distally, and proximal fractures are more likely to isolate the proxi- mal bone fragment from any entering vessels. The more distal the fracture, the less of a chance there is of osteonecrosis. Scaphoid fractures that are treated improperly may result in nonunion and poor outcomes. These injuries, if suspected based on the mechanism of injury and tenderness of the scaphoid, should be immobilized with a thumb spica splint pending further evaluation, even if no fracture is visualized on imaging. Incorrect Answer Explanations The blood supply enters throughout the distal scaphoid, which makes it more likely that a vessel will enter the bone just proximal to a fracture located at the distal pole. This arrangement reduces the likelihood of avascular necrosis of the bone fragment. Fractures of the proximal (rather than distal) scaphoid are more likely to lead to avascular necrosis. The vascular supply enters through the distal scaphoid (not the proximal scaphoid). Fractures of the proximal aspect of the scaphoid are at the highest risk of avascular necrosis. The blood supply, however, enters through the distal pole (not the proximal pole). Key Points The arterial supply to the scaphoid enters through the distal pole. Proximal scaphoid fractures are at high risk of avascular necrosis.

question: Which medication commonly prescribed in the emergency department is most likely to predispose a patient to the development of avascular necrosis of bone?
englishExplanation: Glucocorticoids, including prednisone, have been associated with the de- velopment of avascular necrosis of bone, also known as osteonecrosis. Although chronic use of glucocorticoids places patients at higher risk, limited evi- dence suggests that even short courses of glucocorticoids may predispose patients to this condition, and osteonecrosis is more likely to develop after the use of higher doses of glucocorticoids. Other risk factors for osteonecrosis include certain genetic disorders, trauma, and autoimmune disease. Osteonecrosis may be difficult to identify on plain x-rays, but MRI can help confirm the diagnosis when suspected. Incorrect Answer Explanations Clindamycin is not associated with the development of osteonecrosis. Like many antibiotics, however, it is associated with the development of Clostridioides dif- ficile infection and should be prescribed with caution. Furosemide is not associated with osteonecrosis. However, it may cause elec- trolyte imbalances or, less commonly, ototoxicity. Metoprolol is unlikely to cause osteonecrosis. The most commonly discussed side effects of metoprolol include bradycardia, fatigue, bronchospasm, and electrolyte imbalances.

question: Which organism most often causes osteomyelitis as a result of a plantar puncture wound to the foot when wearing shoes?
englishExplanation:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes approximately 90% of cases of osteomyelitis of the foot due to puncture wounds. Patients often sustain plantar puncture injuries through the sole of a shoe; tennis shoes are most frequently known to provide the suitable environment for P. aeruginosa to grow. P. aeruginosa is also seen in os- teomyelitis in injection drug users and postsurgical wounds, such as infected orthopedic joint prostheses. P. aeruginosa osteomyelitis of the foot is treated with in- travenous antipseudomonal antibiotics, such as cephalosporins or fluoroquinolones. Incorrect Answer Explanations Clostridium perfringens infection is a common cause of gas gangrene (or myonecrosis) and food poisoning. C. perfringens infection is not a common cause of osteomyelitis from puncture wounds of the foot when wearing shoes. Staphylococcus aureus is the second most common pathogen in plantar puncture wounds resulting in infection. Staphylococcus is also a common cause of osteomyelitis that does not involve puncture wounds. Notably S. aureus and Staphylococcus epidermidis account for 75% of postsurgical and prosthesis-related causes of osteomyelitis. Streptococcus pyogenes causes pharyngitis, cellulitis, and, in some cases, necrotizing fasciitis. Streptococcus species are another common cause of os- teomyelitis in the general population, excluding patients with puncture wounds to the foot.

question: Which imaging modality has the highest combined sensitivity and specificity for detecting osteomyelitis?
englishExplanation: MRI is far superior to other imaging modalities for detecting early abnor- malities seen in osteomyelitis, including bone marrow involvement and medullary or cortical destruction, periosteal reaction, edema, soft tissue extension, joint effusions, and articular damage. MRI is 95% sensitive in diagnosing os- teomyelitis. Although metal may cause streak artifact, MRI is still the imaging of choice to diagnose osteomyelitis in patients with metal hardware or joint prosthesis. MRI is also useful in differentiating bone infection from bone infarction in patients with sickle cell disease. Incorrect Answer Explanations CT scan with IV contrast is good for defining bone destruction and the bony cortex. On CT scan, osteomyelitis appears as a lucent area. Gas may be seen in bony abscess cavities. Like x-rays, CT is limited for the early diagnosis of osteomyelitis, and the disease must typically be present for more than 1 week for changes to be apparent. CT may be used as an adjunctive imaging study for surgical planning. X-rays are typically normal early in the course of osteomyelitis but may show bone demineralization, periosteal elevation, and lytic lesions later in the course of osteomyelitis. Lucency is not detected on plain x-rays until about 50% of bone mineral has been lost. Less than one-third of patients with os- teomyelitis will have abnormalities on plain x-rays in the first 7 to 10 days after symp- tom onset. Although it is not as sensitive as MRI, x-ray is a helpful screening tool because it is readily available and can quickly differentiate infection from trauma or malignancy. Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy is more sensitive than plain x-rays in the early diagnosis of osteomyelitis; changes can be detected within 48 to 72 hours after the onset of infection. A radioactive tracer is injected into the bloodstream and areas of increased radioactivity are visualized. Although bone scintigraphy is more sensitive than CT in detecting acute osteomyelitis, it has lower specificity and often requires additional confirmatory imaging. Furthermore, it is less useful in the presence of a fracture. Given the radiation bur- den, technetium-99m bone scintigraphy has been replaced by MRI over the past 2 decades. Although technetium-99m bone scintigraphy has less streak artifact in the presence of metal hardware or prosthetics, MRI is still preferred for its overall in- creased sensitivity and specificity.

question: A 25-year-old patient presents with dull, boring pain to the right knee that has grown worse at night over the last several weeks. The patient denies fever or chills, and routine laboratory work is unremarkable. An x-ray of the area is obtained and shown below. What is the next best step in management? Credit: Copyright 2022 Dr. Pir Abdul Ahad Aziz Qureshi. Image courtesy of Dr. Pir Abdul Ahad Aziz Qureshi and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 69332. Used under license.

options.text: Consult orthopedic surgery for expedited follow-up
Obtain CT scan of the right lower extremity
Reassure the patient that their symptoms will resolve

correctAnswer: Consult orthopedic surgery for expedited follow-up
englishExplanation:
This patient's x-ray demonstrates a “sunburst” type of periosteal reaction near the metaphysis of the femur. In combination with the clinical presentation of dull, boring pain for weeks and lack of fevers, this is most suggestive of osteosarcoma. An urgent referral to orthopedic surgery is important for tumor biopsy and potential limb-salvage surgery. If necessary, further evaluation of osteosarcoma should be done with MRI, although x-ray is often suggestive enough for a referral to specialty services. An osteosarcoma is an aggressive bone tumor usually seen in the second or third decade of life. Osteosarcoma is most frequently found in the distal femur or the proximal tibia or fibula, and it often arises from bone metaphysis. Dull, bor- ing pain that grows worse at night is a classic presentation for this tumor. Osteosarcoma can be aggressive, and approximately one-fourth of patients will have metastasis at diagnosis. Risk factors for osteosarcoma include prior radiation therapy for other cancers and genetic predisposition. Osteosarcoma classically metastasizes to other long bones, to the same bone as “skip lesions,” or to the lungs. Incorrect Answer Explanations Advanced imaging is not emergent and may be completed as an outpatient. If ad- vanced imaging is warranted, MRI is the test of choice. Although CT in the emer- gency department may further evaluate the area, MRI would better elucidate soft tis- sue extension and other staging concerns. A prescription of outpatient antibiotics would be inappropriate in this case. Although periosteal reactions can represent osteomyelitis, the initial treatment of osteomyelitis should be parenteral antibiotics. Furthermore, lack of fever and normal laboratory work are less suggestive of osteomyelitis in this case. Reassurance that symptoms will resolve would be inappropriate and potentially deadly in this case. The “sunburst” periosteal reaction on x-ray is highly sug- gestive of a bone tumor such as osteosarcoma, which is frequently aggressive in its course.

question: In which decade of life would Ewing sarcoma most likely be diagnosed?
englishExplanation: Ewing sarcoma is a bone tumor that affects adolescents and young adults, with a median age of 15. X-ray classically demonstrates a type of pe- riosteal reaction called an “onion peel.” Clinically, patients present with local- ized pain and swelling for weeks to months, and they may have a tender soft tissue mass in the area. The pain is often worse at night or exacerbated by ex- ercise. Ewing sarcoma is an aggressive tumor that is usually seen in the second or third decade of life. Urgent referral to orthopedic surgery is important for tumor biopsy and potentially limb-salvage surgery. Ewing sarcoma represents a family of tumors described as “peripheral primitive neu- roectodermal tumors” due to their histologic characteristics. Ewing sarcoma usu- ally arises from the diaphysis of long bones, although it may be seen in pelvic bones or the axial skeleton as well. They can be extraskeletal and have an associated soft tissue mass. Like osteosarcomas, a Ewing sarcoma classically metastasizes to other long bones or the lungs. Incorrect Answer Explanations Primary bone tumors are uncommon in the first 10 years of life. Leukemias such as acute myeloid leukemia are much more common at this young age and may also result in bone pain. A bone tumor in the seventh decade of life is more likely to be a sec- ondary metastasis from primary tumors in a lung, breast, or prostate. Central chondrosarcoma is a rare primary bone tumor that may present in patients older than 50 years. A bone tumor in the sixth decade of life is more likely to be a secondary metasta- sis from primary tumors in a lung, breast, or prostate. Central chondrosarcoma is a rare primary bone tumor that may present in patients older than 50 years.

question: A patient with a history of lung cancer presents with the x-ray shown below. Which laboratory abnormality is most likely to be seen? Credit: April stock/Shutterstock.com.
englishExplanation:
This x-ray demonstrates an osteolytic lesion that is consistent with probable bone metastasis from lung cancer. Due to dysregulation of the normal bone modeling process, the bone is dissolved by increased osteoclastic activity. As a result, calcium is released into the blood. Hypercalcemia in the cancer patient with bone metastasis should be managed with isotonic saline, bisphosphonates, or monoclonal antibodies directed at inhibiting osteoclast function. Bone metastasis can be osteolytic, as in multiple myeloma; osteoblastic, as in prostate can- cer; or a mixture of both, as in breast cancer. Although osteolytic lesions di- rectly result in hypercalcemia, osteoblastic lesions may also stimulate bone destruction and resultant hypercalcemia. Incorrect Answer Explanations Hyperkalemia is unrelated to bone metastasis. Hyperkalemia may be caused by metabolic acidosis, insulin deficiency, acute or chronic kidney disease, or increased tissue breakdown. Hypocalcemia is rarely seen in patients with bone metastasis. Osteoblastic metastasis commonly seen in prostate cancer may cause hypocalcemia, but even in those pa- tients, hypercalcemia is more common due to stimulation of osteoclastic activity from the dysregulation of osteoblasts. Hypocalcemia may be seen in chronic kidney disease, after destruction of the parathyroid glands, or with vitamin D deficiency. Hypokalemia is unrelated to bone metastasis. Hypokalemia may be caused by increased GI losses due to vomiting, diuretic use, or increased potassium entry into cells, such as in the case of increased insulin availability.

question: A 75-year-old woman with osteoporosis presents with a 2-day history of atrau- matic pain in her right gluteal region that radiates into the pubic area. The pain is difficult to reproduce on examination. She has significant pain with walking that limits her ambulation. A pelvic x-ray is obtained and is read as negative. What is the next best imaging modality to obtain from the emergency department?

options.text: CT scan without contrast of the bony pelvis
MRI with and without contrast of the pelvis
PET scan of the axial skeleton
Ultrasound of the greater trochanteric region

correctAnswer: CT scan without contrast of the bony pelvis
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with nontraumatic pelvic pain that is poorly localized on examination and is most notable with walking. This presentation is quite common for pathology of the pelvic bones. For patients that have a high likelihood of having a pelvic fracture, such as in this patient, a CT scan should be obtained. Patients with osteoporosis are prone to fractures that can occur without trauma or from a minimal traumatic incident. These are often referred to as “atypi- cal” or “fragility” fractures. It is important to note that pelvic x-rays have an inadequate sensitivity (<85%) for identifying pelvic fractures. CT is often helpful to protocolize the scan to optimize bone imaging. Fractures that are diagnosed without a clear mechanism should be suspicious for a pathologic fracture and should trigger further workup, particularly if malignancy is suspected. The most common cause of pathologic fractures is osteoporosis. The bone matrix can become so brittle in osteoporosis that minimal forces can lead to sig- nificant fractures. Metastatic lesions to the bone can cause pathologic fractures and are the second most common cause. Other conditions (eg, vitamin D deficiency, Paget disease, osteogenesis imperfecta, and primary benign and malignant bone tumors) can also lead to pathological fractures. Incorrect Answer Explanations An MRI with and without contrast of the pelvis should not be the next step in this case. Although MRI may have more sensitivity than CT, it is impractical in most emergency departments to obtain an MRI for this reason. Additionally, contrast would not be needed unless there was a high suspicion for infection or tumor. A PET scan of the axial skeleton would not be indicated at this stage. If this patient has a fracture noted on CT imaging, it is likely a fragility fracture from osteo- porosis. However, if additional imaging suggests potentially metastatic disease, then a PET scan would be indicated as part of the patient's workup. This would be done either inpatient or as an outpatient test and is not indicated from the emergency department. Greater trochanteric bursitis and gluteal tendinopathy can be a cause of hip pain in patients. An ultrasound may show an effusion and tendon fraying around the greater trochanter. This usually presents with lateral hip pain and with focal tender- ness around the greater trochanter, which does not describe this case.

question: Which factor confers the highest risk for an osteoporotic fracture?
englishExplanation: Osteoporosis is a condition in which patients have low bone mass and mi- croarchitectural disruption of the bones, resulting in skeletal fragility. In addition to poor bone mineral density, bone fragility is caused by increased rates of bone cell turnover, issues with bone microarchitecture, and abnormal bone geometry. Clinically apparent factors that influence the likelihood of osteo- porotic fracture include advanced age, female sex, low body weight, history of previous fracture, glucocorticoid use, excessive alcohol intake, and to- bacco use. Vertebral compression fractures are the most common manifesta- tion of osteoporosis and are often asymptomatic. Hip fractures and distal radius fractures are also commonly seen. Incorrect Answer Explanations Low BMI, not high BMI, is a risk factor for developing osteoporotic frac- tures. Osteoporosis is, in part, caused by an imbalance of bone resorption and re- modeling, which can lead to decreased skeletal mass. Osteoporosis is more common in women than in men. Up to 38% of women are affected in their lifetimes, compared to only 8% of men. One in three women ver- sus one in five men will have an osteoporotic fracture after age 50. Postmenopausal women are at increased risk. Smoking is associated with increased risk of osteoporotic fractures. The risk is greater in current smokers than in former smokers. Other major risk factors for osteoporotic fractures are corticosteroid use, excessive alcohol use, and history of fractures.

question: What is the most likely location for a fragility fracture?
englishExplanation: Of the sites listed, the forearm is the most common location for fragility fractures. These injuries usually occur from a fall onto an outstretched arm, resulting in a distal radius fracture. Fragility fractures can occur from minimal trauma, such as a fall from standing. These fractures are common in geriatric patients. It is estimated that 10 million Americans older than 50 have osteoporosis, which leads to 1.5 million fragility fractures each year in the United States. The vertebral col- umn, which is not listed, is the most common location for fragility frac- tures overall. Incorrect Answer Explanations In patients with osteoporosis, humeral fractures are less common than distal radius fractures. The ribs, pelvis, and skull are also less likely fracture sites. The most common site for fragility fractures is the vertebral column. Fragility fractures of the pelvis are unlikely. However, the hip (proximal femur) is the second most common site of osteoporotic fragility fractures. In 2000, the hip accounted for 1.6 million fractures worldwide. They always require hospitalization and often result in death (up to 20% of cases) or permanent disability (up to 50% of cases). Only about 30% of patients fully recover. Although traumatic head injuries are common in older adults, intracranial hemor- rhages are more common than skull fractures. The skull is an uncommon loca- tion for a fragility fracture.

question: A 65-year-old woman with stage IV breast cancer presents with an inability to walk due to severe hip pain. She recalls no trauma. There is no deformity on exam- ination, and her vital signs are within normal limits. What is the best initial hip imaging modality?
englishExplanation: A pathologic fracture should always be considered in patients with metastatic can- cer who suddenly develop pain and an inability to ambulate, even in the absence of deformity on a physical examination. This is especially true for patients with cancer that commonly metastasizes to bone (eg, breast, lung, and prostate). A fracture in the setting of minor trauma is also a clue that a fracture may be pathologic. The initial best imaging modality to identify a fracture is x-ray. X-rays will commonly show cortical destruction and lytic destruction at the site of the fracture. Incorrect Answer Explanations CT of the patient's hip may be useful for surgical planning or if the original x-ray is negative and a fracture is suspected. However, CT is likely unnecessary as the ini- tial imaging modality for a suspected pathologic fracture. MRI is very sensitive and specific for fracture, metastatic disease, and os- teomyelitis. However, MRI is expensive, time consuming, and is also often unavail- able in many emergency departments. Therefore, x-ray is a better screening modality for fractures. Ultrasound can be useful in identifying fractures. However, ultrasound — especially POCUS — is operator dependent, and fractures can be missed. Furthermore, the abil- ity to distinguish pathologic from nonpathologic fractures on ultrasound has yet to be studied. In this case, x-ray would be the first imaging modality in a patient with a sus- pected fracture.

question: A toddler with a history of hearing loss and abnormal dentition presents with a re- peat femur fracture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is a genetic bone disorder that can vary in severity and phenotypic characteristics relative to the specific genetic mutation. Some forms of OI are associated with extraskeletal manifestations, such as hearing loss and abnormal tooth development, which is referred to as dentino- genesis imperfecta. The hearing loss associated with OI can be conductive, sen- sorineural, or mixed. Patients with dentinogenesis imperfecta have very weak teeth that are prone to fractures and have either a blue-gray or yellow-brown discoloration. Patients with OI have bone deformity and fragility, resulting in frequent fractures that often occur after minimal trauma. Fractures of the long bones occur most commonly, although patients can also experience compression fractures of the vertebra. Additional musculoskeletal manifestations include ligamentous laxity, scol- iosis, and chest wall and basilar skull deformities. Some subtypes of OI are associated with blue sclera, increased risk of cardiac valve abnormalities, and impaired pul- monary function. Prenatal diagnosis of OI is possible. However, genetic testing may be required in infants and children, particularly when trying to differentiate OI from nonaccidental trauma. Incorrect Answer Explanations Differentiating between OI from nonaccidental trauma in a child with re- peated long bone fractures can be difficult. Although children with chronic disabilities and special needs are at increased risk of nonaccidental trauma, hearing loss and abnormal dentition are more closely associated with OI. Although ge- netic testing is not readily available in the emergency department setting, x-ray imag- ing may help clinicians distinguish between the two conditions. Rib fractures and classic metaphyseal lesions have a high specificity for nonaccidental trauma and rarely occur in patients with OI. Contrarily, x-ray findings of wormian bones, which are small bones found between cranial sutures, are more suggestive of OI. Rickets refers to a condition of abnormal bone mineralization due to ei- ther calcium deficiency or low serum phosphorus. Delayed dental eruption and abnormalities of the dental enamel can occur in the setting of rickets. However, patients with rickets do not typically have hearing deficits. Affected children will of- ten present with skeletal findings of bowing of the lower extremities, craniotabes, and prominence of the costochondral junction, which is known as rachitic rosary. The metaphyseal changes of rickets can be mistaken for nonaccidental trauma on x- ray. Extraskeletal findings in rickets include hypotonia, failure to thrive, and seizures or tetany related to severe hypocalcemia. Transient hyperphosphatasemia of infancy and early childhood is a be- nign condition that is not associated with any abnormalities other than the serum laboratory findings. Clinical presentation is usually that of a healthy child with an incidental finding of an elevated serum alkaline phosphatase. Additional laboratory screening, specifically for bone and liver diseases, will be nor- mal. No treatment is indicated, and serum alkaline phosphatase levels will usually re- turn to normal within 3 to 6 months.

question: An adolescent presents with acute-onset chest pain. Which underlying condition indicates an emergent echocardiogram?
englishExplanation: Marfan syndrome is a disorder of connective tissue, and patients are at increased risk of aortic dilatation and subsequent dissection. Echocardiogram can be diagnostic of aortic dissection, a major cause of morbidity and mortality in these patients. Additional symptoms of aortic dissection include ab- dominal pain; neurologic symptoms of seizure, syncope, or limb paresthesia; and shortness of breath. Additional diagnostic tools to consider when aortic dissection is suspected are an ECG, laboratory studies, and radiographic imaging. Although the ECG may be normal in aortic dissection, some patients may demonstrate ST-segment elevations or electrical alternans. There is no specific laboratory marker to diagnose aortic dissection, but troponin may be elevated if there is associated myocardial is- chemia. A widened mediastinum can often be visualized on chest x-ray and CT scan. Marfan syndrome also affects the skeleton and the eyes. Patients are typically tall and thin with long extremities. They are at increased risk of lens dislocation, scoliosis, joint hypermobility, and pectus excavatum. Incorrect Answer Explanations Achondroplasia is not associated with cardiac complications, and an emer- gent echocardiogram is not indicated as the first-line diagnostic tool for chest pain in this population. Achondroplasia is caused by a gene mutation that prevents normal conversion of cartilage into bone. At birth and in early childhood, these patients will notably have short stature, short extremities, and a disproportionately large head. Patients with achondroplasia are at risk of complications, including spinal steno- sis, cervicomedullary compression, and hydrocephalus. Patients with clau- dication or an abnormal neurologic examination should be evaluated for these complications. Dilated cardiomyopathy, congestive heart failure, and arrhythmias can occur in patients with muscular dystrophy. However, these patients will rarely present with cardiac-related chest pain as they are often asympto- matic until late stages of the disease. Muscular dystrophy is a group of progres- sive genetic disorders that involve skeletal muscle degeneration. Muscle weakness is the hallmark of these diseases. Children with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the most common form, lose the ability to ambulate by the age of 12 years. This inability to exercise is thought to contribute to the absence of classic symptoms of heart fail- ure. Mortality in patients with muscular dystrophy is primarily attributed to respira- tory and cardiac failure. The most common complications associated with spina bifida are neuro- logic. An emergent echocardiogram would not be the first-line diagnostic tool to evaluate chest pain in this patient population. Spina bifida is a neural tube defect and can be categorized as either spina bifida occulta, myelomeningocele, or meningocele. Patients with spina bifida occulta have intact skin overlying vertebral bodies that have failed to fuse. The neural tissue is not exposed in this type of defect. Contrarily, a meningocele is an open neural tube defect in which the meninges herniate through the vertebral bony defect. Similarly, both the meninges and the spinal cord herniate through the defect in a myelomeningocele. The associated symptoms and complica- tions in spina bifida include hydrocephalus, Chiari malformations, lower ex- tremity weakness and paralysis, and bowel and bladder dysfunction.

question: A patient presents with 2 days of atraumatic back pain without any red flag symp- toms. Acute right-sided lumbar radiculopathy is suspected. What is the best initial treatment for this condition?
englishExplanation: Acute lumbosacral radiculopathy is a common complaint, and the first-line treatment is conservative therapy for 1 to 2 weeks. Reassessment for additional therapeutic op- tions and surgery can be ascertained afterward. Conservative therapy consists of nonopioid pain relief (eg, NSAIDs or acetaminophen), activity modification to avoid activities that cause pain, and a progressive return to normal activity. If these conservative measures do not improve symptoms, then physical therapy and systemic glucocorticoids can be tried for another 2 weeks. If symptoms are still present or worsening after that time, or if the patient has progressive neurologic find- ings, imaging such as an MRI should be obtained. Depending on findings from the MRI, spine surgery can be consulted. Acute lumbosacral radiculopathy occurs when there is dysfunction of one of the lum- bosacral nerve roots. Patients present with pain, radiation of pain down one leg, and paresthesias in a lumbosacral dermatome. Patients with atraumatic mecha- nisms do not need imaging in the immediate period unless red flags are present that indicate more serious disease, including older age (>60 years); fever; im- munocompromised state; weight loss; night sweats; a history of or sys- temic symptoms suggestive of cancer; duration of symptoms longer than 6 weeks; and any physical examination findings that suggest cauda equina syndrome such as saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, bilateral symp- toms, or weakness. In the emergency department, patients with red flags can be screened with lumbosacral x-ray, which may reveal bony abnormalities such as frac- tures or significant changes in alignment; however, this is nonemergent. Patients with symptoms that persist for more than 6 weeks can undergo a nonurgent MRI. Patients with concerning findings for cauda equina syndrome should un- dergo an emergent MRI. A CT scan is inadequate to evaluate the soft tissue struc- tures of the spine. Lumbosacral radiculopathy has many causes, but the most common are due to disc herniations, which are often self-limited, or progressive spinal stenosis. Less commonly, lumbosacral radiculopathy can be caused by tumors or other compressive lesions, such as spinal abscesses or hematomas. Most patients with lumbar disc her- niations are between age 30 and 50 years. Sciatica, or pain in a radicular distribution, is present in up to 95% of patients with lumbar disc herniation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Prolonged bed rest is no longer thought to be helpful in patients with back pain; therefore, patients should be encouraged to carry out activities of daily living in a modified fashion. First, they should avoid activities that cause an increase in pain and then gradually increase their activity level as tolerated. Although many patients with acute lumbosacral radiculopathy may need physical therapy, it is not typically recommended in the acute phase in the first 1 to 2 weeks, as it can be painful for patients with severe symptoms. Additionally, many patients with mild symptoms improve with conservative therapy, such as NSAIDS, in the first 1 to 2 weeks. Steroids, either locally injected or taken systemically, are not recom- mended for the initial treatment of acute lumbosacral radiculopathy. Some experts recommend systemic steroids (eg, prednisone for 5 days) if symptoms are still persistent after the initial conservative therapy has been tried for over 2 weeks. Notably, the evidence regarding systemic steroids and acute low back pain is mixed, so these cases should be handled weighing the patient's personal risks and benefits of systemic steroids.

question: Disc herniation affecting which nerve root is most likely to cause a decreased Achilles (ankle jerk) reflex?
englishExplanation: S1 radiculopathy pain radiates down the posterior aspect of the leg into the foot. The nerve root is affected by herniation of the disc at the L5 to S1 level and exits be- low the S1 vertebra. The S1 nerve root is associated with the Achilles (ankle jerk) reflex. Herniation at this level may lead to weakness in leg extension and knee flexion, as well as plantar flexion of the foot. On examination, the patient may exhibit symptoms of decreased sensation to the posterior aspect of the leg and lateral aspect of the foot. Incorrect Answer Explanations The L3 nerve root exits at the L3 to L4 level and supplies sensation to the medial aspect of the knee. This is an uncommon site for herniation. The L3 nerve innervates the quadriceps femoris muscle affecting knee extension. The L4 nerve root exits at the L4 to L5 level and supplies sensation to the medial aspect of the lower leg and foot. The L4 nerve innervates the quadriceps femoris and tibialis anterior affecting dorsiflexion of the foot. Additionally, L4 inner- vates the patellar tendon reflex. The L5 nerve root exits at L5 to S1 and is the most common radiculopathy. L5 supplies sensation to the lateral aspect of the lower leg and dorsum of the foot as well as the webspace between the first and second toes. It provides motor innervation to the tibialis anterior affecting dorsiflexion of the foot and great toe.

question: What is the most common cause of sciatica?
englishExplanation: Disc herniation is the most common cause of sciatica. Sciatica is radicular back pain along the sensory distribution of a particular lumbar or sacral nerve root. Sciatica symptoms may be caused by nerve root compression by the herniated disc. Other possible causes of nerve root compression, and therefore sciatica symptoms, include neoplasm, epidural abscess, fractures of the vertebra or sacroiliac joint, and many others. Incorrect Answer Explanations Epidural abscesses can cause sciatica, but disc herniation is more common. Approximately 47% patients with epidural abscess report radicular symptoms of sci- atica due to epidural compression syndrome. Sciatica is found in one or both legs in these patients. Although spinal tumors can cause sciatica, disc herniation is the more common cause. Patients may report radicular symptoms of sciatica due to epidural compres- sion syndrome. Sciatica can be found in one or both legs in these patients. On rare occasions, vertebral fractures can cause sciatica, but disc herniation is the more common cause. Sciatica in vertebral fractures is related to nerve root compression.

question: A high school football player presents with cervical pain and left-arm paresthesia after a game. An MRI demonstrates a C5 disc herniation without epidural intru- sion. What are appropriate discharge instructions for this patient?

options.text: Require to wear a hard cervical collar at all times
Return to play only when all symptoms are resolved

correctAnswer: Return to play only when all symptoms are resolved
englishExplanation: Cervical disc herniation in adolescent athletes should be managed with care. Much like with concussions, young athletes with cervical disc herniations should be assessed for symptoms and should refrain from play in contact sports while symp- toms continue. When conservative treatment results in a complete resolution of symptoms, then the athlete may return to contact sports. An athlete requiring surgi- cal intervention of cervical disc herniation should follow the advice of the surgeon, who can be more discriminating when deciding whether the athlete can return to play. Cervical disc herniation in young athletes may occur due to similar mechanisms as in adults, including acute injury or trauma (acute onset), or due to degenerative disc disease (insidious onset). Up to 10% of adolescent athletes may have some degenera- tive disc disease. Clinical symptoms of disc herniation include sudden-onset posterior neck pain, referred pain to the arm or shoulder due to nerve root impingement, or di- minished reflexes. More severe symptoms — including gait disturbance, loss of bowel and bladder function, or lower extremity weakness — may be seen in cases with epidural compression syndrome. Incorrect Answer Explanations Occupational therapy may be useful if this patient has prolonged or persistent symptoms, but it is unlikely to be required at this point. Physical therapy may be use- ful in the acute injury setting. Surgical intervention is a later step in cervical disc herniation. It is generally con- sidered only after 6 to 8 weeks of conservative treatment has failed. A hard cervical collar is unnecessary for cervical disc herniation in the young athlete. Soft cervical collars may be used as a reminder to limit activity.

question: A 25-year-old woman presents with pain in her knees, heels, and left ankle as well as limited range of motion in her lower back. She was recently treated for STI symptoms with antibiotics and has since tested negative for gonorrhea; she is oth- erwise healthy and not taking any other medications. Examination reveals inflam- mation of her Achilles tendon. What is the medication of choice to treat this most likely condition?
englishExplanation: The classic presentation of reactive arthritis (formerly referred to as Reiter syndrome) includes arthritis, urethritis, and uveitis; however, this triad is not necessary for making the diagnosis. This patient presents with an asym- metrical polyarthritis following a recent chlamydial infection or urethritis, which is enough to warrant a high level of suspicion for reactive arthritis. The treatment of choice for reactive arthritis is an NSAID, commonly indomethacin. Antibiotics have also been shown to have benefit in postchlamydial reactive arthritis. Long-term combination therapy of rifampicin with doxycycline or azithromycin may be used in addition to NSAIDs. In this syndrome, the Achilles tendon might be in- flamed at the insertion point. The pain patients typically experience is in the weight-bearing joints of knees, ankles, and heels. In addition, the sacroil- iac joints, ischial tuberosity, and ischial crest can be involved and cause pain with range of motion. Diarrhea caused by infection with the invasive GI bac- teria — Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia — has also been known to cause a reactive arthritis picture. The NSAIDs are also the treatment of choice for postdysentery reactive arthritis, but antibiotics have not been shown to have benefit. Incorrect Answer Explanations Antibiotics are not the first-line therapy for reactive arthritis. Chlamydial infections might respond to long-term antibiotic therapy, but ceftriaxone is not an antibiotic typically used in these cases. Although not first-line therapy, the appropriate antibiotics have been shown to improve recovery time in patients with reactive arthritis caused by chlamydial infections. Typically, rifampicin is used in conjunction with either doxycycline or azithromycin, but NSAIDs are still the treatment of choice. Methotrexate is not used for reactive arthritis but may be used in other forms of arthritis, most notably rheumatoid arthritis. Intraarticular or systemic gluco- corticoids may be considered in patients with reactive arthritis who do not receive relief from NSAIDs.

question: A young man presents with back pain that started while performing a deadlift. He describes a sudden “popping” sensation to the back with pain radiating down his right leg. He has no urinary retention or incontinence. On examination, he has normal motor strength and sensation and no midline spinal tenderness. What emergency department imaging is indicated?

options.text: CT scan of the lumbar spine

englishExplanation: Emergent imaging is not indicated because there is no concern for frac- ture, infection, neurological issues, or cauda equina syndrome. This pa- tient presents with lower back pain that started suddenly while deadlifting. Given the mechanism, this patient likely experienced a sudden herniation of the intervertebral discs of the spine, causing impingement of the spinal nerves as they exit the spinal foramina. This is characteristic of lumbosacral radiculopathy, which leads to pain shooting down the leg, or radiculitis. Overall, this patient is at low risk of an acute fracture. His history and examination are inconsistent with acute cauda equina syndrome. Management involves anti-inflammatory medications and muscle relaxants. If these measures are inadequate, physical therapy and corticosteroids may be indicated. Plain x-rays have an overall low sensitivity in evaluating acute fractures or other pathologies of the spine. In the case of traumatic injury, CT imaging is most useful to identify potential fractures. MRI is the imaging modality of choice to evaluate for acute cord compression and the extent of disc herniation. It is also the modality of choice to evaluate for infection, such as an abscess of osteomyelitis. Incorrect Answer Explanations CT scan of the lumbar spine is not indicated in this case. CT imaging is useful in evaluating for acute fracture of the spine in the setting of trauma. However, this patient did not have any direct trauma and does not have an indication for a CT scan. Emergent MRI of the lumbar spine is not indicated in this case. MRI is useful to evaluate for acute cord compression, cauda equina syndrome, or spinal infection. Although this patient does not have clinical features of any of these condi- tions and does not warrant emergent MRI, he may ultimately require nonemergent MRI. X-ray of the lumbar spine is not indicated. Overall, plain x-rays have low sensi- tivity in evaluating back pain, even in the setting of trauma. They can be useful for a gross evaluation of the spinal column and vertebral alignment. However, if there is clinical concern for a fracture, CT imaging should be used. Regardless, this patient does not meet criteria for imaging given a low likelihood of fracture with no other dangerous features on history or examination.

question: Which examination maneuver is used to help diagnose cervical radiculopathy?

options.text: Arm abduction and extension with neck extension while palpating the radial pulse
Arm forward flexion, internal rotation, and adduction with downward resistance
Chin extended, head tilted, and application of axial pressure to the head
Series of gravity-directed head rotational movements

correctAnswer: Chin extended, head tilted, and application of axial pressure to the head
englishExplanation: The Spurling test is an examination maneuver that is used to help diagnose cervical radiculopathy. This maneuver is performed by pushing downward on the head with the chin extended up and the head tilted toward the symptomatic side. A positive test occurs when this maneuver reproduces pain radiating down the affected side. This test works by compressing the intervertebral discs while narrowing the spinal foramina that the cervical nerve roots exit from. Cervical radiculopathy occurs most commonly from nerve root compression. This can be caused by degenerative changes to the cervical spine, termed “cervical spondylo- sis.” It can also be caused by degeneration of the intervertebral discs. Symptoms typi- cally start with pain that radiates down the arm, which may be associated with loss of sensation or motor weakness. There may be loss of normal re- flexes as well. Radicular symptoms without acute loss of function typically have a be- nign cause, and treatment includes anti-inflammatory medications, physical therapy, and corticosteroids. Imaging is not indicated in these cases. However, if there is concern for a more dangerous pathology (eg, fracture, tumor, or infection) or if there is an acute change in motor function or sensation, advanced imaging should be obtained. Also consider stroke and be sure to complete a full neurological exami- nation any time there are neurological deficits. Incorrect Answer Explanations Arm abduction and extension with neck extension while palpating the radial pulse is incorrect. This is the Adson test, which is used to diagnose thoracic outlet ob- struction. This is a condition that causes vascular and neurologic compromise to the upper extremity when the thoracic outlet becomes narrowed or obstructed. When the Adson maneuver is performed, the radial pulse on the affected side will become diminished when the neck is extended and the head is tilted. Arm forward flexion, internal rotation, and adduction with downward resistance is incorrect. This is the O'Brien test. The O'Brien test is used to diagnose labral injuries of the shoulder. This test is performed by having the patient forward flex, adduct and internally rotate the shoulder, and then press up superiorly against the examiner's resistance. Pain reproduced in the shoulder represents a positive test. Series of gravity-directed head rotational movements is incorrect. This is the Epley maneuver. The Epley maneuver is used to treat benign paroxysmal posi- tional vertigo and reposition otoliths.

question: Which finding is an indication for an emergent MRI of the cervical spine?

options.text: Gradual-onset neck pain with intermittent shooting pain down the arm without weakness
Gradual-onset neck stiffness that is relieved with application of heat or massage
Sudden-onset neck pain with fever and left arm weakness in a patient using IV drugs
Sudden-onset neck stiffness and pain with lateral neck rotation after waking from sleep

correctAnswer: Sudden-onset neck pain with fever and left arm weakness in a patient using IV drugs
englishExplanation: Sudden onset of pain with arm weakness and fever should be emergently evaluated with an MRI to assess for an epidural abscess or osteomyelitis, as this clinical scenario is concerning for the development of a cervical neck infection. These infections are emergent diagnoses that need to be promptly treated. Patients who use intravenous drugs are at a much higher increased risk of seeding infections (eg, epidural abscesses or endocarditis) given the frequency with which they inject unsterile material into their veins using unsterile techniques. Sudden onset of any acute neurological syndrome, including loss of sensation or weakness to an upper extremity, is concerning for significant pathology (eg, infection, acute spinal cord syndromes such as infarction, or multiple sclerosis lesions). This is also concerning if there was preceding trauma. X-ray imaging is limited and will miss many significant diagnoses. CT imaging is most useful when evaluating for traumatic injuries of the cervical spine, such as acute fractures or liga- mentous injuries and instability. MRI is most useful to evaluate for le- sions affecting the spinal cord itself or to evaluate for infection, such as ab- scess or osteomyelitis. It is also useful to confirm ligamentous traumatic injuries when CT is inconclusive or negative despite persistent neurological symptoms. Incorrect Answer Explanations Gradual-onset neck pain with intermittent shooting pain down the arm without weakness is suggestive of cervical radiculopathy caused by de- generative changes to the cervical spine. This is usually due to degenerative changes to the vertebral column (termed “cervical spondylosis”) or to the interverte- bral discs, all of which lead to cervical nerve root compression. This does not warrant emergent imaging in the emergency department in the absence of neurological deficits and can be managed conservatively. Gradual-onset neck stiffness that is relieved with application of heat or massage is more suggestive of musculoskeletal neck strain. Most often, this affects the trapezius or sternocleidomastoid muscles. This condition does not require emergent imaging. Sudden-onset neck stiffness and pain with lateral neck rotation after waking from sleep is suggestive of an acute cervical neck spasm or torti- collis-like syndrome. Although this condition is painful, in the absence of neuro- logical deficits or infectious symptoms, it does not require further evaluation with imaging and can be treated conservatively.

question: What disease process causes numbness and tingling to the lower legs that worsens with activity and improves with rest?
englishExplanation: Spinal stenosis is a condition that causes narrowing of the spinal canal and leads to compression of various neural elements, including the spinal cord and spinal nerves. The most common mechanism by which this occurs is degen- erative change to the lower spine, including degeneration of the lumbar discs, arthritis of the facet joints, and spondylolisthesis (ie, slippage of one vertebra onto another). Classically, lumbar stenosis will present with midline back pain and symptoms of nerve root compression, including weakness, numbness, and tingling to the lower extremities. This pain will often be exacerbated by activ- ity and relieved by rest. This is referred to as “neurogenic claudication” or “pseudoclaudication.” Forward flexion of the spine will improve symptoms by opening up neural foramina and relieving nerve root compression. Conversely, exten- sion of the spine will exacerbate symptoms. The diagnosis of spinal stenosis is initially clinical but is usually confirmed with imaging, including CT or MRI. Symptomatic care and physical therapy are the mainstays of conservative treatment, but patients may ultimately need surgical intervention to improve their symptoms. It is important to rule out acute cauda equina syndrome by assessing for urinary retention, urinary or fecal incontinence, and perineal anesthesia, as this is a surgical emer- gency. Additionally, vascular claudication can present similarly to neurogenic clau- dication. With vascular claudication, pain tends to be more cramping and diffuse, which is in contrast to the dermatomal distribution and nerve-like radicular pain seen in neurogenic claudication. There will likely be reduced pulses and signs of poor blood flow to the lower extremities. Vascular claudication is caused by periph- eral arterial disease, most frequently from the buildup of atherosclerotic plaques within peripheral arteries leading to reduced blood flow to the extremities. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cauda equina syndrome is a condition in which the spinal nerve fibers from the end of the spinal cord are compressed. Presenting symptoms of cauda equina syn- drome are weakness and loss of sensation to the lower extremities, uri- nary retention, overflow urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence, and perineal or “saddle” anesthesia. This is a surgical emergency. Symptoms are constant and progressive and do not come and go with activity. Guillain-Barré syndrome is a demyelinating condition that most often af- fects the lower extremities. It classically causes an ascending paralysis that starts in the lower legs and migrates superiorly. These symptoms are constant, progressive, and do not come and go with exertion. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a demyelinating condition that tends to affect the CNS. Symptoms of MS are variable and may include weakness, paresthe- sias, and impairments in coordination and balance. Symptoms do not classically worsen with exertion and improve with rest in a predictable manner, as occurs in spinal stenosis.

question: Which historic or physical examination finding is most consistent with the diagno- sis of costochondritis?

options.text: Pain that worsens when the patient lies flat

englishExplanation: Consistent reproduction of pain with chest-wall palpation is the most im- portant diagnostic feature of costochondritis (also known as Tietze syn- drome). Other, more serious causes of chest pain must also be ruled out. It is esti- mated that as many as 50% of patients who present with chest pain have a muscu- loskeletal source. However, musculoskeletal pain can also occur in the setting of my- ocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, and other serious conditions. Pain caused by costochondritis tends to be localized and sharp. In addition to pain reproduced with palpation, patients with costochondritis may also have symp- toms reproduced with the “crowing rooster” maneuver. This maneuver involves extension and abduction of the shoulders with the patient placing their hands behind the head, elbows facing out to the sides. The head is pointed to the painful side, with the cervical spine in extension. Posterior traction is then applied to the arms in an at- tempt to reproduce chest symptoms. When serious causes of chest pain have been ruled out, patients with presumed cos- tochondritis can be treated with NSAIDs, acetaminophen, and topical medica- tions, such as lidocaine and capsaicin for pain relief. Stretching exercises are also recommended to help relieve the symptoms. Opioids should be avoided in patients with musculoskeletal chest pain. If pain persists for more than 4 to 6 weeks, the patient should be referred to a specialist — such as an orthopedist, physiatrist, or rheumatologist — for further evaluation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Pain that worsens when the patient is lying flat (or is relieved when they are sitting up) is a common finding in patients with pericarditis, not costo- chondritis. Sitting up reduces pressure on the parietal pericardium. Patients with pericarditis also tend to have pain that radiates to the trapezius ridge. Pain that worsens with deep breathing or inspiration often occurs in patients with costochondritis, but pleuritic chest pain is also one of the most common pre- senting symptoms of a pulmonary embolism. Thus, other causes of pleuritic pain may need to be ruled out in patients with risk factors. Coughing can lead to inflammation of the chest wall but is not the most likely finding associated with costochondritis. Presence of a cough should also lead to further con- cern for a possible infectious etiology of pain or, potentially, pulmonary embolism.

question: Pain elicited from which test or maneuver is most supportive of a diagnosis of costochondritis?

Extension/abduction of shoulders with hands behind head and with neck ex- tended; physician applies posterior traction to arms
Passive flexion of shoulder while physician prevents shoulder shrugging
Physician applies downward pressure to top of head with neck in neutral position

correctAnswer: Extension/abduction of shoulders with hands behind head and with neck ex- tended; physician applies posterior traction to arms
englishExplanation: The “crowing rooster” maneuver often reproduces chest symptoms in pa- tients with costochondritis (also known as Tietze syndrome). This maneuver in- volves extension and abduction of the shoulders with the patient placing their hands behind their head, elbows facing out to the sides. The head is pointed to the side that is painful, with the cervical spine in extension. The physician then applies posterior traction to the arms in an attempt to reproduce chest symptoms. In the setting of chest pain, it is important to rule out other, more serious causes. It is estimated that as many as 50% of patients who present with chest pain have a muscu- loskeletal source. However, musculoskeletal pain can also occur in the setting of my- ocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, and other serious scenarios. When serious causes of chest pain have been ruled out, patients with presumed cos- tochondritis can be treated with NSAIDs, acetaminophen (if not contraindi- cated), and other topical medications, such as lidocaine or capsaicin for pain relief. Stretching exercises are also recommended to help relieve the symptoms. Opioids should be avoided in patients with musculoskeletal chest pain. If pain persists for more than 4 to 6 weeks, the patient should be referred to a specialist — such as an orthopedist, physiatrist, or rheumatologist — for further evaluation. Incorrect Answer Explanations The test in which the patient's shoulder is stabilized while the elbow is flexed to 90° and the physician internally rotates the shoulder is known as the Hawkins- Kennedy test. If pain is elicited, the test result is positive. This test is used to diag- nose shoulder impingement syndrome. The maneuver in which the patient's shoulder is passively flexed while shoulder shrugging is prevented is known as the Neer test or passive painful arc maneu- ver. Pain elicited with this motion supports the diagnosis of shoulder impingement. The maneuver in which the physician applies downward pressure on the top of the patient's head with the neck in a neutral position is known as the Spurling maneu- ver or neck compression test. It is used to reproduce radicular pain in the neck. Key Points Extension and abduction of the patient's shoulders with the hands behind the head, the neck extended, and posterior traction applied to the arms (the crowing rooster maneuver) is used to reproduce costochondritis pain on examination. Costochondritis can occur in conjunction with other more serious illnesses, such as myocardial infarction or pulmonary embolism, so it is important to consider and rule out other illnesses occurring simultaneously. Opioids should be avoided when treating musculoskeletal chest pain.

question: A 45-year-old man presents after an outpatient MRI reveals cauda equina syn- drome. What finding is most likely present?

options.text: More weakness in upper extremities than lower

englishExplanation: Physical examination findings that are consistent with cauda equina syndrome in- clude decreased anal sensation (known as saddle anesthesia), decreased rectal tone, lower extremity weakness, numbness or paresthesias, de- creased or hypoactive lower extremity reflexes, and urinary retention. The most consistent finding in patients with cauda equina syndrome is urinary reten- tion, with a sensitivity of 90%. This can be checked easily in the emergency depart- ment with a postvoid residual. The patient may also complain of urinary or fe- cal incontinence, but urinary retention (which can manifest as overflow incontinence) is more common. Cauda equina syndrome is not a true cord syndrome; it is a syndrome that affects the cluster of lumbar and sacral nerve roots that exist distal to the cord known as the cauda equina (or the "horse's tail"). Patient complaints of low back pain and bilateral motor or sensory findings, especially in the saddle or perineal region, should raise suspicion for this condition. Cauda equina syndrome is a lower motor neuron lesion because it involves only the nerve roots, so hyporeflexia might be seen. An upper motor neuron lesion or a mix of upper and lower neuron lesions can be seen with the pathology of the distal spinal cord; this is known as conus medullaris syndrome. Hyperreflexia and a positive Babinski sign are upper motor neuron findings. The sensory changes in cauda equina syndrome are dermatomal and correspond to the affected nerve roots. The classic finding in cauda equina syndrome is saddle anes- thesia involving the buttocks, the backs of the thighs, and the perineum. The most common cause of cauda equina syndrome is disc herniation. Other causes include spinal epidural hematoma, epidural abscess, discitis, tumors, trauma, and spinal stenosis. Urinary retention (and postvoid incontinence) and fecal incontinence are signs of sphincter dysfunction that are common in both cauda equina and conus medullaris syndromes. Incorrect Answer Explanations Abnormal Babinski sign occurs when the lateral aspect of the foot is stim- ulated and leads to extension or dorsiflexion of the big toe. This is a patho- logical sign that signals an upper motor neuron problem. Cauda equina syndrome is a lower motor neuron problem, so the Babinski sign should not be abnormal in this syndrome. Upper motor neuron signs indicate a problem in the spinal cord. Increased deep tendon reflexes are suggestive of an upper motor neuron problem arising from the brain, brainstem, or spinal cord. Because cauda equina is a lower motor neuron problem involving the nerve roots distal to the spinal cord, hyporeflexia (or absence of reflexes) would be expected. Upper extremity weakness that is greater than lower extremity weakness is seen often in central cord syndrome, which is a cervical spinal cord condition. Cauda equina syndrome presents with lower extremity weakness that is often bilateral due to compression of the lumbar and sacral nerve roots of the cauda equina. The upper extremities are not involved.

question: What is the most common etiology of cauda equina syndrome?
englishExplanation: Cauda equina syndrome (CES) is a relatively rare disorder (1 in 370 patients who present to the emergency department for back pain) that results from compression of nerve roots in the lumbar vertebral canal. Disc herniation is the most com- mon etiology of CES, occurring in up to 45% of cases. Nerve roots involved include lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal levels, with L4 through L5 and L5 through S1 being the most commonly involved. In addition to back pain, symptoms of CES include bladder or bowel dysfunction (ie, incontinence), saddle sensory deficit, and sexual dysfunction. Symptoms may occur acutely or in the setting of chronic back pain, making this a diagnosis that is often missed. Prompt recognition of CES is essential, as delays in treatment may result in permanent neurologic deficits. Regardless of etiology, suspicion for CES should remain high in patients who present with back pain and associated lower- extremity neurologic deficits. Incorrect Answer Explanations Malignancy of the spine, either as a primary lesion or metastasis, may cause nerve root compression in a similar manner as disc herniation. Although relatively com- mon, cord compression due to malignancy occurs less frequently than with disc herniation. Symptoms due to neoplastic compression typically develop more slowly than with disc herniation and are preceded by an extended period of pain. As with malignancy and disc herniation, compression from a spinal abscess may lead to CES. Infectious etiologies — including spinal epidural abscess — com- monly cause neurologic deficits, but development of the clinical signs that define CES occurs less frequently with infection than with disc herniation. Traumatic injury is another cause of CES, although less common than disc hernia- tion. Other potential but less frequent causes of CES include spinal anesthesia, aortic disease, and lumbar spine manipulation. Neurologic deficits and pain caused by these etiologies share a common mechanism with disc herniation: direct compression of the nerve roots that comprise the cauda equina.

question: What imaging modality is considered the gold standard in evaluation and diagno- sis of cauda equina syndrome?
englishExplanation:
MRI remains the gold standard for the evaluation and diagnosis of cauda equina syndrome (CES). Based on American College of Radiology recommendations, MRI without contrast is typically appropriate, although contrast may be useful in set- tings such as suspected malignancy or infection. MRI sequences commonly evaluated are sagittal and axial T1, T2, and STIR of the lumbar spine. Evaluation of the entire spine may be performed if malignancy is suspected, as lesions proximal to the lumbar region may be missed if only localized imaging is performed. CES — caused by compression of nerve roots at the lumbar, sacral, or coccygeal level — manifests as a variety of nonspecific symptoms, including back pain, urinary incontinence, bowel dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, diminished lower- extremity reflexes, and lower-extremity weakness. Of these symptoms, blad- der dysfunction is considered most predictive of CES. This dysfunction typically be- gins as bladder sensory change and incomplete emptying with progression to urinary retention and overflow incontinence. Incorrect Answer Explanations CT, although typically more accessible in the emergency setting than MRI, does not offer sufficient visualization of the spinal cord for diagnosis of CES. The use of CT imaging with contrast is currently being explored for use in patients with con- traindications to MRI (eg, claustrophobia, incompatible metallic implants), but this is not currently in widespread use. POCUS, specifically in the measurement of postvoid residual (PVR) volume, has been used to risk-stratify patients with suspected CES. Although PVR volume cutoffs for diagnosis of CES have yet to be established, both low-volume (rule out) and high- volume (rule in) strategies have been utilized. In one study, a PVR volume of <200 mL had a negative predictive value of 97% in the diagnosis of CES. Another study found that PVR volume >500 mL was a reliable predictor of CES. If CES is sug- gested by ultrasound measurement of PVR volume, further evaluation by MRI is re- quired for definitive diagnosis. X-ray is typically more accessible, faster, and less expensive in the emergency setting than MRI. However, the utility of x-ray in the diagnosis of CES is limited given the lack of visualization of the spinal cord and potential compression.

question: What treatment is most essential in the prevention of long-term neurologic seque- lae in cauda equina syndrome caused by a spinal abscess?
englishExplanation: In any patient with cauda equina syndrome (CES), prompt surgical decompression at the site of the offending lesion is the definitive treatment. Although the exact tim- ing of surgery has been debated, decompression within 48 hours of symptom out- set generally leads to more favorable outcomes, including prevention of long-term neurologic sequelae. For patients with advanced symptoms (typically present for >48 hours), surgical decompression may still provide benefit, although surgery may be delayed as full return of function is less likely. If CES is suspected in the emergency department based on clinical history (eg, lum- bar pain, sciatica, bladder or bowel incontinence, or sexual dysfunction), physical examination findings (eg, urinary retention, saddle sensory deficit, lower-extremity weakness, or diminished lower-extremity reflexes) and imaging (MRI), prompt consultation with a spine surgeon is critical in providing the best chance for complete recovery. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although surgical decompression is necessary for the definitive management of CES, symptom relief in the emergency department should not be ignored. Bladder de- compression by Foley catheterization and appropriate analgesia may provide significant patient relief while awaiting imaging and consultation. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics are indicated in patients with CES secondary to spinal abscess, but this treatment does not preclude the need for definitive surgical treatment. Prompt surgical decompression (ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset) remains the gold standard treatment for CES. Dexamethasone IV is often recommended in the emergency department treatment of CES. Dosing is typically in the range of 8 to 10 mg. Although intravenous steroids may improve long-term outcomes in patients with CES secondary to malignancy, their utility in preventing neurologic sequelae in all patients with CES re- mains unknown.

question: Which disease is most commonly associated with inflammation of the sacroiliac joints?
englishExplanation: Ankylosing spondylitis is an inflammatory disorder that is characterized by gradual-onset lower back pain, bilateral sacroiliitis, and limited move- ment of the lumbar spine. The inflammation in this disorder specifically targets where ligaments attach to bones and can ultimately cause new bone formation. This contributes to lumbar stiffness and the appearance of “bamboo spine” on x- rays. Ankylosing spondylitis affects men more than women, and onset of symptoms is before age 45. There is also an association with the development of ankylosing spondylitis and carrying the HLA-B27 gene. Treatment includes administration of NSAIDs and a referral to rheumatology. Complications of this disease include spinal fractures with minimal trauma. Incorrect Answer Explanations Behçet's disease is an inflammatory disease that commonly affects the eyes, skin, GI tract, CNS, and large blood vessels. Bony manifestations like sacroiliitis are unrelated to this disease. Recurrent uveitis and ulcers of the genital and oral mucosa are the most common clinical features. There is a higher prevalence of this disease in people from East Asia, the Mediterranean, and Middle Eastern countries. Treatment includes referral to a rheumatologist for initiation of high- dose steroids and immunosuppressive agents. Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) is characterized by ossifi- cation of the tendon, ligament, and joint capsule insertions. The spine is most commonly affected by ossification, but involvement of the sacroiliac joints is atypical. Patients with DISH are at increased risk of vertebral fracture and spinal cord injury after minimal trauma. Many patients are asymptomatic. Treatment is usually supportive care. Occasionally, surgery may be needed for severe cases. Psoriatic arthritis is a chronic inflammatory condition that affects some patients with psoriasis. There are multiple subtypes of psoriatic arthritis, but the joints of the hands and feet are often affected. Up to 40% of patients may develop spinal involvement, including sacroiliitis, but less often than in ankylosing spondyli- tis. Other clinical features include dactylitis and enthesitis (inflammation at tendon and ligament insertion sites). Treatment includes NSAIDs and a rheumatology re- ferral for immunomodulator therapy.
