question: A patient has disc protrusion at L3 that is causing right-sided lower-extremity neu- rological symptoms. What physical examination finding is most consistent with this diagnosis?

options.text: Decreased sensation over the medial malleolus
Weakness with right great toe extension

englishExplanation: The L3 nerve root provides motor function to the knee extensors and hip adductors and provides sensation to the anteromedial thigh, extending to just below the knee. Thus, weakness with right knee extension would be the most likely physical examination finding in this case. Disc protrusion can be acute or chronic depending on the patient's age and clinical presentation. In younger patients, acute disc herniation or spondylolysis can be caused by trauma, sports, or improper lifting. In older adults, symptoms are typically related to degenerative disc disease or arthritis. Patients will typically present with back pain with or without associ- ated neurological symptoms, depending on the level of injury. Patients who present with sciatica due to a herniated disk generally complain more about the radicular symptoms than about back pain. The majority of disk herniations occur at the L4 to L5 (L5 nerve root) or L5 to S1 (S1 nerve root) level. Understanding der- matomes and myotomes is important in identifying the level of injury and the sever- ity of symptoms. Incorrect Answer Explanations Sensation over the medial malleolus is typically localized to the L4 nerve root. The L4 nerve root provides sensation to the anterolateral thigh, crosses the anterior knee, and wraps around the lower leg to the medial malleolus and the medial aspect of the great toe. The L4 nerve root also assists in knee extension. The ankle jerk reflex is achieved by tapping the Achilles tendon while the foot is slightly dorsiflexed. This reflex is mediated by the S1 spinal nerve root. The patellar reflex or knee jerk reflex is mediated by the L3 and L4 nerve root and may be diminished in a patient with L3 radiculopathy symptoms. Great toe extension, which is controlled by the extensor hallucis longus, is medi- ated by the L5 nerve root. The L5 nerve root is also responsible for sensation over the lateral calf and the dorsum of the foot, including the first and second toe. Sensation for L5 is often checked in between the first and second toes.

question: Which laboratory finding is most likely to be noted in discitis?
englishExplanation:
The ESR in discitis is elevated in 90% of cases, and the CRP is also often elevated. Laboratory workup does not often reveal an elevated WBC. Discitis is an infection of the vertebral disc space, which can also be associated with vertebral osteomyelitis. Patients with suspected discitis should undergo a thorough neurologic examination. If the patient has any neurologic deficits, or if imaging reveals cord compression or evidence of an abscess, neurosurgery should be consulted. MRI with contrast is recommended to best identify discitis and other potential associated infections, in- cluding epidural abscess and vertebral osteomyelitis. The majority of infections are caused by Staphylococcus aureus. A biopsy should be conducted, and blood and urine cultures should be obtained. Incorrect Answer Explanations The WBC count is reported to be elevated in <50% of patients presenting with disci- tis. Thus, a normal WBC count is not a sensitive test in the setting of discitis and does not rule out discitis or another vertebral infection. The CRP is often elevated in the setting of discitis and vertebral infection, as is noted with the ESR. However, it is reportedly not as sensitive or specific as the ESR, and an ESR >100 should warrant a high suspicion for infection. The initial biopsy obtained to culture the infectious organism is only positive <50% the time. Thus, it may be necessary to obtain a second biopsy sample. It is also im- portant to obtain urine and blood cultures initially prior to starting antibiotics.

question: Which laboratory test result is the gold standard for diagnosing gout?

options.text: High uric acid levels in serum
WBCs less than 2,000 and PMNs less than 25% on aspirate

englishExplanation: Gout and pseudogout are classified as inflammatory arthritides and are diagnosed by analyzing synovial fluid collected during arthrocentesis. These two can be identified by the level of the cell count along with the presence of crystals, which indicates a crystal-induced synovitis. If the underlying condition is gout, there are negatively birefringent uric acid crystals on aspirate. If it is pseudogout, there is positive birefringence. Patients with gout or pseudo- gout typically present with acute monoarthritis, most commonly seen in either the great toe or the knee, precipitated by factors such as alcohol consumption, noncom- pliance of diet, infection, trauma, or other stressors. The treatment of choice for an acute attack starts with NSAIDs or colchicine only in the absence of re- nal dysfunction. If renal disturbance exists, recent guidelines recommend oral steroids, and a course of narcotic pain medications may be used if necessary. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although the absence of bacteria on joint aspiration can help make the diagnosis of gout, it is not specific for gout itself and is not the gold standard test result. Only in conjunction with the presence of negative birefringent crystals can the absence of bacteria be used to confirm the diagnosis. High levels of uric acid in the serum can be found in patients with gout, but the level can also be normal during an acute gout attack. Thus, this finding should not be used to confirm the diagnosis of gout. A WBC count less than 2,000 and polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) less than 25% on arthrocentesis indicates the presence of a noninflamma- tory arthritis, such as osteoarthritis. Gout is in the category of inflammatory arthritides, which have a WBC count between 2,000 and 100,000 and PMNs greater than 50% with a negative culture on arthrocentesis.

question: An afebrile 67-year-old man who takes hydrochlorothiazide presents with right foot pain, as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: tacojim/iStock/Getty Images Plus.
englishExplanation:
This afebrile patient has tophi, making a gout flare the most likely diagno- sis. Gout is most common in middle-aged men and postmenopausal women. Additional risk factors for gout include hypertension, obesity, diabetes, a purine-rich diet (eg, meat, seafood, and beer), and the use of cyclosporine, aspirin, or thiazide diuretics. In gout, uric acid builds up in the body, leading to the formation of uric acid (monosodium urate) crystals in the joints. Gout flares oc- cur secondary to WBCs ingesting the crystals, causing cytokine release and inflammation. In 75% to 90% of cases, this occurs in the metatarsophalangeal joint of the great toe (ie, podagra). The gold standard for diagnosing gout is fluid aspiration from the joint, with microscopic analysis showing needle-like and negatively birefrin- gent uric acid crystals. Although laboratory studies such as ESR and CRP can be helpful in ruling out other diagnoses, they can often be elevated in both gout and sep- tic arthritis. Serum uric acid levels are also unhelpful because they can be ele- vated or normal in the setting of a gout flare. Diagnostic x-ray imaging may be helpful in chronic disease, as it may ex- hibit asymmetrical “rat bite” bone erosion that is consistent with gout. Ultrasound may also be helpful because gout crystals may exhibit a “double contour” sign. Gout can be treated in the emergency setting with NSAIDs, corticosteroids, and colchicine. NSAIDs should be avoided in patients with significant renal dis- ease, and oral steroids should be used with caution in diabetic patients. Colchicine should be avoided in patients with significant renal or liver disease because it can also cause significant GI side effects. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cutaneous leishmaniasis is an unlikely diagnosis in this case. Cutaneous leishma- niasis is caused by a protozoan parasite that is transmitted through sand fly bites. The bite site, which occurs on exposed areas of the skin, usually develops into a pruritic papule or nodule that progresses to a painless ulcerated lesion. There may be multiple lesions, and they may take months to years to heal. Although gonorrhea is a potential cause of septic arthritis, gonorrhea is unlikely in this case. Patients with disseminated gonorrhea can develop pain and swelling of one or more joints, but it is often polyarticular and asymmet- rical. It most often involves the wrists, knees, and ankles. Patients frequently present with associated tenosynovitis, dermatitis, and polyarthralgia. Patients with disseminated gonococcal infection frequently have systemic signs of infection but may be afebrile on presentation. Joint fluid aspiration is vital if there is any suspi- cion for septic arthritis. Lyme arthritis is unlikely in this case because it rarely involves small joints. Lyme septic arthritis can occur in the setting of both acute and late Lyme in- fection. Lyme septic arthritis often involves the larger joints (most commonly the knees), and it characteristically leads to large joint effusions. Arthropathy from Lyme disease is often polyarticular and asymmetrical. Patients may also present with erythema migrans, the classic “bullseye” rash. Lyme disease is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, which is transmitted through the bite of the deer tick.

question: Which synovial fluid finding is most consistent with gouty arthritis?

options.text: 10,000 WBCs/mm<sup>3</sup>, 50% PMNs, positively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and negative Gram stain
15,000 WBCs/mm<sup>3</sup>, 50% PMNs, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and negative Gram stain
75,000 WBCs/mm<sup>3</sup>, 80% PMNs, positively birefringent calcium py- rophosphate crystals, and positive Gram stain
100,000 WBCs/mm<sup>3</sup>, 92% PMNs. negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and negative Gram stain

correctAnswer: 15,000 WBCs/mm<sup>3</sup>, 50% PMNs, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and negative Gram stain
englishExplanation:
Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid analysis is key to diagnosing gout. Findings of 15,000 WBCs/mm, 50% polymorphonuclear cells (PMNs), negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and a negative Gram stain are most consistent with gout-induced arthritis. Although the WBC count can be somewhat variable, it should be less than 50,000/mm in the set- ting of a crystal-induced synovitis without septic arthritis; however, septic arthritis can occur when the WBC count is less than 50,000/mm, especially in the setting of immunocompromise, early infection, and certain bacteria (eg, Neisseria and my- coplasma). Consider septic arthritis in conjunction with a gout flare, and administer antibiotics if septic arthritis is a concern. There can be variable percentages of PMNs in gouty arthritis, but arthritis should be suspected if the PMNs are 75% to 90% or greater. Monosodium urate crys- tals are often present in acute gout flares, and they are negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals. Joint fluid in the setting of a gout flare should not have a 3 3 3 positive Gram stain. Cellulitis overlying the potential aspiration site and coagulopa- thy are relative contraindications to arthrocentesis. Arthrocentesis of a prosthetic joint should be done in consultation with an orthopedic surgeon and should only be done if necessary to rule out infection. Incorrect Answer Explanations Synovial fluid findings of 10,000 WBCs/mm, 50% PMNs, positively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and a negative Gram stain are not the best choice be- cause uric acid crystals are negatively birefringent. Calcium pyrophosphate crys- tals are positively birefringent and are diagnostic for pseudogout. Synovial fluid findings of 75,000 WBCs/mm, 80% PMNs, positively birefringent cal- cium pyrophosphate crystals, and a positive Gram stain are suggestive of septic arthritis or septic arthritis with pseudogout. WBC count in crystal synovitis can be variable but should be less than 25,000 (with a positive likelihood ratio [+LR] for septic arthritis in this context of 0.32) to 50,000 (+LR of 7.7). There is also a higher percentage of PMNs and a positive Gram stain, which would be concerning for septic arthritis. Synovial fluid findings of 100,000 WBCs/mm, 90% PMNs, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and a negative Gram stain are not the best choice. The WBC count is greater than 50,000/mm, and the percentage of PMNs is 92%, making this sample concerning for septic arthritis. Although the Gram stain was negative in this analysis, Gram stain is only 29% to 50% sensitive, so a neg- ative Gram stain does not rule out infection.

question: What is the best oral treatment for acute gout flare in a patient with chronic kidney disease?
englishExplanation: Prednisone is the best oral treatment for acute gout flare in the setting of chronic kidney disease. Courses of prednisone 30 mg to 40 mg PO daily (either in single or divided doses) for 5 days can be effective in treating acute gout flares; ta- pered courses can also be considered. Studies show that steroids can be as effective as NSAIDs in the setting of acute gout flares and may potentially have fewer side effects. However, steroids should be avoided if there is any concern for septic arthritis and in diabetic patients with poor glycemic control. In patients without significant comorbidities, other therapies such as NSAIDs and colchicine may be considered. If there is no concern for a septic joint, glucocorticoid articular injection may also be considered. Incorrect Answer Explanations Allopurinol is a urate-lowering medication used to prevent gout flares. It is not the best initial choice because it may potentially prolong the gout flare. Recent small studies suggest that this may not be the case, but this is still controversial. The me- tabolite of allopurinol remains in the circulation longer in the setting of renal impair- ment and may lead to toxic drug reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. Thus, allopurinol should be used with caution in these patients. Colchicine should be used with extreme caution in patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency. It should also be avoided in any patients taking a P-glyco- protein inhibitor. Colchicine has a narrow therapeutic margin. If it accumulates in the body, colchicine can have potentially serious side effects, including cytope- nias, neuropathy, liver failure, and rhabdomyolysis. Colchicine also can have signifi- cant GI side effects, such as vomiting and diarrhea. Indomethacin is not the best answer choice because NSAIDs should be avoided in patients with renal impairment. NSAIDs should also be avoided in patients with a history of gastric or duodenal ulcers or who are on anticoagulation therapy. NSAIDs are most effective when started at the onset of a gout flare and should be continued for 2 to 3 days after the resolution of symptoms.

question: What crystals are found in the synovial fluid of pseudogout?
englishExplanation: Positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals are seen on syn- ovial fluid analysis in patients with pseudogout or calcium pyrophos- phate crystal deposition disease (CPPD). Pseudogout is a crystal-induced syn- ovitis that is caused by deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in the joint. These crystals exhibit positive birefringence on microscopy and are rhomboid- shaped. In patients with pseudogout, the most commonly affected joint is the knee. These patients may exhibit findings of white lines of chondrocalcinosis on x-ray imaging of the joint. Treatment of pseudogout is similar to gout flares, with NSAIDs, colchicine, and steroids unless contraindicated. Incorrect Answer Explanations Calcium oxalate crystals can be present in synovial fluid but are not are not diagnos- tic for pseudogout. Notably, calcium oxalate crystals can be observed in eth- ylene glycol intoxication as ethylene glycol is broken down into oxalic acid. Subsequently, calcium oxalate precipitates in the kidney. The calcium oxalate crystals can then be identified on urine microscopy. Monosodium urate crystals are present in gout flares, not pseudogout flares. The monosodium urate crystals are negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals. Gout most commonly presents with involvement of the first metatarsal pha- langeal joint (podagra), and patients may have tophi, which are nodular deposits of uric acid crystals. Cholesterol crystals can be present in synovial fluid but are not indicative of pseudogout. Cholesterol crystals can be present in states of chronic inflamma- tion, and it is also possible to see lipid droplets on synovial fluid. In that context, the presence of a fracture should be considered.

question: What is most likely to trigger a gout flare?
englishExplanation: Salicylates can increase uric acid levels and have been linked to gout flares. Gout is most common in middle-aged men and post menopausal women. Additional risk factors for gout include hypertension, obesity, diabetes, a purine-rich diet (eg, meat, seafood, and beer), and medications, including cy- closporine, thiazide, diuretics, and aspirin. In gout, uric acid builds up in the body and leads to the formation of uric acid crystals in the joints. Gout flares occur sec- ondary to WBCs ingesting the crystals, causing cytokine release and inflammation. One of the most common locations for this to occur (75%-90%) is in the great toe metatarsophalangeal joint (ie, podagra). The gold standard for diagnosing gout is fluid aspiration from the joint, with microscopic analysis showing needle- shaped and negatively birefringent uric acid crystals. Treatment of gout in the emergency setting involves the use of NSAIDs, corticosteroids, and colchicine. NSAIDs should be avoided in patients with sig- nificant renal disease, and oral steroids should be used with caution in diabetic pa- tients. Colchicine should be avoided in patients with significant renal or liver disease because it can cause significant GI side effects. Incorrect Answer Explanations Angiotensin receptor blockers are unlikely to trigger a gout flare. In fact, angiotensin receptor blockers may help lower uric acid levels, based on recent stud- ies. Diuretics such as thiazide, however, do increase urate reabsorption and can trig- ger gout flares. Although more research is needed, several studies have indicated that supple- mentation with ascorbic acid may reduce serum uric acid levels. However, there is no convincing evidence that ascorbic acid supplementation reduces the fre- quency or severity of gout flares. Caffeine is not a likely trigger for gout flares, and it has been shown to potentially decrease uric acid levels. In contrast, alcoholic beverages and bever- ages that are high in sugar or high-fructose corn syrup have been linked to gout flares. Alcohol metabolism blocks excretion of uric acid, leading to increased levels in the body.

question: A 36-year-old woman presents with bilateral ankle pain that has lasted for a week. She also mentions progressively worsening wrist stiffness over the past few months that improves throughout the day with use. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic, inflammatory polyarthritis af- fecting the synovial joints. Peripheral joints are usually affected in a symmet- ric pattern, and as the disease progresses, proximal joints may become involved. It is an autoimmune disorder that can lead to joint deformities through cartilage and bone erosion as well as ligament and tendon damage. If untreated, RA may lead to permanent loss of joint function in as little as 10 years from onset. RA is also associ- ated with many extra-articular manifestations, such as heart disease, osteo- porosis, and eye involvement. The onset of RA is insidious, and most patients initially complain of hand or wrist stiffness that improves with use throughout the day. Morning stiffness last- ing more than half an hour after sleep or prolonged inactivity is indicative of an in- flammatory arthropathy. The proximal joints of the fingers, hands, and feet are often the first affected, but patients may experience swelling and pain of more proximal large joints, such as shoulders, elbows, and knees as the disease spreads. Incorrect Answer Explanations Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by uric acid crystal deposition in synovial fluid. Gout flares are typically monoarticular with an intense in- flammatory response. Joints in the lower extremities are the most commonly affected. In longstanding disease, gout may present in a polyarticular fashion. Psoriatic arthritis is an inflammatory arthritis associated with the skin disease psoriasis. Joint involvement is often asymmetrical, and distal joints such as the DIPs are affected. The spine may also be involved. In contrast with RA, most patients with psoriatic arthritis are seronegative for rheumatoid factor. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) may present with polyarthritis. It is an autoimmune disease with multisystem involvement. Most patients experience systemic symptoms such as fever, fatigue, weight loss, myalgias, or skin in- volvement in addition to arthritis. SLE is diagnosed based on clinical history and serologic testing.

question: A 38-year-old woman presents with wrist pain. The joint is tender and warm to the touch. A joint aspiration is performed. Which description of the fluid is most con- sistent with an acute flare of rheumatoid arthritis?

options.text: Cloudy and yellow with 30,000 WBCs per mm<sup>3</sup>, neutrophilic pre- dominance, and negatively birefringent crystals
Cloudy and yellow with 95,000 WBCs per mm<sup>3</sup>, neutrophilic pre- dominance, and no crystals
Transparent and yellow with 4,000 WBCs per mm<sup>3</sup>, without neu- trophilic predominance or crystals
Yellow with 20,000 WBCs per mm<sup>3</sup>, neutrophilic predominance, and no crystals

correctAnswer: Yellow with 20,000 WBCs per mm<sup>3</sup>, neutrophilic predominance, and no crystals
englishExplanation:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic inflammatory polyarthritis affect- ing synovial joints. Synovial fluid analysis will show an inflammatory effusion with 1,500 to 25,000 WBCs per mm with a neutrophilic predominance. No crystals will be present as in gout or pseudogout. WBC counts greater than 25,000 per mm should raise suspicion for infection of the joint. All fluid sam- ples should be sent for culture. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cloudy and yellow synovial fluid with 30,000 WBCs per mm with neutrophilic pre- dominance and negatively birefringent crystals is representative of gout. Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by uric acid crystal deposition in syn- ovial fluid. Gout flares are typically monoarticular with an intense inflammatory response, and the most commonly affected joints are the lower extremities. Cloudy and yellow synovial fluid with 95,000 WBCs per mm with neutrophilic pre- dominance and no crystals is indicative of a septic joint. Septic arthritis is a rapidly progressive monocular arthritis due to intra-articular joint infection. Patients may present with systemic symptoms (such as fevers and chills) and hesi- tancy to or inability to range the affected joint due to pain and swelling. Synovial fluid analysis will typically show cloudy fluid with a WBC count greater than 50,000 with a neutrophilic predominance greater than 75%. Transparent and yellow synovial fluid with 4,000 WBCs without neutrophilic pre- dominance or presence of crystals is suggestive of osteoarthritis. Osteoarthritis is a chronic polyarticular destructive joint disease, which lacks systemic symp- toms. It is not an inflammatory arthritis. For patients who present with exacerbations of symptoms, analgesics and rest is recommended.

question: Which is the definitive method of diagnosing rheumatoid arthritis?
englishExplanation: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a polyarticular inflammatory arthritis with an autoimmune cause. As with all patients, the initial evaluation of RA should in- clude a history and thorough physical examination. In RA, peripheral joints are initially affected in a symmetric pattern, and as the disease progresses, proxi- mal joints may become involved. Many patients experience morning stiffness lasting longer than 30 minutes as one of their initial symptoms. RA is a chronic condition, and patients who have symptoms for fewer than 6 weeks should have test- ing performed to rule out alternate causes such as viral illness. Definitive diagno- sis of RA is through serologic testing for rheumatoid factor and antibod- ies against cyclic citrullinated peptide. Incorrect Answer Explanations Arthrocentesis is necessary to diagnose septic arthritis, which is a rapidly progressive monocular arthritis due to intra-articular joint infection. Patients may present with systemic symptoms (such as fevers and chills) and hes- itancy to or inability to range the affected joint due to pain and swelling. Synovial fluid analysis will typically show cloudy fluid with a WBC count in excess of 50,000 per mm with a neutrophilic predominance greater than 75%. Although history and physical examination are essential to make a diagnosis of RA, it is not solely a clinical diagnosis. Fibromyalgia, which is a disorder of pain regula- tion characterized by chronic musculoskeletal pain not explained by another systemic disorder, may be diagnosed clinically after other possible causes are ruled out. X-rays of affected joints may help diagnose osteoarthritis, which is the most prevalent arthropathy affecting older adults. Osteoarthritis frequently affects joints in the knees, hips, hands, and spine. It is a chronic, progressive arthropathy char- acterized by degeneration of cartilage and bone. On imaging, there may be non- uniform joint space loss, subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte formation, or cyst formation.

question: A child with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) presents with persistent fever, cough, weight loss, and night sweats. These symptoms are most likely due to treat- ment with which medication?
englishExplanation: This child's symptoms are consistent with reactivation of latent tuberculosis, one of the most significant side effects of tumor necrosis factor–alpha (TNF- alpha) inhibitors. TNF-alpha inhibitors also increase the risk for other op- portunistic infections. There are multiple TNF-alpha inhibitors used to treat rheumatic conditions, but the most commonly used in the management of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) are adalimumab, etanercept, and infliximab. Generally, they are less effective in treating children with systemic JIA compared to other JIA sub- types. TNF-alpha inhibitors are considered in patients who have moderate to severe disease that has been poorly controlled with other treatments. Specifically, infliximab and adalimumab are routinely used in children whose uveitis is unresponsive to oph- thalmic glucocorticoids and methotrexate. Clinicians should consider administer- ing empiric antibiotics and antifungals in patients being treated with TNF-al- pha agents who develop systemic febrile illnesses. Incorrect Answer Explanations Infection is a risk of corticosteroid use. However, this risk is minimized with short courses and low doses, which is the goal for treatment in patients with JIA. This patient's symptoms are most consistent with tuberculosis infection, which is more likely to result from TNF-alpha inhibitor use than corticosteroid use. However, pro- longed use of corticosteroids in young children can result in adrenal suppression. These patients typically present with symptoms of lethargy, dehydration, and hypotension. They should be treated promptly with stress dose steroids and in- travenous volume replacement with isotonic fluids. Methotrexate is categorized as a conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) and is both an immunomodulatory and immunosuppressive agent. The risk of infection is higher with the use of biologic DMARDs, such as TNF- alpha inhibitors, than with conventional DMARDs. Methotrexate is more commonly associated with hepatic toxicity. Methotrexate remains a first-line treatment for polyarticular JIA but has gradually been replaced by biologic DMARDs for the treat- ment of sJIA. NSAIDs are the first-line treatment for mild to moderate JIA and are not associ- ated with increased risk of infection. There are multiple classes of NSAIDs, and it is difficult to predict how well a child will respond to a particular one. However, aspirin should be avoided in patients with JIA as it is associated with increased gastric and hepatotoxicity. NSAIDs should be administered at the appropriate age- or weight- based anti-inflammatory dose. Trials of NSAIDs as monotherapy for JIA should last no longer than a few weeks before considering either a different class of NSAID or combining the NSAID with an additional agent.

question: What is the correct disposition plan for a child with fever, arthritis, and the rash pictured below? Credit: CDC/James Gathany.
englishExplanation:
The rash in this image has the typical bull's eye or target-like appearance of ery- thema migrans, which is associated with early Lyme disease. Patients with un- complicated early Lyme disease can be treated as outpatients with oral antibiotics. Recommended antibiotics are either doxycycline for 10 days or amoxicillin or ce- furoxime for 14 days. However, the treatment course should be longer in patients with associated Lyme arthritis. Lyme disease is a tickborne illness caused by the spirochete bacteria Borrelia burgdorferi. In addition to the erythema migrans rash, early clinical presentation includes fever, fatigue, and headaches. Latter manifestations include arthritis, carditis, and neurologic involvement. The arthritis associated with Lyme dis- ease usually affects large joints. When treated early, patients usually make a full re- covery. Persistent, worsening arthritis after the initial course of oral antibiotics should be treated with intravenous ceftriaxone. Incorrect Answer Explanations Admission to the hospital for intravenous antibiotics would be indicated in joint in- fections such as osteomyelitis or septic arthritis, but not in the initial course of treatment for Lyme arthritis. Children with septic arthritis and osteomyelitis may present with fever and similar systemic symptoms, but these conditions are not asso- ciated with erythema migrans. Admission to the hospital for pulse corticosteroids would be indicated to treat severe manifestations of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), but it is not indi- cated for treating Lyme arthritis. Macrophage activation syndrome is an indica- tion for intravenous high-dose corticosteroid treatment in JIA. It is impor- tant to consider the potential side effects of prolonged corticosteroids use in children, which include adrenal crisis, hypertension, delayed pubertal development, and mood lability. Discharge to home with oral NSAIDs would be indicated for conditions such as tran- sient synovitis or new onset uncomplicated JIA, but it is insufficient treat- ment for Lyme arthritis. Transient synovitis is a common condition in children that causes hip pain due to inflammation of the synovial lining. Children will present with fever, limp, or refusal to bear weight, often following a viral illness. The physical examination may be difficult, as young children may not be able to local- ize the source of their discomfort. It is a self-limiting disease that resolves without long-term effect. Affected patients should be advised to rest from physical activity, and pain can be treated with oral NSAIDs.

question: A 33-year-old man presents with acute-onset pain and swelling in his joints in both knees, his right hip, and his left heel. When asked, he says he has pain on uri- nation but no penile discharge. He denies previous STIs and other risk factors. A physical examination reveals asymmetrical arthritis, bilateral injected sclera, and photophobia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Reactive arthritis (formerly known as Reiter syndrome) is an autoim- mune condition that develops following infection. The classic triad is conjunctivitis, urethritis, and arthritis, which this patient has but is not re- quired to make the diagnosis. Reactive arthritis is one type of seronegative spondy- loarthropathy that is characterized by an asymmetric, inflammatory pol- yarthritis and a negative test for rheumatoid factor (hence, seronegative). Joint involvement is often present in the lower extremities, especially the heel (lover's heel). Conjunctivitis can progress to iritis, uveitis, or corneal ulceration. Reactive arthritis typically occurs in males aged 15 to 35 years, often 2 to 6 weeks after an episode of urethritis or dysentery. Bacteria that have been linked to subsequent reac- tive arthritis include Chlamydia trachomatis, Shigella flexneri, and Salmonella. Treatment for reactive arthritis is supportive, with NSAIDs as the pri- mary pain control agent. Antibiotics may shorten the duration of symptoms if the patient has concurrent chlamydial infection. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ankylosing spondylitis is one of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies, along with reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and the arthropathy seen in patients with inflammatory bowel disease. There is considerable clinical overlap among these conditions, but some generalizations can be made. Ankylosing spondylitis occurs in young males and usually presents with the chief complaint of back stiffness and pain that has been present for 3 months or longer. In these pa- tients, x-rays demonstrate sacroiliitis and symmetrical squaring of the margins of the vertebral bodies (known as bamboo spine). Symptoms of ankylosing spondylitis do not typically include urethritis or conjunctivitis. Common symptoms of disseminated gonococcemia include fever, arthralgias, migratory arthritis, and pustular or vesicular skin lesions. Gonococcal septic arthritis can present with urethritis and polyarthritis. Both disseminated gonococcemia and gonococcal septic arthritis typi- cally exclude ocular involvement. Systemic manifestations of Neisseria gonor- rhoeae infection often include skin findings such as a vesicular rash. The lesions usu- ally number from 10 to 20 and begin as small red papules with an erythematous pe- riphery. The lesions can be present on the palms and soles. Unroofing the lesions may yield purulent fluid that can be sent for Gram stain, which should show gram- negative diplococci. Blood cultures can also demonstrate the organism. Genital or other mucosal surfaces are typically sterile at the time of disseminated infection. Gonococcal septic arthritis is possible even if urine or genital testing results are negative. Systemic lupus erythematosus is more common in women, occurring 7 to 10 times more often than in men. It typically presents with a triad of fever, rash, and joint pain, but a very wide diversity of symptoms can be seen. The rash is typically malar or discoid. The joints most often affected are the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints of the hand. Oral ulcers, pleuritis, and pericarditis can also be seen. Renal disorders such as proteinuria and insufficiency as well as various neurologic and hematologic disorders are typical. Iritis and urethritis or dysuria are uncommon in the presentation of lupus.

question: An otherwise healthy newborn presents for evaluation of an abnormal popping sound when changing the diaper. On examination, a palpable clunk when abduct- ing the flexed hip is noted. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Emergent surgical consultation for joint aspiration

englishExplanation: A palpable “clunk” while abducting the flexed hip indicates the reduction of a previously dislocated hip, requiring urgent but not immediate ortho- pedic consultation. This provocative maneuver, called the Ortolani test, is done to assess the hip stability in infants with suspected developmental dysplasia of the hip. Similarly, the Barlow maneuver can be used to identify an unstable hip that can be passively dislocated. In this maneuver, a palpable clunk may be detected when the examiner adducts the hip while applying a posterior force on the knee to cause the head of the femur to dislocate posteriorly from the acetabulum. Infants younger than 4 months who have either a positive Ortolani or Barlow test should follow-up with an orthopedist within 1 to 2 weeks and be placed in a hip abduction brace. Additional physical examination findings associated with devel- opmental dysplasia of the hip include asymmetric lower-extremity creases. Although this can occur in normal, healthy neonates, it should prompt further evalu- ation for potential limb length discrepancy when present. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although fractures are a common presentation of nonaccidental trauma in children, the isolated finding of a hip “clunk” is more consistent with developmen- tal dysplasia of the hip, and admission would not be warranted. Nonaccidental trauma is often difficult to diagnose, but concerning components of the history should raise the clinicians' level of suspicion. Examples include a delay in seeking medical treatment, parental reluctance to give an explanation, and an in- jury pattern that is inconsistent with the explanation provided. The clini- cian should carefully examine the child for any signs of acute or chronic trauma. This includes evaluation of the skin for abnormal bruising, burns or abrasions, and careful palpation of all extremities. Emergent surgical consultation for joint aspiration would be indicated if the infant demonstrated clinical signs of septic arthritis, but an isolated hip clunk is inconsis- tent with this. Acute septic arthritis in the pediatric population can have varied presentations but must be considered when any neonate presents with a swollen, painful, and red joint. Affected neonates may also present with pseu- doparalysis and irritability with passive movement of the involved ex- tremity. Prompt recognition of neonatal septic arthritis, early surgical consulta- tion for potential drainage, and expeditious administration of parenteral antibi- otics is necessary to decrease risk for sepsis and permanent joint damage. Laboratory investigation may yield an elevated WBC count, serum CRP, and ESR. An ultrasound often demonstrates an effusion and can be used to guide aspi- ration of synovial fluid. Once blood and synovial cultures have been ob- tained, empiric antibiotics should be administered immediately. In this age group, antimicrobial agents should target Staphylococcus aureus, Group B Streptococcus, gram-negative bacilli, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Outpatient referral for genetic testing would not be indicated in this in- fant whose clinical presentation is consistent with isolated developmen- tal dysplasia of the hip. Developmental dysplasia of the hip can occur in conjunc- tion with other disease processes, such as Down syndrome, but this case describes a well-appearing infant with no additional physical examination abnormalities. Contrarily, genetic testing would be indicated if this infant presented with hemihy- perplasia (ie, an overgrowth of one side of the body when compared to the other). Hemihyperplasia can be associated with genetic disorders such as Beckwith- Weidemann syndrome, features of which include an increased risk for tumor development.

question: An obese 15-year-old boy presented with left hip pain and limping that has wors- ened over the past 3 weeks despite taking ibuprofen. He denies trauma, fever, or recent illness. Active and passive motion of the hip elicits pain. X-rays are shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Courtesy of David Effron, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation:
This patient has a slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), a hip condition most frequently seen in adolescents. SCFE results from a disruption be- tween the epiphysis and metaphysis at the physis, or growth plate, of a grow- ing femur. It is usually seen in boys 14 to 16 years old and in girls 11 to 13 years old. Boys are affected about twice as often as girls. Obesity is the most strongly associated risk factor; other risk factors include endocrine and metabolic disorders. Patients diagnosed with SCFE are at risk of bilateral hip involvement. Clinically, they may complain of hip, knee, or thigh discomfort. X-rays demonstrate displacement of the femoral head in a posterior and inferior direction relative to the femoral neck. This is commonly described as ice cream (the epiphysis) falling off the cone (the metaphysis). Treatment includes internal fixation, sympto- matic pain management, and avoidance of weight bearing. Although most patients with this disorder do well with prompt and appropriate treatment, chronic complications (eg, avascular necrosis, leg length discrepancy, permanent joint dys- function, and chondrolysis) can occur and are strongly associated with greater de- grees of epiphyseal slippage. Incorrect Answer Explanations Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is an idiopathic osteonecrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis. Patients 3 to 12 years old are most commonly affected. This teenage patient is older than would be expected to suffer from Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease. Additionally, the x-ray shows slippage of the epiphysis, which is typical of slipped capital femoral epiphysis, not Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease. Patients with Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease typically present with several weeks of hip or groin pain, and a physical examination might demonstrate atrophy of the thigh mus- cles, painful gait, and limited range of motion of the affected hip joint. X- rays can help confirm the diagnosis and demonstrate a range of findings, which vary according to disease progression (eg, subchondral fracture, bone resorption, or a smaller femoral head epiphysis with widening of the articular space). Septic arthritis is caused by a bacterial infection within a joint. Without rapid identification and treatment, it causes permanent joint damage. This patient has pain with movement of his hip but no other signs or symptoms of an infection. The x-ray is diagnostic of slipped capital femoral epiphysis. Septic arthritis can occur at any age, but the highest incidence occurs in children younger than 3. The hip and knee joints are most commonly affected. Patients may present with rapid on- set of pain, erythema, swelling, and inability to move the joint. Fever and systemic symptoms of infection may also be present. Although serum tests — such as WBC count, CRP, and ESR — can assist in this diagnosis, synovial fluid analysis pro- vides the cornerstone for diagnosis. The Kocher criteria can help distinguish between septic arthritis and transient synovitis. It includes a non–weight-bearing joint, temperature >38.5°C (101.3°F), ESR >40 mm/hr, and a WBC count >12,000 cells/mm. Orthopedics should be consulted emergently for operative treatment and intravenous antibiotics. Transient synovitis of the hip is the most common cause of acute hip dis- comfort in patients 3 to 10 years old. This patient is a teenager, and his x-ray findings are inconsistent with transient synovitis. The cause of transient synovitis is 3 unknown, but it is often seen after a recent viral illness. Patients often demon- strate a limp, painful range of motion, and occasional inability to bear weight on the affected side. No bony abnormality is seen on x-ray, but joint effusion is often seen on ultrasound. Joint aspiration helps to rule out septic arthritis when the diagnosis is unclear. Treatment is supportive care with NSAIDs.

question: A sexually active 24-year-old man presents with polyarticular joint pain in his left knee, right ankle, and right heel. He reports having bilateral eye redness last week that has resolved. What additional clinical finding may have been present?
englishExplanation: Reactive arthritis, previously known as Reiter syndrome, is a syndrome of pol- yarticular arthritis that occurs 2 to 6 weeks after an episode of urethritis, cervicitis, or dysentery. Penile discharge or urethritis from Chlamydia trachoma- tis likely preceded this patient's infection. Reactive arthritis can also follow GI tract infection with Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, or Campylobacter organisms, which typically presents with abdominal pain and diarrhea. Reactive arthritis is generally a disease that affects younger patients. The common phrase that refers to reactive arthritis is “can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree.” The arthritis associated with reactive arthritis is typically polyarticular, asymmetrical, and involves the weight-bearing joints of the lower ex- tremities. The heels can also be affected (known as “lover's heel”), and the fingers and toes may swell and appear sausage-like. Some patients may also have oral lesions that can progress to shallow painful ulcers, similar to the lesions that may be seen on the penis. Patients with reactive arthritis respond very well to NSAIDs, particularly indomethacin. If Chlamydia is suspected, antibiotics should be used as well. Incorrect Answer Explanations Erythema marginatum is a skin rash that is typically seen with acute rheumatic fever and is listed as one of the JONES criteria. Erythema marginatum is not typically associated with reactive arthritis. The erythema marginatum rash typically begins 2 to 5 weeks after an episode of streptococcal pharyngitis as an asymptomatic macule that spreads peripherally before coalesces start to form serpentine patches or plaques. Other JONES criteria used to make the diagnosis of rheumatic fever include polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, carditis, and subcutaneous nodules. Do not confuse this rash with erythema migrans, which is the targetoid rash associated with Lyme disease; notably, Lyme dis- ease may also be associated with joint pain. Palpable purpura is typically associated with Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP), not reactive arthritis. HSP is an Immunoglobulin A-mediated disorder that causes vasculitis involving the small vessels of the joints, GI tract, skin, and kidneys. Although HSP also presents with arthralgias, the diagnosis is made based on the presence of palpable purpura in the lower extremities. HSP also typically affects children. Rectal abscess may be present in a patient with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) but are not typical in reactive arthritis. Typically, the musculoskeletal manifes- tations of IBD are acute, migratory, and asymmetrical polyarthritis. The severity of the arthritis typically correlates with flare-ups. The associated urinary symptoms and conjunctivitis mentioned in this case are more consistent with reactive arthritis.

question: Which medication is typically used in the long-term management of gouty arthritis?
englishExplanation: Gout therapies are divided into acute treatment and long-term prophylaxis. Allopurinol is a prophylactic agent that is indicated for the long-term man- agement of gouty arthritis, but it should not be initiated during an acute attack; notably, prophylactic medications should not be stopped during an acute attack ei- ther. Allopurinol is a urate-lowering medication that can cause acute gouty flares due to the destabilization of intra-articular uric acid during initiation of therapy, which is why it should not be initiated during acute gout attacks. Doses should be adjusted in patients with renal insufficiency. Allopurinol is also used for prevention of tumor ly- sis syndrome and recurrent uric acid or calcium nephrolithiasis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Colchicine is used for acute gout flares and for gout prophylaxis, but it is not indicated for long-term management. Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory medication that disrupts cytoskeletal microtubules and migration of neutrophils. If patients are already taking colchicine prophylaxis at the time of their gout flare, a higher total daily dose of 1.8 mg should be used on the first day of the flare. The most common side effects of colchicine are nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Dose adjustments should be made for patients with renal disease. Notably, patients with hepatic disease or hepatic biliary obstruction should not be prescribed colchicine since it is metabo- lized through the liver. Naproxen or indomethacin are the NSAIDs of choice for treatment of an acute gout flare, particularly in younger patients who do not have kidney, cardiovascular, or GI comorbidities. NSAIDs are most effective when treatment is initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset. The average total duration of treatment for a gout flare is 5 to 7 days. Contraindications to NSAID administration include chronic kidney disease, active gastric or duodenal ulcer, difficult-to-treat hypertension, heart failure, coro- nary artery disease, anticoagulant use, or NSAID allergy. Prednisone is effective in the treatment of acute gout flares, not in the long-term management of gouty arthritis. Prednisone may have a more favorable risk and bene- fit profile in patients with renal insufficiency; however, caution should be taken in pa- tients with a history of diabetes or heart failure.

question: A 70-year-old patient presents with right knee pain, redness, and swelling. X-rays show chondrocalcinosis. What is the most likely arthrocentesis finding?
englishExplanation:
Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate deposition disease (CPPD), also known as pseudogout, results when calcium complex crystals form across articu- lar surfaces and lead to chondrocalcinosis. These positively birefringent crys- tals trigger an inflammatory reaction, causing a clinical presentation that is similar to gout and septic arthritis. Joint cartilage calcification, also known as chondrocalci- nosis, is often seen on plain x-rays, although its absence does not rule out the diagno- sis. Pseudogout tends to affect older patients and is typically seen in the knee. Synovial joint fluid examination shows rhomboid-shaped crystals that are pos- itively birefringent. Treatment is typically similar to acute gout (ie, NSAID, colchicine, or steroid administration). Unlike gout, there are no current medi- cations that prevent future attacks of pseudogout, so the mainstay of therapy is acute pain management. There is no reported history of trauma in this case, so hemarthrosis is less likely. Furthermore, chondrocalcinosis is not usually asso- ciated with trauma. Lipohemarthrosis, which results from an intra-articular frac- ture with escape of fat and blood from the bone marrow into the joint, is typically characterized as a fat fluid level seen on horizontal beam x-rays. The fluid aspirated will be bloody with fat globules floating within the aspirate. Negatively birefringent crystals are typically seen in gouty arthritis and re- main the gold standard for diagnosing gout. Although this patient has symptoms that could be consistent with gout, chondrocalcinosis is more diagnostic of pseu- dogout. The crystals in gout are typically monosodium urate crystals that are nee- dle-shaped and negatively birefringent, whereas in pseudogout the crystals are rhom- boid-shaped and positively birefringent. A synovial WBC count greater than 100,000 cells/mm is more consistent with a diagnosis of septic arthritis. Ultimately, arthrocentesis is performed to exclude septic arthritis, but the chondrocalcinosis makes this less likely. Inflammatory arthritis and septic arthritis can co-exist but is less likely. In this case, the chondrocalcinosis should prompt suspicion of pseudogout, which is characterized by positively birefringent crystals.

question: A 14-year-old boy presents with leg pain after being tackled during football. He was able to continue playing but had persistent pain in that extremity. A physical examination demonstrates intact muscle strength, range of motion, and sensation with mild soft-tissue swelling of the anterior thigh. He injured the same leg years earlier while wrestling. An x-ray of the femur is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Courtesy of David Effron, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation:
This patient has myositis ossificans, or heterotrophic calcification, which is an abnormal healing process that results in extraskeletal ossification of the soft tissue. Most commonly, this disorder occurs at the site of direct trauma where a hematoma forms and then undergoes partial calcifica- tion. Affected patients complain of localized tenderness, swelling, and pain. A physical examination may reveal joint motion abnormalities or a tender mass with or without associated erythema. Most ossifications are located in the arm or thigh. Depending on how long it has been since injury, imaging will reveal calcified densities in the soft tissue that may eventually appear sharply circumscribed and mass-like. Treatment of myositis ossificans is primarily symptomatic, but surgery may be required if joint mobility is affected or the calcification grows to excessive sizes. Unlike myositis ossificans, dermatomyositis is generally unassociated with trauma, and it is often an autoimmune condition in the pediatric group. Osteosarcoma must be considered in all patients with x-ray evidence of soft-tissue calcifications. In osteosarcoma, the calcifications are associated with the bony metaphysis and extend from the center to the periphery. In myositis ossificans, on the other hand, calcification is associated with the bone's diaphysis and is initially located in the periphery of the soft tissue. Subcutaneous injection of illicit drugs, such as heroin, is called skin pop- ping. Skin popping causes localized trauma to the affected superficial tis- sues and results in thickening and abnormal calcification of the skin. However, this patient has no listed history of drug use, and the calcification appears to be within the muscle tissue as opposed to originating from the skin surface, mak- ing this diagnosis unlikely.

question: A 74-year-old woman presents with weakness in her legs and difficulty walking. She has had a rash on both arms for 4 months that has not responded to over-the- counter corticosteroid cream. Which additional finding supports a diagnosis of myositis?

options.text: Distal muscle weakness, abnormal sensation, and loss of bladder or bowel function
Intermittent weakness relieved by rest; normal reflexes and sensation
Proximal muscle and limb-girdle weakness, muscle tenderness, and normal reflexes
Symmetrical ascending weakness, decreased reflexes, and minimal sensory involvement

correctAnswer: Proximal muscle and limb-girdle weakness, muscle tenderness, and normal reflexes
englishExplanation: Myopathies are diseases of the skeletal muscles. In myositis, an inflammatory myopathy, patients typically present with muscle pain, weakness of the proxi- mal musculature, and normal reflexes. Weakness of the hip and shoulder girdles is prominent, and patients classically describe difficulty getting up out of a chair. The degree of weakness is variable, and the muscles are often tender to palpation. Reflexes and sensation are normal. Some patients have an associated rash (dermatomyositis) that classically presents as erythema and swelling over the ex- tensor surfaces and around the eyes. The CK level is elevated, but rhabdomyolysis is uncommon. An elevated CK level is not required for the diagnosis of this condition. Management involves corticosteroids and supportive care. The reflexes are initially diminished, but they typically im- prove over time. Myositis is a disease of the muscles as opposed to one with a neu- ronal etiology; it presents with intact reflexes and normal sensation. Intermittent weakness that is relieved by rest with normal reflexes and normal sensation is a description of myasthenia gravis. In this condition, the number of functioning acetylcholine receptors within the neuromuscular junction is decreased, resulting in disordered neurotransmission. Myopathy and myositis do not typically have intermittent weakness and are not linked to faulty neuro- transmission at the neuromuscular junction. The rash described in this case also does not occur in myasthenia gravis. Symmetrical ascending weakness with decreased or absent reflexes and minimal sensory involvement is a classic description of Guillain-Barré syndrome, an immune-mediated lower motor neuron neuropathy. Tick paralysis can present in a very similar manner. Guillain-Barré syndrome most notably has weakness that is worse distally — given that it has an ascending pattern — with de- creased reflexes. Proximal weakness and intact reflexes are typical of myositis.

question: An intoxicated 52-year-old man presents with altered mental status after using phencyclidine. His laboratory evaluation is significant for a CK level of 5,100 U/L and tea-colored urine. What is the most appropriate treatment?
englishExplanation: Rhabdomyolysis is diagnosed by laboratory analysis that reveals a CK level of at least five times the level of normal (ABEM's normal range is 30-170 U/L) in addition to the presence of myoglobin in the urine. Aggressive intravenous hydration is the mainstay of treatment for rhabdomyolysis. Urine output should be targeted to 3 to 4 mL/kg/hr. No specific type of crystalloid has been shown to be of particular ben- efit. If rhabdomyolysis is left undiagnosed or progresses to advanced stages, DIC and myoglobin-induced kidney injury can ensue. Early in the course of rhabdomyolysis, complications such as compartment syn- drome, hypovolemia, and hepatic dysfunction are known to occur. Electrolyte dis- turbances and acidosis are the greatest threats; hyperkalemia and hypocal- cemia are the most common electrolyte abnormalities and pose the greatest risk for arrhythmias. Kidney failure begins later in the course as the result of myoglobin being deposited in renal tubules and obstructing them in the presence of aciduria. This, combined with hypovolemia, further reduces the glomerular filtration rate and worsens renal failure. The worse the renal failure, the worse the hyperkalemia can be. In severe forms of this condition, prothrombotic substances are released and cause DIC and hemorrhagic complications. Incorrect Answer Explanations There is no evidence to suggest that urine alkalinization is a necessary goal in the treatment of rhabdomyolysis. However, aggressive intravenous hy- dration is necessary, and urine output should be targeted to 3 to 4 mL/kg/hr. Avoiding acidosis is important, so some physicians continue to use sodium bicarbon- ate in conjunction with intravenous fluids to avoid this complication. Bicarbonate should be reserved for those patients with severe rhabdomyolysis. Mannitol and other diuretics have not been shown to provide any benefit in the treatment of rhabdomyolysis. Mannitol may actually cause an osmotic diuresis that can worsen a patient's hypovolemic state. Mannitol should be reserved for pa- tients with volume overload, if used at all. There is no indication that this patient has a UTI, so antibiotics are unlikely to be of benefit. Some antibiotics, particularly macrolides, may actually precipitate rhabdomyolysis either alone or in combination with other medications and risk factors.

question: A 32-year-old man presents with muscle weakness and dark-colored urine after completing a marathon the day before. Which additional finding would suggest that he has an acute renal injury?
englishExplanation: Acute kidney injury in rhabdomyolysis is associated with a rapid increase in serum creatinine and a low fractional excretion of sodium. The develop- ment of acute kidney injury due to rhabdomyolysis is multifactorial and depends upon volume status, urine pH, and the effects of myoglobin on the kidney. The mech- anism of renal injury seems to be fluid sequestration in injured muscle, which causes renal vasoconstriction and leads to renal ischemia. Myoglobin can also form deposits by combining with proteins, which then cause tubular obstruction that leads to renal injury. The likelihood of developing acute kidney injury in the setting of rhabdomyol- ysis can be predicted using the McMahon score. Urine findings of rhabdomyolysis include pigmented granular casts, oliguria or anuria, myoglobinuria, and dipstick urine tests that are positive for blood with no RBCs on microscopic examination. However, the presence of myoglobinuria does not necessarily indicate acute kidney injury. Blood testing may reveal an elevated CK level (although this does not correlate well with incidence of re- nal injury) and an elevated myoglobin (which is the causative agent of renal injury). Incorrect Answer Explanations Blood testing might reveal an elevated CK level in rhabdomyolysis, but this does not correlate well with incidence of renal injury. The correlation between CK and renal injury is stronger in rhabdomyolysis due to trauma than in rhabdomyolysis due other causes such as exertion, drugs, or infection. Electrolyte abnormalities (eg, hyperkalemia, elevated phosphate, and elevated uric acid) and elevated anion gap with metabolic acidosis are characteristic findings in rhabdomyolysis. However, none of these laboratory findings correlate well with the level of acute renal injury, and the level of potassium can also increase in rhab- domyolysis from damaged muscle cells. Urine findings of rhabdomyolysis include pigmented granular casts and myoglobin- uria. Pigmented granular casts are created when heme pigment binds to Tamm- Horsfall proteins; these casts may be seen on urine microscopy but do not cor- relate well with acute renal injury.

question: What serum laboratory abnormalities characterize the acute phase of rhabdomyolysis?

options.text: High CK, high calcium, high potassium, high phosphorus
High CK, high calcium, low potassium, high phosphorus
High CK, low calcium, high potassium, high phosphorus
High CK, low calcium, high potassium, low phosphorus

correctAnswer: High CK, low calcium, high potassium, high phosphorus
englishExplanation: Rhabdomyolysis is a condition that results from the breakdown of skele- tal muscle. Because CK is contained within muscle cells, large amounts are released. In addition, intracellular potassium and phosphorus are re- leased, causing an increase in serum levels. By contrast, hypocalcemia results from a couple mechanisms. First, myocyte membrane damage leads to an influx of extracellular calcium into the myocytes, given a relatively low concentration of intra- cellular calcium. Second, elevated serum phosphorus leads to deposition of calcium- based salts in the damaged muscle tissue, further reducing serum calcium levels. If rhabdomyolysis is suspected or diagnosed, it is imperative that close attention be paid to potential electrolyte derangements. The mainstay of treatment is ag- gressive hydration and monitoring of urine output. Supplemental calcium should not be given in response to low serum calcium levels. Calcium in the treat- ment of hyperkalemia should be avoided unless there is hemodynamic instability or apparent cardiotoxicity. Additional calcium supplementation in the setting of rhabdomyolysis can result in worsened muscle damage and can exacer- bate the pathophysiology. Incorrect Answer Explanations CK levels are elevated, as are potassium and phosphorus levels. However, serum calcium levels are reduced due to intracellular sequestration and calcium salt deposition. CK levels are elevated, as are phosphorus levels. Potassium levels are also elevated due to cellular breakdown and intracellular potassium release. Additionally, rhab- domyolysis can result in renal failure from myoglobin blockage of renal tubules, fur- ther raising serum potassium levels. Calcium levels are low in acute rhabdomyolysis. CK levels are elevated, as are potassium levels. Phosphorus levels are also ele- vated because phosphorus leaks out of damaged cells into the systemic circulation, raising serum levels. Calcium levels are low in acute rhabdomyolysis.

question: A 22-year-old football player presents with sore muscles after an intense workout. His urinalysis results show 3+ blood with no RBCs, a serum CK level of 15,000 IU/L, a potassium level of 5.7 mEq/L, and a creatinine level of 4.5 mg/dL. What is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous hydration with monitoring of serum electrolyte levels
Oral fluid hydration followed by a repeat CK level test
Oral fluid hydration without repeat laboratory tests

correctAnswer: Intravenous hydration with monitoring of serum electrolyte levels
englishExplanation: The best initial treatment would be intravenous hydration with monitoring of serum electrolyte levels. This patient's findings suggest acute rhabdomyolysis, a condition caused by the breakdown of skeletal muscle. Potential etiologies include traumatic injuries, drug use, seizures, intense exercise, and some genetic dis- orders. In this case, intense exercise is the likely cause. Rhabdomyolysis causes large amounts of CK, myoglobin, potassium, and phosphorus to enter the circulation after the breakdown of muscle cells. Myoglobin is filtered into the kidneys and can cause tubular obstruction, leading to acute renal insufficiency. Urinalysis results are typically positive for blood, given the cross-reactivity of that as- say with myoglobin. However, RBCs are often absent. Red-gold casts may be noted in the urine. There are three primary mainstays of treatment for rhabdomyolysis. The first, and most important, is aggressive intravenous hydration, usually with multiple liters of fluid in the emergency department, followed by a high maintenance rate of 4 mL/kg/hr. Reduced rates may be considered for patients with underlying heart fail- ure, end-stage renal disease, or volume overload. The second mainstay of treatment is to maintain urine output at 3 to 4 mL/kg/hr. The third is close monitor- ing of electrolyte levels, which is imperative because rhabdomyolysis can cause hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia. Patients with signifi- cant acute kidney injury in the setting of rhabdomyolysis, as in this case, should be admitted to the hospital for close monitoring and to continue aggressive hydration until their condition normalizes. However, this condition will likely improve with intravenous hydration, which causes increased urine output and potassium clearance. Hemodialysis is only indicated in the most severe cases of rhabdomyolysis. This patient has elevated creatinine and potassium levels. Downtrending CK levels af- ter oral fluid hydration do not necessarily mean that the patient's renal function and potassium levels have stabilized or improved. This patient needs aggressive in- travenous fluid hydration and monitoring of electrolyte levels to ensure his condition does not worsen. This patient has significantly elevated CK, potassium, and creatinine val- ues and needs aggressive intravenous hydration. Oral fluids are unlikely to sufficiently resuscitate this patient and prevent worsening kidney function. Serum electrolyte levels should be monitored periodically to ensure they are improving as the patient is hydrated.

question: An 18-year-old soccer player presents with severe leg pain and tea-colored urine after intensive running drills. On examination, the anterior compartment of the lower right leg is firm. There is severe pain with passive ankle plantar flexion and reduced sensation between the dorsal first and second toes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Ischemic neuropathy of the tibial nerve
Severe muscle strain without compartment syndrome

englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with muscle soreness and pain with dark tea-colored urine in the setting of intensive running drills, which is consistent with rhabdomyolysis. Intense exercise is a risk factor of acute rhabdomyolysis, especially in ath- letes who exercise outside and may be dehydrated. Rhabdomyolysis involves muscle breakdown, causing the leakage of potassium and phosphorus into the blood as well as intense inflammation and calcium deposition in the damaged muscle tissue. One complication of rhabdomyolysis is acute compartment syndrome, es- pecially in compartments like those of the lower leg that are tightly bound by fascia. Muscle breakdown causes inflammation and edema, which can lead to increased in- tracompartmental pressure. As swelling increases, acute compartment syndrome can develop. In this case, the patient has developed acute compartment syndrome of the anterior compartment of the lower leg, as demonstrated by a firm compartment and pain with passive stretch of the muscles of the involved compartment. The anterior compartment of the lower leg contains the deep peroneal nerve, which provides sen- sory innervation between the dorsal first and second toes. Acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency. The pressure needs to be relieved with an emergent fasciotomy as soon as possible to prevent irreversible necrosis and damage. A surgical consult, usually to orthopedics, should be made as soon as compartment syndrome is suspected. The tibial nerve is contained within the superficial posterior compartment of the lower leg and provides sensory innervation via its branches to the plantar aspect of the foot. question: A 45-year-old woman presents with pain, paresthesias, and decreased sensation on the palmar aspect of the first three fingers of her right hand. Her motor strength is intact. Symptoms began after she started a new job as an administra- tive assistant. What is the best next step in management?

Discharge home with a neutral wrist splint
Perform a steroid injection at the carpal tunnel

In CTS, the median nerve is com- pressed as it passes through the carpal tunnel, which can cause pain, paresthesias, sensory disturbance, motor weakness, and muscle atrophy in the median nerve distri- bution. question: Which examination finding is most sensitive for the diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome?

options.text: Abnormal sensation of the finger pad of the fifth finger
Weakened grip strength of affected hand

englishExplanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS), or median mononeuropathy, is the most common entrapment neuropathy in the United States. Although the gold standard for diagnosis is nerve conduction studies, provocative maneuvers can be done in the emergency department. Both the Phalen maneuver and the TInel test are commonly used in the ED for initial diagnosis with moderate sensitivities. The Phalen test compared to the Tinel has higher overall sensitivity (68% versus 50% pooled sensitivity, respectively). The Phalen maneuver is conducted by having the patient hold their wrists in the flexed position with the hands touching each other on the dorsal surface for one minute. If CTS is present, the patient should experience tingling in the distribution of the median nerve. The Tinel test, another approach to diagnosing CTS, is positive when percussion over the median nerve causes tingling in the hand in the distribution of the median nerve. The Durkan test or median nerve compression can also be used and involves compression of the median nerve. Symptoms of CTS are generally unilateral and are worsened by repetitive use, such as typing at work all day. Carpal tunnel syndrome is commonly associated with preg- nancy, obesity, diabetes mellitus, and renal failure. In patients with bilateral symp- toms, CTS usually is related to systemic illness. When examining a patient with sus- pected CTS, it is important to remember that the median nerve causes numb- ness involving the palm and palmar surface of the first three fingers, then splits at the fourth digit and supplies only the radial aspect of that finger, generally leaving sensation of the ulnar side of the fourth finger and the fifth finger intact. Sensory findings generally precede motor symptoms, and the most sensitive examination finding is an alteration in sensation to the distal tuft of the index finger. Initial treatment for CTS is application of a wrist splint and instructions to the patient to reduce activities that make the condition worse. Patients should be referred for surgical follow-up; a surgeon or other specialist would consider steroid injections or surgical management if wrist splinting fails to re- solve the symptoms. Incorrect Answer Explanations Abnormal finger sensation over the fifth digit is not consistent with CTS since CTS af- fects the median nerve. Numbness of the fifth digit would be expected with ulnar nerve entrapment. The median nerve compression will cause sensory find- ings in the palm and palmar surface of the first three fingers. It then splits at the fourth digit and supplies only the radial aspect of that finger, gen- erally leaving sensation of the ulnar side of the fourth finger and the fifth finger intact. A positive Finkelstein test is used to diagnose de Quervain tendonitis, not carpal tunnel syndrome. This test is performed by grasping the thumb with the fingers and then deviating the wrist in an ulnar direction. De Quervain is associated with repetitive movement of the wrist and pregnancy. A patient with CTS might demonstrate weakened grip strength on examination, but this is not the most sensitive finding. It is important to remember that sensory find- ings generally precede motor symptoms.

question: A patient suffers an electric shock sensation that radiates from their wrist to their hand when a physician taps on the palmar aspect of their wrist. What is the name of this test?
englishExplanation: The Tinel sign is one of the classic examination findings in patients with carpal tunnel syndrome. Eliciting pain and paresthesias of the hand and wrist by tap- ping on the palmar aspect of the wrist indicates median nerve neuropa- thy, likely due to compression within the carpal tunnel. Carpal tunnel syndrome is a common peripheral mononeuropathy and should be clinically distinguished from central processes that cause paresthesias. The median nerve traverses through the carpal canal or tunnel of the distal forearm and wrist, covered by the transverse carpal ligament. When a condition causes swelling in the carpal tunnel, the median nerve is compressed, causing paresthesias along its distri- bution — the index and middle fingers, the radial aspect of the ring finger, and the palmar aspect of the thumb. The patient may report waking up at night with burning pain and tingling in the hand. Incorrect Answer Explanations The Finkelstein test is performed to evaluate for de Quervain tenosynovitis. In this physical examination technique, the thumb is cupped in a closed fist, and ulnar deviation reproduces pain along the extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus. The Froment sign tests for palsy of the ulnar nerve rather than the median nerve. To perform this test, the patient is asked to hold a piece of paper between the thumb and index finger. If the examiner is able to pull the paper away, or if the thumb flexes at the interphalangeal joint to compensate for weakness of the adductor pollicis, the test is positive. The Phalen maneuver is also performed to evaluate for carpal tunnel syn- drome, but the technique is different. The Phalen maneuver is performed by hold- ing the wrists in flexion for 30 to 60 seconds. The test is positive if this evokes or worsens hand pain or paresthesias.

question: A patient presents with a 1-month history of numbness to part of the thumb and the first three fingers of the right hand. The pain is worse in the morning. What is the most probable cause?
englishExplanation: When any condition causes swelling in the carpal tunnel, the median nerve is compressed, causing paresthesias along its distribution — the index and mid- dle fingers, the radial aspect of the ring finger, and the palmar aspect of the thumb. The patient may report waking up at night with burning pain and tingling in the hand. Carpal tunnel syndrome may develop from a number of causes, including overuse, edema (as seen in pregnancy and congestive heart failure), trauma, hematologic causes, rheumatologic causes, anatomic anomalies, and infectious causes. A common scenario is overuse, in which the patient recounts a history of re- peated flexing and extending the wrist. In patients with carpal tunnel syndrome, out- patient electrodiagnostic testing may demonstrate a slowing of nerve conduction across the carpal tunnel. This will guide management decisions. Severe forms may re- quire surgical intervention. Incorrect Answer Explanations The symptoms described are consistent with carpal tunnel syndrome, not cubital tunnel syndrome (compression of the ulnar nerve). The ulnar nerve courses through the cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle at the elbow before en- tering the forearm. It supplies cutaneous innervation to the medial palm and to the small finger and medial half of the ring finger. The ulnar nerve is most vulnerable to repetitive stress, inflammation, and trauma in the cubital tunnel. It is the most common ulnar mononeuropathy, and the second-most common compres- sive mononeuropathy. Ulnar compression is possible if tapping on the cubital tunnel at the elbow provokes symptoms. A positive elbow flexion sign is seen when symptoms recur within 3 minutes of the elbow being held in flexion with the wrist in extension. The etiology of Dupuytren contracture is poorly understood. The disorder is char- acterized by fibroblastic changes of the subcutaneous tissues of the palm and volar aspect of the fingers. The ring and small fingers are affected earliest. This condition is found most commonly in men of northern European descent, smok- ers, those who abuse alcohol, and diabetics, but it may also be caused by overuse. Progressive fibrosis may eventually lead to tethering and joint contracture. On physi- cal examination, longitudinal thickening and nodularity of superficial tissues over the distal tendon sheath of the palm are evident as scarring progresses. Guyon canal syndrome impacts the ulnar nerve, not the median nerve. The ul- nar nerve is also vulnerable to repetitive stress, inflammation, and trauma at the Guyon canal. Guyon canal syndrome is caused by entrapment of the ulnar nerve in the Guyon canal of the wrist. It is also called “handlebar palsy,” and symptoms are similar to those seen with cubital tunnel entrapment.
