question: Which examination technique is paired with the correct condition for which it is testing?

options.text: Phalen maneuver for carpal tunnel syndrome
Piriformis test for tarsal tunnel syndrome
Tinel sign at the wrist for cubital tunnel syndrome

correctAnswer: Phalen maneuver for carpal tunnel syndrome
englishExplanation: The Phalen maneuver and the Tinel sign test at the wrist may be performed to evaluate for carpal tunnel syndrome. The Phalen maneuver involves holding the wrists in flexion for 30 to 60 seconds. It is positive when the test evokes or worsens symptoms. When any condition causes swelling in the carpal tunnel, the median nerve is compressed, causing paresthesias along its distribution — the index and middle fingers, the radial aspect of the ring finger, and the pal- mar aspect of the thumb. The patient may report waking up at night with burn- ing pain and tingling in the hand. Incorrect Answer Explanations The Finkelstein test is performed to evaluate for de Quervain tenosynovitis, not for sciatica. de Quervain tenosynovitis involves the extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus tendons of the hand. To perform the Finkelstein test, cup the thumb in a closed fist and deviate the hand in the ulnar direc- tion. In a positive test, ulnar deviation reproduces pain along the extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus. de Quervain tenosynovitis occurs with overuse of the thumb or wrist. It is also often associated with pregnancy, the postpartum period, and activities involving repeated radioulnar deviation, such as us- ing a hammer. Patients will report pain along the radial aspect of the wrist that may radiate proximally and distally. On examination, they will have painful range of mo- tion of the thumb and tenderness over the distal portion of the radial styloid. The piriformis test (also called the flexion, adduction, internal rotation [FAIR, FADIR, or FADDIR] test) does not test for tarsal tunnel syndrome. It is used to detect tightness of the piriformis or other impingement of the sciatic nerve as it passes through the piriformis muscle. To perform the test, the patient is positioned lying on their unaffected side, and the symptomatic leg is positioned in 60 to 90 degrees of flexion at the hip and 90 degrees of flexion at the knee joint. One of the examiner's hands is placed on the pelvis to stabilize it, and the other hand gives pressure on the lateral side of the knee, stretching as far as possible. The examiner performs horizontal adduction while putting pressure on the knee in the direction of the table. During the stretch, the patient may feel pain or discomfort. The Tinel sign at the wrist is one of the classic examination techniques to assess for carpal tunnel syndrome, not cubital tunnel syndrome. It is important to clarify the location being tested for Tinel sign. The Tinel sign can also be performed at the elbow. Firm percussion is applied over the ulnar nerve in the ulnar groove to test for cubital tunnel syndrome. In this case, tapping on the wrist will produce an electric shock sensation that radiates from the wrist to the hand in a patient who is impacted by carpal tunnel syndrome.

question: What is the appropriate initial management of carpal tunnel syndrome?
englishExplanation: For patients initially presenting with symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome, conserva- tive treatment may be offered for mild to moderate disease. Options include wrist splinting, corticosteroids, and physical therapy. Wrists should be splinted in the neutral position; nocturnal splinting is commonly recommended. Local corticosteroid injection can provide relief for more than 1 month and, in some studies, has delayed the need for surgery at 1 year from the time of diagnosis. Patients with moderate to severe symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome should receive outpa- tient electrodiagnostic studies to determine whether surgical referral may be beneficial. Incorrect Answer Explanations Gabapentin is an antiepileptic that is also used to treat neuropathic pain. There is some evidence that gabapentin may be a useful drug in treatment for carpal tunnel symptoms when used in low doses. However, it is not the first-line treatment for carpal tunnel syndrome in the emergency department. Although trauma and space-occupying masses may cause carpal tunnel syndrome, x- rays are not indicated in the initial diagnosis unless the patient's history suggests otherwise. If symptoms are moderate to severe, outpatient electrodiagnostic test- ing may be warranted. For more severe cases of carpal tunnel syndrome, referral to a neurologist to perform an electromyogram may be warranted to assess for severity of median nerve com- pression or damage. However, conservative therapy such as splinting is appropriate initially.

Flexing the wrist and holding it for 1 minute

question: A 32-year-old woman presents with pain over the radial aspect of her right wrist. The examination reveals that the pain is exacerbated when she grasps her right thumb in her palm and ulnar deviates the affected wrist. Pain exacerbated by this motion is diagnostic of what condition?
englishExplanation: This patient has de Quervain tendinopathy, an overuse syndrome that af- fects the extensor pollicis brevis and abductor longus tendons at the ra- dial styloid. de Quervain syndrome is diagnosed clinically by performing the Finkelstein test, as follows: tell the patient to place the affected thumb in the palm of their affected hand (“bend it across”), then tell the patient to deviate the wrist in the ulnar direction (“toward the little finger”). The test result is positive if this motion reproduces the patient's presenting pain, usually at the base of the thumb or radial styloid, and has been shown to be pathognomonic for de Quervain tendinopathy. On physical examination, swelling at the radial styloid is sometimes present. This con- dition is treated with a thumb spica splint and NSAIDs; recurrence might necessitate steroid injections or surgical decompression. Incorrect Answer Explanations The question describes the steps of the Finkelstein test, which is used to diagnose de Quervain syndrome, not carpal tunnel syndrome. In contrast, carpal tunnel syndrome is entrapment of the median nerve that leads to paresthesias along the volar thumb, second and third fingers, and radial aspect of the fourth fin- ger. Traditionally, the tests used to diagnose carpal tunnel syndrome have focused on eliciting the Phalen sign and the Tinel sign. Dupuytren contracture is a fibrosis causing a flexing of the fingers; it is not diagnosed with the Finkelstein test. The finding of this contracture, and possibly the palpation of a fibrotic nodule in the palm, helps make this diagnosis. Lateral epicondylitis, known as “tennis elbow,” is pain at the lateral epi- condyle of the humerus; it does not involve the wrist. The Cozen test can re- produce the symptoms by holding a clenched hand in extension against resistance while the arm is fully extended.

question: A 40-year-old woman presents with a 1-week history of right shoulder discomfort. There is no history of injury or prior pain. Lifting her arm above shoulder level ag- gravates the discomfort, and sometimes she feels it “catch” when she moves. She has no numbness or weakness but says the shoulder occasionally feels stiff. Examination reveals markedly limited range of motion, with tenderness over the insertion of the supraspinatus tendon with some crepitus. An x-ray is obtained and is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Courtesy of David Effron, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation:
The patient's presentation and x-ray findings suggest tendonitis with discomfort at the tendinous insertion of bone. In cases of calcifying tendonitis of the rotator cuff, calcium deposits are usually visible on x-rays at 1 cm to 2 cm proximal to the tendon insertion on the greater tuberosity. The supraspinatus tendon is the most com- monly affected tendon in calcific tendonitis. The calcium crystals form the nidus for inflammation; the etiology is unknown. Women are affected more often than men are, and the right shoulder is involved more often than the left is. The diagnosis is made based on typical history and imaging findings, as described above. Although plain x-ray is often used to make the diagnosis, ultrasound can also be used in certain clinical settings. The initial management of calcific ten- donitis is based on symptom control, as this disease is often self-limited. Oral NSAIDs and physical therapy can be prescribed from the emergency depart- ment, and referral to sports medicine or orthopedics for glucocorticoid injections is also recommended. In refractory cases, special therapies (eg, extracorporeal shock wave therapy) can be tried based on specialist opinion. Notably, only about 10% of cases require surgical intervention. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bursitis does not cause calcium deposits, as seen on this patient's x-ray. Inflammation of the bursa results in localized tenderness, edema, warmth, and limited range of motion of the affected joint. Trauma, infec- tion, crystal deposition, and systemic disease are just a few of the com- mon etiologies of bursitis. Patients with subacromial (subdeltoid) bursitis often complain of shoulder pain with limited range of motion and a history of repetitive activities. Although impingement syndrome can cause similar pain as calcific tendinopathy, there are no pathognomonic changes on x-rays of the shoulder to indicate the diagno- sis of impingement syndrome. Impingement syndrome refers to mechanical com- pression of the rotator cuff between the acromion and the humeral head. Impingement syndrome is an overuse injury caused by repetitive overhead activity, such as with painting, lifting objects, or playing sports that involve overhead motions. A cardinal symptom of impingement syndrome is gradual onset of pain to the anterolateral shoulder over the course of weeks to months. Subacromial pain reproduced with 70 to 120 degrees of arm forward flexion is consis- tent with this syndrome. Although rotator cuff injuries can present with similar pain as described in this case, they are not typically associated with the classic calcific finding on shoulder x-ray. Rotator cuff injuries are common and are seen in both athletes and nonathletes. There is an increased incidence of rotator cuff tears in patients older than 40 years of age. Patients with rotator cuff injuries frequently complain of anterior and superior shoulder pain that is aggravated by full abduction of the shoulder. The physical examination in rotator cuff injuries is notable for weakness of shoulder abduction. For example, the “drop-arm test” is done with passive abduc- tion of the arm to 90 degrees; if the patient is unable to maintain this position, signif- icant tears are likely.

question: A 21-year-old woman presents with right calf pain that is worse with walking. The pain is worse in the mornings and wanes in the evening. She is a runner and has recently started training for a marathon. On examination, she has tenderness 2 to 6 cm superior to the posterior calcaneus, with crepitus on active plantar and dorsi- flexion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Tenderness over the Achilles tendon located 2 to 6 cm superior to the posterior calcaneus is highly suggestive of Achilles tendinopathy. Other clues to this clinical diagnosis include a recent history of increasing physical ac- tivity, using new exercise equipment, and using tendinopathic medications, in- cluding fluoroquinolones, statins, and corticosteroids. Patients with Achilles tendinopathy may experience latency where pain is severe upon beginning exercise but subsequently improves and then returns with increasing severity if activ- ity is continued. Examination findings can include crepitus with plantar and dorsiflexion as well as decreased strength, range of motion, and flexibility of the af- fected tendon. Other physical examination findings that can sometimes, but not al- ways, be seen are palpable nodules and tendon thickening. Erythema, hematoma, and joint effusions are rare. Incorrect Answer Explanations Calcaneal bursitis causes pain at the posterior heel that is similar to Achilles tendinopathy, but the pain and local tenderness is located at the insertion site of the Achilles on the calcaneus. In the context of subcutaneous calcaneal bursitis, pain is located in the subcutaneous tissue overlying the posterior calcaneus; pain located deep to the Achilles is usually due to retrocalcaneal bursitis. Manual isolation of the tendon with palpation of these structures can be achieved to differentiate these disease processes. Symptoms associated with bursitis include lo- cal warmth, swelling, and tenderness. This patient's presentation is more consistent with Achilles tendinopathy, not cal- caneal stress fractures. Calcaneal stress fractures cause pain directly over the calcaneus with generalized pain that develops slowly over days to weeks in the setting of increased stress. Pain may be mild in the morning and worsens with activity. Physical examination findings of calcaneal stress fractures in- clude tenderness over the calcaneus when the heel is squeezed from both sides (also known as the squeeze test). This patient's presentation is more consistent with Achilles tendinopathy than with plantar fasciitis. Plantar fasciitis causes pain at the site of the plantar fascia insertion on the calcaneus, and it is worse with passive dorsiflexion of the foot. Pain is worst in the morning and after long periods of non–weight-bearing. Other signs and symptoms of plantar fasciitis include a preference for toe walking and worsening of the pain with ambulation on hard surfaces. Plantar fasciitis is also associated with an increase in activity prior to symptom onset.

question: A 21-year-old man presents with right elbow pain. Tenderness is elicited while pal- pating the medial elbow with one hand and passively supinating the forearm and extending the elbow, wrist, and fingers with the other hand. What is the most likely etiology of this patient's symptoms?
englishExplanation: Golfer's elbow (otherwise known as medial epicondylitis or elbow flexor tendinopathy) is caused by overuse affecting the medial epicondyle of the elbow and proximal forearm. Repetitive movements lead to microtears of the tendinous insertion of the pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis muscles onto the medial epi- condyle. This causes pain at the medial epicondyle as well as pain with movements that require wrist flexion and forearm pronation. Physical examination maneuvers include the golfer's elbow test, which aims to ac- tivate the affected musculature in order to incite pain. When performed passively, the examiner places a hand on the medial epicondyle and uses the other hand to supinate the forearm and extend the elbow, wrist, and fingers. When performed actively, the patient is asked to flex the affected elbow and supinate the forearm. The examiner will then grasp the wrist and elbow and attempt to actively straighten the elbow against resistance. Both active and passive versions of this maneuver serve to acti- vate the pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis muscles, which function in forearm pronation and wrist flexion. A positive test occurs when pain is elicited along the medial elbow. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient's presentation is more consistent with flexor tendinopathy than with cervical radiculopathy. Cervical radiculopathy is a process affecting the cer- vical nerve root that frequently causes neck, shoulder, or arm pain; weakness; and paresthesias of the upper extremity. Cervical radiculopathy cannot be elicited through passive supination of the forearm with wrist extension but can refer pain to the elbow that is not affected by elbow movement. Maneuvers that can elicit cervical radiculopathy include the Spurling maneuver (ie, recreation of pain with axial pressure applied to the head while bent toward the symptomatic side) and the shoul- der abduction relief test (ie, relief of pain with arm abducted at the shoulder). This patient's presentation is more consistent with flexor tendinopathy, not ex- tensor tendinopathy. Extensor tendinopathy or lateral epicondylitis is also known as tennis elbow. The "tennis elbow test" is an active maneuver that can elicit proximal forearm and elbow pain or weakness on resistance against wrist exten- sion with the elbow held in full extension. The tennis elbow test is similar to the golfer's elbow test in that the examiner places one hand on the lateral epicondyle (where pain is felt) and uses the other hand to provide resistance at the wrist against patient forearm pronation, radial deviation, and wrist extension. This patient's presentation is more consistent with flexor tendinopathy than with radial tunnel syndrome. Radial tunnel syndrome is caused by radial nerve entrapment and can mimic tennis elbow (also known as lateral epicondylitis or exten- sor tendinopathy). Maneuvers that can elicit and differentiate radial tunnel syndrome from tennis elbow include forced flexion of the middle finger's proximal interpha- langeal joint while it is extended; this will cause pain over the extensor muscles in the proximal forearm in radial tunnel syndrome.

question: A 46-year-old man presents with right shoulder pain that is worse at night and with overhead activities. He denies trauma and states that he has been unable to lay on his right shoulder. He denies neck pain. On examination, there is no pain at the bicipital groove. Which provocative maneuver can help elicit the cause of the patient's shoulder pain?
englishExplanation: The empty can test can elicit pain due to supraspinatus tendinopathy or tendon tear. A positive test elicits pain or weakness with resistance of the patient's arm in abduction elevated to 90 degrees and internally rotated. The supraspinatus muscle and tendon function as components of the rotator cuff, which also consists of the infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis muscles. Rotator cuff tendinopathy, impingement, and tendon tears represent the most common causes of shoulder pain in the general population — the supraspinatus tendon is the most frequently involved. Prevalence of rotator cuff disease increases with age, but other risk factors include repetitive overhead activities or sports. The biceps muscle and tendon are also important for shoulder function, and biceps tendonitis can elicit similar symptoms of nighttime shoulder pain and pain with over- head movements. However, this case is less likely to be related to biceps ten- donitis because there is no pain at the bicipital groove. Incorrect Answer Explanations The scarf test, also known as the cross-body adduction test, is a maneu- ver that elicits pain due to acromioclavicular joint dysfunction. It can be performed with the patient's arm held at 90 degrees of forward flexion with the elbow also flexed at 90 degrees followed by the examiner horizontally adducting the flexed arm across the patient's body towards the contralateral shoulder. This results in pain due to compression of the medial acromial facet against the distal clavicle. The Spurling test can elicit pain due to cervical radiculopathy. It can be per- formed by the examiner turning the patient's head to the affected side while extend- ing the neck and applying downward pressure atop the patient's head. Cervical radiculopathy typically leads to neck pain radiating down the arm. The Yergason test provokes pain due to biceps tendon pathology, such as bicipital tendinitis or tears of the glenoid labrum. Although the biceps muscle is also important for shoulder function and biceps tendonitis can elicit similar symptoms, this is less likely in this case since there is no pain at the bicipital groove. The Yergason test is performed while the patient is seated with their elbow held at 90 de- grees of flexion and in a pronated position, with the humerus against the side. The patient is then asked to attempt external rotation and supination of the arm against resistance from the examiner. A positive test reproduces the pain in the bicipital groove.

question: A scleroderma patient presents with mouth sores, throat pain, and severe diarrhea. She has been taking methotrexate 20 mg daily for the past 10 days, although her prescription is for 20 mg weekly. What treatment will this patient likely require?

question: A 58-year-old woman presents with sepsis after a 1-week history of URI. Her medical history is significant for lupus on chronic steroids. She is started on an- tibiotics but has hypotension refractory to fluid resuscitation and norepineph- rine. What is the next best treatment option?
englishExplanation: This patient is iatrogenically adrenally suppressed and is presenting with adrenal insufficiency. She requires exogenous supplementation of steroids and the use of stress-dose hydrocortisone because her chronic steroid use has sup- pressed her endogenous adrenal axis; consequently, when she experiences stressors, her body cannot mount its own steroid stress response due to this suppression. There is a lot of controversy around steroid use in septic shock, and there is cur- rently no recommendation for the routine use of “stress-dose steroids” for all patients with septic shock since it has not been shown to have a consistent mortality benefit. The exception would apply to patients who are on chronic steroids, as their adrenal axis is suppressed and requires supplementation. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient is suffering from adrenal insufficiency and requires exogenous steroid supplementation first versus adding another pressor. Vasopressin is an endogenously released peptide hormone that can be used in adjunct with nor- epinephrine in patients with refractory shock, and it should be considered in pa- tients who do not have adrenal insufficiency. However, vasopressin's use in compar- ison to norepinephrine alone has not shown a mortality benefit. A cosyntropin stimulation test utilizes synthetic adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) to measure the body's response to generate cortisol. A baseline cortisol level is checked followed by the synthetic ACTH, and a repeat level is checked 30 and 60 minutes later. This test is thought to be unreliable in the critically ill patient. Furthermore, waiting for such testing in this hypotensive pa- tient would be inappropriate; stress-dose hydrocortisone would be the next best treatment option. In patients with septic shock, cortisol levels can vary widely and should not be used to direct management. In the critically ill patient, cortisol levels are raised and may present a falsely normal level. Cortisol levels have also not corre- lated with mortality. For these reasons, a random cortisol level can lack the sensitivity to detect iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency. Cortisol levels also vary sig- nificantly during the day and are commonly checked in the morning. In the critically ill patient, this variation may be lost, so even cortisol drawn in the morning for a critically ill patient will not have the same reliability in the non–critically ill patient.

question: A 54-year-old farm worker presents with low back pain of 3 weeks' duration that radiates down his right leg. An examination reveals decreased sensation on the lateral side of the right lower leg, dorsum of the right foot, and the lateral edge of the right foot. The right patellar reflex is normal, but the right ankle reflex is ab- sent. A motor examination is mostly normal, except that he has trouble standing on his toes. Reflexes in the left leg are normal; he denies urinary or fecal inconti- nence. If an MRI of the spine were obtained, what would it likely show?

options.text: Broad-based disc bulge compressing the cauda equina
Herniated disc between L5 and S1
Lytic lesion causing cord compression between L2 and L3
Spinal stenosis with narrowing at L3

correctAnswer: Herniated disc between L5 and S1
englishExplanation: This patient has developed a herniated lumbar disc causing lumbar radicu- lopathy. Based on the physical examination, the affected spinal levels must be L5 and S1, so a disc herniation in this region explains the findings. Most patients with herniated spinal discs recover with medical and physical therapy; operative re- pair should be avoided. Two elements of the examination contribute to pinpointing the spinal level of the pathology: deep tendon reflexes and skin dermatomes. Deep tendon reflexes correspond to certain spinal levels; the biceps reflex is medi- ated by C5-C6, the patella reflex by L2-L4, and the ankle jerk by L5-S1. Spinal levels can also be identified by loss of sensation along dermatomes. In this case, the L5 dermatome runs along the lateral side of the leg and wraps around to include the toes. The S1 dermatome runs mostly along the back of the leg and wraps into the plantar surface of the foot. Because spinal nerves emerge from the vertebral column and extend inferiorly, herniating spinal discs press on the spinal levels above the level of origin (for example, an L5 herniated disc presses on spinal nerves from L4). Not every patient with back pain should be sub- jected to imaging, but it is indicated in certain situations. Red flags from the history that indicate the need for imaging include fever, weight loss, incontinence, elderly, intravenous drug use, and a history of cancer or aneurysm. When a neurosurgical emergency is suspected (cauda equina syndrome or spinal cord compression), MRI is the imaging modality of choice. Incorrect Answer Explanations A large broad-based disc or mass pressing on the terminal fibers of the spinal cord (the cauda equina) causes cauda equina syndrome, which is characterized by a loss of sensation in sacral dermatomes between the legs and in the perineum (saddle anesthesia) and a loss of bowel or bladder continence. This patient has localized, distal neurologic abnormalities and no bowel or bladder symptoms, so a herniated disc at L5 to S1 is more likely than cauda equina syndrome. A lytic lesion, suggesting a neoplasm, is a possible cause of this patient's back pain, but a lesion compressing the L2 nerve root would lead to a decreased patella reflex and anesthesia along the thigh into the medial leg. This patient's examination points to a lesion at the L5-S1 level, so a herniated disc at L5 to S1 is more likely. A lesion compressing the L3 nerve root would lead to a decreased patellar reflex and anesthesia along the thigh into the medial leg. This patient's ex- amination points to a lesion at the L5-S1 level, so a herniated disc at L5 to S1 is more likely. Key Points Deep tendon reflexes and skin dermatomes can help pinpoint the level of spine pathology in patients with low back pain. Low back pain red flags include fever, weight loss, incontinence, elderly, intra- venous drug use, and a history of cancer or aneurysm.

question: A 43-year-old patient has a history of migraines, lumbar radiculopathy, sickle cell disease, and rheumatoid arthritis. An opioid prescription is most indicated to manage chronic pain from which of these disease processes?
englishExplanation: Recurrent pain, such as that experienced by patients with sickle cell disease, is a subset of a chronic pain disorder. In sickle cell disease, pain should be managed similarly to other acute causes of severe pain, with rapid administration of opi- oids. Since this is a chronic illness that causes repeated episodes of severe pain, many patients have a prescription for opioids at home. By the time patients present to the emergency department, they have usually attempted to manage the pain at home without success, and they may require higher doses of opioids compared to those used to treat most causes of acute pain; frequent reassessment is necessary. Empiric administration of oxygen therapy is contraindicated in patients whose Hgb oxygen saturation is at their baseline because it may mask respira- tory depression. There are no physical examination or laboratory findings that reliably confirm a patient is having an acute exacerbation of pain from a vaso-occlu- sive crisis due to sickle cell disease. Patients should be trusted to report their pain accurately. Avoid terminology that may be perceived as judgmental when describing patients with this disease process. Incorrect Answer Explanations Opioids are not indicated in the management of migraine. Effective thera- pies for migraine include NSAIDs, acetaminophen, triptans, and antiemetics. Opioids are not considered a first-line therapy in the treatment of chronic pain from radiculopathy. This is a neuropathic pain that can be ex- pected to respond better to medications such as gabapentin, pregabalin, select anti- convulsants, and certain antidepressants. Chronic widespread pain from rheumatoid arthritis is preferentially treated simi- larly to fibromyalgia — with a multimodal approach rather than opioids. In ad- dition to administration of select antidepressant medications (eg, tricyclic antide- pressants), treatment of rheumatoid arthritis often includes nonpharmacological therapies that address comorbidities and promote healthy lifestyle choices.

question: What is the best initial diagnostic test for undifferentiated hemoptysis?
englishExplanation: Chest x-rays are good initial screening tools in patients with undifferen- tiated hemoptysis. They can locate the cause of hemorrhage in as many as 46% to 80% of cases. Chest x-rays should be the first diagnostic test along with laboratory studies (CBC, PT/INR, and type and screen). In young, healthy patients with nor- mal chest x-rays and a likely viral cause of hemoptysis, the diagnostic workup can stop there with close follow-up. Those with normal chest x-rays and more concerning history will need further diagnostic workup, potentially in- cluding CT scans and/or bronchoscopy. Incorrect Answer Explanations Angiography is not the first-line diagnostic test for hemoptysis. Angiography is often used as a therapeutic option once the source of bleeding has been identified using other techniques (eg, chest x-ray followed by CT scan or bron- choscopy). Although angiography is relatively minimally invasive, it is still more in- vasive than other diagnostic tools and requires the use of intravenous contrast. Because bronchoscopy is relatively invasive, it is not the initial diagnos- tic test for hemoptysis. However, it is a useful tool in hemoptysis because it can be diagnostic as well as therapeutic. Bronchoscopy can be used to locate sources of bleeding and remove blood from the airways. Often, bronchoscopy is synergistic with CT imaging in the diagnosis and treatment of hemoptysis. CT imaging can lo- cate peripheral bleeding that is unreachable by flexible bronchoscopes. A CT scan is often useful as a second step in the diagnosis of hemoptysis in patients with normal chest x-rays. Because most sources of bleeding can be identified on a chest x-ray with far less radiation exposure, a chest x-ray is the pre- ferred initial diagnostic test.

question: A 56-year-old man presents with severe right shoulder pain, a swollen and warm shoulder joint, and fever to 39.1°C (102.4°F). His range of motion is severely lim- ited by pain. Arthrocentesis is performed, and 30 mL of fluid is obtained and shown below. What is most likely to be found in the fluid under microscopic examination? Credit: Hans R. House, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation:
Considering the patient's fever and the pus-like appearance of the shoulder synovial fluid, it is likely the patient has septic arthritis. The most common cause of sep- tic arthritis is Staphylococcus aureus, which typically appears as a gram-positive cocci collecting in grape-like clusters. Other bacteria that can be found in septic arthritis include Group A Streptococcus, Streptococcus pneumo- niae, and, rarely, Neisseria gonorrhoeae (a gram-negative diplococci). Patients with septic arthritis typically present with fever, joint swelling and pain, and limited range of motion in the affected joint, which is almost always monoarticular. Elevated ESR and CRP levels are suggestive of infection. Septic arthritis, especially in children, is not an obvious diagnosis, and clinicians must be cautious about performing arthrocentesis. One set of clinical criteria is the Kocher criteria, which were developed retrospectively to estimate the risk for septic arthritis of the hip in children. But a definitive clinical diagnosis can be made only from a synovial culture, which must be obtained by arthrocentesis. A Gram stain of the synovial fluid might reveal the causal bacteria but is more likely to show only WBCs. The synovial fluid drawn from the septic shoulder is turbid and purulent and has a low viscosity, low glucose, and 30,000 or more WBCs/cm, most of which is polynu- cleated cells. Incorrect Answer Explanations Gram-negative diplococci are the typical appearance of Neisseria species. N. gonor- rhoeae can cause a migratory polyarthritis associated with a vesicular or pustular rash. It can also, rarely, cause a septic monoarthritis, usually in the knee, wrist, or ankle. The most common cause of septic arthritis is S. aureus, which typ- ically appears as a gram-positive cocci collecting in grape-like clusters. Needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals are caused by the precipitation of monosodium urate in the synovial fluid. This is the cause of gout and typically af- fects the first metatarsal phalangeal joint but can occur as a monoarthritis in other joints, including the ankle, knee, and elbow. Although gout can lead to low-grade fevers and slightly cloudy synovial fluid, the high fever and turbid appearing puru- lent synovial fluid in this case is most consistent with septic arthritis. The most common cause of septic arthritis is S. aureus, which typically appears as a gram-positive cocci collecting in grape-like clusters. 3 Rhomboid-shaped positively birefringent crystals are caused by the precipitation of calcium pyrophosphate crystals and are seen in pseudogout. Although pseudogout can lead to low-grade fevers and slightly cloudy synovial fluid, the high fever and turbid appearing purulent synovial fluid in this case is most consistent with septic arthritis. The most common cause of septic arthritis is S. aureus, which typically appears as a gram-positive cocci collecting in grape-like clusters.

question: A patient presents with a fever of 38.9°C (102°F) 2 days postoperative from right inguinal hernia repair without mesh. There is drainage from the wound site with surrounding erythema, warmth, and pain out of proportion to examination. The patient has no allergies to medications. Which empiric antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
englishExplanation:
Most surgical site infections present 5 days or more after surgery. The early presentation of a postsurgical fever with wound site drainage and cellulitis, particularly with pain out of proportion to examination within 24 to 48 hours, is concerning for the possibility of a necrotizing soft-tissue infection caused by group A Streptococcus or Clostridium perfringens. Empiric an- tibiotics should cover a broad spectrum, with clindamycin added for anti- toxin effects. Early surgical consultation should be obtained. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ciprofloxacin and metronidazole are good empiric antibiotics for intra-ab- dominal infection and would be a reasonable choice if the surgical site infection were a later infection, more than 5 days postoperatively. However, the early onset of this patient's symptoms raise concern for necrotizing soft-tissue infection. Ciprofloxacin and vancomycin are empiric antibiotics for superficial skin site infection and would be reasonable choices if the surgical site infection were a later infection, more than 5 days postoperatively, and more superficial in na- ture. Double coverage of aerobes with this regimen is likely unnecessary and could expose the patient to additional risks. Additionally, the early onset of this patient's symptoms raise concern for necrotizing soft-tissue infection. Piperacillin-tazobactam and metronidazole are good empiric antibiotics for intra-abdominal infection and would be reasonable choices if the surgical site infection were a later infection, more than 5 days postoperatively. Double cov- erage of anaerobes with this regimen is likely unnecessary and could expose the patient to additional risks, such as C. difficile infection. Additionally, the early onset of this patient's symptoms raise concern for necrotizing soft-tissue infection.

Adolescent athletes who are involved in sports that require a lot of lumbar extension, such as this patient, are particularly at risk. For symptomatic patients, activity restriction for 1 to 2 weeks is recommended. If pain per- sists after that time period, diagnostic studies are indicated, starting with x-rays. question:
Shared scenario:
A 55-year-old man with a history of diabetes presents complaining of left
knee pain several days following a fall from standing height. The patient
was brought to the ED by ambulance after being found on a park bench
stating he was unable to walk because of the pain. On physical examination,
there are no rashes or external signs of trauma. His left knee is warm,
diffusely tender, and swollen with a large effusion. He has pain on passive
range of motion and is refusing to walk. His BP is 150/85 mm Hg, HR is
105 beats/minute, RR is 16 breaths/minute, and temperature is 102.7°F.
POC glucose is 89 mg/dL.

165.   Which of the following is the most definitive diagnostic test?

options.text: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP)

englishExplanation:
165.  The answer is d. This patient is exhibiting the common signs and
symptoms of septic arthritis, an infection of a joint space. The knee is the
most commonly involved joint, followed by the hip, shoulder, and wrist.
Preexisting arthritis (eg, osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis),
immunocompromised states (eg, alcoholism, diabetes, or cancer), and
sexually transmitted infections are risk factors for the development of septic
arthritis. Patients present with a warm, tender, erythematous, swollen joint
and pain with passive range of motion. Fever and chills are common.
Arthrocentesis is diagnostic with joint fluid demonstrating a WBC count
greater than 50,000/μL with more than 75% neutrophils. S. aureus remains
the predominant pathogen for all age groups. However, in young adults,
gonococcal septic arthritis is common and should also be considered when
selecting empiric antibiotic coverage. Patients with sickle cell disease are
also at increased risk for septic arthritis due to salmonella. Patients with
septic arthritis should receive a first dose of antibiotics in the ED prior to
admission. If a coincident cellulitis is present over the involved joint,
arthrocentesis may need to be delayed, though this decision should be made
in consultation with an orthopedic surgeon, as delay in diagnosis of a septic
joint can lead to significant morbidity.
Plain radiographs (a) should be obtained to identify any underlying
osteomyelitis or joint disease, but are often nondiagnostic in acute septic
arthritis. MRI (b) plays no role in the diagnosis of acute septic arthritis but

may be useful in evaluating for chronic disease, osteomyelitis, and other
musculoskeletal injuries involving the knee. The ESR and CRP (c) are often
elevated in septic arthritis and can be trended to assess treatment success,
but neither is specific or diagnostic. A bone scan (e) is useful in the
detection of osteomyelitis that may not be immediately apparent on a plain
radiograph, but is not sensitive in the diagnosis of septic arthritis.

question:
A 54-year-old man presents to the ED with 2 days of right foot pain
that suddenly worsened at night. The touch of his bed sheets on his foot
made the pain worse while he was trying to sleep. The pain is burning in
nature without radiation. He denies fever or trauma. His medical history is
significant for chronic kidney disease. He believes the pain is due to a gout
flare. Pain began after he recently celebrated his birthday at a local
gastropub known to have the best steak and craft beers in town. Which of
the following is indicated in the treatment of this patient’s condition?
englishExplanation:
289.  The answer is b. Dexamethasone and other systemic steroids are
used in the treatment of gout in patients who cannot tolerate NSAIDs.
NSAIDs are contraindicated in patients with comorbidities, such as peptic
ulcer disease, GI bleeding, renal insufficiency, hepatic dysfunction, or are
on warfarin.
Indomethacin (a), naproxen (c), and ketorolac (e) are all NSAIDs and
would be contraindicated in this patient with renal insufficiency. Colchicine
can be used in patients with renal insufficiency but is less commonly
prescribed due to a narrow therapeutic window and risk of toxicity.
Colchicine should be started within 36 hours of the onset of symptoms and
is associated with side effects including vomiting and diarrhea.
Intraarticular steroids such as triamcinolone acetonide, can be used for the
treatment of gout. Topical steroid ointment (d) is not shown to be of benefit
in the treatment of patients with gout.

question:
A 55-year-old male is the restrained front-seat passenger in an MVC.
On arrival to ED, primary survey is intact. Secondary survey is notable for a
right leg that is slightly flexed at the hip, shortened, adducted, and internally
rotated. Exam is also notable for loss of sensation of the posterior leg and
foot, loss of dorsiflexion and plantar flexion, and loss of deep tendon reflex
(DTR) at the ankle. Patient has palpable posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis
pulses. Patient’s exam is concerning for injury to which of the following?
englishExplanation:
311.  The answer is d. This patient’s clinical presentation is concerning for
a posterior hip dislocation with associated sciatic nerve injury. Posterior
hip dislocations account for 90% of all hip dislocations and often occur due
to “dashboard injuries” in MVCs (ie, posterior force transmitted to a flexed
hip while patient is seated in vehicle). Around 10% of posterior hip
dislocations are associated with sciatic nerve injury—which may present as
above with a loss of sensation of the posterior leg and foot, loss or difficulty
with plantar and dorsiflexion, and loss of DTR at the ankle. Reduction
under conscious sedation should take place within 6 hours to decrease risk
of AVN. Injury to the femoral nerve (a) is typically associated with anterior
hip dislocations and presents as loss of sensation over the thigh, weakness
of the quadriceps muscle, and loss of DTR at the knee. While injury to the
femoral artery (b) is a complication of hip dislocations, this patient is
vascularly intact. The obturator nerve (d) supplies sensation and innervation
to muscles of the medial thigh. The saphenous nerve (e) arises from the
femoral nerve and provides sensation to the anteromedial leg.

A 20-year-old man was brought in by EMS after he was found lying
face down, unresponsive in a field by his friends. He regained
consciousness after a few minutes, but is still confused in the ED. On
examination, you notice the cutaneous lesion depicted in the figure. The
patient denies any recent travel or sick contacts. He also denies any
symptoms except for some generalized confusion. What other physical
examination finding may help confirm this patient’s diagnosis?

(Reproduced, with permission, from Tintinalli J, Kelen G, Stapczynski J.
Emergency Medicine: A Comprehensive Study Guide. New York, NY:
McGraw Hill; 2004:1238.)

options.text: Palpating the cervical spine for tenderness

englishExplanation:
449.  The answer is b. This patient sustained a direct lightning injury as
evidenced by the typical fern-like pattern exhibited (known as a
Lichtenberg figure). Associated injuries include fractures (from muscle
contraction), cardiovascular collapse, burns, blunt abdominal injuries, and
neurologic damage. Tympanic membrane ruptures are a common
associated injury and is believed to be caused by the rapid expansion of
surrounding air generating a pressure gradient similar to an explosion.
Therefore, it is important to check for blood in the ear canals of these
patients. It is important to quickly assess the ABCs of these patients and
establish an airway. Immobilization of the cervical spine is often indicated,
as well as close ECG monitoring. Patients should be admitted for
observation after obtaining a complete blood count (CBC), creatinine

kinase, troponin, basic metabolic panel, and appropriate radiographs of
injured areas. Although 50 to 100 people die of lightning strikes each year
in the United States, most injuries sustained are not lethal. Triage of
multiple victims of a single lightning strike is reversed and patients who are
pulseless or apneic should be managed first. Respiratory arrest may outlast
cardiac arrest as the diaphragm is stunned. This fact may necessitate rescue
breathing for a short period of time in the patient with a pulse to give
appropriate time for the diaphragm to recover.
Orthostatic vital signs (a) more commonly is seen in vasovagal
mediated syncope rather than lightning strikes. Hemoptysis (c) could
suggest PE as a potential cause of syncope and is less suggestive of a
lightning strike. A systolic murmur (d), especially in the elderly population,
could represent critical aortic stenosis. This patient is young with no
medical problems, which would decrease the probability that the syncope
was secondary to valvular disease. Patients who are struck by lightning
often have blunt injuries from being thrown by the blast effect from the
current (a tertiary blast injury). Any patient who presents to the ED with
paralysis should have cervical spine precautions in place, regardless of
whether or not they have cervical spine tenderness (e). Keraunoparalysis is
a transient paralysis of both lower extremities due to a lightening injury that
will self-resolve over hours and is not due to any spinal cord injury.
Initially, such distinction may be difficult to discern so necessary spinal
cord precautions should be initiated.

A 35-year-old man presents with severe back pain that radiates 
down his right leg. He reports that while lifting a heavy box at work 
2 weeks ago, he felt a “pop” in his lower back. He has not been able 
to return to work since the injury occurred. The patient spoke with 
his lawyer and was told to come directly to the emergency department to get an magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). He denies having any other symptoms and reports no significant past medical 
history. During the physical examination, the patient is asked to lie 
on his back, with his knees extended. His right leg is elevated and, at 
50 degrees, he reports severe pain running down the lateral aspect 
of his right leg to his foot. The patient is then asked to sit with his 
knees flexed and legs hanging over the side of the bed. His legs are 
passively extended, with no production of pain. The remainder of 
the physical examination is normal. What is the most appropriate 
next step in managing this patient?

options.text: Computed tomography (CT) of the lumbar spine

englishExplanation:
Several aspects of this scenario point to malingering. The 
most convincing relates to the physical examination findings. The 
straight leg raise (SLR) is the classic test for sciatic nerve root irritation. 
The absence of a positive result generally rules out nerve root irritation. 
To perform the SLR, the patient is positioned supine, knee extended, 
and leg elevated until pain is elicited. A positive result is pain radiating 
down the leg below the knee in a dermatomal distribution when the 
leg is elevated between 30 and 70 degrees. In a patient who may be 
malingering, the SLR can be performed with the patient sitting on the 
side of the bed with knees flexed. Passively straightening the legs in 
this position should produce equally positive results if true nerve root 
irritation exists.

A 54-year-old male with poorly controlled hypertension and coronary artery disease on daily aspirin presents with a swollen first 
metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint on the right foot. You make the 
diagnosis of gout. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient with a presumptive diagnosis of gout?

options.text: Naproxen 550 mg twice daily coupled with daily proton pump

correctAnswer: Naproxen 550 mg twice daily coupled with daily proton pump
englishExplanation:
This patient is moderate risk for gastrointestinal (GI) injury 
due to history of poorly controlled hypertension and daily aspirin use; 
thus an oral nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug (NSAID) coupled 
with daily PPI use is reasonable. If the patient had no cardiac or GI 
risk factors, use of NSAID alone would be appropriate. Colchicine is 
an alternative therapy, although given its side effect profile, another 
NSAID is generally preferred. Allopurinol and febuxostat are medications that may be used to prevent gout attacks but should generally not 
be started during an acute flair and are not typically initiated in the ED 
setting.

question:
Which of the following interventions should routinely be used 
when treating patients with tendinopathies?
englishExplanation:
Patients with tendinopathy should be advised to modify 
their activities (including ergonomic workplace adjustments, when 
pertinent) to avoid exacerbating pain and further tendon injury. Some 
patients may benefit in the near term from a short course (e.g., one 
week) of NSAIDs, although this can result in impaired tendon healing 
in the long term. Thus, their use should be dependent on the circumstances of presentation, such as the severity of pain or comorbid conditions. Intratendinous corticosteroid injections and immobilization 
should not be routinely utilized as they may prove detrimental in the 
long term.

question: A 42-year-old man presents with odynophagia. He reports a constant pain in the middle of his chest that is worse when he eats during the last week. He has never had these symptoms before. His exam is unremarkable. Which of the following is most likely to be discovered in his history?
englishExplanation:
This patient has pill esophagitis, also known as drug-induced esophagitis, a common but often underrecognized cause of acute chest pain and odynophagia. It typically occurs when medications become lodged in the esophagus, leading to localized mucosal injury. Doxycycline is one of the most frequently implicated medications due to its acidic nature and potential to cause caustic injury if not promptly flushed into the stomach. Other medications associated with pill esophagitis include tetracyclines, bisphosphonates, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and potassium chloride.

The condition most often affects younger adults and is more likely to occur when pills are taken without adequate fluids or just before lying down. The injury typically localizes to the midesophagus, corresponding to anatomical areas of compression by the aortic arch or left atrium. Symptoms include acute-onset retrosternal chest pain, odynophagia, and dysphagia. In severe cases, patients may experience hematemesis or melena due to ulceration.

Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on a clear temporal relationship between symptom onset and pill ingestion. Imaging is usually not required, but endoscopy may be performed if symptoms persist or complications are suspected. Emergency department management focuses on pain control, discontinuation of the offending agent, and supportive care. Viscous lidocaine, proton pump inhibitors, and patient education on proper pill-taking techniques are commonly recommended. Rare complications include esophageal strictures, perforation, and bleeding.



Human immunodeficiency virus infection (A) increases the risk of infectious esophagitis caused by Candida, herpes simplex virus, or cytomegalovirus. These typically present in patients with advanced immunosuppression and often include additional systemic symptoms such as fever or oral thrush. In contrast, this patient has localized, abrupt-onset postprandial pain without other systemic signs and normal findings on exam, pointing away from an opportunistic infection and toward a chemical etiology.

Caustic esophageal injury from alkaline substances (B) causes immediate and often severe pain, dysphagia, and drooling. It is typically seen in children or adults with intentional ingestion. There are no signs of acute caustic injury in this patient, and the presentation is less acute than that of a toxic injury from alkaline substances. The delayed symptom onset over several days and the association with swallowing solid food are more characteristic of pill esophagitis than corrosive esophagitis.

Tobacco use (D) is a major risk factor for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma and gastroesophageal reflux disease. While both conditions can lead to chronic esophageal irritation, they typically present with progressive dysphagia, chronic heartburn, or weight loss, not recent-onset odynophagia. This patient’s more acute symptoms and lack of chronicity suggest a more abrupt mucosal injury such as that caused by a lodged or caustic pill rather than the gradual effects of tobacco use.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the treatment for potential eosinophilic esophagitis in the emergency department?

Reveal Answer:
A proton pump inhibitor and gastroenterology referral.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Medication-Induced Esophagitis

Common causes: antibiotics (e.g., tetracyclines), NSAIDs, bisphosphonates
Sx: odynophagia, retrosternal pain
Dx often made clinically, EGD in certain cases (e.g., severe disease, atypical Sx)
Tx: stop offending medication, acid suppression therapy (e.g., PPI)
Preventive measures
Remain upright after taking medications
Take medications with sufficient quantities of water
Use liquid formulation of medication when possible

question: A 47-year-old man with a history of diabetes and morbid obesity presents to the ED with a painful swelling near his umbilicus since yesterday. The pain is worse today, and he vomited one time. He has no fever. He has had swelling in this area before, but it has gone away on its own. On exam, vital signs show HR 90 bpm, BP 147/82 mm Hg, RR 16/min, and T 37.4°C. Near his umbilicus, there is a tender swelling without redness, induration, or fluctuance. As you palpate with greater pressure on the area, he suddenly cries out, and the mass reduces. What is the most appropriate care at this time?

options.text: Consult surgery for emergent hernia repair
Discharge the patient with a surgical referral for elective hernia repair next week
Encourage weight reduction and strict control of diabetes, and provide surgical referral for outpatient evaluation

correctAnswer: Encourage weight reduction and strict control of diabetes, and provide surgical referral for outpatient evaluation
englishExplanation:
An estimated 25% of all people are either born with or will develop a ventral or anterior abdominal wall hernia during their lifetime. Management of ventral hernias needs to take into consideration whether the hernia is incarcerated or strangulated, other risk factors associated with poor surgical outcomes, and the patient’s desire for repair. This patient most likely had an incarcerated hernia that was successfully reduced in the emergency department. An incarcerated hernia is one that does not easily reduce on its own, whereas a strangulated hernia is one with decreased vascular supply leading to tissue necrosis. Although this patient had one episode of vomiting, he is not presenting with signs and symptoms of a strangulated hernia, and reduction was appropriate in the ED.

Now that the hernia is reduced, this patient does not require emergent surgery, so next, the clinician should consider risk factors for a poor surgical outcome. Relative contraindications for hernia repair include morbid obesity, diabetes, and smoking. Patients with these risk factors are more likely to develop an infection and to have a recurrence of the hernia. Therefore, in patients with morbid obesity and diabetes, the most appropriate care plan would be encouraging weight reduction and strict control of diabetes as a priority before and alongside further outpatient surgical evaluation.



Since this patient’s hernia has reduced and he does not have signs and symptoms of a strangulated hernia, he does not require a consult to surgery for emergent hernia repair (A). If he has signs and symptoms of a small bowel obstruction with vomiting, inability to pass gas, and fever, or if his hernia swelling was red or dark with significantly rising pain (indicating strangulation), then an emergent surgical consult would be warranted.

Discharging the patient with a surgical referral for elective hernia repair next week (B) would not be appropriate since the surgeon will likely recommend medical optimization of morbid obesity and diabetes first. It is necessary to set up appropriate expectations for this patient.

No further management (D) would only be recommended for patients who are adamant about declining surgical repair of a nonemergent hernia. Proper outpatient care instructions should be given to this patient to reduce recurrence of the hernia and improve overall outcomes.

One Step Further
Question:
What population of chronically ill patients is prone to developing ventral hernias?

Reveal Answer:
Patients with cirrhosis due to increased abdominal pressure and poor wound healing.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Abdominal Wall Hernia in Adults

Most often acquired through processes that increase intra-abdominal pressure (obesity, ascites, pregnancy)
Evaluate like any other hernia for incarceration, strangulation, and bowel obstruction
Tx
Reduce simple hernias
Strangulated or incarcerated hernias: surgery consultation
Obesity: laparoscopic versus open repair with or without bariatric surgery at the same time
Pregnancy: observation for asymptomatic hernias, surgical repair of highly symptomatic hernia and those with acute incarceration or strangulation
Cirrhosis: medical management of ascites and cirrhosis with surgical repair

question: An 81-year-old man presents to the ED reporting 2 days of redness, tenderness, and swelling along his left jaw. He has a medical history significant for hypertension and diabetes, which are controlled with metoprolol and metformin. His family also notes that they occasionally give him diphenhydramine to help him sleep. They are concerned that he does not eat well or drink enough fluid at baseline, and since this swelling has begun, his oral intake is even less because he can barely open his mouth. His blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg, heart rate is 62 bpm, temperature is 100.6°F (38.1°C), and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. On examination, he is a cachectic-appearing man with erythema, tenderness, and swelling over his left lower face and jaw. He has difficulty opening his mouth due to pain. However, he is able to open it enough to reveal the above findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Suppurative parotitis is caused by bacterial infection of the parotid gland. The hallmark of suppurative parotitis is purulent drainage from the parotid duct. It is a serious condition with a rapid onset. Other symptoms include redness of the skin overlying the parotid, tenderness to touch, fever, and trismus (inability to open the mouth). The most common causative bacteria are Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes such as Bacteroides species, peptostreptococci, and Fusobacteria. Less common bacteria include Streptococcus pyogenes and Haemophilus influenzae. Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas may also be seen in immunocompromised patients. If oral antibiotics are tolerated, amoxicillin-clavulanate, clindamycin, or cephalexin combined with metronidazole are recommended. Patients who have trismus, are unable to tolerate oral antibiotics or comply with outpatient treatment or are immunocompromised require intravenous antibiotic treatment and admission. The risk of suppurative parotitis is heightened by states that decrease salivary flow, which can include medications (e.g., diuretics, antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, phenothiazines, beta-blockers, barbiturates, anesthesia), predisposing oral conditions (e.g., sialolithiasis, oral lesions, duct strictures, tracheostomy, ductal foreign bodies), chronic diseases (e.g., liver or kidney failure, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, Sjögren syndrome, human immunodeficiency virus, cystic fibrosis, hyperuricemia), and other patient-related factors (dehydration, prematurity, advanced age, malnutrition, depression, anorexia, and bulimia). Therefore, activities that increase salivary flow, such as sour candy, hydration, warm compresses, or parotid massage, are also recommended.



While Ludwig angina (A) presents with trismus and fever, it is caused by cellulitis of the sublingual, submental, and submandibular spaces. Physical exam shows edema, tenderness, and swelling beneath the tongue and in the anterior neck. In addition to requiring antibiotics, these patients often require emergent definitive airway management as the tongue may be displaced posteriorly from the edema.

Mumps (B)is a viral parotitis. It is most common in children. Fever, parotid swelling, and tenderness are usually present but typically without warmth or erythema. Purulent drainage is not a common clinical feature.

Sialolithiasis (C) is caused by a stone in a salivary gland. It occurs most commonly in men aged 20–50 years. Approximately 80% of the stones occur in the submandibular gland and 20% in the parotid gland. The pain and swelling are typically colicky and exacerbated by eating. Purulent drainage is not seen with sialolithiasis. Sometimes a stone may be palpated or seen.

One Step Further
Question:
True or false: surgical drainage is required for suppurative parotitis if a patient does not improve on antibiotics within 24–48 hours.

Reveal Answer:
True.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Parotitis

Bacterial (suppurative) and viral (nonsuppurative) causes
Most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, but anaerobes common too
Viral causes can include mumps, influenza, and coxsackievirus
Noninfectious causes: sialolithiasis, alcohol use disorder, diabetes, uremia, certain drugs (anticholinergics, antihistamines), malignancy
Risk factors: age < 1 year, older age, recent surgery or intubation, dehydration, poor oral hygiene, eating disorders
Sx: pain and tenderness with trismus and dysphagia
PE: unilateral, firm, erythematous swelling of the pre- and postauricular areas that extends to the angle of the mandible
DDx: bacterial causes are more often unilateral, whereas viral parotitis is often bilateral
Suppurative parotitis is also associated with purulent discharge, whereas viral or noninfectious parotitis is not
Dx: clinical, but CT can detect abscess
Tx: hydration, often broad-spectrum antibiotics
Complications: respiratory obstruction, septic thrombophlebitis (Lemierre syndrome), bacteremia, osteomyelitis

question: A 66-year-old man with a medical history of hypertension, coronary artery disease, and atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department for sudden vision loss in his left eye 30 minutes ago. He does not have flashes or floaters. He reports no pain or trauma. On exam, both pupils are reactive when the right eye is exposed to light and both pupils dilate when light is shifted from the right eye to the left. Visual acuity is 20/20 on the right and only shadow perception on the left. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s symptoms are consistent with central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). CRAO is characterized by sudden, painless monocular vision loss due to disruption of the blood supply to the inner retina and surface of the optic nerve. It may be preceded by amaurosis fugax. CRAO may arise due to atherosclerotic, embolic, hematologic, or vasculitic etiologies. Carotid artery atherosclerosis is the most common etiology of CRAO overall. This patient’s history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, and atrial fibrillation all contribute to an increased risk of CRAO. Physical examination will demonstrate profound visual loss of the affected eye and an afferent pupillary defect. Funduscopic exam may demonstrate ischemic retinal whitening and classically a cherry red macula. There is mixed evidence regarding maneuvers such as ocular massage, intraocular pressure-lowering medications, or the use of tissue plasminogen activator. Hyperbaric oxygen treatment may be considered. Ophthalmology and neurology should be emergently consulted if there is suspicion for CRAO.



Acute angle-closure glaucoma (A) is caused by obstruction of aqueous humor outflow. Typically it will present as sudden, painful, monocular vision loss, commonly described as hazy vision or halos. Intraocular pressure will be high, and the exam may reveal a mid-dilated pupil. This patient is presenting with painless vision loss, which is not characteristic of acute angle-closure glaucoma. Central retinal vein occlusion (C) also presents with painless monocular visual loss, but funduscopic exam will reveal diffuse retinal hemorrhages, which is not mentioned in this patient. Furthermore, this patient’s risk factors are more suggestive of arterial disease rather than venous disease. Optic neuritis (D) may present with or without pain. Visual loss is typically gradual, and color vision is more commonly affected. Optic neuritis is associated with multiple sclerosis. This patient had sudden visual loss not consistent with optic neuritis. Retinal detachment (E) causes painless vision loss. It may be associated with flashes or floaters or a curtain over the field of vision. Ocular ultrasound may be used to identify a detached retina. Dilated indirect funduscopy is necessary to confirm this diagnosis.

One Step Further
Question:
Which classes of pharmacologic agents can cause a nonreactive dilated pupil?

Reveal Answer:
Cycloplegic and anticholinergic medications.

Rapid Review

Sx: sudden, painless monocular vision loss
Funduscopy: retinal whitening, cherry-red spot, boxcar appearance (from segmental blood flow)
Tx: ocular emergency, evidence unclear regarding optimal therapy

question: A 23-year-old woman presents to the ED due to ear pain. She first developed itching of the left ear 2 days ago that has since become painful. She has recently been training for a triathlon, which has involved running, cycling, and swimming frequently over the last 6 weeks. She has no significant medical history. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals erythema and swelling of the auditory canal on the left. There is a small amount of serous drainage without mastoid tenderness. The tympanic membranes appear normal bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Otitis externa refers to inflammation of the external auditory canal that results from disruption of a protective lipid layer formed by squamous epithelial cells and cerumen. This disruption can occur in the setting of increased temperature, high humidity, or prolonged exposure to moisture. Each of these circumstances allows bacteria to penetrate the skin and establish infection, with Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa as the most common organisms. It is commonly referred to as swimmer’s ear due to its association with swimming, particularly in lakes and streams, and is a likely contributing factor in this patient’s case.

The diagnosis of otitis externa is made based solely on clinical impression and requires no diagnostic testing. Characteristic features include ear pain that may be preceded by pruritus, serous or purulent otorrhea, and erythema and swelling of the external auditory canal. Manipulation of the tragus or auricle will classically produce pain, which is a differentiating factor from acute otitis media, in which these maneuvers often relieve pain. There may also be associated lymphadenopathy or lymphadenitis and local cellulitis.

While some patients with mild cases of otitis externa may improve with acetic acid drops alone, topical antibiotics are the mainstay of treatment for most cases of otitis externa, with fluoroquinolone-based drops most commonly prescribed, though there is no strong evidence to support the use of any particular agent over another. Topical corticosteroids are also commonly prescribed, though data does not suggest their use increases the cure rate. Indications for systemic antibiotic therapy include extension of infection outside the auditory canal, significant immune compromise, and poorly controlled diabetes. Oral ciprofloxacin for 7–10 days is typically recommended, although some patients with malignant otitis externa may require IV antibiotics and hospital admission. Notably, topical aminoglycosides are contraindicated due to their association with ototoxicity and sensorineural hearing loss. In addition to antibiotics, the canal should be gently cleaned using a cotton swab or irrigation and suction to remove any obstructing debris.



Normal appearance of the tympanic membranes bilaterally suggests against acute otitis media (A) in this case, while erythema and edema of the canal suggest otitis externa.

Malignant otitis externa (B), also known as necrotizing external otitis, is a severe form of otitis externa that is most commonly seen in patients with severe diabetes mellitus, immune compromise, or advanced age and typically presents as persistent symptoms of otitis externa refractory to topical antibiotics.

Tenderness over the mastoid process in the setting of known or suspected acute otitis media suggests mastoiditis (C), but no such findings are present in this case.

Otomycosis (D) is a fungal infection of the external ear that accounts for approximately 10% of cases of otitis externa but presents with pruritus as a predominant symptom and usually affects patients in tropical climates or with a history of diabetes mellitus or immune compromise.

One Step Further
Question:
What instructions can be given to patients with otitis externa to enhance drug delivery to the site of infection?

Reveal Answer:
Lie down with the infected side up for approximately 5 minutes after medication administration.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Otitis Externa

Most commonly caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Risks: swimming or moisture exposure
Sx: malodorous discharge, pruritus, otalgia
PE: erythematous, edematous canal with pain with palpation of tragus or pinna
Tx: topical antimicrobials with or without steroids
Necrotizing otitis externa
Complication seen in those with diabetes or immunocompromised
Sx: otorrhea unresponsive to treatment, periauricular pain, swelling
Tx: fluoroquinolone (often IV therapy needed)

question: A young woman with a BMI of 29 kg/m2 presents to the ED with bilateral eye pain and blurry vision. Her vision has gradually become worse over the last few days. She reports no head trauma, seizures, diplopia, or hemianopsia. On exam, her extraocular movements are intact, and her pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light. A noncontrast head CT shows no acute intracranial abnormalities. Her intraocular pressures are 13 mm Hg on the left and 20 mm Hg on the right. Ocular ultrasound shows an optic nerve sheath diameter of 5.8 mm on the left and 6.1 mm on the right. How are these results interpreted, and what is the best next step in management?
englishExplanation:
Eye examination involves specific testing of intraocular muscles, intraocular pressure, visual acuity, visual fields, and pupillary function. Additional testing of the lids, cornea, sclera, conjunctiva, lens, iris, anterior chamber, and vitreous may also be included. Assessing for papilledema provides useful information to the clinician about the possibility of elevated intracranial pressure. When intracranial pressure increases, this leads to bilateral edema of the optic nerve heads. Intracranial tumors, malignant hypertension, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, and hydrocephalus are conditions that can cause papilledema. Papilledema can be appreciated on funduscopic examination and appears as blurred optic disc margins, elevation of the optic nerve heads, and vascular congestion.

Ocular ultrasonography can be used to evaluate certain eye pathologies, including papilledema, retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage, lens dislocation, intraocular foreign body, and retrobulbar hematoma. The optic nerve appears as a linear, hypoechoic structure extending posteriorly from the globe. The optic nerve sheath diameter can be measured to determine if intracranial pressure is elevated. A normal adult optic nerve sheath diameter is up to 5.0 mm, measured at 3 mm posterior to the globe. Though sources vary, on average, a measurement > 5.7–6.0 mm is highly predictive of intracranial pressure > 20 mm Hg. It is important to note that papilledema is the cupping of the optic disc into the vitreous chamber of the eye. It is seen as a hyperechoic mound or crescent in the posterior globe separate from the optic nerve. This is referred to as the crescent sign and is the sonographic equivalent of funduscopic papilledema. The presence of ultrasonographic papilledema with a normal optic nerve sheath diameter is called pseudopapilledema, which can be caused by optic disc drusen (calcium deposits) or inflammatory states such as sarcoidosis, lupus, optic neuritis, or syphilis. In this patient’s case, her measurements (5.8 mm and 6.1 mm) are concerning for elevated intracranial pressure, likely from idiopathic intracranial hypertension. This suggests increased intracranial pressure, and the best next step (after CT imaging) is to perform a lumbar puncture to measure opening cerebrospinal fluid pressure.



Ophthalmology (A) should not be consulted right away, as further diagnostic studies (e.g., CT of the head, lumbar puncture) are indicated to evaluate the cause of the patient’s symptoms. She is more likely to have an intracranial rather than a purely ophthalmologic process.

The patient’s bilateral optic nerve sheath diameters are increased, making an interpretation of normal (C, D), with the next steps of reassure and discharge or searching for alternative causes incorrect.

question: A 17-year-old patient presents with redness and discharge from his right eye. Visual acuity is within normal limits. Which of the following treatments should most likely be avoided in this patient?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with conjunctivitis and should be treated with either ophthalmic antibiotic drops or ointment and warm compresses. Conjunctivitis is an inflammation of the bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva. It can be caused by trauma, toxic agents, allergies, or viral and bacterial pathogens. Common bacterial agents include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus organisms, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Although viral infections are the most common cause of conjunctivitis, it is often difficult to differentiate viral from bacterial causes, leading many clinicians to treat all presentations as bacterial conjunctivitis. Patients typically present with eye redness, lid swelling, crusting of the eye in the morning, and drainage. Pain, loss of vision, and photophobia should not be present. Ophthalmic ointments may provide a soothing effect but can interfere with vision. Drops do not interfere with vision. Corticosteroids and eye patching should be avoided, as these may exacerbate the infection.



Eyelid hygiene measures (A) like cleaning the eyelids are recommended for conditions like blepharitis and would not be harmful. Patients with conjunctivitis should be educated on measures to prevent transmission, including avoiding touching the eye, practicing good hand hygiene, and avoiding sharing towels, linens, and cosmetics until symptoms resolve.

The standard treatment for acute conjunctivitis involves ophthalmic antibiotic drops (B) or ointment (C) and warm compresses (E).

What is the most common cause of viral conjunctivitis?

Reveal Answer:
Adenoviruses.
