الفخ: الخيار B (Osteochondroma) قد يبدو مناسباً ظاهرياً لكنه لا يتوافق مع المعايير السريرية المطلوبة هنا.

question: A 35-year-old man presents to the ED with finger pain. He sustained lacerations to his right hand 5 days ago during a bar fight, and 2 days ago, he started to notice pain and swelling in the right third finger. On exam, his finger is diffusely swollen, erythematous, slightly flexed at rest, and tender along the palmar surface, and he has increased pain on the palmar surface with passive extension of the finger. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment?

options.text: Incision and drainage by a hand surgeon
Incision and drainage in the ED

correctAnswer: Incision and drainage by a hand surgeon
englishExplanation:
Flexor tenosynovitis is an infection in the flexor tendon sheath and is diagnosed by the four cardinal signs of the Kanavel criteria, including the finger held in passive flexion, symmetric swelling of the digit that is commonly referred to as a sausage digit, tenderness along the flexor tendon sheath, and pain with passive extension of the finger. The combination of these signs is very sensitive and fairly specific for flexor tenosynovitis. Infectious tenosynovitis, including flexor tenosynovitis, usually occurs from direct traumatic inoculation or spread from nearby soft tissues but can also occur from hematogenous spread.

Treatment includes IV antibiotics, usually vancomycin and ceftriaxone, and surgical drainage by a hand surgeon.



Admission for IV antibiotics (A) is appropriate in all cases of suspected flexor tenosynovitis. However, it is definitive treatment only in the most mild cases involving only mild pain and local inflammation. These patients can be given vancomycin and a third-generation cephalosporin and admitted to monitor progression and the need for surgical intervention. Once there is severe pain, diffuse swelling, and limited passive range of motion, surgical intervention is warranted for definitive management in addition to IV antibiotics.

Incision and drainage in the ED (C) is appropriate for simple abscesses but not infections involving complex structures like the flexor tendons of the hands, which require specialist intervention.

Oral antibiotics (D) are not appropriate for the treatment of flexor tenosynovitis, given the high likelihood of progression to require surgical drainage, even in mild cases. Patients with mild signs and symptoms may be admitted for IV antibiotics and monitoring. Individuals with more advanced presentations, like this patient, should undergo surgical drainage by a hand surgeon.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the name of the condition that results from fibrosis of the palmar fascia and causes a cord that limits the motion of a finger or area of the hand?

Reveal Answer:
Dupuytren contracture.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Flexor Tenosynovitis

History of penetrating trauma (most common)
Most commonly caused by S. aureus infection
Dx: Kanavel criteria
Tenderness along the flexor tendon
Fusiform or symmetrical swelling of the finger
Pain with extension
Flexed posture of the finger
Tx: IV antibiotics, surgical emergency

الفخ: الخيار A (Admission for IV antibiotics) قد يبدو مناسباً ظاهرياً لكنه لا يتوافق مع المعايير السريرية المطلوبة هنا.

question: Which clinical feature is most sensitive for cauda equina syndrome?

options.text: Diminished strength in bilateral lower extremities

englishExplanation:
Cauda equina syndrome results from lesions compressing the conus medullaris and the nerve roots extending from it (the cauda equina). These lesions most commonly are herniated discs, bone fragments, hematomas, epidural abscesses, tumors, or vascular insufficiency. Spinal epidural abscess is a rare but important infection of the central nervous system (CNS) that requires emergent consideration, diagnosis, and treatment. Spinal epidural abscesses are most commonly found in the thoracic or lumbar areas, where the epidural space contains more infection-prone fatty tissue in a larger area. Risk factors for a spinal epidural abscess include epidural catheter placement, paraspinal injections, diabetes mellitus, alcohol use disorder, HIV, trauma, bacteremia, intravenous drug use, and hemodialysis. The classic triad of symptoms of spinal epidural abscess is fever, spinal pain, and neurologic deficits (may be consistent with cauda equina syndrome). Patients with other forms of cauda equina commonly report low back pain, lower extremity pain, paralysis or paresthesia, saddle anesthesia, impotence, or bowel or bladder dysfunction. Once paralysis is present, it quickly becomes irreversible, thus early recognition and treatment are crucial. Urinary retention is the most consistent finding with a sensitivity of 90%.

A thorough history regarding recent spinal procedures, trauma, anticoagulation, intravenous drug use, and history of malignancy helps aid in determining the cause. Physical examination of the lower extremities may demonstrate sensory or motor deficits. Frequently, clinical features are asymmetric with unilateral signs and symptoms being present. Absent or decreased rectal tone and bulbocavernosus reflexes may also be found. A palpable distended urinary bladder may be appreciated secondary to urinary retention. Laboratory examination may reveal an elevated or normal white blood cell count, and may therefore not be helpful with the diagnosis. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) lab values are typically obtained for evaluation with both being elevated in the majority of cases. However, several studies have found that the ESR has better sensitivity and specificity compared to CRP.

Patients with a suspicious history and physical or lab results concerning for cauda equina require emergency MRI imaging. CT myelogram may be utilized in patients unable to have an MRI performed. A bedside postvoid residual of 100–200 mL without a history of voiding difficulties suggests a neurologic etiology. Treatment relies on early surgical decompression. If a spinal epidural abscess is found, antibiotics should be started as soon as the diagnosis is strongly suspected or confirmed. Vancomycin plus cefotaxime or ceftriaxone are appropriate empiric antibiotics. If Pseudomonas is thought to be a possible organism, then cefepime or ceftazidime should be used in place of cefotaxime or ceftriaxone.



Diminished deep tendon reflexes (A), diminished strength in bilateral lower extremities (B), and positive straight leg raise (D) may or may not all be present in cauda equina syndrome. However, none of these clinical features are the most sensitive for cauda equina syndrome.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common causing organism in a spinal epidural abscess?

Reveal Answer:
Staphylococcus aureus.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Spinal Epidural Abscess

Most commonly caused by S. aureus
Risks: diabetes, IV drug use, recent back surgery, immunodeficiency, endocarditis, bacteremia
Sx: back pain, fever, and neurological deficits
Dx: elevated ESR or CRP
MRI
Tx: IV antibiotics, spine surgery consultation for drainage

question: An otherwise healthy 13-year-old boy with a history of obesity presents to the ED with 1 day of hip pain. On exam, you note an antalgic gait and a right leg held in external rotation. His vital signs are within normal limits. Which of the following findings most supports the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Irregular ossification of femoral head on X-ray
Widened physis at the right femoral head on X-ray

correctAnswer: Widened physis at the right femoral head on X-ray
englishExplanation:
The patient’s clinical presentation is consistent with slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). The most common early finding to support this diagnosis is widened physis at the right femoral head on X-ray. This patient has multiple risk factors for SCFE including obesity and ages between 12 and 15 years old. His clinical presentation of hip pain with an antalgic gait and external rotation at the hip is characteristic of SCFE. X-ray findings associated with the disease include widening of the physis. The classic displacement of the femoral head from the femoral neck (“ice cream off the cone” on X-ray) is a late finding. Treatment is surgical.



SCFE is not an inflammatory process, so the C-reactive protein (A) should not be elevated.

Irregular ossification of the femoral head on X-ray (B) is the classic finding of Legg-Calve-Perthes disease. This condition is more common in younger patients, typically between 4 and 9 years of age.

Joint effusion on hip ultrasound (C) is a common finding in transient tenosynovitis of the hip, which is associated with a recent viral syndrome in patients 3–10 years old.

One Step Further
Question:
What percent of Legg-Calve-Perthes disease is bilateral?

Reveal Answer:
10%.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE)

Male adolescents 12–16 years old with obesity
Displacement of the capital femoral epiphysis from the femoral neck through the physeal plate
Clinical: progressive limp and hip or knee pain
PE: loss of hip internal rotation and flexion
Dx: X-ray will show apparent posterior displacement of the femoral epiphysis (scoop of ice cream slipping off cone)
Tx: non-weight-bearing and urgent orthopedic consultation, surgical fixation

الفخ: الخيار A (Elevated C-reactive protein) قد يبدو مناسباً ظاهرياً لكنه لا يتوافق مع المعايير السريرية المطلوبة هنا.

question: Which of the following history or physical exam findings may be seen in an individual with the diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis?
englishExplanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of inflammatory arthritis of the spine. Sacroiliitis is usually apparent on X-ray but may require an MRI if suspicion is high. A patient will usually present with chronic back pain before the age of 45. It is often associated with enthesitis, synovitis, and dactylitis as well as extra-articular manifestations including uveitis, psoriasis, and inflammatory bowel disease. A patient with chronic bloody diarrhea and chronic back pain has a higher likelihood of having ankylosing spondylitis. It is associated with the gene HLA-B27. Features consistent with inflammatory back pain include age of onset < 40 years, insidious onset, improvement with exercise, no improvement with rest, and pain at night.



Psoriasis, not eczema (B), occurs in about 10% of those with ankylosing spondylitis. There is more frequent peripheral joint involvement with those who have psoriasis.

Patients with ankylosing spondylitis will usually have improvement of back pain with exercise, not increased pain (C). Back pain is also worse at night, not during the day (D).

One Step Further
Question:
What are the acute and chronic treatments for back pain from ankylosing spondylitis?

Reveal Answer:
Anti-inflammatory medications like NSAIDs and disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs for chonic disease and to prevent relapse.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Ankylosing Spondylitis (Radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis)

Sx: low back pain that is most severe at night and morning stiffness that improves with exercise
PE: limited spinal mobility, decreased lumbar lordosis
X-ray: squared vertebral bodies, multiple vertebral fusions (bamboo spine)
Lab results: increased ESR, positive HLA-B27
Treatment options include NSAIDs, physical therapy, TNF-alpha blockers
Associated with uveitis, aortitis, IBD, psoriasis, apical pulmonary fibrosis
Diseases associated with HLA-B27: PAIR
Psoriatic arthritis
Ankylosing spondylitis
Inflammatory bowel disease
Reactive arthritis

question: In which setting is initiating allopurinol inappropriate in the treatment of gout?
englishExplanation:
Gout is caused by the deposition of uric acid crystals in the synovium, bursae, tendon sheaths, skin, heart valves, and kidneys, which can lead to arthritis, tophi, kidney stones, and gouty nephropathy. Typically, patients present with acute, exquisitely tender, monoarticular arthritis. The joint is usually warm and erythematous. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is most commonly affected. Detecting negatively birefringent, needle-like crystals in the synovial fluid from an arthrocentesis confirms the diagnosis.

Allopurinol is a urate-lowering medication used for the long-term prevention of gout attacks, but it should not be initiated during an acute gout flare if the flare is not yet controlled. Starting allopurinol can rapidly shift serum urate levels, which may worsen or prolong the acute attack. The preferred approach is to first treat the flare with NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids until symptoms improve. Once the acute attack is resolved and inflammation is controlled, allopurinol may be started with prophylactic colchicine to reduce the risk of flare during initiation.

The risk of triggering or aggravating a flare occurs because changes in uric acid concentrations destabilize urate crystals within joints. Therefore, guidelines emphasize stabilizing inflammation before initiating a urate-lowering agent. If a patient is already on allopurinol at the time of a flare, the medication should not be discontinued, but starting it during an active, uncontrolled flare is inappropriate. After resolution, allopurinol can be initiated at a low dose and titrated upward as tolerated.



While caution and dose adjustments are required, allopurinol is not contraindicated in chronic kidney disease (B). Proper dosing and monitoring can safely facilitate its use in gout management for patients with impaired kidney function, so it would not be inappropriate to start in a patient with a GFR stage of G3a.

Ethanol metabolism blocks kidney excretion of uric acid, which increases the risk of developing gouty arthritis. However, allopurinol is not contraindicated in individuals who consume ethanol (C).

Hyperuricemia (D) is present (usually > 8 mg/dL) in patients with gout, and when symptomatic, these patients should be treated. Allopurinol is used to decrease uric acid production, thus managing hyperuricemia effectively, and there is no contraindication based on the level of serum uric acid.

Colchicine (E) can be used in combination with allopurinol to help decrease the likelihood of a gouty flare while the uric acid level decreases after an acute attack has subsided. Colchicine decreases inflammation associated with lactic acid production and phagocytosis of urate. It terminates most gouty attacks within 6–12 hours but is limited by GI side effects.

One Step Further
Question:
What are the nodular deposits seen in gout?

Reveal Answer:
Tophi, which can be seen in subcutaneous tissues, tendons, cartilage, and bone.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Gout

Mono- or oligoarticular arthritis caused by uric acid crystals
Risk factors: male sex, age > 30 years, obesity, metabolic syndrome, CKD, dietary factors
Sx: podagra (acute onset of pain in the first MTP)
PE: hot, red, tender joint, tophi
Lab results: needle-shaped crystal with negative birefringence, uric acid can be low, normal, or elevated
Treatment
Acute: NSAIDs, steroids, colchicine
Chronic: allopurinol (first line), febuxostat, probenecid
Can be triggered by loop and thiazide diuretics
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي الخيار A (Acute attack of gout) بناءً على المعطيات السريرية: In which setting is initiating allopurinol inappropriate in the treatment of gout.
الفخ: الخيار B (GFR stage G3a) قد يبدو مناسباً ظاهرياً لكنه لا يتوافق مع المعايير السريرية المطلوبة هنا.

question: A 16-year-old healthy boy presents to the ED for 6 weeks of progressive, dull, atraumatic pain just proximal to his right knee. Examination shows a full range of motion of the right knee without effusion, and there is a tender, palpable mass in the distal femur. X-ray is as shown above, and laboratory evaluation is significant for alkaline phosphatase of 225 U/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
englishExplanation:
This X-ray shows a destructive, sclerotic lesion with periosteal reaction and sunburst pattern, characteristic of osteosarcoma. This is the most common primary bone malignancy in adolescents, often affecting the metaphyseal region of long bones like the distal femur. This patient’s age, presentation with localized pain and mass, and elevated alkaline phosphatase all support this diagnosis.

Osteosarcoma is a primary malignant bone tumor with a bimodal age distribution. It most frequently affects adolescents between 16 and 18 years old during periods of rapid skeletal growth, and a second peak occurs in adults > 60 years old, often in the setting of predisposing conditions. Known risk factors include genetic syndromes such as hereditary retinoblastoma (RB1 gene mutation), Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53 mutation), Paget disease of bone, and prior exposure to ionizing radiation or alkylating chemotherapy.

The tumor most commonly arises in the metaphyseal regions of long bones, with the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus being the most frequent sites. Patients present with localized, progressively worsening bone pain that may be accompanied by swelling or a palpable, tender mass. Symptoms may develop gradually or be noticed following minor trauma. Despite the aggressive nature of the tumor, constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats are uncommon and may suggest alternative or advanced disease.

Initial evaluation should include plain radiographs, which often reveal classic findings such as a mixed lytic and sclerotic lesion with periosteal elevation, producing a characteristic sunburst or hair-on-end appearance due to aggressive periosteal bone formation. The Codman triangle, another radiographic feature, represents subperiosteal new bone formation at the tumor margin.

Laboratory findings may include elevated alkaline phosphatase and lactate dehydrogenase levels, both of which correlate with tumor burden and may have prognostic significance. Definitive diagnosis requires a biopsy, ideally performed after consultation with an orthopedic oncologist to prevent compromising future surgical margins. Staging with chest imaging (CT scan) and bone scintigraphy or PET scan is essential, as the lungs are the most common site of metastasis.

Treatment involves a multidisciplinary approach, typically starting with neoadjuvant chemotherapy to shrink the tumor and address micrometastatic disease, followed by wide surgical resection. Limb-salvage surgery is preferred over amputation when feasible. Postoperative (adjuvant) chemotherapy is administered to reduce the risk of recurrence and improve long-term survival, which varies depending on factors such as tumor size, location, response to chemotherapy, and metastatic status at diagnosis.



Chondroblastomas (A) are benign tumors of the cartilaginous epiphyseal plate. They affect a similar area, most commonly the distal femur and proximal tibia, but present with restricted range of motion due to epiphyseal involvement, and X-ray findings show a well-circumscribed lytic lesion without periosteal reaction. Treatment often involves surgery to eradicate joint obstruction.

Ewing sarcoma (B) is another malignant neoplasm of the diaphysis of long bones that presents with pain, fever, and a hard mass. It can be differentiated on X-ray with classic onion skinning of the periosteum. Treatment would be similar, with surgery and chemotherapy.

Osteomyelitis (C) is an infection of the bone, which would typically present with fever, acute-onset pain, and elevated white blood cell count. An X-ray may show cortical destruction in advanced disease. Treatment would require intravenous antibiotics and orthopedic evaluation.

One Step Further
Question:
What is appropriate empiric antibiotic treatment for osteomyelitis in a patient with sickle cell disease?

Reveal Answer:
Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone (or another third-generation cephalosporin) to cover increased risk of Salmonella infection.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Osteosarcoma

Most common malignant bone tumor
Typically occurs in individuals 10–20 years old or > 65 years old
Sx: pain, swelling that often awakens the patient at night
X-ray: Codman triangle, sunburst pattern
Most common location: long bone metaphyses

question: What treatment should be initiated for a patient who presents with a crush syndrome and rhabdomyolysis?
englishExplanation:
Patients with crush injuries and rhabdomyolysis should be aggressively resuscitated with intravenous fluids. Rhabdomyolysis is a life-threatening condition characterized by skeletal muscle breakdown and the release of intracellular contents into the circulatory system. Muscle damage leads to third spacing of fluid into muscles. Intravascular volume contraction from this sequestration, in turn, leads to acute kidney failure. In rhabdomyolysis, aggressive fluid resuscitation and volume expansion are critical to avoid myoglobin-induced acute kidney failure. Volume expansion results in increased blood flow to the kidneys and increased glomerular filtration. In turn, the kidneys excrete the toxins from cellular breakdown, including myoglobin, into the urine.



Acetazolamide (A) and furosemide (B) are diuretic agents that can increase urine output, but they also lead to further intravascular volume depletion.

Sodium bicarbonate (D) administration can be used in certain types of rhabdomyolysis (severe creatine kinase elevation or muscle injury) but does not take priority over fluid rehydration.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the classic urine finding in rhabdomyolysis?

Reveal Answer:
In rhabdomyolysis, the urine dipstick will be positive for blood, but there will be no (or few) red blood cells on microscopy.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Rhabdomyolysis

Risks: trauma, heat, alcohol or drugs, exercise
Dx: creatine kinase > 5 times the upper limit of normal
Lab tests
Urine: tea-colored, positive for blood, negative for RBCs, myoglobinuria
Hypocalcemia (most common), hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia
Immediate ECG
Tx: IVF, bicarbonate (select, severe cases)
Complications: DIC, acute kidney failure, compartment syndrome, hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia
Return to activity: afebrile, symptoms absent, heme-negative urine

question: A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department with knee pain. This morning he slipped on the ice and felt a pop in his knee. On physical exam, his left knee appears to have a moderate effusion with limited range of motion and medial joint line tenderness. An X-ray of the left knee is performed. A pedunculated, bony exostosis with well-defined margins is seen along the distal lateral femur on the anteroposterior view of the knee. What is the most likely diagnosis of the bone lesion?
englishExplanation:
An osteochondroma is a benign bone lesion. It is an outgrowth of the growth plate and is made up of bone and cartilage. It often develops in childhood or adolescence and grows larger over time until skeletal maturity is reached. Osteochondromas are the most common benign bone tumor. Many lesions are asymptomatic and incidentally found on radiographs. Some may present with a painless mass while others may develop mechanical symptoms, such as a catching sensation. On X-ray, osteochondromas appear as a sessile or pedunculated outgrowth along the surface of the bone. They are most often seen in the distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal femur, and proximal humerus. Treatment most often is observation. However, osteochondromas may be surgically resected if symptomatic.



Aneurysmal bone cyst (A) is a benign bone lesion seen on X-ray as an eccentric and lytic lesion most often in the spine or metaphysis of long bones.

Osteoid osteoma (C) is a benign bone lesion seen on X-ray as intensely reactive bone around a radiolucent nidus most often in the lower extremities.

Osteosarcoma (D) is a malignant bone lesion seen on X-ray as a lytic, destructive lesion, a heavily ossified and lobulated mass, or a blastic and destructive lesion depending on the subtype.

One Step Further
Question:
What part of the bone contains the growth plate?

Reveal Answer:
Metaphysis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Osteochondroma

Benign tumor found on external bone
Most often in children and adolescents
Found near end of long bones
Distal femur is most common site
Asymptomatic, so typically found incidentally on imaging
Monitor for symptoms and with serial imaging for changes

question: A 19-year-old man who is employed in construction presents with pain in his thumb and wrist for 4 months. He states the pain worsens while he is working. Examination reveals pain along the radial surface of the wrist with forced ulnar adduction. What initial management is indicated?

options.text: Corticosteroid injection into the first dorsal extensor compartment
Surgical release of the dorsal extensor compartment
Wrist X-ray with ulnar deviation view

englishExplanation:
De Quervain disease is a repetitive strain injury that is often work-related. In this disorder, the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons found in the first dorsal extensor compartment of the wrist are inflamed and enlarged. Patients commonly present with pain on the radial surface of the wrist, which is increased with movement of the thumb or ulnar deviation at the wrist. Patients may have decreased grip strength as well.

Finkelstein test is considered to be pathognomonic for de Quervain disease. It involves ulnar deviation of the wrist with the thumb in full flexion. This movement creates severe pain over the radial styloid. First-line treatment is with rest, splinting (thumb spica splint), and NSAIDs.



A corticosteroid injection into the first dorsal extensor compartment (A) may be offered by an orthopedic surgeon if conservative measures are not helpful in alleviating symptoms, but it would not be a recommended first-line treatment and would not be performed in the ED.

MRI of the wrist (B) is not necessary to diagnose de Quervain disease, but it is useful if a scaphoid fracture is suspected.

Surgical release of the dorsal extensor compartment (D) is indicated for patients with refractory symptoms.

Wrist X-rays with ulnar deviation (E) are not often indicated for patients with nontraumatic wrist pain but may be helpful in patients with trauma. Ulnar-deviated wrist X-rays are used to image the scaphoid.

One Step Further
Question:
What is intersection syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
An overuse tendinopathy manifesting with pain to the radial side of the wrist 4–8 cm proximal to the site of de Quervain disease.

Rapid Review
De Quervain Tendinopathy (Tenosynovitis)

Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons
Cause is generally unknown
May be associated with overuse or repetitive movements of the wrist or thumb
Pain along radial aspect of wrist and with abduction of thumb
PE: pain on ulnar wrist deviation while passively flexing the thumb to the palm (Finkelstein test)
Tx: thumb spica splint, NSAIDs, local glucocorticoid injections (severe symptoms)

question: Which of the following children is most likely to have Legg-Calvé-Perthes?

options.text: 11-year-old boy with 3 weeks of left knee pain with a tender prominence below the patella
14-year-old boy with 2 weeks of right thigh pain who favors external rotation during hip flexion
6-year-old girl with 1 month of limping and right knee pain without a history of trauma
8-year-old boy with an abnormal gait and unilateral limited hip abduction and internal rotation

correctAnswer: 8-year-old boy with an abnormal gait and unilateral limited hip abduction and internal rotation
englishExplanation:
Legg-Calvé-Perthes is a pediatric disease characterized by idiopathic avascular necrosis of one or both femoral heads. It most commonly occurs in prepubescent boys with a 4:1 incidence compared to girls. Ages tend to range from 4 to 10 years old. There are no specific risk factors known for the disease. The mainstay of diagnosis is a pelvic radiograph. Frog leg views are controversial as they may cause further injury in another pediatric femoral disease, slipped capital femoral syndrome, that presents very similarly to Legg-Calvé-Perthes. Normal radiographs do not preclude the diagnosis. Timely diagnosis and treatment equate to good functional outcomes.

Patients commonly present with an insidious onset of limping with hip, thigh, or knee pain. Examination may reveal limited hip abduction and internal rotation and, in severe cases, limb length discrepancies. Treatment is with immediate non-weight-bearing status on the affected limb or limbs and referral to a pediatric orthopedic surgeon. Most cases are nonsurgical.



Young girls with an insidious onset of prolonged limping with knee pain (C) may have Legg-Calvé-Perthes. However, boys greatly outnumber girls in terms of incidence (4:1). Thus, this patient is not the most likely of the answer choices to have Legg-Calvé-Perthes. Children with

knee pain and a tender prominence below the patella (A)are most likely to have Osgood-Schlatter disease. It is defined as apophysitis of the tibial tubercle and is more common in athletic or active children between 10 and 15 years old.

Puberty-aged boys with leg pain and obligate external rotation during hip flexion (B) most likely have slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). SCFE is more likely in puberty-aged boys who have overweight BMIs or have hypothyroidism. As with Legg-Calvé-Perthes, the diagnosis is with pelvic radiographs but will show femoral epiphyseal displacement and not avascular necrosis. Treatment is with surgical fixation.

One Step Further
Question:
Patients with advanced cases of untreated Legg-Calvé-Perthes may have what two physical exam findings?

Reveal Answer:
Limb shortening and proximal thigh atrophy.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Legg-Calvé-Perthes Disease

Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) of proximal femoral head or hip
Boys > girls, peak incidence 4–8 years of age
Symptoms: unilateral > bilateral, insidious onset, intermittent limp (worse after activity), hip, thigh, or knee pain
Associated with obesity, SGA, breech delivery, familial, glucocorticoid use, SLE
Dx: X-ray (can be normal during initial stages), MRI
Tx: casting, surgery

question:
A 29-year-old man, with no significant medical history but occasional alcohol and cocaine use, presents with acute onset bilateral flank pain that is worse on the left side. He also notes blood in his urine. Vital signs are BP 120/70 mm Hg, HR 85 bpm, RR 14/min, and T 98.2℉ (36.8ºC). His WBC count is 7,500/µL, creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL, and urinalysis is shown below:

Color: brown

Glucose: negative

Bilirubin: negative

Ketones: 40 mmol/L

Specific gravity: 1.017

Blood: 3+

pH: 5.5

Protein: 30 mg/dL

Leukocyte esterase: 1+

Nitrite: negative

RBC: 0–2/hpf (negative)

WBC: 3–10/hpf

Epithelial, squamous: 6–30/hpf

Bacteria: negative

What is the pathophysiology behind this patient's most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bacterial invasion of the bladder wall leading to hematuria
Disruption of the urothelium by a malignant mass causing bleeding
Inflammation of the glomerulus due to immune complex deposition
Obstruction of the ureter by a calcium oxalate stone causing hydronephrosis
Release of myoglobin from damaged skeletal muscle leading to acute kidney injury

correctAnswer: Release of myoglobin from damaged skeletal muscle leading to acute kidney injury
englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation and laboratory findings suggest rhabdomyolysis, a condition characterized by the breakdown of skeletal muscle tissue, releasing myoglobin and other intracellular contents into the bloodstream. The pathophysiology involves muscle injury—here likely triggered by cocaine use, which can cause vasoconstriction, ischemia, and direct toxicity to muscle fibers—leading to cell membrane disruption. Myoglobin, a heme-containing protein, is nephrotoxic and can precipitate in renal tubules, especially in acidic urine (pH 5.5 in this case), causing acute kidney injury (AKI). The urinalysis showing 3+ blood but only 0–2 RBC/hpf indicates the presence of heme pigment (myoglobin) rather than true hematuria, a classic finding in rhabdomyolysis. Elevated creatinine (1.3 mg/dL) further supports early AKI, and ketones may reflect dehydration or metabolic stress, common in this setting.

Risk factors for rhabdomyolysis include trauma, extreme exertion, drug use (e.g., cocaine, alcohol), seizures, and metabolic disturbances. Cocaine, as noted in this patient’s history, is a well-documented cause due to its sympathomimetic effects and potential to induce prolonged muscle contraction or ischemia. Symptoms typically include muscle pain (here, flank pain likely from paraspinal or abdominal wall muscle involvement), weakness, and dark urine (due to myoglobinuria, perceived as “blood” by the patient). Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) levels (not provided here but implied), and urinalysis findings.

Treatment focuses on aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline to prevent AKI by maintaining kidney perfusion and diluting myoglobin, targeting a urine output of 200–300 mL/hr. Urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate may be considered to reduce myoglobin precipitation, though evidence is lacking, and this therapy is generally no longer recommended except in exceptional circumstances. Monitoring for complications like hyperkalemia or hypocalcemia is critical.

Complications of rhabdomyolysis include AKI (up to 50% of cases), electrolyte imbalances (e.g., hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia), and disseminated intravascular coagulation from the release of prothrombotic substances. AKI results from direct tubular toxicity, obstruction by myoglobin casts, and hypoperfusion, with the patient’s creatinine elevation signaling early renal stress. If untreated, severe cases can progress to kidney failure requiring dialysis, compartment syndrome, or cardiac dysrhythmias from electrolyte shifts. In this case, the patient’s normal vital signs and modest creatinine rise suggest early detection, improving prognosis with prompt fluid therapy.



Bacterial invasion of the bladder wall leading to hematuria (A) suggests cystitis or urinary tract infection, which could cause hematuria and mild flank pain if ascending to pyelonephritis. However, the urinalysis shows no nitrites, minimal WBCs (3–10/hpf), and no bacteria, ruling out infection. The 3+ blood with scant RBCs points to myoglobinuria rather than bladder inflammation, and the cocaine history better aligns with rhabdomyolysis than a primary infectious process.

Disruption of the urothelium by a malignant mass causing bleeding (B) implies bladder or kidney cancer, which could cause hematuria and flank pain. However, the urinalysis shows a discrepancy between blood (3+) and RBCs (0–2/hpf), inconsistent with urothelial bleeding, which would produce visible RBCs. The patient’s young age (29) and lack of chronic symptoms or risk factors (e.g., smoking) make malignancy unlikely, and cocaine use is not a typical precipitant for cancer-related bleeding.

Inflammation of the glomerulus due to immune complex deposition (C) points to glomerulonephritis, which can present with hematuria and proteinuria. However, the urinalysis lacks significant RBCs (0–2/hpf) or red cell casts, hallmarks of glomerular bleeding, and shows only mild proteinuria (30 mg/dL), insufficient for nephritic syndrome. The patient’s history lacks systemic signs (e.g., rash, arthritis) or chronic conditions linked to immune-mediated disease, and cocaine is more directly tied to rhabdomyolysis than glomerulonephritis in this context.

Obstruction of the ureter by a calcium oxalate stone causing hydronephrosis (D) suggests nephrolithiasis, which can cause flank pain and hematuria. However, the urinalysis shows 3+ blood with only 0–2 RBC/hpf, inconsistent with true hematuria from a stone, which typically shows numerous RBCs. Additionally, cocaine use is not a direct risk factor for stones, and the absence of colicky pain or imaging findings (not provided but not implied) makes this unlikely. The pathophysiology of stones involves obstruction and irritation, not muscle breakdown or myoglobin release.

One Step Further
Question:
What class of medications is often associated with rhabdomyolysis?

Reveal Answer:
Lipid lowering medications (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Rhabdomyolysis

Risks: trauma, heat, alcohol or drugs, exercise
Dx: creatine kinase > 5 times the upper limit of normal
Lab tests
Urine: tea-colored, positive for blood, negative for RBCs, myoglobinuria
Hypocalcemia (most common), hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia
Immediate ECG
Tx: IVF, bicarbonate (select, severe cases)
Complications: DIC, acute kidney failure, compartment syndrome, hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia
Return to activity: afebrile, symptoms absent, heme-negative urine

الفخ: الخيار A (Bacterial invasion of the bladder wall leading to hematuria) قد يبدو مناسباً ظاهرياً لكنه لا يتوافق مع المعايير السريرية المطلوبة هنا.

question: A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency department with mild lower back pain and right heel and ankle pain for several days. He reports no trauma and does not report fever. He is healthy otherwise but does report that he had dysuria a few weeks ago. He did not seek medical care at that time as his symptoms improved after a few days. He reports no other preceding symptoms. On exam, he is well appearing. You note paraspinal muscular tenderness in the lumbar spinal area. His right heel has point tenderness over the insertion of the Achilles tendon, and he has mild pain with range of motion of the ankle. He has mild swelling but does not have any redness or warmth to the ankle. Testing for which organism is most likely to help with the diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with back and joint pain that could be muscular in nature but with swelling and pain in the ankle is more likely related to arthritis of some sort. He is young and healthy so a detailed history should be taken to evaluate for preceding causes of arthritis. In a well-appearing patient with arthritis, a history of preceding urethritis or enteritis should be sought after as both can lead to reactive arthritis, which is likely the presentation in this patient. Patients with reactive arthritis generally present a few weeks after the initial infection and frequently all symptoms of the previous infection have abated (abated dysuria in this patient). The genital pathogen that is most frequently associated with reactive arthritis is Chlamydia trachomatis. If patients have not already been tested for urethritis, they should undergo such testing. Treatment consists of treating the underlying infection and treating arthritis with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications.



Escherichia coli (B) is a frequent cause of enteritis and has been implicated in complications such as thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura but it is not frequently a cause of reactive arthritis. The clinician might consider that Escherichia coli could be the cause of a urinary tract infection leading to this patient’s dysuria. However, it has not been implicated in causing reactive arthritis.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae (C) is a cause of urethritis and can lead to disseminated gonococcal arthritis, but usually the presentation is different in that patients are ill appearing, frequently have fever and chills with a disseminated rash or lesions, and the arthritis is usually a polyarthralgia.

Salmonella (D) enteritis can lead to reactive arthritis along with several other enteric pathogens. However, this patient does not report a history of enteritis and it is not as common as reactive arthritis from C. trachomatis.

One Step Further
Question:
Which type of patients have a genetic predisposition for developing reactive arthritis?

Reveal Answer:
Those with HLA-B27 haplotype.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Reactive Arthritis

Risk factors: male sex, HLA-B27 positive, history of recent GI or Chlamydia infection
Sx: acute asymmetric arthritis
PE: conjunctivitis, arthritis, urethritis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum (lesions on palms and soles)
Lab results: may show positive stool cultures or Chlamydia NAAT
Tx: NSAIDs
Mnemonic: can’t see (conjunctivitis, uveitis), can’t pee (urethritis), can’t climb a tree (arthritis)

question: Which of the following is a risk factor for development of carpal tunnel syndrome?
englishExplanation:
Carpal tunnel syndrome, or median mononeuropathy, is the most common of all entrapment neuropathies. The median nerve arises from the brachial plexus with contributions from C6–T1 nerve roots. It passes through the carpal tunnel, which is formed by the transverse carpal ligament superiorly and the carpal bones inferiorly. The median nerve provides both motor and sensory innervation to the hand. Carpal tunnel syndrome develops when there is compression of the median nerve as it travels through the carpal tunnel. Compression can occur from a number of processes, including the presence of mass lesions, edema or inflammation, and fibrosis of the tissue that surrounds the tendons. Risk factors for development of carpal tunnel syndrome include obesity, female sex, and comorbid conditions such as diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis.

Sensory symptoms of pain and paresthesias predominate, although weakness may develop later in the course of disease. Symptoms may be bilateral, are often worse at night and are exacerbated by activities that involve flexing and extending the wrist. Pain and paresthesias are typically limited to the wrist and hand but may extend proximally to the forearm. The most sensitive finding is abnormal sensation of the distal palmar tip of the index finger. Normal sensation on the ulnar palmar side of the ring finger with abnormal sensation on the radial palmar side of the same finger is the most specific finding.



There is conflicting data regarding the association between advanced age (A) and smoking (D) and the development of carpal tunnel syndrome.

Despite the commonly held belief that prolonged computer use (C) increases the risk of carpal tunnel syndrome, this has not been shown to the be true in most studies.

One Step Further
Question:
What hand muscles are innervated by the median nerve?

Reveal Answer:
Abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, and the first and second lumbricals.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

Risk factors: repetitive hand and wrist use, female sex, obesity, pregnancy, hypothyroidism
Pain and numbness in the first, second, and third digits, especially at night
Caused by median nerve compression
PE
Phalen sign: reproduction of symptoms with wrist hyperflexion
Tinel sign: reproduction of symptoms with percussion over the carpal tunnel
Carpal compression test: reproduction of symptoms within 30 seconds of applying direct pressure to the carpal tunnel
Hand elevation test: reproduction of symptoms after raising hands above the head for 1 min
Tx: wrist splint in neutral position, glucocorticoid injection, oral glucocorticoids, surgical decompression
Classically associated with prolonged computer use
Recent studies show moderate-quality evidence that computer use was not associated with carpal tunnel syndrome
arabicExplanation:
ليش: الإجابة الصحيحة هي الخيار B (Female sex) بناءً على المعطيات السريرية: Which of the following is a risk factor for development of carpal tunnel syndrome.
الفخ: الخيار A (Advanced age) قد يبدو مناسباً ظاهرياً لكنه لا يتوافق مع المعايير السريرية المطلوبة هنا.

question: A previously healthy 10-month-old girl is identified as having a transverse fracture of the distal right tibia. During a review of the child’s electronic medical record, you note an orthopedic clinic visit at 7 months of age for a transverse fracture of the upper left humerus. Which additional history most strongly supports osteogenesis imperfecta in this patient?

options.text: History of a clavicle fracture at birth

englishExplanation:
Fracture is considered one of the most common signs of child abuse, occurring in over half of maltreated children. Distinguishing fractures due to child abuse from those associated with osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is a significant challenge for clinicians. Low-impact fractures with very minimal trauma remain the hallmark feature of OI. OI is an uncommon congenital disease, yet it is considered to be the most common inherited disorder that primarily involves bones.

There are four main types of OI (types I–IV), and they are based on clinical, radiological, and genetic features. The severity level for the various forms of OI ranges from mild to lethal. The main skeletal features of OI include bone fragility, osteopenia, and skeletal deformities, with growth delay and short stature. Extraskeletal manifestations include dental abnormalities (teeth are discolored, chip and wear easily), bluish discoloration of the sclera, laxity of the joints (hypermobility), laxity of the skin (easy bruising), and deafness, which is mainly due to a defect involving the ossicles of the middle ear.

Approximately 85% of OI cases are caused by pathogenic variants in genes encoding type 1 collagen (COL1A1/COL1A2). Most people with OI inherit the condition in an autosomal dominant form. However, gene defects may also arise sporadically. Given this pattern of inheritance, there is often a positive family history of fractures, short stature, and early-onset osteoporosis in extended family members. The involvement of genetic and orthopedic specialists is key to evaluating and testing individuals suspected of having OI.



Clavicle fractures (A) are the most common birth-related fracture in all infants. It is associated with a difficult vaginal delivery, shoulder dystocia, and increased birth weight.

When severe, OI can impair mobility due to pain, fractures, deformity, and muscle weakness, but developmental motor delay is nonspecific. Most children with OI do not have delayed gross motor milestones (B).

Children with OI usually have normal growth in mild forms or short stature in severe forms due to vertebral compression and scoliosis. A height > 95th percentile for age (C) suggests a diagnosis other than OI.

Widened wrists and bowed legs (E) is more commonly seen in skeletal dysplasias or rickets. Rickets results from impaired mineralization of bone and presents with widened wrists and ankles from metaphyseal widening. Bowed legs can be seen in both rickets and OI. Recurrent low-impact fractures are possible in children with rickets, but they are less predominant in rickets than in OI.

Reveal Answer:
Autosomal recessive.

question: A 5-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with difficulty ambulating. Her parent states that she has always been active, but over the past few months, she has had episodes in which she reports pain in her knees and refuses to go to school. Her symptoms generally improve as the day goes on, and she is able to play with schoolmates after school but often runs with a limp. A recent clinic visit showed that she was dropping off of her growth curve despite a nutritious diet and unremarkable basic metabolic panel and complete blood count with differential. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s symptoms of intermittent polyarthralgia, improvement in symptoms as the day progresses, and decreased weight gain are most consistent with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (formerly called juvenile rheumatoid arthritis). This rheumatologic disease usually affects children under the age of 7, more frequently girls. Children will have episodes of joint pain and swelling accompanied by malaise.

Oligoarticular arthritis (≤ 4 joints) involving the large joints is the most common presentation. Other subtypes include systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and polyarticular arthritis. Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis is diagnosed clinically and is typically a diagnosis of exclusion. Laboratory results depend on the specific type of arthritis. Patients are treated with anti-inflammatory drugs, steroid injections, and physical therapy. Refractory cases usually respond to disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs such as methotrexate.



Functional pain (A) and weight loss can be manifestations of stress in pediatric populations and could present as pain and unwillingness to take part in a certain activity. This patient’s continued limping despite enjoyable activity makes this less likely.

Lymphoblastic leukemia (C) can also present with weight loss and joint pain secondary to metaphyseal expansion from neoplastic lymphocytes. However, this patient’s unremarkable CBC with differential makes leukemia unlikely.

Osgood-Schlatter syndrome (D) also causes knee pain and swelling, but symptoms usually worsen as the day progresses. The syndrome is more common in boys and rarely affects girls below the age of 8.

One Step Further
Question:
What other screening should be done in children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis?

Reveal Answer:
Around 20% of children develop anterior uveitis and should be regularly screened with slit lamp exam.

Polyarticular: five or more joints
Oligoarticular: one to four joints, uveitis
Complications: joint damage, macrophage activation syndrome
Tx: NSAIDs, intra-articular corticosteroids, other DMARDs (methotrexate, TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6 antagonists)

question: A 25-year-old woman with a history of ulcerative colitis presents with progressive lower back pain over the past few months. She states that the pain is worse when getting up from a sitting position or first thing in the morning and improves with activity. She has not taken any medications to help with this pain. She reports no radiation of the pain, fevers or chills, weight loss, urinary incontinence, or urinary retention. Her exam is unremarkable except for tenderness at the bilateral sacroiliac joints. What is the best next step in management?

options.text: Obtain MRI of the lumbar spine

englishExplanation:
This patient presents with signs and symptoms consistent with sacroiliitis. Referral to physical therapy for instruction in back exercises, as well as NSAIDs, such as naproxen, are the initial management for this condition. This patient has a history of inflammatory bowel disease, which is associated with spondyloarthritis. It may also be associated with uveitis, psoriasis, synovitis, enthesitis, and dactylitis. Patients are often positive for the HLA-B27 gene. These patients should be referred back to their primary care clinician or rheumatologist as symptoms may be refractory to the initial treatment and may require different NSAIDs, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors, or local steroid injections.



An MRI of the lumbar spine (A) is not indicated, given the patient's presentation. Indications for emergent MRI of the lumbar spine include signs or symptoms consistent with cauda equina syndrome, spinal epidural abscess, spinal hematoma, or spinal cord injury.

Obtaining procalcitonin (B) is not indicated in this patient, as bacterial infection and sepsis are unlikely. Procalcitonin may be helpful in following the response in the treatment of sepsis. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are acute phase reactants that may be elevated in a patient with this presentation.

A prescription for infliximab (C) may be a step up in therapy if the patient does not respond to the initial treatment of NSAIDs and physical therapy followed by sulfasalazine or methotrexate. Infliximab is a TNF inhibitor. This medication would most likely be prescribed by a primary care clinician or rheumatologist.

One Step Further
Question:
What are the symptoms of reactive arthritis?

Reveal Answer:
Uveitis, urethritis or cervicitis, and arthritis, which can be recalled by the mnemonic “can’t see, can’t pee, can’t climb a tree.” This triad makes up only a small subset of those with reactive arthritis.

question: A 17-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after being struck in the arm by a baseball. On physical examination, he has ecchymosis and swelling over the right medial epicondyle. He is most likely to have decreased sensation of which of the following dermatomes?
englishExplanation:
Examination of the upper extremity is critical in patients with traumatic injuries in order to determine underlying pathology. Understanding the upper extremity dermatomes helps facilitate accurate diagnosis, management, and response to therapy. Sensation of the fifth (or little) finger and medial half of the fourth (or ring) finger assesses the C8 dermatome. Imaging may be needed to rule out an underlying fracture. Isolated medial epicondyle fractures usually occur in children and adolescents and often result from posterior elbow dislocations, repeated stress (e.g., throwing a baseball), or a direct blow. Examination findings include pain and swelling over the medial epicondyle and painful elbow flexion or forearm supination. Nondisplaced or minimally displaced medial epicondyle fractures are managed nonoperatively with early range of motion. Complications include ulnar nerve palsy and avascular necrosis.



Sensation of the tip of the third (or long) finger assesses the C7 (A) dermatome. This also grossly assesses the sensory function of the median nerve. The skin overlying the medial epicondyle is innervated by the T1 (or first thoracic) dermatome (C) and is part of the ulnar nerve but is not typically altered by injury at the medial epicondyle. The T2 (D) dermatomal distribution includes the medial upper arm from the anterior midline to the posterior midline, excluding the skin overlying the deltoid and axilla.

What two structures are involved in a Monteggia fracture-dislocation?

Reveal Answer:

question: A 53-year-old man presents with a report of numbness in his right hand for 4 months. He says he notices the numbness upon waking in the morning, but it gets better when he shakes his hands around. He indicates the numb areas are on the first, second, and third digits of his right hand. Which of the following tests is the most sensitive for detecting the underlying issue?

options.text: Downward pressure applied to the affected limb while at 90 degrees of abduction, 30 degrees of flexion, and thumb down
Flexion of thumb with pressure applied to the hand in an ulnar direction
Pressure applied over the transverse carpal ligament for 30 seconds
Repeated tapping of the space between the medial epicondyle and olecranon process, with the elbow of the affected limb flexed and the arm externally rotated

correctAnswer: Pressure applied over the transverse carpal ligament for 30 seconds
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with signs and symptoms consistent with carpal tunnel syndrome, which is the most common entrapment neuropathy of the wrist. It is caused by compression of the median nerve and is associated with numbness and weakness in its distribution. Patients typically present with numbness, pain, and paresthesia of the first three digits that is worse at night and with activity but improves when shaking their hands out.

Median nerve compression testing (Durkan test) consists of direct pressure applied to the median nerve at the carpal tunnel. Findings are positive if this maneuver reproduces the symptoms, and the test is 64% sensitive and 83% specific for the diagnosis. Another good clinical test is the hand elevation test, which has the best diagnostic accuracy compared to other provocative tests. The hand elevation test is performed by having the patient raise their hands above their head for 1 minute. The finding is positive if it reproduces the carpal tunnel syndrome symptoms.

Conservative treatment with wrist splinting and cortisone injections often relieves symptoms. Referral for orthopedic management is indicated in patients with recurrent or refractory symptoms.



The empty can test is a maneuver performed to evaluate supraspinatus integrity when a rotator cuff injury is suspected. It is performed by applying downward pressure to the affected limb while at 90 degrees of abduction, 30 degrees of flexion, and thumb down (A).

Flexion of the thumb with pressure applied to the hand in an ulnar direction (B) describes the Finkelstein test and is diagnostic of de Quervain tenosynovitis.

The Tinel sign is used to identify ulnar neuropathy by repeatedly tapping the space between the medial epicondyle and olecranon process, with the elbow of the affected limb flexed and the arm externally rotated (D).

One Step Further
Question:
When is emergent orthopedic consultation required for carpal tunnel syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
When acute onset of symptoms occurs over hours, suggesting the presence of acute median nerve compression from fracture or infection. This requires emergent decompression.

question: What is the most serious complication associated with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, particularly during the initiation of treatment?
englishExplanation:
The most serious complication of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), especially during early treatment, is macrophage activation syndrome (MAS). MAS is a potentially life-threatening condition characterized by excessive immune activation, leading to high fevers, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, coagulopathy, and markedly elevated ferritin levels. It can be triggered by JIA itself or by immunosuppressive therapy.

JIA is a chronic inflammatory condition that affects children < 16 years of age. One subtype, systemic JIA, presents with daily, high-spiking fevers for at least 2 weeks, arthritis involving multiple joints, and a characteristic erythematous, macular rash that appears on the trunk, palms, and soles. Additional systemic features may include hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, serositis (pleuritis or pericarditis), and fatigue.

Laboratory evaluation is often nonspecific and may show elevated inflammatory markers, anemia of chronic disease, and leukocytosis. The overlap of fever and joint pain can mimic septic arthritis, necessitating arthrocentesis to exclude infection. As a result, many of these patients are hospitalized for diagnostic evaluation, synovial fluid analysis, and initiation of treatment in consultation with a pediatric rheumatologist.

Treatment includes NSAIDs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs such as methotrexate, and biologic agents in refractory cases. Approximately 50% of patients go into remission, while the remainder may develop chronic, progressive joint disease with the risk of permanent joint damage and functional disability.

Severe complications include interstitial lung disease, pulmonary hypertension, and lipoid pneumonia. The most life-threatening complication is MAS, a form of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. MAS presents with spontaneous bruising or bleeding, hepatomegaly, elevated liver enzymes, cytopenias, neurologic symptoms (e.g., lethargy, seizures, coma), and shock. It can occur early in the disease or be triggered by infections or medications. High-dose glucocorticoids are the mainstay of MAS treatment, with additional immunosuppressive therapy required in severe or refractory cases.



Myeloproliferative disorder (B) is not commonly associated with JIA and is not a recognized complication of the disease or its treatment.

Sepsis (C) is a concern in patients who are immunosuppressed but is less directly linked to JIA than MAS and typically arises later or with more profound immunosuppression.

Widespread osteoporosis (D) can occur with long-term corticosteroid use but is a chronic complication, not an acute, serious, early threat like MAS.

One Step Further
Question:
What treatments, besides disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, have helped decrease the incidence of growth restriction and osteoporosis in patients with juvenile idiopathic arthritis?

Reveal Answer:
Recombinant growth hormone and vitamin supplementation, particularly with calcium.

question: A 12-year-old girl with a history of obesity presents to your ED with left thigh pain over the last 2 weeks causing her to limp. While stepping off a curb, the pain suddenly worsened, and she is now unable to walk. She reports no recent trauma, fevers, or other ill symptoms. Your exam shows a normal exam except for pain over her anterior left hip and decreased range of motion at the left hip. You obtain a complete blood count that is normal, as well as an anteroposterior view of the pelvis that shows a slight widening of the physis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Crutches with weight bearing as tolerated
Joint aspirate of the left hip

englishExplanation:
A slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is the most common adolescent hip disorder and is caused by a relatively weak proximal femur physis (i.e., growth plate) that cannot support the child's weight. It may slip slowly, presenting in an ambulatory patient with weeks of knee, thigh, or hip pain, acutely in a patient now unable to bear weight, or a combination of the two. Trauma can worsen an SCFE, causing an acute or chronic picture, but the trauma is typically minor for the degree of symptoms as seen in this patient. An anteroposterior view of the pelvis may show only mild widening or irregularity of the physis. A SCFE is best visualized with a frog-leg view of the pelvis, which shows displacement of the femoral epiphysis, often described as the image of ice cream falling off a cone. If you are concerned about an associated pelvic fracture, obtain a cross-table lateral image instead, which can show the posterior displacement. These patients should be kept non-weight bearing and admitted for surgical pinning by orthopedic surgeons.



A patient with an SCFE should not be allowed to bear weight so sending the patient home with crutches with weight bearing as tolerated (A) can worsen the slip.

A joint aspirate of the left hip (C) is appropriate when ruling out a septic joint but is less likely than an SCFE in this patient based on the lack of fever and normal complete blood count.

An MRI of the pelvis (D) is useful if you suspect osteomyelitis and would make the diagnosis, but it is unnecessary in this patient as the presentation is more consistent with SCFE.

One Step Further

What is the most common complication of slipped capital femoral epiphysis that is reduced with surgical pinning?

Reveal Answer:
Avascular necrosis.

question: A 48-year-old woman presents to the ED with progressive neck pain over the last 6 weeks. The pain radiates down her posterior arm to the dorsum of her forearm. She reports numbness and tingling of the forearm and third digit. On examination, she has mild weakness with pronation of the forearm and decreased triceps reflex. What is the likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
The distribution of symptoms (posterior arm and forearm radiation, numbness of the third digit, triceps reflex reduction, and pronation weakness) is characteristic of C7 radiculopathy. C7 innervates the triceps and contributes to wrist extension and finger extension. Involvement of the third digit is highly suggestive of C7 nerve root compression.

Cervical radiculopathy refers to a constellation of neurologic symptoms, most notably pain, sensory disturbance, and motor weakness, resulting from compression or irritation of one or more cervical nerve roots. This condition most frequently arises from intervertebral disc herniation, degenerative spondylotic changes, or a combination of the two. Less common causes include foraminal stenosis, facet joint osteophytes, trauma, and space-occupying lesions such as tumors or abscesses.

The cervical nerve roots exit the spinal canal through the intervertebral foramina above their corresponding vertebral bodies (e.g., the C7 nerve root exits between the C6 and C7 vertebrae). Posterolateral disc herniation is the most common anatomical cause of root compression and typically occurs at the C5–C6 and C6–C7 levels. These herniations can result in both axial neck pain and referred or radicular pain, sometimes accompanied by occipital headache due to upper cervical involvement.

The C7 nerve root is the most commonly involved and characteristically produces radiating pain from the neck through the posterior arm and forearm to the dorsum of the hand and third digit. Patients may also report discomfort along the medial border of the scapula, reflecting referred pain from the affected nerve root. Sensory deficits typically involve the dorsum of the forearm and the middle finger. Motor findings include weakness in forearm extension and pronation, due to involvement of the triceps and wrist flexors. A diminished or absent triceps reflex is a hallmark physical examination finding.

Evaluation begins with a thorough neurologic examination, focusing on sensory mapping, myotomal strength testing, and deep tendon reflexes. While plain radiographs may show degenerative changes or reduced disc height, MRI is the diagnostic modality of choice due to its superior ability to visualize soft tissues, including nerve roots, intervertebral discs, and spinal cord.

Most cases of cervical radiculopathy are self-limited and improve over weeks to months with conservative treatment, including physical therapy, NSAIDs, and activity modification. Corticosteroids, either systemic or via epidural injection, may be used for more severe symptoms. Surgical intervention (e.g., anterior cervical discectomy and fusion) is reserved for patients with intractable pain, progressive neurologic deficits, or spinal cord compression.



C5 radiculopathy (A) would affect the deltoid and biceps, leading to shoulder pain and decreased biceps reflex, not triceps weakness or third digit symptoms.

C6 radiculopathy (B) presents with pain radiating to the lateral forearm and thumb, with biceps and brachioradialis reflex involvement.

C8 radiculopathy (D) affects the medial forearm and fourth and fifth digits, often impairing finger flexion and grip but not pronation or third-digit sensation.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the Lhermitte phenomenon?

Reveal Answer:
A transient, electric shock-like sensation that radiates down the spine and often into the limbs, typically triggered by flexion of the neck, most commonly associated with cervical spinal cord lesions, including multiple sclerosis, cervical spondylosis, radiation myelopathy, vitamin B12 deficiency, and cervical tumors.

question: A 22-year-old man presents with chronic back pain. He notes it has gone on for his whole life and is the most severe in the morning. As he exerts himself or lifts boxes at his job, he notes his symptoms improve. Physical exam reveals reduced mobility in all directions of the spine with no midline tenderness. An erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 35 mm/hr. A radiograph is performed, and the results are shown above. The patient is requesting a work note for a month off from work. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a rheumatologic cause of back pain more common in young men. It classically presents with back pain and stiffness that is worse in the morning and relieved with exertion and exercise. AS may also affect peripheral joints and other areas, including the eyes (uveitis), heart, lungs, and kidneys. Patients will have reduced mobility of the spine. Initial diagnostic workup may include plain films of the lumbar spine (demonstrating a bamboo spine) or sacroiliac joint (demonstrating sacroiliitis). The most accurate diagnostic test is an MRI of the sacroiliac spine. Human leukocyte antigen B27 testing can also support the diagnosis. Inflammatory markers can be elevated in AS. Treatment is centered on exercise and physical therapy. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, acetaminophen, and immunomodulators, such as infliximab, adalimumab, and etanercept, can be used to control symptoms.



Malingering (B) should be suspected when a patient has concerns that do not line up with the exam or normal physiology and the patient is seeking secondary gain. While this patient is requesting a work note (secondary gain), his reduced spinal mobility and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate suggest against this diagnosis.

A muscle strain (C) is the most common cause of back pain after heavy lifting and is worsened by lifting, bending, and twisting. There may be palpable tenderness over the muscles. This patient’s symptoms improve with lifting rather than worsen.

Spinal epidural abscess (D) is a life-threatening cause of back pain that is more common in immunosuppressed patients and patients who use intravenous drugs. Patients will present with back pain, malaise, and fever and will have elevated inflammatory markers. While this patient’s erythrocyte sedimentation rate is elevated, his other symptoms suggest a diagnosis of AS, and he lacks risk factors for spinal epidural abscess.

Reveal Answer:

question: A patient presents to the emergency department for a painful, swollen finger. Which of the following features, if present, would be most consistent with a diagnosis of flexor tenosynovitis?

options.text: Localized swelling along the flexor tendon
Pain on passive extension of the affected finger
Percussion tenderness isolated to the distal phalanx

correctAnswer: Pain on passive extension of the affected finger
englishExplanation:
Flexor tenosynovitis is a surgical emergency that requires rapid bedside diagnosis to expedite appropriate care. Penetrating trauma precedes most cases, although the injury itself may have been innocuous, leading to bacterial seeding of the deep tendon sheath. Skin flora, such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus spp, are most commonly identified. On examination, Kanavel signs may be identified that can help with the diagnosis of flexor tenosynovitis: pain on passive extension of the affected finger (often the first finding), finger held in partial flexion, tenderness of the full tendon sheath, and fusiform swelling of the digit. These findings are due to progressive inflammation of the tendon sheath. Kanavel signs have a sensitivity of approximately 90% in the diagnosis of flexor tenosynovitis. Patients with findings concerning for this diagnosis should rapidly be treated with intravenous antibiotics such as vancomycin plus extended-spectrum penicillins. They should have emergent hand surgery consultation, as this infection can rapidly spread through the fascial planes of the hand. Inappropriate management of flexor tenosynovitis can lead to loss of function in the affected hand.



Fingers are typically held in partial flexion rather than full extension (A) in flexor tenosynovitis.

Fusiform or symmetric swelling, rather than localized swelling (B), would be seen in flexor tenosynovitis.

Percussive tenderness will involve the full length of the digit and tendon sheath and will not be isolated to the distal phalanx (D).

One Step Further
Question:
Which antibiotic is recommended for the acute treatment of closed fist injuries (fight bite) of the hand?

Reveal Answer:
Amoxicillin-clavulanate.

Rapid Review

History of penetrating trauma (most common)
Most commonly caused by S. aureus infection
Dx: Kanavel criteria
Tenderness along the flexor tendon
Fusiform or symmetrical swelling of the finger
Pain with extension
Flexed posture of the finger
Tx: IV antibiotics, surgical emergency

question: A 15-year-old boy presents with 2 days of finger pain and swelling after pulling off a hangnail. The pain has progressed and he is having difficulty performing simple tasks. The finger is shown above. On exam, there is tenderness of the distal phalanx with a small area of fluctuance. He is able to articulate the finger at both the metacarpal and interphalangeal joints with no significant discomfort. He reports no fevers, nausea, nor diarrhea. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this condition?

options.text: Surgical washout of the tendon sheath

englishExplanation:
This patient presents with paronychia, a soft tissue infection of the fingernail. Paronychia is the most common hand infection in the United States and begins as cellulitis of the paronychium but can progress to an abscess of the deeper structures, which necessitates incision and drainage. The most typical causative organism is Staphylococcus aureus. Risk factors include finger trauma such as nail biting, manicure, or forcibly removing hangnails. Diagnosis is made with clinical exam. When paronychia involves abscess, the purulent material should be drained to facilitate healing. Untreated infections can spread to deeper structures such as the pulp (felon) or the flexor tendon (flexor tenosynovitis).



Antibiotics (B), either oral or topical, are often used in the treatment of paronychia. In simple cases of isolated cellulitis, antibiotics are sufficient. However, progression to abscess requires drainage as the first step in management.

Warm compresses (D) and soaks are the traditional treatment for mild paronychia limited to cellulitis. However, there is little evidence to support their efficacy.

Surgical washout of the tendon sheath (C) is indicated for flexor tenosynovitis, which also presents with finger swelling and pain. However, this patient’s symptoms are localized to the distal finger and he does not have pain with range of motion of the digit or along the flexor tendon.

One Step Further
Question:
How does the presentation of paronychia contrast the presentation of felon?

Reveal Answer:
Paronychia usually begins dorsally and laterally whereas felon begins on the volar surface and has a more severe presentation.

Acute
Bacterial infection around nail folds
Most commonly caused by S. aureus
PE: redness, tenderness, and purulence of lateral nail fold
Tx: antibiotics, warm soaks, I&D often needed
Chronic
Inflammatory disorder of the nail folds
PE: redness, tenderness, and swelling > 6 weeks
Tx: corticosteroids ± antifungals

question: Which of the following symptoms is most consistent with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis?
englishExplanation:
Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) is characterized by fever, arthritis, and rash occurring in children up to 16 years of age. All sexes are affected equally. The fever, present in > 95% of patients, is described as quotidian (one high spike of fever per day followed by normal temperatures for the rest of the day). Constantly elevated temperatures should prompt investigation for an alternative diagnosis. Arthritis typically affects more than one joint. While the wrist, knees, and ankles are most commonly affected, any joint can be involved. An erythematous, macular rash is also commonly seen and is most noticeable when the child is febrile. Although not diagnostic of sJIA, patients will often have leukocytosis, reactive thrombocytosis, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Diagnosis can only be made after excluding other etiologies of the patient’s symptoms (e.g., septic arthritis). Fever must be present for > 2 weeks and arthritis for > 6 weeks before a definitive diagnosis can be made.



Lymphadenopathy (B) can be seen in sJIA but is only present in one-third of patients.

The arthritis is polyarticular or oligoarticular in the vast majority of patients. Monoarthritis (C) is much less commonly seen.

The classic rash in sJIA is a faint, erythematous macular rash which is typically present when the patient is febrile and recedes when the patient has defervesced. A purpuric rash (D) is not characteristic of sJIA.

One Step Further
Question:
What organism is most commonly implicated in septic arthritis?

Reveal Answer:
Staphylococcus aureus.

Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (Formerly Juvenile Rheumatoid Arthritis)

Autoinflammatory disorder
Dx (of exclusion): persistent, unexplained arthritis in one or more joints for ≥ 6 weeks in children < 16 years old
Clinical types
Systemic JIA: fever (quotidian pattern) ≥ 2 weeks, LAD, arthritis, rash (salmon colored on lighter skin and erythematous or hyperpigmented on darker skin, transient with fever)
Polyarticular: five or more joints
Oligoarticular: one to four joints, uveitis
Complications: joint damage, macrophage activation syndrome
Tx: NSAIDs, intra-articular corticosteroids, other DMARDs (methotrexate, TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6 antagonists)

question: A 12-year-old boy with a history of obesity presents with groin and proximal anterior thigh pain. He has no pain below the knee. Physical examination shows a significant decrease in internal rotation of the affected hip. Radiographs show a widened growth plate. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Atraumatic pediatric hip pain or limp is usually caused by acute transient synovitis, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, or slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). SCFE is a fracture in the physis (growth plate) of the femoral head, which leads to slippage of the overlying epiphysis. It usually occurs during adolescent growth spurts. Predisposing factors include male sex, obesity, and increased sports activities. The typical age range is 10–14 years for girls and 11–16 years for boys.

Patients present with pain in the anterior proximal knee or thigh that is exacerbated by activity. On exam, there is a loss of hip internal rotation, particularly with the hip flexed. Patients typically walk with the involved extremity externally rotated. Anteroposterior and frog-leg radiographs show “ice cream falling off the cone.” All cases warrant urgent orthopedic evaluation for stabilization surgery. Patients should be non-weight-bearing and restricted to bed rest until then. Complications of untreated disease include chondrolysis and osteonecrosis.



Acute transient synovitis (A) is considered the most common cause of childhood hip pain or limp. It is most common in boys aged 3–6 years. Radiographs are normal. Treatment includes NSAIDs and relative rest.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (B) is a group of arthritic conditions affecting children, which typically presents with joint swelling and pain over a longer duration and does not involve widening of growth plates.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (C) is avascular osteonecrosis of the femoral head. It occurs more commonly in boys aged 4–10 years. Radiographs show a small, sclerosed femoral head and widened joint space.

Osgood-Schlatter disease (D) is a common adolescent condition in those active in sports. Repeated microtrauma occurs at the apophyseal cartilage between the anterior tibial tubercle and the secondary ossification center of the patellar tendon. These patients present with anteroinferior knee or superior shin pain and tender tibial tuberosities.

One Step Further
Question:
Which endocrinopathies predispose adolescents to slipped capital femoral epiphysis?

Reveal Answer:
Hypothyroidism and growth hormone deficiency.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE)

Male adolescents 12–16 years old with obesity
Displacement of the capital femoral epiphysis from the femoral neck through the physeal plate
Clinical: progressive limp and hip or knee pain
PE: loss of hip internal rotation and flexion
Dx: X-ray will show apparent posterior displacement of the femoral epiphysis (scoop of ice cream slipping off cone)
Tx: non-weight-bearing and urgent orthopedic consultation, surgical fixation
