question: Which of the following structures runs through Guyon canal?
englishExplanation:
The Guyon canal (or Guyon tunnel) is the tubular fibromusculofascial space through which the ulnar nerve travels as it enters the wrist. It is anatomically separate from the carpal tunnel through which the median nerve and several flexor tendons traverse. The ulnar and radial walls of the Guyon canal are formed by the pisiform bone and fibers from the volar carpal ligament, respectively. The roof consists of a thick fascial layer that is continuous with the hypothenar and palmaris brevis fascia. This fascia is not unyielding, and the contents within the canal are subject to compression from various causes.

Repetitive trauma such as cycling, golf, baseball, or pounding objects with the palm of the hand can lead to numbness or tingling in the ulnar aspects of the fourth digit, the fifth digit, and the ulnar aspect of the palm of the hand. This is likely due to swelling and subsequent hypertrophy of the tissues around the tunnel or from fibrosis or bleeding within the tunnel. Other causes of compression include displaced bone, tumors, or ganglion cysts (as may occur in the carpal tunnel).

Treatment involves splinting the hand to immobilize it and orthopedic referral for nonemergent surgical decompression.



The axillary nerve (A) supplies motor innervation to the deltoid and teres minor muscles. Compression due to hypertrophy of the bordering muscles of the axillary nerve commonly presents as shoulder pain and paresthesias.

The recurrent branch of the median nerve (B) is a motor branch that innervates the thenar muscles. Injury to this nerve can cause loss of function of the thumb and is sometimes referred to as the million dollar nerve because of the likelihood of high litigation if injured during carpal tunnel surgery.

The superficial branch of the radial nerve (C) crosses the anatomic snuffbox on the dorsum of the wrist and supplies sensation to the skin over the radial two-thirds of the dorsum of the hand, dorsum of the thumb, and dorsum of the index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger proximal to the distal interphalangeal joint.

question: Which muscle attachment is inflamed in lateral epicondylitis?
englishExplanation:
Lateral epicondylitis, commonly referred to as tennis elbow, is an inflammatory condition involving the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. The lateral epicondyle is the site of origin for the wrist and digit extensors and the forearm supinators. Muscles that originate at the lateral epicondyle include the extensor carpi radialis brevis, extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, and extensor carpi ulnaris. Lateral epicondylitis is often the result of repetitive supination of the forearm.

Patients present with focal tenderness over the lateral epicondyle, proximal wrist extensor muscle mass pain with resisted wrist extension and the elbow in full extension, and pain with passive wrist flexion with the elbow in full extension. Treatment includes NSAIDs and activity modification. A counterforce brace placed distal to the elbow and physical therapy are often helpful.



The abductor pollicis longus (A) and extensor pollicis brevis tendons are found in the first dorsal extensor compartment of the wrist and become inflamed in patients with de Quervain tenosynovitis. Patients commonly present with pain on the radial surface of the wrist, which is increased with movement of the thumb or ulnar deviation at the wrist. It is diagnosed clinically. The Finkelstein test involves ulnar deviation of the wrist with the thumb in full flexion and is most often positive in patients with de Quervain tenosynovitis. First-line treatment is with rest, splinting (thumb spica splint), and NSAIDs.

The flexor carpi radialis (C) and the pronator teres (D) both originate at the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Medial epicondylitis, which may also be referred to as golfer’s elbow, presents with focal tenderness over the medial epicondyle, proximal wrist flexor muscle mass pain with resisted wrist flexion and with the elbow in full extension, and pain with passive terminal wrist extension and with the elbow in full extension.

The triceps (E) tendon inserts on the olecranon. Triceps tendinopathy will present with pain and tenderness of the posterior elbow that is worse with extension of the forearm.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
The ulnar (medial) collateral ligament.

Tx: bracing, NSAIDs, avoid overuse activities

question: Which of the following is a characteristic of pseudogout?

options.text: Metatarsophalangeal joint is most commonly affected

englishExplanation:
Pseudogout, also known as acute calcium pyrophosphate (CPP) crystal arthritis, typically presents with acute monoarticular or oligoarticular joint pain, swelling, warmth, and limited range of motion, most commonly involving the knee or wrist. Systemic symptoms such as fever and leukocytosis may be present, particularly in older adults, and the presentation can closely mimic septic arthritis or gout, making diagnostic evaluation essential.

The definitive diagnosis of pseudogout is made by identifying CPP crystals in synovial fluid using compensated polarized light microscopy. CPP crystals are characteristically rhomboid-shaped and exhibit weak positive birefringence. Under polarized light with a red compensator, CPP crystals appear blue when aligned parallel to the polarizer axis and yellow when perpendicular, which is the opposite pattern seen in monosodium urate crystals in gout, which demonstrate strong negative birefringence.

Treatment in the ED is primarily supportive and aimed at reducing inflammation and pain once septic arthritis has been excluded. First-line treatments include NSAIDs, colchicine, or systemic or intra-articular corticosteroids, with therapy selection guided by patient age, kidney function, and comorbidities.

Long-term treatment focuses on controlling recurrent flares and addressing associated metabolic conditions such as hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, or hypomagnesemia.



Crystals (A) are present in pseudogout.

The metatarsophalangeal (B) joint is most commonly affected in acute gout. In pseudogout, the knee is most commonly affected, followed by the wrist.

Uric acid (monosodium urate) crystals (D) are needle-shaped with negative birefringence and cause gout, not pseudogout.

One Step Further
Question:
What are other crystal arthropathies besides calcium pyrophosphate?

Reveal Answer:
Calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) deposition disease, calcium oxalate arthropathy, cholesterol crystal arthropathy, and cystine crystal deposition.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pseudogout

Mono- or oligoarticular arthritis caused by deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals
Lab results: rhomboid-shaped crystals, weakly positive birefringence
X-ray: chondrocalcinosis
Tx options: intra-articular steroid injection (one or two joints), NSAIDs, colchicine, systemic corticosteroids
Notes: associated conditions include hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesemia, and hypophosphatemia

question: Developmental dysplasia of the hip in patients under the age of 6 months is primarily based on physical examination findings in the absence of recent trauma to the hip or knee areas. What two diagnostic physical maneuvers are considered to be strongly suggestive of developmental hip dysplasia?
englishExplanation:
Developmental dysplasia of the hip is unlikely to be the primary cause for an ED visit for an infant < 6 months of age since most related symptoms occur after the child starts to bear weight and walk. Before 6 months, parents may be aware of the possible abnormality due to routine screening by primary care clinicians. They may have only been told that there is a “click,” a “clunk,” or a “loose joint” in the hip that will require monitoring. Parents may notice that the child’s legs appear asymmetrical in their range of active or passive hip motion or one leg appears shorter than the other. When the dysplasia involves both hips, diagnosis may be more difficult because the asymmetry may be very subtle. Restricted internal rotation of the hip is the most sensitive sign of pediatric hip pathology but is not specific to developmental dysplasia of the hip. Another sensitive but not specific marker is skinfold asymmetry in the groin, below the buttock, and along the thighs.

The findings of the Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers are considered to be cornerstones of the diagnosis in this age group, but they become less reliable as the child ages. The Ortolani maneuver includes stabilizing the pelvis with one hand while the other hand slightly abducts the hip, then placing the index and long fingers over the greater trochanter and gently pulling up on the thigh, simulating a maneuver that would reduce a dislocated hip. The presence of a click or clunk during the maneuver is abnormal. The Barlow maneuver attempts to identify a lax or loose hip joint that could be prone to dislocation. It involves stabilizing the pelvis with one hand while placing the thumb of the other hand over the lesser trochanter of the hip on the inner aspect of the thigh. The thumb then exerts downward pressure on the thigh, pushing it to the table. Any abnormal movement between the femoral head and the acetabulum is significant. Both maneuvers can be difficult to perform well or to interpret without significant experience. Therefore, if the child has not been actively screened for developmental dysplasia, the presence of asymmetry in range of motion, leg length, or skinfolds should cause the emergency physician to refer the patient to their primary care clinician within several weeks for further evaluation.



Essex-Lopresti and Monteggia (A) are two types of forearm fractures.

Romberg and Thessaly (C) is also incorrect. The Romberg test is used to evaluate the cerebellum and vestibular system, while the Thessaly test is a very sensitive and specific test for meniscus tears of the knee.

Tinel and Phalen (D) tests are used for the evaluation of carpal tunnel syndrome.

One Step Further

What are the known risk factors for developmental dysplasia of the hip?

Reveal Answer:

question: A 14-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a painful and swollen great toe. This is his third visit to the ED for the same concern. He has tried placing a cotton wedge and using dental floss to raise the nail after soaking his foot in warm water several times per day for the last 2 weeks without improvement. There is granulation tissue with mild erythema but no drainage or abscess formation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
englishExplanation:
Onychocryptosis (ingrown toenail) is a common occurrence in which the edge of the nail plate penetrates into the skin along the nail fold. This most often occurs in patients with poorly fitting shoes, who have nail trauma or a pincer nail deformity, or who excessively trim the lateral portion of their nail.

Mild cases of onychocryptosis involve minimal redness and only mild to moderate pain and can be treated conservatively with a cotton wedge under the nail fold. This should be done three times per day after soaking the affected foot in warm, soapy water for 10–20 minutes. There are other methods described, including using dental floss, toe taping, and nail bracing, with the ultimate goal of relieving pressure by pulling the nail fold away from the nail.

Severe cases often have significant erythema and even purulent discharge, not typically from infection but from the inflammatory response to the nail, which acts like a dermal foreign body. When conservative measures fail, partial nail or spicule removal is accomplished using a digital block and nail clippers or scissors along the affected edge, removing the lateral portion. Conservative measures are preferred, as nail removal can result in abnormal nail regrowth with repeat spicule formation. The patient should also be referred to podiatry for further care.



A foot X-ray (A) will evaluate for a foreign object which is appropriate in cases of a felon but not necessary for patients with onychocryptosis.

An ingrown nail can lead to paronychia, which would be diagnosed if a collection of pus was evident. The treatment for paronychia is incision and drainage (B). In the case of an ingrown toenail, which commonly occurs on the lateral edge of the great toe, this will not treat the underlying cause of inflammation: the nail acting as a foreign object.

Antibiotic coverage such as oral cephalexin (C) is often prescribed but has not been shown to change outcomes in patients with onychocryptosis.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
Topical antibiotics and warm water soaks.

question: A 47-year-old man with hypertension presents to the ED with persistent right eye pain and swelling after finishing antibiotics for an eye infection. His eye hurts when moved. He has right periorbital edema and erythema, pain on lateral gaze, a dilated nonreactive right pupil, and intraocular pressures of 42 mm Hg (right eye) and 12 mm Hg (left eye). Visual acuity is shadows (right eye) and 20/40 (left eye). What is the best next step in treatment?
englishExplanation:
An emergent lateral canthotomy is indicated as this patient has elevated intraocular pressures and evidence of optic neuropathy. When acute orbital compartment syndrome is suspected, no further testing or treatments should delay immediate lateral canthotomy. Retrobulbar hematomas, either from surgery or direct ocular trauma, are the most common cause of acute orbital compartment syndrome. However, orbital cellulitis, orbital emphysema, and tumors are possible etiologies. In this case, the patient most likely has postseptal cellulitis leading to compartment syndrome of his left eye.

The most common physical exam findings of acute orbital compartment syndrome include acute unilateral optic neuropathy with evidence of changes in visual acuity and abnormal pupillary reflexes, limited extraocular movements, elevated intraocular pressures (typically > 30–40 mm Hg), or any combination of the above.



While an emergent ophthalmologic consult (B) should occur immediately, this consult should not delay the procedure and can be called by an extra team member. As noted above, no further imaging or treatments, such as an orbital computed tomography scan (C) or parenteral antibiotics (D), should delay a lateral canthotomy.

What diagnosis is consistent with a pale retina and “cherry red spot” on eye exam?

Reveal Answer:

question: A 21-year-old woman presents with left shoulder pain and limited range of motion. Her examination reveals the left arm to be completely abducted with the elbow flexed and the hand behind her head. Which of the following maneuvers will bring therapeutic relief?
englishExplanation:
Luxatio erecta is an inferior glenohumeral (shoulder) dislocation. The mechanism of this injury is extreme abduction that is sometimes accompanied by downward force on the humeral head, causing it to break through the weak inferior glenoid rim. The arm is then positioned in full abduction with elbow flexion and the hand is held behind or on top of the patient’s head. The humeral head may be palpable in the lateral chest wall. Reduction is usually successful with upward (cephalad) axial traction in line with the humerus, along with countertraction. An audible clunk signifies successful reduction. The arm is then immobilized at the patient’s side. This type of shoulder dislocation is rare and often associated with significant soft tissue trauma or fractures of the proximal humerus. Concomitant rotator cuff injuries are also common. Operative management may be required if the dislocation is irreducible. For successful reductions, orthopedic follow-up is needed.



Abduction and internal rotation (A) only recreates the mechanism of injury and will not reduce luxatio erecta.

Downward (caudal) axial traction (B) is not feasible, as the arm is fixed in abduction and will not be successful in reduction.

Hyperpronation (C) is a method of reducing radial head subluxation (pulled elbow) seen in pediatric patients.

question: A 16-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a painful finger that was accidentally slammed in a car door. On exam, he has tenderness, swelling, and bruising under his right second fingernail. Which of the following is an indication for nail trephination?

options.text: Nonpainful subungual hematoma with intact nail folds that was noticed 3 days ago
Painful subungual hematoma with a loose nail fold on the right side from an injury yesterday
Painful subungual hematoma with intact nail folds from an injury 5 days ago
Painful subungual hematoma with intact nail folds from an injury yesterday

correctAnswer: Painful subungual hematoma with intact nail folds from an injury yesterday
englishExplanation:
Subungual hematoma is a common injury, particularly in children. It is defined as blood under the fingernail or toenail. It is a traumatic injury caused by a blow to the nail. Patients typically report throbbing pain, and they will have a black discoloration under the nail. Pain can be relieved with nail trephination. Nail trephination is indicated for any subungual hematoma that is < 48 hours old, is not spontaneously draining, shows blood trapped under the nail with intact nail folds, and is painful. Subungual hematomas associated with fractures, extensive nail bed injury, or infection should be referred for specialty evaluation.

Nail trephination can be performed with an electrocautery device, an 18-gauge needle, or a mesoscission device. Using electrocautery, the clinician simply punctures the nail in the center of the hematoma while avoiding the lunula and the nail matrix. When using an 18-gauge needle, the clinician should twirl the needle while applying gentle pressure until blood is expressed. The mesoscission device bores multiple holes in the nail over the hematoma. Alternatively, a 29-gauge insulin syringe could be advanced proximally and parallel to the nail plate, just underneath the nail, while applying gentle suction on the syringe until the hematoma is drained. Most patients receive immediate relief from the pain after nail trephination, and there are few complications from the procedure.

Nonpainful subungual hematoma with intact nail folds that was noticed 3 days ago (A) suggests a different condition that has a similar appearance to a subungual hematoma. A painless lesion is usually not blood but a subungual melanoma, junctional nevus, or subungual epithelioma. Nail trephination should not be performed on these lesions.

A painful subungual hematoma with a loose nail fold on the right side from an injury yesterday (B) will not benefit from nail trephination because the loose nail fold already allows drainage of the blood.

Trephination of a painful subungual hematoma with intact nail folds from an injury 5 days ago (C) also has the potential to fail because, after 5 days, the hematoma is most likely already clotted, and trephination will not be effective.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
False.

question: Which of the following is the greatest risk factor for the development of contrast-associated acute kidney injury?

options.text: Exposure to contrast more than once in 48 hours

englishExplanation:
The greatest risk factor for the development of contrast-associated acute kidney injury (CA-AKI) is preexisting kidney insufficiency, with patients having a serum creatinine > 1.5 mg/dL at greatest risk.

Exposure to radiocontrast agents is a common cause of hospital-acquired acute kidney injury. Kidney perfusion can be decreased for up to 20 hours following radiocontrast exposure. The ensuing injury can range from a mild nonoliguric rise in serum creatinine to severe kidney failure requiring hemodialysis, which is less commonly seen.

A rise in serum creatinine > 25% of baseline occurs within 3 days of exposure and resolves within 10–14 days. The risk of developing CA-AKI is nearly negligible in patients without any risk factors.

However, patients with risk factors such as preexisting kidney insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, age > 65 years, volume depletion, and multiple myeloma have a significantly greater risk of developing kidney injury (up to 10–20%).



Age > 65 years (A) makes patients more susceptible to CA-AKI if there are other comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease, but age alone is not an independent or primary risk factor. The decline in kidney function with age is gradual and does not universally predispose patients to injury unless other contributing factors, such as underlying kidney disease, are present.

Diabetes mellitus (B) is frequently cited as a risk factor, but its significance diminishes when controlling for baseline kidney function. Patients with diabetes are at increased risk, primarily because of coexisting diabetes-related nephropathy. In the absence of kidney dysfunction, diabetes alone does not substantially elevate the risk of CA-AKI.

Repeated contrast exposure within a short time frame (C) may elevate risk, particularly in susceptible individuals. However, this factor is situational and less predictive than underlying kidney disease. While cumulative nephrotoxic effects can occur, preventive strategies can mitigate this risk, and many patients tolerate repeated studies without incident if baseline kidney function is intact.

Reveal Answer:

question: A 5-year-old boy presents to the ED with fatigue after having diarrhea and abdominal pain 5 days ago. On physical exam, he is noted to have pale conjunctiva. Lab tests reveal hemoglobin 7 g/dL, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, and platelets 50,000/µL. Urinalysis shows proteinuria and hematuria. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is defined by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and kidney failure. It is one of the more common causes of acute kidney injury in children. The main cause of HUS is Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli. Other potential causes include dysregulation or mutations in complement proteins and Streptococcus pneumoniae. The pathophysiology is driven by the development of microthrombi leading to glomerular thrombotic microangiopathy and cortical necrosis. While most cases of HUS occur in children, adults can be affected as well. Patients will generally have a prodromal illness with abdominal pain, diarrhea, and vomiting approximately 1 week before the development of HUS. Laboratory findings are characterized by a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes on peripheral blood smear. Platelet counts are usually around 40,000/µL, and the degree of kidney involvement ranges from hematuria or proteinuria to oliguria. Diagnosis of HUS is mainly made based on clinical and laboratory findings. Management is supportive, focusing on the correction of electrolyte abnormalities and dialysis if needed.



Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) (A) is a pathologic and excessive activation of the coagulation cascade, causing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia similar to HUS. However, abnormal coagulation studies, including prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time, distinguish DIC from HUS. This patient also presents with elevated creatinine and preceding gastrointestinal illness making HUS more likely.

While gastroenteritis (B) caused by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli leads to HUS, most cases of gastroenteritis are self-limiting and respond to simple intravenous or oral rehydration.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) (D) is caused by an abnormality in ADAMTS13, resulting in abnormal platelet aggregation and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. TTP is more common in adults and is less likely to cause kidney failure when compared to HUS. The classic pentad of TTP includes neurologic symptoms, fever, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and kidney dysfunction.

What is the treatment for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura?

Reveal Answer:
Plasma exchange.

Clinical triad

Thrombocytopenia
Acute kidney injury
Most commonly caused by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC), S. pneumoniae, HIV, complement deficiency
Tx: supportive (RBC transfusions, fluid and electrolyte management), dialysis (if necessary)
Avoid antibiotics if E. coli suspected

question: A 55-year-old man presents with perineal pain. He has a long-standing history of hypertension and uncontrolled diabetes. He states 2 days ago, he noticed a “zit” and redness on his inguinal area and scrotum. He was seen by a different clinician yesterday, who started him on an antibiotic for cellulitis. Today the patient states the pain is worse, and he is now having fevers and chills. Vital signs are remarkable for a temperature of 39°C, HR 120 bpm, RR 23/min, BP 96/57 mm Hg, and SpO2 of 94%. Physical exam is remarkable for ecchymosis that extends from the medial right thigh and perineum to the right buttock. There is notable erythema with an indurated mass, patchy ecchymosis, and crepitus on palpation. Based on the presentation above, what is the best next step in management?

options.text: Administration of a 30 mL/kg bolus of normal saline
Emergency surgical consultation and broad-spectrum antibiotics

correctAnswer: Emergency surgical consultation and broad-spectrum antibiotics
englishExplanation:
Fournier gangrene is necrotizing fasciitis of the perineal, genital, or perianal anatomy. Often the process begins as a benign infection or simple abscess but quickly becomes virulent and results in microthrombosis of small subcutaneous vessels, leading to the development of gangrene of the overlying skin. Risk factors include diabetes and alcohol use disorder, as these result in an immunocompromised host, with male patients being most commonly affected. Early in the disease course, patients may report genital pain or perineal pain, often with associated pruritus. As the disease progresses, the pain may improve or completely resolve due to nerve damage or death. Crepitus and ecchymosis can occur, or the area may appear benign.

Diagnosis is often clinical as no lab study is sufficient to make the diagnosis. A high index of suspicion is required to prevent a delay in diagnosis. Treatment consists of emergency surgical consultation for debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics, such as piperacillin-tazobactam, imipenem, or meropenem with vancomycin. Clindamycin is another agent that should be given as it helps reduce toxin formation.



Even though establishing IV access and administering a 30 mL/kg bolus (A) will likely be a part of the patient’s management, these are not the best next steps in management. Emergent surgical consultation is warranted to ultimately treat the disease process.

Admission for intravenous vancomycin (B) would be appropriate management for failed outpatient treatment of cellulitis. However, this patient has findings concerning for necrotizing fasciitis requiring surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Imaging should not delay emergent surgical consultation. A CT scan of the pelvis (C) will often identify the disease, but MRI has the highest sensitivity. This is not required, however, and the best next step in management should be emergency surgical consultation and empiric antibiotics.

One Step Further

True or false: Fournier gangrene is most commonly due to methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

Reveal Answer:
False. It is most commonly polymicrobial.

question: Which of the following best describes the genital findings in primary syphilis?

options.text: Shallow, tender ulcerations preceded by a burning sensation
Single 1–2 cm painless ulcer with a raised border
Small, shallow painless ulcer with tender lymphadenopathy

correctAnswer: Single 1–2 cm painless ulcer with a raised border
englishExplanation:
Syphilis is a sexually acquired infection caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum. The characteristic lesion of primary syphilis, the chancre, appears after an incubation period of 10–90 days. It is described as a single papule that develops into a 1–2 cm painless ulceration with a raised border and a clean base. It appears at the site of inoculation which is typically on the genitalia or the mucous membranes of the mouth. It lasts about 3–12 weeks and then resolves spontaneously. It may become painful if there is a superimposed bacterial infection. Diagnosis is made by identification of spirochetes with darkfield microscopy or serologic tests such the Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) test or rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test. Positive serologic tests should be confirmed with the fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) test. Treatment for primary syphilis is with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly.



Multiple painful papules that ulcerate (A) are characteristic of chancroid, a sexually acquired infection caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. The ulcers are typically 1–2 cm in diameter and have an erythematous base usually covered with a gray or yellow purulent exudate. Treatment is single-dose therapy with azithromycin or ceftriaxone.

Shallow, tender ulcerations accompanied by malaise, headache and myalgias (B) are characteristic of a primary herpes simplex infection. Patients with primary herpes may also experience local burning and itching, dysuria, and tender regional lymphadenopathy.

Lymphogranuloma venereum presents with a transient small, shallow ulcer with tender lymphadenopathy (D). It is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. Treatment is with an extended course of doxycycline twice daily.

Reveal Answer:
Jarish-Herxheimer reaction.

question: What is the most common presenting sign or symptom of pediatric nephroblastoma?
englishExplanation:
Wilms tumor, or nephroblastoma, is the most common childhood abdominal malignancy. The median age at diagnosis of Wilms tumor is approximately 3.5 years. The most common presenting sign is a painless abdominal mass, which is seen in 80% of children at presentation. Other signs and symptoms include abdominal pain, hematuria, urinary tract infection, hypertension, fever, anemia, and respiratory symptoms in patients with lung metastases. Laboratory testing should be performed to evaluate renal function and electrolyte status. A CBC should also be performed to evaluate for significant anemia. The initial imaging study of choice is renal ultrasound. Management of Wilms tumor is with immediate nephrectomy followed by chemotherapy. Patients may receive postoperative radiation therapy. With current multimodality therapy, approximately 80–90% of children with a diagnosis of Wilms tumor survive.



While patients with Wilms tumor may have frank hematuria (A), it is not the most common presenting symptom.

Malignant hypertension (B) may be seen with renal vascular compression in bilateral Wilms tumor or renal cell carcinoma in adults. However, it is a very rare presentation.

Recurrent urinary tract infections (D) are a risk factor for renal abscess and may also be seen with a large Wilms tumor causing urinary obstruction. However, it is less commonly seen than a painless abdominal mass.

Reveal Answer:
Initial treatment with phentolamine or phenoxybenzamine followed by a beta blocker.

question: Which of the following is the most frequent complication to occur during hemodialysis?
englishExplanation:
Hypotension is the most frequent complication that occurs during hemodialysis, affecting patients during 50% of treatments. It is typically the result of a reduction in circulating intravascular volume and the patient’s inability to compensate for such changes by shifting fluid from the interstitial and intracellular compartments to the vascular spaces. Antihypertensive medications, especially beta-blockers, can contribute to the development of hypotension as well. The majority of cases of hypotension during dialysis are transient and resolve with simple measures such as decreasing the filtration rate or giving a small bolus of intravenous saline. Those who do not respond to such measures should be evaluated further for other possible etiologies of hypotension such as sepsis, myocardial infarction, or pericardial tamponade.



Air embolism (A) is an uncommon complication of hemodialysis and can present with symptoms such as acute onset of dyspnea, chest pain, hypotension, and loss of consciousness.

Disequilibrium syndrome (B) can occur during or just after hemodialysis and is due to rapid changes in body fluid composition and osmolality. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, headache, and muscle cramps and can progress to altered mental status and seizures in more severe cases.

While hyperkalemia (C) is common in patients with kidney failure, it is not a complication of hemodialysis.

Reveal Answer:
Staphylococcus aureus.

question: Which of the following clinical presentations would be most concerning for underlying bladder cancer?

options.text: A 24-year-old woman with dysuria who currently smokes cigarettes
A 3-year-old boy with gross hematuria and a palpable abdominal mass
A 32-year-old man with a benign medical history who presents with unilateral flank pain and microscopic hematuria
A 72-year-old man with painless, gross hematuria and a history of prior pelvic irradiation for prostate cancer

correctAnswer: A 72-year-old man with painless, gross hematuria and a history of prior pelvic irradiation for prostate cancer
englishExplanation:
While malignancies can originate from any part of the urinary tract, the urinary bladder is the most common site. In the United States, urothelial cell carcinoma accounts for 90% of cases of bladder cancer, which totals nearly 83,000 cases and 17,000 deaths annually. The majority occur in patients > 65 years, and the incidence is four times higher in men. The most important environmental risk factor is cigarette smoking, though other implicated factors include exposure to arsenic, chlorine, opium, and various other chemicals, including those contained in hair dye, paints, diesel exhaust, and certain plastics and cements. Prior pelvic irradiation also increases the risk, such as in the 72-year-old man with a history of previous prostate cancer and pelvic irradiation.

Painless, gross hematuria is the most common presenting symptom of bladder cancer. Pain is usually due to the effects of locally advanced or metastatic disease. Suprapubic pain is commonly the result of local invasion, while upper abdominal or extremity pain may result from abdominal lymphadenopathy or liver or bony metastasis.

Definitive diagnosis of bladder cancer requires direct visualization with cystoscopy and tissue biopsy, but imaging in the ED may help to identify or rule out a benign cause of the symptoms. CT urography is often used to ensure dedicated imaging of the urologic tract. Treatment is variable and involves a combination of surgical and medical strategies ranging from surveillance to chemotherapy and local resection and is based on the type and stage of cancer, as well as the patient’s age and expected prognosis.



While cigarette smoking increases the risk of bladder cancer, the case of a 24-year-old woman with dysuria (A) suggests an alternate diagnosis, such as cystitis. Bladder cancer is rare in patients < 35 years old.

A child with an abdominal mass and hematuria (B) should prompt suspicion for Wilms tumor. Bladder cancer in children is rare.

Ureterolithiasis typically presents with unilateral flank pain and microscopic hematuria (C), so this combination of symptoms in a young adult is not likely to be attributed to bladder cancer.

Reveal Answer:

question: Which organism is the primary cause of epididymitis in patients < 35 years of age?
englishExplanation:
In adolescents and adults < 35 years, Chlamydia trachomatis (along with Neisseria gonorrhoeae) is the primary cause of epididymitis. Chlamydia can spread from the urethra to the epididymis, causing epididymitis in patients with a sexually transmitted infection. In contrast, in older patients, particularly those who are not sexually active, complicated urinary tract infection with uropathogens is a more common cause, especially in those with prostate disorders.

Signs and symptoms include testicular pain, scrotal erythema, and swelling that is typically unilateral. On examination, there is palpable swelling and tenderness of the epididymis, and accompanying findings may include testicular tenderness, scrotal erythema and swelling, urethral discharge, and hydrocele.

Up to 15% of epididymitis cases are complicated by chronic pain that is usually idiopathic and often unresponsive to antibiotics. Other complications include decreased fertility and, rarely, a testicular abscess.



Escherichia coli (B) is a common cause of epididymitis in individuals with urinary tract abnormalities and those who use a catheter. It is the most common cause of urinary tract infections in female and male patients.

Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi (C) and is a sexually transmitted infection characterized by painful genital ulcers and inguinal lymphadenitis. It is not associated with epididymitis.

Mycoplasma genitalium (D) is mostly seen in the genitourinary tract of female patients and can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease or urethritis, but it is not a common cause of epididymitis.

Neisseria meningitidis (E) is not a cause of epididymitis. However, Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a common cause of epididymitis in individuals < 35 years of age, along with Chlamydia trachomatis.

True.

question: Which of the following findings on urinalysis is most consistent with a diagnosis of acute interstitial nephritis?
englishExplanation:
Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN), most often due to a hypersensitivity drug reaction, presents abruptly with signs and symptoms of acute kidney injury. Patients may have malaise, nausea and vomiting, and oliguria. Classic symptoms of rash, fever, and eosinophilia can be seen in cases due to drug reaction, although most patients do not have all three cardinal symptoms. Cases caused by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are also less likely to present with classic symptoms compared with other agents. Urinalysis findings include pyuria, microscopic or gross hematuria, eosinophiluria, and mild proteinuria. Urinalysis findings alone can not confirm or rule out the diagnosis. A definitive diagnosis is made based on kidney biopsy. Treatment includes removal of the offending agent in cases of drug-induced AIN. Kidney function generally returns to baseline over weeks, although chronic kidney insufficiency can occur.



Glucosuria (B) in combination with proteinuria and kidney insufficiency points to diabetes-related nephropathy.

While some degree of proteinuria is commonly seen in AIN, proteinuria > 3 grams/day (C) is uncommon. This degree of proteinuria is seen in nephrotic syndrome.

Red cell casts (D) are diagnostic of glomerular disease, but are not seen in AIN.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the treatment for nephrotic syndrome in children?

Reveal Answer:
Prednisone, diuretics for respiratory distress or significant ascites, and salt restriction.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Interstitial Nephritis

Etiology: medications (e.g., NSAIDS, antibiotics, PPIs), infections, autoimmune disorders
Can be asymptomatic or present with Sx (e.g., fever, rash)
Labs: ↑ Cr; WBCs, RBCs, and WBC casts in urine sediment; eosinophilia
Tx: discontinue offending medication; consider biopsy and glucocorticoids if kidney function does not improve

question: A patient presents with scrotal swelling suspicious for hydrocele. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention at this time?
englishExplanation:
As the testicle descends during fetal development, an outpocketing of the peritoneum follows. This is known as the processus vaginalis testis, which normally pinches off after complete descent to form the tunica vaginalis testis. Any fluid accumulation in the tunic vaginalis testis or in a persistent processus vaginalis testis is called a hydrocele. Hydroceles, although commonly self-limited in newborns, can occur at any age and almost always present as painless, unilateral scrotal swelling of acute or insidious onset.

Typical examination findings include a fluctuant, ovoid, nontender mass about the testicle, making direct palpation of the testicle difficult. A hydrocele transilluminates on exam. What widens the differential in hydrocele is the possibility of having swelling about the testicle or swelling about the spermatic cord. Other diagnoses that can be associated with it include epididymitis, trauma, tumor, and torsion of the testis or an appendage. If the swelling extends proximally to the inguinal ring, the clinician must consider an indirect inguinal hernia. In any case of scrotal swelling, color Doppler ultrasonography is the first diagnostic test recommended.



Serum and urine studies (A) are not warranted in hydrocele but may be helpful in any urinary tract infectious condition.

A computed tomography scan (B) is not the initial diagnostic test in evaluating scrotal swelling.

Simple aspiration (C) is typically unsuccessful because the fluid rapidly accumulates, though it may be effective if combined with use of a sclerosing agent (e.g., alcohol). Excision of the hydrocele sac is the most common surgical procedure.

Immediate surgical consultation (D) is not necessary for hydrocele, although it is required if testicular torsion is suspected.

One Step Further
Question:
Which disease caused by lymphatic obstruction commonly results in chronic hydrocele (elephantiasis)?

Reveal Answer:
Filariasis, a parasitic disease caused by nematodes (commonly Wuchereria and Brugia species) and transmitted by black flies and mosquitoes.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Hydrocele

Presents with painless testicular or scrotal swelling, right > left
PE: fluid around the testicle that transilluminates
Consider ultrasound if Dx uncertain
Common cause of scrotal swelling in children and adolescents

question: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a fever and lower back pain. His symptoms started yesterday and have been gradually worsening. His temperature is 102°F (38.9ºC), and his physical exam is notable for severe pain when examining the prostate. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
englishExplanation:
Prostatitis occurs when bacteria from sexual transmission or hematogenous/lymphatic spread penetrate the prostate. Patients will typically present with fever, chills, dysuria, increased urinary frequency, lower back pain, and the sensitive and specific exam finding of an exquisitely tender prostate on rectal exam. Patients who are reliable without comorbidities such as immunosuppression can be treated with a prolonged course of oral antibiotics including trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, ciprofloxacin, or levofloxacin. Otherwise, patients with severe symptoms or medical comorbidities will often require hospitalization and IV antibiotics.



Ceftriaxone and doxycycline (A) could be an appropriate antibiotic regimen in a younger patient presenting with prostatitis or in an older patient presenting with prostatitis in the setting of a risky sexual history to cover for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis.

Doxycycline (C) could be appropriate to treat a vector-borne disease such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever or Lyme disease or may be indicated for Staphylococcus aureus coverage in cases of cellulitis with an associated abscess. Doxycycline could also be used to cover Chlamydia trachomatis.

Gentamicin (D) can be given in addition to ciprofloxacin but is an insufficient treatment by itself for prostatitis. It could be added to treatment if the patient is severely ill, demonstrates signs of severe sepsis, or has bacteremia.

One Step Further
Question:
What is a potential complication of untreated or severe bacterial prostatitis?

Reveal Answer:
Prostatic abscess.

PE: boggy and exquisitely tender prostate
Most common causes
Sexually active: N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis
Nonsexually active: E. coli
Tx
Sexually active: ceftriaxone IM and doxycycline
Nonsexually active: fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX for 4 weeks
Avoid vigorous prostatic massage, which can lead to septicemia

question: A 52-year-old woman with a history of obesity and type 2 diabetes presents to the ED with medial knee pain for the past several weeks. She describes the pain as a dull ache that worsens with activity, particularly going up and down stairs. She reports no trauma, mechanical locking, or instability. On examination, there is tenderness over the anteromedial proximal tibia approximately 2–3 cm below the joint line, with pain elicited by resisted knee flexion. There is no joint effusion, erythema, or warmth. What is the most appropriate next step in care?

options.text: Recommend quadriceps strengthening exercises and NSAID therapy

correctAnswer: Recommend quadriceps strengthening exercises and NSAID therapy
englishExplanation:
This patient's exam is most consistent with pes anserine pain syndrome (PAPS), also known as pes anserine bursitis, a common cause of medial knee pain, particularly in middle-aged and older adults with risk factors such as obesity, osteoarthritis, and diabetes. The pes anserine bursa lies beneath the combined tendons of the sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus muscles at the medial proximal tibia. Repetitive stress, valgus knee deformity, and poor biomechanics can contribute to its inflammation. The condition typically presents with anteromedial knee pain that worsens with activities such as climbing stairs or transitioning from sitting to standing. Unlike intra-articular pathology, PAPS does not cause significant joint effusion, instability, or mechanical symptoms like locking or catching.

The diagnosis is clinical, based on localized tenderness at the pes anserine bursa without significant joint involvement. Imaging is not routinely necessary unless an alternative pathology is suspected. First-line treatment includes conservative measures such as NSAIDs for pain relief, ice application, and most importantly, quadriceps and hamstring strengthening exercises. Strengthening the quadriceps reduces stress on the knee joint and improves biomechanics, which is essential for long-term symptom relief. Physical therapy emphasizing stretching and strengthening is highly effective in preventing recurrence. Most cases improve with these conservative measures, making this the best initial management step in the emergency setting.



Septic arthritis typically presents with acute-onset severe joint pain, warmth, swelling, and systemic symptoms such as fever and would be an indication to perform arthrocentesis (C) and initiate antibiotic therapy (A). Gout and pseudogout also usually cause acute-onset, severe joint pain with significant swelling, erythema, and warmth. This patient lacks these inflammatory findings. Her symptoms are chronic and localized without joint effusion, making infection and crystal disease highly unlikely.

Radiographs (B) are unnecessary unless there is trauma or significant concern for structural joint damage. This patient’s symptoms are localized to the pes anserine region and do not indicate acute bony pathology.

Immediate orthopedic consultation (D) is not necessary for PAPS, as it is a nonemergent, soft tissue condition that typically responds well to conservative management. Orthopedic referral is generally reserved for cases involving significant structural damage, such as ligamentous injury, complex meniscal tears, or fractures, none of which are present in this patient.

One Step Further
Question:
What organisms should be of highest consideration when treating septic bursitis?

Reveal Answer:
Skin flora including Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species.

Rapid Review
Pes Anserine Pain Syndrome (Anserine Bursitis)

Pes anserinus refers to the insertion point of the sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus muscles
Risks: knee osteoarthritis, obesity, knee malalignment, diabetes
Sx: pain around the medial knee with activities such as rising from a chair, ascending or descending stairs, or lying in bed with one knee pressing on the other
PE: tenderness over the upper medial tibia
Dx: clinical
Tx: weight reduction, quadriceps strengthening exercises, NSAIDs
Refractory pain may benefit from corticosteroid injections

question: A 78-year-old man is brought to the ED from his nursing home for confusion. His vital signs are within normal limits for his age. He is thin but unshaven and malodorous. He is awake, alert, and oriented only to person and place. His blood glucose is 89 mg/dL. What is the next most appropriate step in diagnosis after completing a head-to-toe examination?

options.text: Contacting the patient’s family for further information
CT of the head without contrast

correctAnswer: Contacting the patient’s family for further information
englishExplanation:
In a patient with altered sensorium, the next best step after obtaining as much information from the patient and prehospital personnel and performing a thorough physical examination is to attempt to contact the patient’s family to obtain further information that may elucidate the cause of the mental status change. Mental status is the clinical state of one’s emotional and intellectual function and can include appearance, behavior, attitude, thought content, perception, mood, affect, insight, judgment, and level of alertness.

Delirium is a transient alteration in attention and cognition that generally develops acutely (i.e., over days rather than weeks or months) and often has an underlying systemic, toxic, or primary neurologic cause. Symptoms are often intermittent, fluctuate throughout the day, and typically become worse at night. Clinical features that may be present include visual hallucinations, tremors, tachycardia, asterixis, diaphoresis, hypertension, and emotional outbursts. The primary method for diagnosis is obtaining history from family, caregivers, other health care providers, and spouses. Information obtained from these ancillary sources can help differentiate causes of delirium and may guide diagnostic and therapeutic intervention.



Further historical information should be gathered in any case of altered mental status or delirium prior to placing a consultation for admission (A).

Ordering a CT of the head without contrast (C) may be indicated, but a history and physical examination should be completed prior to neuroimaging in the absence of clinical findings that might suggest an acute stroke.

Similarly, serum chemistry and urinalysis (D) may be appropriate, but a thorough history should be obtained prior to diagnostic workup.

One Step Further
Question:
What syndrome should be considered in a patient with altered mental status with mydriasis, urinary retention, anhidrosis, and flushed skin?

Reveal Answer:
Anticholinergic syndrome.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Delirium

Diagnosis
Fluctuating disturbance in attention and awareness
Additional disturbance in cognition (e.g., memory, perception, language)
Develops over a few hours to a few days
Clinical findings provide evidence Sx are a direct consequence of a medical condition, medication, substance, toxin, or multiple etiologies
Treatment
Main intervention is to treat underlying condition
Environmental interventions
Medications
None approved by FDA
Haloperidol (if IV, needs QTc monitoring) or atypical antipsychotics
Benzodiazepines should generally be avoided, except for substance withdrawal and other specific contexts (e.g., potential role for delirium in palliative care or if antipsychotics are contraindicated), as they are an established risk factor for exacerbation of delirium

question: An 8-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a report of gradual-onset vague lower back pain and lower extremity paresthesias. Her symptoms are worse during gymnastics practice. The pain does not wake her at night. On exam, she does have some pain with extension of the back, but she has a normal gait, normal range of motion, and no point tenderness. Her back appears straight when bending forward, and there is no posterior pelvic tilt. She has normal sensation in her legs. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
englishExplanation:
Careful attention is needed in young children with back pain as it is not a common concern and often signifies pathology. Back strains and lumbar herniation are less frequent in children compared to adults. However, an injury to the vertebral pars interarticularis is common. Spondylolysis is a fracture or separation from the pars interarticularis, commonly from overuse. When bilateral pars defects occur, the lumbar spine slips anteriorly in a process called spondylolisthesis. Occasionally, this can result in spinal cord compression or injury. It typically presents as a gradual onset of vague lower back pain and is frequently seen in patients with repetitive hyperextension of the back, such as figure skaters and gymnasts. They usually have normal range of motion and a reassuring exam, although pain on back extension is common. Spondylolisthesis is typically diagnosed with an X-ray of the lumbar spine.

Treatment varies based on the degree of lumbar slip, but most patients are treated conservatively with stretching exercises, ice, warm baths, and over-the-counter analgesics. They are usually followed as an outpatient by orthopedic surgeons. Only those with signs of cauda equina syndrome (e.g., urinary incontinence, saddle anesthesia) need emergent intervention. Back pain in children can also present due to neoplasm, bony metastasis, inflammatory arthritis, pneumonia, pneumothorax, nephrolithiasis, or a vaso-occlusive crisis in patients with sickle cell anemia, who are also at risk of osteomyelitis of the back. Rarely, back pain in children is due to an aortic aneurysm, most commonly seen in patients with Marfan syndrome. History and physical exam findings indicating a dangerous cause of back pain include children < 4 years of age, patients with associated fever, weight loss, worsening pain, pain at night, or those with evidence of neurologic dysfunction.



Back strengthening exercises (A) are not routinely recommended in children with back pain, but stretching exercises are sometimes used to provide relief in patients with spondylolisthesis.

An MRI of the lumbar spine (B) can rule out many serious diagnoses that cause back pain, but plain film radiographs are usually recommended as the initial starting point. An exception could be made when the history or exam suggests a spinal epidural abscess or hematoma, transverse myelitis, osteomyelitis, or a spinal cord lesion.

Back pain in young children is uncommon, and while the history and examination may suggest spondylolisthesis, the degree of lumbar slip will change treatment. Thus, reassurance and discharge (C) are less appropriate than an X-ray.

One Step Further
Question:
What physical exam finding suggests severe spondylolisthesis?

Reveal Answer:
Posterior pelvic rotation noted by loss of gluteal contour.

Rapid Review

Pars interarticularis: between the lamina and pedicle, where the facet joint is located (neck of Scottie dog)
Spondylolysis: fracture of the pars interarticularis
Spondylolisthesis: defects in posterior arch lead to vertebral anterior displacement
Clinical: lower back pain radiating to buttocks or posterior legs, radicular symptoms
Worsened by spine extension and during physical activity
Dx: plain AP and lateral radiographs
Tx: NSAIDs, PT, surgery

question: A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset back pain on the right side. He was lifting a box when it started. He has no radiation of pain down his legs and no numbness, tingling, or weakness. He has a 20 pack-year smoking history. His medical history includes osteoporosis and hypertension. Physical exam is notable for an absence of midline tenderness when palpating the spine. When the patient is placed in the recumbent position and his knee is kept straight while the right leg is elevated, the patient experiences sudden worsening of his pain with radiation down the right leg. He has 5/5 strength in the lower extremities and intact sensation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
A herniated disc (or nucleus pulposus) is a common cause of back pain that presents with back pain that typically radiates down one or both of the legs and is worsened with bending or flexing the spine. It most commonly occurs after heavy lifting or trauma but may occur spontaneously. The diagnosis can be made clinically with the classic history and physical exam findings. When the spine is flexed, the reproduction of pain with radiation down the legs is highly suggestive. The straight leg test can be suggestive of radiculopathy. With the patient lying in the recumbent position, when the ipsilateral leg is lifted while the knee is kept straight, a reproduction of symptoms is supportive of this diagnosis. With an appropriate history and exam, the diagnosis can be made and therapy can be started with analgesia, physical therapy, weight loss, and smoking cessation. The confirmatory test in uncertain cases would be an MRI of the spine, though this test should not be routinely ordered in the ED.



Cauda equina syndrome (A) presents with lower back pain and neurological symptoms, including asymmetric lower extremity weakness and paresthesias, urinary and bowel retention or incontinence, saddle anesthesia, and loss of rectal tone. The diagnosis is made based on the clinical presentation and MRI of the spine demonstrating compression of the cauda equina (the end of the spinal cord, typically L1–L5). Compression fractures (B) occur more commonly in patients with advanced age and those with risk factors such as osteoporosis. It presents with midline back pain, often after trauma or heavy lifting. The diagnosis can be made with a CT scan or an MRI, which is more accurate. Compression fractures are generally treated conservatively with analgesics and physical therapy. Some patients are candidates for vertebroplasty, which may alleviate symptoms. This patient’s radicular findings are more consistent with a herniated disc. Muscle strains (D) are one of the most common causes of back pain and present with pain with bending or twisting of the back, often with tenderness and spasms of the muscles along the spine. Management is centered on analgesia and physical therapy. Muscle strains are not typically associated with a positive straight leg test.

One Step Further
Question:
What imaging study should be ordered when working up a spinal epidural abscess?

Reveal Answer:
An MRI of the entire spine with and without contrast.

Presentation: abrupt onset of pain that is severe and exaggerated by sitting, walking, standing, or coughing
Pain radiates from the buttock down the posterior or posterolateral leg to the ankle or foot
PE: pain on straight leg raise test, tenderness in the sciatic notch, limited ROM
Diagnosis confirmed by MRI
Most commonly caused by herniation of the nucleus pulposus into the lumbar spinal canal
Most common location L4–L5 or L5–S1

question: A 42-year-old man is concerned about redness in the eye. The patient had food poisoning last night and vomited multiple times overnight. Today, he saw bleeding in his eye, as seen in the image above. What is the appropriate management of this condition?
englishExplanation:
This patient has a subconjunctival hemorrhage. These hemorrhages occur when a blood vessel ruptures under the surface of the conjunctiva. On physical examination, the hemorrhage is flat and bright red and does not cross the limbus. These hemorrhages may occur spontaneously or as a result of Valsalva maneuvers or trauma. In this case, the patient reports multiple episodes of vomiting over the night preceding recognition of the hemorrhage. The hemorrhages do not cause any long-term sequelae and treatment is aimed at reassurance. A subconjunctival hemorrhage is typically painless without any associated decreased vision or photophobia. If these symptoms are present, other diagnoses should be pursued.



An anterior chamber evaluation (A) is part of the complete physical examination of the eye using the slit lamp. The anterior chamber may develop inflammatory changes and debris in keratitis. Additionally, subtle hyphemas (collection of blood in the anterior chamber) may be difficult to see without inspection of the anterior chamber. However, this patient's exam is not consistent with a hyphema.

Coagulation studies (B) are indicated in patients on anticoagulation therapy. However, in the routine evaluation of a subconjunctival hemorrhage, these tests are not necessary.

A complete blood count (C) to measure platelets is indicated if there is concern for thrombocytopenia in the patient. This may include patients with other areas of active bleeding, patients on chemotherapy, or patients with marrow-suppressing diseases.

How long does it take for a subconjunctival hemorrhage to resolve?

Reveal Answer:
10–14 days.

question: A 13-year-old boy presents because his parent noticed a progressive left-sided limp over the previous 3 weeks. The patient states that he has pain in his knee. On exam, you elicit pain on internal rotation of the hip. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
The patient has a slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). SCFE is a Salter-Harris type 1 fracture of the femoral capital epiphysis. The X-ray will show the classic posterior and inferior displacement of the head (capital) of the femur. SCFE occurs in males twice as often as females, is commonly seen in children > 10 years of age, and classically presents in children with obesity as subacute hip pain with a limp. Some underlying metabolic disorders such as hypothyroidism, panhypopituitarism, and hypogonadism are also risk factors for the development of SCFE.



Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (A) is avascular necrosis of the femoral head, usually seen in young school-aged children. Hip pain and limp are early signs. Radiographs may be normal. It occurs bilaterally in 15% of cases and occurs more often in sickle cell disease. Malignancy could also present with subacute symptoms. Most osteosarcomas (B) arise as solitary lesions within the fastest growing areas of the long bones of children. The top three affected areas are the distal femur, the proximal tibia, and the proximal humerus, but virtually any bone can be involved. The most common presenting symptom of osteosarcoma is pain, particularly with activity. Septic arthritis (C) is the most common cause of painful hips in infants and typically presents as acute monoarthritis in an ill-appearing baby.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the Klein line in relation to slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)?

Reveal Answer:
A line drawn along the superior border of the femoral neck that should intersect the femoral head. If it does not, suspect SCFE.

Male adolescents 12–16 years old with obesity
Displacement of the capital femoral epiphysis from the femoral neck through the physeal plate
Clinical: progressive limp and hip or knee pain
PE: loss of hip internal rotation and flexion
Dx: X-ray will show apparent posterior displacement of the femoral epiphysis (scoop of ice cream slipping off cone)
Tx: non-weight-bearing and urgent orthopedic consultation, surgical fixation

question: A 22-year-old man presents with upper extremity weakness. He notes that he was drinking heavily last night, and when he woke up this morning, he was unable to move his hand. On examination, he has normal strength in the biceps and triceps but weakness of the wrist extensors, finger extensors, and brachioradialis. What injured nerve accounts for his symptoms?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with findings consistent with radial nerve palsy. The radial nerve arises from nerve roots C5 through T1 and courses along the humerus in the spiral groove of the upper arm. Compression at this site can lead to radial mononeuropathy, which is commonly seen in intoxicated individuals who sleep with their arm draped over a hard surface, leading to the term Saturday night palsy.

On examination, triceps strength remains intact since the radial nerve gives off its branch to the triceps before wrapping around the humerus at the spiral groove. However, there is weakness in the wrist extensors, leading to wrist drop, and weakness in the finger extensors and brachioradialis muscle. Sensory deficits occur in the radial nerve distribution, primarily affecting the radial aspect of the dorsum of the hand.

The diagnosis is clinical and based on characteristic motor and sensory deficits. Treatment involves wrist splinting, physical therapy, and pain control. Most cases resolve spontaneously over weeks to months as the nerve recovers from compression.



The median nerve (A) is responsible for the motor function of the flexor muscles of the anterior forearm compartment (except for the flexor carpi ulnaris and part of the flexor digitorum profundus), the thenar muscles, and the lateral two lumbricals. Compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel of the wrist will result in pain and paresthesias in the distribution of the median nerve.

Musculocutaneous nerve (B) innervates the coracobrachialis, the biceps brachii, and the brachialis. Injury to this nerve will result in weakness of elbow flexion with associated sensory loss over the lateral forearm.

Ulnar (D) neuropathy at the elbow is the second most common compression neuropathy and results in sensory loss and paresthesias over the fourth and fifth digits and weakness with finger and wrist flexion.

One Step Further
Question:
Which neuropathy is seen in chronic alcohol use?

Reveal Answer:
Symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy in the lower extremities.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Radial Nerve Palsy (Saturday Night Palsy)

Risks: arm compression, overuse (repetitive overhead arm movements), distal humerus fracture
PE: weakness of the wrist extensors, wrist drop, weakness of the finger extensors, and sensory deficits potentially over posterior forearm, dorsal hand, lateral fingers
Tx: splinting the wrist, physical therapy, and pain management

question: A 66-year-old man presents to the emergency department with weakness in his left hand. He has a history of chronic drug and alcohol use and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He indicates he noticed this weakness upon awakening yesterday morning and came to the emergency department today because it has not improved. He reports no other symptoms and has difficulty relaying events around when this weakness occurred. He had been drinking alcohol the other night. He has full function in his left shoulder and upper arm but has difficulty extending at the left wrist and has mild decreased sensation on the dorsum of the hand. Neuropathy of which nerve is the cause of this patient's symptoms?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with a focal mononeuropathy which is most likely due to nerve compression. Focal mononeuropathy can occur at any compressed point along a peripheral nerve. Traumatic peripheral nerve injuries can cause significant disability, so early diagnosis and prompt follow-up are important. Radial nerve neuropathies are usually caused by trauma or compression in the mid-upper arm. One common cause is external compression of the nerve during sleep. This can occur if the patient's head is resting on the medial aspect of the upper arm or if the arm hangs over a bench, for instance. Sedation or alcohol intoxication may prevent the patient from awakening when the warning signs of paresthesias develop. On examination, the triceps retain full strength, but patients develop weakness of the wrist extensors, finger extensors, and brachioradialis. Sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand may also be present.



The long thoracic nerve (A) is a pure motor nerve that, when damaged, leads to paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle, resulting in scapula winging. Trauma to the long thoracic nerve can occur from a direct blow to the shoulder or lateral chest wall. This patient's presentation is not consistent with a long thoracic nerve injury.

The most common form of any focal mononeuropathy is carpal tunnel syndrome with compression of the median nerve (B) at the wrist. The most classic presentation is pain, paresthesias, and numbness along the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, and middle finger, as well as the radial aspect of the fourth finger. Weakness and wasting of the muscles of the thenar eminence may be noted on exam. These findings are not evident in this patient.

Cubital tunnel syndrome is the most common ulnar nerve (D) mononeuropathy occurring with injury of the nerve as it courses through the elbow. It results from compression of the nerve at the medial epicondyle. Classic symptoms include tingling in the fifth and lateral fourth fingers with weakness of the intrinsic muscles of the hand. This patient's symptoms are not consistent with an ulnar nerve neuropathy.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common systemic cause of noncompressive focal neuropathy?

Reveal Answer:
Diabetes.

PE: weakness of the wrist extensors, wrist drop, weakness of the finger extensors, and sensory deficits potentially over posterior forearm, dorsal hand, lateral fingers
Tx: splinting the wrist, physical therapy, and pain management

question: A 55-year-old woman with lupus presents with bilateral leg swelling. She notes that for the past few months, her shoes have felt tighter, and her legs have slowly become visibly swollen. The patient reports no shortness of breath, chest pain, or leg pain. Her vital signs are notable for a BP of 180/100 mm Hg. Physical exam reveals clear lung sounds, normal heart sounds, and pitting edema of bilateral lower extremities. Her lab results reveal hyperlipidemia, and her urine is positive for proteins. What is the mechanism of the most likely cause of this patient’s leg swelling?
englishExplanation:
This patient with systemic lupus erythematosus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, proteinuria, and bilateral pitting edema most likely has nephrotic syndrome due to lupus nephritis. In nephrotic syndrome, loss of albumin in the urine leads to decreased intravascular oncotic pressure, which allows fluid to shift from the vascular space into the interstitial tissues, causing edema.

Bilateral lower extremity edema refers to the palpable accumulation of excess fluid in the interstitial space due to an alteration in capillary hemodynamics. This condition can be categorized based on its onset as either acute or chronic, with each category having distinct underlying causes.

Acute bilateral lower extremity edema may develop suddenly and is often associated with conditions that cause rapid fluid retention or shifts in intravascular volume. Acute heart failure is a common culprit, leading to increased hydrostatic pressure and impaired venous return, resulting in fluid extravasation into the interstitial tissue. Acute kidney insufficiency can also contribute by reducing the body’s ability to excrete sodium and water, leading to fluid overload. Additionally, certain medications, including calcium channel blockers, NSAIDs, and corticosteroids, can induce fluid retention by affecting vascular permeability or kidney function.

Chronic bilateral lower extremity edema, on the other hand, evolves gradually and is often a manifestation of long-standing systemic or local conditions. Chronic heart failure remains a leading cause, in which sustained elevated venous pressures due to impaired cardiac function result in persistent fluid accumulation. Cirrhosis, particularly in cases of severe hepatic dysfunction, can contribute through hypoalbuminemia and portal hypertension, leading to fluid leakage and secondary sodium retention. Chronic kidney insufficiency results in similar fluid retention mechanisms seen in acute kidney dysfunction but develops over a prolonged period. Venous insufficiency is another frequent cause, in which dysfunctional venous valves and increased venous pressure contribute to fluid pooling and capillary leakage. Pregnancy, due to increased plasma volume and mechanical compression of pelvic veins by the enlarging uterus, can lead to dependent edema in the lower extremities. Malnutrition, particularly in cases of severe protein deficiency, reduces oncotic pressure and promotes fluid extravasation. Mechanical factors such as pelvic compression from tumors or other obstructive processes can impair venous and lymphatic drainage, exacerbating fluid retention. Dependent edema, often seen in individuals with prolonged immobility or bed rest, results from gravitational pooling of fluid in the lower extremities. Chronic medication use, including vasodilators, steroids, and hormonal therapies, can further contribute to persistent fluid retention.



Congestion of lymphatic vasculature (A) is the mechanism behind lymphedema. Lymphedema causes chronic swelling of extremities but generally is nonpitting and should not have other laboratory abnormalities.

Decreased intravascular sodium (C) is not a cause of lower extremity edema, but increased sodium is a proposed mechanism in nephrotic syndrome.

Increased intravascular hydrostatic pressure (D) is the mechanism behind lower extremity edema in venous congestion, heart failure, and pulmonary hypertension. In nephrotic syndrome, there is no congestive pressure forcing fluid out of the capillaries.

One Step Further

Which pulmonary condition causes bilateral leg swelling?

Reveal Answer:
Pulmonary hypertension.

Acute: acute heart failure, acute kidney insufficiency, medications
Chronic: cirrhosis, chronic heart failure, venous insufficiency, chronic kidney insufficiency, pregnancy, malnutrition, pelvic compression, dependent edema, medications

question: A 42-year-old man presents with lower back pain that started acutely while lifting a couch. He reports pain radiating to the right posterior calf. He reports no bowel or bladder incontinence. On examination, he has decreased plantar flexion at the right ankle and numbness of the right lateral foot. Impingement of which nerve root is responsible for his findings?
englishExplanation:
Radiculopathy results from irritation or compression of a nerve root that leads to weakness, numbness, and paresthesias in a specific distribution based on the nerve root involved. The leading cause of radiculopathy is disc herniation, most commonly at L4, L5, or S1. Most disc herniations are posterolateral, resulting in irritation or compression of the lower nerve root as it exits the neural foramina (e.g., compression of the S1 nerve root with an L5-S1 disc herniation). Patients with an S1 radiculopathy present with pain that radiates down the posterior aspect of the leg into the foot with some degree of accompanying weakness with plantar flexion of the ankle (gastrocnemius), leg extension, and knee flexion. Sensation is affected on the posterior aspect of the leg and the lateral aspect of the foot. The Achilles reflex may be absent. All patients with lower back pain should also be assessed for signs and symptoms concerning for cauda equina, such as bowel or bladder incontinence, saddle anesthesia, and bilateral leg pain and hyporeflexia. MRI is the modality of choice for evaluating back pain concerning for disc herniation and nerve root compression, infection, or malignancy.



Compression of L3 (A) results in weakness with hip flexion and adduction with decreased sensation of the anterior thigh.

L4 (B) radiculopathy presents with weakness with knee extension and decreased sensation of the lateral thigh, anterior knee, and medial leg. There may be a decrease in the patellar reflex on the affected side.

Compression of L5 (C) results in the most common radiculopathy of the lumbar spine. Patients present with back pain that radiates down the lateral leg with weakness with dorsiflexion of the foot and extension of the great toe. Sensation will be decreased in the lateral aspect of the lower leg, the dorsum of the foot, and the webspace between the first and second toes.

One Step Further
Question:
True or false: the straight leg raise test is considered positive if it reproduces pain in the back.

Reveal Answer:
False. A positive test results in radicular pain below the knee of the affected leg.

question: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a skin lesion, as shown above, which has developed over the past week. He also reports joint pain and diarrhea during this timeframe. Which of the following conditions is most likely given this patient’s skin findings?
englishExplanation:
Ulcerative colitis presents in a patient with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea and can include extraintestinal symptoms such as arthritis. Symptoms are limited to the colon (versus the entire gastrointestinal tract in Crohn disease). There will typically be gross blood in the stool, and radiography may demonstrate a “lead pipe” sign, particularly when this pathology is chronic. Other diagnostic tests include a perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody test and colonoscopy. A dermatologic manifestation of ulcerative colitis is pyoderma gangrenosum which presents with an inflammatory ulcer with undermined borders that may occur at any site on the body. This skin finding is associated with inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, leukemia, and chronic active hepatitis (among other inflammatory diseases).



Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection (A) can present with ecthyma gangrenosum, which occurs secondary to perivascular bacterial invasion of arteries and veins in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue.

Rheumatoid arthritis (B) is a potential etiology of pyoderma gangrenosum, however, epidemiologically, this is more likely to occur in a middle-aged woman with morning joint stiffness.

Streptococcus pyogenes infection (C) can cause necrotizing fasciitis which presents with crepitus, pain, erythema, purulence, and a rapidly progressing infection (over hours).

One Step Further
Question:
What vitamin deficiency in Crohn disease can cause a megaloblastic anemia and decreased proprioception?

Reveal Answer:
Vitamin B12 deficiency from terminal ileum involvement.

As disease progresses or moderate disease: add glucocorticoids (topical, oral)

Complications: toxic megacolon, ↑ colon cancer risk
